My position is fairly clear with respect to these matters. I voted for the second reading of the bill; therefore I went on record as being in favour of the principle of the bill. I have favoured such legislation all my life. I had to make a decision some years ago in the provincial legislature, when the revenue of Nova Scotia was only $7,226,000 or thereabouts, while to-day it is about 240 per cent above that, more than $17 million. We had certain social legislation before us for consideration and for enactment, if possible. We had to choose whether we would make a grant for mothers' allowances for the benefit of children, or whether we should adopt old age pensions. The financial position of the taxpayers of Nova Scotia at that time was such that we were not able to adopt both, although we were in principle heartily in favour of doing so. We gave our preference to mothers' allowances, although it did not bring us the political kudos which we would have received if we had enacted old age pensions. It involved an expenditure of about $360,000 a year, which was a very large sum in those days, when our revenues were small and we were operating under a deficit. We passed a mothers' allowances act because it had as its basis the assistance of families, particularly the assistance of children. My record from that day to this has been sympathetic to any measures which have as their purpose the benefit of the children and the family, and that is why on principle I support this measure, although there are many features of it which I do not like.
There is also before the committee the question of the constitutionality of the bill. I have a record with respect to that as well. I am in agreement with the view expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Yale and several other laymen, also the legal opinions expressed by some members of this house. There is certainly a doubt as to the constitutionality of this bill. I do not see why there should be; I do not see why we should have to give any attention to a discussion as to whether this measure is consti-

Family Allowances
tutional or not. I myself have grave doubts how, as the hon. member for Yale expressed it this afternoon, this parliament can vote and administer money for the benefit of children in the home, when we have been told for the last fifteen years that it was unconstitutional to do so for the benefit of the old people in the same home. I am at a loss with respect to that.
Matters of social legislation and unemployment insurance were before our legislature during the time I had a seat in that chamber. I went on record at that time with reference to these questions. The late Hon. Gordon S. Harrington was leader of the party of which I was a member in the house. He proposed an amendment to the speech from the throne, in 1936, placing himself and myself on record. I had the privilege of seconding that resolution. I am going to put it on Hansard to-night. It was opposed by the premier of the province of that day, now the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services and hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Macdonald), the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. McGarry), now in this house, and the members of their party. If that motion had been adopted and made effective at that time there would have been no need for this discussion now with regard to the constitutionality.
I wish to read the amendment that was proposed at that time. While it does not refer in precise words to the measure that is now before the house it does so in effect. On March 12, 1936, the Hon. Mr. Harrington moved and I seconded the following motion:
This house regrets that the speech from the throne fails to indicate that the government of Nova Scotia has proposed or consented to a precise and specific amendment to be made by the parliament of Great Britain to the British North America Act, to empower the parliament of Canada to proceed at once with a centralized dominion-wide much needed social programme of maternity benefits, unemployment insurance, health insurance, accident insurance, widows' pensions, old age and invalidity pensions.
Which amendment being seconded by Mr. Black, and a debate arising thereon, after some time spent in such debate, and the amendment being put from the chair, there appeared for the amendment 6 and against the amendment 18.
No action was taken at that time, and in the following year the proposal was made again by the Hon. Mr. Harrington, supported by myself in the provincial legislature. We went farther. We felt that it was most important in the interests of the people of the province that there should be a clear understanding of what our responsibility was. It was clearly recognized that it was not financially possible for Nova Scotia as a province, to undertake these measures which were so urgent and
pressing, that we made a proposal to the government of the day that they support such a resolution, make it unanimous, and submit it to the federal government. They refused to do so and there have been years of delay and uncertainty. I will read the resolution which was proposed at that time on March 17, 1937. It was moved by Mr. Harrington as follows:
Resolved, that the British North America Act should be amended to empower the parliament of Canada to create and administer a social security plan consisting of accident insurance, health insurance, unemployment insurance, widows' and orphans' pensions, old age and invalidity pensions and incidental and allied matters.
Which would include the matter of family allowances now before the house. An amendment was proposed by the attorney general, the Hon. Mr. McQuarrie, a follows:
Whereas paragraph 12 of the speech with which this session of the general assembly of Nova Scotia was opened reads as follows:
"My government feels that the recent decisions of the privy council respecting the validity of certain legislation enacted by the federal government in 1935 will necessitate a review of those sections of the British North America Act assigning jurisdiction to the dominion and provinces respectively. In any conference for this purpose my government will ever seek to secure the advancement and promote the welfare of the people who are its immediate care."
And whereas, while these decisions have declared that the jurisdiction to enact certain types of social legislation resides in the provinces, it is desirable that measures of this nature should be dominion-wide in their application.
And whereas this house approves of the announcement of the Prime Minister of Canada in the House of Commons on February 16 that the government of Canada proposed to appoint a royal commission of inquiry to investigate the whole system of taxation in the dominion; to study the division of financial powers and financial responsibilities between the dominion and the provinces; and to make recommendations as to what should be done to secure a more equitable and practical division of-the burden so as to enable all governments to function more effectively and more independently within the spheres of their respective jurisdictions;
And whereas this house believes that the scope of social legislation should be extended;
Be it therefore resolved that this house express its view that the investigation to be undertaken by the said royal commission of inquiry, should include the reallocation of the cost of social services, unless in advance of the sittings of the commission an agreement as to these matters shall have been reached between the dominion and the provinces ensuring that measures of social security affecting Canada as a whole shall be adopted at the earliest possible date.
Eight years have now passed, and the members of this house as well as the people of the country do not up to this day know
Family Allowances

just where we stand. The proposal made at that time was not submitted in any political sense but on its merits, and that proposal was that there should be specific amendments to the British North America Act, which in , my opinion every province would have approved, and that those amendments should be enacted in order that the federal government would have the necessary undisputed authority to bring in legislation of this kind, to bring in unemployment insurance and other social measures which it was not within the competence of the provinces to enact and administer or which they were not financially capable of undertaking. If that had been done the people of the country would not have been deceived and much needed social legislation would not have been delayed for years. They have certainly been deceived for years on this question of constitutionality. The question has been thrown back from the federal government to the provinces and from the provinces to the federal government, so that we have not known where we stood.
The hon. member for Lake Centre the other day, in a most admirable speech, one of the ablest speeches I have heard in this house, placed the situation clearly before the house when he asked that, in view of the uncertainty that surrounds the subject, a special case be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada. It is only fair to the members of this house, especially the laymen, and to the Canadian people, that this be done. If that is refused, then I suggest that we go back to our proposal in Nova Scotia of 1936 and 1937 and accept the motion made at that time by the late Mr. Harrington and his associates and hav.e that proposal enacted so that we may have a specific amendment to the British North America Act. If that were done, there would be no doubt in the years that lie ahead as to what our authority is, and we would be able to pass legislation that would be effective and concerning which there would be no shadow of doubt. That is the position I have taken over the years and that is the position I take to-night.

I wish to clear up one question that arose in connection with the second reading of the bill on July 27. The Prime Minister interrupted me and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre said that it was propaganda that I was advocating at that time. It is seldom that I have spoken in this house without having my facts before me and when the Prime Minister interrupted me I said that the facts could be found in a book that could be procured from the parliamentary library. I have checked the facts, and I find

that in "Who's Who" for 1913 the statement is made that the right hon. Prime Minister was engaged upon the investigation of industrial relations under the auspices of the Rockefeller foundation from 1911 to 1917 and wrote "Industry and Humanity" in 1918. That was all I said. I did not say that he had given up his residence in this country, because I knew then, as I know now, that many men have been overseas for the last four or five years without having given up their residence in Ottawa or elsewhere in Canada, and the elections act provides that they may vote in their own constituencies. The Prime Minister has told us many times of the confidence that the people of Canada have reposed in him, but I would point out that at times this has been by means of an antiquated electoral system. The Prime Minister like many other hon. members was not elected by the majority of the ballots in his own constituency of Prince Albert. He was short some 1,160 votes.

I was only correcting the impression that took place on second reading of this bill. I have pretty well covered the matter now. I just wish to say that there are some seventy-four members in this house who have been elected to the present house without a majority of votes cast, although in 1919 the Prime Minister's chart, or whatever you wish to call it, did suggest some alterations in our electoral system.
When I spoke on second reading of this bill I said that I did not think it was constitutional. I repeat what I said a year ago, in 1913, in speaking on social security, and as has been well pointed out to-day, it is passing strange to me, if the federal government could not pay old age pensions direct but had to pay them through the provincial governments, how in the world they can profess to pay this grant, family assistance for young children, direct. I do not know. I fail to see where one can differentiate or draw the line between old people and babies in this legislation. As the hon. member for Lake Centre so well argued this afternoon, I think this matter should be referred to the supreme court and there should be a decision, because certainly if it is found to be unconstitutional at a later date, after we have started to put it in operation, it will

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: The hon. member has tried again this evening to leave the same impression he sought to leave the other evening, which was to the effect that I was in another country during the years between 1914 and 1918. He has read from the introduction to the book which I had written entitled "Industry and Humanity", that the work of research was carried out at the instance of the Rockefeller foundation. The hon. member perhaps has not known that the Rockefeller foundation has men carrying on investigations in all parts of the world, and that in many instances there is no obligation on the part of the investigators of the foundation to reside in any one place rather than another. It is true I was retained by the Rockefeller foundation to make certain researches. But the writing of the book which my hon. friend has referred to and the researches I made in connection therewith were for the most part carried on in this very city. I have allowed to pass in previous years this story that I was out of Canada during the last war. It has been repeated-*
It was not denied until at the time of the last election.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: No. It was denied when I became leader of my party and has been denied many times since; but I have made it a general rule on matters of this kind to allow people to say what they please and not to pay any attention to them. But this thing has gone a little bit too far. It has gone to the extent where people of this country have come to have an entirely erroneous impression. I told the hon. member the other night that I had written every line of that book in this city and I wish to repeat that to-night. I want to tell him, if he needs to be told, that if he will go to the city hall here he will find that I have paid my taxes every month in this city from the year 1900 to date. If he will go to the Imperial Realty company he will find that I was living at the Roxborough every month of the years to which he has referred to-night. It is true that my duties took me occasionally to the United States to visit large industries in my endeavours to help in avoiding industrial complications-disputes in war industries and in helping to further a maximum production of munitions of war.
On a point of order-

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: I am going to answer the hon. gentleman; I have a right to answer him.

On a point of order, I have the same rights in this house as the hon. Prime Minister. May I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that you were pretty rigid in your ruling as to our sticking to the issue. What has this to do with the bill we are discussing, whether the right hon. the Prime Minister was living in this country or in the United States during the last war? What has that to do with this particular issue?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Tory propaganda, that is all.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

You would never know it from what you said to-night.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext:
May I say further to my hon. friend that during the greater part of the last war I was a member of the executive of the Canadian patriotic fund, and if he or any other hon. members will take the care to look at the record of the patriotic fund they will find I was present at more meetings than any other single member. During that time I was assisting in every possible way I could, having regard to circumstances which I could not avoid.
Just one further word with reference to what the hon. member for Souris said the other evening. He said that I had placed party before country. At that time he was referring to the words with which I concluded the debate an evening or two before, namely, that I hoped to be able to leave to this countiy, to my party and to my country an honourable name. Because I said party first, then country, he found it necessary to go out of his way to refer to me as "A man who puts party before country." Perhaps my hon. friend might be interested in knowing that where there are two words and one wishes to emphasize one word more than the other, one usually leaves the word to be emphasized to the last, and where there are two words, one of which refers to something which is greater than the other, one usually, if one is complying with the elementary rules of composition, allows the word expressive of the greater entity to follow the lesser. It may be helpful to the hon. member to keep that in mind from new on. That is the reason why I placed the

word "country" at the end' and the word "party" before it. I regard my country as more important than anything else.

(b) "child" means any person under the age of sixteen years who is a resident of Canada at the date of registration and-
(i)	who was.bom in Canada and has been a resident of Canada since birth; or
(ii)	who has been a resident of Canada for three consecutive years immediately prior to the date of registration; or

I take it that the intention of the amendment is to cover the cases of children born overseas whose fathers are in the Canadian forces. Is it the intention that the amendment shall cover the case of a child born to a Canadian soldier who may be in an army of occupation on the continent after the war?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: It covers the cases of children bom overseas, but while they are resident in Canada, not for the period of time that they are overseas.

Will it not cover the case of a child in Great Britain? I believe there are many thousands of children of Canadian soldiers who have been bom in Great Britain. The suggestion made by several other hon. members early in the debate was that the parents of those children should be covered. Canadian troops may be in Great Britain and 
on the continent for some years to come, and I suggest that the family allowance should be payable in respect of the children of those men.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: My hon. friend is aware that, under the dependents' allowance board, at the present time provision is made for children such as those to which he has made reference. In the opinion of the government, if more is needed for their protection the best method in which to provide that protection would be under the act which already exists for that purpose. My hon. friend will see that payments under this measure will be made throughout Canada. It is hoped it will not be necessary to make payments under this measure outside Canada. However, payments under the dependents' allowance measure, already are made outside Canada; and if further payments are needed, in the opinion of the government it would be better if the necessary provision were made under dependents' allowance than to try to make any further amendment to this measure.

In respect of the child of a soldier living in Canada, dependents' allowance is now paid. The same is true of a child in Great Britain. Under this measure a child living in Canada will receive family allowance. The family allowance will not be paid, however, in respect of the child living in Great Britain. As I understand the Prime Minister's present suggestion, it is that the dependents' allowance would be increased in respect of a child living in Great Britain. I should like to know why children are not treated the same in both cases. Why cannot that be done?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: This bill does not come into effect until after July of next year. In the interval conditions may arise which, at the moment, cannot be anticipated. But if there is any injustice in any way with respect to any Canadian child born overseas it can readily be met, as I have said, under the dependents' allowance measure, when the time comes; or, if it were preferable, it could be met under some ' regulations under the present measure.

I take it that it is the object of this bill to encourage the rearing of healthy young Canadians. If that is so, then it seems to me that these sections-and I have been able to give them only a cursory reading 

are restrictive, and that we are by these sections limiting the children to whom this shall be paid. We are limiting it, because of the changes in residence, in respect of the parents.
Let us take a case in point. This child is born in Canada and has been resident in

Canada since birth. Then the parents moved, we will say to the United States, perhaps in search of work. They return a year later and take up their residence in Canada again. Under these regulations would that child not be debarred until it had been here for three consecutive years?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext:
No. There is another section-perhaps my hon. friend has not seen it-which states:
. . . whose father's or mother's domicile at the time of such person's birth and for three years prior thereto was in Canada, and has continued to be in Canada up to the date of registration.

That does not cover it. I draw attention to the words "has continued to be in Canada up to the date of registration." That is the point I am getting at. It seems to me to deprive the child of the benefits, under those circumstances. It is the child I am thinking about, not the family.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Here there are four classes, under which it has been felt that we would include all the children who were residing in Canada, except those who were 'born outside Canada, and -who would not be included until they had been in Canada for three years. First of all, if they were born in Canada, and have remained here, they are covered. If they are born of persons who were not in Canada, but whose domicile or home is in Canada-but born away from Canada-they -can be registered as soon as they get back here. And that, incidentally, would take care of merchant seamen.
It might well happen there would be men in the forces who are not domiciled in Canada. But they are in Canada's fighting forces, and they should have the same privilege as if their domicile were here.
Then there is the class who were not born in Canada, but who have been admitted, to Canada, and have been here three years. It was felt, with respect to outsiders, that they should not merely by getting in become entitled to family allowances. A certain period should elapse, wThich would show that they intend to remain here.
I do not think it would be possible under that provision to exclude any who should be included unless, in the view taken by the hon. member for Vancouver South, it should also be paid outside Canada to children born of members of the forces. But, with respect to that, if anything unfair results from paying the allowances to children of members of the forces in Canada, it can be dealt with more conveniently by increasing the dependents' allowance; because there are boards there to determine overseas who are the persons who can receive dependents' allowances, while if it were left generally payable to any
child who could claim that one of his parents was or had been a member of the forces, it would be very difficult to arrive at proper decisions.
There would have to be some controlling agency to determine who are to receive the benefits. That controlling agency exists already in the form of the boards administering dependents' allowances. It would be much simpler for the time the children will remain overseas to arrange for an increase in dependents' allowance than it would be to have another separate agency to distribute the allowance.

Why could not the dependents' allowance committee in Great Britain deal with family allowances as well? I presume they will have to do much the same thing in Canada.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Because this paragraph, as it is, is so broad that it would give rise to claims which the boards administering dependents' allowance would not recognize. They recognize claims for persons who have been living together as man and wife for a period determined by the regulations, but do not recognize other possible situations; whilst this is intended to apply to all children in Canada.

I realize that there might be some administrative difficulties, and there would certainly be some cases in which it would be improper to pay allowances. But I suggest it is unfair to the great majority of men in the forces who are overseas and who have children there. A man who was married in Great Britain and perhaps at the present time has two children-and I believe some of them have two or three-is, in my opinion, entitled to the family allowance. I do not see that there is any reason why there should not be a family allowance paid in respect of his children. They are Canadian children, just as are children here in Canada. I do not think administrative difficulties should deprive that man of the allowance.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It would be unfair only if the amount were not paid. There will not be any unfairness in paying an equivalent amount as an addition under dependents' allowances, if in dollars and cents it is the equivalent. There would not be any unfairness in not calling it by two names.

The dependents' allowance is paid only by order in council.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

Which was passed under the War Measures Act.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.
Family Allowances

But this family allowances measure is primarily a peace-time measure. The man overseas should have the same rights as people in Canada.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: So far it is not intended to provide for children who are going to live abroad. It would be quite proper to provide for them by an increase in dependents' allowances while they are there because of their fathers' connection with the armed forces of Canada. If, after the war is over, they decide to remain abroad it would not be the purpose of this law to provide them with allowances while living abroad.

I agree with that, but there will probably be a Canadian army in Europe after the war. We shall probably have troops in the army of occupation and there will be many Canadian troops remaining in England after the war on military duty. It will take a long time to get even the present families back to Canada and I suggest that allowances should be payable in respect of children of those men.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Dependents' allowances will be paid and will have to be paid so long as the men remain in active service overseas. It will be quite a simple matter to equalize the benefits for them so that they will not be inferior to the state they would be in were they in Canada and receiving money from two different sources.

Then it is plain they are to get a second dependents' allowance, something of that type?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If there are children of Canadians who are still in the forces when this becomes operative they should not be discriminated against; they should get as much money as they would if they were in Canada.
Can the Prime Minister give us an assurance that the children of the men in the armed forces will be paid the same amount of money as the children in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: I cannot say whether I will be in the next parliament or not, and I am therefore not in a position to give any undertaking as to how this measure will be carried out. If I am here to assist in carrying out -its provisions, I shall certainly see first and foremost that justice is done to the men of the armed forces.	*

Supposing a Canadian woman, for instance, a Canadian nurse marries a'man who is not a Canadian. I know of girls who went to South Africa who have

married South African men. If they come back to Canada would they have to put in three years residence?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No; it is the father or mother.

They would have to wait three years. Paragraph (iv) reads:
Who was born while his father or mother was a member of the naval, military or air forces of Canada or within twelve months after his father or mother had ceased to be a member of such forces.
In the case of the nurse, she would have to leave the service to be married, and if she did not return within a year then they would have to wait three years.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If the child were born more than- a year after she had left the army and she then came back to Canada, that child would have to wait three years because she would then come in as an immigrant under the Immigration Act. If the child were born within a year from the time she left the army, that child would come under paragraph (iv) of this section.

I have a case upon which I should like a little clarification as to the status of the children of the union. A man and woman were married before war broke out. He enlisted in the first brigade that went overseas and his wife followed him overseas. They have had two children since they arrived there. What would be the status of those children of that soldier?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Just as soon as he got back-

When they get back home would their ages start from the registration in Canada or the registration in the old country?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: At the time of the registration in Canada.

This man is a soldier, and he cannot come back, but his wife decides to return to Canada. He is still a Canadian and his children are Canadian, even though born in England. If the children of a soldier, who cannot come back to Canada, who are born in Great Britain, decide to come to Canada, would their ages start from the registration in England?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The ages would start from the time of the registration in England, but the payments would start from the date of the registration in Canada. Until the children get back to Canada, their cases should be taken care of under the dependents' allowances, but as soon as they get back they would not have to wait three years before becoming entitled to family allowances.

Family Allowances

Supposing a child was born in 1941 in England and does not return to Canada with his parents until 1945. Would the age as far as Canada is concerned start from the date of registration in England, where the child must be registered, or from the date of its return to Canada?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	There are two
registrations, one for the purpose of determining the age, and the other, a special registration, to determine whether one is entitled to come under the family allowances measure. When that child would get here he would be four years old and he would receive $5 a month until he had completed his sixth year; that would be for two years after he got back, and then he would draw S6 a month.

I am still not clear about one point. Sometimes we have cases under the old age pensions regulations where an old age pensioner goes away, perhaps to Great Britain, thinking he may be able to live there with some relations. He comes back again after breaking his residence for a year and finds that he is no longer eligible for old age pension. I am thinking of a case of this kind. A family may register their children on July 1,1945, and then, later, because of family necessity or the need of work or something of that sort, they move across the border. They remain there for fifteen or sixteen months and then come back. Would not those children under these four clauses be denied family allowances?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: They would if domicile had been abandoned, but if they had merely gone abroad with the intention of returning that would not change their domicile. Had we used "residence" only, the result that the hon. member fears would have happened, and that is why we used both residence and domicile. If one goes away with the intention of coming back, his absence would have no such effect.

But they do not always know what they are going to do, whether they will change their residence or domicile. Whenever they come back it may be held that since they had left the country to get work, we will say, they had actually abandoned their domicile. I am asking this question because there will be the odd case and it is the odd cases that cause trouble in the public mind. Somebody says, "I have been a Canadian for three, four or five generations, and just because I happened to be away for a year or so I am denied benefit under this bill." We have had such cases with old age pensioners.
Domicile is a question of intention and it can easily be inquired into. If such a one went away with the intention of abandoning his Canadian domicile for good, he would forfeit his right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to quote
an example along that line in connection with old age pensions. I am thinking of a person who came from England and has lived in Canada for a total of forty years. At the age of fifty-five he returned to England for a visit, intending to return to Canada shortly. While in England he became ill and had to remain there for four or five years. Although his intention had not been to stay in England, when he came home it was stated that for the purposes of old age pension his 20-year period between the ages of fifty and seventy years had been broken and that he could not qualify for an old age pension, until some years after the age of seventy. A person in that situation feels it very keenly. He says: "Here I am a British subject and a Canadian citizen and because of this technicality I fail to qualify." If this clause in this bill stands the way it is, it will be only a matter of a few years * before we shall have similar cases brought to our attention as members of parliament. Canadians of several generations will come to us and say: "I went- away, not intending to stay, but something happened and I had to stay, and now I bring my children back, and although they qualified before I went away I find that now I have to wait three years before they can qualify again." It seems to me that in view of cases such as we have indicated the Prime Minister might reconsider the wording of subparagraph (i) so that it would read "who was born in Canada and is resident in Canada at the time of registration."

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext:
The clauses
have all been very carefully considered, but there will be cases arise and one cannot see at the moment how they may be interpreted. It depends undoubtedly on what the whole motive of the bill may be and in the carry-* ing of it out in accordance with what would be equitable treatment. I cannot imagine that this measure would be administered in a way that would prejudice any child who has a real ground for receiving benefits under its provisions. But may I direct the .attention of hon. members to this point. You can sometimes say too much in acts of parliament and by so doing convey an impression that is far from the one that is intended. My hon. friend the. leader of the party has spoken of families that might go to the United States for a short time and then come

Family Allowances

back. I can. conceive of cases where families might leave Canada, for example, if there was a gold strike in California or something of the kind, and the father might wish to go there and take the chances, and might stay there for a couple of years and then come back. If the attempt is made to cover every class of case that may arise, the measure might soon be rendered unworkable. To deal as my hon. friend suggests with cases of the kind might encourage people to leave Canada instead of causing them to remain here, and one of the purposes of this measure is to encourage families to stay in Canada and help build up the country. There is power to make regulations under the bill. The regulations will be submitted to this house and to parliament. The government will have to report on all the regulations that are made. If there are injustices they will be remedied at the right time, but to attempt to anticipate every circumstance would make the legislation unworkable.

I realize that there is
a great deal in what the Prime Minister says, but the difficulty is that the letter of the law is often adhered to rigidly, and it is because of some of our experiences with old age . pension cases that we are anxious about this.
I know it was not the intention of parliament to say to an aged person who comes from Alberta to Ontario with a view to being with the only relatives she has-I am dealing with a particular case now-"You cannot get the old age pension unless you go back to Edmonton and apply for it there." I have a case that I have been dealing with for six or seven months, and this old lady telephoned me recently and said, "I suppose I will have to spend part of my last one hundred dollars to go back to Edmonton." That is the kind of case I have in mind where the letter of the law is applied rigidly and leads to difficulties that were never intended, I think the letter of the law in this case is pretty rigid, but I must confess that to widen it to the extent my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggests would be, as the Prime Minister indicates, opening the door very wide indeed. But I should like to see some further consideration given to the phraseology of this clause. I am not suggesting any wording at the moment.
Mr. .ST. LAURENT:	The case suggested
by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would qualify a child who was born in Canada while his mother was on a visit to Canada. If she returned to her home in, let us say, the United States and then came back, her child could be registered immediately,

whilst if the child had been bom at his home and then came to Canada he would have to wait three years. I think that is a distinction which should be made. He should not get any special benefit because- of the fact that while his mother was touring Canada he was born. I think it will be found that all the cases that could be covered have been covered. Hon. members will notice that this language is much broader than that used in the Old Age Pensions Act. Some of the difficulties which arose under the old age pensions legislation arose because a portion of the pension is payable by the provinces and each province wants to take care only of its own. Provisions are being made this year to clear up that situation and to remedy many of the difficulties which have arisen in the administration of the Old Age Pensions Act.

With reference to
paragraph (c), is it intended that orphanages, homes for children and the like are to be entitled to this payment? I notice that in section 4 (1) it is provided-I omit the portions that are inapplicable:
The allowance shall be payable ... to a parent .	.	. or to such other person as is
authorized by or pursuant to the regulations to receive the same.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	It is not intended
that allowances shall be payable to institutions. It is intended that payments shall be made to a parent. If the hon. member will look at paragraph (f) he will see what parent means:
"parent" means a father, stepfather, adoptive father, foster father, mother, stepmother, adoptive mother, foster mother or any other person who maintains or has the custody of a child, but does not include an institution.
The intention of the bill as drafted is not to substitute the allowance payable under this bill for the provision that is now being made by the provinces for the care of children in institutions.

Section 5 refers to an agency.
It says:
The allowance shall be applied by the person receiving the same exclusively towards the maintenance, care, training, education and advancement of the child, and, if the minister or such officer as is authorized by regulations in that behalf is satisfied that the allowance is not being so applied, payment thereof shall be discontinued or made to some other person or agency.
What does that mean?

Family Allowances
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That was intended to cover such welfare organizations as have been rendering so valuable and patriotic a service in the administration of the dependents' allowance. Hon. members know there are some cases where the dependents' allowance, instead of being turned over directly to the person who would normally receive it, is paid to a welfare agency which disburses it and sees that it is used in the manner that was intended.

Then this is not intended to cover an institution?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is not intended to cover an institution. I suppose there might be a case where a parent would be receiving an. allowance and would be using an institution as a boarding house where the child was actually living. He would have to show that he was maintaining the child in order to get the allowance. But it is not intended to pay the allowance for the purpose of relieving the provinces of what they are now doing in the institutions for those who are not cared for by their parents.

There really is no definition of "institution" in the bill. It reads:
(c) "institution" shall have such meaning as may be prescribed in the regulations.
I think that is very poor draftsmanship, and I should like to know why "institution" is not defined in the bill.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It was left in this form because it was felt that it would be difficult to make a description which would fit the cases of all the nine provinces. Administrative machinery will have to be set up, and the intention is not to substitute this for the disbursements which are being made by the provinces now, under subsection 7 of section 92, of the British North America Act, for eleemosynary institutions which are within their exclusive jurisdiction; and it was felt that in setting up the machinery it would be possible to ascertain what would be the proper description to fit the various kinds of institutions doing that work in the various provinces. In my province there are institutions of a certain character in some places; there are others of another character, sometimes in the same place. Up to a few months ago my own home was alongside a Protestant orphans' home, which was an organization under the direction of the Church of England. There are institutions in the city of Quebec under the direction of the Roman Catholic church, some under the direction of the Salvation Army, some under the direction of the Independent Order, Daughters of the
100-358i
Empire, and one under the direction of the Ligue des Jeunes Filles-all getting subsidies from the province to assist them in the work they are carrying on; and it was felt that it would be dangerous to attempt by statute, without an investigation over the country at large, to make a definition which would fit them all.

Is it the intention that any of these institutions will get the allowance?
_ Mr. ST. LAURENT: No; it is the intention that institutions which are financed by provincial authority will not get the allowance. These institutions, by subsection 7 of section 92 of the British North America Act, are under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. It is intended here that the allowance shall go to the children who are maintained by individuals, those individuals being of a class described in section 2, paragraph (f), as "parents".

I am still in doubt as to just what the minister means. I can understand very well that an institution financed by a province shall not be entitled to any allowance for the maintenance of a child. Do I understand! that any organization, orphanage, home for children, and the like, which is maintained by a church organization, is to be entitled to an allowance,, when the parent pays any amount to that institution for the maintenance of his children?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The allowance will be paid to the parent and he will make his arrangements with the institution.

In case a child is found on the street, it is taken, of course, to whatever institution the police have for taking children to and then is handed into the possession of some organization, the Children's Aid Society, or some such body. I am not very familiar with that part of it, although there is some activity of this kind in Toronto. Then that society hands such children over to people who will adopt them; whoever adopts them gets the money?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

There are other cases- I know of a number-where homes are operated by good, ordinary, humane people, usually motherly women, and they look after, perhaps, three or four of these children and raise them. Would they be entitled to receive the allowance?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If they do so, not as an. institution which would come within subsection 7 of section 92 of the British North America Act, but as adoptive parents, they
56%
Family Allowances

would get it. It is not the intention to insist upon legal adoption. Hon. members will see that the definition is quite wide. It includes adoptive mother, foster mother or any other person who maintains or has custody of a child. It is the fact which is intended to be looked to rather than the legality of the proceedings under which the child has been taken into a private family.

What about a child of unknown parentage in an orphanage?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: An orphanage will not receive the allowance, but if a child of unknown parents is adopted by an individual, the individual adopting the child will receive the allowande.

lit view of the fact that orphanages so often are in charge of provinces, would the provinces benefit to any extent?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No.

They would not get anything?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have already had some representations on this very point from the constituency I represent. A number of people whom I know are concerned about the assistance which some of these orphanages and homes may or may not receive. In part their concern will be covered by the minister's statement that where parents or others are paying for the keep of children in homes, they will-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The parents will receive the allowance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Fine. There is another angle to it which, it seems to be, might be investigated further. The aim of this whole measure is to improve the conditions surrounding the children of Canada.
To put the children back in the home. That is what I would think it was for-rather than in institutions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the proper course to pursue where the parents are living-
And where they are not living.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
-and wherever it is possible for this to be done. The hope of all of us in supporting this measure is that the conditions surrounding all the children of Canada, the houses they live in, the clothing they wear, the food they eat, will be improved. Why should not children in orphanages have the same opportunity of some slight improvement as a result of the money which we are voting under this measure? That is our

primary concern, not so much assisting the family budget, although that is the way you achieve the purpose in view. Our primary concern is to improve the conditions of the children. I have already been asked, for example, whether certain orphanages and homes in Winnipeg will receive this benefit so that the children in these homes may have better conditions.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It was felt that these orphanages and like institutions were expressly declared by subsection 7 of section 92 of the British North America Act to be a provincial responsibility, and it is a responsibility which is being discharged by the provinces. I know that in my province these institutions now receive sixty cents per day per infant. I think that amount is paid up to a certain age; I did not inquire as to what the allowance was when children get beyond four or five years old. It used to be forty cents; it was increased to sixty cents because it was found that forty cents a day was not sufficient to provide for them adequately. But the provision which is made is fixed at what is necessary for their upkeep, and we would have no way of saying that the provinces would have to continue to make the same provision as heretofore, or to make such additional provision as the increase in the cost of living might require, and it would be merely taking for the federal exchequer a burden which is already being carried by the public through the provincial exchequers. It was felt that if this were done there would be a much better chance of getting children back into individual homes where the surroundings are perhaps more congenial than they are in the institutions.

What about an orphanage in a province that receives no support from the province?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If it receives no support from the province, the province is not discharging the responsibility which the British North America Act has put upon it.

What about children
whose parents send them to an institution for one reason or another? Would the parents be allowed to turn the money over to the institution?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Certainly. Not only will they be allowed to do so, but the institutions will insist upon their doing so. Institutions, I know, do now accept children of parents who are not providing for them and who are supposed not to be in a position to provide for them. If it is the opinion of

Family Allowances
the institution that in respect of a child the parent is receiving from the government a certain sum of money, the institution will insist on getting it or will not keep the child. But the money will go from the federal treasury to the parent, who will have to apply it for the children. Under the other provisions the hon. member will see that if the children are in an institution and the parent is receiving money and does not apply it to the maintenance of the children, they will be cut off.

If the money is given to the institution by the parent, how does the government know that the money given for a particular child, or for two or three or four . children, went to the children's upkeep? How will the inspector know that the money is spent on them?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The government will not know that, but it will know that that money is being used for the benefit of the child. Whether that is the money which is used to buy the milk or the porridge that the child does consume, or whether it is not, the government will know that it is used in the institution for the maintenance of the child. But it will not attempt to identify the commodities bought individually with that money.
Will they be sure of that all the way through?

Does that mean that as far as children's aid societies, maintained under provincial laws are concerned, they would not be entitled to any part of this?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not as against the crown.

Or in any way?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	They would be
entitled as against the parents whose children are being aided. It would be stipulated that they should receive it, but they will not be entitled as against the crown to receive it direct.

But suppose the parents
are dead or cannot be found and the institution itself has the responsibility for these children? They would get no assistance under
this?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, because they are performing ,a work specified in subsection 7 of section 92, and it is a provincial responsibility to maintain those institutions. Up to the present they have been maintained. This is a measure for the assistance of children living in individual homes.

Having regard to the explanation given by the minister-of the reason designated that these institutions shall not receive any payment, which is to prevent any question of constitutionality being raised in this regard-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is not to prevent any question of constitutionality being raised but to prevent any suggestion that the federal government is trying to control the conduct of those directing these institutions. They are not under federal authority but under provincial authority. It is intended under this legislation to see to it that the money which is voted is expended for the purpose for which it was voted, and it was not felt desirable to attempt to exercise any control over the institutions which are expressly put by the constitution under the jurisdiction of the provinces.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In further answer to the hon. member for Lake Centre, I may say that both in Ireland and1 in New Zealand, where no constitutional question could arise, the institutions maintained by the state are not recipients of familv allowances.
- *

What administrative organization is planned for checking these cases? There will have to be many investigations and continual checking. What organizations are to be set up to do that work?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: What is planned is to have first of all a registry and the registration will constitute the title until something else is showm. It will operate, I hope, as satisfactorily as the administration of dependents' allowances. There have been enlisted now almost a million persons and a large proportion of them are married. There are a great many family allowances being paid under the name of dependents' allowances, and that has been going on since 1939. It has not required any elaborate machinery. It has operated in a manner that has caused little or no complaint; and it is hoped that there will be, if perhaps not to the same degree, at least to a satisfactory degree, the same willingness on the part of the Canadian public to be of service during peace as there has been manifested during war. There is not a city in Canada where public-spirited citizens have not spent a lot of time to assist in the proper administration of dependents' allowances, and it is hoped that the same public-spiritedness will continue to exist. No doubt there will have to be some machinery, just as has been provided to administer dependents' allowances, but it is not anticipated that there will be anything of a different
Family Allowances

nature, andi this will be spread over the whole country. I cannot say just what organizations will be used1, but it is not the intention to set up an entirely new organization which will be giving full time in every little village to the administration of family allowances.

Can the minister give an example of the organizations that would be used?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: These matters have not been determined. They have been discussed and are being discussed, and it is because it is felt that it will require a great deal of investigation and consideration that power is being asked to provide all these through regulations. But what I have in mind for the village in which I was born, for example, and where I still have a brother and sister residing, is that the postmaster or the secretary treasurer of the municipality would probably be the local officer attending to it, and it would add very little to the other work which that kind of official is performing. That is the way in which these things are done under the dependents' allowance scheme. The officials available where the work has to be done are those who are looked to to do it.

About what number of people ' would be required to administer these allowances?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I could not even make an estimate.

The government must have some idea of how many new civil servants will be required.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: From statistics that were given here the other day, at the present time over 600,000 cheques a month are being distributed to dependents of members of the forces. Now, it may be that two or three times that many cheques would have to be distributed. The task will be a little larger.
It is not a task of a different kind. A lot of experience has been gained in the administration of payments to be made for children through the operation of dependents' allowances.

The government must have some estimate of the personnel that would be required. About how many civil servants will be required to administer family allowances?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: So far as I know, no estimate has been made of how many civil servants will be engaged in administering this. There are quite a number already in the Department of Finance who will be controlling

it, but the details of the machinery required have not been determined; and what was stated to tire government was that it was not a problem different in nature or kind but only different in magnitude from that which had to be faced in the distribution of allowances to dependents of men in the forces.
I take it that there has been no estimate of the number required to administer the measure. Has there been any estimate of the cost of administering it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If I may answer my hon. friend as well as I can I should point out, following what the Minister of Justice has said, that there has been a great deal of experience in connection with the administration of dependents' allowances. Under the dependents' allowances regulations 609,854 cheques are issued each month. They are issued from Ottawa'. They are issued by the treasury officials, and it is estimated that it takes something like forty officials to issue 100,000 cheques and to keep 100,000 accounts. It is estimated, as the Prime Minister said, that if every family having children entitled to receive family allowances receives an allowance this will mean something like one and a half million cheques. That would be just to write the cheques?

Free?

I should like to ask one question that has been confusing me somewhat, but perhaps it is clear to the other hon. members of the committee. I was wondering if the parliamentary assistant would clear up this point, because the question has been asked me on many occasions, and I am sure other hon. members have been asked with respect to the kind of machinery which will be in operation in connection with those above that salary level.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If I might make a correction of a figure I gave the hon. member for Vancouver South I would say that the number of treasury officers estimated to be needed is 600-not 900.
Family Allowances

This bill does not purport tp deal with the income tax situation, as the leader of the opposition no doubt understands. It will be noted that section 8(1) says:
Nothing in this act shall preclude such adjustment of the deduction on account of a dependent child from tax payable under the Income War Tax Act as may be necessary to avoid duplication of benefits under the Income War Tax Act and this act.
By that provision the legislation aims to warn recipients of cheques that they are not going to get both family allowance and full allowance for their children under the Income War Tax Act. But that is not being dealt with in this bill. I am informed it is the intention of the government that that will be dealt with by way of an amendment to the Income War Tax Act to be introduced at the next session of parliament, which will certainly be held prior to the coming into force of family allowances, on July 1, 1945.
If I might answer my hon. friend briefly on one point, I would say this. Both in his speech the other day and again to-night, he mentioned the figure of 81,200 as being the limit of income above which a person would not benefit from family allowances. I do not know if he was using the figure as an illustration, or if he used it as a definite top level. But from the tables I have seen, some people in peculiar circumstances, getting as much as $5,000 income, will benefit from family allowances. The number of people getting over $1,200 a year of gross income who will benefit from family allowances will be much greater than those above that figure who do not benefit from those allowances. But, as I have said, that is a matter which is not to be dealt with now.
Would the parliamentary assistant give some' further explanation on that? It is important.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is not intended to be dealt with under this legislation. That will be dealt with by an amendment to the Income War Tax Act, and when the amendment is introduced it will be fully explained to the house. I will be quite frank and say it is not easy to explain the operations of family allowances and the income tax deductions in respect of children, so as to avoid duplication. That is not a simple thing to do. It is not a simple thing to work out, in view of the changes made by legislation this year. That is still being worked out.
The purpose, however, is to make it quite clear and that is the intention of this section, -that no one shall benefit both from family allowances and from the Income War Tax 
Act, and that no one will be worse off than he is to-day. Those people receiving the full allowance for their children, to which they are entitled under the Income War Tax Act, will not receive any allowance by way of family allowances.
In answer to the hon. member who asked whether cheques would be sent out to those people who could not possibly benefit from family allowances, I can say that that is still under discussion with the income tax authorities. It may be easier for . all concerned: to send cheques out to everyone, and then have a final adjustment on the income tax return, rather than sort out in advance the number of people who could not possibly benefit under the family allowances measure. That number, I might tell the committee, is something under 200,000. There are fewer than 200,000 taxpayers who are in a position where they cannot benefit at all under the measure.
Fewer than 200,000?	^

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:

Family Allowances
However my hon. friend has referred to his case, and I might refer to mine. Perhaps this will help to illustrate just how much easier this whole business may be to administer than would at first appear. The provisions of this measure relate only to families. There will be no necessity of keeping track of those individuals who have no families. Where there are families, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the chances are that already registrations will have been made, and those registrations will help to verify other matters of registration, will verify information given as to numbers, and the like. Children must be registered when they are born, and families dio not move as readily as individuals. That is an important fact to keep in mind in connection with the administration of this measure, and the difficulties surrounding its administration-or rather the limitation of the extent of those difficulties. I mention, this only because it throws some light on that aspect of the matter.

For the last half hour the discussion has been entirely irrelevant. We are dealing with definitions, and particularly to the definition of "institution". I would ask hon. members to confine their remarks to that.

Before leaving this paragraph I would ask the parliamentary assistant whether or not the decision as to the sending of a cheque to a person who, perhaps, is in a three- or four-tbousandi-dollar income tax bracket, would not depend upon the person himself. For instance, if I wish family allowances to be paid to my wife, instead of my having the privilege of deducting it from my income tax, I shall make that application. If I do not wish to have it done in that way, I will not make the application. Will not the matter work out through the volition of the taxpayer, rather than through the arrangements made by the department? If I wish my wife to have it, I shall apply for it. If I do not wish her to have it, I shall take my deduction. Is that not the way it will work out?

That might be the solution to the problem in my mind. I take it that the application vvould be made and the cheques issued. Perhaps the suggestion of the hon. member for Trinity would, cure the problem. Those of us who would normally be entitled to exemption under the income tax might decide that there is no point in having cheques come in and then having them go right out again. There would thus be duplication and trouble to the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The number of taxpayers in Canada is estimated to be 2,000,000. The figure of 181,000 will fluctuate from year to year. Since the income tax is now on a pay-as-you-go basis it might well be that the income tax authorities will advise that the only way in which to handle this is to pay every one the allowance and adjust it at the end of the year. But the suggestion made by the hon. member for Trinity is certainly one that is being considered.

It would fluctuate from
month to month, too.

I believe we are on the
clause giving the definition of "institution." I am disappointed that the government has not found it feasible or possible to arrange that these allowances shall be paid to children in orphanages. Those of us who have had any experience in raising a family know that the allowance which is intended to be paid would in no way provide for the proper upbringing of a child. As has been stated previously, this is considered to be a provincial responsibility.
In the province from which I come there are several orphanages. I believe the oldest and largest is situated in the constituency the Prime Minister represents in this house. I am sorry I have not the amount of assistance the province has given to these institutions, but I know that in years gone by, had it not been for the help received from the district from which I come, the children in this orphanage in the constituency of the right hon. gentleman would have had extremely slim living and a very hard time to get along. In later years a fraternal organization has carried on a province-wide appeal for assistance for this institution.
There is also another institution in the southern part of the province at Indian Head which is sponsored and supported by another fraternal organization. I want to point out to you. Mr. Chairman, and to hon. members of the committee that the small sum being given under this legislation is not going to provide any child with a proper upbringing. This

Family Allowances

allowance is to be paid to some people who can take it along with other money they have earned and yet place a child in an institution. As the Minister of Justice pointed out, this is properly done if it is to the advantage of the child. By this bill we are attempting to provide for the children of parents in unfortunate circumstances and I submit that there could not be any more unfortunate child in this country than the one who has lost both parents and must of necessity be in an orphanage. Consequently, I say I am disappointed that the government has not seen fit to work out some system whereby it would be possible to give this little bit of assistance to the children in these institutions.

I think it will be
found that in a great number of cases the child who has been left an orphan will be taken by relatives, perhaps a cousin or an uncle or an aunt. When this small assistance is being given, the child would not be placed in an orphanage. It may mean that children will be kept in the homes of relatives who oould not otherwise afford to keep them were they not receiving the help to be given under this bill. Will the definition of "child" cover an Eskimo or Indian child?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: I would suggest that if the committee would keep to the particular clause we are on we would make greater headway. There is reference later on to that and I think the question could be asked more appropriately at that time.

I understood the Minister of Justice to say some time ago that allowances under this bill would be paid to an adult who sponsored a child in an orphanage. Would that mean legal adoption or could you just sponsor a child?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It would not be sufficient for one to say that he would sponsor any child who came along. He would have to come within the definition of paragraph (f), but if unable to keep the child in his own home, he would have the child maintained in an institution where he would be paying board. He would have to be more than in loco parentis?

I happened to be out of the chamber, and I am not sure that the question I have in mind has been brought up under this section. Paragraph (c) reads:
"Institution" shall have such meaning as may be prescribed in the regulations.
I do not understand why it is necessary to adopt that form. This is supposed to be an explanation, but it is really no explanation at all. It is simply handing over to the people who will draw up the regulations the power to say what it means. In the other paragraphs of this section ,we find definitions of "child", "maintains", "minister", "parent", "registration" and so on. There is no attempt made in this section to explain the meaning of "institution". It says:
"institution" shall have such meaning as may be prescribed in the regulations.
Is what we mean by "institution" so complex that it cannot be explained in a paragraph just as "child" is explained in paragraph (b)? This takes the whole power away from parliament to define an institution and gives the power to the person who will draw the regulations. Is this committee incapable of defining "institution", or is there anything improper about it that we cannot deal with it here? Is this one definition out of them all beyond us, that we cannot say what the word means? It is a common thing in this house to say, whichever party is out of power, that the government is governing by order in council, but orders in council are not nearly as bad as the abuse of the power to make regulations. Orders in council, many of them, are just matters of passing a resolution, and they must be passed by thousands in time of war. The real damage, if damage is done, is done by abuse of the power to make regulations. This power to make regulations generally appears at the back of an act where it is scarcely noticed, and it gives the framer of the regulations power almost to make an act that suits him. It is generally provided that the regulations must be laid on the table, but has any hon. gentleman had the experience of trying to get something that has been laid on the table? I was referred to three different people when I tried to get something that had been laid on the table, and finally I was told that I might get it in a few months hence if I am lucky. I would1 ask whoever is in charge of the bill to explain why it is necessary to take all powers away from this parliament to define such a simple ordinary word as "institution".

speechtext:

On section 2, paragraph (d)-"maintains".

Could the Minister of Justice explain why this provision is inserted?

"maintains" means maintains wholly or substantially.
There was no agreement at the time whether it was 51 per cent or 51J or 60 or 75 per cent, and - so it was said that there may be some other way in which it will be possible to determine who will get the allowance. It is not to be divided, one portion going to one person and another portion going to another. There should be some way to determine in a practical fashion what will appear as to be reasonable as to what "substantially" means. It may not be the same in every locality. Hon. members will see in a later clause that the allowance is paid only while the child is being maintained. speechtext:

speechtext:

Do I understand that the regulations will be sufficiently broad to give "substantially" a meaning that it has not had before, or some meaning which is in contravention of the meaning of the word? speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to suggest an amendment to this paragraph. I hope that the Prime Minister will give it consideration. Frequently the tendency is to look with suspicion upon amendments from the opposition side, but I would suggest that this paragraph, and also, if I may refer to it at the moment because it is related to it, section lil (a) of this bill might be amended so as to put the choice of the mother first, as the one to receive the allowance. I would point out that in the two amendments which I intend to propose I leave the governor general in council with the power it has under the sections as they are now worded, to make varying arrangements in different provinces or for different classes of persons. But it seems to me that, in view of the experience of countries where family allowances are in effect, which in most cases is that it has been found desirable to make the payment to the mother, and in view of the considerable feeling here that that should be the case, we should try to word the bill so that the first choice will be the mother. Would you, Mr. Chairman, be lenient with me to the

point of letting me read to the committee and particularly to the Prime Minister, the two amendments I would propose? First:
That section 2 (f) of Bill No. 161 be amended by removing the words "father, stepfather, adoptive father, foster father," from their present position and inserting the said words after the words "foster mother" in line 31.
If that were done, the section would then read:
(f) "parent" means a mother, stepmother, adoptive mother, foster mother, father, stepfather, adoptive father, foster father or any other person who maintains or has the custody of a child, but does not include an institution.
Legally that would not change the picture at all, but it would, so far as wording is concerned, put the mother, or the person taking the place of the mother, first, and I think it is more than likely that in the case of most of the provinces and in the ease of most classes of persons the desire will be to have the cheque sent to the mother.
Along with that amendment it would be necessary to make a change in section ill (a), and I hope you, Mr. Chairman, will permit me to read my proposal at this point so that the Prime Minister will have the whole proposal before him. I suggest that when we reach section 11 (a) it be made to read:
(a) provide generally that payment shall be made to the mother, stepmother, adoptive mother or foster mother, without limiting the right of the governor in council to provide in respect of any province or any class of cases that payment shall he made to the parent prescribed in the regulations.	.
I point out again that legally that does not change the situation. The governor in council might, under the wording which I have laid down, provide that payment would be made right across Canada to. the father, but it would put the mother first at least as far as the wording is concerned. I think it might have the effect of encouraging provincial authorities to think in that direction and, I suggest, this would be more desirable. If it were not for the different concept of civil law that we have in the province of Quebec-I am not objecting to that in any way; I am simply stating a fact-I think it would be desirable to follow the practice of other countries where family allowances are in effect, and make it payable only to the mother; but because we have that different concept, which we respect, in one province of this country, I suggest that rve should word this bill not in ironclad language, but nevertheless so that the primary emphasis will be placed on the parent to whom I think it is desirable that the allowance be paid in all _ provinces where it is possible, namely, the mother. I read the second amendment so that

Family Allowances
the Prime Minister may know just what I have in mind for the later section. At the present time I move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort, the amendment I have sent to the Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: As the hon. member has said, the order does not make the slightest difference in the legal effect. If that is the case it seems to me there is a very strong reason for following in this statute the course followed generally in the statutes of Canada.
