If it were going to have any real effect in the direction which my hon. friend thinks is desirable, namely, that this government or the provincial governments were more likely to put the emphasis on the mother than on the father, there might be some point to it; but I submit that it is better to hold to what is customary in statutes and allow the arrangement itself to be made in accordance with what may appear to be best in the different localities concerned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I might say to the Prime Minister that I regard1 the amendment to the later section, to which I have already referred, as the more important one. My reason for introducing this amendment at this point is that if my amendment to section 11 (a) were accepted by the Prime Minister and the government, it would then make the wording of this section seem a bit odd in its present form. Maybe I am counting on too much in hoping that my amendment to section 11 (a) will be accepted, but I dare to hope that. I just want tc say to the Prime Minister that I did not feel that his argument that this statute is following other statutes on the law books of this country carries quite the weight he attached to it. This is a different kind of measure. This is a measure such as we have not yet on the books, concerned about improving the conditions of all the children of the country. As he knows, despite his bachelorhood, it is the mother who is closer to the children in their younger days, and' I urge there is a real argument for payment being made to the mother. I suggest that this statute should be looked upon as something new and different in Canadian legislation.

In connection with that, the Prime Minister has pointed out that it would not make a bit of difference as to the order* I was reading the other day that in New Zealand they found it worked out better in the payment of allowances to make them payable to the mother only and
that, as I understand it, is the law in New Zealand to-day. In Australia, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said, the payment can be made to institutions but not to institutions that are wholly or mainly maintained either by the national or by the state government. In that connection I would ask the Prime Minister whether consideration has been given the question, whether or not in the interests of the maintenance of the children it be directed that the payments be made to the mother.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext:
Yes, decidedly so, and that is the reason for paragraph (a) of section 11, under which the governor in council may make regulations to give effect to and carry out the objects of this bill and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, .to provide generally or in respect of any province or any class of cases, that payment shall be made to the parent prescribed in the regulations. Speaking generally, we see a great deal to be said for that particular objective; but in bringing it about it has been thought that the end will perhaps be best served by having the regulations made after there has been opportunity of conference between officials administering the federal measure and officials in the different provinces. ' A good deal- has been said about the desirability of conferring with the provinces on matters of the kind, and that end would be well served if ithis were one of the questions that would come up for consideration between the two.

subtopic: CANADA AND LABRADOR - EXCHANGE OF NOTES BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES AS TO PAYMENT OF EXPENDITURES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA AND LABRADOR - EXCHANGE OF NOTES BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES AS TO PAYMENT OF EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I wish to table an exchange of notes between Canada and the United States of America constituting an agreement respecting the payment of expenditures on defence installations in Canada and in Labrador, signed at Washington, June 23 and June 27, 1944; three copies in English and three in French.
The exchange of notes which I have just tabled, dated June 23 and June 27, 1944, between the Canadian ambassador in Wash-

ington and the Secretary of State of the United States constitute an agreement under which the Canadian government undertakes to reimburse the United States government for certain works which the latter have constructed in Canada. It covers also certain United States expenditures at the base constructed by Canada at Goose Bay in Labrador.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) informed the house in February of the government's decision to reimburse the United States government for permanent improvements which they had made to airfields on the northwest staging route and in the northwest generally. Then in April the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) stated that as part of an understanding which he had reached with the secretary of the treasury of the United States in connection with the Hyde Park declaration, the Canadian government would reimburse the United States government for permanent improvements which they had made to other airfields in Canada and for the telephone line from Edmonton to the Alaska boundary, which was also built by the United States. The exchange of notes which I have tabled is an agreement between the two governments on this subject and, with its appendices, goes into considerable detail as to the amounts spent in various localities.
It has been agreed that Canada will reimburse the United States to the extent of 76-8 million dollars, United States funds. This covers construction costs incurred by the United States government on works of permanent value on the northwest staging route, the flight strips along the Alaska highway, the flight strips along the Mackenzie river, the airfields in northeastern Canada, the airfield at Mingan, Quebec, the airfield at Goose Bay, Labrador, and the telephone line from Edmonton to the Alaska boundary. An additional 13-8 million dollars spent by the United States on these projects is not being repaid by Canada, since, while necessary for the prosecution of the war, it represents wartime expenditure for United States purposes and provides nothing of permanent value; for example, temporary barracks and other housing facilities. However, all these works, whether of permanent or non-permanent value, are relinquished to the Canadian government and it is I am sure a source of satisfaction to both governments that a specific agreement has been reached regarding the disposition of these facilities.	.
I should also point but that in addition to reimbursing the United States for the outlays under reference Canada has assumed substantial expenditures for the construction of war-

Defence Installations
time facilities which were originally made on the understanding that we would be reimbursed by the United States. Our expenditures under this head in Canadian funds will total 34-7 million dollars. Thus including our reimbursements to the United States and the expenditures which we are making ourselves the amount expressed in Canadian dollars which the Canadian government is spending on the airfields and related projects mentioned in the exchange of notes is of the order of 120 million dollars.
Hon. members will observe that all of the foregoing expenditures were incurred in connection with defence installations in northwestern and northeastern Canada. Both are vital areas in the joint defence plans of the United States and Canada. Through the permanent joint board on defence far-reaching defence measures have been taken to close these back doors of the continent against attack by Germany and Japan. In concept and in execution the defence plans for these areas represent one of the most effective examples of cooperation among the united nations. At the same time these facilities have become links in the offensive plans of the allies. Planes fly across the northwest to the Pacific theatre of war and across the northeast to Europe.
Considerable information has already been given to the house and to the public about the northwest staging route, but for reasons of security little information about the northeast staging route has so far been made available. The need for a northeast staging route was originally suggested to Canada by the United Kingdom government in August, 1940, with the suggestion that the matter be discussed with the United States. Long-range bombers were already being ferried across the Atlantic through the Newfoundland airport at Gander, but this airport was congested and there were no facilities for ferrying short-range bombers or fighters which were beginning to come off United States assembly lines in considerable volume. Following discussions between Canada and the United States the United States proceeded to investigate the possibilities of establishing airfields in Greenland while Canada proceeded to reconnoitre Labrador. In June, 1941, Mr. Eric Fry of the topographical survey, who had been seconded to the Royal Canadian Air Force, discovered an ideal site at Goose Bay, North West river, and a preliminary survey was made. A United States army air force party subsequently examined and recommended the site. By agreement with the government of Newfoundland construction was begun by Canada almost immediately and the field was in use before winter closed in.
It was subsequently agreed by tne governments of Newfoundland and of the United Kingdom that Canada should be given a ninety-nine year lease to Goose air base for defence purposes; that this air base should be available to the Royal Air Force and to the United States air forces for the duration of the war and for such time thereafter as the parties might agree to be necessary or advisable in the interests of common defence; that the question of civil air use should remain over for settlement after the war, but that in any event civil and military aircraft owned by the government of Newfoundland should have rights to use the base on terms not less favourable than aircraft owned by the government of Canada.
In the meantime, the United States, by agreement with the Danish minister at Washington, had in April 1941 assumed responsibility for the defence of Greenland and had begun constructing airfields there which were to be available to other "American nations," which included Canada. Shortly afterwards the United States also made an agreement with Iceland for the defence of that island, and airfields were rapidly constructed there. With the completion of Goose airfield and the Greenland and Iceland fields, a staging route was available for relatively short-range aircraft.	.
With .the entry of the United States into the war on December 7, 1941, the strain on the existing ferry routes became even heavier. In May, 1942 the United States army air force proposed to the permanent joint board on defence the establishment of air routes over northeastern Canada to ferry long, medium and short-range aircraft to Europe. From the factories of the United States Pacific coast aircraft would be ferried across the Canadian prairies to The Pas and Churchill. From this Hudson bay port planes would fly to Southampton island, Frobisher bay, Greenland and Iceland and from there to their destination. Planes from another great focal point of United States aircraft production in the midwest states would fly across Ontario and Quebec to Fort Chimo on Ungava bay at the northernmost tip of Quebec and from there would link up with the other north-east air route at Frobisher.
These two channels were to be in addition to the ferry route already established to the United Kingdom via Goose bay, Greenland and Iceland.
Another purpose for the speedy construction of the route was to permit forces from interior
570S
Defence Installations

points to be rushed to the defence of Greenland and Iceland should the occasion arise. While this defensive phase of the war now seems remote, members will recall that in the summer of 1941 the German battleship Bismarck operated in this area, and, as is also well known, the Germans established weather stations on different occasions in Greenland.
On June 9, 1942, the permanent joint board on defence approved of the proposal of the United States army air force. It recommended immediate construction of the proposed airfields on Canadian territory, either by the Canadian government or by the United States government with the approval of the Canadian government. Facilities of the new routes were to be made available to the Royal Air Force.	.
For several reasons the Hudson bay leg of the northeast route has not been used to the extent anticipated and the original plans were never completely implemented. As the submarine menace was mastered there was a parallel improvement in the shipping situation, permitting the transportation of more aircraft by ship. Increased facilities at Goose air base and at Newfoundland airports permitted a greater flow of aircraft through these fields. Amazing technological advances, which increased the flying range and reliability of aircraft, as well as improved meteorological ' services, made the route from Goose air base more serviceable for short-range planes. The successful allied landing in North Africa made it possible for aircraft used in this area to be flown over the southern route, thus relieving the pressure on the northern route. As the fortunes of the united nations rose in the north Atlantic theatre the threat of enemy action against the northeastern section of this continent diminished.
In reaching this agreement for repayment for expenditures incurred for these defence facilities in northwestern and northeastern Canada and Labrador, the government had two considerations in mind. In the first place, it is believed that, as part of the Canadian contribution to the war, this country should take general responsibility for the provision of facilities in Canada and in Labrador required for the use of Canadian, United Kingdom and United States forces. In the second place, it was thought that it was undesirable that any other country should have a financial investment in improvements of permanent value, such as civil aviation facilities, for peace-time use in this country. I am happy to say that our views on this subject were understood by the government of the United States and the agreement which I have tabled is the result of this understanding.

speechtext: On the orders of the day.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ADVERTISEMENTS IN CONNECTION WITH CAMPAIGN FOR RECRUITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was asked with regard to a couple of recruiting advertisements which had been published, one in English and one in French, and the question was whether the French one was a correct translation of the English one. The answer is no. The situation is that there was no intention that the advertisements in French and in English should necessarily be duplicates, any more than that there was any intention that the advertisement in French should be a translation of the advertisement in English or that the advertisement in English should be a translation of the advertisement in French.
There is a central committee having to do-with recruiting publicity and recruiting campaigns generally. That committee has two what might be called subcommittees, consisting of experts in advertising and publicity, one committee to deal with French-speaking areas and the other to deal with English-speaking areas. Each of these committees prepares copy appropriate to the particular area to which the particular advertisement is being addressed and, as I say, there is no attempt to translate one series of advertisements in- the one language into the other language.
It happened that eight advertisements were to be selected, and eight advertisements were selected, eight in English by the committee having to do with English-speaking, Canada, and eight in French having to do with Frenchspeaking Canada. Three advertisements in French were actual translations of the English advertisements. None of the advertisements in English, so far as I know, was a translation of the French advertisement. I think that that disposes of the question of the advertisements being translations or being uniform. There was no suggestion and no attempt that they should be uniform. They were suggested by committees who know the areas and the conditions which might hinder recruiting and had in mind the matters that could be put before a particular area to deal with those particular conditions.
There was a suggestion in the question- that was asked that punches were pulled in connection with the French-speaking advertisements. I can say that no instructions, direct or indirect, by implication or otherwise, were given, nor was there any intention, directly or indirectly, to pull the punches in connection with French-speaking Canada, any more than in connection with English-speaking Canada.
Canadian Forces-Recruits

Each set of advertisements was dealt with on its merits by advertising experts who were supposed to know their job.
I want to refer the house to just one advertisement. It is a translation of one advertise' ment that was published in French Canada. This is it:
Let's Repeat the Heroism of Vimy and Ortona
Let's March to Victory Together!
"Yes, you, chum, come on and join the ranks. If you have blood in your veins, you won't let us down. Do you want us to make you a present of victory without taking any part in [DOT]it? Surely, you have more pride than that. Surely, you want to do your bit. We must win the war, we have to be in great number, you've got to be there.
"You'll lead a real man's life in the army. Let's march together in the footsteps of the heroes of Vimy, Coureelette, Passeliendale, Dieppe and Ortona. Join the infantry. Be a ^volunteer. Volunteers are the best soldiers.
That was an advertisement that was published in the French language. There is no point whatever in taking No. 8 advertisement which was published in the English language and comparing it with No. 8 in the French language, because there was no intention at all to synchronize them in the matter of tone or in the matter of matter, or in the matter of argument or appeal. The situation is that the matter has been dealt with by publicity experts and the recruiting staff with a view solely to achieving results.
Mr. J. C,. DIEFENBAKER (Lake Centre): There is one supplementary question I would like to ask following the minister's statement. He stated that these advertisements are made appropriate to the conditions and the areas in which they are disseminated. By that does the minister imply that the advertisement "Have I the guts?" was appropriate to the areas in which it was distributed? I would also ask whether these advertising committees that he mentioned go ahead without any control from the minister, or are any of these matters submitted to him? Do the men in charge of recruiting submit nothing to the minister in connection with the recruiting campaigns that they are waging? The statement made by the minister that these advertisements are appropriate to the conditions and areas in which they are distributed is a most strange and peculiar statement.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY

speechtext:
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act. 1936, to provide that the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation shall devote the whole of his time to the performance of his duties under the said act, and that he shall be paid such annual salary as may be determined by the governor in council.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Canadian Broadcasting Act

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
I wanted the minister to make an. extended statement as to the purpose of this resolution, and also to give the details, or such details as he can, so that we shall have some idea as to the principles upon which the bill will be founded.
Mr. LaFLECHE: This bill is a result of long observation by myself-if I may mention myself first-and by the chairman and the members of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. During this long observation and study of what was necessary to better the position of the corporation, it was ascertained by all that perhaps one of the weaknesses of the past was that the organization was not complete, in that the chairman of the board of governors- in other words, the gentleman occupying the top position in the corporation

was a parttime officer only and not at all times available to consider matters and to help arrive at quick decisions. In the setup of the corporation as described in the Canadian Broadcasting Act of 1936 the general manager is chief executive officer of the board; he has to carry out the policies laid down by the board. The general manager has not the power to make or decide policy; only the board of governors may do so. It has been found time after time in the administration of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that questions have come up which required very quick replies and decisions. It was asking too much of the general manager to require that he should, without authority, take it upon himself to make decisions on these points as they came up. In addition to that, the business of the corporation has increased very much. The people of Canada take a much greater interest in radio than ever before. With the years-with the few years, really, since radio broadcasting became popular and a matter of the every-day life of the people of this country-there has grown up in Canada, as in other countries, not only 'a great use of the radio but a great interest in radio, which means that the business of the corporation has increased a very great deal in volume and importance because of the more vivid interest attached to the matter by the people of Canada.
It has been found by those whom I have already mentioned that the machinery of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation must necessarily be rounded out by giving to the board of governors a fqll-time chairman so that the nominal head of the corporation shall be the real head and shall be accessible at all times to persons wanting to do business with the corporation. I am of the opinion more-

over that some of the troubles in connection with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the past, those things that have been criticized about the corporation, have been very largely if not solely due to the fact that the top man in the organization, the chairman of the board of governors, has not at all times been accessible both to the public and to the officers of the corporation. It has been manifestly unfair, I believe, to the gentlemen who have held the .position of part-time chairmen of the board to demand of them that perfection of administration which all of us without exception have wanted very badly. With this amendment I am very hopeful, I am sanguine, that the business of the corporation can better be attended to, more expeditiously and with a far greater degree of fairness to the officers of the corporation. I submit, that it is not fair to demand an immediate decision on policy of a man who is general manager and who has not the power to decide policy. This amendment would rectify that situation and would protect, to that greater extent, a property which has become very valuable to the nation. I think, Mr. Chairman, that this action is quite necessary and in that I am in wide and, I believe, very good company.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
I have not been on the radio broadcasting comimttee for more than two years, and have missed very greatly the deliberations of the committee during the time that I have not participated in them. I felt, during the committee's deliberations from time to time, that the viewpoint of members of the house was very valuable, and I believe a good deal of advantage was gained by virtue of the meetings that were held. I have followed with some degree of care its deliberations this year as well as last year. One of the things that always struck me, one of the difficulties that radio has faced in the .past, and I advance this suggestion to the minister, has been that there have been too many bosses of radio. That was a complaint that I made previously, and I am not sure that this resolution upon which a bill is to be founded cures the situation. This would appear to set up another boss of radio and to put him in the position of a paid boss at that. One of the reasons, of course, why the corporation failed to live up to all the advance notices and1 expectations that many people bad of it was that it was never given a proper chance, during at least a part of its existence, to render the kind of service it should to this country. I know it is being remedied, and for that I commend the minister; but for a long period there were noticeable absentees from among the members of

Canadian Broadcasting Act
the board of governors. From time to time vacancies were allowed to drift, one of them for eighteen months before it was filled1, and in many instances for shorter periods there were important vacancies on the board. I am glad that the government has seen fit to take a step in the right direction with regard to the appointment of representatives of labour and of agriculture on the board. But for a long time the board of governors was not the strong body that radio really needed . in Canada to make a success of it. Coupled with that, an unfortunate situation arose with regard to the whole of the corporation's activities, and that has made the task of bringing the corporation back to its proper position not a very easy one.
I am not sure that I agree with the minister-that the appointment of a full-time paid chairman of the board of governors is a step in the right direction. My belief is it is not, but rather that it is a retrograde step, because I do not think that by simply paying the chairman of the board of governors you accomplish the ends which are needed at this time. You have a general manager, and no doubt an assistant general manager will be appointed as well; and then you have a paid chairman on top of that. In radio, as in other things, as I pointed out two years ago, too many cooks spoil the broth. We had an example of what was going on at that time, and I hope the minister will pause and review the position and give careful, thorough and diligent consideration to the question whether or not this step now really achieves the ends which we have in mind. I know that in this session there is not likely to be a motion for concurrence in the report of the broadcasting committee, although it would have been helpful if such concurrence had been moved and we could have discussed at the same time as we are discussing this resolution the provisions and recommendations of that committee. I understand it was not unanimous in its report.
So far as the appointment of a new paid officer in the corporation is concerned, I think the minister ought also to consider something which I brought to his attention in a previous debate in this house, and it is this. With the commercial revenues rising in the corporation, with two networks now in operation across Canada, with the rising revenues everywhere so far as the corporation goes, I think the board of governors and the minister must consider taking one of two courses. First of all consideration should be given to keeping within the ceiling which was set previously by the minister who is now the Minister of Munitions and Supply, namely, a ceiling of onehalf million dollars per year of commercial revenue. If the policy of the government is to allow the ceiling to be raised to two or three million dollars, then I believe the radio licence fee, which has always been a difficult fee to collect, should be abolished once and for all. in that connection, if my memory serves me rightly, the cost of raising and collecting the radio licence fee is greater than the cost of collecting any other tax in this country. I believe that it cost something like $536,000 to collect the radio licence fee last year. The collection of that tax does not justify the tremendous expenditure involved. It may be perfectly proper to have a radio licence fee in certain circumstances, but with the mounting revenue and with commercial programmes providing an ever-increasing revenue for the corporation, the time has come when the government must either revert to its previous decision with respect to the ceiling on commercial revenue or abolish once and for all the radio licence fee.
I desire to say no more on the resolution at the moment except to express that very material doubt. I do not think that the move which is now being made to pay a man who is to be the chairman of the board the sum of money which newspapers suggested, $15,000 will meet the difficulties-of course I realize that at odd times their speculation is not correct, although in most circumstances they have the happy faculty of being able to prophesy fairly accurately. I know that the minister will not be able to state the salary this morning because I understand it has not been set; nor has the person who will become the permanent chairman actually been decided upon. I should like the minister to give careful consideration to the position, because I for one am not convinced that the additional expenditure is going to meet the situation as may some alternatives which may be suggested during the discussion on the bill.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
This is the first opportunity that one has had of expressing an opinion regarding the report of this year. The report of the committee is not under discussion and therefore I do not propose to discuss it in detail, but I wish to say that I am generally in approval of the report that has been presented to this house. My reservation lies exactly in the resolution which is now before the committee. I am not convinced that the appointment of a full-time chairman is going to work out and be of benefit either to the corporation or to the country. I am afraid of this divided authority. We had an unfortunate experience two or three years ago when the corporation, because of the inability of the then general manager to do the job that
Canadian Broadcasting Act

was expeeted of him, found it necessary to divide the authority in three ways, and I think the experiment was most unfortunate. I am afraid that this proposal will lead us into difficulties. I realize the necessity, as the minister has said, of having quick decisions made.
The criticism that I have heard of the corporation in the last year is that there seems to be nobody, and quite understandably, who can give a quick decision. After all, the responsibility for the policy of the corporation cannot lie in the hands of one man. It must lie in the board of governors, and we must have a strong board of governors. The board of governors having decided the policy, it seems to me that the official general manager of the corporation ought to be the person to carry out that policy. The government and the corporation will invite criticism in this way; there is no effective governing board, but rather a dictator in the person of a chairman who will make the decisions from time to time. From the point of view of the government I think that is dangerous; from the point of view of the corporation* I think more so, because in my opinion the divided authority between the chairman and the general manager will lead us into more difficulties.
I concur in the views expressed in that regard by the leader of the opposition. I am glad that the amendment is only in this one particular. I am glad that the committee of this year, as in former years, expressed its faith in the soundness of the radio act, and that this resolution covers just one detail of the statute; but I am afraid of it. I should be remiss in my duty if I did not rise and say that in my opinion we are apt to run into more difficulties. We have experienced that before. I repeat that I would have preferred to see a strong board of governors with a strong general manager. I believe that the corporation has in its own service one, two or three men any of whom would have made an excellent general manager. I do not think that any prejudice there may be against one or more of these men should stand in the way. We have men in the organization who could have fulfilled this function well, and I am sorry that this alternative has been proposed. A strong board of governors with a general manager is in my opinion preferable to the method suggested by the resolution.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on the proposed resolution. If the resolution passes the committee this morning you are going to open up the whole set-up of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation Act of 1936. When that act was passed the regufMr. Coldwell,]
lation of radio was comparatively in its infancy. A commission had been appointed. It went to Japan and other countries and made a report to the government. I am absolutely opposed to the division of authority in connection with this system. While I realize that the present minister has been most active and has made some salutary changes in the short time he has been in office, yet I have noticed in the set-up of any public body, especially a public utility or a public ownership concern like this, that the main point is to have someone as a strong administrator with a free, hand to administer the property. In my opinion this board is not necessary at all; this board should never have been appointed in the first place. A strong sole administrator should be appointed to administer the system. He should have a free hand to choose his staff, and over the programmes and everything else. I am opposed to the recommendation of this committee, because I believe it will lead to a lot of complications, duplication and interference by a chairman of the board with the chief executive officer and generally will cost more money. It will lead to jobs and all that kind of thing. I believe it would be far better if the chairman and the board were abolished altogether and the system administered by one responsible head. In the past this system has given the public many headaches. I notice that during the past three months some of the speeches delivered over the radio have been published. Recently one such speech was widely criticized in the press, because it 'was bound on the most costly paper. Some of the speeches have to do with contentious matters, and are in the nature of propaganda. I do believe it would be far better to do without a chairman so that he will not sit around the establishment all day long, interfering with the heads of departments, because that is all he will be doing. In the past the chairman has been very largely a figurehead, also the governors; they have been providing jobs and interfering with the proper administration of the system.
I am sure this committee did a great deal of good work and gave much time to these matters. However, I should like to refer to one or two points before this amendfnent is carried. In the first place there should be a consolidation of the act, and it should not be amended piecemeal in this manner. I do not know the present acting general manager personally, but I have had some correspondence both with him and with the minister to which they replied very promptly in' the ordinary course of business, and they have both been most attentive to their duties.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
The whole system of broadcasting has been changed by the war. When parliament framed the act of 1936 a great deal of it was copied from the B.B.C., though all the British legislation was not adaptable to this country. I do not believe we should have a chairman, drawing a salary of ten or fifteen thousand dollars a year and just sitting around retarding-progress. I noticed not long ago it had been recommended by the governors under section 24 of the act that four new French language radio stations be established in Canada. Before this amendment is acted on and carries I should like to find out where those stations are to be located and at what- cost. In the beginning of this act we had a system, to which objection was taken by my former leader. I believe that one of these gentlemen at the start said he wTas going to make this country bilingual by radio, and all that sort of thing. I do not know why bilingualism should enter into the set-up, because this system was supposed to give equality of treatment to all classes of citizens no matter what their nationality.
As I see it, this division and duplication of officials will be a waste of money. If you look at the way a railway or any large corporation is administered, for example, generally it has one man who is responsible for the way that system carries on. I am absolutely opposed to the recommendation of the committee; I believe it is a step in the wrong direction, and that any changes whatever in this act should have awaited the result of a general election.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
I am not going to discuss this resolution. I never had very much faith in part-time employees; that has been my experience. I rise at this time, however, to make a few observations on the report of the committee, and I do so for this reason. There is mot very much use appointing officials of any kind unless their decisions are carried out. We in Nova Scotia require improved radio facilities. Not a station in that province is provincial in the sense that it can carry provincial broadcasts, and even the handling of network programmes has been rather poor. For at least the last five or six months I have understood that the corporation has had a plan under way for the setting up in Canada of a second national network, and I felt that to be a move in the right direction. In reading over some of the proceedings of the broadcasting committee I understood that Doctor Frigon, the. acting general manager, had told the committee on June 28 that it was the intention of the corporation to set up in the city of Halifax the nucleus of a second
network under which- improved facilities would be made available in that city. I was also informed from Halifax that a transmitter was installed for that purpose, and that the only thing necessary to make available the facilities already decided upon was the passing of an order in council by the federal government. Evidently this order in council has not been passed. Those of us in that province who are interested in improving radio network facilities thought it would be merely a matter of time, but evidently the matter now is at a standstill.	,
I endeavoured to obtain some information through questions placed on the order paper a few days ago. The answers to those questions were tabled, but they were anything but satisfactory. I am not going to read the questions at the moment; they are available to hon. members in Hansard. In most cases the minister replied that the subject matter was still under consideration and no decision had been reached, but one question was not answered at all. I asked whether any steps had been taken by the C.B.C. toward the establishment of a new publicly-owned station, and whether a transmitter had been installed for that purpose. The part of the question dealing with the installation of the transmitter at Halifax was not answered at all. The information I was given from Halifax was that a transmitter had been installed and could be put into operation in a matter of three hours. Therefore I am taking this opportunity to obtain information, not because I want to be critical or because I want to hold up the measure but because I am interested in obtaining better radio facilities for the province of Nova Scotia. I am not quarrelling with the service given in the past; it has been as good as could be provided with the facilities at the disposal of the employees of the corporation in that province. I think they are doing an excellent job, but I am concerned about improving it.
We are now asked to approve the appointment of a full-time chairman. I do not quarrel with that. I am quarrelling with the fact that an official like Doctor Frigon should attend a parliamentary committee and definitely state that the nucleus for a second network for the province of Nova Scotia has been decided upon; that some of the equipment should be installed, and then at a moment's notice have the work come to a halt, with nothing more done about it and confusion reigning in regard to that matter as far as my province is concerned. A great many people are writing me in this connection. I do not care whom you appoint; unless the administration making the appointment are
Canadian Broadcasting Act

prepared to support that man, no matter how capable he may be, if there is machinery behind the scenes holding him back then the net result will be that he will be discredited with the public whom he has tried to serve. It seems to me that any time a man in public life, employed by the government, doing a job for the people of Canada, makes a public statement, he should be supported one hundred per cent by those who have authority to do so.
I should like the minister to elaborate on the answers to the questions I asked in regard to this matter, because I must endeavour to answer them to those in Nova Scotia who want these facilities. I do not want to make trouble; I merely want to satisfy them that this matter'is being looked after and that in due course these facilities will be established. I want also very frankly to tell the minister this. In some of the letters that I have received I have been told definitely that political forces in Halifax are endeavouring to set up a privately-owned station to be used exclusively for political purposes, and that that is what is holding up the installation of a publicly-owned and operated second network in Halifax. If the minister can assure me that that is not so, that there is some war-time necessity holding up the necessary equipment, I am prepared to take his word, but as the matter now stands it requires considerable clarification.
Mr. MeCANN: Mr. Chairman, this resolution has to do with one of the recommendations made by the committee on radio broadcasting which carried out its investigations this year. Anyone who has been interested in the inquiries carried on during the past three years will readily see that because of the growth of the corporation it has been almost physically impossible for one man as general manager to carry on all the duties expected of him. The legislation to be based upon this resolution will not be very far from that contained in the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936. That act made provision for a chairfh-an of the board of governors, a general manager and an assistant general manager. The only difference I can see in this resolution is that the chairman of the board will be a full-time rather than a part-time officer. The bill to be founded upon the resolution will also fix the salary to be paid to whoever takes the position.
Because of the demand of the public for improvements in radio services there has been a great growth in this corporation since 1936. Men who would be capable of acting as chairman of this board are hard to get. This position requires a man with some imagination as

to the possibilities of the development of radio. Partly due to the war many executives are engrossed in their own particular affairs; they find that all their time is necessary to carry on and protect their own businesses during the years of the war.
This country has been fortunate in the *men who have acted as chairman of the board of governors, and in the governors themselves. These men have given freely of their time and services. They receive no salary apart from their expenses, although the chairman receives a small honorarium. In my opinion the corporation has reached a position where it -needs the full-time services of some one who understands the business.
It is physically impossible for a man. like Doctor Prigon, the general manager, to carry out all the duties for which he is responsible. He is one of the best radio technicians in this or any other country, but he also has to carry on the business of an organization with a budget of about $5,500,000. Do the njembers of this committee realize that there are over 800 people in the employ of the corporation, that there are ten stations that belong to C.B.C.; that there are two short-wave stations, that another short-wave station is to be built, and that the corporation has supervision over 79 private stations? Doctor Frig-on has been looking after the technical work of the corporation, and his work has been doubled because he looks after the French programme. It is absolutely impossible for him to carry on. If he attempts to do so, sooner or later he will have a break-down and we shall have no one coming up in the corporation who is in position to do his work.
It is simply a matter of the allocation of the work. Doctor Frigon has stated in evidence that it is necessary to have some one who can give bis full time to the corporation. Mr. Morin, who was chairman of the board of governors, has also made this suggestion. I do not need to quote him, because I do not believe I should deal with the report of the committee at this particular time. I am quite prepared to back up the recommendation that there should be a full-time chairman of the board who would be paid a salary commensurate with his ability and the work he has to do. The chairman of this board would occupy a position comparable to that of a supreme court judge or the chairmen of other boards that have to do with public business.
It is not going to be easy to get someone who can carry on this work. With the increased growth of the corporation there will be sufficient work for a full-time chairman of the board and a general manager. The one will have to do with the making of policies. He will call the board together and policies

will be determined. He will interpret those policies. It will be the business of the general manager to carry out the policies. I think the division of the work will be quite simple. This is the only extension of the Canadian Broadcasting Act contemplated by this proposed legislation.

speechtext:
I wonder if the Prime Minister would mind giving the committee the underlying reasons for the particular amounts mentioned in this section. On second reading considerable stress was laid on the fact that those in the higher income brackets were already being given what was tantamount to a cash allowance by virtue of the income tax exemptions for children, amounting to S10S per child up to eighteen years of age. I am not suggesting that that should necessarily be the basis, but the Prime Minister did indicate that as one of the arguments he advanced in support of the bill. In view of that .$108 income tax exemption which the Prime Minister said was really in the final analysis a cash allowance, may I ask how the amounts mentioned in this section were arrived at as the proper allowances for those in the lower income brackets: $5 per month for a child less than six years of age, and so on up to $8 per month for a child thirteen
but less than sixteen years of age. I would also ask about the allowance in the case of larger families. I raise that question only because a different base for allowance is provided for in the income tax exemptions for taxpayers in the higher income tax brackets, where an exemption is provided with respect to children in the family up to eighteen years of age. I think that some reconciliation as to this section's provisions is in order.
There is another matter I might as well mention now while I am on my feet. It seems to me that the most expensive period of a child's maintenance and support is after fourteen years of age and from then on to sixteen and for the next three or four years. At least those of us who are parents realize that when children reach these ages the cost of their maintenance and support mounts rapidly.

My hon. friend will realize that the experts in the Department of Finance have very carefully considered the relationship of this measure to the income war tax measure, and some of the figures that have been arrived at have been as a result of considering all the implications and possibilities that may arise in that regard. The point that my hon. friend has stressed has been that under the income tax measure a larger amount is conceded by way of exemption for children over sixteen than is given in the form of allowances under this measure. Not only the finance department but others who have considered this class of measure hold, I believe, the view that there should be some recognition of the fact that something may be owing to those who are paying money into the treasury which would not be owing to a like extent to those who do not contribute to the treasury at all. I would add that this is the first attempt at a measure of this kind. It is based on experience already gained from the dependents' allowance administration, and undoubtedly further experience will go far to show what further readjustments may be advisable.
As to my hon. friend's point about the expenses increasing as the children get older, I am not experienced in these matters and I have to take as correct much that others tell me; but my recollection of my early days was that as one became older one was able to help one's parents by sharing some of the general burden and that might offset what my hon. friend finds is necessary in the way of extra expenditure as the children get older. I do think it is true, as I said on the second reading, that as a family increases in numbers what has served former members of the family can help in part to serve other mem-

bers and as children get older they in turn are able to help their parents in household ways as they cannot do when they are younger. Did my hon. friend have any other question?

speechtext:
In view of what the Prime Minister has just said it might be well to offer an observation. Too many people fail to recognize the changes which have been brought about in our economy by the coming in of an age of abundance Fifty or sixty years ago it was possible for the family to keep cows and supply milk to the neighbours, keep chickens and supply eggs, and do a variety of other things to supplement the family income, and in those days it was in a way an economic asset to have an addition to the family when the child was able and willing. But the coming in of the age of abundance and of the machine age has negatived all that in most cases. For example, in our ordinary towns it is impossible to keep cows and sell milk to the neighbours. In most cases there is a law prohibiting it, and in many other cases, even if the milk were there, the neighbours would1 not buy it because they would be buying from the dairyman who comes right to their door. A similar changed situation exists with respect to a large number of other economic activities in which boys and girls participated in the days when the Prime Minister was a boy and when I was a boy not so many years ago. I believe that that whole situation should be taken into account. You frequently hear people exclaim quite indignantly against this whole policy of social services and talk about "the time when my grand-dad went out into the woods and threw off his coat and rolled up his sleeves and carved a living". Well now, my old grand-dad could do that, because there were woods then that he could go into, there was free pasture where he could let his cows run, and it was possible for him to go out and catch fish, and shoot game; and many other conditions existed which gavt my old grand-dad a chance to do such tlpngs. But let my old grand-dad's grandson go out and try to do these things, and see what happens to him. Then there is another simple illustration. My old grand-dad's wife could knit stockings and send the child to school with knitted stockings: you let my old

grand-dad's grandson's wife try to do the same thing, and see what happens.
A great variety of changes has come over the world which renders it very necessary that these social services be offered and that they be munificent. I have said once before in connection with this measure that I consider it wholly inadequate. These -allowances are not enough. The Prime Minister said, or implied, that the young girl or the young boy could probably help around the home. That is quite , true, but by helping around the home that young child can add hardly twenty-five cents to the family income. Many of the things which children used to be able to do and which were a valuable service to the parents, such as running the wringer, the washer and the churn, are now no longer available to them. There are electric washers or some equipment of the sort in the average home which render the services which a child can give its parents of far less direct financial and economic value than in the old days.
Probably there are very few members who are in a better position to speak with authority on the subject of raising children than I am. The Lord blessed me with twelve children- for which I am very thankful-and he also blessed me because of those twelve children with an abundance of experience, and a lot of it in the school of hard knocks. So that speaking from experience I say that we can very profitably make these allowances a great deal larger, and then we would not be doing too much to aid those who are raising a future generation in this country.
Perhaps while I am on my feet I should say a word or two on a subject which hardly seems to be directly in points but which has a bearing because of changed conditions. Fifty or sixty years ago grand-dad could stay around the home and there were always a lot of things which he could do to help out the family. He could feed the cow, feed the pigs, take care of the chickens, and do a lot of other things to help the family economy along. Because of changed conditions which have been ushered in through the age of abundance, the age of machines, grand-dad can find hardly anything about the place to do which will enable him to make any substantial contribution to the economic 'well-being of the family. This is hard on grand-dad-it grieves him terribly-it is hard on the family, and it renders essential the payment of more and more generous old age pensions.

It is not that children are any less ready to take care of their parents, or that the older people are any less ready to support themselves: they are forbidden to offer the support and to give the support, because of changed conditions over which they have no control whatever. .If we expanded our pensions to the elderly to S50 per month and brought down the age at which they received the pensions to sixty yearSj we would still leave plenty of room for actual hardship in Canada among elderly folks. Mr. ST. LAURENT: May I say one word about this scale?-because I have had, a lot of correspondence about it and I know that considerable public interest surrounds the scheme. The answer-and it is a complete answer-is that given by the Prime Minister. This bill has been prepared in the light of the experience which the government has gained over a period of nearly five years during which dependents' allowances to the families of the men in the services have been paid. That scale has been a sliding scale, providing $12 per month for the first child and S12 for the second child. $10 per month for the third child, and for the fourth, fifth and sixth, $8 per month each, and no further benefit beyond the sixth child; making a total possible dependents' allowance for children of $58 per month to a man who, in order to have that dependents' allowance for his children, is required to assign fifteen days' pay per month; and hon. members know that the rates of pay to the men in the services are in no wise comparable to the rates of pay which are being received by civilian wage-earners. There is in addition a separation allowance to the wife of $35 per month. The whole of the income available for the family of a service man has been computed and has been compared with the whole of the income which would be available to a like man in a civilian occupation, and it seemed from the experience gained during those five years that it was something which met with satisfactory results to have a diminishing scale as the number of children in a family increased. It was that reason which motivated the setting of these figures in this bill. Now it is intended to improve conditions throughout the land,' but to do so in a reasonable fashion, and if the experience which has been acquired over
the past five years should prove that it did not provide a satisfactory solution for civilian families, it will be possible to rearrange things.
There is in the dependents' allowance a limitation that does not go beyond the sixth child. While in the service the ordinary man is of an age group that does not go above a certain level, in the civilian population there are heads of families of all age groups, and a limitation on the number of children provided for by allowances would have implied a declaration by parliament that that was the maximum number of children that might be desirable in a Canadian family, and it did not seem that it was a good thing to have that either expressed or implied in any law enacted by the parliament of Canada. The population of Canada is in large part sprung from families in which there was no limitation as to numbers, and there are still, as the hon. member for Lethbridge pointed out a moment ago, a considerable number of families maintaining the traditions of past generations, so that it did not seem that it would be proper for parliament to say that it was not desirable to have a family exceeding so many persons. For the families in civiliain life, the whole available income for expenditure will be comparable to that which is made available to men in the forces by means of pay, separation allowance and the dependents' allowances; and I think it is a reasonable attempt to bring about a situation which will realize the objective expressed in the resolution-a greater degree of equality of opportunity for all the children in Canada.
There is the other point mentioned by the leader of the opposition, that the amount of $108 allowance off the tax is larger than even the twelve monthly payments that would go to a child of fifteen. It is somewhat larger, but it is also a fact that in a family it is a proportion of the revenue that is expended on each member, and prior to the war the situation was such that those with the higher incomes got a greater reduction in income tax than those who were paying tax on a lesser amount. But it was found that there was an amount beyond which, under the stress of war, the tax should not be further reduced, and the S10S was arrived at on a basis of $400 per child with the old rates. That would give an exemption of $80, at an average tax rate of 20 per cent; and that is the portion that is now deductible from the graduated tax. The other $28 is seven per cent of $400 for the national defence or normal tax, and the income tax act is so arranged that it is only when you, get into the relatively high brackets that you get the full benefit of the $108. You
Family Allowances

get $28 per child off your normal or national defence tax, but if you have, say, five children, you should get five times $28, or $140; but you have to have $2,000 income to have a normal tax of $140. If you have only $1,800 you do not get the full $140 but only the amount that is determined by the calculation of your normal tax on what your income is. And it is so with the graduated tax. You take from the graduated tax first of all $150 as an allowance for being a married person, and then if there is enough of the graduated tax left to make up $80 per child you get the benefit of it. But you have to reach a relatively high level of income-and when I say a high level I am speaking of the population at large, a level of income which is more than that of a very substantial portion of the population-before you get the full benefit of $108 exemption per child. It was felt that on the whole the calculations made by the experts of the finance department and the Department of National Revenue showed that these figures were a reasonable attempt to realize the objective of the resolution and to bring about as near an approach to equality of opportunity as past experience justified.

I was merely seeking information in regard to what looked like a difference in the treatment of different classes, rather than making any advocacy with respect to amounts, because I had nothing at all to say in that regard. The minister's explanation has cleared up considerably one or two points in my mind with reference to the question. As he points out, the income tax payer in the brackets above SI ,200 running to $2,000 does not actually get $108 allowance, which of course brings this much more closely into line, and I hope the minister will realize what my point was. I thought I saw a situation there which was irreconcilable with the other, but I did not rise to advocate any change, because the one thing which of course this bill does not really cover is the point which I rose to make in my speech on the second reading. I realize the difficulties that governments face, but the question of need is not taken into consideration in this matter in the same way that it might normally have been. There are certain families I know of who are almost comparable in point of numbers and ages and because of that they would be entitled to the same kind of consideration under this act. In one particular family I know the cost of raising them has been at least four times the cost of raising another with the same number of children, in the same town and in the same circumstances, the only difference being that in one case the ravages of disease left their impress. In many

instances it would be wholly inadequate, a mere drop in the bucket, while in the case of families where health has played a greater part than in others the allowances might be viewed in a different light. That was one of the reasons why it struck me that in the best use to which this public money could be put, greater stress should be laid on the whole question of the need of families that were to be helped. I felt, and I believe many in the chamber felt, that there should have been some reasonable arrangement with the provinces as to where the money could be utilized to the best advantage instead of simply having a general standardized scale such as this, because it might have met the situation better; although I readily realize that situations arise where parents must have some cash. At no time did I advocate that there should not be cash paid in the circumstances where it could be used to best advantage. I think there would be agreement in the committee on this point; in some instances there ought to be supplementary arrangements made in connection with health programmes and so on. However, the question of need is one which is not covered in the bill. The policy which is laid down and the structure of the bill indicate that evidently that is not a possibility at the moment. I do wish to leave this one point with the government. There will be a dominion-provincial conference some time this fall. I am hopeful that this will not be such a rigid system that there will not be some way by which the provinces may play their part, and that underprivileged families will be considered.
May I say this one word in closing? I come back to it again because I feel very keenly about it, and the Prime Minister made some reference to it on second reading of the bill. I do not want to be misunderstood when I say 'this. There are parts of this country in which the standards of wages are too low. Those parts of the country are making it difficult for industry in other parts to compete successfully on the general market in Canada and elsewhere. I am fearful that this measure will start out to subsidize families before a proper wage level has been actually set across the dominion. It may be that that is an exaggerated position to take; but it seems to me that the family allowances scheme will work only if wage levels across Canada are equalized so that everybody in Canada will be on an equal basis to start with, with the exception of children. It seems to me that that is an almost unanswerable argument. That is one of the reasons why the amendment was framed in the way in which it was by us on second reading. If one part of Canada is to have

Family Allowances
family allowances they ought to be ready to raise their wage levels so that those allowances could not possibly be a substitute for a higher wage level. I realize the difficulties connected with it, but this is one argument that is very difficult to get around. If wage levels in Canada were brought up to a proper standard, nobody could say with the same force that some form of family allowances should not be recognized.
I was struck by the arguments that were presented on all sides of the house with respect to the question of equal pay for equal work. If we accept that theory, as I think most people do, then as matters stand at the present time a penalty is attached to a man who has a large family. There is an injustice to the parts of Canada that have a high scale when they have to compete with low wage areas. I have not gone into this question very deeply. It may not be confined to one province-I am not sure that it is. Regardless of'whether it is confined to one province or not, I think we should have a proper standard of wages in Canada so that even the people without any children may have a decent standard of living and there shall be no sagging below that minimum. Once you have that level, then bring in a proper and workable scheme for family allowances. At the present stage of our history it does work a comparative injustice to other parts of Canada that have a high wage level. I advance that argument without any special feeling in the matter, except that I do say there are arguments there based on premises which are difficult to get around. It has been difficult for me; to get a satisfactory answer, and I think that applies generally throughout the country. -
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I will not surprise the leader of the opposition -by saying to him that I have been just as troubled as anyone could be by the apparent discrepancy in some wage levels in civilian industries between my province and the one in which his constituency is located. I have been met with the objection, with research work behind it, that there was a very close approximation to equal pay for equal work, and that the unit cost of labour entering into a commodity was as high in the province of Quebec as in any other province, because of the fact that apparently there was not as efficient work being performed during the. same number of hours. I know for a fact that during a certain period that was true in our shipyards, but I am glad to have seen great improvement come about, and I am now in touch with research work that is being done in civilian industries for like improvement. of output.
We would certainly be entitled to complain in my province if we were required to do work of the same value for less compensation. In order to justify an increase in the hourly pay for which we are asking we shall have to be able to show that we are capable of giving service for the additional pay. These are subjects that are being carefully examined into to determine the number of man hours that go into a given commodity. I know that the same situation does not exist all over the province. I know of two printing shops. The one that has the best installation does not deliver as much output per man hour as the other that has not as modern an installation. These things are being inquired into now and they are being attended to as well. Therefore I am of the opinion that that is the proper basis. There can be no objection, and should be no obstacle either from labour or from employers, to obtaining for our workers the same hourly rates as elsewhere just as soon as it is satisfactorily shown that their output is equal to that for which these hourly rates are being paid elsewhere.

I should like to call the attention of the Prime Minister to one point, and I think this is the only section on which I can mention it, though I have read the bill over eight or ten times. Section 3 has to do with monthly allowances, and provides for the payment of money out of the unappropriated balance in the consolidated revenue fund from July 1, 1045, in respect to children resident in Canada and maintained) by their parents, in amounts of $5, S6, $7 and $8 according to age. The point I wish to make would
Family Allowances

relate also to several other bills of last week amounting to a billion dollars in all, and while perhaps the Prime Minister may not be able to give me an answer to-day he might consider the suggestion. Of late years we have made a practice of drawing upon the unused portion of this consolidated revenue fund, and shortly before the war I introduced a bill which was based largely upon the laws of other countries, embodying a principle which has been in operation in many of our provinces and municipalities since confederation, proposing that on these questions of great national importance the people who pay the taxes should be consulted. That has been found to be a very good1 principle in votes on money by-laws in the administration of the provinces and municipalities. The explanatory note to bill No. 11 of 1939 contained just two short paragraphs, which I should like to read:
This bill is enabling legislation similar to that for many years in vogue in democratic countries. It is found to be in the public interest and most useful, permitting the submission of important national questions to the wisdom and judgment of the electors.
The provinces have used it extensively for years through the municipalities, thus providing an opportunity for giving the public a voice in government policies. It will create a prerogative of checks and balances and make for government "of the people by the people and for the people." The governor in council can be thus enabled to submit to a vote any matter of a national importance.
The bill was read a second time and considered by the election committee who took evidence and heard the clerk of the house and others. I recognize that to adopt this principle the measure now under consideration, the election act, would have to be amended. Everyone agrees that this provision dealing with children, and the other bills that have been brought in, deal with domestic matters of the greatest magnitude, matters which must be dealt with if we are to have a happy people and happy country. Everyone, both inside and outside this house, wants to help our poorer people. I do not know of anyone who does not believe in the Christian doctrine as set out in the tenth chapter of St. Mark, -where the Lord referred to children, to the duty of the state toward the children, and all that sort of thing. I believe the adoption of a principle of "this kind would be in the interests of the government itself. Some very able men have come up to the government benches from the municipalities; I would mention particularly the hon. member for Huron-Perth, who was a former mayor of his municipality. All those who have been active in municipal affairs realize the salutary effect this provision has had in keeping down 
the tax rate, and in protecting both the ratepayers and the government. I do not ask the Prime Minister to give a decision on this matter right away. I do not want to act unfairly in bringing up this suggestion at this time, but I believe it would be in the public interest if consideration could be given the matter and a reply made before the bill is given third reading.

Unlike the hon. leader of the opposition I am not satisfied with the explanation given by the Minister of Justice for the scaling-off principles included in section 3 of this bill. I feel that the argument advanced by the minister just before the luncheon adjournment to the effect that the scaling-off principle applied in connection with the dependents' allowances to families of service personnel also applies here does not altogether fit the case. In connection with dependents' allowances an attempt is made, whether or not the government measures up to it, to meet the full cost of maintenance of the families. of men in the services. As the Minister of Justice pointed out; the amount allowed for a child in the first instance is $12 a month rather than the $8 we are allowing here. There are also the other amounts, such as separation allowance for the mother and the assigned pay which the soldier must send home. I suggest that the situations are not comparable. What we have here is only a token payment toward the extra cost of maintaining children in a family, and because that payment does not meet the additional cost of each additional child it seems to me unwise and unfair to reduce it as the number of children increases.
- Another argument that has been used in support of the scaling-off principle was advanced by the Prime Minister when he moved second reading if not also on some other occasion, when he contended that the

Family Allowances
average cost of maintaining children in a family drops as the number of children increases. While in a 'sense that is true it does not tell the whole story by any means. Let me illustrate my point by giving some figures by way of example. Let us assume a married couple getting along on the meagre income of $100 a month. When the first child is born it would cost at least $20 a month to maintain it. This allowance will provide only $5 a month for that child when it is born, so the family allowance does not meet the additional cost of maintaining that child but only provides a token payment. Let us go on. The second child is born. Accepting the Prime Minister's argument that the cost of maintaining the second child will not be as great as the first, because there will be some things that can be used again, still it will cost $18 a month to maintain the second child. That brings down the average to $19 each, but I point out to the Prime Minister that the extra $18 it will cost to maintain the second child is not, there. The family still has only the $100 a, month income it had in the first place, plus the allowances for two children which will total $10. So the deficit in the cost of maintaining the entire family mounts with each child, even though the average cost of maintaining the children in the larger family may drop. It is. a case where the average has no practical significance. Suppose, for example, that a family has five children, and that it costs to maintain those children $20, $18, $16, $14 and $12 respectively per month. That makes a total of $80 a month, or an average of $16. But we must remember that the family has only $100 as a basic monthly income, plus such sums as may be received under the family allowance measure. In other words, the deficit grows as the family increases.
Here is the point I have in mind. The fifth child born into a home comes in at a decided disadvantage as compared with the Canadian child who is the first or second child in another home. We should remember all through our consideration of this measure that our concern is with Canadian children as such. If we are concerned with Canadian children, we are concerned with every Canadian child whether he is the only child in a home or whether he is the fifth or tenth. I suggest that with this scaling-off principle included in this section we are penalizing the children who are born into large families wherever they may be.
There is also another scaling-off principle in this section which provides for lesser grants of money for younger children. I am not so
sure from such experience as I have had that it can be said that children of tender years cost less to maintain than those who are a little older. I suggest that it is of extreme importance that children in their first two or three years should have everything possible provided for them so that their health will get a good start. It could be argued that there should be extra money the first year or two for this purpose. I speak out of some experience on this matter. It so happens that I was bom in the midst of a depression into a home haunted by the spectre of unemployment. That spectre had already taken its toll before I arrived in the loss of two other children from malnutrition. If I may say so wtihout inviting a jibe from some of my political opponents in the chamber, I am told that it almost cost me my life as well.
I want to emphasize the importance of giving every Canadian child the best possible start. Frankly I do not not like the leader of the opposition to be able to say that he has three eight-dollar children whereas other Canadian children will be considered as only five-dollar children. I hope the government will reconsider these two scaling-off principles. I was pleased to note from the remarks last night of the parliamentary assistant to the Prime Minister that there are still some matters to be settled about this whole arrangement. He was speaking particularly about the relationship between this measure and the Income War Tax Act, but I took from what he said that study has still to be given to a great many feaures of this plan before it is put into effect.
When I was speaking on the second reading of the bill I suggested that we would probably pass this bill in its present form but that before it came into effect there would be an amending bill to implement some of the results of the study that will still have to be given * to the measure. I hope there will be further study given in the interests of the main purpose of this bill which is to provide the best chance possible for Canadian children. In this study I hope it will be decided to revise the scaling-off principles to which I have referred.
