I was interested in
hearing what the Minister of Justice had to say this morning with respect to the rates. From what I gather, these rates were arranged by the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue and were based on purely financial considerations. The minister went to some pains to say that no consideration had been given to any differential in the standards of living between different parts of Canada. I have been a member

of the social security committee of this house which has been sitting for several years and I know that witness after witness has appeared before that committee and said that one of the great drawbacks to family life in Canada was the income differential in different parts of Canada, and the differential even between one family and another living in the same community. I was just going to give an example. In a long brief presented by the United Textile Workers of the American Federation of Labour to the Quebec war labour board they point out that the textile worker in the province of Quebec is receiving an average weekly wage of $20.80, whereas the worker in all industry in the city of Toronto is receiving an average weekly wage of $32. There is a very great discrepancy between rates of pay, and until you lift the pay of the textile worker in the province of Quebec or in the textile industry generally you are going to have a differential between the standard of living of the worker and his family in Toronto and the worker and his family in the province of Quebec. I think that some consideration should be given to that point.
Here is another point. Over and over again witnesses have testified before the social security committee that the infant mortality and maternal mortality rates increase tremendously with the birth of the sixth or seventh child and furthermore that the cost of sickness increases very considerably in the larger families. But this bill by its provisions decreases the allowance to larger families. I do not know whether that is sound or unsound, but if this measure is based on what is likely to be the need, the allowance to the larger family should be increasing rather than decreasing; because witness after witness proved before the social security committee that the larger families have greater need of hospitalization and sickness benefits than the smaller family.
I am not going to go into the question of other services, but it appears on the face of it that these rates were brought about by the Department of Finance without any consideration of the human needs of the families concerned.

Let me finish. The first thing the hon. member should do is to compare likes. If he compares the average weekly wage of workers in the province of Quebec with the average weekly wage of workers in the province of Ontario he will find that the differential is not $12 as he seemed to imply, but in the neighbourhood of two or three dollars, and a considerable part of that differential is due to the different classes of industries in which the people of Quebec are engaged as compared with the people of Ontario. Other reasons for the difference were given by the Minister of Justice just before the recess. Although we are wandering a long way from the provisions of clause 3, I thought I should point out the unfairness of the hon. member for York West comparing wages in probably the lowest paid industry, not only in Quebec but right across Canada, with the average wages paid in all industries in Ontario. If he compares like with like he will find that the differential is less than ten per cent in like industries, and there are various reasons for that.
May I deal for just a moment with the suggestion which the hon. member made that the government in arriving at this schedule of allowances has proceeded on the basis of financial rather than human considerations. I do not know just what the hon. member meant by that. I notice that he did1 not give any explicit answer to, the hon. member for Parry Sound who questioned him about it. Does he mean this: that somehow the government of Canada or the administration that is to be set up under this act is to find out what the relative needs of each family are right across Canada and then pay the family allowance on that basis-is that it? If so, then surely, on the

Family Allowances

illustration, he gives, the people of the province of Quebec, having lower wages, should receive more proportionately than the people of the province of Ontario, who have a slightly higher average weekly wage. That is where that argument leads him.
But my suggestion to the committee is this, that you cannot do what is suggested by the hon. member for York West, or what was suggested' by the leader of the opposition, except in one of two ways. Either you can try to make provision for a family allowance or children's allowance in kind, or you can do it by the application of a means test. Those are the only possible alternatives to doing it in the way proposed in this bill. Let us look at each one of them. If you want to provide assistance in kind to children, you are going back, I suggest, to some such setrup as was adopted by a former administration during the worst period of the depression. It led1 to every kind of unfairness and every kind of effort to get around the regulations; it reduced the self-respect of the recipients; it was paternalistic in an extreme form; it was a reversion to the days when the rich man took a basket of necessaries to the poorer people in his community. That, would be a retrograde step. What is more, it would be impossible for this parliament to do it, or to approach doing it. When it is suggested that instead of the proposal before the committee we should have some other proposal, we may ask if that is not really a suggestion that we should not do anything at all, because the suggestion is one which can be carried out only by some other agency. Payment in kind will not be accepted by the people of Canada; it would be retrograde in the extreme.
The only other way to relate payment in the way suggested by the opposition is to have a means test, whereunder family allowances will be paid1, not on an equal basis for every citizen, varying only with the age and number of his children, but in proportion to the income of the family. That, too, would lead to a kind of policing in connection with the bill, fin interference with individual freedom, and a degree of regimentation, which the people of Canada would not stand for.

In New Zealand they have a flat-rate wage which runs right across all industry. The differential for skilled workers and unskilled workers is not more than five cents an hour. The average earnings of the people at the top wage level and at the bottom wage level in New Zealand do not vary by much more than ten per cent. The whole economy is on a very level basis. If you have it on that basis it is possible to apply a means test of the kind they have in New Zealand without unfairness and without interference with the liberty of the individual. We have only this test, that the people who get the full benefit from the allowance for chlidren under the Income War Tax Act do not get a duplicate benefit from the family allowances. Apart from that everyone is treated alike.
One word in conclusion. The greatest single factor in creating differences between one family in Montreal and another family in Montreal, or even between one family in Montreal and another family in Toronto-is neither, their wages nor their health; it is the number of their children. Taken by and large across the great bulk of the population, nothing so much affects the relative economic position of families as the number of their children. That is why this measure is introduced at this time; it is an endeavour to correct that disparity by attempting, in part of course, to bridge the gap between wages and the number of children. Wages are related, as we know, to work done. This measure is relative to the number of children, and it is in an endeavour to equalize the position of the great mass of the people of Canada that this measure is introduced. When we have an increasing scale for children of higher years, and a reduction for the number of children over five, we are simply trying to make this as scientific as it can be. I share the experience of the leader of the opposition in having three children, but it is within my knowledge, as I think it is within the knowledge of all hon. members who have children, and it is the experience of all social workers, that on the average the cost of caring for, maintaining and educating a child rises fairly steadily from birth until at least the age of fifteen.

In our case we have our legislation in that regard codified partly because of the fact that we are a federal country. That criticism is insincere, because they ought to know that when the head of a family earns more than $1,200 per year he is subject to income tax. Now he may deduct $108 a year for each child. Minister has to face. As a member from that province I receive letters of complaint all the time from people who are not well-informed. Every one of those families will receive the family allowances.

He can use it to build a better home, or if he intends to rent, he can obtain a home possessing more hygienic facilities. If one of his children shows special talents he will be able to keep him in school longer than he otherwise would. There are many things that the fathers of our families will be able to do with this grant.
I talk with knowledge on this matter. I know there are many heads of families in my own district who will be delighted to receive these allowances. It will be just found money: tresor trouve. Those who understand the laws of psychology and sociology will understand the benefits to be derived. These people understand the danger in the present movement against the capitalists. This dangerous underground1 movement is going on from the west to the east; it is pervading the whole world. Our legislators should try to prevent this movement from coming to the surface and getting hold of the administration of our country. We should have parties based on sound principles of government. This country should be governed , by either the Tories or the Grits. I am frank about that.
Let us be sociologists. Let us work together to try to help the larger families. Let us be willing to, take a few pennies out of our pockets to enact this social security measure. The families in Quebec did not expect to get this legislation. If we were not in the midst of such a terrible struggle I think I could say something that would open the ears of my colleagues about the patience of the people of Quebec. We are patient. We did not ask for this legislation. Our sociologists came here and suggested that this would be a good policy, but we never made any threats as to what we would do if we did not get this legislation. It comes as a gratuity and the fathers of our large families will be very much pleased.
I recall the day when I was a young fellow. I was the fourteenth boy in a family of seventeen and I am proud of it. Had my father, who was a very humble farmer, lived to this day I know he would send a letter of thanks to the Prime Minister of this country for giving him help in raising his family. What did he do? At the age of thirteen years he gave me my inheritance. Do hon. members know what it was? It was the king's highway. That farm is very narrow but it is very long and full of hardships. I am glad that I followed that road. When I was passing through those difficult times I said to myself that whatever talents Providence would give me would be used to help relieve the hardships of others. If I am to leave public life, the fact that I have contributed by my vote toward the passage of this measure to help the young children of large families make their way in life, will make me feel that my, life will not have been in vain.

That is correct; but if you will bear with me for a moment I think you will find that I am pretty closely on the section. Certainly there are textile workers; I cannot say whether they are exclusively on cotton or not. There are cotton textile workers in the city of Hamilton, for which I have not the figures at hand, but I think they pretty well bear out the general principle, which is understood by everybody who knows anything whatsoever about industry, that wages are considerably higher in Ontario than in Quebec.
What is feared by some people in regard to these family allowances is that they will tend to crystallize the situation in Quebec, namely, continue the lower wages there which the people in Quebec, the people in Ontario and elsewhere in Canada would like to see raised

Family Allowances
so that the people in Quebec would have a better standard of living because of what they earn and contribute to industry, and would not compete unfairly with industrial workers in other parts of the country. I understand that in recent years practically the whole cheap furniture business has gone to Quebec, much of it from Ontario, because of the lower wages in the province of Quebec. If these family allowances are to be paid on the rates set forth in the schedule, with which I have no complaint generally, they may nevertheless tend to cause a shift in employment because of certain industries in the lower wage class moving from Ontario to Quebec and thus favouring one province of this great country over another when it comes to employment. Naturally that is something looked at with askance by the people of Ontario, particularly the industrial workers. What is the solution of it? I do not suppose that in a federal state such as Canada we can definitely and clearly rectify the difficulty and make certain that further damage will not be caused by the granting of these family allowances. However, I believe that the government should be cautioned on this point, should be warned, if I may use that expression, that the people in the other sections of Canada will watch to see just what effect these family allowances have on the relative wage scales and the tendency for certain industries to shift to the lower wage scale areas in this country.
The second matter I wish to mention is this. I do not put this forward too seriously in a sense, and yet I think the committee should be apprised of the fact that there is in the minds of many of us, and I hope in the minds of all of us, a very great difference between a man who has earned money being allowed a certain deduction for the maintenance of his children and the man receiving an allowance or what even might be termed a hand-out from the state for the support of his children. In the one case the man has earned the money by the sweat of his brow or the work of his brain in open competition with his fellow Canadians; in the other case the man has not earned the money but is being given it by the state. I see no way of rectifying the situation exactly. One does not ask for greater consideration to be given to children of taxpayers than to children of those who do not pay taxes; yet in this regard I believe it is an integral part of the bill that we should know definitely what the changes in the income tax regulations are to be. What we have been given is the very general statement that a parent will not be allowed to benefit through receiving the income tax deduction or tax credit, as it now is, and certain family allowances. Yet an income tax schedule should be available to all, so that those who receive $1,200 and over, but are not given the full $108 exemption to which a larger income would entitle them, may know exactly what their position is, and so that all may be fairly dealt with. This matter of income tax regulation is just as vital as any other provision in this bill; and while I do not want to use the term "half-baked legislation", it certainly does indicate that the government or the Department of Finance, which is responsible for the income tax act, as yet has not found out exactly how it is to be handled. Otherwise there could be no possible reason why the actual mechanics of it should not be given to the members of this committee, so that we might understand them and be able to answer the many questions which have been addressed to us by our constituents.
The other point is in regard to where the money is to come from. I suppose it is merely going to come from the general pot, but undoubtedly it will prevent certain reductions in taxation which otherwise might have been made. However, we cannot have our cake and eat it at the same time, and we must realize that we are going to pay for these family allowances through taxation. Yet I believe the government should give us a clear indication, perhaps not in percentages but at least in principle, of where the money is to come from; whether it is expected that it will come from income tax directly or from some form of indirect taxation. This statement does not apply only to family allowances; it applies to the whole generality of these appropriation bills which we are putting through the committee at the present time with such abandon. In this committee and this house we have little regard to how much we can raise; we simply go ahead and make our coat with no regard at all to our cloth. We do not know what our total financial requirements are likely to be in the post-war years. This all ties in with a matter which I believe is of first importance; that is, if we are to have full employment after the war we must have incentive for our people. If they are taxed too heavily it means that people will not be given a reasonable reward for the risk and enterprise which they show, and we shall come to the point where the state will be running everything. So that I urge upon the government that they outline to this committee not only where the $200,000,000 or $250,000,000 required for this measure are coming from, but that- they give us some idea-it might as well be brought in now as at some later time-where all the money is to come from and approximately

what the total budget is likely to be in the year after the war, say, when we shall no longer have direct war expenditures. Otherwise it is impossible to know whether we can with the most complete faith vote for measures which involve hundreds of millions of dollars, without knowing where the money is to come from; whether it will come through a continuance of the printing press methods, or from borrowing from the banks as in the past we have borrowed a certain proportion of our national expenditures.
To give some indication of the lack of information possessed1 by hon. members in regard to these financial expenditures, as yet we have been given no information whatever with respect to the $848,000,000 which the Minister of Finance announced would be spent on matters of which he could give no details. Perhaps that should be more properly brought up under another bill, but at least it will give hon. members an appreciation of the little or no information we are given by the government in regard to the very important matter of how we are to finance our expenditures or even how we are to spend our money. I would remind hon. members that $848,000,000 is not less than 160 or 170 per cent of the normal pre-war budget; yet we have had only the barest indication that this money will be spent, and we are not told on what it is to be spent. In the same way I believe we should be given full details, at least in principle, as to what our total expenditures will be, so that we may have an over-all picture, before we go at the matter piecemeal, appropriating $200,000,000 here and $200,000,000 there, without knowing whether or not this country can afford to go ahead with these measures.

I should like to refer to just one point asked by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. Several hon. gentlemen on the opposite side have implied that the granting of family allowances is going to have the effect of keeping wages in the province of Quebec at. a comparatively lower level than in the province of Ontario.
I suppose there is nothing more intricate than an understanding of the factors which enter into the determination of rates of wages; they are in part international, in part national and in part local, and arise from many causes. One thing, however, is apparent or, I believe, has become apparent in recent years, since the prejudice against the organization of labour has begun to disappear and large visioned employers have begun to see the wisdom of such organization. That is, wages have only risen appreciably where labour has been strong enough to organize. In the matter of organi-

zation, there is perhaps nothing that enters so effectively to prejudice their position as the obligation the workers have to consider when they are carrying on a struggle to improve their conditions. In a province in which there are small families, where great numbers of those employed are unmarried, it is relatively easy for labour to organize, and, if that should become necessary in order to improve the condition of labour, to strike and refuse to work until wages are more in accordance with the service rendered. But where you have a condition in any part of the country where wages are relatively low and where there are large familes, the wage-earner is confronted with the most difficult situation possible as far as improving his condition is concerned. When he is driven to the point of refusing to work unless he can get better pay he has to consider not himself only, his wife and possibly one child; he has to consider the fate of five, ten or fifteen children, and he finds himself in a position where there is practically no option between allowing some of his family to starve or giving up the struggle to improve his condition altogether.
This allowance to children where there are large families will help remove that impediment. It is going to help place those large families above a bare subsistence level, and often a condition worse than that, because the standard of living frequently degraded because of the small incomes which heads of large families are able to obtain in relation to the obligations they are called upon to meet because of the size of their families. When this law goes into effect the head of a large family will have at least some provision which he can be sure his children will receive if he finds himself driven to that desperate position which labour at one time or another has reached in whole or in part when it has tried to improve its condition, namely, having to choose between starving or working, because that is all what lies at the basis of success or failure in most strikes. I do not for one moment hesitate to say that the effect of this legislation will place those who have large families in a relatively stronger economic position. They will not, because of this legislation, be economically weaker, relatively, than their brothers in other provinces. They will be appreciably stronger than they have been in the past and, as a consequence, will be able to fight for wage standards in their respective provinces comparable with those existing in other provinces. In that way they will help bring about what all hon. members have said is very desirable, and which I personally think most desirable, namely, uniformity of rates of

pay for equivalent work in all parts of the dominion. So that my argument is that, far from deploring that this legislation is quite likely to further an inequality in labour rates of pay for all parts of this country, we should view it in entirely the opposite way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
Under this bill the allowances are payable to parents with respect to children and to parents who maintain children wholly or in part. The payment is to be made to a parent as defined in the bill and he must maintain the child in order to qualify. Once you have a parent who maintains a child, then he is qualified under the bill. He would receive the allowance and could, I think quite properly, make an arrangement with a boarding school, a child welfare organization or anyone else whereby the child would be boarded and supported. The parent may pay the necessary amount to the institution and still continue to receive benefits under this bill. The allowances to be paid are payable to parents who maintain children.
It is contemplated that in a small number of cases it may" be necessary, on the application of a child welfare organization or a provincial or municipal welfare officer, to consider whether or not in the special circumstances of a given case the allowances should not be diverted from the one parent to another or from the parent to a guardian appointed by the court or to some other person. Such other person may conceivably be an agency or organization.

speechtext: The only comment I wish to make with regard to this bill can be most appropriately made under this clause. I personally am concerned that we give recognition to the people whom next to the children we have uppermost in our minds. It is in recognition of the greatest financier that I have ever known, my sainted mother, that I rise in my place at this time and recall the sacrifices that she made, her industry and the heartaches that she had when I was a boy. I think of the hundreds of mothers, legitimate and others, who have consulted me in my professional capacity during the last twenty years. I am most concerned that this money which is to go to help children shall in very truth and fact go to those who are most anxiously concerned to help children-the mothers of those children. I would feel much happier if it were embodied right in this bill that parliament says that the money shall in the first instance go to the mother of the children, and only to others when it is established by proper authority that the mother is not a fit and proper person to receive the money wherewith to take care of her children. I feel keenly and strongly on that phase of the matter, and I know that many other members of this house and literally thousands of people outside are most anxious and concerned lest the benefits of this legislation be lost by reason of the fact that this government will make it possible for these funds to be diverted by officials or others from what I believe to be and what I believe humanity believes to be the proper and appropriate recipient of the money, the one who cares most for the weal, welfare and happiness of those whom this measure is designed to help1-little children.

There is a question bearing on this section that I would ask, but before doing so may I say how glad I was to hear the opinion just expressed by the hon. member for Calgary West. I trust that he will support me when I move an amendment to section 11 (a), which I indicated last night that I would propose when we reached that clause.
My question on section 4 is this: Will the allowance be paid at the beginning or at the end of the month for which the payment is being made? I have a reason for asking this question. Personally I feel that the provisions of section 4 are generally quite good, but from our experience with the old age pension measure we know that one unhappy situation arises. A person who qualifies for the old age pension had his seventieth birthday, we will say, the second day of January. Because of the wording of the Old Age Pensions Act he does not draw his first old age pension cheque until the last day of February. There is" a lapse of almost two months from the date that he qualifies before he receives his first cheque. That may not seem veiy much to some people, but it is a source of a good deal of disappointment and feeling to those who are affected. I have run into quite a few cases of that kind. As I see it, the wording of this section will produce the same result if the payment is made at the end of the month. Chi the other hand, if payment is made on the first day of the month for which the payment is specified, there would not be that two months' lapse.
Let me point to another type of case. Supposing the child is born about the twenty-eighth of the month; the father is excited; it is the first time it has happened, and he neglects to register until the first or second of the next month; then the payment is not made until the end of the following month. It is a pretty long lapse of time between the birth of the child and the receipt of the first cheque. I wonder whether the parliamentary assistant could answer me on that point.

The hon. member is concerned now with a minority, and it is a small minority of cases where the parent does not look after the child properly. This bill has two provisions which expressly deal with that. There is the provision in section 5, under which it is declared:
5. The allowance shall be applied by the person receiving the same exclusively towards the maintenance, care, training, education and advancement of the child, and, if the minister or such officer as is authorized by regulations in that behalf is satisfied that the allowance is not being so applied, payment thereof shall be discontinued or made to some other person or agency.
In this, I may say, the bill provides along lines similar to section 20 of the Australian act and section 29 of the New Zealand act. In addition there is this provision in section 11:
11. The governor in council may make regulations to . . .
(b) provide that where, by reason of age, infirmity, ill health, insanity, improvidence or other reasonable cause of disqualification of the person to whom the allowance is payable or in other special circumstances, payment may be made to another suitable person or agency.
There, provision is made for diversion, and I should say, further, that it is contemplated that in the administration of these provisions the provincial child welfare agencies and child welfare officers will play a very big part in drawing to the attention of the family allowance administration any case where there

In regard to subsection I, I feel, as I stated when I spoke on the second reading, that there is an inconsistency between section 8 (1) and section 7. I do not complain against the taking back or the withholding of the allowance from those in the higher income brackets, but I still feel, as I said hefore, that further consideration should be given to the whole question of relating this family allowance scheme to the income tax structure, which I feel is wrong. I was glad to hear the parliamentary assistant say last night that this is a phase of the question on which the officials are still doing a great deal of study. I hope their study will not be confined to the various ways of working things out within the provisions of section 8, but that they will give consideration to divorcing the payment of allowances from the income tax structure altogether. That structure is not sacrosanct. It is something of a hodge-podge in the way it has grown up. Certainly it is likely to undergo changes in the post-war years, and the family allowance scheme should stand on its own feet, with a view to its inclusion later in an over-all social security plan. speechtext:
As the hon. member for
Cape Breton South indicates, this power given to the governor in council to make regulations has relation to section 6 of the bill, which reads:

6. If any person is dissatisfied with a decision as to his right to be paid an allowance or as to the amount of an allowance payable to him or as to any other matter arising under this act, he may appeal against such decision to a tribunal to be established and conducted in accordance with regulations, and the decision of the tribunal shall not be subject to appeal or review by any court of law.
As a matter of administration it will be necessary to decide in some eases whether or not the child is the age his parent claims, whether or not the child has been resident in Canada for three years or was born in Canada, whether or not the child is a child in respect of whom the allowance may be made. Also it may be necessary to decide whether or not the parent is maintaining the child wholly or substantially, and sometimes even which parent is maintaining the child. All these matters will have to be decided as matters of administration, and it was not thought fair that such important matters should be left exclusively to be decided by administrative officials. Consequently provision was made for an appeal, and the word "tribunal" was used, although what was intended was something more in the nature of a committee. As I understand it, it is under contemplation that committees will be established in each province, probably of an honorary nature or at least not of a permanent nature, and not of a purely judicial nature, but committees of people who, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested, would be experienced in welfare matters, and they would have these cases submitted to them for decision, in much the same way as the local committee of the dependents' board of trustees act with respect to the claims for allowances made under that measure. In other words, there would be an appeal from the purely administrative official to a committee of citizens who would be chosen because of their interest in public questions and their knowledge of public welfare matters, who could be trusted to be fair and to make each decision in the light of all the circumstances of the particular case.

speechtext:
I just want to say to my hon. friend that from an administrative point of view it would be hopeless to allow appeals to the courts in a multitude of small cases which in the nature of things should be decided administratively. There is even greater justification for excluding references to the courts here than in the case of
workmen's compensation allowances, pensions under the Pension Act, dependents' allowances for the dependents of members of the armed forces and other similar payments.
There is no more justification for allowing appeals to the courts in this case than in these others. As my hon. friend knows, in a measure of this kind it would make confusion worse confounded to have that particular procedure adopted. But there is a further fact to be considered. The moneys paid under this bill are in the nature of grants. There is no contractual relationship being established. If there were there might be reasons for appeal to the courts; there might be reasons for having the courts interpret and decide. If my hon. friend wishes to introduce the courts into this legislation, I am afraid he will be only helping to make it anything but agreeable in the eyes of those who may hope to benefit by it, and until it is shown that decisions by a tribunal under this measure would not be as fair as decisions under tribunals such as are established in the case of workmen's compensation, and dependents' allowances, we can afford to leave the question of appeal to the courts where it has been left in the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext: In reply to the Prime Minister, may I say that the argument I have advanced has repeatedly been advanced by the Canadian Bar Association and, I may add, during the period when the Minister of Justice was president of that association. I do not believe there should be appeal on questions of fact, but I believe, when a decision is made by an administrative tribunal which deals with the rights of individuals and which may determine those rights contrary to the law of the province concerned, that in such cases there should be the right of appeal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext: I do not think this should be allowed to pass without a further word. Here we are passing legislation which is new. We have had an opportunity to examine with the utmost care legislation already adopted in New Zealand, Australia and Ireland, and I think it is interesting to let the committee know the situation with regard to this matter in those three countries. In each of those countries there is no appeal except to an administrative officer, a single administrative officer appointed under the provisions of the act or the appropriate social security measure.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext: An appeal from a tribunal to that officer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
Not at all; an appeal from an inferior to a superior administrative officer. Here we have gone farther and provided for
Family Allowances

appeal from an administrative officer to a committee or tribunal of citizens to be appointed and to be independent. I submit that is a fairer provision and it is a provision which goes further than the legislation in the other countries mentioned. It is the kind of provision which will give the citizens of the country the safeguards they should have.
My hon. friend keeps harping on the constitutional question and interference with provincial rights in one respect or another. There is no provision of the bill which interferes in any way with provincial rights, and I cannot conceive of any administration by those responsible which will amount to interference with provincial rights. In the case he mentioned, namely,''where a guardian is appointed by a provincial court to administer the affairs of the child, I cannot conceive of any administrative official paying anyone but that guardian except in the most unusual circumstances. But if by any chance he did, that would not be an interference with provincial rights in any sense whatever.| It would be the exercise of powers conferred under this measure. It would not change the position of the guardian in any sense or interfere with the jurisdiction of the provincial court. It would be carrying out the provisions of this legislation which gave the administration power to say to whom the payment should be made.
It is essential that payments be dealt with in this way because here we are dealing with 3,500,000 children, and it is impossible to lay down in this or in any other measure, no matter how long we work at it, the terms and conditions on which the payment should be made so as to cover every special case. It is essential that there should be not only discretion in the individual case but power to pass regulations to deal with classes of cases. In this connection may I mention how far they have gone in Ireland. We have not gone so far, but it does indicate the attitude in their legislature toward this kind of problem. Section 19 of the Irish children's allowance act of 1944 reads:
If in any respect any difficulty arises in bringing into operation this act the minister, with the consent of the Minister of Finance, mtty by ofder do anything which appears to be necessary or expedient for bringing -this act into operation and any such order may modify the provisions of this act so far as may appear necessary or expedient for carrying the order into effect.
In this bill .we have provided, as has been provided in the case of the Pension Act and every other similar act I have knowledge of, that the governor in council shall have power to pass regulations. It is provided that these
[Mr. Claxton.l
regulations shall be laid on the table of the house and shall be published, and that gives hon. members and citizens of the country the safeguard of publicity. But also, as the Prime Minister has indicated, it is contemplated that the regulations will be drafted and laid on the table of the house at the next session before the measure comes into operation, so that hon. members will have an opportunity of seeing them then.

speechtext:
My hon. friend speaks
of administrative bodies. I have had some experience in connection with workmen's compensation. Under the -old scheme of things, prior to the establishment of workmen's compensation in Ontario in 1914, there was the old common law approach where a man could go to the courts. What were the results? The biggest part of the damages awarded injured workmen went to the legal fraternity for prosecuting the case or conducting it before the courts. I am convinced that since the inception of workmen's compensation with an administrative body, and notwithstanding appeals from other people outside that there should be the right of appeal to the courts, no resolution or demand has come from any responsible labour organization. They have always taken- the position that while the number of problem cases is less than a fraction of one per cent, if appeal were allowed to the courts almost every case in the very nature of things would be challenged by the employer. That might be said truthfully also about widows' -pensions, if access had been given to the courts in connection with such pensions or soldiers' allowances. I think it is fair to say that all these administrative bodies engaged in connection with social measures, unemployment insurance, for instance, function better and to the advantage of the working man and woman without resort to the courts. They get the money instead of the legal fraternity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
That is the usual
answer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext: It is the practical answer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
It is a frivolous kind of answer and we are not dealing with frivolous matters now. So far as the parliamentary assistant is concerned he has not covered the situation at all. New Zealand has had a similar act in effect since 1926. I would ask him to point out where there are any similar

Family Allowances
provisions in the act of New Zealand. Australia has had an act since 1941. I would ask him to point out similar provisions in that act. Let me say to him that the example of Eire is scarcely applicable to the situation in Canada. In Eire there is no divided jurisdiction such as exists in this country as between the dominion and the provinces. There has been little experience in the operation of the act which was passed in Eire during the present year; therefore the argument which the parliamentary assistant advances scarcely covers the point that I endeavoured to make.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
The regulations are covered in the Australian child endowment act by section 29, and 1 shall read it:
The governor general may make regulations, not inconsistent with this act, prescribing all matters which are by this act required or permitted to be prescribed, or which are necessary or convenient to be prescribed, for carrying out or giving effect to this act, and in particular for prescribing matters providing for or in relation to-*
(a)	the manner and form of any claim, the person by whom and to whom and the time within which claims shall be made, and the information and evidence which may be required and accepted in connection with any such claim;
(b)	the general conditions governing the grant, payment and administration of endowments;
(c)	the manner in which endowments may be paid or applied; and
(d)	penalties not exceeding a fine of twenty-five pounds or imprisonment for three months, or both, for any breach of the regulations.
If lion, members will look at the New Zealand act they will find that their social security act deals with the various provisions regarding social security. Only sections 28 to 32 deal specifically with family benefits, as they are called there. In other words, they have only five sections dealing with this whole measure specifically and they are in such terms that almost all of them could be included in two sections of our bill, sections 3 and 4. These, however, are supplemented by general sections applicable to the whole bill, and one of them, namely section 140, gives power to make regulations. It reads:
(1)	The governor in council may, from time to time, by order in council, make all such regulations as in his opinion are necessary for the purpose of giving full effect to this act.
(2)	All regulations purporting to be made under the authority of this section shall, until revoked, have the force of law as if they were enacted in this act.
(3)	AH regulations made under the authority of this section shall be laid before parliament within fourteen days after the making thereof if parliament is then in session, and, if not, shall be so laid before parliament within fourteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session.

speechtext: I should like the committee to be informed rather fully of what is in the government's mind with regard to the holding of this registration, whether it is to be carried out entirely by the officials appointed under this measure, or whether use will be made of officials of the welfare departments of the provinces and other officials of the provinces.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENTS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN UNDER SIXTEEN
speechtext:
The form of registration that is receiving favourable consideration at the present time from governmental officials is this. They hope that it may be possible to use the facilities of the post office and of its employees in order to conduct the registration. It is hoped that it will be done in this way. Forms will be distributed to the letter carriers and deliverers of rural mail. These forms will be made available in sufficient numbers that a form of registration will be left at every house or residence where there is a family that might be entitled to these benefits. At the same time there will be publicity in the press to draw attention to what is being done, and other forms may be obtained at any post office. The forms will be explained; in themselves they will be simple, containing probably^ not more than seven, eight or nine questions. Probably a statutory declaration or affidavit will be required with some supporting evidence as to the birth of the children. Those forms when completed by the parents will be collected by the postal carriers and sent from the postal headquarters to the local office of the administration. At that local office the registration will be effected; addresses and ledger sheets will be prepared, and all the necessary machinery prepared in order to send out the cheques. At the local office also the registration forms will be checked with vital statis-
tics information from the provinces; spot-checked in other ways; checked with the local welfare officers of the province, if their cooperation can be achieved as it is hoped it will be. Throughout all that operation the only employees it will be necessary to appoint under the measure will be those in the local offices actually charged with registration and administration, together with the treasury officials necessary to make out the cheques, and the officers of the governments necessary to supplement any investigation carried on by provincial or other agencies.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE AND DEVELOP TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an extremely important bill touching an important phase of our national and international life. Despite the fact that it is late in the session and that there is a desire on the part of some hon. members to hasten along with the business I feel that this measure should be given close attention and consideration by the house. The importance of international trade, on which this bill has a definite bearing, is recognized by almost all Canadians. It is of particular importance to us, and as we look forward to

Export Credits Insurance

the post-war period we cannot but be keenly interested in any measure that proposes to provide for the revival of export trade and the development of our international economic relations.
The purposes of the bill are set out in the preamble and, as I see it, those purposes are really two. The preamble reads:
Whereas it is desirable to promote the revival of trade by establishing a corporation to insure against loss caused by insolvency, delays in collection and transfer difficulties in connection with the export of Canadian-produced goods, and during the period of transition from war to peace by providing for loans or guarantees to governments of other countries or their agencies;
Therefore, His Majesty . . .
And so on.
The two important provisions referred to in that preamble are to be found by referring to sections 13 and 22 of the bill. Section 13 indicates that under the terms of this bill the government wdll have power to "enter into a contract of insurance with an exporter to insure against the risk of loss involved in a contract for the export of Canadian-produced goods." That is one phase of the machinery proposed under the terms of this bill, that the government shall have power to enter into contracts to assist exporters in the development of foreign trade.
The other important feature of this bill is found in section 22, where we learn that the government may make guarantees to other governments or their agencies to assist them in the purchase of Canadian-produced goods during the three years immediately after the coming into force of part II of the bill. This second feature of the bill is in a partial sense a continuation of the mutual aid principle which we have followed to a considerable extent. during the war. That is a principle which has received support from almost all the members of this ho'use, and we welcome the suggestion that that principle is to be carried over in part for-at least three years into the post-war period.
The other feature of the bill is also commendable so far as its aim. and objective are concerned, namely, the development of foreign trade, but I am not so sure that it is commendable as the best way of achieving that purpose.
I said a moment ago that the importance of international trade can hardly be overemphasized so far as Canada is concerned. I should like to place on the record a statement in this connection which was made by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation at its first annual convention in Regina in 1933. At

that time the C.C.F. drew up what is known as the Regina manifesto, clause 5 of which reads as follows:
External Trade
The regulation in accordance with the national plan of external trade through import and export boards.
Canada is dependent on external sources of supply for many of her essential requirements of raw materials and manufactured products. These she can obtain only by large exports of the goods she is best fitted to produce. The strangling of ou.r export trade by insane protectionist policies must be brought to an end. But the old controversies between free traders and protectionists are now largely obsolete. In a world of nationally organized economies Canada must organize the buying and selling of her main imports and exports under public boards, and take steps to regulate the flow of less important commodities by a system of licences. By so doing she will be enabled to make the best trade agreements possible with foreign countries, put a stop to the exploitation of both primary producer and ultimate consumer, make possible the coordination of internal processing, transportation and marketing of farm products, and facilitate the establishment of stable prices for such export commodities.
I remind the house that that is not some statement which was prepared recently in the light of present conditions. That statement was issued by this party at its first national convention, eleven years ago, and I submit that every word of it still stands as a valid and basic statement so far as Canada's foreign trade is concerned.
When we talk about the importance of foreign trade, I think the question should be asked once in a while as to what it is that makes foreign trade so important. As a matter of fact the question has been answered in part during recent debates. The important, thing about international commerce, if it is conducted on a basis of freedom of exchange, is that the people in various countries are enabled to produce the things which they are best capable of producing and, by trading those products, achieve mutual gain. That principle is the underlying idea so far as free trade is concerned .and there is no question that the principle itself is still sound. But there are some things which free traders-those who give us the theory behind it and claim that that is the essence of their gospel-seem to have forgotten. - One is that it is quite possible even under free trade for cartels and monopolies to be set up and dictate world prices with the result that the advantages of free trade accrue, not as they should, to the people of the countries which enter into free trade, but rather to those who dictate the policy of trade throughout the world.
I should like to have the privilege of quoting briefly from an address which was delivered in

The liberal economists, still under the influence of the heady vintages of 1890, continue to debate the dead and varied issue of free trade versus tariff. That issue has long been superseded-[DOT]

I said a moment ago, I regard the aim and purpose of the bill as the revival of trade in the immediate post-war period. The preamble states that. To achieve that purpose the bill sets out two proposals. One is dealt with in section 22 along mutual aid lines, and so far as that part of the bill is concerned I express my wholehearted support of it. As a matter of fact, when the bill for mutual aid, and the bill in connection with UNRRA were before the house, I expressed the hope that the principle of mutual aid might be carried into the post-war period. I am glad to find that the principle, at least for three years, is woven in part into the text of the bill that is before us. But with respect to the other provision of the bill, namely, that trade might be revived in the post-war period by the method of insurance contracts with private exporters, under which the government would bear any loss, leaving the exporter the opportunity to enjoy any gains, I am not in agreement. As a matter of fact I do not see how anyone who argues the case for free enterprise and insists upon the fact that free enterprise must be given its rein because it takes the risk can really support this measure. Similarly I would point out that from our viewpoint it is against the best interests of the country as a whole, and because of the importance of trade to Canada I am not satisfied with a Liberal administration, which has had so much to say about the importance of international trade and the principle of free trade, coming in at this stage of the game and giving us only this as a means of reviving so important a phase of our life as international trade.
Your Honour has questioned my right to deal with the other matter and I take it that I must accept your ruling, but may I add this other sentence or two in conclusion to that phase of my remarks. It seems to me that free trade by itself is not enough. It is a good principle. It is as sound to-day as it ever was, but if the people of Canada are to have the things that accrue from free trade we have to take this further step of
setting up import and export boards so that we can plan our foreign trade, plan our bulk purchases in such a way as will be to the best interests of the people of Canada as a whole. Along with that we must take steps to see to it that the purchasing power of our people at home is increased and that our people are put in a position to buy the things that can be brought into this country in return for the goods that we sell under the provisions of this bill.
If Your Honour had not restricted me somewhat I would have taken time to read some quotations along this line from the very interesting booklet that I have in my hand entitled, "The Mid-Continent and the Peace". This booklet, as some hon. members may know, was prepared at the request made in 1941 by the then Premier of Manitoba, Hon. John Bracken, and the then governor of Minnesota, the Hon. Harold Stassen, by economists of the universities of Manitoba and Minnesota. The economists who did this piece of research were Professor William J. Waines of the university of Manitoba and Professor Arthur L. Upgren of the university of Minnesota. I could have given half a dozen quotations from this booklet showing how they face the problem of foreign trade, and of western agriculture in particular, in the post-war period. It is their contention that tariffs must be lowered by all means, but it is also their contention that there must be planning of trade as between this country and other countries. First of all I should say that it is their contention that the United States and Canada should be more closely integrated as an economic unit, and that in addition to that there should be planning of trade between this north American economic unit and other countries. They also point out in a definite way that if we are to facilitate the economic rehabilitation of other sections of the world we must improve the standard of living of our industrial communities here at home. We must become an increasingly larger market for the goods that may be purchased from other communities. I notice you are restless, Mr. Speaker, therefore I think I had better not push your patience any farther. I have only continued because I really felt that what I have had to say was relevant to this very important matter of international trade. I am not satisfied that this bill, brought in by a Liberal administration goes far enough in recognizing its importance to Canada in the post-war period.

Well, the mutual aid principle is somewhat different from the principle found in section 22 of the bill. Section 22 of the bill authorizes the government to guarantee the obligations of foreign governments which purchase goods in Canada, to make loans to foreign governments which purchase goods in Canada, and to purchase or acquire securities issued by foreign governments for the purchase of goods in Canada. The mutual aid legislation is based on a different principle. Under the mutual aid legislation there is no money obligation whatever on the part of foreign governments, and in that respect it is certainly inaccurate to characterize section 22 of the bill as being based on the mutual aid principle. But what I take particular exception to is his summary of the principle which he alleges is contained in part I of the bill. If I understood him correctly, he said that it contemplates the assumption of losses by the government of Canada, leaving profits, if such are made, to private exporters. That is not so.
The effective section of the bill is section 13. Section 13 provides for the setting up of insurance. It provides for the insuring by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation of private exporters, or, for that matter, it might be public exporters, it might be government boards, although perhaps that would not be entirely appropriate. The main purpose of the bill in part I is to insure private exporters against loss, but on a commercial basis. It is not an assumption by the government of losses, leaving profits to private exporters. May I refer to my colleague's speech made when he introduced the legislation on July 28, at page 5518 of Hansard. He said:
Ihe Export Credit Insurance Corporation that is to be set up in Canada is intended to develop for the assistance of Canadian exporters an insurance business of this kind, and it is tilt intention that it shall operate on a selfsustaining basis, but that it shall be essentially non-profit-making.

In the operation of import and export boards it is possible to relate the prices of the commodities imported to the returns from the commodities exported. In other words, experience has shown that the internal price of a commodity may not bear any relationship to the external price of that commodity in the country to which it is exported. On the other hand, imports from the country or group of countries into the country receiving the imports can be related, within the importing country, to its own internal price level. In that way you could even up the losses with the profits that may accrue as between various types of commodities. Consequently, under an import-export system it is possible to escape the kind of loss-although, of course, conceivably you may have another kind of loss-against which this bill is designed to give protection as far as the individual exporter is concerned.

The statement I was just about to make, I think, covers the points raised by the hon. member.
It is intended that the premium income should be sufficient to cover all claims. The premiums will be set in accordance with the risks involved. Some loss may be incurred during the initial stages when experience is being gained, but it is intended that the scheme should stand on its own feet and require no permanent financial assistance from the government.
The insurance scheme will offer no new means of actually financing foreign trade, because it is proposed that the existing facilities of the banks will be used for financing and collecting bills of exchange. It is expected, however, that the insurance scheme will increase the willingness of these private institutions to finance export transactions and thereby place our exporters in a stronger competitive position. Moreover, it is expected that the banks will find it to be in their own interests to assist the administration of the scheme by providing information concerning the standing of foreign importers. This information will be augmented by reports from the various trade commissioners and commercial attaches, the Bank of Canada and other sources.
The risk to be insured is the risk of loss as defined in section 13 of the bill. The details of contracts will be worked out by the directors of the corporation, subject to the conditions imposed including inter alia, adequate premiums to cover probable losses and the acceptance by the exporter of some portion of the risk. The portion to be thus assumed by the exporter will depend upon the nature of the goods, the standing of the importer and other factors.
It is expected that until the corporation gains experience, it will restrict its contracts of insurance to only the better known forms of bills of exchange. The chief risks to be insured will pertain to solvency of the foreign importer, w-hich is the exporter's principal risk, and the transfer of funds. In connection with the latter risk, it would be possible to have a situation where a foreign importer may have discharged his indebtedness to the Canadian exporter by meeting his bills in the local currency of the foreign country but, because of exchange controls or other unforeseen developments, it might not be possible to transfer the local funds to Canadian dollars. I have not made a close
study of the bill, but I wonder whether the ministers have considered this aspect of it, which goes rather to the whole principle involved. We have new lending organizations coming into being this session very rapidly, involving the lending, as in part II of the bill, of government money. Under our industrial development bank we have set up as a board the governor of the Bank of Canada and his entire staff. They constitute the board of the new industrial development bank. While I have some reservations about the provisions with regard to that bank, I think that is an excellent idea, and in entrusting to the governor and his staff the duties under that measure they are being put in the proper place. Then we have the farm loan bank and that, as will be recalled, is to be administered solely by the Minister of Finance. He administers all the duties under the farm loan bank bill, and that requires the Department of Finance to keep close tab on loans the banks are making under the limited right to lend, and the Minister of Finance there is entrusted with the right of vetoing any class or type of loan which the chartered banks are about to engage in. So that there the Minister of Finance is the hand that controls that type of farm loan.
Now we come to the bill in question, and we are setting up under section 3 an entirely new type of organization to consist of the deputy minister of trade and commerce, the deputy minister of finance' and the governor of the Bank of Canada. That is a third composite type of control to look after the banking business that is to be done with the taxpayers' money. I am not for the moment critical, but I am wondering whether the Minister of Finance and his colleague have given thought to whether or not we should spatter out three different types of banks-because this is in part II really a bank lending to foreign governments, a departure indeed

or whether we should not use in the matter of lending, where the taxpayers' money is to be lent, the entire facilities and personnel of the Bank of Canada, who are trained in lending money, taking security and all that. While the present Minister of Finance has displayed
Export Credits Insurance

great ability in connection with some of the factors that deal with banking and commercial banking, it does seem to me that the true function of the Department of Finance has been in the past, and ought to be maintained in the future, that of controlling perhaps the amount in his budget that we tax the people for, and the amount that we are to borrow, and the various types of loans which have been so successfully handled on the part of the present Minister of Finance-and that is a real man's job by itself. The Minister of Finance should, I think, have full time to spend on that branch of the nation's business, budgeting for taxation, budgeting for borrowing, and he should not begin to assume, as he has done entirely under the farm loan bank, the functions of controlling banking, as he is in part assuming through his deputy minister and wringing in the Department of Trade and Commerce and using as a third the governor of he Bank of Canada.
Glancing at section 22 of part II, which is ;he lending branch of this departure under this 3ill, I find that the draftsman has eliminated the governor of the Bank of Canada entirely. Under subsection 1 of section 22 it is provided that "during the three years next ensuing after the coming into force of this part of this act, the governor in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce may, if he deems it advisable" and so on, guarantee obligations in foreign countries. Why leave out of that very important task the one man in Canada who ought to be best equipped because of his necessary study of the financial systems of foreign countries? Why drop him?

It would be entirely inappropriate to delegate that most important function or set of duties to the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada is set up for an entirely different purpose. It was never contemplated for a moment that it should be passing upon the advisability of entering upon this important transaction. There will be all kinds of delays under this bill. I have had some experience in that line in the last month. We have an export board in New Brunswick that handles the export of potatoes. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: KILLING OF CANADIAN SOLDIERS AFTER CAPTURE BY GERMANS IN NORMANDY
speechtext:
Mi leaker, I would ask for the attention of th	use to a statement
that 1 am about to mai	It is my sad duty
this morning to inform i. y. members of the circumstances in which nil eteen members of the Canadian forces were ki.led in Normandy. What I have to say is apart altogether from any other matter of a like nature to which I have previously made reference.
In the early days of the invasion it was reported to the supreme commander of the allied expeditionary force that some Canadian soldiers had been shot after capture by the enemy. At the request of the Canadian commander, a court of inquiry composed of officers of the British, United States and Canadian armies was promptly convened. That court has now reported, after most careful investigations, that one Canadian officer and eighteen Canadian other ranks who had been taken prisoner by and were in the custody of the German army were murdered by members of the 12th S.S. reconnaissance battalion of the 12th S.S. panzer division, under the direction of certain of their officers. These Canadian soldiers had the status of prisoners of war and as such were entitled to protection. There is no doubt that they met their deaths in a manner and under circumstances clearly in violation of the well recognized laws and usages of war and of the provisions of the international conventions
Privilege-Mr. Picard

on the treatment of prisoners of war. In short, they were wilfully murdered by members of the enemy's forces.
The other governments of the commonwealth have joined with the Canadian government in a request to the Swiss government that the results of the inquiry by the court be brought to the attention of the German government, that a demand be made on the German government for an immediate and searching investigation and that the German officers and men responsible be punished. The governments of the commonwealth have also asked the Swiss government to demand that the German government promulgate strict orders to prevent, in future, a repetition of such an occurrence.
As I have said, we have put the findings of the court into the hands of the protecting power. We have asked them to take appropriate action. In the circumstances, this is all that I am able to say on this subject at the moment. There is nothing more that can usefully be said at this time and I hope hon. members will understand the desirability of avoiding unnecessary discussion. I shall conclude simply with the statement that this house humbly pays its sincere tribute to the valour and honour of the dead and expresses its deep and heartfelt sympathy to the families who have been so sadly bereaved. I may say that the next of kin have been notified but that no names are being published.

MB. PICARD-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. BRUCE IN DEBATE ON JULY 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. On July 31, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) referred to me in such words that I feel I must correct the record. I will not repeat all that was said in committee yesterday when I first brought this matter up, but I should like to quote what the hon. member said as reported on page 5674 of Hansard:
I know the hon. member for Bellechasse has a head of hair which is still black, but I venture to say that he cannot show any better record in this or the last war .than the one to which I have just referred.
This, Mr. Speaker, is, in the hon. member for , Parkdale's usual manner, an insinuation that I did not perform my duty either in the other war or in this one. I object to that insinuation.
I should like to say a word as to my own record and exercise the same right as the hon. member and put it on Hansard. I wish to state, in the same place where the insinuation was made, that in the month of May, 191S, when I was only eighteen years and eight months of age, I enlisted. I have here in my mind a photostatic copy of my enlistment papers on which I find the signature of my father, which authorization was needed as I was still a minor.
I have also photostatic copies of my medical papers dated May 20, 1918, on which, after the usual data, is written, " Declared unfit by medical board, mobilization centre M.D. 4- categors' C3." This photostatic evidence shows that in the last war I did what I thought I should do-I enlisted. I am sorry that systolic murmurs and a mitral lesion were such as to prevent me from joining the service.
At the outbreak of this war I was a few months past forty years of age. I submit that if at the age of eighteen years I was unfit for the reasons I have mentioned, the only contribution I could have made at forty years of age would have been in the nature of administrative work. Instead of that I did what the hon. member said he had done. In the words of the hon member, " my presence in this

Export Credits Insurance
house is due to the fact that I hope to contribute some war service by being here." The hon. member has put a part of his record on Hansard and I now have explained my own position in the last war. I will consider the incident as closed and forgive the hon. member for the use of such derogatory remarks against my compatriots and myself. " They may be ascribed to inexperience and lack of aptitude," to use the words of a great historian as applied to the hon. member for Parkdale.

I think the purpose of this measure is clearly set out in the preamble; that is, that it is desirable to promote the revival of trade and particularly during a period of transition. Before the war Canada traded with a great many countries, including practically every European state. The war has brought about a condition in Europe of complete disorganization, and the problem so far as our external trade is concerned with these countries and their particular problem within their own boundaries is to get their economic life reorganized so that they can proceed on a more secure basis after the war terminates. Years ago I had a good deal of experience, if I may modestly say it, in export business. There were certain places where exporters would not sell grain because of the risk involved; there were other countries with which, by virtue of their reputation for paying their debts and meeting their obligations, business proceeded on a secure basis. Let us picture for a moment the conditions which will exist when the war is terminated and these countries, particularly in Europe and the far east, attempt to get their economic life reestablished. What shall we find? We shall probably find that the old firms, for instance in European countries, with whom Canadian exporters did business year by year, have disappeared.
But individuals of these firms may still be alive. They may endeavour to get their business reestablished and import goods that the people of their country need for the ordinary affairs of life. What will happen? Let me give an illustration: You may have a country like Norway, which has suffered tremendously during the war. Norway may want to import certain types of machines or machine tools or goods of another character to get her own economy reestablished. This
Export Credits Insurance

measure provides a method of giving encouragement, or getting the wheels going again. It is founded after all on two simple principles, the first principle that of insurance and the second, in part II of the act, the principle of direct government intervention. Let us suppose an exporter in Canada gets an inquiry from a firm in Norway for one hundred thousand dollars' worth of machine tools. He says, "Can I safely take that risk? I know these people; they are honourable, they are good people. But what assurance have I that when I ship the goods with a draft attached to them they will be able to meet the draft on the other side so that I shall be paid for my goods?" That is where this measure steps in, as I understand it. The exporter in this case can take out a policy of insurance that he will receive payment for his goods. A premium is charged to him on the insurance and he doubtless adds to the price of his goods the cost of the premium he pays to the corporation. Well, the goods are shipped. He receives payment. The premium remains in the insurance fund. You can duplicate that scores or hundreds of times with machine tools or grain or pulp and paper or any other commodity we may be selling from Canada.

For instance, one might have in mind the Scandinavian countries, where the sense of business integrity and personal honour is high. The reputation of those countries for meeting their obligations has been good. Obviously the risks in dealing under this measure with nationals of countries of that kind are much less than w-hen dealing with governments or peoples of countries, the standard of business integrity of which might not be nearly as high.
In my view this is a very constructive measure. It is true that in the end we may have some loss. In the meantime, however, it is a mechanism for getting much needed goods and supplies to these devastated countries, for purposes of their reconstruction. I say to the committee-and I am sure every member will agree-that it is of great importance to Canada that countries like Belgium, France, Norway, Denmark and Holland be reestablished and get going again in a normal fashion. Perhaps we are not so greatly concerned with selling goods in the next year or two; but if we have long vision, as we should have, we must be concerned with what our opportunities will be ,for trading with those countries, not two years from now, but possibly five years, ten years or twenty-five years from now. In my view,this measure will help to bring about the desired end.

speechtext:
As was pointed out last night by the Minister of Finance, this is not a mutual aid measure at all, in the sense in which we have been discussing mutual aid in the house in the past two or three years. Mutual aid was simply a provision of goods by the Canadian government to countries which could not otherwise pay for them, so that those countries might wage war more effectively. This measure is on a different basis. For instance, it contemplates, under part II-and reference was made to this last night-that if for example the government of China gets a loan of $100,000,000 from the Canadian government, either directly or through the guarantee of Chinese bonds which may be bought by Canadain nationals, the loan will be paid. That is expected on the part of both parties to the contract. But that is not the condition in connection with the mutual aid bills we have had under consideration. Under part I of this bill the goods are shipped, the insurance premium is paid, and all is done under the expectation that the draft- against such goods will be paid. The insurance principle is to provide that- if, in any event, something happens as a result of which a particular shipment is not paid for, these funds can be called upon. Precisely the same principle is applied in connection with the insurance of our homes. For instance, for the last forty years I have had my home insured, but I have never had to call upon any insurance fund. During that time however, I have had the protection. Perhaps someone else
Export Credits Insurance

who carried insurance suffered a fire loss, and collected from the insurance company. The same simple principle is found in this bill.
