It does seem to me that one point about the bill which is most important is the ability of the Canadian government to check the credit rating of the firms or governments abroad. Under part. I of the bill the Canadian government, through the new corporation, is going to underwrite risks, is going to stand behind the credit of foreign importers. This means that the Canadian government has a very heavy responsibility for determining whether or not the foreign firm is solvent and likely to pay its bills. In pre-war years the obligation to determine the solvency of a foreign importing firm rested with the Canadian exporter and his bank. It was very much their business to find out whether or not they were likely to be paid. Now that responsibility is being partially shifted to the Canadian government, and I doubt very much whether the Canadian government or this new corporation will have the proper facilities for determining whether or not a firm abroad is apt to pay its bills. In any event it is of vital importance that the government and this corporation should have those facilities. It is even more important in connection with transactions under part II of the bill, because there we are talking about big money. We are not concerned about a deal for S100.000 between a Canadian exporting firm and a Belgian importing firm; we are talking about a loan of S100,000.000 to China. subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE AND DEVELOP TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
I wish to confine my
remarks to part I of the bill because I think part II has to do with politics and government considerations rather than with strictly business considerations. If the government will admit that under this measure they are endeavouring to stimulate employment or, as
Export Credits Insurance

the hon. .member for Rosetown-Biggar says, create great profits for our people; if the government foresees the possibility of losing a substantial amount of money in carrying out that purpose, then I would understand this bill a little more clearly. However, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated that the rates to be charged for the insurance policies issued on these foreign credits will be adequate. That means that taken over the balance there will be a sufficient measure of gain to offset those credit risks which prove faulty. If it is true that this new enterprise is going to run without loss to the taxpayers of Canada, then I see nothing about the nature of the business which cannot be undertaken by the chartered banks under their present set-up.
They have been engaged in foreign trade for a great .many years. We have become the fourth or fifth largest trading nation of the world in peace time and we have no such institution as is contemplated by this bill. But the chartered banks were able to carry on their financing with complete satisfaction not only to the country but to the business men and industrial companies and natural products companies, who were able to carry on and meet their bills successfully. If there is to be . any substantial loss I do not see what the purpose of the legislation is, and yet, if it is going to be of help to business or in job creation, I want to be among the first to be numbered among the supporters of this measure. We should have more information as to what is contemplated. My own feeling is that some of these measures that are brought down by the government are nothing more than brain waves of civil servants or deputies who think they see a way to be helpful, and they, having the confidence of their ministers, propose a bill and the first thing we know it is brought down, all under the guise of something that is going to be helpful in the post-war period. I characterize the Industrial Development bank as being in that class to some extent, and for all I know this measure may be somewhat the same.
I have no doubt that a good deal of the mail of the Department of Trade and Commerce is from small manufacturers and business men in Canada who would like to get into foreign trade. Everybody is not suited for that trade, even though he may think he would like to get in it and get some gain from it. So that many of these letters have to be discounted as being an impossible situation. One of my friends who is working for the government at the present time told

me that a large number of small companies in Canada were thinking of getting together to form an export association in order to take advantage of some of the possibilities which one firm in itself was too small to take advantage of and could not make the necessary contacts, but they felt that if they had an organization in their particular trade or industry they would be able to get somewhere. I dare say that there are many small companies that could better their interests along these lines.
I should like to say a word about the ideas put forward by the Minister of Mines and Resources when he said, and he was backed up by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that this new government corporation would set up facilities for checking the credit risk of these foreign importers. The minister as he pursued his explanation admitted that they would have to use the banks in the foreign countries. All those banks have correspondent relations with our own chartered banks. The managers know each other, and it is not unusual for them to do business together over the telephone because they have complete trust in one another. You have that system already set up and there is no need, as I see it, to Set up a duplicatory system. It is quite true that our trade representatives whom we maintain in various countries can be helpful, but their information is also available to the banks. Our trade representatives have a multitude of duties to perform and I do not see how it would be possible for them to have the same intimate contact which the banker in a foreign country can have in regard to the credit standing of a particular importer. The confidential relationship which exists between banks gives to our bankers, and through them to our own exporters, an intimate and accurate knowledge which is not possible under any other system. Certainly we have had no indication to the contrary.
There is also the point about how much 3taff is going to be required In carrying out the functioning of this corporation, particularly as set forth by the minister, and also what the cost of that will be. May I point out that every time that we set up one of these government corporations or committees we withdraw from productive employment anywhere from one hundred to a thousand people, as we are doing under the family allowance measure. The nation will be that much the poorer. We must economize in the use of our man-power in the post-war period.
Is it the intention of the government to establish the head office of this corporation in Ottawa? If department officials have to be

consulted by exporters it would seem to me that Ottawa would be the last possible place where one could get efficiency and promptness of action, and as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton says, time is of the essence of these contracts. I do not see how any civil servant, even though he be the deputy of a department, could say to an exporter when he comes to see him and lay his plan before him: Yes, that is all right; go ahead

because the deputy has to think of a lot of things, of an opposition that is going to criticize if something goes wrong, and so forth. You just cannot bring business into politics or politics into business and have efficiency and have business function satisfactorily to the people. So that I feel that if we could possibly use the chartered banks we would be much better off than if we were to try to set up this system, which will lead to a lot of duplication. Certainly I would hope that the head office of the corporation would be in Montreal, where most of the exports take place, with branch offices in Vancouver and some other large cities.

We have not passed the Bank Act and we could put through the necessary amendment. It is a little difficult to understand how this house can be asked to allow the government to charge a rate which it will not allow the banks to charge. I think that the suggestion of the minister, while no doubt based on facts, is preposterous. It means that the government is going to be allowed to take more out of the individual, because it is needed, not because they want a profit, than the bankers can charge under the Bank Act, which has the imprimatur of the government. The answer to the whole _ thing is that the government is hamstringing the banking system of this country so that it cannot engage in the export business because its rate is limited
to five per cent, and that is not sufficient, and the minister has just admitted it. The minister has clearly admitted that there should be another amendment to the Bank Act whereby the banks should be allowed to charge an adequate rate for foreign credits.
I should like to know how much staff will be necessary under this measure. There is another small point. If some of these risks go bad, as the Minister of Finance has just suggested they may, the government will no doubt take over the rights of the exporters and sue the importer in a foreign country. Once again we are in danger of getting into international complications. There is another difficulty. No international complications are likely to arise when a private firm in this country sues a private firm in another country. But once you get governments mixed into the thing you have rights and wrongs being decided, and matters of opinion, and of course nationals will always side with their own people; so that while I would not like to go so far as to say that this would be a fruitful source of international discord, I believe that if business can be carried on by private enterprise in one country with private enterprise in another country you are likely to save yourself a great deal of trouble.
I do not think there are any other points which I wish to raise at the present time. If this measure were going to be helpful at all to industry and would assist in creating jobs I should be whole-heartedly for it, but I still feel that the government has made out no case for it, and I suspect that it is the brain-wave of some person who has not had a great deal of practical experience.

speechtext:
Listening to the hon. member for Rosedale, the hon. member for Vancouver South and other hon. members opposite, one would think that we were living in a perfectly normal world, one which had not been engaged in a war of unprecedented destructiveness for four and a half years, and in which war had not produced chaos both in the form and in the character of government and in the economy of a great many countries engaged in or directly affected by the war.
The present legislation is to assist in recreating a healthy world out of a sick world.. When the international household is such that all
Export Credits Insurance

its members are sick in varying degrees, one must call in doctors, submit to the ministration of nurses, and follow many regulations as to conduct, nutrition and so forth, and if the household submits to the dictates of the doctor and the nurses who are in charge, recovery may come fairly quickly, with the result that normal channels of intercourse between nations can be reestablished. The most desirable state is, of course, a condition of affairs wherein the Canadian exporter can seek the importer in the foreign country who wishes to purchase and pay for the goods which the Canadian has for export. But I would point out something w'hich is occasionally forgotten, that any measure which has for its purpose the encouragement of exports is of necessity also a bill for the encouragement of imports, because the one is a corollary of the other. When one mentions exports and imports it is something like raising the question which came first, the egg or the hen. No one can answer that. But of necessity, when we encourage the export of Canadian goods we-quite properly and in the best interests of this country- are encouraging imports.
Take this bill and consider it. I realize it is a measure which is forced upon this countiy because of the practical difficulties which Canada and other countries will face in the post-war period.

The bill will permit the small exporter to export without assuming a risk which, because he has so little knowledge of conditions in the country with which he hopes to trade, might result in his ruin. The large corporations, with their ability to spread the risk because of the volume of their business, can more easily assume in the post-war world the risks in carrying on export business. It seems to me therefor that this bill will enable the small exporter to carry on business with the aid of an agency which for a certain premium and under certain conditions will assume the risk. On the other hand, realizing that in the post-war world it may be quite impossible for the exporter or the corporation under this bill to assume the risk of dealing with some individual importers in foreign countries-

If we have confidence in the integrity of the government in power in the foreign country we ask it to place its guarantee on the standing and financial ability of its importer to pay, and the matter is arranged between governments. But I do urge that the committee consider the purpose and the necessity of the measure in the world in which we are living and in which we shall continue to live for an uncertain number of years. The bill has merit and should be supported if we are sincere in desiring to get export trade back into normal channels, not only in this country but in the other countries with which we hope to trade.
Let me remind hon. members of the opposition that while this measure may present problems as regards accepting the guarantee of a foreign government, we should put ourselves in the position of that foreign government when it in turn is called upon to guarantee on behalf of some private importer in that country payment for the goods which he proposes to import. In my opinion other governments will not continue longer than necessary to pursue that method of doing business, because countries do not like to assume that type of obligation. So that this measure is a stop-gap, based upon realization of the conditions in which wTe are living and the practical difficulties which Canadian trade will face in the post-war years, and is a very sensible and practical attempt to help solve that problem.

What I desire to say has a definite bearing .on the bill. But, I submit, so did the remarks of the Minister of Mines and Resources and of the Minister of Finance. What I want to know is this. While this is an insurance corporation, what liaison is there, what machinery is it proposed to set up between this corporation and the international bank or the organization that will eventually come out of the Bretton Woods conference? No matter what you do in any trade, particularly in international trade, the most important thing you have to make sure of is what you are to be paid in. It is all very well to say that you will be paid in something; but you have to be paid in something that is translatable into something else with which you can pay your costs of operation in Canada. Whether that will be gold or some other currency, I do not know; but it is vitally important that before we can reestablish any degree of international trade some idea of a basis of currency has to be decided upon, and this bill, while I appreciate that it is an insurance measure solely, has as far as I can see no clause in it which effects a liaison with the international bank. I think this is very important, because there will be two sections of the world after the war is over, apart from the north American continent, which will probably be able to pay in a currency that is valid to us, namely gold. South America is building up considerable gold resources, and so is the orient. Now we are going to have to deal in a different way with the oriental and the South American countries from the way in which we shall deal with the
European countries, where the ravages of the war have been if anything more thorough than in the orient.
That is one question. The second is this. The Canadian exporter, I think, with all due respect, does know his business. Canadian export trade before the war was built up to such a degree that we had a greater per capita export trade than any other country in the world, and I venture to say that the government will find, and find amazingly soon, that despite the terrific ravages of war, the Canadian exporter will be able to pick up the threads of his business if he gets the support of the government-and I approve the bill. I do not think however that under the bill as I have read it sufficient recognition is taken of the innate ability of the Canadian manufacturer and exporter. I do not think that is sufficiently considered. In my own riding before this major war broke out I was told by several manufacturers that the incident on the Marco Polo bridge, which led to the Sino-Japanese conflict, was eventually the cause of unemployment to nearly 200 persons in that district. I mention that because foreign and external trade is one of the most vital things we have to encourage in Canada. We must oil the wheels and get the machinery working again. That is of prime importance. But we must realize that the men who are in this business will probably be able to pick up the threads of their business again with the support of the government, and we do not want to court the danger of having the individual importer or trader abroad feeling that he is dealing with the Canadian government. We have to make sure that the Canadian exporter believes he has the government behind him, but we must take care that the trader abroad does not feel that he is dealing with the government of Canada, because if he does, then I submit that when the trader feels he is dealing with the government he will take a different attitude, particularly in external trade, than if he felt he was dealing with another trader with whom his good will counts more than anything else.
This bill also appears to overlook the tremendously important work that was done by the Canadian insurance companies, particularly in the orient. They knew the conditions, and while the greater part of the insurance was life, nevertheless our insurance companies carried more business than the insurance companies of both the United Kingdom and the United States combined. Here are these companies who do know the conditions of trade in the orient and of financing in that part of the world, and the orient will be one of our big spheres of trade in the future. A
Export Credits Insurance

close liaison should be made in this bill between our private insurance companies and this corporation, because if we are to get back to international trade on anything like the scale we had before the war and anything like the scale necessary to maintain our economy on a high level we have to make use of our people who have built up this external trade and use them to the fullest extent possible. This bill omits certain clauses that should be inserted and I have some doubts as to whether it really appreciates the difficulty that lies ahead.

This section provides for the board of directors which is to be made up of the deputy minister of trade and commerce, the deputy minister of finance, the governor of the Bank of Canada and four others. I should like to know if these four other directors are to be chosen from the business world or from the civil service.

Of the other four directors, one would be the general manager of the corporation and the other three may be chosen from either the civil service or the business world. A decision has not been made on that as yet. It is conceivable that the deputy minister of fisheries, the deputy minister of agriculture or some outsider who is prominent and experienced in a particular line would be appointed, or perhaps it would be someone from some other business source.

Will these four other directors be on a full-time basis, or will they just be called in for directors' meetings?

There would be an opportunity under this section to appoint such persons as I mentioned this morning in the amendment?

Subsection 3 provides that the aggregate amount to be paid to directors shall not exceed $3,000. If they are all civil servants, and I trust they will not be, I presume the $3,000 would be adequate, but it would not be if you are going to take directors from the business world. If men of that type are going to be called in they will have to be given more adequate remuneration. Business executives are willing to come down to Ottawa to spend all their time for a dollar a year because of the war emergency, but a different set of circumstances will obtain after the war. Many of these men will have to return to their private businesses in order to recoup themselves and get reinstated in their own industry. If the government hopes to get men who will be of some real assistance to this corporation there should not be this limit of $3,000. The amount should be large enough to compensate them, because there is not the same honour in serving on a board like this in ordinary times as there is serving the government in war time.

Why is this provision inserted that the Civil Service Act may be overridden? It is another case of weakening the merit system in the civil service. As I read it, this clause gives the corporation power to hire employees without going through the civil service commission.
This section gives the civil servant protection so far as superannuation is concerned.

The minister is referring to subsection 2, but I am referring to subsection 1, which clearly gives the corporation power to by-pass the civil service commission. In other words, appointments may be made

I quite appreciate the point my hon. friend is making, but in the selection of the personnel it is not proposed to go through the civil service commission. It is proposed that we shall be able to pick the most capable men available, and many of them will be required for only temporary service.

establish offices or employ agents in any part of Canada, and if necessary may employ agents elsewhere than in Canada for purposes of enforcing any right which as a result of a contract of insurance may be vested in the corporation.
I do not understand what type of agency is in contemplation. What type of agency is to be engaged beyond Canada?

Subsection 2 requires each officer, adviser or employee to take an oath of fidelity and secrecy. Is it usual in this type of crown corporation to insist upon an oath being taken?
I am told that it is the usual custom.

I am wondering whether it is, because private business does not find it necessary to swear its officer to secrecy. I have the idea that this is one of the novelties imported by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who requires of certain dollar-a-year men a vow of secrecy-that without the permission of their superior officer that they will never reveal anything they observed or heard while in the government service. It says "purchase, acquire or guarantee any security issued by the government or by the agency of the government of any such other country to any person in Canada for payment of the cost of Canadian-produced goods exported or to be exported to such other country". Surely that is a guarantee. We are putting ourselves in the position of guaranteeing the security of another country for the payment of Canadian goods. Let us say a south American country has a bond issue and in order to purchase Canadian goods a portion of that bond issue is guaranteed by the Canadian government. We shall find ourselves in this position, that part of a foreign bond issue is guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada and part of it not guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada, and I think we shall be in a very dangerous position in consequence of this clause. I should like to reply to the criticism of my remarks advanced by the Minister of Finance

last evening after I had spoken along this line by repeating that I feel there is a strong element of the mutual aid principle in this section. The minister suggested that I was wrong, because in this section of the bill there is not the kind of mutual aid that we have had during the war period. I would point out that it is still mutuality, only of a different kind. During the war period we have aided each other mutually in this respect, that from Canada we have sent goods and materials in return for the greater cost in terms of suffering that some of our allies were paying. In mutual aid during the war we are helping each other by contributing to the common cause things that may be different in kind. As I see it, under part II of this bill in the post-war period we are still going to try to help each other, by contributing to the common cause of rebuilding the world. We in Canada are going to help rehabilitate some of the war-torn countries; in return for the help we give them in that way they are automatically going to help us by providing markets for some of our surplus products; and to the extent they become rehabilitated they will also help us by being able to pay for those products in sending us some of the goods they produce, which will improve the lot of our people. In other words, an element of planning is being injected into world trade under the terms of this section. The government have said, and I congratulate them on it, that it is not their intention simply to sit down and wait for the years to roll by in the hope that things will somehow readjust themselves. The government have said that they are going right to work in an effort to revive our trade with these war-torn countries by lending them money and helping them get rehabilitated, so that we may get affairs back on a more satisfactory basis. speechtext: Perhaps the minister wishes to speak first?

speechtext:
Yes. Mr. Speaker, this is a similar bill to the one passed by this house a few days ago with reference to agricultural products. It differs only in that the word "agricultural" is replaced by the word "fisheries" in all sections of the bill, and there
[The Chairman.]
are minor changes in section 9 which are necessary to cope with the fisheries trade as against the agricultural industry. Of course there is also a difference in the amount appropriated, which is $25 million, instead of $200 million for agricultural products.
This legislation is to provide the government with powers to meet a situation which has not yet developed but which may have to be faced later on. Whether the necessity arises will depend upon many factors. First, there are the external trade relationships, which may be very' different; there are the international monetary stabilization arrangements, and the level of food requirements throughout the world in the immediate post-war period, as well as other factors which may arise and which I cannot foresee. At the present time we are not in a position to say exactly what trade relationships are going to prevail, nor can we yet foretell what will be agreed upon among the nations as to monetary stabilization, nor do we know what fisheries products will be affected and where the pinch is going to be first felt.
But. Mr. Speaker, although we do not know exactly all that we are going to do, we know exactly what we are not going to do; that is, we are not going to let the prices fall to the low levels to which they fell in 1920, and again in 1932, 1933, 1934 and a few other years.
It follows, then, that it will be impossible to describe the mechanism which will be employed in the application of this measure in any but very general terms. It is important that the underlying principles be elastic enough to cope with the situations as they may arise. Knowing that certain degrees of elasticity are necessary in order to meet the complex situation which may arise, we have been careful to place the significant powers in the hands of the governor in council, so that we may have the benefit of close coordination and cooperation with all the ministers of the government.
Now I come to the bill itself. The main section is, of course, section 9. The devices used to support fisheries in this bill are of two kinds. First there is, under section 9, subsection 1(a) and (b), provision that the fisheries prices support board may prescribe prices at which they will be prepared to purchase such commodities as may be named by the governor general in council. This, while not being exactly a floor price, will have the effect of ensuring to the primary producer the prices which the government is going to set for certain commodities, because if we are ready to pay more than the merchants are going to pay of course we will get the products.

Fisheries Prices
The second device, under section 9, subsection 1(c), is what we call a deficiency payment. The deficiency payment has already been in use under the salt fish board in 1939 and 1940 and was found to be workable. The feature of the deficiency payment is that under this scheme there is no interference with the natural fluctuations of price brought about by the laws of supply and demand. At the end of the year or of the season the board determines what the average price is to the producer of the fish on which a price has been set. If that average price is deemed to be too low to support and reasonably maintain production, the board, with the >
approval of the governor in council, sets a value on the unit commodity which in its judgment will bring sufficient return at this price to the producer, the difference between the average price and the value which it has set.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR STABILIZATION, PURCHASE OF STAPLE PRODUCTS AT APPROVED PRICES, ETC.
speechtext: In other words, it is just a new way of paying a subsidy.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR STABILIZATION, PURCHASE OF STAPLE PRODUCTS AT APPROVED PRICES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is not a subsidy, and later on I want to say why it is not, because there is a danger in paying a subsidy. This relates to exactly the policy of this bill. Section 9, subsection 2 is as follows:
(2) In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection one of this section, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for fisheries by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from fisheries and those from other occupations.
This is the policy of the bill. At the end of the year, as I said, there would be a calculation made as to the average price, and if the unit commodity has been sold below that average price the difference is paid between the average price and the price at which it should have been to give a fair return to all those who have sold this commodity.
I will give an instance. If A lands fine fresh cod and gets S3 per hundred and B lands stale cod and gets only $1, while C lands medium quality cod for which he receives $2 per hundred, the average price will be $2 per hundred pounds. If the board finds that it takes a price of S3.50 per hundred pounds to support the fishermen properly and to keep them in the fisheries it will pay the difference between the average price, which is $2, and the prescribed value, which is $3.50, which difference would be $1.50, which would go to every individual who had been fishing. This would give an incentive to the fishermen to sell at. as high a price as possible and it would deter fishermen or processors or wholesalers, I will not say from cheating but from trying to get more money from the government than
they should. This would result in A, who has looked after quality, receiving $4.50 per hundred, B receiving $3.50, which would be the price stipulated by the board, and C, who did not pay any attention to the quality of his fish, receiving $1 plus $1.50, or $2.50. As I say, this would provide an incentive, and, basically this method did work very well. It worked in 1939-40 with the salt fish board. Of course, these two methods cannot be applied at the same time 'with respect to the same commodity; one or the other will have to operate.
We are told that half the world is underfed to-day and half the world was underfed even in the years preceding the war. If the war brings a new world order, I do not think prices will fluctuate as they did between 1920 and 1939. There is no reason why people should starve in one country while commodities are burned or otherwise destroyed in other countries in order to keep up prices. Through international bodies, such as combined food boards, UNRRA or others which might be established, food could be distributed in the world so as to raise the level of nutrition almost everywhere to a reasonable standard. I do not think we have been producing too much of any kind of food, but I do believe the distribution has been altogether wrong. If it had been done through international arrangements as we are doing to-day, the present war might have lacked one of its pretexts and might even have been avoided. I could give instances of writings which were published a few yearn before the war but I do not wish to prolong the discussion. However, just to mention one, the French author Claude Farrere, an academician, wrote a book on "The Tragedy of Asia," in which he said that the country which has no commodities necessary for the life of its citizens has the absolute international right to go and take those commodities elsewhere by force if they are not being developed by the nation in whose country they exist. This is quite different from our conception of honesty between nations. The world had reached the stage where great writers were expressing sentiments like this.
I repeat what I said when the resolution was before the house. It is my hope that this legislation may never be necessary. Perhaps I am too optimistic; if so, at any rate the legislation will be a good tool in the hands of the government. The expansion of fisheries has not been great during the years of the war in comparison with agricultural production. Fisheries were handicapped by lack of labour and boats. However, I must pay this compliment to our fishermen. They have done marvelously well with the instrument they had.

Fisheries Piices
I desire to put on Hansard, with the consent of the house, for the information of members, a few statements showing quantities of fish caught between 1939 and 1943, giving both dollar value and quantity.

Yes; it includes eastern Canada, inland and west coast. In 1939 eastern Canada produced in value $16,797,306; in 1942 it produced $28,219,379. There is a great difference in prices, which in 1942 were much above those of 1939; but as

I wish now to refer to the inland fisheries, because many people may think they are not as important as they actually are. I know the hon. member for Davenport believes in their importance, and I must admit he is absolutely right. The quantities of fish caught in the last few years in inland fisheries amounts to seven per cent of the total production of fish. The value of fish caught amounts to eleven per cent of the total, which shows that the fishermen and the producer's and the merchants are certainly right up to their business. The figures show that with only seven per cent in quantity the value amounts to eleven per cent.
In 1939 the total marketed value of fish from inland fisheries was $5,579,627, whereas in 1942 it was $8,761,981. The catch in 1939 for the whole of Canada amounted to 10,638,535 hundredweight, and in 1943 amounted to 12,373,921 hundredweight. This latter figure is an estimated amount: we have not the exact figure. These figures prove that there is no danger of the markets being glutted, because it has not increased in proportion to the increase in agricultural production-and I am not suggesting at all that the production of agricultural products is sufficient to flood the market. They will certainly dispose of what they produce.
May I also, with the permission of the house, place on Hansard a table showing the prices of fish as landed, for the east coast, west coast
and inland fisheries. This table gives prices for east coast cod, lobster, herring and mackerel between 1926 and 1943. All hon. members will know that during that time there was, at the beginning, a very serious decline in the price of fish. For example, in 1926 the price of cod was $1.96 per hundredweight. In 1932 it was $1.01, and in 1942, $2.88. I believe in 1943 it was about $3, although I have not the exact figure.
I understand the minister is quoting prices to the producer.

Yes, prices to the primary producer. In 1926 the price of lobster was $12.24. That price went down to as low as S6.12 in 1933. Then it increased to $12.19 in 1936. In 1938 it fell to $9.11, and went up again to $10.47 in 1941 and $13.88 in 1942.
The herring prices have not fallen to as great an extent as have other fish prices. The price went from 54 cents in 1926 to 45 cents in 1936 -that is the lowest figure-and 70 cents in 1942.

Mr. Speaker, in the discussion of this bill, which the minister has so ably explained, we are handicapped because we have not before us- except from memory-the data the minister has placed on the record. We cannot very well work out a reply based upon figures at which we have had only a fleeting glance.
When this matter was before the house on an earlier occasion I expressed some criticism with respect to the conditions under which the bill might operate. At that time it was presented in a somewhat vague form. Now, however, when it is in the shape of a concrete bill, there will probably be no opposition to the passing of it, any more than there was to the passing of the bill dealing with agricultural products. But there probably will be considerable criticism of the method by which it is proposed to carry out the provisions contained in the bill.
No one could reasonably object to the theory-if I may be pardoned for calling it a theory-of putting up the sum of $25,000,000 to help correct a condition of low prices in the fishing industry. Perhaps my calling it a theory could hardly be justified, when the proposal is one of spending $25,000,000 to boost an industry. What I am anxious about is-if, when and how it can be made to work.

Fisheries Prices
At this stage I should like to make a few remarks following what the minister said in connection with the bill itself, because. of course I could not anticipate what he was going to tell us. He suggested, and I hope correctly, that we were coming to the beginning of a new era, a new world. I am sorry to have to say so, but experience and history tell us not to be too optimistic. We thought these great thoughts about a brave new world after the last war. Until the millennium comes; until the doctrines laid down by Christ come into practical operation, I am afraid human nature will remain as it is, and human nature has a disposition to endeavour to get ahead t the expense of the other fellow.
The minister made allusion to the way in which a small fish board worked in the east in 1939 and 1940, and said that that legislation had worked well. Quite so; and this bill will work well if we continue on a rising market, or, in other words, if we do not need this measure. But there is a world of difference between setting floor prices on a rising market, which any one can do, and dealing with these prices in a time of depression such as we had in the early thirties. Unless I am grossly mistaken I believe the minister is basing his policy on a wrong premise, although perhaps that is the only one available to him. He uses the word "average," and says that at the end of the year he is going to average prices and find o.ut what has been paid. Then, as I understood, although of course I may be wrong, in some way he is going to pay something additional to those producers who have not received the average price, and in that way make up the difference to them. That word "average" goes to the root and ruination of the whole situation. It is a word beloved of governments. When you are dealing with the government you must almost always do things on an average, but you cannot do them in that way in real life. We cannot all live up to the same ideals; we cannot all live on the same income, and we cannot all produce fish or potatoes or anything else at an average cost. That is humanly impossible. At the end of the year the minister can tell us the average pricq obtained for cod or salmon or potatoes, but that does not solve the difficulty that one man can produce potatoes at $40 a ton, while another man, working no harder, can produce them for half that cost. The same applies in connection with various fish markets. It might be the wrong average, but let us suppose the average was correct. The average of anything is an exact medium between the highest price or higher prices and the lowest price or lower prices; but you cannot live on an
average. You have to live on what you can get. The demand would immediately arise: "You fixed an average on salmon of ten cents," we will say for the sake of argument, "and you cannot produce it in the east or the west for less than fifteen cents." But the government says that the average price was ten cents. Then the fishermen of one district say, "We sold below the average and lost money. We were nearly ruined; we had to scrape very close." I cannot see any virtue at all in dealing with things on an average basis. I would suggest, rather, that you use the best statistics available and say that a certain class of fish is worth perhaps ten cents a pound, that you will keep the price up to that figure and let the man who has been selling for less than that simply drop out. But that makes it pretty tough on him, and the whole purpose of the bill is to protect him.
Then the minister made another point. In dealing with the returns from the fish he said that for various reasons, particularly lack of labour, the production of fish had gone down. It is a little difficult to figure out the relative production when it is expressed in such a low unit as hundredweights, but I woud suggest that there is very little complaint on the score of decreased production. In the east, if I took down the minister's figures correctly, there was actually an increase in quantity. There was a slight reduction in the west, but I suggest that it was not due to lack of labour, because the people out there made a special effort to increase production and in most cases succeeded in doing so. The fact that there was a comparatively small reduction in the quantity of fish caught does not arise at all from lack of labour. People who are familiar with the fishing industry in the west know that the quantity caught depends very largely upon the size of the runs. You might put out a million fishermen and if the run was not there they would not catch any more fish than a couple of hundred fishermen. The famous big run in the Fraser river every four years used to be four and five times the size of the run in other years. No one knew why, but that was the fact; the sockeye run in the Fraser river was enormous every fourth year. Then there is the run of pink salmon. In the majority of places in British Columbia the pink run, which is the second biggest run, occurs only every second year, and as yet no man has discovered the reason for it. So that it would not matter whether you put out a million fishermen; in the off year you would not get any more pinks than what comparatively a few fishermen could handle.
That applies right down the line. I have seen a large fleet go out to catch pilchards,
Fisheries Prices

which they use in the reduction plants. Owing to the current, the heat of the water, or some other reason, the catch might be only a fraction of the catch the year before with fewer boats. Sometimes the pilchards will come within gunshot of the refinery door, almost begging to be taken in; at other times you will have to go two or three hundred miles away and then have difficulty in finding them. I remember that on one occasion the government hired an aeroplane to hunt for them, and they were discovered away down the Pacific coast near California, far from where they are ordinarily found. So that the slightly smaller production of fish on the west coast is not due to any lack of fishermen. I emphasize that particularly, because perhaps in months to come this will be trotted forward as a reason for putting the Japs back in the fisheries. I assure the minister that more fishermen took out licences last year, after the Japs were eliminated, than previously. That is a positive statement; more fishing licences were issued in British Columbia after the Japs were eliminated than before, so that any slight decrease in production was not due to the absence of our yellow brethren.
This bill was brought in very hurriedly, as is only natural at the end of the session, and before we had time to consult the people most concerned. In order that I might get the views of those people, immediately the bill appeared I sent copies of it to the three largest unions of fishermen on the west coast, asking their opinion. Yesterday I had a letter from two of the unions; I have not heard from the third. I should like to quote from the joint reply. They wrote sensibly and at some length, and I should like to mention some of the salient points. They said:
While Minister of Fisheries Bertrand undertook that when the time came to appoint the board, he would recommend that one of the three members of the board would be a fisherman, he refused to commit himself that such would be the case.
Ignoring for the moment the merits of the bill to meet the situation which it is designed to remedy, it is clear that the contemplated composition of the board is hardly adequate.
The stated purpose being to assure die fisherman an adequate return for his labour, surely there can be no reasonable objection to stating in the act that some members of the board shall be directly chosen by the fishermen themselves. And since there are so many differences in conditions between t'he Atlantic and Pacific fisheries it would seem, too, that either there should be two boards-eastern and western-* or a larger board to provide adequate representation for both coasts.
A board of five members, consisting of representatives of fishermen and the trade from each coast with a chairman representing the Department of Fisheries would seem the most practical

solution. A quorum could consist of three meeting at either coast, and we hope that the bill will be amended along these lines in committee before it is passed.
And later on:
We see no harm, in the principle of the bill. It represents at any rate a recognition that some protection must be provided the fisherman against the vagaries of unregulated economic conditions. We share the hope expressed by the minister that it will not be needed but we would emphasize that hopes alone are insufficient. . . .
Legislation to meet post-war conditions in the fishing industry will need to include measures for conservation of fisheries, marketing of products and regulation of fishing including licence limitation, on all of which matters the fishermen's organizations are now' in the process of preparing a considered programme.
That is a very moderate presentation. I wish to make some comments of my own. I do not see why there should not be some provision in this bill for something like the participation certificates in the wheat business. If the government is to take over large quantities of fish and there is a change in the market conditions or what-not and they reap a substantial profit, I think the fishermen would be entitled to participate by means of participation certificates.
The second matter which I should like to mention has not been referred to by the fishermen. The government is not going to fix a price for fish; it is going to fix a minimum price, and I am afraid that there will be a dangerous trend on the part of the trade to accept the minimum price as the basic price. They will say, "You want ten cents but the minimum is five cents a pound; I tell you what we will do; we will give you five cents, the government price." I am afraid an attempt will be made, unfairly I grant, by those in the market to buy fish cheaply. They will say, "Well, the government have put a price of five cents on fish which is equivalent to saying that you can produce it at that; we will give you that and no more." I think the government should take cognizance of that fact. It is not as though they were fixing the price of fish right on up the line; they are simply fixing a minimum, and the trade may say, "The government experts have said that you can produce fish at five cents a pound, and we will pay no more."
My idea w'ould be not to have a minimum but to fix a price for each grade of fish. That could! be fixed according to what experience and statistics showed was a reasonable level. Then the government could supplement it by subsidies. It could subsidize, as my hon. friend said, up to that amount. You would then get away from the danger of having the minimum price regarded as the basic price.

speechtext: A subsidy would only make things more difficult.

That would be the minister's funeral; not his funeral, but his problem. I am a great believer in letting people run their own affairs. When it is necessary to finance them, do it in such a way that they will not be interfered with. We should not set, say $100 as a reasonable wage for a fisherman because some are liable to sit down and not do anything. I would not let the government run anything. I would not let them run even a funeral because they would be liable to bury the wrong man. Let the people run their own business because they are familiar with it. The greatest incentive in the mind of man is the profit motive. If I hustle out at two o'clock in the morning and attend to my job of fishing, I will make a success of it. But if I can sit down and whistle and say that the government has to take care of me, the whole thing will be a complete failure. Why should the industrious, hard-working fisherman be penalized directly or indirectly because the other fellow is willing to take advantage of these provisions and have the government take care of him? If you are going to pay a man an income he will not get out and hustle, but if you say that pilchards are guaranteed worth $4 a ton at the wharf he will be encouraged to go out and get all the pilchards he can.
It will be noticed that in this brief of the fishermen's union their primary criticism is that there is to be a board of only three men. I raised) this point when the resolution was before the house. This board is to control and set prices in connection with an industry huge in volume and with utterly divergent conditions on the east and west coasts. On the east coast there are fish of which we do not even know the names of. A man named one to me the other day and asked me what I thought it was. I told him I thought it was some kind of a flat fish, but it turned out to be a shell-fish.
The minister has said that it is his intention to recommend that one of these men shall ibe, not a fisherman but a man representing, the fishermen. That recommendation will be subject to, the governor in council; they may turn him down. I know of one man who was selected to represent the fishermen whose financial interests were absolutely opposed to the interests of the fishermen. However, he was said to represent the fishermen because he knew of their situation.
Men should be appointed who are practical fishermen. They should be appointed by the government, but selected by the fishermen.
The fishermen's unions are well organized and they are in position to be responsible for these appointments. The man selected by the government may be a funeral director. He will be appointed because the government thinks he is a suitable man to represent the fishermen. He may have the brains of a Churchill, but how can he deal with such different conditions as exist on the east and west coasts. Not only are conditions different, but the seasons, the runs and the fish themselves are different.
I think the suggestion put forward by the fishermen is a reasonable one, that'the board should consist of five members. There would be one man from the trade and one from the fishermen on each coast, and then the chairman could represent the Department of Fisheries, making a total of five. I think that is a moderate request and one which I hope the government will heed. The last day this matter was being discussed the minister said that he would recommend that one of these three members should represent the fishermen. But he did not say that it would be a man nominated by the fishermen; he said that it would be a man to represent them. That man might be a college professor, and in any event the provision would have to be put into the bill before it would count.
I can remember a former Minister of Mines and Resources telling me that a certain thing meant so-and-so when I asked about it in the house. But six months afterwards when I went to the officials and told them they were not carrying out the promise made to me by the minister, they replied that he was not bound by what he said in the house, that he was bound only by the act.
A further criticism I have to make is in connection with section 9 (i), which gives the board power to appoint commodity boards or other agents to undertake the purchase and the disposition of fisheries products. That is a large order. There is no restriction. A tailor may be sent out to handle crabs or lobsters. God help him and God help the people who will be under his control. Who are these men to be and how are they to be appointed? They are to have unrestricted powers. There should be some restriction or at least some qualification for the men who are to run these boards. They should know something about what they are doing.

speechtext:
If this private conversation is finished I can go on. If the minister can guarantee that he will be running this bill, then I shall be perfectly satisfied because I know he will run it wisely and well. But there are always doubts about human actions. A man may die, or he passes on, and it is possible that this might be enforced by somebody who had not his policy or his determination. to look into everything.
Paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of section 9 give the Board very wide powers to prescribe prices, to purchase directly by means of agents, to pay to the producer the difference between the price prescribed by the board and the average price. Prescribed by the board? Who is going to prescribe it? The board consists of three men,, only one potentially a fisherman. Who is going to fix the prices and give the difference to the fishermen? The board have also power to purchase the fish directly. What are they going to do with it when they purchase it? You have to store it somewhere. Suppose somebody wires to Ottawa, "We have two thousand tons of pilchards on the Pacific coast and the reduction plant will not take in any more." What are you going to do? The government cannot store them in the fisheries offices. Yet you have to do something about it and you have to act quick, or the industry will come to a deadlock while people are sending wires back and forth between Ottawa and the Pacific coast.
Section 11 gives the governor in council power to make regulations. That means this three-man board, which includes a representative of the. processors and a representative of the government, who by and large is generally more or less favourable to the processors. Anyway those two would be a majority of the board and they would have power to make the regulations. I submit that this is absolutely unfair. We are not passing a bill if we do that, but an enabling bill to allow these two men to make an act to suit themselves because the regulations will be the whole crux of the bill. This bill does not even contain a clause that has been put in several other bills, notably the one we passed yesterday about agriculture, providing that the regulations must be advertised. No publication of these regulations is provided for, and the consequence is that no man will know the regulations until they are applied. Then you ask, what about it? And the answer you will get is: It is done by regulation. It will take two weeks to find out who passed the

regulations, what they mean and where they are. It is hard to get copies of regulations. The regulations which are to be made under bill No. 168, for the support of the prices of agricultural products, provided by section 12, under pressure from, farm members in the house, would not become law until published in the Canada Gazette. If you cannot handle things in a democratic way but must handle them in a bureaucratic way, at least we must have publicity so that we can know what the conditions are. Eventually we do get the Canada Gazette out there, but if the regulations are not published we would have to trust to some typewritten document or to something we saw in the newspapers which does not give a correct picture of the facts. But if the regulations are advertised in the Canada Gazette, at least we shall know where we are at.
It comes back to what I said before and to what the unions advocate, that the board should consist of five members, and I would add On my own that the regulations should be advertised in the Canada Gazette as soon as they are arrived at.
Then as to the title of this bill, on the outside page these words appear: "An Act for the support of the prices of fisheries products during the transition from war to peace." But those words are not put in the title of the bill on the inside page, where it says, "This act may be cited as the Fisheries Prices Support Act, 1944". Which is to govern? Perhaps what is printed on the outside of the bill may govern; I do not know. But the words outside most certainly do not appear in the title. This measure might be terminated overnight by order in council. Most of the other bills of this kind that we have been passing, under which regulations are to be made, have said that they should continue in force during the conduct of the war and for six months thereafter, or something of that kind. Here is a man, we will say, who has spent a lot of money equipping himself for some phase of the fish business. He has bought nets, and you cannot get a net for much less than a thousand dollars. Perhaps he has bought a reduction plant. He has been benefited by these subsidies, for that is what the payments under this bill amount to, and perhaps he has been kept alive by them, for sometimes they make the whole difference between a man staying in business or going out. Then all of a sudden he gets a notice, not even by air mail, saying, "This thing ends next Monday and you can do what you think best." He is left to do what he thinks best about his

Fisheries Prices
investment. There should be some protection given. They should get at least a season's notice, perhaps one year's notice from the time that that decision is made. You cannot expect men to spend a lot of money on equipment when there is no certainty that they will ever get their money back again. At the beginning of this war we know how manufacturers were reluctant to invest capital in new plants to produce munitions so long as their profits were limited to five per cent. They would not spend a couple of million dollars to get the machinery that was required to make guns unless they had some protection, because at any moment the war might come to an end when they had turned out only one gun, and they would be ruined with all their money tied up in this machinery and plant which was left on their hands. Accordingly provision was'made for them.
One other point on which I hope the minister will elaborate is this. The success of the bill will depend in part upon what is done with regard to the export trade. That is a very important element. He does not mention that in the bill. But I do not see how you can coordinate prices suitable for Canadians and possible outside markets which may disappear at any time. That is why I suggested the use of participation certificates. There might be a boom in prices in Europe or elsewhere and the government might come out and say: We will take over this product, and afterwards make good money. Some cognizance ought to be given to the export trade.
It does not seem clear to me from section 9 whether the government will allow the fishermen to run their own business or whether the government in order to keep prices up to a reasonable level will decide to take over the business and run it themselves. That opens up possibilities of enormous expense and dosses. Suppose somebody at Ottawa says to these so-called ignorant fishermen on the Pacific-coast, "I know your business better than you do and I will take over and run the whole thing. I will take over the whole salmon run." The first thing he would need would be a cannery. Would he build more canneries, or would he buy out existing canneries? The cost of that would be enormous. The same is true of reduction plants. They cost a lot of money and you have to have, not one, but half a dozen. If you go into that business it opens up possibilities of enormous loss, and I warn the government against it because the local people, the men in the business, are the ones best able to handle it. Someone at Ottawa may decide that he will go into the whaling business.
Does anybody in Ottawa know how to catch whales off the Pacific coast? He may know something about catching a whale on the Labrador coast, but not on the Pacific coast, where I have seen a large fishing boat come in towing five and six whales. You have no time to write to Ottawa for instructions how to handle them because they have to be handled right away. Similarly, if you get a man from the Pacific coast, his knowledge of lobsters, for instance, would not be very great.
Suppose this three-man -board took the notion to take over the whole salmon run, what would it mean? It might be done for a year or two, and with apparent-I say "apparent"-profit; and then the government, having found they had made a complete mess, and that they could not run it so competently with government officials as it could be run by the experience and incentive of personal ownership, would do-what? They would hand it back to these people. Whether they rented the premises or put up competing establishments, they would hand the business back to the people from whom they took it and say "go to it", possibly with the market gone and with the reputation of the product also gone. Of course the government says, "The department won't do foolish things like that." But I know a department not a hundred miles from here that allowed processors to put up a product marked "canned finnan haddie" and put in it hake and pollock and another inferior fish called cusk, and it has mined the market for canned finnan haddie. If they are capable of doing (hat they are liable to put up something marked "canned salmon" and have cusk in that as well. Do not let the government go into large business of which they are ignorant. The government's job is to regulate and control; let the people who know best, run their business. If I were a member of one of these fishermen's unions-one branch of them is the cooperatives, and it is the very finest type of organization-I wmuld certainly hate to see the whole control and organization of markets, perhaps in the United States and elsewhere, taken over by the government and handled, possibly by a gentleman of the highest intelligence and honesty, but whose whole experience may have arisen from running some other branch of industry, perhaps fishing in the Atlantic. It would be the greatest mistake to put in such a man to run this business on the Pacific coast, and remember there is not only one; there are eight or nine different phases of the industry.
I said, when we were discussing the resolution on this subject, that it seemed a rather poor reason why we should endorse the legis-
Fisheries Prices

lation when it was hoped it would never be used. Now I understand from what the minister said that perhaps it would never be necessary to use it, and I quite agree; but if it should be necessary I submit that this bill is not definite enough in its proposals, and above all it is just asking for trouble when you appoint a board to run an industry with about ten different branches, duplicated sometimes on each coast, and sometimes not, and it is problematical whether the board will include even one practical fisherman. There is no question about this, because the minister is on record in Hansard of July 25, at page 5315, as saying that he would not commit himself to it, but that his intentions were to recommend that one member should represent the fishermen. The government will pick out men-it might be one of us-and say, "You are competent to represent the fishermen." But he does not guarantee even that.
