maintopic: PRICES1 OF FISH AS LANDED EAST COAST
speechtext:
I want to express first a word of commendation to the minister for bringing forward this bill. I should also like to congratulate him on the concise and brief way in which he explained it to the house. It was very clear, and I believe we all agree that it is a step forward for the security of the fishing industry. The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Neill), in his inimitable way, and rather facetiously, criticized the bill. Perhaps some of his criticisms will have a salutary effect, but I have come to the conclusion from the numerous criticisms he has made that he is " seeing ghosts." However, it is a matter of providing for the future, and there is always some uncertainty about that.
This bill is similar to the farmers' bill which was put through this house a few days ago. That measure was not intended to interfere with free enterprise. One hon. member, I believe, referred to it as the "if, as and when" bill. I believe that that is a good description of both measures. It means that if the occasion arises we shall have legislation which we can invoke for the purpose of keeping up the standard of living of the fishermen, so that

Fisheries Prices
they will not suffer as they did in the past, owing to depressions and absence of markets. It will put the resources of the nation behind the fishing industry in times of peril.
The fishermen are doing very well now. I do not think there was ever a time when our fishermen received better returns than they do at present. I might add that in so far as the run of fish is concerned, of which mention was made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, fish are extraordinarily plentiful on the Atlantic coast, and this, added to the price, means that fishing is now in a really buoyant state.
I do not think we should interfere with the fisheries so long as the prices are fair. We must realize that fish is a very perishable product; it must be handled quickly, and marketing organizations, transportation and equipment are essential in this industry. The firms who are handling the business on the Atlantic coast, at least in some of the centres, are well equipped for these purposes. I must say, however, that there are parts of Nova Scotia where equipment is not so good and transportation is slow, where entrance to the markets is such that there is danger of deterioration in the quality of the fish before they can be put into the proper storage. This organization is wanting in many parts of the coast. In my county it is well developed, especially in the 'towns of Lunenburg, Liverpool, also in Halifax and some parts of Cape Breton. I know it will be difficult to put a floor price under fish. Seventy per cent of the fish is exported to foreign countries, and anyone who is acquainted with foreign trade knows that the price in the foreign market will largely determine the price of fish, so that a floor price is something that might not work to the advantage of the fishermen. But this bill does not fix a floor price. In effect the government says, "We stand by, and if the price received is not sufficient to give the fishermen a decent living we will supplement that price. Furthermore, if there is not a sufficient market we will buy the fish ourselves and use the resources of the country in order to stabilize the situation and sell the fish to the best advantage of the industry."
It will be recalled that some years ago we had a price spreads committee, which developed afterwards into a royal commission, and that commission investigated price spreads in Canada. Fish was in the forefront, from the point of view of the price paid by the consumer and the price paid to the primary producer. There was a wide spread, and people expressed concern in many places over the difference between what they paid for the fish that appeared on their tables and
what the fishermen received on the coasts of Canada, That is something that is not well understood by the uninformed. The price paid the primary producers is paid for an article that is different from that for which the price is paid by the person using the fish. For instance, fish must be processed, and in the processing a great dteal of it becomes offal; also, in the drying of fish a great deal of the weight is lost by the elimination of water. To the uninformed a picture is presented which is not quite intelligible, so that a wrong impression may be created.
However, one thing that this board might do, and in my opinion can do, is to see to it that this vexed question of price as between producer and consumer shall receive its attention, and the board can deal with it in a definite way and for a specific situation. This feature will always be a factor and, in my opinion, one of the factors that will operate not only for the benefit of the fishermen, and the industry generally, but also in the interests of the country. It will create an intelligent idea of what price spreads mean in connection with fishery- products. When you set a floor price the dealer might go to the fisherman and say, "I will give you so much for your fish." The fisherman says that the fish is worth more than he is offered, and the other replies, "That is the government price and I am giving you the government price." A floor price is, therefore, apt to be regarded as the price that should be paid. That, I think, is something that is carefully guarded against in this bill because it is not intended to set a floor price. What is said to the fisherman is this:	"If
you do not get enough we will buy the product or make up the loss to you, and in that way we will see that your price is brought up to the level at which it should be in a fair economy." That shows a scientific approach to the question and in my opinion it is an admirable feature of the bill. For that reason I think it should receive the enthusiastic support of all elements in the industry and of people generally.
There will be difficulties of course. I suggested to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the other day that he might anticipate embarrassment from other countries dumping products into Canada if we had this sustained price. There has been considerable criticism in Nova Scotia about the dumping of fish from Newfoundland. Fish comes from Newfoundland into Nova Scotia, and they have a lower standard of living there in Newfoundland than we have. One of the difficulties of the fishing industry in our province is that we are in competition with countries where there
Fisheries Prices

are lower economic standards-such countries as Iceland, Norway and Newfoundland. All these countries, the European countries especially, are economical in their living and in their work, and they seem to be able to enter these foreign markets and in the past have done so perhaps more advantageously than Canada was able to do.
There is another thing to be considered. In our reciprocity agreements there is a paragraph that provides that if you stimulate industries in certain ways so as to disarrange the exchange, or if you try to stimulate your business in an artificial way, the result may be a cancellation of the agreement. But there is also a clause that provides that anything that is done for the social or physical welfare of the people in the way of social security or health shall not be regarded as a subsidy. For this reason I was enthusiastic about family allov'ances, because I can see among the fishermen along the coast of Nova Scotia that the man with a large family who has been unsuccessful in his industry will have something coming from his country to sustain his family. It will not become a part of any countervailing trouble with another country so far as trade arrangements are concerned. Family allowances will be especially good for the fisherman because they will make him more secure and place him in a better position with regard to export trade. Suppose some year world prices fall very low-and we must remember that we market our fish in the world market. The fisherman has his backlog of family allowances, and he will be in a much better position to stand the strain of some of those prices than he otherwise would be. And so, above everything I can see, there is nothing to compare with family allowances, so far as the fishermen along the coast of Nova Scotia are concerned. It is a floor under the family.
There is another feature of the bill which I think is important. It does not fix things in a static way. It is flexible, so that it can be used if, as and when it is needed, in order to stimulate the trade in the country. In my view this is a step forward.
The fishing industry in my county has been cooperative for many years. I believe the success of the fishing industry in the county of Lunenburg, which I have the honour to represent, has been for years a romance in industry. I say that because it has beeh outstanding in its success, it has been outstanding in the community it has built up, and it has been outstanding in that it has survived the depression of other years. To-day it is growing in a way which bids well for the future.

I do not quite agree with the minister in his statement of the production theory. There was a time when it was hard to find a market for fish, and I think that day will come again.
I do not believe in immense production, just for production's sake. Industry is for a purpose, that purpose being to sustain the people of one's country. In so far as it sustains the people of the country it should be promoted. And, so far as I can, I wish to keep it that way.
Many Lunenburg fishermen, operating in h :ooperative industry, own shares in vessels. That was done in this way: The vessel is divided into sixty-four shares. A young man might want to have a vessel. He might consider himself equipped to be a skipper of a schooner, and if he felt that way he would go around to get people to take shares with him. If they had confidence they would take shares; he would then go to his crew, and his crew would take shares. And if one man did not have the money he would say to another man, "Let us join .notes in the bank; you take part and I will take part and we will put it into the vessel."
I attribute the success of the Lunenburg fisheries to that cooperative effort. .That was cooperation between capital and labour; it was not a class movement. It was a movement where each shared in the' industry, where each had an incentive to work, and where each and everyone had a stake in the success of what was going on.
This went on until the depression. Then, when the depression came along, the fisherman who did not have very big resources, did not as a rule retain his share in the vessel. He took an opportunity to sell. When the vessel lost money he was even more anxious to sell, because he could not afford to bear the loss. As a result, the merchants got control of most of the vessels. I think that was to the detriment of the fishing industry, and I hope that the industry will be developed in the future so that, so far as possible, the men will have a stake not only in the production, but in the venture as well. In that way we would have the cooperation in a healthy form, and one which gives the best results.
In connection with the production of fish let me remind the house that in the last three years we have tried to build fishing vessels. However, the navy, the air force or the army have come along and said, "We would like to have this vessel"-and they, would simply say, "We will simply change her over, to suit our requirements." For that reason there has been no opportunity to build vessels for fishing purposes along the coast of Nova Scotia,

Fisheries Prices
because to a great extent the shipyards were engaged in the war effort. That, of course, is the way it should be. Furthermore, if one looks up the records he will find that men along our coast are either in the army, the navy, the air force or the merchant marine. There are very few men left-certainly there are no young men. It is nothing short of phenomenal that we have kept up our production, in view of the conditions we have had to face.

maintopic: PRICES1 OF FISH AS LANDED EAST COAST
speechtext: We have exceeded it.

maintopic: PRICES1 OF FISH AS LANDED EAST COAST
speechtext:
Yes, production has really increased. As my hon. friend has pointed out, there are some years when there are no fish, and in those years you cannot get production. That is true on the Atlantic coast, as well as on the Pacific coast. Some years there are lots of fish, and other years the fishermen have to go further to sea to get their catch.
Taking it by and large, the activities of fishermen in the last few years have been most commendable. And let us remember this, that the fishermen who go out along the coast of my province are fishing in dangerous waters. While the merchant marine and other vessels sailing the Atlantic are subjected to the dangers of submarines, and that sort of thing, the fishermen must be there like sitting ducks, fearing at any time to be destroyed. While I am pleased to say that none of them has been destroyed by submarines, at least two of our vessels were run down by convoys on their way to Europe, resulting in a loss of a number of men from my home town.
I cannot let this opportunity pass without adding a few words about the beam trawler. The beam trawler is an efficient machine; there is no doubt about it. But do not. forget it is centralized control. Fishermen cannot own beam trawlers. Beam trawlers will be controlled and' managed by the big fish corporations, and we have facilities in both Lunenburg and Halifax. And on the score of beam trawlers, so far as my county is concerned, I can say that we will be in the vanguard of progress at any time.
But there is the human element to consider, and I think one of the great purposes of the beam trawler is to get clear of that human element. While there is a scarcity of fishermen at the present time, it is a war condition I have been in public life and associated with fisheries and fishermen all my life, and my chief concern has been to get a place at the table where those fishermen can get food and employment. For that reason I do not want anything to happen that would make less labour in the fisheries along the coasts of Nova Scotia, or otherwise be a detriment to supply and demand.
Another matter Mr. Speaker.
It seems to me we have arrived at a time in Canada where we will have to make a decision. The fishing schooners along our coast are paying enormous amounts in income tax to the exchequer of this country. The fishing industry in Lunenburg is a cooperative industry. The set-up, however, is not quite in conformity with the act of parliament which permits cooperatives to function without taxation, and also allows the setting up of reserves so that they by statute pay nothing to the w7ar-time exchequer. Government ownership also is in this class.
In Ontario they have their hydro system, which pays no federal tax-and naturally so. It is a provincial concern. The other day we heard that Quebec was to take over a power company-and I am not complaining about or criticizing that. But about $8,000,000 in taxation which formerly came to the federal treasury will not now be paid. In fact, we are told that similarly Saskatchewan is taking over the hydro there, and in that way they will get clear of income tax. Then, the wheat pools in the west can have their reserves.
Furthermore, the companies which finance them are free of taxes. But the fishermen in Nova Scotia, who are really cooperative, must pay the government thousands of dollars in income and excess profits taxes. The country cannot continue in that way, in the interests of either private or cooperative industry. A country cannot be half slave and half free. If some of us must pay taxes while others go free, we are working for the people who operate businesses and do not pay taxes. Therefore, if the revenues of this country are to be protected; if business is to be kept stable and free and to be judged upon its merits, the government must come to some decision as to whether some industries in this country shall pay no taxes while others pay the shot for running the country's affairs. I do not believe industry should be free of taxation, unless it needs stimulation. I have no objection to this, kind of assistance being given the small cooperatives, where a few people try to get together and get ahead. I am all for some concession to them. But when they get into the realm of big business, when they go into pool insurance, pool wheat marketing, pool elevators and all that sort of thing, then I say the position should be reviewed. If we are to judge business on its merits; if we are in favour of free enterprise, then let it be free. If it is free, then let us have a free field and no favour. That is my doctrine and philosophy. I believe the time has come when we should seriously review the conditions that exist throughout Canada, with regard to the activities of provincial
Fisheries Prices

governments and other activities in various parts of the country that at present are tax free.
May I refer to export trade? We hear a great deal about export trade, Mr. Speaker. Of what does it consist? We sent to other countries food and materials for their people. Those people feed on and use our products; then they say that in order to have a balanced economy they must send back to us goods which will be sold in our country, and by this circulation we are supposed to bring about a healthy economy. Well, the thought occurs to me that if this be so, and it is, why not bring many of these people to our country, feed them at our own table here in Canada, and let them work with us? If we had twice as many people in this country we would not need as much export trade. I think the immediate problem of the future is immigration; I believe we must have selected immigration in order to have a population large enough to sustain our economy and carry our overhead. Mark you, I am not against export trade; I am all for it, but we should have both. In the United States they have 130,000,000 people, who provide a great home market. They also have a great export trade, and the home market and the export trade work together. It seems to me that in the immediate future wre in this country must give consideration to that matter.
I am afraid I have gone a little far afield, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to say that I like this bill because it is flexible; I like it because it is not a frozen statute that contains great detail but because it provides a stand-by that can be used as a lifeline in time of peril. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni does not like a board of only three members. Well, we have a supreme court in Canada that has only a small personnel, and its decisions affect the whole country. The Minister of Agriculture said the other day that there would be advisory boards all over the country. We must have orderly control if these things are to operate properly. They cannot be let go haphazard ; there must be some supreme authority. That supreme authority is the government, and they appoint a board. It seems to me the government can control a board of three much better than they can control a board of, say fifteen. I want the government to be in control. These advisory boards all over the country will bring various matters to the attention of the central board, where I hope they will be intelligently dealt with. I will say that the fishermen must be represented on all these boards.
I want to tell you that down in my county we have fishing skippers who can take their place anywhere, who know the fishing game and who know all about business. I could name many men who would adorn this board and bring to it practical experience that would have a salutary effect, giving it balance and helping it work for the good of the fishermen. I have faith that this will be done; I am sure that will be so if we who represent the maritimes can exert any influence in the matter.
This measure is intended to prevent disaster to the industry and poverty to the fishermen in times of financial peril. If it accomplishes that purpose it will be a good measure. I say we should try it out; put it through, and we will not have the fishermen coming to us later on saying, "We get poverty prices for our fish, while other people in this country are prosperous."

maintopic: PRICES1 OF FISH AS LANDED EAST COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take my stand beside those who favour this legislation. Representing as I do a constituency where a large number of the people depend upon the fishing industry, it gives me great pleasure to support this measure. I support the principle of this bill on its second reading on two grounds. First, I favour the recognition of federal responsibility in the matter of fisheries and, second, I favour this immediate measure for the benefits that the fishermen will derive from the legislation.
I should like to refer briefly to the history of government responsibility from confederation on and indicate the difficulties that have been experienced because of the attitude taken by both federal and provincial governments. These difficulties end to-day in this measure which indicates a breaking of new ground, so to speak, by the federal government. The British North America Act gave jurisdiction over the seacoast and inland fisheries to the federal government. Immediately a bouncing procedure began where this jurisdiction was tossed back and forth between the federal government and the provinces. We find the federal government saying, "True, we have jurisdiction in so far as seacoast and inland fisheries are concerned, but that means only jurisdiction with regard to regulation and control; the responsibility
fMr. Kinley.]

Fisheries Prices
for the individual fisherman, to see whether he is prosperous is not ours; that is for the provinces under property and civil rights and the general responsibility of taking care of the individual."
In the midst of that argument the British Columbia fisheries case was decided by the privy council. Under that case the rights to fish in tidal waters were decided as belonging to the Dominion of Canada, not to the federal or provincial governments. In other words, fisheries in tidal waters were considered to be the right of the people of Canada as a whole, not of the dominion or provincial governments. That simply complicated the matter a little further, and the bouncing procedure between the federal and provincial governments continued until 1935. I do not want to make this a political speech because the matter is more serious than that.
In that year we were in a great depression. From 1930 on, the responsibility had not been recognized by either the provinces or the federal government, and nothing had been done to take care of the fishermen while they were going through the depression. On October 3, 1935, we find Mr. Bennett, then Prime Minister of Canada, addressing a public meeting in Bridgewater, in the constituency of the then Minister of Fisheries. Mr. Bennett made this terrible admission, according to a report in the Halifax Herald of October 4, 1935:
Turning his attention to fisheries policies of the Conservative party, the Prime Minister declared an immediate survey of the entire industry was essential, to spur the industry along a forward march of progress. The remedies he suggested, were: first, we must have better knowledge of the requirements of the people who buy our fish. . . . Second, trade commissioners should have complete knowledge of the fisheries. . . . Third, we must find out how we can assist the fishermen. I confess I do not know. I tell you, frankly. . . . Fourth, we shall continue extensive advertising to make your fish better known.
I think he was telling the truth. Because of this lack of responsibility by any government the Department of Fisheries at Ottawa had become nothing more than an unwanted child thrown from one minister to another. Sometimes a real minister was in charge of the department; sometimes only an acting minister was at its head. The result was that we had Mr. Bennett saying that he did not know how to assist the fishermen. The department had been unable to deal with the situation, to find out what the remedies should be. The same thing can be said of the previous administration.
In March, 1937, when I spoke in this house I referred to what I thought was the first
thing that had to be settled, namely, the responsibility for the industry, whether it belonged to this government or to the provincial governments. I placed the fishing industry in the same category as our agricultural industry and I contended that our fishermen should be treated the same as our farmers. That is now being done by the measure before the house. At that time I said:
I realize that it would be unreasonable for me to ask for discrimination in his favour. We cannot favour one against the other. I therefore propose, briefly, that we follow the policy adopted to take care of another primary industry in another part of Canada.
Then I went on to refer to the farmer. I felt that the first thing that had to be done in order to take care of the fishing industry was to remedy the terrible conditions existing. This is a great day for the fishing industry when we find a measure of this kind before this house. We have had bill No. 168, providing minimum prices for the farmer, and we now have bill No. 169, making .the same provisions for the fishermen. There is some difference in the amounts, but perhaps that should be so. One after the other these industries are coming into their own; measures have been introduced to take care of the primary industries of fishing and farming. I am happy to stand here to-night as a member of this house representing my constituency and support this measure.
This measure is necessary. I should like to indicate the situation that existed in 1935 at the end of the great depression. Let me give again some figures that I gave previously to the house indicating the earnings by different boats:
The status of a large number of fishermen in the maritimes has become desperate. For example, in one district in my riding, which was once a prosperous and successful fishing district, the catch for 1935 followed the general trend. I want to see it improved. I should like to give some examples of the earnings of some of the fishing boats. I shall not give the names, referring to them only by number.
Boat number one, with a crew of twenty-two men, fished for fourteen weeks. It stocked $4,000, and the average share per man per week was $4. Boat number two, with a crew of twenty-one men, fished nine weeks. It stocked $2,272 and the average share per man per week was about $2. Boat number three, with a crew of eighteen men, fished twenty-two weeks. It stocked $4,600 and the average share per man per week was about $1. Boat number four, with a crew of twelve men, fished thirteen weeks. It stocked $2,100 and the average share per man per week w'as $4.50. Boat number five, with a crew of six men, fished thirteen weeks and the average share per man per week was fifty cents.

Fisheries Prices
That was a general picture because those were not isolated cases. They were not the worst cases; they simply showed what was happening in the fishing industry when men were making from fifty cents to $4 a week over a period of ten, fifteen or twenty odd weeks. That was the condition facing the industry. That was the condition after we had had a period of prosperity following the last war.
I should like to indicate further the number of people who will be affected by this measure. We have approximately 80,000 fishermen in Canada, engaged in an industry that produces from $30,000,000 to $75,000,000 of fish each year, depending largely upon the prices at which the fish is selling. There is no great variation in the quantity of fish caught, but there is a great variation in the prices paid for the fish. That is why I support this measure. I think it is necessary.
We have on the Atlantic coast what are known as fishing banks, an area of 75,000 square miles, the greatest cod and haddock fishery in the world, bar none. On the pacific coast we have one of the greatest salmon fisheries in the world. These are assets which the Canadian people have to take care of, and the people engaged in this industry have a right to look to this and other governments for assistance when conditions beyond their control make it impossible for them to gain a decent and proper livelihood.
A word as to Canada's position in world fisheries. Canada exports about seventy per cent of its fish products. Canada produces only about four per cent of the world's production of fish. I am quoting from the 1937 figures which were given by the United States tariff commission and I believe that they are approximately correct. They show that the total world catch of fish in 1937 was approximately twenty-five billion pounds, of which twenty-five per cent was produced by Japan, seventeen per cent by the Soviet Union, ten per cent each by the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway; four per cent by Canada, three per cent each by France, Germany, Spain, Newfoundland and Iceland, and nine per cent by other countries. Norway, Canada, Newfoundland and Iceland were primarily engaged in producing fish for export. So that we are just a part of the world's picture. How can we expect, therefore, that the individual fisherman can stand up by himself without assistance in a competing world when conditions over which he has no control make it impossible for him to, carry on?
Let us look for a moment at what happened after the last war, and let me say that I think
[Mr. Pottier.J
the same thing is going to happen after this war. Speaking in this house on May 25, 1939, on the bill to establish a salt fish board and giving it my support on these same grounds, I said:
During the period, of the war

I was referring to the war of 1914-18, and it is my considered opinion that in a general way we shall face the same situation after this war, and should be ready to meet it.
-owing to disturbances in Europe interfering both with the fishing grounds and European fishing operations, there was in Canada a favourable reaction upon our fishing industry. There was increased demand and prices went up. After the war, however, and since that time they (other countries) seem constantly to have gained ground to our disadvantage.
I went on to show what the government of Norway had done in voting $3,000,000 as bounties for the three-year period beginning in 1920, and I showed what other countries had done. I summarize the situation in this way.
Bounties for fishing operations were given by Germany and Japan. Bounties on exports were given by France, the Irish Free State, Italy and Newfoundland.
Grants for the construction or repair of vessels were made by Germany, Japan and Newfoundland.
Grants for the construction of freezing establishments were made by Japan and Norway. Government loans and guarantees were made by France, Iceland, the Irish Free State, Italy, Netherlands, Newfoundland, Norway, Portugal, the United Kingdom and Denmark.
One after another these countries were priming their fishing industry, granting assistance of various kinds which made it impossible for the Canadian fisherman who did not have this assistance to carry on.
Promotion of the home market was undertaken by Denmark, France, Germany and Japan.
Other aids by governments of different countries were preferential transportation rates; tax or duty exemptions; emergency relief; other governmental aid such as in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.
I am going to take codfish as an illustration of what happened generally in the fishing industry. It will show the trend of what has happened in our fisheries since the last war. I have a table taking five-year periods, showing the weight of the fish caught in

Unless something is done, we shall fall .back from the 1943 price of 3-3 cents per pound to the prices we had in 1939, 1936 and 1931, when the returns to the fisherman were respectively 1-2 cents per pound, 1-2 cents per pound and 1-3 cents per pound, or approximately one-third of present prices. But the point I wish to make is that we have gone up from a price of 1-2 cents before the war to 3-3 cents to-day, owing to the war and other causes which I have indicated. I emphasize that point because we do not want to go back to where we were before, and that is why this measure is so necessary to prevent a return to the low prices that we had before the war.
The United Maritime Fishermen had this same thought in their minds in the brief which they submitted to the Minister of Fisheries this year. I should like to quote the following passage from their brief:
In the past years, especially during the period between 1923 and the beginning of the present war, the fishery of the maritime provinces was in a state of chronic depression. Ample evi-deuce of this is to ibe found in the fishery statistics. These figures indicate that in 1939, which was not by any means one of the worst years, 30,524 fishermen in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick received for their total landings of fish the sum of $7,467,919 gross, making an average of $244 each.
Out of this had to come the fisherman's operating expenses.
Just imagine what a terrible situation you have when the average person in an industry gets $244 a year, and out of that has to pay his operating expenses, bring up a family, and carry all the other responsibilities incidental to him as a member of the community I
We cannot allow the fisherman-and a number of these after the war will be returned men-to be left on their own responsibility,
having to compete not only with individual fishermen of other countries but with the advantages these other countries will give to their fishermen in turn.
This measure will protect the price to the fishermen to the tune of $25 million. The important powers under the bill itself are contained in section 9, subsection 1, subparagraphs (b), (c), (d) and (e), to which I will briefly refer.
The first power is:
(b)	to purchase directly or by means of agents at such prices any fisheries product if such product on inspection meets standards as to grade and quality prescribed by or under any act of the parliament of Canada.
The second is:
(c)	to pay to the producer of a fisheries product directly or through such agent as the board may determine the difference between a price prescribed by the board with the approval of the governor in council for such fisheries product and the average price as determined by the board at which such product is sold during a specified period if such average price is below such prescribed price.
The third power is:
(d)	to sell or otherwise dispose of, directly or by means of agents any fisheries product purchased by the board.
The fourth power is:
(e)	to package, process, -store, ship, transport or export, directly or by means of agents, any fisheries .product.
Increase or decrease in the price of fish depends on a number of things; among others, on production, markets, processing methods, marketing and general conditions in the country itself, as well as general world conditions. That is to say, prices tend to increase if there is a decrease in production; further market# are found; improved processing methods are brought into play; orderly marketing is taken advantage of, and there is general prosperity in this and other countries. If, however, there is temporary overproduction, loss of markets, loss to other commodities owing to better processing, disorganized marketing and general depression, then the price of fish will decrease.
Generally speaking, I take it that if there is temporary overproduction or loss of market, the board will purchase to take care of the oversupply. If there is loss to other commodities owing to processing or disorganized marketing, the board has power to process or organize marketing. If a general depression takes place then the board can pay the producer an- amount toward assistance to a price to make up for the general depression.
I know some will say that we depend on export markets and ask, how can the government control prices in view of that fact; how
Fisheries Prices

are you going to get around the difficulty of placing prices for different areas, different conditions, different qualities of fish, and a hundred other arguments? I am not afraid of these, because I have come to the conclusion that any matters of this kind can be adjusted and expedited if sufficient good will, effort and energy are spent by those who try to put them into effect. If, on the other hand, the people who are affected realize that these conditions and regulations are for their general benefit, you will have no difficulty in bringing such conditions and regulations about and having them put into effect; and I believe that this measure will be worked out with that end in view. I would say this about the officials of the fisheries department, that they know the fishing industry, have the fishermen's problems at heart, and are willing to grapple with them. On the one hand we are going to have officials who are inspired by this resolution, and on the other hand, the people in the fishing industry realize that this measure is being brought about for their benefit. Under these conditions I am convinced that the necessary measures will be made effective and benefit the fishermen. I have no doubt that this measure will prevent prices of fish going for starvation wages or earnings. That is the point in which I am interested. I do not mean that this measure will hold the price of fish on the market; I mean that it will bring about returns to the fisherman which will enable him to carry on.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the inscription over the entrance to these buildings has now a different meaning to me. I have in the past often wondered, when passing under that inscription, "The wholesome sea is at her gates, her gates both east and west", whether one could correctly say that a wholesome sea was one which produced hunger and want to those who went down to it.
This measure, if it is put into effect, will enable those of us who live in our kingdom by the sea to say with the rest of Canada, as in the poem, "There is a Land":
And 0. her skies are bright and blue,
Her waters bright and pure;
There's balm within her forest shades All world-Worn men to cure:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west,
Then is it strange that we should love,
This land, our land, the best?

It is the view of our members that if the fishery is to be reconstructed upon a basis which will provide freedom from want for the fishermen some means must be devised to maintain fish prices on a parity with other commodities.

I am rather suspicious; I like to be definite and to leave no loopholes or guessing about legislation. To approach the problem of the fisherman on that basis is, in my opinion, wrong. These people have suffered since confederation, they have been the forgotten people of Canada. This has not been an industry in the true sense of the term, it has been simply a relief measure which has kept practically all the fishermen and their families in the breadline since its establishment. To think of reestablishing this industry only during the transition from war to peace means that we are simply going to reestablish it under the conditions that existed prior to the outbreak of war. It cannot mean' anything else..
Hundreds of fishermen are in the services and they will be coming back. If it is intended merely to route them back into the industry, then I think the approach is wrong. Anything we do should be definite and permanent with the complete reorganization of the industry as the end in view. Our aim

and objective should be the establishment of conditions and income in the industry that will guarantee a decent livelihood for those employed in it. I am not in accord with this term which indicates a makeshift and temporary arrangement pending the reorganization of the industry back to what it was prior to the outbreak of the war. Anyone who considers that Canada's rehabilitation- programme is to cover merely the transition from a war economy to a peace economy is thinking in terms of what we had- when the rvar broke out.
Second, we must remember that it is not in the immediate post-war period that the fishing industry will need assistance. speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Transport) :
maintopic: PRICES1 OF FISH AS LANDED EAST COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is gratifying to note that this measure, which is advanced by the government to alleviate the situation of the fishermen during the immediate post-war period, has met with the approval of practically every hon. member who has spoken, and has been endorsed by the official opposition. Criticism was offered in regard to two or three points, but I believe it arose from the fact that those offering it were not fully appreciative of the objects of this measure. The hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) claimed that this legislation is in direct contradiction to the economic law of supply and demand. Well, that is so. It is purposely designed in that way because of many factors, other than the general law of supply and demand for fisheries products, that come into the picture.
Hon. members must not overlook the fact that until a few years before the war eighty per cent of our fishery products were exported, with only twenty per cent consumed in Canada. Just before the war home consumption increased to thirty per cent and exports dropped to seventy per cent. However, when it is realized that seventy per cent of the products of this industry must be sold in a dozen different markets, under conditions which this country cannot control, it will be seen that some extraordinary artificial measures are required to counteract the workings of the law of supply and demand. We have the factors of restrictions, tariffs, the financial ability of the purchaser to pay or to supply goods in return for the imports of our fish, and other factors over which we have no

Fisheries Prices
control but which unfortunately work to the detriment of those engaged in this industry. That is the basic reason why in the past the fishermen, although they had at their disposal an unlimited source of supply and a means of production relatively not too extensive, nevertheless could not realize a sufficient return to enable them to maintain a standard of living in our country comparable with that enjoyed by other classes of industrial workers.
For these reasons governments in the past have tried to find remedial measures. Attempts were made to secure special treatment for our products in certain countries through trade agreements. Other governments tried to compensate the fishermen by means of loans to make up the deficiency in their returns. Other governments established cold storage plants on the Atlantic coast. Finally, just before the war, the government applied to the salt fish industry the principle which, among others, is contained in this legislation. So that we have the benefit of the experience gained through the measure of control and help given the salt fish producers in the east to justify us in continuing that control and assistance and in extending it to the producers of other varieties of fish, provided that certain factors are taken into account and certain conditions met.
It is claimed that this legislation does not comply with the requests made last spring by the united fishermen of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Well, it may not comply with those requests in the terms in which they were presented; but I submit that in preparing for the immediate post-war period we must take into account the factors which may work against the distribution of the products of the fishing industry. We must prepare for the period when world conditions will be unsettled; when we shall not know what will be the trade relationships between the various countries of the world, what will be the tariff situation, what will be the financial position of the countries that may desire to purchase our exports of fish. Therefore we must take the necessary precautions against a recurrence of the conditions which came about immediately following the last war. I grant that this cannot be looked upon as a permanent measure to improve the condition of the fishermen. It is designed to assist them in the period immediately following the war, when we cannot tell what will be the condition under which they will have to sell their products. By this legislation we say, "So far as this country is concerned, we will take care of the products of your industry
and will assure you a return which will enable you to continue in that industry and at the same time maintain a decent standard of living." That is what this measure is designed to accomplish, and nothing more.
As to meeting the demands of the fishermen and assuring them a measure of security, I repeat that as far as it is possible to guess what the future may be, this is the only legislation this parliament and this country could devise to take care of the situation, irrespective of the conditions that may exist in other countries or in the markets of the world over which we may not have much control when the war is over. After all, what the fisherman and those engaged in this basic industry want is an assurance that whatever may be the condition outside Canada, this country will see that they get a fair return, no matter if that must be accomplished by a violation of the economic law of supply and demand.
In normal times seventy per cent of the production of this industry cannot be absorbed in the home markets; it must be exported. If that condition were reversed; if seventy per cent of the production could be consumed in this country, then the law of supply and demand could work. The industry would obtain a sufficient return to enable it to take care of the thirty per cent which would have to be exported, either at a loss or at no profit.
I was surprised at the criticism offered by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that this legislation will provide no benefit for the fisherman and will not help to alleviate his situation in the post-war period. I am afraid the hon. member has not studied this legislation; I am afraid he has not considered the purpose of this bill. This bill has been introduced to meet a situation which should be well known to the hon. member for Cape Breton South. As I say, for many years from seventy to eighty per cent of the production of this industry had to be exported to markets over which we had no control. Only from twenty to thirty per cent was consumed by markets in this country over which we had control.
I submit that the government has tried to find a means of relieving that situation. As I said previously, the government extended loans to fishermen and built some cold storages. Those may not have been sufficient to meet present-day conditions, but they were sufficient to meet the conditions which prevailed in those days when seventy per cent of the fish produced on the Atlantic coast had to be exported. Only a small quantity was exported in fresh or semi-fresh state; most of it had to be
Fisheries Prices

processed, dried, cured, salted or canned in order to meet the requirements of the export markets. It is true that we have since opened up and developed markets for fresh fish in Great Britain and the United States. It is hoped that we shall be able to keep those markets and, if that is so, this legislation will not be required to maintain the price of fish. This legislation is found necessary in anticipation of losing those markets or of their demands being decreased.
Section 9 (c) of the bill maintains the principle which was established by the salt fish board. During its operation that board worked to the advantage and benefit of the fishermen, because the great bulk of the exports could not be exported at a profit or even at the cost of production. I submit that the criticism of this legislation advanced by the hon. member for Cape Breton South was not to the point. This legislation being a measure temporarily to relieve a situation cannot be construed and looked upon as a measure permanently to establish prices in markets over which we have no control and which are quite uncertain at the present time.
I submit that this measure will go a long way toward relieving a situation which has been deplorable and which has concerned all governments for many years. They had tried to solve this problem but unfortunately have been unable to do so, owing partly to public opinion and partly to conditions over which they had no control. Now, however, we are establishing a principle whereby those who are willing to help themselves will be helped, and I am sure that this measure will be of great assistance to the fishing industry.

That makes.it almost unanimous because it was an hon. gentleman over on the other side that I heard saying that it was the greatest bill ever introduced. That makes, I think, three members who are of that same mind. Let me dwell for a moment on that-the greatest bill ever brought down in the interests of the fishermen.
My memory goes back to some legislation that was brought in even by those evil people, the Tory party, which was of great value to fishermen. The ancestor or father of the present hon. member for St. John-Albert was at one time Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as the portfolio was then, called. His party was in power and he came out to British Columbia to look over the fishing industry. The member representing the district which I now represent was a supporter of the minister, and the minister looked upon the work of that gentleman and said that it did not look good to him. He said: "There will be no more of this system." Most of the cannery men there then belonged to the same party as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of that day. They had a perfect cinch. The law then was such that they could build a cannery, and then see

Fisheries Prices
somebody and get a licence for the cannery. But they got more than that. They got a complete guardianship, so to speak, or control over a large area of water, water which belongs to the people of Canada, or to the people of the world if it is outside the three-mile limit, and not a fisherman could put a net into the waters allotted to the person who got the licence without his permission. The result was that since the fishermen had to live they went to the cannery man and got put on his list. There were so many licences to a cannery, perhaps twenty or thirty, and one of the first conditions imposed before a fisherman could get a licence was that he had to sell all the fish he caught in that water to the cannery and at the price fixed by the cannery man. Aou could not sell it to anyone else or you would not get on the list the next year. The licences were handed out, not to individual fishermen, but to the cannery man or to the man who had been successful in obtaining a licence covering a large area of water, and he farmed out these licences to the fishermen under the conditions I have mentioned. Mr. Hazen saw that that was not good, that it was not democratic, and that it was leading to a lot of graft. You can see all the implications possible. He said: "I am going to stop this." And in defiance of his own supporters and the opposition of a great many of his friends out there he said: "Hereafter anyone can get a fishing licence and the fisherman can fish anywhere in Canadian waters and sell his fish to anyone he likes." If that were not the greatest boon that was ever enacted for the benefit of the fishermen on the Pacific coast, I will tell you of another.
This was a boon also, and incidentally it was also a product of the Conservative party. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), who at one time was minister in connection with military matters, was, at the time I am speaking of, Minister of Fisheries. A condition existed in British Columbia which I had been trying to remedy for years and years, but I never got anywhere because the parties who were behind this custom were strongly entrenched here. Then new circumstances arose and it struck me that the time was right to try once more to get the situation remedied. There was a law at that time that any man catching sockeye salmon, the most valuable and expensive salmon in British Columbia waters, from a certain area down near the Fraser river had to sell the fish to the local canneries at the price fixed by the local cannery men. There was a gentleman's agreement that the price should not be lower than seventy-five cents below the price obtainable in Seattle. They could always have got
a much better price in Seattle. But that was the law. You could not sell the sockeye salmon where you could get the best price. I thought that was rotten. Finally the present hon. member for Yale became head of the fisheries department and I said to him, "If I bring this matter up in the fisheries committee, what about it? Are you going to put your brute majority on and kill it?" He said, "If you can get the committee to approve your suggestion, I will not interfere." I put it to the members of the committee who were representing the fishing districts, and they could not believe it. They said, "Is it true that a man can catch fish legally and must sell it to a particular person?" I said, "Yes." They voted for the remedy and the thing went flying through the committee. Again I approached the hon. member for Yale and said, "The committee has approved. Now what about you? Will you damn it when it comes up for concurrence in the house?" He said, "No, I will not interfere if you can get the house to support it." And the house did support it, and that was the biggest boon the fishermen ever got. It must have meant hundreds of thousands of dollars in the pockets of the fishermen because they could then 6ell their fish in the open market and get six bits for a fish that they formerly sold for thirty-five cents.
^Those were two boons for the fishermen that were obtained through Conservative governments. But Liberal governments have also been responsible for legislation favourable to the fishermen. In 1922 I had not been here for three months before the Liberal government passed a measure cutting the number of licences issued to Japanese down by forty per cent and later by further cuts. That was a very big thing for the white fishermen. Then there was a reduction of customs duty on fishermen's nets and gasoline engines. Then the Minister of Customs of that day arranged that the fishermen could get their gas two cents cheaper per gallon than anyone else. All those things are to the credit of the Liberal government. The Liberal government also inaugurated, after spending money in investigating, the building of reduction plants, which has been the means of employing many people and of bringing in thousands of dollars of revenue to the country. They also provided that no reduction plant could be started unless a guarantee was given that it would be staffed entirely by white men. That was another great advantage to our white men on the coast. Again, in the east, the government put up cold storages in the maritimes and paid for a collecting boat so that the
Fisheries Prices

fishermen cquld get their fish quickly together. The salt fish board of a year ago is another case in point. I do not think it is fair to say that this bill is a bolt out of a blue sky, and the first and only benefit to the fishermen. I suggest that any one of these things would have been of far greater importance than the best that can be hoped for from this legislation, which, as we are told, is to meet a need which has not yet arisen, and which we hope will not arise.
It has been said that many hon. members have spoken wholeheartedly in favour of the bill, but I hoticed some said that there were improvements they would like to see. I hope the minister will take notice of these suggestions, more particularly the suggestion made by one of the hon. members for Halifax when he took his courage in both hands and said that he thought there should be a board of five. I believe the hon. member for Cape Breton South said something along the same lines. The minister cannot possibly be wrong if he raises the number to five. He will get the hearty appreciation-shall I call it the heartfelt approval?-of the people in western Canada, and apparently it will also meet with credit in the east; and with these changes, and one or two others which may be suggested as we go along, I think he will get a very feasible bill. Almost the whole benefit will depend upon the way in which it is handled and carried out, and as long as the present minister holds this office I am satisfied that it will be done in a reasonable and businesslike way.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Fisheries prices support board.
Mr. BERTRAND (Laurier); Mr. Chairman, I wish an amendment to be made to this section. I understand the point of view which some hon. members have been putting forward. that the board should consist of five members, and I am content to accept an amendment which would say that the board would be of not more than five.
That section 3, subsection (1) be amended by striking out the word "three" in line 16 and inserting in the same line the following, "not more than five."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall this amendment
carry?

Will this likely include
the nomination of someone representing that eleven per cent of production or of value contained in the inland waters?

It is possible. The hon. member will understand that we shall have to choose the best men from where they are, and that we want the primary producers to be represented. We cannot now say who the members are to be. This bill will come into force as soon as it is passed. Some of the sections will come in force by proclamation, and we have some preliminary work to do. It is my intention, as represented to me by my officials, that the chairman of the board shall be appointed now and shall make a survey of the field, and that as soon as this is done the other members will be appointed, and I intend to have representatives from primary producers and from the trade.

Has the minister any
prospective chairman in mind?

No, I have
not. Members of the board may give their full time, or some of them may not give their full time. We have not yet decided. But we are going to have the trade represented, and also the primary producers.

I quite appreciate what
the minister has said, and when this afternoon he kindly referred to my own interest in the fisheries in inland lakes all over Canada I said to myself that perhaps when this section came up he would get out of a jam of giving two representatives to the west coast and one to the east coast, or vice versa, by increasing the number to five so that he could give each coast two, and escape the further dilemma by giving one representative to the inland lakes fish producers.

The hon.
member may be sure that there will be a man on the board who knows very well the problems of the inland fisheries.
Amendment agreed to.

There is a consequential amendment required to paragraph 5 of section 3, in order to make a quorum' of the board three instead of two. I move:
That in paragraph (5) the word "two" be struck out and the word "three" be substituted therefor.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 4-Officers, clerks and employees.

I have been following
fairly closely the bill which was introduced with respect to the support of agricultural prices and the bill which is now before the committee with respect to the support of the

prices of fisheries products, and I should like to know from the minister in what respects or in what sections the two bills do not follow each other closely. Do the terms and provisions of this legislation differ from those of the measure in support of agricultural prices?
I might say that in most instances I have found them: similar, but in case there is some difference I think the committee ought to know -what it is.
Mr, BERTRAND (Laurier): I explained, when I made a general expose of the principles, that it is absolutely similar to the agricultural bill except that the word "fisheries" replaces the word "agriculture", and that in section 9 certain paragraphs had to be modified in order to meet the exigencies of the fisheries trade instead of those relating to agricultural products.

Should there not be a consequential amendment to subsection 5 of
section, 3	.
Yes. That was made.

Section agreed to.
Sections 5 to 8 inclusive agreed- to.
On section 9-Powers of the board.

This, I believe, is the section where there are the dissimilarities from the bill which relates to agricultural prices. Would the minister indicate the changes in this bill as compared with the agricultural bill?
Well, I should have to read both. I know that wherever in the agricultural bill the word "agriculture" occurs, in the present bill "fisheries" is substituted.
I understood the minister to say that there was some more important change than that.

Yes, in subsection I (a), which reads:
(a) to prescribe from time to time with the ' approval of the governor in council prices at which the board may purchase fisheries products;
The similar subsection in bill No. 168 reads as follows:
(a) to prescribe from time to time, with the approval of the governor in council, prices at which the board may purchase agricultural products in the market.
It was found necessary, I suppose, to put "in the market" in the agricultural products bill because they are bought in the market instead of being bought from the primary producer. In the bill we left it to be purchased
Fisheries Prices
wherever it was found to be convenient. The other differences have references to replacing the word "agriculture" by "fisheries".
Is it intended to read each of these paragraphs of subsection 1 and to take them paragraph by paragraph?
That can be done if it is so desired.
I think it should be done, because this is really the meat of the whole bill.	[DOT]

I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South; it is the meat of the whole bill.
Paragraph (a) agreed to.
On section 9, subsection 1, paragraph (b).

What does the minister propose to do with respect to deciding upon quality? There is no food product that is more perishable or that more quickly deteriorates than fish if it is not properly caught, processed, preserved, looked after, shipped and put on the market. It quickly becomes worthless. I should like to know what standard the minister is setting and how he proposes to decide on the quality and preservation of the fish to make sure that it is perfectly edible.

In past years, it has been found that the inspection of fish products should be more stringent than ever and that they should be classified. One of the difficulties is that "sometimes the fishermen, owing to their manner of fishing, their engines, which are not very strong, and their boats, which are not properly equipped, cannot land their fish fast enough. I was myself in Halifax last year when a schooner came in with 350,000 pounds of fish. It was a very hot day following other hot days and, although the schooner had gone to sea with a scowload of ice, it had all melted. The catch was very good but the captain stayed too long at sea. He wanted to fill the holds and, when he came to Halifax, although he had 350,000 pounds, it was found on inspection that much of the fish -was not first class. We realize that if we are to help the fisheries we must see to it that the fish is landed in the best possible condition, processed immediately and shipped to the centres of consumption >'n proper edible condition. The problem of the fisheries for me and my officials is to see to it that the fish is landed and placed before the consumer in the best possible condition so that there will be no difficulty in selling it. That is why we have set forth in paragraph
Fisheries Prices

(b) the conditions upon which quality will be established. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman means, how we are going to do it and how we are going to keep the fish in proper condition. All that will have to be done by the agents, most of the time, because the government has no refrigeration plant of its own. However, we shall see to it that the agents who are appointed will take the necessary steps to ensure that the product is in first-class condition.

Would the minister consider an alteration in the words dealing with the matter to which reference has now been made? Where standards have not been established, fish may be purchased "by the board or its agents on such basis of quality as the board may designate." That is putting far too much power in the hands of officials. I have supreme suspicion of official-made regulations, because they are far too often made for the convenience of those who carry them out rather than for the practical benefit that is to be derived from them. I cannot give the exact legal word's, but it is customary in a case like this to use language of this kind: "may be purchased by the board or its agents -on such basis of quality as the custom of the trade and/or the board may designate." That would give power to the minister after all. It would help him, or whoever makes the regulation, to take notice of the custom of the trade. It might be that an inferior class of fish, which has been well known and has always had a certain grade attached to it, or which has been designated by some name, could be sold in bulk without being put up in boxes. Certainly, at any rate, the custom of the trade would be a protection against any bureaucratic rule being passed which would make the bill unworkable. It might read: "by the board or its agents on such basis of quality as the custom of the trade and the board may designate", or it might be made to read "as the board may designate after taking into consideration the custom of the trade". If you include the words "custom of the trade" you , give that added protection, and you may be sure that the custom of the trade will be a wise and reasonable one.

I do not think we can accept the suggestion, because we want the fishermen to land their fish in the best possible condition and we want the board to help the fishermen to raise the standard of the fisheries. As to the custom of the trade, the board will consist of men who will know it perfectly. I do not think we can accept the suggestion. There would be room for a good

deal of litigation if the custom of the trade happened to admit of a quality inferior to the standard which the board would require.
Suppose the regulations set a standard that cannot be lived up to.

We cannot
suppose that the extremes are going to happen. The men 011 the board will be reasonable men and I am sure that they will pass regulations that will be reasonable.

Paragraph agreed to.
On section 9, subsection 1, paragraph (c).
I should like to ask two questions. First, what is meant by producers of fisheries products? A fisheries product is defined. Then, what is a producer of fisheries products?

The man who
catches the fish.
The fisherman?
What does the paragraph mean?
The hon. member was not here when I gave my explanation on second reading?
If the explanation was given then, I shall read it in Hansard.

The same principle is applied here as was applied by the salt fish board in 1939-40, and which worked out very satisfactorily for the fishermen. This is a paragraph which gives to the fishermen an inducement to produce fish and sell it at as high a price as possible. There is always danger of collusion between fishermen and purchasing agents or processors. Under this paragraph the average price of a unit commodity is made after the season is over. If we find that the price is not sufficient to give the fishermen a fair and decent living we will fix the same price at a certain amount, and the difference between the average price and that amount will be distributed to all the fishermen. If a fisherman has produced very good fish and has sold them at a higher price than the one which we believe would give the fisherman a fair and decent living, he will receive the difference, and have the higher price.
Was it the same grade of fish?
Yes, the same fish, caught at the same tide and shipped at the same time.
And the same grade?

Yes. One man was paid the highest price, and the other received nothing, because it was reported to him that the fish were not marketable. Under those circumstances would both shippers be protected by this measure?
And shipped to the same dealer in the United States?
I could not say positively about that.

I would suggest to the man whose fish were said to be no good to prove that they were good, if they were absolutely the same as those shipped by his neighbour who received the high price. However, I do not think a single instance like that can be set up as a guide. If one of the fishermen had supplied smelts which were not as good, he would have to suffer, because we do not want to subsidize fishermen who are not careful. That would be an inducement 'for them not to be careful about their fish. The essence of good fishing business is to be careful in handling the products.
Let us suppose there are two open seasons for a certain kind of fish. How does the minister arrive at an average price?
If there are different seasons, and the fish are not sold at the same price in both seasons, we take the average.
You have an average price for each season, at the end of each season.
Yes.
The prescribed price, as I understand it, is not set at the begining of the season.
It is at the end of the season.

If the hon. member will look at section 9 he will see that we have the power to buy at a set price. We go on the market and we say that we will buy at that price. Therefore fish are going to be thrown on us if the market does down. That is one way of protecting the fishermen. The other way is by the deficiency payment, which I explained a moment ago, and which was tried by the salt fish board. However, we are not going to use the two tools, if they may be so described, at the same time for the same commodity. We have to use one or the other.

Paragraph agreed to.
Paragraph (d) agreed to.
On section 9, subsection 1, paragraph (e).

Does the department propose to have paragraph (e) made effective; if so, how is it to be carried out? In the speech to-night by the hon, member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare this was represented as being a very important feature in the bill, the government having authority to do the things set out in this paragraph. Is it the intention of the department to have the board exercise the authority given under this paragraph?

Paragraph (e) is consequential to paragraphs (a) and (b). The board1, having the right to purchase, has the right to package, process, store, and do everything that shall be found necessary, either through agents or directly. When section 9 comes into force it might be that the government at that time would have more than one refrigeration plant. It might have a number of them.

Paragraph agreed to.
Paragraphs (f) to (h) inclusive agreed to.
On section 9, subsection 1, paragraph (i).

I have an amendment to paragraph (i) and, without any preliminary discussion, I move, for the purpose of guaranteeing representation on the board by the producer:
That section 9, subsection 1 (i), of Bill No. 169 be amended toy adding thereto the following words: "provided that any boards appointed under this subsection shall include representatives of the primary producers."
I may tell the hon. gentleman that this will be done with

No.
Fisheries Prices

or without the amendment, so that I am not even going to object to the amendment moved by my hon. friend. I accept it.

As I understand it, the amendment refers to "representatives of the primary producers." I was somewhat impressed with the argument along this line by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, as I am always greatly impressed with the arguments advanced by that hon. gentleman. He pointed out that this really does not mean very much. Actually the government can put in anyone, even someone in the department, to represent the producers, so that this looks like a pretty hollow sort of amendment. I should like to have seen it with a few more teeth. As it stands now, the producers can be represented by anyone. Perhaps it is the intention of my hon. friend that the producers themselves should have some say as to who will represent them, but, as I see it, the amendment does not go that far. I believe it lets the government out entirely.

I have in mind that the
fishing industry of eastern Canada, at least, is an organized industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is quite clear in the amendment.
My conception of this amend-is that it would refer to someone from the maritime fishermen's union, for example.

Of course the government will have to choose the members of the board, but this representative will be a man from the primary producers. No doubt we might accept suggestions as to whom he should be, because we want good men, but we must retain the power of appointment.

At least the minister will agree to consider suggestions put forward by fishermen's unions as to who should represent them.
Amendment (Mr. Gillis) agreed to.
Paragraph as amended agreed to.
Paragraph (j) agreed to.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
On section 9, subsection (2)-To maintain returns from fisheries.

I should like to ask the minister for a further statement with respect to the marketing of fish products. I understand that some seventy per cent of our fish products are sold in foreign markets. Has the minister fully canvassed the effect of

government bonuses and assistance in regard to fish that will have to be marketed in other countries, in competition with the products of those countries or other imports? This is an important matter, on which I think we should have a definite statement from the minister.

I do not think that question is relevant to this subsection, which contains a direction to the board to see that these prices are set in such a way that a fair relationship will exist between the returns from fisheries and those from other occupations. It has nothing to do with exports, although I suppose prices might be set for fish that we would have to export. I do not quite understand the question my hon. friend has put to me.
Under this bill the government is going to spend a certain amount of money in order to help the fisheries. I have no doubt that most of the time, if we have to use this legislation, we shall lose money on the resale of the fish we have to buy. According to the law we shall be buying it because prices are too low, and by purchasing it we shall necessarily increase the return to the fishermen. So that when we sell it we shall lose. We might accidentally make a little profit, but the $25,000,000 is to be there to enable us to help the fishermen if prices go too low.

Will you not have cold
storages?

We will use
agents, and they will be the people in the business.
And they have cold storage facilities?
Yes.

The minister has hardly answered my question. I want to know if he has investigated the effect of this bonusing or assistance by the government on the marketing of these fish products in foreign countries. Some seventy per cent of our fish products are marketed in that way, and I want to know if the minister has considered whether we would be prevented from selling in such markets by virtue of the fact that we are bonusing the production or subsidizing the sale of these fish products? .

Well, it is not a subsidy. This has been done under the salt fish board, after the season is over, through the deficiency payments. A subsidy is a payment to all members of a certain class at the same rate, and it is decided in advance. Here the payment is decided after

Questions
the season is over, and it has not been considered as a subsidy in carrying on the affairs of the salt fish board.

Would that apply only to the West Indies market, or has it direct application to the marketing of fish products in the United States? I understood that the United States had stringent laws and regulations with respect to the importation of subsidized commodities.
The United States does not apply any such regulations against our salt fish.

I suggest that the last two lines in this subsection are pure windowdressing and do not mean anything. The subsection reads:
. . . the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for fisheries by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions-
That is fine; that is what they are to do. The rest of it is just pure moonshine:
-and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from fisheries and those from other occupations.
Take a bishop, for instance; how are you going to compare the two, or a blacksmith?
You have to take people on the same level.
It does not say so.
I might tell the hon. gentleman that the idea behind) those words may be found in the brief of the United Maritime Fishermen which the hon. member for Cape Breton South read a few moments ago.
I think the idea is that if a fisherman has to pay $10 for a barrel of flour while he only gets a couple ,of dollars for his fish, the board will take that into consideration.

What I am concerned about is making this board permanent. I am not satisfied with this from war to peace arrangement and I am going to move the following amendment:
That section 9, clause 2, of Bill No. 169 be . amended by striking out all words after the words "board shall" in line ten and substituting therefore the following words:
"ensure adequate and stable returns for fisheries by promoting orderly marketing and shall secure a fair relationship between the returns from fisheries and those from other economic activities.
Rather than a temporary measure, I would like to see it made permanent.

I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
