speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the serious labour situation existing in Montreal at the present moment, will the Minister of Labour give full details as to the causes of the dispute which led to the present transportation tie-up, and the efforts which have been made or are now in contemplation by the government to settle it?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE-CAUSES AND MEASURES FOR SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member gave me notice of this question. It will be recalled that this is the third walk-out of Montreal tramways employees in recent months.
The differences have developed mainly because of union jurisdictional disputes by reason of the fact that some of the employees belong to any one of three different unions, and also due to differences of opinion between the company and its employees in respect to payment of a bonus based on revenue. That is a short and broad history of the dispute.
Since the wartime labour relations board was created the matter of union jurisdiction has been clarified, and the representatives of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees and Other Transport Workers have been certified as the proper bargaining agency for all operational employees.
Since the decision was given by the labour relations board in April of this year, negotiations have been going on between the union and the company with the object of agreeing on the terms of a new contract to replace one made with a committee of employees some years ago. Negotiations in the first instance were direct between the company and the union and at this stage agreements were reached on a number of points.
There had been previously a discussion in regard to payment of a bonus based on earnings of the company, to which I referred a moment ago. The matter was submitted to the national war labour board and the decision of the board was that the bonus was to be paid. Early this week approximately $1,800,000 was paid by the company to the employees in respect of the decision of the national war labour board.
There is also outstanding a question of rates of wages, although it does not enter into the present dispute, which under the law has to be

submitted to the regional war labour board of the province of Quebec, with the right of appeal, of course, to the national war labour board by either party.
There exists to-day the matter of approval of proposed rates of wages, which matter is before the regional war labour board.
The present situation is that agreement has been reached or directions have been given on all the outstanding matters except rate of wages and some of the terms of the agreement.
While all of the details of the terms of the agreement have not been ironed out, the matter which caused the strike is that the union demands that the company require all new employees to join the union within thirty days of the date of employment. This the company refuses to do, giving as its reason, first, the belief that it is the duty of the company to see that men employed by them have freedom of choice as to what union they join, and, secondly, because of the legal advice given to the company that a contract requiring men to join a particular union would- be contrary to the laws of Canada and the province of Quebec.
Agreement has been reached on many of the points as a result of a recommendation made by a board of conciliation set up by the Department of Labour under the wartime labour relations regulations in connection with the voluntary check-off, which was further agreed to yesterday at a conference at which I was present between, the company and the employees.
On the point which has created the strike, the members of the board of conciliation were divided, each one of1 the three members expressing a different point of view. The report of the board of conciliation was given publicity by the department, and when it became clear that no agreement was in sight, I wired the two parties as follows:
Regarding the matter of the Montreal Tramways and the position taken by the solicitors for the company. My understanding of the -matter is that differences between the company and the men could be cleared -up except on the question of one .point and in this connection on behalf of the -men you are asking that new employees be required to join and remain members of the union during the life of the contract.' The position taken by the company in this respect being that this would involve the company in an act which was contrary to the laws of the province of Quebec. I have consulted with the Minister of Justice and after doing so am proposing to you that the department appoint a superior court judge as a commissioner to bring in a report on the matter which would constitute advice among other things as to the legal status I respectfully urge your consideration of this suggestion and that you

Montreal Tramways Strike
request your committee to aecept the proposal as one which would be of definite assistance in helping to bring about a settlement of the dispute. If the foregoing is acceptable I will appoint commissioner immediately. If the proposal is not acceptable I would suggest that you and two or three others representing the men come to Ottawa together with representatives of the company to discuss the situation with me. Kindly advise.
In response to this wire I was advised by the company that it would accept the proposal for the appointment of a commission and I was advised by the union that the proposal was not accepted.	.
Arrangements were made for representatives of the company and the men to see me and officers of my department and a lengthy conference was held with them yesterday. At the conference yesterday some points of difference were cleared up-that is the check-off I mentioned a moment ago-but on the main point as to whether or not new men would be required to join the union within thirty days of the date of their employment, agreement was not reached.
In addition to the proposal that I appoint a commissioner, two other proposals to settle the dispute were made. The first was that the matter be arbitrated by a board of three men. one to be appointed by the company, one to be appointed by the men, with an independent chairman on the understanding that the decision would be binding on both parties. The company' offered to agree to this proposal, but representatives of the union stated that the proposal would not be acceptable to the men. The second proposal made yesterday was that the company sign the agreement with the disputed clause included but with a rider that the clause would not come into effect until it was stated by the Supreme Court of Canada that it would be proper and legal for the company to enter into this agreement.
I promised on behalf of the government that if this proposal was accepted the government would refer the matter to the supreme court for a decision on two points: (a) whether or not. the dominion wartime labour relations regulations superseded the Public Employees' Dispute Act of the province of Quebec, and (b) whether or not the company could legally enter into the contract asked for by the union. This latter proposal was acceptable to the company and was in part acceptable to the union. However, the negotiations broke down because the union demanded that the terms of the paragraph go into effect immediately and if found illegal by the court would be cancelled, whereas the company took the position that they could not put the paragraph into force until the matter had been clarified by the court.
The department has been giving a great deal of attention to the whole case. I would say that I do not know of any labour dispute within my memory in which greater efforts have been put forth with a view to settlement. In saying this I have in mind all governments, and I have some knowledge of different governments which have been in power-and I am not speaking in a personal sense. We went through the normal procedure of certification and established a conciliation .board, and when the men, could not agree to the terms of the recommendation of that board we sent, a judge who tried to compose the differences. In addition to that, we sent the chairman of the wartime labour relations board last week to try to compose this difference, and of course there was the long conference I had yesterday in the final stage. The officials of the department have been in constant touch with the situation. I think that about covers the ground.

It is quite true there have been recent reductions in airgraph postage rates from ten to five cents, and the air-letter form for prisoners in Germany has been reduced from ten cents to five cents, while the air-letter form to prisoners of war and internees in the far east has also been reduced from ten cents to five cents. To Italy and Sicily the rate was 60 cents for the first pound and $1.10 for three pounds and following pounds much higher than our rate. The actual cost of handling these parcels in Canada, paying cost of transportation overseas, and land charges, exceeds 12 cents. We are actually handling these parcels at less than cost at the present time. In view of the fact that any reduction would cost approximately a quarter of a million a year for every cent of reduction, it is not felt that a reduction can be made at this time unless more favourable rates can be negotiated.

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendment made by the senate to bill No. 163, to amend the Special War Revenue Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: May I ask the minister if the government is satisfied with this amendment, and what was the reason for the change?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. C. ABBOTT (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The government is satisfied with the amendment. The change is a minor one, having to do with the drafting of the bill. The section in question is section 113 of the Special War Revenue Act, relating to the requirement with respect to the keeping of records and books by persons who are collectors of taxes or who are required to affix or cancel stamps. The section as originally drafted read:
Every person required, by or pursuant, to this act, to pay or collect taxes or other sums or to affix or cancel stamps shall keep records and books of account in English or French at his place of business in Canada in such form and containing such information as, in the opinion of the minister, will enable an audit to be made to establish the amount of taxes or other sums that should have been paid or collected or the amount of stamps that should have been affixed or cancelled.
The senate amendment has taken out the words "as in the opinion of the minister will enable an audit to be made" and substituted the words, "as will enable the amount of taxes or other sums that should have been paid or collected, or the amount of stamps that should have been affixed or cancelled, to be determined." It is a minor amendment, and is entirely satisfactory.

I am not quarrelling with the point raised by the minister; it is immaterial as far as I am concerned. AVhat I am concerned about is that I interpret the bill as it now stands to be merely a temporary measure, because it definitely states that these functions are to be carried on only during the period of transition from war to peace. That is the part with which I am quarrelling. The amendment I propose would strike out the words dealing with the transition from war to peace conditions, and make at least this part of the bill a permanent set-up that can be carried forward into the peace. As I see it, the operation of this measure could be terminated at any time, or at least this feature of it, if someone should determine that we had made the transition from war to peace, which might merely mean that when the war is over, when demobilization is complete and all the soldiers are back in this country, we shall have made the transition from war to peace without the necessary adjustments in our economy to take care of the measures which this bill is designed to meet, namely the reestablishment and organization of the fishing industry, and the endeavour to establish parity prices for the fishermen. This measure, as provided under the present -section, can be terminated at any time. The minister's statement that the department would "endeavour" to ensure is immaterial. I thought it was better to say "ensure" than "endeavour". Some very weak endeavours can be made, and they do not accomplish much. But if the language in the bill is emphatic, and gives instructions to those who will be administering it, then there is a greater pressure on the administration to do something about the provisions contained in the bill. They would do more in that way than if they were just weakly told that they should endeavour. The purpose of my amendment is to give permanency to this provision rather than just to make it a transitional provision to be effective in the period between war and peace-a period which could be defined as concluded when demobilization is completed.

speechtext: I am advised that there has been nothing since notice was given that item 442 would be amended. I say that I am so advised. The minister is in the banking and commerce committee but will be here in a moment, and perhaps my hon. friend would like to have his question stand until the minister is here.

My purpose in making the inquiry was that I was anxious to know whether agriculture and industry, both being affected, had made representations to the government since the provisions of the legislation became kftown.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There have been no representations from agriculture.
Or from industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. There were immediate representations from industry, that some tariff concessions must be made on materials entering into the manufacture of parts. I think that covers the field.

This section provides that the act shall be deemed to have come into force on June 27 last and its provisions are retroactive-a wrong principle-to that date. The bill also gives the officers of the department power to interpret all the items in the schedules attached, which gives them the force of statutes. That is too much power to put into the hands of the executive. Revenue statutes should be construed strictly, and they are so construed by courts of law. But we are leaving it to departmental officials to interpret these various items in the schedules. As a parliament we are delegating our authority to the executive, just as we have been doing all this session in connection with almost every statute passed by this house. This house just passes on the general principle and then we leave it to departmental officers to say what the regulations shall be and what the inter-

pretation shall be in all these matters affecting trade and commerce. That is one of the objections that business and trade and commerce are having to contend with to-day. They have great difficulty' in getting an interpretation of the custom tariff. It is a most elaborate affair to make application to the department for an interpretation. There are delays, and artificial burdens and barriers are placed in the way of large and small business.
I have protested against this before, and I intend to continue to protest against it because we are building up in this country a bureaucracy that makes it impossible for any business man to conduct his business.
These regulations and restrictions are becoming intolerable, and more than that, penalties are provided for violation of the regulations. The Habeas Corpus Act has been suspended and the Bill of Rights and the legal clauses of magna charta. These regulations and restrictions not only interfere with the liberty of the subject but make things an offence which never have been considered an offence in peace time. In Great Britain twenty thousand people have been fined for infractions of their regulations, and three thousand people have been imprisoned. Such a thing never happened in time of peace' and if I am the only member to rise in his place and protest against this I am going to do it. although I realize that both the minister and his parliamentary assistant, who is doing very good work, have a very difficult task. I can say that as a private member of the house. I wish to give the department every support but I do hope that when the budget is brought down next year parliament will not delegate its authority in this way. In the British house the same objections wrere made when Sir John Anderson, the chancellor of the exchequer, presented his budget with similar schedules to what we have here. Several members took part in that debate and forced the government to make changes to make the schedules more specific so that parliament would not be a mere rubber stamp, and by these schedules and rules that is all we are here. I hope that I have not offended any member's dignity. I do not want to ask the leader of my party here to have to rise in his place and defend me. I have made this suggestion, Mr. Chairman, in all' sincerity to the ministry and the department, and I hope that before another year goes by we may see an end to this intolerable situation and say in exact words what each item is and means. Our friends in the far east corner have been talking about a new and a better world to come. I say, let us get back to the days of 1939 and try to restore

Customs Tariff
the freedom and liberty we had then. In those days the business man, large and small, had a chance to do business.

Has the minister given
further consideration to the representations that were made on the resolution stage as to the date on which these items will become effective? The date fixed here is September 30, but representations were made that the date should be moved forward. Has further consideration been given to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Intensive and prolonged
attention has been given to that question with the result that we are all of the opinion that the date, September 30, cannot possibly be changed, and I will give the reasons.
In the debate which took place on the evening of July 20 some hon. members expressed dissatisfaction with order No. 421 of the wartime prices and trade board in which directions were given respecting the lowering of ceiling prices on repair parts for agricultural implements to become effective after September 30, 1944. Some fears were expressed that certain importers could import large quantities of these repair parts between June 26 and September 30 free of duty and exchange tax and by continuing their sale at ceiling prices up to the effective date of the order thereby defeat the purpose of the budget amendments, which were designed to lower the prices of these repair parts to the farmer. I have looked into the question carefully and have reached the conclusion that the board has taken not only the most practical course in all the circumstances, but as well, the one which will most effectively give the farmer the benefit of this policy at the earliest possible date. In the first place hon. members should understand that upwards of 80,000 pricing items are involved in this change.
I have just sent up to my office for a few of the lists to show them to the house. They are appalling in their magnitude, and if mem- -bers could look at them they would see the principle on which these prices are made up and how impossible it would be for any government body to go over them quickly, take out of the prices there the amount which is represented by war exchange tax and duty, and create a new price list; or, for that matter, for the companies themselves to do it. Certainly it would be impossible for the companies to do it and get out new price lists.
Let me repeat. In the first place, hon. members should understand that upwards of eighty thousand pricing items are involved in this case. There are well over ten thousand dealers throughout the country who handle the sale of these repair parts, and all of them work
from price lists issued by the implement companies setting out in detail the price of each item. These price lists do not indicate which items are imported and which are of domestic manufacture. There is considerable variation in this respect between different companies, as some manufacture domestically items which may be imported by other companies, and vice versa. The percentage of the price which represents exchange tax and duty also varies between each company and between the individual items; that is to say, there is no uniform percentage applicable to the extraordinarily lengthy list of repair parts, so that each and every item has to be adjusted in accordance with whatever pricing formula may have been adopted when the duty was applied and when the war exchange tax was levied. Consequently, it is not possible effectively to pass on desired price reductions without a complete revision of these price lists, and as I have indicated this is a task of considerable magnitude. I am informed that in normal times the preparation, printing and distribution of these price lists would take from four to six months and under present day conditions the difficulties are appreciably greater. Notwithstanding this, however, the board has set the effective date at September 30, which would appear to be the minimum period possible. I want to say that the strongest representations were made that that date would have to be later than September 30 because of the great difficulties involved, but that the board insisted on getting it back to September.
May I interrupt the minister? Prom whom did he receive these representations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From, I think, the implement companies. I do not think it was the dealers; I think it was the implement companies.
It was not from the agents; it was from the implement companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think so. The implement companies are the ones who have to get out the new lists.
Here are some of the lists. There are thousands and thousands of different items with very small amounts charged for each. I have opened this just at random. Here are some items:
No.	Price	Description	CodeGK 1508	, .. .18	adj. washer....	. RTGK 1503	... .68	connection ....	. RTGK 1519	... .08	stud 	. RTGK 1524	,.. .15	collar	. RT
There are thousands and thousands of these which would have to be adjusted, perhaps by a cent or half a cent or something of that
Customs Tariff

kind; and the task of a government body to do that., and pass on this, and do a job which would be at all respectable or would stand up, is impossible to perform.
I should like to know how it is that it is so easy for them to make any increase. That applies to what has happened in years gone by.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it is not easy. I shall come to that.
The second point of interest is that potential imports during the three months period are strictly limited because of quota restrictions and the physical difficulty of obtaining supplies under present day conditions. The production of these parts in the United States is under a rigid production schedule which cannot be altered without government approval. For these and other reasons having to do with production under wartime conditions I can assure the members that no increase in imports can possibly take place over this three months period beyond what had been already # scheduled.
The real point at issue, it seems to me, is whether or not the procedure followed by the board has carried out the wishes of government. On that point I am completely satisfied, namely, that having in mind the practicalities of the situation the price reduction is being made effective as quickly as possible and in a way to secure the best benefit to the farmer consumer. It is difficult to forecast precisely the actual results because it is impossible to obtain the actual inventory position of the larger number of dealers involved in this trade. In one test case made, however, which is regarded as representative, the following results were apparent:
Inventory in hands of dealers, on
July 1, 1944	 $494,604
Imports allocated July to Sept. 30....	178,000
Total available for sale	 672,604
Estimate of sales during period		325,000
Estimated inventory on Oct.	1	 $347,604
In this typical example it will be observed that farmer consumers will receive a price reduction on purchases after October 1 on inventory totalling $347,000 and have paid the old price on only $178,000 additional. One further point is that as at June 30 the great bulk of inventory is in the hands of these 10,000 dealers and not in the hands of implement companies. It would be manifestly unfair to reduce maximum prices in such a way that these dealers should take the loss involved and I understand from statements made by some hon. members during the former debate that no such desire is in their minds.
TMr. Ilsley.]
Could the minister tell me how many dealers in the country there would be who would have to take the loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ten thousand.
The dealer would not take that loss; it would be the companies, and if they would divide that up like they do when they slap it on for us, I do not think there would be very much difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the price were brought down as of June 26 it would have to be a reduction of the price which the dealer would charge, would it not?
The point is that a large number of these dealers carry on consignment; they do not pay for the parts until they are sold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would want to look into that affirmation. There are not ten thousand agents, or anything like it, of implement companies selling parts. As I understand it, hardware stores and even blacksmith shops and dealers all over the country are in this business. To put a compulsory price reduction in effect on June 26 so that they sell at a loss is something which we cannot contemplate. Whatever hon. gentlemen want to do with the implement companies you could not do it with these dealers.
One other possibility, however, was examined by the board, namely to investigate the possibility of making the price reductions effective immediately and refunding the dealers for the tax and duty already paid. This course was found to be quite impracticable. As already pointed out, the inventory could not be identified in any event, and further, the administrative task of trying to deal with claims from ten thousand dealers involving some eighty thousand items seemed quite impossible.
One final point is the assumption made by some members that the implement companies and dealers were permitted to add the tax immediately when it was imposed in 1940 and thereby profiteered at the expense of the farmer. I am unable to find that such a criticism is warranted. The same difficulty about getting out amended price lists existed at that time. The question the hon. gentleman asked was a perfectly intelligent one. He said, how could they amend their price lists so fast in 1940 if it takes them so much time in 1944? That is an intelligent question; the answer is that in most cases they did not. I will go on.
Moreover, section 6 of the War Exchange Conservation Act specifically prohibited the adding of the tax to any items on which tax

Customs Tariff
had not been paid. But as I have pointed: out, it was impossible to identify the parts in the hands of dealers between those on which tax had been paid and those on which it had not. Consequently, there may have been cases in which individual dealers took improper advantage of the situation in respect of.specific items. There was considerable diversity of method in regard to the practice followed by the implement companies. In one case, for example, prices were increased immediately by a flat percentage and this increase continued for a couple of months, after which it was cancelled and refunds made to purchasers in that period. Ultimately the revised prices went into effect at the beginning of 1941. In other cases the time lag varied from six to ten weeks and as previously stated the price and procedures followed between the companies were by no means uniform.
I hope hon. members will agree that in a pioblem of this complexity the board, in passing order No. 421, has followed the best course for all concerned, and that it has the additional great advantage of achieving a uniform price reduction on a specific date.
This question was raised the other night and it has given me a great deal of trouble. I wanted to see if we could institute a two-price system, and was satisfied, before I had gone into it very far, that it was absolutely impossible to do so. We could bring the date back from September 30 to August 30, in which event there would be a larger proportion of goods on which the implement companies and dealers would take a loss and a smaller proportion on which they would obtain a profit. I took that up with the board and Mr. Gordon gave it his personal attention. He went over the question thoroughly because he was most anxious not to leave his board open to the accusation that they had done something in the interests of the implement companies and against the interests of the farmers. He was anxious to see that the directions which I gave to. the board in the budget speech, to ensure that the advantage of this reduction was passed on to the farmers, should be carried out. It was impossible, for the reasons I have stated, to take precisely the items that came in on June 26 and make a lower price on these items. It was impossible to institute that two-price system on these 80,000 items. It was utterly impossible to examine the inventories and find out what they were and how many were brought in before and how many afterwards, even if it were desirable to have a two-price system. Therefore the only thing to do was to set a date and to say, " Whenever you
brought it in, whether you paid tax on it or not, if you sell it after that date the new price has to go down, and whatever you sell before that date you can sell on your existing price list." That was the only practical way of doing it. I discussed the matter with a member of this house, a member on this side who is very much interested, and I think I can say that if he were here he would say that he concluded it was the only practical method to adopt. Then it comes to a question of the date, and we cannot administratively do it before September 30. Even if we could, however, taking the instance I have given, it would be unjust to the dealers-forget about the implement companies-to move the date back too far because they take a loss on too large a proportion of the inventory and have too small a profit to offset against it. I have done the best I can in the circumstances. I know what will be said about it and I shall not be there to answer as I have done to-day. But that is the best that I can do.

I agree with the minister
that he has done all he can; I am prepared to say that. He did what he could, knowing the circumstances as he does. At the same time, I would point out to him that his advisers in all probability have paid too much attention to one side of the picture and have ignored the other. They have given him some sort of idea as to how many repair parts would be brought in from June 26 to August 30,1 suppose. Have they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could get that, but they have not given it to me. I do not know.
They could bring them in without duty and have them with the other stock piles and make a profit on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They took what they regarded as a typical case and I gave the figures just now. Certainly the farmers as a whole do not lose and the dealers do not profit on the selection of the date of September 30. I could get figures such as the hon. member has asked for but they would be estimates. We know how much can come in before September 30; it is the balance of the United States allocation and it is strictly limited. They cannot speed up imports. There was a fear that they would profiteer by getting parts from the United States and selling them before September 30 but they cannot do that because we know exactly how much the country can get from the United States and the quantity is limited. However, I can find out roughly, though there would be a large element of estimate in it, how much their floor stock was
Customs Tariff

on June 26. I am assured that there will be a large volume of parts on hand on September 30 on which they must take a lower price. In this case, the estimated inventory on October 1 is 347,604. Some of these parts do not sell for years.

Has there been a greater quantity of these imported parts brought in since this came into force than last year? How much difference is there between importations under the new regulations and those previously?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not the information
but I am positively assured that the amount is limited. It is not at the option of t}ie importer or of Canada. It is allocated by some combined board in Washington. We can get so much, and we can get the remainder of our allocation for a certain period, and that is all that can come in.

The impression seems to be abroad that the companies have taken advantage of the situation and brought in more repair parts than they did previously. Whether that is right, I am not prepared to say. The minister should know. So far as the implement dealers are concerned, we should not leave it to them to assume responsibility for the loss; they must be protected where implements are in their hands. But it is the companies bringing implements in now that we should get after.
What action is the government taking to check the new list that will be used on September 30 to see that they too reflect the necessary reductions? Are they taking action?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. That is the responsibility of the wartime prices and trade board. They must assume their full responsibility and see that the directions I gave in the budget speech are carried out. To the extent that the laid-down cost to the importer is reduced, that reduction must be passed on to those who purchase from the importer.

When I discussed this matter before, I was satisfied, from experience I have had with dealers, that the implement companies of this country are a very up-to-date outfit. Every week they receive a return and they know exactly how many parts there are in every warehouse. These warehouses are supplied so that the farmer gets service. There is keen competition. In every little hamlet in the western provinces the companies know exactly how many spare parts there are available and where. I complained to the min-

ister because they had the figures. They are up-to-date figures. They could put their finger on any repair part. The implement companies are up-to-date going concerns. If I go to Winnipeg and ask for some repair part they might say they have not got it, but they ask me to wait a minute and then they tell me that there is a dealer in Saskatoon that has it and that they will get it down for me. They know their business thoroughly. They are in a position to be just a little cleverer than the minister in finding out the figures. I agree with the minister and I appreciate what he has done for us. I am sorry that he did not put gasoline engines on the list. I had a special interview with him and told him about it. If a mower or binder is essential on a farm, so is a small gasoline engine. I am awfully disappointed that the minister was not able to put gasoline engines on the list. If I call up any of those companies in Ontario or western Canada and ask them if one of those little gasoline engines is on the agricultural list they will say "yes." I would like the minister to give further consideration to it.

I should like to remind the minister that while it is quite true that a hardware store here or a private dealer there may have some parts and may continue to sell some of them, yet by and large the bulk of the repair parts are handled by the machine companies. As the hon. member for Selkirk has pointed out they are handled by their agents, but the stock belongs to the company. All that the agent has to do is to give an accounting of what he has sold. The articles that remain belong to the company. The company knows where they are and how much the agents have on hand.

I do not think that is' quite a correct statement. When the parts come in to the implement dealers they buy them. They are responsible for the sale. It may be that what is left over after a certain period is taken back by the implement companies.	[DOT]

There is something in what the last speaker has just said. I think there are a number of service men who are required by their respective companies to carry a stock of repair parts. I believe that most of those parts are paid for by the individual dealers. They are not on consignment. But the point is not really a pressing one at this time, because I do not think that we as a parliament should attempt to put a loss on the manufacturer any more than on the dealer by virtue of a change in the customs tariff. The hon. member for Selkirk

Customs Tariff
hit the nail on the head and spoke with some knowledge of the business when he said that an inventory is kept by the dealer and by the company whom he represents of all stock on hand from day to day, and that they are well informed at all times. That being the case I do not think the difficulty or the impracticability that the minister has mentioned of ascertaining the stocks on hand at different dates would be as great as the minister seems to suggest. I believe it could be ascertained very easily. Regardless of the date on which the price is changed and the tariff is dropped, if a dealer or manufacturer has stock on hand on which he has paid duty I believe he should be refunded that amount by the government.
During the last war a great deal of difficulty was caused when the tax on motor cars was dropped. Many dealers had motor cars on hand on which they had paid the tax, and it was not refunded. It took some years before it was actually adjusted and the tax rebated to the dealer. I do not think the. minister's difficulties are anything like what he thinks they are in respect to refunding any customs duty that was paid and in ascertaining what stocks are on hand either in the manufacturer's plant or in the dealer's hands. These people would be very efficient in finding out just how much they have on hand on which the various customs duties have been paid. The minister would be well advised to explore the possibility. He will find that exact and reliable information can be given at any date as to what stock is on hand.

With respect to the list that the minister has in front of him, there is no doubt that it is large and detailed, but the greatest reduction that will come about in repair parts will come from the removal of the war exchange tax. It would be a very simple matter for them to use the old books that they had before the war exchange tax was put into effect. Is the ten per cent war exchange tax on gasoline engines being removed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
I cannot understand why not. It is a protective measure as far as manufacture in this country is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. member talking about imported engines or domestic engines?

Imported engines. I am talking about the small gasoline engines used on the farm. They are imported. They are engines made for the John Deere company, the International Harvester and Massey Harris in the United States. I really cannot see why
the war exchange tax should not be removed, even though you might have to change the tariff. The war exchange tax is a temporary war measure placed into effect for the conservation of exchange. If I understand the situation aright, the measure was not introduced in order to protect industry; therefore I cannot see any reason why it should not be removed so far as it applies to gasoline engines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The war exchange tax yields us $128,000,000 altogether. We cannot give that up as a jvhole. There are all kinds of people who ask us to pick out this item or that item and take the war exchange tax off it, because it would reduce their costs so much. We just have to turn them down. Up until the time we took it off agricultural implements, as that term has always been understood, and as they are grouped in the tariff, we did not remove the war exchange tax at all except as a means of keeping the price level down, enabling the price ceiling to be observed. We made an exception in our tariff treatment of agricultural implements. I must repeat that I cannot be pushed inch by inch into a general revision of the tariff. I am sticking to agricultural implements; that applies to duty and war exchange tax. There are people all over this house who would make a remarkable speech so far as their constituents are concerned by saying: I should like to have the war exchange tax off this, I should like to have the duty off that. But we cannot go on that way. The hon. member is not the only one who wants the war exchange tax off; farmers are not the only ones who would like to have the war exchange tax off. There are all kinds of people who would like to have it off, but that cuts into a revenue item which yielded us nearly $130,000,000. I am not prepared to let that go.

Probably the minister
might look upon the gasoline engine as being a little different from any other machine, because it is an essential agricultural machine. It is a great labour-saving device to the farmer. If he will look at the peculiar position in which we find ourselves so far as labour is concerned I think he will realize that it is of great interest to the agricultural industry, and on that basis alone he would be well advised to give serious consideration to a reduction in the tax on gasoline engines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, I presume it would create some popularity with some people; but hon. members must remember that this house is simply demanding that we pour out money for many purposes-

Canadian Broadcasting Act
And we are suffering because you are doing so voluntarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and they must have a little regard for our desire to preserve some revenue items.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We are just pushing you on your own free trade principles.

I do think the government should reconsider their position with respect to what are classed as agricultural implements, if gasoline engines are not included. While they may not have been agricultural implements thirty years ago, certainly they are to-day. The list of agricultural implements must be changed to meet changing conditions in agriculture, and anyone who operates a farm of any size at all knows these engines are a necessity; they are used for a dozen different purposes. I believe any farmer will agree that if they are not classified as agricultural implements, certainly there should be a revision of the list as it applies to our tariff. I will ask the minister to give serious consideration to going over the present list of agricultural implements and1 bringing them up to date to comply with modern conditions in agriculture.

Section agreed to.
Schedule A agreed to.
Schedule B agreed to.

a second time I want to ask just one question about it. I believe this proposal which comes to us from one of the committees-I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker; I thought we were in committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
A number of matters no doubt will come up for discussion when this bill goes to committee, but before that is done I should like to again register my objection to this method of improving the set-up of the Canadian broadcasting corporation. During the debate on the resolution I tried to make it clear that the appointment of a full-time chairman will not remedy our broadcasting difficulties. I think I made it clear, too, that instead of this being a step in the right direction I believe it to be a retrograde step. We have been placing the cart before the horse in connection with the C.B.C. for a good many years, and as a result the real meat of the problem has not been really tackled since the beginning of the w'ar.
In 1940 and 1941 appeals were made for the setting up of a committee on radio broadcasting. The government in its wisdom-though I regret to say they did not display wisdom in that connection-time and again refused to accede to the request of the opposition for such a committee. During that period while the searchlight of public inquiry was kept from this corporation it drifted into a position which in 1942. when the committee met for the first time, clearly showed that the affairs of the corporation should have been properly inquired into and investigated before. The report of the committee on that occasion was not in my opinion a true representation of the conditions that existed. Many of us at that time found it impossible to make that report unanimous, because we felt that it did not go far enough in castigation, first of all of the government itself which in the final analysis had the real responsibility for radio having come to such a position. There was scarcely a word in the report in censure of the government. Why, you would think. the government had practically no responsibility, and that it had carried out perfectly what little responsibility it might have had. As a matter of fact, however, the government failed in its primary duty of keeping the board of governors complete, let alone seeing to it that the right men were appointed. The ranks of the board of governors were almost continually decimated, because the government did not fill them as vacancies occurred.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
The committee of 1942 did not bring in the sort of report I would have brought in, or the sort of report that would have been brought in by several others who were on the committee. That report made it as easy as possible for the government. This is not intended as a reflection upon those who served on the committee. It is a statement of fact, as I saw it; the committee did not criticize the government as much as it should have been criticized. Now we find that while that report should have been enough to compel every member of the board of governors to resign, they all stayed where they were. It is true that some changes have occurred through the efflux of time, but the fact is that the government has only temporized with the real root of the problem, and I say we are still temporizing with it.
The present position in my opinion is a disgrace and a scandal to Canada. I cannot find words strong enough to indicate my feelings with respect to it. I do not know of a single reason why this great corporation, charged with heavy responsibilities in both peace and war, should be left without a general manager ever since last September. This means that we will have been without a general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for a period of almost twelve months. Time after time in this house during the present session we have called-I have done it myself-for the appointment of a general manager. If a general manager is of any use to the corporation, he should be appointed. And if there is no use for a general manager, there should not be one. It should be either one thing or the other. But there is no excuse for one of the major corporations controlled by this government, one of the major corporations under the aegis or control of this government, being left in that condition.
There is, of course, a grave difficulty, from the legal point of view, as to just where this corporation does fit in as a government enterprise. I have dealt with that matter before, and I shall not discuss it again now. But I do say this: Here we are now being asked to appoint a paid chairman for this corporation, after having allowed the general managership to remain vacant for almost twelve months. Is there any wonder that some of us would like to speak with some feeling in this matter?-because I do not think what is being done is fair to public ownership broadcasting in Canada.
From time to time I have expressed my views clearly with respect to public ownership of radio broadcasting. I think the set-up which exists with respect to private enterprise having its share and its fair opportunity
100-368*
alongside a public ownership corporation will perhaps not meet with criticism if regard is had for the interests of Canadian listeners and the Canadian people generally. But while we believe that-and I say this as emphatically as I can-we also believe that the whole texture, the whole fabric, the whole structure of public ownership radio broadcasting is imperilled and endangered by the fact that we have allowed this managerial condition to exist. How long would a private broadcasting corporation, a private station, or any private enterprise be able to get along if they allowed their general managership to remain vacant for a year? It would not be tolerated at all.
I was hoping some plan would be laid before the house long before this under which the position with respect to the managerial or executive staff of the corporation would be such that the public would at least have confidence in the way in which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is being operated. We have had no intimation from the minister or the government or from the board of governors as to when a general manager for this corporation will be appointed. We do hear rumours through the newspapers to the effect that the assistant general manager is likely to be moved up. We hear the rumour, too that a new assistant general manager is to be appointed. We are now asked by way of legislation, to add to the corporation a $15,000-a-year job. I must say however that this is only rumour, and I do not wish the minister to take it that I suggest that will be the amount. .But people are wondering why we need another $15,000-a-year job on top of the jobs which never have been filled in the corporation. It seems to me that that is a ridiculous proposal, until there is some plan and some scheme whereby radio can again be put on its proper footing.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation ought to have a great future in this country. I have been fearful and I have been anxious with respect to that future. On many occasions I have been criticized; but no one has ever heard me criticize, except for the purpose of trying to make our radio system a better system for the people of Canada. Because I believe if we were ever to reach the position where this public ownership broadcasting enterprise were denied its proper place, we would be talcing a retrograde step for the whole of the dominion.
All this temporizing and all this delay and all this drift is not good for our radio system. I do appeal to the minister, I do urge upon him with all the emphasis I can command, and with every conviction, to make sure that.
Canadian Broadcasting Act

we do have a set-up of broadcasting in Canada which will be a credit to the country, to the government, to parliament and to the corporation itself.
There will be some who will say that my criticisms in respect of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are pretty severe. But my criticisms of that corporation are not half as severe as the criticism of the corporation which has been emanating right from the corporation itself. Up until recently one could not help hearing the criticism which came from those who were within the corporation. I do not like to hear that. We in parliament have a responsibility to see that this broadcasting set-up works; I do not think we can make it work by making effective the foolish policy and the principles set out in a bill such as this. We are loading up the corporation with more jobs. We are loading up the corporation with more paid men. I would like to see the paid men who are already in there placed in a position where they can carry out the job, instead of allowing jobs to remain vacant, not merely from day to day, from week to week, but from month to month, stretching almost into a year. It is not fair to the country; it is not fair to the public, and it is not fair to the corporation. And if my castigations of the corporation's policies in the past and at the present time are severe and strongly worded, they arise from convictions which I hold' sincerely. Because if there is one single thing I should like to see [DOT]come from heavy criticism of the Canadian Broadcasting System it is that we: should finally emerge with a better publicly controlled enterprise, one giving the kind of service originally envisaged by the act, a service which the fathers of the broadcasting system in this country actually intended it should be. That should be the object of every one of us so far as broadcasting in general is concerned.
I leave this message with the minister. We need a change with respect to the whole set-up of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This bill does not suggest the way in which that can best be done. For that reason I cannot support the measure, nor is my party able at this time to do so, although we would like to have some plan or some scheme set forth which would really solve all the problems which so badly need solution..

The house resumed at three o'clock.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
I wish to express to the minister my appreciation of some of the changes which have already been 
made by the corporation. Radio is a public utility of very great magnitude and of great importance to the people of this country. It is one of the means of communication between the families of soldiers at home and the boys overseas, but like every other great invention, use is one thing and abuse is another.
I have been a friend and admirer of the minister for many years for the part he played in the last war and for what he did for the soldiers in our district, but I must say to the minister that before he took charge of his department there was widespread dissatisfaction with the conduct of this great public utility. On the other hand, it has been a revelation to the people of Canada what this great public utility could do if properly administered.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, there should be no board at all. I remember when the act was passed in 1936. At that time the former leader of my party objected to what had been said at the first meeting of the board. Some of the officers had set out to do something which was illegal under the constitution. They announced with a great flourish of trumpets that instead of making the corporation serve all the provinces they were going to use it for the benefit of one province and were out to make Canada a bilingual country. I have never believed that was to be the peculiar function of radio. I believe in equal rights for all the provinces.
The vast possibilities of the radio and of this organization are perhaps not realized yet throughout the country. It is spending about five and a half million dollars a year. It controls about seventy-five per cent of the stations, has two short-wave stations and one more is being built. The organization comprises 749 to 810 employees. So that it is a large corporation.
Radio affects the lives of people of every class morning, afternoon and evening, in peace time and in war, in matters of trade, industry and commerce, amusements, music and education. On Sundays particularly a splendid service could be given if rightly used, free of advertising.
I would point out that we are not getting the return we should get from the licence fee of $2.50. I think it would be interesting to have figures as to prosecutions for nonpayment of the licence fee. I am told that a large number of owners of radio sets in the city of Ottawa do not pay the licence fee, also a large number in Quebec and many other places throughout Canada. Perhaps the minister would give us figures on the number of prosecutions in the different provinces for non-payment of the licence fee.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
The corporation was set up in 1936. Previously the head of our party had appointed a royal commission which travelled all over the world and investigated radio in different countries, visiting Japan among others, and then the commission made its report. The Corporation was set up but it was never intended to be like the laws of the Medes and Persians, unchangeable. The set-up of the corporation from 1936 until now has been weighed in the balance and found wanting.
Talk about appointing a chairman! It was announced over the radio that the chairman was to get a salary of $15,000 but according to the bill the governor in council is to fix the salary. The trouble with all these boards is that there are too many figureheads. Yesterday I was listening to a debate in this house on controls and advisory boards. We are appointing boards and committees all over Canada whose members serve without salary. My hon. friend the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) who is not in the house to-day -I think he is away at the election-and the admiral of the fleet of the bay of Quinte, the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario (Mr. Fraser), have criticized the appointment of dollar-a-year men to these boards and have told how they occupy needed hotel rooms and crowd the trains travelling to and fro. It would be better to pay some of these men five or ten or fifteen thousand dollars a year salary than pay some of their expenses. There are lots of people who would serve on the corporation without salary. The corporation should be abolished. There should be no board and no chairman. There should be just one chief executive officer. A departmental store runs a bigger business than is run by the corporation and does it without all these boards and executive officers.
I believe that the committee has done a splendid work. One good thing it has done is that it has brought this corporation's affairs and every dollar of its expenditure under the control of parliament, and that has had a salutary effect, although up until two years ago the fact remains that if we asked questions in parliament about any official of the board we could not get an answer because we were told in those years that the corporation was independent of parliament. [DOT]
Some of the radio programmes give one a headache. Some people turn the radio off because it reminds them, our soldiers' families particularly, too much of the war. I appreciate that the minister 'has made in some ways a very fine contribution in improving the system, and I hope that he will be able to eliminate some of the abuses. I believe a
recommendation was made to the minister three or four months ago that applications for licences to run four new broadcasting stations should be approved by the board of governors, but no action has been taken.
Many of the employees of the corporation are appointed under the patronage system. It is hard to get technical men for some radio work because radio is still in its infancy. We cannot measure in the future its ultimate possibilities, if rightly used and applied, for the happiness of our people. Nothing has contributed more than radio to the education of our people except the motor car, which has also contributed to their education. But as I said, use is one thing and abuse is another. I wish the minister and his department every success, but I fail to see the necessity for appointing a chairman. It will be a duplicate system, not needed. He will be nothing but a figurehead. He will come and look around the offices all day long and worry everybody who is connected with the system. But nowadays we are appointing boards for this and boards for that, and chief executive officers of all kinds who are unnecessary and only add to the cost of governing the country and lessen efficiency of a concern that should be administered from the commercial aspect.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take very long in discussing this bill. First of all, the good things that have been, said to-day about the work of the C.B.C. are well deserved. In the past two years the employees of the corporation have given a good service to the Canadian people and are doing worth-while work. We can all be proud of the w'ork that the C.B.C. has done. Looking back over the. years one realizes how the taste in good music and in drama has improved, the interest that has been awakened in discussion groups and so on, because we have this great broadcasting service. It is not a profit-making organization in the sense that broadcasting systems in some other parts of the world are. This is a great national service, and I am glad to note that the corporation is constantly improving its facilities. The establishment of a second dominion broadcasting radio network is, I think, a step in the right direction. I hope that a friendly rivalry will develop between these two networks and that between them they may improve the service that is given to the Canadian people. Knowing as I do the tremendous benefit this is to people who are shut in, I feel that the establishment of a corporation free from large advertising and interested in raising the standards of radio in this country is something for
Canadian Broadcasting Act

which the parliament that established the present broadcasting system will deserve praise.
I have never been convinced, although of course I have heard discussions before the radio committee, that what is now proposed in this bill is the the best thing for the corporation. I have no doubt the bill will be passed by this parliament, and that if it is passed- speaking as a member of this house and, perhaps, as the leader of the party associated with me-there will be no sniping; we will do all we can to see to it that the chairman of the board and the new method are given a fair trial; we shall give them all the support we possibly can. But as I have said before, I am' fearful of a divided authority in the corporation. We had a long discussion of that two years ago, and I do not intend to repeat the arguments then advanced against that divided authority. It is necessary to-day only to say that divided authority in the past was bad for the corporation, and I feel that this step to-day is in the wrong direction. It may be argued, of course, that the chairman of the board will be a full-time employee of the corporation. But the chairman of the board can scarcely be an employee; he is at the head of the board of governors, and as such he must lay down the policy, as the mouthpiece of the board of governors, to the responsible official of the corporation. It seems to me that he cannot act in a dual capacity, that of a paid employee of the corporation and that-of the policy-making head of the corporation; and I would ask, in the appointment of another official-because as I understand it the broadcasting act is not to be changed in any other particular; we shall still have a general manager and an assistant general manager, and under this bill we shall have a chairman'- where is the authority going to lie? It is said, of course, that the authority will lie largely in the chairman, who will decide policy on behalf of the governors. But if we do that we rather minimize the importance of the board, because the new chairman will be virtually the board of governors.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext: They will be just rubber stamps.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
As the leader of the opposition suggests, they may become merely rubber stamps. I would much prefer to see the government review the board of governors and see to it that a really strong board is appointed. I am not implying that the present board is lacking in strength, though I think it could be improved in some respects. A few years ago we 'had a board of governors which was not particularly strong, and which, for one

reason or another-one .member because of ill-health, and some for other reasons-could not give the attention to the corporation it deserved. As I said at the outset, when this measure is adopted we shall endeavour to give the new chairman all the support we can in the carrying out of his duties; yet I feel that this divided authority is not in the interests of the corporation or of the general public. If the new chairman is to be regarded as a public relations man, that again is a different thing. Perhaps the corporation has not gone in for public relations to the extent it might have done, and has suffered on that account. I believe people are not aware of the splendid work which 'has been done by the corporation. I do not want to prolong the discussion. I merely rose to say-I have been a member of the committee for three years, have attended pretty faithfully its meetings, and have made it, if I may so put it, something of a hobby or an interest-that I am doubtful of the wisdom of this proposal; nevertheless if the house adopts it we will do all we can to make the new chairman feel that 'he has the support of everybody in this house.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
It appears to me that the party of which the hon. gentleman is the leader have repudiated the policies laid down by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett in 1932 in connection with radio broadcasting in Canada. They have taken a different course entirely and would now seek to put the blame on the government with respect to the conduct of this institution. I submit that the government has discharged its duty entirely and absolutely in setting up an independent, publicly owned corporation and providing it with a good workable statutory foundation, leaving it to the chief executive of the board of governors to run things. They should not be blamed for any mistakes which the board of governors might make, when you have a board deliberately designed to be free from political interference. I think that at the bottom of this is a subtle method to put in a spoke for the private broadcasters of the country. They appear to lose sight of the fact that the private broadcasters in Canada have no vested interest in the airways of the country, or in radio frequencies, which are the property of all the people and if any utility should be publicly owned and managed, that utility is the one that is concerned with radio broadcasting. The growth of the corporation has necessitated that there should be more than one man, a general manager, to carry out its operations. The functions of the corporation have increased, and you have the matter of laying down policies, the matter of executing those policies.and carrying on the business of the corporation. All that is meant by this measure is that instead of there being a part-time chairman of the board that man should give his full time to the duties which are assigned to him. That is only a matter of policy with respect to the allocation of the work that the general manager shall do and the allocation of the work to be done by the chairman of the board of governors, and it will not be a one-man corporation. The people of the country do not want it to be such. The board of governors will be advisers to the chairman and the chairman of the board1, along with his advisers, will make policies under the broadcasting act. To me nothing could1 be simpler than that set-up. It does not make much difference what you call them, whether you have a chairman of the board and a general manager with the position of assistant general manager, or whether you have a chairman of the board who shall have his particular functions, and a general manager.
The criticism from the leader of the opposition has been that that particular position has not been filled. That is quite true. But under the act the assistant general manager, in the absence of the general manager, steps up to that position in the conduct of the functions of general manager. It so happens that the assistant general manager is the technician of the corporation. In addition to that, he has charge of broadcasting in the French language. As a matter of fact, in this country, by virtue of our racial differences, it is necessary to have two almost complete and entirely different systems, and if radio is to carry out the function for which it was created in Canada, that of developing something truly Canadian along educational and cultural lines, then the people of the French language must be given equal rank with those who speak English, so far as radio is concerned. That is only fair. That is the only policy which, if carried out, will tend to promote unity and goodwill in
Ccinadiari Broadcasting Act

this country; and any deviation from that policy is bound to have exactly opposite results. Dear knows there are enough differences in this country without making more at the present time. The policy of the government and of ipeople in public life should be as far as possible to placate differences, to see that they do not exist, and to see particularly that there is no reason why new differences should arise.
I think that the set-up proposed in this bill is one that will work out in the interests of greater efficiency and will make for better broadcasting programmes so that the use of radio broadcasting will fill a better office than at present and make for the general welfare. I am therefore prepared to give the matter a trial and to support the bill in its present set-up. I do not for a moment condone the action of the board of governors in not having made a recommendation with reference to the filling of the position of general manager. Since the resignation of Doctor Thomson, that particular position has been vacant. It is the duty not of the government but of the board of governors to see that the recommendation is made to the government to fill the position, and I join with the leader of the opposition and those who are critical of the board in that regard, and go so far as to say that the board has been neglectful of its duty in not having submitted a recommendation so far. But that is water under the bridge. We have the present position before us. What are we to do now to improve the position of the corporation? I submit that the greatest benefit would be for the board to submit a recommendation as soon as possible, and that is what we recommend in the report of 1944-that they submit a recommendation as soon as possible that the position of general manager be filled and that there should be a full-time man at the head of the board of governors who would be a public relations man and who would determine policy. In my judgment, only by creating that position or one similar to it can radio broadcasting make progress and help to attain the position which we all so much desire to see achieved.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
As a member of the radio committee which was presided over by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. McCann), I may possibly be allowed to pay him a tribute for the manner in which he discharged his responsibilities as chairman in giving an opportunity to all to express themselves, and in displaying throughout the period of the present session, to which my experience is confined, a fairness which I think should be referred to in the house.
So far as this bill is concerned I am not at all impressed by the arguments that have been advanced by the minister as to why another highly-paid official should be appointed to the hierarchy of the national radio system, because I believe it will result in bifurcation of authority that will lead to uncertainty rather than to a strong unified administration of this great instrument of public education. The reason I say that is this. On August 1 tie minister made a short review of the reasons why this official should be appointed. At page 5712 of Hansard he said:
The general manager has not the power to make or decide policy; only the board of governors may do so. It has been found time after time in the administration of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that questions have come up which required very quick replies and decisions. It was asking too much of the general manager to require that he should, without authority, take it upon himself to make decisions on these points as they came up.
When the minister concludes this debate I should like him to explain whether under the new set-up there will be any greater convenience in securing the opinion of the board of governors than there is to-day. Then the next sentence is surprising to me:
In addition to that, the business of the corporation has increased very much.
Does this not signify that not only the general manager but also the chairman, who from now on will be a full-time official will be looking after administration? I find it difficult to understand why it is necessary to have two highly paid officials, each discharging practically the same responsibilities, if what the minister stated the other day is correct, except that the chairman will have something to do as well with the question of policy.
It is in connection with the extension of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the work it is doing that I wish to make a few references this afternoon. My remarks have to do with the question of advertising, and that certainly is a matter of policy and will be one of the matters that will have to be considered by the broadcasting corporation in the years to come.
I think that, the corporation has done a good job in the dissemination of cultural and educative programmes for the benefit of the people of Canada; but I do not understand why it should continue to be expanding its advertising programmes; for if it continues to make the inroads in the next year or so that it has in the past, and at the same rate of increase, the press will not be able to remain as independent as they are to-day. Freedom of speech cannot exist without

Bennett, a former prime minister of this country. As long as our system permits private companies to operate, those private companies have the right under the law to have their point of view heard and considered even though that point of view is contrary to the point of view of the national board, and that consideration should be given by an independent body.
As far as a full-time chairman is concerned, it is not that $15,000 matters very much. After all, during the last five or six days and the next two or three days parliament will have voted expenditures amounting to $2,300,000,000 for the post-war period. The matter of the $15,000 may be unimportant, but there is a principle at stake here. It is this: why the divided authority? Why appoint two men, who will have to be strong men in order to occupy positions such as- these, one directing executive administration and the other directing matters of policy? A third appointment will be required to act as an umpire, if the views of these two men are to be finally resolved one way or the other.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext: That is exactly the function of the board.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
Then if that is the function of the board there is no necessity for having a full-time chairman; the present system would be sufficient. The management still would be able to obtain the views of the board of governors as a whole, and I am sure very few problems would come up from day to day of such great importance that their decision could not be delayed until the board of governors was called together. There have been difficulty and uncertainty in the past due to the fact that the membership of the board has not been kept complete, but my fear is that in future we will have the difficulties that always arise under a divided authority such as we have here, in that neither official will be circumscribed as to the jurisdiction he may exercise.
It is my intention, Mr. Speaker, to vote against this bill. If it becomes law, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said, we all hope it will work out, though fearful of the dangers that may be ahead in a bifurcated, divided authority, with no clear indication as to the limits of the work to be undertaken by each of these officials.

I cannot altogether agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when he sajrs that as a government institution it is not a profit-making organization, because I am informed that last year it was one of the greatest profit-making institutions in Canada,

It may not have been its motive. When one looks at the operations of the board of governors for the last three or four years he is struck at once by the confusion and the turmoil which has prevailed.
