The government having got into a most unhappy tangle only two or three years ago with the general manager and the assistant general manager, and having permitted a year

Canadian Broadcasting Act
to go by without appointing a new full-time general manager, and having permitted long periods of time to elapse without filling vacancies on the board, we do not take kindly words such as were uttered this morning by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) when he said, "There are things, such as motors for farm implements, which we would like to exempt from the customs tariff, but we cannot give away all our revenue." In the light of these words, the board of governors, inefficient as it has been, cannot now come forward and say that it will appoint another man at a big salary. The day has come in parliament when we should consider with great care any possible economies. We should give that matter more thought and attention than we do at the present time. We. should see thoroughly justified before us and thoroughly proven to us the necessity for appointing any more chairmen with divided authority to a body which has not sufficiently justified the purpose behind its creation.. I say the board of governors is in that position.
While serving on the committee I felt, and I still feel, that the strongest possible case should be made out for the appointment of a high-salaried full-time chairman of the board of governors, before hon. members give their approval.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking for the Yukon and for the whole north country may I tell the minister that the Canadian radio broadcasting system, so far as we are concerned, simply does not exist. This condition may be due to a lack of managing ability or poor equipment but the fact remains that up there we cannot receive any Canadian broadcasts at all. We get the programmes from the United States stations. We listen to Seattle Chicago, New York and San Francisco, but we cannot get programmes from Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa or Vancouver. In short, so far as we are concerned there is no radio at all in Canada. We hear nothing Canadian over the air. Programmes do reach us from London, England each night-but not from Canada. If the board of governors or the chairman cannot make a better job of radio broadcasting than they have up to date, then I do not see why there should be an additional appointment at greater cost to the country. Surely this is a disgraceful state of affairs. So far as we are concerned the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation might as well not exist, it would not be missed by us because we never hear it.
With the magnificent revenues we heard mentioned to-day the corporation should have better management and better equipment.
100-369i
Certainly it should have equipment capable of transmitting messages over long distances, messages which at the present time are confined to exchanges between Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces. Radio broadcasting in Canada should serve the whole country.
I hope the minister will give this matter his attention, and see to it that either a change is made in personnel, or an improvement is made in equipment.
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): Mr. Speaker, the day before yesterday when the principle of the bill was under consideration it was most encouraging both to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and, to an extent, to myself, to hear some of the eulogistic comments of hon. members, some of whom have reversed their positions to-day.
At the outset may I express my appreciation of the work done by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the past year. It is true that a number of persons have criticized the corporation in one respect or another. They have been heard. I am not certain that in all cases their true position as critics has been understood by those who have heard the criticisms.
As was pointed out this afternoon, there is in this matter a question of legitimate interest. I quarrel not with those who have vested interests. I quarrel not with those who have the ambition to launch into private enterprise and to succeed. But, Mr. Speaker, I say clearly that to-day I have the duty of protecting the interests of the people of Canada against those who criticize the policies of the corporation, and I intend to continue defending that which belongs to the nation. In saying that I hope no hon. member will disapprove of my readiness to defend that which is Canada's.
There is such a thing as giving a dog a bad name. That is a popular way of saying something which to an extent-not a very wide extent-I think has happened in Canada within the last year in regard to the corporation. I do not think it is good to criticize without realizing just what the situation may be or the effect of one's criticism, particularly of a matter that is in the Canadian national interest.
It is with the greatest pleasure, Mr. Speaker, that I express on this occasion my very deep gratitude to those who have acted as governors on the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Knowing much more of the individuals who now compose the board of governors than of their predecessors, I wish to extend to them not only my thanks but my gratitude for their diligence, their
Canadian Broadcasting Act

care and their rectitude in handling a piece of property that belongs to the taxpayers of Canada. I was not well acquainted with those who comprised previous boards of governors of the corporation, but as a citizen of this country, as one who many years ago was very much in favour of an attempt to bring into being a state-owned radio system in Canada, I have taken a particular interest in radio matters since radio has become such an everyday part of our life, and I have therefore been able to appreciate the difficulties of the problems confronting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and therefore in a position to admire the manner in which those concerned have tackled their problems and found solutions for them.
I suggest that perhaps too much mention has been made of the situation in the corporation for some time before I had the honour of becoming Minister of National War Services and therefore the minister to whom the corporation reports. I hope I shall be pardoned for pointing out that things could not very well have been otherwise when there was this anomalous situation of having a part-time Chairman and a full-time general manager whose duty was and is-although it is a different person doing the work-that of chief executive of the corporation, an executive officer but not a governor, and therefore having nothing to do with deciding what should be the policy or policies governing the corporation. I say that it is surprising to have noted how well the corporation did get along when there was such a fault, in my opinion, in the set-up of the corporation. I cannot conceive of how any other corporation proceeding day and night with something of interest to all Canadians could have" got along as well as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation did under a set-up where the head of the body, empowered to make policies, was not present at all times, and therefore not available either to the public or to the officers of the corporation.
I heard with great interest the day before yesterday and to-day the fears that were expressed on the point of divided authority. But the very purpose of this amending bill is to do away with any possibility of divided authority. I suggest that in the past there has been ineffectiveness due to this faulty set-up making possible divided authority in the organization of the corporation. Now I am seeking to rectify that situation. I do not like the idea of such an important body -being headed by an officer, whom we will call the chairman, who is not at all times available for the conduct of the business of the corporation. But divided authority comes when the set-up is not defined, and divided authority comes when
f.Mr. LaFleche.]
the set-up is faulty. I think that there has been a fault here, and I am surprised to note that it was not corrected a long time ago.
I would like to see a full-time chairman of this board. I definitely believe it is essential that there should be such an officer, and I am in good company in so believing. It may not be proper to cite the deliberations of the committee of the House of Commons this year on radio broadcasting, yet I think I am entitled to say that all who gave evidence on this point were very much in favour of the appointment of a full-time chairman of the corporation. The board of governors passed 3, resolution, and passed it unanimously, I am assured, to the effect that it would be well that there be a full-time chairman of the corporation. Surely the members of the board of governors must know what is necessary. They must have realized, although they do not say so in their resolution, that there might be this danger of divided authority, but they passed the resolution nevertheless. I was very glad indeed that the board made that recommendation, because I want to see during the time I am the minister to whom the corporation reports that there is a sound advance in the affairs and well-being of the corporation, as well as a sound advance in all matters pertaining to radio in Canada.
It is regrettable that certain hon. members have deemed it wise or necessary to make clear t'heir stand on this point before I was given an opportunity of bringing these further facts to their attention. The day before yesterday I spoke very briefly, and there was a good reason for that, one of lack of time. I stated then that I would make further observations at this time.
I have thanked the members of the board of governors, and now I should like to say something about the House of Commons special committee on radio, of which I have had the honour of being a member both this year and last, under the distinguished chairmanship of the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann). Something has already been said about his excellent work and I readily and heartily endorse what has been said in that respect this afternoon. I should also like to say that the members of these two committees were most diligent and most careful in their work, and there was a great deal of evidence to sift. I have only one point on which to be surprised and that is that after hearing all these things there were some members this year who could not see their way clear to supporting this bill. I suggest to the hon. members of this house that it is hardly

Canadian Broadcasting Act
possible to have been a member of the committee this year and not have come to the conclusion embodied in the principle of the bill now under consideration.
An hon. member who spoke earlier this afternoon mentioned, either directly or indirectly, privately-owned broadcasting stations, also the press. I think it may be repeated-because it has already been stated- that the views of the owners of the privately-owned broadcasting stations have never as much as this year been so carefully heard and considered. It was my pleasure and privilege to be present at the annual convention of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters last February. It was there that these statements were made that never before had they been so much encouraged. It may be beside the point, but it is my conviction that all engaged in broadcasting in Canada deserve and have the right to be heard, and above all have a right to believe that decisions made on matters concerning them are made with the full knowledge of the facts. With a full-time chairman it will be easier for the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to make much further progress in that regard.
Coming back to this question of divided authority, one which has been mentioned so often during this discussion, I should like to place the position before the house by using a very simple comparison. In any well organized body there must be a head; he must be the effective head, and he must be ready at all times to conduct the business of the corporation. As this question of divided authority has been based upon the two positions of full-time chairman and general manager, may I say, with due deference to the gentlemen who have occupied the position of general manager, that. it is not correct and it is not good business that a servant-the general manager-be the master of the corporation. I would want to put the general manager beyond the possibility of believing even for a moment that it would be his duty to assume the functions of the real head of the corporation.
There were other questions raised. I am sorry the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) is not here. I should have liked to thank him for his kind remarks. I point out to this house that oftentimes the hon. member from Broadview acts and speaks in the true meaning of the name of the constituency he has represented so long in this house. I could wish nothing better for the hon. member
for Broadview or for any other human being than that he and we should continue to strive to our utmost always to have a broad view.
It might be well to acquaint this committee that all these questions and many more than have been touched upon to-day were gone over most carefully by the House of Commons special committee on radio broadcasting again this year. There were twenty-five meetings; in the proceedings of that committee a great deal of valuable information is to be found; and I suggest to those who do not seem at the moment to favour this particular bill that they would, upon reading the reports, come to believe that the conclusion that some such measure as is now provided for in this bill is necessary.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South ' (Mr. Gillis) the day before yesterday in his kind way took me somewhat to task for not giving him a fuller reply to the questions he had put a few days before. I assure the hon. member that in the circumstances I went as far as I possibly could to give him as good and complete a reply as could be given. Circumstances since that time have not changed. I must therefore in all frankness say through you, Mr. Speaker, to the hon. member that the situation remains the same. When there is a change I shall be very glad to acquaint him with the facts. The answers I gave are the best, I think, anyone could give under the present circumstances.
I hope that those who have been kind enough to promise their support of the fulltime chairman when appointed will carry out their promise to the best possible effect. I know they will. I know also that the full-time chairman and the corporation require the good will and the active support of all Canadians who are ready to help out in something of very material value to this /country.

I am informed that a transmitter for the purpose was installed but what was holding the matter up was the passing of an order in. council. I made inquiries and found that the necessary order in council had not been passed. Perhaps the minister has

answered the questions as best he can in the light of the information he has, but I am informed-if I am wrong, or if the people who are advising me are wrong, I want to be given that assurance-that the reason that C.B.C. station has been held up is that certain people in Halifax who have an old franchise dating back seven years which they have never made use of are resurrecting that franchise and installing a station privately owned.
These people have not the equipment. I understand they are arranging to purchase a second-hand transmitter from Edmonton or somewhere in the west. Now that is not the kind of service I visualize for Nova Scotia. I want to see that service installed by the government of Canada through the medium of a network already established so that we may look forward to the same kind of service in that province as the rest of Canada enjoys where there are publicly owned stations. I am perhaps biased to this extent, that the group with which I sit believe that service can be best performed by the government of Canada under proper supervision and. fully responsible to the Canadian people, whereas small groups who are promoting this matter for the purpose of making a profit are not interested in public service but in furthering their own ends.
It cannot be said that I am interested in this matter from any personal consideration, because the people who are writing to me are not concerned about, the organization to which I belong but about the service that is to be rendered, and they have asked me to try to get some information. I will not pursue the matter further. I will simply ask the minister if through his department he will continue to investigate the question and when he has any further information as to the possibilities of going ahead with what the acting general manager intimated would be done in Halifax he will inform the house, or someone who is interested in the question in Halifax.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
Perhaps I may add a word to what the hon. member has said and the minister can reply to both of us at the same time. I am as much interested in complete coverage of Nova Scotia as the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I have sat as a member of the radio committee for the past six or seven years and have endeavoured to follow its proceedings as carefully as possible and to give my best judgment on all matters pertaining to the carrying out of the duties

Canadian Broadcasting Act
of the committee, and have passed on suggestions respecting administration so far as the board of governors is concerned.
We in the maritime provinces have not had the coverage which I felt we should have had. Representations were made to the board of governors, and on various occasions the question was brought .up in committee. I was happy to have the support of all members, and finally we had a 50,000 watt station, CBA, established at Sackville which was to have given us as complete coverage as was given the rest of Canada. We were pleased to get that, and it has given us fairly good coverage, but the people were not entirely satisfied in certain sections of Nova Scotia and I made suggestions on more than one occasion, particularly when the second network was proposed, that in addition to the sustaining programmes carried by CHNS at Halifax and other stations in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, a second network should be given to such stations as Sydney, represented by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I am surprised that the hon. member did not support me in my request for better coverage for that section of Nova Scotia. I also suggested that we might possibly have the dominion network extended to include a station in Charlottetown or in some other section of Prince Edward Island. I understood there was an application before the board of governors in 1938 which was granted but not immediately put into effect. It had to be revised and it was revised. The application was again put before the board of governors and the Department of Transport with a view to giving, as I suggested, greater coverage to the city of Halifax and the surrounding districts. I believe if that suggestion is carried out-and I hope it will be-we shall have greater coverage and better service in sections of Nova Scotia which are not being served as efficiently as they might be without a second station.
I am not sure that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself should spend the money to open up a new station at Halifax if a second privately-owned' station could function and give the service which is needed. That is a matter for the board of governors to decide. I do feel that we should have another outlet in Halifax. I have supported it; I am supporting it to-day. I am strongly in favour of increased facilities at Halifax to give a more complete service.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South has stated his position in regard to public ownership. His leader has gone on record as stating
that he believes in both public ownership and private ownership of radio. I take the same stand. I have been a strong supporter of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I believe that on the whole we are getting good programmes when one considers that radio has to broadcast for sixteen hours a day. I think we are getting as good programmes as we could get from any other system on the North American continent. It is true that we have not the expensive and high class programmes, but by arrangement with the United States networks, and through the medium of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's channels, we have been able to take full advantage of these very fine programmes. We are not in a position to pay for these programmes ourselves. Certain hon. members have criticized the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation this afternoon for extending their commercial activities, for carrying a large amount of advertising. It is impossible for Canada to enjoy that excellent type of programme unless we have the added revenue to produce them. If we are to use the medium of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as it was intended, to educate our people, to .give them the finer type of musical programmes, then we must of necessity have a greater revenue to provide the people of Canada with those programmes.
We have in Halifax at the present time a fine station, CHNS. It carries the No. 1 network programmes, the Trans-Canada sustaining programmes. In addition they initiate splendid programmes by using local talent to good advantage. But we should have a second outlet carrying the dominion network, or the No. 2 network, which would give us still greater service. There is an opening there that could be used to good advantage if we had an outlet for the second network in Halifax. If the hon. member for Cape Breton South has in mind, as I have, a second station or outlet in Halifax, then 1 am anxious to cooperate with him and support him. But if he wants to block the granting of the licence which has been on file since 1938 and which I understand was recently renewed, then of course, he and I differ. I am all for greater coverage, whether it is through the recognized Canadian broadcasting channels or through a proposed privately-owned station, in competition with CHNS, but which because of that competition would bring about better programmes and better coverage in our province, particularly in Halifax.

May I just say one word to the senior member for Halifax? It is cot

my intention to block anyone. What I am endeavouring to do is to stop someone from blocking what has already been recommended by the acting general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. speechtext:
Let me say just a word, since the senior member for Halifax referred to my views on this matter. I have always said that I believed in both freedom of the press and freedom of the local community station; but I believe we must have a national broadcasting system complete from coast to coast under public ownership and control, and the broadcasting corporation must complete as rapidly as possible its own chain of stations to give sendee to the people of Canada and to pick up the channels allotted to Canada in the Havana agreement. I have said many times that I believed the high power channels ought to be in the hands of the corporation. The hon, member suggested, although perhaps a little more widely than I would be prepared to accept it, that the local community station ought to be maintained because it can give a local community service. The matter to which the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred was dealt with by the acting general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on June 28 of this year in reply to a question of the senior member for Halifax. The question was:
Because of the bringing into being of this second network will it add more outlets of your own at C.B.C. stations?

Doctor Frigon's answer was:
Well, it means that CJBC, Toronto, is now on the dominion network and we are providing now for a provincial outlet in Nova Scotia, Halifax. The report has gone to the minister.
Q. That is, you are making capital expenditure so as to carry out services of the second network?
A. Bight.
Q. Are there any others besides the one in Nova Scotia?
A. There is only one station, CJBC, which was not on the network before and which is being placed on the dominion network, and the one which we are building to provide an outlet in Halifax for the dominion network.
From that I took it that this was to be a C.B.C. owned station, when Doctor Frigon made the statement that this station would complete the outlets in Nova Scotia, as it were. My hon. friend suggests that since that time an old charter has been revived and an attempt' made to block the building of a station for which arrangements had been made and a transmitter secured. I think -that is the point my hon. friend wants the minister to look into and report upon.

subtopic: CHAIRMAN OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PROVISION FOR FULL-TIME SERVICE AND ANNUAL SALARY
speechtext:
There is no difference between the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and myself in regard to coast to coast control by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That was set out in a report brought in in 1932, and finally carried into effect by the establishment of stations in the maritimes. It will be recalled that the report stated that five 50,000-watt stations were to be erected throughout Canada to serve from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to give complete coverage, and we are getting that complete coverage to-day. The only difference of opinion is in regard to the coverage as far as Nova Scotia is concerned. For years I have advocated better coverage in certain sections of my province which did not appear to be receiving the C.B.C. news and other items of interest to which I thought they were entitled. When I spoke a moment ago I mentioned Sydney, Halifax and Charlottetown, because I thought that would give us complete coverage, but I neglected to refer to Yarmouth, the extreme western point of Nova Scotia. I still hope another outlet will be set up in Halifax. To be quite frank, if there is a private company willing to undertake the cost of constructing a station and able to give the service we want, by all means let them go ahead and give us what we have been asking for so many years.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Golding in the chair.
359. Departmental administration, $425,590.

I understand that some
little latitude is allowed under this item to 'discuss railway matters generally, and I do not see any other item in the estimates under which I might properly bring up a matter which should have been mentioned much earlier in the session, when the weather was cooler than it is to-day. I should like to draw to the minister's attention what may seem like a small matter but something that means a great deal to those involved. During the frigid weather those employees of the railways whose duty it is to look after sleeping-car and other tickets have to carry on their work under most difficult circumstances. After watching their work for a year or two, I finally made some inquiries on my own initiative; the matter was not brought to my attention by any of the employees themselves. I found that these men were working under conditions which I do not think should be permitted by the railway companies, and I believe it would be only necessary for the minister to bring the matter to the attention of the companies in order to have the situation dealt with before cold weather comes again. They work in that part of the station just at the entrance to the tracks, where it is very cold and draughty in the winter time. These men have to perform clerical duties and do some writing in addition to their ordinary work as conductors. I believe the minister should give consideration to having some sort of heated booth or office erected for their use. Thpse men should be able to work under conditions as favourable as those that exist at the union station in Toronto, or the station in Montreal. I mention the matter because this seemed to be the only item under which I could bring it up. Last February I was told that some negotiations were under way in order to have the situation remedied, but later on I noticed that it had not been corrected. Therefore I would ask the minister to bring the matter to the attention of the railways so that the conditions under which these men work may be remedied. The stress and strain under which these men work, due to the tremendous traffic, is something which members of parliament who have to travel a good deal may understand somewhat better than some others who do not have occasion to travel as '"ch.
These railway workers deserve high commendation in this period of war. I have said before, and I repeat-and I do this as an old railway man, because in my early days I was employed by a railway company-that there is no group of workers whose tradition is better or who work with better spirit than do the railway workers.
I think the point I have raised need only be brought by the minister to the attention of the company to see to it that this branch of railway workers may operate under more favourable conditions in this time of war. It is bad enough for them to have to handle so ' much traffic, without having any added burden. Frankly, I do not know how they have done so much. We always considered that even before the war railway workers had plenty to do. But now, in wartime, they are handling at least three times the traffic they had before the war, and they are handling it efficiently and without complaint. In most cases the service seems to be just as good as it was in peace time. Surely these points ought to be sufficient to ensure that this comparatively small improvement be made. Let us have them operate under the best conditions we can give them.

I believe what I should like to say at this time might properly be said under this item. The minister will have noticed that yesterday a report was tabled in which the situation in Ottawa, the capital city, was discussed. In that report special attention was drawn to railway crossings in Ottawa. I believe, too, that the condition found in this city is also found in other communities.
When we are considering matters connected with reconstruction and rehabilitation I suggest that it would be wise at this time if the minister were to give special thought to the relocation of tracks, and1 particularly the providing of overhead rather than level crossings, as they now exist. He might consider particularly the situation in Ottawa, and the detrimental effect these level crossings have on the whole economy of the city.
I believe it is contemplated that large sums will be spent in the post-war period on reconstruction and rehabilitation. I can think of no better way of spending that money than to spend it in making improvements in our transportation systems, and eliminating the dangerous conditions which develop from level crossings in heavily travelled areas. I would urge that the minister give this matter his immediate attention, and that it be drawn to the attention of the railway officials. This is a bad condition, and particularly in Ottawa.
Supply-Transport

May I first of all thank the leader of the opposition for what he has said in respect of the railway employees across Canada. I am sure no one will disagree with him, or with anyone who says that particularly during this time of war the railway employees of Canada have done a marvellous job. In fact, in view of the handicaps under which they have had to labour-shortage of rolling stock, shortage of material and shortage of man-power-it is difficult to understand how it has been possible for them to accomplish this huge task of transportation of not only people but war materials. However, that task has been accomplished, and stands to the credit of the management, as an instance of cooperation between the management and the employees of the railways.
Then, the leader of the opposition has recommended a certain measure of comfort which should be given to some of the railway employees who are detailed to look after passengers at the gates in the Ottawa station. I understand that this matter has been brought to the attention of the operators of the station at Ottawa, and there has been consideration as to the best means of remedying the condition. I hope some means will be found of giving more comfort to these men who have to stand hour after hour, sometimes well into the night, in all kinds of weather.
Then, the hon. member for Carleton has mentioned an interesting subject, involving the cooperation the railways should give the city of Ottawa in elaborating upon the programme to beautify the city. This matter has received considerable attention from both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway company. There has been consultation between the officials of these two railways which enter Ottawa, and some progress has been made in connection with reaching an understanding as to how trackage should be relayed.
Another matter which has received attention from the board of transport commissioners is that of level crossings. The condition in and around Ottawa is bad. I am not disclosing any government secret, or any secret of the board when I say that this situation is being taken into account in connection with postwar reconstruction. I know that the citizens of Ottawa, and the managements of the two railway companies are keenly interested in correcting the very bad situation which has developed from level crossings in and about Ottawa.

I should like to take only a few minutes to refer to the work of the minister's department, and to the general

satisfactory war effort of the two railway systems. When war broke out it was predicted by the critics of our railway systems that the last war had been a terrible load for the railways of Canada, and that in this one, which would involve possibly five times the freight and passenger traffic of the last war, the railways would not be able to handle the job. They pointed out that there was a scarcity of rolling stock; difficulty in connection with labour conditions, difficulties in getting war materials, shortages of cars, adverse climatic conditions, and several other factors which would cripple the war effort of our railways. That prediction has proved groundless. So far I have not seen any historical sketch of the part our railways have played in the war effort, but I know it has been a glorious part-and that includes both the large railway systems of Canada. The record has not been written yet, but when it is written it will be one of the most glorious chapters in the history of railroading in Canada, if not on the American continent. Our railway transportation systems, with their subsidiaries, are closely interlocked with those of the United States, and labour conditions and conditions with respect to getting equipment are similar on the railways of both countries. I was glad to see a statement in the National City Bank railway review of the two wars for October, 1943, dealing with the magnificent work that is being done by the railways of the United States and Canada during this war. The review says:
In world war 1 the railroads buckled under the strain of a traffic burden which, at its peak in 1918, totalled 405 billion ton-miles of freight and 43 billion passenger-miles. In 1942, with 35 per cent fewer locomotives and 26 per cent fewer freight cars, they handled 638 billion ton-miles of freight, an increase of 58 per cent over the 1918 movement, without anything remotely resembling a major car shortage. In the same year they moved 54 billion miles of passenger traffic, exceeding the 1918 volume by 26 per cent.
The splendid survey of north American railways goes on to refer to the impossibility of using the Atlantic because of the U-boats and says that the railroads of the United States and Canada have had to replace the shipping services on the Atlantic and those that formerly used the Panama canal. It gives a fine summary of the organization of the freight and passenger traffic movement and the volume of war traffic in Canada and the United States. I have not seen any similar statement regarding the two railway systems in this country except what is conveyed in the annual budget of the Canadian National Railways and its subsidiaries, which

Supply-Transport
is referred to a select committee of the house. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has also done magnificently in moving freight and passenger traffic and in handling ocean and hotel services during the war, and it is a great pity that civil aviation is being divorced from the railways. The great mistake that Britain made between the two wars was in separating civil aviation from railway and water-borne traffic and in giving a monopoly. British railways and ocean shipping have a magnificent record in this war.
I have a suggestion to make to the minister. I have been over in the United States during this war only once or so for an occasional week-end, and I notice that on the New York Central lines running between Buffalo and Cleveland the empire state and others have overcome the shortage of sleeping berths on their trains at night by setting aside two or three coaches in which passengers can reserve chairs for a small increase in the railway fare. We have some very fine railway cars on the Canadian National, not as efficient or as good in rolling stock perhaps as the cars on American railways; we seem to give on the Canadian National American subsidiaries all the good cars and none to Ottawa, but I think we might well reserve a few cars in which chairs could be rented for the night by those who could not obtain a berth. There are many members of parliament who want to leave Ottawa and go home on Friday or Saturday night and who find they cannot get a berth. In the United States you pay a new fare as a railway -ticket of about fifty cents for the privilege of getting a seat reserved, where as good a sleep can be had. We could do the same thing on our trains running between Montreal and Ottawa and Ottawa and Toronto, and all over Canada. The trains running, some in the daytime, from Montreal and Ottawa to Toronto and western Ontario pull from twelve to fifteen cars. I do not suggest that we adopt the system they have in the United States here in the daytime, although we could do it in part, but it would be a great convenience at night. There is a great deal of difficulty in getting accommodation at the union station in Ottawa, as well as at the offices on Sparks street, where the railways have such courteous officials. I hope that the minister will see if they can adopt my suggestion.
The conditions at the union station in Ottawa with close tracks and trains running in and out, invite disaster. There should be some better way found of handling the traffic at the station. I referred to this matter in connection with the Ottawa bill. The difficulties are largely due to the war and to heavy traffic, but there should be some way of regulating the passenger traffic so that there will be less danger of accidents. A barrier might be placed in some part of the station where people could say good-bye to those going off on the trains. The station officials are overworked and underpaid and working long hours and doing their best to handle a difficult situation, just as they are at the Toronto union and other stations, but it is a wonder that people have not been injured before now. There is a fine lot of officials at the union station in Ottawa, and I sympathize with them and with the trainmen on the trains. Only a small number of the public are hard to handle and in war the public are apt to be at times critical, and some of their criticism is not fair, as the minister knows. Unless something is done we may have an accident at the Ottawa union station, and it is the duty of the government to prevent accidents. That is all I have to say about the railway system.
I saw a very nice sketch of the minister in a navigation paper the other day and the tributes it paid to the minister were well deserved.
There has been a tremendous loss of life on the highways. Yesterday the announcement was made that there had been five or six hundred level crossing accident deaths, and the announcement was made in Ontario yesterday that in Ontario alone 7,595 people had been killed on the highways in the past few years. I referred to this the other day in connection with the minister's estimates for marine services.
On July 27 I asked the minister a question as to what steps had been taken to prohibit the sale of gasoline for motor launches and other marine craft which carry passengers for hire and which have not been licensed and have not been inspected by any federal authority as to navigation safety. I also asked if the Minister of Munitions and Supply had any control over small craft and what had been done to regulate such craft by refusing gasoline. I have a letter here which refers to the danger to passengers being carried on small boats and motor launches. I am not going to give the name of the writer because he might lose his job. The letter is written from Sturgeon Point and says that over thirty people sometimes crowd info one of these boats and a captain who has been on the lake for a great many years says that he has never seen anything on the lakes so fraught with possibilities of tragedy. He quotes the manager of a very large branch of a bank in Toronto as saying that he had seen over
Supply-Transport

thirty people in this small boat and he wondered why they were allowed gasoline. There was a disaster at Port Stanley and an accident from this cause at Midland the other day. I do not like to bother the Minister of Munitions and Supply, but he has some control over the gasoline situation and I would ask him to take steps to safeguard the public from this menace.
In conclusion, having travelled on the two railway systems of this country, I wish to pay my tribute to all officers and employees on our two great railways who work so well and have rendered such a magnificent effort in this war at the risk of their lives. An intolerable traffic situation has been brought about by the war and these men have borne the burden and heat of the day. They work long hours at only fair wages, and they handle the public and the very heavy traffic in a magnificent way.

I should like to inquire what headway is being made in regard to the construction of the causeway or bridge over the strait of Canso. I understand that the department and the Canadian National Railways had engineers making a special survey with respect to the construction of this work. Premier MacMillan when he was in Ottawa a few weeks ago advocating the construction of this causeway, gave it as his conclusion that the causeway itself could be constructed for S3,000,000, the drawbridge for 81,000,000 and the diversion of the railway and the building of the track across the bridge and causeway for another $500,000. or a total cost of $4,500,000. What headway is being made in the construction of this causeway? Have plans been prepared so that this work can be proceeded with without delay, at least after the cessation of hostilities?

Regarding the remarks made by the hon. member for Broadview with respect to the steamer which was plying on Sturgeon bay without complying with the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act and the regulations made thereunder, for his information I may state that as soon as I received his letter I brought it to the attention of the steamships inspector of the district, and I am informed that either yesterday or to-day the boat is to be inspected under the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. Also for his information, in view of the number of accidents which have happened lately on inland waters-the waters of the great lakes or the St. Lawrence-I refer to section 387 of the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, part VII, and there I find that it is the duty of each owner of any craft which has to be inspected under

the act to apply for inspection and apply for a licence. He can well understand, I have no doubt, that with the long coastline we have it is impossible to retain an army of officers to prevent any person from using a boat for carrying passengers unless the boat is inspected and licensed before passengers are taken. But recently we have tried to use the services of the local authorities, the local police and the mounted police, in order, to check on those who violate the regulations and carry passengers in craft which are not safe, or are not inspected, or are overloaded, or otherwise are operating in defiance of the regulations.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Cumberland as to the Canso causeway, for his information I may state that we have received representations from the premier on behalf of the province of Nova Scotia and also from public bodies in the Cape Breton area, and the matter is under consideration. No definite plans have been made. In the past there were some surveys, and attention has been given to the general principle of the proposition, but there having been no detailed surveys, no detailed plans have yet been made. This is a project of such magnitude that it could not be undertaken under present-day conditions, and it will have to await the end of the war before receiving consideration from either the province of Nova Scotia or the dominion government.

Is not the project of constructing that causeway one which would come within the jurisdiction of the ministry of reconstruction? The reconstruction committee definitely recommended the carrying out of that project as a post-war measure.

I believe that when that ministry is organized and is formed, to it will be transferred all projects of this kind for coordination and execution, but I still believe that the duty of surveying and planning, all the technical work required to bring the project to the point of execution, will have to be carried out by those government servants who are particularly qualified to do that work, and I believe that the engineers of the Department of Transport are those who will be entrusted with the duty of making those final surveys, tests and plans.
It was surveyed back in 1906.
Before that.

There is another project of great interest to the people of the maritime provinces, especially Prince Edward Island. The only reason I mention it is that publicity is given by the minister

Supply-Transport
and his department, or anyway through the press, that engineers have been sent to the maritime provinces to make a survey with respect to a causeway or a tunnel connecting New- Brunswick with Prince Edward Island. Has the minister any statement to make as to what progress has been made? Have these engineers actually undertaken this work, in accordance with the publicity; if so, have they reported; if not, when is the report expected?

Some attention has been given by the department to the matter of establishing between the mainland-that is New Brunswick-and Prince Edward Island either a causeway or a tunnel, and engineers of the department who in the past have been familiar with the conditions and have carried on surveys have been instructed to renew their investigations. There has been associated with them an eminent Prince Edward Islander, Mr. Lea, who is well known, I am sure, to the hon. member for Cumberland; he has an office in Montreal. Mr. Lea was retained by the department early in the summer and has been doing some work in cooperation with departmental engineers on this project.

Would the minister state the names of the departmental engineers, and also advise the committee whether this Mr. Lea and his associates are actually on the job at the site making surveys, and if they have made any interim report?

The engineer from the department who has been entrusted with that work is Mr. D. W. McLachlan. I know that late in the winter or early in the spring, in cooperation with Mr. Lea, he carried on an investigation into ice conditions. I am sorry I cannot say to what extent their work has progressed, because I have not seen any report of the work following the spring investigation.

Another project of very great importance to that part of Canada and to all Canada is the building of the Chignecto canal. This was projected by the early settlers in a small canal hundreds of years ago, and it was followed up from time to time, in the days of Sir Charles Tupper and of H. J. Logan as well as of my predecessor who ably represented Cumberland for ten years, Mr. R. K. Smith. It is recognized that it would have been a great commercial project, and during war years it would have been of great military advantage if we had had such a canal. It would have been partly paid for in avoiding the loss of the steamship Charlottetown, the ferry boat that operated between
New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Had it not been necessary for that ferry boat to proceed all round Nova Scotia, if it could have crossed on this canal, that misfortune would have been avoided. Has the minister a statement to make as to whether the department has taken steps to get information regarding the construction of this very important work?

I am just as much
interested in the construction of the Chignecto canal as the hon. member for Cumberland, although it happens that I am more remote from the locus than he is.. In my opinion it would be quite an improvement to navigation and transportation by water in the east. The project has been receiving the attention of the country for years, ever since confederation, and has been studied by engineers who have made conflicting reports as to the advantage of the canal and the cost. A year or so ago public opinion woke up again and demanded that this construction should be proceeded with as a valuable post-war undertaking. I heartily endorsed that and suggested that the old surveys should be looked up and that a modern plan and detailed estimate of the cost should be prepared. Unfortunately, the engineers of the department who could be assigned' to that study have been busy in war work and the little time they have had has been given to the Prince Edward Island project.

I appreciate very much the interest of the minister in this matter. I regard it as very essential from the point of view of the adequate defence of Canada and of the United States in time of war. When- this last survey was made at the instance of my predecessor, Mr. R. K. Smith, the cost was larger than expected, and it was felt by many at that time who had investigated the cost that it had been purposely swollen by some in order that there might be greater justification for not proceeding with the construction of the canal. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I rise at this time to seek the support of the Minister of Transport in connection with a matter that I intend to stick with until it is properly settled. In my persistence, I suggest that I am only following the example set twenty years ago by the Prime Minister in a similar situation, and I am sure that no member on the government side can criticize me for doing that. I refer to the case of the Canadian Pacific railway employees whose pension rights have been . curtailed or denied because of the time they were out on strike in various parts of Canada in 1918 or 1919. As the minister probably knows, I have already spoken on this matter in the house on two occasions this year, so that it will not be necessary for me to repeat the details I placed on the record on May 1 and on July 24. I hope I can enlist his interest in this cause to the point where he will study the material I placed on Hansard on those occasions and the other material he can get in connection with the subject. He may recall that I first wrote to him about one case, which I selected out of many hundreds, on February 8. He was good enough to get in touch with the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway company about that case and he wrote to me a couple of times about it. His second letter was dated March 4, 1944. However, he simply reported to me that the president of the company had explained that technicalities stood in the way of doing anything about the case to which I had drawn his attention. A little later I wrote to the minister again seeking confirmation from him of something I knew to be a fact, namely, that the Canadian National system did the right thing in connection with its employees who were out on strike at Winnipeg at the same time. I refer to 1919. In the minister's letter to me, dated March 28, 1944, the concluding paragraph reads:	.
With reference to your second question, Canadian National railway officials inform me that, "participation of Canadian National railway

employees in the Winnipeg strike of 1919, does not affect the eligibility for pension, under the rules, of those employees who were involved, and who returned, at the termination of the strike, to their former positions."
That letter was signed by the Minister of Transport. Nevertheless when it seemed that I was not making much headway on this matter by taking it up with the Department of Transport I decided I would see what could be done by treating it as a matter of labour relations, which is what it is. Accordingly the detailed material that I placed on Hansard was given during the discussion of the labour estimates, and again I would refer the minister to the debates on the two days which I have already indicated. My reason for rising now is that in addition to the interest that I hope the Minister of Labour will show in this matter, plus the interest that I hope the Prime Minister will display, I should like also to have the interest of the Minister of Transport. I am so thoroughly convinced as to the justice of this case that, as I said when I first rose in my place this afternoon, I intend to stick with it until these men, at least those who are still alive, win their rights.
I have before me the most recent letter that I have received in connection with one of these cases, one that came to my desk this morning. As a matter of fact I receive letters dealing with this matter in almost every day's mail. This is one paragraph from the letter I received this morning:	.
Since writing you last one of our machinists here has been retired. He started working in the dining-car service as a boy in 1891- He was apprenticed in 1893 to the machinist trade in Medicine Hat, coming here-
That was to Kenora, Ontario.
.-in 1907. Fifty-three years of service and no pension, and in bad shape with high blood pressure.
I am of the opinion that we must take situations such as that seriously. Here is a man who has given fifty-three years of service to a company. Because of a technicality that the company is able to use, because of participation in a very short strike in 1918-in this case the strike lasted only eighteen hours-this man is denied a pension. My notion is that the minister is sympathetic with the position that I take and that the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister are likewise sympathetic. They all agree with me that something ought to be done. My hope is that I can persuade these three members of the government not just to display sympathy but to try to do something about it.

Will my hon. friend explain the technicality so that we may understand what it is all about?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes, I shall be glad to do that. The technicality is that there is a rule, known as clause 8 in the pension rules of the Canadian Pacific Railway company, which says that no one is entitled to a pension unless his last entry into the service of the company occurred before he reached the age of forty years. There is nothing in the rule about strikes. On its own the company made a decision that those who were out on strike in 1918 or 1919 broke their service with the company and that, therefore, when they came back after that they were denied their pension rights if they were over forty years of age. Not only did those who were over forty years of age lose all their pension rights, but those still under forty lost such rights as they might have acquired in the years prior to 1919.
Including seniority?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am not sure at the moment about seniority, but I believe they lost that too. The point under discussion is their pension rights. As an example, we have men who had worked ten years prior to 1919 and who were under forty when they returned to work. They are able to qualify for a pension, but when they retire their pension is computed only on the basis of the years they have worked since 1919. They lose such rights as they had acquired by their work in previous years.
Did the company make the rule?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, the company made the rule. As a matter of fact they made it first in 1903 and it was rewritten in the new by-laws that were drawn up in 1936 ' and came into effect on January 1, 1937.
When I was referring a moment ago to the men who had about ten years' service prior to 1919 I wanted to add that in that group there are a great many returned men of the last war. Those men feel particularly keen about the injustice done to them. I know of several men who had just come back from the front a few days before the strike broke out. Some of them did not want to go back right away; they wanted to wait a few days for a bit of a rest. The company implored them to come in and start work because they were busy. The strike took place in two or three days. As a matter of fact some of the men hardly knew what it was all about. They found themselves out, and in due course
they lost the rights that they had built up in the ten years prior to 1919. Those men are in this position: if they had not responded to the company's plea to come back to work, if they had stayed at home for two or three days' rest they would not have been involved in the strike, and they would have retained their pension rights. I might as well be frank and say that these men make comments of this kind: "Is that what we went and fought for? For a private company's right to do this kind of thing to us?" I am told that the ex-servicemen in the employ of the company still resent very keenly the particular injustice that they feel was done to them. They spent three or four years away fighting; they came back ready to take up their jobs with the company and the company wanted them back, but the company takes advantage of rule 8 which is in the pension by-laws and asserts that participation in the 1919 strike is a break in service.
I could take the time to go into the details of the strike, but I do not think it would be desirable. It seems to me that the unanswerable argument as to the justice of ignoring the strike for pension purposes is the action taken by the other major employers who were involved, the Canadian National Railways, the dominion government, particularly the Post Office Department, the Manitoba provincial government and the Winnipeg municipal government whose policemen were out. All these other major employers have completely disregarded participation in that strike so far as pension rights are concerned. I know that some of the C.P.R. men have given up hope long ago of justice being given. But despite that loss of hope they still hang on, still discuss it in their union meetings, still discuss it amongst the servicemen around the Weston shops, and they dare to hope that the government will yet be able to persuade the company that they ought to do the fair and proper thing with them. In the discussions that were had with the union representatives in 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939 the company used an argument that I do not think was justified, and certainly is no longer valid, namely, that they could not afford it. It was suggested that if the fortunes of the company were better something might be done. Well, the fortunes of the company are a great deal better to-day. The minister will realize that from the figures I placed on Hansard on a former occasion. To be fair to these men and to the country I suggest that the company should reconsider its position in this matter.

What does my hon. friend suggest the government could do?

Mr. Chairman, I crave a few minutes of the time of the committee to place before the Minister of Transport a situation which obtains in part of the constituency I represent, and which also extends into Saskatchewan. Since this is possibly the last opportunity I may have to address this august assembly at this session, and in deference to the large number of French Canadians residing in Athabaska, may I ask permission of . the committee to address the chamber in French. I assure hon. members who do not understand that language that there is no political aspect, whatsoever to the question I am about to discuss.
Supply-Transport

(Translation): Mr. Chairman, I wish to support a request submitted four or five years by a large number of people from northeast Alberta for an improved service on a branch line running from the town where I live, Bon-nyville, to Beaver river, a distance of about thirty miles. This is an extension of the Canadian National line which is to be built later- immediately after the war, I hope-to connect up with another section of the same system coming from Saskatchewan.
The section I am referring to was built in 1930 and 1931. Grading has been done on a further distance of about forty-five to fifty miles but has never been used. On this branch line only one train a week is run. At every session, for the last four years, during which I have had the honour of representing that part of the country, I have urgently requested the directors of the Canadian National Railways for an improved service. Again, very recently, with the support of one of the ministers, we paid a visit to the directors and the manager of the Canadian National Railways in Winnipeg and Edmonton, but, so far, our request has been turned down because it is claimed that the traffic is not heavy enough to warrant a two-train-a-week service; and I was asking three trains weekly. The reason given by the directors is not acceptable. It is easy to understand that if there is no train there will be no traffic. One train a week is so inadequate that the greater part of what is produced in that district is hauled by truck, and the committee knows that new trucks are very hard to obtain. Trucks that have been used for four or five years are becoming more and more defective.
That is a live stock area. Take, for instance, hogs which are raised in large numbers from Bonnvville to a point in Saskatchewan that lies 35 or 40 miles away. Those among us who raise cattle will readily understand that our people cannot keep those animals longer than one or two days after they are ready for the market. If a hog is over a certain weight the quality begins to decrease. Those breeders are compelled to deliver their hogs at once if they want them to qualify for grade 1, which represents $3 for each animal, and ensures a better classification.
I ask the minister to help us in our representations to the company. Nobody knows better than I the tremendous task performed by the railways and the efficiency with which they are doing it. A great many experienced employees have left the company to fight the great battle and they have had to be replaced

by men who had been superannuated. I realize that with the large increase in the number
of passenger and freight trains, the railways' task has more than doubled, and I commend them for the work they have accomplished. However, there is such a ground for complaint in that district. That is a matter which affects not only farmers in the Bonnyville area, but also a large number of people as far away as Saskatchewan. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that this committee as well as the minister and his department will support my request that pressure be brought to bear upon the Canadian National so that the people who took up land in such a remote district in the expectation of a railroad that had been promised for ten or fifteen years, may get such a service at least over that distance of thirty miles.

Mr. Chairman, I have a great deal of sympathy for my hon. friend from Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) and for the plan he has just submitted. As I told him, I shall be glad to make a point of pressing this scheme with the railway management. I might be held back by what he just said, namely, that the railway section would connect Bonnyville with the beaver kingdom. I would hesitate to introduce my hon. friend to the beaver kingdom!
Oh, no! I don't belong to that family.

Nonetheless, this matter has not failed to attract the attention of my department or of Canadian National Railways officials. There and, elsewhere, we cannot satisfy everyone and give them the service they want, and that for two reasons: the first is that there is a shortage of equipment and the second, a shortage of manpower. I have no doubt, however, that when conditions get back to normal, we will be able to comply with the request of the citizens of Bonnyville and of all the good folk represented by the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, just before the committee rose at six o'clock I was pleased to hear the minister express sympathy with the project of building a canal across the Chignecto isthmus, the matter having been brought up a little earlier by the hon. member

Supply-Transport
for Cumberland', who gave, I thought, an interesting and capable review in arguing why the canal should be built. Since I have made a very careful survey, so far as a layman can do, across the isthmus from Baie Verte to the bay of Fundy side, a distance of about seventeen to nineteen miles, I think I ought to say a word in support of the proposal. It is five years since I made my own personal inquiries into the matter. I have always been in favour of the canal being built. It has been a subject which has been before this house since 1870. It was one of the first canal projects proposed in the parliament of Canada, a matter of seventy-five years ago. So that I think it is about time, after seventy-five years of argument, that this job should be got on with.
From my own personal investigations there is-I am speaking from memory-a small chain of lakes, some more or less lengthy, in that region, and when Mr. R. K. Smith' was a member of parliament in this house my memory was that I had heard him make a speech on this project, but on looking up Hansard I do not think it was during my term here, between 1930 and 1935, but earlier that he gave an exhaustive and well delivered address in . favour of the building of the Chignecto canal. He also spoke of these lakes which I saw myself. Mr. Smith argued in favour of building the canal. He stated that it was not a difficult engineering problem from the Baie Yerte end until you come to the bay of Fundy, but that there, where the high tides come in, the engineers might find some diffi-cutly. I would say from my own observations that the argument put forward by the hon. member for Cumberland here to-day is a good one. If the canal were built it would save at least five hundred miles in going from the nearest New Brunswick port, which I believe is Shediac, to Saint John, as compared with the present route from Shediac around Nova Scotia to Saint John. That is a big saving in distance and time.
When I referred to this matter on a previous occasion I put on the record the distance that would be saved in going from Saint John to Montreal, and if the canal were built it would provide a much safer route for shipping. I also pointed out what it would mean in going from Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, to Boston. I think this house should do everything it can to increase the prosperity of the maritime provinces, and here is one way of doing it because a canal across the Chignecto isthmus would shorten the distance between Charlottetown and Boston by hundreds of miles and be a much safer course for ships to follow than going around by the ocean.
Not to prolong the matter I just wish to say, after hearing the hon. member for Cumberland and the sympathetic reply of the minister, that I hope that between now and the next session of parliament-if the minister is minister in the next parliament-he will avail himself of whatever opportunity he has to study the reports of the different commissions, and there have been many from 1871 down to the present time, and study also the plans that have been submitted for the building of this canal. I have examined those plans carefully. Indeed, I took them with me on my journey to New Brunswick to survey the area between Baie Yerte and the bay of Fundy. I shall be much pleased, if I am here at the next session of parliament, if the minister is able to submit to the house, if he is then Minister of Transport-

It will be handy when
he is in the opposition anyway.

I shall be glad if he will prepare himself between now and the next session to further this project for building the Chignecto canal in favour of which he has spoken so sympathetically. I am convinced that the country owes it to the maritime provinces. I am convinced that it will bring a larger measure of prosperity to the maritimes than they have to-day. It will provide a much safer and much shorter route and would provide for the producers on the bay of Fundy, such as the plaster rock miners and the coal mining people in my hon. friend's riding of Cumberland, a much shorter, safer and faster route from the coal mines and plaster rock mines to the main markets of central Canada. We should do everything we can to encourage greater trade, faster trade and more trade between all of the maritimes and upper Canada.

I am glad that the Chignecto canal project has become a national project rather than a maritime or local one through the support-and the enlightened support-of the hon. member for Davenport. I am sure that he has full knowledge of the possibilities of this canal as a national project to improve communications between the maritimes and from the great lakes around the coast to New England and other United States ports. It would provide a shorter and a safer route, would be of great benefit to trade and would improve relations between different parts of Canada and the United States.
The hon. gentleman is right in saying that the building of the canal has been mooted for many, many years, definitely since confedera-

tion, since 1870. I find on. looking at the report that was made by a commission in 1933 that the project has been studied by several different commissions ever since 1822. Administration of the Transport Act-
SCO. Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada-administration, maintenance and operation, $285,105.

What is the function of this board of transport commissioners, and what have they done for the Dominion of Canada in the last two years to justify what we have spent on them? The minister might tell us who they are.

The duty of the board of transport commissioners for Canada is to perform the functions vested in the board by the Transport Act and by the Railway Act, with the object of coordinating and harmonizing
[Mr. Michaud.?
the operations of all carriers engaged in transport by railways, ships, and up to this date, aircraft. It will be noted that there is no duty assigned to the board in respect of transportation by motor trucks or motor vehicles, or by other methods of transportation except railways and ships.
The personnel of the board consists of one chief commissioner, one assistant chief, one deputy, and three commissioners. The main functions of the board and the personnel of the board are to administer the several sections and provisions of the Transport Act and the Railway Act which have regard to coordination of traffic, rates of transportation both of persons and goods, safety appliances and devices, and generally coordinating the functions of the respective railways and ships engaged in transportation.
Could the minister tell us anything which this board has done within the last two years that is worth while?
How long has it been since the board of transport commissioners reviewed the freight rate schedules which obtain in western Canada?
I cannot give the exact date. I have not that information before me.
Would the minister suppose that it has been attended to within the last ten years?

Oh, yes. I believe there have been applications within the last few years. I am not so sure that there was a general revision of the rate structure within the last ten years. The board acts generally on applications by interested parties.

I should like to draw to the minister's attention a case in point. To illustrate the highly discriminatory freight rates that exist with respect to western provinces like Alberta and Saskatchewan, one can ship 100 pounds of barbed wire by rail from Montreal to Vancouver for 75 cents but if one wishes to send the same barbed wire from Montreal to Edmonton it costs $1.98. The whole freight rate structure affecting Alberta and Saskatchewan is shot through with absurdities like that. The time is overdue when something should be done about this matter, and I believe this board ought to go to work on it and make sure that certain provinces are given a better chance to live.

The board is constituted for the purpose mentioned by my hon. friend and any public body or person having any complaint or grievance regarding freight rates can submit that grievance to the board. They
will hear the complaint and pass upon it and adjust the situation to the general freight rate principles that prevail in the country.

Can the experts in the department tell the minister of one or two cases that have been referred to the board within the last five years in which there has been an adjustment in favour of Alberta or Saskatchewan?

I do not know of any,
but if there were any applications or representations and a hearing has been held and a ruling given it will appear in the annual report of the board of transport commissioners, which is tabled in this house each year.

As a member of parliament I appreciate being referred by the minister to certain reports, but being himself a member he knows that if the members of this house undertook to read one-half of the reports that are put into their hands there would not be very many members; there would be so many corpses. We have to depend upon ministers to give us an idea of the essential features of the reports that are submitted by them. I appreciate the answers that the minister has given, but I repeat, the time is overdue for a revision of the freight rates in western Canada so that they will have a less injurious bearing upon Alberta and Saskatchewan. As between freight rates for export and freight rates for inland carriage there is a difference that has been recognized by transportation and shipping companies and all public bodies. There is a differential between commodities that are moved for export and those that are moved for home

consumption. The matter has been argued many times within the last twenty-five or thirty years, but the principle has never been changed, namely, that there should be a differential. As to the differential in rates on goods transported for home consumption as between Montreal and Vancouver on one hand and between Montreal and Calgary, on the other, I cannot give any explanation why there should be a differential, if there is any. Of course, in considering the freight rate structure of Canada competition between rail transportation and water transportation must be considered. There are competitive rates and there are rates that are not competitive. As regards the rates between two points which are served by both rail and water, since water rates are always lower than rail rates the railways have to make their rates between such competitive points the same as water rates in order to get business.

The view is generally held by people who are well informed that the freight rate structure in Canada in many respects establishes a tariff wall around Alberta, both importing and exporting, and there is no joke at all about it. The situation in Saskatchewan is just as serious. Anyone who imagines that a sound Canadian economy can be erected on a situation like that is capable of imagining pretty extreme things. I repeat, the time has come for a thorough overhauling of these rates.
