Marine services-
366. Marine service administration, $15,542.

I wish to ask the minister a question on this item. In doing so, I am being consistent with the stand I took in 1940 and 1941, when I maintained that Canada should have a merchant marine service of her own. I was quite satisfied with what was going on, until I read the statement by the minister about the first of the year that the service would not be continued. I am not asking that the government operate these boats, but I maintain that Canada should have a merchant marine service of her own, sufficient at least to carry some of her merchandise from Canada to overseas ports.
As I understand it, we now have seventy-five boats built in Canada, totalling about 542,000 tons. These are administered by the Fark Steamship company. Fifteen of those boats are oil tankers; fifty-one are 10,000-ton boats and nine are 4,700-ton boats. That is the total capacity of Canada's merch-ent. marine at the present time, and I maintain that it is not sufficient for our requirements.
I do not wish to delay the committee too long, but I shall take time to give some indication of what tonnage will be required in Ca.nada in the very near future-in fact, as soon as we can get to it. Prime Minister Churchill said some time ago that in Great Britain they were going to build 3,000,000 houses, and more recently he has announced that they will be building 5,000,000. We have noticed reports as to damage in England at the present time, and it is.possible that the amount mentioned by Mr. Churchill would not be any more than sufficient.
I wonder how many of us realize just what 5,000,000 houses in Great Britain mean in the way of construction, and the supplying of lumber, most of which will have to come from Canada. It means that if the housing plan upon which Great Britain is embarking is to be carried out they will have to build a house in Great Britain every twenty seconds for ten years. That will mean that an enormous amount of lumber from Canada will have to be secured. Quite recently they placed an order for two billion feet, one billion of which is to be supplied in each of the next two years. More than 300 boats will be required to carry that item alone from Canada to Great Britain. Then, to name only a few of the other larger items, 7,500,000 tons of wheat will have to be moved from Canada, and that will require another 250 boats. So that, all told, I claim that Canada should have at least 5,000,000 tons of shipping operating out of Canada, and at the very minimum we should have 500 of

Supply-Transport
those 10,000-ton boats. Up to the present time we have only seventy-five operating, and fifteen of those are tankers.
In my opinion our position has changed entirely since the last war. During that war Ihe Scandinavian countries were neutral, and as a result they built up a large merchant fleet. The consequence was that their flags were seen flying in every port of the world. Many of their ships were coming to Canadian ports. To-day the situation is entirely reversed. In this war their merchant boats have pretty well disappeared, and ours have come in. We have built a fleet-possibly a small one-of our own. In addition to that we have now in Canada a large personnel trained in sea-going occupations, men who will wish to follow the sea when the war is over.
So that, as I say, the situation is now entirely changed. As nearly as I can estimate it, it will require about 40,000 men to transport Canadian goods to foreign countries. How many of those 40,000 men are going to be Canadians? Canadian boats flying the Canadian flag and operated by Canadians should be in every port of the world. I am not saying tliat our Canadian boats should carry every bit of lumber or every bushel of grain shipped from Canada. Certainly we might have to get some outside service. But we should be carrying at least a fair proportion in our own boats, and bringing back a fair proportion of materials from abroad.
In my view Canada can no longer stand idly by and see this service go to ships outside Canada. Now is the time for us to take advantage of the situation, and now is the time for the government to declare a policy. I say this, despite the fact that we entered the merchant marine service some time ago and, I understand, lost somewhere in the neighbourhood of 8100,000,000. "But that was a puny effort, an effort which in my opinion was destined to nothing but failure, because there was no strength in the organization and no vigour behind it, and the class of boats put into the service were not the boats which could perform the services required.
Only yesterday we debated a bill setting up export credits, to help in connection with the export of our goods. But there is no export credit that is as important to a Canadian exporter or producer as the fact that there will be a regular service from Canada to every port in the world. In our own small way in British Columbia we export to Australia and New Zealand, and before the war we exported to Japan, China and, to some extent, to South Africa. That trade, however,
was only intermittent. The South African service was very poor, and we had to depend almost entirely on foreign boats.
That is all I wish to say on the matter to-night, but as long as I am in the house I am going to advocate giving a chance to our sailors who have learned to sail the seas, and to love it. These men will want to stay at that work, and they should have an opportunity of operating our boats, carrying our goods, and carrying our flag and our good will to all parts of the world.

I should like to describe to the minister a condition I have found at our public dock in Belleville, Ontario. Practically all the facilities at that dock are appropriated by one firm. As I recall it, the dock was erected in 1935 by an expenditure of public money, and I would understand that it was erected for the use of the general public. I contend that it should be made available to the public. I have noticed that at the present time there are upwards of 3,000 tons of soft coal covering practically the entire surface of the dock. This pile is replenished as quantities are taken out of it, with the result that the content remains practically constant. The entire length of the dock is covered with the coal, right out to the water's edge, leaving only a bare catwalk along the front.
This situation renders it impossible for other coal dealers in our city successfully to tender on contracts with our large purchasers of coal for public buildings. It is an indisputable fact that only those having the advantage of waterborne freight can compete successfully on orders of that kind. This is a condition which has stood for some considerable time, and one which merits supervision better than it has had up to date.

With regard to the Belleville dock I understand that it is operated under a local board. We have received no complaint through the board as to the facilities of that dock being monopolized by one firm, but I can assure the hon. member that we will look into the complaint, and if it is possible to remedy the situation we will see that it is remedied.

The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) has raised a very important question as to the maintenance and expansion of our merchant marine service after the war. Several times I have heard questions asked in the house of different ministers as to the policy of the government with respect to the merchant marine service after the war, but as yet we have received no definite answer as to the government's intentions. I think this would be a good time to hear from the government just what it proposes to do in the matter. I heartily endorse everything that the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) has just said, and there is no need of my repeating it. Would the minister mind taking five minutes to inform the committee as to the policy of the department with respect to the maintenance and expansion of the merchant marine service after the war? Are the government doing any thinking about it? Have they any policy on it?

There is quite a divergence of opinion as to what will become, after the war, of the merchant ships built and owned by Canada. It is impossible to state at the present time. But there is no difference of opinion as to whether Canada should retain as many of these ships as can be used for the trade of Canada. Whether our Canadian merchant marine should be operated by the government or by individuals or by private companies is another matter.
The opinion I expressed last January was my opinion as between operation of the Canadian merchant navy by private control and operation under government control. At the end of this year we are going to have close to three hundred merchant ships owned by Canada. Some are leased and operated by our allies. Some are operated by a crown corporation, Park Steamships, and some by the Canadian National Steamships. After the war Canada will have a large merchant marine, close to three hundred ships, we hope. Before the war we had thirty-seven. So that the number of Canadian merchant ships registered in Canada has increased almost ten times since the war began. I agree that most of these ships will be required for carrying out of this country the goods which will have to be exported,
Mr. Michaud.]
' and some of them will no doubt be bringing back return cargoes, but no one who has had any experience or has any knowledge of shipping can expect that our imports and exports will all be carried exclusively by Canadian ships. That is an impossibility.
I did not advocate that.

No, I know, and I have
never advocated doing away altogether with the Canadian merchant marine. The opinion I expressed was based on our experience after the last wrar, when the government operated the ships. I still believe that all our merchant ships will be needed and will be operated after the war. But as to a definite policy governing the future, that has not yet been determined by the government. It is under consideration and has been for some time by a committee of civil servants, experts, and we have not yet received the final report of the committee to enable us to determine what policy should be followed after the war.

I am sure that the statement just made by the minister will be appreciated by the people of Canada, because this is the first time that Canada has been given any idea that we shall have three hundred merchant ships in the Canadian service by the end of the year. I would refer the minister to a return tabled in the house on May 3, which speaks about the Canadian National steamship company. That company has six 4,700-ton boats out of the sixty altogether that are being operated. The Canadian National Steamships have six of the smaller boats.

We certainly do not want to repeat the mistakes of the last war. There is no doubt in my mind that after the last war the Canadian merchant navy was sabotaged in the interests of private shipping companies. We certainly should guard against anything of that sort this time.
I,	too, am glad that the minister has at least said something definite on the matter. What we are now discussing is a very important part of our post-wrar plans, and definite plans should be being made now as to what we are going to do in the matter of maintaining and expanding the Canadian merchant marine. Study should be given now as to how we can best utilize the ships which we have built with the taxpayers' money with a view to providing, among other things, opportunities for those who have taken to the sea since the war began, and who may desire to follow that calling after the war. I have heard it stated several times in the house, and I think rightly so, that Canada is going to

Supply-Transport
play a great part in the first four or five years after the war in helping to feed and rehabilitate European countries, and perhaps the British isles to some extent, and I think these three hundred ships, with the crews now employed on them, if they want to follow that vocation, might very well be utilized in that service. Now is the time that someone should be studying the matter and laying plans so that we may be able to go into that phase of rehabilitation, ready to carry out our plans immediately after the war is over.
I have no intention of pursuing the matter further. I have read a good deal and have files about what happened to the Canadian merchant marine after the last war, and it is not a nice story. I believe it is very well known. We need to guard against a repetition of this experience. As I say, it is not a matter of deciding whether operations are to be carried on under a system of private enterprise or under government ownership. If the Canadian government now own these ships, they have spent the money which has trained the personnel that are operating them; if the government is going to make millions of dollars available to UNRRA for the purpose of rehabilitating the European continent, it should be the responsibility of the Canadian government to see to it that every bit of machinery they niyw have should be utilized. If private shipping companies want to go into the business for commercial purposes, that is entirely up to themselves.. We now have an organization which should be fully utilized, and whether we intend to continue it for years after the war is over is something which can be determined as we go along. In the posh-war period the whole organization should be used to its fullest extent, and now is the time to plan and be ready.

As I have already said,
this problem is being examined by what we consider the best talent that can be got together, to give it consideration and make a report upon which the policy of the government will be based. There is no intention on the part of the government to sabotage any ships of our merchant marine, ^here is, however, one point I would bring to the attention of the hon. member. He spoke of forty or forty-five thousand men being employed or finding employment in our merchant marine after the war. When one remembers what number of men is required to man one of these ships, I cannot see the possibility of utilizing forty-five thousand men. Admitting that after the war we shall still have our complete quota of ships built during the war, the number will be not more than three hundred, and 100-370J
it takes only fifty men to man one of these ships, so that at the most fifteen thousand men will find employment. That is the utmost number we can expect to employ even if we keep our merchant marine intact and all our ships are returned to us after the war.

I should like to correct
a statement. I said that forty thousand men would be required to move the goods produced. That does not mean to say, forty thousand Canadians. I followed that up by asking how many of these will be Canadians?

I am interested in the statement that the minister is going to maintain a merchant fleet of three hundred ships after the war. I should like to have a statement from him as to whether in operating this fleet he will maintain the wages of the crews who will operate them at a scale that is appropriate to Canadians. If, in so doing, he comes in competition with low scales of wages of competing ships, how is he going to deal with that situation. How is he going to compete with the ships of Great Britain- not that that will be so very difficult, although heretofore they have operated with a much lower wage scale than is acceptable to Canadians-and with the Norwegians, the Swedes, the Finlanders, the Greeks? Last of all I would ask the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) how he would propose to operate these ships in competition with the Japanese or other orientals whose scale of living is very much lower than is acceptable to Canadians.
It is all very well to say that we want to operate these ships-I am in agreement with that sentiment-to carry our own products. But we have the financial problem of how we are to get paid for our goods and how we are to be paid for the carrying of these goods. I assume also that Canada will insure these goods along the lines of the bill which was recently before this committee, so that we shall furnish our own insurance and it will no longer be business for other countries. Is it that all we shall ask the motherland and other countries to do is to pay for Canadian goods shipped by us in our own bottoms, manned by Canadian crews and insured by ourselves? I should like the minister to explain how we shall be able to maintain a proper scale of wages in the operating of these ships and enable importing countries pay for our products.

The hon. gentleman has just touched upon a very important angle of the whole problem, and one of several items which have to be taken into consideration, and indeed are being considered, by the board
Supply-Transport

which is now studying our post-war merchant shipping problem. I know it will be difficult to adjust all these factors which enter into the whole problem, and it is impossible to state what will be done until the committee has-studied the subject from its various angles and has presented to the government a suggestion which may have to be integrated in the general policy to be adopted by the government.

Just a word on that. I quite agree that there are two principal difficulties which will be encountered. The first was referred to by the hon. member for Cumberland, and is connected with the varying rates of wages and standards of accommodation which the crews of other countries have. It is true that a number of countries before the war started were running ships at one-third of the cost at which Canadians could operate. There are countries which have a lot of shipping tonnage, members of whose crews would bring their food and their own dishes and the like in a trunk across the Atlantic, looking after themselves, at an expense of a few cents a day for maintenance, while we were trying to set up standards for our ships which are wholly out of proportion with the standards of these competitors, so much so that, as I said, our ships were costing from the point of view of personnel about three times as much as the ships of other countries which I need not name and which have a large tonnage.
There is another problem. You cannot expect to have your ships go into a country to take your goods and bring back their goods with your shipping on every occasion. They want to have a shipping fleet and to transport their goods in their own ships. The problem is full of difficulties. I can quite understand that it will need a lot of study, and I hope the committee will find a solution.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a complaint with respect to the failure to appoint a light-housekeeper in my constituency on the He au Haute, at the head of the bay of Fundy. Mr. John T. McCormick is the person to whom I refer, and from information I have, the greatest discrimination has been practised against him by the department or by someone in the government service. This position of lighthouse-keeper became vacant in the ordinary course. The previous occupant had given good service, had reached the retiring age and retired, and the civil service commission advertised for applicants. A number of applications were received and examinations were held. Mr. McCormick headed the list of applicants. He was recommended for appointment by the civil service commission and notified of his appointment subject to confirmation by the department. He was notified at that time that he must vacate within seven days the position he hfeld. That position was captain or mate with the merchant marine in the north Atlantic service. I believe he was drawing about $240 a month in this position. The remuneration attached to this position of lighthouse-keeper is much less, but it had the attractive feature of permanency. He agreed to accept it. He was a man of good character and had splendid service in the last war. I believe he had and still has the support of every returned man in the county of Cumberland. He gave up his position and to this day has not been confirmed in the appointment.
After leaving his position with the merchant marine service, he waited around for some months expecting to be notified to report for duty. He obtained temporary employment on the provincial police force of Quebec. That shows his standing and his capabilities. My complaint is that there has been gross discrimination against him as a returned man of the last war. This man is entitled to the position and to compensation by the department because he had been notified that he must vacate the previous position he held. I bring this complaint to the attention of the minister and the committee. If the minister is not able to reply to-night I ask him to look into the case and see that justice is done to Mr. MacCormack.

I have no recollection whatever of this case. There are 1,139 light-keepers in the service. Most of them were appointed by the civil service commission. I have no recollection of having seen any correspondence or of ever having the matter brought to my attention. However, I shall look into the case.

I think the minister's department is responsible. His appointment had been recommended by the civil service commission or the Department of Transport. He was told that he must vacate, within seven days, the position he was holding, which he did. However, it is impossible to prevent some people from operating craft which are unseaworthy. We have a staff of forty inspectors in the department at present, and we are eleven short. We cannot get people to take these jobs. Some of our inspectors left to undertake war work. We have advertised for competent people to take these positions, but have received no replies.
Did I understand the minister to s&v that he was eleven inspectors short?
Yes.

Probably that accounts for the fact that in some cases inspections have not been made for quite some time.
(Mr. Stirling.]
That may be so. We have advertised through the civil service commission in an attempt to fill these jobs, but have received no applications.

One year.
Is any penalty provided if the equipment is found deficient?

There is no penalty provided for deficient equipment, but there is a penalty for using a boat that has deficient equipment. Have charges been laid
against any of these ship owners?

Yes. An accident occurred not long ago; an investigation was held, and on the report of the commissioner I found the matter sufficiently serious to bring it to the attention of the attorney general of Ontario. In that case I know a charge has been laid and an arrest, made.

revenue during the year ending March 31, 1945. The minister should make it perfectly clear that this does not give a true picture of the situation. It may have been that when the item was reduced from $490,000 to $200,000, the amount of the deficit was underestimated.

Last year we voted
$200,000 to take care of the deficit. In 194243 we had a surplus of $112,120.75. We did not have to expend the appropriation for that year. In 1943-44 we had a deficit of $347,872.90.

Is there any report issued by the Hudson Bay Railway company so that members of the house can see it? Just in that connection I should like to suggest that inasmuch as this railway is operated, as I understand it, by the Canadian National Railways, under their supervision, for the Hudson Bay Railway company, and indirectly

for the government, the report of this railway should be submitted, along with the reports of the Canadian National Railways, the T.C.A., and Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Limited, to the regularly constituted parliamentary committee on wholly-owned government railways. For instance, I think this committee, and the railway committee, if it had it within its purview, would be interested to know why it was that in 1942-43 this railway, with an income of $1,113,000 and expenses of just $1,000,000, was able to show $112,000 profit, and yet in 1943-44, with an income of $660,000-$400,000 less-the expenses were actually, if I gathered the minister's figures correctly, a few thousand dollars higher. Yes.

It appears to me that our American cousins have sense enough to use a road which we ourselves do not use as much as we should. We have that road there and it has not in the past been made use of to the extent that it should have. I contend that it was a good thing for the united nations' cause that we had that road there, and Americans have made good use of it and have shown its value. The government has invested a lot of money in it, and I think it should be continually searching for ways to make this endeavour a paying proposition. I believe that in the interests of the country generally and in western Canada in particular it is very important that the administration continually have their eyes on
[Mr. Jackman.3
this venture for the purpose of seeing in what way more use of it can be made in order that we shall not have these continual deficits year after year. Like many who come from western Canada I believe that good use can be made of the railway and that it can be converted into a profitable venture.
How much wheat was shipped over the Hudson Bay railway last year?
Nothing in the last five years.

None for the last three
years.
WThy is that?
No convoys.

If I lived in Alberta or Saskatchewan I might know it, but I suspect that there are no convoys to take the wheat out of Churchill. I understand that there is no consumption of wheat at Churchill, that the wheat which is being shipped over the railway is for export from the port of Churchill, and for the last three years, for obvious reasons, no convoys have gone to Churchill to take the wheat to Europe.

What my hon. friends on this side of the chamber have been saying about the use of the road is important, but at the present time it cannot be used as an export route, for the reason which the minister has just announced. I made a very careful survey of the whole area from the Pas to Churchill. At Churchill, I might say, there is a wonderful elevator which was built by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. It is one of the finest elevators in the world, but it cannot be used now, for the reason outlined, that no convoys are available to ship wheat from the port to the old country. The explanation of the increased freight revenue during 1942-43 is quite simple. The Americans were building a great airfield there. It was mentioned here the other day in a report that these airfields are to be taken over. A tremendous traffic was going on; it was almost impossible to get from the Pas to Churchill, but of course when the airfield was completed that traffic slowed up, and for that reason in the following year the freight was much less.
I endorse what some of my hon. friends have said regarding this route. It is to be hoped that after the war the magnificent elevator will be put to good use in handling western wheat.
Someone said that Canada put a lot of money into the road. Well, Canada did, but

Supply-Transport
the three western provinces alone put nearly fifty million dollars into it. The Dominion of Canada put in a lot of money, but the major portion was contributed by the three western provinces. I sincerely hope that after the war things will so develop that the road can be used commercially for the exportation of wheat.
Who owns this railway at the present time?
The people of Canada.
Are all the shares in the hands of the dominion government?
It is not an incorporated company; it is a public work built by the country and owned by the country, and it is operated for the country by the Canadian National Railways.
How much wheat was shipped out of that port in 1939 and in 1938?
In 1939, to the value of $154,142.16.

It sounds like an
appallingly small amount for a national railway, does it not? Could the minister give an explanation why more was not shipped out in 1939? Was more shipped out in 1938?
How much wheat was shipped out of Canada in the meanwhile by other railway routes?
I do not know.

This seems on the face of it altogether too small an amount of wheat to be shipped out of that port. Western Canadians have the idea that this railway is being damned with faint praise; in other words, that it has been sabotaged. We should like to have some information from the minister to reassure us that such is not the case.
If my hon. friend will guarantee that the wheat when delivered at Churchill will be taken care of, I will guarantee that more wheat will be shipped over that road.
Could the minister give us any reason why the wheat when it gets to Churchill could not be taken care of?

Because the shipping
companies will not take it out of Churchill.
Why not? We want to find out the reason for that. That is what we are here for.
They prefer to ship over other routes.

There must be some other reason why the company prefers to ship over other routes. There seems to be plenty of evidence that the railway is a good one and that there is a good, route through Churchill. Why should we find so little grain carried over that route? Why should shipping companies be averse to using it?

Surely the hon. member is aware that the government does not route grain or other goods. The owners or shippers or buyers ship their own goods by whatever way they see fit and over such routes as are cheapest to them and whereby they can get their goods to the point of destination quickest and cheapest.
The Department of Transport exercises no influence in that regard. Is that right?

Perhaps I may be allowed to speak for a moment with reference to a route that I know fairly well. A transportation route is an avenue that is open to the shipping public. There are several avenues for wheat from the west. There is the avenue to Fort William and Port Arthur and down the great lakes and the St. Lawrence to Montreal and then to the ocean. The Hudson bay route is an alternative. The use of the route depends on the cost of shipping grain from point of origin to point of consumption, which may be in the United Kingdom or on the continent. Grain will follow the cheapest route, and an eighth of a cent a bushel is sufficient to transport grain by one route or another. The Hudson bay route is there, and it depends on its effect on prices whether grain is shipped by that route or the other. If the cost of shipping by the head of the lakes and through the great lakes gets out of line, the least bit above the cost of shipping by Churchill, shippers will use Churchill. I think that since the west has the protection of the route it is not very serious whether large volpmos go by that route every year. If rates on the great lakes are high, a very large volume moves through Churchill; if rates on the lakes are low, a small volume moves through Churchill. It is an alternative route, and the western producer has a choice of routes and therefore can take advantage of whichever route is cheapest.

The railway is merely an instrument in the hands of the Canadian
Supply-Transport

west for preventing exploitation by any companies that might be transporting Canadian wheat.
It has that effect, yes.

If that is the light in which we are to look on the route, then it is well that we should know that. We know the amount of money we are spending for the maintenance of that route as an insurance against exploitation.

I am glad to see that there is an increase in the expenditure on this railway and the terminal at Churchill. Some of it may be to make up the difference between earnings and the cost, but I think the minister would be well advised to see that the route is kept in order so that when the war is over it will be ready to serve the public. I think it will prove to be one of the great outlets for western Canada, one of the very best and cheapest. We had before the committee on agriculture this year a statement with respect to grain shipped from there. Last year the elevators were full of Canadian wheat board grain, and a great deal of it was shipped out and the capacity filled again. But, as has been pointed out, owing to convoy service now, they cannot use it for shipping grain. I heard the head of one of the largest steamship companies in Britain say a year or so before the war broke out, speaking in Regina to the board of trade with reference to this route, that there was no question in the world that, with the improvements in radio equipment and direction for shipping, that port could be kept open for three months longer than it has been up to the present time and that it would serve as a great route so far as shipping grain to Britain is concerned. The cost would be nearly three to four cents a bushel cheaper and that would be in its favour. But at the present time the chief shipping interests are centred at Fort William and Port Arthur and they would naturally direct a great deal of their shipping there. As an outlet for western Canada it is one of the coming routes. One of the largest shipping concerns in Britain declares that after the war, with the improvements that have been made in radio equipment for directing ships, that port will be available for shipping for three or four months longer in the year. I am glad to see the minister increasing the estimates, and I hope the route will be kept in proper repair so that when the war is over it will be available.

What the Minister of
Munitions and Supply said a moment ago with regard to grain moving according to where the

shippers and exporters desire it to move holds water to a certain extent, because we know that certain departments of government do from time to time encourage trade in one way or another. Were any
other architects consulted as to utilizing coal and the ordinary steam power plant that is used in other boats of this type?
Is my hon. friend aware that Prince Edward Island is quite likely to become a great producer of oil? '

I hope that may be so, and I am told there are possibilities that my county of Cumberland may become a great oil producer also. But it is recognized that there, is a world shortage of oil at the present time. We had evidence before the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment that the supply of oil in sight will be sufficient for only fourteen years at the present rate of consumption. Therefore, with *coal supplies sufficient for hundreds of years right at hand, it seems only an ordinary business precaution to give the preference to coal rather than oil, even if the hope of the Minister of Munitions and Supply should be realized, as I hope it will be, and a great oil reservoir should be found on Prince Edward Island.

I am going to say something about this item, although I would not have done so if I had thought the minister could get through his estimates in toto to-night. I have made several trips to study this matter of transportation between the mainland and the island, and I should like to satisfy myself that this new ship is of the proper design. I must admit that from its picture it is a fine looking ship. I would remind the minister that between St. Ignace

and Mackinaw, the strait between lake Michigan and lake Huron, a strait a little over nine miles wide, in the winter time gets badly clogged with very heavy ice. I believe that strait is approximately the same width as Northumberland strait. I should like to know if the department saw to it that the designers of this new ship of ours consulted those who were conversant with similar conditions, and with the designers of the six boats that cross from St. Ignace to Mackinaw. One of these boats, I believe it is the Sainte Marie, appears to load and unload at both ends. The ship is so designed that the main deck front end can be lifted up to allow the railway cars to roll oft". I do not know whether this new ship is of the same design. Perhaps in the opinion of the architect or engineers who designed the new ship, their design is the only type that can safely navigate this strait. If that is the case, their judgment should be accepted. But if a ship could be designed to load and unload at both ends it seems to me it would be able to take on and discharge its cargo much more rapidly than the new ship may be able to do. I am not going to criticize the new boat in any way, for it seems to be very smart. It is a big ship, with tremendous power; it has nearly three times the power of any of the fine ships that cross from St. Ignace to Mackinaw, but its internal design must be totally different from that of those ships which cross the difficult nine-mile Mackinaw strait in .the winter time, where ice piles up so high that two or three ships have propellers fore and aft to cut through ice.
Every ship in service on Mackinac strait, even the smallest one, will carry more automobiles than this new ship will carry. According to the figures submitted by the department, the new ship will carry only sixty motorcars. I hope the time will come when motor traffic to and from the island will amount to many more than sixty automobiles per trip. In contrast, the smallest ship crossing the strait of Mackinac carries seventy-two automobiles, while one of the largest carries one hundred and eleven almost twice as many as this new ship is designed to carry. Then this new ferry is designed to carry only nineteen railway cars. That may be sufficient; I do not know whether a train going to Prince Edward Island would consist of more than nineteen cars, but I hope the time will come when trains going to and from that island will have twice that many cars. These ships crossing from St. Ignace to Mackinaw carry as many as twenty-four railway cars.
All I am going to say is that the island is entitled to the best this country can give it,

Supply-T ransport
and I know we have a sympathetic minister.
We have not always had ministers who were as sympathetic to the island, but the present minister is, and I hope he will look into the particular matters I have drawn to his attention. There is no reason why the capacity of a brand new ship should be so much smaller than the capacity of the smallest ship on the Mackinac strait route. This new ferry is to be 372 feet 6 inches over all, while the smallest ship crossing the strait of Mackinac is about 250 feet long, but has greater automobile and car capacity. Why is that? Does the strait of Northumberland require a ship so strongly built, or with a much greater capacity for passengers? I note that the passenger capacity is larger, and I am glad of that because this is a glorious island.
What is the draught of the Mackinac ships?

The smallest one is twelve feet aft, and the largest one is twenty feet aft.	I have looked into the matter very
carefully because, like other hon. members, I have long felt that the island has not had what the fathers of confederation promised it. I realize that the minister is sympathetic, and as long as he is in power he will, I hope, see that they get more than they have been getting.
As I said a moment ago, the largest boat, ChieJ Wawatam, is 4,500 horse-power, and the horse-power of the new Canadian ship is 12,000. That is a very heavy horse-power, and the speed of sixteen and a half knots is good. That is a smart speed at which to cross the strait. May I congratulate whoever is responsible for that speed, because the old Prince Edward Island had a knotage of only 124. The islanders-they like to be called the islanders -are entitled to the fastest and most up-to-date transportation which can be secured between the island and the mainland.
I know if the minister examines the docks at Borden and Tormentine he will say, the same as I did, after careful examination, "These docks are not what this great country of Canada should provide for this magnificent and beautiful island, for its traffic to and from the mainland." If I were designing a dock-[DOT] and of course I am not a dock architect, although I have seen many docks in Europe and on the North American continent-I would certainly see to it that boats could go into and out of the dock much more rapidly than they can to-day. If conditions would permit ib-and I do not say they will permit it-I would have ships that would load at one end and drive straight off the other end if desirable.
I should like inquiries to be made about that. This might not be suitable at that point, but if it is we should certainly have it that way.
The minister, being sympathetic to the island and its rights, should not hesitate to pay the cost to have adequate and proper docks built at Tormentine and Borden, so as to increase speed in loading and unloading. He ought not to hesitate during his term of office to see to it that the islanders get what they have been asking for for such a long time, and that is fast traffic, fast loading and fast unloading. All this will help commerce. At the present time it is almost too much for the ordinary tourist to take a big car over there. I have been over several times with my car, and I have never crossed on boats crossing that strait without becoming furious before I got off at either end of the crossing. I do considerable travelling, and a lot of driving; I have driven several hundred thousand miles, and I become furious when I have to go along on an upper deck and drive my motorcar around a narrow passage.
While there is still time-and I believe there is time-we should see to it that this fine new ship, with its beautiful design, is built with regard for speed of loading and unloading at each side of the strait. This should be considered, even if it will cost more money, because it would give the islanders a fair deal. Let us not worry about a few extra dollars, because this is not an investment for only one year. It is for many years. The docks can be vastly improved for greater speed in loading and unloading. I suggest that the designer, or whoever is responsible, should visit many other places to see how quickly loading and unloading can be carried out. For instance, he could go to Toledo, to discuss the matter with the Toledo Shipbuilding company, which perhaps has had much experience in building such ships for such purposes.
I am glad that a Canadian company is building this ship, and that Canadian workmen are doing the work. There is no reason why we cannot build as good ships here as are built anywhere else, and there is no reason why our workmen cannot do as good work as other workmen are doing-and I know they can do it. Therefore I am very happy indeed that the ship has been built in Canada by Canadian workmen, and designed by a Canadian designer.
If it is at all possible the minister should look into this matter to have some alterations in design if practicable, so that the number of cars crossing that channel may be greater than called for in the design. Sixty is not enough. I am referring, of course, to motorcars. The
Supply-Transport

number of freight cars to go aboard the ship when crossing the channel should be more than nineteen.. That is not enough, either.
A large amount of money is being spent- not too much, but certainly a large amount. But I would say that even more should be spent, if required, to give the island people a square deal.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister answers I have a question to ask. It is represented to me that a ferry boat was put into service on lake Ontario, since the beginning of the war, and that it is a boat of dimensions perhaps larger than those of the new ferry serving Prince Edward Island. That boat is powered with coal-not Canadian coal, but coal brought in from the United States.
The ferry boat now under discussion is being designed to use oil which, in all probability, will also be imported, despite the fact that in the post-war years the coal mines of Nova Scotia will be more anxious than ever to secure a market for their product. Has the minister any information with respect to that new ferry boat? If not, will he make inquiries and advise the committee at a later sitting?

I have no information regarding that new ferry boat, the name of which has not been given to me. But I know that the most modern icebreaker that is being built in the United States is built on exactly the same principle as the one which has been designed for Prince Edward Island.
I can assure the hon. member for Davenport that all the considerations he has set forth have been taken into account by the department, the architects and the engineers, and we are trying to give the island the best boat Canada can produce, and a boat which will give service under the conditions under which it will have to operate. The boat could not stand a draught of more than nineteen feet.

How many
feet?
Nineteen feet. So that the boat has to carry its load and its own machinery, and has to develop enough power to break the ice.
Will the docks require alterations?
The docks required will be taken care of.
Is this boat designed to go both ways, back and forth?

It will go back and forth,
but it will turn around.
It has not propellers at both ends?
It has an icebreaker bow.
It will have propellers at both ends.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, August 4, 1944
The house met at eleven o'clock.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: Yesterday I directed a question to the Minister of Labour with respect to a serious situation in western Canada in connection with harvest help, but owing to the confusion he did not answer me. I would call his attention again to the matter. There is a very serious situation in Saskatchewan where they need 8,000 or 10,000 extra men to assist in taking in the harvest. subtopic: HELP FOB WESTERN WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Last year we were faced with the same problem. As I recall, the then member for Weyburn moved the adjournment of the house in connection with what he considered a matter of urgent public importance. We got the crop off in western Canada last year and we got if off in Ontario and the maritimes with some difficulty in view of the man-power situation which confronts every nation that is doing its duty in the present war. I am confident myself that we shall get the crop off in western Canada as we did last year. Last year we had a movement from Ontario to the western country. It was a movement of such a character that we reached the stage where the western people said, "We don't want any more help." We intend to follow the same policy this year. In addition to that, the crop condition in the Dakotas is not as good as it was in years past. We anticipate a movement from the Dakotas into western Canada to swell the tide of harvesters engaged in the work of getting the crop off this year. In connection with that movement we are paying return transportation costs both from Ontario and from the Dakotas, and of course there is the policy that has been in operation for the last two years, of leave where possible from the armed forces. I am convinced that the cooperation that has been displayed in the past and is being manifested at the present time will satisfy my hon. friend and the result will be that the crop will be got off in western Canada.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CONDITIONS RESULTING FROM DRY WEATHER IN SOUTHERN ALBERTA
speechtext: May I direct two questions to the Minister of Agriculture. First, will the minister tell the house what measures he is taking to meet the feed situation facing beef producers of southern Alberta because of the drought conditions prevailing in that area? Secondly, has the minister considered the advisability of buying from southern Alberta producers the beef and lambs and of shipping them to the east where feed is ample?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: CONDITIONS RESULTING FROM DRY WEATHER IN SOUTHERN ALBERTA
speechtext:
I received yesterday afternoon the communication which was referred to by the hon. member for Lethbridge, from the Card-ston Cooperative Association, and I have writ-' ten to them this morning stating what the usual practice is in connection with matters of that kind. We are making and have been making since the beginning of the summer full investigations in connection with prairie farm assistance as to what the nature of the crop is, and I intend to check that immediately when I go to the west in a few days' time. In addition to that, the practice in the past has been, and so far as I know it still is the policy, both provincially and federally, that when there is a shortage of feed grain in any particular locality application is made to the provincial government for any assistance that is required to move grain from one part of the province to another. If the job becomes one that is so considerable that the provincial government cannot undertake it, then means of access to the federal government is always open to the provincial government, and I would suggest therefore that if there are any conditions such as have been spoken of by the hon. member for Lethbridge so far as the southern part of Alberta proper is concerned, the procedure is for those who are interested to make representations to the provincial government and they in turn no doubt, in due course, will make whatever representations to us they see fit. So far as the matter of cattle is concerned, there is a much higher floor price established now under the present arrangement in connection with all kinds of beef than has ever been established in any preceding year and a provision is made under which, even if it is not necessary for the government to enter the field itself, stock can be handled to better advantage this year than
in any previous year. I suggest that any live stock organization in the west ought to take advantage of that fact and proceed to market their live stock in the best possible way and if there is any necessity for government consideration of any difficulties that may arise 1 am sure that consideration will be given.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DISCUSSION OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DISCUSSION OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The business for this morning is the discussion of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. On Fridays His Honour the Speaker leaves the chair for the house to go into committee without any question being put; but I believe it would suit the convenience of hon. members, and also enable the debate to proceed in a more orderly fashion, if I were to introduce a motion that His Honour the Speaker do not leave the chair until there has been a general discussion on the question of external affairs. If that meets with the approval of the house, I would move that the provision of standing order 28 in relation to Mr. Speaker leaving the chair on Fridays without putting any question, be now suspended in order to allow general discussion on external affairs. This .would mean that after hon. members have had a chance of speaking on external affairs and delivering such addresses as they may have in mind, His Honour the Speaker could then leave the chair and the house go into committee and take up the various items in detail.

speechtext: This is the first intimation that I have had of this motion. It had not occurred to me that the discussion on external affairs would be in the nature of a full dress debate. I fancy that the situation which has now developed would throw the whole matter into a full dress debate, thus preventing the asking of such questions as I had in mind. If the Prime Minister and the government can see their way clear to agree to it, I see no objection to Mr. Speaker leaving the chair and the house going into committee; those who desire to make speeches could do so, and those who wish to ask questions would feel free to get in the usual way the information required. speechtext: First of all, may I apologize to my hon. friend for not having mentioned to him my intention to introduce this motion. speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DISCUSSION OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DISCUSSION OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

It does not seem to me
that this is a desirable change to make in what we have been accustomed to in the past. I know of no reason for departing from the procedure we have adopted in past sessions. As the Prime Minister has said, he did not give any intimation to the opposition of the suggestion that he has now made, nor does he exhibit any desire to use the force of his majority to put it through. I take it that he is ready to withdraw this motion if it does not met with the approbation of the house. May I say to
my hon. friend that my motion does exactly what has been done in previous years.

speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DISCUSSION OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will look over what has been customary in the debate on external affairs-and that has been the chief reason why I made this motion to-day-he will see that before the estimates were considered in detail there was a general discussion with the Speaker in the chair. It was because I expected, unless I made a motion of this kind, my attention would immediately be drawn to the fact that I was departing from the custom of previous years that I anticipated a possibility of this kind. Buit the house itself regulates its own business, and possibly it might be understood that, after I have made my statement, hon. members will have an opportunity to make statements of their own if they so desire before we go too much into detailed discussion. In that way we can carry out the objective even though we have no formal motion. In those circumstances I am quite prepared to withdraw the motion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
May I say first of all that I regret that the discussion on external affairs matters should have been delayed until this particular stage of the session. No one regrets that more than I do, but it has been due to circumstances over which I personally and the government have had little or no control. Possibly the circumstance that accounts most for the fact that external affairs matters are being discussed now rather than earlier in the session is that I was obliged, as lion, members know, to leave Canada for a month to be present at a meeting of prime ministers in London. That absence was responsible for some matters of legislation being held up for final decision until after my return. The government naturally felt it important to bring forward this legislation as rapidly as possible. The important debates that took place on other subjects also consumed a great deal of time-the debate on the address, later the debate on the war appropriation, which was a very lengthy one, the debate on the budget; all these matters had to be disposed of in the sequence to which I have referred. Then, as hon. members are aware there was a good deal of social legislation, legislation in which it was necessary for me to give my time almost exclusively to the house in the course of the discussions. There were dhe matters related to the creation of the Department of Veterans' Affairs, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Reconstruction, and later the legislation with respect to family allowances. These matters have occupied the time continuously up to the present, together with some other matters of importance.
However, I think any inconvenience that may have been caused is more than offset by the extent to which matters of external relations have been discussed throughout the session, not all at once but at different periods. In time of war questions relating to foreign affairs will come up almost every day, in one way or another, and this session' has been no exception in that regard. For example, a large portion of the debate on the address was devoted almost exclusively to matters pertaining to foreign affairs. I believe hon. members will recall that during that debate some very important questions with respect to cooperation within the empire, and the like, were discussed at great length. Again on the war
appropriation measure matters pertaining to foreign affairs were discussed at length, and to a lesser extent on some other measures. The fact that the meeting of the prime ministers in London was concerned largely with foreign affairs had the result that members of this house were fully informed of the position taken by Canada at that conference, as far as it was possible to have the discussions made public by the reports that came from the conference itself, and which rvere released here. Then we have received here the prime ministers of New Zealand and Australia, who discussed very freely and openly matters relating to the conference, Canada's position as compared with that of the other countries, and so on. On all these matters I think hon. members are as fully informed as they would have been if this discussion had taken place at an earlier time.
Then I should remind hon. members that from time to time I have been asked to make a statement on some particular aspect of foreign affairs, and in most cases I have been able to give the statement so desired. In addition many returns have been asked for, and a very large number of questions have appeared on the order paper. These returns have been brought down; the questions have been answered, and in that way I believe hon. members have been kept fully informed as to the outstanding aspects of policy and matters of which they would wish to have knowledge in relation thereto. However, this morning I should like to follow the custom that has prevailed in previous years, and yery briefly review the progress of the war since I last made a statement, anticipating as well as I can the subjects on which I think hon. members will wish to have further information.
It is now almost two years since the first major offensive by forces of the united nations began a new phase of operations. This phase carried the allied war effort across the great divide from uncertainty of victory on the one side to certainty of victory on the other. The initiative then seized, in the Solomons, in the western desert, then in North Africa, has never been relaxed. Rather has it been maintained and greatly extended.
Two months ago the war of liberation was carried to one of the many parts of Europe which had been under Hitler's control for nearly four years. While the northwestern wall of the nazi-controlled fortress was being breached, and the breach held, the gigantic summer offensive of the armies of the Soviet Union has'hurled "back the enemy on a scale never dreamed of in modern warfare. With the exception of a limited area in the Baltic republics, the Soviet forces have recovered

nearly all the territory which was occupied by nazi forces following the treacherous invasion launched on June 22, 1941. This tremendous drive is now being carried across Polish soil into Germany itself. In Normandy the great struggle for liberation is being fought out by combined United States, British and Canadian forces. The next few weeks, if not days, may witness battles which will go far to decide the fate of the German stronghold now beset from east and west and south.
When I reviewed the progress of the war last July it was on the very eve of Canadian landings at Pachino, in Sicily, at the beginning of the battle for the liberation of Italy. Following a campaign of thirty-eight days, which saw the complete defeat of German forces on that island, Canadian forces were in the van of allied landings on the mainland. The unconditional surrender of Italy shortly after removed this unhappy partner from the axis alignment. In the heavy fighting which pushed the nazi forces steadily northward, Canadian troops have had an important part. At the beginning of 1944 the 1st Canadian division was supplemented by other units, and by the establishment of headquarters of a Canadian corps in the field. In May this Canadian corps reached its full fighting strength, and up until the liberation of Rome it took part in many important actions.
The Canadian corps was and is a part of the British 8th army. It was moved secretly from the Adriatic front to engage the enemy. The move had decisive results. In the landings both in Sicily and Italy, and in many subsequent operations, concentrations of the Royal Canadian Air Force and ships and men of the Royal Canadian Navy have cooperated fully and effectively. In like manner the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Royal Canadian Navy have cooperated fully and effectively in the invasion of Europe from the north. AVherever they serve, from now until the day of final victory, we may be sure that all the armed forces of Canada, rigorously trained and superbly equipped, will continue to strike telling and relentless blows in the cause of the world's freedom. I might also mention the heroic and far-reaching service on the part of Canada's merchant navy, which throughout the war has played a vital role.
The spectacular progress of the Red armies in pushing back the German enemy, and the initial successes of the allied armies in Normandy and Italy, should not obscure the importance of allied offensives elsewhere. In the battle of the Atlantic increased air coverage over vital routes and new methods of combat

have made possible a greater concentration of weapons against the U-boat menace than ever before. The bridge of ships upon which victory depends has been kept intact. The menace of the U-boat may never entirely disappear during war-time. Since the beginning . of the year, however, in the north Atlantic, the number of U-boats sunk by the combined resources of escort vessels, carrier-based aircraft and land-based aircraft has been at least five times the number of merchant ships lost by enemy action.
In the western .Pacific, Japanese forces are being steadily hemmed in and driven back from the fringes of a vast area of sea and islands. It is of interest that in an area where what at first was a war of survival, and for many months a war of attrition, has now become in part a war of liberation. In a part of Netherlands New Guinea, for example, Netherlands civil affairs officers are already at work in the first sizeable area of Dutch soil to be wrested back from the Japanese. United States task forces have been reducing Japanese outposts by the occupation of strategic islands, of which Saipan, Guam and Tinian are recent examples. The air war against Japan has been pursued actively from land as well as from sea. From lately-constructed bases in China new super fortresses of the United States 20th air force have rained destruction on some of the most important industrial areas under Japanese control. On land also, on the Indo-Burmese front, dogged efforts are being made to whittle down the Japanese lines and keep open the supply routes to China upon which her own military effort against Japan now so largely depends.
As might be expected, the weight of Allied bombing over Europe, the relentless patrolling of European seaways, and now the actual fighting on land, have aroused the resistance movements. These movements have been kept alive through underground channels in many European nations whose governments are in exile. It is known, for example, that full-scale fighting by underground warriors in some parts of France has engaged large numbers of nazi troops who might otherwise be serving elsewhere. In Yugoslavia the "partisan" forces serving under Marshal Tito have taken control of extensive areas, and at least one constituent assembly has met in the midst of a country still outwardly under nazi domination. In still other countries, always at great personal risks, organized sabotage of transportation and communication facilities has slowed down the enemy's plans. These underground forces have played a vital part throughout the war in hampering the enemy,

and in the war of liberation now entered upon in earnest, they will continue their efforts ever more strongly for victory.
Recent events in Finland and Turkey are significant of the crumbling of the German positions at both ends of the eastern front.
Behind this bare recital of offensive successes and operational gains lies a meritorious story of realistic planning for the strategic needs of total war. A year ago I spoke of the then public achievements of the latest meetings at Casablanca and at Washington between Mr. Churchill and President Roosevelt. Last August there was the historic conference at Quebec, and between August and the end of the year there followed meetings at Moscow, Cairo and Teheran. Of the outcome of these meetings I should now like to speak briefly.
It has been said that Casablanca and Quebec were primarily "councils of war", where strategic decisions of the highest importance were taken involving the war in Europe and the war in the far east. It was the war still at the planning stage, but all of the combined declarations of 1943 were calculated to impress the neutral nations of Europe, and even more the German satellite states, with the determination of the allied powers to stop at nothing short of victory over the axis.
The organization of total war for victory always has had some contemplation of the period following the end of hostilities. This necessity is reflected in the communiques issued following the Cairo and Teheran meetings, where for the first time in this war the Generalissimo of China and the Premier of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics were brought into direct conference with Mr. Churchill and President Roosevelt.
The Cairo meeting made it clear that Japan would be fought and defeated, and that those possessions which were added by force of arms to the empire of Japan over the past half-century would be taken from her. The meeting at Teheran envisaged the early prospect of frontal attacks upon the nazi stronghold in Germany-attacks from the east and south and west. The United States, Great Britain and the U.S.S.R. did not go so far as to specify what losses a defeated Germany was to suffer. But some guidance on this point had been given by the meeting at Moscow, at the end of October, of the foreign ministers of the Soviet Union, the United States, and Great Britain. Dealing with the case of fascist Italy-, then already but a glimmering remnant of Mussolini's once-pompous empire, Mr. Molotov, Mr. Hull and Mr. Eden stated that:
Allied policy towards Italy must be based upon the fundamental principle that fascism and
all its evil influences and emanations shall be utterly destroyed, and that the Italian people shall be given every opportunity to establish governmental and other institutions based upon democratic principles.
The Moscow conference gave many leads for the future organization of a peaceful world order. In particular, in a four-power declaration to which China also was a party, these nations pledged their joint efforts to bring about the unconditional surrender and disarmament of their common enemy, and to take all necessary measures to provide against the violation of terms imposed upon that enemy.
They likewise agreed not to use their military forces after the war in other states except after joint consultation, and to confer with each other and other united nations on the regulation of post-war armaments.
To carry on cooperation in war time as collaboration in peace time, Great Britain, the United States and the U.S.S.R. further expressed their "unanimous recognition . . . that it was essential in their own national interests and in the interest of all peace-loving nations to continue the present close collaboration and cooperation in the conduct of the war into the period following the end of hostilities, and that only in this way could peace be maintained and the political, economic and social welfare of their peoples fully promoted." With this objective in mind they set up two continuing bodies, representing the three powers to which have been given important functions. The European advisory commission has been established in London to make joint recommendations to the three governments regarding armistice terms and the nature of the post-war supervision to apply to Germany. The advisory council for Italy with headquarters in the liberated zone has already been set up. Provision was made for representation on the council of the French committee of national liberation and the governments of Yugoslavia and Greece.
Perhaps of greatest continuing interest was the so-called Moscow declaration on general security. In outlining a part of the pattern of post-war international society, the three nations envisaged the necessity of establishing a general international organization, based on the principle of the sovereign equality-' of all peace-loving states and open to membership by all such states, large and small, for the maintaining of peace and security.
On the strength of these several conferences, there is hope that the united nations will carry into the post-hostilities period the machinery of military, political and economic collaboration which has been so extensively developed under stress of war.

The first object of our external policy must continue to be to win the war, and to win it at the earliest possible day. It is more true than ever, more urgent than ever, that we in Canada should bend all our efforts to the supreme task of winning victory at the earliest possible moment. We have now been fighting, on a scale of increasing magnitude and intensity, for more thah four years. Of the people of Canada as a whole, I think it can be said that we have never mistaken or doubted the real issue in the world-wide struggle. For this reason the planning which has shaped the war effort of Canada since 1939 has been constantly aligned with the changing needs of war. This planning has been directed towards victory for the united nations. It has also been concerned with the responsibilities which will fall to Canada on the morrow of victory, and with the tasks of Canada as an emerging world power in the society of-free nations.
I shall now speak more particularly of postwar world organization.
We are rapidly approaching, if we have not already reached, the military climax of the war against Germany. We are at or near the peak of our effort, when the courage and resolution of every service man and every civilian is being put to the severest test. The Canadian Navy and the R.C.A.F. have long been heavily engaged against the enemy, but never before in such numbers at the same time. Most formations of the Canadian Army are now in action in Italy and in France in the midst of the ordeal for which they have prepared themselves so patiently and so well.
At times like these it is hard to look beyond the immediate fortunes of the fields of battle and consider with a detached mind the problems which we must solve after military victory is won. The price paid for victory has indeed been high during the five long years of war. It will be still higher before fighting stops. We must see that what we get for that terrific price is not the bitter fruit of disillusionment. We must spare no effort to secure a result which will bring peace and prosperity in our time, and in the time of those who succeed us. We must turn our minds, even in these days of military climax, to the organization of peace with the same sort of vigour and determination that has been devoted so successfully to the organization of war. .
The organization of peace was one of the chief subjects which was discussed at the meeting of commonwealth prime ministers in May. Mr. Churchill on May 24 gave to the British House of Commons an outline of the views which had been considered at that meeting. President Roosevelt in a statement of June
[Mr. Mackenzie Kine.l
15 indicated that he had a similar conception of the means which should be adopted to give effect ito the fourth paragraph of the Moscow declaration of last autumn. A lot of hard thinking is being given to these problems in Moscow, in London, in Washington, in Ottawa and in the other capitals of the united nations. Mr. Cordell Hull has announced that they will be discussed in Washington this month by representatives of the four largest powers.
I said in the House of Commons last January that it was indeed true beyond question "that the peace of the world depends on preserving on the side of peace a large superiority of power so that those who wish to disturb the peace can have no chance of success." In recent weeks the Germans have added to their armoury of weapons a new instrument of blind destruction, the use of which may serve to underline the thought which I then expressed. The "flying bomb" of to-day is a weapon in its infancy. If it is developed with all the resources and ingenuity of modem science, we may find in a few years that it has become an engine of war which without warning and in no time at all could be used to destroy peaceful countries from afar. The weapon which the Germans are using so indiscriminately against southern England may be as crude in performance in comparison with its successors as was the tank first used in battle on the Somme in September, 1916, in comparison with the latest tanks now in production.
We must indeed preserve a large superiority of power on the side of peace. We shall have that power among the united nations from the hour of victory. We must- keep it in the first place to disarm our enemies and prevent a revival of barbaric militarism in their countries. We must keep it also not only to meet dangers from other quarters which might arise, but to further constructive solutions of the problems which give rise to such dangers.
Canadians should, I think, approach these great questions of the organization of security with two main objects in mind: first, that the methods adopted should be as effective as can be contrived; and, second, that they should safeguard the interests of Canada and commend themselves to the Canadian people so that they can secure steady public support.
There is no constitutional cure for the diseases of international society. Indeed, perhaps one of the errors into which many people fell between the two ware was to feel that the establishment of the league of nations had somehow itself removed the danger of war.
