I am asking the question in all sincerity. I do not relish the interruption of the minister. The question I ask is this: Is Canada backing out of participation in the world council? Certainly she is not represented at Washington. There is a distinct difference between those two situations. In the first place we have the British commonwealth one of the four powers, and in the second place Great Britain one of the four powers. Which is right? Which is the proper

policy? It is not yet too late to decide. Is the fourth power on the council to be Great Britain or is it to be the British commonwealth? The Canadian people are entitled to know. They are entitled to have the record kept straight. Is Canada to have a voice in this world council?
You see, Mr. Chairman, we have taken part in three wars within the last fifty years beside the other British nations. To-day we have nearly a million men under arms; and in this present war, as in the others, members of the commonwealth have fought as one. I suggest that they should take their part in maintaining the security of the world in the same way. again as one. In my opinion the British commonwealth should be the fourth power, just as Mr. Eden and Mr. Curtin have suggested. I presume the Canadian forces will be helping to maintain security in the postwar years-and on that point the Prime Minister made no declaration to-day, by the way-yet Canada will be put in a subsidiary position. The British government will be making the decisions-they will have to because Canada does not want to be a party -and Canada will be informed of what is happening and will follow along just as we did before this war. Canada will be what the Prime Minister described this morning as "one of the rest" of the united nations. That situation, Mr. Chairman, is not sound.
The Prime Minister suggested to-day that the problem be met by providing what he calls functional representation. In other words, where Canada is primarily interested she should be called into the council, or where Norway is interested she should be called in. Well, this functional representation is the old hobby-horse that the Prime Minister trots out whenever he is faced with this problem of whether we are to work together as a commonwealth or whether Great Britain is to carry the responsibility. I submit that his proposal of functional representation is ineffective. My suggestion would be that some method must be devised for representation of Canada on this world council, or at any rate for empire consultation beforehand on the questions that are to come up. Because whether we like it or not in effect the representative on that council, even though he is only supposed to be representing Great Britain, will speak for all the British nations. We will find that we are more or less bound by what he says, whether we have a representative there or not. I believe that the secretariat proposed by Mr. Curtin would have been a great help in paving the way for agreement between the British nations as to what stand should be taken. I know that proposal was rejected by our own Prime Minister in London, and I think improperly so.

Supply-External Affairs
Prime Minister Curtin explained to a press conference in Ottawa the implications of setting up an empire secretariat. A report- of his statement says:
He thought there would be favourable results from a continuing conference of empire representatives at a central -point, where background information, communications and files could be kept for a moment's notice. He likened his idea to a newspaper morgue where background was compiled and was ready for use. He spoke of the need for definite decisions being reached at empire conferences and not just preliminary work done.
His proposed consultative body would do the preliminary work and the more frequent prime ministers' conference would be ready to take definite decisions and not merely start study of any question which arose.
The attitude of the Prime Minister to-day on this question of the set-up of a world council is entirely negative. He emphasizes all the difficulties surrounding the making of such arrangements. It is defeatist. It looks like a return to the old isolationist and nocommitment policies which were indulged in by this government up to the very day of the outbreak of the war. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister's policy in this regard is unsound and unfair to the Canadian people.
My third thought concerning Canadian foreign policy has to do with the setting up of a world organization. We all agree on the need of some such organization. I do not suppose there are very many hon. members of the committee who would not support the setting up of an organization, and Canada must take her fair share. There is mention in the speech from the throne of Canada's participation in a world organization. I shall read it to the committee, because it seems to have been forgotten by the government. It is as follows:
My ministers believe that the time has come when all the nations now united in the common purpose of winning the war should seek unitedly to ensure an enduring peace. The dangers of future aggression can be removed, and world security attained, only by a general international organization of peace-loving nations. You will accordingly be invited to approve of Canadian participation in the establishment of an international organization to further national security through international cooperation.
No steps have been taken to get the approval of this House of Commons to Canadian participation in the establishment of an international organization. I do suggest that the committee was entitled to the details of the way in which Canada would cooperate in setting up such an organization. I ask the Prime Minister to make during this debate a declaration of the position that Canada will take with regard to a world organization. I hope it is not going to be a case of Canada's
making no commitments except to a complete world league of nations after everyone [DOT] else has thrown in his hat.
The Prime Minister also should explain whether or not the Canadian government favours some type of regional organization. When we were given the government's air policy, that was part of it. It was said there should be regional councils for the control of international flying; but there has been nothing said by the government about regional councils in connection with this world organization. If they are in favour of regional councils, in which regions will Canada participate? We are not only an American nation; we face the Atlantic, the Pacific and the Arctic, and it will not be easy to decide just what should be our relationships with any regional councils that may be set up.
In connection with this question of a world organization one approach has been made by this government which in my opinion is dead wrong. That is when the government says in effect that to strengthen the British empire would prevent any world organization. The Prime Minister used words to that effect in his speech in this house on January 31 of this year, when he said that making any further concentration in regard to the British empire would run counter to the establishment of effective world security. In his speech before the British houses of parliament he used words to the same effect. I have here a reprint of that speech; the Prime Minister said that in considering new methods of organization, and he was referring to new methods of organizing the commonwealth, we cannot be too careful-and I really think those words "we cannot be too careful" sum up the government's foreign policy-
-we cannot be too careful to see that, to our own peoples, the new methods will not appear as an attempt to limit their freedom of decision or, to peoples outside the commonwealth, as an attempt to establish a separate bloc.
As a result of that speech we had such newspaper articles as the one in the Vancouver Sun which I hold in my hand, the headline of which is, "King Calls for World Unity Plan, Not Empire Bloc." The Prime Minister seems afraid that the nations of the empire might work too closely together, as though that were possible. No one at that conference, and no one elsewhere in the empire, is attempting to form a bloc in the accepted meaning of that word, which is the forming of some organization as against everybody else. As a matter of fact we have in the empire the model for a world organization. Here we have nations actually working together, as we hope all nations will be able to work together in a
Supply-External Affairs

league of nations. I think the better attitude was that taken by Prime Minister Curtin, who when he went back to Australia told his people:
Our readiness to associate in a world organization does not lessen the realism of our membership of tile British commonwealth.
As Progressive Conservatives we believe in strengthening the empire. We believe that working more closely with the other empire nations will not in any way hamper our working with the other nations of the world to build a new world order, and will not prevent us from working closely with the United States of America. Other nations expect us to work together in the empire. Why should Canada, under her present leadership, always be so frightened lest we may upset the other nations? It all reminds me of the government's attitude before the war, when the Prime Minister was always threatening us about Japan; when he said if we did this or that we would have Japan making war on us and we would upset world peace. Actually all the time Japan was just going ahead making her plans to attack us when she saw fit to do so. Our position, as the Progressive Conservative party, is set out in this portion of our creed, which reads:
The British Partnership.
We affirm our loyalty to the king and our faith in the British partnership. We accept t'he responsibilities together with the benefits of this partnership. The guarantee of freedom, security and opportunity for Canadians will be found in the strengthening of the British commonwealth, its closer association with the United States of America and our other fighting allies and in t'he application of the principles of the Atlantic charter.
My fourth and final thought on foreign policy has to do with the Pacific. Practically nothing was said by the Prime Minister this morning about Canada's foreign policy in the Pacific. You would almost wonder whether there was a war on with Japan, when as a matter of fact Canada was the first nation to declare war. For example, what about the Pacific council which was set up some years ago, and which met in Washington? After a good deal of prodding and coaxing Canada asked for membership on that council. What has been done? Has it been meeting? What has been going on? We are entitled to know. Then in January of this year Australia and New Zealand entered into an agreement to collaborate on Pacific affairs, and in that agreement appears this paragraph:
The two governments declare their desire to have the adherence to the objectives set out in the last preceding clause of any other government having or controlling territories in the Pacific.
Canada is a nation on the Pacific. Is Canada to collaborate with Australia and New Zealand under the terms of this agreement? Then what about an air line to Australia and New Zealand? We in the Pacific coast province of Canada are vitally interested in having air connection with those dominions. Is Canada to be represented at the very important conference to be held in Australia in the near future dealing with the war in the Pacific? What part are we to play in the war against Japan? What preparations have been made? One hears rumours to the effect that Canada is very backward in making adequate preparations for her part in the war in the Pacific. These are questions which should have been dealt with by the Prime Minister this morning, and I hope they will be dealt with by him before this debate ends.
The right hon. gentleman mentioned the pan-American union and said he thought that before Canada became a member of that union the people should1 have a more complete understanding of what membership would mean. Last year I advocated that Canada should join the union, subject to the one proviso that thereby we wore not to be taken as weakening our connection with the British commonwealth of nations.

I thank the Prime Minister. I think perhaps he made a wise suggestion to-day when he said this was a matter on which the Canadian people should acquire further knowledge before a stand is taken. But he went on to say that this was the responsibility of other people, not the responsibility of the government. Surely if the government believes that we should eventually join the pan-American union the government itself should accept responsibility for telling the Canadian people just what that membership will entail.
This morning the right hon. gentleman also dealt with the problem of the Japanese in Canada. That subject hardly comes under the Department of External Affairs at the moment, but he made a detailed statement in regard to it. I was pleased to learn that at last the government is treating this as a Canadian problem. It has been a Canadian problem from the start, because it was the federal government that allowed the Japanese

Supply-External Affairs
people to come to Canada years ago, but ever since then hon. members from British Columbia have found it impossible to persuade their fellow members of the house that this was really a Canadian problem. Now, however, it is recognized) as a problem for the whole of the Canadian people. And the Prime Minister's statement this morning was hardly in accordance with the statement he made during the debate in connection with giving votes to Japanese. On July 17, as reported at page 4937 of Hansard, he made a statement which worried me a great deal. This is what he said:
The persons of whom my hon. friend is speaking are still citizens of British Columbia. They have moved or been moved from British Columbia temporarily for reasons connected with the war. They have been moved through arrangements effected by the government as a war measure which was deemed necessary for reasons of security and in part for the protection of these very Japanese themselves. In most cases they are not persons who have voluntarily left British Columbia to reside in some other province. They are still citizens of British Columbia.
That was going very far, and judging from that statement I took it that the Prime Minister might be thinking of returning them all to British Columbia at the end of the war. Of course we would violently object if such action were taken. However, the Prime Minister to-day made himself clear on that point. During the course of the debate on the Japanese question, when the Prime Minister was in Great Britain, I placed certain questions before the ministry, questions which have never been answered until to-day-and indeed they are not all answered now. These were the questions:
Is it the plan to remove all the Japanese from British Columbia, or are some to be left there, and. if so, how many?
Are they to be kept out of the province of British Columbia for good? Can the minister give us assurance that they will not be sent back to British Columbia?
Are any plans under way for returning any of these Japanese to Japan? If so, what group or groups?
What does the government propose to do with those Japanese in other provinces if the government of any province requests their removal after the war?
One of the questions which was not dealt with this morning particularly was the one as to what the government proposes to do if other provinces request the removal of Japanese after the war. It is all very interesting to have people from other provinces say that this and that should have been done for the Japanese, and that British Columbia was wrong in asking this or that. But at the same time, this very city of Ottawa has refused to
allow Japanese to come here. And the same was true recently with respect to Toronto. Different centres in eastern Canada have refused to have anything to do with the Japanese, which is not a very helpful attitude so far as settlement of the problem in the future is concerned.
The Prime Minister said this morning that the policy is to spread the Japanese across Canada. He mentioned that perhaps there should be a numerical limit placed upon those who could remain in British Columbia. I suggest to him that the only way in which the question of keeping the Japanese out of British Columbia can be handled is to maintain the protected zone into the post-war years, and to extend it to cover the whole province.
I do not believe a scheme can be worked out under which a certain limited number can go into the province. There will always be the question of checking that number. A sounder and much more effective way would be to make the whole province a protected zone. That could very well be done on the basis of national defence. Keep Japanese Canadians away from the Pacific ocean where they can come in contact with Japanese ships and Japanese merchants coming to our ports.
The Prime Minister said the government proposed to encourage the movement of Japanese to other parts of Canada. I suggest that that should be started at once. Under the present law Japanese in eastern Canada cannot acquire land. They cannot buy a business. They cannot set themselves up in business and yet many of them are merchants. Unless some provision is made to allow them to resettle on a permanent basis, the Prime Minister will be disappointed in his attempt to spread them across Canada.
The Japanese should be resettled on a family basis. They are a great people for family life; families of Japanese like to stick together. So far there has been very little attempt made to bring whole families away from British Columbia. As of June 30-only about five weeks ago -there were still two-thirds of the Japanese in British Columbia. Only about one-third had been moved out, and the exodus from our province had practically stopped. I hold in my hand a newspaper clipping dated July 5, setting out a statement by George E. Collins, general superintendent of the British Columbia security commission. Mr. Collins points out the following:
Whether voluntary movement of Japanese to self-supporting jobs outside of British Columbia will continue depends on the future attitude of the Japanese themselves.
Substantial exodus of Japanese during the past several months has now come to a virtual

Supply-External Affairs

stop. Advice from the camps indicates this has been caused .by lack of a definite statement oi federal government policy on the Japanese question.
It may be that with the announcement made to-day by the Prime Minister it will be easier to persuade the Japanese to move away. But in any event I suggest that the resettlement policy be commenced at once.
I have no further facts to place before the committee to-day. In conclusion may I go back to what I consider the most important thought and suggestion, and that is the one respecting the objective of the Canadian people and the destiny of Canada. Is it to be to play only a secondary role among the small nations of the world, or is it to become a great world power, standing beside Great Britain in the British commonwealth of nations? I hope and I believe that the decision will be in favour of the latter.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon for the first time this session we meet to discuss in any extended way the Department of External Affairs. I ami not blaming the Prime Minister or the government, because I think all hon. members realize that this debate has come on at the end of the session because of pressure of business and also to meet the wishes of many hon. members. Therefore I am not making any criticism of the government because the debate has not been called until this stage in the session.
In spite of what the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has just said, we are meeting in the parliament of one of the lesser powers, one of the smaller nations. I look forward to the day when Canada may become a great nation; but in the light of the present world situation we are one of the smaller nations. In this war we have played a remarkable role, a role of which I think this nation may well be proud. Others of the lesser powers look to Canada at this time as the leading member of that group of powers. I think that in spite of what the hon. member has just said, because we are not at this time a nation of 30.000.000 or 50.000,000 people, we ought to assume the role we can play so well at this time, as at least one of the spokesmen for that group of nations which within the united nations can be described is the lesser powers.
I offer no apology for speaking of Canada, in her relationship to the world, as one of the lesser or smaller nations. That does not mean that I do not believe that one day Canada may assume the role of a great power. I hope when that day comes that instead of being a

rival of other great powers we may be able to cooperate with great powers of the world for the general good, the preservation of world order and universal peace.
It is impossible in the short space of time at one's disposal this afternoon to do more than refer briefly to some of the international developments which at the moment are of great concern to our country. It is unfortunate that we cannot go into these matters a little more fully, because the developments we are witnessing now are of interest not only to Canadians of the present but to future generations. The decisions we make now, the manner in which we handle questions and problems that arise, are bound to have tremendous repercussions upon the future of this country and I believe of the world.
It is a matter of satisfaction that because of the fighting qualities of our soldiers, our sailors, our airmen and those of the united nations, we can confidently look forward in the not too distant future to the collapse, at least of the German nazi regime and the German military power. Then let us hope that there will follow7 the fall of Japan and the making of peace. The part that Canadian service men have played in this and the efforts of our civilians and farmers deserve the gratitude of all the people of our country.
I think we are all in agreement that the German war machine must be crushed and dismantled; so thoroughly must the job be done this time that never again can German militarism plunge the world into war. When we come to treat with Germans, as ultimately we must, we shall have to treat with somebody. My hope is that we may yet find in Germany reborn peoples' organizations like trade unions, cooperative societies, farmers' groups and the Christian church whose leaders have resisted, even in the underground, the threat not only to their own freedom but to the freedom of the world. I think it would indeed- be folly to attempt to negotiate any sort of peace with the great landowners, the great industrialists or the junker class, with those people who have been responsible for the promotion of German militarism in the past, with their trusts, their cartels and so on. They were indeed the economic army which enabled Hitler to rise to power. We may find that there are many German people who if given free rein will assist in dealing effectively with these anti-social forces. The difficulty is that the war has now lasted for five years and such forces in Germany at the moment are probably quite small. We cannot place them all in the same category. Let us not forget however that many of their peoples'

Supply-External Affairs
leaders were first to fall victims to nazi and fascist aggression. In fact the first organizations in Germany that were destroyed by nazism were trade unions and the cooperative societies. The leading thinkers of the Chris-lian churches also found themselves behind the barbed wire of the internment camp.
Whatever foreign policy we pursue, either now or in the future, ought to be unyieldingly democratic. When we have to deal with the people in the enemy countries we should deal only with those forces which have struggled unswervingly against fascism and nazism. I think many people have been alarmed at what appeared to some of us to be the monumental errors that were made in North Africa, and more recently in Italy, the attempts that appeared to be made to pin Europe down in all directions to, if I may use a Latin phrase, the status quo ante. That is the kind of policy I think Canada should endeavour to end. It seems to me that the greatest mistake we can make is to underestimate the patent desire of all the enslaved peoples of Europe to bring about basic social and economic changes and to rebuild their countries on the basis of true economic and social democracy. The misery that these people have undergone under the nazi heel and their consciouness of the bankruptcy of their old leaderships and of the old order leave them determined to embark upon entirely new social concepts in the place of the dictatorships and the fascist movements which destroyed them.
Unless basic social and economic changes are brought about and democracy is allowed to flower in full in all fields, we are headed once again for world war No. 3. If we return to the old ways of mass unemployment-when I say "we" I mean the world generally, not this country alone-of trade strangled by all kinds of barriers, of industry regulated through selfish cartels, and of economic tensions which mankind cannot endure, w.e shall find ourselves faced with the threat of war and ultimately war itself.
As one reads the newspapers to-day he realizes the unquenchable spirit of the underground movement in Europe, especially in France. These people have fought consistently against the nazi and fascist aggressors. They have risked their lives every day and the lives of their families. They have done this not only in guerrilla warfare, but, as we have reason to know in this country, by giving shelter to some of our boys who have been brought dowm in their midst. There is an outspoken demand for a better world to follow this war. Any plans that we make should be for their social betterment as well as our own. At the moment we are giving this idea 100-373J
recognition to a greater extent than ever before, because we read constantly of supplies of arms and food that are being given to the underground movement in France. The successful prosecution of the war should mean for the people of the liberated areas the fullest participation in their own affairs at the earliest possible date. We in Canada should look for our natural allies among those people-yes and among those Germans in exile or who have worked underground, in order to combat in the future the threat of any revival of the nazi and fascist menace.
The hon. member for Vancouver South mentioned the absence of references to the orient and the Pacific area. We cannot neglect the orient and the Asiatic peoples. Indeed all dependent peoples cannot be sidestepped by Canada, as a responsible member of the united nations and as a responsible member of that association to which we are all proud to belong, the British commonwealth of nations. I do not think it was done deliberately this morning.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I was going to deal with another phase altogether, the phase referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Exploitation, which we often refer to as imperialism, in all its forms wifi have to be rooted out, will have to go. The exploitation of one people, whether it be in China, India or anywhere else, by another group of people or by another nation creates friction which will inevitably lead to war. In the new world into which we are moving we have to see to it that we do not return to that kind of exploitation. In my opinion the basic cause of imperialism, whether it is to be found in Malaya, in Bolivia, in China or anywhere else, is the chronic inability of our present economic system to distribute the goods which science enables it to produce at the present time. It is part of the motion-the perpetual motion if you will-of our capitalist economy that we thrust fatally towards this kind of imperialism. I am of course using the word "imperialism" in the economic sense. We not only stretch out abroad but we also do it at home, and strife is the consequence.
I should like to remind the committee that in the immediate future we shall have to reckon with a large portion of the world's population which for a long time has been
Supply-External Affairs

depressed and exploited. What are there?- 450 million people in China, 370 million people in India and millions elsewhere. I suggest that for the post-war period we should be making such plans as will lead all these people to assume as rapidly as possible the full responsibility of nationhood. Where we have backward peoples-and let us recognize the fact that there are backward peoples who are not immediately capable of governing themselves-my opinion has been, and is, and I think Canada should work for this, that we should give them a helping hand; that no group of people should be returned to a position of being subject to any one power, but that there should be some form of international organization, or, as it is sometimes sailed, third-party intervention or supervision to see that the responsibile nations are doing the kind of job which democratic peoples would have them do. As a matter of fact the recent proposals of the British colonial office for regional international commissions to supervise the affairs of all dependent peoples are a move in the right direction. They seem to me to show a new spirit, and I think they are worthy of consideration. But it must not be like the old mandate system of the league of nations which gave Japan, for example, the opportunity of acquiring mandates over islands and territories which she was able to use as fortified bases and is to-day using very effectively to conduct a war against ourselves, the united nations and the world.
For better, as I believe, or for worse the world is headed towards more internationalism and more international supervision of many of the economic and social activities of mankind.
Before turning from the problems of the dependent peoples I may refer briefly to one of the nations which is associated with us in our own commonwealth, and that is India. We have, it seems to me from my reading and what I have been able to learn, failed to mobilize the masses of that great country for the prosecution of the war as we might otherwise have done. Perhaps that is not surprising, after the manner in which we have neglected Indian opinion in the past. I have said before, and I repeat this afternoon, that another attempt should be made to reopen negotiations under the supervision, not of any ane power, but of the united nations, for the immediate settlement of this problem, so that we can mobilize public opinion there not only at the moment but for the good of the world in the years to come.
Turning from the problems of the dependent peoples to those of what I will call again the smaller nations, we must, I think, as one of 
these nations endeavour to avoid at all costs anything like a big power world. It ought to be obvious to all of us that the great powers of themselves cannot maintain peace, for by themselves they must necessarily engage in delicate manoeuvres to balance each other. In other words, to turn the world over to the big powers would simply mean to go in again for a balance of power policy, and along the road of balance of power-and history supports me in this-lies war. The four-power Moscow conference in 1943 foreshadowed, and I quote the declarationthe necessity of establishing at the earliest practicable date a general international organization based upon the principle of the sovereign equality of all peace-loving states-
All peace-loving states.
-and open to membership to all such states, for the maintenance of international .peace and security.
Later on, at Teheran, much the same sort of view was expressed by the great powers- the principle of the sovereign equality of all peace-loving nations; and that, I take it, is the desire of all democratic people. Even that organization however is foredoomed to failure unless it fulfils two basic conditions. First, it must rest upon the foundation of social and economic justice everywhere in the world. We cannot have peace by force and maintain it indefinitely. The only kind of peace that the world can have is peace which is based upon social and economic justice everywhere, and this entiails not only economic collaboration among nations in trade, exchange, investments, shipping and so on, but also democratic and economic planning within the nations for the full utilization of all our human and economic resources for the satisfaction of human need.
I think the second foundation upon which peace must rest is that any world organization must be democratically representative of all peoples great and small. Domination by the great powers, Mr. Speaker, inevitably awakens the distrust of the smaller powers-it is bound to do so ultimately-while big-power dominance inevitably leads the dominant powers to seek security in what? In their own might- and to jockey among themselves for selfish advantage. Now, true collective security on the other hand looks to collective action of all the peace-loving nations for the stamping out of aggression within the world community, It embodies the conception of nations standing in defence not just of their own immediate interests but of an orderly world in which all people are free to flourish and to live.
Canada is at war to-day, not because Great Britain is at war, not because of any specific

Supply-External Affairs
aggression against Poland'-no doubt these two factors influenced this parliament-but because, in spite of the grave doubts that many people had of the intention of the governments that were then in power in England and France, the governments of Chamberlain and Daladier, our people believed that the common people of Britain and France recognized that this could be made a war to end recurrent dangers of nazi and fascist aggression and assist in the destruction ultimately of militarism. Thus Canada's obligations to the ideal of a lasting peace are very definite. What are they? First, allegiance to the idea of a democratic and international organization in which some phases of national sovereignty, particularly those involving the use of force, are merged in a collective system of security. And then the abolition of national armaments and their pooling in an international police force, that of course by progressive steps. No one anticipates that there can be complete disarmament of the nations for a considerable period after this war, but that should be something at which we should aim; and, what I think is perhaps most important of all, the planned use of economic resources everywhere to raise standards of living throughout the world and for the elimination of insecurity, poverty and exploitation and the attainment of selfgovernment by all peoples.
These, I think, are our general obligations. What are the specific problems of Canadian foreign policy? First of all I say this, that clearly in regard to the British commonwealth-and we all want to maintain the closest association with the peoples of the British commonwealth-public opinion in Canada, I am sure is overwhelmingly against the idea of forming a commonwealth power bloc against which undoubtedly counter power blocs would ultimately be pitted. But that does not mean, of course, the rejection of the idea of constructive cooperation within the commonwealth, nor does it mean that there are not fruitful avenues open to a British commonwealth nation in ways of cooperative endeavour. There are many such avenues. For instance, we might have some common investment policies coordinated within the commonwealth along the lines proposed not so long ago by the international labour organization, and provision might well be made for the mutual exchange of social security benefits for persons moving from one part of the commonwealth to another. That would make people realize that we were one in a manner in which perhaps nothing else could make us realize our unity.
It is along these lines, of which many more examples could be cited, of progressive cooperation in its best forms that commonwealth relationships will thrive in the future. If they do not thrive along these lines I do not think they will thrive at all; and to complete the circle of friendly understandings that exist between Canada and the British commonwealth and Canada and the United States, we might well conclude a treaty of cooperation and non-aggression with the U.S.S.R.-our northern neighbour-a significant fact we sometimes overlook. We always look to the south and talk about our great neighbour stretching all across the southern boundary of Canada, but these days we should remember that we have another great neighbour touching us very closely, and the aeroplane has made that neighbour very close indeed. That neighbour is Russia. I would suggest to the Prime Minister, if it is possible that a treaty be negotiated along the lines of the British .twenty-year pact, a treaty which more than anything else probably has helped to allay material distrusts and paved the way which we hope will lead to a more durable international understanding and international organization.
Then of course we must not forget that we are within the western hemisphere. The Prime Minister this morning referred to the pan-American union. I agree with him that our people know very little about it. Indeed, our people have taken too little interest in foreign policy. Even, members of this house have taken too little interest in foreign policy and external affairs. But in spite of what the Prime Minister said- this morning I think we should, when the opportunity occurs, enter the pan-American union. It would not weaken our ties with the British commonwealth or anyone else. On the contrary it would strengthen our position in this hemisphere and bring us into closer relationship with peoples whose cultures resemble more closely the culture of one great element in our own population. It is true that the pan-American union is a union of republics and we are not at least formally a republic. Great Britain is often referred to as a crowned republic. I think that in her governmental methods she is a crowned republic.

I think that probably if Canada expressed a desire to enter the union she would receive an invitation to do * so very soon.
May I say to the Prime Minister that we very heartily approve of the steps that have been taken this year to raise the status of our ministers-our legations into embassies and our ministers into ambassadors. That is a step in the right direction. Quite as important however as all the relationships to which I have referred is the problem of integrating Canada's own economic life into the developing world economy. Questions of trade arise, of the domination of cartels, investment, currency stabilization, labour legislation, immigration and all the rest of it, and it seems to me that all these problems are part of external relations and require definite integrated economic planning. Canada should be doing everything in her power to promote public organizations that will assist her in these fields. She should give every support, and I think she will, to such agencies as the I.L.O., UNRRA, and other war-created planning boards in foodstuffs, raw materials and investment control. She should finally bend every effort towards the creation and support of effective international agencies to supervise such functions as post-war aviation, shipping and communications. All such measures are directed to the end that habits of international cooperation, in place of national competition, may gradually develop, and that wider loyalties than we have to-day toward the international community may be built in the minds of men. May I say that when I speak of that wider loyalty it does not mean that there is any diminution of one's loyalty to one's own country, or any lessening in the patriotism that
[Mr. Coldwell.l
one has to one's own land. Indeed in my opinion the widening of patriotism into fields beyond our own borders makes one even more patriotic to what the people in the south sometimes call " all God's children." Therefore I say that such policies are directed, too, toward the kind of settlements that are envisaged in the Atlantic charter, a world-and these are the words of the charter-in which there will be " the fullest cooperation between nations in the economic field with the object of securing for all, improved labour standards, economic advancement and social security." The following article of the charter forecasts conditions " which will afford assurance that all men in all the lands may live out their lives in freedom from fear and want."
Of course there are reactionary minds here and there in the world-they so express themselves in newspapers and magazines-that are talking in terms of a retreat from the Atlantic charter. For our part we ought to continue to strive for the goals the Atlantic charter holds before us, believing, as I do at least, that they can be achieved-it is not impossible-through economic planning among nations as the counterpart of economic planning within nations.
We have had a discussion this session on air transport, civil and military, which is of urgent concern to Canada; for this country lies across the cross-roads of the world, the airways between the new world and the old, between Europe and Asia. In addition, as we have seen from the statements that have been made from time to time by the Minister of Munitions and Supply and lately by the Prime Minister in the house, Canada has a huge capital investment in air facilities of all kinds, and, what is more important, a precious investment in many thousands of skilled young men. I am going to express an opinion which is shared to the full by one of the great parties in Great Britain, the Labour party-for I have the official outline of their policy here- that an- international air force should be created,' supreme in the air, financed and controlled by a body under a new international organization- representative of world ajuthority. It should -operate from international bases under the control -of that authority. For if we are in earnest about stamping out aggression, some such measure is essential. The aeroplane to-day is a blessing or a menace, as we make it. It can virtually destroy civilization. By the same token we need an international authority to control civil aviation, because it is so easy for civil aeroplanes to be turned very rapidly into military transport planes or bombers.
Canada's interest in maintaining world- peace is a compelling one. We are bounded on the

Supply-External Affairs
southern and northern boundaries by two powers whose resources predestine them to major roles in the post-war world. The friendliest of relations between those two powers ought to be the urgent concern of Canada's foreign policy. The geographical position of Canada has conferred upon Canadians in this twentieth century the advantages of occupying a pivotal position in the unfolding of the future and in world affairs; but we must recognize that it has conferred upon us also the gravest of responsibilities. Therefore, I say, Mr. Chairman, that we should spare no efforts to promote an expanding world economy grounded on social justice and dedicated to lasting peace.
Now may I come to the domestic problem that was raised, the problem of the citizens of the Japanese race who are in our midst. I do not know why this problem is always called "the Japanese problem". We do not speak of the second, third or fourth generations of Germans as creating a German problem, but we speak of the Japanese problem. I am in the fullest accord with the Prime Minister when he says that any person of Japanese origin who has been disloyal to this country should be denied the right to live here when the war is over. They should be interned now and deported to their country when this war is over like any other alien of similar attributes. But in my opinion it is copying the policies of Hitler to discriminate against any people because of their race, colour or creed. I have attended enough international conferences where able men from the orient have been present to have learned that the discriminatory treatment of Canadians by birth of Japanese origin has placed in the hands of the Japanese war lords a weapon of propaganda which may cause us to lose many thousands of lives. I know too that the treatment of East Indians, British subjects, in this country, who are denied the rights of British citizenship because they are coloured, has been one of the most potent weapons used by the congress party in India against the British authorities. I know too that the discrimination against our Chinese citizens is felt keenly by those of the same race who are in other parts of the world as well as in our own.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has given expression to what every hon. member of this house feels to be a condition precedent to bringing about satisfactory relations between the nations of the world; that is, that unless it is possible to arrive at a measure of social and economic justice, as a result of collaboration between the nations of the world, any projected world organization is likely to experience the frustration which attended attempts to build and guarantee peace during the last two decades. At the end of the last war our country took the position that economic and social matters were not properly within the terms of reference of the conference which was then convened to design the structure which it was hoped would preserve the peace of the world during the years following. The view was held that while political matters were properly within the terms of reference, matters involving the economic phases of the problem were not to be considered in the same light. I think we are all agreed that the experience of the last twenty-five years has shown that unemployment in the devastated and dependent territories of the world, as well as in the more fortunate countries, is a problem of world interest which must be solved first if the political problem is to be dealt with satisfactorily.
This government, headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenize King), has not waited till the end of the war to lay before the nations of the world its views with respect to recurring phases of international organization. Canada's representation at the food conference held in Virginia was notable. Harold Laski, writing recently on the projection of a world organization, referred specifically to the contribution made by Canada at
Supply-External Affairs

the conference in Virginia, and later at the Atlantic City conference in connection with UNRRA. So that long before the end of hostilities we have appreciated our obligations to the other nations of the world. I could mention, and I do want to mention, apart altogether from myi own contribution, the work of Canada at the very important twenty-sixth meeting of the International Labour Organization, recently held in Philadelphia. Perhaps here I may be permitted to pay tribute to the Canadian delegates to that conference, those who were advisers, those who represented the workers and the employers, and those who represented both provincial and federal governments. I believe Canada did make a contribution at that conference and, as I want to show later, something developed there to illustrate the fallacy of the kind of argument advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver South. More recently we had Canada's contribution at the international monetary conference, which brought great distinction to. this country. Since that time I have met in this city a number of delegates to that conference from other countries, who have spoken in the highest terms of the work of the Canadian delegates. If one did not know some of the personalities involved these tributes might be considered almost extravagant. One distinguished gentleman of the United Kingdom delegation said in my presence, speaking of two of our people at that conference, that no delegates from any other country stood higher in the esteem of the conference generally or in the measure of the contribution they made. These are practical contributions.
At this point we are discussing the theoretical basis of the future world order, of the future political organization of the world; but during the past two and a half years representatives of our government, civil servants and others who have been coopted to serve along with these two groups have been applying Canadian foreign policy in a practical and definite manner. It is regrettable that we, along with the other constituents of the commonwealth and the empire, should sometimes have it suggested that because a certain viewpoint is taken it can only mean disloyalty to the crown and to the institutions fashioned and given to the civilized world by British genius. The suggestion is that because you may have a certain conception of the development of the commonwealth, thereby you aire trying to contribute to its liquidation and break-up.

, Mr. MARTIN: I hope the Prime Minister will not consider that I do not fully appreciate the value of the contribution he made recently when speaking to both houses of parliament in London, but I believe the unique contribution he made then came about not so much because he said anything that was really new but because of the way in which he said it, the circumstances under which it was said, and the time at which he made his statement. After all, his statement was a continuation of the foreign policy that has been in existence throughout the development of this country. It was a development of the foreign policy of Laurier, and particularly of the foreign policy of Sir Robert Borden. One has only to read the Marfleet lectures given,by Sir Robert Borden at the conclusion of the last war to see that the course followed by the present Prime Minister in London was in line with the foreign policy of this country under successive governments and successive prime ministers with various political affiliations. There is no attempt to bring about a diminution in the strength of the empire or of the commonwealth. At this stage I think it is well to make a distinction, .as Mr. Churchill himself makes it, between the empire and the commonwealth. He defines the empire as being the United Kingdom and the colonial empire, and the British commonwealth as being the United Kingdom and the self-governing dominions. No attempt is made in any way to destroy the strength of those two combinations or of either of them if they are interchangeable, as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has suggested. Rather the idea is to strengthen them, to bring the British commonwealth in line to work with the nations of the world, instead of standing aside as a strong power bloc pitted against the whole world.

Supply-External Affairs
This policy is not based upon a failure to appreciate what the British commonwealth may mean to the world. Anyone who suggests the breaking up of that commonwealth is speaking in unrealistic language. No one is suggesting that; rather the suggestion is that we should maintain it. The way to maintain it is through a policy of inclusion rather than one of exclusion, and that was the policy enunciated by tTie Prime Minister in London. And that that is a sound view seems to me, in the light of the appraisal made of that speech, to be generally accepted. I have gone carefully over the periodicals, and have had press clippings from newspapers reviewed, and the unanimous view-well, I should not say the unanimous view-but the extent of the view throughout the whole commonwealth in support of the Prime Minister's statement at Westminster recently is so overwhelming that one wonders whether it is necessary at all to spend much time on the point.
It is generally admitted that the only hope for the world, particularly having in mind Moscow and Teheran, is by the pursuit of that kind of policy. It is not an attempt to refuse to speak with one voice, but rather to be able effectively to demonstrate that if it is possible to speak with one voice, that one voice has arisen as the result of consideration in each individual country within the commonwealth. In that way, if you can say to the nations of the world that these problems have been thought out at Ottawa, at Canberra and at Cape Town, just as well as at London, and you have coincidentally the same kind of view, then that kind of one-voice has been and is a voice of strength, and a voice with persuading influence in the councils of the world.
We had an example of that recently at the International Labour Organization. Canada took a certain view with regard to the projected future of the International Labour Organization. Great Britain had not yet expressed her view, nor had Australia, nor had New Zealand. Canada's view was much criticized in many quarters, although, later, without any consultation, except by way of informal discussion, Great Britain took the same stand, Australia took the same stand and New Zealand took the same stand.
I suggest that if at one time we had said, "Here is the view of all of us at once", it would not have had the same effect that it did have, coming as it did as the result of individual deliberation on the part of the various self-governing dominions. It had more effect than it would have had if it had been given as a common expression of opinion, or the expression of view of the whole bloc.
If you can impress other nations of the world -and that is what we must do-that we are simply trying to bring about a healthy contribution among the nations of the world, looking at these matters from our own particular point of view, and always bearing in mind that our own point of view in the big things ig not necessarily different from the point of view of the United Kingdom government, we are more apt to have the kind of influence we desire than we would have under the policy suggested, as I gathered, in the observations of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green).

speechtext: The hon. member did not follow my suggestions very closely, then.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
I read very carefully the speech delivered by the hon. member last year, and I must say that I did not see much difference between that speech and the one delivered this afternoon.
Surely our strength is this: surely the strength of the British commonwealth of nations is that there has been allowed to grow in the various self-governing dominions a measure of autonomy which has affected the personalities and mature developments of those dominions, as a result of the extension of the principle of autonomy. In freedom we have grown-not grown apart, but we have grown to march still within the same grouping, that grouping which is called either the British empire or the British commonwealth of nations.
For instance, when this parliament declared war in 1939, as a result of its own free decision, that was a more effective answer to our enemy than if we had been called into it automatically through the exclusive act of the United Kingdom government. That demonstrated that the liquidation of this commonwealth is not at hand, but that it is stronger, as a result of the extension of the principle of freedom, which freedom has tended to develop each of the units known as selfgoverning dominions.
I think surely the time has come when we should be able to demonstrate to the world that, apart from a few extremists here ' and there, in this country there is no desire to break away from that grouping, when the whole trend in the world is toward grouping- toward larger groupings, as well as toward maintaining the same commonwealth grouping. Surely nothing is to be gained from the suggestion that the Prime Minister of this country, or that any individual serving in the government of this country, is motivated by instincts less sincere than those of persons
Supply-External Affairs

who take the opposite view. In the view taken by the Prime Minister it should not be considered that he was expressing simply his own view. He spoke, I think, for Canada, and for the great majority of Canadians. But he also spoke the language which was uttered by another distinguished prime minister of a self-governing dominion. Mr. Fraser cannot be said to be less interested!-always having in mind the geographic position of New Zealand-in the continuity of the solidarity of the British commonwealth of nations than is the hon. member who took a view which, I suggest, is opposite to the one I am trying to set forth.
So that I think we ought to realize that in the disturbed conditions of our world, we will be called upon to deal with matters affecting the future of civilization. We should not allow some of our differences on commonwealth direction to cause us to lose our perspective. These differences have been shown in the past to be less real than at first glance would seem to be the case.
To suggest that the policy of the present Prime Minister or the government is an isolationist policy, as was suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South, is, I find, very difficult to reconcile with the criticism the hon. member makes it the first instance, and the action he proposes in the second. If the Prime Minister had followed the line which the hon. member for Vancouver South has suggested the result would have been out of line with the present trend among the united nations.
Of course, no one can seriously contend that at this time in the history of the world any government can afford to have an isolationist policy-and least of all any government in Canada. We cannot afford that in Canada, dependent as we are, almost to the extent of forty per cent of our national income, upon trading with other nations in the world. This country least of all can afford to be isolationist, and this government certainly has not given any indication that it has any desire to be isolationist.
I think it will be seen, and the records will show that the first statement made by any prime minister within the British commonwealth with regard to the desirability of setting up a future world organization based upon the recognition of the interdependence of states was the statement made by the present Prime Minister of Canada. It was a statement fully in harmony with the action taken at Moscow, at Teheran and recently in London. No one can suggest seriously in this chamber-and I am sure that upon reflection

the hon. member for Vancouver South would agree that he was not really serious in his suggestion-that this government is isolationist.
