speechtext: I meant exactly what I said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
No one in this country can suggest that we could be isolationist in a world in which, as Mr. Willkie has said, no point is more than sjjtty hours distant from the farthest point. This is a world in which, because of the developments of science, we have been brought together to such an extent that unemployment has ceased to be a national problem and has forced us to be as much concerned with the fortunes of the dependent areas of the world as we must be with our own. I think one can dismiss summarily the suggestion that we are committed, to a policy of isolation. On the contrary I think we recognize the realism of the moment. We recognize that on the shoulders of certain great powers rests, because of their power, the opportunity of shaping things to come. We say, as the Prime Minister said this morning, and as he has said on other occasions, that the peace of the world cannot be maintained simply by a supremacy of power. On the other hand, the peace of the world cannot be maintained by overlooking the realities of the situation. These realities were dealt with, for instance, by Walter Lippmann, in the book to which the hon. member for Vancouver South referred last year and likewise in Mr. Lippmann's book published a few weeks ago. We must take into account the realities if we are going to avoid mischief and the kind of mistakes made a.t the end of the last war. Our ideal must be a world organization.
The peace of the world can be maintained through the agency of conference, and law on the same analogies and principles by which the peace of the community is maintained. But in the building up of this peace mechanism ,we must not overlook the strength and the bargaining position of the great powers. To do so would be to step into a situation which would defeat the very purpose we all have in mind in maintaining world peace through organization on a world basis.
Canada will have a great role to play. Canada did play a role during the last two decades by being one of the leaders among the small powers, by interpreting to the great powers, either in the council of the league when it was in existence or by other approaches, the wishes as well as the aspirations of the smaller powers. That we shall do in our ascent from the status of a small nation to what must be the ambition of every Canadian, that of a great power, as

Supply-External Affairs
suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South. In building this world organization we should note the experience of the older world political organizations. We have the experience of the League of Nations. While it is fashionable to criticize the league and say that it failed, that it did not avoid war, the fact is, as Prime Minister Churchill has said, it was not the league that failed, it was so many of its members who failed its ideals. However, that does not mean to say that the covenant of the league was perfect, that the structure of the league was satisfactory. There were weaknesses.
This government in line with the declarations of the governments of the United Kingdom, of the U.S.S.R., of the United States, has gone on record in favour of a world political organization. There is to be a world assembly which will fulfil the legislative function of government. There is to be a council which will fulfil the executive arm of government. With regard to the assembly I trust that the Canadian government in making proposals, either vicariously or directly, in respect of the discussions to be pursued in Washington in the near future or later, will not feel bound to the letter of the law as we were in connection with the covenant.
Perhaps such things as the rule of unanimity, perhaps such things as the rule of the two-thirds vote on certain occasions, both in the council and in the assembly, will be found not to be necessary. Perhaps we shall not find it necessary to have a written constitution, and, if we do have one, I trust it will be more elastic and less rigid than the covenant. There you have the conflict between the civil law lawyer and the common law lawyer. Whatever we do in framing the theoretical base of the organization, let us do it in such a manner as not to find ourselves faced with constitutional obstacles from which there are no remedies at the time.
With regard to the council one must take into account the actual situation. The great powers must find their places, but it is hoped that in the extension of the principle of functionalism Canada will be able to play her part along with the smaller nations. This principle of functionalism is not as anaemic as the hon. member for Vancouver South has suggested. The principle which was enunciated by this government has been carried forward in other international conferences during the last two and a half years. It was recognized at t'he food conference at Virginia, it was recognized at UNRRA, it was recognized at the I.L.O. and it was recognized recently at
the international monetary conference as the correct approach to international matters in our day.
Then there is the third phase of the world organization, the judiciary.. The permanent court of international justice still continues to be a reality, and it is inconceivable that the principle of the judiciary in terms of a future world organization should not have its proper place. Undoubtedly there will have to be some modifications in the present constitution of the court, but the principles underlying it are principles which need as ready acceptance as the other components of the world organization.
In recapitulation, may I say that I think the Prime Minister expressed the view of every member of this committee when he said this morning that the first job is to win the battle, the winning of a war Which was not of our making or of our desire. After that, we must make sure, in so far as man can make sure, * that we set up those agencies by which it may be possible to maintain the peace of the world or to minimize the occasion of war. I suggest that these ideals should ever be foremost. But alongside of these ideals should be the ready acknowledgment of the realities of the moment and of the inherent intricacies which attend foreign affairs generally.
We cannot retreat now. We might be said by some to be building up a supranational government, a super-state, but the latter is not the intention. There is not any desire or any intention of interfering with the normal course of national development but rather it is to see that extravagances in national aspiration are curbed and disciplined in the common interest which in this time and age becomes the interest of men and women all over the world.
I think this government has made an excellent start in this new phase of its foreign policy. It is in line with the aspirations of our people and with those of thinking men and women throughout the world. It now becomes its task to make sure that its policy is detailed and directed in the light of the developments which will soon come upon us. Much work has been done in this country by private agencies and by government officials who have been studying these matters for months and several years. The time is now running when we shall have to place these proposals of ours alongside the proposals of other nations. We must make sure that we develop toward a healthy phase of internationalism without which there can be no peace for any of us.
Supply-External Affairs

In conclusion, may I say that the recent conference of workers, employers and governments at the international labour meeting in Philadelphia in May and April of this year laid down on the part of forty-two countries- as good a cross-section of united nations and associated powers opinion as one could find- the indication of a desire in each country that the respective governments should be enabled by their own action to arrive at satisfactory social security measures, that they should set into being, following collaboration among themselves, those forces as a result of which the trade of the world might be restored to its former momentum with proper regulation and encouragement, thereby providing work for their people.
That is a great challenge. In the light of the conditions of the world as we see it, it will be a difficult challenge to meet. That the challenge must be met goes without saying, but it will not be met unless we fully appreciate the dangers involved and the realities-the terrible realities-of the situation. It can be met. We can have social security here at home. We can have a high level of employment such as the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell) and we on this side envisage. We can have economic comfort and security for our people. Let us not make the mistake of assuming that these things can be done by our own effort alone. Unless there is international collaboration on the highest level these things will not be. For that reason we in this house owe a duty to those we represent of seeing to it that our foreign policy is made along lines which will encourage not a policy of exclusion but a policy of inclusion, whereby we shall not drift apart, but whereby all nations, the British commonwealth itself, its self-governing dominions, and the other units of its empire will march in unison with all the nations of the world, making sure thereby, and only thereby, the world peace which all of us desire.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
There has never been a programme before this house which has evoked wider differences of opinion than that which affects this great question of external affairs. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who have had a long and colourful career in relation to this subject, may remember that we who sit on this side of the house have alwaj's pursued a consistent policy in foreign affairs. This is an appropriate and historic day upon which to discuss the question. On the 4th of August, thirty years ago, the first great war, with all the destruction it caused, broke out. May I point out that

the period between the two wars, when we threw away our defences and friends, was also most destructive, and nearly destroyed civilization.
I should like to see Canada give some recognition to the achievements of the great generals who in this war have done so much to save civilization. If we followed the example of the' United [DOT] States, which has on two or three occasions elected as president one of its distinguished soldiers, we might well appoint General Montgomery as Governor General of Canada.
In examining the history of Canadian policy in foreign affairs it is important to make sure that we understand what the term means. Since the last war "external affairs" has been invested with a number of new meanings and has included many new activities in the way of appointment of ambassadors to many countries. So far as our party is concerned, one hundred years ago, in 1844, the founder of our party, Sir John A. Macdonald, laid down the principle of Canada's connection with the mother country as our policy, and we intend to continue to support the British connection and all it means and has meant down the ages for freedom and civilization. That policy remains in force, I believe, to-day.
Foreign affairs has been referred to by the writer of a text-book on the subject as largely a matter of what one might call a chartered accountant's policy, by which you strike a balance sheet of assets and liabilities, and decide as a country what commitments you have to meet and what you will be able to do with them in the event of war. That is a very good definition. As I see it, the foreign policy of this country should be based on two principles.
The first is, to give the people all the information you can. On March 21, 1939, a few months after Munich, I took the position in this house that as far as possible the people should be told everything about the real facts of the coming war situation. That has been a good policy in the past. When a grave situation lies before us in external and foreign affairs, commitments are made, as Britain did two years before the war, t6 Poland, Greece, Czechoslovakia, and other countries, and this bound the dominions, because when Britain is at war Canada is also at war. I believe that the people should be told the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and that any foreign affairs policy should also be based on the preservation of human liberty the world over.
After all, Britain is not fighting this war for any selfish motive. While the government of our great ally and supporter to the south

Supply-External Affairs
is not responsible for statements made in the United States senate and house of representatives, one remembers that statements have been made there during the debates on lease-lend that this was not their war, that it was Britain's war. Neither Britain nor the United States went to war for personal reasons. Britain went to war in honouring her pledge to Poland. The United States, our great ally, and Russia went to war because the one was attacked at Pearl Harbor and the other was invaded. Britain seeks no gain from this war in territory and no special privileges; nothing but honour and justice and the preservation of liberty and freedom for the whole civilized world.
I believe that two or three years ago I suggested to the Prime Minister that we should give the other branch of parliament, meeting in another place, some more work to do. It would be well, I think, to follow the practice in Washington and London and have that other branch go into this matter of foreign and external affairs. After all, they have over there some former premiers and members of parliament of both parties; they include men of wide experience; and we might strengthen our position somewhat and stimulate better discussion if such an arrangement were adopted. The Prime Minister gave two or three times the very reasonable reply that he would take the matter up with the leader of the senate.
Much was hoped from the great conference of premiers held last May in London. At that time a vast armada had been assembled in Great Britain. Thanks to our control of some bases in Northern Ireland the battle of the Atlantic against the U-boat had been won. Nobody knows what the world owes to those brave men of the dominions who on land, on sea and in the air saved civilization at Dunkirk. At the time these magnificent preparations were all but completed there occurred the conference in London at which our Prime Minister represented Canada and addressed both houses of parliament, where he got a great reception, approved by the people of Canada. Everybody thought that something would be done to lay down a constitution and a programme for the empire and to provide some policy for after the war.
The visit of the prime ministers to London came at a time when the invasion of Normandy was about to be launched, with such grave consequences to Europe and to the world at large, and no doubt the prime ministers were told about it and all about foreign affairs. But when you talk about foreign affairs to-day you must remember that everything you plan depends upon one eventuality, namely, victory in this war. Without victory in this war everything that is being said on this whole subject here is beside the point. In my opinion, on this whole question of foreign affairs and a common foreign policy for the future, so far as coordination and cooperation are concerned, the results attained at the conference of prime ministers were not what the people of Canada had expected. It is true that our Prime Minister addressed the conference and so did Prime Minister Churchill. I have not at my command at this moment all the information with regard to the conference, but in my opinion the results achieved on that- occasion did not meet with the approval of all the Canadian people-certainly not with the approval of a great many people in this country.
It is true that Mr. Churchill made the statement that it was not necessary to write down in black and white all the sentiments which were shared in common by the prime ministers who met in conference in London, since the provisions of the statute of Westminster had been written down in black and white. He pointed out that fraternal relations had emerged from the common association of the different parts of the empire as well as of the United States and Russia in the waging of this war. Speaking in the British House of Commons on April 21 last, Mr. Churchill said that he had never conceived that fraternal association with the United States would militate in any way against the unity of the British commonwealth and empire, and he referred to the twenty-year treaty that had been made with Russia. Let me quote what he said:
I have never conceived that a fraternal association with the United States would militate in any way against the unity of the British commonwealth and empire, or breed ill-feeling with our great Russian ally, to whom, we arc bound by the 20 years treaty. I do not think we need choose this or that. With wisdom, and patience, and vigour, and courage, we may get the best of both. We have often said of our own British empire: "In my Father's house there are many mansions."
The results of the conference of prime ministers were, in my opinion, disappointing to a great many of the citizens of this country, because, after all, when we are discussing foreign affairs we must remember that everything depends upon common action as between the mother country and the dominions. Without such unity there can be no empire policy. Indeed, a great many people are of the opinion that as a result of that conference reliance will no longer be placed on united action within the commonwealth for the defence of the British empire, but that instead we are
Supply-External Affairs

postponing appropriate action now and what is vital for consideration by some new international order, some new league of nations.
I suggest that unless the dominions are united to the mother country now, in this time of war, we shall have little to do at the peace table, because the dominions and the mother country must hang together. If they do not they will hang separately. No one part of the commonwealth can act alone, for the simple reason that it does not possess the armaments necessary to support its position. That is what we have to consider in connection with any fundamental principle of foreign policy.
Look at the commitments which the mother country has made at different times and you must realize that if you are to make commitments you must have the force to support them. That will mean in the future, after the war, that not only Britain and the dominions but the United States and Russia will find it necessary to have a large navy, air force and army in keeping with the commitments which have been made.
I do not believe in any new league of nations, nor do I think that you need look for one. If that is your idea, then you may expect another war twenty-five or thirty years hence. The old league was a sham and failed absolutely. At the conference, I suggest, Canada should have supported the stand taken by Premier Curtin and Premier Fraser, with certain limitations, of course, because I believe there is something in what the Prime Minister said about fraternal relations. But it would have been better, in my opinion, if we had had some form of empire secretariat for collaboration. We are spending $5 million on the League of Nations, with all the offices they have. If wTe had had a combined secretariat, taking in the mother country and all the dominions, it would have served a very useful purpose, particularly in the postwar period, because it would ensure close collaboration, especially with civil aviation what it is. Civil aviation to-day is one of the great agencies for binding different countries together. I believe that some such plan was given to the conference but they were not unanimous on it.
As regards what has been said by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and others, I believe that on this question Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser were absolutely right. In my opinion we would be on the wrong track altogether if we adopted the suggestion that has been made for participation in a pan-American plan, which is a new sort of league. The hon. member for Essex East is running true to form because he has always been a believer in ideas of that sort based on

leagues, and separatism and isolation. Well, he is entitled to his opinion, but I suggest that the British empire will be on the wrong track again, as in 1919, if it follows that line. Internationalism should start within the family of British nations. If we are to have internationalism let us start within the British empire. How is it that more of the dominions are not willing to make an agreement of that sort? We are not real internationalists if we are not ready to join with other branches of the empire, the other dominions, as one family in- a united empire policy of cooperation and collaboration with the mother country. Why should we not have a league of nations of our own? As has been well said to-day, the only league of nations that has ever achieved any success is the British empire. The United States knows that; the world knows it; and out of this war there should emerge a great league of nations, namely, the British empire. If we have something of this sort there is hope for us in international affairs, but if each separate dominion undertakes to deal with foreign countries along its own lines we shall not succeed. That is a policy to which I am absolutely opposed.
As Lord Milner said in 1919, speaking at Oxford, it was a -most' strange anomaly to hear that the self-governing parts of the British empire should be joining a league, binding themselves by a formal tie to a number of foreign nations, when they had theretofore been unwilling to enter into similar obligations with one another. There is a great deal in that. At the conference of prime ministers there are many matters which should have been dealt with and which I should like to have seen discussed, such as defence, security, reconstruction, trade and commerce, migration within the empire, civil aviation, empire preference tariffs, and so on.
The Prime Minister to-day gave the committee an elaborate address with a great deal of valuable information, but I suggest, that in our foreign policy the main object should be to wmrk with the people of the United States and Russia. Only by so doing can the peace of the world be maintained.
At the same time the coming British empire and Great Britain cannot throw overboard the several countries in Europe that have been overrun by the axis, and look to the mother country to defend them. Britain cannot throw these countries over. They have been loyal to us in two wars. They are looking to Britain for a post-war lead. I believe we should continue to merit the confidence of these people which Britain and the dominions

Supply-External Affairs
enjoy. We can make a great contribution as an empire by this unity which Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser propose. In that way we shall have a larger voice in the world to come. We have had long traditions of friendship with many countries in Europe, Norway, Belgium, Denmark, Sweden, France and Greece and those other countries. We cannot ignore them in the world to come. In particular we should be on the most intimate terms with France, that glorious country, where so many' of our own men of the last war sleep their last sleep till the resurrection morning. France is a great nation. It will always be a great nation as was said by the late King Edward VII of Great Britain. He said that Divine Providence had designed that France should be our near neighbour and always our friend and our ally by geography.
I do not believe that the great general who is the prime minister of South Africa, Jan Christian Smuts, did the empire any good when he gave an interview at the guild hall, in which he said that France will only be a second-class power after this war, because France will always be a great nation. It will rise again. Events that have taken place in Italy have proved that. We saw the military genius of the French soldiers in Italy, and General de Gaulle has given us a demonstration of the integrity of France in this war. I believe that the time is coming when General de Gaulle will be looked on as one of the greatest Frenchmen. I was glad to see the reception that General de Gaulle received here a while ago. He represents the real spirit of France. Look at the reception he got in Normandy. He and his officers deserve all the credit for the uprisings which have been taking place there.
When fhis war started and after France was invaded, not a single colony of the splendid colonial system of France failed to come to her assistance. The French have a wonderful colonial system. We have a little bit of it in this country. France went all over the world and developed a great many fine French colonies. When the war started not one French colony of the great French empire failed to respond to the call of the mother country, France. They had the utmost loyalty and devotion to her. I hope that General de Gaulle w'ill get the renewed support of the government of Canada, because we have in the past been depending too much on Mr. Ristelhueber and Vichy and Petain. Washington has even now been acting in the same wayr. As Mr. Churchill said in this house, ninety-five per cent of the people of France supported General de Gaulle. We saw what
he did in the St. Lawrence when he went in at the request of the inhabitants and seized the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon and protected Canada and her shores.
I am sorry to see that in Normandy and in France our ally, the United States, are doing something that I had never heard of before, issuing American currency for use in France to pay for their troops in Normandy. That is against international law and will not be a good thing for the allies. It will not conduce to the allies working together unitedly in this war because it will do harm to our French allies and should not be gone on with.
There has been altogether too much hush policy about the brutal murders on the part of the axis powers. We had the same in the last war. We all know the way in which they have been carrying on and murdering all these people. I believe, as the members of the British House of Commons and the press of Britain have said, that the gestapo police force and everyone else of these murderers should be rounded up and put to death immediately. Russia is acting. They will not wait for any trial by an international court such as has been proposed by some people. They punish them the minute they arrive and catch them. That is what should happen. I hope Canada will support such action.
There are many other problems to which reference might be made. So far as these treaties are concerned, we had them between the two wars and they were disastrous. We saw many' democracies go under. We saw democracy crushed in Germany, Austria, Jugoslavia, Greece, Italy, Spain and Portugal. They all went out. None of them had democratic constitutions.
We may rejoice that in 1939 before the war started we had a visit from our gracious King and Queen. The great reception which was given to them showed the popularity of the monarchy in Canada. There is one thing to be said about the British monarchy, it has won a glorious record in this war in the way it has kept the different countries together. The loyalty of the dominions and of public men has been most commendable.
I believe that the dominions should continue to play a much larger share in foreign affairs than we have ever done in the past. If we had a united policy and approached the peace table with that policy we would play a much larger part in world affairs. We have no need to apologize for what this empire has done. Next to the Christian church to-day it has been God's greatest single gift to humanity. The British people and the British empire down through the ages have
Siipply-External Affairs

of a misconstruction of the war debt situation, because, after all is said and done, after the last war, like the United States, England was a creditor nation when the war ended. In less than twenty years after the war she had lost great sums through unpaid war debts, and she left German reparation payments out of the picture entirely. The United States by that time had manoeuvred herself into the position of receiving most of those payments.
Great Britain was not a defaulter; her debts were paid. My point is that these isolationist representations in respect of war debts have never been adequately answered or challenged. Britain does not even guard 'herself against those representations. But my prediction as to lease-lend settlement is that unless we are very careful, we shall have the same trouble after this war in bringing about a settlement. I believe that the British empire exists, in spite . of geography.
As I said last session:
While Canada, as Mr. Churchill said, has made a glorious contribution in this war in material tilings, food and munitions and supply, it is in its man-power overseas on land, sea and in the air, that the sons of Canada in battle have so gloriously rewritten the whole history of courage in this war as to win the admiration of the whole civilized world. We as a people have not 'had in this war real national selective service, nor any real equality of service nor of sacrifice.	Our policy in
relation to this was everything by fits and starts and nothing long. We were three years too late in starting a real selective service policy, and have now one that is not national, not selective, nor is there in it any equality of service or of sacrifice.
Further, what Canada has done since before the close of the last century, she has done voluntarily, of her free will and under her own status, sovereignty and autonomy, namely gone to the aid of Britain in her hour of peril.
In the South African war a few thousand went from Canada, but Britain paid the total cost of it.
I do hope that in days to come, instead of discussing foreign affairs for the first time on the 145th day of the session, we may have it at some earlier time, or that a committee of the other chamber might deal with it. I hope that we may have a real discussion. I realize, of course, the heavy work the Prime Minister and his brilliant young assistant from Vancouver have done since the war started.
I wish to say in conclusion that the world does not know yet nor does civilization realize the great service given, by Northern Ireland when they permitted the use of their bases. This matter was referred to at the time of the last war. As Mr. Lloyd George said, we would have lost the last war if we had not had those bases. Had not our ships been able to use the southern channel, and so get

to Queenstown, where would we have been in our campaign in Normandy only for the Ulster bases and the victory over the U-boats in the Atlantic? Where would we have been if we could not have used these ports? The Eire bases belong to the empire. We should have protested years ago about not having the use of them.
And after almost four years in this war the commander of the United States forces, General Eisenhower, and President Roosevelt have notified Eire that they want them to check the axis raids on Atlantic shipping. The axis aid in Eire gave them a light across the channel to destroy Coventry and Cardiff, as Eire aided Germany. I should like to see the day not far distant when we would close up our useless embassy in Dublin altogether. I fail to see why we need one there, particularly in this time of war. Australia and New Zealand have none and join the United States in a protest against the way Eire aided Germany.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, to save time-and sweat-I shall try to shorten my remarks. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this morning used an expression which caught my ear. I wrote it down. He said, "We should seek to lower the tempo of nationalism." More power to him, if he does it. But before he starts on that great enterprise, he would gain the gratitude of all of us if he would lower the temperature of this chamber.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext: Hear? hear.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
It is disgraceful to see that 245 members have no more sense than to sit here in a temperature of 95 degrees, with our coats on-because our dignity, forsooth, does not allow us to take them off. We had a cooling system put in here some years ago. It never did work, and it has not worked since.
When I first came here members sitting on the back benches could not see to read, because of the arrangement of the lighting. It took me-I happened to be one of the victims -two years to have that fixed. And it was almost a whirlwind job to have it done in two years. It is not good for us and it is not good for the country that we should have to legislate, and conduct our debates in a temperature like this. But it will go on, I suppose, as long as the house sits.
With much of what the Prime Minister said in the earlier part of his speech this morning. I agree. Particularly do I agree with that

Supply-External Affairs
portion of his speech in which he endorsed the statements made by the five prime ministers of the different nations, and also with his remarks on the paivAmerican situation. I will not go further into that, however, because I wish to discuss in greater detail the policy announced with regard to the Japanese, which is so important to us in British Columbia.
The other night when he announced his intention of having this matter discussed, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked for a delay which, with his usual courtesy, the Prime Minister granted. But I think they were wrong. What the leader of the opposition should have asked for was a day's delay after the Prime Minister had spoken. Then we would have been in a position to see in print exactly what his remarks were. To-day, however, having heard them verbally only once, we are not in a position to give his address the genuine or careful consideration to which it is entitled. Several days are always left between the speech from the throne and the debate, and on many occasions the matters contained in the speech from the throne are not as important as the policy the Prime Minister announced this morning.
Also, I should like to study it, and understand all its implications-because I just caught certain phrases which, perhaps years hence, might prove qualifications or modifications of what I thought the policy was. Some of the statement I think had qualifying clauses which might considerably change the meaning when it comes to be interpreted in days ahead.
However, as I gathered it, the Prime Minister laid down three basic lines of policy in regard to the Japanese situation. One was that it would be unwise to let all the Japanese return to British Columbia. If I am not strictly accurate in my understanding, the Prime Minister can correct me. I am stating only what I gathered. The second point was that all those of Japanese origin proved guilty of disloyalty should be deported, and the third one was that there should be no further immigration.
I shall comment on these three, what the Prime Minister called basic policies. As regards the first, my conviction is-and I believe this is the conviction of ninety per cent of the people of British Columbia-that every one of those of Japanese origin should be repatriated at the end of the war. The argument against doing that to them all does not seem to be any stronger than the argument for doing it only to those suspected of disloyalty, because, to amount to anything, it would have to cover those who are only
suspected. If a man has been proved guilty of disloyalty or treason, of course he is in gaol and he does not need to h.e deported. Therefore, if the provision amounts to anything it will have to apply to those who are suspected of disloyalty. In one case it covers as much as the other. If you are going to deport 200 people, you might as well deport ,2.000 or 22,000. If you are going to repatriate only those who are convicted of disloyalty you will have to get a conviction of treason against them. Then, if you did that, they would be in gaol and the need for their repatriation would not arise.
There would be objection to the suggestion that they be spread out among the provinces. I have in my hand a copy of an agreement made by the British Columbia security commission. This is just the same as the government because the government gave them power which they never should have been given. They were turned loose with every kind of power but that of sending people to the gallows. They were given the power to run this particular business. This particular agreement bears the signature of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), giving his approval to it. One section of the agreement, outlining what the commission will do, reads:
The commission agrees to remove or to have removed from the province, upon the termination of the state of war now existing between Canada and Japan, the Japanese temporarily placed or maintained within the province pursuant to the terms of this agreement, as requested so to do by the province.
That is the agreement with Alberta, and I understand that there are similar agreements with other provinces. They may not be couched in exactly those terms, but they mean the same. The arrangement with Manitoba was not in the form of a signed agreement; it was arrived at by an exchange of letters, but they agreed to do exactly the same thing.
If you take these people away from Alberta, where are you going to send them? Are you going to break faith with the people who let them into Alberta on that understanding? Are you going to send them back to British Columbia where you have said already that they must not be allowed to creep in again. There is only one thing to do with them, deport them. You cannot coerce Quebec or Nova Scotia or any other province to take a certain number of these Japs. Those provinces would not like it and you would not expect them to do it. I understand from the grapevine that some of the provinces that took them in in good faith because they were in need of labour are beginning to realize that their philosophy and system of life, their
Supply-External Affairs

ambitions and the goal toward which they are working, are not in harmony with those of the province. They are looking forward to the day when those Japanese will be taken away.
I suggest that this policy will be unworkable. They should all be repatriated. If you are going to do it in a partial way, then you can do it in a complete way. The Prime Minister has suggested setting up a commis-* sion to find out those who are disloyal. I presume this will mean that each man will be asked to take an oath of allegiance to the king. I predict that that will be taken by ninety-nine and a half per cent of them just as glibly and as unconcernedly as we would take an extra cup of tea if our host pressed us to have one. The occidental oath means nothing to the oriental. He has his own ideas about what is binding. I believe they tried a similar thing in the United States, and a surprising number of those who had been born in the United States refused to take a false oath. Some of them said that they were neutral and others said that they stood by their emperor whose country they had never seen. I should like to quote what Kipling said:
The stranger within my gate,
He may be true or kind
But he does not talk my talk-
I cannot feel his mind.
I see the face and the eyes and the mouth, But not the soul behind.
Another verse reads:
The stranger within my gate,
He may be evil or good,
But I cannot tell what powers control- What reasons sway his mood;
Nor when the gods of his far-off land Shall repossess his blood.
That was said by an able man who knew what he was talking about. The Prime Minister and everyone who has studied this question knows that the oriental is not capable of being assimilated with the white race. That is the answer to those who say, "Why do you treat the Japs differently from the Germans or Italians?" They do not assimilate. They simply look forward to the day when all countries and races from Hawaii to Alaska will be governed by their emperor. I have seen that in translations of some of their propaganda. Intermarriage is the only way you can assimilate, and the records show how very few cases there have been of intermarriage, and how unsuccessful they have been. There is some difference between oriental and occidental blood which will not permit them to mix. At any rate they do not want to mix with us.
Once the Prime Minister has admitted, as he has to-day, the salient fact that British

Columbia will have none of them after sixty years experience and after sixty years has proved that they cannot and do not want to marry with our race, then I submit that there is no other logical course open to him than to go the whole length-the opportunity will never happen again-and get rid of them. History records cases where such repatriation has been highly successful. When the Turks defeated the Greeks in 1921 all the Greeks in Asia Minor were sent into Greece, and Turks were moved into Asia Minor. Something like 400,000 people were moved, and we are talking of repatriating only 22,000. That repatriation of 400,000 worked very well. The families of some of those Greeks had lived in Asia Minor for a thousand years, but they were sent away.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
At six o'clock I was referring to the precedent of removing people in large bodies. I cited the incidents of the Turks and the Greeks, totalling something like four hundred thousand, who were exchanged over a wide area. For some of them the district had been their ancestral home for a thousand years; yet circumstances justified the policy of removal, and it worked. I suggest that it might also be worked out in the case of removing Japanese in Canada. If four hundred thousand people can be successfully transferred in another part of the world we do not need to make a fuss about removing twenty-five thousand, especially as most of them are not beyond the second generation or, in a very few instances, the third generation.
An attempt has been made to play up the fact that the Japanese have not been convicted of sabotage. No, they have not, to any extent; but if the Japanese army had landed in British Columbia, what would the story have been then? I notice that advocates of the Japanese in dealing with this subject always talk about them as "Japs". But they are not Japs; they are British subjects; that is the argument, at any rate. These advocates never talk about "British subjects" not getting a square deal; they always talk about "the Japs" as not getting a square deal, thus recognizing that they are not British subjects. It may have been noticed that when a deputation of them came here to ask for the vote, as they did before a parliamentary committee some years ago, they did not ask that it be

Supply-External Affairs
extended also to Chinese and other orientals; they only wanted the privilege for themselves. As I say, they regard themselves as Japanese and are so described by their advocates. If they are British subjects, in that case they come under the ordinary law, or should do so at any rate.
The Japs who lived around Pearl Harbor had nothing but love for their white brothers until the war struck them. How are you going to prove that they are loyal? Ask them to get up and sing "God Save the King" and take an oath of loyalty? Of course they will do that. An oath means nothing to them. They would just as readily sing "God Save the King" as "Heil Hitler", and with just as much sincerity and intention of being loyal to one authority as the other.
I have mentioned this incident before, but I want to do it from a different angle. A man who held quite a good position as a doctor in Pearl Harbor had a summer home close to where I lived, and he employed a Japanese couple whom the family regarded as thoroughly reliable people. I am perfectly certain that if they had been asked six months before the war whether these Japs were loyal, these white people would have said, "Certainly. We have known them for twenty years. They could not be anything but loyal; they have been so' faithful to us." But came the day of Pearl Harbor, and a United States detachment came along and took the Jap man out and shot him. There was ample proof that he had been a traitor all the time. He had obtained plans of Pearl Harbor, and also in his portmanteau they found charts of the ports and waterways in the district of British Columbia where they lived. The Jap woman expressed regret to the family; she said, "You have been just like a father and mother to us, but we had to do it because we serve the emperor." Yes; they had been loyal to United States institutions, but when they came within the orbit of a greater loyalty, that to their country of origin, why, then it was quite a different story.
It reminds me of a story, or rather of a tradition. In Scotland it was the habit of the kings to go around and listen to the grievances of their subjects. Any criminal had the right to claim a hearing from his king. The monarch visited what we would' now call a penitentiary, and all the prisoners wanted to be interviewed. They all said that they had been treated horribly. They had been "railroaded" to prison; yet all of them were as innocent as a yoke of oxen, and if the king would only let them go it would be lovely. But one man remained silent. The king asked, "What is
the trouble with you? What injustice do you complain of?" The man answered, "My lord, I have not had any injustice; I stole a horse and I am punished for it." The king said,
What! you stole a horse! You are a regular villain;" and he turned to the gaoler and said, "I will deal with the cases of these innocent people the next time I come around, which will be about five years from now, but I direct you to throw out this wretched criminal, who stole a horse and who admits he stole a horse. I will not have these innocent men polluted by a blackguard like that. Throw out the man who says he stole a horse".
So it is with the Japanese. Put them in court and ask them if they will be loyal; why, they will be loyal to anything you could mention-for the time being.
The Prime Minister says that we must in some respects follow the policies of the United States. I would accept that counsel with a great deal of caution. Their problems, though in some sense analogous, are not identical. For one thing, the proportion of Japanese in Canada is far greater than in the United States, although in numbers there are many thousands more in the United States. At any rate we are running our own affairs and we are not obliged to follow anybody else's policy.
I believe the Prime Minister's second basic policy, to report only those convicted of disloyalty, is untenable, because ever since they have seen that the white man is holding his own they have been careful to avoid sabotage. It will not do to issue certificates to people as being loyal because they will sing "God Save the King." Oh, but, we are told, this is absurd; you will have to get some evidence; you cannot indict a whole nation. You cannot ask a man to prove his loyalty. A Jap can get some person who has dealt with him for twenty years, to say, "I know Homatka; he is all right; he has bought groceries from me," and unless you can get convincing evidence that he ought to be in the penitentiary, he is turned loose with a certificate that he is, so to speak, a white man.
A few weeks ago I saw in a Vancouver paper that one of the officials, an inspector who was connected with the job of taking care of the removal of the Japanese-I have not the cutting here, but I can speak from memory -gave testimony that the third generation of the Japs were the worst to handle, because they were better educated and knew what their so-called rights were, but they were just as firmly embedded in the traditions of their forbears as were the first generation. This man rather favoured the Japs; he said that
Supply-External Affairs

they had not done any sabotage; but he did say" that the third generation was worse than the previous ones.
The Prime Minister also suggested that, even if it were found that a Jap was guilty of certain things, it would be very natural for anyone to be stubborn in defence of his own property, which is an easy way of explaining, perhaps, subversive action. I am rather afraid of a commission or a man to whom these duties are committed going out with that point of view. The Prime Minister himself does not handle these things; he is more or less in the hands of his officials.
There was an official appointed, of course, by the government, to handle the situation out there in the matter of removing the Japs. His name was Trueman. Before he left Toronto on his way out he said that he was familiar with the situation and that the whole trouble was caused by mob hysteria on the part of the white man. There is a nice, competent commissioner to decide whether these men are loyal or not. Can he look into a Japs soul? But he knows before he starts that this is all due to the mob hysteria of the white man. That official ought to be fired.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
Well, no, but he ought to be sent to live with his "friends."
There is one thing the Prime Minister said with which I entifely disagree. He warned us of what repercussions might occur affecting our Canadian soldiers or sailors in Japanese hands if the Japs did not like the way we treated the Japanese here. That might well be so, if the proposal was to perpetrate brutalities or injustices or anything of that kind upon these men. But this is a totally different thing. I have had considerable experience in dealing with native races, both with them and where they live, in all parts of the world, and I know from experience that the best way to treat them is with strict justice. If you give the native more than justice, the native mind is such that he thinks you are afraid of him; he fancies he can take liberties with you. But if you deal out to him even-handed justice; if he knows that when he does wrong he will be punished, then he will be a much better man, and he will not only respect you but realize that it pays him to play the game. I am very sure, on this point, that our men in Japan will not suffer because we treat the Japanese here justly. If we were to treat them unjustly, the consequences would certainly be different. In any event, what we propose is part of the peace terms, and it will then be too late to do anything very much. People who know the situation will endorse

what I say, that the way to deal with a native is not to pamper him and show that you are afraid of him, but be just, by all means. What keeps the population of India, with its teeming millions, under the control of a handful of men, some of them no more than lads just out of Eton? The answer is, the "face" of the white man. They have great regard for "face" in the orient. You must keep face with them and live up to your traditions, and you must be fair. But once you begin to weaken or give any hint of being afraid, that moment you have lost your power.
The Prime Minister's third line of policy was to stop immigration from Japan. I welcome that most sincerely. He knows how urgent I have been on that point during the last twenty-three years. There seemed, however, to be some qualifying phrase in what he said in this regard; he said something to the effect that it was for a time at least, that it was subject to revision, or something of that sort. He also used a phrase which I did not like when he said something to the effect that the whole policy, of course, would always be subject to circumstances which might arise. Well, that rather undermines the entire force of what he said in this connection; it undermines the full force that we might otherwise attach to the declaration of policy which he gave to the committee this morning. However, when we see Hansard to-morrow morning we shall know then exactly what the Prime Minister said and we shall then be in a position to see the full force of his statement. I appreciate fully the attitude he takes against further oriental immigration, but I am afraid he is leaving too many loopholes in the other branches of his policy to have it very effective.
He says that he will spread them all over Canada. I suggest that if you have cancer in your little finger you are not going to do your body any good if you do anything that will result in spreading that disease throughout your system. Similarly, if you start little centres of shintoism with its evils, such as the Japanese devotion to their emperor, all over Canada, where will you end? And where are these people to be sent? We in British Columbia do not want them and we may take the perfectly selfish attitude and say, "It is all right so far as we are concerned if you send them to other provinces; they will not bother us any longer." But that is not fair, because we know these people and others do not. I do not see how it can be done because every province into which they have penetrated has received a pledge that they will be removed whenever the province so asks. They hold a pledge from the dominion government that these people will be taken away

Supply-External Affairs
whenever those provinces ask that this be done. Where then will they go? I read this afternoon that there will be a request that they be taken away from Alberta. Well, they cannot be taken back to British Columbia. As I say, we do not want them, and we have the Prime Minister's promise that they will not be sent there. Will they be sent to Ontario? Oh, no; Ontario does not want them. Well, where are they to go? We shall certainly hold him to his pledge to keep them out of British Columbia, but at the same time we do not wish them on others. That would be like the mayor of the small town, when it was reported that a case of smallpox had come to town, meaning expenses of isolating those who were affected and cost of nurses and guards and all the rest of it; he had them put on a train going out of town just to keep things quiet and to shift them to some other place. That was all right for him and for the people of his town, but we do not want to play a trick like that on our neighbours so far as these Japanese are concerned.
Some philosopher or statesman, or whatever he was, once said that under a democracy the people eventually get the kind of legislation they want. I hope that is indeed true. I assure the government that we in British Columbia certainly want the elimination of the Japanese population, and now is the time to get rid of them. The chance will never come again. The Prime Minister told us that they will not come back to British Columbia and we stand by that; his word has been given. But, I repeat, we do not want to be selfish. On one occasion the Doukhobors were annoyed by those little animals known as gophers; and since they did not believe in taking life they caught the gophers on their place, put them in a box or something of that sort, took them a few miles down the road to the property of someone who was not a Doukhobor and turned them loose. Well, if we are beset by pests of any sort we do not want to turn them loose on other people. We may say, "God help you, but it is all right for us; we have nothing to worry about- now." But that, I repeat, is not the proper attitude to take.
After all, many of us came from the east where we have friends and relations and we do not want the people in this part of the country to go through the experience we went through. I do not think it will be possible to settle the Japanese elsewhere for the reasons I have given. That is the first point I wish to make. Secondly, I do not think it will be possible to test their loyalty individually, because that is something you cannot prove. You can judge them as a nation on their record. You cannot
prove what is in a man's mind or soul or what he will do under any given circumstances.
The third point is with reference to the stopping of immigration, and that is one thing for which we can hold up both hands. I heartily congratulate the Prime Minister on that. But that is not enough. When our soldiers come back, with the recollection of the atrocities which their comrades have suffered, it will cause a very great deal of hard feeling in British Columbia at least, and for the sake of the Japanese themselves it would be better for them if they went back to their own country. With the knowledge and education which they have acquired here they could do well and elevate their own people and be prosperous in their own way.
I foresee trouble. I am not one of those who say, "Wait until the soldiers come back and they will use their bayonets." Not at all; I shall support law then as now. But it will be a very unpleasant situation and nothing but trouble will arise, so that for the Jap's own sake they should be taken away. I am speaking for those whom I know and whose welfare I have at heart; I have no axe to grind or votes to get. But it would be a great thing for Canada in the future if the government took this opportunity, which will never come again.
By the way, I did not mention one item when the Prime Minister said we would have to guide ourselves in some respects by the policy of the United States. I hold in my hand a copy of a bill which has been introduced into the house of representatives, being an act for the deportation of Japanese aliens. It will be seen that they are paying some attention to this matter in that country. The bill was introduced on May 9, 1944, and referred to the committee on immigration and naturalization, and the man who introduced it writes to tell me that he has good hopes of its passing. He ought to know; I do not know. However, it shows that there is feeling there too, and I suggest that it might be well for us to give them the lead instead of waiting for them to show us the way. At any rate, let us manage our own affairs. British Columbia is solidly against the presence of the Japanese now or in the future. A great many have been moved away, but there is no way of keeping them out unless you deport them. Does Nova Scotia want them? I do not think so. Does Prince Edward Island want them forced on that province, or can they be forced on the people there? I do not know the answer to that, but I hope the Prime Minister's actions will be more decisive than the
Supply-External Affairs

manner in which he pronounced his policy, because there was rather too much qualification in what he said. However, we shall see tomorrow what he actually said, and in the meantime I want to make it clear beyond the shadow of a doubt that what British Columbia wishes is to get rid of the Japs, dead or alive.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
Now that my hon. friend is speaking on this question, I think this is an opportune moment to clear up exactly what I meant by stating that there should be consideration, in any policies we may have, of the policies of the United States. These are the exact words I used:
Moreover, we shall attempt in so far as it seems desirable to maintain a policy that can in a sense be considered as part of a continental policy in handling the Japanese problem. The situation in the United States is in all essentials the same as our own-
I believe I interrupted there and said, in most essentials.
-and to the extent which seems desirable we shall endeavour to ensure that our policy takes account of the policies which are being applied south of the border. There is no need for an identity of policy, but I believe there is merit in maintaining a substantial consistency of treatment in the two countries.
I stand by every word of that, because I feel that in relations with the orient this country cannot afford to do anything other than carefully to study the implications of policies in the United States towards the orient. Sooner or later their policies in relation to ours are going to affect, for better and for worse, the relations between our part of this continent and the orient, and' the United States and the orient. What I have' in mind is this: We have all in international affairs to take a long range view. I, for one, will say that I believe it will not be long after the war is over before the business community of this country, the manufacturers of this country and the producers of this country, will be anxious to secure all the markets that they can possibly get, and the markets in the orient will be among the markets that they will be seeking. I think that very few of them will hesitate to make sales in some parts of the Japanese empire, or what may be left of it, if there is possibility of securing a market. One thing I am perfectly sure of is that the Americans are not going to hesitate to seek to get into all the markets of the orient and to establish themselves firmly there. I believe a government that did not recognize that it was most important to see that we are, at least, as fair and reasonable in our treatment of the nationals of an enemy

country as the very powerful country to the south may be, would not be taking the view that was in the national interest of Canada.
That is what I mean by saying that I feel that when the day comes that another effort will be made to bind up the wounds of the nations of the world, in establishing a new world order, we should be careful to see that meanwhile we have not taken positions which will not be forgotten even by our enemies.

speechtext: I might just say one word to that. I think the time for that logic is past. It is exactly twenty years this month, I think, since the United States passed a law prohibiting entirely the immigration of Japanese into that country. We did have and still have a limited immigration law allowing so many to come in. The same argument was used twenty years ago as is being used to-night that we could not afford to antagonize and lose the chance of getting the trade of the orient because, if we did, the United States would reap at our expense. The United States did take their courage in their hands and cut immigration right off. They said, "No more immigration". I remember using that argument to the Prime Minister in urging that we should do the same thing, that that was our opportunity and that it would make no difference. Time proved the truth of it. We did not get any more business because we allowed a certain amount of immigration. They did not cut off and boycott the United States on account of their action. Trade will go where it is most profitable. You may not like the kind1 of boots or the colour of the hair of the man in the grocery store at the corner, but you will go down there and buy rather than walk ten blocks farther down the street, particularly if the price is right. Trade will always follow that policy. Have we not been relying too much on that trade idea and thereby sacrificing our traditions of the white man and so forth, all for the fear of losing some trade? As I say, trade will go where it is profitable to go. Are we going to win a bloody war and then sit down and lose the peace by fighting for markets here or there? I am grieved indeed to hear the Prime Minister take the attitude he has to-night. I think the time has gone past for that.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
They declared war the moment it favoured them.
Mr. A. W.. ROEBUCK (Trinity): I hone that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) will not expect those who follow him in this debate to take part with him in his discussion of the Japanese question, and certainly not to follow him in some of his logic or attitude. It seems to me that the hon. member loses a little of the influence he might otherwise possess in this house and in the country by too evident a dislike for the subject of his remarks. What he fails to appreciate in the policy of the Prime Minister is that it is guided not by likes and dislikes. We all have a right to like whom we please; kissing goes by favour, but statesmanship is based not upon favour but upon justice. I caught the words from the hon. gentleman himself that the way to treat the oriental is with strict justice. Of course that is right. It is not whether we like the Japanese or dislike them; they are human beings and have certain rights, and those rights must be respected, not for their sakes but for our own sakes.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
Why will not
Toronto take some of them?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
I think Toronto has a
number of Japanese-Canadian citizens. They are not Japanese; they are Canadian citizens of Japanese origin.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext: Your province will not take them.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
Our province has not the power to do otherwise than to take them, and there are a fair number of Japanese Canadians, and some who are not Canadians, in the province of Ontario at the present time. I am not going to defend the Japs, but I find it difficult to imagine that anyone can be so bad as the bete noire of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. It may be so, but it does not make any difference whether they are good, bad or indifferent; our job as legislators, the Prime Minister's job as a statesman guiding the affairs of this country, is to deal out evenhanded justice to everybody. When it comes to immigration into this country we have a right to say that this one shall come in and that that one shall not. The Prime Minister is within his rights when he says that there shall be no more Japanese immigration to this country, but when it comes to dealing with Canadian citizens born in this country or nationalized by us in a solemn way by legal
process, that is another matter. These people are Canadian citizens and have a right to be treated as Canadian citizens.
Mr. O'NEILL: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
Certainly.
Mr. O'NEILL:	Would the hon. member
consider that a person born in this country and holding dual citizenship is a good Canadian citizen?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext: All you have to do is to show that and you can cancel the Canadian nationality of the individual; but you must not punish'the innocent because of the guilty. There may be some who have dual nationality, who owe a loyalty to the emperor of Japan and who attempt to show the same attitude toward the king of England. It cannot be done. If you can show that, there is no difficulty at all in cancelling the British citizenship, and I rather think you could) cancel the nationality of even a person bom here, although I am not so sure about that. My point is that you must not do these things by rumour and assumptions. Even-handed justice requires that we prove such charges against the guilty individual and not in a broad way assume that all must be guilty because of some national characteristics. I have found even in my short experience that usually characteristics attributed to large sections of a community, to groups, to nationalities, to races and so on, have very little foundation in fact. They are usually fictions. For instance, there is a fiction that the French are excitable, the English phlegmatic, and so on; I could mention many more. Usually these are not based upon facts but upon assumptions. The French are often phlegmatic and the English excitable. So that perhaps it may be with those of Japanese origin who have had the benefit of long years of association with Canadians and of Canadian training. It may be that they are not quite so bad as, say, the military clique who guide the destinies of Japan. It is not my intention to-night to argue the question of the Japanese or to constitute myself their champion.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext: You sound like it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: * AUGUST 4, 1944
speechtext:
I am the champion of
democracy, of justice and of right, applied to anybody; and I am not going to imbibe here the violent prejudices of the hon. gentlemen from British Columbia.
