speechtext:
Nevertheless, I trust that the Prime Minister and the Department of External Affairs are giving active consideration to this matter. I know that strong representations have been made to the undersecretary of state for external affairs. I have before me a copy of the memoranda from which the hon. member for Trinity read earlier this evening and which was presented to the under-secretary by the Canadian Palestine committee. I may say that that committee is made up primarily of non-Jewish people. I am very happy to notice from the letterhead that not only are the leader of this group and I, as well as certain other members of the C.C.F. included in the membership of that committee, but there are several other members of this house. I think I should mention them and congratulate them upon their interest in these oppressed people. The ones whose names appear on the letterhead are the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand), the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black), the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) and the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Ross).
The fact that people of this calibre, if I may use that phrase, are associated with this organization is an indication of the feeling that many of us have for the plight of these people. We are in the midst of a war against Hitlerism. The terrors of Hitlerism first fell upon these people, and I think it is safe to say that no human beings in the world have suffered to the extent they have. I suggest that the least we can do is to exert all our efforts to relieve any part of their sufferings it is possible to relieve. There is this immediate situation which has been drawn to the attention of the Prime Minister, and I hope he will give it his further active consideration.

Mr: R. T. GRAHAM (Swift Current): In view of the fact that a number of hon. members will soon be going back home, I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make a statement with regard to the marketing programme that will be in force this year respecting wheat and other grains.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DELIVERY QUOTAS-PROGRESS OF PARTICIPATION PAY'MENTS
speechtext:
It has been suggested by the hon. member and by others that I make a statement on the grain delivery quotas that have just been put into effect in western Canada, and also upon the progress of the participation payments.
Initial quotas have been established on wheat for 1944-45 of five bushels per authorized acre, and on oats and barley of five bushels per seeded acre. No quotas have been placed on rye and flaxseed.
By the time the new crop deliveries commence in volume, the quotas at individual points will be adapted to the available space as in previous years, with due regard to acreage, yield and various market factors.
As was provided last year, producers who have barley suitable for malting purposes, and whose sample is accepted by the buyer, will be given a special permit to ship and deliver one car lot of malting barley over and above their present established quota.
By the close of the crop year on July 31, producers at nearly 90 per cent of the country points in the prairie provinces had been able to deliver the whole of the marketable quantities of their 1943 crops. At some 260 stations, however, the available space did not permit delivery of the balance of the 1943 crops, and at these stations open deliveries of wheat and oats from the old crop have been extended until August 15. Producers who were unable to deliver their barley on past open quotas, owing to lack of space at their delivery point, may apply to the Canadian wheat board for special permission to deliver.
With respect to the 1940-41 crop participation payments, up to the present approximately 225,000 requisitions have been received from
producers, and approximately 170,000 cheques have been issued. The remainder of the 1940 cheques, based on requisitions already received, should be sent out within the next two or three weeks, with the exception, of course, of those requisitions which, for one reason or another, require adjustment. Immediately thereafter it is planned to start writing cheques for the 1941 and 1942 crops, which will go out in one cheque. At the same time, the Canadian wheat board will make arrangements for replacing lost certificates, of which there is a tremendous number.
The magnitude of the whole task will be apparent when it is realized that between duplicate and original certificates, approximately 10,000,000 certificates will have bee" handled.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext:
I should like to address a question to the Minister of Labour. According to an item in the Ottawa Journal this morning some progress has been made toward settling the Montreal tramways strike. I notice the article contains a suggestion that the minister might get some legal interpretation of the point at issue which precipitated the strike both in Halifax and Montreal, namely, the objection of the employers to accepting the union's
Montreal Tramways Strike

proposal for the maintenance of membership clause in their agreement. Is the minister in a position to inform the house whether he has had some legal interpretation of section 20, paragraph 1, of order in council 1003, in order to clarify in the minds of the public the point that caused the strikes, so that we may have some reasonable understanding that there will not be a repetition of this in the future?

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: The points at issue in Halifax and Montreal are entirely different. In Halifax the point at issue is the check-off and maintenance of membership clause. Whoever gave my hon. friend the information, it is incorrect. The company and the organization in Montreal have agreed to the maintenance 'of membership clause and the check-off. That has been agreed to with certain reservations.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: It is a matter of interpretation.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext:
No, it is not. Now that the hon, member has raised the point may I say that it has gone abroad that the Department of Labour has the power to call strikes or stop them. The only people who have the power to call strikes are the organizations themselves; and by the very nature of things that responsibility must rest on the organization involved or the employer as the case may be. But to try to get from under and to blame the Minister of Labour, whether it is the provincial minister or the federal minister is unfair. I have been in this game long enough to know that that is the old technique that has been carried out ever since I have been a trade unionist. Let us be frank and honest about that. I think I know something about leadership. I am convinced of this, that there are good men, able to give the right kind of leadership, and the rank and file will go down the line-that is the trade union language. I have had some connection with the tramways organization in Montreal over the last thirty years. I knew personally the man who organized that union, Magnus Sinclair, the vice-president of the Amalgam^ ated Street Railway Employees of America. At that time he was assisted by "Bill" Mahon, who has been president for over forty years. Until recently they enjoyed what one might describe as reasonably satisfactory relations such as one expects when negotiations are going on between the employer and the employees. I think that should be made clear. I sat in convention with these men. I did not call the strike in Montreal, neither did the
fMr. Gillis.l
Department of Labour. We did everything humanly possible to prevent the third walkout in the last seventeen months. We used all the machinery that had been agreed upon by employers and employees in this country to settle industrial disputes. I think I said this before in the house, that when we drafted the labour relations code, neither the employer nor the employee approved the principle of compulsory arbitration up to the negotiations for the first contract. It was all based on the principle of conciliation.
As I said before, I know it has been hinted that I, as minister of the crown, should have said to this company: "You have to recognize the closed shop." Well, I am not going to do that.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: They are not asking for that.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext:
I know what they are
asking for. I have sat through the negotiations, and when I say that I am moving in a goodly company. To begin with, under the legislation I have not the power to say to the employees or to the employers that they should recognize the closed shop. I remember a speech delivered by President Roosevelt in 1941 when he was addressing a conference of union and steel officials in Washington, I think. I got in touch with Washington yesterday and obtained a short transcript of his remarks, in which he made this observation:
I tell you frankly that the government of the United States will not order, nor will Congress pass legislation ordering, a so-called closed khop.
My hon. friend knows that no government, even if his party should be fortunate enough to form a government and he should be the minister of labour, is going to pass legislation saying to a man that he has to go to a particular church or to belong to a particular fraternal society or to a particular trade union. Once, a government takes that position, in my judgment democracy no longer functions.
So far as the labour relations code is concerned I take this position: provided that the employers and the employees mutually agree on the terms of a contract, my own view is they can do it. It so happens in this case that the company stepped in and said: we believe it is illegal; we believe it is in contradiction of the legislation that was passed recently by the province of Quebec to stop strikes in public utilities. There is nothing new about the position taken by either the lowest or the highest in the land in this regard. There is nothing new in an appeal to the

Labour Conditions
courts in connection with what they think is their just rights. I think that is elementary and fundamental.
The president of the union has notified my department-and I think this will cover the point raised by the hon. member in regard to legal interpretation-that the men have told him that they will not return to work until an agreement has been made that all men employed and all men who are employed in the future shall be required to become members of the union. On the other hand, the company has stated that in its opinion the resentment which would be stirred up amongst the public in Montreal if the company agreed even to the modified agreement which was previously under consideration, would be so great that the management would have to retire. Certainly the company would not be prepared to grant the terms now being asked by the men. I have explained the legal position. I hope I have made myself clear to my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: You had a legal opinion on it?

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: No, I am giving my own opinion; I am not speaking for the courts.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: It is not a legal opinion?

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: I have no intention of pursuing this matter, Mr. Speaker, but we are at a great disadvantage; the minister can debate the issue while we cannot. What I wanted to clarify in my own mind, and for the sake of the people concerned, was the legal position within the meaning of the labour code. It seems to me that if the position of the strikers is legal, then the employers are in an illegal position and should be handled accordingly. Somebody is in an illegal position.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: Is my hon. friend in favour of the closed shop?

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: As you understand it, no; as I understand it, yes.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: Then how do you understand it?

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: I do understand it, and you do not; that is the trouble.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: It is not as simple as my hon. friend states; I want to be clear on that point. He is going a long way when he says one party is in an illegal position. At the moment I am not discussing the merits of the matter.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: They cannot both be right within the meaning of the code.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN SETTLEMENT OF MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE
speechtext: Then let us get it clear in this way. In Halifax they had a board of conciliation, and the employers turned1 down the report of that board. In Montreal they had a board of conciliation and the employees turned down the report of the board, which was quite within their rights under the code.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That is perfectly correct. The bill which this resolution seeks authority to introduce is a long and complicated one. It therefore seems desirable for me to explain at some length the provisions of its various parts at this time. Consequently, I propose to make a speech on the resolution which perhaps ordinarily I would make on moving second

Housing
reading of the bill. I think this procedure will make it possible for hon. members to get a clearer understanding of the various provisions of the bill and to be in a better position to discuss these provisions when we go on with the second reading. I can assure hon. members I shall limit myself to exposition of the provisions of the bill and the principles underlying it rather than attempt any extended argument.
I also do not think it necessary to weary the house by giving any historical or analytical background or any elaborate statistical information in regard to the housing problem, what we have done in this field in the past and what is being done in other countries. If there is one thing upon which all parties in this house agree it is on the importance of placing a house building programme and the improvement of housing conditions well up in the forefront of the general programme of reconstruction which we are preparing for the post-war period. Furthermore, hon. members now have at their disposal the very elaborate report on housing and community planning prepared by a subcommittee of the advisory committee on reconstruction. While all hon. members may not agree with all of the recommendations contained in this report, nevertheless they will find it a very convenient compendium of information in regard to housing experience and legislation in Canada, Britain and the United States, the dimensions of the post-war housing problem in its various aspects, the need for and principles underlying community planning, and other pertinent aspects of the housing situation. I shall therefore assume that hon. members have this report as a necessary background for the purposes of this debate and will confine myself to a rather simple outline of the proposals which we are making in the bill which will be brought down when this resolution has been passed.
The housing programme to be outlined is a programme of general application. It was not thought feasible in this legislation to make special provision for any particular classes in the community, such as members of the forces oi their dependents, ex-members of the forces, or those belonging to any occupational group. As the house knows, Wartime Housing Limited is also carrying on an emergency programme for the provision of houses on a rental basis to dependents of members of the forces in so far as the availability of materials permits and needs in particular localities develop.
I am not in a position to state what specific provision will be made otherwise than under this bill for those now in the forces as and when they are demobilized. This, however, is
a separate question, which will, to the extent that it is not covered by this legislation, be dealt with separately. In saying this, I wish to make it clear that apart from the wartime housing programme I have mentioned, I am not intimating that there will be a separate and additional housing programme. I am merely indicating that if and when a statement is made in reference to the special problems of demobilized members of the forces, it will be made by another minister.
The present bill will contain six parts. Part I will deal with the construction of houses to be owned by prospective home-owners; part II with the construction of houses for rental purposes, and also with slum clearance; part III with rural housing or houses on farms and in small and remote communities; part IV with loans for the repair, alteration, modernization or extension of existing homes; part V with housing research and community planning; and part VI with a number of general provisions.
Let me deal first with the provisions of the bill regarding the construction of houses for home ownership. In this part of the bill we follow in general the pattern established by part I of the National Housing Act, 1938, but with some important additions and modifications. The way in which this part works is as follows: The prospective home-owner who has a lot on which he wishes to build a house or a builder who wishes to build a house for sale to a prospective home-owner goes to an approved lending institution with the plans and specifications for the house, details of the location of the lot and other pertinent information. The lending institution ascertains the cost and appraises the value of the land, checks the plans and specifications of the building in order to see that they conform with the minimum standards laid down by the government, checks the estimated cost of production, the credit-worthiness of the borrower, et cetera; and after all this work has been done, if it is willing to participate in a loan to facilitate the construction of the house, submits the application with the supporting material to the national housing administration for its examination and approval. We may then approve the plans and the application as they stand or require certain necessary modifications. If we approve the application, a loan is made jointly by the lending institution and the Minister of Finance with the first m'ortgage or hypothec running jointly to the two of us. The proceeds of the loan are then paid out in instalments and provision is made for inspection of the house at various stages during its construction in order to assure that the builder or contractor completes the
Housing

construction of the house in accordance with the plans and specifications which .have been approved. The loan is repaid by monthly instalments which cover not only payment of interest and amortization of principal but also the annual taxes on the property and in case of any loss incurred in respect of the loan, the loss is shared in agreed proportions between the minister and the lending institution.
Hon. members will note that this procedure requires that the minister enter into contracts with approved lending institutions and that these contracts must contain the various provisions governing the making of loans, supervision of construction, the terms of the mortgage and the repayment of the loan, the steps to be taken in case of default, the sharing of losses, and other matters specified in the bill. In the new bill we are extending the definition of a lending institution that may be approved by the governor in council for the purpose of making loans under the legislation, to include not only insurance, loan and trust companies but also trustees of trust funds, building societies, credit unions and other cooperative credit societies authorized to lend money on the security of real or immovable property. We are also defining "cost of construction" in a somewhat broader sense than previously in order to take into account a fair and reasonable value for work done by the owner of the house himself, and also to provide for a fair appraisal of land, where the land has been acquired by gift or demise, and to include development cost and carrying charges where the land has been held by a builder for a considerable time.
The house will also be interested in the terms upon which loans may be made. The new contracts will provide that a joint loan shall not be less than 50 per cent of the lending value of a house-incidentally, lending value is either the estimated cost or the appraised value of a property, whichever is the lesser-and it Shall not be more than 95 per cent of the first $2,000 of lending value, plus 85 per cent of the amount by which the lending value exceeds $2,000 but does not exceed $4,000, plus 70 per cent of the amount, if any, by which the lending value exceeds $4,000. Let me give some illustrations of the way in which this works out: If we are considering a house with a lending value of $2,500, the minimum loan under this formula would be $1,250 and the maximum loan would be 95 per cent of the $2,000 plus 85 per cent of $500, or a total of 93 per cent. On a house with a lending value of $3,000, we could make a loan of $2,750 or 91$ per cent; on one with

a lending value of $4,000 we could make a maximum loan of 90 per cent; on one with a lending valu<j of $5,000 we could make a maximum loan of 86 per cent; and on houses with a lending value in excess of $5,000 the maximum percentage of loan would gradually scale down. I think this formula is as sound a one as can be devised. It is true that representations have been made by the building industry and others that we should increase the value of a house on which we could make 90 per cent loans to $5,000 or $6,000 or even a higher amount, and the subcommittee on housing recommended 90 per cent loans for houses with a lending value up to $6,000. The adoption of that recommendation would mean that a prospective home-owner would only require an equity of $600 to obtain a $6,000 house, whereas under our formula he would require an equity of $1,000. It does not seem to me sound that an individual who has only been able to save $600 should be encouraged to buy a $6,000 house and assume the obligations of a $5,400 mortgage. Nor do I think that at least in the vast majority of cases would that represent sound lending.
Other essential points relate to the rate of interest and to the period for which the loans will run. As I have already announced to the house, the new contracts will provide for an interest rate to be charged to the borrower of not in excess of 4J per cent. This low rate is made possible by the government advancing its 25 per cent share of the joint loan on a 3 per cent interest basis, the lending institution obtaining a return of 5 per cent on its share of the loan and for the work which it is required to do. Under the Federal Housing Act in the United States, the maximum interest rate allowed on home mortgages is set at 4t per cent but there is also a mortgage insurance premium charge determined by the risk involved and limited to not less than one-half of one per cent or not more than one per cent of the original face value of the mortgage. Under that act also provision is made for the instalment payment of such initial service charges and appraisal and other fees as the federal housing administrator may approve.
Under our new contracts the maximum term of loan will be twenty years in the ordinary case, but if there is sound community planning and adequate zoning restrictions in respect of the area in which the house is to be located, the loan may be made for a term not exceeding thirty years.
Let me illustrate what these new terms mean for a person wishing to build a house with a lending value of $4,000. The down payment

Housing
would be $400, leaving $3,600 to be financed by a joint loan. In the ordinary case this is payable in twenty years, the monthly carrying charges, including principal and interest, being $22.61. If the house is to be built in an area which has been adequately zoned and planned, the loan might be extended for thirty years, in which case the monthly carrying charges would be $18.04.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Does that include taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
No.
In addition, of course, there would be taxes, one-twelfth of which are payable each month along with the instalments of interest and principal.
As to sharing of losses on joint loans made under the provisions of part I of the act, there is a provision that regulations to be made by the governor in council may establish classes or categories of loans based on the ratio of the joint loan to the lending value and on the location of the houses, but the maximum amount of the loss to be borne by His Majesty in respect of any class or category of loan is not to exceed 15 per cent of the aggregate amount of the share of the said lending institution in all joint loans within the class. Hon. members will note that this provision will enable us to establish a number of guarantee pools in order to encourage the making of the type of loan which from our point of view is most desirable. In other words, we can provide a higher pool guarantee for loans on small homes where, the percentage of loan to lending value would be very high, and also a higher guarantee for loans made in smaller or more remote communities or in what the lending institutions might regard as less desirable residential sections of our larger towns and cities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: It is the same guarantee, as I recall it, as was given in connection with the home improvement loans. It is the same percentage, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
It was fifteen per cent. We are proposing under this legislation to make it five per cent for home improvement loans. But the two are not exactly comparable.
Conversely, we could provide for low poo! guarantees in the case of the larger loans and loans made in the best residential areas. Our desire will be to make regulations and adapt these regulations from time to time in such a way as to get loans made which are in the public interest but which might not otherwise be made.
Cooperative housing projects may also be financed under part I of the bill. In such
projects the cooperating tenant-owners normally own the project collectively by the device of either a corporation or a trustee holding title to the project. The loans to be made to such corporation or trustee repr&-seating the tenant-owners will be based on the same general provisions as apply in the case of an ordinary loan to a home-owner except that the shareholder of the corporation or the beneficiary of the trust will have to assume responsibility not only for the monthly instalments of interest, principal and taxes payable in respect of his cooperative apartment but also his pro rata share of additional payments required for operating costs and instalments of interest, principal and taxes where one of the cooperators fails to pay his share.
Perhaps the only other provision of part I of the bill to which I need to call attention at the present time is the section which appropriates the necessary funds for the making of these loans. The bill asks for an appropriation of $100 million in order to make loans under this part and to pay losses in respect of such loans or in respect of loans made under the Dominion Housing Act or the National Housing Act. This, it will be noted, will enable joint loans to be made in the total amount of about $400 million and for a total construction programme exceeding this amount by the amount of the borrowers' equities in respect of the loans less the cost of land. I need not say that this will give a very substantial impetus to employment and business activity in the post-war years.
It may be of interest to hon. members to know that under the dominion and national housing acts up to July 31, 1944, we had made 21,839 joint loans amounting to $87,388,517 in total. These loans provided accommodation for 26,443 families. And so far the net loss incurred by the government under the operation of both these acts has amounted to only $970.
I now come to part II of the bill, which deals with housing for rental purposes. Under this part there are four types of project or activity provided for: first, the financing of ordinary or commercial rental housing projects; secondly, the financing of low-cost rental housing through limited-dividend housing corporations; thirdly, the authorization of certain life insurance and other designated lending institutions to invest a limited proportion of their funds in low-cost or moderate-cost rental housing projects and to hold and manage such projects; and fourthly, the assistance we are proposing to give to promote the clearance of slum or blighted or substandard areas.
Housing

In the first type of case loans will be made jointly with approved lending institutions, in somewhat the same way as under part I * of the bill, to persons who desire to construct either single family dwellings or a group of single family dwellings or a multiple family housing project to be rented to tenants on a commercial or economic basis. The ordinary apartment house would come within this category. As in the case of part I loans, the government will advance 25 per cent of the amount of the loan and the interest charged to the borrower will be 4| per cent. But the maximum amount of loan is not to exceed 80 per cent of the lending value of the house or project and we may take a chattel mortgage or assignment of rents or other form of additional security in order to protect adequately the interest of the crown in the loan. Such loan will in the ordinary case not exceed twenty years but may run up to twenty-five years where there are sound community planning and adequate zoning restrictions. The usual provisions for assuring sound plans and specifications, for adequate supervision during the construction process, and the sharing of losses will also apply.
The second type of project provided for is the low-rental housing project intended to be rented to persons of low income, perhaps at rates less than economic rentals for the housing accommodation provided. These are to be developed, constructed and managed by limited dividend housing corporations. Such projects would be similar in nature to the so-called Montreal housing project whjch I described to the house some weeks ago. The limited dividend housing corporation must provide equity capital equal to at least 10 per cent of the cost of the project, limit its dividends to not more than 5 per cent, agree to provide competent and independent management, keep books and accounts in a form to be prescribed by regulation, permit inspection of the project at any time and comply with other appropriate conditions laid down in the act or in the regulations made thereunder. The loan made by the dominion will not exceed 90 per cent of the cost of the project and will bear interest at the rate of 3 per cent per annum. It may run for a period not exceeding the useful life of the project to be fixed by the minister and in any case not exceeding 50 years. It must be secured by a first mortgage and hypothec upon the project given in favour of the crown. Such supervision of the rentals to be charged by the corporation may be provided for as will assure the maintenance of the low-rental character of the project. In addition, any province, municipality, social agency, trust or lMr. TMey.t
person may make contributions to a rent-reduction fund to be held by the limited dividend' housing corporation and to be used only for the purpose of reducing the rentals that would otherwise have to be charged. Need for the project by reason of shortage, overcrowding, congestion or the sub-standard character of existing housing accommodation in the municipality or the metropolitan area in which the project is to be located must be established and the area must be adequately planned and zoned. Finally, the contract between the minister and the corporation will provide for the disposition of surplus earnings and will require that- the project shall not be sold or otherwise disposed of without the approval of the minister. If the project is sold with the minister's approval, any surplus from the proceeds of sale over and above the limited dividends and1 the return of the original investment shall be paid to such person or expended in such manner as is provided in the contract or as the minister may direct. In other words the intention is that no capital profits shall accrue to the shareholders of any limited dividend housing project.
The third type of project under the new bill involves one of the most interesting and most radical departures from previous practice in this field. It provides that .notwithstanding any restriction on its power to lend or invest money contained in any other statute or law, any life insurance company subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, may subject to certain specified conditions invest its funds to an aggregate amount not exceeding 5 per cent of its total admitted assets in Canada in the purchase of land and the construction thereon of a low-cost or moderate-cost rental housing project, including such buildings or such accommodation for retail stores, shops, offices and other community services, but not including hotels, as the company may deem proper and suitable for the convenience of the tenants of such rental housing project, and thereafter may hold, maintain, repair, alter, demolish, reconstruct, manage, collect or receive income from, sell or convey, in whole or in part, land so acquired and the improvements thereon.
Certain conditions must be complied with before the minister gives his approval to the investment. The project must be in accordance with or in harmony with an official community plan satisfactory to the. minister. It must be designed to provide housing accommodation for families of low or moderate income. Before any project is proceeded with the company must submit an, application to the minister for his approval accompanied by

Housing
maps, plans and specifications, estimates of cost, estimates of probable income and such other information as may be required. These safeguards are for the protection of policy holders as well as to promote desirable housing developments. In order to give a reasonable degree of security to the investment, which is something new for Canadian insurance companies, the bill will also provide for a limited guarantee by the government. If the company agrees with the minister to keep satisfactory records open to his inspection at any time, to establish a reserve consisting of all net earnings in any year in excess of 6 per cent, and to repay out of this reserve any advances made by the minister under a guarantee, the minister may guarantee to the company, for as long as it retains ownership of the whole of the project, a net return in any year after the completion of the project of 24j per cent per year of the cost of the project for a period not exceeding the estimated useful life of the project and in any case not exceeding 50 years.
Two or more life insurance companies will be allowed to join in the development, ownership' and management of a rental housing project of this type and the governor in council also may designate other approved lending institutions, such as trust and loan corporations under the jurisdiction of parliament as eligible to invest not more than 5 per cent of their assets in Canada in projects of this type.
I think it will be quite obvious to honourable members why we are making provision for this type of project in our new housing legislation. One of the great weaknesses in the house-building industry in Canada is the absence of a substantial number of companies with competent management and with sufficiently large resources to acquire large blocks of land, particularly in our larger cities where land values are high, and to develop such areas in a comprehensive way providing all necessary community and incidental services. As some hon. members will be aware, several of the states of the United States have allowed life insurance companies to embark upon this type of project and a number of such companies have developed several very large and very attractive projects. I trust that we will see similar developments undertaken by a number of our Canadian companies.
The fourth feature of part II of the new bill is intended to assist municipalities in clearing slums. This will be done by empowering the government to make direct grants for that purpose. We believe this is the most direct and effective way of getting the job
done. Conditions will be attached to the grant, but these will be of a character which are obviously necessary in order to assure the development of the area along sound lines. First, the land acquired and cleared must be developed under a master plan approved by the local municipality. Second1, the land must be sold either to a limited dividend housing corporation or life insurance company, which has agreed to build a low-cost or moderate-cost rental housing project thereon. Third, the acquisition and clearing of the land must be approved by the provincial government concerned. It will be apparent that in most cases, particularly in the larger urban municipalities where slum areas are acquired and the buildings presently upon them demolished, the cost of the land so acquired and cleared will usually be too high to provide the site for a low rental or moderate rental housing project. Our problem therefore was to find some way of dealing with this excess acquisition cost, of getting the cost of the land down to the level where it would make feasible a low cost or moderate cost rental housing project. The bill will therefore give authority to the minister with the approval of the governor in council to make a grant to the municipality concerned of 50 per cent of the amount of what I have called the excess acquisition cost, the remainder of this excess acquisition cost to be borne by the municipality or jointly by the municipality and the government of the province concerned.
I have described rather briefly the essential provisions of part II of the act. The appropriation section of this part will authorize loans up to $50 million; that is to say, advances of the government's share of joint loans made through approved lending institutions for the construction of commercial renting projects and the government's 90 per cent loans to limited dividend housing corporations. It will also provide for grants for slum clearance purposes under the conditions I have described not in excess of $20 million. It is rather difficult to estimate the total amount of house *construction which will thereby be made possible; it depends on the extent to which the $50 million is divided between loans to limited dividend housing corporations and loans made through lending institutions for commercial renting projects because in the latter case the total loan, including the lending institution's share, will be four times the amount of the government's advance. It is also difficult to estimate to what extent low" cost or moderate cost rental housing projects will be proceeded with by life insurance companies and other designated approved lending institutions under the special provisions I have
Housing

described. If the life insurance companies were to take full advantage of the full limit of the investing powers now made possible for them, they could embark upon projects costing something in excess of $150 million.
Part III of the bill deals with rural housing. This is one of the most difficult phases of the housing problem in Canada and we have made special efforts to deal with it in a practical manner. One hindrance in the past has been the 'extra expense involved in making loans to farmers and to other persons in small and remote communities, including fishing and lumbering villages. This we propose to meet by authorizing the minister to make payments to the lending institutions of up to $20 in respect of each loan, together with other reasonable allowances for necessary travelling expenses incurred by the employees or agents of the lending company.
As I have already said, loans to urban house builders will be repayable in monthly instalments. Quite clearly such terms are not suitable to all farmers. It will therefore be provided that farmers may repay housing loans in such a way that the periodic instalments of interest and taxes will accord as nearly as may be practicable with the probable receipts of income by them from their farming operations.
Another very practical difficulty in the field of rural housing arises from the fact that a substantial percentage of Canadian farms are already mortgaged. To meet this situation the bill will provide for consolidation with an existing mortgage loan of a new loan made for the construction of a house upon a farm. Such consolidation, of course, assumes that the lending institution which is to make the loan for the construction of the house will also be the same institution that holds the existing mortgage on the farm. If this is not the case, presumably the only way in which the problem can be met is for the lending institution to acquire the existing mortgage. The government's advance in respect of such consolidated loan will, of course, be limited to 25 per cent of the amount of the loan necessary to build the house and the share of loss assumed by the government will also be the appropriate portion of the new loan made for the construction of the house.
The funds required for making housing loans to farmers and persons in small or remote communities will come out of the $100 million appropriation under part I of the act. In this connection, however, I should point out that in the farm improvement loans bill there is provision for loans to be made by the chartered banks to finance the construction of houses by farmers, including the construction of cottages for farm labourers. Such loans are limited in amount to $3,000 and no mortgage will be
[Mr. Dsley.l
taken except in the case where the loan exceeds $2,000 and runs for a period longer than five years. Hon. members will remember that the farm improvement loans bill provides an appropriation of $250 million for all kinds of purposes for which loans are authorized under that legislation. I suspect that because of the greater convenience of the local bank, a great many of the small loans made for farm housing, particularly for farm cottages, will be provided under the provisions of the farm improvement loans bill.

Yes, but the interest rate is moderate in both cases.
I have dealt so far with financing the construction of rural houses. This is an essential part of a sound rural housing programme but it is by no means all that is required. Already, under the farm improvement loans bill, provision has been made to facilitate the extension of rural electrification and for the purchase on favourable terms of the electric stoves, refrigerators, washing machines and other equipment that contribute so much to the amenities of life on the farm. In part III of the housing legislation, which I am now discussing, we are taking another step forward by authorizing the minister to enter into contracts with manufacturers for the experimental production of plumbing and heating equipment and other component parts of houses. Actually we have already encouraged building equipment manufacturers to devote extensive study to the development of standardized units of equipment which would have high efficiency and low cost. This clause will enable us to push this type of encouragement to a much greater extent. More important still, the bill will authorize the minister, with the approval of the governor in council, to guarantee or underwrite the sale of a specified number of standardized units of equipment

Housing
or component parts manufactured for installation or use in farm or rural houses. The significance of this provision will, I think, be immediately apparent to hon. members. Let us say that as a result of extensive research an equipment manufacturer designed a bathroom unit or a heating unit specially suitable for rural homes. The manufacturer would not know whether he could sell a dozen, or a hundred, or a thousand, or ten thousand of these units to farmers, and the natural tendency would undoubtedly be to produce them on a small scale which would mean a high cost per unit. Under this new provision we could guarantee that the manufacturer would sell, say five thousand or even a larger number of the units in question and thus assure that the particular equipment would be made available to farmers at the lowest possible cost. I believe that this provision should make an important contribution to improved rural housing and we are asking parliament for authority to enter into contracts of the character I have mentioned, subject to the limitation that the aggregate amount of the contract or contingent liabilities assumed by the crown in respect of such contracts does not at any time exceed $5 million.
Part IV of the act deals with home improvement and home extension loans and represents a reenactment with some improvements and extensions of the old Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act which was passed in 1937, and which proved so successful. Under that act 125,720 loans were made for the repair and modernization of existing urban and rural homes and the total amount of such loans was $49,959,055. Certain losses were incurred in respect of 1,231 loans, and claims have been paid to the lending institutions in the amount of $447,511, of which amount $44,763 has been recovered by the Department. The net loss represents a percentage of -806 per cent. Up to March 31, 1944, 98-4 per cent of the principal amount of the loans made had been repaid, leaving $811,652 outstanding, or 1-6 per cent. This represented the government's contingent liability in respect of the loans as at that date. If not another dollar were repaid in respect of these loans, our total losses, it will be noted, would be less than 2^ per cent.
Loans under this part are made chiefly through the chartered banks which have offices all over the country, but certain instalment credit agencies may also be approved as lending institutions for this purpose. In the case of what we call a home improvement loan, the principal amount of the loan must not exceed $2,000 in the case of a single family dwelling, or $2,000 for the first family housing unit and
an additional $1,000 for every other family housing unit in the case of a multiple family dwelling. In the case of what we call a home extension loan, the principal amount of the loan must not exceed $3,000 for the first family housing unit which is to be added to the existing house and $1,000 for each further addition. Loans under this part are for either three or five years.
Under the old home improvement loans bill the rate of interest to be charged was expressed as a discount of 3i per cent for a one-year loan repayable in equal monthly instalments, which worked out at an effective rate of 6-02 per cent. In the new bill we are providing for a rate of interest not to exceed 5 per cent per year simple interest, and no fee, service charge, insurance premium, or other charge of any kind can be levied as long as the borrower is not in default.
The total amount of loans which may be guaranteed is not to exceed $100 million but the operation of this part of the act may be terminated at any time by the minister with the approval of the governor in council. In view of the highly successful experience under the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee. Act, the guarantee is for an amount not in excess of 5 per cent of the aggregate principal amount of the guaranteed loans made by any bank or approved instalment credit agency. Under the old act this pool guarantee was 15 per cent.
In this connection it must be remembered that the old act covered repairs, alterations and additions to both urban and rural homes. Such repairs, alterations and additions to rural homes will in future be financed by loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act where the pool guarantee amounts to ten per cent of the total loans made by any bank, and the total amount of the loans to be guaranteed, as I have already indicated, is $250 million.
I come now to the two concluding parts of this long and comprehensive piece of legislation. Part VI contains the usual provisions relating to staff, regulations, reports and proclamation. The only provision to which I would draw your attention is that relating to insurance. The intention under this clause is to enable a borrower to take out reducing term insurance to pay the outstanding amount of his loan in the event of his death before the loan is fully repaid. In certain cases the purchase of this type of insurance may be made mandatory.
To return to part V, this relates to housing research and community planning. If I had time I would like to deal at length with these provisions as they may prove to be of the very greatest importance during the years that
Housing

Housing

surely we are dealing with a fixed asset of great importance to the life of Canada, and I would hope that we might be able, in connection with this most socially important fixed asset, the homes of our Canadian people, to match the amount of money that we have been able to put into fixed assets for the very necessary task of prosecuting the war. I hope that the minister will indicate at some stage of this debate, perhaps when we go into committee of the whole on the resolution a little later, whether this amount of money is one appropriation of $275,000,000 or whether we might expect it to be regarded by the government as the first of several annual appropriations. If it were the latter over a period of, say, ten years, it could be used to make a real contribution to the solution of Canada's housing problem; but if this is the total amount of money which the government feels should be appropriated out of public funds for solving Canada's post-war housing problem, I fear we shall fall far short of meeting our basic needs in this field.
If I took down correctly the figures which the minister gave when he was speaking just now I believe he said that up until the end of July of this year the total amount of loans advanced by the government under the Dominion Housing Act of 1935 and the National Housing Act of 1938 was $87,388,578, and that these loans provided housing accommodation for 26,443 families. I take it he meant that that many housing units were built, whether they were individual houses, suites or other types of accommodation. If the lending by the government of a little over $87,000,000 during the lifetime of these acts has made available only 26,000 dwelling units, it is to be assumed that ihe lending of $100,000,000 for the building of houses for prospective owners will not provide much more than 30,000 housing units. Further, even if one were to take the entire amount of money set out in this resolution, which is less than 8300,000,000', and to treat it generously on the proportion of the figures already given, the highest total number of housing units that one could foresee would be about 90,000. That is too generous an estimate, because not all of this money is availabale for new homes. It is a rough calculation, obviously made on short notice, because I simply took the figures the minister gave a short while ago. But I should like to set that calculation of 90,000 or even
100,000	prospective housing units Which may be realized under this legislation against the housing needs of Canada as set out in the Curtis report, published by the advisory committee on reconstruction.

On page 151 of this report, following a discussion of the matter in considerable detail, the committee gives a table showing the needs of a Canadian housing programme for the first ten years of such an effort. It is given in detail, but I shall refer only to the totals. The committee states that in the first ten years of an effective housing programme' we should provide for 606,000 urban, non-farm homes and in addition should provide for 94,000 homes in farm areas, or a total of 700,000. I suggest that the house take note of the wide gap between the ninety to one hundred thousand homes that may be built under the legislation to which the minister has referred, according to the calculation I have made, and the seven hundred thousand indicated in the Curtis report as Canada's need for new homes. The table on page 151 goes a bit further and gives the unofficial British programme for housing for the same ten-year period as well as the official New Zealand programme. I need not give the figures set out for those countries, because the important feature is in the next two columns, where the committee has apportioned the British and New Zealand figures to our Canadian situation. The committee says that on the basis of that apportionment, to equal the British programme we in Canada should be producing 921,000 homes, or to equal the New Zealand programme we should be producing 756,000 homes in the ten-year period to which I have referred. It may be that when we are in committee, or on second reading, the minister will be able to indicate other measures that will supplement what is before us at the present time. I hope he will; but I am pointing out that what is before us now-

The whole question of the interest rates on houses built under these acts is to us a matter of concern. I still have the hope that the

government may find it possible to arrange for a lower rate of interest, even if they consider it necessary to retain some of the other protective measures to which the minister referred, so that the legislation might better meet the needs of our people. I feel very keenly that further consideration should be given this whole question of interest rates. In that connection, and apropos of the other reference made by the minister, I should like to give a quotation from the ministry of housing in New Zealand. The minister referred to the desire on the part of the government to keep to a minimum the loss to the treasury as far as this whole project is concerned. Our minds run in different channels on that point. I cannot feel that the country as a whole is losing if we build homes. Despite the fact that it was done for war purposes we like to think that there is increased wealth in the country because of the fixed assets we have created as a result of our war expenditures. I feel in the same way that when we spend money on the building of homes for the Canadian people we are gaining, not losing. In this connection, after the labour government of New Zealand [DOT] opened its housing account with the reserve bank of New Zealand on July 1, 1936, just after it was first elected, the housing ministry of that country issued a statement in which it said, in part:
We are out to create assets against this reserve bank credit, and to the extent that we succeed in giving the nation sound assets, so we will have demonstrated the sanity of socialist finance.

I commend our line of thought to the min. ister and suggest that he consider that the proposition upon which he is embarking now, namely the investing of public funds in the building of homes for the Canadian people, will not in the real sense involve any loss at all but will mean an increase in real wealth which in turn will contribute to a better life for our people.
Another point to which I should like to refer is the necessity of any housing programme being directed primarily to the needs of people in the lower income brackets. The Curtis committee dealt with this to some considerable extent, pointing out that there are altogether too many people in Canada in these lower income brackets, and the result is that far too many people at the present time are called upon to spend disproportionate amounts of their incomes for rent. We feel, as part of a programme of economic planning, that public funds should be used to relieve that situation. The theory behind that is not strange to the present government. It is very similar to the principle behind family allowances. As a matter of fact that principle is found in part in this housing measure, but it does not begin to go far enough.
, Let me quote from page 110 of the Curtis housing report:
The most striking fact is that average family income (from wages) among one-third of all metropolitan tenants is only a little over $700.
Then there is a reference to table 25. The paragraph continues:
In three cities it is substantially higher than this average, but in six cities actually lower.
And then reading further down:
Desirable minimum income levels have been examined in general terms in the report on social security. For a more or less representative family of five persons the assistance or subsistence minimum for the bare essentials of healthy living requires an annual income of $1,135, assuming urban conditions comparable to those in Toronto.
And later, dealing with tenants in urban communities, the report has this to say:
About 50 per cent of the families living in metropolitan areas throughout the dominion ,pay a disproportionate rent, and in six cities more than half of the families strain their budgets in some degree by paying an excessive proportion for their housing needs.
What I am driving at in these quotations is that a proportion of the money the government appropriates for housing larger than is given by this measure should be for those in the lower income brackets who are doing what this report says, namely straining their budgets and paying disproportionate amounts for rent. The measure before us provides $100,-
Housing

000,000 to assist in the building of homes for prospective home owners. Although providing some help to that group, the measure will not meet the problems of those referred to in the quotations I have read from pages 110 and 120 of the Curtis report.
Of course I realize that behind all this is 'the government's theory that if houses are built, in some way or another the increase in the number of houses, even if they are expensive houses for those who can afford to own them, will result in those who are down at the bottom, in the slum areas, or without housing accommodation at all, benefiting from the increase. It does not work out that way. We should approach the problem more directly, in fact through a public housing authority. A larger proportion of the money should be appropriated by the government directly for slum clearance, and should follow along the lines which, as indicated in the closing portion of his speech, have been turned down by the minister and the government.
I was glad to hear some of the things the minister had to say this morning, but I was very sorry to hear others. For example I was glad to hear that credit unions and cooperative societies are to be included in the list of approved lending institutions. But I was sadly disappointed to learn from the minister's statement that the government had decided not to consider, beyond the one provision he announced, assisting municipalities in connection with housing. I was glad he made that one provision clear, because it certainly was not clear to me from a reading of * the resolution that the 820,000,000 mentioned therein for the aid of municipalities is only for the purpose of enabling municipalities to buy land which is now slum area, but Which is valued high.
I cannot agree with the minister when he takes the position that it is possible to -lend money to limited dividend housing corporations to build low-rent housing projects, confident that arrangements can be made to supervise and take care of them, and yet that on the other hand administrative difficulties are too great to consider doing the same for municipalities. Particularly in western Canada, from where I come, there has been a tremendous growth in the belief and conviction that municipalities and cities should be going directly into the matter of slum clearance and housing projects. In my city there is a keen social conscience in respect of this matter. The same is true of many cities throughout the west, and I am sorry the government has not yet seen fit to provide ways and means of cooperating directly with cities and munici-

palities in connection with slum clearance and the building of houses. I hope that matter . may yet be considered, either by this government or by whatever government succeeds this one.
Another feature of the resolution which gave me considerable annoyance but which I shall not discuss in detail now-because of some of the comments made by the minister which to some extent allayed my fears-is the very small amount provided for rural housing. I shall have to study more closely what the minister said, to see whether my fears are really set aside. It is my understanding he stated that under other legislation housing might be carried out in rural areas. But certainly so far as this measure is concerned, only $5,000,000 for the farming areas of Canada, out of a total of $275,000,000 was about the unkindest cut of all. The Curtis report's recommendation is that the proportion of money spent on farm housing as compared with urban housing should be in about the ratio of one to six. I would point out that $5,000,000 out of $275,000,000 is a proportion of one to fifty-six. That, by itself, is pretty bad.

of the realization that housing is a rural problem as much as it is an urban one. Thus far we have thought of housing in terms of slum clearance in congested areas, but it is equally important that the people on our farms should have better homes to live in.

I hope that what we have here is only the beginning of a housing scheme that will go into the rural' field as well as the urban, and that from this beginning we will make real progress until we are able to provide for the people on our farms proper homes with the amenities and conveniences that farm people think the city people Have, but which many of them are still denied.
I shall not detain the house further at this point except to say that while we welcome this measure even in the dying days of the session and will give it our support, we certainly think that it does not even approach a solution of the pressing problems of those in the lower income brackets who are most in need of housing. We are sorry that it is not a move more in the direction of a public housing authority. We are not satisfied with the method the government is employing, namely, to assist private lending institutions to do the job. I do not say that because we have any particular, grievance against private lending institutions-we can discuss that on another occasion-I say that because we feel that the method adopted will not get the job done. One of the vital necessities in Canada is a broad, imaginative, far-reaching housing programme on the basis of which we will really launch out to rebuild our cities and the rural areas of this country so that our people will have an asset of real worth in homes worthy of the sacrifices that have been borne during these war years. This measure is welcome, but it leaves much to be desired.

Mr. 'Speaker, I wish first of all to commend the minister for the great improvement he has indicated in the present housing act over what was provided in the former one. The other part of his speech which interested me most was that dealing with the provision for low-cost housing projects. This is one of the greatest needs in this country, and if such projects are undertaken they will do more than anything else to relieve the poor people in our cities particularly those with large families. Not only do we have people living in substandard houses in our slum areas, but we have overcrowding of those slum houses. On a number, of occasions I have seen families of four and five living in one room, and I have also seen two families of ten people, living in a single room. It was necessary for these people to go out into the yard for their conveniences. Their water was drawn from a tap outside which was frequently frozen up during the winter.
I cannot see how conditions such as these can do other than increase delinquency and crime with its added cost on all municipalities for the upkeep of police forces and penal institutions. I am not sure whether the minister is sufficiently generous in regard to the interest rates to be charged to those who will borrow money to provide this type of accommodation for our lowest income group. That class of individual is unable to pay an economic rent, and the difference between what he can pay and the economic rent will have to be made up by somebody. I think it would be economical for this government to subsidize either the housing authority or the individual so that these people may live in decent houses at rentals they can afford to pay.

Speaking on this subject in the house last week or a couple of weeks ago I suggested to the government that the interest rate to be charged on loans under this act should be reduced to two per cent or less, and I did so because I knew that the rent to be

Housing
charged is largely determined by the rate of interest paid for the money. It has been shown that if the wages paid to labour employed on the site in the construction of a housing project were cut in half, the annual cost of the 'housing produced would be reduced only about ten per cent. - If the cost of materials entering into the production of housing were cut in 'half the annual cost would be reduced by only fifteen per cent, but the reduction in financial charges, interest and amortization by half would effect a greater reduction in annual cost than cutting in half the costs of both materials and labour.
The United States housing act embodies a plan for producing new housing at rents equivalent to those charged in the slums. It accomplishes this by authorizing the federal government to perform two separate-financial functions, that of banker and that of donor of annual rent subsidies. As banker the United States housing authorities lend to the local housing authority for the purchase of its bonds up to ninety per cent of the capital cost of a project. After the project is completed the United States housing authority assumes its second financial function; it grants annual subsidies in an amount sufficient to cover the difference between the annual economic rent and the rent which low income families can afford to pay.
The local housing authorities in the United States have been able to market bonds running up to the year 1985, which they sell at interest costs that average less than two per cent. The way has thus been paved for establishing a public housing programme in the post-war era on a basis of financing which will ultimately relieve the federal government almost wholly of responsibility for providing capital funds. I see no reason why this plan now in operation in the United States of America should not be made available for this unfortunate group of our citizens in the low income brackets.
The minister spoke about the loan to the Montreal housing authority which was arranged through the good offices of Mr. George W. Spinney, and I hope his example will be followed in Toronto and in other cities. Am I right in assuming that the rate charged for the money to that authority was three per cent?

As a measure of public health and social advancement, low rental housing projects will have a direct influence in improving conditions of life for the low wage-earner in urban areas and will be a factor in increasing the employability of our workers in a period in which their employability has been greatly reduced.

The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that we require 125,000 houses to be built in the rural areas of this country within ten years after the end of the war, of which 100,000 will be replacements of homes already existing. I saw the statement made recently that if an endeavour was to be made to raise the standard of living of the rural residents of Canada, at least fifty thousand homes should be built in this country during the first full year after the war. We all realize the difficulties in the way of carrying out such a programme, but I do feel that they should share at least on an almost equal basis with the urban centres, to the end that conditions now existing in the country areas of Canada may be remedied as soon as possible.
In that connection I might mention that a complete survey of the situation was made by Mr. Forsey, director of research for the Canadian Congress of Labour, and was published in the Canadian Unionist in the latter part of 1943. He pointed out that in twenty-seven Canadian cities of thirty thousand population and over there were 150,000 overcrowded households containing one million people; that in fourteen of the twenty-seven cities at least twenty per cent of the houses needed external repairs, and that farm, housing was in a much worse condition. When this programme is brought in, when we have an opportunity of seeing the bill in its entirety and the plan of operation, I hope we shall have a plan which will hold out a new hope for Canadian people in the lower income brackets, and that the rural people will be given an opportunity to have a greater share in those better things of life which in the past have been denied them.
We are all in agreement with the principle of the resolution. I have risen for only one purpose, and that is to ask that in carrying this measure into effect the farm population of Canada shall receive a fair share of the moneys to be appropriated for housing and thereby be given an opportunity to raise its standard of living to a point approximating that enjoyed by the vast majority of people living in the urban centres of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this resolution as a means of bringing relief to that large section of our people who have no decent homes. And when I use the expression "decent homes" I believe I am using a very mild one, because many of those people live in places which could scarcely be called homes.
In Montreal the situation is particularly serious. Last year Jacqueline Sirois of the Montreal Standard made a special investigation into the housing situation of that city. She made her report in four newspaper articles,
[Mr. Hi1>y.l
in which she pointed out that about 6,000 familes in Montreal at that time lived in stores, shacks, public halls,i warehouses, and summer cottages unfit for winter habitation; seme even lived in boats. She reported that sheds were rented for as much as $15 a month, and that some people living in stores paid rents as high as $48 a month.
Out of these 6,000 families, 1,200 lived in stores, 400 in garages, warehouses and public halls, 4,000 families doubled up and 200 tripled-that is, there were three families in each small home. Since Jacqueline Sirois made that report the situation in Montreal has by no means improved. That condition came to a head in May, 1944, when many people had to leave their homes and had nowhere to go. Many of them of course had no alternative but to take summer homes. We are again going to have a very serious situation when the summer homes have to be closed down, owing to their unfitness for winter habitation.
No doubt the housing crisis in Montreal was aggravated by the fact that tens of thousands of workers came to our city to work in the war factories. But that is not the whole story. To complete it let me say that between the years 1925 and 1942 there were 140,000 marriages. Those people went looking for homes. During that time only 54,000 housing units were built-and this was before those tens of thousands of people flocked to Montreal.
In that city we have always had crowding. The figures show that 24-4 per cent of all homes in Montreal were overcrowded-and when I say overcrowded I mean more than one person to a room. Let us compare that figure with 12 per cent overcrowding in Toronto. That is, we in Montreal have a condition twice as bad as the one in Toronto. Outside Montreal the overcrowding is even worse. In Quebec City 31-8 per cent live in overcrowded homes, and in Hull 34-5 per cent.
Let me show how closely this condition of overcrowding is linked with the health of those communities. The number of children in Montreal who die in their early years is double the number in Toronto. There we have the answer-double the overcrowding; double the number of deaths among children. And where overcrowding is even worse-in Three Rivers -with a percentage of 34-7, the number of deaths among children stands at 118 per thousand live births. The figure in Montreal is 71 per thousand. Again these figures are in proportion to the extent of overcrowding. I am not a medical doctor, but these facts are simple and clear. Anyone who studies social problems will understand what this has meant to us in the province of Quebec.

Housing
I should like also to stress the small percentage of homes in Montreal which have central heating. I have lived in houses with no central heating units. I have lived in houses where we had a stove in the kitchen and perhaps another one, a heater, in the hallway. In the mornings we would get up in cold bedrooms. We would go to the kitchen, finding it warm. This passing from one place to another, from one temperature to another, brought about colds. I have no doubt this condition exists in many homes across Canada. Colds are often followed by complications. In Montreal only 36 per cent of homes have central heating, or are heated by furnaces, whereas in Toronto the percentage is 94. In Hull only 16 per cent of the homes are heated by furnaces. Again we can see how these conditions affect health.
I have placed these figures on the record because I believe it has been announced in Montreal that a building scheme, for the erection of modern homes, is to be undertaken. According to reports, however, these homes are not to have central heating. I would say that at this time for any government to advance loans to any group of people to engage in a housing project for the building of homes without central heating is criminal.

Another objection I find to the scheme is that there is not sufficient provision for using the provinces.
