subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two things as to which I should like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to assure the house before this bill is given a second reading. I am quite sure that all the members here are anxious that proper housing at proper cost should be provided for those people whose need is greatest, and if we have the assurance from the minister that that will be done under this scheme, I am confident that it will receive the enthusiastic support of every member here.
Housing is one of the great costs of living, and there must be some assurance given that the people whose income is such that they cannot pay for this housing will be given the opportunity to get a home of their own. Basically and fundamentally our problem is an economic one. The people of Canada can afford only that type of housing which they can pay for out of their income, and only a certain portion of their income can be allotted to housing. If we are to have a repetition of Wartime Housing, with its costs, I am afraid that Canada will live to regret the day she proceeded along those lines. There is little assurance that the people are going to be able to meet the obligations of rental, or the obligations of purchase.
There is also this important thing to be said in regard to the whole scheme, and that is that the costs of building these houses may be much too high. The costs of production, the cost of materials, of lumber and cement are much higher than they should be in Canada. Are these excessive costs to be borne by the people of Canada when they are out of line with what they should be in a land which can provide itself with all the lumber and cement and building materials that the people need? We can provide all these things out of the natural resources of this country merely by applying to them the labour that is so abundant in this country; but as it is now we have to pay toll to those who have control of these natural resources and the power to extract from the purchaser whatever they wish to charge.
Another thing that bothers me in reading over the bill is that it in no way suggests that adequate housing will be provided in those places where housing is needed most. The Minister of Finance has the power to join with approved lending institutions in making loans under certain conditions for the construction of houses, but apparently it is
Housing

the lending institutions who are going to decide where they will provide these homes.
I am dubious about where the farmer in Canada is going to come in under this scheme. Housing conditions in most of our cities and in certain rural areas are disgraceful. We have had placed on the record to-day what is happening in one of our largest cities in the matter of housing. If one takes the trouble to go into the city of St. John, New Brunswick, or into almost any rural area in that province, or into any rural area in any other province, one will find housing conditions which are disgraceful. The problem of providing rural housing is not met by this legislation, so far as I can see, and that is where there is a great need for housing. The people in the rural areas, who are performing the work that they do for Canada, require better housing if they are going to maintain agriculture on the standards which it should reach. Many of these people are living in isolated areas and require special attention in the matter of housing.
The trouble in Canada has been that the economic condition of the farmer has not received proper attention in the past, and there is no assurance that it will in the future. I am quite sure that under this bill the lending institutions will not lend money, even with government assurance, in areas where they are not absolutely sure that the farmers will return it. I do not see any solution for better housing conditions where they are vitally needed, namely, in the rural areas of Canada. I will not bother to put the records on Hansard again; this has already been done on several occasions. What assurance can the minister give us that the distribution of any benefits which may accrue from this bill will be equitable across Canada, and that the loans will not all be made possibly in one particular area where for the time being economic conditions are good, even in rural areas? Adjacent to cities that dairy farming, for instance, may be a profitable business in these days, and the farmer makes a little more money; but that does not mean that the other agricultural producers in more distant places are not in great need of housing. Is there going to be special consideration for the larger income groups? The people I am thinking about, on the other hand, are in the northern parts of Saskatchewan, in the backwoods of New Brunswick, in the more isolated districts of British Columbia. That is where housing is required in the rural parts of the country. There is provision here for slum clearance where the government lends to limited dividend corporations to assist in the financing of [Mr. Castledon.l
low rental housing projects. Is there similar provision for the agricultural needs in the matter of housing?
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement in reply to some of the questions that have been brought to his attention?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

speechtext: With regard to agriculture, I do not think that the minister's statement gave us sufficient assurance that the distribution of the benefits of the scheme will extend to the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Very extensive provision is made for loans for the purpose of building and improving farm buildings. In the first place, provision is made under the bank act and under the farm loan improvements bill. That was all explained to the house at the time that legislation was under consideration. Under this legislation the farmers are eligible to the same extent as anyone else for loans under the housing act. Moreover, we recognize that many farms have mortgages on them, the mortgage covering a good deal more than the house; they cover the farm as well. And so provision is made in the bill for the consolidation of the mortgages if more money has to be lent by way of mortgage. Moreover, special provisions will be found in the bill to encourage lending institutions to lend in remote areas and places of that kind. I mentioned that in the speech I made this morning in introducing the resolution. They consist of special fees and payment of travelling expenses, because there will be extra expenses of investigation in certain cases. Those are provisions that will be found in the legislation. But if we were to undertake to make sure that there is a distribution of money equally province by province or something of that kind we could never satisfy anyone that the distribution was equitable-never. subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Is there provision here for groups of people who go together to build houses in a cooperative way similar to what we find in Nova Scotia?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

For loans from a loan company, or directly from the government?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: What about the other point I brought up? Is the minister in a position to answer the question about the actual efficient operation of the plan so as to make sure that our people will really get dollar for dollar value for what they buy in housing, taking into consideration the excessive cost of cement, lumber and building material?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: The whole struggle we have made ever since the beginning of the war has been to keep prices down. That does not apply only to building materials, however; it applies to everything.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Would you say you were very successful in war-time housing costs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I have no reason to think that War-time Housing incurred excessive costs in the building of houses. I do not think we have been particularly successful in keeping prices down in building materials, fn fact, we have been less successful in regard to lumber than anything else. I would say that. I know that is the opinion of the price control authorities, but that does not mean that we have not tried and tried desperately. There has been a great increase in wages, of course, in the logging and lumbering industries, and that has reflected itself inevitably in prices.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: There was little money spent in western Canada in comparison with other parts of the dominion having regard1 to the economic conditions that existed out there in the years before the war, and I do not see where in this measure provision is made for supplying houses in areas where they should be supplied, in depressed areas. You have to meet the same conditions in every part of Canada, no matter what the local conditions are. You have to give the same consideration to special conditions which may exist in different areas in Canada. After all, the person who lives in one of those areas needs housing just as much as if he lived in an area where economic conditions are better. There is difficulty in meeting these conditions, but some consideration should be given the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: This does not provide for subsidizing housing in selected depressed rural areas. It does not do that, and I do not know that any scheme does. I have not seen any.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Does not the minister think there should be something to take care of such conditions? The conditions are there. The people are living under those conditions and raising families. The health of the people in those areas is certainly not equal to the average for the Dominion of Canada. So long as we allow people to live there, we should make some effort to see that conditions are better in those areas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not know the situation in my hon. friend's province, but in my province you cannot prevent people from living in submarginal or marginal locations. Just what the government should do in respect to housing in those circumstances I do not know. We certainly are doing something very substantial for large families. I think the important thing is to give those people a chance on their income rather than to subsidize the houses. The administrative difficulties would be terrific. If you start selecting places here and there and subsidize housing in the depressed areas in the country there will be charges of inequality. The important thing is to get the income levels and the incomes of the people up and let them avail themselves of reasonable and general schemes such as this.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I agree to some extent with what the minister has just said; but what some others have in mind is this: Some plan should be worked out in cooperation with the provincial governments under which instead of people picking out a piece of land and putting a shack on it they will be given the opportunity to build a house; and by means of cooperation something might be done to enable them to support a family and to undertake some obligation. I am very familiar with my own province. We have had people move up in the north country where there is a lot of bush and trees. As the minister suggests, these people are not making an economic living. They are living in little shacks and log houses. The land is good. More has to be done, probably by the provincial government, to make use of the high powered machinery we have to make that land economically usable-in other words to help them to clear land so that they can put in a crop and get a return that will enable them to assume some obligations. But the condition is there. Health and other social conditions are exceedingly poor in those areas. I have seen housing conditions in my own province
Housing

that are indescribable. I remarked to the Prime Minister the other day that in his own constituency in the northern part of the province there are indescribable housing conditions. A bill like this, of course, does not help the situation very much. What we need is cooperative undertakings so that people can make a living on land that is good and assume some obligation to build decent houses; in other words, cooperative effort.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: A person of low income in the city cannot afford to build or buy a house, but he can obtain one at low rental. The farmer's income is sometimes the lowest in the whole of Canada. subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

by other hon. members in favour of more rural houses. I am in agreement with the principles but probably not with the details of some of the suggestions. subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

I am not going to enter into an argument with the minister on this, but I cannot altogether agree with him.
I do not believe the people of Canada agree with him. I believe the soldier should be in a preferred class and that the people of Canada will back the minister and this government or any other government in placing them in a preferred class to become house-owners. I do not know the average age of the soldiers, but I presume it would be from twenty-five to twenty-seven years. We presume and hope that they all want to get married when they come back and become house-owners. With regard to the landlords-and I suppose I am m that class since I have rented my farm and my house-I suppose they are the ones to whom preference will be given. Maybe I should be given preference: since I have no house in Ottawa and I have rented the one I own in the country. I should not be con-

sidered in the preferred class rather than the man who at nineteen or twenty-one years of age went overseas to fight. He has sacrificed everything, every possibility of earning the necessary capital to make a down payment to acquire a house, in order that I might live in safety here. I believe it is the duty of Canada to give him at least a fifty per cent preference, because he has done all he could to ensure our safety at home.
I shall not be here when some of these measures are discussed further and I have not the knowledge to speak on monetary reforms, but I wish to assure the minister that the province of British Columbia has been fairly well represented in the banking committee at least so far as volume is concerned. We might be further represented in this house when this bill is considered, if we thought money could not be found in some way to cut the cost in half as far as these soldiers are concerned. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Before this session is over I believe the hon. gentleman will find that the provision we are making for the soldiers will be considered adequate by this house and by the people of Canada. I quite agree with the minister, and I regret that he did not see fit to bring this legislation before the house much earlier in the session in order that I might pass upon it. At the moment I am not speaking as a Liberal member or as the member for Fraser Valley; I am speaking as a returned soldier member of this house. I do not believe family allowances or anything else can be as important as the steps we take to endeavour to meet our obligations to the men serving overseas in our behalf. The government may bring in legislation that will provide what I suggest is lacking in this measure. Legislation may be brought in to provide what is lacking in other measures that have been or may be passed before the session is over. I
have no way of judging as to that, but as a returned soldier member of this house I consider it my duty to bear in mind at all times that the first interest of the Canadian people is their obligation to the men who are overseas.
This is probably the first time I ever got ahead of my friends to the left, at least that is what they will claim, who always say, " We brought this in." I am glad the minister has stated publicly to-day, in his responsible position as Minister of Finance, that the government ig bringing down legislation along the lines advocated in 1940 by the returned soldier member for Fraser Valley, so that the soldiers may be adequately protected.

Or partly an open
space?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: You might have too much land then in proportion to buildings to make the scheme practicable from the economic standpoint, but if you did not there would be no reason why that could not be done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I think it should be made perfectly clear, and the public ought to know, that whatever may be said in favour of this resolution it does not meet the acute housing situation at present facing many parts of Canada. I read in the newspapers last week, and brought the matter to the attention of the minister when I inquired as to the introduction of the housing legislation, that in the city of Toronto there were no less than 800 families who would face acute housing problems before the end of the year. The newspaper report showed that a large number of those families were families in which the breadwinners were either overseas or in the armed forces.
The minister was good enough to indicate some time ago when the legislation was going to be Introduced, and gave a skeleton outline of it, so that those who might utilize the facilities afforded by the legislation would have an opportunity of doing so ahead of the actual introduction of the resolution. On that occasion I raised what I thought was a pertinent question, one which should not be overlooked. I pointed out that it is all very well to provide the necessary financial arrangements for a housing programme, but that we must also have the materials with which to build the houses. Priorities is one of the real difficulties now facing those who would build houses. Materials in short supply are a powerful impediment to meeting the housing situation.
Not long ago the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply made a statement in which he warned the people in Canada not to become too optimistic about a building programme for the coming autumn. On June 30 the parliamentary assistant said that in 1944 the housing programme must be limited, and went on to give the reasons. He indicated clearly-at least it was clear to me- that any programme of housing would be considerably impeded by virtue of the fact that materials were not available. I am quite ready

Housing
to believe that there may be a shortage of many materials required in any housing programme. I have in mind such things as furnaces and construction materials in general. My point in rising at this time is to indicate that I should not like to have the public feel that this housing legislation-in the long-term view, excellent in many respects-would before the end of the year provide any real help to relieve housing. When I say that I have in mind the situation as to materials.
May I endorse the statements and arguments respecting our armed forces personnel which have been made in this debate. It is important that, no matter what civilians may be entitled to, we keep in mind the fact that those who have done the fighting in this war are the ones who have first claim upon the generosity of the government and parliament. In my opinion, and I believe in the opinion of everyone in the house-because this is not a matter in which there is any division politically-those who have done the fighting must have the first consideration and must be the first concern of those who have power to do something for them. That must be so in this as in other matters. As a nation we cannot afford to do anything less than the best for those who are giving their best for us.

minister help me think through this matter, as it affects my constituency. Suppose in the city of Lethbridge there is a truck driver, the father of three children, who, by means of all manner of effort with his truck, is able to make $900 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is what I want to know. I would not think he could.

speechtext:
What we are trying to find out is whether this building provision is interested in people or in money. If it is interested in people, it will build homes for people; if it is interested in money, it will build homes for bankers' dividends. That is the fact. In my opinion it is designed to pay bankers' dividends, and not to build homes for people at all. The amount a man can save surely does not enter into it. With his three children and a wife-and his family
might grow to seven children, children Canada needs badly-the question is: Are you going to make provision to give him a home in which to rear those children? He has been prepared to make sacrifices to rear them. I want to see how it will work out. This man gets $900 a year. Can he qualify for one of these loans, by any means of which the minister can conceive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: He cannot get a loan unless he can make a down payment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, you see, that immediately rules out a huge percentage of the people of Canada. If I remember correctly, the figures given this morning by the hon. member for Parkdale indicated that fifty per cent of the wage-earners of Canada were getting less than $1,000 a year. It is the wage-earners of Canada who are the men who are rearing Canadians of to-morrow. They are the men who are rearing the soldiers for the next war.
Mr, ILSLEY: Better not go too far. Would the hon. member suggest that we provide loans to the extent of one hundred per cent of the value of the property?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Is not that the way the housing scheme I had in mind would work out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Let me deal first with the hon. member for Lethbridge.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Let me have the minister's question again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member suggest that in certain conditions or circumstances we should advance loans to one hundred per cent of the value of the property, so that a person applying for a loan would not be under the necessity of putting up anything for himself? He could get title to the property, and the government, or a lending institution-or somebody-could take a loan for the full hundred per cent of the value of the property. And if so, to what persons would we extend that concession? First of all, should we extend it at all? The most I have heard suggested has been ninety per cent. Does the hon. member suggest one hundred per cent?	.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Does the minister mean one hundred per cent of the value of the home he is going to build?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The value of the house and lot.
Housing

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not see any way in which we are going to help substantially the vast percentage of wage-earners in Canada unless some such scheme is devised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: And the hon. member is in favour of it, is he?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I am in favour of it, yes. That is the only way in which you can help the people who need it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: It would be interesting to find out how many members in the house are in favour of it. I should like to know that, as a matter of practical interest. Members get up and make very fine speeches, mentioning individual cases, and they say: What is the government going to do for this man? How much money are they going to give him? They gay: If you do not do something for him, there will be a lot of people you will not be doing anything for. I ask hon. members to put themselves in a practical position once in a while. I know the hon. member for Lethbridge would make a one hundred per cent loan, and' I am glad to get that from him.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: For these low wage and salaried people a scheme in cooperation with the municipalities should be undertaken whereby-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: And the provinces.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: And the provinces, if you will. I am thinking of the organization which is closest to the people at the moment, the municipal organization. A scheme should be worked out whereby houses are erected and rented, or I would prefer to have them sold to purchasers on a rental basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Without any down payment?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Without any down payment. I think there are many families to whom homes must be sold or rented and who are not able to make a down payment. We must face the fact sooner or later that this scheme does not help that type of person.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Renting is a different thing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I think it would be better to sell on a rental basis. The people should feel it is their home.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Is that not the way it is done in many city schemes? Are the homes not sold on a rental basis? Do they not pay $25 per month, a portion of which goes to pay for the cost of building?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not ashamed to say that the first home I owned I purchased with a very small down payment. I paid for

that home on a rental basis and it took me a number of years to do so. Schemes have been worked out in many countries, especially in Great Britain, where the amount of rental purchase is no more than the ordinary rental for the same class of property. I think this is the right time to do this. I do not see how we can meet the situation the hon. member for Lethbridge was talking about, the truck driver with a wife and three children and earning less than $1,000 a year, by any other means. That man could not pay his expenses and obtain a home on any other basis. I think we should encourage the ownership of homes rather than rent them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I think the minister realizes the reason why I say that the money should be advanced to the extent of one hundred per cent. I am not saying that the dominion government should advance all that money; it might be advanced through the cooperation of the provinces and the municipalities. The minister knows quite well that every dollar of that money could be created by the Bank of Canada without any cost at all, and it could be advanced to the provinces and the municipalities without any cost to Canada. Under this scheme you are simply putting into use money which has been made already by people and put into savings. No endeavour is being made to use the financial power of the country to help individuals to get homes. The government's interest is not in human beings, it is in the savings which have been accumulated by men who have been fortunate enough to save money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. gentleman means.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: This is simply to enable people to put savings to profitable use.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, no, not at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: If that were not the case the government would have provided a scheme under which the ordinary individual like the truck driver I mentioned could obtain a home, but it has not done that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Is there a housing shortage in Lethbridge?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
There is a housing
shortage in every area in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: All of them?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am speaking about the constituency I represent, and I would say that there is hardly an area in my constituency in which there is not a housing shortage. My constituency is not an industrial constituency where war work is being carried on. The housing shortage must be simply tremendous

Housing
in areas like Toronto, Montreal, Halifax and other centres. We must bear in mind that new Canadians are growing up all the time; they are getting married and must have homes. The figures given by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose) concerning Montreal are impressive enough. If I remember aright, he said that in Montreal 140,000 couples had been married while only 54,000 homes had been built. It does not take a very astute intellect to work out the situation that will develop in Montreal, and a similar situation has developed in various parts of Canada.
What are we doing to meet the needs of these young folk who are getting married? This scheme should be such that they can take advantage of it. A sound arrangement would be one where young people who are ready to assume the responsibilities of married life could go to the proper agency in their community and say, "We want to build a home and this is what we are able to do." The agency would send out a representative to make sure that they w^ere as they represented themselves and then would say, "If you had to rent a home in this community you would pay $25 a month; you cannot: get a home for less; we will endeavour to make arrangements to have a home built for you; you *will pay $25 a month and at the end of twenty-five years you will #vn your home." Perhaps that period could be twenty years. If they had to leave within ten years to go somewhere else that agency should be ready to take over the home, discharge their obligations and give them whatever equity they might have.
That would be a common sense arrangement; that would be a workable arrangement. It 'would give hope to young people who wished to marry. I do not want to go into another matter while we are on this subject, but it must be borne in mind that it must be made easy for young people of Canada to marry and raise children. There are tens of thousands of young people who do not dare marry because they cannot see how they can make it go; they cannot see any hope of getting a home. Why should not this housing scheme be drafted to meet the needs of the hundreds of thousands of young people who are our greatest possession. There is nothing at all in this scheme to meet the needs of those young Canadians. Practically every one of our returned soldiers will be in that position when he returns. What are we doing for them? '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The overwhelming majority of those people will have $300 or $400 saved, and $400 is all you need to build a $4,000 home under this scheme.
Mr MoNEVIN:	I wish to make one
observation with respect to the housing shortage. I should like to refer particularly to a condition which is due to the centralization of our war industry in large cities like Toronto, Winnipeg and Montreal. I can go out through the country and find many villages and hamlets where there are vacant houses. I know of one hamlet of ten houses of which three are vacant. One house is equipped with electricity and running water, and the whole three are 'good dwelling houses. The same condition prevails throughout Canada. I think we should bear that in mind. If there is a great shortage of housing in Montreal, Toronto and other large cities, a survey should be made of the small villages and hamlets to find the accommodation that can be used this winter if there are people without homes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I quite realize that a
survey could be made to find vacant houses, but could these people find something to do in order to make a living in -those small communities? As a matter of fact this condition is not due to the war. It was present before the war. You have only to read the census figures of 1931 to realize that. I remember a report being made to this parliament; I have a copy of it in my office at the present time. It showed the housing conditions in Canada as revealed by the census figures of 1931, and I was particularly interested in the figures for the city in which I lived at that time, the city of Regina. Even at that time, when there was no war, the congestion in Regina was such that there was an average of two persons to every room in that city. That condition may have improved since or got worse; I do not know, but what I am pointing out to the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, is that -this condition is not due to the war. We had a shortage of several hundred thousand houses in this country before the war broke out.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I was not speaking from
that angle at all. The suggestion had been made that there might be eight hundred families in Toronto without shelter this winter. You cannot get enough houses built under any scheme between now and Christmas to take care of people in those circumstances, and I was saying that we had in Ontario, in the small municipalities, hamlets and villages, a substantial number of good, habitable houses now vacant which would enable us to take care of an emergent situation. I am in full
Housing

accord with what has been, said of the necessity of a large housing scheme for the Dominion of Canada as one of our post-war objectives.

speechtext:
How much money
would this truck driver have to have to qualify for the loan?
Mr. ILSLEY':	If he co.uld build a house
for $2,500, he would require five per cent. We advance ninety-five per cent if it is over $2,000, and I think it is ninety per cent if it is over $3,000. I gave the figures this morning. He puts up very little if the cost of the property is only $2,500. At $3,000 we advance a little over ninety-one per cent, and at $4,000, ninety per cent.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

And how long would
he have to repay the loan?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to continue the discussion I was having with the minister about twenty minutes ago when the committee got off on another tack. I think the minister has received wrong advice about the municipalities. I am speaking from my experience in western Canada, where, as I said this morning, there is a keen social conscience on this matter of housing. I feel that there will be general disappointment that the government has taken the obstinate view that it will not consider assisting in the setting up of municipal public housing authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister said this
morning that the matter had been considered and that the government had made the definite decision that it did not propose to assist municipalities in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

Is there anything more
obstinate about that than in the hon. gentleman's own position?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
So long as we are both
obstinate I do not mind.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
With the good humour
now prevailing we may get somewhere. I was going to ask the minister whether consideration had been given to any other level

of public authority, for example, provincial or federal. I take it that representations have been made to the government for assistance to the municipalities, and that that has been considered and turned down. Has the government any alternative to this indirect method of working through private lending companies? Has it considered setting up federal or provincial housing authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think the setting up of provincial authorities was considered. It must be remembered that we have had a pretty sad experience in dealing with certain of the provinces so far as recovery is concerned. There are four provinces all of which owe us large sums which apparently they 'have no intention of paying. When it comes to relations between the dominion government and other public authorities we naturally are getting a little bit careful. But I am not-putting it entirely on that ground. There are disadvantages in advancing money and putting other public authorities in this country in debt to the dominion government. It can lead to a very serious situation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: For what purpose were these moneys advanced?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
There is always a reason why they cannot repay after they have signed their names.
Mr. COLD'WrELL:	It was a national
calamity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, I know. All the fertility of the human intellect comes right into play in finding reasons why solemn obligations signed by inferior jurisdictions in this country will not under certain conditions be honoured, and we are absolutely powerless to do anything about the matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: These were national calamities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: And the hon. gentleman will argue that they should not pay back the advances, just as they argue. But the fact remains that the advances are not repaid.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister uses the word "recovery", and then speaking in another vein he talks about the amount of money that a person must have before he can be assisted in building a house. He has a different approach to this matter from that which some of us take. I feel that we should come at this matter directly, and that should not seem entirely strange to the government, in view of the family allowance legislation which the government brought down. The government in bringing down that measure has taken the position that children need assistance and that

Housing
the thing to do is to put cash directly into the hands of the families concerned so that they will be able to feed and clothe their children better. Again, the minister in reply to the hon. member for Fraser Valley said that we should not be critical of the government's programme with respect to service personnel until everything had been brought down, and he referred to the war service gratuity legislation that is yet to come before the house. There again we are to have an attempt on the part of the government to meet an economic problem directly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I did not say
"attempt".

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
At least we are agreed in this that we shall be glad to see the legislation brought down. I feel that in the matter of housing we should not think in terms of financial losses in connection with any programme as a result of which houses are built. If we build houses in Canada we increase the wealth of this country; we increase the goods and services available to provide a good life for our people, and I feel that what we should be doing is to be working through public authorities to build houses and make them available either on a rental basis or at prices at which they can be purchased at practically rental rates, so that our people can enjoy life in their own homes while they are living, instead of spending all their lives in trying to save up the necessary dollars so as to be able to buy a home in which to die.
I should like to say this to the minister. When a soldier enlists we do not ask him if he has enough money to buy a gun or a tank. We do not ask a young man who enlists in the air force if he has enough money to make the down payment on a Lancaster bomber. We directly provide him with this necessary equipment, as essential to the job in which he is engaged. The minister has discussed the financial nature of these things a number of times in the house and has objected rightly to the criticism of the opposition when they tried to argue that we are going bankrupt by doing these things.
The minister said that when we increase our production and devote a large part of it to a great cause we are not going bankrupt, and if we are not going bankrupt in doing that, when we are producing war goods, there is no reason why we should go bankrupt in the production of an essential peace-time undertaking such as homes for our people. I am convinced that the day will come when the principle of governments going indirectly into the providing of homes for the people through the medium of public housing authorities will prevail. I am sorry that what I
thought was a first step in that direction in ;his resolution has been exploded by the minister's speech this morning. I think he got the wrong advice so far as the municipalities in the west are concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I wish to ask just two questions. First, will the machinery provided in this resolution, in other words the funds, which will be made available to the lending institutions, be administered through the present National Housing Act? Secondly, will the machinery that is being set up take in the credit unions, for example, as an approved lending institution? That institution has gone into housing, in Nova Scotia particularly, to some extent. In discussing the matter the minister definitely indicated that this machinery would not be available to the municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Nova Scotia has a very good provincial housing act, and the authorities there have done considerable excellent work in the field of cooperative housing. Would the machinery now being set up be available to the provincial government to expand the existing legislation they have in that cooperative housing field? They operate to some extent with the credit union movement in the province, and I should like to know whether the funds now being made available can be used provincially, in that province at any rate, to augment and expand their present legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not understand the latter part of the question. No money will go to the province; none of it will go to the province. The hon. member asks whether credit unions will be approved as lending institutions. If they have the power to lend on real estate, yes; we propose to make them eligible as lending institutions. I do not want to make my statement so sweeping that it will be used against me in case some cannot qualify, because there are some private lending institutions that cannot qualify for one reason or another. Nevertheless, the cooperative lending institutions are to be put on the same basis as the private institutions as far as eligibility is concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: The whole credit union movement in Nova Scotia will qualify because they are tied into a central organization.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
There are one or two comments I wish to make on what the minister said a moment ago. He said that the interest on this money which would be advanced to the prospective home builder
Housing

would be 4i per cent. I do not hesitate to say that this is a little over twice too much. No home builder in the country should have so pay more than two per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Why two per cent?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not say that it would not be well to make it less.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I would make it one or nothing if I were in the hon. gentleman's place. The money will not cost anything; it will be debt-free money issued by the Bank of Canada. Why charge anything? That is, looking at it from my hon. friend's point of view.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I did not want to alarm the minister by going too far. The simple fact of the matter is that this question must be understood definitely by the rank and file in Canada, because it is not understood at the present time: The Bank of Canada does print this money without any cost and the money could be advanced.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Order. Let us confine our remarks to the resolution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: If what I am saying is not relevant to the resolution, then nothing is. You could not get anything that would be relevant to the resolution if what I am saying now is not to the point. It would be impossible to get anything that would be more pertinent. The hon. member for Park-dale, if I recall rightly, pointed out that in the United States the rate was 2 or 2i per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I shall have to wait and see what was said.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I am depending on my memory, but he read an excerpt from the report, I believe, of the Purvis commission in which it was pointed out that in the United States the rate was as I have stated.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: He is generally wrong.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
He may be right. Certain it is, however, that 2% per cent is enough; it is as high as anyone should pay. The money can be created absolutely debt-free by the Bank of Canada and the minister will not deny it. The only argument he has ever given against the use of the Bank of Canada for the creation of money is that it will cause inflation. Well, seeing that we have created an abundance of goods for war purposes, and that we shall be able to produce enormously

after this war, I suggest that it would be nonsense to talk about inflation after the war. The goods and services will be there.
I wish to make another comment on what the minister said about the provinces owing money and not paying it back. I do not knoiv what the situation generally will be in this regard, but I would point out that the Bank of Canada was established for the purpose of creating money in the Dominion of Canada and it has been given the absolute power of issue. It can therefore create money without any gold behind it. If it cannot create money and advance it to the provinces without loss to the dominion, then I suggest that it is impossible to reason at all. Why we should1 w7orry about the provinces failing to pay back certain moneys it is difficult to understand. There must be a completely changed attitude towards this whole aspect of finance. The sooner members come to realize that, the sooner they will be in a position to save the country from communism. We cannot go on with the antiquated notions about finance that have filled the minds of members of this house and of the administration. We must acquire a modern realistic attitude toward money, and then- we shall see that this proposal with respect to providing money to home owners at 2i per cent is quite feasible.

speechtext: I do not know what foundation there is for the statement which the hon. member has made with reference to Soviet Russia, because the fact is that Soviet Russia uses approximately the same monetary system as we employ.

I wish to say a few words on the provision made for slum clearance, which has been substantially qualified by the minister in his remarks this morning. Slum clearance is something everyone talks about but nobody does anything about, and the reason is that unless the municipadities are able to develop a programme of slum clearance and prosecute it, the situation remains without anybody being in a position to move on it with any effectiveness. Slum clearance is probably one of the finest examples of the danger of obsolescence fastening itself on to a community through the practice of always thinking of everything in terms of the investment of money. In slum clearance and in the futures of cities there is probably something more important than the individual dwelling houses. I think the more important thing is the environment and the surroundings of the dwelling houses themselves. We have moved along to a time when the number of hours that people work is comparatively small

Housing
compared with the number of hours that they have in the way of leisure time. You will hardly find in a Canadian city anything like adequate accommodation for the healthy cultural occupation of lqisure time.
I do not know how the figure of $20,000,000 was arrived at, but certainly that amount would not go very far in slum clearance throughout Canada. I should think that you would be able to spend much more than that in the city of Montreal alone. You could spend a good deal of it even in a young city like Vancouver which has not the obsolescence that the older cities have. There are whole areas in that young city that are outmoded to-day. As a matter of fact they were not properly built and they should be cleared away. In my opinion one effective method of slum clearance is to establish in the school areas not merely a school and playground, but a school with all the requirements of the social life of that school centre. Each school should be equipped not with one mediocre bit of ground for the children to play on, but with several divisions of playgrounds. It should have its gymnasium; it should have its stadium; it should have its swimming-pool; it should have its skating-rink, of course; it should have its theatre and its music centre; it should have its accommodation for music and for art, not merely for the children but each school centre in that section of the city should become as well as a centre of education, a centre for cultural entertainment for the whole community. What would it cost? How could it be paid for? It could be paid for in the same way that we pay for our highways, our parks, or those things that we must have in war time and in peace time that never reproduce a dollar of money dividends, but could produce enormously in the dividends of culture, better citizenship and better community life in a sounder, national economy. I know it is easy to say that we cannot afford these things. When the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, suggests that the Soviet Union are adopting the same kind of monetary system that we are-

That is a very different matter. They are using it in an entirely different way. They are putting and will continue to put the emphasis on public expenditure, not on investment to make money, but on investment to provide better accommodation for the people. It is one of the great fallacies of our whole public economy that we insist on putting everything out in the hope that it is going to be paid back either by
some profit-making enterprise or by some levy of taxation. I happen to know some of the needs of our Canadian cities. I happened to be one of the mayors who formed the first mayors' conference in the west which became the mayors' conference of the Dominion of Canada. That conference has been actively organized and represents the municipalities of Canada in close cooperation with a similar organization in the United States. They have told us in this parliament through our reconstruction committee that they have not the money either in taxable reserves or in resources to carry on any programme of substantial expansion that would improve either the cities or provide post-war employment.
When you come to split this $20,000,000 how are you going to allocate it? How much is to go to Vancouver, how much to Halifax? Charlottetown is also included, I take it, as well as Montreal and Toronto.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: Not the rural areas?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOB CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I would not say that because it included municipalities and that probably takes in a great many rural areas. How are we to divide it? How far will it go round and what impression will it make on the slum condition of our cities? If some programme could be worked out whereby the dominion government would finance municipal schemes not merely of slum clearance but of community betterment, then I think we should be moving along the line where the days of slums in Canada would be done away with.
I fear that I see in this $20,000,000 and in the remarks of the minister this morning the same old attitude that prevailed in 1930 to 1935 and from 1936 to the outbreak of the war when the dominion government under two great parties stood with their backs to the wall flatly refusing to recognize as their responsibility those things which had been imposed upon provincial and municipal authority and which neither provincial nor municipal authority had the means or the powers under the constitution to finance. In my opinion, of all the violations of the true spirit of our Canadian constitution we find the greatest one in the selfish attitude of the federal parliament to the junior departments of government. I find no better expression of that same weakness, shall I say, in our national administration than in the attitude expressed in this bill in connection with slum clearance, and in the utter indifference on the part of the federal authorities to any desire to become associated with provincial and municipal governments in making conditions in the cities better for the masses of the people. What do slum
Housing

conditions and the pitiable living conditions that exist in our cities cost us sis a nation? What do they- cost in health; what do they cost for the maintenance of machinery to prevent the crime that is bred there; what do they cost in the general deterioration of the productive capacity of the whole community? It is not something you can measure accurately, but the actual losses sustained from those conditions are infinitely greater than would be the amount of money required to remove them.
I want now to plead with the government and the minister that this excellent programme, as far as it goes, be strengthened and made much better by carrying it along to the point of taking power to cooperate with tfye province of Quebec, for example, and the group of municipalities making up the great city of Montreal, in order to do a real job in improving conditions in that great Canadian city- which will become greater as the years go by -to make it a model, and to carry that programme clear across the whole of Canada, from Montreal to the Pacific and from Montreal to the Atlantic. The federal government should embark upon a programme of that kind, for the federal government is the only authority that has power to create the money that can and must be employed if that sort of undertaking is to be pursued. You see, no municipality has a Bank of Canada. No provincial government has any power to raise money other than by taxation. We in Ottawa, in the federal parliament, can raise money by borrowing; we can raise money by taxing; we can raise money by issuing Bank of Canada notes, or we can raise money by borrowing bank deposits. Here we have power to create and issue the money of the people of Canada; and for some parts of the programme, such as the one I am discussing at the moment, we [DOT]must find some way of financing other than by borrowing, which is merely deferring taxation, or by direct taxation because throughout Canada to-day we have in our municipalities a level of taxation that has converted a large part of our investments in municipal real estate from investments to liabilities. I do not know of a city in this country, unless there be one or two of the very small ones, that has any reserve of taxing power; in fact they have all levied taxes far in excess of the actual value of the property itself. So that if all we are going to have in the way of slum clearance is this $20,000,000, then as far as slum clearance is concerned, as far as any improvement in the poor conditions that exist throughout our Canadian cities is concerned, one of the hopes for the post-war period can now be abandoned.

I went into the idea of establishing community centres of the kind I have described. Of course they would vary in cost. Take a community such as Ottawa; probably you would have to build a dozen or more such centres. In Vancouver we would have to build a much larger number, but the lowest cost at which I could arrive, using the most ordinary equipment, was in the vicinity of $150,000 per unit. To do it as it should be done would cost probably $500,000 per unit. Then, to bring all these various centres under one common centre, where you could have playgrounds, theatres, general stadia affording facilities for competitions, and that sort of thing, would cost a very large sum. I should say that in my own city of Vancouver it would cost a good many million dollars to do that job right, at least somewhere in the vicinity of $10,000,000. Why, we have no more chance of raising that $10,000,000 from real estate taxes, or from any reserve of taxation that may be left to that community, than we would have of flying to the moon. The taxable resources are not there, but the unfortunate living conditions that should be remedied may be found everywhere in that young Canadian city.
It is a remarkable thing that men can think in terms of putting up $60,000,000 for a battleship which can be sunk in ten minutes; but when you come along and say that you would like to have $10,000,000 invested in the city of Vancouver to improve the living conditions of the children particularly and the people generally, men will shudder at the idea of giving a community that kind of protection, which is better than the protection given by a battleship in time of peace and even better than the protection given by a battleship where it may .mean the winning of a war. Why should it be that only under pressure of war do men move to find the means for protecting the life of the state? What is more important in the life of the state than the standard of living of the people? In raising and protecting that standard the government performs its full function. But oh, no; we must have some financial complex about these things. We have to be smart business men when we are in the Department of Finance; we have to stand up and say, "We are careful and cautious; we do not put money out here unless we are sure it is going to come back. We have made some investments in the provinces, and now we find them reluctant to pay them back, even though the bond has been signed." Well, we appointed the Sirois commission to look into this housing situation, and to look into provincial and municipal powers to finance obligations which the dominion government had imposed upon

Housing
them. The Sirois commission's report made a definite recommendation that the time had come when the whole programme of financing provinces should be revised, because provincial and municipal governments did not have the means to carry out programmes of slum clearance, and a great many other things.
I regret that this housing bill had to come before the house at this late date in the session, because it involves one of the most important phases of our post-war programme, not merely because we should take advantage of the opportunity afforded to improve life in our cities, but because it is in that field that probably the largest measure of unemployment relief is to be found.
Would it not be possible for the government to provide under this measure at least the power to work out those schemes of improving our cities? Let me plead on this basis: Will not the federal government assume and recognize that life in the cities is the very root of Canadian democracy? If it deteriorates and goes down, it cannot help having a serious effect upon the life of the nation. Would not the government recognize, with its superior financial power and strength, that there is a great, growing, national need in which it can serve, in full cooperation? If it is prepared to go as far as it has gone, to the length of saying that children should be given $9 a month to guarantee that they receive the right kind of food, surely it will follow along the same principle and say that in the "east ends" and in slum areas not only should those children have clean milk, and enough of it, but should have the right kinds of playgrounds and environment, the right kind of air in their schools and in their homes.
Does anyone believe for one moment that to do that kind of thing is beyond the capacity of the people of Canada? Will anyone say that there is a member in this chamber, or a citizen in the dominion, who would suggest that we shall not have the men available in the coming post-war period to build those playgrounds, swimming tanks and gymnasia? Does anyone believe for one moment that we shall not have enough instructors to administer those playgrounds? Out of the army alone we shall have back, this time, between 600 and 800 of the most highly-trained physical instructors the Dominion of Canada has ever had.
What are you going to do with them? Does anyone think for one moment that we shall not have the materials? Are we to revert, as we are reverting under this $20,000,000 programme, to where we were in 1936, with idle men, idle materials and jobs crying to be done, because somebody in the Department of Finance has said, "Oh, if you issued $50,000,000 to the Bank of Canada that would be inflation,"
or, "If you issue $200,000,000 to the Bank of Canada that would be inflation." Are we to go back to that kind of nonsense again, or are we to shudder under a load of debt we have piled up, and say that we have won the war from the aggressor and lost the nation to the debt dealer?
That kind of thing is not going to go on when this war is over. And if this government thinks for one moment that it will be allowed to fail to accept its responsibility for slum clearance, and its responsibility for the betterment of conditions throughout Canadian cities, it is making a very serious mistake. It is making a mistake in the light of a magnificent programme where cost seems not to have been of the least concern. And I would judge from the remarks of the minister this afternoon that we have not heard the best of it yet. That is still to come. Shades of the Hon. Charles Dunning I We have $200,000,000 for this; $300,000,000 for that-and we total it up and find that hardly a day goes by that we do not appropriate at least $100,000,000, or more! Why, they scared the living daylights out of the editorial department of the Ottawa Morning Journal by bringing in an appropriation in one week that totalled $1,200,000,000- and all for the betterment of the people of Canada!
What a pity it is that there are just a few little things we cannot seem to digest! Two hundred million dollars for family allowances- and $20,000,000 for slum clearances! If we can give $200,000,000 for family allowances, then we ought to be able to give $200,000,000 for family homes, and for the environment around family homes that will make that $9 a month we are giving the children a real national investment.

The hon. member for
Vancouver-Burrard has made his usual attack upon the Department of Finance. He has been doing so throughout the whole session in the banking and commerce committee, and out of it; and I have got to the place where I must say publicly that I resent it. I am not speaking now in defence of myself. Rather, I am offering a few words in defence of departmental officials of the Department of Finance.
This afternoon the hon. member said that we spend $200,000,000 for this and $300,000,000 for that, and a billion for this and a billion for that-and that is admirable! Apparently the Department of Finance is functioning well when it spends or consents to the expenditure of these very, very large sums of money. He says, "If you can do that for one thing, you can do it for everything. There is no reason why you cannot, do it for everything, because you have the Bank of Canada to turn on the printing presses and turn out the money."
That is his argument. Then, with regard to the $20,000,000 for slum clearance he asks, "How is this figure arrived at?" I can say it was not arrived at on any basis of compilation or calculation. We thought that if the plan under this measure worked out, if the municipalities and the provinces were interested in it, we could very well increase the amount by further appropriations, just as further appropriations have been made in the past for purposes of the old housing act. If it does not work, then we shall have to resort to something else or adopt some other scheme. I do not know; there is not much reason why it should not be $50,000,000 instead of $20,000,000. if that would, make it look any better, but I do not believe that between now and next spring we shall have any opportunity to. spend more than $20,000,000. This summer, this fall and this winter there will be very little slum clearance take place because of the tremendous shortage of materials and labour in the country, as is known to every one. I am not going into this question of the unlimited, indefinite availability of what is called debt-free money.

I am prepared to deal with that. I heard the hon. gentleman state in the banking and commerce committee what he would have done during the war and what he would do in the peace to come. It is surprisingly little different from what we have done or what we are prepared to do. When the hon. gentleman comes down from the heights of oratory to the valleys of practicability he has to admit that we have done about what any intelligent group of persons would do. Other countries have financed the

war much as we have. They have financed it by taxation to the extent of the capacity of their peoples to pay, as we have done in this country. They have even borrowed to the extent of their ability to borrow from the public, as we have done with great success. Then, for a comparatively small and insignificant margin they have borrowed either from the central bank or from the chartered banks, depending upon which they thought was the best way to borrow. I am prepared to argue that the manner in w'hich we have borrowed has been to the advantage of this country as compared with the alternative method of borrowing from the Bank of Canada.
I do not want the people of this country to get the impression that it does not make any difference the amount you borrow from the Bank of Canada, that it does not make any difference how much money you turn out on the printing presses of the government. That is the oldest of all fallacies; that is the oldest of all exploded nostrums, the idea that you can turn out money indefinitely. Let people read the history of the French revolution. Let them read the speeches of those eloquent gentlemen like Mirabeau himself, who advocated the issue of assignats. Each issue was argued for as being-

I am not arguing and I do not say that a moderate expansion of the credit base is not feasible. That is what we have done during the war and before the war. There was a steady improvement in conditions between 1934 when the Bank of Canada came into existence and 1939. The steady improvement in employment figures and farm and wage incomes and so on was parallel to the expansion of the credit base during those years. I do not say that that should not be done after the war; but this idea that it can be done to an unlimited extent and that because we spend $200,000,000 here and $200,000,000 there we should spend $200,000,000 on everything, and that we are nibbling down and displaying a finance department complex and all that kind of thing simply because we

do have some caution, at times,-that I say is an idea which is most dangerous for this country.
As I say, I think $20,000,000 is all right for the time being, but so far as I am concerned the $20,000,000 may be increased for this purpose later on. It is the one place in the legislation where perhaps the amount might have been larger, but the bill provides and contemplates a large expenditure of money and I think we had better continue with that as it is now. As I say, if we cannot get along with the $20,000,000, we can supplement it at another session of parliament.
Mr. MeGEER: There is one comment I should like to make in reply to the minister. I have never suggested that there is no limit to the amount of money that you can use simply because you have the power to print money. I am not unfamiliar with the history of John Law and the assignats. As a matter of fact I am not unfamiliar with the history of money as it has been written from the dawn of civilization.

I wonder if we cannot try to stick to the resolution?
Mr. MeGEER: Yes, we will stick to this. When a nation has the power to create money and the creation of money stands between the removal of slums and the continuance of slums, then there must be something wrong with a nation that will refuse to create money to be used to improve a condition that should be improved and would make for the betterment of the community at large. I resent the suggestion that I have no understanding of the problem of maintaining balanced finance in the community. I have listened to men talk about the security of money under the gold standard, and that has gone by the board. That was the only thing that was fought for two hundred years ago in France and during the civil war. We have abandoned that kind of thing and to-day we are operating on a straight managed paper standard. We have proved in this war that we can carry on an enormous programme of inflation and still maintain a balanced economy; we have proved that prices can be held comparatively easily.
I am glad the minister admits that this is one place where the figure might be larger. Let me draw the attention of hon. members to one important thing that he said. He said that this figure was arrived at because it was thought it would be enough, without any survey or computation being made; it was just picked out of the sky.

How do you know
that?
Mr. MeGEER: The minister said so. I think I am right.
Mr. IiLSLEY: We did not make a survey, we did not circularize the municipalities to consult them on the policy and find out how much they would take.
Mr. MeGEER: As a matter of fact the municipalities had already been before the reconstruction committee and had laid a great deal of information before that committee of this parliament. If you had appointed a committee of competent architects and engineers who could have been secured in the areas affected you could have had a complete story of what should be done and what was needed to be done. You could have laid out, not a one year or a next spring programme, but a five or ten year programme.
That has been done in the United States and it is one of their great reconstruction programmes. Every city in the United States has been surveyed and a report made of the total cost. Planning has been made over a long period of time. I think it is important for this committee to know just what it is hoped may be started on that phase of the housing scheme. But it certainly is no indication that there is any real policy or plan. How can these things be financed if they are not to be financed with Canada's national currency? We cannot go on much longer piling up debts for war, or for war on slums. We have come to about the limit of that kind of financing which says that it is fine to use a printing press to issue national debt but unsound to use a printing press to issue national legal tender currency. If we insist on sustaining this debt-claim system, we are putting our feet in the path that led Europe to disaster; make no mistake about that. If you think there is any soundness in piling up debts at the rate of two and three billion dollars a year, which comes down to nothing more or less than this, that you are making promises you cannot keep by issuing promises that you do not intend to keep; if that is sound, all I will say is that it has not been found sound in any other country that has been forced in due course to come to flat repudiation and all the disasters that have afflicted those countries which have gone on blindly believing that they can accumulate over the nation a burden of debt that no individual will accept.
Where is the man in Canada who will say that it is healthy for him individually to be under a load of individual debt? No one will agree with that. Yet we are now called upon

to believe that the thing that is bad for us individually, is going to be good for us collectively, and because we are a little afraid now that we are getting our debts too high, we cannot clear slum conditions within the cities of Canada. I think we can do that, and I think we can do it without increasing debts. I think we can do it through a wise policy of national cooperation with our provinces and municipalities and by a wise administration of our managed paper currency, which is now the only basis of money that we have in the Dominion of Canada.
