I would think that this phase of the resolution and this phase of the legislation is really much more important, than the phase of helping the lending companies in financing homes at a profit. That seems to be where we have rather lost our balance in the housing legislation. We seem to think that if we bolster up the lending companies and associate with them by way of guarantees making it possible for them to lend more, even though the rate of interest is reduced, that is the major part of the government's

participation in housing. Here is one particular issue on which I disagree with the Department of Finance. I think it is far more important for the Department of Finance to cooperate with the municipal and provincial governments in doing a public job, in building better schools, better houses and better community surroundings. If the government goes ahead and does that part of the job and maintains the national income, and does it without too great a burden of taxation, it will be found that people are able to build their own homes without having to pay any interest at all. I know a great many young fellows in my own part of the country who saved up their money-school-teachers or mechanics- and built their own homes in the evenings and on their holidays and never paid a dime of interest to anybody. That does not apply to everybody, but I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that that is the type of people who make the very best kind of citizens. This thing of piling up a load of interest-bearing debt where a man pays out in interest more than he pays for the land and materials and the labour that goes into his house is just the kind of thing that has carried whole communities to disaster. Why should the Department of Finance become, as it is rapidly becoming, the mainstay, the main support, the helping hand, the guiding light and the guardian angel of all the debt-piling bodies in Canada? That is where we are going to on this housing legislation. All the way through it is helping the financial organizations.

I do not think so. I think slum clearance and allied subjects are on the list of questions to be taken up at the dominion-provincial conference, where agreement will have to be reached on some phases

Housing
of the matter with the provinces and municipalities. This particular provision in this bill is not a slum clearance proposal nearly so much as it is a housing proposal. Slum clearance here is merely incidental to the other provisions of the bill which provide that a low dividend housing corporation or a life insurance company may undertake a project and, if it does, it may do so under the terms set out in the bill. If it is a low dividend corporation the dominion government will lend ninety per cent of the cost of the project at three per cent on certain conditions, the conditions being that the low dividend corporation can make no capital gain out of the venture, that the rates of return will be limited to five per cent. The financial resources of municipalities are wholly inadequate for any large-scale post-war public works programme such as probably will be required.

This, even presuming that the fiscal and tax reforms urged in the earlier section of this memorandum, have been implemented. For, taking a realistic view of the situation, it is apparent that the volume of financing required for the kind of a post-war public works programme likely to be needed is completely beyond the limited revenue or credit resources of local and/or provincial governments.
Moreover, the scope of the problem-urban reconstruction-has gone far beyond the proportions of a mere local responsibility. It is a matter affecting virtually all the urban communities, and involves more than half the population of the country. Only the fiscal capacity of the federal government will be adequate for the task in hand. The question as we see it is not whether the federal government will assume the responsibility, but rather, on what terms, and what conditions, and for what kind of local public works.
It is not our responsibility to put forward or recommend a specific proposal concerning federal financing of local public works. The federal government in due course will announce its own policy in this regard.
In general however, we believe:
1.	The federal government should stand ready to extend loans to local governments at the lowest possible interest rates, and for extended periods, consistent with the nature of the specific project for which the money is required.
2.	In some instances it will be in the national as well as the local interest for the federal government to make an outright grant to cover in whole or in part the cost of certain kinds of local public works.
3.	The proposal, referred to earlier in this memorandum, for the matching with federal dollars of post-war municipal reserve funds earmarked for "approved public works" has much to commend it.
4.	The principles incorporated in the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, 1938, whereby the federal government financed, at low interest rates, self-liquidating local improvements, are sound, and might well form the basis for an extended national improvement act for post-war reconstruction.
5.	We agree with the proposition that federal government financing of local public works or housing should be restricted to those municipalities having a master town plan.
6.	We believe there is point to the suggestion that the federal government should encourage the preparation of local public works plans by agreeing to underwrite the cost of preparing the detailed plans for public works projects which have been mutually agreed upon as being potentially possible and desirable, whether or not the project is eventually proceeded with.
Such a procedure would permit the accumulation of a shelf of possible local post-war construction reserves, adequate for any eventuality, without unduly burdening the limited financial resources of local communities with1 the cost of preparing expensive detailed plans. The cost of preparing the plans would of course be a charge against any project eventually proceeded with.

Before we take up these sections one by one I should like to make a few comments. I have seen the reprinted copy of the bill, with the amendments made in committee. While I suppose very seldom in our parliamentary history has a bill been given the lengthy consideration this bill was given in committee; while I personally found it impossible, because of duties here and elsewhere, to attend the meetings of that committee with any great regularity, I have tried to read most of the transcripts of the proceedings there. I find those proceedings so lengthy that it is indeed rather difficult to sift through them, but certain matters of fundamental and outstanding importance were brought before the committee during this lengthy inquiry.
In m.y opinion this inquiry has been, most important because of the implications of our banking system in relation to our post-war

problems. Most of the time was spent in going into the report of the Bank of Canada and hearing evidence from the governor of the bank, the minister, the deputy minister and other officials, as well as representatives of the banks, largely based on the material brought before the committee or perhaps I should say brought out in evidence by the committee from the governor of the Bank of Canada and other witnesses. Two or three things struck me forcibly. Hon. members will recall that in his report as governor of the Bank of Canada Mr. Towers said that a million more persons than in 1939 will have to find employment in the immediate post-war period. Later on in his evidence before the committee he said, as will be found at page 84 of the proceedings, that one and a 'half million more persons will be available for civilian employment than are employed in the sector of civilian employment at the present time. He meant when we come to the period of demobilization following the war. This entails, of course, a tremendous financial and economic problem; and if we are to solve that problem it means that we must engage in vastly increased production or that we must spread the production out over a vastly greater number of people, which means new social and economic problems. At the same time, as that is spread out over more people by shortening hours or in some other way, if we reach the stage where we are producing greater quantities of goods, it involves the distribution also of increased purchasing power and, as Mr. Towers pointed out, a very high level of new capital investment. It is that about which I wish to say something this evening. At page 85 of the transcript of evidence Mr. Towers suggested that we shall require the enormous sum of one and a half billions of dollars of new investment a year, indefinitely, if we are to maintain a national income of the present high level, or approaching the present high level of about seven and a half billions of dollars annually. That is the annual investment he said would be required in order to maintain full employment. This is found at page 85 of the transcript of evidence taken before the committee on banking and commerce.
What has struck me throughout, when we were dealing with these enormous figures and were faced with the enormous problems these figures involve, in terms of goods, services and distribution, was simply this:	Is it possible
for our present system of private enterprise to accomplish all this?
Another point which was brought out clearly in the committee was this:	Surveys show
that it is unlikely that private enterprise

Bank Act Amendment
itself will be able to carry this tremendous load. I wonder too if it might not be unwilling to carry that obligation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS

He said:
It has been estimated that the maintenance of .full employment after the wrar would require capital investment of one and a half billions per annum. There are inevitable qualifications to such estimates; but they are intended to and do serve the purpose of giving us a general idea of the magnitude of the problem.
I think that was taken to be an estimate.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Yes, it was. But I think Mr. Towers, in placing that before the committee, did so with his personal approval. That is perhaps a minor detail in the discussion. However, I am glad the minister mentioned it, because I do not wish to quote Mr. Towers as having said anything he did not actually say. But at least the James committee gave that impression.
In the last couple of months some interesting surveys have been made which have a bearing on this problem. One survey deals directly with the banking problem. On May 29 of this year the Financial Post published a survey of 2,400 of the largest manufacturing concerns across Canada. In those 2,400 manufacturing concerns were included eight of our major industries. The Financial Post listed them as follows:	Animal products, including
packing, and so on; vegetable products, including canning, dehydration and the like; textiles; wood; paper; iron and steel; non-ferrous metals, and non-metallic minerals. Those are eight of our major industries in Canada.
The Financial Post showed that the 2,400 industries combined created one-seventh of the entire national income in 1939. They were asked what they thought they could invest in capital outlay immediately following the war, and the figure they gave for the three years after the war was an average of $106,000,000 a year. That is, they estimate that they will spend approximately one-fifteenth of the one and a half billion dollars that the James committee suggested is required after the war to maintain full employment.
Let us bear in mind, too, that the survey indicates clearly that they feel they can invest this $106,000,000 annually, only provided that there is an, attempt made to maintain both full employment, and a high level of export trade.^ Hon. members will recall that the other day when discussing the family 100-378i
allowances I made the statement that the social security measures were to be welcomed.
I pointed out, however, that we were erecting a. superstructure of expenditures on social security measures without laying, first of all, an economic foundation. I am, not suggesting that those social security measures should wait until we lay that economic foundation; but I am suggesting when we are considering social security measures we ought at the same time to be considering also the economic foundations upon which they must depend.
My criticism of this bill, as it comes from the committee, is that it fails to take into account these problems, and to lay the financial foundations which in my opinion are necessary to meet the grave problems which will arise shortly. I say, "shortly", because I hope that we are nearing the end of this great war.	-	'
If the Financial Post survey in in any measure correct, it means that somebody, somehow, has to fill the tremendous gap between $106,000,000 and the one and a half billions we require for capital investment annually. Of course there are many other industries, many other manufacturing concerns in the country which will invest in capital expenditures after the war. But when we consider that the big industries which were surveyed were able to see expenditures only to the amount I have indicated to the committee, then it becomes obvious at once that at very best there will be, in any event, a tremendous gap which the government itself will have to fill.
This nation, then, has to look forward to the making of very large expenditures in order to maintain anything approaching full employment. Sometimes I am asked, and quite properly, "What is your definition of full employment?" There are a great many definitions. Sir William Beveridge gave one which was quoted in the house the other day. But the simplest definition I know is that full employment means that every able and willing worker has an opportunity to do productive work at a reasonable level of income. That being so, the government has two functions in this respect. First, it must finance useful projects to create necessary employment and second, it must distribute adequate purchasing power in order that the products of industry may be distributed among the people.
As I have read the evidence given before the committee on banking and commerce, the thought that has struck me is that under the present financial system, under the system this bill maintains, mounting indebtedness to the
Bank Act Amendment

private banks must be involved. The government must sell bonds or other securities, treasury certificates and the like, to private banks, in exchange for bank credits which create a deposit against which the government writes cheques in order to meet many of its obligations and expenses. No matter what our views are regarding banks and banking, I think that looking back over the last few years we have been struck by the growth of the government's indebtedness to the private banks. This has increased sharply in the last fifteen years, or since 1930. It seems that whether it is during a peace-time depression or a wartime prosperity the trend has been the same. Not only has it been the same, but what I think is equally important, it has been continuous, whether in the pre-war depression or in the present unhealthy war prosperity. I think the statistics prove this assertion.
Let us look for a moment at the statistics, and again I refer to the evidence before the banking and commerce committee. The Bank of Canada statement shows that the bank holdings of dominion and provincial securities rose from S316 million in 1930 to $1,234 million in 1939. That was a sharp increase. But by the end of 1943 they had risen to $2,627 million. What is equally significant is that they comprised almost one-half of the total assets of all our chartered banks. This creation of debt on the part of the public to the private financial institutions also creates an exceedingly dangerous situation in which there may be, in the postwar period particularly, the thing which we call inflation.
We were told before the banking and commerce committee that loans and securities created bank deposits, and that bank deposits constitute from ninety to ninety-five per cent of our medium of exchange, namely the available cheque money. An attempt, and a very successful one, has been made during this war by means of victory loans to draw off a good deal of purchasing power which might otherwise have punched the price ceiling. But in spite of our victory loans drawing off a considerable amount of purchasing power from our people, bank deposits have risen-I will use round figures-from over $2,000 million before the war to something like $4,500 million at the present time. Apparently full employment under the present financial system cannot be achieved without an increasing accumulation of debt to the private financial interests and at the same time a grave threat of inflation to the country.

But in any event there was a considerable increase to $4,500 million. The facts conveyed by that statement constituted the paradox which faced the committee and which occupied practically all its time. May I suggest that this bill offers no solution at all. Some amendments seeking to deal with the problem were offered, but they were rejected by the committee on the ground that they would hamstring the banks. No amendment or suggestion was adopted that, in my opinion, will meet the situation with which we are now faced.
I should like to mention the principal amendments that were rejected. The first was to prohibit the banks from dealing in government bonds and securities. The second was to maintain cash reserves of one hundred per cent against demand deposits. The third was to prohibit the banks from issuing demand deposits as a substitute for the lawful currency of Canada. Those were the three suggestions made, I think by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and the hon. member for Parry Sound. The fact that must have struck the committee-I know it struck me forcibly-was that apparently on the present basis the chartered banks could not operate without government business. That was the evidence given before the committee. I should like to quote the deputy minister's statement on July 18, as it appears on pages 1242 and 1243 of the evidence, when he said that the banks, if forced to give up their government securities, would go into the red several million dollars each year; that they would lose about $35 million in interest, which would more than wipe out their net earnings of $31,600,000 which they made last year, before taking care of losses or paying any shareholders' dividends.
That illustrates the degree to which the banks are dependent upon government business, public business, instead of private business, and I think it warranted the observation

Bank Act Amendment
made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard who is reported on page 1244 of the record as follows:
... if the banking business could not function as a private enterprise servicing private enterprise it must depend upon the earnings from public finance and public enterprise . . . then is it not pretty nearly time that they become recognized as an institution that had evolved into a state public utility that should be operated as such.
The evidence before the committee confirmed my opinion that this bill to extend the charters of the private banks should not be proceeded with, but that the banks should be made public utilities or, as we suggested on second reading of the bill, that they be nationalized. How they should be operated under a nationalized or socialized plan is a .natter which the committee could have gone into exhaustively had it been empowered to do so on the second reading. But we could not inquire into that particular suggestion, because the house had already rejected it, and therefore very little discussion of it occurred in committee.
Those are some of the few observations I wish to make on this particular bill at this time, but I wish to refer now to some of the amendments made and to say also that there are in the bill some new sections with which we are in hearty agreement. The amendment that would require the banks to disclose their inner reserves every ten years occupied several weeks of the time of the bank and commerce committee and was finally rejected on the advice of the minister. But the testimony before that committee brought out the fact that the banks can currently escape-I say currently escape-some of the excess profits taxes. The minister himself brought out the fact that two or three banks had set aside higher inner reserves than he thought were warranted, and he suggested ah amendment which would meet that situation in the future. I want to say to the minister that his contention that publication of the inner reserves would shake public confidence in our banks and banking system was not a good reason.

But the total effect was that a rate, as he gave it, of 11-781 per cent was charged. That is given at page 381 of the evidence. I found it difficult to follow the minister's reasoning when he urged the committee to drop subsection 2 of section 91 on the ground that it could not be defined in language sufficiently clear to leave no loopholes for the banks. It did not seem to me that it was beyond the powers of the legal advisers of the government and the clever draftsmen who frame so much of our legislation to find language that would block the loopholes and also prevent small loans from being charged an effective rate of interest that was considered too high. That there is a necessity for these small loans from the chartered banks I think no one will dispute. I think they have served, so far as they have gone, a very useful purpose in spite of the charges-I will not use the term "interest rate"-that have been made. People without collateral often need a small loan of two or three or four or five hundred dollars for an operation or something of that sort or because of sickness, and the banks have been making these loans, but what I think is serious is that they have been making them at an effective rate of interest higher than the rate of interest allowed by the act and in that sense have been practically doing something that is not legal under our legislation. Unfortunately the bill as now before the

committee does not meet this need of the borrower for a small loan or legalize the methods used by the banks.
In my opinion the necessities of the postwar situation to which I referred at the outset of my remarks do not- warrant the renewal of the bank charters for ten years. This bill ought not to be adopted with that clause in it at the present time. Why? Because many new economic developments will have to be faced in the near future. As I remarked earlier, we have just adopted in this, house a necessary but expensive social security programme. We have accumulated during this war an exceedingly heavy debt, and while interest rates are much lower than they were on the war debt at the end of the last war, nevertheless those debt charges constitute a tremendous burden upon this country of
11,500,000	people. As I suggested earlier, because of the gaps that may be found through the inability or unwillingness of private enterprise to assume certain risks and do certain jobs, we shall have to make very large governmental expenditures for projects which we must undertake as a nation in order to meet the needs of our people.
All this, Mr. Chairman, will certainly require significant changes in our fiscal policy, and this means that we have to face significant changes in our banking policy. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle to limit the life of the charters to the next two years was before the committee and voted down. I supported that motion and will do so again, although I felt we would have been much wiser to have extended the charters just now, pending further parliamentary investigation or even investigation, suggested by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, by royal commission, for just one year instead of two years; because a royal commission could go into more phases of banking policy and the proposals regarding banking than our narrower terms of reference and the vote in the house would allow us to do.
But this proposal for a two-year extension was rejected by the committee who, I think, were probably persuaded, many of them, to vote against it because they believed that the parliament of Canada had at all times the power to review the charters whenever it so wished. This bill, however, is regarded by a good many people as a contract between this parliament and the banks. It requires the consent of gentlemen in another place-gentlemen who are not elected to parliament but who are appointed for life-and before it could be reopened their consent would be necessary; and it is not impossible that they

Bank Act Amendment
might object, indeed they might withhold their consent, to the reopening of the question of bank charters at any time within the next ten years.

I will not say what I was going to say, because once or twice when I have expressed myself with regard to the other place I have been accused of making threats and I do not like to be accused of making threats. I think, however, it is altogether likely that we would have some difficulty in that direction.
Some members of the banking and commerce committee were frankly of the opinion, an honest opinion, that the banks had done a good job and should be left alone to continue that job for another ten years. I do not agree with that. One hon. member, however, gave what I thought was an interesting reason for binding the country to a ten-year contract with the banks. He felt that there were dangerous trends in the country that threatened the existing banking system, and he said:
Let us renew these charters for ten years and fortify to the limit of our capabilities against the disruption of the banking system of Canada.
That will be found at page 1496 of the evidence. When I heard that-and I did happen to hear it-I thought this was a clear demand upon this parliament that we tie the hands now not only of this parliament, which is in its dying days, which, according to the Prime Minister, will not go beyond, we will say, next April or May, but also the hands of the parliament which the people of Canada may elect to succeed this one. I say that an attempt to do that kind of thing is wrong because it tends to thwart the will of the people, and such an attitude is not in conformity with the democracy we are at the present time fighting to preserve.
Those are the principal comments I wish to make on the bill at this time. It will be readily seen, from what I have said already, that we oppose this bill because we do not believe it to be in the best interests of the people of Canada. It is binding the country to the same kind of financial economic system which we had before the war and which has been found wanting, and thus we cannot support this bill to extend the charters of the banks for another ten years.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
I think It might be well to review the history of the bill which is before the committee. It is, of course, the bill that renews the charters
of the commercial banks for the traditional period of ten years. The resolution preceding the reference of the bill and the proposed amendments to the committee on banking and commerce was discussed in the house and the general principles embodied in the bill were approved by this house. When the bill reached the committee on banking and commerce the task assigned to the committee was, of course, within the principle which the house had approved, to give the consideration, with care and deliberation, to the proposed amendments. The task was further to consider any other amendments or suggestions that came before the committee, generally with the purpose of improving the bill itself and the operations of the chartered banks.
I come from western Canada, and it is common knowledge that we in the west have believed for many years that financial wealth and therefore financial control and direction have been centralized too much in eastern Canada. We remember the happenings in western Canada during the period of the great depression that had such a terrible impact on the economy of the three western provinces. In addition it has been my lot in life to champion without exception the cause of the consumer and the producer class in this country; therefore I do not appear before this committee as the champion of any large corporate enterprise as such. In all the research work that I have had an opportunity of doing and in all the committees that I have taken part in I have attempted to maintain at least a balanced mind with regard to the matters under deliberation and not to adopt the attitude of wholesale condemnation in order to correct some of the things that should be corrected in the banking or other systems of this country.
In the course of the committee's many sittings dealing with this particular bill I took the opportunity of bringing to the committee and to the representatives of the chartered banks some of the criticism that I thought should be levelled at the past record of the chartered banks, particularly in western Canada. For instance, I pointed out that I found that, when the depression period emerged, the banks pursued too restrictive, a policy particularly toward the small borrower and producer in this country. That was partly brought about by the necessity of the banks putting themselves in a liquid position to meet possible demands and their inability to realize on larger loans made in eastern Canada for the development of more or less large corporate concerns. I felt that in pursuing that policy to the extent that they did the banks
Bank Act Amendment

had failed to discharge their primary function, namely, lending to take care of the current business of this nation, and that had they not been involved in large loans to large corporations they might have pursued a less restrictive policy toward the farmers of western Canada and, I presume, elsewhere when the depression came upon us.
Then I suggested that the banks in periods not necessarily of inflation but in boom times are inclined to follow the crowd and to make unwise expansions in lending policy. .1 hope the banks have learned a lesson and will apply the lesson and see to it that their policy in the future is a more temperate one in order to check boom conditions and in order to do what they should do to check the effects of depressions 'when they come about. In addition to that I pressed the banks to realize that they are national institutions, and that wherever they do business they should realize the conditions under which the producer in that particular area has to carry on his business. I was speaking particularly of the western farmer. The western farmer has long ago discovered, as we all have who have resided in that section for any length of time, that the words "annual business" is not a proper term to apply to the type of business the western farmer has to carry on because of climatic conditions. It therefore seems to me that any banking system must in its banking policy take into consideration the conditions under which its borrowers must carry on their business, and that the period of the loan and the time of repayment should not necessarily be one year, but should be that period in which a reasonably good farmer attempting to discharge his obligations can reasonably be expected to repay the loan he has obtained from the banks. In other words, I believe that the chartered banks must reach a decision. Either they must decide that they are not national in their lending policy, that they do not believe that western Canada offers a fair field for their banking activities, and that therefore they are withdrawing, or they must recognize the conditions under which the farmers of western Canada are operating and fit their banking policy to discharge that national duty toward that particular class of borrower.
As I listened in the committee to the statements of the senior officials of the chartered banks, it did appear to me that they are attempting to fit their banking policy into the actual conditions which we know in a given period of time obtain in western Canada. These were the criticisms that I thought were fair

and proper to bring to the attention of the committee and of the officials of the banks when they appeared before us. But may I say, Mr. Chairman, that these criticisms did not blind me to the fundamentals of the Canadian picture with regard to the necessity of commercial banking institutions. The record of the Canadian banks when compared with that of any other banking system in the world is a record that by and large we can take the greatest pride in. I hold in my hand a statement of the chairman of the reserve bank of the United States which draws attention to the fact that in the period of the depression in the United States, the same period that I have referred to as the thirties- some 9,700 United States banks failed. There is not one hon. member who has lived as long as members of the House of Commons have lived who cannot imagine the terrific disaster that came to so many communities in that great country to the south as a result of those failures. In addition to that a great many other banks had to be saved by the action of the President of the United States in declaring a bank holiday. In other words, when we compare the record of our Canadian banks and the practices under which that banking system is operated with the record of the banks in the friendly country to the south of us which is economically very much like our own, we realize that the Canadian banks have a record that merits a great deal of approval so far as the safety of those banking institutions is concerned.
What are the primary purposes of a commercial banking system in a country such as ours? I think it is obvious that it is wise and proper to have safe depositories for" the savings of the people. It is wise and proper, and in my opinion necessary, to have commercial banks to carry the current accounts or the checking accounts of the business men and the people of this nation, and to act as a clearing-house for the vast multitude of business operations that are settled between individuals every day in this country. The banks, of course, have performed that function for this nation. Then there are other services that the banks perform in the ordinary course of their banking business. One is a safe depository for valuable papers. We all know it is a very wise precaution for anyone who fears fire or other disaster to see to it that important documents are kept in a safe depository, and the banks give us that service at a very reasonable charge.
Until quite recently the banks discharged another important function. They were given the right, subject to taxation and certain

Bank Act Amendment
limitations, to issue our cash in the form of bills in denominations of $5 and upwards. For many years that was a valuable part of the business allotted to the banks under the aot. As hon. members know, however, it has been considered wise gradually to diminish the power of the banks to issue currency; that right is now being taken over by the Bank of Canada, and by 1950 the chartered banks will have lost that function and will no longer have the right to issue any part of the currency used in this country.
Then, as I have said, it is the function of the chartered banks to collect the savings of the people and, having collected them, to make those savings available by way of loan or by way of investment to individual or corporate enterprises in this country, of course subject to the limitations of the Bank Act as to the things in which the bank can invest and the security on which it can make loans. That, of course, is a very important function, and a very difficult one to discharge properly. Henry Mencken in his book, "The History of Religions", makes the point that the acceptance of the biblical ban upon usury, otherwise known as interest, held back the progress of the world for three or four hundred years, as he puts it. One can easily see that making available to productive enterprise the collective savings of the people has been a great agency in bringing about the great expansion of business that has taken place during the last two or three hundred years. The average individual would never think of making a loan, because the amount of money at his disposal would not be of very much use in any particular development. Through the agency of the chartered banks, however, on the one hand we provide a safe depository for the savings of the people and on the other we collect the results of their thrift and make it available at rates determined by parliament to the nation in order to develop and expand our commerce, add to the national income, increase the nation's wealth, and improve the welfare of the people as a whole.
There is one factor which I think is often overlooked but which I feel is of vital importance. The banks can exist and continue in business and discharge the duties we have imposed upon them by the Bank Act only as long as they are able to retain the confidence of the people. Confidence is the greatest asset any banking institution can have. That is why it seems to me that the founders of this nation were wise when they decided not to grant a monopoly to any bankers, but to see to it that the institutions which were given the right to collect the savings of the people and guarantee their safety, and to lend these collective savings to productive enterprise, were 100-379
such as would protect those savings as far as might be humanly possible. While the record of the Canadian banks has been good, it is unfortunately a fact that there have been failures. Quite a number of men have considered, as some do to-day, that the banking business is a bonanza; that by some formula one can easily grow wealthy if he merely succeeds in getting a charter under the terms of the Bank Act. The records, of course, show that those banks which departed from policies of reasonable safety in discharging the duties for which they were created and which were unable to retain the confidence of the people in their integrity, finally ended by being merged with or taken over by some other bank or went into bankruptcy, sometimes with the shareholders losing all the money they had invested.
Then, when one considers the widespread use our people make of the services offered by the Canadian banks I think we would be blind if we did not realize the necessity of maintaining some such institutions as the commercial banks of this country. More than four million of our people have deposits in the chartered banks amounting to less than $1,000 each. This shows the widespread use of the banks by those who have not great wealth. If we consider the deposits up to $5,000 each we find that the aggregate of such deposits is almost as great as that of deposits of under $1,000. And that figure of four million people does not represent all those who are interested directly or indirectly in these deposits. I recall that an hon. member who sat beside me in the committee said that in his family of four, consisting of himself, his wife and two young children, there was only one bank account, but that his wife and two children had as much interest in his account as he had. So that the number of those interested in the safety and well-being of these banking institutions could be multiplied considerably.
Our approach to the consideration of the renewal of the charters, I suggest, should be this. What functions are the banks supposed to perform? They are a quasi-public utility, as we all admit and as the banks agree. Having decided what those functions are-and I have tried to give them to the committee-then it seems to me our task is to decide whether or not those functions have been performed with reasonable efficiency and at reasonable cost to the nation. The hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, is not here at the moment, but he put the matter before the committee very plainly, and I agreed with him. In my opinion, after having followed very carefully indeed all the evidence presented by the officials of the banks, the governor of the Bank of Canada, the deputy minister and others, on the

Bank Act Amendment

whole, subject to the criticisms I have indicated, the banks have discharged the duties imposed upon them in a very efficient manner indeed. It was brought to our attention that in the year 1943, a comparatively good year for the banks and much above the average for the preceding fifteen years, the banks made a net return of only 6-03 per cent on the shareholders' equity. I submit to the hon. members of this committee that this is not an unreasonable return on that equity, and that, quite obviously the banks are not charging the people of Canada too much for the services that we think are necessary properly to conduct the country's commercial and financial business.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned some of the amendments which were dealt with by the committee, and which were approved and recommended to this committee of the whole house. One .was a reduction of the rate of interest from seven per cent to six per cent. That is a very real advance toward reducing the cost of money to those requiring to use bank services when borrowing money. It is only one per cent, but let us remember that one per cent is a very considerable reduction when one applies it to the total of the sums lent throughout this country by the chartered banks.
In addition, from the point of view of one who represents an agricultural constituency I was delighted, of course, to see the provision for encouraging loans to farmers at a rate of five per cent, for the purpose of making specified farm improvements.
I do not intend to go into detail in respect of this particular provision, but it, too, is an amendment to the Bank Act which should be of great value to the farming community. This type of loan has been encouraged by the government's undertaking to guarantee against loss in loans made to farmers for those specific purposes, and to the extent of ten per cent of the aggregate amount so lent, and limited by a total over-all amount.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to another amendment suggested by the minister, and that was the matter of small loans. While I do not think the hon. member meant to be unfair, yet I thought he did not deal quite correctly with the history of that amendment. As hon. members know, under the Small Loans Act, that type of loan is repayable on monthly instalments without security, and the rate is roughly two per cent a month. In order to make available a cheaper source of money the minister suggested that we include in the Bank Act a special section enabling the banks, if they saw fit to do so, to make loans on the same terms to the same

type of borrower at a final cost of approximately 9| per cent. The committee discussed that particular amendment at great length. The objection to it, expressed by a number of members, was that while everyone in the committee felt that we would be performing a very real service to the smaller income group needing loans of that kind, it would be difficult indeed to remove from the minds of the public the suggestion that the banks might include in that particular category farmers and others who would be entitled by other provisions of the bill to a lower rate of interest.
The minister reluctantly-he did not urge it -suggested that in view of the criticism it might be wise for the committee to consider withdrawing that particular amendment. I say to this committee that, in common with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I was very reluctant to agree to the withdrawal of that particular amendment. I must confess, however, I did agree with the minister that, in the light of the discussion, it was wise to do as he suggested. The basic thing we wished to accomplish was to assist in providing a source of loans to persons who must borrow under those conditions, at a lower rate of interest than is available to them from any other source. My opinion is that while the amendment was withdrawn, inevitably common sense will cause it some day to be put into the Bank Act, so as to encourage the banks to carry on that type of business.
There was another reason. We were advised that the Canadian Bank of Commerce and one other bank-I believe it was the bank of Montreal-were already carrying on this type of business, and within the terms of the Bank Act as at present framed. The committee noted that while we were withdrawing the amendment, the banks were undertaking voluntarily to attempt, under the terms of the Bank Act as amended, to carry on the very type of business we wished to encourage. So that was another important reason why we adopted somewhat reluctantly the suggestion that the amendment should be withdrawn. That is, the banks are experimenting in the field of small loans, and will accomplish the desired purpose of giving that class of borrower a cheaper source of money if, in an emergency, he needs it.
Then, we provided for a better system of returns to the inspector general. And in the matter of inner reserves, which was discussed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, an amendment was made to the effect that the Minister of Finance is now charged with a statutory duty to make a report to the Minister of National Revenue if he considers that the inner reserves are higher than necessary for the purposes for which they are kept.

Bank Act Amendment
This amendment is, of course, to make it clear that the chartered banks are not escaping the taxation from time to time imposed upon them by parliament.
I shall for the moment deal with the so-called inner reserves. They are sometimes called "inside reserves," and some who wish to criticize use the term "hidden reserves". As I listened to the evidence regarding these reserves I was convinced that the banks pursued the same policy as any large corporation pursues in the matter of its reserves. The only difference is that they are dealing with the value of loans rather than the value of inventory in the shape of stock or merchandise. These inner reserves are created, outside of that portion which is put into reserve through surplus realized from sale of its stock, by a proper evaluation of the assets each year. If some of the loans have an element of risk which would appear to lower their value, then the value of those loans is depreciated, and the difference between the total amount of the loans and the depreciated value constitutes these so-called inner reserves.
This is a perfectly proper system, guarding against risks which are inevitable in banking. Despite all the rumours and the discussion which has taken place on that particular item, in my opinion no one need fear in the least the setting up of inner reserves. It is a perfectly proper safeguard, and particularly on the part of an institution which must in our interests-not its own-maintain the confidence of the people in the integrity and safety of that institution in which the people's money is deposited.
In addition, I think it is not generally known that these banks do not operate without strict supervision. As we know, they have their own auditors and, in addition, they have shareholders' auditors. Those auditors are appointed to go over all the books of the banks. They have access to every bit of information, including that connected with inner reserves. The decision in respect of the choice of the shareholders' auditors is that of the Minister of Finance.
In addition to that, we have the inspector general, whose duty it is to keep fully informed as to the position of each of the banks, and as to all matters connected with the business of those institutions. Therefore we have a government official responsible to this parliament to see to it that there is a continuous check kept on the banking institutions of the country, so that the position of the depositors, the borrowers, the shareholders and the public may be protected. And, mark 100-3791
you, the public have a very real interest in the safety and welfare of these banking institutions.
As the work of the committee developed we left, I think unwisely, the task assigned to the committee by the house, that is, the consideration of bill No. 91 and the suggested amendments thereto, and we ranged far and wide into matters that had nothing to do with the Bank Act, matters that had to do with government financing and the general financial policy of this country. I should like to summarize briefly some of the suggestions that were made.
As every one knows, the C.C.F. stand for the socialization of the commercial banks of this country. I must commend the members of that particular group who were on the committee for recognizing that prior to the bill being sent to the committee the house had decided against them on the principle and therefore the committee was not the proper place again to press their theories that the banks should be nationalized. Yet we know that that is the declared policy of the C.C.F.
But I want to point out that the recognized policy of the C.C.F. is to nationalize the banks, not for the reason given to-night by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, but in order to secure the control over money and credit that will permit them to nationalize everything else that they may wish to nationalize. It is a means to an end, and that is the manner in which we must pass judgment upon the advocacy of nationalization by the C.C.F.
I am not going to deal at length with the Social Credit standing because with due deference to the members of that party I must admit that throughout the whole course of the committee I remained a little puzzled as to exactly what the Social Credit members wished to do with regard to the banking system of this country. Like us, they uphold the advisability of leaving the commercial banking business of the nation, particularly the lending part, in the hands of the present privately owned institutions. They feel, as we do, that under the Bank Act and under proper supervision the banks can perform much better and more efficiently the duties of a banking system than could a government-owned system.
In addition we had presented to us by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and the hon. member for Parry Sound certain theories that they held with regard to the financial policy that should be pursued by this country. I have not the time to go into the wide range of thought that was brought before the committee by those two members. The hon. member for Parry Sound suggested that
Bank Act Amendment

we should take over the $2,700 million of dominion securities now held by the banks and give the banks in lieu thereof Bank of Canada currency and provide for a one hundred per cent reserve to guard against inflation. He contended that that would be a great thing for this country.
As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar pointed out, it was made quite clear to us that if we followed the suggestion of the hon. member for Parry Sound, the interest that the banks would have lost by the taking away of the investment of the savings of their depositors in that type of security

it is the safest in the world and we want the banks to be safe in the matter of their investments- would have more than wiped out the total net earnings of the banks in 1943. In other words, we would have had to face the necessity of destroying our commercial banking system or force the banks into some other means of obtaining revenue. I think that would be unfair, unwise and inadvisable, and for this reason.
While all the people of this country through the medium of taxation, contribute to paying the interest on government securities, this would not be the case if we adopted the suggestion. Our taxes are raised on the principle that those who earn more should pay more than those who earn less. They are based on the measure of the income of the individual. If we attempted to take away this source of revenue from the banks and allowed the banks to add to their service charges, to the rates of interest on their loans and to other charges they might concoct in order to replace the revenues lost, this load would fall upon the little people, the people with small savings who use the banks in the way I have mentioned and on those who otherwise use the services provided by the banks. It would be quite inequitable. It would be transferring from the total population to a few-part of the load of carrying on the banking system of the country.
When I turn to the suggestions of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard I hesitate to attempt to give to this committee exactly the plan that he thinks necessary for the proper carrying out of the banking system of this dominion. I think, of course, that he is fearful of the debt load which has mounted steadily and to a considerable extent during the war years. However, I think all of us realize that this war has to be paid for in one way or another. It is the annual cost of carrying that debt and to whom the interest is payable that is important.
The record of the financial and banking practices of Canada during the war is some-

thing that we should be extremely proud of. What other country in the world can face the financial obligation of carrying on this war to victory with greater assurance? The financial policy pursued by this government, the integrity of our banking system has permitted us to carry on this unprecedented effort with the least strain of any country I know of. I consider, too, that we shall be able to face with confidence the post-war period and the problems which the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has properly raised. We shall be able to meet those problems and finance them with more courage and optimism than any other country. Credit for this is due to the elasticity of the financial policy and banking practices of this country and their ability to expand for any purpose. I believe that if there is any country in the world that can be reasonably proud of the financial policy that has been pursued and the banking system that is in vogue, it is Canada.
It emerged during the evidence before the committee that Australia tried the experiment of financing its war effort by the issue of national currency. They realized in fairness that when that national currency came to a bank in the shape of deposits, those deposits were not an asset of the bank. They became a liability and it cost the bank money to service them. They ran the risk of making the investments -and loans that we speak about, and, believe me, they are not without risk. That is one of the major mistakes it seems to me that is made by most people who consider this problem. Deposits are a liability of the bank, and it costs the bank considerable to service them.
When we consider the number of branch buildings, the rentals paid, the cost of maintenance, the staff, the risks of robbery and other risks incidental to the banking business it is obvious that the banks which in 1943. a good year, earned only 6-03 per cent, are not agencies for the creation of vast profits, as they are somtimes pictured to the people of this country. We do injury to ourselves when we do not make sure not to distort the facts.
I find myself in hearty agreement with the committee in reporting this bill as amended to the house. There was the question of the appointment of a royal commission to examine the questions raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and others. I do not believe anything emerged in the committee that would disturb my conviction that we have learned a great deal in the last two decades and we are applying what we learned to the banking system of this country.
There is prevalent, however, a widespread misunderstanding and a lack of appreciation of what is involved in such matters as the

Bank Act Amendment
government borrowing from the banks in order to carry on its business. I have mentioned Australia. After Australia made that experiment they found that in fairness they had to give to the Australian banks three-quarters of one per cent as a service charge for the service which the banks performed in connection with government policy, and by a coincidence that is exactly the rate which the Canadian government in the early part of this war arranged to pay to the Canadian chartered banks for the money which it borrowed. Because of this widespread misapprehension and misunderstanding of what is involved, while I would not say that I recommend the appointment of a royal commission I think it would be fair for me to say that I would recommend to the government the careful consideration of the appointment of a royal commission, if they can secure the proper personnel, to bring up to date the investigations made by the Macmillan commission in 1933 and to review the whole question of our banking and financial policy, and thus help to clear the minds of our people with regard to these matters.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make several observations before this measure carries. I do not believe that the committee should have recommended that the banks' charters be renewed for ten years. As the hon. member who has just taken his seat has indicated, I think there is great need for a careful and thorough investigation into the whole matter of the financial and economic system which is being pursued by Canada. In a country so bountifully endowed with natural resources as is the Dominion of Canada we ought not to have witnessed the spectacle of upwards of one million unemployed during the depression. It is argued by advocates of our existing financial system that what occurred in the depression years was a phenomenon which was in Canada largely the result of certain actions which had taken place outside Canada and that, therefore, Canada should not be held responsible entirely for the great depression. I listened with a great deal of interest to the evidence given in the committee and I failed to find any thoroughly satisfying reason why we should altogether accept that explanation. I cannot escape the conviction that if Canada had been entirely an island separated completely from the rest of the world it would have been possible to have devised and erected a financial and economic system in Canada which could at least have enabled the people of Canada to enjoy the results of the potential economic activities
of the people of this country. For example, if the people of Canada could produce all the milk that the people of Canada could possibly use, it ought to have been possible for us to enable all the people of Canada to have all the milk that they could use; and if that was not possible we ought to know the reason why. If the financial system of the country is not responsible for our inability to give the people of this country the means to use the goods we can produce, then we ought to know what is responsible.
Here was a country, Canada, in the depression, capable of producing all the enormous output which we have shown we were capable of producing, vast amounts of grains and foodstuffs of many different kinds, together with tremendous quantities of manufactured goods of one sort and another-a wrar effort which has commended the admiration if not the astonishment of practically the whole world, including ourselves-and the only reason for all this seems to be that we have been able somehow or another during this war to liberate into our body economic money and that we have been able to dispose of our products at reasonable prices, even if we had to give some of them away to the Germans. I submit that to any individual of ordinary intelligence that poses a problem which should challenge him to the greatest possible effort to explain why it was that whereas we could do the wonderful things we have done during this war, we could do nothing to put our people to work or keep them at work during the depression or at least supply them with the necessities of life.
I believe that the flaw lay in our economic system or in our financial system. I am not prepared to say that it was entirely the fault of the banks or of the banking system. But if it was not the fault of our banking system it was certainly the fault of some other aspect of our financial system. My feeling in the banking and commerce committee was that it would be an excellent thing for the committee to go into that whole matter and' find out what was the trouble. The majority of the committee thought I was wrong in that respect, but I still believe that the committee should devote a great deal of time to determine why it was that our banking system signally failed during the depression and why it was that we were unable to distribute the goods and services which we unquestionably were able to produce if we could have disposed of them at fair prices all during those dreadful years of the 1930s.
I raised the question several times in the committee, but somehow or another I always
Bank Act Amendment

seemed to be out of order, that our main problem in this generation is a problem of distribution. We have solved the problem of production. Once or twice I endeavoured to point out to the committee that the United States, for example, in 1935, with its industrial equipment as of that time, was capable of producing enough goods and services to supply every family in the United States with $4,400 worth of goods and services a year, but for .some reason or another the United States did not produce those goods and services and did not supply the people with them. The result was that whereas the United States could have been the richest, the most prosperous and happiest nation in the world, actually it was one of the most wretched countries in the world, following the same financial system under which we suffer. It had 23,500,000 people on relief and' between eleven and fifteen million unemployed. If the tragic failure of the United States in 1935 to produce the goods and services which it could have produced, and to enable its people to gain access to those goods and services, was not the result of a faulty banking system, then I .suggest that it is the problem of this generation to find out what it was the result of.

Whatsoever there was in the remark that the Chairman finds objectionable I withdraw without qualification.
I was going on to say that if there is any one subject that we ought to discuss at this stage in our history it is this question: what is the matter with our financial and economic system, which has made it so that we were unable during the 1930s to use our natural resources, both material and human, to produce a high standard of living for our people, whereas, from 1939 to 1945, we have been able to use those resources, material and human, to produce one of the most magnificent war efforts which it would be possible for a Canadian to conceive of? That question needs to be explained. It is my judgment that it should be explained in the committee, and the

Bank Act Amendment
question whether or not this bill passes for ten years or for one year is one that ought to be determined by considerations of the deficiency, on the one hand, or the success, on the other, of our financial system as it has been established since the last time we granted the banks a renewal of their charter.
In addition to our failure to distribute our goods, I think a good deal of attention should be paid to the matter of debt. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has spoken with great eloquence and effectiveness regarding this serious aspect of our economy at the present time. Consequently I do not propose to go into any great detail with regard to our debt.
I think the hon. member who spoke just before me rejoiced over the magnificent war effort of Canada and said that it ought to be paid for and had to be paid for, and the only way in which we could pay for it, I gathered he implied, was through the accumulation of an enormous debt. I do not believe that we should have an enormous debt financially as a result of a war like this. The war is paid for with blood and tears and material. And when that payment is made there certainly should be no financial debt. Why, in the days before Canada was, the savages fought wars; all they used was the resources at their disposal, material and human; and when they finished their wars they had no national debts hanging over them. Now, it seems a most strange situation if we, with civilization to help us, using our materials and men as freely, as they did, and losing just as heavily as they did, have a debt accumulated for all generations to carry and to endeavour to pay off. I 6ay, therefore, that the fourteen billions of public debt which ihis country is likely to owe by the end of 1944 constitutes a challenge to this generation. I do not believe that the members of this house can lightly neglect that challenge, nor do I believe that the members of the committee can afford lightly to disregard it. There should be some means or other whereby we could liquidate that debt and make our war effort a real pay-as-you-go effort, I am still of that opinion and still believe that the committee neglected its duty in failing to study the question of debt and to make recommendations to the government with respect to a policy which might possibly enable the government to conduct a war like this without the accumulation of public debt.
Another matter which I believe must give all thoughtful members grave concern is the prospect of unemployment. A responsible committee in the United States, appointed
some time in the early days of 1942, if I remember correctly, to examine into the whole question of possibilities after the war, reported early in 1943 that shortly after the war closed there would be twenty million unemployed in that country. I expect a similar condition to exist in Canada. I think the president of the Bank of Canada in his report this year to the minister indicated that in his opinion there was grave concern on this score. When we come to unemployment we come to a problem of failure to use our human resources. It ought to be possible for a country like Canada to use its human resources to produce goods and services to be distributed among the people so that the people of Canada may enjoy a high standard of living.
If the Dominion of Canada is unable to use its human resources and its material resources to produce goods and services to distribute among the people to give them a high standard of living, that fact must be conclusive evidence that something radically wrong exists. Whether the thing that is wrong lies in the banking system or whether it lies in the general financial and economic system that is used is a matter which, of course, will require a great deal of study to determine. But I think it certainly is a matter of finance because distribution is a matter of finance. We cannot employ men unless we can use resources, and we cannot use resources unless we can get money. We cannot get money unless we use our financial system. If the banking system is the major element in our financial system, and it appears to be so, then unquestionably there must be something wrong with the banking system, or there must be oome-thing deficient in our financial system independent of the banking system. What that is I believe we ought to study with the greatest thoroughness.
My remarks to-night merely indicate the reasons why I believe that we should not now pass this bill giving the banks a charter for ten years more until we have some of those vexatious questions cleared up. If we grant the banks charters , for only one year, for example, then every year they will come to this parliament for a renewal of their charters, and every year we can conduct an examination into their business and into the way in which they conduct it, into the financial system of this country in an endeavour to determine its deficiencies and consequently keep ourselves in a growing condition. But if we pass the Bank Act for ten years, then we shall not have all that study every year. Everybody will tend to rest on his oars. The banks will go back

Bank Act Amendment
to their business of banking, and what will happen to the country I tremble to contemplate.
I had the privilege of sitting in this house from 1935 to 1939, and I must say that one thing that struck me almost with despair in contemplating the government was the way in which they seemed to shrug helpless shoulders and wave hopeless hands whenever they were urged to do anything about the unemployment that we had in this country. They seemed to think that nothing could be done. If we pass this bank bill, giving the banks a renewal of charter for ten years, we shall be preparing the stage for a repetition of just that very thing. It may be argued, and it will be argued, by some government advocates that the government is now bringing down a great many social services, and that consequently conditions will not be as they were before. We are to have family allowances now. We are to have floors under agricultural prices. We are to have an industrial development bank. We are to have farm credit arrangements. Presumably all these things are to improve conditions, but I ask, Mr. Chairman, what will happen if it is discovered that this country is unable to dispose of its products and consequently a serious unemployment situation develops shortly after the war and revenues begin to fall off and the government finds itself unable to collect enough revenue to pay the interest on the accumulated debt and at the same time to service all these new social services which we now have the stage set to give to the people? Where is the money to come from? Surely every hon. member of our committee must be realistic enough to recognize that this question needs very careful consideration. Suppose it should be discovered that there was not enough money in the consolidated revenue fund to pay the family allowances and to pay the interest on the accumulated debt; which way would the members of this committee vote? To pay the interest on the debt or to pay family allowances? That is a question which cannot be answered by just lightly waving the hand. I found all during the committee stern opposition to the idea that it would be in any way safe for us to create money debt-free.
I confess that I can see no other way in the world in which the revenues of this country can be supplemented sufficiently to enable the government to discharge its responsibilities to the holders of our debt and its responsibilities to the people in the matter of social services. I can see no other way in the world in which the revenues can be supplemented except by the creation of debt-free money, and 
no one has taken the trouble to show me any way of supplementing it. No one did in the committee.
Somehow or another everybody seemed to take it for granted that as soon as the war is over all is going to be well. As the father of boys returning from that war, I do not find these assurances of optimism at all satisfying to me. My greatest anxiety at the present time is whether or not my children are to be able to find employment after this war. I enabled them, as far as I could, to qualify themselves to fit into the economic life of the country, but I remember 1934 and 1935. I was elected to this parliament in 1935, and I resigned my position, just a little high school position with a salary of $1,300 attached to it. Just three days after there were 735 applications for my position and among the applicants were a good many Ph.D.'s. Nothing that has been said in this house or in the committee has been sufficient to reassure me that there will not be a return after the war to conditions similar to that. There has been no change whatsoever in the financial system, either advocated or hinted at by the government. The Bank Act is not seriously changed.
I will challenge anyone to show any change in the present Bank Act which would make the banks operate materially differently from the way in which they have operated in the last term. As a father in this country I find these considerations very serious.
Without desiring to delay this committee any farther, I just wish to say that I believe this committee ought to exercise the greatest care before it decides to renew the charter of the banks for ten years, and clamp down upon this country a financial system which may not by any means be the kind of thing we shall want in this country to meet the changed conditions in which we may find ourselves within probably just two years.
