subtopic: FELICITATIONS AND GOOD WISHES ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ACCESSION TO LEADERSHIP OF LIBERAL PARTY

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FELICITATIONS AND GOOD WISHES ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ACCESSION TO LEADERSHIP OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext:
It is refreshing for public -men to pause during these days of heavy war-time burdens, anxieties and responsibilities and to observe fittingly occasions of importance in the lives of others. To-day I rise to recognize the twenty-fifth anniversary of the elevation of
tMr. Graydon.]
the present Prime Minister to the leadership of the Liberal party, because I feel that it is singularly appropriate that some of us outside that political family circle should join with those Canadians of a different political complexion to pay a tribute and to do honour to one whose length of service in the public arena as a chieftain exceeds that of any national leader in the world to-day.
In lighter vein as befits a happy occasion such as this, may I go so far as to say that to-day is actually the silver wedding anniversary of the marriage of the Prime Minister and the Liberal party. While the happy couple were joined in holy wedlock exactly a quarter of a century ago, it could in all fairness be said, I think, that the courtship was a somewhat long and at times a spectacular affair, and that his success in that earlier race was the result of a technique overwhelming in its consequences and surprisingly successful for a bachelor. In short, the Prime Minister wooed and won, and what is more, during the intervening period since it may well be noted that the well-known and comparatively industrious committee of another place has been provided by virtue of this union with no grist for its matrimonial mill to date. The admonition "till death us do part" so far has been strictly observed.
Akin to the experience of many families, prior to this new era of family allowances, floor prices and high levels of national income, the matrimonial pathway of these political honeymooners was not always strewn with roses, although flowers there were in abundance at times. There were those troublous periods in the uncertain twenties when the political home had to be shared by other political families to make ends meet. The early thirties saw the mortgage foreclosed, the sheriff in possession and the title almost lost; but the breadwinner kept his chin up and his courage undaunted until in the middle thirties the political stock market went soaring once more and reached new highs never known before by these humble speculators. The happy couple, visibly much happier now, repossessed themselves of their political belongings, got back their home, and rejoiced in being able once more to have the spare room of the house free from the political tenants of an earlier time, although it should be pointed out that meanwhile some of those tenants had changed their names and had themselves become legally adopted and full-fledged members of the household. Success after success met the family endeavours until in the early forties the family had grown to unheard-of proportions, almost to the point,

The Prime Minister
one imagines, of parental embarrassment. The normal flow of succeeding events has, however, somewhat lessened the housing congestion, and the neighbours, who think they know, are saying that there are signs of new factors in the ofling which are apt further to remedy the crowding difficulties. Upon that aspect, of course, I could not on such a happy occasion as this be expected to comment.
Meanwhile some of the family have started little homes for themselves-at this point one cannot help recalling those who have left to live down in the southeast corner of the political garden. Then again it might not be amiss to point out that in the old party home itself there are said to be some of the bigger and older boys who should really be setting up separate homes for themselves as well right now. With their somewhat playful vigour they are said to create problems in the home which tax to the limit even the gentle, forgiving and patient disposition of the parents, to say nothing of the other members of the family as well. But these are not affairs for us who are only neighbours to discuss. Therefore I pass on to more serious things.
In the days that are to come, as in the past, the Prime Minister will have in full measure our good will and our genuine wishes; but with respect to wishing him good luck I should perhaps make one reservation, and one only. It is the reservation which was aptly inserted by the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe when he congratulated me in 1941 upon my elevation to the national chairmanship of our party. As between political adversaries but who were close personal friends his word had a depth and breadth of meaning not readily measured by ordinary yardsticks.
On this occasion, so close to a general election, perhaps the Prime Minister will not mind if my native political caution prompts me, without diminishing the warmth of my personal sentiments, to repeat Mr. Lapointe's observation and say to him as Mr. Lapointe said to me, "I wish you luck, but not too much." As house leader of our party I convey on this occasion warm and cordial felicitations to the Prime Minister. This day will be a prized and treasured one for him and his friends; but we as political neighbours in the great Canadian community perhaps may be excused for taking the liberty of looking over the fence to have a little share in the enjoyment of to-day as well.
In conclusion may I say that regardless of the issues which sometimes appear to divide us, in the field of politics or otherwise, let us ever keep in mind that we are all Canadians,
striving to do and to give our best in the interests of a greater Canada, of a strengthened British commonwealth and empire, moving toward the goal of a better world of peace and plenty in the days ahead. With that thought in mind, this nation and this parliament, with a keen appreciation of the serious war-time responsibilities resting upon his shoulders, salute the Prime Minister on this, his day of days.

subtopic: FELICITATIONS AND GOOD WISHES ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ACCESSION TO LEADERSHIP OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think one of the glories of the British democratic system is that men may differ and yet feel the warmest personal regard for those with whom they differ. To-day I rise on behalf of those associated with me to endorse what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has said in regard to this anniversary of the right hon. the Prime Minister's accession to the leadership of the Liberal party. We wish him long life. We know that the contribution he has made to this country throughout a very long public career will be remembered in future histories of our land. We wish him, therefore, many happy returns of this day, and we do so sincerely. We hope he may be spared to give counsel and advice no matter what the political circumstances of the future may be. We join therefore in the tendering of best wishes to the Prime Minister.

subtopic: FELICITATIONS AND GOOD WISHES ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ACCESSION TO LEADERSHIP OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext: Once in a while, Mr. Speaker, a man lives long enough to be rewarded for his efforts. To-day I believe the Prime Minister is privileged to enjoy the reward of long and earnest effort. So many fine things already have been said that for me to try to add anything I believe would be something like gilding the lily. I will just conclude by saying that we wish to join with those who have congratulated the Prime Minister on this very happy day; we wish him long life and great success-but not too much.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FELICITATIONS AND GOOD WISHES ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ACCESSION TO LEADERSHIP OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker and hon. members of the House of Commons, in the twenty-five years I have had the honour of being leader of the Liberal party in Canada there have been many events and many occasions to which I look back with gratitude and pride. I think I can say quite honestly that no occasion, no event in that long period of time, has meant more to me than the welcome I have received this morning from my fellow members of the House of Commons, and the pleasure I have derived from the eloquent and extremely generous words which have been uttered by the leader of the opposition and the leaders of the other parties opposite.
The Prime Minister

I need scarcely say to Mr. Graydon, Mr. Coldwell and Mr. Blackmore-and I use their names because these gentlemen are intimate personal friends-that I have been deeply touched by their expressions of good will, the more so in that they have been shared in such a generous way by all associated with them in the parties which they represent. I thank you, gentlemen, with all my heart for what you have expressed this morning.
Looking back over the whole of the past twenty-five years there is nothing for which I have reason to be so grateful as the unfailing loyalty and constant support I have received from the members of my own party. I doubt whether in the history of politics there has been an instance in which the leader of a party has been more fortunate in the continuous and unfailing support he has received over such a long period. May I say also that I appreciate equally the good will that has been extended to me during that time by hon. members of this House of Commons who have belonged to other parties. In that again I think I 'have been perhaps far more fortunate than most men in public life. While I can recall occasions on which situations have developed that have been trying and difficult for all of us, I must confess that looking over the past twenty-five years what comes most to my mind next to the fidelity of my supporters is the magnanimity of most of my opponents in this House of Commons, and the friendships which I have been privileged to share with them. If twenty-five years ago to-day, when I was chosen leader of my party, I had known that my course would run over so long a period, during times such as we have since experienced; if I could have had a vision of the responsibilities which would come upon one's shoulders over that period of time, I doubt if I could have seen my way to accept so great a responsibility. But-
Heaven from all creatures hides the book of fate,
AH but the page prescribed, their present state.
Fortunately I have been able to take a day at a time, a month at a time, a year at a time, and it has stretched out now to twenty-five years.	-	.
For these years of public service in the parliament of Canada I can only feel a sense of the deepest gratitude. Apart from all else, public life offers two great rewards, perhaps I should say two great opportunities as well as great rewards. The greatest opportunity is that of public service. From long experience I know that no motive lies closer to the hearts of men who enter public life than the desire to serve their fellow men. That I think has been true of all or mostly all men who have

entered public life in our country. They may have differed as to the methods, but the motive was the same. I sometimes think we do not realize how great this opportunity is. I sometimes think that a member of parliament who does not happen to be a member of the ministry, or who is in the opposition, does not begin to comprehend the great part he is privileged to play in shaping the future and the destiny of his country. After all, it is ideas that count for most, and it matters little the source from whence they come; if the idea be right and sound it will tell for all time. That opportunity and that reward one has in public life. Having had the privilege to serve as leader of my party for twenty-five years and enjoyed the great opportunities which have come with that position, I am profoundly thankful to Providence for all that this has meant and for having been able to reach this day with that full 'measure of health and strength which, happily, I still possess.
The other great opportunity and reward of public life are the friendships which one forms with members of both houses, with members of this House of Commons and of the Senate, and with others associated in the work of parliament. In the very nature of things we are here brought more closely together than are corresponding groups anywhere else. We are drawn together in the realm of ideas and ideals, and it is upon ideas and ideals that the great community of friendship itself is based.
I can think of nothing richer in a man's life than to have been privileged to share over a quarter of a century the close friendships which come through membership in the House of Commons. I do not forget that I have been longer in parliament than I have been leader of my party. To-day I believe there is only one member in the house, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), who has been in the House of Commons a longer time than I have been. And, looking at the list of privy councillors in the Parliamentary Guide, I find that there are only two who precede me, one of them Sir William Mulock, who is in his hundred and first year, and the other Sir Allen Aylesworth, who is in his ninetieth year. I do not know whether that signifies that greater age is to be attained by those who remain, but it does bring the thought that whether remaining time be long or short, one has reached a place of very high honour in the company of those who have served in public office in this country.
I agree with the leader of the opposition that there are occasions on which the real spirit of the House of Commons asserts itself in a very noble way. This morning is one of those occasions, and I am sure it is one which

The Prime Minister
will be remembered by future parliaments, and which will no doubt help to exert its influence upon our public life. I do hope that in our public life we will keep, above everything else, that note of chivalry [DOT] which I believe to be more necessary in our day and age than it has been at any time previously.
Hon. members will I think agree that in the years I have led my party I have had my fair share of criticism. But I would also say that perhaps no other man in Canadian history over that period of time has been more kindly treated than I have been by the press of this country. Sometimes when very cruel things are said there comes to my mind the observation made by that great leader of the Conservative party, Sir John A. Macdonald, who told his audiences many times that the sticks and stones were to be found in greatest number under the trees which bore the most fruit. There is a lot of truth in that. I should like on this occasion also to recall something which Sir Wilfrid Laurier said on more than one occasion-something of which I have thought very often-that it does not do to cherish resentments in public life. I should like to go a bit further and say that I feel it does not do to create resentments in public life. In fact I can think of nothing so destructive of what is best in the spirit of a nation than any attempt to create prejudice or resentment, whether it be toward individuals, toward classes, toward races, toward religious denominations or toward other countries or other people. In politics, as in other walks of life, it is, I think, a cardinal sin to do aught in the way of detraction that can be avoided, and to lend oneself to perversion of the truth. As we help to maintain high standards in public life, so we help to secure the future of our nation.
May I say at once I am conscious that in the play of politics, back and forth; at moments of earnest pleading for particular causes, one from time to time often says things that he regrets. One never regrets the charitable or kind or generous thing one has said, but inevitably I believe one does come to regret any word which may have caused pain to another. If words of mine in the course of this past twenty-five years have inflicted a wound in the breast of any man, I would ask him to forgive me. May I assure all hon. members that in the years I have been in parliament I have tried to avoid that kind of thing, and have sought as best I could to interpret aright the views of others. I know I have slipped on occasions, and I should not like those particular slips to be remembered. However, I do feel that
the joys of friendships which have been so much more a part of public life will endure long after these other things are forgotten.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has referred to my state of bachelorhood. A law which I believe to be one of the greatest, is the law of compensation. As my hon. friend has said, it is quite true that this is a sort of silver wedding without a bride. On the other hand, what I have lost in the way of a personal family, I have more than gained in the political family I have had around me all these years.
Sometimes I hear it said that I am a lonely man, that I have few friends, that I see few people. I just wish some of those who hold this mistaken view could get a truer glimpse of my inner nature. I imagine there is no man in Canada who for these twenty-five years has been less lonely than I have, or who has enjoyed greater or more numerous friendships. True, one becomes isolated more or less in affairs; but I do not see how any man holding a position of responsibility at a time like this-if that man takes his responsibilities seriously-can for one moment do other than take-every opportunity he possibly can get to prepare in respect of those questions which have to be discussed in parliament, to study the great issues of the day, and to make sure that as few mistakes as possible are made. That, of necessity, deprives one of very much in the way of personal associations. May I say this to hon. members that there has been no privation of which, owing to pressure of work as it has been from day to day, month to month, and year to year, I have been more conscious in recent years than the inability to keep in personal touch with members of all parties in parliament. This has been to me a deep privation. I have lost much of the' richness of life through being unable to see, in a personal and intimate fashion, members of this parliament coming from all parts of Canada, members of the press and others. And what is true of parliament is also true, in even larger measure, of the people of Canada, so far as getting about to different parts of the country is concerned. This has been, due to a realization of the great trust which has been imposed upon me; the responsibility of seeing that in every way the things of greatest importance at the moment, and at all times are given first attention. I should like to thank hon. members for their understanding of this situation.
May I say one or two words in conclusion. First, a word about this House of Commons. I believe that there has been no parliament in
The Prime Minister

the history of Canada which as a whole has been worthier of great responsibilities, and has measured up to great issues in a finer way than the present parliament. Everything considered, having relation to the times in which we are living and our responsibility to them, I do not believe that the membership of any parliament in Canada's history has measured up in better fashion than have the members of this war parliament, nor has the average of ability and earnestness of purpose been higher than has been the case with those who occupy seats on both sides of the house.
I do pray that for the sake of our country, for the sake of the great empire of which it is a part, for the sake of the world of to-day, every effort will be made from every quarter to bring into this parliament the best men we can have to occupy the seats here. I can see nothing so serious for the nation than that by any chance the standard of ability and integrity and high purpose should be lowered in any way or from any cause. I believe it is the highest form of patriotism that we should put forward every effort to bring into future parliaments the best men and the best women that can be obtained as representatives of several communities.
Looking to the future, I hope that our parliaments will become more and more representative, that we shall have more and more of those who represent rural parts of Canada as well as the working classes, that we shall have in addition to the professional and business representation a good representation of those brave men and women who have been serving their country with their lives during this great war. I hope that we will see more women in the House of Commons as the days go by. They know the problems of the home perhaps more intimately than men, and it is the problems of the home that are the problems of the nation, and a solution of the problems of the home will prove, I believe, a solution of the problems of the nation.
Then this last word, if I may express it this morning. I have great faith in the future of Canada. I think we are the most fortunate country in the world. I believe that Canada increasingly will become a great world power and, what is even more important, I believe she will become a great beneficent power in the world. I have no fears about the future. Having been spared to live through these past twenty-five years and having witnessed what Canada has done at times of the greatest stress in the history of the world, one would be a pessimist indeed who did not believe that this country will rise and prove equal to any occasion.

I hope that in times to come the association which we enjoy in that great association of nations which comprises the British commonwealth may continue, may endure, as it is one of the greatest blessings to this world. I hope that the friendship which we have for the great country to the south will continue to grow strong and remain firm through time. I hope above all that the good will which this country has helped to create with other nations in other parts of the world will strengthen and develop so that, as the years go on, mankind may witness throughout this globe more often the way of true brotherhood among nations as well as among men.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation in respect to the hospitalization of our wounded as provided by the Department of Pensions and National Health has been a matter of controversy over a period of the last couple of years. I know that the statement has been made that the wounded until discharge are the responsibility of the defence services and that upon discharge the wounded become the responsibility of the Department of Pensions and National Health. As a matter of fact we know that the wounded arriving from overseas are sent to the hospitals of the Department of Pensions and National Health for treatment.
It is a well-known fact that one of the chief hospitals in Ontario, and perhaps in Canada, is the old Christie street hospital in Toronto. That hospital before being taken over was a factory, and was taken over towards the end of the last war only as an emergency to meet an emergent situation.

subtopic: WOUNDED
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Who took it over?

subtopic: WOUNDED
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
It was taken over by the union government, and therefore both sides will have to share in that responsibility. It was never intended to remain as a permanent hospital to take care of the wounded. As I said before, it was taken over only to meet an emergent situation. But surely in the intervening years since then, there has been ample time for the minister and his department to find other and proper accommodation for our wounded, both of the last war and for those who will be returning from this war. What has been done?
We are now in the fifth year of this war. The situation at Christie street hospital was so bad and so serious that last year representa-

tions were made to the Department of Pensions and National Health to have them acquire some other property and build a suitable hospital in which to take care of our wounded. It was only after a great deal of public pressure and much effort on the part of the Canadian corps and veterans' organizations, by groups of citizens, the board of trade, the city council and other bodies, and the holding of meetings and the making of public protests, that ultimately the department agreed to accept free from the city of Toronto a considerable acreage of land just outside the city for the purpose of building a suitable hospital upon it for the care of our wounded. That land was acquired last November, and the first sod was turned by the Minister of [DOT] Pensions and National Health on Armistice day, 1943. It is now over nine months since that ceremony took place, and yet no building has been started on that property.
It was pointed out many months ago that the United States had built many large military hospitals and that the plans for those hospitals could be easily secured by an application to Washington. No such application was made. If these plans had been secured, a local architect could very easily have adapted them to our purposes here and, by letting contracts on a cost plus basis, the work of building the hospital could have been begun as soon as the frost was out of the ground last spring. I do not believe anyone can dispute that. I know that as soon as a firm of architects in Toronto were engaged to make plans for these buildings they worked very hard, day and night, with a staff at their disposal to get these plans ready. Therefore I attach no blame whatever to the architects, engineers or other technicians who have been engaged for all these months on this particular undertaking.
Within the last week or so we have seen a notice in the press that at last-at long last-a unit is to be built at Sunnybrook park, and that unit is to accommodate nurses -it is a nurses' home-together with a building for up-patients, and some engineering works. It seems to me an extraordinary thing, since we have had so much delay, that those responsible for this undertaking did not decide that the first building to be put up at Sunnybrook park should be an active treatment unit. That is what is most urgently needed, and I have no doubt that, if energetically undertaken by a competent man of affairs who has a practical knowledge of building, these buildings could be completed by the end of this year. But we have still the spectacle of Christie street; and if anyone doubts the situation there, as has been

described to this house on more than one occasion by myself, and other hon. members, I ask him to look at the illustrations in the Toronto morning paper; although some members of the government do not regularly read it, perhaps they look at the pictures. These photographs, appearing in this morning's issue, illustrate very clearly what the situation at Christie street is. If they have not seen this newspaper this morning I will send a copy over to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). In one room in that building are 82 patients. The beds are so close together that a nurse can scarcely get between them to carry out her duties. If the windows are opened, dust, dirt, steam and smoke from passing trains enter and cover the sheets and patients with smut. Not only the noise of the trains but the noise from surrounding manufacturing plants make it impossible for anyone to sleep during the daytime, and only after great exhaustion can they sleep at night. Yet on that property the department is willing to allow a neurological building to continue to house our nervous patients.

speechtext:
Perhaps it should not be necessary to refer any more and any longer to the situation at Christie street, which is so well known to members of this government. But I could not deal properly with this subject if I had not alluded to conditions there; and
if I may continue for a moment I should like to answer something which has arisen, namely that it has been announced that many thousands of beds are available for our wounded. I am informed that beds are now vacant in Christie street hospital for the first time in months, because wounded who need treatment have been moved out of those beds and sent to their homes so as to allow others to use them. The fact that within recent w'eeks the minister has announced the acquisition of a building in Peterborough, formerly used as a hostel by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, which will accommodate some three hundred and fifty patients, and has also taken over a hostel in Kingston which he states will accommodate two hundred and fifty more, making a total of six hundred, would indicate that the serious situation about which I complain is more widespread than simply the city of Toronto.
Now we come to the city of Montreal. Some months ago it was revealed by Doctor Wilder Penfield of that city, an eminent neurological surgeon-possibly the greatest neurosurgeon on this continent-that although he had offered this government the opportunity of building an addition to his hospital to accommodate the neurological patients who were returning from overseas and who required the services of an expert neuro-surgeon, that offer was turned down. Had it been accepted, it is only fair to assume that that building, of one hundred-bed addition to the present neurological institute, would have been completed and ready for this serious type of cases arriving from overseas. In my opinion that showed a total disregard by the head of this department of what might happen to these cases and a neglect to take advantage of a golden opportunity to give our wounded, suffering from head injuries or spinal injuries, the privilege of profiting by the skill of a great surgeon in this specialized department of surgery.
I am not familiar with the situation in othei places, but I am informed that it is not very much better. From what we read we know what is going on overseas. We know that our forces have suffered heavy casualties in Normandy and Italy. Although the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has not given out the total number of casualties to date suffered in Normandy, we know that the colonel of the Black Watch was killed, and we know that the Royal Regiment of Canada suffered severe casualties. I do not think it will be long before we shall learn that the Queen's Own of Toronto will also have suffered heavy casualties in that theatre of war. I cannot imagine anything more callous than to sit idly by and refuse to provide the very

Canadian Forces-Hospital Accommodation
best type of accommodation for those who are willing to offer their lives to protect our freedom and to save our civilization. That has been the situation in regard to this department. Surely the minister of this department, a veteran of the last war, should have known years ago that we would have casualties. We always have casualties in a war. He should have commenced years ago to build hospitals of a modern type suitably equipped and ready when the time came to be occupied by our wounded men. This he has not done. Therefore, I say, Mr. Speaker, that he has failed in the discharge of his great and onerous responsibility to our wounded.
I do not think that the people of this country will accept the bald statement that he made on Saturday and again to-day that we have thousands of beds available. I should like to ask if in that number are included the two thousand beds stored in the Rawlin-son warehouse in Toronto, which were placed there some years ago for air raid precaution purposes, or the other similar beds in storehouses in other parts of Canada. What we want is a sufficient number of modem hospitals with adequate equipment and every facility to treat our wounded men when they come home. Anything less than that will not satisfy the Canadian people.

speechtext:
May I say that we supported the hon. member in his move to adjourn the house to discuss this matter of public importance, because, while we have no definite knowledge of the situation which has been outlined, we felt that if there were any suspicion in the country that the very best that ought to be done was not being done, it should be aired at once.
We too feel that perhaps the preparations that have been made in the past to take care of the wounded of the present war and the veterans of the former wars have not reflected credit on this country. From information I have been able to obtain in former years I agree that the situation as to Christie Street hospital has not been very creditable. I had hoped that we might do better for the men who need the best of care in our hospitals. May I add that I think the policy of the immediate past with regard to providing military hospital accommodation has been mistaken. We should have viewed the necessity of military hospitals from a broader angle than this house was prepared to view it. Instead of building temporary accommodation for men who were in training, we should have seen to it that we were preparing for the present and the post-war period.
The minister said he was prepared to make a statement on these matters. While that

statement could have been made when the estimates were under discussion, it is just as well, since the matter has arisen this morning, that the opportunity has been afforded to the minister to reply.

speechtext: I had no idea that this question was coming up this morning. However, I wish to strongly support the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce). As the minister knows, I have been to see him personally on many occasions concerning this matter. I do not propose to go into that again at this time. I have been- fortunate enough to see what the United States is doing on this continent and at the bases she has obtained under lend-lease in the West Indies and elsewhere, with regard to this problem. I have seen the magnificent hospitals she has built. I feel that we have not been properly apprised of the necessity of continuing these old and temporary hospitals. We see that the United States, Australia and other countries have built magnificent hospitals during the war. The question I cannot help asking myself is, why have not we, who were in the war two years before the United States, built hospitals? I know the condition in my own district; I know the conditions in the hospitals; I have been in them on many occasions. That is the inescapable question. Why have not we been able to do what the United States is doing? Surely care of the wounded is our first obligation, our No. 1 priority in social security.

It
is not my intention to delay the house for very long, Mr. Speaker, in seconding the motion moved by the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Bruce). I merely wish to support what the hon. member has said, and to emphasize the urgency of the situation. I am not particularly condemning the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), because after all this is a matter of government responsibility. I do not believe anyone on the government side is more sympathetic to the returned men than is the minister. But for a long time there has appeared to be a strange and unfortunate contrast between the speed with which we can clear airfields and build barracks for soldiers; the speed, indeed, with which we can manufacture guns we did not think we could build, and the hesitancy with which we make provision for those gallant wounded men who are certainly the most important citizens of this dominion. In the same general way it rather irks me to think of the speed with which we talk about provision for the post-war period; the speed with which we put through family allowances, if you will. Some hon. member says "speed," so perhaps I should modify that statement by saying the speed with which the suggestion of waiting a year was agreed to. Unfortunately I was not in the house at the time to vote against the measure; however there is certainly a great difference between the speed with which we go about our post-war planning for those who are well and the lack of speed with which we build hospitals for those who have been wounded. In one instance the first
sod for the construction of Sunnybrook hospital was turned nine months ago. I do not blame the Minister of Pensions and National Health for this situation; I blame it on the government of the day, and indeed as a member of this parliament I must assume part of the responsibility myself if I do not press for its early construction.
I do not want to say very much about Christie street hospital, Mr. Speaker, since you have suggested that perhaps enough has been said in that regard, but I believe it is just as important to look after the gallant men who are undergoing treatment in that hospital as it is to look after people in any other part of this dominion. It almost makes one hang his head in shame to think of that hospital being maintained in that location, whether by this government or the previous government. Personally I do not think it ever should have been located there. However, I understand in the first place it was undertaken as an emergency measure. Anyone who has driven through that district as often as I have; anyone familiar with it, as I am sure seventy-five per cent of the members of this house are, knows the clatter, the dust and the din that are to be found in that district at all times. It is not a fit locality for the hospitalization of any class of our citizens, let alone our returned soldiers. These men should1 not be cared for in a hospital as wards of the state; they should be given every consideration as the leading champions of our national cause in this, the greatest and most important moment of our history.
I do feel that we should demonstrate in the building of hospitals the same speed that has been shown in the construction of war plants; and I believe our hospitals should be located in the most appropriate places. I believe the Sunnybrook hospital is in a very satisfactory location. Why should not our returned men be given accommodation equal to that provided for our ordinary citizens at the Toronto General hospital, or at the hospitals in Montreal, Halifax, and other places? I am told that more than one-third of the patients in Christie street hospital have been there since the last war, some of them unable to move. Many have grown so accustomed to the noise, the dust, the trains passing by and the grinding, rasping din of the metal manufacturing plant right next door that they have become reconciled to the situation, comforting themselves with the thought that they went through worse conditions when they were wounded overseas. But they should not be expected to endure that sort of thing indefinitely. I believe it is a national obligation on those whp have remained at home to pro-

vide for our wounded soldiers, not merely adequately but generously. It is not enough to say that we have eighteen hundred beds available; in a short time we may have twenty-eight hundred men come back wounded. I doubt if anyone can say that there will be no emergency we cannot meet, in view of the hesitation with which we have gone about making our preparations.
The leader of the opposition has mentioned the proposal advanced by the premier of Ontario, who has said that the province is willing to forgo the use of the hospital at St. Thomas, which I understand will provide some 1,700 beds. I suggest that this accommodation could be used in an emergency, and that suitable accommodation elsewhere might be found for members of the R.CA.F. who are there at the present time, because it does seem that we can make preparations for war a great deal faster than we can take measures for the protection of our returned men. I submit that this is a national emergency, because it affects the morale of our people at this most critical hour. It is bound to affect the enlistment of volunteers, who after all are the only members of our forces who are fighting. We should regard this as an acute national emergency in this hour of greatest crisis. This war may be over soon, as far as Europe is concerned, but in any event we may anticipate the early return of many men who have had their lives blighted by critical wounds. I repeat that before we go on making preparations for peace-time luxury of those who have not been overseas, we should make sure that we are well prepared to meet any emergency that may arise in connection with our returned men. We should have not merely sufficient but ample accommodation, so that these men may be looked after properly, not eighty in one room but one in each room. If this country can vote half a billion dollars for the post-war paternalism which has been suggested in this house, then we cannot afford as a nation to allow these boys to suffer when they return, and not have for them something better than placing eighty of them in one room, with all the dust, din and noise that is involved in the Christie street hospital situation.
I shall not detain the house longer. I should like to hear from the Minister of Pensions and National Health. Again I say I believe he is sympathetic to the returned men. But the responsibility is upon this whole government; therefore it is their first duty and our first duty to see to it that these men have not only a doubtful sufficiency, but adequate and surplus space. Everyone knows that if there are more beds than are required, there

are many places in Canada where they can be .used, because hospitalization in Canada has been short for the last several years.
Let us therefore have a surplus so that we may be sure that if five thousand more return than we expect, we may have ample provision for them. When we have done that, we can look after those to whom we seem to give so much paternalism in the post-war period.

The chief differences which arise, in my view, are in connection with the sincerity of some allegations made. During the last two or three years when the estimates of my department have been before the committee allegations have been made with respect to hospitalization at Christie Street hospital. I did not hear any criticism during those five years when hon. gentlemen opposite were in the government.
But now, of course, the criticism has been vociferous and frequent. I have been many times in that hospital, and I must say I have never seen the slightest justification for

Forces-Hospital Accommodation
the attacks which have been. made. We need Christie street hospital at this time, and we require it until we have the new hospital at Toronto. We commenced last November arrangements for the construction of Sunny-brook hospital, which will be one of the biggest-if not the biggest-in Canada, when it is completed. And I can assure the house that not one hour has been lost in connection with all the preparations made for Sunnybrook. The first contract was let for $2,800,000, and the contract has been let for the first stage of *construction. We will proceed as fast as it is humanly possible, the same as has happened in other parts of Canada.
A new hospital is being built in Montreal- the Currie hospital. Then there is the hospi-. tal at Deer Lodge, and the new hospital at Calgary, also a new hospital in Edmonton. We have a new hospital in Regina, and in Vancouver we have a new hospital, with extensions. In Ottawa we have a new wing on the civic hospital.
The hon. member for Parkdale has spoken about the neurological centre at Montreal, about which I spoke earlier in this session. We have had consultations with the defence ministers. The defence services also have their own hospitals. The Department of Pensions and National Health has gone into the whole matter. In the last two years at least we have had a central committee on war hospitalization. This committee is composed of some of the most brilliant medical men to be found in Canada. They are able to consider and appraise every suggestion, and they review all suggestions in connection with the building and construction of hospital accommodation. This is not entirely a government committee. Rather it is a committee composed of the most expert and brilliant medical men in Canada. They pass upon every single new wing or new building erected in the country. The government does not authorize alterations or new construction until they have been recommended by those on the committee. I think some hon. members will know the personnel of that committee, and they will realize that it is composed of the most eminent men in medicine, in surgery and hospital administration to be found anywhere in the country. They are eminently able, and have been in charge of the work of passing upon the recommendations of departments.
In regard to neurological centres, may I say that we have accepted their advice, and these centres have been formed in four or five different places in Canada. The hon. member ..for Parkdale has said that we have not used the services of an eminent surgeon in Montreal, whom I have had the honour of complimenting in this house. We have been using his services for years in the Department of Pensions and National Health; we are using them to-day, and we hope we shall have the privilege of using them as long as they are required.
In no instance have we neglected to carry the advice of the best medical opinion in Canada. I still say we are meeting the situation properly, although that situation has changed recently because of two events. First, there was the new attack upon the old country, by new methods, and second, there was the matter of increased hospital ship accommodation. There may have to be a revision in the estimate made by the experts of the three defence departments in regard to casualties returned to Canada. That has been foreseen, and the condition is being carefully considered.
The Minister of National Defence, along with the other two defence ministers and myself, engaged an expert some time ago to review the whole situation in Canada in the light of the new conditions which now prevail. But if it comes to a desire of rendering every humane service and every other possible service for those boys, this house may rest assured that as long as I am in charge of the portfolio I now hold, that will be done.
May I add that my colleagues in the three defence services-all three-are gallant comrades who know what casualties mean. They learned about casualties in the last war, and I have had the most complete and marvellous cooperation. We have been meeting day after day for some months, especially in the light of the new developments in Europe. Those developments impelled us to review the whole situation.
I must say that a committee of the cabinet deals from time to time with these problems. The cooperation of every member of the government has been missing at no time. Any suggestion the committee has made to the government has been immediately endorsed by every single minister of the crown. I have had the fullest possible cooperation. Looking over the numbers of casualties-which I cannot reveal at the present time-and the construction programme now under way, and the bed accommodation we already have- taking account of the average stay in hospital we can care for about 20,000 new patients between now and Christmas. I must say on my responsibility that I am assured and I am confident that there will be proper accommodation for the boys requiring it. That is the first responsibility of any government, and certainly it is a responsibility which has been met by this government.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should say a word in connection with this matter from the point of view of the army, the navy and air force which are responsible for their own casualties up to a certain point. So far as the army is concerned, that point is when men in army hospitals are found not to be reparable within a reasonable length of time- that is, when it is found that men will not be back for service within a reasonable length of time. When that point is reached the thing to do is to have them make the change-
over to civilian life and go to the care of Pensions and National Health. That is the general division of responsibility.
The army in connection with its responsibility of taking care of casualties when they first come home, unless they have injuries which can immediately be designated as of the irreparable nature I have spoken of, has its own hospitals all over Canada to which these men are sent. I want to say with regard to the army hospitals that we have felt, having regard to the word which we get from overseas-not so much as to the number of casualties, because I think we have anticipated the number of casualties all right-on account of the possible speed with which there will be an increase of evacuations from the United Kingdom as a result of conditions there, and on account of possible increased shipping accommodation, that we should increase our facilities. Plans have been made in a number of cases to increase facilities. Perhaps I could put it in another way by saying that we should speed up the provision of those facilities in case there should be any increase in evacuations from the United Kingdom. The army is doing this and I may say that we have regarded it as being so important that we have brought in a man from the outside to deal solely with the matter particularly from the engineering and construction angle, to see that the plans, which are being made are dealt with promptly and to see that every possible pressure is put on the situation so that there will be no possible lack of accommodation so far as the army is concerned for any number of casualties which can reasonably be expected to come.
While the army is doing that I want to say something else. We have never taken the position, neither Pensions and National Health, nor the army, the navy, or the air, that we are all separate departments each working within its own watertight jurisdiction and paying no attention to the necessities for coordination and integration of these hospital services. We realize that, if it is possible to avoid it this country does not want to be unduly expansive in connection with hospital accommodation. That is to say, we could take the position that the army, navy and air should have sufficient hospital accommodation of all types, and then have Pensions and National Health duplicate the facilities for their purposes. We have not done that. Sooner or later, and probably sooner, the service hospitals will be evacuated to Pensions and National Health.
We have felt rather that we should put at each other's disposal the facilities both of

accommodation and personnel that are available. In other words, we have felt that we should pool those facilities. In that connection Pensions and National Health have repeatedly provided accommodation for certain service personnel even though they were still on the strength of the services, and we appreciate their having done so. On the other hand-I am speaking for the army but I think the same can be said for the other services- we have provided professional personnel and nursing personnel in certain Pensions and National Health establishments in order that patients might be cared for and that the strain on the personnel might be relieved.

I think that is just as natural as it is for a man to be grateful for something some one has done for him, it is just as natural as any instinct in humanity. We are all just as anxious as we can be to see to it that these facilities are the best that can be provided, [DOT] that they are provided on time, that they are provided where most needed and that they are adequately staffed.

That officer returned and made a report, which I presume was in due course reported to the premier of Ontario and led to the letter which he sent to the Prime Minister of Canada. I remember a complaint which was made to me-I am not going to say by whom but it was by a very distinguished gentleman, who complained bitterly that the air force were closing down in London in order to make it into a hospital for army purposes when St. Thomas was right there beside them and they could just as well use that. I have another observation to make to the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) and it is this. Speaking in the house on August 4 the hon. member for Parkdale put a question

to the Minister of Pensions and National Health in these words, at page 5902 of Hansard:
Owing to the alarming reports in regard to the lack of accommodation for our wounded who are returning from Normandy and Italy, and the fact that he announced two or three days ago that he has taken over hostels in Peterborough and Kingston for the purpose, I wonder if he would tell the house why it should be necessary in the fifth year of the war to scurry about to get accommodation in any old building for our wounded.
I ask the house to pay particular attention to these words that the hon. member used: "to scurry about to get accommodation in any old building for our wounded." On that point, which is related to the motion the hon. member has made this morning, I want to say to him that so far as the hostel at Kingston is concerned which the Department of Pensions and National Health has taken over, the description "any old building" is entirely inappropriate and inapplicable. My hon. friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health will recall the time when I approached him with regard to the use of that building for our wounded returned soldiers.
I had watched that building from its earliest days, when it was erected by the Department of Munitions and Supply as a hostel for women workers in the city of Kingston. I had seen conditions change there so that the need for that hostel was not nearly so great as before. I had observed how splendidly it would adapt itself to the purposes of a Pensions and National Health hospital. My hon. friend sent down his officials and doctors; they looked at the building and agreed completely with the representations I had made, and they took it over for use as a hospital. I am prepared to say that it will make a magnificent hospital-well equipped, well furnished, and well situated-and it is entirely incorrect and unjust to refer to it as "any old building which is to be used as a building for Canadian soldiers".
Another point I wish to clear up, and which is related somewhat to this matter, is a statement in a newspaper last week that the three ministers of defence had lost confidence in the Minister of Pensions and National Health and therefore had set up demobilization committees of their own. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this house that in no degree have we lost confidence in the Minister of Pensions and National Health. On the contrary he shares completely, I think, the confidence of the ministers of national defence. Why did we set up these committees in our various departments? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) speaking to
Questions
this house some weeks ago, gave the reason. He said that there are two phases or stages in the lives of men in the services, two different stages in their histories. The first is while they are under our control, while they are in the services, and during that stage we in the services must do everything we can to look after them, including their repatriation to Canada, the preparation of the various sendee documents, arrangements about pay and discharge and the like. When they are discharged they become the care of the Minister of Pensions and National Health. The setting up of committees by the three defence services was done solely with regard to the first stage: it was done so that we might attend more carefully to the great mass of detail which must be attended to before you can get men out of the service, including transportation to Canada, proper documentation, and finally, discharge. Then the Minister of Pensions and National Health takes over; and so far as I am concerned I am happy to be able to say here, that, instead of the minister's losing our confidence, our confidence in him has grown as we have observed in recent months, and indeed ever since he assumed office, the great thoughtfulness, the generosity and the sympathy he cherishes for all men who are in the armed services.

speechtext: ,	-SUGGESTION AS TO ADJOURNMENT

I understand that there is a dinner to-night to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I suggest that since this is a most unusual occasion, and no doubt the Prime Minister's friends will wish to attend) that dinner, we should not sit to-night.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was about to rise
Business of the House

to speak on this matter, which I had already mentioned privately to the Prime Minister, and make a similar suggestion in connection with it. My information is the same as that of my hon. friend; it is that a great many hon. members desire to attend, and if the government's business is sufficiently advanced I should think there would be no objection to allowing an adjournment at six o'clock to-night until to-morrow morning; perhaps in any event we can pick up in the succeeding days any time which is missed. speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I express my appreciation to my hon. friend the Leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) and to my hon. friend the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Graydon)' for their courtesy in suggesting that the house do not continue with business this evening. If there are any hon. members who feel that they would be inconvenienced by the house not sitting, I would personally much prefer that somehow or another we would keep a quorum on this side to continue with the business. However, I do know that all hon. members on this side have been looking forward to being present with myself and colleagues this evening, and the courtesy of the house in causing us to feel that we may have the evening free is something which all of us would deeply appreciate.
I might say that had I assumed for a moment that the business of the house would not have been over by this time I would have been the first to ask that no engagement of any kind be arranged for this evening. When, some months ago, some hon. members kindly suggested that a dinner might be held on August 7, the time looked so far distant that I thought it was safe to say that I felt we might count on being together that evening. However, I do appreciate the suggestion of adjournment at six o'clock this afternoon, and would thank hon. gentlemen opposite on behalf of members of my party for making it possible for all of us to have this evening together.
As to the business, I would say that if we were not sitting in the mornings as well as the afternoons I would hesitate to accept the kind proposal which has been made, but as we are sitting morning, afternoon and night it will I believe be possible for us to conclude

the business of the session without losing much time in virtue of not sitting this evening. Again I thank hon. members.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: RELEASE OF MEN FROM EQUIPMENT AND PERSONNEL SECTIONS R.C.A.F.
speechtext: I should like to direct a further question to the Minister of Labour in connection with a matter that I raised on Saturday in respect to which he suggested that I take it up with the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). This matter has to do with a letter sent throughout the country indicating that men in the ground crew of the air force have been advised that opportunity will be given to them to secure discharge from the air force provided that they are needed in industry or on farms. These men want to know the situation with respect to this order. Once they get their discharge from the air force and apply to go into essential industry will they be subject to call-up under the N.R.M.A.? The rumour is about that they will be subject to that call, and so far no information has been given thereon. It is a matter that falls strictly within the Departs ment of Labour.

maintopic: RELEASE OF MEN FROM EQUIPMENT AND PERSONNEL SECTIONS R.C.A.F.
speechtext:
I have made inquiries and find that there has been no change in the policy which has been followed in the Royal Canadian Air Force in matters of this kind. It has always been the practice so far as the Royal Canadian Air Force is concerned to consider an application from a man to be given his discharge in order that he may return to essential industry, provided that he can be released without interfering with the training programme, and provided that the recommendation was received from national selective service confirming the applicant's statement that he was needed for some essential work. The order which the hon. member has heard about is simply an order standardizing the practice throughout Canada as to what routine would be followed. With respect to the question as to whether a man receiving his discharge would be called for service in the army, it is a fact that under such circumstances a man might be called for service in the army, but if such were the case he would probably be given his postponement

Income War Tax
by the mobilization board on presentation of the same set of facts which prompted a national selective service officer to recommend his discharge from the air force in the first instance.
We have a satisfactory interdepartmental arrangement, and I do not know of any case in recent months where a man who has been given his discharge from the Royal Canadian Air Force to return to essential service has been called for the army.
Regarding farm leave, Royal Canadian Air Force this year has adopted the same practice as has been followed by the army, namely, men who apply for farm leave may be granted it to enable them to work on any farm, whereas in previous years the man had to specify what farm he was going to, and unless the farm was owned by a member of his family, leave was not extended. I think that answers my hon. friend's question.

When we were discussing the budget resolutions one point that I raised was in connection with income tax exemption for unusual medical expenses. I pointed out that the provisions of the Income War Tax Act did not permit the allowing of all the kinds of medical expenses that taxpayers have to incur. I suggested that one way to provide desirable relief to the taxpayer would be to lower the five per cent figure to three per cent or to two per cent. When we were discussing the matter in the house the parliamentary assistant indicated that our representations at least would be given consideration. I am

Mr. Speaker, I have already taken up with the department the grievances of the sleeping-car conductors, the porters and others who wait on the public. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that the application of this tax is most unfair and unjust to this class of people. In some

cases and in certain localities, arbitrary amounts have been added to the incomes of porters back to the year 1942, after they had paid their taxes, this arbitrary levy being for the tips or gratuities they were supposed to have received from the public. If this is a proper tax on this class of people, of whom there are thousands all over Canada including not only sleeping-car porters but waiters, people in hotels and others who serve the public, why are they not advised in advance that this is income which is subject to taxation? In some cases it has been represented to me that these people have advised that they did not receive such earnings; that they were not regular porters but were on casual trips in connection with the transportation of service personnel, who as a rule do not give tips. I was able to get an adjustment in one case by having the man concerned add to his income for 1942 the maximum amount he had received in the form of tips, which was far less than the amount charged.
This taxation is not fair from another point of view. The small gratuities that are given these servants of the public are from the residue of the earnings of people who already have paid taxes. It is not untaxed earning or income, but comes from what is left. Therefore it should not be again subject to income tax. This is a real grievance on the part of this class of people, who are not allowed to deduct expenses when away from home.
I wish to bring another matter to the attention of the department; that is, the unfairness of the present tax on electrical energy. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that on two previous occasions I tried to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which con-[DOT]cerns a number of my constituents, and others who reside not only in my constituency but as well throughout the city of Windsor. In this matter the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), who is attending a very important meeting outside the chamber, has joined with me on several occasions in discussing this matter with the responsible minister and with the officials of the Department of Finance, to see if there might not be some remedy for the grievance of which I am about to speak.
This matter concerns some 2,500 to 3,000 citizens in the city of Windsor, who for the most part earn their incomes by working in the city of Detroit. I have no doubt that this border situation is not peculiar alone to that city, but is a condition which may be found at other border points. These people
feel, and I join with them, that they suffer a grievance in respect of the administration of the income tax in so far as earned income in the United States is concerned. Perhaps the minister would appreciate if I were to state the three grounds upon which the application for redress is made. They ask:
1.	That substantial tax-free allowances be made for expenses incurred in the United States which come out of income earned in the United States, the said money never entering Canada, and that these allowances should be comparable to those employees of the British Supply Council in North America.
2.	That the ten per cent premium on gross salary be removed, but if charged at all, be on net salary, after all deductions have been made and,
3.	That the tax should be levied on net salary or earnings, not gross, plus ten per cent as at present.
That is the way in which these people have stated their case. I prefer to state it perhaps in another way, one which fo* my purpose would be clearer. The general problem is that most of these men and women, who are earning salaries well within the range of $2,000 or $3,000-there may be exceptions, but for the most part they are relatively small wage-earners-find that they are forced, in the normal carrying out of their occupations, to spend a considerable portion of their money each year upon food and travel in the United States. True, if they brought all of that money back into Canada in American currency it would be valued at a rate ten per cent higher than the Canadian dollar, due to the discount rate. The fact is, however, that a good portion of that money is necessarily spent in the United States. Yet for income tax purposes, they are charged on it. Let us say, for instance, that a man's salary is $3,000. If he were to bring that $3,000 into Canada it would amount to $3,300. Actually he does not get that $3,300, because, as I say, he has spent some of it in the United States. And yet he is charged on the total amount but which in fact he never brings into Canada, and which in fact he never gets.
While I recognize the administrative difficulties, I do submit strongly to the minister that there can be no justification for charging income tax, no matter how small or how large the amount may be, on a sum of money which is actually never received. That is the situation. They get the money and bring it into Canada, but if they spend it on meals and other necessities in Detroit, they spend American money which, having in mind the locale of the expenditure, is still one dollar and not $1.10.

These people are known as commuters. They are valuable citizens, many of whom not only since the war but for a considerable number of years have worked for the most part in the neighbouring city in the United States, and are an asset to the community and to this country. All they are asking is that having in mind the nature of their work and the circumstances under which it is undertaken, they shall not be placed in a discriminatory position. They are not asking for any special privileges.
They feel, first, that they should be allowed as a deduction from gross income the expenses necessarily incurred in the United States in the earning of this income. They have to pay travelling expenses to and from Canada, provide themselves with food while there, and they are subject to other incidental expenses from which there is no escape. The minister might say: You are asking for something that is unreasonable, something that is not accorded to any other class of the Canadian community. One recognizes that answer. The fact is however that these people are in a special class, and I suggest they might very well be dealt with in the same manner as certain persons employed by the United Kingdom Treasury Delegation, and also another group covered by an order of the treasury board dated April 27, 1944, section 3 of which order reads as follows:
That the appropriate United States expenses allowances may be deducted for income tax purposes under common services notice No. 78, paragraph 5.
This privilege has been granted to all persons employed in the United Kingdom treasury delegation, and I think it is also applied to people in the British supply council in the United States, who are chargeable with Canadian income tax. If there is one group for which such allowance should be made, I think it is these commuters who have a special set of circumstances attending their occupations. They feel, and this is a strong argument and one which I think is unanswerable, that it is unfair to be charged the exchange addition upon that portion of their income which they have to pay out in the United States in connection with commuting to the United States. That is money which in fact they have not brought into Canada and cannot bring into Canada. It seems to me that we are imposing there a tax that just simply cannot stand in equity.
Their third request is in conformity with the principle applied by the department to persons in the British Supply Council and the United Kingdom Treasury Delegation. My constituents consider themselves comparable

to these people and feel that they should have a tax-free allowance granted to them in view of their special situation.
I can only add in this connection that these people are working alongside United States citizens. Many of them have bought Canadian victory bonds but because of their continuous contact with United States citizens they are obliged to invest some of their earnings in United States liberty bonds, and in a corresponding way in United States war certificates and the like. They have to make contributions to charitable organizations and patriotic organizations in the United States within their means. They are taxed on the total amount of their earnings as though the total amount plus the ten per cent premium which the United States dollar commands was really in their hands. To the extent of these necessary expenses, they never have that income.
I urge the minister to reconsider the submissions that have been made' to him by the Secretary of State, by this organization and by myself, and review the matter in the light of the representations which I am taking thq time of the house to make to-day only because this is a small but very important section of the community which I represent, made up of ordinary men and women earning no great income but who find themselves discriminated against. I do not think this discrimination is justified, and I ask the minister to reconsider the whole matter in the light of these further representations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) has brought up the question of commuters. I have had a great deal of correspondence on this subject with the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) and the matter has been given very careful consideration. The hon. member for Essex East says that he has a grievance in respect to "the administration" of income tax, but I should like to read from section 3 of the act which defines income. It reads:
For the purposes of this act, "income" means the annual net profit or gain or gratuity, whether ascertained and capable of computation as being wages, salary, or other fixed amount, or unascertained as being fees and emoluments .	.	. whether derived from sources withinCanada or elsewhere;- and shall include the interest .	.	. and also the annual profit or
gain from any other source, including
(e) personal and living expenses when such form part of the profit, gain or remuneration of the taxpayer or the payment of such constitutes part of the gain, benefit or advantage accruing to the taxpayer under any estate-
Section 6 of the Income War Tax Act sets out the deductions that may not be allowed from income. It says:
In computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed, a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of
(a) disbursements or expenses not wholly, exclusively and necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the income;
(f) personal and living expenses.
Commuters are much in the same position as other workers in Canada. While the persons referred to cross the international boundary, there are many other people in Canada employed in places other than where they reside. Those Canadian citizens who have to pay train fare, perhaps street car and automobile expenses, are not allowed to deduct those expenses from the salaries they receive. Commuters are in the same position. They go to the United States but -they are no more entitled to receive their travelling expenses for going to and from their work than are other Canadian citizens who have similar expenses.
Another complaint is that the salary received is taxed with the exchange of ten per cent added. The first section I read provides -that income is taxable when received from sources within Canada or elsewhere. In all cases where wages or dividends are received by a Canadian taxpayer, the Canadian value of the amount received is estimated for tax purposes. Consequently when wages are received in United States funds, ten per cent is added to find out what the Canadian equivalent is for taxation purposes.
I quite agree that the commuters feel that they have a considerable grievance in that if they are working in the United States all day they have to buy some of their food in the United States with United States currency, and they say: We cannot -bring back this United States money on which we could receive the ten per cent. But the difficulty is that under the act they are not allowed to make any deduction from income for personal or living expenses, and consequently the amount which they spend on their lunches in the United States is not allowed as a deduction under the act as it now stands. Their income is the gross amount that they receive. It is a matter that can be given further consideration. I know that it is causing a great deal of hard feeling among those who work across the border, and I can assure my hon. friend that we will explore any means that can be adopted to grant any relief that is possible. But I do not think that anybody will expect that the whole principle of the act dealing with the question should

Income War Tax

be changed in order to accommodate a small group. If we created a precedent in a case such as this it would have very far-reaching effects indeed, and affect not only commuters crossing the international border, but workers in all parts of Canada who have to travel any distance in going to and from their work.
Another point that was raised -by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was the taxation of railway porters. That raises very much the same point, as to whether they should be allowed a deduction for personal or living expenses incurred while away from home. The act definitely states that that shall not be allowed as a deduction. There is a difference in the treatment of some of the railway workers. The members of the running trades are not paid a salary but are paid on a mileage basis. Many years ago-I do not remember how many but I would say ten or fifteen years ago-representations were made by the railway workers and the income tax division agreed to treat the members of the running trades, who were on a mileage basis, as though they were paid on a commission basis, which would allow them to deduct their expenses. That was accepted at that time by the railway workers organizations, and that ruling has been continued to date. It is to my mind questionable whether that ruling would stand up under fire, and whether we are not wrong in allowing the running trades to have that exemption which they have been receiving. Certainly rather than broadening it out to permit the deduction of living expenses from salary, which is not allowed in any industry in this country, I think we would be well advised to review the original ruling in regard to the running trades and perhaps we might find that they were not entitled to the exemption which they have been receiving. But to hold their case up as an example that should be followed in the case of other employees is not sound, because it is not .allowed in any other industry in this country.

Why are conductors and porters who are away from home part of the time and have to keep a room and pay their living expenses at the other end of their run not allowed to deduct these essential expenses from their earnings for taxation purposes?

They are if they are on a
mileage basis, but where they are drawing salary, that expense is not allowed as a deduction from their earnings for taxation purposes. If in addition to their salary they were given an additional allowance to cover their necessary expenses while away from home, that
