would be included as income and be taxable. One of the deductions that is not allowed is any allowance for personal or living expenses.
The hon. member for Cumberland brought up another point, and that was the inclusion of tips as income. That is a matter that has recently come to light. I think that possibly in the days of lower taxation and higher tax exemptions careful scrutiny was not given to items of that kind, but to-day with the tax exemption standing at $660 and with war taxation higher the income tax division has found itself forced to scrutinize more carefully the returns that are filed and the sources of income from which taxpayers receive their remuneration. Under the definition of income in the act, income means the annual net profit or gain or gratuity, and so forth. I quite agree that if a taxpayer has not kept an adequate record of the tips he has received it is very difficult for him or for the income tax division to know what his income is. I agree that there may be many men who. are engaged on troop trains who may receive little or nothing in the way of tips. I would like to have these cases brought to the attention of the department because we do not want to inflict hardship on individuals. While we want to collect all the taxation that is owing, nobody wants to have a man forced to pay more than he is legally bound to pay.

I should like to say a few words regarding paragraphs (u) and (v), section 1 of the bill, providing for the right to deduct, in determining the amount of the income tax, expenditures which are made by any company or other body in respect of scientific research. The sections as they stand are as follows:
_ (u) "scientific research" means any activity in the field of natural or applied science for the extension of knowledge;
(v) references to expenditures on scientific *research include all expenditures incurred for the prosecution of. or the provision of facilities for the prosecution of, scientific research and reference to scientific research relating to a *business or a class of business include any scientific research that may lead to or facilitate an extension of that business or, as the ease may be, business of that class.
It is generally recognized that the productivity of many industries in this country might be increased by the application of scientific research. In this connection Canada during the years has lagged behind other countries which could be named. No doubt the purpose of defining the term "scientific
research" and also of making provision that amounts expended in connection therewith should be deductible, is to improve the productivity of industry in this country by permitting of research taking place. But the section as now worded applies only to natural and applied science, and as it now stands, I submit, does not go as far as it should to make effective the intentions of those who have drawn it. The purpose, as I say, is to increase productivity by means of research. Productivity and its increase depend on two matters. The one is technological, the standards of plant and equipment and the utilization thereof; that is now covered by the amendments suggested in this bill. But the second factor is as important, if not more important, namely the investigation into the efficiency of the worker with a view to increasing his enterprise and his success. It is a psychological matter; it is a matter which is not comprised within the terminology of this section. This definition of scientific research takes into consideration the technological side but not the matter of the human element; and my submission is that if it is the intention, as it must be, of the department to permit of scientific investigation in order to increase production, it should also make provision for an investigation into causes- psychological causes, if you will-which explain such matters as absenteeism, elements of behaviourism, and the like. It has been said that as far as accidents in industry are concerned, all that this will permit will be an investigation into the causes of accidents, without permitting scientific investigation of the reasons why workmen act in certain ways which result in accidents, and it is in the spheres of psychology and behaviourism that science believes there can be a substantial reduction in the number of accidents.
Dalhousie university has done a great work in this connection, in investigating not the technological end of it, but the scientific end in so far as the mind (is concerned. I submit that if we recognize that much can be done to increase production by scientific investigation. we should also recognize that the whole field should be available to industrial research and give it the right to make deductions from *its income in furthering that very necessary work.
It might be said that the definition is the same as it is in the United Kingdom. That is often given as an explanation in this house for not making changes. But the situation in the United Kingdom is very different from the situation in Canada, for over there, numbers of outstanding leaders in industry and in business have set aside large sums of money for
Income War Tax

investigations such as this. We all know of the investigations in this connection which have been carried out by endowments created by Lord Leverhulme, also the work which 'has open done through grants made by Lord Nuffield, the motor car manufacturer. No such endowments have been made in Canada. I therefore suggest that consideration be given to amplifying the definition of "scientific research". To that end, and to make the provision effective, because as it now stands "scientific research" is narrowly defined and non-inclusive, and I submit will be almost non-effective in the carrying out of the purposes which the bill has in mind unless the definition is widened sufficiently to encourage investigation into these psychological matters, I wish to move an amendment to the definition of "scientific research" in section 1, paragraph (u), by adding thereto the following words:
and includes research in problems related to the working conditions of the employee in the taxpayer's industry.
I wish to commend the hon. member for Lake Centre for raising this question-

I suggest that the time has come for us to interest ourselves in this field. Many universities in Canada have been carrying on research into industrial relations with the view of improving conditions in industry itself, particularly for the employees. They have done,this at a great disadvantage because of lack of funds. The Carnegie institute and other benevolent organizations make sums of money available. It should not be placed on the basis of charity. If we are prepared to enhance the future of industry from the technological standpoint we should consider the human element. Dalhousie university has done great work in that direction, and so has St. Francis Xavier, largely at their own expense. If the provision contained in the amendment were included in the bill to encourage the industries of Canada to con-

tribute to the universities that are carrying on this work, and if it were permitted as a deduction for taxation purposes, there is a chance that we might be able to get the funds from industry itself to meet this very necessary need. I believe that educational research into relieving conditions, promoting the health of the workers, clarifying in the minds of the employers and in many instances the employees what should be proper bargaining arrangements, would pay dividends.

speechtext:
I should like to put forward the reasons why it is felt that this suggestion could not be accepted. As hon. members of the committee probably know, the suggestion has been made to the minister and has been very carefully considered. The first point that I wish to make is that the proposed addition to the definition of research within the meaning of the section includes research in problems related to the working conditions of the employees in the taxpayer's industry. That and the definition as it stands are not mutually exclusive. In other words, if research into working conditions can be brought within the meaning of science, either natural or applied, then I take it it would come within the terms of the definition as it stands. The difficulty, of course, is where to draw the line. I would not be particularly afraid of employers making contributions, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South has indicated, to genuine research to improve working conditions if I were absolutely sure that that privilege would not be abused. But, after all, research of that kind, if you include it in the -category of scientific research, might well be extended to pseudo-research into marketing activities to improve the sale of products, advertising, promoting, any form of activity of that kind which might lead to expanding or increasing the employers' business.
As the hon. member for Lake Centre has pointed out, the section is similar to that in the English act. The definition of scientific research which we have taken is, I think, very similar to the definition contained in the English act. It is a new departure for us, and I think it was a new departure for them. We

Income War Tax
are allowing a deduction from taxable income; in other words, we are saying the taxpayer's money or the money which would otherwise be paid in taxes may be used for these particular purposes. In taking a new step of that kind I think we should be pretty careful to see that it does not lead to abuse, particularly when the tax rates are as high as they are at the present time, which of necessity creates a pretty strong incentive to include as an expense anything which can possibly be included. The provisions of the section do not exclude any expenditure which can qualify as necessarily incurred for the purpose of earning the income. Of course it has no effect on donations which an employer may make for charitable or educational purposes. It may well be-I do not know

that an association or a group may be formed for the purpose of conducting research into labour relations or something of the kind, and that a donation to that type of organization might qualify as a charitable donation.
I merely wish to emphasize the point that the proposed amendment is an addition to a privilege which now exists, whereby the employer may deduct an outlay necessarily incurred for the purpose of earning income, and is an addition to a privilege which he now has of making donations for charitable or educational purposes. I feel and I believe that the minister feels that when we are introducing this provision into the law for the first time it would be dangerous to extend the definition beyond the scope "natural or applied science," which, after all, is a pretty clear, well-defined and easily understood field If we extend it, as suggested in the proposed amendment, to research in problems relating to working conditions, which I grant is very desirable, it seems to me that in logic we should extend it to a good many other problems which may and do arise in connection with industry and which are of equal importance to labour relations.	*

I agree with my hon. friend that a great many of the items to which I referred would be properly deductible as expenses. Frankly, as I have said before, in introducing new legislation of this kind, really for the purpose of stimulating and encouraging scientific development in the generally accepted meaning of that term, the minister is not willing to extend that to what could be a very much wider field.
