We merely wish to extend the same privileges in the field of research to the working people of this country who produced the wealth. This paragraph makes provision for industry to carry on technical research and development. I think the development of the people who work in industry is just as necessary as the development of speedy methods-because that is all we have got out of it in the past. It is time we began to consider the human element in industry. As the hon. member for Rosedale pointed out, twenty-five years ago the Prime Minister wrote a book entitled Industry and Humanity-and he did a good job of it. But I am reasonably sure he did not do it on his own; a good deal of research was necessary. I am reasonably sure he was assisted in that. The thing we are asking for in the amendment is the very thing the Prime Minister emphasizes all through that book- consideration for the human element in industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not wish for one
moment to minimize the importance of study and research into the questions referred to by the hon. members for Cape Breton South and Lake Centre. I say however that that is foreign to the proposal put forward here. Here we are suggesting that in order to encourage scientific research the taxpayer should be allowed to deduct from his income the amount so expended. Now, if work of the kind referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre and by other hon. members comes within that definition, then of course it can be deducted.
Well, does it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I would say in certain
aspects it does not. And I say it does not because I do not think it is in the realm of science, pure or applied. If we wish to extend our taxation provision to include contributions or payments for the study of employer-employee relations, well and good. I should think myself that a considerable amount of expenditure made by individual employers for that purpose could very well come within the description of expenses necessarily incurred for the purpose of earning the income. I should think it would not need any very elaborate provision in the Income War Tax Act to spell out that type of work. But in any case I suggest to the committee that it does not come within the same field of scientific research. It is research, investigation and study, if you wish, in the field of employer-employee relations. But that is not a division of scientific research, at any rate, which was contemplated in this proposal. I should think a very large amount of expenditures along lines urged here
Income War Tax

to-day might-very well form part of the expenditures of an employer which could be charged by him as expenses wholly or necessarily incurred for the purpose of earning the income. I feel it is not desirable to tack on to the definition set out in the bill, which deals with scientific research as any activity in the field of natural or applied science for the extension of knowledge, the one addition of research into problems relating to employer-employee relations. If it comes within the definition of scientific research, well and good; but if it does not, it seems to me it is a different subject altogether.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I wish to say only a few
words in this matter, because my name has been mentioned several times. It will be recalled that about two weeks ago I brought this matter up, when the resolution was being considered, and asked whether the particular project which Professor Richter of Dalhousie university had in mind would come within the resolution then before the house. While I did not ask for an answer, my observation was worded so as clearly to imply that in the administration of the matter covered by the resolution it might be extended to the particular work *which Professor Richter hopes to have undertaken.
In any event the discussion we have had to-day will do a great deal of good, because it has brought to the attention of the committee at long last the necessity of doing something in the field of employer-employee relations. I believe the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, no mean lawyer himself, has indicated that there is the opportunity of considering this matter as an expense wholly necessary for purposes of earning the income. Knowing the progressive nature of the deputy minister, I have no doubt that he will look sympathetically upon the work being done at Dalhousie. This matter is important. I have had considerable discussion with Professor Richter on this matter and I think the problem which confronts him will commend itself to the committee.
We are in the pioneering stage of labour organization in comparison with the United Kingdom and other places. We want to put labour-management relations upon a satisfactory basis whereby the worker will be sure of beng guaranteed his rights as well as of having an opportunity to shoulder his obligations. We are away behind some other countries. In the United States there are schools of industrial relations that are of tremendous help to the workers' movement and to that country, and we must have .that kind of encouragement in Canada. Here is an academic man who has had considerable experience in the maritime provinces and who wants to do

something very special, not only for the workers but for an orderly relationship between workers and management, something which in turn is related to government. I think this matter should be encouraged to the full.
How did he go about it? He said, "I have no money to do this work, which is important," and he addressed himself to particular industries and asked for assistance. They have taken the attitude that they will help him, provided they get a deduction for income tax purposes. I do not commend that particular attitude which makes it a condition that they get an income tax deduction. I would much rather that they saw this as a matter over and above the realm of income tax deduction, as something that will enhance their own particular business as well as improve the problem generally.
In my part of Ontario at Western university, through its affiliated college of Assumption, there is a school where labour-management relations are being taught. I know what they have been doing. At the university of Toronto, my own university, they would like to extend their work in this very important field. I suggest that the loophole suggested by the parliamentary assistant, namely, the consideration of this as an expense wholly necessary for the earning of the income, be used. When we think of the amount of money spent by industry in pure research, perhaps not too much, in advertising and in all that sort of thing as compared with, the small amount spent by industrial plants in trying to improve labour-management relations, I felt that I must add my voice in support of this matter. That is w'hy I have risen.
I feel that labour-management relations in this country should be on the most satisfactory basis possible, one where the workers will be given every opportunity of organization as a means of protecting themselves and at the same time an opportunity of sharing in the responsibility of the management of the industry in which they are employed. I think nothing but good could come out of a very generous interpretation of this section by the deputy minister. I strongly urge that in making his decisions in the future he continue to earn the generous reputation he has won for himself.
Does the hon. member think this would enable the deputy minister to make a decision to include the provision we are talking about?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I understood at the outset that there was no answer given to my question because of its wording, but I then understand there would be no question that under

Income War Tax
"scientific research" this matter could be brought in. If there has been a definite ruling against that view, I would say that it was stretching or altering the meaning of the phrase "scientific research." I would think that "scientific research" is sufficiently broad to include this kind of proposal. However, if a decision has not yet been made I think if I were sitting down with the deputy minister and able to argue with him for a few minutes I could win him over. But assuming that I could not, I would then resort to the argument that this should be considered as expenses wholly necessary for the earning of the income. If he did not concur in that argument, I would proceed under the provision for grants to educational and charitable institutions. In that instance you would be limited to five per cent. There is the difficulty. I would prefer to see the matter dealt with unambiguously here. However, if that cannot be done I do hope that there will be an interpretation along the lines I have indicated to permit this important work being carried on.
The matter of silicosis was brought up by the parliamentary assistant-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are dealing with the amendment having to do with labour-management relations.

That is exactly what I am talking about, Mr. Chairman, if you will bear with me. Coming as you do from a mining district, you will know that silicosis is an industrial disease. Doctor Robson and Mr. Denny carried on experiments in silicosis at the McIntyre mine, as a result of which experiments aluminum therapy was developed. It is thought that with the use of aluminum therapjr silicosis will become almost an extinct disease. I would think that is paramount as a scientific development. If we can destroy or eradicate a serious industrial disease, then every encouragement should be given to the work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That would clearly be considered in connection with this section.

I am glad to know that because I think it is vitally important.
I should like to refer to another piece of scientific research which also had to do with mining and industrial conditions. I refer to the rock bursts which have occurred at certain of our deeper mines. A committee was appointed and some experimental work was carried onf Experts were brought in from the deep copper mines in Michigan and from the mines in India, in Mysore and other localities, to try to solve this problem of
rock bursts in our Ontario mines. A definite and scientific study was made with the idea of improving working conditions. I would say that this work of a scientific nature carried on in an endeavour to eradicate rock bursts should come under this legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not think there would be any question about that.
You think it would come under if?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: From your description I think it would be clearly within the provisions.

I am very glad. If these rock bursts are eliminated there will be an improvement in working conditions because they have been killing men. Every encouragement should be given by the government to this work in order that everything humanly possible can be done to eliminate this hazard. I must say that conditions have improved considerably, but there is still some danger. These are conditions that have faced the mining industry. Silicosis is the forerunner of tuberculosis and the .patient seldom recovers. It is one of the worst of the mining diseases. Rock bursts are also very serious. These are two aspects of scientific research to improve conditions underground and conditions under which the miners work which are included in the bill, and, I think rightly so. But let us say that you have in some industry bad lighting caused by vibration or something of that sort, and you get a group of engineers in to improve the lighting conditions in your plant. That helps the plant by improving the conditions under which the men work. Surely if one is allowed the other is just as scientific and should be allowed as well.
The Workers' Educational Institution is doing excellent work to bring about better housing and better health conditions. It is working in conjunction with the trades unions, the university of Toronto and the Ontario government and, in my opinion, is doing excellent work. Surely we should allow the scientific work that is being done by the Workers' Educational Institution and by the universities to be included. I understand that the work done by the Nuffield foundation is allowed as a deduction from income tax in Great Britain, and that the work done by Lord Leverhulme is also allowed as a deduction. If they find that advisable in Great Britain I think it would be well for us to do it here, because it leads to greater efficiency to have these private organizations doing research work of this kind instead of having it

Income War Tax

done by a national organization which would have to set up its own office staff and equipment. _ They find it cheaper and much more efficient in Britain to have these things done by people like Lord Nuffield and Lord Leverhulme.

The other day I had a call from Doctor Richter, a professor at Dalhousie university, who is interested in the provisions of this bill for research, and he left with me a little memorandum which I should like to read in order to present the matter intelligently. He says:
, It is generally recognized that the productivity of many industries could ibe greatly increased by the application of scientific research.
We are all agreed on that. The memorandum goes on:
Canada lags in that respect behind other countries. The government bill, therefore, aims at encouraging research by declaring as deductible the expenses for scientific research prodded the research is directly or indirectly related to the taxpayers' business. Another restriction is implied by the term "scientific research" as used in the bill: only expenditure for research in the field of natural and applied science is deductible while all types of social research are excluded.
The distinction is arbitrary and unfair and may seriously impair the effect of the clause as a whole. The purpose of the measure is to increase industrial productivity by means of research. Productivity is determined by two factors: one is technological, the standard of plant and equipment and their utilization. The second factor is just as important: the human element in industry, the efficiency of the worker and the contribution which they make to the success of the enterprise.
The bill as it stands is only concerned with the technological elements of production and disregards the 'human factor. This is not in keeping with the repeated statements of the Prime Minister about the aims of the government's labour policy.
The distinction made by the bill will often prove unworkable and may cause some great injustices. The clause applies, for instance, to research on problems of speeding up production. It denies the tax privilege to research concerned with the effects of the speed-up on the worker.
Research on the technological causes of industrial accidents is covered by the clause, research on the causes of accidents brought about by the behaviour of the worker is excluded. This is all the more regrettable as it is mainly the second group of accidents which, according to expert opinion, is capable of further reduction.
The whole field of industrial morbidity which is concerned with health conditions in a particular industry will have to do without the tax privilege and will probably remain as neglected as it is at present.
The clause as it stands militates against the smaller firms. Large industrial concerns have for a long time through their personnel departments _ conducted research on the "working conditions of the employees and have always regarded the expenses involved as deductible. 
If, however, smaller businesses join together for that purpose or commission a university to do the research for them, they will be hampered by the present bill.
The proposed amendment attempts to remedy these defects by extending the tax privilege to research on working conditions of employees in the taxpayers industry. The technological and human factors of production are thus treated alike. An unwarranted use of the clause is made difficult by the concise definition of the purposes of research.
The terms used in the government bill are taken from recent British legislation. But conditions in Canada require a different approach. In Britain Lord Nuffield, Lord Leverhulme and other benefactors have made ample provisions for research on the conditions of industrial workers. No such sources for the financing of that type of research exist in Canada and as a result the country lags sadly behind Britain. It is the purpose of the amendment to facilitate the provision .of the necessary funds in this country.
I have an amendment here which I understood was to have been submitted by somebody, but I was not in the house at the time and I do not know just what has happened in regard to it.
The memorandum I have read is from this teacher at Dalhousie university, and while I cannot speak with a knowledge of all the facts I should like to see encouraged the research activities of these smaller universities which coordinate the practical and the theoretical, bringing the activities of the worker and the teacher together. That is a splendid thing and they have been doing that at Dalhousie university for the last two years with beneficial results. It seems to me that anything that can be done to forward the search for knowledge, especially on the practical and humane side, should be done, and I hope that the minister will see his way clear to considering this appeal and, after consultations with his officers, that he may be able to bring in something to meet the conditions outlined in the memorandum.

The hon. member for Cape Breton South has brought up the subject of silicosis. A great deal of money has been spent by the mining industries in my riding and in your riding, Mr. Chairman, on research into silicosis. I forget the exact figures but they run into the millions. I think the mines do not always get credit for what they are doing along this line. A year or so ago the statement was made in the house that nothing was done in the way of research by the mines, and it would surprise hon. gentlemen to know just how much has been and is being spent on research by the mines to improve the health conditions of their workers.
I do not think rock bursts can be eradicated altogether, but the mining companies in my

Income War Tax
district and in your district, Mr. Chairman, where the rock bursts are not quite so bad have spent thousands and thousands of dollars to prevent them. They have the finest machinery to try to indicate where rock bursts are coming and with such success that for the last two or three years no man has been killed from this cause, thanks to these very delicate instruments which scientific workers have produced. I do not think rock bursts can be eliminated; they arise from pressure; the deeper one goes, the more pressure there is from the sides, and this cannot be stopped. But if you can find out when they are coming and get the men out of harm's way you have accomplished a wonderful thing, and I know that no pains are being spared by our mine operators in this direction.
I wish to make this correction: it was not I who raised the question of silicosis.	*

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Right. I raised it myself, Mr. Chairman, much to my sorrow I may say.

What I am concerned about, and what I said was, that we make an appropriation federally for the department of industrial hygiene. Not enough money is appropriated in that field by the dominion to achieve anything. What the provinces are doing is all to the good. I agree with the parliamentary assistant to this extent, that I am reasonably certain that most of the matters raised by the hon. member for York West, and also the question of silicosis, are covered. But that is not the angle from which I was arguing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe that the parliamentary assistant brought in a point of order on the amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before you rule on the amendment, Mr. Chairman, will you give someone else a chance to speak on the point of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Well, nobody so far has spoken on the point of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with
respect to the point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Davenport has the floor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On the point of order, the only reason why I did not speak-
The Chairman gave me the floor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Speaking to the point of order, if I may, the reason why I did not ri*
'before was that I thought the Chair was ignoring the point raised by the parliamentary assistant.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not ignoring the point of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I would call your attention, Mr. Chairman, to a rule which I have cited before, citation 502 of Beauchesne, third edition:
A private member may move that certain specified taxes foe readjusted and that the scope of tax exemptions foe enlarged.
I called attention to that rule in connection with an amendment made in committee of the whole on a resolution on July 19, and, as reported in Hansard, page 5092, you replied to me in these words, immediately after you quoted citation 502:
That principle applies to the committee on the bill only and not to ways and means.
My point on this amendment is that you did not allow citation 502 as applicable when we were in committee on a resolution; you said at that time that it applied only to committee on the bill, and that is exactly where we are now. We are in committee on the bill, and I submit, upon your own ruling, citation 502 applies to the present situation and that this amendment is in order.

I gather from what has been said that some objection has been taken to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lake Centre. If it were accepted, paragraph (u) would read, that " 'scientific research' means any activity in the field of natural or applied science for the extension of knowledge, and includes", the hon. member adds, "research in problems related to the working conditions of the employee in the taxpayer's industry". I would say that the parliamentary assistant, if he has the authority to do so, would be well advised to accept the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre. It entirely fits in with what I interpret to be the purpose and value of this clause.
When I was home two weeks ago or more, I had occasion to see a man who was long employed at a foundry. Those who know anything about foundry life know that employees too often have been sadly affected as a result of the conditions under which they have to work, particularly in the moulding shop. I know there are those who will say that the moulding shop is conducive to health. That is so in respect of the ordinary small moulding shop, but in the big plants where large machines are used to do moulding work, in spite of every effort of the manufacturers of these large machines to eliminate the
Income War Tax

effects of rapidly revolving wheels and sand throwers, men have been and are being affected therewith. A man who died recently was found, upon post mortem examination, to have his lungs largely congested with material which had accumulated year after year until it finally caused his death. But the man to whom I started to refer, whom I visited a short time ago, also worked in a foundry, and in spite of every effort of the operators of the plant and the inspectors of the Ontario government to eliminate the effects of internal injuries in foundries of this kind, he contracted a disease which caused him to break out every ' so often with red spots and compelled him to lay off work. He is now off permanently. After a while his body used to heal up, but the trouble recurred until finally his body was so badly affected in this and other ways, through whatever it was took place in the plant, that he could not carry on any longer. I went to see the workmen's compensation board in Toronto. They are a fine board and are doing wonderful work in the direction of eliminating causes of disease in industrial plants. Away back in the early nineteen-hundreds I was a strong advocate of workmen's compensation and, as I said some days ago, I was very glad to see it finally enacted, I believe in the year 1914. The workmen's compensation board have developed quite a technique of ascertaining causes of disease of men in industry, and I hope their activities will be greatly extended.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If I may interrupt my hon. friend, I have been listening very closely to his description, and I believe that work of the kind he is referring to would come within the definition of "scientific research" as contained in the bill.
It seems to me that the hon. member for Lake Centre is clarifying the section by having it include research into problems relating to the working conditions of employees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I know the hon. member for Davenport was not able to be in his seat at the time, but I discussed this matter at some length after the hon. member for Lake Centre and others had spoken. I pointed out that I felt the government could not accept the amendment as drafted, but that I thought a great many cases which had been cited by various speakers would come within the definition as it now stands; that is to say, if it were within the language of natural or applied science, and certainly investigations into the health conditions in a specific plant, what was causing disease and so on, when conducted by a properly qualified scientist, 
would, I think, clearly come within the language of the section, but it is to prevent its being extended to outside associations to conduct general inquiries, let us say, into working conditions as such. I pointed out that it would be impossible to draw the line there; that you would need to extend it into investigations into marketing conditions and that sort of thing. I discussed the question at some considerable length, and I am sorry my hon. friend was not here at the time.

I do not wish to prolong
the discussion-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: To be specific, I think the things my hon. friend has been describing would come within the definition in the bill as it stands.

I am talking from practical experience. I am not talking about something I do not know a good deal about, because I have been connected with the business and know a lot about it. I may have forgotten a lot since I left it. It was a big business, and I saw a lot happen to men that should never have happened to them. I cannot understand why the parliamentary assistant will not include the hon. member's amendment, because it is inclusive and covers what I have in mind. I cannot see that it is being covered by simply saying "scientific research", because it would take a Philadelphia lawyer to protect the working men on that basis.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My short answer was that if the research into problems relating to working conditions was scientific research, natural or applied, then, of course, it comes within the provision of the section as it stands. The real effect of the amendment is to extend the definition of scientific research.
Is that not all to the good?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am sorry; I argued this before. Where are we to stop in this thing? It may be important to encourage, let us say, research into marketing conditions or sale problems or efficiency or a dozen other things that arise, how to operate a plant more efficiently, and so on. I am repeating what I said before; a good deal of this work I am sure comes under the heading of expenses necessarily incurred to earn income. If so, the taxpayer does not need to rely on this section at all. He can rely on the ordinary law. The same thing applies to charitable donations; but this is expanding the existing law to encourage research of a scientific character, scientific research, either natural or applied. That is the purpose of this section, and it was

Income War Tax
never intended to go any farther than science as the term is generally accepted. As I say, it does not extend to things like marketing problems or efficiency engineers, or what have you.

I am not thinking of marketing problems. I am thinking only of the working men. The difference between my hon. friend and myself is that I have been associated with working men in the plants for many years, and have had a keen knowledge of many other plants manufacturing subsidiary lines of brass, copper, steel and iron. In my experience I have seen men's health being ruined, and they have been unable to obtain any redress because the people from whom they sought to obtain redress have always been able to engage a brigade of lawyers to combat the men and take their hides off, if necessary. The poor man never had a chance until-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I return to what I said. If it is investigation into the health of the working men it may come under the head of scientific research.

I am sure the hon.
member will admit that I ought to know something about plants.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I not only admit it; I freely concede it.

If this section includes allowances to companies or firms they should know about .it. They would then develop means of protecting the lives and health of the workingman in their plants, and they ought to be able to deduct the cost of investigations looking toward the protection of the lives of the working men. If this section goes that far that is far enough for me. I agree with the argument of the hon. member for Lake Centre, but if the parliamentary assistant will not accept it he has the power to reject it. I am thinking only of the men in the manufacturing institutions. I am not talking about mines; I am not competent to talk about them, but I am competent to talk about the effect on the health of men in industry. I have seen so much distress amongst working men brought about by the conditions under which they work in large plants that anything I can do to make it easier for them I am always glad to do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Citation 551 standing order 60, of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, reads as follows:
It is fundamental principle that no resolution or amendment to increase a charge upon the people can be moved with the speaker in the
chair; it must be initiated in committee by a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
That ruling applies also to committee of the whole.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned citation 502 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, which is as follows:
A private member may move that certain specified taxes be readjusted and that the scope of tax exemptions be enlarged.
That, of course, applies to public bills. When I gave my ruling the other day I do not know whether I qualified my statement by saying that it applied equally to private bills in committee of the whole. Citation 500 states:
Though it is the function of the committee of rvays and means to impose rather than to repeal taxes, examples of the repeal of taxation effected in this committee are to be found upon the journals. Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee; but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year.
Citation, 501 is as follows:
No augmentation of a tax or duty asked by the crown can be proposed to the committee, nor tax imposed, save upon the motion of a minister of the crown; nor would an amendment to extend the imposition of a tax to persons enjoying an exemption therefrom be now permitted.
There are dozens of decisions that have been rendered by Speakers to the effect that no private member has the right to. amend a public bill to increase public expenditure. The amendment we are discussing uses these words: " 'scientific research' means any activity"- these are the words on which we must concentrate our attention-"in the field of natural or applied science for the extension of knowledge." I listened attentively to the statements made by the parliamentary assistant in which he said that this phraseology' might be almost wide enough to include what is contained in the amendment. At the same time I believe he objected to the fact that he thought the language of the amendment might result in an increase in the expenditure of public money. If it is in order I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant on what he based his argument that it might result in an increase of public funds?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I shall do it very readily. If the amendment has any meaning at all, in my opinion it is extending the exemption or the deduction. It is extending the class of cases in which the taxpayer may deduct from his income, which would otherwise be subject to tax, certain expenditure which he makes, and
Income War Tax

thereby in effect it would reduce the amount of taxes which he would pay. That, very briefly, is my submission as to the manner in which it affects the revenue.

May I now speak to the point of order. If what the hon. member says is correct-and I accept his statement that it will extend the scope of tax exemptions -then my submission is that the amendment which I moved is in order under citation 502.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am not an expert in
parliamentary procedure, as I have said on numerous occasions, I do not know whether or not citation 502 is a precedent which has to be followed. The Minister of National Revenue points out that the language there is, " that certain specified taxes be readjusted and that the scope of tax exemption be enlarged," whatever that may mean.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre brought up a similar point which I decided a few weeks ago, but perhaps my statement at that time was not sufficiently clear. After listening to the argument of the hon. member for Lake Centre and the statement of the parliamentary assistant, I am sincerely of the opinion that the adoption of this amendment would mean an increased expenditure of public money, and consequently I rule it out of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to say a further word in connection with section 1 of the bill. This section amends section 2 of the act, which is the section setting out the various definitions and terms used throughout the income tax legislation. As a matter of fact, before I finish I should like to offer an amendment that will add a definition to section 2 of of the Income War Tax Act.
I do so because of the discussion we have had already in regard to sleeping-car conductors and sleeping-car porters. The Minister of National Revenue spoke on this matter on second reading, and indicated that the difficulty arises from the wording of the relevant section in the act. That relevant section is section 5, paragraph (f), found on page 13 of the most recent office consolidation. It reads:
5.	"Income" as hereinbefore defined shall for the purposes of this act be subject to the following exemptions and deductions:
(f) Travelling expenses, including the entire amount expended for meals and lodging, while away from home in the pursuit of a trade or business.
It is in defining "trade or business" that the income tax division has drawn the line between railway conductors, for example, and sleeping-car conductors. The Minister of Finance ad-

mitted that this was a very fine line when he referred to the matter on July 12 of this year. At page 4788 of Hansard he said:
It may be argued that "trade or business" includes profession or salaried occupation; but here again the income tax division have been thoroughly consistent and uniform throughout in ruling that "trade or business" does not include salaried positions; they regard that as meaning trade or business in a different sense. The line is very fine, but they have tried to draw it between what they called trade or business on the one hand, and salary which is not a trade or business on the other.
Then the minister uttered these further words, which I suggest were an admission that we have a case:
Most unfortunately it seems to run through the railway employees, and that is the reason for the difficulty which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned this evening. . . .
I still cannot see why the income tax division should not regard the work of a railway sleeping-car conductor as very similar to the work of a railway conductor, as a trade or business; and as such the expenses incurred by the one while away from home should be treated in the same way as the expenses incurred by the other. But if the income tax division has that difficulty it seems to me the only thing to do is take care of it by an amendment to the act. I should like to suggest an amendment defining "trade or business" in such a way as definitely to include all railway running trade employees, whether they are on a mileage, wage or salary basis. It strikes me that the best place to have that definition is in section 2 of the act, and in order to get it there I am moving an amendment to section 1 of bill No. 180, which is now before us. My amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, is as follows:
That section 1 olf bill No. 180 ibe amended by inserting after subsection (1) (w) thereof the following additional subsection:
(x) "trade or business" includes employment in any of the railway running trades, whether on a mileage, wage or salary basis.
In the light of what the chairman did with the last amendment I suppose I may as well anticipate that he might not accept this one as in order. If that should happen, I suggest that the Minister of National Revenue give consideration to accepting this amendment and moving it on his authority as minister. When he spoke a short time ago, if I understood him correctly he based his whole case upon the difficulty of interpreting section 5(f) of the Income War Tax Act in any other way than is now being done by the income tax division. If that is the problem this parliament can clear

Income War Tax
up the difficulty for the income tax division by adopting this amendment. I have said already that if this amendment were adopted it would add another subsection to section 2 of the act, which would define "trade or business" in the manner indicated, which would then have its effect upon the words "trade or business" where they appear in section 5(f).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the hon. member realizes that this amendment is out of order because of the changes it would bring about in the Income War Tax Act. He qualified his remarks by asking the Minister of National Revenue to adopt the amendment, but as far as that is concerned the amendment is certainly out of order on the grounds I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would you permit either the parliamentary assistant or the Minister of National Revenue to comment on my suggestion?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Certainly.

The hon. member suggested that I should move the amendment, but I am not prepared to do so. It would mean granting an exemption on account of travelling and living expenses while away from home to one class or group of salaried workers in this country, and I am not prepared to recommend that one group should receive a benefit under the taxation laws which is not given to other groups paid on the same basis.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I thought I protected
my amendment against that argument by using the word "includes" rather than the word "means"; in looking through section 2 of the Income War Tax Act I find those words used alternatively, depending on what is desired. By using the word "includes" I did not cut out any other group, but made it definite that in addition to such railway running trades employees as are already included these others, namely sleeping-car conductors and porters, would be covered as well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Of course the effect of the
amendment would be to override section 6(f) and, by implication, to override the provisions of section 3, which defines "income." As the Minister of National Revenue has pointed out it would, in effect, be providing that a certain class of salaried employees, namely the railway running trades, who are paid on a salary basis, would be allowed to deduct certain expenses which other salaried employees of the country are not allowed to deduct.
The remedy, I should think, if a remedy is necessary, lies with the method of payment. The reason why certain railway employees are
allowed to deduct these expenses is that they are paid on a mileage basis, and they are allowed to deduct certain expenses incurred in earning that income. But they do not come within the definition of salaried employee.
As the Minister of Finance has pointed out time and again, since the Income War Tax Act was first adopted in 1917, persons in receipt of salary or ascertained income have never been permitted to deduct expenses incurred in earning the salary. My hon. friend's suggestion is adverse to the rule which has been followed, and I think properly followed since the act was first introduced.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant suggests that the proposed amendment overrides the effect of section 6, paragraph (f) which states that no deduction can be allowed for personal and living expenses. I should like to point out that section 5, paragraph (f) of the same act states that all travelling expenses, including the amount spent for meals and lodging while away from home, in pursuit of a trade or business, may be allowed.
A further point is that there is nothing in the act about salaried employees not being engaged in a trade or business. Thus the decision that "trade or business" covers people on a mileage or wage rate, but does not cover people doing similar work, who are on a salary rate, has been made by the income tax division, according to the statement of the Minister of Finance himself. My proposal is that since a difficulty has arisen because of a line drawn by the income tax division-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is not quite so. This is a matter of legal interpretation, the legal meaning and use of section 3, which has been interpreted by the courts in England, at any rate, along the lines I have indicated. Section 3 is one of the fundamental sections in the Income War Tax Act, and is the defining section as to what shall constitute income.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The distinction is still unfair.
Are we dealing with the whole section, or only part of it?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I read it all.

Before it
carries, it is understood that the discussion on the first section of the bill shall be fairly wide, and that general matters may be brought up.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not too general, I am afraid.

I have already discussed to-day the unfairness of taxation on electrical energy in different parts o'f Canada.
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I cannot allow a discussion of that kind to proceed under this section. I am sorry to say that, but my hon. friend placed his views on record in the debate on second reading. *

I wish to have a statement from the minister or the parliamentary assistant as to whether they are going to allow the condition to be perpetuated, under which Ontario and Quebec are relieved of taxation, and Nova Scotia is taxed to the extent of a million dollars a year. The city of Montreal and the surrounding territory are relieved of about $6,000,000. Surely there is nothing fair or just in that. I want a statement from the minister in regard to it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is not in order to discuss that matter on this section and, as my hon. friend knows, he is not entitled to demand a statement from me on that now. I can tell the committee this, that this question of the taxation of privately owned utilities companies is not a new one. It has been brought up in the house before. However, the question as to whether privately owned utilities companies will or will not be subject to income tax is a matter of government policy, which will be announced in due course. It is not relevant at the present time.

It is a condition wfiich is becoming more aggravated all the time. Hon. members are entitled to a declaration from the minister or from the government with respect to it. The question as to the basis of taxation of electricity has been left altogether too long.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I rise to a point of order again. If we are to make any headway with this bill I suggest we must stick as closely as we can to the section under consideration. If not, we shall be here forever.

On the point of order, the hon. member for Cumberland is quite right in his view that under section 1 a general discussion can take place. And yet, when the parliamentary assistant starts reading lectures as to taxation-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not at all.

I say that this matter could have been brought in long ago. We are placed in the position, as members of the House of Commons, of being asked in the dying days of the session to deal with hundreds of millions of dollars worth of expenditures, and with most important legislation brought down in a rush, so that full consideration cannot be given to it. And yet
 '
the parliamentary assistant is endeavouring to read a lecture to hon. members on this side of the house.
The point I am making is this: Here we are in the last few days of the session, being asked to deal with expenditures and with bills with which we have not had time to become fully conversant. There is no necessity for hon. members to become annoyed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Oh, no, I was not annoyed, at all.
It is not an offence that is so uncommon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Appearances were misleading.

WTe have a very heavy responsibility, so far as these discussions are concerned. They are almost restricted to members of the opposition, hon. members to the left of the chair, who Endeavour to assist the government and to see to it that the interests of individuals are protected. The parliamentary assistant should not endeavour to brush hon. members aside simply by suggesting that we are endeavouring to-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If I gave that impression I wish to remove it at once. I did not wish to read a lecture to anybody, and I did not intend to indicate any desire to rush anything. But I must point out to the committee that the resolutions on which this bill is founded were laid before the house on June 26. Hon. members have had an opportunity to study them since that date. They have known what the government's proposals in the budget have been since that time.
I am free to confess that the bill was available to hon. members only two or three days ago; but on the other hand lawyer members in the committee will realize that the drafting of a bill of this kind is a task of considerable difficulty, and it cannot be carried out until the resolutions are brought to a final stage.
The resolutions were passed only about ten days ago. I certainly do not wish to leave the impression that I am attempting to restrict discussion. After all, however, we are in committee on the bill and we are discussing the section which deals with exemptions. It may be that I was wrong in saying that the question of complete exemption from income tax for certain types of companies should not be discussed under the bill, although it certainly does not come under any of the specific provisions. It might come under another section.
In any event I cannot allow to pass unchallenged the statement that we are rushing

Income War Tax
things through. I believe we are trying to expedite business as much as possible. I do not think it is fair to say that this legislation was brought in at the last minute, because the provisions have been known to hon. members for at least six weeks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section carry? Mr. BLACK (Cumberland): Do I understand that it is the wish of the minister, his parliamentary assistant, and the government, that this basis of unfair taxation of electrical power generated by private enterprise and by government plants shall be perpetuated; is that the policy? Users must pay heavy taxation running as high as twenty-five per cent, or fifty per cent when they are served by private companies. That is imposed on industries, agriculture and households served by these companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I must rise to a point of order. I do not wish to appear rude, but I must ask for your ruling, Mr. Chairman, whether it is relevant to discuss under this section of the question of the taxation of privately-owned power plants?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must say that I cannot find that it is relevant. I think hon. members will agree that I would be the last person to try to curtail the discussion, but we are dealing with section 1 of bill No. 180. I believe the hon. member for Cumberland made a very strong statement this morning on the case he has mentioned, and I know hon. members of the committee will want to avoid repetition as much as possible. I hope it will be found possible to keep to the section.

I subscribe to your ruling and I appreciate what you say about my position being clear and strong. I ask for a statement from the government or from the minister, representing his own views if he cannot speak for the government, as to the policy of perpetuating this unfair basis of taxation that exacts $1,000,000 from the province of Nova Scotia and $150,000 from my own constituency which is not charged other places in Canada. The small industries in my part of the country have in any event to pay higher costs than those in areas served by great power developments. This is unfair, and I think we should have a declaration from the government as to whether it is their purpose to perpetuate and aggravate this unfairness.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Payment upon retirement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Subsection 7 that is to be added implements resolution 10, the purpose of which was to try to take care of the situation of a married woman having an income just over $660. Under the previous wording of the legislation she and her husband might have to pay more in taxation than was intended.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the income of the wife was $670, the extra $10 would be very much less than the combined tax on herself and her husband.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This gives her the right to pay in that $10 and for her husband to retain his married status.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Correct.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
All right; under this heading at the resolution stage I raised the case of the married lady doctor and the married nurse who are also discriminated against and I had hoped that the matter might be covered by a section such as this.
I take it that that has not been done. Before the minister or the parliamentary assistant makes a reply on that angle, I should like to call their attention to rule 2 on page 70 of the office consolidation of the act, which states toward the end:
. . . that a husband shall not lose his right to be taxed under rule one of this section by reason of his wife being employed and receiving any earned income.
As I understood it, it was desired to draw a line between earned income and investment income.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think substantially that is correct. Section 22 of the bill amends rule 2 to which the hon. member referred.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
But it does not change the part to which I was referring. When we were at the resolution stage I drew 1he attention of the parliamentary assistant to the case of the married lady doctor receiving fees. She is not regarded as coming under this rule 2, whereas a married lady doctor working for a clinic and receiving a salary is considered to come under rule 2. I have been contending for a change in the legislation to take care of that case, and yet it seems to me that the difficulty is in the interpretation made by the income tax division. If the parliamentary assistant will turn to page 4 of the office consolidation he will find that clause (m) states that "earned income" means salary, wages, fees, and many other things as well. I emphasize the word "fees". I want to know why it is that a married lady doctor receiving fees directly from patients is treated differently under rule 2 from a married lady doctor who works for a clinic and receives a salary. Under the definition on page 4, "earned income" means salary, wages and fees. The same argument applies
Income War Tax

to married nurses, as between the nurse who works for a hospital on salary and the nurse who takes private cases and receives fees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The part of the rule to which my hon. friend referred which states, "by reason of his wife being employed and receiving any earned income" has been interpreted to mean a wife employed by an employer and paid wages or salary. The nurse or doctor who was operating independently would deduct expenses from the gross earnings, and that is the reason for the distinction. As my hon. friend said, he raised this point on the resolution stage and I answered him at some length as well as I could. I am afraid there is not much I can add to what I said at that tme.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Was the matter considered?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Oh, yes.	,

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Apart from the technical argument the parliamentary assistant has used in reply to me, has he any moral argument to offer in connection with the case I put to him?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not wish to repeat what I said before. At that time I said that perhaps this was an unsound provision put in there, but it was inserted because we wanted to encourage the employment of women in war industry.
All industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All industry, if you will, but particularly in war industry. It was found that some of them were not prepared to work if their husbands lost the benefit of the special taxation provision.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I suggest that doctors and nurses are particularly necessary.

In replying to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the parliamentary assistant said that the original intention was to distinguish between earned income and investment income on the part of the wife. This is clearly a case where that original idea or intention is not carried out, and -I submit it is nothing less than faulty draftman-ship on the part of the department. It should be changed to include income received by the woman as long as it is earned.

May I ask the parliamentary assistant if some arrangement could not be made to take care of the case of a wife who *receives income less than S660 from Great Britain after paying income tax there? I brought to his attention the case of a wife getting an income of about $800 from Great Britain upon which she had to pay a tax there of $300. ^ She was really getting less than $660 in Canada, yet here she had to pay tax 
*on the basis of the full income payable to her in Great Britain. That means that under this provision she would still have to pay approximately $200, although she was receiving in Canada only about $300 or $400.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My hon. friend spoke to me about that the other day, and I had hoped to have looked into the particular case to which he referred, but I must apologize to him because I have not yet done so. I have his representations, and I will discuss the matter with the officials and see what administrative action can be taken in a case of that kind.
It does seem to me very unfair that she should be taxed in that way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I'll have it looked into.

May I ask the parliamentary assistant a question with respect to subsection 6 of section 2? Am I right in understanding the subsection to mean that where a man has served a company for a long time and then retires and is given a gratuity of, let us say, $750, for taxation purposes he will be taxed to the extent of one-fifth of that amount, or $150 in five instalments?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is spread over five years. As the law now stands, it is all taxable in the year in which it is received, but it was felt that this worked an undue hardship in a great many cases. This was discussed at some length on the resolution stage. An amendment put forward at that time proposed that it should be based on the expectancy of life. The provision now is this. Let us say the amount is $1,000.
Take my figure of $750.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We will take $1,000 because it is a little easier to divide by five. It would be taxable to the extent of $200 in the year in which it was paid and in each of the four years thereafter if the recipient lived. It would be spread over the five years. It would be considered as taxable income only to the extent of one-fifth of it in each year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Just one further word to the discussion we have had on subsection 7 of section 2. Since we are not going to get through this bill to-day, will the minister give further consideration to amending section 22 when we come to it by deleting the words "being employed and" in the last two lines. That would cover the case of the married lady doctor and the married nurse. I do not ask the parliamentary assistant to reply now.
I would rather he would think it over.

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will bring my hon. friend's representations to the attention of the minister.

Since the department has not seen fit to change that subsection whereby any lump sum given to an employee on retirement is to be spread over five years instead of ten years or on life expectancy, I just want to say that as it stands it is nothing but a rank injustice to a small class of Canadian taxpayers.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Service pay and allowances.
Would the parliamentary assistant let me know on what resolution the rectification of the present injustice was based?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There was no resolution covering the provisions of subsection 1 of this section relating to the armed services. The effect is to put male and female members of the services on the same basis.
Is it necessary to introduce a resolution preceding a provision of this kind? What is the procedure in that regard? This is a rank injustice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am not an expert on procedure, but I understand that the general resolution is sufficient in law to justify any amendments which the government may see fit to make. In practice, however, the custom has grown up of outlining in some detail the major amendments which it is proposed to make in the form of separate resolutions. Subsection 1 does not impose any new tax but just provides relief, so that for that additional reason I think the amendment could be made in the bill itself without the necessity of preceding it by a resolution. That applies only to subsection 1.

This question of taxation of service pay and allowances brings up the question of taxing the members of the auxiliary services overseas such as the Y.M.C.A., the Knights of Columbus, the Salvation Army and the Canadian Legion. I think the present situation is very unfair to these men. As I understand it, they are taxed on four-fifths of the money they receive, although in Normandy and in Italy they are actually with the invading troops in the Canadian army who, of course, pay no income tax at all. I know that some consideration was given to this question, and I do not wish to take up time to-day in discussing it further, but I do think the present situation should be remedied, and it could be done by order in council. I cannot
for the life of me see why these men should be taxed at all, especially those who are with the invading forces. Can the parliamentary assistant tell us what the present position is?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think I touched on this when we were discussing the resolution. The matter has received extensive consideration. I have also considereed it personally. I took part in conferences with representatives of the auxiliary services on this question. Briefly, why complete exemption is not granted to the auxiliary services is that in no case is complete exemption granted under the Income War Tax Act to a person with the status of a civilian. We do not grant exemption to the merchant seamen or to the ferry pilots, although they are engaged in a very hazardous occupation, because they have the status of civilians. If the auxiliary service people were service personnel, as I understand they are in the United States, they would automatically benefit from the exemption which is given to service personnel, but after the fullest consideration it was decided that in order to maintain the line of distinction between service men and civilians they should not be completely exempted. There are only about 200-odd involved, and they are treated on substantially the same basis as the officers of the merchant navy and the ferry pilots. It was done by order in council with respect to the merchant navy and the ferry pilots, because it was felt that this provision need not be included in what is a permanent taxing structure.
In effect these men are in the forces. The men in Normandy or Italy cannot be treated as civilians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The army can cure that very easily by taking them into the army and .making them members of the forces, but I am advised that the auxiliary services do not wish to be included officially as a part of the armed forces. I was told that at the conferences of which I spoke. The men of these auxiliary services are given pension privileges and other benefits. However, their legal status is that of civilians, and the income tax act has never granted complete tax exemption to any class of civilians.
I understand that civil servants who go overseas are protected against the tax by getting an additional allowance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have no information on that.

That is what I am told, and I think they should be protected too, but
Income War Tax

surely these men of the auxiliary services who are actually with the fighting troops should get the same consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They have received special consideration, and the consideration which has been given was decided upon after, I can assure my hon. friend, the fullest discussion.

I know, but the auxiliary
services are not satisfied and the men serving with them are not satisfied. What is the situation with regard to dominion civil servants overseas?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am afraid I have not any information as to that. I would have to make inquiries and see if I can find out. I am not quite clear; did my hon. friend say that they were receiving some special non-taxable allowance or something of that sort?
The living allowances they get are not taxable, or the expense allowances.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Of course my hon. friend knows the law is quite clear on the point. The section was amended last year or the year before.
I believe the effect is that they get compensation for the tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not know of any special treatment given to any special class of civil servants. The officials point out to me that the officers of the auxiliary service forces do not take into account as taxable income their living allowances. There is a provision, subsection 4 of section 3 of the act, which reads:
Provided however that the living allowance paid to persons who are serving outside of Canada but are maintaining a self-contained domestic establishment in Canada and who are either employees of the government of Canada or members of the Canadian naval, military or air force in Canadian active service forces shall not be deemed to be taxable income up to_ such an amount as may be determined by the minister in his discretion.
The auxiliary service forces benefit from the same sort of provision in that the proportion of their pay which represents living allowance is not included in the amount subject to tax, and I think that either one-third or twenty per cent of their actual pay is treated as a war risk element and is not subject to tax.
Their allowance, I believe, is lower than the allowance payable to the civil servants?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It may be, but I do not * know.

Section agreed to.
IMr. Green.]
On section 4, subsection 1-Deductions for superannuation or pension fund.
Would the parliamentary assistant explain paragraph (g), subparagraph (ii) ? Does that mean that the employee can contribute $300 in respect of previous years before he came under the plan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. That is to take care of the cost of the plan, which, let us say, is found to need additional moneys. The employer can make contributions to the plan in order to make it actuarially sound; those are allowed. This section allows a similar contribution to be made by the employee up to the amount of $300 a year.
That is in addition to the current $300?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Oh, quite; it is in addition to the current $300, and if they came in late or something of that sort, and wanted to make up previous contributions, they could do so to the extent of $300 a year.

Do I understand that the employer for the current year can contribute $300 in respect of the employee which the employee does not know about? As far as taxation is concerned the employee can contribute $300 which is also deductible. This provision allows him to put in a further $300, over a series of years, if he wishes, in order to make up any deficiency on his part in respect of the fund; in other words, $300 from the employer which the employee gets the benefit of although he does not know anything about it; and now the employee is allowed to contribute $600 from his received income and pay no tax whatever on that in order to make up the back portion of the fund and keep it running? I must say it is quite generous, although I am not objecting to it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
My hon. friend's summing
up is quite correct.

Subsection agreed to.
Subsections 2 and 3 agreed to.
On section 4 subsection 4-Unusual medical expenses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already spoken about this. This is a clause where, in spite of charges to the contrary, the government has not only listened to representations which have been made by all sides of the house but acceded to them in some respects. If the committee will bear with me for a moment-it is one minute to six o'clock-I should like to conclude this section. The government has done this in three ways.

Labour Conditions-Strikes
First, it has lowered the floor from five to four per cent, largely to take care of matters which were raised, such as drugs, some travelling expenses and the like.
Then, the upper limit, which was not touched on by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, has been increased fifty per cent. In other words, the ceilings have been increased from $400 to $600 in the case of a single man and from $600 to $900 in the case of a married man, with a corresponding increase of $150 for each child; and certain items such as artificial limbs, spinal braces, braces for limbs, and aids to hearing, have been included, the reason being, as suggested by a number of hon. members, that these were felt to be a type of special aid which was particularly expensive and which could be looked on as being an unusual expense and coming within the general theory of the benefit which is conferred therein. I hope that the section as it now stands will provide a further measure of relief in these difficult cases.

Subsection agreed to.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
