subtopic: STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the serious situation created by the strikes now in progress at the Halifax shipyards and on the tramway system in Montreal.

subtopic: STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have been considering
the proposed motion of the hon. member and in view of the fact that the business of the house, as indicated last evening, is to be that I leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply, when this matter might be discussed, I think there is sufficient urgency for the hon. gentleman to proceed.

subtopic: STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitated to
hold up the house at this stage of the session, realizing that the government desires to get through this week if possible, and I think
members of this group join with him in that wish. However, I felt that the situation in Halifax and Montreal, because of the serious interruption of two very necessary war organizations, warranted a discussion at this time of the factors involved in the two strikes mentioned. The Halifax shipyards, a very necessary industry, have been tied up for the past two weeks, affecting some three thousand personnel. In the tramway situation in Montreal, I feel that the tying up of this transportation system affects indirectly every war organization in that city, in that it makes it extremely difficult for a large percentage of the employees in the war plants to get to and from their work. I appreciate the fact that the government has taken some emergency measures in that connection by making army vehicles available to transport as many as possible. Nevertheless there is still a serious interference with the operation of war industries in the city of Montreal.
The point with which I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, is that these two matters have dragged on for the past couple of weeks. There is a possibility that the house will adjourn this week, and I think it is necessary that the government should make some definite pronouncement on their present labour relations regulations as affecting the two situations mentioned. I do not think there is any other agency in Canada which can at the present time decide one way or the other as to the legality or otherwise of the issues involved In the two strikes. I would say particularly for the benefit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) that all during the process of fighting, war labour relations in Canada have constituted one of our most contentious problems. On several occasions the government has passed orders in council which did not solve the problem satisfactorily.
Most of us who are primarily interested in labour problems were pleased when the Prime Minister announced the setting up of a body to take evidence, in order to compile into one labour code the wishes, hopes and desires of those interested in labour relations. Our understanding was that dt was to be a labour jurisprudence in Canada. Accepting it in that light we felt that labour laws were being laid down by the national government, and that to some extent we were going to have control of labour relations across Canada, in cooperation with the provincial governments. That was our hope. That was the way we felt order in council P.C. 1003 was to be applied. I did not think there was going to be any room for quibbling on the part of anybody, once the
Labour Conditions-Strikes

machinery set up by the code was followed out. The natural or common-sense thing to expect was that those concerned would legislate and adjudicate within the terms of that order in council.
In my opinion the situation at Halifax is very clear. On the part of the employers in Halifax there has been a flagrant violation of public authority. For four years the employees in the shipyards have been endeavouring, with every means at their disposal, to lay dawn a collective bargaining agreement. In the last analysis they followed the terms of order in council P.C. 1003. A government-appointed conciliation board was set up, and within the terms of the labour code decided that the maintenance of union clause and check-off, requested by the employees of Halifax shipyards, was legitimate and desirable. Their decision was rendered accordingly. That, may I say, was a unanimous decision. But the employers at Halifax refused absolutely to accept that unanimous decision of a government-appointed board, with consequent disruption in a very necessary industry.
I know of no agency which can settle that problem in Nova Scotia unless it be the federal Department of Labour. All the legal machinery which can be provided has been set up; a government-appointed commission has made its decision, and the employers have refused to accept that decision. Someone in authority has to make a declaration in the Halifax shipyards case.
The situation in Montreal is somewhat different. To the best of my knowledge, for the past two years all the machinery provided by government legislation has been followed in determining a bargaining agency in Montreal. The point at issue in my opinion is this. Under order in council P.C. 1003 a vote was taken. The bargaining agency in Montreal was determined legally by majority rule, by the employees of the Montreal Tramways union. The Canadian Brotherhood' of Railway Employees was selected. If we stick to majority rule in managing the affairs of this country, then as I understand this code no small groups within the country or within an industry should be permitted the prerogative of carrying on an agitation on the side so as to disrupt and interfere with that which in my opinion is the principle of democracy. This is what happened1 in Montreal. As I understand it, for the past year the bargaining agency has been interfered1 with. Disruptive tactics have been, carried on within the industry for the purpose of defeating the decision of a majority of the employees of the Montreal Tramways
[Mr. Qfllis.1
company.' I am told further that some of the difficulties and some of the stoppages of work which have taken place were not strikes called by the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees, but rather were promoted on the side. This is done very easily, because I have seen it done on many occasions. It may be carried out at the behest of a company in order to discredit a legitimate bargaining agency forced upon the company by a majority of employees.
In the agreement for which they ask at the present time the union demand a union shop, in order to give them union security, and to place in the hands of the executive board of the union, when it signs an agreement, sufficient authority to enable them to guarantee to the operating company a continued observance of the agreement. If the union officials are going to give that guarantee-and any trade union official who signs the agreement has to guarantee it, and work to that end; otherwise the agreement would be no good- then those union officials must be in a position to exercise some supervision over their membership, along lines of discipline, so as to guarantee the observance of the agreement.
The tramways operators in Montreal take the position that there is compulsion, in that they are demanding a closed shop, and that it is foreign to their set-up. In a statement issued to the press a few days ago, Mr. A. R. Mosher, President of the Canadian Congress of Labour, stated definitely and clearly that what they are now asking for by way of union agreement is already in effect in the tramways organization. For example, they have a benevolent association. Every employee, when employed by the Montreal Tramways Company, is obliged-and remember that this is a company-controlled benevolent association- to sign a card to the effect that he is willing to pay $3 a month to that company-controlled organization. He must do that whether he likes it or not. One of the terms of his employment is that he must be prepared to sign his willingness to a check-off for that purpose. If the Montreal Tramways can set a precedent of .making membership within an organization they control obligatory upon anyone receiving employment, surely there is no reason why, in the present situation in Montreal, in which there has been friction and disruption, union officials representing the designated bargaining agency-the agency certified by the government, decided by a majority vote of employee and familiar with the difficulties of administration-should not ask for union security. I say there is no reason in the world why they should not, and that is the point at issue.

Labour Conditions-Strikes
I do not wish to labour this matter at great length. The position of the government is this. When it issued order in council P.C. 1003 it definitely decided as to the machinery with respect, to union certification, how contracts may be arrived at, and what is and what is not permissible. In the tramways case the employers take the position that the agreement asked for by the employees is illegal under the terms of order in council 1003. The union take the position-some of them sat in on the preparation of this code-that under section 20, subsection 1, the matter is clearly defined. I understand that during the discussion of this clause they were assured by those who drafted it that there was nothing in it that prohibited or prevented the employers and employees from writing agreements that were suitable to themselves.
I think in order to settle this matter, and settle it before the house closes, in order to start these two necessary war organizations in operation again, either the Minister of Labour or the Prime Minister should make a definite declaration in this house that neither the Montreal nor the Halifax situation are beyond the scope of order in council 1003. If the government would make that statement, then the union or the employers concerned would be in a position, if they wanted to take the reverse attitude to test the legality of the situation in the courts. We would at-least be moving somewhere.
I know the situation very well in Nova Scotia. In Halifax the question of the checkoff is at issue. The employer there is the Dominion Iron and Steel company. They have had check-offs in the whole coal and steel set-up in that province during the last thirty years. If the attitude of that small section of the company in Halifax is sustained, the chances are that the labour relations which have existed for thirty years will be interrupted. I know the steel workers and miners are watching it closely and I do not want to see the industrial set-up of that province disturbed.
My request is that some declaration should be made by either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Labour in order to give the warring factions a chance to have the legality of this matter decided by the courts.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, having the honour of being one of the representatives of Halifax city I feel that I should say at least a word in connection with this matter. I am going to be quite frank and say that I am not in the same position as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in my knowledge of labour affairs. I have not gone across the country taking part in strikes in various sections, nor have I been actively associated with any trade union. But I do business in the city of Halifax, and I am happy to say that so far as labour is concerned my relations have been very pleasant. I believe I have had and still retain the confidence of labour to a very considerable degree. I want to retain, if not their support, at least their confidence, because I believe it is a good thing fqf, our country to have sound leadership in so far as labour is concerned. This is nothin^pew that I am saying, because I have always believed it.
I am anxious to see this strike settled as quickly as possible. My approach to this question is a little different from that of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I am not going to deal with the question as it affects the Dominion Iron and Steel company's interests throughout Canada; I am not going to deal with the Montreal situation, but I do want to say that the Halifax shipyards industry has been important to the war effort. It has been an asset to us for many years. I remember during the last great war the splendid work done by the Halifax shipyards and its employees. I remember also the strike that took place, I believe in 1919, following the last war.
Wonderful progress has been made by the Halifax shipyards in the construction of two destroyers for the Canadian government, and they have also done splendid work in connection with repairs. Like many other citizens of Halifax, I am hopeful that that work will continue throughout the entire war period and into the peace.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South has stated that a board, was set, up and I understood him to say that it made an unanimous finding. My understanding is that that was not so; that there was one dissenting voice, and that the whole question rested on the matter of interpretation. I am not in position to give a legal interpretation, nor would I dare to do so. I have confidence in the ability and' knowledge of the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). Notwithstanding the fact that there may be some criticism from certain labour circles, I feel that on the whole our present Minister of Labour stands high in the regard of the large majority of trade unions throughout Canada.
We should appreciate the fact that this department has at its head a former labour man, one who for many years has been associated with trade unions and who still holds his trade union card. We are fortunate
Labour Conditions-Strikes

to have a man of that type, and I think labour should recognize the fact that there is a man of that type at the head of labour affairs at such a critical time in Canada's history.
I should like to say a word with regard to the conduct of the men at Halifax. They have conducted themselves in a splendid manner, and I hope they will continue to do so. It is unfortunate that a strike should take place at Halifax. I am not thinking of the present effect alone; I am thinking of the future. We want to keep all these trained shipwrights and other kindred trades in Halifax. I hope that the port of Halifax will play a great part in the post-war period. I know there will be a large number of ships turning at Halifax and for that reason I want to see these shipyards and other ship repair plants kept at a high state of efficiency in order that we may carry on the trade between Canada and other countries which is so essential to the welfare and future of Canada.
I discussed this matter with my colleague from Halifax and we have both been following the matter closely. I wrote the head of the union at Halifax stating I was anxious to see a settlement made as soon as possible, and I gave the same reasons as I am giving to-day. I would not attempt to take it on myself to place the responsibility on any one particular party. I do not believe that the people who have followed the dispute will agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South that the blame should be put directly on the Minister of Labour or on this government. The machinery which is necessary to look after matters of this kind has been set up. I am sure that the minister and his officials are following closely what is taking place, and it is my sincere hope that the strike will be brought to an end at the earliest possible moment.

I pointed out that this labour difficulty not only affected the

employees in Halifax but was a matter' of very great concern to labour organizations in other parts of the province. In the town of Springhill we have a labour organization that has been functioning for many years in a community that is as stable as any mining community in all Canada, with as high a standard of citizenship as you will find anywhere in this country. They have enlisted in this war, as they did in the first great war, in as high percentages as anywhere else in Canada for service in any theatre. But these labour men in Springhill are very jealous of their rights and the principles for which they stand. They are in sympathy and in accord with the action that has been taken by their brother organizations in Halifax. They have asked me as their member to make representations on their behalf, and I have done so.
I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) that nothing could be more unfortunate than to have a stoppage of work on naval ships at this time. It is doubly unfortunate that it should come as we approach the climax of the war, with victory for ourselves and our allies in sight. We all realize how essential it is that there should be a united effort on the part of all that victory should be achieved in the very shortest possible time. There is also the question of setting a standard for all our people in Canada and for our allies everywhere and that our fighting men should know that we are back of them to the full. I am very anxious, Mr. Speaker, that the government make every possible effort and concession in order that these unfortunate labour difficulties may be adjusted without any further delay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the
constructive approach of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), who has been in constant touch with me with reference to the labour dispute in that city, and also of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black). I do not think that I can add much to what has already been said.
For over a generation the American Federation of Labor held a contract with the Montreal street railway company. Then there was a jurisdictional dispute which some say caused a strike or a couple of strikes there. Eventually the present organization, the C.B.R.E. was designated as the bargaining agency, and it is only human that this organization should want to consolidate its position.

Labour Conditions-Strikes
Let me say frankly to the house that I am a trade unionist by heritage and conviction. My father was a trade unionist, and my views on compulsion I got with my mother's milk when I was a boy in the old country. I do not believe in compulsion. I do not believe in compulsory cooperation. That is fundamental and I cannot change my ground on that.
So far as the company and the men's organizations are concerned, I have already pointed out clearly that there is nothing than can compel them to come to a mutual understanding and agreement. But what they want me to do as Minister of Labour is to say that the men shall belong to one organization or to another. Frankly I cannot go that far.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South has said that we have had difficulties in the labour field in this dominion. But looking at it in a big and broad way I think it will be agreed by hon. gentlemen that we have had less labour difficulties in this country than there have been in any other of the united nations. Labour difficulties are continually occurring in every country, in the country to the south of us, for example, in Australia, and even in Great Britain, notwithstanding the fact that they are being bombed all the time. But I think it should be said for the trade unions of this country that they have measured up to their responsibilities.
I was in the last war and I do not know what happened on the industrial front in Canada during that war, but I must confess that when I was landing at the Dardanelles I would not have liked to think that people were going on strike back home for what I considered conditions that did not warrant a strike such as is taking place in the city of Montreal to-day. I say that frankly. I think that there is an obligation on both the company and the employees there to settle their differences so that this great metropolitan centre can move ahead and play its part in the war effort.
With reference to the code, it was drafted in cooperation with employers and employees throughout this dominion. The very principle which the hon. member for Cape Breton South has just enunciated was opposed by these two great partners, employers and employees, in the industrial life of this country. They laid down the principle of conciliation, and in conciliation there must be give and take. I know something about conciliation. I was chairman of a grievance committee for fifteen years when I was working in a plant whose president was the father of the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson).
Relations between employers and employees must be based upon character, not upon the gun, not upon compulsion. I know that Sir John was a pretty tough individual to deal with; he was an old Scottish character. But eventually we got an agreement with the company which exists to this day. It is not a closed shop agreement. The men employed in that industry are probably as well paid and enjoy just as good conditions as any workmen in that calling in this country. I feel that with that spirit of tolerance and good will both the labour disputes which have been mentioned this morning can be satisfactorily settled, but it cannot be done by the state dictating to one side or the other or dictating to the men the organization to which they shall belong. It would be the beginning of despotism in this country if the government should start to dictate to one side or the other. I am trying to be absolutely fair. I hold no brief for the Montreal Tramways company, except that I know people who have been associated with them for over a generation in the negotiation of their contracts.
We suggested arbitration. It was agreed to by the company and turned down by the men. Then we suggested setting up a commission with a high court judge. That was agreed to by the company but turned down by the men. Then I suggested the reference to the supreme court, but the organization insisted on the closed shop aspect of the agreement going into force before a reference to the courts. I think we did everything which was humanly possible to bring these difficulties to a conclusion so that there might be harmony in that particular community.
I have nothing further to say on the dispute except this, that anything which can be done will be done to bring this dispute to a conclusion, affecting as it does an industry so necessary in connection with the successful prosecution of the war.
Let us now review the Halifax situation. There you had a board of conciliation. In that case employer and employed agreed to all the terms of the contract except what is known as the check-off and the maintenance of membership clause. In that case the majority signed a report with these conditions. The employer of course did not want to go along with the check-off and the maintenance of membership. In the city of Montreal the reverse is the case: the employees turned down the report and the recommendations of the conciliation board. There you have the perfect example of conciliation and give and take. I believe in give and take; I have always believed in it; I have always preached

Labour Conditions-Strikes

it. It is part of my creed that in industrial life you must have that degree of conciliation which made the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act a pattern in industrial relations in this country. A degree of conciliation is necessary. I do not think you can shake an employer by the throat and call him a scoundrel, and expect to make an agreement with him. Neither do I believe that an employer can try to destroy the men's organization and yet maintain industrial harmony. That is elementary and fundamental; and I hope I shall never live to see the day in this country when the government says to either employer or employee, "This is what you have got to do, or else-".

The position we are trying to point out is that the government has laid down a labour code, P.C. 1003, dated February 17, 1944. A dispute has arisen and workers are on strike in Montreal because a provision of this order in council, found in section 20(1), is not clear. We are asking the government to make the position clear.
I was going to say a word about the situation in Halifax. I wish to correct one statement made by the senior member for Halifax when he accused the member for Cape Breton South of placing the blame on the government for both these strikes. As a matter of fact, in the Halifax situation I think the public generally recognizes, and it is the position we take, that the blame rests upon the employers. We feel on the other hand that in the Montreal situation the blame rests on the government for failing to make clear that provision two weeks before the strike occurred, at which time they were asked to clarify it. In the Halifax situation there has been arbitration and a decision has been made in favour of the employees. The employers have refused to abide by that decision. The minister knows our position. We feel that the pressure of public opinion should compel them to abide by that decision, but otherwise we do not maintain that the government should step in and enforce the decision, because the minister would reply quite properly that that would cut both ways. But if the production of the Halifax shipyards is essential to the war effort

and there is a stoppage because of a strike which has occurred as a result of the employers' refusal to accept the decision of the government's board, we suggest that the thing for the government to do is to step in and take over the plant, at least for the time being, [DOT]so that production can be restored.
And so, in spite of all the interruptions, I hope I have answered the questions put to me by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. My answers are definite. In Halifax, if the company refuses to abide by the board's decision the government should take over the plant. In Montreal, the government should make absolutely clear whether a collective agreement is legal or illegal under P.C. 1003.

speakeroldname: Mr. PAUL MARTIN (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Knowles) obviously did not clearly follow the minister as he spoke. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) made a constructive suggestion in dealing with the matter. He recognized that this was an important matter at the present time and he hoped that the minister would be able to clarify it. The minister made that clarification and I can only ' repeat what he said. My purpose in rising is to observe that I cannot follow what the hon. gentleman who has just spoken really meant by insisting that the minister should state whether or not, within the terms of this code, it was possible for the fullest contractual powers to subsist on the part of parties who sat down to negotiate a collective agreement. P.C. 1003, recognized by the leaders of labour throughout Canada to be a real step in setting out, in regulatory form, the kind of order one wishes to see obtain between labour and management in this country, is admittedly not a perfect document. It is a document which, when it was announced by the Minister of Labour, was said to be capable of improvement in the light of experience and practice.
When this particular section was drawn, as the minister said, it was drawn not in some corner hole of the Department of Labour. The history of this code is an interesting one, about which enough has not been said in this house. Following the inquiry launched by the then chairman of the national war labour board, at the instance of the Minister of Labour, a full investigation was made into the whole field of labour-management relations. Labour organizations from all over the country were heard, including representations made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South and his colleague from Vancouver, over a period of three months, and after that inquiry

Labour Conditions-Strikes
took place a report was made by the board. That report was carefully considered by officials of the Department of Labour and by gentlemen representing employers and others representing employees. There was the fullest consultation with labour and with employers, as evidenced by the statements of Mr. Mosher, president of the Canadian Congress of Labour, Mr. Bengough. president of the Trades and Labour Congress, Mr. Charpentier, of the Catholic Syndicates, and others. Here was a document setting out the relations between labour and management, a document arrived at after the fullest possible consultation with Labour, as the Minister of Labour (Mr: Mitchell) said when he tabled order in council 1003, and when he thanked labour and mentioned specifically the presidents of the great national organizations and the help they had given the administration in trying to establish at long last, on a national basis, a labour code which -would recognize and protect the rights of labour and at the same time extend to labour the opportunity to exercise its obligations. I remember very well when section 20 was discussed with the representatives of labour, and it means exactly what it says. That is why I cannot understand the insistence of the hon. member who has just spoken. Section 20 provides:
No person shall, with a view to compelling or influencing a person to join a trade union or employees' organization, use coercion or intimidation of any kind-
Labour is the first to recognize the merit of that provision. You cannot use coercion or intimidation, either as an employer or as an employee; but if two parties, sitting down around a conference table, management on the one hand and the workers on the other, carrying out the processes of contract, wish to agree on anything, within the language of this section they may do so.
-but this subsection shall not be construed to prohibit the inclusion of any provision in a collective agreement.
So that on analysis of what the Minister of Labour said I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will find that he and the minister are in full accord. He would not compel anyone to join a union, nor would the minister. However, he would allow the parties to a dispute or the parties to a collective agreement, workers and management, to sit down and agree upon anything; and the minister has said in regard to the particular dispute at hand that if the management and the workers in the plant at Montreal, or any other plant, wish to have a closed shop, there is nothing illegal about it under P.C. 1003.. Can anything be clearer than that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The parliamentary assistant says that if employer and employee wish to agree on a closed shop there is nothing illegal about it, but the question is this: can the employer under P.C. 1003, apart from what he may or may not want to do, refuse to agree to- a closed shop agreement on the ground that it is illegal?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: On reflection I believe my hon. friend will see that this question is-I was going to use the word "absurd", but I will say instead that it is not very carefully considered.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is what the strike is all about.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: STRIKES AT HALIFAX AND MONTREAL-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour said that und'er P.C. 1003 a closed shop agreement can be concluded. If the company does not interpret the code as the minister does, or as the workers do, and says it is going to test it in the courts, we have no power to prevent anybody from testing any law in the courts of this land. Speaking for myself I would say the company's position would not be justified by a thorough, careful perusal of this section, but no one in this country can stop any party from saying to the courts, "We do not agree; we dispute that this is an illegal act." That is the right of every free citizen in every free country, and if this company chooses to follow that course the hon. gentleman would be the last ' to deny them the right to settle the matter in the courts. But the issue is clear. The Minister of Labour has stated what has been the policy of the government through the years in regard to .the sanctity of contracts. If people wish to negotiate an agreement covering a closed shop they may do so; under the code there is nothing illegal in such an agreement. I do not think the matter could be clearer.
Motion withdrawn.

I understand from a press report that a group of officials are leaving by air to-morrow for Churchill and the other bases which the minister mentioned. I am sorry that the minister found it impossible to accede to the request that he received from the mayor of Winnipeg that a representative of that city or of the province of Manitoba be included in this party. When the minister replied to Mayor Coulter and also to me in the house he said that the party would in-

Supply-Transport
clud'e only military and technical personnel and that there would be no place in it for a representative of the city of Winnipeg or the province of Manitoba. I imagine that the request was made by Mayor Coulter because the press dispatches regarding the trip said that a study was to be made of possible postwar uses of these bases. Mayor Coulter is a mild sort of person and has accepted the minister's explanation as to why no representative of the city or of the province can be taken along, but I am not so easily satisfied. The city of Winnipeg occupies a very important position on the world air map, both of the present and of the future, and I feel that Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba should be represented right at the start in the study that is to be made of these northern and northeastern bases with a view to their possible post-war use. I shall have something further to say about the airport at Stevenson's field, Winnipeg, when we get to the appropriate item, but I still hope that the minister will agree that a representative of the city of Winnipeg or of the province of Manitoba be taken along on the trip that is to start to-morrow. '

In connection with the taking over of these airports at Churchill, Greenland and other places which the minister mentioned, I should like to secure a statement from the minister in regard to the disposal of the surplus goods or equipment that the United States government may have at these various airports. While there has been a denial by members of the government that on the northwest staging route there was destruction of equipment, scarcely a day passes but letters are received by members of this house from people living in Dawson Creek and on up there testifying that there was destruction of very valuable equipment and placing the responsibility upon the dominion authorities on the ground that the dominion authorities had refused to the United States government the right to dispose of its surplus equipment because it was brought into Canada without payment of duty. Personally I have no knowledge of the matter but I have read about it in the Edmonton press and have also had numbers of letters on the subject, which has become a very vexed question. I would like to ascertain from the minister what the plans of the government are with regard to the disposal of surplus or excess property, equipment and the like when these airports are officially taken over by the Canadian government.
There is another matter, a smaller one. Recently Prairie Airways Limited at Moose
100-383	bevi
Jaw was taken over by the Department of Munitions and Supply to be operated by them so far as the repair depot is concerned. I have received reports that certain lumber and other materials are being destroyed instead of being sold, even though this material has value. The informants state that certain quantities of material, lumber and the like, were removed from the premises, and representations have been made to the effect that it could have been made available for civilian uses and ought not to be destroyed. I also point out that six of the employees who were acting as guards, all of them returned soldiers of the last war, received notice that their services were no longer required and were replaced by men of military age who combined the duties of guard with looking after the storing of the planes and the like. I would like to know what is going to be done to assure these returned men who were discharged of placement elsewhere. They have not the mechanical qualifications that would enable them to work in armament factories, but they were able to do the work they were doing as guards. Their removal from their positions has aroused no little resentment.

As to the disposal of United States material on the northwest staging route, negotiations are proceeding between the Canadian and United States governments to the end that War Assets Corporation will act for the United States government in disposing of movable assets. A representative of War Assets Corporation is now in that territory, cooperating with Major General Foster, who is the administrator of the area for the Canadian government. It is hoped that War Assets Corporation will be in a position to dispose of United States assets, for the account of the United States government. My hon. friend will appreciate that the Canadian government has bought only the immovables from the United States government; that the movables are the property of the United States government, and are for disposal by the owner.
My hon. friend said that the Canadian government has prevented local officers from selling materials locally. United States army regulations probably prevent army officers from selling government material, just as is the case in Canada. My hon. friend will appreciate that the sale of materials owned by a government is a matter which cannot be handled carelessly. The United States has followed the same practice as has the government of Canada in setting up a disposal agency for the sale of government war material. However, reports from Major General Foster indicate that the destruction of materials by the United States government was a comparatively minor matter;
Supply-Transport
no very important stores were disposed of. I may say that ours is an official report, not something received by way of gossip.

Moose Jaw has an overhaul plant operated by Prairie Airways Limited. It was expanded with government assistance, and probably the ownership of the government in the plant is larger than the ownership of Prairie Airways. Incidentally, Prairie Airways was acquired by Canadian Pacific Air Lines subsequent to the original negotiations. There has been a reduction in the volume of overhaul work. This plant is wholly a private operation. The government has not operated and is not now operating the plant, which is operated by Canadian Pacific Air Lines. The plant is still in use, and has not been declared surplus to government requirements. If there has been disposal of government material, such disposal has been wholly illegal; if there has been disposal of privately-owned material, the situation is quite in order. A private firm can dispose of its material as it likes. The department has received no report that government material has been disposed of, but if it has, that will undoubtedly come to light in due course.
When the plant is no longer required for the purpose for which it was built-and my hon. friend will appreciate that air training has been reduced substantially and that therefore overhaul work has been reduced substantially-and when the plant is reported as surplus to requirements, it will be turned over to War Assets Corporation for disposal in the usual way.

speechtext: Will the minister make a statement with respect to air service operations at Amherst in the post-war period? The board of trade and others are interested in it, and I believe they are having a meeting this week to discuss the matter. As the minister knows, this airfield is within the town boundaries, and the location is as favourable as that of any airfield in Canada. It was built after substantial contributions were made by the town of Amherst. It had the good will and cooperation from the beginning of the minister himself and of Mr. R. P. Bell, director general of aircraft construction. The town of Amherst has a large investment and a great interest in it and they are now anxious to know what their position is, having regard to the Aeronautics Act and the policy of the government and the minister, in the post-war period, in securing and maintaining an air service to utilize this field and serve the town of Amherst and the surrounding community.	*

speechtext: The field at Amherst is an airport which will be suitable for post-war commercial operation. At the moment it is busy with operational work connected with the war. When the airport is no longer required for the overhaul of aeroplanes, and for flight-testing of new aeroplanes, it will be declared surplus to the requirements of the war amd turned over to the Department of Transport. I feel sure that at that time it will be converted without difficulty into a unit of a system of commercial aviation. Amherst is an enterprising city with considerable, mail and passenger potentials, and I feel sure that one of the air lines in that area will desire to give service to the town. Certainly the government will be wholly favourable to civilian service when the time comes.

There are two or three other questions I should like to ask the minister. They have to do with the establishment of a route between Winnipeg and Edmonton. Something was said about that a few months ago, that an air line was to be established there, but lately we have heard nothing about it. When is it expected that this air line will be put into operation, and has consideration been given to the inclusion of Prince Albert in the route? It would not mean the addition of many miles, but it would be very helpful in connecting with the private air line which operates into the north from Prince Albert and giving people from the north an opportunity to travel on the route from Saskatoon and Winnipeg. To-day the situation is that there is only one passenger plane each way each day, which does not provide the service that Prince Albert, I submit, should be entitled to by reason of its strategic position.
In that connection I would ask the minister whether it is intended to hardsurface and improve the runways in Prince Albert and Saskatoon. Recently there was a suggestion that this would be done. The situation to-day, so far as Prince Albert particularly is concerned, is that for at least a month in the spring and also to a lesser extent in the fall it is very difficult to use the air field because nothing has been done to render it available at all seasons of the year. Prince Albert is the jumping-off place into northern Saskatchewan, and if it had had anything like the facilities that are available in 'one or two other cities in adjoining provinces the amount of air transportation would have been multiplied very considerably. Before the war what held back its development was the fact that it did not have the necessary all-weather air facilities.
As far as Alberta is concerned, it has those facilities with the result that people who desire to go into northern Saskatchewan, in connection with mining development and the like, find to-day that it is almost a necessity to go to Yellowknife, which is immediately north of the northern boundary of Saskatchewan. I do not raise any objection to- the- facilities in Edmonton because it has a great air future; and as regards Winnipeg, Stevenson field as it stands to-day is a monument to lack of vision on the part of our authorities with regard to post-war development of aviation in Canada but I ask that in the post-war development Saskatchewan be given an opportunity to expand in that direction. Representations have been made from time to time to the government by the Prince Albert board of trade. An implied promise of action was given

During the course of the war, Prince Albert has been served by an excellent transport service, one of the few successful smaller operations in Canada. It has had regular service, every day in the month and every month of the year, since the war began. The airport is adequate for the present service. The curtailment of operations in the north resulted from the curtailment of gold mining operations in northern Saskatchewan as the hon. gentleman knows. We hope and expect that the revival of gold mining following the end of the war will result in operations into the north from Prince Albert on a greatly increasing scale.
So far as Saskatoon is concerned, the present airport is hard-surfaced. Extensions of runways in length are required, and will be undertaken as soon as any programme of improved civilian fields can be undertaken. As regards the service between Winnipeg and Edmonton, the radio beams are nearing completion. Some improvement in fields is proceeding, but I cannot give the date for the commencement of the service. As a matter of, fact, Trans-Canada Air Lines is very short of equipment, but when that equipment is available, we hope to be ready to put on a first-class direct service between Winnipeg and Edmonton. That route will involve a decided improvement for air traffic in and out of Prince Albert.

speechtext:
I desire to move an amendment to this section, to provide that any provincial government, upon the authorization of the legislature, shall be empowered to ask the dominion government for a charter to establish a provincial bank. The amendment is as follows:
That section 12 of ibill 91 be amended by inserting immediately after section 12 thereof the following new sections:
12a. The government of any province which has been duly authorized by its legislature so to do, may apply under this act for an act ol incorporation of a bank in the form set forth m schedule B(l) to this act, and the act of incorporation shall be construed to confer upon the bank thereby incorporated all the powers, privileges and immunities, and subject it to all the liabilities and provisions set forth in this act except those specifically excepted in the act of incorporation.
12b. The following sections of this act shall not apply to any bank incorporated under the provisions of section 12a of this act, that is to say, sections 11, 12, 20, 33, 35, 37, 39 40 41, 42, 45, 40, 47, 48, 49 and 50.
Before offering'reasons why this amendment should be incorporated in the act may I point out that as the amendment is drafted it will be noted that the provincial legislature will pass legislation authorizing the provincial government to make application to the dominion parliament for an act to incorporate a bank. The dominion government will then be requested to incorporate a bank in the same form as that in which the commercial chartered banks have been incorporated. In view of the fact that both the dominion and provincial legislatures will have concurred in the incorporation prior to the charter being granted, the question of jurisdiction does not arise. .
It will be remembered by those who were called upon to become familiar with the whole situation that when Alberta applied for a charter in 1940 and the matter came before the banking and commerce committee the request was denied upon the advice of Mr. Varcoe, who maintained in brief that the act would be ultra vires of the Dominion of Canada because it would impose certain liabilities upon the provincial government.

Bank Act Amendment
What I have just said indicates that if the matter is proceeded with in an orderly fashion, and with wisdom, there need be no infringement whatsoever upon the British North America Act; there need be no reason why the act should not be allowed, certainly not upon the grounds which the committee found substantial in the last instance.
May I point out that the sections referred to in the suggested clause 12 (b) relate to formalities which would not be applicable to a provincial bank. Those sections relate to the following subject matters, and I would review them briefly. Section 11 has to do with the qualification for provisional director; section 12 has to do with stock books for subscriptions; section 20 has to do with the qualification of directors; section 33 has to do with the allotment of shares; section 35 has to do with share personality; section 37 with calls on shares; section 39 with the recovery of calls; section 40 with a fine for failure to pay a call; section 41 with actions to recover calls; section 42 with conditions for the transfer of shares; section 45 with the sale of shares under execution; section 46 with the transmission of shares; section 47 with the transmission by marriage of female shareholders; section 48 relates to sections 46 and 47, by reference to the documents required; section 49 has to do with transmission by will, and section 50 with transmission by decease. Therefore it will be seen by hon. members that while a considerable number of sections of the act are proposed to be made non-applicable in the case of the provincial bank charter, nevertheless no impairment whatever is proposed of the general purpose and effectiveness and formality of the Bank Act. Now may I point out to hon. members why the province of Alberta is so insistent- in requesting that it be granted the right to have a bank. Be it noted that this amendment is not a request for the granting of a charter; it is merely to provide enabling legislation. Several times since coming to this house I have contended that there need be no conflict between the dominon and provincial governments with respect to the constitutional competence of either, if the dominion passes enabling legislation and allows the provinces to cooperate by passing similar legislation, or legislation which becomes in order in cooperation with the dominion under the enabling legislation. This legislation is to provide authorization to a legislature to incorporate. There is no imposition of liability on the province by the dominion.
May I deal briefly with the question why Alberta wants to have a bank, and why I say the house should pass an amendment to
the act under which any province in Canada may have a chance of having a bank of its own. In 1940, when the banking and commerce committee was examining Mr. Low of Alberta, in connection with the proposed granting of a charter to Alberta in that year, questions were asked as to why Alberta wanted a bank. I should like to read Mr. Low's remarks in that connection. I turn to the evidence taken before the banking and commerce committee on Tuesday, July 16, 1940 where, at page 5, I find this:
Mr. Casselman: W'hat need?
The Witness:	That covers, Mr. Chairman,
very much ground; but we are of the opinion and we think our opinions are sound in this respect, that there should be an institution in the province of Alberta sponsored by the people of the. province in a cooperative way which will endeavour to increase the industrial possibilities of the province, which will make it possible to stabilize prices of certain commodities whose main market is in the province of Alberta, and which will eventually prove to the whole of the Dominion of Canada, if not to the world, that the control of credits should be vested in the government of the country and not in private institutions.
And farther down on the same page, the following questions by Mr. Thorson:
Q. How will it accomplish the purpose you have in mind?
A. Well, in the first place this bank certainly would operate on a more extended policy of ' credit issue. That is, if a man or an institution or a community or a corporation cannot put up adequate security they should be entitled to their credit, and there will be no such thing as premature withdrawals of credit to render men and corporations helpless as we see to-day all around us.
May I comment just there that one of the most serious disadvantages from which Alberta suffered during the depression was the disastrous fall in prices from what they had been, when Alberta incurred most of her public debt, to what they were in 1931 and 1932. This fall in prices rendered it impossible for people who were in debt to discharge the responsibilities they had assumed when they contracted their debt. This brought about undesirable conditions of various kinds.
I shall now proceed with Mr. Low's evidence, at page 7 of the report:
By Mr. Cleaver:
Q. I understood you to say quite distinctly a moment ago when you were stating the objects and the need for your bank that the need was that the present banking institutions were not extending credit where it was required by credit-worthy individuals?
A. True.
Q. I take it from that statement you intend to extend greater credits than the existing banks are now extending?
Bank Act Amendment

A. Not necessarily, but -more -honourable ones. Would you mind if I qualified your statement?
Q. Yes.
A. In time.
Q. I also understood you to say that you are not going to withdraw these credits abruptly after loans were granted

they would not be abruptly recalled?
A. Unless there is a mighty good reason for so doing.
Q. If having made generous loans you undertake, or your policy will be not to require payment of them, if your depositors want their money which they have deposited in the bank, -how do you -propose to obtain it for them?
A. We propose to keep adequate reserves to meet the demands -for repayment by increasing the capital structure.
Hon. Mr. Hanson: Mr. Chairman, Mr. Low has in part answered one point, one question I raised concerning the necessity for the -bank. He says in effect, if I understand him correctly, that -one of the reasons why this bank is required is because the present chartered banks do not extend sufficient credit -to the people of Alberta; is that not a correct statement of your position, Mr. Low?
' A. Partly, yes, Mr. Hanson.
I do not propose to read at greater length from the hearings of the committee. Hon. members who find themselves interested may read the proceedings and gather information for themselves.
I believe what the dominion government has clone at this session of parliament indicates just how sound was the position taken by Alberta in 1940. It will be recalled that there has been before the house at this session a bill to enable the freer granting of loans to farmers. The government of the day takes a good deal of credit to itself for having introduced that measure. At the same time there is to-day before the banking and commerce committee bill No. 7, for the establishment of an industrial development bank, the object of which is to enable the Dominion of Canada to extend loans to industries for fixed) capital, where those industries would not be able to obtain loans from the chartered banks or from other lending institutions in the country. I feel safe in saying that those two measures alone indicate that Mr. Low was on absolutely unchallengeable ground when he made the statements he did make; and the Alberta government was completely justified in asking for a bank to enable it to grant credit more freely, more discreetly and on better terms than were being granted to the citizens of Alberta throughout- the depression, and than they have been granted even up to the present time-perhaps even notwithstanding the war.
Other provinces have suffered seriously by reason of a faulty or unsatisfactory financial system, or a faulty administration of that system by the banks. To show that Alberta
TMr. Blackmore.]
is not unreasonable and is not alone in making her request that she be given greater control over credit in that province, may I turn first to the submission by the government of the province of Nova Scotia to the Rowell-Sirois commission, as published in February, 1938. At page 82 of that submission hon. members will find the following words:
The Jones commission appointed distinctly to consider the relations of Nova Scotia with the dominion and the general effect of federal1 policies on provincial economic development, emphasized throughout the whole of its report that, as was expressed by Premier Taschereau of Quebec at the dominion-provincial conference in 1927,-
"To have a happy and prosperous Canada, there must be happy and prosperous provinces, and the latter could do more for Canada than could the federal authorities."
I should like to emphasize those last words of Mr. Taschereau. He said that the provincial governments could do more for Canada than could the federal authorities. I have maintained that steadily and consistently ever since coming here. I proceed with Mr. Taschereau's remarks: '
The provinces were more in contact with the people, educating them, building their roads and looking after their health. The provinces enacted compensation laws in favour of workmen and had control of the judicial machinery.
I continue quoting from the submission:
Doctor Innis likewise stated in his complementary report:
"We are convinced from a wide variety of evidence that the trend towards centralization in railways, banking, finance and industry tends to become less efficient in relation to the outlying areas and must be offset by a definite reversal in terms of development policy. Increasing centralization must be offset by increasing devolution, if the more distant regions are to guard effectively their interests. No province has -been exposed more directly to the effects of the national policy and no provirice deserves more careful consideration as to a policy of development. . . .
I quote now from page 83 as follows:
The federal government could not ask a . greater sacrifice of a province and it cannot refuse sympathetic consideration to measures which will involve a restoration of unity.
I contend that at this time i-n the history of Canada the dominion government could hardly do anything more calculated to restore the confidence of the provinces than to grant to the provinces the right to have provincial banks under their own control. These banks would foe under the control of the dominion financial system; they would obey all laws and submit to inspection by the dominion authorities, but they would be under control of the provincial governments. I continue:
It may be urged that centralization of policy in the dominion is in the best interests of the

Bank Act Amendment
province rather than devolution and lest we should be misinterpreted it should be said that we are favourable to centralization as to matters of coordination and we regard the federal government as becoming, to an increasing extent, a clearing house as to matters of general policy -a clearing house which can effectively be used with control over funds. On the other *hand, we have been forcibly struck with the callousness, lack of sympathy, and general disregard of broad policy, which has characterized federal supervision.
I do not know- how the dominion officials could be more roundly or emphatically condemned fo* their past policies than they are in the closing words of that paragraph which I have just read. That was the submission of the sober, staid province of Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia has not yet asked for a bank, but the main reason is that she has not come to see that it would be in her best interests to vote Social Credit.
May I turn from the submission to the Sirois commission to the words of two prominent members of this house which were uttered as late as yesterday in the banking and commerce committee. First I should like to refer to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenberg (Mr. Kinley), who said: "Centralization has been-"

speechtext: The Minister of Finance raised a point of order which was well taken. We are now discussing bill No. 91, while the hon. member is discussing a bill which at the moment is before the banking and commerce committee.

subtopic: SUPPLY OF REINFORCEMENTS TO CANADIAN ARMY
subsubtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
My understanding of
the point raised by the minister is that he was objecting to my quoting the exact words which were uttered in the committee by an hon. member. I am not going to discuss the industrial development bank any further, so that I shall not be out of order in the future.
I have no desire to be out of order; I do not need to be out of order to establish my case, because it is too strong for that. The fact is that the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham) pointed out that Saskatchewan had suffered from centralization. That indicates that Saskatchewan has been suffering from the disability about which Alberta complains.
I turn now to the submission of the province of New Brunswick to the Sirois commission, which was published in April, 1938. I quote from page 49 as follows:
In this connection it is well that the commission should bear in mind that the Canadian banks have been centralized in Ontario and Quebec. Prior to confederation and for some years afterwards we had our own banking institutions in this province and our people were able to obtain money for the encouragement of industry here.
The head offices of these banking institutions were removed, after confederation, to Montreal and Toronto where they were situated more immediately in touch with the financial interests by which they were controlled.
The result has been that industries in New Brunswick have not been able to obtain financial assistance in cases where such assistance would enable our local industries to compete with those in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
Pertinent cases may be cited where local industries in this province have been destroyed because of the difficulty of financing and we submit that finances have been withheld as local industries might come into competition with similar industries in the last mentioned provinces.
There is the advice of New Brunswick given in 1938. May I read a passage from the submission of Alberta to the Rowell-Sirois commission. At page 37 of Part II I find the following words, commencing with the second paragraph:
When it is borne in mind that this overriding control by the central bank is exercised in conjunction with a debt-creating system which
Bank Act Amendment

progressively places everything under the control of finance because of its prior debt claims against the community, something of the enormous and extraordinary control of the highly centralized banking system can be appreciated.
This has been very clearly demonstrated to a started world by recent events in this province. Even governments are expected to submit to the domination of these financial rulers. And as unsatisfactory as it is that this centralized control of all human activity should be exercised by a group of institutions in the dominion, the situation becomes fantastic when it is fully realized that the centralization of control is continued through central banks to a coterie of alien financiers exercising supreme domination of the system on an international scale.
May I read again from page 53, where those who prepared the brief are making suggestions:
In order to implement the policy of electors, the following specific proposals should be adopted to rectify the faults in the financial system which have been examined in previous chapters:
(a) A provincial credit authority under government control to be established in each province to supervise the administration of policy as decided by the people.
I omit paragraphs (b) and (c) as not being particularly pertinent to the matter under discussion and continue with (d):
(d)	The note issue to be regulated by the volume of financial credit released, instead of the present procedure of an arbitrarily limited note issue unnecessarily restricting the issue of financial credit by the banks.
(e)	Banks to continue the administration of the financial system under the jurisdiction of the dominion government and subject to the control of policy by the people of each province through a provincial credit authority.
[DOT]	(f). Banks to discontinue the practice of
charging arbitrary interest rates and to be compensated adequately for their services to the community on an equitable basis.
(g) The careful preparation of an interim scheme to be undertaken so that the application of the general proposals outlined above can be introduced smoothly and without dislocation to the social life of the province.
I think that is sufficient to indicate quite clearly that the need, if not the actual demand, for more provincial control over the credit administration of the provinces is evident throughout the dominion. Here are four.provinces at least which have expressed a sense of disability, directly or indirectly, and one of them has asked specifically for the right to have a provincial bank.
May I draw attention to one other aspect of this question before I resume my seat. Hon. members are familiar with the fact that in the province of Quebec there is a Quebec Savings bank. This bank applied to the dominion government for the renewal of its charter, and on I'riday, July 28, 1944, the application for the charter was under consideration by the banking and commerce committee. Among other things we learned that this Quebec

Savings bank had first been granted a charter in 1846 by Lower Canada, that it had another charter granted in 1871 by the dominion government, The nature of the bank was such that it very closely but not entirely resembles the sort of bank that Alberta has in mind. I should have liked to quote from the proceedings of the committee, but I presume I would be out of order in doing that; I would refer hon. members to pages 1534 and 1536 of the committee's proceedings, where, in reply to questions which I asked, the witness gave evidence which would justify one in assuming that'the Quebec Sayings bank is akin to an ordinary bank in its operations and in its powers. Now if an ordinary bank in a province can be granted a charter by this dominion it seems to me a most astonishing thing that a whole province is to be denied a charter to conduct a provincial bank. In Ontario there is a provincial financial institution which is called the Province of Ontario Savings Office, which was incorporated in 1921.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word in support of the amendment. For the last several years we have had one province of Canada requesting permission to establish a provincially owned bank in order that the bank may fulfil some of the needs of that province. While I do not entirely agree with the reasons advanced by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Black-more), that is a matter of detail. The broad

Bank Act Amendment
principle is that a province has asked for a provincially owned bank and the request has not been favourably received. It may be argued that there has not been time to go into the matter very thoroughly and so on and so forth, but in my opinion the attitude of the house generally has not been favourable towards the incorporation of a provincially owned bank under this bank act, and the request has always been met, as the hon. member for Lethbridge has said, with the objection that there are certain provisions of the Bank Act which would have to be changed as they make it virtually impossible to organize such a bank. In the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Lethbridge he meets those objections; as far as I know he meets them completely. While he was speaking I have looked through the sections which he proposes to delete from the act, all of them having to do with the transfer of shares, the directorates, the records and so on of the chartered banks; and if those sections are deleted-I do not know if there are any more which should be removed, but no doubt he has gone through the act very carefully-it would seem that the sections which stood in the way will be pretty well eliminated from the act if this amendment is passed.
I believe that with the expansion of public enterprise and cooperative enterprise in the provinces, the need of developing their resources to a greater extent than some of those resources have been developed in the past, and the decentralization of industry or the establishment of industries in parts of the country where they have not yet been established and where great resources exist, as in the province from which my hon. friend comes, which is perhaps the most richly endowed province in Canada in this respect, these suggestions would enable a province to do for itself that which the chartered banks have been unable or unwilling to do for it.
I am not going to enter into a long discussion of this matter; I do not think that at this stage it is necessary. All I want to say is that we of this group have supported the hon. gentleman in the past when he has brought before us the request for consideration of the establishment of a provincially-owned bank in Alberta, and we intend to support that request to-day by supporting this amendment.

subtopic: SUPPLY OF REINFORCEMENTS TO CANADIAN ARMY
