speechtext:
I regret very much that this matter comes so late in the session and I almost feel like apologizing to my colleagues in the house for participating in a discussion of this kind at this stage in the proceedings; but it should be remembered that we were here for months before the Bank Act was introduced. While it did go before the banking and commerce committee; while it can be said that it has been under lengthy review there, in the light of all the circumstances surrounding the Bank Act in 1944 there were a great many things I felt should have been most exhaustively investigated which were not investigated at all.
I should like to mention just one other point. If this Bank Act passes, it passes for a period of ten years; and unless the government of the day sees fit to reopen it there will be no opportunity for parliament to discuss this act again for anothef ten years. So far as I am concerned personally, having definitely made up my mind not to contest another election, this will be possibly the last time I will have an opportunity to speak on the Bank Act in the parliament of Canada. Believing that men come and go like bubbles on a stream but that a sound idea once established in the minds of people will go on forever, I do want to take the opportunity to-day of placing some facts upon the record.
To understand section 59 of this bill you must read along with it section 75; and if I am right in my interpretation of those two sections read together then it is section 59, coupled with section 75, that vetoes and nullifies and makes impossible the execution of the declared policy of the government. That policy, enunciated from time to time in this house, is that the parliament of Canada, through the Bank of Canada, shall control ,'he issue of currency and credit in terms of public need, not private gain. If you will look at section 75, subsection (e), you will find that there the banks are empowered to-
(e) engage in and carry on such business generally as appertains to the business of banking.
It is under and by virtue of that clause that the banks are empowered to issue bank deposits as a substitute for national currency in the form of Bank of Canada bills and in the form of coin. It is under the bankers' interpretation of this section of the act that we find them able to create and issue a bankers' form of money. In section 59 you find that the banks are required to hold five per cent of their deposits in Bank of Canada cash, and that must be held either in the
[Mr. Blackmore.J
bankers' tills or on deposit with the Bank of Canada. On the face of it section 59 seems to provide security for depositors, and it is assumed that it also imposes a restriction upon the power of the banks to issue bank deposits as an effective medium of exchange in Canada. But upon examination of the practice established and in vogue, the five' per cent reserve is really an authorization for the piling up of $100 of bank deposits for every $5 of Bank of Canada cash which the banks hold. If that section is allowed to remain as it is to-day the bankers, with the cash reserves they have on hand, can increase and inflate the bank deposit buying power in Canada by double the extent of the bank deposits that are now in issue.
According to the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada for April and May, 1944, the chartered banks have in their tills and on deposit with the Bank of Canada $501,000,000 of Bank of Canada cash. That supports total deposits of $5,297,000,000. But the evidence before the banking and commerce committee was that this is a maximum or a minimum reserve. That is, in their practice the bankers have decided that what parliament has fixed as a minimum is not a safe reserve basis, so they say, "We have fixed as our right and privilege, as bankers, a reserve not on the basis of five per cent but on the basis of ten per cent." Therefore, on the evidence given before the banking and commerce committee, and on the facts which are not disputed, the banks are free to inflate the bank deposit buying power of Canada to the extent of $5,000 million on the reserves as they stand to-day. That cannot and will not be disputed as a fact.
In the face of these facts I submit that any man who will say this parliament has any control, either through the Bank of Canada or otherwise, over the power of our chartered banks to inflate bank deposits to promote a stock boom or any other form of inflationary activity, is uttering what is obviously an utter absurdity. Is it good enough for parliament to say, "We can trust to the wisdom of our bankers"? In the light of the experience of the past is it safe to say that for the coming period of ten years we can give the control of the issue of currency and credit to men who are interested primarily in private gain, and then ask the people throughout this Dominion of Canada to believe us when we say that parliament is in control?
Of course there has been controversy and disagreement; probably there is no subject upon which men will disagree more definitely or so divergently as in the matter of monetary theory and monetary policy. There is always

Bank Act Amendment
great danger in the use of power; and the power to issue money as the medium of exchange of a nation and its .people is the greatest power the government possesses.
What have we done with that power? We have given that power away to a group of men whose business is that of lending money at interest. Human nature being what it is, what would one naturally expect as the outcome and result of that kind of monopoly? Well, one would expect money to be organized in its flow so that it would always be in demand. The people will have to borrow it, because its supply is not adequate either for the needs of government or for the needs of trade. Will anybody suggest we have had enough money to finance this war? Will anybody suggest we had enough money to finance during the last depression? And, looking out on the to-morrows, is there anybody under this present system who does not view with grave concern the danger of the ever-mounting pyramid of debt, and the danger which has swept other countries into the disaster of repudiation, and internal as well as international strife?
To give that power away to a private monopoly, without having absolute control over what that monopoly might do, is an evidence of bad government. And it is because we have maintained a monetary system in the hands of private entrepreneurs that we had a series of booms and depressions, scarcity of money in peace time and abundance of money in war time, and always the very thing one would expect from the monopoly we have created and the power we have given them-an ever-amounting pyramid of unpayable debt.
Of course if the debt dealers are going to control the issue of currency and credit it will be issued in terms of private gain, the debt dealers dealing in debts. And if they have power to create debts they go on creating them until disaster overwhelms them-because that kind of monopoly has invariably the seed that breeds its own destruction.
What is the answer to the debt situation to-day? "Oh," we are told, "we can go on." "How long?" "We do not know". "Well, if you do go on indefinitely, what will happen?" According to your bank governor you will impose an intolerable strain upon the economy of the nation. When is that intolerable strain to come, and when it does come, what is the consequence and what is the remedy? The answer is "We do not know." That is all we can get in the committee on banking and commerce.
Sections 59 and 75, as interpreted, establish a monetary system beyond the control of the
Bank of Canada and beyond the control of parliament;. They establish a monetary system which vests in private monopoly the right to control the issue of the medium of exchange of both the government and the people, in terms of private gain.
Like all men. I was interested in how money is created. One of the most common questions one hears is this: Where does money go to? How does it come about that at certain times we have an abundance of money, ana at other times it disappears? Why is it that money, in its circulation, rises and falls? Well, in 1939, I examined the governor of the bank, and elicited this interesting information from him, as it appears at page 76 of the evidence of the committee on banking and commerce:
Mr. McGeer: Am I right iu saying that a bank deposit can be created in this way? A banker can purchase a dominion government bond by accepting from the government, we will say a bond for $1,000, and giving to the government a deposit in the bank of $1,000?
Mr. Towers: Yes.
*
Mr. McGeer: And in law all that the bank has to hold in the way of cash to issue that deposit liability is 5 per cent?
Mr. Towers: Yes.
Do hon. members realize what that simple transaction means? It means that the Bank of Canada hands over to the bank of Montreal $5 in Bank of Canada cash. The Bank of Canada with that S5 can buy 85 worth of bonds; but when the bank of Montreal gets it it can buy, on its own practice, 850 worth bonds. And the answer is not complete when it is said that we are borrowing some money from the banks at three-quarters of one per cent. That is only a partial answer. It has nothing to do with the actual operation. Can we conceive of a sane man owning a bank and then giving that bank's money over to another institution, and that institution's being able to use that same money to buy the bonds of the original bank to the extent of ten times-or, as by law, twenty times- the value of that money? We are the Bank of Canada. We own every dollar of that stock. It is the people's bank, and we are the people. Yet with a bank capable of issuing real money, we use that bank to bonus a private banking monopoly to carry out the practice of purchasing government bonds by exchanging the noninterest-bearing debts of the chartered banks for the interest-bearing debts of the government of Canada. And you call that a sane monetary system-a sound monetary system? It is a monetary system which has neither sense nor reason or logic to sustain it.
Let me give you an illustration of what that means in the cold terms of factual reality as
Bank Act Amendment

they exist to-day. Our government now has sold to the Bank of Canada approximately one billion dollars' worth of securities. It is somewhat more than that, but I will use the round figure. The Bank of Canada in turn has issued a billion dollars' worth of Bank of Canada cash into circulation. The fact is that there is no debt with regard to that billion dollars. Those bonds are owned by the Bank of Canada and the Bank of Canada is owned by the government of Canada. That is an instance where internal debt is owed by all of the people, through the government, to all of the people. That is a debt that can be cancelled out as a mere bookkeeping entry. But there is another $3,000 million which this and former governments have issued to the chartered banks of Canada, There is an instance of a debt owed by all the people of Canada, through the government, to some of the people of Canada. Once we became the owners of the Bank of Canada why did we ever continue the practice of borrowing through the chartered banks? I think I summarize correctly the answer when I say that if we did not do that we would suffer the consequences of inflation.
I agree that there is always the danger of inflation, but it is not confined to currency alone. You can have inflation of debt, you can have inflation of prices, you can have inflation of commodities. You have had all those things. When you get a superabundance of wheat that you cannot sell, you have inflation of wheat. You can have an inflation of capacity to produce. Inflation can never be summed up in one term alone, that of inflation of currency. When you want to deal with rising prices you do not depend any more upon the manipulation of international or internal monetary systems; you move directly, as the MacMillan committee pointed out you could and should back in 1931, and which we have . demonstrated in this country can be done, to the direct control of prices. If you want to prevent over-production, you move to the direct regulation of production. If you want to maintain your international trade in balance you no longer depend upon the uncontrollable movements of gold; you ' set up your international trade organization and1 you carry on your international trade in exactly the same way that a sound merchant carries on his business. You examine what you can consume at home and what can be sold abroad and then you move to regulate and control your international trade. In that way and in that way alone can you control the international buying power of your own medium of exchange.
You get an inflation of debt because you have had the converse to the issue of currency.

I am amazed at men who say that they fear the use of the printing press to create national currency as the buying power and medium of exchange of the people. The same mien have no fear at all of the danger of using the printing press to secure a medium of exchange to carry on the affairs of government by issuing interest bearing bonds. No one seems to worry about that. The simplest of all principles of economics that we can understand as individuals is to keep out of debt. We have to do that in our homes and we have to do that in our businesses. We try to keep out of debt by thrift and by denying ourselves. If that is sound for the individual, how can it be unsound for the nation which can be nothing more than a group of individuals? See where that has taken us.
I am going to put on the record again the statement made by the Hon. Charles Dunning in 1939 in his budget speech. It is to be found on page 3150 of Hansard of April 25, 1939. He said:
Let no one think that I have changed my mind in regard to the necessity of a balanced budget. Doubtless I will remain the target equally of two extreme schools of thought; on the one hand, those who believe that budget balancing is an outworn fetish, that a nation can continue to do what would soon bring an individual to disaster, and on the other hand, those who believe that governmental expenditures should be ruthlessly slashed regardless of the social distress and the cumulative deflation which would thereby be caused.
And later on;
In times of depression, as I have already shown, increased expenditures on the part of governments are a sheer social necessity. Nevertheless, no nation can go on indefinitely with a budget heavily unbalanced without sooner or later providing a real, not an imagined, basis for fear as to the soundness of the country's financial position. If that fear should take root, nothing which a government could do short of taking over gradually the whole field of private enterprise, could offset the slowing up of private enterprise and the reduction in employment and incomes to which fear and uncertainty would give rise. Canada has had ten years of unbalanced budgets.
That was the warning from one who was held in this house and throughout the country as being one of the greatest ministers of finance we have ever had. He made that statement with a budget I think of $580 million of expenditure and $520 million of revenue, or a deficit of $60 million. Was there neither truth nor wisdom or common sense in that statement? Our Minister of Finance gives us a budget to-day of $6,000 million with a deficit of approximately $3,000 million. Where is the end? That is because this parliament under section 59 and section 75 of the Bank Act has-given away the power of this nation to create its own money to a

Bank Act Amendment
monopoly of debt dealers who think in terms of issuing bank deposits as a substitute for money, only in terms of private gain and not in terms of public need.
Let me put on the record a summary of the evidence taken in 1939 and agreed to by the governor of the bank. I read from page 90 of the evidence of the standing committee of this year, where I am examining Mr. Towers:
Q. Then if I just give a short summary of what- I think we agreed on in 1939, it might cover the situation. We agreed first that our medium of exchange was created under the laws of parliament and consisted of the following: (1) metal coins minted by the mint; (2) Bank of Canada bills issued by the Bank of Canada, and I think that we agreed that that was our national currency and represented about 12 per cent of the total amount of medium of exchange in use; (3) chartered bank bills issued by the chartered banks; and (4) credit entries constituting debt obligations of the chartered banks to customers of the chartered banks and called bank deposits. Those I think we agreed were the four types of media of exchange that constituted the money of Canada. I think you agreed to that.-A. Yes.
Q. I think we also agreed that the government were able to finance public enterprise by using (1) national currency; (2) by taxation; (3) by borrowing from the people; and (4) by borrowing from the chartered banks. Those four methods are, I think, the only four available to government as a means of financing. We agreed on that, I think. Is that right?-A. Yes.
Q. I think we also agreed that our paper money issued by the Bank of Canada for domestic purposes was just as good as gold.- A. Certainly.
Q. Yes.-A. Provided reasonable restraint was exercised.
Q. Oh, yes. Of course, gold has a bad habit of bouncing around. Somebody has suggested that it might go to $65 an ounce. It has already bounced from $20 to $35. I think we also agreed that, as the law is to-day, a chartered bank with $50,000 in Bank of Canada cash was able to purchase interest-bearing bonds from the government to the value of $1,000,000 by giving the government a credit of a million dollars in the bank's books. We agreed on that. We also agreed that under bank practice, the bankers hold 10 per cent of all cash reserves, so that under banking practice a banker with $100,000 in Bank of Canada bills can purchase $1,000,000 in interest-bearing bonds by writing into the books of the chartered banks a credit to the government of $1,000,000. We agreed on that, did we not?-A. Yes.
Q. And we also agreed that the chartered banks do not lend their depositors' savings. That is right?

A. They do not lend their liabilities.
Q. They do not lend their liabilities, and they do not lend their depositors' credits or savings?-A. That is right.
Then, a little further on:

That evidence gave beyond a shadow of a doubt the answer to the question of the people who are mystified by this sudden appearance and disappearance of money. Under section 59 and section 75 this parliament has given to this monopoly the power to lend money into circulation and to create inflationary conditions, and then to withdraw it from circulation and precipitate deflationary conditions. With that power, as Mr. Towers has outlined it, in their possession, and having in their possession sufficient reserves under section 59 as it now stands to increase their issue of currency by $5,000 million, we have no control over the inflation of currency through the Bank of Canada or through any other medium of government. If you are afraid of currency inflation, if what we have heard in support of the taxation policies of the government is sound, if it must be necessary to take the people's money away from them to reduce circulation, then it cannot be reasonable and logical to leave a power of this kind in a private monopoly which, under section 59, has unbridled authority to control the economic bloodstream not only of the nation but of the people in every part of this dominion.

Quite true. You will find
it fully discussed in the English Macmillan report. They reported that these controls were ineffective, that the controls consisted of, first, the bank rate. Assume you are starting off to set up a banking system. You set up your merchant banks around the national central bank. The merchant banks must borrow from the central bank the cash reserves which they use to issue their bank deposit medium of exchange. If the chartered banks are borrowing
Bank Act Amendment

from the central bank, then, if you raise the rate of interest, their inclination is to pay off their loans. If you lowpr the rate of interest their inclination is to borrow more, and so by the rise and fall of the so-called bank rate, which is referred to in Mr. Towers' Bank of Canada report this year, but is admitted by Mr. Towers never to have been in operation as an effective factor of control since the Bank of Canada commenced operations-there is no dispute about that. So the bank rate is out.
The first of the two other controls which incidentally are also incorporated in bank rate policy is the buying of securities. When the Bank of Canada goes into the market and buys a bond from an individual or from a government it sends its money into circulation. Sooner or later that money will be deposited in a chartered bank, and it then becomes the chartered bank's money. The chartered bank banks the money and gives to the depositor a deposit liability in its books. That is what is called an easy money policy, because it gives to the chartered banks cash reserves free of any interest rate at. all and subject only to whatever liability there is to the depositor, the liability for servicing the depositor through the cheque system. But the money goes from the Bank of Canada free. Now, selling securities is the opposite of that. When the Bank of Canada sells securities it calls for payment in Bank of Canada cash. But there is no power in the Bank of Canada Act by which it can compel the chartered banks either to buy or sell securities. If a bank says, or the public says, "We do not want to buy," or if a bank says or the public says, "We do not want to sell," there is no power to compel it to do either. But we have carried on an easy-money policy to this extent: In addition to the 1500 million which the banks have on deposit, another I860 million of Bank of Canada cash is circulating nobody knows where, perhaps in the pockets of the people, perhaps in their possession, but every dollar of it is a potential chartered bank reserve over which this government through the Bank of Canada has. no control at all.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard talks very fluently about the mounting pyramid of debts, and coupled with that he mentions the danger of repudiation. He has used phrases about "drifting over the Niagara of debt into the whirlpool of bankruptcy", or something like that. Now if these statements are not true, if there is no foundation for them, they certainly should not be made at a time-of all times-when the country is at war.
What is the issue between the hon. gentleman and ourselves with regard to this "mounting pyramid of debt"? It became apparent in the banking and commerce committee-I can give the citations from the evidence if it is desired that I should do so-that the hon. members for Vancouver-Burrard, Leth-

Bank Act Amendment
bridge, and Parry Sound and myself were agreed that in time of war it was necessary for any country to tax its people heavily, so as to withdraw from them purchasing power which, not withdrawn from them, would lead to inflation. It was agreed by these hon. gentleman and myself that in addition to heavily taxing the people we should conduct great borrowing campaigns and persuade people to save and buy bonds, carry on the kind of campaign we have carried on for the sale of victory bonds and war savings certificates, for the same reason, the reason being that if we did not in some way channel back to the treasury the excess purchasing power created by war conditions, we would lose control of our price level, as so mahy other countries unfortunately have done.
With regard to the balance, the very small balance proportionately, which cannot be raised by taxation or by borrowing, there is a difference of opinion. The increase in the holdings of the chartered banks of this coun-[DOT] try of dominion government securities between August 1939 and December 1943 was SI,440 million. The difference between the attackers of this system and the upholders of this system is this, that instead of increasing the holdings of the chartered banks by $1,440 million between August _ 1939 and December 1943, the banks should not have been permitted to increase their holdings of government securities at all, that the securities should have been held by the Bank of Canada and sold to the Bank of Canada instead of to the chartered banks; so that under the system which we have adopted we are or were at the end of December, 1943, if bonds held by the Bank of Canada are not regarded as debt, more heavily in debt to the extent of $1,440 million than we would have been under the system advocated by those who are attacking us. That is the issue: instead of our direct debt being something like $11 billion as it was at the end of 1943, had the other system been adopted our direct debt would have been slightly less than $10 billion. Under one system we are drifting over the Niagara of debt into the whirlpool of bankruptcy, with possible repudiation; under the other system we are living in a heaven of debt-free money and not creating debt claims.
I h'ope hon. gentlemen have followed these figures, because it must be clearly understood that the attackers of the system of financing this war would themselves have created an enormous internal debt, would have been obliged to create an enormous internal debt, only slightly smaller than that which we have created.
But, they say, why create that balance? Why buy bonds from the chartered banks instead of from the Bank of Canada? Now, we could have sold our bonds, to cover that proportionately small balance, to the Bank of Canada instead of to the chartered banks, but had we done so, leaving section 59 as it is, I think it is generally admitted that we would have had grave danger of a most serious inflation, because of the multiplication of deposits which would come, based on the increased cash deposits in the chartered banks. In order to avoid that we have what is known as the 100 per cent cash ratio suggestion, which is that after a certain date or with regard to certain deposits the banks should not be allowed to lend money or undertake deposit liabilities to the extent of five or ten per cent of their cash reserves, should not be able to lend any money at all or lend any deposits based on these cash reserves, but that those cash reserves should be put back in the Bank of Canada. That is what is suggested. But what, happens? The government borrows its money from the Bank of Canada and spends that money into circulation. The persons who receive that money put it in the chartered banks and the chartered banks incur deposit liabilities, which liabilities cast upon them very substantial expenses, and they are denied any opportunity of recouping themselves for any of those expenses at all.

I refer to Australia. That subject was not pursued very far. In Australia they did borrow from the central bank after a certain date instead of going to the chartered banks for their borrowings. Mind you, they tax very heavily in Australia, and everyone admits that we must do that. And they borrow very heavily in Australia, and everyone admits that we must do that. But as to the residuum, the margin, the balance, they borrowed from the central bank instead of from the commercial banks, and the result was that this money went out and into the commercial banks, into the banks doing commercial business-because the central bank does some commercial business too in Australia. They found that in order to prevent the evils of a great multiplication in deposits and prevent a rise in the price level, they had to provide for the deposit of all cash increases in those banks after a certain date back into the central bank, *which is the 100 per cent reserve ratio system. They adopted that plan in Australia, although they did not give it that name. That was what they did about the end of 1041. But what did they do next? They saw it was so unfair to the depositors in the commercial banks and to the commercial banks themselves, casting upon them burdens of servicing

the public without giving them any revenue out of which to do it, that they' decided to give them some revenue, and so they paid them three-quarters of one per cent per annum on this amount which they compelled the banks to deposit back in the central bank. Independently of experience in Australia, we in the Dominion of Canada, in the summer of 1942, found that we had to borrow from the chartered banks. We had tried desperately to avoid any bank borrowing, but in the summer of 1942 we had to borrow from the chartered banks.

Perhaps I should complete
my forty minutes first, then, because when the hon. gentleman takes the figures of debt; when he paints this appalling picture of the debt this country is incurring, he does not take the debt to the banks only. He takes figures like eleven billion dollars, fourteen billion dollars, sixteen billion dollars and twenty billion dollars. He counts all this valuable, wholesome borrowing from the public, which he himself advocates, in piling up this debt which he condemns. When we reached this point in the banking and commerce committee ; when the hon. gentleman was pinned down after the lengthy speeches he made and asked. "What would you have done"? he said he would have taxed, in the severe way that I have mentioned; he would have borrowed, only he would have borrowed more than we did. But then for the balance-and there might not have been any balance if he had borrowed so much more, and the debt would have been greater than it is at the present time-r-he would have issued national currency. That is, he would have borrowed from the Bank of Canada instead of from the chartered banks; and he thinks that by some magic, for that is all it would be, he would gain something for the country by borrowing, from a government institution instead of from privately owned institutions. My contention is that the interest obligations of the public, if they do the fair thing, will be the same under both systems; and that the principal obligation, certainly if one comes to the deposit liability of the central bank to the chartered banks, would be the same under both systems.
The hon. gentleman in his speech used a phrase which is so attractive and so hard to answer in a sentence or two. He used these words: "If we can issue bonds; if we can use the printing presses to print bonds, why can we not do that to issue currency?" The * difference between the two is just this, that when you issue bonds you borrow money from people, reduce their bank deposits and transfer them to the government account; you do not increase the total amount of money or circulating medium in the country. But when you talk of printing money to the amount of a million dollars and paying your contractors, your civil servants and so on, you have increased the circulating medium of the country by a million dollars; and if that goes into the chartered banks as reserves it may be

multiplied quite a bit beyond that. Yet I know that very question is troubling hon. members of this house. They Say, "If you can turn on the printing presses for bonds, why can you not do it for dollars?" The reason is that in one case you are borrowing; you are taking back the purchasing power of the people, getting it away from them so that they will not exert that irresistible upward pressure which otherwise their spending would exert, while in the other case you are not lowering their purchasing power at all.

Yes, you are increasing it. That is the reason for doing it under one system rather than the other. In his speech the hon. gentleman said that we must not have deficit financing. I want to say that in due course, after we pass through the war and the immediate post-war period, I hope to get into a position where there will not be any deficits in Canada. We can do that if we can get private investment up to the level at which it ought to be, and if we can keep a healthy, well-balanced condition of prosperity in this country. The hon. member quotes Mr. Dunning back in 1939 as saying that if the fear should become rooted that there are always going to be deficits and that the economic fabric is being destroyed, it will be destroyed. That is why I do not like these speeches, which, if they were taken seriously, might result in that fear becoming rooted.
There is no ground whatever for alarm with regard to the debt we have accumulated so far. I should like hon. members to read the figures I put on the record on July 11, 1944, which appear at page 4718 of Hansard, showing that on March 31, 1944, the net annual carrying charge on Canada's direct and indirect funded debt was only $183,509,355 if the surplus of the Canadian National Railways is regarded as a factor in arriving at the net annual carrying charge of the debt. If it is not so regarded, the charge is $219,149,355. On March 31, 1939, the net carrying charge was $149,651,990 and on March 31, 1920, it was $164,349,572. What is there in figures like that to justify these alarmist utterances, this talk about a Niagara of bankruptcy, the fear of repudiation, and so on? This country will not repudiate. It is nowhere near the place where there is any cause for alarm. A year or two ago I used to be afraid for the success of our victory loans when I heard speeches of this kind, but I am glad to say that the people of the country did not take them very seriously. They have faith in the future of the country and they know that the annual carrying charges are well within our capacity to look

Bank Act Amendment
after. The hon. member talks here at times about the spending of money in huge sums on the building of public works in every part of Canada

the trans-Canada highway, works to block the strait of Belle Isle, a causeway across the strait of Canso, and so on, and so on, having no fear at all about the expenditure of money. But the moment he comes to an actual expenditure of $183,000,000 he goes back to these gloomy and despairing predictions about the future of the country, and the inability of the country to carry the burden.
This country can carry a burden of very much greater debt. He says that we do not know, that we will not say how big a debt it can carry. He says that we will not say what the point is when, the intolerable strain will be too'heavy. No, we do not say that. I believe they have had in the United States great arguments about the amount of debt the United States can carry. I do not think that government ever said, and I do not think any government in Canada can say dogmatically. We have to see how conditions develop in this country.
I would be foolish to stand up here and say that if in 1950 we have a debt of twenty billions of dollars we cannot carry it, or say that if in 1955 we have a debt of twenty-five billions of dollars we cannot carry it-or we can carry it. I would be foolish to say that, because I cannot predict the conditions which [DOT]will exist. But we do know that we have to do everything within our power for the promotion of private investment and, if that is not sufficient, public investment, and by other means-by sound, social security measures, and otherwise-to see that the people of our country attain full employment or at least attain high employment in the post-war period. I feel that we shall be buoyant under the same national economy and financial system which has been adopted in other countries. I am thinking of countries like Great Britain, like the United States, like New Zealand. I am not quite sure about the situation in South Africa, but I imagine it is the same there. Those are countries which have adopted substantially the same system which we have in Canada. That is to say, in time of war they tax heavily and they borrow heavily.
The hon. members who have attacked this system in the banking and' commerce committee concede that if we are going to prevent inflation in Canada we have to tax heavily and borrow heavily. I do not complain about that situation, but I do complain about the sweeping statements about the creating of debt, the iniquity behind our
banking system, and the necessity of having debt-free money, when the very ones who suggest these ideas admit themselves that we will not have it in time of war, and probably cannot have it after the war, either.
Next the hon. member made some statements about his policy after the war, which was practically the same as his statement with regard to banking during the war. The hon. member said something about deposits being out of control. He said that the Bank of Canada's controls are entirely ineffective. He pointed out that we have $501,000,000 deposited in the chartered banks in cash reserves, and that they can issue or create deposits on this up to $5 billion. That is correct. Then he says that they have unbridled authority to do what they like.
A reserve in cash which must be about ten per cent is a pretty effective control, I can tell this committee.

The Bank of Canada controls it. The Bank of Canada absolutely controls the amount of cash reserve. I have tried to make that clear, time after time. If those cash reserves now in the hands of the banks were to turn into an expansion of deposits, the Bank of Canada could take that out of the banks by the sale of securities. And when the hon. member says that no one can make anybne buy securities, and no one can make anyone sell securities, he is missing the fact that there is always a sale for securities, at a price.
The Bank of Canada can sell securities and buy securities, and by that method they can control the amount of cash reserves in the bank. If the cash reserves in the bank are reduced the amount of cash deposited has to be reduced, or the bank cannot continue in business. And if the cash reserves in the bank are increased, the bank will indisputably increase its loans and increase its deposits, because otherwise it could not profitably continue in business.
I have just touched on a few of the points introduced in the discussion. 1 have not said much about what has happened in the banking and commerce committee, because I wished to have these proceedings completed. However, I have taken this opportunity again to place on record the views which we hold, and which I have repeatedly expressed and justified in the house and outside the house, .views which I think are fairly generally accepted the world over, and views which are sound.

Mr. Chairman, in the discussion this afternoon something has been said about the time the bill was introduced into the house. If my memory serves me correctly, the Minister of Finance introduced the bill on May 2. It was referred to the banking and commerce committee on May 16, and on May 17 that committee gave Bill No. 91 precedence over all other business. The bill was finally passed in the banking and commerce committee on July 27. Therefore that committee spent two months and ten days in the discussion of this very important bill. I do not think any member of that committee or any member of the house can say that there' was not ample time for a full review, investigation and discussion of the provisions of the bill which renews bank charters for another ten years.
I should like to make only one or two observations with respect to the provisions of this bill. I am very much in favour of those provisions which extend longer term credits to the great agricultural industry in Canada. I regard the banking business as a commission business. The banks have their capital; they have their reserves, and they have a deposit business.
This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said that in answer to questions asked the governor of the Bank of Canada the governor had said that the banks did not lend their deposits. That is true; he did say that. Bht the governor further explained that the banks lend the proceeds of their deposits which, I suggest, places an entirely different construction upon thip situation.
The Minister of Finance has effectively reviewed the situation as far as the issue of Bank of Canada money is concerned, through the chartered banks. However, after two months and ten days of discussion the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard had some suggestions, which I regarded as his final suggestions. I find that on Thursday, July 20, seven days before the bill passed the committee, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said this:
Mr. Chairman, yesterday the matter arose in connection with a liability that would be created or that some seemed to think ryould be created by the Bank of Canada taking over the savings deposits.

No, it is not. It may be just slightly larger than the percentage we have financed on a similar basis. I do not agree with the hon. member's contention that when you finance through the Bank of Canada you finance without interest. When you issue Bank of Canada money it goes out in cheques to working men, to soldiers, for the payment of dependents' allowances and so on; it goes into the chartered banks in the form of deposits and becomes a liability of the
banks to the Canadian people. If you take the savings deposits at one per cent, that is _ not debt-free money.
During the discussion in the banking and commerce committee something was said about the great emancipator of the United States, Abraham Lincoln. It was said that Lincoln had financed the civil war by the issue of greenbacks. According to my recollection Lincoln did issue about $450 million in greenbacks, but later on about $103 million were withdrawn and the remaining part of the issue was absorbed by the rapidly developing, young and new country. But do not forget this, that in that same civil war the Confederates of the southern states issued very large amounts of fountain-pen money or paper currency that we hear so much about to-day, and I do not think more than one or two per cent of that money was ever redeemed. They papered their back kitchens with it and put it on their gate-posts, et cetera. That should not be forgotten.
But the most important point that I have in mind in connection with the financing of the war by our great and strong neighbour to the south is this. Lincoln was a great emancipator, one of the great presidents of the United States, just as our great neighbour to the south has a great president to-day in Franklin D. Roosevelt; but I am convinced of this, that had Lincoln discovered some method whereby you could finance a war without cost the people not only of the United States but of Canada and of Britain and of Russia would be using that system to-day. But what do we find? From June 12 to July 5 of this year the United States government authorized a loan issue of $16 billion. That was their fifth victory loan. Of that $16 billion, $6 billion was allotted to private subscribers and $10 billion to what we would call our special list. The result of the loan was that approximately $6 billion was subscribed by individuals and the $10 billion was oversubscribed by about $3 billion. So that our neighbours to the south, even in the light of the experiences which they had had under President Lincoln, found it necessary to borrow from June 12 to July 5 of this year a victory loan, not of one billion dollars or of two billion dollars but a loan of nineteen billion dollars. There is perhaps some difference between the rates of interest paid in the United States, in this country, in Soviet Russia, and in Great Britain but the fact remains that the major countries, not including China, who are fighting on our side in this war are all following a somewhat similar system of financing. That is why I have not been convinced by what I am sure were

the lucid arguments of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and the hon. member for Parry Sound.
Something was said in the discussions in the banking and commerce committee about bank deposits and I wish to touch upon that. According to the census of 1941 we had in the Dominion of Canada heads of families numbering 2,516,762. That represents the number of families in Canada at .that time. We had employed at that date 2,115,299 males and 699,492 females, a total of 2,814,791 employed persons. The number of people employed and on the payrolls right now is higher than that, but I could not get the exact figures for a more recent date, so that I am taking the figures of the 1941 census. At the close of 1943 we had in the Canadian chartered banks demand deposit accounts numbering 738,300 and savings deposit accounts numbering 4.662,100. There was a total of 5,400,400 deposit accounts. Of course, there may be considerable duplication because some people would have one or two or perhaps more accounts, but I think I am perfectly safe in saying that, on the average, we have in the Dominion of Canada a bank account for every family, and I think that is a very good showing.
I have no particular interest in bankers, particularly big bankers, but what I kept firmly in my mind during the entire discussions in the banking and commerce committee was this, that these ten chartered banks have within their coffers somewhere between four and five billion dollars of deposits of the Canadian people's money, and it is in order to protect those deposits of such a large number of our people that I have been prepared, after lengthy and full discussions, to support the motion to renew the bank charters for a further period of ten years. I do not think this is a time when we should do anything to increase a feeling of uneasiness. We have inserted in the Bank Act wide and new provisions to enable the banks to lend money to farmers, fishermen and many others. That, it seems to me, is an additional argument for adhering *to the ten-year rule. I believe that any wavering in this regard is a sign of weakness, indecision and distrust. If it is a good thing to continue, why cast doubts about it and say, "We will give you a lease of life for two years. We are not brave enough to destroy you, but we may get courage enough and facts enough in the future to do you some damage when you come back to this house."
In the difficult days ahead the banks should be enabled to function without the insecurity of impending destruction. If anything is wrong, now is the time to change it. Recurring revisions of the Bank Act have always brought changes, and this revision is no exception. The banks mush accept -these changes. My general opinion is that -the banks have done a fairly good job. They are restricted by law. There are some things they cannot do, But we restrict them to make them safe ; we limit their services to a certain sphere so *that they shall serve the public in the way we intend them to do.
Are the banks efficient? Let us compare them with others. This is a competitive world. Other nations have banks and similar financial institutions. Is there any place in the world which can give us fuller knowledge or teach us more of the mechanics of the operations of banks? In the great republic to the south, a few years ago, the banks were closed. They were unable to perform the functions for which they were intended. They did not have the stability- nor did they enjoy the general advantages which are possessed by the Canadian banking system, which is based on the Scottish system. For that reason the banks in that rich country, the United States, failed to function. They could take a lesson from the Canadian banking system.
Another reason why I think our banks are efficient is that they do business in other countries. When you make a product which you use yourself it must be fairly good, but when you can export it to other countries and they are willing to use it you know it must be efficient because it meets the competition
Bank Act Amendment

of the world. Our banks have gone to other countries; they have branches in London, in New York, in Paris, in a number of the South American states and other countries, and are doing business there, and they are missionaries of Canadian trade. To disturb a situation of that kind would be a very foolish act on our part at the present time.
Not every business in Canada is restricted to ten years, because we give charters to other corporations. Moreover, limited liability is a privilege to any institution because it absolves the members from certain obligations with regard to personal liability so that they can carry on. Their charters continue indefinitely. One of the reasons for incorporating a company is that when a man dies his business carries on and there is not the same confusion as ensues upon the death of a man who has been carrying on a personal business. Why then, seeing that the banks are subject to greater control than any other business, should we be so particular; why should' we be afraid to extend their charters at this time after they have shown a good record, and have continued to do business successfully, and have given us evidence that they will render as good service both within and outside Canada in the immediate days to come as they have done in the past.
In this revision some changes have been made. The banks had a maximum interest rate of seven per cent and we have reduced it to six per cent. Do you know what was said in that regard? It was said that the banks are doing most of their business at six per cent now so that the reduction will not hurt them. In other words, as a result of their efficiency, they were reaching the point which we would compel them to assume by legislation, and when they get the legislation it will not hurt them a bit.
Furthermore, we have extended their powers and increased their responsibility in lending money to fishermen and farmers, so that they can lend money on floating property, which has always been regarded as too hazardous for the banking system. It was difficult to get money on floating property. This is something I regard as advantageous to my constituency because we make our living on the sea, and anything in the Bank Act which will stimulate the marine business of the country will receive my support, because I believe it is in the interests of the people I represent.
As regards farmers, we have an amendment which will allow greater liberty in the making of loans to this class. That is in the interests of the country: it. is a sfen forward.

That is something else we have incorporated in the Bank Act this year to bring it into line with the progress that is being made generally.
There has been a change with regard to the qualification of directors, and that I think is a good idea because there might be some misunderstanding in the country. It might be felt that the banks are the citadel of weaRh in Canada and that men with big bank accounts, men who are dealing in financial matters, are the only ones who should run the banks. The banks themselves agree that they should draw upon labour and the producing and farming community and lower the qualifications for directors so as to enable the banks to take advantage of that added strength which would come from below. I am sure that will be of assistance and will prove of great value. I think parliament did the banks a good turn in this regard and the banks have so accepted it.
There was some discussion about small loans. There are small loan companies charging two per cent for money under certain conditions.

speechtext:
In presenting my views
on what to me are the two most important features of this bill to be dealt with by this committee, I desire to make my personal position very clear, as I have endeavoured to do on previous occasions. I have no quarrel with the bankers of this country as men and citizens. They are a worthy, patriotic, hardworking group of men. My quarrel is entirely with two features of the system under which the private banks are operated. And let me say that there can be no reflection upon any member of this committee, any member of this house, any member of this government or of any previous government within the lifetime of any member of this house in regard to the creation of the system which I believe is outmoded and must be discarded. This system was brought into existence by our forefathers. No living member of the House of Commons had anything whatever to do with its creation; nor is it necessary in this discussion to place any blame on our forefathers for having created this monopoly. Conditions then were entirely different from conditions of to-day. Trading was on a small and crude basis. There were no railways., It could scarcely be called the horse-and-buggy days; it was largely the day of the oxcart when the present system came into the hands of the bankers. Highways as we have them to-day were practically unknown, and from Ottawa to Toronto was a two weeks' journey. There was no electricity, gas. telephone or telegraph. There were no motorcars and no branch banks. The currency of the country was in pounds, shillings and pence. The industrial life of Canada as we know it to-day had not developed at all.
I comment on this because we are all more or less inclined to be averse to changing existing conditions. Let no man tell me, however, that %the change in our whole economic structure and way of life since the time this system was inaugurated has not been progressive, radical and so great as to be almost unrecognizable. I think it was Mr. Morris Wilson who, ten years ago, when asked why this system should not be changed, smiled and offered to the committee of that day, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for York-Sunbury, the reason, " It has just always been this way." In modern times that, I submit, is not good enough.
I present two main objectives which I believe must be given effect to, if we are to protect the people in the next ten years. Both of these come under the reform set out in sections 59 and 75. The first is to retake from the banks, for the Canadian people, through
Bank Act Amendment

the government, the right to create and control currency and credit, and the issue of money. The second is that, hereafter, when new money has to be created, it shall be issued into existence through the Bank of Canada, instead of being borrowed into existence through the private banks, by the use of debt borrowing securities.
My submission is that we should do no borrowing whatsoever from the private banks for public financing or for government needs. We shall thereby destroy what is at present a toll-gate privilege now enjoyed by the banks, of collecting from the government interest on new money issued with the backing of our national credit, by pretending to lend us money which they do not possess but which, in reality, is our own money, our own credit or our own medium of exchange.
Let me put it in another way, as it was put by the present Prime Minister in parliament in 1933, and repeated in 1935 on the public platform. This is a policy which I used in my campaign when seeking election. This is the first time since 1935, in a period of ten years, that there has been a chance to amend the Bank Act. I appeal to the committee, to all political parties, to accept this-not because it is the language of the present Prime Minister, but because it is the very best and soundest economic doctrine which could be presented for the benefit of our people. He said:
Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit shall be restored to government-
That was in 1935. Who had that control? He said that until it shall be-
-restored to government, and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of 'sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile. To regain for the nation what has thus been lost will continue to be the first objective of Liberal effort.
Again I quote the Prime Minister, as recently as June 20 of this year-1944-when he spoke upon introducing into the house bill No. 82, to establish a department of reconstruction. He referred to it in this language:
.	.	. restoring and increasing the capital
equipment of the nation . . .
And then added:
It is in connection with this economic reconstruction that the new department of reconstruction of the federal government will be primarily concerned.
I do not believe there is a member in the house who does not recognize the need for post-war reforms, as against the old order of things. I think every hon. member would
IMr. Slaght.l
agree that we are not going to allow our men to come back to the conditions they left. Who will gainsay that, among all these reforms, the question of economic reform does not stand at the very threshold and, in the language of the Prime Minister, must be our primary concern? Are we to go back to the days where we are to be asked by the treasury department as we were in peace time, when we desired to increase old age pensions-a small item, but an important one-"Where will the money come from?" If we are to go back to those days, then the picture we are all seeking to bring into being must disappear.
I quote further the language of Mr. Graham Towers, the governor of the Bank of Canada, contained in his annual report issued in February, when he warned us that there lie ahead, to be solved by the government, problems of unprecedented magnitude. Before I conclude I shall ask the Minister of Finance, and I shall also ask my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party, who may oppose the reform I suggest, what their remedy would be. What have they to suggest?
We at least have a remedy. I recognize that some may not agree with it. Some may find hidden within if dangers which outweigh the virtues. But we must all agree in the face of language like that from the governor of the Bank of Canada that our problems of government in the economic field are of unprecedented magnitude. If there is any member who will quarrel with those solemn statements by our Prime Minister and the governor of the Bank of Canada, so far as I am concerned he must give me an alternative remedy capable of operation.
Please do not misunderstand my position. I would preserve for private banks-and there, for the moment, I would disagree with my distinguished friend, the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party-the right to carry on the commercial banking business of this country, - and the right to lend up to the amount of their own capital, and in addition an amount equivalent to the time deposits-that is, the savings deposits- of their customers. But beyond such limits the banks ought not to be allowed to lend money, except to the extent that they have a full cash reserve, either in currency or in credit.
This policy I suggest will save the country from going farther down the path of an ever-increasing public debt, one which has already reached an appalling total. Mr. Graham Towers admitted to me, at page 159 of the evidence, that by the end of this year, 1944, it would reach the sum of S16 billions. This amount includes dominion, provincial and

Bank Act Amendment
municipal borrowings, on all of which, let us not forget, the taxpayer must pay interest. I suggest that we must call a halt, or run into national disaster, the disaster of repudiation.
It is all very well for the Minister of Finance to say that we can go on in this way, that we have only just started, and that Canada is a virile nation. He is not going to put me into the position of belittling Canada's great reserves, or her capacity to finance, by using an argument of that kind. I suggest, however, that the amount is staggering and appalling. The figure for interest this year, as given by Mr. Towers-and it will increase by $40,000,000 next year-is $280,000,000. That is what we have to pay to carry the dominion's load alone.
But do not take my word for it. Only a few days ago, on July 4, in the committee, Doctor Clark, the distinguished deputy minister, who is here to-night, made this admission to my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. This is what appears in the evidence:
Q. [DOT]-I think you will agree with me we cannot go on pyramiding debt, interest-bearing debt of the people of Canada indefinitely?
A. Not indefinitely.
Then what is the remedy my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party offer? I have heard none in the banking and commerce committee. What remedy do our hon. friends in the group of Liberals in that committee or in this house, headed by certain of my hon. friends who are so solicitous for their Progressive Conservative friends offer? I must except the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. Is it to keep tax-free the inner reserves which the banks refuse to disclose?
I will touch on that in a moment because the Minister of Finance spent a little time this afternoon in trying to imply that if we took this monopoly away -from the banks and gave it back to the people of Canada it would be disastrous to the banks. He contended that that is what would happen if we did not keep on borrowing nationally from them in the future. Mark you, I am not suggesting that we take anything away from them by paying in cash the debt of $2,700,000,000 which we owe them now and on which they are collecting $40,000,000 a year and will continue to collect that, as far as I can see, during the life of all the hon. members of this committee. In my judgment it will be a long, long year before Canada can ever hope to repay any principal money of the vast obligations we have undertaken.
I asked for remedies from those two groups. It is true that the C.C.F. suggested a remedy to parliament, but parliament rejected it. That aspect is not under discussion in this debate because my hon. friends of that party
bowed to the decision of parliament when this bill was referred. I am not going to spend any time in discussing whether they are right or wrong, but they had a remedy. I want to say to those members who may have deep apprehension about that remedy and the incidents that will flow from it as to industry as a whole, that it is a dangerous thing-

speechtext: It is a proposal, not a remedy.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
It is a proposed remedy. I hold no brief for them, but they believe it is a remedy that will cure. No doubt it would in part cure some of the evils of the present bill, but it would bring with it matters which in my judgment would be detrimental to our future economic possibilities, so much so that it may be that we dare not accept the good in their proposal because it would bring down around the country a whole house of cards containing much more evil. As I said, I am not going to argue that or express myself on it to-night because we shall hear a good deal about it between now and the next election.
I suggest that if you agree with the Prime Minister, if you agree with Mr. Graham Towers, you will believe with them that it is a problem of such terrific magnitude that someone must produce a remedy. I should like to hear from the Minister of Finance and his friends as to what their remedy is. I think I have heard it in the banking and commerce committee and you have had a smattering of it this afternoon. He has no cure or remedy; it is hopeless! Seventy-five years ago we gave away this monopolistic right to create money. We are now going to go on borrowing from the banks debt-laden money to fill Canada's needs, when wre can step to the Bank of Canada and borrow it without interest. I must comment upon what the minister said when he exhorted the committee not to "wreck the banks." That was his expression. Why, he says, if you carry on what these monetary reformers are suggesting you are going to wreck the banks! He was commenting upon what he called the extravagant language of the hon. member for V ancouver-Burrard.
He said, 'Why, the chartered banks, the private banks would have to impose service charges upon our people in order to permit them to service the money the Bank of Canada would issue for the public need." I agree with him that these funds would flow very promptly into the coffers of the chartered banks. I had not intended to deal with that here, but let me do so. Why in the world should not the people who receive service from the banks pay for it? Is it bad economic policy to see to it in your national set-up that those who receive benefits which are not conferred
Bank Act Amendment

upon all the people should pay for them? Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, what the evidence in the committee disclosed. I do not want to spend too much time on this because I do not think it is worth an argument.

There are 11,000,000 people in Canada, so that there are 6,500,000 who have no bank accounts. Somebody will say at once: Oh, the children are in that. Of course they are in that, but a very large number of people in Canada are paying taxes who have not and never had a bank account of any kind in their lives. When you say to me that such and such a man would be too poor to have an income upon which to pay taxes, let me reply that the poor people in this country are paying enormous taxes through the sales tax which they pay on everything they wear, and on everything that their children wear, boots and shoes and suits and so on. In this country, because of our climatic conditions, children require practically three outfits a year, and it may interest hon. gentlemen to know that last year this government collected $304,000,000 in sales tax. So do not tell me that the little fellows, because they are not paying income tax, are not paying taxes at all. Under the present system these little fellows are paying the taxes for the services which the big firms are getting for nothing. Let anyone rise in his place in this house and support that state of affairs. I only bring it to your attention, Mr. Chairman, to wipe out what the Minister of Finance thinks is an answer when he is asked to take back from the bankers what the British North America Act gave to the people of Canada. I do not agree with him and I do not think this committee should agree with him.
I had intended to give one or two extracts because, strange to say, when you suggest that we have given away to the private banks the right to create money some people do not believe you. I am going to give two or three pretty effective quotations. I give you a few sentences from what Governor Eccles, president of the federal reserve bank of the United States, had to say:
The banks can create and destroy money. Bank credit is money. It is the money we do most of our business with, not with that currency which we usually think of as money.
Then Mr. J. M. Keynes, now Lord Keynes, who has been representing Britain on the Bank of England's delegation at Bretton Woods, had this to say:
There can be no doubt that all deposits are created by the banks.

Bank Act Amendment
The Encyclopaedia Britannica says:
Banks create credit. It is a mistake to suppose that bank credit is created to any important extent by the payment of money into the banks. A loan made by a bank is a clear addition to the amount of money in the community.
I am not going to give further references, because I understand that the Minister of Finance and I are agreed on that broad general economic statement. But I want these facts reported to parliament, and to my mind they do not leave the slightest shadow of doubt as to what the situation is.
The figures on the ten chartered banks made it clear that their original paid-up capital was $145i million. Their rest or reserve fund- that is, the disclosed rest or reserve fund-is $136J million, or a total of S282J million. They have private bank notes in circulation, a privilege which we gave them to create money at the mere cost of printing and paper, to the amount of $40 million. That privilege is going out of existence. The banks have been notified gradually to reduce the amount until it will be wiped out altogether. Then the banks have hidden reserves about which the minister said nothing at all when he was painting the pitiful plight of the bankers, and these hidden reserves have been accumulating year after year out of earnings, and they are tax free in the current year in which the earnings are collected. We do not know, and parliament does not know to-day, how much that accumulated fund of hidden reserves taken out of earnings amounts to. It may be thirty million dollars or it may be three hundred million dollars.
In passing, let me say this. To my mind the attitude of the bankers and the attitude of the advisers of our Department of Finance in supporting them in refusing to disclose their hidden reserves to the committee on banking and commerce when the banks came there after ten years for a renewal of their charters was most unwise. I asked the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, "How much have you tucked away in your vaults out of current earnings each year as hidden reserves? What is the total amount now of that hidden reserve fund?" He said to me, much more politely than this-this is not- his language but it was" this in effect- "It is none of your business." He would not tell me. Accordingly I turned to the Minister of Finance, who does know-and it was said by Mr. Tompkins that he does know what these aggregate total hidden reserves are-and I asked him to tell that to the committee on banking and commerce. The minister said in effect: This is a very serious matter, and I should like to ponder it; I
think I need a little time to decide whether I should disclose it or not. He took from the 25th of May to the 6th of June, twelve daj's, and then he came back to the committee with a nine-page statement and refused to tell the committee or parliament the aggregate amount of those hidden reserves of the ten chartered banks on December 31. What do you make of that?
I thought the banking and commerce committee-and I have the terms of reference here-was a fact-finding committee, given full power to bring witnesses and to secure evidence on the subject on which we had to report back to the House of Commons, and so it is. The advisers of the Minister of Finance were brought in-and I will tell you in a minute how I know they were brought in to assist him in preparing a statement which he doubtless believed in with the utmost good faith, and I want no misunderstanding on that score-and they would not tell the committee what the hidden reserves of the ten chartered banks are which have been accumulating for fifty years. I asked why? And what do you suppose was the reason? Parliament ought not to know; the people of Canada ought not to know. The shareholders of the individual banks do not know because their directors and auditors conceal it from them each year. None of these three bodies ought to know, they said. Why? Because they might misunderstand it.
The first smoke-screen that was set up in support of concealing the hidden reserves was that if the banks disclosed last year, and the year before, their hidden reserves and then two years hence they admitted any serious loss it might check the confidence of the public in the bank, if you please. So I bowed to that, which was vehemently put forward by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, not by any Liberal I might say, and then I said: "Mr. Minister and Mr. Banker, tell this committee of parliament what is the aggregate total amount of the hidden reserves of all the ten banks on December 31. Is it thirty million dollars or three hundred million dollars?" And I framed a resolution which was put to the banking and commerce committee, that this committee require the bankers to disclose to parliament the gross amount of the hidden reserves of all the ten chartered banks-that and nothing more. Now what excuse they will give this time I do not know.
I invite the Minister of Finance to disclose the aggregate amount to this parliament tonight. But no more hush-hush. How can a parliament deal with applications to renew
Bank Act Amendment

charters for ten years andl consent to be told by the bankers who seek this monopolistic privilege, " Parliament is not going to know from us-and we have got the minister converted to our view-point-and members of parliament are not going to know how much more earnings the banks take in every year and put away as hidden reserves, and escape payment of taxes on them in the current year." Has the minister any God-given right to know what my hon. friend the chairman of the banking committee does not know? I venture to say he knows a good deal about the economics of banking. I venture to say that in bringing his good judgment to bear on whether we should renew the charters, it was important to know how much over fifty years has been tucked away as hidden reserves. There may be $300 million of Bank of Canada cash in there in that respect. What blessed reason is there that they should in 1944, coming for renewal of charters, hide the truth from parliament? To my mind it is the blackest thing acquiesced in by any body of men, as destroying the supremacy of parliament, that has happened in the last hundred years. Who is there who will tell me why he should know and you should not know? Are your constituents less entitled to weigh your conduct in renewing the bank charters than the constituents of the hon. member for a maritime constituency? I thought that this was the place where the people's representatives were to learn the truth, and that any black pall of secrecy was done away with long ago in British parliaments conducted1 on British lines. Therefore I say to this committee, when we are told, "Do not bow to this reform and take back this monopolistic privilege to create money, because you will wreck the banks," and in the same breath we are told, "You are not old' enough or wise enough or you cannot bring good enough judgment to bear if we disclose to you the lump sum of money which' is tucked away tax-free in ten years"-tax-free, I should say, in the year in which it was earned-the people of Canada are not going to be content with that attitude.
I beseech the members of this parliament in this matter to remove the stain which will rest upon us if we pass these bank charters for ten more years, dissolve this house and1 then, going home to our constituents, have to tell them from the public platform or wherever we meet them, " We signed on the dotted line and we did not ask the bankers to tell us what in each year were their earnings which they tucked away as hidden reserves." [Mr. Slaght.l
To my mindi-and I put the point in all friendliness-we made a mistake in the banking and commerce committee. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has said that he may not sit in this house again. I say the same thing, under present conditions. I have not made up my mind. But I am going to find it difficult to come back here and support a policy of renewing bank charters, when bankers have told us, " It is none of your business what we have tucked away in hidden reserves and escape taxation on." I love my party, perhaps as well as any man on this side of the house. Let us see where we are going in this thing. Let us stop while there is yet time; and if the committee do not agree with me and my colleague in the matter of having the public exercise their right under our constitution to do government borrowing from our own bank, let us reach that decision after our Minister of Finance, whom I invite and beg to do so, has disclosed the real financial situation of the ten chartered banks.

At six o'clock the hon.
member for Parry Sound brought up a point of order, which was that he thought we ought to stick to section 59, which deals with cash reserves of the bank, and while I shall perhaps go farther afield than this section indicates, I think he has done the same. I want to read this section so that there will be no mistake about it:
Cash reserves
59. The bank shall maintain a reserve which shall, as provided in the Bank of Canada Act, be not less than five per centum of such of its deposit liabilities as are payable in Canadian dollars and such reserve shall consist of a deposit with the Bank of Canada and of Bank of Canada notes held by the bank; and the bank shall also maintain with the Bank of Canada or elsewhere adequate reserves against liabilities elsewhere than in Canada and furnish such information as may be required by the minister from time to time to satisfy him that such reserves against liabilities elsewhere than in Canada are so maintained.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, in quoting this section, said that the law required that a reserve of five per cent should be maintained against this sort of banking business, and he said that the bankers, with a disdain born of greater knowledge, decided that they would not conform with the law but they would use ten per cent. In my business, where

Bank Act Amendment
we deal with materials and have to take into account stresses and strains, we always allow for what we call a margin of safety to provide against disaster. For instance, if engineers tested the elevators in this building for 2,000 pounds, do you imagine they would allow you to put 2,000 pounds in these elevators? They would test those elevators for 3,000 pounds-

speechtext: More likely, six.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
