-and then they would probably allow you to put in a weight of 2,000 pounds. If I build an engine of 150 horsepower, I always have a margin which I can use in an emergency; probably it would develop 165 or 170 horse-power. So with a boiler; if you are going to test a boiler for 200 pounds, do you think any engineer would allow you to put steam into that boiler up to 200 pounds? The boiler would first be tested for, perhaps, 300 pounds, and then he might let you use it with a safety valve up to 200 pounds. Much the same principle applies here. My hon. friend misquoted the act. The section does not state that the reserve shall be five pep cent; it says that it shall not be less than five per cent. The bankers in their wisdom think they should have a margin of safety, and put it at ten per cent, and the hon. member uses that fact as a reason for arguing that the bankers are disdainful of the laws we create to control them.
There is a distorted opinion in the country of what banks can do. Some people have the idea that banks can create money ad libitum. According to the hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard, they can create money with a fountain-pen. If that were true, I do not see why bankers would have to stay in business very long, why they do not get rich and be done with their vocation altogether.
I do not intend to explore this realm of banking on a plane which almost comes into the region of mystery; I am going to get back to the old country store. You know a great deal can be said for the old country store; in the old days it was a place where a good deal of sound philosophy and many wholesome truths were learned. They are the people who must be convinced about the banking situation and therefore we had better talk in language that they will understand. The old country store was a good institution and performed many duties that usually belong to the bank, and until the days when the chain stores took away their cash business and compelled them to deal only in credit the country stores were found throughout the country almost at every corner.
Suppose a man were helping in the building of a railroad in some country district. The farmer wanted to use his team on the job and he would call up the storekeeper and ask for a double harness. The storekeeper would say, "All right; it is worth $100 and I will send it over. I will charge it on the books." He then instructs his bookkeeper to charge John Jones with $100 for that harness. A few days afterwards the contractor calls up the merchant and says that he would like to get some potatoes. The merchant calls up John Jones and tells him that he would like to have 100 bushels of potatoes for this man who is engaged on the road. The price, let us say, is $1.25 a bushel. And so he credits John Jones [DOT] on his books with $125 for his potatoes. Now there are two transactions. He calls up the contractor and tells him that he is going to deliver 100 bushels of potatoes and asks him if he will give him a cheque. The contractor sends the storekeeper a cheque which he puts in the bank and the bank gives him credit for $125. The contractor in turn wants some money and he calls up his debtor, who sends him a cheque which the contractor takes to the bank and deposits it and is given credit for the money he places there. Now all these transactions have been completed and there is no cash, no Bank of Canada money involved. Who says that is getting something for nothing? Who says that is not a splendid way of doing business?
The bank is a place where you exchange obligations; it is a credit exchange, and when it performs that function and collects a service charge therefor, it seems to me it is carrying on in a way which is beneficial to the business of the country. Take a manufacturer. I want to buy a certain quantity of raw material and I send him an order and get thirty days credit on that raw material. The man I bought it for makes a draft through the bank and I accept it at thirty days. When the draft is due the banker charges that to my account on the debit side and sends a credit along for the manufacturer, and the goods are dispatched. Is there anything wrong about that? There is no money used. A week afterwards I have to pay my men and I send a cheque to the bank and get $1,000 in bank notes. That is where you need real money, for pay envelopes. I go to the bank and they charge that to me. And so the transaction goes on.
Every transaction involves a debtor and a creditor; one brings and another takes. You can read that in any of the books on economics. The hon. member for Vancouver-

Bank Act Amendment

Burrard said! that a bank could buy- a $50 Dominion of Canada bond and all they hadi to do was to make an entry in their books; they did not need to put up any more than $5 as a reserve against it, in other words, 10 per cent. So far so good, but the hon. gentleman did not follow that transaction through. Suppose the government owes my hon. friend $50 and issues him a cheque on that bank and he takes it to the bank. He can demand for that cheque fifty Bank of Canada bills, or he can give it to the banker with instructions to have it placed'to his credit, thus transferring the credit from the bank to himself, or he can take the cheque to another bank and cash it. If he takes the cheque to another bank the first bank must meet the clearing-house the next day and give Bank of Canada bills for the cheque. It will be seen, therefore, that the hon. member went only half way in telling about such a transaction; he did not follow it all the way through. If he followed it through he would find that the bank must meet their obligations or be in peril at the clearing-house when they get there.
As I said before, the bank is the medium for the exchange of the country's business. It is true it creates deposits and credits and there is an enormous amount of business done without money at all, but a distorted idea is conveyed that the banks create money, that in their function as an exchange for the business of the country they create money, which is only credit and confidence. We must not break down credit as an institution for carrying on the business of the country. This five per cent reserve is a reserve against break-down. It is what one might call a degree of safety in the exchange of confidence and credit. Nor must we forget the power of association. The Creator Himself when he made the world had regard for the power of association. To make life it takes two people; one man cannot make life. Two people have to be properly equipped to make life; every living creature is of the same kind, and so is most agricultural production. Money is the economic bloodstream of the nation, and to control the economic bloodstream you need association; because there is power and there is virtue in association. I might do something that was criminal if I did it alone, but if I did it in association with others, and if it were done in a manner agreed upon, that would be all right. I say, therefore, that we had better be careful above a government-monopolized bank working all by itself instead of having a bank working in association with the people of Canada for the purpose of carrying on the business and commerce of the country.

My hon. friends say that there should be a 100 per cent reserve. What would you think of the country storekeeper who, when he charged the harness on the books, told his bookkeeper instead to go and get $100 in cash and put it in the safe so that he might have a reserve against the harness, or who, when he sold the potatoes, ordered his bookkeeper to go and get $125 in cash and put it in the safe so that he might have a 100 per cent reserve in that transaction? To hear our friends talk, to hear what some people said before the banking committee, one would think that banking was the only function in this country. There is a feeling that if you could fool with money, and have an easy time with it, you would be happy and the business of the country would be all right. Banking is only the handmaiden of business in this country; it is only the instrument that business uses for its convenience. As a rule, any troubles from which the country suffers do not come from banking; industry and business support the country. Banking in itself, in my opinion, will have very little to do with the prosperity or advancement of the nation.
Then the hon. member for Parry. Sound, with considerable heat and! fervour, almost in the style of a stump speech at election time, referred to these inner reserves. He pretty well rang the changes in regard to them, and his words could create a good deal of alarm in this country in this connection. He calls them secret reserves.

They must disclose their reserves to their auditors, and to the auditor appointed by the shareholders. They must satisfy Mr. Elliott, the commissioner of taxation. Then, by virtue of an amendment adopted this year they must also disclose their reserves to the Minister of National Revenue. These inner reserves are something like the stand-pipe that you see at the point where the water-main comes into a town, to control the flow so that it will be even, regardless of any rise or fall in the level. These controls all have their purpose; every machine must have some control. In any machine there is motive power and there is a means of control. Your automobile has an engine and a steering-wheel, but it also has a brake and other methods of control. All these things are for good and intelligent

control. The banks are in competition. Do you think one bank should know what the other has in its inner reserve?

I will permit any intelligent question, for I believe we should search for the truth; truth will make men free. The hon. gentleman says that he wants only the aggregate. Well, that is the entering wedge. Supposing, for instance, I owed, the bank 850,000. The bank might say to its auditor, "This man Kinley owes us 850,000. We do not think we will ever get it, so that we had better set up a reserve against it," to which
100-385^
the auditor would reply, "Yes, I think you should." Well, if you are going to pursue this thing t,o the bitter end you have to get down to names. The directors have a meeting; they tell the shareholders the news. It comes back to my home town that I owe the bank 850,000 and they do not think they are going to get it. In the first place that will destroy my credit. In the second place, if I find that they do not expect to get their money, I may never pay them. So that you see it is a bad thing in more than one way.
What is our interest in these inner reserves, anyway; what is the public interest in them? We can have only one possible interest; that is in connection with taxation. We are told that ordinary businesses have inner reserves, and I know they have reserves of inventories. I know most industries to-day will make a conservative inventory because of uncertainty as to the future. You may say that is evading taxation, but is it? These inventories are bound to get into the money stream of the business in a short time, and if you make them too large this year you lose out next year. The thing will balance in a few years because eventually it gets into the money stream .of your business, and it will not do you any good unless you>
go into a field of lower taxation in the immediate future. I do not have to disclose the reserves of my business to this parliament. First I have to satisfy my own auditor, who is very careful not to do anything he should not do, because his reputation depends upon how well he carries out his duties and how well he obeys the law. Then I must satisfy the income tax officials who go over my books, and who are experts. Finally I must satisfy the minister. An ordinary business does not have to disclose its inner reserves, and it is a feature of our income tax laws that you may not divulge what people pay in income tax. It is not fair to do so in a competitive system.
Therefore I say that as regards these inner reserves of the banks having any effect on the taxation of this country, that is a matter conjured up for the purpose of frightening somebody, and I do not think those who want to be fair about the matter will consider it for a moment. Why, the shareholders' auditor, one of the most eminent members of his profession in the city of Toronto, was most positive in stating that the interests of the shareholders and of business and industry generally were protected by keeping these reserves secret except from those who should know. The Minister of Finance is a public servant who is expected
Bank Act Amendment

to protect the people of this country, and it seems to me sufficient if he and his officials have this information.
On the other hand we have in this country one branch of business which has large reserves and which does not pay any taxes. I recall that we have in western Canada large organizations doing business running into millions of dollars. At first they were mutual companies that were allowed to divide their profits among their shareholders and those who were cooperating. Then they decided that they should have reserves, and obtained that privilege under the law. They went ahead and built up reserves amounting to millions, and they are exempt from taxation while the banks pay millions of dollars of taxes to the government of Canada. Then take the Canadian National Railways, since we talk so' much about government ownership. What taxes did the Canadian National ever pay to the government? Do you not think the Canadian National is a better railway because we also have the Canadian Pacific? Our ventures into public ownership in this country have been a sorry story of deficits. It took a war to bring the Canadian National out of the red, and we are not very sure of what may happen when the war is over. It seems to me that when we get into the realm of ' government ownership we get into the realm of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. They want to nationalize the banks of Canada, and make them government-owned banks, government monopolies. I think a government monopoly is about the worst kind of monopoly one can have.
We are told that monopolies in this country are terrible. I am not so much afraid of monopolies. They are defenceless when parliament wishes to deal with them. It did not take the Minister of Munitions and Supply long to tell the Canadian Pacific what they were to do with their air lines. He told them- that the air lines were to be preserved for the young men coming back.
What I am afraid of is that we might lose our free parliament. As long as we have a free parliament to deal with monopolies, we can deal with them; but if we have a government that owns monopolies, and a government that runs monopolies for the service of the country, we lose our free parliament, and we have a monopoly which is supported by the government. The people would get very little from it.
Something has been said about debt-free money. Some persons would abolish interest. The wages of money might be high in this country, but in my opinion the wages of

money are fair. Let us suppose I have a house. I want to rent that .house, and you come along and give me $50 a month for the rent of it. That would be a fair rental. However, after a couple of months you come to me and say, "Look here, I think I can build a house. I think I could live cheaper and save some money if I built a house." I say, "All right, I will lend you the money to build the house." You get the money and you build the house. You live in the house and you save money-and that, of course, is a splendid thing to do. You take some responsibility when you do that. You have paid the rent for my other house, but now you do not want to pay me interest on my money that I gave you to build the house in which you are living. Somebody, possibly, made you believe in debi>free money.
This matter of debt-free money is only a matter of dilution. A farmer may bring 100 quarts of milk to town. When he milks his cows, one day he gets only seventy-five quarts, and he says, "Well, we will put it under the pump, fill it up, and we will have 100 quarts." But that is not more milk, and he cannot be paid for 100 quarts. If they catch him they will put him in gaol. That is w'hat is meant, and I am getting it down to the place where people can understand it. We have had this thing up in the air so long that we had better get it down to the place where people can understand this kind of talk.
You talk about inflation! My dear friend in the corner, the hon. member for Lethbridge, tells us about debt-free money. I have some of his debt-free money, right here-or I had some. I do not think I can spend it. This was debt-free money that was issued-prosperity certificates.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon and this evening we have heard a great deal about two sections which have been held over, namely sections 59 and 75, in connection with this renewal of the Bank Act. There were about forty-five sessions of the banking and commerce committee. The pros and cons of arguments, back and forth, have been set out by different members of that committee, by representatives of the banks, by the retail merchants' association and by other organizations which appeared before the banking and commerce committee.
This afternoon and this evening we have heard two speeches by two eminent Canadian lawyers. I want at this juncture to say a word about the eloquence of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and to refer to several statements by the hon. member for Parry Sound as being simply unadulterated shadowboxing. I can vouch that the hon. member for Parry Sound could with his eloquence and his experience argue the case for the renewal of these bank charters with just as much merit as he has the ideas which he has accepted and which in my opinion are absolutely unsound.
I should like to deal with this matter from two or three matter of fact points of view, but I will adhere as strictly as possible to the two sections under discussion. Before proceeding, may I say that this matter should be analysed in a cool, businesslike way without using words like "dark secrets" and "hush, hush" or applying to the business of banking inferences that are absolutely unfounded and without reason.
In the first place the banking business of this country is a highly scientific business. It is no different from many other businesses because all the corporations in this country are the children of government. Companies operate under charters issued either by the provinces or by the dominion. They are permitted to conduct certain types of business, not only for ten years but perpetually as long as they comply with the taxing laws of the country and the articles of their incorporation. I submit that no business is subjected to such close scrutiny year in and year out, particularly every ten years, as the business of commercial banking. The business of banking is scrutinized not only by government officials and by the inspector general; it is subjected to the closest scrutiny by the Minister of Finance and his officials.
Bank Act Arhendment

The question of inner reserves has been mentioned; and I submit that an endeavour has been made to create a bogey, to arouse suspicion in the minds of the Canadian people that there is something hidden, something uncanny, something the people of this country should know in connection with hidden reserves. In analyzing this matter of the renewal of these bank charters we must consider whether the banking business of Canada is being properly conducted or whether it is not; whether the banking business of Canada is making undue profits or whether it is not; whether the banking business of Canada is serving the purpose that commercial banks should serve in the interests of the people of this country, both depositors and borrowers, or whether it is not. I submit that the banking system of this country is being conducted in a highly efficient manner, consistent with the best banking experience and brains not only in Canada, but in the great republic to the south, or even, as some hon. members have said, in the Scotch banking system.
Let me deal for a minute or two with the matter of incorporation and also with the question of whether the chartered banks are making excess profits. As was set out in the evidence submitted to the banking and commerce committee, the profits of the Canadian banks average only 6-2 per cent. Not only do they not compare favourably with many other financial, industrial and commercial enterprises, but they represent an extremely modest profit. It happened to be my good fortune to sit in the banking and commerce committee of 1934 when the bank charters were renewed, and I have endeavoured as much as possible to absorb the discussions that took place in the many meetings of the committee during the last three months.
Let us look for a minute at the position of Canada's chartered banks. The word "monopoly" has been used time and time again in the committee and in this house. It is said that we are being asked to renew the charters of what has been termed a monopoly. I submit that the position of the Canadian chartered banks is not an enviable one in comparison with that of Other industries. I have in my hand the statement of Lake Shore mines. With a capital of $2,000,000, this company showed a profit of 134-8 per cent in 1936. They do not have to have their charter renewed every ten years or to make reports to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue and the inspector general. Not only is this corporation a child of the government, but under its incorporation it can develop the natural resources of Canada. Therefore let

us not call the banks a monopoly. Let us not point to the banks as making immeasurable profits. If we are going to discuss the profit motive, let us take the picture as a whole and stop pointing just at the Canadian chartered banks.
I wish to say a few words in connection with the hidden reserves of the banks. It was in reference to the hidden reserves that the hon. members who preceded me used the language I quoted a moment ago. As I say, that language has been used not only in this house but repeatedly in the banking and commerce committee. It has been broadcast throughout the length and breadth of Canada that there is something sinister, something we should be suspicious about in connection with these hidden reserves. There is nothing mysterious about the hidden reserves.
It is not a question of hidden reserves; it is a question of the method of accounting that is used not only in the banking business but in industrial and commercial businesses throughout Canada. We had as a witness before the banking and commerce committee Mr. Clarkson, one of the leading accountants in Canada. His evidence corroborated what I say, that this -method of accounting is quite common. I am going to read from one bank statement and compare it with the statements of some commercial companies. The banks carry on exactly as do the commercial companies. They take in their inventories which are composed of loans, portfolios, assets and the like, with reserves to protect themselves against loss in any one year. That is all they do. There is nothing secret about it. There is nothing funny about it. It is a system followed by every company in the Dominion of Canada. Let me compare for a moment the financial statement of Canada Steamships Limited and its subsidiary companies with a bank statement. I am reading from the 1943 consolidated balance sheet of the Canada Steamships company, and this is what it says:
Accounts receivable, less reserve.
That is exactly what the banks do. There is nothing funny about it. They simply take in their accounts receivable and their other assets, less reserves.

Let me say this to the hon. member for Parry Sound, that the reserves of the banks are scrutinized by the banks' auditors in exactly the same way as reserves of industrial companies are scrutinized by their auditors. There is no difference. That evidence was given before the banking and commerce committee.
Let me go one step farther. An hon. member said this evening that the shareholders had not the right to know what the hidden reserves of the bank are, but evidence was given before the committee that upon request the shareholder had the right to ascertain through the directors or the auditors what the reserve of the bank was at a given time. It is also provided in the act that the banks are required once a year to submit to the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Finance and, I believe, to the deputy minister of finance, or at all events to ' a third person, what amount has been set aside as hidden reserves.

That is what I thought. As has been stated, these reserves are to protect the banks against losses on loans and declining prices and are submitted to the careful scrutiny of the three gentlemen I have mentioned. On that point, Mr. Chairman, have we in this country
reached the stage where the people of Canada cannot trust the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue, a deputy minister, and probably the governor of the Bank of Canada, no matter what government happens to be in power?	If we have,
certainly there must be a weakness in our democratic system somewhere. So far as I am concerned, as a customer of the banks I am perfectly happy to have the reserves of the banks scrutinized in that way.
Reference has been made to the cash reserves of the banks and it has been proposed that 100 per cent cash reserves be held by the banks. I do not think the hon. member for Parry Sound is really serious in what he suggested because he knows perfectly well, for it has been repeatedly stated, what an impossible situation it would toe if the banks had to carry 100 per cent Bank of Canada cash against their deposits. Let us analyse for a few moments what the banks really are.
To me and, I believe, to most hon. members there is nothing funny about this banking business. The banks are simply the bookkeepers of the nation. They are the retailers of credit. There is nothing funny about money. I can take this blank cheque that I have on my desk, fill it out for five or ten dollars, write my signature and hand it to the Postmaster General and he will give me a ten dollar Bank of Canada bill for it. Why? Because he is satisfied that behind that cheque I have in the bank of Montreal a credit, created through selling lumber, apples or something else and depositing the proceeds in the bank. The banks are a repository of the stored-up energy and production of the people of Canada. That is another reason why confidence in our banks should not be jeopardized by anything that is said here by any hon. member. Previous speakers, notably the Minister of Finance, have pointed out all the ramifications that would be involved in insisting upon the banks carrying 100 per cent cash reserves. As the minister said, it would be an impossible situation.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard stated that the government of Canada had no control over the chartered banks. I remember well the submissions that were made to the banking and commerce committee in 1934; I am quite willing to give credit to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard who, along with many others of us at that time, advocated the establishment of a national bank, and in consequence the Bank of Canada was set up. The banking system in no other country in the world has made as much progress, so far as government control is concerned, as has the Canadian banking system
Bank Act Amendment

since 1934 and on through the years to 1937, when we took over the whole stock of the Bank of Canada. I submit that under the set-up of the Bank of Canada the government of Canada has ample control, practically total control, over the flow of money and credit in the Dominion of Canada, Anyone who has studied the financial system knows perfectly well that the Bank of Canada controls the flow of money and credit throughout this dominion.
I listened attentively to the statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and the hon. member for Parry Sound. But it is a bad thing to put people to doing things to which they are not accustomed. With all due respect to my hon. friends, I must say that they are first-class lawyers who can argue on either side of a case with equal dexterity and facility. There is no question in my mind as to that. I prefer to take the opinion of gentlemen who have spent their lives in the banking business of this country- managers of banks, the Minister of Finance, the governor of the Bank of Canada, the deputy minister of finance, the gentlemen who make it their lifelong business to handle the banking requirements of the people, who understand not only those requirements as respects our banking system but also the ramifications of the foreign connections of the ' banking of the dominion. It is a bad thing at this time to create any suspicion in the minds of the people of our banking system. It is also unjustifiable. We have the most flexible banking system in the world, one which stood up during the years of depression; a system which, unlike the banks of the United States, did not go by the wayside. Our banking system is flexible in the set-up of its branches across the country. The branch banks not only serve the people in the communities in which they are established, but are repositories of the savings of the people of those communities, and can transfer credits to different parts of Canada where those credits are required. Our banking system provides the flexibility required by a country such as ours. It can serve the fisherman on the east coast, the grain grower of the prairie provinces, the lumberman of British Columbia, because the collection and flow of funds are made possible through the branch bank set-up. I repeat that it is a bad thing to try to shake confidence in this system, because I do not believe any of the allied nations possess banking systems which have been as successful as our own in handling the demands of the present war.
At this time I wish not only to make reference to the splendid way in which the chartered banks are handling the demands 
of industry, agriculture and the services of the dominion, but to pay tribute to the foresight, the tenacity, the judgment, and the never-ceasing application of thought and untiring effort which the present Minister of Finance has given, not only to the banking system through the Bank of Canada, but to the whole financial set-up of this country in the prosecution of the war. As somebody said the other day, and as is acknowledged beyond the dominion, the pattern of finance, the success in controlling inflation, the application of our price ceiling, the application of wage and salary controls, have not only been a matter of pride in Canada but recognized in the United States and Great Britain as models of efficiency. I do not believe any other banking system in the world has served, under the direction of the officials I have mentioned, the purposes of the prosecution of this war as effectively as that of the Canadian banks.
After all that has been said in connection with this bill, not only in this chamber this afternoon and evening, but in the long sessions of the banking committee, I do not think it is necessary for me to go into further details in connection with our banking system, except to say that unless somebody can submit evidence such as, I claim, has not so far been presented, there is no reason why these bank charters should not be renewed for the next ten years. Personally, as a member of this house, I would consider it extremely disastrous should anything occur to hold up the renewal of the charters of these banks for any less period than the banks have been granted in the past. Do not forget that we shall be shortly entering the great post-war period. ' The last thing we want is any uncertainty in connection with our financial set-up. The last thing we want to do is to inject into the management of our financial system anything except experience and capable management, under the assurance that there will be no interruption with the operations of the banks for the next ten years.
As I said a minute ago, there are ample safeguards. There is no question of the scrutiny of the banks, no question of their solidity, no question as to their ability, in all of the ramifications of the country's business, to handle it efficiently. I submit that neither in this committee nor in the banking and commerce committee has any reason been advanced why these charters should not be renewed. All along the greatest emphasis and stress have been applied to the matter of these hidden reserves. Some of my hon. friends have dW'elt on these things. The Min-

Bank Act Amendment
ister of Finance this afternoon refuted the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vanco'uver-Burrard in the banking and commerce committee. The hon. member for Parry Sound followed with this hidden reserve stuff. I say not only to you, Mr. Chairman, but to the hon. member himself, let us get away from this talk of hidden reserves. Let us acknowledge what it is. Let us accept the statements we have received andi admit that there is nothing sinister about the thing.

That is not the word to use. As my hon. friend knows, these statements are submitted every year to the Minister of Finance, to the banks' auditors and to the inspector general of banks, and they decide, after Biey have checked the inventories and the portfolios of the banks, whether or not, they have taken too much depreciation on their stock in trade.
As regards the two banks referred to by the hon. member for Parry Sound, when the investments in the portfolios, when the lending accounts were checked by the competent auditors and submitted to the Minister of Finance, he cjjid not gum-shoe; he did not catch them. He scrutinized the accounts as any business man would scrutinize a statement, as I would scrutinize a statement submitted by my own bookkeeper. Anyone would say to a business man, "You have too high an inventory reserve of merchandise," or "your inventory is not high enough, and you must go and change it for this reason of that." And the reasons are given. It is not a matter of catching anybody. As I say, that is not the word to use in business. You might use that word in a police court, but this is not a police court; this is a matter of analysing the business statements of financial institutions doing business in the interests of the people of Canada, acting as their trustees, the repositories of their savings, institutions trusted by the people of this dominion. No one was caught. The Minister of Finance decided, on the advice, I suppose, of his deputy minister or of the governor of the Bank of Canada, or probably of the Minister of National Revenue, that these inventories were taken at too low a figure. The market had moved up over a period, or some loans may have been paid over that period. And so they said to the banks-not with a -38 calibre revolver in each hand, but as businessmen dealing with other businessmen: Call in your auditors and let us discuss the matter; in our opinion these inventories are too low; your reserve for depreciation or for bad debts is too high, perhaps, or whatever it might be, and we suggest to you as businessmen that they should be reduced. And they were reduced. There is nothing funny about that. It is not all a dark mystery. It is all clear.

I will tell you what took place. I submit to the hon. member for Parry Sound that the minister explained that through the stress and burden of victory loans in connection with war finance and the handling of the domestic business of Canada he was two or three months behind in seizing an opportunity to
Bank Act Amendment

scrutinize these statements. Naturally, with the stress of work and lack of time, he was three months, or two months, or whatever it was, behind. It was not because of anything that was said in the banking and commerce committee, because the statements would have been checked, as there is an obligation under the act to check them every year. It was because of overwork on the part of the Minister of Finance. I say to my hon. friends in this house: Why try to permeate and saturate this whole question and to cover it with suspicion. This is not a matter of porchclimbing; it is a matter of discussing an important function, obligation and responsibility of certain institutions, and it is the duty of the intelligent representatives of the people of Canada to come to a judgment in this matter.
There were over forty sittings of the banking and commerce committee where the whole question was considered, and I suggest that we should decide now whether the charters should be renewed or not. If we have not discussed the matter sufficiently to be in a position to reach a conclusion, it is for one of two reasons; either lack of mentality to absorb on the part of certain hon. gentlemen, or straight obstruction on the part of some other hon. gentlemen. It can be for only one of those two reasons, because you cannot carry this thing on forever. Every question has been asked that could be asked; every witness has been called who was requested; the zenith of courtesy has -been extended to members of the committee; there has not been a general manager of one bank who objected to any question; there has not been a question directed at the deputy minister or the minister himself to which they have refused to reply. They were as open-minded as they could be, and I suggest that no effort should be made to tar this queston, to tar the whole subject with suspicion and to try to spread suspicion across the dominion. We as businessmen and as members of parliament can unquestionably make our decision., and I for one have come to my decision, namely, to vote for the renewal of these bank charters for another ten years. In .my opinion that is what should1 be done in the interests of the banking institutions, in the interest of the depositors and in the interests of the borrowers and of the people of Canada who are receiving from the chartered banks the best banking service given to any population in any country in the world.
Let me say in that connection that, notwithstanding what has been, said in this committee and in the banking and commerce 
committee, the dominion to-day is paying only a service charge on over one billion dollars which it is receiving through the Bank of Canada and1 the Canadian chartered banks. I have not tried to remember the exact figure, but the service charge is 1-2 or 1-3 per cent. Surely the labourer is worthy of his hire. The banks are retailers of credit. They have a function to perform; they have thousands of employees across the dominion, and the government as borrower has to pay a service charge for the service it receives. There is no mystery about that. You cannot do funny tricks with money. You cannot make money out of paper unless you have something behind the paper. No one has ever done that successfully and no one ever will.
I repeat, in conclusion, that there is every reason why hon. members should renew these charters. Let us get away from the uncertain position in. which the banks have found themselves for the last three or four months. Let us renew these charters so that the banks can get on with their business and so that the people of Canada may enjoy full confidence in them, in a banking system which has rendered excellent service and over which there is, in my opinion, ample control through the Bank of Canada.

"Look at the terrific profits
of that mine; 600 per cent in one year." I believe the bank of Nova Scotia paid sixteen per cent during a certain number of years, but we must remember that while the stock of the bank of Nova Scotia had a par value of $100, it had been selling for more than $200 for some years. To compare the sixteen per cent profit paid by the bank of Nova Scotia with the two or three hundred per cent paid by the Lake Shore mine is unfair, and I do not think is a proper comparison to make as to the payment of profits.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a
popular thing with the masses to attack the banks. We are approaching a general election. I do not think any hon. member will make any speeches in defence of our banking practices and banking system unless he is actuated by the most sincere motives, and feels compelled to do so.
As we look at the picture, the allied nations are fighting a war of survival, fighting the costliest of all wars. It is no exaggeration to say that during the first three years of this war we were fighting with our backs to the wall. The best financial brains in Great Britain, the United States and Canada have been directing this war from a monetary point of view, and I think I am safe in saying that these men have devised what they believe to be the best method of financing it. Recently in the banking and commerce committee Canada's financing of the war effort has been under what might be called a two-pronged attack. I will deal with the lesser attack first. That was in regard to inner reserves. Under these circumstances, I think at least we should be careful of our facts. As I listened to the hon. member for Parry Sound talking about hidden reserves this evening I was positively shocked to hear him state that the banks might have tucked away in their vaults $300,000,000 of Bank of Canada cash as these hidden reserves, as he calls them. I well remember the hon. member in the banking and commerce committee referring to hidden reserves as loot, and in another place he said that sums of money were tucked away.
I am going to make a statement which I think will shock the hon. member for Parry Sound, but I know it is positively true. I say that not a bank in this country has not disclosed in its financial statement, for everyone to read, eveiy security that it holds, every dollar of its cash, and the value of all its bank property. I picked out at random from my banking and commerce folder the statement of the bank of Montreal, on which I should like to make some comments. The assets of any Canadian chartered bank in the main are
Bank Act Amendment

these. First there is the bank property, their real estate, furniture, office fittings and the like. Next comes their Bank of Canada cash, in the form of deposits with the Bank of Canada or aotual cash. Their third asset is securities.

speechtext:
What has the bank of
Montreal in its hidden reserves, and of what do they consist?

speechtext:
I shall be glad to follow
through, but I have thought this thing over, and I believe we should approach this matter in a studious, careful, quiet and sane manner, that we should not get in any passion about it.

speechtext:
Not at all, but that is a

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext: Mr. Tompkins, the inspector, says that there is.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago, when I was interrupted, I had come to the third form of assets which a bank holds, namely securities and bonds, Dominion of Canada bonds. The fourth form of security is promissory notes, as well as any collateral, which they hold with them, for the repayment of loans which they have made to customers.
Let hon. members look at any bank statement-and I say this without fear of contradiction, although I know it will be a shock to the hon. member for Parry Sound. I know the hon. member did not intend to mislead the committee, but I say that he did mislead the committee when he said that any bank had a dollar's worth of security or a dollar's worth of cash in any of its vaults in the form of inner reserves.
I come now to the fourth item of bank assets. The fourth item is securities in the

form of promissory notes which a bank holds, in order to secure repayment of loans which it makes. Now we come to the place where inner reserves arise. In this instance I am reading from the financial statement for 1943 of the bank of Montreal, and I find this item: "Current loans and discounts, less estimated loss provided for"-and then the item extended is 8215,000,000 odd.
That statement simply means this, that the bank of Montreal holds promissory notes for loans which it has made to customers in excess of 8215,000,000. But it just shows $215,000,000 in the statement, because bankers know they are in a hazardous business. Every year they take losses. They know they may not be able to collect the par value of the notes which they hold for loans they have made; therefore they must make a compensatory adjustment, and if they are to have a true financial report they must make a compensatory adjustment to bring down the total par value of loans to the actual amount which they will finally recover. That is the inner reserve - item; it is simply a bookkeeping item. There is not a dollar of security behind it. There is not a dollar of cash there. There is no hidden loot.
Why, to hear some hon. members talk one would think that the banks of this country have hidden away in some corner of their vaults, piles of stocks, currency and securities for hidden or inner reserves. Nothing of the kind happens. They do not hold a dollar of cash, and they do not hold a dollar's worth of securities under this item of hidden reserves. It is simply a bookkeeping entry, simply a writing down of the amount of their loans from par value to the amount which the experience in banking tells them they will 'finally collect. You can pick up any bank statement and you will find that item, or a ' similar one-"less estimated loss provided for."
When I approached this problem in the committee on banking and commerce and I found that the banks were not required to report to the Minister of National Revenue, the taxing minister, the amount set aside as an item to protect them against loss they would eventually have in the collection of their loans, I did not think that was proper. I thought banks should be placed in exactly the same position as all other industries in this country. I thought banks should have to report to the Minister of National Revenue the amount they had set aside in the reduction of the par value of their loans, in order to reach the true value of their loans. I moved an amendment, but when the minister indicated

Bank Act Amendment
that he was bringing in an amendment to provide for what I had in mind, I of course withdrew my motion.
We have to-day in the Bank Act the fullest possible protection in that regard. The Minister of Finance has no option. The act says that the Minister of Finance shall report the amount of the inner reserves to the taxing minister, so that the taxing minister will at all times have full information.
With that amendment in the Bank Act the banks of this country, so far as inner reserves are concerned, are in exactly the same position as every other industry. One can pick up tne financial reports of canning companies, steel companies or other industries in Canada, and he will find that they all make a similar compensatory deduction for anticipated loss, and that they do not disclose the amount to the general public.

We cannot both be right, but I say positively that every bank in this country reports in its financial statement every

dollar of cash, every dollar of Bank of Canada deposits and every dollar of securities in the possession of the bank, and that the so-called hidden reserves item is simply a bookkeeping entry.

speechtext: What would the bookkeeping entry represent?

speechtext:
I am sorry if I have not made that clear. The bank may show a net value of loans of $215,000,000. They have reduced that by the amount of their estimated losses with respect to the loans. Those loans are secured by promissory notes, but actually the amount would be in excess of $215,000,000. They set up a reserve or a cushion between the par value of their loans and the amount which they show as the actual value of the loans. It is simply and purely a bookkeeping entry.
The major part of the attack in the banking and commerce committee was that we were all wrong in the way in which we are financing this war, that we have created an unbearable load of debt, that we are on the way over Niagara falls into the whirlpool of bankruptcy. The complaint has been not only with respect to the interest of the debt but equally with respect to the capital. In the light of present-day conditions when hon. members make a statement of that kind they know there are many gullible people who think the wealthy are holding out on them and all that sort of thing; they know there are many gullible people in Canada who will believe these statements even though they are wholly untrue. I think the least these hon. gentlemen can do when they make statements of that kind is to give us their proposal.
Time after time in the banking and commerce committee I asked the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard to tell us, please, what his proposal was. Was his proposal that for every dollar of the cost of the war we could issue Bank of Canada cash, debt-free money as he calls it? Was his proposal that we can finance this costliest of wars without any cost? I think he should tell us. Is it his proposal that a limited amount of Bank of Canada cash in addition to the amount that has been printed should be and can be issued? If it is a limited amount, I think he should tell us how much.
Our Minister of Finance demonstrated clearly this afternoon that while from a physical point of view we could issue as much Bank of Canada cash as we have paper and printing ink, it would not be debt free; it would not be costless; it would cost just as much in the long run to finance in that way as in any other way. I do not intend to go into that phase of the matter at all because it has been ably answered already, but there is one

point which has not been covered and to which I should like to call attention. If we started the printing presses of this country to print Dominion of Canada notes, not for the purpose that they were intended to be printed but to pay our debts, I think the people of Canada would have something to say, I think the people of Canada would have a reaction as to the value they would place on. those notes.
Keeping in mind the fact that there is not a dollar of gold behind our Bank of Canada notes; keeping in mind the fact that the value of those notes can be retained only as long as the public retains confidence in them, I suggest to the hon. members for Vancouver-Burrard and Parry Sound that the issue of those Bank of Canada notes is in the nature of a trust. The Dominion of Canada through its parliament has entrusted the Bank of Canada with the creation of a medium of exchange.	The power	to	issue	Bank	ofCanada cash was not given in order that the Dominion of Canada could pay its debts with that cash. The reason why the Bank of Canada is	empowered	to	issue	Bank	of
Canada notes is to supply to the people of this country a medium of exchange so that they will not have to carry on their trade by barter and the exchange of goods.
I suggest that just the minute any government departed from that fundamental principle and started to issue Bank of Canada cash for the purpose of paying government debts instead of for the purpose of supplying the people of this country and the business life nf this country with sound money as a medium of exchange, just as soon as that happened the people of this country would have something to say as to whether they would put any value on that kind of money.

speechtext: Would the hon. member tell us what sound money is?

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS

It is a medium of exchange to permit the farmer who has a beef cattle to sell, to obtain a medium of exchange, which can be used anywhere in Canada instead of having to drive in the beast ^o the grocery store and obtaining credit there for it or bringing back goods to the value of the beast.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
The hon. member is on the all-important question right there.

So long as the Bank of Canada confines the issue of Bank of Canada cash to the amount necessary for the carrying on of the business life of this country, then you have sound money.
Mr. BLACIvMORE: How can you tell how much is necessary?

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext: This afternoon the Minister of Finance referred to the fact that to-day we are carrying a much heavier load of debt with a very much greater amount of interest. The fact is that in 1920 we were financing dominion government bonds, issued to pay 5} per cent tax free. The rate of interest at that time ranged from 5i per cent to not lower than 2J per cent. Obviously the endeavour to balance the budget that took place between 1920 and 1930 resulted in the collapse of the whole economic structure of the Dominion of Canada as elsewhere. When that collapse came, refunding took place all the way down the line until the general interest rate was reduced from 5i per cent to 3 per cent, and in some instances the rate was lowered to three-quarters of one per cent.

The minister overlooks the fact that we have now reduced our interest rate in some instances to a level where it is just about equal to the operating costs of servicing money. But do not forget this. If we had used our own money we would not have incurred any debt.
Of course the assumption is that there is no. way by which a government can finance public enterprises unless it borrows its own credit, its own money. Let me give the committee one example of its fallacy which is based on indisputable facts. We were always told in Canada that this was a young country, that we had not the accumulations of savings which were required for our capital investments, that we therefore had to go into the realm of international finance, to London, Paris or Berlin.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext: Or New York.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Or any place where large sums of money had accumulated over the centuries from large numbers of people. What happened when this war came? Did we go to London to borrow capital to build up the war organization? No, we did not, and we certainly did not go to Berlin or Paris, and we did not go to New York. The first thing we did was to lend England $700 million. Then we assumed the responsibility of our own

Bank Act Amendment
army, our own navy, our own air force, and a new munitions industrial organization. How did we finance that? Did we go.to London? Not at all. Instead of London being the rich uncle as we had assumed in the past, London was the poor relative. Not only did we lend $700 million, but we gave $1,000 million of goods and services. How did we finance that, because that required an enormous capital investment in plant and equipment and organization? Then the next year, because some people objected to a gift to Britain, we made it a billion dollar gift of mutual aid for the various nations.
Will anyone say again that, in the light of our experience in financing our enormous war programme between 1939 and 1944, we shall ever have to go abroad again to raise money to build railways or municipal buildings or provincial highways or harbour facilities? We have proven that Canada, as far as financing the development of her own resources w'ith her own intelligence and her own labour is concerned, is independent of the world.

I want to put on the record before the house adjourns an amendment which I propose to section 59. The amendment reads as follows:
That section 59 be amended by adding thereto a new subsection, to read as follow-s:
"The bank shall not hereafter create or issue bank deposit credit in place of or as a substitute for the lawful currency and coinage of the Dominion of Canada unless the amount so to be created or issued has been authorized by a board consisting of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, and the governor of the Bank of Canada.
Bank Act Amendment

That does not mean that every time the banks create a new loan they will have to get that authorization. They can budget for three months or six months or a year. They can be stopped from doing what they did in the stock boom period of 1929. I examined the manager of the bank of Montreal on what happened in that particular period. The banks were behind the stock boom and the banks were definitely responsible for the collapse that came in 1929. In Canada it required several hundred million dollars of inflation of bank deposits to support that boom, and that boom was supported by the creation and issue of several hundred million dollars of bank deposit money. Who is to know what the law is with respect to this section? The explanatory note says: "This implements in part budget resolution No. 8." That is not the effect of it in my opinion. Budget resolution No. 8 regarding dependency allowance and tax credits is most unfair, unjust and inequitable and it bears most hardly on the small man, and on those with a fixed income. They are taxed all along the line. Wait until you see the income tax next year with all these millions of relief resolutions and social security provisions which are being put over this parliament in the dying hours of the session. Nobody in this committee understands what section 23 means. I doubt whether the financial critic
Income War Tax

of the opposition knows what it means. I doubt whether some members have even read this section. I want to protest against the way in which these things are clipped through the committee. I did so the other day in connection with a related bill. So far as the dependents are concerned, the tax credits allowed are not what they should be. Take housekeepers, for instance, referred to in section 23. The Minister of Labour brought down a return the other day, which was never mentioned in the newspapers, indicating the great lack of domestic help in the homes of this country and the great dearth of nurses who are badly needed in our hospitals. That situation is becoming intolerable, and the dependents' meagre deduction allowances are partly to blame for it. It is time we called a halt. We should know what these clauses mean.
The budget speech should be fixed by statute within sixty days after parliament opens. Here is the one hundred and nineteenth day of the session, and these resolutions are brought down. Nobody knows what they are: What is going to be the result? When are we to file income tax for 1944 under the statute, including the schedule about dependency and that kind of thing? The allowance under section 23 for dependents is not large enough, considering what it costs to keep a house today. I urge there should be more liberal allowances all along the line for those who are keeping a household. In the city I come from there are a hundred) thousand people with no houses who have moved into apartments, and it is the main taxpaying city in the main taxpaying province of the country. Some of the provinces pay little or no income taxes. This is a tax which for the most part involves the two industrial provinces. It is absolutely unfair that this kind of taxation should be imposed, applying to some and not to others. There is no attempt at equality of service or sacrifice.
Further, the lawyers cannot tell you what the law is, nor can the doctors or the physicians. Take section 23, rule 5: you have to look at "Rule 5 of section one of paragraph A of the first schedule." Who here this morning has ever seen the schedule; they are amending a schedule you have never seen; and section one of paragraph A of the schedule is amended "by replacing the period at the end) thereof with a semicolon," if you please! We are learning grammar here from the department; a semicolon makes all the difference in the world. Then "the following words are added", and we are told that it follows resolution 8, and on page 18 we find "provision for housekeeper." Such a provision is unfair and unjust
[Mr. Church 1
to those who keep a house. Why should there be any limitation in this connection? Does it not cost one person as much as another to keep a house of the same kind? I agree as to the proviso in the third paragraph, regarding the self-contained domestic establishment, for the reasons given in rule one of the section. But the whole thing, Mr. Chairman, should be simplified. I do not see why it is necessary to have these rules and provisoes and explanations referring to schedules in the statute. It would be more fair and just and more would be obtained in the long run if this government adopted the old income tax method of the municipalities and had the tax imposed on the aggregate net income received by the taxpayer. By setting a percentage of the man's income for tax purposes, be it 10 per cent or 12^ per cent or otherwise, he would know what he had to pay. To-day one does not know anything about it.
Only yesterday we had an election, and there seems to be a demand that income tax shall be restored to its proper place, where it was prior to 1917, namely to the municipalities. If this system of income tax goes on much longer I do not see where the taxpayer is going to be, because he has had to pay almost two and a half years' income taxes in a year. I wish to protest again against this proceeding;-against the method and manner of passing the amendments; the limited allowance made for tax credit for dependents; the construction put on domestic establishment; and, fourth, the system and method of taxation, the rules and regulations which are read into these amendments after we pass the principle of the Income War Tax Act, and all those things. If, as we hope, this bill will pass this morning, I doubt *whether this afternoon any member of parliament will be able to tel! you what the law is. The departmental officials all over Canada will need a volume the size of the revised statutes to tell them what the law is. We are going too far. Section 23 is fittingly numbered, it is a "skidoo" section, that is what it is; it allows some relief and others no relief; it treats one class of domestic householders one way and another class another way. speakeroldname: Mr. D. C. ABBOTT (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I gave a detailed explanation when we were on the resolution stage. But capital employed, as the committee knows, is defined in the act. Additions to capital employed were permitted only in respect of accumulated surplus, if that surplus had been capitalized by the issue of stock dividends. These profits of accumulated earnings left in the business since the end of the standard period-the end of 1939-may be included in "capital employed" up to the end of 1943, or the beginning of 1944. Excess Profits Tax

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am not quarrelling with the basis for the ascertaining of the amount of income. My question has to do with the basis for ascertaining the foreign tax and whether the full amount of tax paid in other countries is allowed as an exemption in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The basis for ascertaining
the tax is that the taxpayer takes credit for all the taxes paid in a foreign country with respect to income on which he is taxed in Canada for income tax or excess profits tax purposes up to. but not exceeding, our rate of tax on the same income. In other words, if the income of a Canadian taxpayer from all sources anywhere in the world is $100,000, of which $50,000 is derived from the United States, he would be taxed in Canada on his gross income of $100,000 from the two countries. He would estimate his tax at the Canadian rates and then he would deduct from that tax when ascertained the income tax paid in the United States with respect to the $50,000 earned there, provided that that tax was at a rate not exceeding the Canadian rate. That is the tax position with respect to the Canadian taxpayer. He would pay that tax whether the income was earned at home or not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I felt from the explanation of the parliamentary assistant that he was assuming that the phrase, "in respect of the income of the taxpayer derived from sources therein" applied to section 6 which is now before us, but my point is that it is not there and I felt it was an oversight.

case may be the amount paid abroad provided that tax rate is not greater than the Canadian rate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

This item deals with the national harbours board, a matter in which I am particularly interested because of the large number of men employed on the water-

Supply-Transport
front at Halifax. On a previous occasion I made a suggestion to the; Prime Minister which he was good enough to say was a helpful one, and later he indicated that the Minister of Transport would consider my suggestion.
f felt that the time was opportune for the Department of Transport, through the national harbours board, to take complete control of the labour situation on the waterfront at Halifax and at other ports which are under that board. I Would respectfully urge that the minister give this matter his earnest consideration. We all know that there is a great amount of money invested in the operations of the national harbours board. In 1943 the board had a revenue of $10,861,081 and an operating income of $5,583,507. I feel that the investment is sufficiently large, particularly when we take into consideration (he assets of the national harbours board amounting to $224,892,400.27 to warrant the closest supervision so far as the labour situation is concerned. Instead of having a large number of concerns looking after labour on the waterfront I believe that greater efficiency of operation would be secured if my suggestion were adopted, and I think it is particularly important at a time like this when Canada is at war and the quick dispatch of our ships both entering and leaving the ports is so necessary.
I could enlarge upon this but I indicated my views on a previous occasion and I shall not take up further time now. I will content myself by urging the minister to give favourable consideration to establishing a policy under which the waterfront workers, such as the longshoremen, the freight handlers, checkers and casual labour, would receive a guaranteed weekly floor wage. The situation in the past for many years has been that large numbers of men will come into Halifax and other ports and take work for short periods, at fairly good rates of pay, but I Think it would be much better for the men themselves and result in greater efficiency in the operation of the ports if the men were guaranteed a weekly wage spread over the entire year. I hope the minister will give that suggestion very serious thought.
I thank the hon. member for Halifax for having brought this matter to my attention. It is a very important question, and I can assure him that it will be given every consideration.

The senior member for
Halifax has raised an important question. The commission was set up by order in council after consultation with the Department of Labour and the unions concerned.

What the hon. member for Cape Breton South is referring to I think is the temporary wartime arrangement which has been made under order in council to take care of the war business in the harbour. Does not that commission handle it?
So far as war work is concerned.

Perhaps I can throw a little light on the question raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I would be the last to want to interfere with any satisfactory arrangement that any labour union has at the port of Halifax. The hon. member is right in part in saying that there is a floor wage. There is a floor wage for what is known as the pool, which consists of approximately six hundred to seven hundred men. My thought was rather that if all the waterfront activities were brought under the national harbours board it would lead to greater efficiency in the port's operations, and the labour unions which the hon. member has in mind would still continue to enjoy their present bargaining rights. They would be dealing with one organization, namely, the national harbours board, instead of with a large number of employers. I feel that my suggestion would be a move in the

direction of greater efficiency in the handling of freight both incoming and outgoing to the port of Halifax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would like to add a word to what my colleague, has said. There is one class of our waterfront employees at Halifax who I think will be entitled to a better deal at the very first moment an opportunity presents itself, and that is the freight handlers, particularly those who are handling wharf freight. Prior to September, 1942, this class was employed by thet Canadian National Railways, but because of considerations arising out of the war it was deemed advisable to have these men employed by a stevedoring company to whom the handling of freight was given by the railways. This situation has been tolerated during wartime, but I submit that, now the end of the war is in sight, different principles must apply. These men should once again become employees of the Canadian National Railways. Many of them were employed by the railways as long as thirty years. They enjoyed certain benefits owing to the relationship to the Canadian National Railways; for example, they were entitled to temporary and yearly passes. While they were not permanent employees they had many of the rights and benefits which permanent employees of the Canadian National Railways enjoy. Some of them lived outside the city. Their passes enabled them to travel to and from work free of charge.
There are one or two other observations I wish to make about national harbours board operations at Halifax. Halifax has been called during the war the world's busiest port. It looks very much as though its activities may continue, if not on the same scale, upon a very large scale, for some years after the war. But because of the activities in Halifax during the past few years there has been no time for national harbours board to take care of ordinary maintenance of harbour works, let alone new construction. I wish to suggest, for the consideration of the minister and officials of the harbours board whom I see in front of him, several matters.
In the first place, there should be a new deep-water pier in place of existing piers three and four at the deep-water terminals. The existing wooden piers are quite old and are now almost a fire hazard. They could be replaced by a large pier, or even, if deemed advisable, by two small ones. That is something which should be taken in hand at the earliest possible moment.
Another matter: at pier 9, in the northern part of the city, an extension was made during the past year. Most of the pier, however, is of timber construction, built almost forty
!Mr. Isnor.]
years ago, and its period of usefulness is now approaching an end. Consideration should be given to the construction of a new and more permanent type pier.
A new transit shed is required at pier 26. It is true that at the moment the open dock at pier 26 is under lease to one of our large corporations, but the time will likely soon come when they can release it and possibly confine all their operations to pier 9, where they are also operating. In that case pier 26 with a new shed could be used as an ordinary pier for the transit of cargo.
We hope that Halifax will become a very important fish centre after the war, and much more important in this respect than it is to-day. It is now the centre of very considerable fishing activities, but it is contemplated that these will increase, and I would suggest for the consideration of the minister and his officials that the cold storage plant be extended. Additional freezer space is required at the plant, and the new fish pier should be constructed in its vicinity.
One other matter which I suggest should be taken into consideration by the minister is the coordination of the fire services in Halifax harbour. Unfortunately a fire occurred on the national harbours property during the past winter, and a considerable delay occurred between the time the fire was first known to exist and when the alarm was sent in. A very full investigation was made by the fire marshal of Nova Scotia, and one of his recommendations was that the fire services of the Halifax-Dartmouth area be coordinated. On several occasions I have asked questions on the floor of the house or through the medium of the order paper with regard to Stevenson field at Winnipeg, because in the view of those of us from that city the time is overdue for an enlargement of that field and particularly for an extension of the runways. A year ago when I pressed this matter under this very item the Minister of Munitions and Supply insisted that the runways at that field, in their present condition, are long enough for the largest planes that might wish to use the field. I quoted from one of the Winnipeg newspapers and made the statement that some of the larger planes that had sought to use the field had found it difficult to do so. I was in a very difficult position because I felt that some of the information that had been given me was in the nature of a military secret and so I was unable to press my point. Instead I had to let the minister's statement stand, that in his view the runways were long enough. Now, with the information that has been released about the purchase by Canada of bases in the north built by the United States government, and also with the information that has been released regarding the number of American planes that have been flown over Canada to the Soviet Union under the terms of lend-lease, perhaps we are in a position to discuss this matter much more freely. What I was told before, when I spoke about the matter a year ago, was that on two or three occasions some very large planes, American Flying Fortresses, had landed on Stevenson field but that the pilots who brought the planes down found that, although they made successful landings, they brought their planes to a stop so close to the end of the runways that they felt they did not wish to continue bringing these planes down' on Stevenson field. That information was given to me by an official in the city of Winnipeg, but knowing myself that it might be in the nature of a military character I did not feel free to continue the argument with the minister last year. I understand that as a result of the experience of these pilots in finding the runways at Stevenson field not long enough for Flying Fortresses an arrangement was made whereby the United . States government constructed a larger airport with larger runways at Edmonton. Consequently some of these larger planes which might have flown via Winnipeg and thus helped to build up the route through that city were flown instead through Edmonton and on fo Churchill and thence to the Soviet Union.
I have no desire to say anything that could be interpreted as critical of the future of Edmonton as an important airport on the world air map of the future I have no doubt

that Edmonton will be a place of great importance in that respect, but I feel that the same is true of Winnipeg. Winnipeg is at the very centre of the Trans-Canada route. We have large facilities there at the present time, but the people of my city feel that we have been given the go-by so far as plans for enlarging that field are concerned. Perhaps I should qualify that by saying that there have been plenty of plans drawn. I have seen them. Plans have been laid on the table of the house in response to motions on the order paper. But that is all that has happened. Nothing further has been done, despite the fact it is desirable to know what is to be done so that the necessary property can be purchased and any railway lines moved, if that should be . necessary.
In reply to my representations on behalf of enlarging Stevenson field and extending its runways under this item, the minister's reply last year was, as I have already said, that the runways at Stevenson field were perfectly long enough for any plane to land there. When the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) was making representations-the other day on behalf of certain airports in Saskatchewan, the minister made a slightly different reply to him. The reply on that occasion was that it was due to shortage of material and man-power. Now that the story of what has gone on in the past few years with respect to flying planes across this country is out in the open I hope that the government may reconsider its position so far as Stevenson field is concerned; that instead of a statement to the effect that nothing is necessary there, we shall have active consideration given to enlarging the field and extending the runways. I hope the fact that if this field is enlarged and the runways

improvements and enlarging of runways. I have no doubt that in the near future it will be necessary to enlarge them again, and possibly to revise the whole set-up and make it a much more modern airport than it is to-day, although I am told it is a very good one now.
