subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OP BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Last night I was pointing out the necessity for this measure of control over the issue of bank deposit credits, as a substitute for Canadian currency. I would draw the attention of hon. members to the inflationary condition which existed between 1926 and 1929, and the deflationary condition between 1929 and 1932, which followed the line of the flow out of bank deposit money, and its withdrawal.
From 1926 to 1929 bank deposits were increased by $335,000,000, and from 1929 to 1932 they were withdrawn to the extent of $338,000,000. It was that amount of money, that amount of inflation of bank deposits, and that deflation of bank deposits that played a preeminent part in the stock boom and collapse.
To-day, under the law as it stands in section 59. the banks have issued $5 billion of bank deposits. They have, as the evidence before the banking and commerce committee shows,, issued that on a ten per cent reserve of cash, holding, as they say, $501,000,000 of Bank of Canada cash on deposit in the Bank of Canada, or in their till. They therefore can now,

Bank Act Amendment

of bank deposits that was required to start the last boom and to precipitate the last depression.
I know that it is easy to say that men are eloquent and that their oratory runs away with their intelligence, but I have never been ashamed of what talents I have. I have tried to use them in whatever public service my friends and neighbours have elected me to. I am not alone in advocating monetary reform. I would like to add to the list a few names of people who have advocated monetary reform, because we must be all crackpots together.
Woodrow Wilson said in 1911:
The great monopoly of this country is the money monopoly. So long as that exists, our old variety and freedom and individual energy of development are out of the question. The growth of the nation and all our activities are in the hands of a few men who. by reason of their own limitations chill, check and destroy a genuine economic freedom.
Senator Elihu Root, recognized as one of the greatest councillors that ever spoke in the United States Senate, predicting what would happen and what did happen in 1933, said when the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 was being passed:
This bill (the Federal Reserve Act) proposes to put in pawn the credit of the United States. We are setting our steps in the pathway that brought Rome to its fall.
Louis D. Brandeis, the distinguished American counsel at the Pujo commission in 1907 and afterwards an associate, justice of the Supreme Court of the United States, said:
We must break the money trust or the money trust will break us.
Following these statements, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, after he was elected in 1933, said:
Nature still offers her bounty, and human efforts have multiplied it. Plenty is at our doorstep but a generqus use of it languishes in the very sight of the supply. Primarily this is because the rulers of the exchange of mankinds goods have failed through their own incompetence. Practices of the unscrupulous money changers stand indicted in the court of public opinion, rejected by the hearts and minds of men.
The money changers have fled from their high seats in the temple of our civilization. We may now restore that temple to the ancient truths.
Lloyd George, describing Roosevelt's fight for monetary reform, said this:
The intrepidity with which he is fighting against the machinations of the established and arrogant priesthood of the golden calf is being watched with a thrill of admiration by those who. all the world over, have been suffering from its thraldom. If lie wins he will have rendered a service to mankind which will exceed that of Lincoln when lie abolished a more limited slavery.
But his task is even more formidable, for the hierarchy he has challenged is powerful and

its janissaries in all lands are'federated in a well-knit, well-drilled and well-equipped brotherhood in arms. They play into each other's hands -they fight each other's battles. If they fail, they will share each other's ruin-if they succeed, they will divide the loot among themselves.
In London and in Paris they are unassailably entrenched. To adopt the Scriptural quotation, "Judas is their law giver. Industry is their wash-pot and over successive ministries have they cast their shoes."

It is Lloyd George's, and
he is talking about President Roosevelt. Listen to what he says:
The President has resolved that this verse shall no longer apply to American governments and American producers.
And we sit here and pass a bill that gives away for ten years the right of this nation to create and issue and use its own money, and we accept in its place a form of money issued by a private monopoly for private gain. I speak a word of warning to this government, because I want you to know that you have no special dispensation here. My own humble opinion is that the situation in Canada is such that we face a more terrible division of opinion than we have ever faced before in our history. Monetary reform is marching in the vanguard of the ambitions of the common people for a better Canada. Do not make any mistake about the votes in Saskatchewan and in Alberta. They are the people's votes and they are economic votes. The people in both these two great provinces have completely repudiated the old political parties.
I read a book in 1925, written not by a monetary reformer, not by a crackpot, but by one of the most astute and distinguished business men in the United States, a great philanthropist and a great success. Edward A. Filene, famous in Boston and throughout the world, published "The Way Out" in 1925 and he has this indictment to offer of the private money system:
It is clear beyond need of explauation that most of the sins for which the modern revolutionist indict our social system are :sins of the financial point of view, not of the administrative. I could bring numerous instances to show how the substitution of the banking for the administrative point of view affects good relations between employer and employee and seriously hinders social progress. As an astute critic of our social system has said:	"An
adequate study of the modern political organ that has grown out of the ancient business of exchanging and storing money must soon be undertaken."
For the fact is that the administration of credit has become one of the greatest forces of

Bank Act Amendment
social control in modern times. Credit is the lifeline of the business system which feeds, clothes and shelters mankind. It is therefore a species of social treason not to regard its administration as a public responsibility and a creative opportunity. The real rulers of modern society are not the men who own the most but the men who exercise most control over enterprise, namely the men who administer the world's money.
I think it is true to say that the slow and, to my mind often sinister, encroachment of the .financial upon the administrative point of view in business and industry has given the mod<ern revolutionist one of his best arguments.
In his May day speech of 1942, Premier Stalin of the Soviet Union had this to say:
The German army is a blind tool in the hands of these gentlemen and is called on to shed its own blood and the blood of other peoples and to cripple itself and other peoples not for the interests of Germany, but for the enrichment of the German bankers and plutocrats. That is what the experience of war tells us.
In reality the German fascists are enemies of European culture, and the German army is an ai-my of medieval obscurantism, called upon to destroy European culture and assert the slave-owing "culture" of the German bankers. This is what the experience of war tells us.
Emil Ludwig, who has just written a magnificent sketch of our own Prime Minister, writing the life of Stalin, makes these observations:
I am irresistibly attracted by the social justice of the world. Though I am convinced that the power of personality is greater than that of numbers and I cannot be taken for a Marxist, the foundation of the Soviet Union appears to me as the greatest event produced by our century till to-day. The Russians are the only people that have broken the reign of money.
Stalin is so outstanding as a colonizer and general that he towers above most of our contemporary leaders-no matter what his end is [DOT]going to be. Probably he will be the only dictator who survives the war. Who fears that Stalin's victory will bring wrorld revolution is not aware of the fact that we are in it already.
We are following in the same steps that brought Germany to disaster. It was the debt load which precipitated the invasion. to extinguish us. It was the debt load and the impossibility of advancing the Russian masses that compelled the Kerensky government to collapse and permitted Lenin to take over. And do not make any mistake about the programme that Kerensky had. He had a programme of social justice, of independence and freedom and of national development infinitely superior to anything which has been presented by the budget of this parliament. But it was too late. Do not make any mistake about what brought Mussolini into power in Italy or caused the revolution in Spain. It was the idea that you could go on financing by issuing debts based on the assumption that
it was. sound business to pay off promises you could not keep by making more promises that you knew you would not be able to meet.
We can, of course, balance our budget. But how are we going to finance our municipalities? How are we going to finance our provincial governments? How are we going to maintain the national income at the level estimated by some to be, to-day, over $10,000 million a year? We must maintain a monetary system that can circulate a medium of exchange created and issued by the government, not by a private monopoly.
I just want to say in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that you will find confirmed beyond any question as to how we are financing the war if you will examine page 6 of the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada. He says:
During 1943, the Canadian deposit liabilities of the chartered banks increased by $748 millions. In addition, total active note circulation (including Bank of Canada notes) rose by $161 millions, making the total expansion in the volume of money, therefore, $909 millions during the year.
Why did we not have $909 million of Bank of Canada cash? We did not need to have any debt. They say, "Oh well, if you did that the banks would have to service it through the exchange system." That is perfectly true. But why should the government pay interest charges and pile up unpayable debts for the purpose of bonusing the banking system? That is what you are doing. You are bonusing the banking system by clamping on the nation hopeless and impossible debts, and that in itself could never be justified. If anybody wants to put his money in one of our chartered banks and have them look after it and have them service it by transferring it under a cheque system, why should not that individual pay for that service? Why should the nation go into bankruptcy or accumulate unpayable debts to allow a person getting a service that is worth something to escape paying for it? If large corporations like departmental stores or general stores and merchants of all kinds want to use the banking system as their exchange headquarters and to facilitate their business, why should not they pay for that service? In Australia, of course, they have changed to 100 per cent cash reserve, and that means that when you have a deposit in a bank in Australia you have money in the bank behind it. But in Canada you have the promise of a banker to pay, and all the money he needs to have to make that promise good is five per cent of your deposits. Of course Australia is paying a service charge, but they cannot accumulate debt when they'issue national currency and pay a service charge on it.

The hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) was generous enough, and indeed generous, when he stated that there were two sides to this matter. I shall try in a lew words-a very few words- to present, shall I say, the other side to that to which we have been listening. I think there is need, Mr. Chairman, for just a little bit of sober thought about the nature of money. What is money? Well, it may be anything in form, but in essence, I suggest, it is a claim on goods. We want money only because of w'hat it will buy.
Now we have several conditions of life. Unfortunately we have learned that there is such a thing as crisis. There is such a thing as war need, and money for war need. And what is that? A need for claims on goods. Our government has not been peculiar in the matter of war finance; it has followed, as I see it, a rather common pattern of financing war, and it has done so in three ways, first of all by the usual method of taxation, which in effect is a conscription of claims upon goods. War needs were insatiable. The government went on to borrow future claims on goods and as I gathered from the Minister of Finance last night in his very able speech, it borrowed in several ways, first directly by way of loans from the people, from individuals and from voluntary associations. And then it borrowed from institutions such as the banks -and the banks were only one of several institutions. It borrowed from them claims on goods, or moneys, if you like, that had been deposited with them as trustees.
But the government went a step further, and all governments practically have done the same thing. It went on to write out claims for itself by way of the issue of money through the central bank, and of course that may be done in various ways.

I have no Objection to anybody asking questions or intervening in what I have to say, because the matter is a controversial one and it is most important that we get at the truth of it. The government, I say, proceeded in three ways. First they taxed and taxed and taxed, and then they borrowed and borrowed, and then they issued what is commonly called fiat money. I take it that the objection from my hon. friends who have spoken so strongly on the subject is that they did not issue enough of the fiat money. But there is a further objection. They look forward, as we all do, with apprehension into the future.
Again we have a difference of opinion and I wish to be perfectly frank in stating my opinion. My trouble is not with the money of the future. I may be accused of being orthodox in my views, and sometimes orthodoxy in these days is not regarded as a virtue, but I contend that all marketable production can be financed. My trouble is to foresee production. I have no trouble about finance, because I realize that it will follow naturally.
A Scandinavian economist, whose name I believe was Pierson, likened money to a shunting engine. It went up the tracks and *pulled down cars and put them on the main highway and away they went. Now, you will never solve this problem by multiplying the number of shunting engines. What counts is the load in the cars.
I want to come right down to the issue in this thing. I hear a great deal about monetary reform. I never used the word "crackpot", never in my life, and I have never used the words "funny money", but I do object somewhat when people tell me they have a new idea, that there is something new in the idea that the state should finance itself by issuing its own money, fiat money.
The hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. McNevin) spoke yesterday about greenbacks. Well, we might go back to the war of 1812. We might go back still farther, as the Minister of Justice will recall, to France in the revolutionary days when that theory swept the people. I am not going back that far, for history does repeat itself. I have listened and listened to the suggestion that we should serve ourselves and our future by issuing money, and I think of the words that were written by an eminent monetary economist. The name may be familiar to some hon. members-Ludwig von Mises. During the critical days after the last war he was professor of economics in the university of Vienna. He is in this country now. He has written a book recently, and was somewhat surprised to hear us-I do not mean in this
house-in this copntry saying the very things that were said after the last war in Europe. This is one of the things they said: Why should not people issue fiat money; why not more money and more money? He said then that it was regarded as a wicked thing to think that the state could not build railways, could not build anything and everything that it wanted to build because it had to borrow from capitalists and the money interests. I am giving his statement in digest form. I have it here, and if the committee wishes I shall read it later on in detail. What I am interested in is the result of that policy; what was the result of issuing fiat money as it was issued then? In 1923 there came chaos to Europe and particularly to Germany. Why did it come in the form in which it came? Remember; go back a little, if you do not mind my adopting the school-teacher attitude. Money is a claim on goods. At the time fiat money was regarded as a species of taxation. Fiat money is a species of taxation, but it is a bad species. It is a disguised absolutism, because when the Minister of Finance brings down a taxing bill we in this house ask ourselves, upon whom is the burden going to fall? And our constituents judge us by our . answer. We in this house have adopted the policy and the principle-and it has been adopted in democracy generally-that the burden should fall according to the ability to pay, the capacity to pay.
What happens when the state issues fiat money of the sort we are discussing? Nobody really knows where the burden is going to fall. The impact of it nobody can see, but we are certain of this. We are certain it is going to fall hardest of all on the people with fixed incomes. It falls hardest of all on the wage-earner. I am going to give the committee some figures as to what happened in Germany. It is very easy to know what brought about the collapse in Germany in 1923. I maintain that it was not the increase of debt; it was the increase in the amount of state money issued, fiat money. This is what happened. The number of unemployed in Germany was relatively small in 1923. Real wages were falling lower and lower between April and October. In October of that terrible year the wages of trained and skilled worker for one week were just about sufficient to buy a hundred pounds of potatoe|; nine or ten hours of work were necessary to pay for a pound, not of butter, but of margarine; to buy a pound of butter a man would have to work hours longer. A hundred pounds of fuel

briquettes took the pay of twelve hours' work; a pair of ordinary boots took six weeks and a suit of clothes twenty weeks.
In commenting on that state, Professor Bruck, who was then on the staff of University college in Wales, said:
We have to bear these facts in mind as a background for the fearful convulsions in which Germany was involved at this time. She was shaken by the fear of revolutions by both communists and national extremists. At this time mass-psychology and ideology were shaping themselves into the antagonistic ideas which clashed during the next period and came to a head in January, 1933.

Well, let us look at that for a moment. We have price control. We have it as a war measure, and for more than one purpose. I would assume that one purpose is to divert the earnings or claims of the people, as far as can be done, to war services. The other is to keep prices down. We are used to the word "ceiling", although some people are not used to that word when it is applied to wages. On the whole however we take it, and take it well. We do so because we think of those boys overseas who have much heavier burdens than we have. But there is a different outlook when peace comes; you have a different problem of control. We must remember that we can have price control, and that they can have it in Russia much easier than we can have it in Canada. Whatever else we may be, we are an almost maturely developed country. There are something like a million articles in modern commerce, and they cannot be controlled by a central authority, no matter what the capacity and capabilities of the price control board may be.
I have quoted from von Mises. I want to give the committee his considered opinion, for I have the highest respect for him, and I know everyone who is interested in international economics holds him in highest opinion. This is his conclusion:
A government that sets out to abolish market prices is inevitably driven toward the abolition of private property. It has -to recognize that there is no middle way ibetwen the system of private property in the means of production combined with free contracts, and the system of common ownership of the means of production. It is gradually forced toward compulsory production, universal obligation to labour, rationing of consumption and, finally, official regulation of the whole of production and consumption.
This is the road that was taken by economic policy during the war. The eta.tist, who had jubilantly proclaimed the state's ability to do everything it wanted to do, discovered that the economists had nevertheless been quite right, and that it was not possible to manage with price regulation alone. Since they wished to eliminate the play of the market, they had to go farther than they had originally intended. The first step was the rationing of the most important necessaries; but soon compulsory labour had to be resorted to and eventually the subordination of the w-hole of production and consumption to the direction of the state. Private property existed in name only; in fact, it had been abolished.
And when that had been done the form of government had to be changed. Because,

May I say a word or two about the European situation. The Europeans were asking the question, "Why not create money to advance national projects?" after the last war. An all-important matter has to be raised and understood. As a whole the European countries are' "have-not" countries. Germany was a narrowly restricted country with 66,000,000 people as compared with Canada, almost an empire in area, with but 11,000,000 people. Who can draw a parallel between the conditions in Germany and those in Canada?
First of all let us bear in mind that the European countries had large populations and relatively meagre resources as compared with Canada. Having that in ,mind let us turn to what happened in Germany. In the first place, Germany was a small country with a large

population and with relatively meagre resources. In the second place, Germany was exhausted as a result of a most disastrous war. In the third place, she had had fastened upon her the terms of the treaty of Versailles which were positively ruinous. They demanded the delivery of the very goods and services which would have supported the money that Germany could issue. They demanded railroad cars, railroad ties, coal and many other commodities to be delivered in almost impossible abundance. At the same time they demanded the delivery of a great deal of gold. How could you judge a country which was in the condition Germany was by ordinary monetary standards? Any one who attempts to compare what happened in tragic Germany in 1920 with what might happen in blessed Canada with her boundless resources and small population simply is not capable of forming a correct judgment. Germany's great lack was goods. In normal times Canada can produce more goods than her people can possibly use. Our problem is one of distribution.
May I turn to the taxation aspect of money? The hon. member for Ontario said that the creation of money was a form of taxation. Mr. Chairman, I emphatically challenge that statement. The creation of money will not constitute taxation unless that money causes a rise in prices. Money will not cause a rise in prices if there are already more goods on the markets than there is money in the economy. To create money to equal the goods on supply is not a form of taxation in any sense of the word because it does not cause a rise in prices. I challenge the hon. member to question that.
The question was raised as to price control. We realize fully that price control is not always easy. Let me draw this to the attention of the hon. member for Ontario. You can always bring down the price of a commodity by increasing the amount of that commodity beyond what the people can use. As a simple illustration, if we have a bumper crop of potatoes in Canada, the price of potatoes comes down. The same thing will happen with any other commodity you can name. If you want to bring down prices, you increase production and then your prices will not go up. The main difficulty then will be of putting floors under your prices.
I think this is one of the points the hon. member for Ontario made. By using a scientific method of price control prices can be completely controlled. First, let there be abundance of production* of every kind the nation can produce to the point at which there is more of each kind of commodity than the

people can use. Then prices will not rise because of demand. You will have no inflation. If you put floors under the prices you will keep them from falling too low. If there is a tendency for prices of manufactured goods to rise prices can be brought down by means of a government subsidy or by discounts with compensation. By the use of price floors and discounts with compensation the price levels of the community can be brought into alignment and thereby prices can be almost completely controlled.

The figures from the "Canada Year Book" for ten years up to 1941 show an average dividend payment of about ten per cent, and that is on top of- the reserves which they have been tucking away and hiding and on which they are getting freedom from taxation in the current year, and which they will not tell us. If we had those, you have no idea what secret reserves would be added to the picture. By reference to exhibit 10, page 117 in the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee, it will be found what rates of dividends were being paid by the banks in the early thirties, when people were in dire distress and riding the rods, when numerous failures were occurring, and the stock market was in the depression of 1932.
Here are the rates of dividend paid by the chartered banks in that year: 12 per cent, 14 per cent, 12, 12, 12, 12, 8 and 12.

The period I have mentioned includes the worst depression we have ever known, but the banks sailed merrily along so far as paying dividends was concerned. In the second place they built up their reserves over a long period to just about the original capital. In other words they have doubled their money. Mind you, that is only the disclosed reserves. If we had the other reserves brought into the daylight it might appear that they have trebled or quadrupled their money. The minister knows but, as the little boy says, he won't tell. He won't tell parliament. I discussed that yesterday. I am not blaming the banks for building up cash reserves equal to their capital by their thrift and business ability. I think it is a splendid thing to do. They have built three thousand buildings scattered all ovdf Canada; excellent buildings, valued by themselves at $70 million and all paid for. The next item is that they have had for years and still have the use of some $40 million of their own bank bills, created by paper and printing ink and lent out at five and six per cent, and have added the profit on these bills to their annual intake. In addition to that let me point out that some fifteen or twenty years ago they were paying dividends as high as fourteen or sixteen per cent on their capital, and at the same time piling up the hidden reserves. Over a considerable period of time, on top of these figures, they were paying for many years income tax of their staff out of profits and deducting that from their profits before those profits were taxed. They have a substantial and satisfactory pension fund for their emplos^ees in which they have set aside out of profits, in the last fifteen years, $22| million. I do not complain of that; I think it is a splendid thing. I only wish we could provide for our civil servants on the same basis. But I want to answer this question about wrecking the banks.

That does not seem to be the opinion that is held. Let us not forget that out of 114 million people there are 51,000 shareholders, and some of the shareholders are corporations, who in turn represent many shareholders who share at second hand in the rich dividends that the banks are able to declare.
They try to frighten us by saying that if you take away this privilege of lending to the government, they may stop paying to the savings depositors 14 per cent, which is the nominal rate, but which Mr. Towers states works out at only slightly more than one per cent as representing what the savings depositor secures. It was suggested that this is a burden on the banks and that if we clipped their wings at all by taking this monopoly from them they would reduce the interest rate. I am not alarmed by that, and I again quote the Minister of Finance at page 2546 of Hansard:
There can be no doubt about the competition for deposit accounts; even though the banks pay the same rate of interest on deposits there are other ways in which the keen competition manifests itself.
So that the banks are only too happy to get savings accounts deposits. If you have read, as I did in the last three-months before the committee sat, the advertisements in the press of the chartered banks you will recall that they pointed out what great virtue there is in having competition among the banks, and they invite savings deposits. They invite you to accept their service. It must not be .forgotten that we run a savings deposit account in our post office department. I was greatly intrigued by the alarm set up by the hon. member for Northumberland, Ont., who said that it would not be safe to deposit money with the post office savings department because the building might burn down or it would be an inducement for robbers to enter the post offices and steal the money. That is the type of argument that is being sought out and put forward on the floor of the House of Commons in opposition to the retaking of this monopoly privilege which in my view the banks should never have enjoyed.
Let me suggest this. The banks may have to reduce their dividends slightly for the first year if this amendment carries. They may have to stop piling up further hidden reserves at the rate they have been doing and the

amount of which they refuse to tell us. They may have to drag out into the open some of these hidden reserves. But so far as other results are concerned there is nothing to interfere with the shareholders of the banks. There is nothing unfair to them or to the people of Canada, and such fears are purely, imaginary and conjured up. They will not stand investigation.
Let me put to you in a word what rights the banks would still have left to themselves [DOT]if this horrible calamity which is going to wreck them were put into effect. I will tell you in a nutshell what they could still do. We do not interfere in any way with the remunerative business the banks do in carrying on legitimate commercial banking by lending to industries and to the business men of the country, which we are told last year, with their loans abroad, as well as in Canada, produced a revenue, on loans and discounts, Of $55 million on an original capital of $145,500,000; nor will this amendment interfere in any way with the excellent business they do in exchange commissions, service charges and other current operating earnings. That is an item they insert, and last year the ten banks had a revenue of $35 million from these sources, which would not be interfered with. The amendment we propose will however have the effect of forcing the banks to bestir themselves to lend their money to the general public in a greater degree instead of sitting back and locking up government securities in their vaults and folding their hands complacently with the knowledge that they cannot lose. That, I suggest, would have a healthy effect on Canadian industry and prospective borrowers. Let me give some figures which I think may startle hon. members although we are familiar with them in the committee.
What our amendment, if carried, still leaves the banks the right to do business on is this: $145,500,000 original capital, on which they would be allowed to lend, and $136 million of reserve, a total of $282 million. On April 30 last, as taken from the official figures, the private banks had savings deposits of $2,254 million, which with the two items mentioned makes a total of $2,536 million, or roughly speaking $24 billion, which after our amendment carries they will be entitled to lend to the people of Canada but not to the government of Canada.
Let us see what their needs have been in lending to the public during the last ten years. First, it will interest you to know that their lendings in 1944, on April 30 of this year, their outstanding loans to the public, were in Canada $962 million only. That is a

Bank Act Amendment
bit low. I want to be fair about this. It is a bit low because the government itself has been financing industry to such a large extent that the needs of private borrowers have been less. But get these figures: $962 million is the total that the banks had out, lent to private persons or industry in Canada on April 30, a couple of months ago. They had lent abroad an extra $197 million, in Nassau and Cuba and in their foreign branches, making a total of money on loan of $1,159 million. I showed you that they would have $2,600 million under this plan. But, you may say, back through the years it may be they were lending the public a great deal more than that. Let me hurriedly give you the facts. In 1938 their total loans, Canada and abroad, were $1,191 million; in 1939, $1,236,000,000; in 1940, $1,317,000,000; in 1941, $1,497,000,000; in 1942, $1,367,000,000 and in 1943, $1,333.000,000. In each of these years they would still have only about one-half of the money left to lend to the public in future years if we do not wreck them by the amendment being put into effect.
A word about service charges; I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard covered that sufficiently this afternoon. I entirely agree with him. What hon. member in this committee will say that the man who receives the benefit, the large corporation that gets the major benefit out of being serviced by the splendid banking system ought not to pay for it? Under the present system all the taxpayers of the country pay it in the interest they pay on the bonds that the government of Canada have lodged in the vaults. All the taxpayers of Canada pay the service charge regardless of who gets the most benefit. I should like to have an hon. member of this committee rise and defend the continuation of that system. Somebody says, why should they not pay it all, because the little fellows, the poor people, the under-dogs have not bank accounts anyway? They have not sufficient income to come within the lower brackets of the income tax. I say that there are 958,000 Canadians who are in the two lower brackets; that is, the unmarried man from $660 to $1,200 and the married man from $1,200 to $1,800. That group constitutes 958,000 taxpayers out of something over two million in Canada who pay a total of $882,000,000. The two groups I have mentioned paid $S7,000,000, a small amount but it is big to them. Taxes bear more heavily on them. They are not based on such a heavy ratio on the little fellow as on the big fellow, but on top of that every man who has a little family pays an eight per cent sales tax on everything that he buys for his children, and he has to buy three outfits
in a year. We are to-day taking a part of the salary of the little fellow to bonus, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said, to finance the private banks of Canada. I want to quit this sort of thing. I think it is time we quit it. It is not a good enough reason to refuse to vote for this amendment to say-

One or two statements
made by the hon. member for Ontario should not, I think, be allowed to go unchallenged. He dragged out the old bugaboo of German inflation. "Germany's Master Plan," written by Joseph Borkin, who has been for many years economic adviser to the anti-trust division, department of justice of the United States, particularly with regard to foreign international cartels, and Charles A. Welsh, who is an authority on international trade and finance and is a cartel expert for the office of price administration, outlined how Germany had merged economic and air commands, and marshalled light metals and gas and everything else for the purpose of establishing world conquest. At page 9 they say:
How perfectly these tactics interlocked in the design is evident in the sucession of manoeuvres which made up German policy during the 1920's. A planned inflation liquidated the cost of the first world war. .
A planned inflation was carried out in 1920 as the first step toward liquidating the debts so that they could move with the same managed currency to build the greatest war machine in the world. It was the accumulation of debts that demanded the inflation which liquidated them, not the inflation that caused the collapse of the debts. I take it that those gentlemen are probably in a position to speak with even greater authority upon that particular issue than the hon. member for Ontario. He also referred to the fact that fiat currency is dangerous currency. We have had a fiat currency since 1928. Mr. C. E. Neill, vicepresident of the Royal Bank of Canada, refutes the statement of the hon. member for Ontario with regard to his ideas of the supply of money in relation to the distribution of goods and with regard to his ideas about fiat currency. May I place on the record Mr. Neill's statement taken from the annual report of the Royal Bank of Canada in 1932. This is what he says:
These wide fluctuations in the money value of output are clearly a monetary phenomenon which, if properly understood, could he prevented. Over-supply of individual commodities could explain the decline in the value of one commodity in relation to another. Overproduction of agricultural products in relation to manufactured articles would justify a decline
Bank Act Amendment

in the price of farm products as compared with the products of industry, but when the average
of all prices declines this can only be explained by an undersupply of that in which prices are expressed, i.e., money, and it would seem that if the effective supply of money is kept in the right relation to production of commodities the phenomenon of a declining average price level will not occur.
He then goes on to say:
If on the collapse of the stock market boom the principal central banks of the world had decided that drastic contraction of currency and credit was not to be permitted, a drastic fall in the price level could not have occurred. Thus the countries with fiat currencies, such as Argentina, Uruguay and Spain are not suffering anything like as acutely as the gold countries.
I take it that Mr. C. E. Neill, because of his position, is probably a better authority than the hon. member for Ontario. I wish to put one more quotation on the record in answer to the old wheeeze that you cannot get something for nothing. On April 24, 1939, Mr. M. S. Eccles, chairman of the federal reserve system, explaining how the $15,500,000,000 of gold was paid for by the treasury of the United States, made this statement:
The process by which the treasury acquires gold and puts it into use involves a number of technical steps, partly the result of custom, partly the result of law and regulation. Reduced to simple terms they are as follows:
1.	The treasury receives the gold

usually at a United States assay office or mint-and issues a cheque in payment for it.
2.	The cheque is deposited by the seller of the gold at his bank, which gives him credit in his deposit account.
3.	The bank deposits the cheque in the federal reserve bank and receives credit in its reserve account.
4.	The federal reserve bank charges the cheque to the balance which the treasury maintains with it.
5.	The treasury replenishes this balance by crediting gold certificates to the federal reserve bank in exchange for deposit credit.
At the conclusion of these five steps the matter stands as follows:	The treasury has
possession of the gold: bank deposits and bank reserves have both been increased by the amount of the gold: and the treasury's checking balance at the federal reserve banks, reduced by the purchase of the gold, has been restored by credits based upon the gold.
The purchase of the gold has cost the treasury nothing.
If you can get $15,500,000,000 in gold into the treasury of the United States for nothing, by a sane management of the national currency power, you can do something of the same kind here.
Then, one word in regard to the argument that this amendment is inflationary. All this amendment proposes is to give the Minister of Finance, the governor of the Bank of Canada and the Prime Minister power to say to the banks. "A ou cannot inflate your bank

deposit money, and you cannot issue money to the amount of eight, nine or ten times the amount you have." This is to prevent that kind of inflation which caused the last disastrous collapse. It is not to create an unlimited -supply of money, but rather to place the government, in its intelligence and understanding, in a position to stop this pyramiding of debt, to use national currency in terms of private need, and to substitute that process for the one of allowing bankers to issue a fiction of money in terms of bankers' greed.

Well, I propose to seek shelter in the word of an economist from the London school of economics, Professor F. A. Hayek.
We are marshalling our authority, and it is for the committee to decide, not which are the better authorities, but which carry the most conviction. Professor Hayek, writing in 1932, in the midst of the depression, said:
There is no reason to assume that the crisis was started by a deliberate deflationary action on the part of the monetary authorities, or that the deflation itself is anything but a secondary phenomenon, a process induced by maladjustments of industry.

As will be recalled, I quoted some of them in the banking and commerce committee, drawn from the economic committee of the League of Nations, and the hon. member was good

Bank Act Amendment
enough to say that they were a valuable contribution to the discussion. Professor Hayek went on to say:
To combat the depression by a forced credit expansion is to attempt to cure the evil by the very means which brought it about: because we are suffering from a misdirection of production, we want to create further misdirection-a procedure which can only lead to a much more severe crisis as soon as the credit expansion comes to an end.
I wish now to refer to another matter. I am not satisfied with the statements of the hon. members for Vancouver-Burrard and Parry Sound. This word "inflation" is a bad word. It is something like the word "toadstool"-it has no scientific meaning. But I think in the way the term is now used I can use it to point out that the inflation in Germany was not brought about, solely at least, by a parcel of crooks. There were honest men in Germany-then, at any rate. And there were honest men who advocated the issue of state money to solve their problems.
I spoke of the opinion of von Mises. I have now before me an exact quotation of the arguments of honest men, such as we have here to-day in the house, as to the objective and the desirability of issuing more and more state money. He said that this was their argument:
Let the state create money, and make the poor rich, and free them from the bonds of the capitalists! How foolish to forgo the opportunity of making everybody rich, and consequently happy, that the state's right to create money gives it! How wrrong to forgo it simply because this would run counter to the interests of the rich! How wicked of the economists to assert that it is not within the power of the state to create wealth by means of the printing press!
And during this debate I have thought of these next words several times:
You statesmen want to build railways, and complain of the low state of the exchequer? Well, then, do not beg loans from the capitalists and anxiously calculate whether your railways will bring in enough to enable you to pay interest and amortization on your debt. Create money, and help yourselves.
Those were the statements of men who at that time in that country honestly-quite honestly-believed that they were doing the best thing in the interests of the public.
I should like to say just a few words about the topic discussed by the hon. member for Parry Sound, namely that of hidden reserves- sometimes known as inner reserves, undisclosed reserves or secret reserves. If our banks are wrong in having them and if the Minister of Finance is wrong in permitting the banks to have them, certainly we in Canada are not alone, because they are the
general practice wherever there is a good and efficient banking system. It is the general practice throughout the world.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words about the amendment and about some of the remarks made to the committee in support of it. The hon. member for Parry Sound has made two speeches, one last night and one this afternoon, which have been dealt with to some extent by other speakers, but some of the points are still outstanding. The hon. gentleman, both in the banking and commerce committee and in his speech last night and again this afternoon, repeated with great emphasis the allegation that depositors or others using the chartered banks should pay for that privilege, and that if a system is established under which they do not pay the full services charges, that is unjust to the general body of depositors and discriminates

Bank Act Amendment
against them in favour of what are called the wealthy corporations. An argument is built up on that and members are virtually being challenged to rise in their places and say that there is no justice in the present system.
Just consider the situation. A depositor establishes a deposit in a bank. That is money. It may be argued by Social Crediters and others that it had fountain-pen origin or something of that kind. But when a depositor is in a position to make a deposit in a bank, that is money. It is as exactly good as legal tender. He is entitled to legal tender for it and he is in a position to get it.
Why does he deposit that money in a bank? Ordinarily if he deposits it in a current account he expects bank services in connection with the deposit. He expects to be able to draw cheques upon the account, to get his money out when he wants it, to put other money in to add to the account, and so on. These services cost something. They cannot be rendered unless the bank has the necessary equipment, the buildings, the staff that knows its business, and so conducts its business that it is in a position to be able to discharge its obligations in reference to the deposit at any time. Almost anyone would think, if he were depositing his money in a bank and getting these services, the bank should be able to make use of the money deposited and get what benefit it could from the use of that money before a charge against the person making the deposit is made. I think almost anyone would say that that was fair. If the government were to step in, as is suggested here, and take the total amount of that deposit away from the bank, move it to the Bank of Canada and hold it there without paying any interest on it, that would be depriving the bank of any opportunity of earning anything by using that money and thereby depriving the depositor of the benefit of the use of his money. It would be taking that away from the depositor. I submit that that is unfair, and in the only jurisdiction in which this system has been adopted, in Australia, the unfairness of it was recognized and the government paid the service charge. It was not sought to throw the service charge on the person using the bank. To do that would be equivalent, as I said in the speech in which I introduced the Bank Act, to putting into effect a compulsory loan without interest from the depositor or from the bank or from both.
But in another aspect it is imposi g a tax upon those using the banking facilities. When I say it would fall wholly upon the depositor, the banks might, of course, pass the burden on to other classes, to their savings depositors or to their shareholders or to their employees,
but the natural body upon whom the burden would fall would be those using the facilities of the hank; that is the depositors.
In the amendment before us it is proposed that steps be taken by which dominion government securities, amounting to about $2,700 million, now owned by the banks would be taken from the banks, and the banks would be deprived of their interest charges which amount to about $39 or $40 million, with the result that the banks would be heavily in deficit and would have to pass on a large part of that to those using their facilities. Is that a good tax? Is it a better or a worse tax than the kind of taxes out of which the interest is paid?
The hon. member for Parry Sound says that it is a better tax. He says it is a better tax than the sales tax. I think it is generally appreciated that the great bulk of our revenue of $2,750 million is raised from income tax and from excess profits tax. But the hon. member for Parry Sound picks out the $305 million that is raised from the sales tax, a very substantial part of which is fictitious because it is on government purchases. But he picks out the sales tax and says: We are making the humble purchaser, the man who buys boots and shoes and clothing for his children pay, through the sales tax, on the things he has to buy, for what the big corporations using the banks ought to pay. But it is not only the big corporations that use the banks. There are five million bank accounts in Canada, a large number of them savings accounts, and some of them current accounts. To put a gigantic service charge, such as this would be, upon those using the facilities of the banks would be to impose the most unsound of all taxes. It would be what is called a regressive tax. It would have no reference whatever to the ability of the person to pay it. It would bear most heavily on small persons and businesses. It would be a tax that would be pyramided in the normal course of events and it would make its appearance in the price. If it did not make its appearance in the price, it would be at the expense of the government. A large part of the service charge would fall upon the government itself. It is one of the greatest users of banking facilities in Canada at the present time. Judged by any standards that apply to sound taxation, it would in my judgment be a very bad tax.
I am glad, however, that the issue has been driven to that point because that is the point where it ought to have been from the beginning. We have been discussing this matter for the last two or three years. First those who were advocating this system of borrowing
Bank Act Amendment

from the Bank of Canada thought it would be just money saved; there would be no expense to anybody in borrowing from the Bank of Canada; it did not cost the Bank of Canada anything because they did not have to service deposit; therefore it did not cost anybody * anything. That was just too good to be true.
It was just reached for and brought down out of the air. But when the proposition is analysed it is found that somebody has to bear a burden substantially equivalent to the very moderate interest that we pay on these loans. Somebody has to bear the burden and it is a question whether that burden should be shifted or not. The issue becomes clarified when members argue on that instead of basing their arguments on other considerations. If the hon. gentleman could establish by anything in the evidence anywhere that the banks are making excessive profits, he might very well argue that the banks should bear a portion of that burden. But there is no such evidence whatever. We knew the importance of that and that is why we had the table compiled which appears on page 2550 of Hansard of May 2, 1944. The figures in that table are concrete. They show the average of the years from 1929 to 1943. They show that for the past fifteen years between 1929 and 1943, including some bad years and a great number of good years, the ratio of shareholders' net income to the total published shareholders' equity was 5'09 per cent, and if inner reserves were regarded as unpublished shareholders' equity it would be less than 5-09 per cent. It would not be that much. Nobody, I think, can argue that a 5-09 per cent return over a fifteen year period on shareholders' equity justifies any contention that the banks of this country are making excessive returns. In 1943 the return was a little higher than that; it was 6-03 per cent, and that was a year of admittedly heavy earnings. But these figures are certainly no justification whatever for the contention made this afternoon that the bankers have been profiteering at the expense of the Canadian people.
There have been many errors of statement in the speeches which have been made. For instance, the hon. gentleman talks about their well-earned published reserves". It has been repeatedly pointed out to the hon. gentleman that about one-half of these published returns were not earned; they were subscribed. They were premiums on stock. Why, then, refer to these reserves as "well-earned"? "I do not begrudge it to them", he

said, "these well-earned published reserves". As a matter of fact something over $60 million of that was subscribed1.
Then we have this reference to the "smokescreen" of the banks put on by their "advocates". Those of us who have views about what ought to be done with reference to the banks of this country are not advocates of . thfe banks; we are simply expressing what we consider to be in the public interest. As to this reference to inflation as a "bugaboo" and a "spectre", there is nothing of the bugaboo and the spectre about inflation. Inflation is one of the greatest dangers which can confront any country in time of war, and many countries have been utterly unable to cope with it. And if we were to take the steps which were advocated two or three years ago, namely, a large borrowing from the Bank of Canada, section 59 being as it was, we would have been taking a course which inevitably would have led to a very serious degree of inflation.	*
May I now refer to inner reserves, which have been dealt with by a number of speakers. I was confronted with a very great and very grave responsibility when the hon. member for Parry Sound in the banking and commerce committee .called upon me to do what had never been done by any other finance minister in the history of this country, and what no banking and commerce committee which had considered the matter-and several of them had-would ever take the responsibility of doing; that is, to say that there should be no system of inner or undisclosed reserves in the banking system of the Dominion of Canada. I had to take a very great responsibility when the hon. member started out by wanting the inner reserves of the Canadian Bank of Commerce disclosed. The general manager of the Canadian Bank of Commerce said that he did not know whether it would be proper for him to disclose them or not. Thereupon the hon. member turned to me and asked me to take, the matter under consideration. I took the matter under consideration, made inquiry as to what was done in other countries and the reasons for the practice which had been adopted in this country, and came to the conclusion, as I had every right to do, that it was not in the public interest to disclose the reserves of the Canadian chartered banks. I came to that conclusion for, I believe, very good reasons, indeed, for the same reasons by which finance ministers everywhere have come to the same conclusion when the question came before them for consideration. I have had an opportunity of discussing these matters with the

Bank Act Amendment
finance ministers of two other countries, and with a very highly placed treasury official of another country who, for a purpose of this kind, would be practically the same as a finance minister; and they all have the same story. They say they get the information; they watch the situation very carefully, but they do not publish those reserves, and they do not publish those reserves for two or three reasons.
In the first place, publication, is bound to give rise to serious misinterpretations and misconceptions. One need only listen to the debate in this house to realize how intricate and difficult the matter is and the misunderstandings which are bound to arise as to what is there. After all, there is nothing there except a write-down of the assets to a conservative valuation. There is no shareholders' equity there at all. If the inner reserves are correctly appraised they will all be required to meet bad debts and losses on securities on realization.

speechtext: There is no pot of gold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OP BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, says, there is no pot of gold. But once you call them "inner reserves", and particularly if you add adjectives such as "secret", "hidden" and so on, it is regarded and would be regarded by a good many persons as a sort of treasure trove which could be drawn upon by the pubfi'c, especially when times were good, when it did not look as if the reserves were needed, and when there was not any apparent danger of decline in the value of loans and securities. But? far more important than that is the danger of fluctuations in reserves, that they might go down and down and eventually disappear, and then the published reserves would have to be resorted to, as they were once in the history of this country, in 1933. And when hon. gentlemen say that that did not do anything to impair confidence in the banks concerned-for all of them were not concerned- they are not making a statement in accordance with the evidence before the banking and commerce committee or with the facts. The evidence there indicated that the banks concerned suffered to some extent from lack of confidence and withdrawal of deposits. But whether they did or not, nobody in his senses would want a repetition of that experience. Nobody would want successive or repeated resorts to published reserves, or publication of the lowering of the level of the inner reserves. These are reasons for my coming to the conclusion I did.
The hon. gentleman talks about the banks having been "caught" in an attempt to evade taxation. The hon. member for Northumberland, Ont., dealt last night with that part effectively and very truly. This year it was late-after the banking and commerce committee met-when I went over this matter with the inspector general of banks; and I came to the conclusion, after conferences with the deputy minister of finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada, that I did not agree with the valuations placed upon securities in certain of the banks-in two, perhaps three. That does not 'justify language such as the hon. member for Parry Sound used about the banks having been "caught", and I think in other places he talked about their being obliged to "disgorge". It merely means that the judgment of their auditors, who are quasi public officials, and of their directors, who I think exercised their responsibility, differed somewhat from the judgment of the governor of the Bank of Canada,, the deputy minister and myself. But there has been no evasion of taxation responsibility by the banks, nor will there be as long as I have anything to do with the matter. These inner reserves are reported every year, like the other affairs of the banks, to the inspector general and are discussed with the finance minister.
The hon. gentleman said, "Very well, but we are proposing a remedy. What is your remedy? It is admitted that there will be great problems during the next few years. At least we have a remedy."
I want to state my agreement with the hon. member for Ontario when he says that monetary remedies are not the most important. The monetary policy is not the most important policy of a country. The most important policies are those which result in the stimulation and maintenance of production, the raising of the national income and a fair and equitable distribution of the national income. If I were to'outline what I should like to see in this country in the post-war years-I do not think I have the time to do it fully this afternoon-I would say that we must make sure that we take steps for the stimulation and expansion of export trade, and there are a great many ways in which it can be done; we must make sure that we take steps to ensure the maximum volume of private investment, and there are a great many ways in which that can be done; steps for the stimulation of domestic consumption, and there are a great many ways in which that can be done; and for a programme of public expenditure if it is necessary; that is,
Bank Act Amendment

if private investment and private expenditure fall down so that a programme of public expenditure is necessary.

With regard to the amendment, it proposes that a board be set up consisting of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada, to pass upon, control and regulate loans, investments and securities made by the banks-at least those that would result in the creation of deposits. That, I gather, is the proposal, and it applies to each bank. As regards the wording of the amendment, I do not think it is good. I think it is in language of monetary

economics rather than in the language of legislation. But if that is what the amendment means, that this board is to pass upon all loans, upon the limit of the loans that may be made by any bank, the limit of securities that may be bought by any bank, it seems to me it places a virtually impossible task upon a government board. I cannot imagine the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada being able to do that intelligently or effectively. It would mean a quota for each bank. The bank of Montreal could make loans and buy securities up to a certain amount; the bank of Commerce could do likewise. But there would be no limit upon their calling in loans. There would be no limit upon the restriction but there would be upon the expansion. It is based upon the theory that our present control, the control of the volume of cash reserve by the Bank of Canada, is ineffective, and it certainly has not been proved that that, control is ineffective. I could not imagine that kind of interference with the management of the banks on the part of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada. I submit to the committee that no case has been made for it and I shall have to decline to accept it.

May I say one word arising
out of what the minister has said. I will not detain the committee. On the last point he said that monetary policy is not the most important policy in a country. I wish to read what his leader said in that regard:
Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit shall be restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.
I leave the two opinions to the judgment of the committee.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OP BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
I shall take only a few minutes. I did not wish to intervene during the discussion that was going on with regard to monetary theory between certain hon. members and the minister. In my view the amendment now before the committee is an attempt to place under the control of parliament, to some degree at least, monetary policy and particularly the policy of making loans and creating deposits, and to that extent I am in agreement with the proposal. We have heard a very great deal in the last two or three months about money and monetary systems. In my opinion the whole discussion before the banking and commerce committee and in this

Bank Act Amendment
house drives us more and more to the inescapable conclusion that there is no satisfactory way of bringing our monetary system under the control of this parliament except by the national ownership and control of our banking and' financial system. The alternatives that are presented to us are pretty much those of continuing as we are, on the one hand, and on the other, of bringing the monetary and financial system under the control of parliament through the socializing of the banking system. That, of course, has been our view throughout. I have before me a copy of the Regina manifesto, which we approved in 1933, calling for the socialization of finance. I quote:
Planning by itself will be of little use if the public authority has not the power to carry its plans into effect. Such power will require the control of finance and of all those vital industries and services which, if they remain in private hands, can be used to thwart or corrupt the will of the public authority. Control of finance is the first step to the control of the whole economy. The chartered banks must be socialized and removed from the control of private profit-seeking interests.
That is from the Regina manifesto of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. That was our view in 1933 and is our view now, and the more this discussion has gone on the more we have been driven to the inescapable conclusion that if we are to deal with this power which is called financial, the only way to do so is to take the control out of private hands.
With regard to some of the other points in the discussion, mentioned in connection with this amendment, I merely want to say this. It is almost impossible to compare monetary policy under different systems within different nations with the system which we have in our country. We have heard' some discussion to-day about what happened in Germany. Well, the men who brought about inflation in Germany may have been honest, but the effect was to destroy the equities of many people in physical property and to transfer, in effect, properties from one group of people to another in that country, with the result that they were free of debt and able to start all over again and build up their war machine, as has been pointed out here several times.

I will not say whether they did it deliberately or not. We have not access to their minds and therefore I am going to leave that an open question.
The Russian monetary policy was mentioned yesterday and the rates of interest in Russia have been mentioned from time to time. But again let me say that it is almost impossible to compare the monetary system in Russia with the monetary system in this
country. After all, in that country the value of money was deliberately destroyed. Money as a commodity ceased to exist and the money in the pockets of the people meant very little indeed in our terms. The financing of this country is done in an entirely different way. When we make comparisons I think we make an understanding of our own system a little more difficult. We cannot compare things that are unlike. The purpose of money in the Russian economy is money of account and, to only a small degree, money of exchange. Certainly money is not a commodity to be bought and sold and lent at interest as it is with us.
Perhaps the governor of the Bank of Canada placed before the banking and commerce committee a point of view that we should keep in our minds. He said:
The real cost of government expenditures is the use of labour and equipment required to carry out projects. When the question is asked if we can finance a certain government expenditure, the fundamental problem is whether we can afford to devote a certain amount of our productive resources to the projects in question. The problem of how the government can obtain the money which will give it title to the labour and equipment ... is not the fundamental question.

speechtext: The fundamental problem is the problem of the resources, of the equipment and of labour under a proper plan. If you have these things there is no reason in the world why money cannot be found to move the goods and services from the producer to the consumer.

resources and if you can plan your production and control your goods, then through your financial system the money can be found.

It will arise and be distributed through the process of production. It is intimately connected with this. I presume that one of the reasons why we are so much interested to-day in this question of money and of financing is our experience during the years of depression and the fear of the future. I had intended to place this thought before the banking and commerce committee at the appropriate time, but I am going to put it before this committee now. From time to time some of us are accused of being unduly pessimistic about the future; that we are promoting the psychology of fear
Bank Act Amendment

and all the rest of it. That is not true. I do not believe there is any reason why we should be afraid of the future in this country if we have a proper economic system and a proper monetary system to move the goods and services around. I do not think there is any need for fear, but I point out that that fear arises in the minds of people who are intimately acquainted with the present economic system. For example, a short time ago Mr. Roger Babson issued a report, as he frequently does, and that report as most hon. members know is regarded by a good many business men in this country as a guide and almost as a sacred document. His weekly report for May 1, 1944, must have come as something of a shock to his well-to-do subscribers. It contained a supplement entitled "Mr. Babson's Personal Message to Parents with Boys in the Service". This is what he had to say. Remember, when I read it, that Mr. Babson is a supporter of the Republican party, and consequently the injection of the Republican party into this opinion is only of significance because of Mr. Babson's association with that party.
Within a reasonable time after world war II, the United States should have a few years of good business, stimulated by a complete Republican victory in 1948. But sometime after 1950, we will again be in a violent business depression accompanied by great unemployment. This could result surely in another new deal victory in 1952, if not in a bloodless revolution of some kind. Much depends upon the -then existing economic conditions in Russia. If Russia's collective system with her planned economy has failed, we have little then to fear here. Otherwise, we are destined to suffer from violent United States inflation and the unwise legislation which may make stocks, bonds, mortgages, and bank accounts of little value.
These are not my words. They are the warning words of Mr. Roger Babson. In discussing the Bank Act it seems to me that we ought to see to it that as much authority as possible is preserved to this parliament. That is why I am going to support the amendment. 'I support it because I believe it is an attempt to put the responsible ministers, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, together with- the governor of the Bank of Canada, in a position where they can influence monetary policy in this country in the postwar years. I do not wish to delay the committee, but there are two or three other things that I should have liked to have said. However, I see it is six o'clock.

speechtext: I am in the hands of the committee and the minister. Many hon. members have been brought to order in the discussion of section 59. However, if it will shorten the discussion or' make it more direct to the clause before the committee I would be in favour of the hon. member's proceeding.
