speechtext:
I believe that all I
have to say, or all I think I should say at this time, can be said in about thirty minutes, and I believe it would be well worth while for me to do so. However, Mr. Chairman, if you feel I should not proceed I shall bow to your ruling.
As I was proceeding to say, the general argument of the Minister of Finance before the banking and commerce committee, and in this committee of the whole, has appeared to be that it is just as expensive to finance with debt-free money as it is to finance with borrowed money. I am not going to argue that aspect of the question, except in a general way.
Let us suppose that we are on an island where gold is to be used as money, and let us suppose further that the rulers of that island have found a gold mine which has yielded choice nuggets. I wonder if they would find it impossible to finance their affairs with the nuggets they could get without any debt at all. I wonder if it would cost as much to finance their affairs with solid gold' nugggts as it would with money they would have to borrow from the banks. It just does not make any sense, does it?
I think in the light of the situation, as this illustration presents it, it must appear reasonable to the minister and to members of the committee that where money can be obtained by the simple process of printing it, and when we know so much to-day about financial controls, what causes inflation, and various other things which pertain to sound money, it must surely be more economical, and it must be possible to organize so that it will be more economical to finance with money we can obtain without a debt.
I do not propose to argue that matter. The minister has presented his case, and it is a clash of opinion. What I would like to lay before the committee in the few minutes at
my disposal is a general statement as to the feasibility of having debt-free money. May I read for the information of the committee a statement found in a book I hold in my hand entitled, "The Canadian Banking System," by James Holladay. This book was published in 1938. At page 140 I find a passage which, I believe, sets forth some truths for the Canadian people. It states:
The Bank Act of 1934, however, sets up a specific quantitative reserve which the chartered banks are required to hold against their deposit liabilities. In form, this reserve must consist of a deposit in and notes of the Bank of Canada. In amount, it must be equal to five per cent of the deposit liabilities in Canada. As a result the chartered banks, as a group, can legally create deposits amounting to $20 on the basis of a one-dollar reserve. A much larger secondary expansion is made possible, however, for the Bank of Canada is required to hold only a twenty-five per cent reserve against its liabilities, which in turn constitute the reserves of the chartered banks.
Consequently the Bank of Canada can expand a dollar into four dollars of liabilities which, if borrowed by the chartered banks, will enable them to lend an aggregate of $80 against a primary deposit of one dollar. This compares with a possible legal expansion of $28.50 under the federal reserve system in vogue in the United States.
Briefly put, this simply means that the Bank of Canada can take paper and ink and print a one-dollar bill for whatever it costs to print a one-dollar bill. And when it prints that dollar bill it has a dollar which belongs to the Bank of Canada. Nobody owes it to anybody. This one-dollar bill can be expanded into four dollars by the Bank of Canada, and the four dollars can be expanded by a chartered bank-the bank of Montreal, for instance-into $80. This means that on a basis of a one-dollar bill which the Bank of Canada creates we can erect a structure of $80 in money, in the Dominion of Canada. And every dollar of that has been created in Canada and belongs to the people who created it. In the light of that fact surely there is a tremendous reservoir of financial resources available to the government of the Dominion of Canada. The contention of the monetary reformers is simply that by some mechanism the capacity to create money should be exercised by the state, for the state, and used for the benefit of the people as a whole. The great problem which confronts us nowadays is that of distribution. Surely the money which could be obtained by this method of money creation and credit expansion can be used to distribute the goods which Canadian people are able to produce. That would seem to be just pure common sense, would it not?



Bank Act Amendment
I have referred once or twice in this house to the experiment which was conducted in the last war. If hon. members will take the report of the royal commission on banking and currency which was published in 1933 and turn to page 22, paragraph 47, they will find an account of the creation of $26,000,000 of bills by the dominion government during the last war. That $26,000,000 belonged to the dominion government; it was created by the treasury department; it constituted no debt and Canadians have never paid a cent of interest on it and do not now. That money was spent into circulation for various governmental purposes and was just as good money as any which was taxed from the people or which was borrowed from any lending institution. That is a striking illustration of the power to create money and the power to use it safely. On the same page, paragraph 51, there is a statement which I think is valuable to us at the present time. I read:
But extensive use continued to be made of the power to issue dominion notes to the banks against approved securities with the result that it was decided in 1923 to make this part of the Finance Act mechanism a feature of the normal Canadian financial system. In introducing the new legislation, Mr. Fielding, the Minister of Finance, made the following brief explanation of its purpose:
"The act (Finance Act) was adopted as a war measure, -and no doubt was exceedingly useful in the financial operations during the war. It may be said that the war being over we no longer have any need for the act, but experience has shown that the act is still required; indeed, I am inclined to think that something of the kind will have to become almost a permanent part of our financial system."
A former Minister of Finance of this government of Canada, realizing the value of the mechanism of creating dominion notes, recommends that device in 1923 for use in peace time. His recommendation has not been accepted or acted upon. I submit that that recommendation ought to be reviewed with the idea of finding out what benefit there is in the recommendation. May I refer to the work of a man who, I believe, is worthy of some respect, Paul H. Douglas, Professor of Economics at Chicago university. In a book entitled, "Controlling Depressions", published in 1935, he refers to what should be done in order to keep the economy in sound condition, and on page 278 he makes these recommendations:
(3) A nationally managed system of currency and credit until such time as an international system may be perfected.
(5) The creation of credit by this socialized agency should follow two main principles; (a) to provide, so far as possible, employment or [Mr. Blackmore.l
useful work for those thrown out of their jobs by business depressions, and (b) to stabilize in a rough manner the general price level.
(11) The use of a social dividend to consumers or an increased expenditure upon cultural services if the amounts distributed to the purchasers of mass production goods are not sufficient to consume at a profit to industry and under competitive prices the mass production goods and services which are turned out by industry.
Hon. members will recognize that what Professor Douglas is recommending is in fact a form of Social Credit system. He is recommending that money should be created and used to stabilize prices, to increase the consumption power of the people, and generally to improve economic conditions by the employment of men and so on. When one recalls the remarks of Liberal members such as the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg and the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, apparently designed to ridicule the idea of debt-free money, one cannot escape the thought that these members really ought to inform themselves a little more before they set themselves up as authorities on this whole matter. Here is a man worthy of consideration, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard indicated this afternoon.
May I turn to another man who, I think, is worthy of a good deal of thought and consideration. I refer to Vincent C. Vickers, of Armstrong Limited of Great Britain. This man wrote a book which he finished almost on his deathbed entitled, "Economic Tribulation". I should like to read some passages which I consider worthy of real attention on the part of hon. members of this committee and others throughout the country. First of all, let me read who Mr. Vickers was;
Vincent Cartwright Vickers was born on 16th January, 1879, and educated at Eton and Magdalen college, Oxford. He was a deputy lieutenant of the city of London, a director of Vickers, Limited, for -twenty-two years, and a director of the London Assurance from which he resigned in January, 1939. In 1910 he was made a governor of the Bank of England, and resigned this appointment in 1919. Later, he became president of the economic reform club and institute.
He died on 3rd November, 1939, after a long illness during which, against time and with failing strength, he was working and writing on economics. A few days before his death he wrote: "My keen desire to help up to the end has been the sole incentive which still enabled me to carry on perhaps a few weeks longer."
That indicates that this man had been well trained, well educated and had a wealth of experience in affairs, apparently with a great deal of success because he had been promoted to high positions. This should have given him the opportunity to know a great deal about

Bank Act Amendment
finance and industry and business generally. In the light of that fact, let me read from the foreword as follows:
Ever since that day in 1926. when, not in arrogance but with humility, I felt it my duty to explain to the governor of the Bank of England, Mr. Montagu Norman, that "henceforth I was going to fight him and the gold standard and the Bank of England policy until I died"-(and well I remember the words of his reply!)-I have been an ardent money reformer. Some few years afterwards I resigned my long directorship of Vickers, Limited; since when I have spent much time and money in advocating the necessity for a reform of the monetary system.
Further, on the same page I read as follows:
I bear no ill-feeling towards my own class or any other class. I seek neither notoriety nor kudos. If someone can change my convictions I shall be only too ready to alter -them. But in fifteen years nothing whatever has occurred to make me alter my views. I still believe that the existing system is actively harmful to the state, creates poverty and unemployment, and is the root cause of war.
This personal confession is merely to demonstrate that I have seen both sides of the picture. My opinions are based upon my own experience and knowledge. I am to-day in the unique position of being absolutely and entirely devoid of animosity and wholly disinterested. I feel myself no longer under any restrictions *whatsoever, except to guard against doing harm to my country or giving offence to anyone.
Vincent C. Vickers.
I think the words of a man who has had experience of this sort and who approaches his subject with such humility and earnestness ought to be of some value to us in this critical time.
May I read now from page 70 of "Economic Tribulation", to show some of the things which he has to say to bankers as a class. He is speaking to the bankers:
1.	I ask you to remember that you are dealing to-day with a general public of a far greater education and of a more thorough knowledge of affairs, of foreign policy and of financial policy, than they have had in previous times; and that the majority of these are conscious that, in some way or another, the key that locks them out from the enjoyment of the good things in the world's shop window is money.
2.	That, because the public come into contact with the monetary system mainly through the medium of banks, they naturally tend to blame the banks for the difficulty; not realizing that they are, in large measure, tied houses-tied, that is, to the monetary system, and that, however great or small the faults of banks, it is in reality the system which is at fault.
3.	That banking is an industry working for profit, just as a gas company or any other utility company works for profit. And the people, realizing this-erroneously, perhaps-do not believe that any essential supply company should, at one and the same time, have control of the volume of its output and control of the
100-388J
price of its output, when the supply of its product is essential to the lives and welfare of those masses of the people who are dependent upon that product.
4.	That, whilst it may be possible, having regard to the immense power of money, artificially to maintain and uphold the present position for some months or for some years to come, against the rising revolt engendered by the present system, yet the time must eventually arrive (as it did in Russia, as it has in Spain, and as it may do in France) when the mass of the people will insist upon their right to possess a much larger Share of the country's available wealth, and when they will insist also upon a much nearer approach of to-day's poverty to to-day's wealth. With all earnestness and honesty I implore them to think of this nossi-bility and to take warning in time; to recognize what is inevitable, and to decide: Whether it is best to continue the present regime and, with the power of the press and with the power of money, to continue to fight for its supremacy; or, alternatively, whether it may be best to recognize that, for the good of the country, the maintenance of the empire, the benefit of the British world community, and for their own benefit, they should immediately take steps to associate themselves with those who are demanding reform of the monetary system. This refers more especially to the controllers of the system, embracing the whole of that particular section of the community which deals in, manages, and controls money, credit, and finance, and whose business mainly depends upon the indebtedness of others.
There are two other recommendations, Nos. 5 and 6, which in the interest of brevity I shall not read at this time but which I would recommend hon. members to read at their convenience. The whole of this appeal to the bankers strikes me as being so sensible, so humble and earnest and so sound that I think this House of Commons should be advised as well as the bankers themselves as to the matter under discussion when Mr. Vickers speaks.
I turn now to page 74 and read some of his suggestions for future policy:
1.	State control and state issue of currency and credit through a central organization managed and controlled by the state.
2.	Stabilization of the wholesale price level of commodities. That is to say, a fixed and constant internal purchasing power of money; so that a pound will buy to-morrow what it bought yesterday; an honest pound, not a fluctuating pound. And this can be done by so issuing and regulating the volume of available credit and currency that it shall at all times be adequate to permit of the purchasing power of the consumer being equated with the volume of production: not by limiting the purchasing powder, but by firstly increasing purchasing power more in proportion to the productive capacity of industry.
May I pause there to point out that the attitude taken there is exactly the attitude taken by the Social Credit movement? Our contention has been from the beginning that the cause of our trouble was that there was

Bank Act Amendment
too little purchasing power in the hands of the people and that measures should be taken to put purchasing power into their hands to enable them to purchase the goods that were available. I go on:
3.	Fixation of foreign exchanges -by foreign exchange equalization funds, and agreement with empire countries and all other countries willing to fall into line; and, once this was accomplished, the removal or diminution of trade barriers which to-day protect the countries from the results of a bad monetary -system.
4.	Any additional supply of money-
Debt-free money. I interpolate that.
4.	[DOT]-should be issued as a clear asset to the state; so that money will be spent into existence, and not lent into existence.
The minister will recognize that as being exactly the contention of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the hon. member for Parry Sound, Social Crediters and the various others in this house. I go on:
5.	The fluctuating quantity of gold lying in the vaults of the banking system should never be permitted to govern the volume of credit and currency needed -by the country.
6.	The elimination of slumps and booms; and more direct procedure -for eliminating unnecessary poverty.
7.	The abolition of the debt system where all credit is created by the banks and hired out at interest to the country.
May I point out there that that is exactly the contention of the monetary reformers in this house, that debts should be eliminated from our economy, and our contention is that they can be, just as this man indicates, by the right sort of management of our financial system. I go on:
8.	Absolute state control over all foreign lending; and the adoption of the general principle that our foreign trade should -be so conducted as to preserve-
(a)	the interests of the home market,
(b)	the interests of -the empire countries and the English-speaking nations,
(c)	the interests of foreign nations,
and that this -principle should particularly apply in the case of home production and foodstuffs.
There is the advice of an eminent man of great experience, Vincent Cartwright Vickers. If I might impose on the committee to read just a few more extracts from another publication I shall have an end to speaking on this particular subject for this year.

speechtext:
I can realize how glad members are to hear that, but they would have four times as much cause for rejoicing if they *saw through the meaning of all this and therefore were in a position to enable this country' to face the future with a measure of confidence which it certainly does not have now as it faces the future.
[Mr. BlackmoreJ
The next publication from which I propose to read excerpts is a report of the London chamber of commerce on "General Principles of a Post-war Economy". Whatever may be said regarding the London chamber of commerce I think almost everyone will recognize it as an organization which is worthy of a measure of respect and of consideration. On page 3 of a little pamphlet which they issued I read as follows:
The chamber submits that constantly raised tariffs, -the imposition of quotas and prohibi-tioRS, -and other signs of growing economic belligerency between the nations in the in-ter-war period, were not the result of stupidity nor ill will but were, on the contrary, imposed for most compelling reasons. They represented attempts by the nations to defend themselves against very real and -pressing dangers. The chamber is_ convinced that until those dangers are recognized and removed, a direct attack upon trade barriers Can serve no useful purpose but will, on the contrary, merely -increase fear. In short, trade barriers are not themselves the disease but merely the symptoms of the disease.
May I interrupt there to comment thus? We read a great deal in the newspapers nowadays as to the desirability of lowering tariffs. The London chamber of commerce points out that to lower the tariffs without removing the causes of the tariffs would simply spell disaster. May I read again from the report, as follows:
It is widely admitted that there was something radically wrong with our economic system. I-t w-as palpably absurd that nations should be desperately anxious to export more of -their real wealth to other nations than they received in return. It was equally -absurd 'that men in want of the necessaries of life should be denied the money with which to buy them because there was a superabundance of -those necessaries and -therefore -their services were not required to make more. There has not, however, been the same readiness -to recognize that there must he a serious error in our economic thinking in order to produce, in action, absurd results.
May I comment again, that the thing which astounds me in this house is that there seems an indisposition on the part of so many hon. members to recognize that there must be something radically wrong with our system? There seems to be no desire to try to find out what that something is which is wrong, or what the remedy should be. Monetary reformers may be quite wrong in their analysis and their diagnosis of the disease, and they maybe quite wrong with respect to the remedy which they prescribe; but it certainly -would be a comfort to hear someone in the house offer an alternative remedy which would have as good reason for being considered as our proposal has. Strangely enough, neither in the banking and commerce committee nor in

Bank Act Amendment
this house have I heard any recommendation which seemed to offer any hope of solving the problem.
May I now turn to page 9 of this excellent little booklet and read as follows:
When, however, it is remembered that even wealthy nations have a large percentage of their population underfed, ill-clothed and ill-housed, it is clear that these would be the best recipients of this alleged surplus wealth. What is necessary is to improve the technique for the internal provision of money, so as to convert this human demand into effective demand.
May I interpolate here that this is exactly the contention of the Social Credit movement, exactly the contention of monetary reformists? What is needed, may I repeat, is "to improve the technique for the internal provision of money, so as to convert this human demand into effective demand." But may I recall now what was brought out in the quotation which I placed on Hansard from the "Canadian Banking System", which indicated how easily this country could obtain money to provide the internal purchasing power, and then ask hon. members to put those facts along with this statement and consider the whole question in the light of those facts? May I go on to read:
The chamber considers that it is a perversion of export trade to employ it for the purpose of exporting domestic unemployment and dumping it on other nations which already have their own problem to solve. These surplus exports might confer a benefit on some countries if they were sent as a gift; and the recipient country had an internal financial mechanism capable of distributing enough purchasing power to its people to enable them to buy excess imports of consumers' goods in addition to, instead of m competition with, the goods already there. They are, on the contrary, used for the purpose of getting other nations into unpayable debt; and moreover, the recipient nations have not the mechanism for distributing additional purchasing power to buy them so that they do, iu fact, displace goods already in the market, and cause distress selling and a slump in prices.
There is a passage which contains profound wisdom. I make no further comment; I merely commend that to the most earnest attention of all members of the committee. May I now read further, on page 10:
Instead of trying to equate supply with effective demand, the chamber advocates that, in future, effective demand should be equated with supply. There can be no such thing as genera] over-production, of which complaint was made after the last war, although of course there can be over-production of a particular commodity in relation to others. The real trouble is under-consumption.
The fundamental problems then, which a satisfactory system must be designed to solve are:
(1) The elimination of the fear and hostility resulting from the struggle of all nations to obtain an "active favourable balance of payments", the penalty of the vanquished being economic servitude to the victor. This struggle has resulted in attempts by all the nations to restrict imports by barriers to trade, and to increase exports by subsidies and other artificial means, and by the use of political and economic pressure.
(2) The distribution internally of the purchasing power necessary to enable the nations to-consume the whole of itheir own production:	if this were done they could
equally consume the goods of other nations which they might exchange for their own production. This problem is closely connected with (1) because an excess of exports over imports furnishes an excuse for increasing effective demand within a country (through the distribution of wages) without increasing the number of goods awaiting consumption in the domestic market.
I will burden the committee no further with quotations.

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of bill No. 183, to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses, the improvement of housing and living conditions, and the expansion of employment in the post-war period.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I imagine that one reason why the last bill, bill No. 134, with reference to credit to farmers, went through so quickly was that it was given a thorough study in the banking and commerce committee. The first comment that I should like to make at this stage of bill No. 183 is that it is so voluminous and so important that I feel it, too, should have been referred to a committee for thorough study. However, since that was not done there are two or three comments I should like to make.
First of all I may say that because this legislation will result in the building of some
houses in Canada and because housing is sorely needed in this country we shall support the measure when the vote is called. However, a number of features about it are very disappointing to us. To me the feature that is most disappointing of all is found in section 12, subsection 2, paragraph (b). By that provision the government insists that no assistance will be given to municipal public housing authorities to undertake on their own behalf the construction of low-rental or other housing projects. This matter was discussed when we were in committee on the resolution preceding the bill. At that time the minister said that he did not believe the municipalities could handle such projects with the efficiency that he ascribes to limited dividend housing corporations and to life insurance companies.
We take sharp issue with the minister on that point. In fact, I feel the stand he has taken is in the nature of an insult to municipal government in this country; and as a former alderman of the city of Winnipeg I resent the suggestion that municipal governments are not competent to undertake projects of this kind.
In addition to that, it seems to me that this provision of the bill is flying in the face of the whole tendency of this day in the matter of housing problems. I need only mention municipal housing projects in Great Britain, and in other places, to which I shall refer more fully when we are in committee, as outstanding examples of what can be done by municipal public housing authorities.
Further, as I said when the measure was at the resolution stage, I am satisfied there is a growing conviction among members of our city councils and municipal bodies that this is a social problem of the first magnitude which they should be tackling. They are the ones who should be encouraged to go in for the construction of housing projects. In my view they are the ones who can be counted upon to get the job done. They are closest to the people who require housing, and I still hope that the government will see fit to reconsider this part of the bill.
In Winnipeg at the present time a sum of $70,000 has been allocated from a housing fund left over from some years ago, and as a result the municipal authorities in that city are building a small number of houses. A short time ago in Winnipeg, during one of the moving periods when the housing shortage was particularly acute, the council renovated an old building, making it into suites of which we were not too proud but which were at least
Housing

clean and fit for decent habitation. The city is renting those suites to people in need of accommodatoin, and the managing of the project has been quite satisfactory. I am satisfied that Winnipeg is competent to carry out a municipal housing project, and I feel sure that is true of other municipalities as well.
When one looks at this provision in section 12 he realizes at once that it is in line with the underlying principle of the entire bill. Hon. members in this group contend that the problem of housing should be approached directly through the medium of public housing authorities. The stand taken by the government is that private lending institutions and private life insurance companies should have some of their risk underwritten, and that they should be encouraged to enter into housing projects. If, then, even on a limited basis any profit is made out of this very serious situation, that profit is to go to private interests. That, we consider, is in direct contradiction to the trend of the times. We feel, further, that that is not the way to get the job done.
When faced with the demands of war this government went directly at the problems facing it. When it decided to bring in a piece of social legislation to assist the children of the country, the government went at it in a direct fashion, by providing family allowances which, after next July, are to be paid directly to families in which there are children. But in facing this problem, that involving the need for housing accommodation in Canada, the decision has been to go at it in an indirect fashion.
Thus, apart from my dislike for the fact that some profit will be made out of this extremity in our country, and apart from the fact that the risk is being lessened if not effectively removed-a condition which seems to question the supposed virtue of private enterprise-* there is the fact that, in my opinion, this legislation will not result in getting the job done in the way it ought to be done.
The other outstanding disappointment in the legislation is the lack of any comprehensive plan, either in the bill or in the comments thus far from the minister. We feel that this matter of housing, both from the point of view for its need in the country and from the point of view of providing a large measure of employment in the post-war period, is one of the most important matters facing us at the present time. In our view what we should be doing is planning the rebuilding of our cities, and the revamping of the kind of homes in which our people in rural Canada must live. In other words, we should be getting a vision of a new kind of life for our people, one which

will express itself in the very best kind of homes modern technologists can devise, and also in providing adequate employment for our people after the war.
Committees have studied the problem. In particular I draw attention to subcommittee No, 4 of the James reconstruction committee, which was headed by Professor Curtis of Queen's university. That committee presented some of the basic considerations which should be faced, and went so far as to indicate the number of homes required in Canada in the next ten years, if we are to face up to the housing problem. The figure given in the Curtis report is 700,000. That report indicates that it can be determined where, in what cities and in what parts of the country houses should be built.
This legislation not only falls far short of providing 700,000 homes, but does not approach the problem of building those homes, with any plan as to where they should be built to meet the most pressing needs of our people. I have not the Curtis report before me, but one quotation I placed on record the other day is to the effect that the very first thing which should be done in approaching Canada's housing problem is to plan our towns and our country so that the construction of houses will be rational and will help to meet the needs of our people.
These, then, are the features about this bill that disappoint us. First of all, the municipalities have been snubbed by the provisions of section 12, which suggests that something is to be done about slum clearance, but which turns out to be only a bagatelle. Worse than that, the municipalities are to be assisted to buy land in slum areas for clearance only on the condition that they resell the land to a limited dividend housing corporation or a life insurance company. That feature is bitterly disappointing to us, and I say that after some little experience in the municipal field1.. We are also disappointed that the government has not seen fit to go at the housing problem directly, but has gone at it in a roundabout way by underwriting part of the risks of private companies. Perhaps worst of all is the failure of the government to bring down a definite plan for the remaking of our cities and towns and the building of houses on the basis of a programme designed to meet the needs of our people. Apparently houses are to be built only on the decision of private lenders and private insurance companies where the risks are the least and where profits, even on the limited basis provided, can best be made.
We suggest that that is not good enough for a generation of Canadians who dare to believe

Housing
that after the sacrifices they have borne during the past four or five years the time has come to rebuild Canada and shape a good life for our people. We shall vote for the measure because it will result in the building of some homes and Canada needs homes badly, but we hope that the time is not far distant when a government of the day will bring down much better housing legislation than we have before us in bill No. 1'83.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the most important bill that has come before this parliament this session. A general housing scheme is of national importance to our urban, suburban and rural communities. I wish to support the principle of the bill because I think if it is given a fair trial it will prove to be of great advantage after the war to those who are without homes. In the city from which I come nearly 100,000 people have had to leave their small homes and move into apartments, and we are becoming somewhat of an apartment city. The bill goes much farther than I had expected it would, and I am glad.
In 1935 I moved a resolution in the house on housing and reconstruction and an elaborate report was made. The government of the day was defeated, but the present government came in and in 1937 and 1938 the National Housing Act was introduced. The present minister has done a great deal of good work. About $83,000,000 has beeen spent by the banks with the government providing up to fifteen per cent, and this has done a great deal of good, not only in. the outskirts of the city but in the city itself.
At the present time there is a great scarcity of houses in our urban, suburban and rural communities and I am glad that this bill has broadened out considerably. It is intended to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses, the improvement of housing and living conditions, and the expansion of employment in the post-war period. That last is a very important .part of our reconstruction work.
The plan is quite elaborate. On August 5 the minister gave a detailed and excellent description of the wide features of this bill. The old National Housing Act of 1938 has been broadened out and made more effective. A man may own a small lot. He goes to a loan company, and in conjunction with the government they lend him money after an inspection of the property is made and specifications of the proposed house drawn up., That money is lent jointly by the government and the lending agency. The applicant repays in monthly
instalments which cover interest, fixed charges and taxes on the property. If there is any loss it is borne jointly by the government and the lending agency.
There is nothing that would create better health and happiness for the people than the provision of up-to-date housing. One of the main causes of ill health is poor housing conditions. I am glad to see the improvements that have been made in the bill. I am glad to know we are to have a modern system adapted to future needs, something that will improve public health. I have received many letters from men who are overseas. I received a letter recently from a soldier now in Normandy who formerly resided in. Eglinton riding. His wife has been living in a small home for four years, and he complains to me that she has received an order to move out by September 1 and cannot find another home.
This condition was explained to the government last Friday to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the Postmaster General and the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I do hope that there will be some way to get the necessary materials and labour for this work. This is a most urgent piece of workin fact it is a war work. It is needed to provide homes after the war for the large number of soldiers who will be returning to Canada. In the city from which I come there is only [DOT]062 per cent of vacant houses. Five hundred soldiers have received orders to move out and applications are being heard by the county judge under the overholding tenants7 act of the province. These people have no place to go. Last week the government came along and agreed to build five hundred houses for soldiers.
We should have had this bill years ago. As hon. members know, every country in the world is suffering from a lack of houses and there has been a lack of employment for those in the construction industry. On May 12 Mr. Churchill brought down a programme for the construction of 500,000 prefabricated houses in the old country. I hope that something will be done this session or after the session to see that Canadian industry gets its share of that business. I hope that the construction industry of this country will be greatly helped. I say again that this is the most important bill that we have had and I hope that there will be no delay in putting it into effect.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this late hour of the session we have before us this bill, one of the most important that has come before this house this session. I am going to be brief because it is too late to discuss a bill of this magnitude and it would not be fair to take up much time

Housing

in doing so. But I do want to place myself behind the proposal of the government to go on with this large scheme of rehousing and reconstruction. If I had any fault to find with the measure it is that the government is late in bringing it in.
Last fall, on November 25, a very large group of housing men came to Ottawa and presented a brief to the reconstruction committee, recommending the construction of some 300,000 houses in a five-year programme. I would have thought this bill would have been brought down much earlier in the session because the government was thoroughly conversant with the programme that had been presented, and if that had been done I believe that we could have had the programme under way now. Certainly we can do very little under this legislation to satisfy the demands for housing this year. The minister is familiar with the different presentations that have been made for housing construction during the last year and prior to that by the city of Toronto through the mayor and various members of the board of control who have been here on quite a number of occasions, one of them being last week. I wish to thank the minister for his kindly and courteous reception of that delegation from Toronto last week, when I believe that he undertook to provide money for the construction of five or- six hundred houses. [DOT] I believe that it had been previously agreed to build one hundred houses and the programme was changed or added to so that five or six hundred houses will now be built. The minister was exceptionally kind and courteous to the delegation, and apparently they went away quite satisfied. It is only right that the minister should have been as kindly and courteous and generous as he was to the delegation because the housing problem in Toronto is one of very great magnitude. I am not going to detail it here to-night because that has been done on many occasions. I will merely say that the demand for houses is very great.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) spoke of receiving several letters to-day. I received three letters myself to-day from returned soldiers. One of these soldiers belonged to that famous Toronto family which was widely pictured in the Toronto Telegram and the Toronto Star only a few days ago. I refer to the Seggie family on Harvie avenue, who have seven sons serving in this war. One of them returned from overseas just a few days ago and he was one from whom I received a letter to-day asking by what means he would be able to obtain assistance, from whatever organization I presume is to be set up under this bill, to proceed

with the erection of a cottage. He has a wife and small family, and is at present housed in two or three small rooms. That only serves to emphasize that the demand for housing accommodation in Toronto is very great indeed.
I would like to say a great deal on this subject because I have made an exhaustive study of it. But it is too late to say much now. I made my own survey of the housing programmes of many of the large cities of the United States:	Richmond, Virginia;
Memphis, Tennessee; Cleveland, Detroit, Washington and a score of other cities. I went carefully into their programmes and went out to see the various sites where they are building their houses, and I had prepared myself to give to the house what I had hoped would be a constructive address advocating housing.
But the minister has brought down his bill, and every minute that I take up I feel would only be delaying the actual starting of work under this bill. I do not want to do that. I am afraid that if I got started on the subject I would take too long because I have studied the matter exhaustively, and so I feel that I should simply urge the minister to proceed as rapidly as he can and in every way possible to get along with the actual construction of housing under this legislation.
When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was speaking he presented a request similar to what we have been asking for in Toronto, namely, that the federal government supply a sum of money to the municipality to assist them in providing housing. But that may not be in order. In any event I do not think it is provided for in the bill. But I can tell the minister this, from what I have seen in travelling around Ontario and other parts of Canada, that the demand for housing is far greater than I have heard anyone express here. Perhaps the minister knows. I feel sure that he must know that under the circumstances there is not a minute to lose.
Without taking up further time, Mr. Speaker, having said what I have said, I urge the speedy passing of this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to hold up the passing of the bill, but I should like to take a few moments to answer the criticisms made of the bill by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and also to make one or two suggestions which I think will be helpful.
I have felt for many years that one of the most important things we can do to help build

Housing
a strong virile nation is to see that our people are properly housed. Quite recently, and many times before that, I have urged that just as soon as this war is over and we are able to do it, active steps should be taken to improve housing conditions in Canada.
The lowest reliable estimate that I have heard as to our present housing shortage is 300,000 homes. I entirely agree with the policy which the government felt it had to follow during war time. It was felt that on account of the demands of war the people should double up and get along as best they could with our present housing accommodation until the war was over so that we would not be using vitally needed war materials and labour in the building of new homes during the war. But now that we can see the end of the war in sight it is gratifying to me that the government has seen fit to bring down such a comprehensive and all-inclusive housing bill as we have now before us. I do not see how it could have safely been brought down a day sooner. In fact, it may be that even this year, under the present housing act we may run into acute shortages of material and labour. With this new enabling legislation put on the statute books many people will want to get started at once to build homes, but I am afraid that they will find acute shortages of both materials and labour this year.
The criticism of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as I understand it, is twofold. In the first place he says that the present measure is one to add profits to lending companies rather than to supply homes to Canadians. I do not think I need to answer that argument. If my hon. friend will take the time to read the bill I think he will convince himself that no lending company is going to get wealthy out of lending its money and servicing its loans at 4i per cent.
As to his other criticism I believe I can speak with a little personal knowledge. He has in effect said that the government has practically insulted the municipalities by more or less by-passing them in this scheme. My first answer to that is this. To my way of thinking, the major part of any housing scheme is one that will supply homes to owner occupants. That is one suggestion I make to the government. As soon as this war is over I should like to see an all-out publicity campaign across Canada for every man to own his own home. The major part of the scheme is to supply Homes to owner occupants; the tenant part of the scheme is a very small part. I believe that we have in Canada a
type of citizen who wants to and should own his own home; we should have as few tenants as possible.
I well remember that in Ontario we had a housing scheme after the last war. At that time I was mayor of my home town, and pressure was put on me to have a rental scheme under which the homes would be owned by the municipality. To that I was strongly opposed, for this reason: a municipal landlord is the worst type of landlord you can have. In the first place, maintenance and repair costs are much higher when the landlord is the government or a municipality. Tenants do not take the same care of the property.

speechtext: And it costs twice as much.

Yes. The second point is that when a municipality or a government attempts to do anything it always costs more than when the project is built either by owners who are going to occupy the homes or by privately owned corporations. There is another point which I hesitate to bring up, but it is incontestably true. Tenants do not pay their rent to a municipality or a government as they do to a private landlord. After the experience of municipal housing in Ontario after the last war, I congratulate the minister upon the fact that he has not embarked upon the kind of scheme which was such a failure in that province.
It may be that in the city of Winnipeg and one or two other municipalities they were fortunate enough to have as chairman of their local board someone who was more than ordinarily clever, who spent all his time on the work, and made a success of a such a scheme. But looking at the whole picture, I can tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre of dozens of municipalities in Ontario which have sustained losses and are thoroughly disillusioned with their venture into municipal housing for rental purposes.
As to the criticism regarding slum clearance, I believe it was two-fold. In the first place the amount was not large enough to suit my hon. friend; I believe he called it a mere bagatelle. Well, to me it seems quite an amount to be provided in the first year of the coming into force of the measure. Hie other complaint was that where a slum clearance scheme is entered upon, the land must be cleared of the slums and new homes built which must be resold to a limited-dividend corporation. Am I right?

No: if the hon. member wants to be fair, that is not quite what I said. I quoted the wording of section 12, subsection

2 (b), which is to the effect that after the land has been bought and cleared it must then be sold to a limited-dividend housing corporation or a life insurance company so that they and not the municipality, may construct the project.

speechtext: In order that I may have that clear, what is my hon. friend's complaint in regard to the dividends being limited with respect to a project of this kind?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext: I was not objecting to the dividends being limited; I was objecting to corporations being set up with the privilege of making dividends at all out of our housing extremity, instead of having it tackled directly by a public authority.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, as I understand the proposal in the bill, the services are to be supplied at cost; the reason why the dividend is limited is to restrict it to actual cost; and I do not believe that you would find any municipality willing to supply these services and put up the interest, for the carrying charges.
I have some rather decided views on slum clearance, and I should like to take a moment to express them. I think it is a most futile thing to spend millions of dollars in clearing a slum and then allow another slum to build up in the very same city. The way to clear a slum is to remove the cause. Obviously no tenant lives in a slum as a matter of choice; he lives there only as a matter of necessity because he cannot afford decent housing accommodation. Therefore I say that the physical clearance of a slum has very little appeal to me. I think we should make housing accommodation available to the extent necessary to supply it at less than an economic rental to those unfortunate groups in our society who cannot afford to pay an economic rent; I refer to old age pensioners, mothers on widows' allowance, part-time war pensioners, war veterans with a fifty per cent pension who cannot get employment; and I would restrict the utilization of any low rental scheme to these limited groups.
Generally as to slum clearance, once you remove the cause of the slum; once you supply decent housing accommodation for the people who are now living in slums, neither governments nor municipalities will have to clear those slums; they will become depopulated because people will move out of them and the owners will have to tear them down at their own expense. I repeat that it is futile to tear down slums without removing the cause and then allow other slums to develop in the same municipality.

In this connection may I say I am very glad that the municipality is tied into this scheme, for this reason. Many slums in our large cities are located in an area midway between the business section and the residential section, on land which is being held for speculative purposes, the owners hoping that it will grow in value and eventually be in demand for business uses. That is no place to build more homes; such areas should not have people living in them at all. Gnce you provide decent housing accommodation in an attractive part of the city at a rent which these unfortunate people can pay, your slums will become depopulated and the owners themselves will pull them down.
With regard to this bill, I compliment the minister and his advisers upon drafting what, in my opinion, is one of the finest housing acts that I have ever read or that has been passed by any country to this day. Ever since 1936, when I first came to this house, I have taken a great deal of interest in housing. I am free to admit that housing was one of the things which motivated me in seeking election in 1935. At that time we had 60,000 of the building trade in idleness on relief, and a serious shortage of homes. I felt that something should be done about it, and I was willing to try to do my part.
The National Housing Act of 1937 has done a wonderful job. Under that act we have built something like 20,000 homes which are practically all owner-occupied. And while the government participated in the cost of those homes, the losses to date are less than ten cents a house. I am very glad indeed that the minister and his advisers have chosen to build the new act on the firm - foundation of the National Housing Act and to simply expand that project.
The reduction in interest rate is very gratifying and will pull down substantially the monthly payments. The increase in the amortization period is very gratifying and will also tend to that end. When you cheek the figures you find that a man to-day under this bill can build a house costing $4,000 and puts up only $400 of his own money; and do you know what the monthly payments are? They are $18.04, and at the end of thirty years he owns that home which under normal conditions would rent from $35 to $40 a month. Yet this man, on the payment of $400 as a dowm payment, plus $18 a month, in thirty years, instead of having a collection of thirty years' rent receipts owns his own home.
Another feature about the bill that pleases me immensely, and one that I have been urging for some time, is that provision is to

Housing
be made whereby the unpaid balance of the loan is to be taken care of in the event of the death of the bread>-winner. Term insurance will be made possible so that if the breadwinner is taken away, the widow will own the home without encumbrance. That is a decided advance. Think of the sense of security and independence a man will have who has bought a home under this legislation and knows that if anything happens to him his wife and family will have a home clear of encumbrance.
Another feature I like is the extension of the list of lending companies. Under the old act the lending companies were restricted to insurance companies, loan companies and trust companies. Now the list has been very much broadened; trustees and trust funds may come under the measure, as well as building societies, credit unions and cooperative credit societies. Then there is provision for the owner who wishes to do part of the work on his own home. He can do that and be allowed for it in the cost of the home.
There is another provision whereby men may group together, so that a group of individuals collectively may build homes for each other. There was such a cooperative arrangement in the town of Oakville in my riding, where men working at the basket factory wanted to build a number of homes for themselves, and they all chipped in and helped in taking out the foundations and doing labouring and carpenter work and painting. That sort of thing was cumbersome under the old act, but now provision is made whereby such things can be done.
The next feature is the one which to me is the most important in the bill. The down payment has been reduced to a point where everyone in this country who wishes to do so can start to buy a home for himself. In the case of a home costing $2,000 a man has to make a down payment of only $100 and he is on the way to become the owner of his own home. In the next group, from $2,000 to $4,000, the down payment is fifteen per cent on the second $2,000, and over $4,000 the down payment on the excess of $4,000 is thirty per cent. This is only as it should be because, if a home costs seven or eight or ten thousand dollars, there should be a substantial down payment before work is started.
I like the measure also because it recognizes the fact that we need a good many new homes oij farms, whereas the old act has no such provision.
I have taken a good deal more time than I had planned and I apologize for doing so.
I wish to close with two suggestions. I should
like to see a nation-wide campaign put on for every man in this country to own his own home, and in furtherance of that campaign I should like to see a provision made whereby a man can buy a second-hand house, a house already built, and finance it together with improvements to it in the same way exactly as he finances a new home. Obviously there are a good many homes in the country which are tenant-occupied. I suggest that it would make for a happier people if every man owned his own home and I do not think secondhand houses should go into the discard. We should make provision for these tenants to buy the houses in which they now live, and make the necessary improvements and repay the cost of the house and of the improvements on a monthly payment basis in the same way as new homes are paid for.
My other suggestion is this. I fear that we shall run into a great scarcity of material. Already scarcity has caused a distinct stiffening in the price of lumber and other building materials, and I would urge upon the minister and his department that steps be taken to organize for and make available building materials in large quantities in the immediate post-war period.

speechtext:
At this late hour I do not intend to delay the house for more than a few minutes. I have already spoken on the resolution stage and said some of the things I wished to say. I then expressed approval of the bill and congratulated the minister upon the great improvement over the bill introduced in 1938. As I said before, much that we have in this bill should have formed a part of the 1938 measure, because of the recommendation in the Purvis report in 1937 that provision be made for the unfortunate individuals in the lowest income group who cannot afford to pay an economic rent. However, there is no use now in complaining of that omission.
I am glad even at this late date that we have such a comprehensive bill, but I should like to make one or two suggestions with reference to it. First of all, this measure, which after all is a very important health measure, should receive careful consideration and support. I do not think there is any single factor which contributes more to the sound health of our people than good housing. We all know that overcrowding is a source of ill health and danger from infectious diseases and produces many social evils that we should like to avoid.
This housing measure is to be administered by the Department of Finance. We all know how hard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Housing

Ilsley) has to work. I suggest that we relieve him of this part of his work by placing the housing act and the administration of it where it properly belongs, namely, in the Department of National Health and Welfare. It is not in any sense of the word a financial measure and hard-headed financial men should not be responsible for its administration. We want a humanitarian such as we hope will be in charge of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Therefore, I am suggesting that the Minister of Finance be relieved of some of his onerous duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What about the Minister of Reconstruction, would he not be the man?

speechtext:
No; I prefer to have it under health as it is in England, because, after all, it is a health measure. In considering all the items that go to make up good health, I believe that this is the most important of all. In the consideration of the national health act in the special committee on social security a good deal was said about the importance of decent housing in promoting good health.
I am glad to know that the minister has made provision for a central bureau for technical research and many other matters connected with the promotion of good housing and community planning. That is undoubtedly very important. I do not intend to attempt to go into the details of the bill, but I should like to comment upon the interest rate charged on money to be used in the construction of those low rental houses. May I congratulate the minister upon reducing the rate to three per cent. In so doing I think he has done a very great service to the community. As I said before, he might take a leaf out of the book of the United States housing administration and reduce the interest still lower to two per cent, and further to arrange to purchase bonds of those housing companies which would enable them to carry on their work more satisfactorily in their effort to meet the needs of a large portion of our population. In my opinion, the amount set aside for this purpose is not sufficient, and should be increased to 8100,000,000, instead of $50,000,000.
Now I should like to say a word about slums. I entirely approve the proposal of a grant for the clearance of slums. It is much more far-reaching than the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) seems to indicate. My chief criticism is that a sufficient amount has not been allowed, and that it should be $50,000,000 instead of $20,000,000. There are slums in every large city in Canada. They are the breeding place of infection, immorality and criminal tendencies. I believe that all these

places should be cleared out as speedily as possible and replaced by suitable, adequate, decent houses for these unfortunate people. The municipalities have not the money to undertake this work. Unless they are assisted by the federal government I am afraid this work will not be done.
The hon. member for Halton spoke about this measure as being the most advanced measure in the world. Although I heartily approve what the minister is doing, I am afraid I cannot be as extravagant as that in my praise. Great Britain has built many houses over a long period of years. Since the last war she has built some three or four million houses. She has under contemplation, following this war, the building of from four to five million more houses. Continental countries, such as Sweden, Austria and some of our enemy countries have been building houses for twenty or twenty-five years. The method that was suggested here a few days ago of prefabricated houses had its origin in Europe and has been carried out successfully there for a number of years. Therefore we are by no means the most advanced country in the world in so far as providing housing for our people is concerned. We are making progress; we are a young country and we cannot do everything at once. I think great commendation should be given to the minister for bringing forward as good a bill as this. I hope that it is only a beginning, and that in time all our people will have decent houses in which to live. I do not know that I need delay the house longer to-night. My views on the housing problem were published in a report ten years ago, and all I need say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, is that this measure has my hearty approval.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to go on record as entirely supporting the bill. My only criticism is that it does not go far enough. It has, however, one defect which I think should be pointed
out to the minister at this early stage of the discussion. The defect is that sufficient recognition is not taken of the three governing bodies, namely municipal, provincial and federal.
This is a bill to assist in the construction of houses. Section 12 provides remedial assistance to do away with slum areas and congested conditions which have developed as a result of our industrialized civilization. In my view, insufficient attention has been given in the bill to having proper town plans prepared. Town planning is just as important for a man who builds a $4,000 or a $5,000 house as it is in connection with a definite scheme of slum clearance.
Section 12 (2) (a) gives slight reference to the necessity for having a plan. Slums in many of our cities to-day are not composed of cheap houses. Rather they are composed of areas which years ago were residential sections. But because those residential sections have been improperly or unscientifically constructed they have deteriorated to slum conditions. Hon. members will know of cities right across the dominion where this condition has developed. Older residential areas have become blighted areas because they were not properly planned. They were constructed without consideration for transportation, for access to arterial highways, for schools, or for industrial planning. The consequence is that we have* a destruction of investment.
This bill proposes the expenditure of a certain amount of money. Whether that amount is adequate or not I shall not now discuss. I am of opinion that a great deal more will have to be spent to do a real job, but I shall not discuss that feature at the present time. However, when we spend these sums of money we must be sure that we are making a good investment. We cannot be sure of that until we have secured the cooperation of the provinces and municipalities, so that the houses built will be houses which will not deteriorate through industrial blight.
The city of Toronto has made a master plan. They took several years to do so, with the result that the plan is in my opinion an excellent one, and demonstrates just how alive and awake municipalities are to this pressing need for housing.
The city of Montreal has quite recently gone into the business of making a town plan. The recent issue of the Journal of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada, in connection with a survey and replanning of Montreal, has four significant things to say in this matter.
Homing

I shall read them, because I believe they are of importance to every municipality in the country:
Montreal, like all other cities which grew during the development of industry and trade ' in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, is characterized by four typical deficiencies:
(1)	There is no planned relationship between working districts and residential areas from the standpoint of easy communication. The transportation system is consequently unduly large and complex.
(2)	The prevailing west wind was not considered in the location of industrial and residential areas, hence industrial smoke and fumes pollute the air over most of the city with ill effects to the health of the community and obvious aesthetic undesirability.
(3)	Houses in the residential areas are built too densely and are oriented without regard to sunlight, and are, therefore, predestined to become slums.
(4)	Recreational areas are lacking where they are most needed.
The correction of such deficiencies must begin with the separation of city elements according to functions and the coordination of these elements by a transportation system.
While I think this bill is a step in the right direction, we must see that the houses we are going to build will be permanent investments. Let us see that they will be the dwelling houses for numbers of years of those people for whom they are built, and let us build them so that we may not find in a number of years that, because of an undesirable change in industry or in transportation or for other reasons, the areas in which we/have built houses and in which we have made investments have become blighted areas. That is very important. We must in every instance insist that wherever these new homes are built there must be a proper and coordinated town plan so that the investment will be a permanent one.
A proposed draft bill has been offered by the province of Quebec architectural association and this can be found in the July issue of the Journal of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada. I do not intend to go into it in detail because it is much too long. It sets out all the salient facts with regard to the necessity of having our investment made in a properly planned way. In the reconstruction period there will be no more important industry than the building industry. The building industry probably more than any other can solve the problem of unemployment. We must see to it that the building industry has a plan prepared for it now, so that when demobilization takes place there will be year round work for all. I wish to emphasize again that before we go ahead and commit ourselves we should act in a scientific manner and not build houses haphazardly all

over the countryside without seeing that they will maintain their value and usefulness as dwellings.
Mr. DOUGLAS G. ROSS (St. Paul's): Mr. Speaker, for many years I have been connected with the Toronto Housing company, a semi-philanthropic institution in Toronto. This is a limited-dividend company which was set up in 1913 by some public-spirited citizens. The dividend was limited to six per cent and the capital stock was about $100,000. The city guaranteed the bonds of the corporation to the extent of eighty-five per cent, which meant that there was roughly $800,000 of bonds and $100,000 of stock. The company went along very nicely until the depression of 1931-32. The bonds were floated in New York.
Two developments were carried on, and the rentals of the units ran from $20 for a one or two-roomed unit to about $40 for a six-roomed unit. The idea was to have accommodation for various sized families. But the depression came along in 1932 and vacancies increased. Also the exchange rate was against us. Dividends had to be discontinued. Many families in Toronto were doubling up; vacancies increased; the company finally got into difficulties, and at the present time it owes the city of Toronto quite a lot of money.
Some provision should be made in this bill to refinance companies like this and put them on. a proper basis. This company has had the experience of running these projects and I really think it would be a good idea to put it on a proper basis. The ten per cent exchange works against us in paying the interest and also the principal in the United States. If the company could be reorganized to take advantage of this three per cent provision it could get out of its difficulties. I am sure it would be quite willing to reduce its capital.
One clause in the bill provides for the ratio as between rentals to be charged and the family income, and states that it shall be such rate as the minister may deem to be fair and reasonable. In any housing projects that are carried on, provision should be made for different sized families. There are many low income families with two or three children and provision should be made for them. I do not think we should have all units the same size.
Ever since I have been in this house I have advocated slum clearance. There are slums in my constituency, as the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) knows. A large part of the survey referred to in his book

Housing
was carried on in that area. We have not been able to do anything about these slum areas and they are becoming worse and spreading. I am glad to see provision made here for this work, but I do not know whether the $20,000,000 provided will be sufficient.
There must be cooperation between the federal, provincial and municipal authorities. Those three bodies must enter into this whole project. After all, the municipality is controlled to a large extent by the provincial government. I have no more to say except that I endorse this bill which has been a 'ong time overdue.

speechtext:
1.	Canada has an observer on the joint committee of non-munitions committee and the London food committee.
2.	Canada is a full member of the combined production and resources board and of the combined food board which deal with the allocation of industrial and agricultural products amongst the united nations. On UNRRA, the agency dealing with relief and rehabilitation requirements, Canada holds the chairmanship of the supplies committee. On other committees operating in more limited fields, Canadian interests are protected in some cases by full membership, in others by an observer and in others by working arrangements with operating subcommittees.

Close contact is maintained between officials of the centre and the Canadian trade commissioner in Cairo. These provisions enable Canada to be specified as a source of supply for any commodities or materials in the supply of which Canada is interested.
The Indian supply mission has a representative in Ottawa working closely with the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Munitions and Supply.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN INTRODUCTION OF MEASURE FOR WAR SERVICE GRATUITIES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN INTRODUCTION OF MEASURE FOR WAR SERVICE GRATUITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will doubtless have noticed that in to-day's Votes and Proceedings there appears notice of a motion in my name relating to war service gratuities to be paid to members of His Majesty's Canadian forces who served on active service during the war and to assist them in their reestablishment, having regard to the length, sphere and terms of their service. I should like to have the bill presented to hon. members at as early a moment as possible.
If we followed the ordinary procedure it would be necessary to wait until to-morrow to advise the house that His Excellency has been informed of the subject matter of the resolution, and it would not be possible to proceed in committee of the whole with the resolution until later. Unless there i9 an objection to my so doing, I would ask leave of the house to introduce a motion which would enable the house to take up the resolution in committee to-day, with the understanding that if the resolution carries the bill itself will later be distributed so as to be available for hon. members for second reading and discussion of its provisions at another sitting of the house. If this course meets with the approval of hon. members I would ask the permission of the house to introduce the following motion: [DOT]
That notice of the resolution standing in Votes and Proceedings with respect to payment of war service gratuities be deemed sufficient, and that the said resolution be considered in committee of the whole during to-day's sitting of the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN INTRODUCTION OF MEASURE FOR WAR SERVICE GRATUITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can see no
objection to meeting the Prime Minister's suggestion with respect to having the resolution advanced this stage so that we can discuss the resolution to-day. I would like, however, to point out that it is one hundred and twenty days since on January 27 this measure was mentioned for the first time in the speech from the throne. While it may be quite a good argument to say that legislation which is perhaps not properly classed as a war measure should be left to the end of the session and that war measures should be given preference, this proposal is definitely both a war and peace-time measure and one which in all propriety should have been before us long ago. It is six and a half months since it was first envisaged in the speech from the throne; and as I understand from the Prime Minister's suggestion to-day, and in this I think he is quite right, it is doubtful whether the bill even yet is printed and ready for distribution.
I am not anxious to have to make the observations which I am making this morning. Few people in the house are more weary than I am or more anxious to see the house come to a conclusion reasonably soon; and I suppose most hon. members who understand the strain which members generally, and those who are leaders in the house particularly, are under during this time of rush and pressure of legislation, will recognise the significance of the remarks I now make. At the risk of being unpopular with some hon. members, since the pressure is so great to have the house rise at the end of the week I do not relish
Business of the House

the idea of suggesting, but I do suggest, that we shall have to give this proposal the full measure of consideration to which it is entitled, no matter how long we have to sit. More than that, I cannot see how we can very well give this bill full consideration and still end our session on Saturday night. No matter what the personal inconvenience to members of this house or to any of us, it is pretty small compared to the inconvenience that the men this measure is designed to help have to endure for us while they are serving overseas and in other places. Parliament should give this measure the fullest consideration to the end that it will be the best measure we can possibly present to these men and women when they come back. If it is possible to do that before the end of this week, by all means let us do it. But let us not hurry this legislation; let us not be accused of hastening it just for purposes of speed. Rather let us make sure that whatever time and whatever money are necessary shall be allotted to a measure which is so very important that I regard it as perhaps the most important to come before this house at the present session.
I do not think we would ever forgive ourselves if we were inconsiderately to push this bill through or give undue signs of haste. After all, it has to do with the lives and the future of men and women who are our No. 1 citizens. Definitely we owe this to them. I know the government will be in thorough agreement with what I have said, but I thought it only fair to point out to the public and to the house generally that, whatever happens, this measure must have the fullest consideration regardless of the inconvenience to members. Whatever responsibility there may be, in all fairness the government must share it, because this measure should certainly have been before the house for consideration long before this.
