May I say at once to the leader of the opposition that I greatly appreciate what he has said by way of accommodation to enable us to bring in this resolution immediately. I hope that hon. members of the house are in agreement with the leader of the opposition to have the resolution introduced at once and the bill brought in later. With regard to the bill being printed may I say to my hon. friend that I have a copy of it in my hand. It has been printed but there are one or two clauses which the government would like to look over before .having the bill distributed. There will be no delay in having the bill distributed.
With my hon. friend, I wish it might have been possible to have this important measure brought down earlier in the session. It is a war measure, but as my hon. friend will see, its provisions relate more particularlj- to the post-war period. I mention that only by way of explanation. The session has been a very heavy one. Some ten weeks or more were occupied in discussing the war appropriations and that accounts in part for there having been some delay in the introduction of this measure.
The measure is one that affects five departments of the government. As hon. members are well aware, the ministers of defence, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Pensions and National Health, all of whose departments are affected by the measure, have had exceptional duties to perform during this latter part of the session and along with their officials have been giving every moment of their time to the immediate questions that are before us. I mention that as one of the reasons why it has been impossible to bring this measure before the house sooner.
May I say to the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) that when a similar measure was enacted after the last war it was not brought before parliament at all, it was enacted by order in council,

Canadian Forces
and that not until after the war was over. The present administration took the view emphatically that we should not attempt to enact a measure of such importance by order in council even if its introduction involved lengthy discussion here. We felt that hon. members of both houses had a supreme right to consider and to be immediately associated with the enactment of a measure of as great importance as this. For that reason we have brought it in as part of the programme announced in the speech from the throne.
Let me say further to my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, that I agree with every word he has said about the time that should be devoted to the consideration of this measure. No one in the house is more anxious to see the session ended than myself, and I am sure there are some members of the administration who are even more anxious than I am because in many directions they have carried heavier loads than I have. But that should not cause us to fail to give the measure every consideration that this House of Commons should give to what I think, along with my hon. friend, is perhaps as important as any measure introduced, not only during this session but during this parliament and I might say during any parliament of Canada.
I believe that the measure is one that will commend itself to all members in this house. I think the view of the House of Commons generally with regard to the recognition to be given to the men who have offered their services at the risk of their lives is a view that is held in common, namely that there is nothing that we can do, having regard always to what the public interest makes possible, that could be too much in the way of recognition for the services that they have rendered and are rendering.
Apparently the house is agreeable to proceeding with the resolution, so that I shall move, seconded by the Minister of Mines and Resources:

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That in order to recognize the service of members of His Majesty's forces who have served on active service during the present war and to assist them in their reestablishment having regard to the length, sphere and terms of their service, it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide:
1.	That to every member of the naval,
military or air forces in Canada, who, during the war which commenced on the tenth day of September, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine, has enlisted for general service in such forces or who, pursuant to the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, may have been at any time obligated to serve without territorial limitation, or who has served in the Aleutian islands, there be paid, subsequent to the retirement or discharge from the forces of such member:	.
(a)	the following as a war service gratuity in respect of the period during which such member was enlisted or obligated for general services or served in the Aleutian islands:
(i)	for every 30 days of service in the western hemisphere, excluding the Aleutian islands, $7.50;
(ii)	for every 30 days of service overseas, or in the Aleutian islands. $15;
(b)	for each six months of service overseas, or in the Aleutian islands-7 days' pay and allowances;
(c)	subject to certain conditions, a reestablishment credit, to be available for specified rehabilitative purposes, equal to the total amount of the gratuity payable under clause (a) of this paragraph.
2.	That a similar gratuity and credit be payable to persons domiciled in Canada on or after the tenth day of September, 1939, who subsequent to that date served on active service in any of the naval, military or air forces of His Majesty other than those raised in Canada who resume residence in Canada within one year of the date of retirement or discharge from any of such forces; subject to there being deducted from any such gratuity or grant any
War Service Gratuities

' benefit of a similar nature which any such person has received or to which he is entitled from any government other than Canada in respect of his service.
3.	That the said gratuity and credit shall not be payable to any person who has been retired or discharged from the forces by reason of misconduct.
4.	That payment of the said war services gratuity may foe made under certain conditions to or on behalf of the dependents of members of the forces who have died either prior to or subsequent to retirement or discharge from the forces before receiving such gratuity in whole or in part.
5.	That the said gratuity and credit shall not be subject to attachment, levy, seizure or assignment, or to taxation.
6.	That the amounts required under the said measure be paid out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.
_ 7. That the expenses necessary for the administration of the proposed measure foe paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament for such purpose.
8. That the governor in council may make regulations governing all matters relating to the payment of gratuities or the making of reestablishment credits available and the evidence to be required in support of applications therefor, .to prescribe penalities for breaches of the said regulations and generally to give effect to carry out the objects of the measure.
He said: The proposed resolution implements the policy set forth in the speech from the throne, respecting war service gratuities and measures to supplement the existing rehabilitation programme. It is designed to give a token expression of the gratitude of our country, in so far as anything can begin to express the country's feelings, to all the men and women of Canada who in the present war have voluntarily offered their services at the risk of their lives. It is with a sense of deepest obligation to the fighting forces of Canada that, on behalf of the administration, I beg leave to introduce the resolution.
Gratuities represent an attempt to recognize a service upon which no price can ever be placed. Those whose services are involved have not thought of their duty as something which would entail a monetary reward, but as I shall seek to explain, the proposed war service gratuities will be both an acknowledgment and an encouragement: an acknowledgment of burdens borne and sacrifices endured; and an encouragement to the men and women who, having voluntarily given their services, have survived the vicissitudes of this the most terrible of wars in the world's history' and may soon wish to resume those civilian occupations which were laid aside by them by the onset of war, or to enter upon new callings as a means of providing a livelihood through the years to come.
I should like to make it clear that gratuities are not to be confused with rehabilitation and 
reestablishment, though they will contribute to these important ends. This measure is the crowning feature of a comprehensive rehabilitation programme which provides for several carefully considered forms of assistance. These include:
A.	Maintenance allowances to veterans and their families in the form of
1.	out of work benefits if employment is not immediately to be had, and unemployment insurance if employment is interrupted;
2.	temporary incapacitation grants;
3.	"awaiting returns" grants to farmers and fishermen;
4.	vocational training grants;
5.	university training grants;
6.	post-graduate training grants;
7.	unemployment insurance benefits.
B.	In addition, under the Veteran's Land Act, assistance is given for land settlement and fishing.
C.	Employ'ment assistance is afforded through
1.	compulsory reinstatement in previous employment ;
2.	preference in civil service competitions;
3.	veterans' welfare officers.
D.	The provisions of the National Housing Act are of benefit to veterans as well as civilians.
The provisions for pensions and medical treatment have been steadily broadened over the past five years. At this present session veterans' insurance legislation has been enacted.
The measure provides cash, and credit which may be converted into cash; for approved rehabilitative purposes. It is an advance over former gratuity and bonus legislation in that, while it gives to the veterans a nucleus of funds which they may use according to their own best judgment without official restraint, it also provides an equal amount to be used directly in rehabilitation. By way of illustration, I might mention: purchase of a home under the national housing act; purchase of a business; purchase of tools and implements of trade; any other purpose soundly recommended as practical and contributing to reestablishment may be approved by the minister.
I think it can be said, and with pride, that in so far as there can be such a thing as generosity towards those who have been prepared to risk their all in war, no country has been more generous in its recognition of the services of men and women in the armed

War Service Gratuities
forces than Canada has been. The rehabilitation programme, set in motion in Canada while the war is still being fought, has been widely commended abroad; and some aspects of it have served as a model for certain of the allied powers. Beyond the question of acknowledgment altogether, there is the concern of the present administration that the already comprehensive provisions should be improved wherever possible. Only constant attention will ensure the sympathetic and efficient reestablishment of veterans in civil life.
Some of Canada's fighting men have been on active service for nearly five years. They deserve, as they will have, a first claim upon our resources for reestablishment. Throughout its various measures for reconstruction and social security, the government is seeking to ensure that there shall be for those who have thus served our country and the cause of world freedom abundant opportunity and security in body and mind.
This measure is the culmination of an earnest desire to provide for service men and women what we believe the nation will expect any government to provide. It is a rounding out of measures provided over nearly five years of war. In the many years I have been in parliament I can think of no measure which it has been my privilege to introduce which has afforded me as deep a feeling of pride and satisfaction to introduce as the present measure. It is one to which I believe the response of the parliament and people of Canada will be unanimous, whole-hearted and sincere.
I have already mentioned that the bill based on the resolution is the work of five departments, namely, the three defence departments, the finance department and the Department of Pensions and National Health. I should perhaps add the Department of External Affairs, as well. Explanation in detail will be given by the ministers of national defence and the Minister of Pensions and National Health.
The total cost of the gratuities and reestablishment credits is very difficult to estimate. Assuming that the service of the present members of the armed forces is extended to March 31, 1945, gratuities in an amount of something over $400,000,000 would be payable.
I wish to pause here to say that by assuming that the services of the present members of the armed forces is extended to March 31, 1945, I do not wish to imply that the war will extent that long or that it may not extend considerably beyond that period. I only mention that date in order to enable hon. members to see the basis on which the estimate has been arrived at.
In estimating the cost of the reestablishment credits provided by this bill, which are in addition to the gratuities, it is necessary to take into account the present programme of benefits for discharged men under the Veterans' Land Act and under various orders in council providing for vocational training, university training and so forth.
The estimated amount of the reestablishment Credits which will be set up under this bill for the benefit of discharged members of the forces will be approximately $350,000,000. Some veterans will, however, take up their credits, either in whole or in part, in benefits under the Veterans' Land Act or under various schemes of training. To the extent of these offsets, the $350,000,000 estimate which I have mentioned will be reduced.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I take it from the language used by the Prime Minister when he introduced the resolution that the ministers of other departments would be prepared to make further statements with respect to this programme. Whether these will be formal statements is something which the house must of course leave to them.
I have no desire at this stage to go into any of the details of the resolution, because it has been in our hands only a few minutes. Because of that I do not think hon. members are in a position at this stage to make other than general observations. When the resolution reaches the committee stage we shall have an opportunity to ascertain the true picture and to learn the details of the proposal and the methods by which this laudable object which the government has in mind will be attained.
I wish to say that it can be echoed and reechoed that whatever material or financial compensation we give to the men and women in the armed forces we cannot fully discharge the obligation that rests upon this parliament, this government and the country. This measure I am sure is one of the items of legislation which will find a favourable response not only in the purses and in the minds of the people of Canada but in their hearts as well. The sacrifices that men and women make in their service on the fighting fronts cannot be measured by the yardsticks ordinarily employed.
In addition to making sure that our men and women are given a hearty welcome when they come back, the question of jobs, the question of the rehabilitation programme, the question of cash gratuities such as are sug-

War Service Gratuities
gested here, and the rehabilitation credits, are the least that we as a country must provide at this time.
Hon. members will recall that during past sessions while the war has been in progress and before I became leader of the opposition in the house I suggested that from the beginning of the war there should be set aside a nest egg to be put beside the service pay and allowances of the men in the armed forces so that at the end of hostilities they would have something that they could call their own, something on which they could lay their hands that would be more tangible than educational advantages and many of the other things that go toward helping the men when they come back. It is very important to them. If that suggestion had been carried out they would be assured of some cash in their hands to do the things that they will find it necessary to do when they come back.
Then there is this other thought. While these men and women have been away, opportunity has been afforded to the civilian section of our population to put away something for a rainy day through the medium of victory bonds and the high level of our national income. That has not been possible for the men and women in the armed forces. A measure such	as this,	which	envisages	theplacing of cash	in the	hands	of men	andwomen when they come back, will be a step forward in equalizing the positions of the men and women in the armed forces and the civilian population. Actually there can never be an equalization of their positions, but this, I say, is a step in that direction. The men and women in the forces will at least feel that as a nation we	are trying to	take up	theslack that they	lost in	the opportunity	for
earning which might have been theirs had they stayed at home. Because they made it possible for those who remained here to live in security and safety, let us by this measure try to do something by way of compensation for them. Let us try to equalize their financial position, although actually we cannot equalize it no matter what we give them in dollars and cents. I am confident that the resolution will have the general support of the members of the house.
Of course close study will have to be given to the details of the measure, but from the broad general point of view of helping these men with cash gratuities it will be only the question of the distance and the degree to which the government will go that may bring out any issue as far as members of parliament are concerned. We may find that the government have not gone far enough. We may find
CMr. Graydon.]
that by certain changes in the bill, when it is brought down, we may be able to do something even better in behalf of these men than is called for in this measure. But this will be a signal occasion, I think, and one time when this House of Commons will try to do its best, each member in his own way and in his own right, to see that this measure does what is proper, not just in relation to what this nation can afford but in relation to what these people deserve when they come back. I believe that must be the sole consideration.
During the difficult period of stress and strain of this war, particularly when this nation, the empire and the united nations were in such danger, there was not a member of this house or a citizen of Canada who would not have been willing to throw aside every bit of his material resources, every hope for the future, every business possibility, in order that these men who were serving in the areas of danger in our behalf should have everything they required and more. So that while in connection with other legislation we may have to apply other yardsticks it seems to me that the true yardstick by which we must measure this legislation is what these men and women require and deserve when they return. When we have established that, we will find the money; we will find the materials and the resources, or we shall have failed to live up to the pledges we have made and the requirements of the time in which we live.
This is our first obligation. It is too bad that it has come before us at this late stage of the session, but it remains our first duty. I hope hon. members will pardon me if on an occasion like this my emotions are perhaps more conspicuous than they might be. Looking back over the period between the last war and this war we realize that as a nation we cannot afford to have a single man or woman return to civil life in Canada dissatisfied with what we are prepared to do for those who have fought for us. It seems to me that is a cardinal principle, not only so that we may play fair with them but that we may have a future of which Canada can be proud. It seems to me this will be of major significance to our future, because we shall only have a Canada that is worth while if we have done our duty to the men and women who have made it possible for Canada to survive.
I want to close by repeating, with all the emphasis and conviction I can possibly summon, what I have said before in this house. I am quite sure most of us feel that during this war-time period we civilians have done little, no matter what may have been our station in life. It is all very well for people to say that the responsibilities of civilian life have been

War Service Gratuities
heavy. Of course there have been great responsibilities, but they have been responsibilities without corresponding dangers. I think I can speak for every member of this house when I say we realize that we have done little while they have done so much. That fact, I think, will prompt the House of Commons to support this measure, not because we are satisfied that it has gone as far as it should but because we believe it is a step in the direction of discharging an obligation which is greater and more important than any other obligation resting upon the citizens of Canada to-day. Let us see that when parliament adjourns we shall be able to look back upon this session, whatever may have been its other achievements, and say that at least we, as citizens of Canada and representing other citizens of this dominion, have not hesitated to go as far as possible to meet the demands of this moment, to recognize the sacrifices that have been made by others in order that we might live and progress and still have a worthwhile Canada for ourselves and our children in the days to come.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I think we can all agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) that the house will -give unanimous approval to this measure. As has been suggested, it is something that should be done, and I am glad the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has brought this measure before the house instead of adopting it by order in council. I believe this is the proper [DOT] thing to do, and I believe it is also the courteous thing to do because it gives every hon. member of this house an opportunity of sharing in what is intended to be a tribute to the men and women who have served at great cost but which still must necessarily fall short of adequate recognition. I want to say, however, that while we are doing this we should not forget that it will only tide them over temporarily ; that it is our duty as a parliament to see to it that conditions in this country are such that after this amount has been expended, or the other gratuities have been used up, men and women will have the opportunity to earn a decent living. That is the real obligation we owe to the men who have fought to preserve the democratic way of life in our own country.
I am not going to say very much more. The bill is not before us; thi3 resolution foreshadows it. There is one omission, however, to which I should like to draw attention at this stage, in case it can be rectified before the bill is discussed. I notice that Canadian nationals who resume their residence in Canada after having served in the armed forces of Britain will be entitled to these benefits. That is good. But there is one group of men who
I think deserve well at the hands of this country, and who are not included unde this legislation. I refer to the merchant seamen, who again and again have undertaken risks that are equivalent to those which have been undertaken so often by the men in the Royal Navy and on the field of battle; and those risks have been continuous. I suggest to the government that before this bill is discussed some further consideration be given that point. There are too, of course, the men in the ferry command, who are excluded from a great deal of our wartime legislation. The ferry command is a small group, and the merchant seamen as far as Canada is concerned is not a very large group. I think they should be given some consideration. May I say to the house without emotion and in the coolest of words I can muster that I think every individual in this country will support the government wholeheartedly in this rehabilitation measure.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words regarding this particular resolution, coming as I do from a district which in the last war sent 55,000 soldiers overseas and which in this war has the largest representation of any city and county in Canada. During this session we have been dealing largely with material things. We passed a billion dollars for certain agencies. Only the other day, after all these years, we provided a small gratuity for the Fenian raid veterans. The men who came back from the Fenian raid and. northwest rebellion were given a little grant of land which many of them never saw. Then we tried to take care of those who went overseas in the last war. When you consider the three sections of this resolution you cannot help thinking by way of comparison, of what has been provided for family allowances. All that a man can get under subparagraphs (a), (b) and (c) is S540 for three years' service. What is that as a gratuity to a soldier who has served in Sicily and Italy and Normandy under the intolerable conditions that exist, under what was simply a hell on earth?
I am disappointed in the amounts provided by this resolution. For the past few weeks we have been dealing with material things in many bills involving millions. I have been visiting the homes of many people who have lost their loved ones in this war. I represent, in part of my constituency, a poor man s district. Many of these men served in the Fenian raid, others have belonged to the militia down through the years, and their sons and grandchildren are now serving overseas.
War Service Gratuities

Why should not this gratuity be large enough to put these people in the position they were in before the war? That should be the principle governing the payment of gratuities. They should be put back in civil life to a position where they can make a success of life and be able to send their children to high school. Just recently I received a letter from a soldier in Normandy who has since been killed in action. He told me that many of the young men overseas never expect to see their families again.
I have seen many of them go overseas and many do not return. This young soldier quoted what Saint Paul wrote from Rome in II Timothy as he was about to be brought before Nero a second time. Those were very troublesome times in the history of the Roman empire. Saint Paul wrote to Timothy:
Thou therefore endure hardships as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.	.
No man that warreth entangleth 'himself with the affairs of this life: that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
This country did not have to choose these men. Many of these soldiers went with the first and other divisions as volunteers; in fact nearly all were volunteers. Is this all we have to offer them when they come home for what they went through?
I notice that this is a different scale from the one we used when we were dealing with war workers, and I wish to pay a tribute to what all war workers have done. At the same time a soldier cannot even get gasoline for his car when you see all these young people going home from camp over the week-end. Some of them will be killed before the war is over.
In my opinion these gratuities do not go far enough, they do not provide sufficient for reestablishment. They are much less than the gratuities provided in the civil estimates. Nothing has been done for the parents of those boys who have suffered the extreme barbarism of the axis powers, the prisoners of war who have been shot. We should pay the parents of these boys a gratuity of $5,000 or $10,000 for the brutalities that have been practised on their boys and then collect from Japan and Italy and Germany in reparations at the conclusion of the war.
There is no provision in this resolution for the young people who rushed to the colours in the early days of the war, who went over to join the Royal Air Force and all that kind of thing. They, and all Canadians in the imperials, should be included. Even the maximum amount that would be paid under sections (a), (b) and (c) will not exceed the sums that some of our soldiers' families have

been paying in interest to shark loan companies at the rate of two and a half per cent per month. These families have had to give chattel mortgages and bills of sale on all they possess.
With thgse gratuities many of these soldiers when they come home will not be able to clothe themselves and send their children to high school. I started with the school board and I have been intimately in touch with the secondary school system since that time. I have been talking to high school principals and soldier families about this thing. One of .them commanded one of the most distinguished regiments that went from the Toronto district in the last war and he is now the principal of the largest collegiate in Toronto. I was talking to him about it the other day and he told me that if something more ' is not done by way of gratuity than was done in the last war some of the youth of the schools whose parents were in the forces might not be able to attend secondary schools but would have to go to work.
I think some of the soldier widows of this war should be given homes which are to be provided by the Minister of Finance in addition to the total of this gratuity. I realize the government have a difficult problem on their hands and I believe in many ways they have done the best they can under the circumstances. I do not believe that these small allowances will commend themselves to the wisdom and judgment of the country especially when the people are expecting us to do our duty at a time like this.
I am disappointed in the resolution because it does not go far enough. It does not provide for a proper system of housing and for a high cost of living bonus to be paid to all dependents of soldiers and adjusted from time to time to include better allowances for their children and protection from unemployment after the war. That is what is covered by a resolution of mine that has been on the order paper since the war started. There should be some provision for a moratorium from foreclosure and eviction as well as more adequate and improved housing for soldiers and their families at low cost. This is only a start and not at all what I had hoped for. It is only pin money in any event.
Mrs. CORA T. CASSELMAN (Edmonton East): Mr. Speaker, as I read the resolution it applies to all members of His Majesty's forces and makes no distinction between men and women, and so I take it for granted that women are included at the same rates as the men, and I express my deep appreciation of that. I think it is only fair and just that the

War Service Gratuities
women should be given this gratuity at the same rates as the men if they have given similar service.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Except those who have seen service in the Aleutian islands.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I am going to refer to that. It applies to men who have been obligated by order in council for service without territorial limitation, and different rates apply.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Suppose within a few weeks of the end of the war an N.R.M.A. man decides to go active; would he be entitled to the gratuity?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: He would get his gratuity, for the time that he was an enlisted man.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: But not for the time he was under the N.R.M.A.?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
That is right, and if an order in council were passed within one week

War Service Gratuities

of the end of the war, the same thing would apply. It is only after a man is obligated either by enlistment or under N.R.M.A. to serve without territorial limitation that he is entitled to the gratuity.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It only covers the period of universal service?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
That is right. It does not apply to men unless or until they have enlisted for general service or the area of their service has been extended to include universal service, to use my hon. friend's expression.
Next it includes those'who have served in the offensive operation in the Aleutian islands. In reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Yorkton, assuming that the service in the Aleutian islands did not last for six months would the gratuity be proportionate to the length of service there, the Minister of Justice has just advised me that in the draft bill the gratuity does apply proportionately.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Every woman in the service has enlisted. They are all volunteers. Is that not right?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Then they would come under this as volunteers.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Is the gratuity payable to men who have already been discharged?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: In other words, the provisions of the bill will be retroactive?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Then there seems to be no
mention at all of the men who are serving in the merchant navy, or in the corps of fire fighters, or in the auxiliary services such as the Legion, the Knights of Columbus, the Salvation Army and the Y.M.C.A. Is it the intention that they should be entitled to the gratuity? I think these groups have not been treated fairly throughout, and I would urge upon the government that provision be made to pay them the gratuity.
One other question, which has to do with clothing allowance. As the Minister of National Defence knows, there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction over the smallness of the clothing allowance. I should like to know whether there is any intention of increasing that allowance to a reasonable amount, or whether this gratuity is to be taken as covering that expense also.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
In connection with a short statement which I intended to make with

respect to the bill, I had it in mind to mention the matter of clothing allowance, on behalf of my colleagues and myself of the defence services. The matter has been considered, and what is proposed to be done is to amend the regulations by increasing the clothing allowance to make it an allowance towards clothing of $100 fiat for all ranks, that is including the officers. May I add that that is arrived at, not by any meticulous computation of the cost of a collar or a shirt or a pair of socks or boots or an overcoat or things like that, because some people require more and some require less. It is felt that the best that can be done is to arrive at what appears to be a substantial-a very substantial-contribution towards outfitting, and leave it to the individual to decide whether to spend more or less than that.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I do not think anybody will contend that $100 will enable a man going out of the forces to equip himself with clothing for civilian life. I doubt if any hon. member will contend that; and my submission throughout has been that men should be entitled to enough to enable them to go out and equip themselves with clothing. I do not understand why the government has not'' made *that provision.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I made this announcement at my hon. friend's suggestion. We are not on the bill, and I suggest that if we want to discuss clothing allowance I should be glad to do it at any appropriate time. But is this really the time to discuss the merits or demerits of the proposal? I made an announcement which I thought would be regarded as a pretty satisfactory solution of this matter. It compares with a grant of $35 in the last war, when money would not buy as much as it will buy in this war. There was an increase to $65 some time ago, and it will be further increased to $100. That is considerably ahead of, at least, Australia and New Zealand, although I am not saying that we should set them up as a yardstick.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
They do not have to buy
overcoats over there.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
At the same time, we do have some regard to what other people are doing.
As I said a minute ago, we are not attempting to take a man who has not a stitch of clothes-if you can imagine a man of that kind-and fit him out from head to toe; nor are we taking into consideration personal desires or preferences or degrees of comfort or of style that a man wants. We are saying, "There is $100 on account of an outfit; you

War Service Gratuities
do anything you like with it." We are not asking him to buy clothes, and my hon. friend knows, as most other hon. members know, that a good many men will not use the money to buy clothes, because many of them-and here I am speaking from some personal experience and knowledge-have their civilian clothing yet. I do not think it can be assumed that a man will have no civilian clothing when he comes back. I hope that with this explanation we can leave the clothing grant at the present time-if my hon. friend wants to discuss it later we can do so-so that we may get on with the resolution.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Will the difference be paid to the men who have already been discharged and have received only the smaller amount?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: No, there has been no provision made for that. As my hon. friend knows, the $65 was not made retroactive-or rather it was made retroactive, I believe, to November or some such time, but not to the beginning of the war.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The minister did not deal with my other question, with regard to the merchant navy, the fire fighters and the men of the auxiliary services.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: As my hon. friend sees, they have not been included in this bill. The persons with whom we have been dealing are the members of the armed forces; that is what this bill was intended to cover. I heard what my hon. friend said, and the same question has been raised by others. But these services, as my hon. friend sees, are not included in the resolution.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Will the government give consideration to providing for these men?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I am not in a position at the moment to speak on that point.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I would point out to the minister that in Normandy to-day, and in Italy, the men of the auxiliary services and, I believe, the fire fighters, are serving with the troops.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: And some of them have been killed.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
They should be treated in the same way as the troops. As to the merchant navy, we all know what they have done in the war. Probably the war would have been lost but for their services. I suggest that some provision should be made for them, if not in this bill, perhaps by order in council, because that is the way in which provision has hitherto been made for them.
Paragraph 4 of the resolution says:
4. That payment of the said, war services gratuity may be made under certain conditions
100-3P0i
to or on behalf of -the dependents of members of the forces who have died either prior to or subsequent to retirement or discharge from the forces before receiving such gratuity in whole or in part.
Could we have some idea what is meant by that paragraph? Is it only to cover the cost where a man dies after being discharged and before actually getting the money, or are there other types of cases which are to be covered?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It would be better, I think, if the committee saw the bill. If I remember correctly, the only condition in this connection which is provided for in the bill is that the amount may be paid to someone other than a dependent to be administered for the benefit of the dependent in certain cases. I think that is the only condition.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It really is not very extensive.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It does not cover very -many cases. .

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It is a procedural situation which does arise sometimes when it is thought best to make payments to someone for a dependent.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver South is quite right in deprecating the fact that the merchant navy, the fire fighters and the auxiliary services are left out of this. I cannot understand why a man coming back from the fire fighters' organization, for example, to practically a strange country, should not be treated exactly as one of the service personnel. He has all the problems of rehabilitating himself, yet he is without the protection of the legislation which we are providing. As to the merchant service, I never could understand the attitude of completely ignoring them. In my opinion the merchant navy has made the greatest contribution to this , war of any service, either on land or in the air, yet they are completely left out of everything. Your air force, your army, and the rest of them would have starved to death in Britain had it not been for the merchant navy.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Everybody would have lost the war if it had not been for somebody else-in every case. [DOT]

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I am not going to argue that with the minister, but that is a plain statement of fact. They have all made their contribution in their own field; there is no doubt about that. You could not have landed the army or the air force in Britain or Italy or in France without the services of the merchant navy, because they would have starved to death otherwise. The greatest contribution has undoubtedly been made on the water. How-
War Service Gratuities

ever, I will not argue about that. Evidently the government has made up its mind on the question. I rise to ask the minister one question; others have anticipated other questions I might have put. Paragraph 1 (c) of the resolution reads; "subject to certain conditions, a reestablishment credit, to be available for specified rehabilitative purposes, equal to the total amount of the gratuity payable under clause (a) of this paragraph." I have received many letters from men in the service who have mortgages on their homes. They are finding it difficult to make the payments. When they come home, can this gratuity be used for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
There are two distinct portions of the resolution, one having to do with cash and the other with credit. This is intended as far as possible to remove the inequality existing at the present time. We have already made provision under the reestablishment order P.C. 7633 in particular, and in connection with the Veterans' Land Act, for benefits for ex-servicemen, first of all on the land, secondly on small holdings, and thirdly in fisheries. Then there are these specific benefits indicated in P.C. 7633. Men who come back and are not able to avail themselves of the specific benefits already provided by this parliament will find ten different headings, which will be analysed in the bill, giving them an opportunity of accepting certain reestablishment benefits such as paying for a home, paying for furniture, paying a part of the premium on returned soldiers' insurance, and various other benefits which are all specified. It is intended to be a constructive provision for the returned fighting men as well as for the nation,
Mr. GI'LLIS: This is applicable only to those who are not being helped by some other method?
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver Centre); Not necessarily at all. The two might in certain cases be supplementary one to the other.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I have in mind individual Canadians, men of Canadian nationality who, not having been able for various reasons to join the Royal Canadian Air Force, paid their own way over and joined the Royal Air Force or the Air Transport Auxiliary, or entered some branch of the army, not Canadian. As Canadians, however, they either proudly made the supreme sacrifice or came back disabled after serving in the British army or any of the allied armies. Is there any provision for such men?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: In paragraph 2 of the resolution.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Is this simply an
amount which they can borrow with interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: No. This is an amount that is placed to their credit. If they are sick or if they choose to do so they can take advantage of one of about ten different benefits in regard to reestablishment. This amount is there for that purpose, over a number of years if necessary.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Repayable?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It is a straight gift. It is a reestablishment grant.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Hon. members have very properly lauded the service of the men engaged in the merchant marine, and it seems to me a notable circumstance that in this case they are omitted. I agree with the Minister of National Defence that it is easy to argue that this set of people could not have done so and so without the help of that other set of people; but, as he has also said, they have all worked as a team. If they have worked as a team, then under this legislation certain members of the team are receiving certain grants which others are not. I think arrangements should be made either in this or in some other measure to prove that the services of merchant seamen, without which the troops could not have reached France on two occasions, should be recognized. Will the minister explain paragraph 1 (a). It says "for every thirty days of service in the western hemisphere." Does this apply to enlisted men or women engaged in service between the Atlantic and the Pacific? To whom does it refer-everyone in the active army?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: My hon. friend speaks of the active army. That term has been used very loosely by the public and many people have the impression that the active army means solely volunteers. Everybody w'ho is full time in the Canadian army is in the active army, so that in that sense (a) does not apply to everyone in the active army. I may say that (a) (ii) applies to persons mentioned in the first part of the paragraph, those who have enlisted for general service in such forces or who, pursuant to the National Resources Mobilization, Act, 1940, may have been at any time obligated to serve without territorial limitations, and it applies, to use the phrase of the leader of the opposition, only to those who have enlisted or obligated themselves for universal service, and for the time only for which they enlisted or were obligated for universal service and served in the western 'hemisphere or the Aleutian islands. That is the application of (a) (ii).

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Let us leave out the
application of the National Resources Mobil-

War Service Gratuities
Ration Act and consider only those who are enlisted in the Canadian Army. It leaves out the reserve army and the enrolled people. Do all the rest of them come in under this? Those who belong to units or batteries or service units which subsequently perhaps have gone overseas or perhaps have not gone overseas- does it cover all of them?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes. But my hon. friend must be careful. He says " which subsequently have gone overseas."

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: They come into another category.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes; that is it. They come in under (i). The time spent by them in Canada comes under (i) and the time spent by them overseas comes under (ii). The scheme of the last war was not this scheme. Under the scheme of the last war, if a man had been overseas any time at all he became tagged as overseas and got the overseas rate based on the whole period of service, with a limitation of three years. This is different in that it actually gives a man credit for service in Canada at a certain rate and service overseas at a certain rate It is a double rate overseas plus something else-that is, plus seven days pay and allowances for six months of service overseas or in the Aleutian islands, and that is pay of rank. This is also in addition to the present rehabilitation grant which is paid to every man who is discharged and which consists of one month's pay and allowances of rank.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: This is over and above that.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Will that be continued?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That will be continued, and it is over and above the clothing allowance I have mentioned.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
This includes the
veterans guard?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes. -

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
In connection with paragraph 1, subparagraph (c), would it not have been fairer if that reestablishment credit had been made equal to the total of the amounts set out in subparagraphs (a) and (b)? I note that it applies only to the amount set out in
(a)	. Would the minister explain why a' person cannot get up to the total of both (a) and
(b)	?

the seven days, which amounts to about $50,000,000 based upon the pay and allowances of those who have served.
Mr, GREEN: A man who served overseas should be entitled to get the full amount as a reestablishment credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: He is. The other is a special category.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The total of (a) and (b).

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It is based entirely on the months of service.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Is the gratuity payable in cash on discharge, or will it be paid at so much a month?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The gratuity is payable in instalments monthly at the rate of pay and allowances which the man was receiving at the date of his discharge.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It is not to be paid in a lump sum?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Is there any power taken to pay it in a lump sum?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I do not remember that
.there is.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Is paragraph 2 wide enough to cover the case of the young Canadian who enlisted in the Royal Air Force in 1937 or 1938? Many young Canadians did that and took part in the battle of Britain. I do not believe this paragraph is wide enough to cover them. We had that same condition to meet when we were amending the Pension Act of 1941, and we put in a special clause to take care of those very men who had gone over before there was any sign of the war. I notice the language of the paragraph is as follows: ". . . persons domiciled in Canada on or after September 10, 1939." I suggest that is not wide enough to cover these young men who went to the Royal Air Force.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I am taking a note of that.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Does the minister think that
is the case?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
