speechtext:
Yes, that is right. It
depends, of course, on his intention. That is the test of domicile. It may be that he was domiciled in Canada. As a matter of fact I think the phrasing is taken from the order in council of 1918, but I shall look into that and see.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I think it should be cnecked up. .

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
With regard to merchant seamen and the auxiliary services and the fire fighters, as I said before, this measure is intended to be a special measure for-members of the armed forces. I am not sure whether in the regulations of at least the Department of National Defence the auxiliary service officers might not be included'. My hon. friend shakes his head. I have in mind a situation which came up the other day which makes me think they might be included. But obviously merchant seamen are not included. Obviously fire fighters are not included. Another group that my hon. friend has not mentioned is the pilots of the ferry command.
I think you could extend the list not ad infinitum but to a considerable distance to show, to use my hon. friend's reference to my expression, that everybody- is a member of the team somewhere; but there is some place where you have to say: "Yes, you are a member of the team, but you are doing something else." Munition worker's in Canada are members of the team, but they are not included in this bill. Therefore it depends' altogether on the importance and risk and so on of the work that is being done. I yield to no one in my admiration of the work of the merchant seamen and of other classes as well. As I said before, I am not in a position to say that the government will give consideration to putting it in this bill. I should not think that would be the proper place for any provision to be made for them. The Prime Minister is carrying the bill and I am speaking in his presence. Certainly we shall discuss the matter of inclusion to see whether some separate provision could be made for others in these classes.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South with respect to paragraph 2. I can- appreciate the fact that domicile means much more than residence. At the same time the word "domicile" does not seem a clear enough distinction between Canadian citizens who may not have been domiciled in Canada on that particular date and may not have been resident in Canada, and others. As I read the paragraph it may throw

those benefits open to persons who were not Canadian citizens although they may be domiciled in Canada. I believe the word "domicile" should be checked very carefully to see that it does bring in the right class of people.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I do not think it is intended to limit it to Canadian citizens who were resident in Canada on September 10, 1939.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: What will be the position of -members of the three services whose service has been partly on this side and partly on the other? A sailor is a typical example. A sailor is afloat at times and at shore establishments at other times. Is he covered for the whole time of his service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Perhaps I can illustrate the statements of my colleagues -by taking a specific case. Take the case of a private soldier in the army who had one year's service in Canada and two years' service overseas. If that man had twelve -months' service in Canada he would receive $7.60 a -month, or $90. For the twenty-four months overseas at $15 a month he would receive $360. In other words the total gratuity payable to him immediately, or within a few months after discharge, would be $450.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Would he not come under subparagraph (b) ?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: He would first come under subparagraph (a). Then of course in addition to that he would get seven days' pay and allowances for each six months overseas, which would give the private soldier another $77. In other words that -man would have a total of $527. plus one month's rehabilitation grant, plus clothing allowance. In addition to that, to answer the hon. member for Yorkton, that man would be entitled to a rehabilitation credit of $450 over and above the amounts that I have mentioned. In other words he would be entitled to a credit equal to his cash gratuity, which credit he might use to make a deposit on a house, to pay insurance premiums, to buy furniture, to do any one of the various things mentioned by the Minister of Pensions and National Health. That is over and above the cash grant. That credit in itself is a straight grant without any interest, without any loan, without any repayment or anything else, but it must be used for certain specific purposes.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: If he were an officer it would be correspondingly higher?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
No; it is a flat rate. Officers and men get the

War Service Gratuities
same gratuity. In the matter of the rehabilitation grants, they are based on pay and allowances and go, of course, according to rank.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
That hardly answers my question with regard to the sailor who is sometimes afloat and sometimes at a shore establishment.
Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City)': The same principle would apply, as I see it, though I should like to think that over a bit. Take the sailor who has served six months at Stadacona barracks at Halifax, and say a year and a half at sea. I would assume he would be credited with six months at the rate of $7.50 and eighteen months at the rate of $15.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
And after that period suppose he is attached to a shore establishment for possibly a year?
Mr. MACDONALD (Kingston City)': Then he would go back to the $7.50 rate. These things would all show on his papers, and the matter could be calculated exactly.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I should like to pursue the inquiry about the payment of this money, because there seems to be a good deal of confusion here. I understood the Minister of National Defence to state that this money would not be paid as a lump sum in any instance. How i^ a young man to be able to buy furniture or a home or anything else if that is the case? I know many of these people are just waiting to come home and get themselves set up.
. Mr. RALSTON: I think my hon. friend is under a misapprehension. What I said was that the cash gratuity, the basic gratuity, was payable in instalments. The reestablishment credit, which is equal to the basic gratuity, is there in a lump sum and can be drawn upon for any of the specified purposes in such sums and subject to such limitations as will be provided in the act. In connection with the reestablishment grant of one month's pay and allowances, the provision is that it shall be paid on the same basis as the pay and allowances the man was receiving at the time of discharge. This means that the credit is there and he can get that credit in the form of a cash grant, but he gets the gratuity in monthly instalments.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Then from what the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services said, and using his figures, a man would get $450 as a credit which could be used for the purposes I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: But if he wanted to buy both furniture and a home he would have to wait for his gratuity, for a period of six months or so. He could not use both these amounts of money to establish a home and furnish it; he would have to wait for the gratuity.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes, but the amount of the credit would be available to him immediately.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is the $450, but he must wait for the remainder.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The cash gratuity is paid in instalments.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
The navy minister gave
the house the impression that these two sums were available, but actually they are not. The credit is available, and the rest of the money is paid in instalments. The man gets the credit and the instalments will be used to pay off the credits undoubtedly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I am sorry if I was not understood. Let me take again the case of a man with one year of service in Canada and two years of service overseas. His total gratuity is $450; that is cash which will be paid to him in monthly instalments. In addition he is entitled to a rehabilitation credit of $450 which he can use for certain designated purposes, and which as I understand it will be paid to him in a lump sum at any time within a certain period of years, I think three years or perhaps even up to ten years. Having been given his gratuity of $450; having obtained his pay and allowances for one month; having obtained his clothing allowance; having obtained his allowance of seven days' pay and allowances for every six months overseas-having obtained all that money within the first few months, he can come back any time within a certain number of years and get another $450 with which to buy furniture, pay insurance premiums, make the down payment on a home, buy tools or do various other things set out in the bill. That is the lump sum payment.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
What check will be made to
see whether this money is really used for the purpose stated? I understand that it can be used only for certain purposes, but what will be the result if the man uses it for something else?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
The total amount is to his credit and must be used for one of these approved projects, which are all set out in the bill which will be introduced If the total amount of his credit is not
War Service Gratuities

used for one of these purposes, the rest of the money can be used for another of these ten schemes.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
The
navy minister mentioned a man in barracks at Halifax, say, and a man who would be at sea. Would Newfoundland be considered at sea or in Canada under this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The man has been ashore in Newfoundland?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Then he would be considered to have been in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes; it would, be in the western hemisphere; and the measure provides that for every thirty days of service in the western hemisphere the gratuity shall be $7.50. I do not say that if a man happened to come in for two or three days, as they often do, while his ship is turning around, that would be worth bothering with; I am referring to the man who was permanently stationed there. He would get the $7.50 rate.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
That
is the man in the barracks in Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes, I think so.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Then consider the man at sea. Would you count a man at sea as soon as he got on board his ship, whether or not he is in harbour?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Order. I should like to read citation 439 of Beauchesne:
The object of the resolution recommended by the crown is to give the house a first opportunity to discuss the advisability of making a certain expenditure. The details of the projected measure are not then disclosed and debate is confined to the resolution which should not be lengthy. . . .
Direct questions, I believe, should not be asked at this stage.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Here we are in the dying cays rf the session and we are being choked off from asking questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Order; I hope the hon. gentleman will get the meaning of what I have just said. I am only citing the rule to the committee, and doing nothing else. I am not dictating or trying to choke off discussion. I am saying it is out of order to ask direct

questions which could be more easily answered on the bill itself, when the ministers haVe their officials in front of them.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I was only trying to get it definite in my mind as to who were concerned in this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The western hemisphere includes the continents of North and South America, the islands adjacent thereto, and the territorial waters thereof, including Newfoundland, Bermuda and the West Indies. It will be noted that Greenland, Iceland and the Aleutian islands are thus, for the purposes of this bill, considered to be overseas. That is quite clear, I think.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is all right. Now I want to find out about the man at sea. I understand the government considers a man at sea only when he is out of the harbour, or is a man at sea as soon as he is assigned a ship?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I would have to think that over. I have a note here, but I do not know that it is very clear. It states that duties performed outside the territorial waters of Canada, or in a seagoing ship of war, are held to be overseas. I would think that service in a harbour probably would not be classed as seagoing service.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Then
a man who was on a ship for a year might be classed as being at sea for only four or five months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Yes; I think that would be possible; I believe my hon. friend is right, though I am not sure.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The minister was going to tell us whether boys in the navy would count their time from the time they got on the ship and until they left or from the time the ship left the harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Overseas service is defined as service involving duties to be performed outside the western hemisphere and includes service involving duties required to be performed outside of Canada and the United States of America and the territorial waters thereof in aircraft or anywhere in sea-going ships of war. If that man was on a sea-going ship of war he would be entitled to a gratuity on the higher scale. If he was on a ship in a harbour which

War Service Gratuities
was not a sea-going ship, he would receive a gratuity on the lower scale. That is my interpretation.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: If he were on the triangular run from Halifax would he include all the time he was in port at Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
For only a day or two?
Mr. FRASER (Peterborough West)1: A few-days.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I would say he would be included.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Before the recess a question was raised with regard to air force men who left Canada in 1937 and 1938. I feel that the resolution as it now stands does not cover these men. Section 2 provides that gratuities shall be payable to persons domiciled in Canada. Anyone who left Canada in order to join the permanent force or the Royal Air Force I presume would have lost his domicile, it being a matter of intention. If he were joining only a volunteer force the situation would be different.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Those men who went over before the war enlisted under what were called short-term commissions, and they intended to come back to Canada. Speaking generally, I think they would retain their domicile.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I realize that those who took short-term enlistments or period enlistments would not lose their Canadian domicile, but I am thinking of those who joined permanent forces, whether the British regular army or the Royal Air Force, to make it a career. I believe they would lose their domicile and I suggest that consideration be given to that particular phase. This morning the Prime Minister stated that this measure was to be a tangible expression of gratitude by the Canadian people to those who have voluntarily served.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I should like to say, in so far as one can express gratitude for so great a service.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I appreciate that that was in his mind, as it is in mine. Some reference was made to the fact that this system is much more extensive and comprehensive than that in effect anywhere else. Will the minister tell us something of the system recently adopted in the United States of America with reference to mustering out pay? To what extent is this plan modelled on the legislation which became law in that country within the last few months?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: What my hon. friend has said with regard to air force personnel will be taken into consideration.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I wanted to cover the navy and the permanent army also.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I have not the particulars of the mustering out provisions in the United States, but speaking roughly their mustering out pay varies from S100 to S300 depending on the length and sphere of service. These payments apply up to the rank of colonel; it is a flat rate, the same for everyone up to the rank of colonel.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I have the act here, but I do not know whether it includes all the amendments.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: As I remember it, the bill at first provided for payments from $100 to $500, and the maximum was reduced to $300.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The United States legislation is more generous as to short-term service, but not so generous as to long-term service.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: There is a floor under it.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It is $300 for persons who have been on active service outside the United States for more than sixty days.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I thought the service had to be eighteen months.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: This is the act of 1944, and it provides that those who perform active service beyond the continental limits of the United States or in Alaska shall receive $300 if their service is for sixty days or more. If their service is within the confines of the continental limits of the United States and is sixty days or more, they receive $200. Anyone who has served less than sixty days receives $100. It is difficult, Mr. Chairman, to know the entire position without having the bill before us. I do not want to contravene any rule, but we are trying to get this through.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: They are not my rules; they are the rules of parliament.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Your interpretation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I just enforce the rules.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I hope no harm will be done if we happen to contravene a rule, particularly when we are cooperating in order to have this matter brought before the house as quickly as possible.
Paragraph 4 of the resolution states that payment of a war services gratuity may be made under certain conditions, and some explanation of it was given this morning. However, I could not follow the minister exactly

War Service Gratuities

as to the conditions under which it would be payable. Where a soldier was killed on active service a year ago and his widow or other' dependents are receiving a pension, will the gratuity be paid in addition to that pension?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is so.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Some mention has been made of men serving in the navy. What is to be the rule for the men who are flying in the western hemisphere? Under the income tax law a man wdio spends so many hours in the air, even though he is serving in the western hemisphere, is entitled to exemption just as though he were overseas. Are the men who are flying in Canada or in the territories adjacent to Canada to be treated as overseas or as men who are serving at home?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: If the service involves duties required to be performed outside of Canada and the United States of America and the territorial waters thereof in aircraft, they would be regarded as overseas.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is, the men who are flying on the Pacific coast would be treated as though they were serving at home and would not be entitled to the $15 but will be paid at the rate of $7.50?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I said that if the service involves duties required to be performed outside of Canada and the United States of America and the territorial waters thereof-
I am reading from the bill-they will be treated as overseas.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Will the minister amplify that statement? He knows about the men flying on patrol on the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean men flying out over the Pacific?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes. Will they be treated as overseas?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: If the service includes duties required to be performed outside of Canada and the United States of America and the territorial waters thereof.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I am afraid that that language would not cover them. I suggest that the government give further consideration to treating all the men who are flying in the same way as the lads who are on service overseas.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: All the men? Men flying in Canada?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes. I have another question. Is this act to be administered by the Department of Veterans' Affairs or by the Department of National Defence?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I must ask hon. members to adhere to my ruling that questions cannot be answered until the officials are here to assist the minister. We are on the resolution, not on the bill. *

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Apropos of your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I understand that the idea of discussing a resolution in committee is that the views of the members may be expressed before the bill is introduced. The government may adopt some of the changes which may be proposed in the discussion, so that I think that we are in order in discussing the various provisions of the bill and asking for an explanation of the provisions.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: May I add a word, Mr. Chairman. This resolution comes into the house under different conditions from most resolutions. We have tried to facilitate the bringing in of the resolution. When a resolution is before the committee the broad principles upon which it is based are brought out, information is given in answer to questions, the discussion goes out to those affected by the proposed provisions of the measure, and their reactions come back to us in this house. In this case, sir, if you extend the latitude that is ordinarily given in discussion of a resolution it will, I am sure, meet the wishes of the house and of the country. This is one of the most important measures to come before the house, and I would not like to see the Chair put in the position of even appearing to prevent a full examination of the proposals of the government.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I believe that the Chairman of the committee is simply seeking to draw the attention of the house to the rules. At the same time may I say that I agree with the leader of the opposition' and others who have spoken as to the special circumstances of the moment, and I hope that the Chairman will give every reasonable latitude for discussion at this time. The Chairman is in a very difficult position. One day he is knocked about for having gone too far, and the next for not having gone far enough.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I wonder if I might have an answer to my question as to which department is to administer this act. There are certain provisions, for example, the ones having to do with the reestablishment credit, which perhaps could best be administered by the new Department of Veterans' Affairs. Which department is to administer the act?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Under the bill the minister will be the Minister of Pensions and National Health or the Minister of Veterans' Affairs. It is quite possible and probable that the

War Service Gratuities
payment of the cash gratuities will be made by the service departments. That Would probably be the most convenient method, because they have the pay accounts and know exactly the pay and allowances which would be payable on the day of discharge. But the long-term administration will be under the Department of Pensions and National Health or the Department of Veterans' Affairs.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: There has been considerable discussion of paragraph 2 entitling persons domiciled in Canada on and after September 10, 1939, who subsequently go on active service, to the gratuity. In the Pension Act the yardstick is much more elastic as to domicile. I have not the act before me but my recollection is that the domicile required in Canada is a period of four years. I would suggest to the minister that in reconsidering this paragraph, which he has stated he will do, he consider the advantages of making the provision as to date of domicile much more elastic so that it would take in those who left Canada before the war, even though they joined the permanent forces of the United Kingdom. I think if we borrow the provision that is contained in the Pension Act, and which specifies a period of four years preceding the outbreak of war, it would facilitate matters. I recommend that thought to the minister before the bill is brought down.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I will take that suggestion into consideration, along with that of the hon. member for Lake Centre.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services will recall that in the assembling of convoys at Halifax and other ports, particularly during the period when the merchant marine were being outfitted with guns, a large number of gunners served on these merchant marine ships who were not in uniform but were certainly acting as gunners. Are they included in this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to merchant mariners who are gunners?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: There has been a good deal of discussion in the house from time to time, as the minister knows, with respect to the merchant marine. In the matter of the income tax, first of all, they have not been given, to my mind, plain ordinary justice. On the other hand the government has its own argument with respect to that, and evidently its decision cannot be changed. But here is a situation which I think we may properly discuss on the resolution, to give the government an opportunity to amend any bill which they have already drafted, and with a possibility of doing justice to these men in the merchant marine. I believe everybody in the house has practically the same point of view on this subject. An hon. member from the maritimes, when the position of these men as compared with those in the navy, especially during the height of the submarine menace, was discussed under the income tax resolutions, indicated that while the navy had at least a gun to shoot back with, the merchant marine simply had to take it, without proper defence. That struck me as being an impressive argument for comparable treatment. I believe the minister should give the assurance that before the bill is brought in consideration will be given to the case of the merchant seamen, or justice will not be done to a class of citizen that has done more and performed tasks under conditions of greater danger, than many who will receive the gratuity. That is no reflection upon those who will receive it. If those who not only individually but as a class, performing their duties under such dangerous conditions, are refused a gratuity, while those who are not subjected to equally dangerous combatant conditions are to receive it, the government will be open to criticism, which as opposition leader I have a duty to point out so that the government and parliament may avoid the occasion for it. There may be reasons why these things cannot always be done as those of us on the outside think they should be, but I believe the government will have to show good and sufficient reason for failing to make this provision if the public mind is to be content on that score.

My hon. friend will realize that there is some merit in

giving separate and distinct recognition to the armed forces of Canada. That consideration was in the mind of members of the goverment when this 'bill was being framed. There was no intention of ignoring anyone; in fact it was recognized that, once the bill was introduced, the claims of others would be very strongly pressed, and the government felt that for that if for no other reason the bill should be confined to the armed forces.
What hon. gentlemen have said about the recognition which is given to others is something which the government would be only too ready to consider, and will be helped in its consideration by what has been said. What I wish to make clear is that there is no intention in this measure, by not mentioning merchant seamen, that they are necessarily to be merely ignored. In connection with the armed forces information is available in the departments to-day of the nature and extent of their services and the reason they should receive this and that, which has not been available to a corresponding degree in respect to the merchant seamen. It may be that a little time will be required to give to the case of merchant seamen the consideration which it should receive. I just want to make it clear to-day that the fact that they and other classes which have been alluded to as not being mentioned in this bill does not mean that they are being ignored. The government's desire has been to have this special recognition to the armed forces, with the knowledge that suggestions would be forthcoming as to further recognition which might have to be given.
May I mention also that the war is not over yet. We do not know how much longer it may last, and I would recall the fact that, even for the forces for whom we are making provision to-day, no provision was made for gratuities after the last war until some time after that war ended. So that there is ample time in which further to consider the many matters which have been mentioned this afternoon.

speechtext:
I am getting a little clearer insight into thi= subject than I had at the outset, but the minister of pensions has just made a remark that brings out precisely the point I have been trying to clarify in my own mind. He says that when the bill comes down it will be found to provide for the purchase of a home, and he goes further and adds, under the National Housing Act. I know of scores of young men who are anxiously waiting to buy homes when they come back. Perhaps preliminary steps are being taken now to assist them. They expected that some assistance would1 be given them, but now we find that in large part it is diverted into the form of monthly payments. It is on a monthly basis. The minister speaks of purchasing a house under the provisions of the bill, and then he qualifies that by referring to the National Housing Act. There are many ramifications of this whole question that have to be considered. Young men are coming back and will want to get married. During the time they have been overseas they have had no opportunity to save anything apart from the odd $50 bond. The young men who have stayed on the farm or in the factory have had a greater opportunity in this direction and many of them have taken advantage of it. These young men are about to step into a new state of life and they are anticipating that they will have a job to go to and that they will use this assistance to buy a home and furniture. I do not think we should attach all the strings to it that apparently we are putting on. We must not do anything that will impede them in their progress towards reestablishment in civilian life.
The Prime Minister has referred to the $900 as a token of gratitude. I appreciate the fact that we cannot express in dollars and cents all that we should like to do for these men. On the other hand, the illustration given by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services has more or less put the matter in summarized form. He has spoken of the $900 plus a month's pay and one or two little things. What worries me is the fact that we are attaching too many strings to this benefit that we are extending to the young men who have been overseas for two or three or four years. They will want to know where they are going to get the money to get started. That is what concerns me. I wish the government would give this whole question very serious consideration and try to look at it from as broad a point of view as possible.
I would remind the government that a great many fire fighters as well as men engaged in the merchant marine and in the auxiliary services have already been killed. I am sure the ministers themselves are aware of the casualties that have occurred in all these services. The fire fighting service has been recognized in the matter of pension rights. There have been casualties among the fire fighters who are now on the coast of Normandy, and the casualties among the men of the merchant marine are untold.
Reference was made to the fact that you could not go on extending this. The Minister of National Defence said that you had to draw the line somewhere. Apart from the fire fighters, the men of the merchant marine and those in the auxiliary services, I do not know of any other groups, certainly there are not many, who could make the claim that these particular groups can.

Other claims would be infinitely small. Having in mind the fact that pension rights of certain groups have been recognized and we are already paying pensions to the dependents of certain men, and the fact that the dependents at home of men overseas or in the extra services have had no opportunity whatever to save money, I say that this is little enough; in fact I should like to see the amount increased to help these men become established in home life in Canada. I urge on the government therefore the importance of removing all barriers from the $900, for example. All barriers should be
War Service Gratuities

removed entirely, because I know that there are scores, yes, thousands of these young men whose sweethearts at home are waiting anxiously for them to come back and they would like to use this money. We cannot do enough to help these men and I do not like to see it held up in monthly payments. I want to see them get it so long as they make proper use of it. I urge the government therefore to consider these qualifications very carefully. I suggest that we should go to the other extreme rather than put any barriers in the way of the men who are coming home shortly.

At the beginning of the war, for the first year of hostilities, there were a great many men in the army who were called out under what was known as G.O. 139 -general order 139. They were referred to as being called out. They happened to be doing specialized jobs in most cases. I presume that the date of this gratuity will take effect from the day they were called out, because it was before the active army was formed. It was in the days when the Canadian forces were known as the Canadian Active Service Force. I believe nearly a year elapsed before the active army actually came into being.
Another question that needs to be clarified is the position of men who are discharged to Department of Pensions and National Health. A man is wounded and sent to military hospital. He is then boarded out of the army and discharged, but left in a Department of Pensions and National Health hospital for a period of six months or a year or longer. .Provision should be made in the resolution for the period of time the service man spends in a Department of Pensions and National Health hospital. That time should be included in his active service. I do not think it is included in the resolution. While the man is in the hospital he is not on war duty but he is still definitely totally engaged; his whole being is there; he cannot be in civilian life. I suggest that that time be included in -the bill.
A word with regard to domicile. After the war ends a number of Canadians may not wish to return immediately to Canada. Some of them may wish to serve with the army of

occupation in enemy territory. Some of them may wish to remain in England, possibly for educational purposes. Some may be offered employment in England. There should be no stigma with regard to domicile after the war. This amount should be paid irrespective of where the Canadian active service force man or the Canadian service man is domiciled after the war.

speechtext: I had to leave the committee for a few moments, and it may be that the question I am about to ask was dealt with during that time. However, since the question of combatancy is not the actual test in regard to the gratuities, and since the line is drawn in regard to overseas service-

Yes, perhaps that is more expressive than the word I was about to use. In any event geography rather than combatancy is the test, and naturally there will be some borderline cases that will cause the govemrhent no end of concern. One such case comes to mind in connection with the air force. Men who have served in Canada in instructional work, and perhaps in reasonably dangerous lines of endeavour in connection with the air force, will find themselves in receipt of gratuities under this act on a much lower scale than some noncombatants who have been overseas but in some cases in perhaps no more dangerous surroundings, if one can properly put it on that basis. No doubt the one man would be more definitely exposed to the dangers connected with combatancy than the other might be, but still the gratuity would be much less in the one instance than in the other.
I fancy that is a matter to which the government have given a great deal of study, for it is a, real difficulty that will have to be faced if we are to have justice and avoid discrimination. Has the government considered the possibility of utilizing some discretionary power to avoid those injustices which in the very nature of the test applied under this act, that is geography rather than combatancy, may arise from time to time and which would be very embarrassing in the administration of the measure. I know how difficult it is to deal with these matters of discretionary power, but I was wondering whether or not that point had been considered by the government and, if so, whether any solution had been arrived at which does not appear in the resolution as it is now on the order paper.
[Mr. Senn.l
In that connection I would point out that many of the airmen who are doing pretty dangerous work here in Canada would be overseas if the department would permit them to go. I suppose there are literally thousands upon thousands of airmen in Canada who are desperately anxious, who have been pleading and urging and doing everything short of committing a crime to get overseas. These instructors and others find themselves subject to the payment of income tax, except under certain circumstances in which they are given relief, and now we find that those non-combatants overseas, some of them in not much more dangerous circumstances than exist here may be granted a much larger gratuity under the terms of this legislation. I do not want it to be understood that I desire to interfere with those overseas who come within the higher gratuity category. That is not my purpose at all in rising. I am only attempting to clear up the point in regard to the men in Canada, to see if it is not possible to increase the gratuity they will receive under the terms of the bill which will be founded upon this resolution. I point out the more favourable position of the non-combatants overseas with respect to the income tax, and other matters, only to show the possible injustice that may be felt by some airmen here in Canada. Certainly I have no desire to interfere with what may be received by those who are overseas. They deserve it but would the government care to make any comment with respect to this point, and indicate how they arrived at this position?

I assure my hon. friend that, as he anticipated, we gave very careful study to the matter of the differentiation in rates and the principles on which it should be based. In the first place danger is a factor. Men fighting in Italy and France probably have been, in many circumstances, in much more danger than anyone else, but the question was whether we could separate the degree of danger. I do not think my hon. friend will find many men in Canada who have endured the dangers that our men in England endured in 1M0 and 1941, at the time of the blitz. Neither do I think he will find many people in Canada enduring anything like the danger being endured to-day during the blitz of robot bombs. Neither do I think he will find men in Canada who have endured the danger which was endured by men in England on antiaircraft work on the coast, in endeavouring to keep the enemy away in the days when the bombing was so severe. We endeavoured to see if there was any possible test of combatancy, but, as my hon. friend has anticipated,

War Service Gratuities
it was extremely difficult to find any such test. So we had to take geography to indicate the theatres in which danger was most likely. In the second place, we coupled with that, separation, which we regarded as a factor to be considered. That is to say, it is one thing for a man to be in Canada, even though he may be in dangerous work, and to be able to get his seven or fourteen days' leave every six months and go home to his family, and be in touch with Canadian affairs. It was quite different with a man even in England, who also got his leave but whose leave only gave him an opportunity to go to London, or to go north, or to enjoy the hospitality of friends. It did not give him that which men prize above everything else, the opportunity to get home and see his loved ones.
The idea of general area of danger, and the idea of separation, were two of the factors which led the government to come to the conclusion that the only way we could make a distinction-not a fine or accurate distinction-which would appeal generally, was to deal with two classes of service; that is, service in the western hemisphere and service overseas. I think we were backed up in that by the fact that in their mustering out provisions the United States, to which the hon. member for Lake Centre has referred, used exactly the same test. Service in the United St.ates was considered as being one thing and service in other geographical areas was dealt with at another rate. In South Africa no difference is made as to service; they pay the same rate to all.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: What is the rate in South Africa?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
For European men it is 30 shillings per month of service; for European women, 15 shillings per month of service; for coloured personnel, 10 shillings per month of service, and for native personnel, 5 shillings per month of service. In New Zealand they have adopted a simple formula which appears to be applicable to all their troops. They have added a shilling a day to the man's pay and made it retroactive to the beginning of the war. However, this is not paid to him; it is treated as a deferred credit to be received by the man after the war. There again no distinction is made as to service. I have mentioned the United States, South Africa and New Zealand. Then lastly, in the last war exactly the same distinction was made as we are making here, that is, overseas service was one thing regardless of whether it was in France or England, and Canadian service was another.
That is why we have arrived at this distinction. I admit it is not precise; I admit it does not take account of many special situations, but it seems to be the best you can do unless you have a most complicated system of boards which would try almost every individual case to arrive at the degree of danger in which a man served. Someone has suggested that the test should be that a man has been within rifle shot of the enemy, which would be a little over a mile. One can see how difficult it would be to apply that test in connection with each particular . individual.
What my hon. friend has said about men in the air force is perfectly true. It is just as true of the army. There are literally thous- * ands of men in Canada who would much rather be overseas but who have worked hard in Canada in order to train others. There are men who have been located at outposts which while they may not be as dangerous as service overseas have been under pretty grim conditions. The same thing applies to the navy. There are many thousands of men in Canada who would rather be at sea. However, it is just the luck of the draw, as they say. The fact that they have been nearer their families is at least some compensation for the lower rate that will be paid.

I think we all appreciate the difficulty in drawing a line, but on the assumption that further consideration may still be given to this matter I would call the attention of the government to the manner in which the line is drawn in the Income War Tax Act. Section 4 refers to excepted incomes and paragraph (t) reads:
The service pay and allowances of-
(i)	members of the Canadian naval, military and air forces while in .the Canadian active service forces and overseas on the strength of an overseas unit outside of the western hemisphere, and
(ii)	members of the said forces while on active service in Canada, or anywhere in the western hemisphere, whose duties are of such a character as are required normally to be performed afloat or in aircraft.
Apparently the same problem which the government has been confronted with here confronted them with respect to income tax exemptions, and the section I have quoted would seem to indicate that the decision arrived at then is slightly different from the decision arrived at now. If the present decision were comparable to the former one the members of the forces whose duties are such as are required normally to be performed afloat or in aircraft would be included with those who have served overseas without regard to geography. You have here
War Service Gratuities

a group of service personnel who for income tax purposes have been treated the same as the service personnel overseas. It will be a bit of a surprise to them to discover that they are not to be included in that same category in this legislation. If further consideration is to be given to the question as to where the line is to be drawn I hope the government will refer to the section of the income tax legislation to which I have referred.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Individual demobilization, not the demobilization of the forces. There is one thing about which I do not believe there has been an announcement by the Canadian government, and that is the question as to how demobilization is going to be proceeded with and what plans have been arrived at by the special directorate that was set up by the government to deal with the matter. All of us I think have received letters from men who have been overseas, some of them for almost five years, endeavouring to secure information as to whether or not the government has a plan for orderly demobilization. In England the matter has been clarified by Mr. Ernest Bevin, who, speaking of the demobilization plans, said that the point system that was used in the last war was not to be used in this war, but that the general principle in Great Britain would be, to use his own words, "first in, first out." Is the minister in a position to deal with that? It would go a long way towards improving the morale of our men overseas, some of whom have been for five years removed from their families and their loved ones and all that is near and dear to them, if they were made aware of the fact that in any demobilization plans they are not going to be held over there in an army of occupation unless they wish to do so; that service in the army of occupation should be applicable to those with the shortest service, and that the men with the longest service will have the first opportunity to come back to their homes.
This morning the Prime Minister was asked whether it was intended that when the war in Europe is over our armed forces in Europe will be sent elsewhere or returned to Canada. I will not go into that question because the Prime Minister, if I understood his meaning aright, said that that was a matter that could not now be decided because of defence considerations and the like. But if the Prime Minister's statement as reported the other evening was a correct one, that there will be no election held during war time and there will be no postponing of the life of parliament, he must have had in mind, to synchronize those two statements, that the war in Europe is about over or will be over before April 1, 1945. If that be so, this is possibly the last opportunity that will be available to members of this house to ascertain just what the government's demobilization plans are. A full statement should be given to the house and the country on the whole plan of demobilization. The Minister

IFar Service Gratuities
of National Defence on a previous occasion answered me most fairly when I suggested that a similar system to that worked out in the United States should be available in Canada, under which, after a period of active service-I believe in the United States it is nineteen months of active service-the men in the army are given the opportunity, subject to the exigencies of war, to return to their loved ones for a furlough. The minister pointed out the difficulties arising from the general war situation and also the shipping difficulties at the time. But this is a matter upon which our men overseas would like to get information. As it is now, they have been over there several years without hope of returning home until the conclusion of hostilities and even then there is the uncertainty because no one knows whether the principle of "first in, first out" of the United Kingdom will be adopted. It is a serious matter and one upon which the men in the armed forces and their dependents in Canada would welcome a statement.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I am sorry that I cannot make a statement to the house now as to a plan of demobilization. I do not think any country yet has made a statement on its plan of demobilization. My hon. friend mentioned the general principle of "first in, first out", and that general principle is certainly an objective to work to. But there are many difficulties in connection with that principle, and one of the difficulties is the matter of units. I am speaking particularly of infantry units, as an infantry man myself. There is the difficulty of breaking up units by withdrawing men of so many years service and leaving the others there. There are two sides to it. It is a matter which the chief of staff in the United Kingdom, who is over here now, is discussing with us while he is here. I therefore cannot make any statement as to a plan of demobilization except to say that it is and has been receiving the most active consideration. For the last six months at least we have been giving this whole matter constant study and examination both here and overseas. We expect that we will have a plan of demobilization which will be as satisfactory as possible. No plan can be wholly satisfactory to everybody. I remember in the last war that when I received the news that soldiers were to be withdrawn according to their occupations I was completely disgusted because that meant the breaking up of units, and the idea was abandoned.
I know that the point system to which my hon. friend referred has been most severely criticized in England. It was a system that
took into account and gave so many points for long service, so many points for essentiality of civilian occupation, so many points for being married or single and points for various other things. It was excellent in theory but it just did not work. When you are bringing home units, there is the question of esprit de corps and certain traditions to be thought of. When you bring a unit back to its home town the men feel that they should have the privilege of being met by their fellow citizens, and their fellow citizens in turn feel that they should have that opportunity.
I can only say that the matter is engaging our most intensive attention and we are satisfied that a plan will be worked out which will be the best possible under the circumstances.
With regard to individual leave-for that is really what my hon. friend was speaking of- I have studied the system in the United States, and no doubt my hon. friend has the same information on it that I have. The system there is not as broad as my hon. friend's statement would perhaps indicate. The system is that leave is granted to certain particular individuals, and there are three principal classes, as I understand it. One is the class that has undergone extraordinary hardship or privation or difficulties in a most intensive theatre of war; in other words, those who are broken down by their service but would not be discharged as medically unfit. Another is the class that is needed at home for instructional purposes. The third is the class of those who have been successively wounded. Those I think are .the three main classes. The information I have is that up to date the number who have been granted leave under that scheme have amounted to something like one to one and a half per cent. I have here with me certain plans and certain arrangements which we are endeavouring to work out with the adjutant-general with regard to that same matter. But with the situation as it is at this moment in Italy and Normandy I feel that I should not discuss the matter of leave at the present time. Hon. gentlemen will understand why. I believe our men both in Italy and in Normandy understand that. I hope the day is not too far distant when the opportunity may be given. I do not think there is anything I can usefully add to that.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED-FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I appreciate the explanation which has been given, but here is the thing which the men in the army overseas want to know. I know that the special directorate on demobilization has given serious consideration to the whole question of demobilization, but has a decision been made on
War Service Gratuities

the question as to whether or not the N.R.M.A. men serving in Canada will receive their discharges and be permitted to enter civil life before those who serve overseas are returned to this country? It has important consequences because if seventy or eighty thousand N.R.M.A. men in this country, all of whom are in the same position under the law as other enlisted men as to their right to reinstatement in civil positions, are discharged before the men from overseas come back, many of the positions which would ordinarly be available for the men serving overseas will have been taken by those who under compulsory service served only in Canada. As I understand the provisions of the law as to reinstatement, as soon as a man is discharged from the forces he is entitled to go back to his former employer and demand reinstatement in the position he previously held. Unless there is a plan, the position of affairs will be this. Some of these men in the N.R.M.A. took positions vacated by men who voluntarily went on active service. If these N.R.M.A. men are discharged before the men who are overseas, they will be able to insist on their reinstatement in the positions which they previously held to the detriment of the volunteer for overseas service.
I do not doubt that our overseas forces will be satisfied with legislation such as is brought before the house to-day. It is all to the good and is not at all a matter of party politics. As the Prime Minister has said, the plan has been worked out to cover the entire gamut of demobilization and rehabilitation, and this resolution is for the time being the concludihg chapter. I repeat that all this is to the good. One thing remains: the men in the armed forces want to be assured of a job with fair pay when they return. Legislation such as this, although helpful and necessary, is merely of the nature of a stop-gap. Without there being a plan for demobilization, seventy thousand men overseas, who otherwise would have positions available to them when the war is over, will be denied positions to which they are entitled if the men who were called up and did not volunteer to go overseas are discharged first and enabled to take over these positions. I should like to hear a declaration of the government with reference to this. It would complete the picture regarding demobilization. Not only would you have a rehabilitation plan-and this is a most commendable one, with which all of us are in agreement-but you would say to the men who serve overseas, "You are not going to suffer because you. volunteered. Your positions will be available to you, and no one else
(Mr. Diefenbaker.]
who was called up and did not volunteer will be allowed to preempt a position which should rightfully belong to you in the post-war world."

I know my hon. friend does not expect me to announce a demobilization plan piecemeal, and I do not think I should do it. I agree thoroughly with my friend in this particular-I found it when I was in Italy -that in spite of what we are doing in this bill, the men over there are not much concerned with the matter of a war service gratuity as they are with having a job and having the chance themselves to be able to work out their own destiny. Export Credits Insurance
men being discharged from the services as to where they fit in under the rehabilitation regulations. I sent out a questionnaire containing seventeen questions. I communicated with army officials through the Department of Pensions and National Health and had these questions answered very clearly, and I have clarified the matter in the minds of most of the people who wrote to me. But I would ask the minister if the provisions of the resolution now before the committee are affected in any way by the type of discharge a man may receive. Here is an example of what I have in mind. A considerable number of men are coming back from overseas and being sent to their various military districts. In many cases they are held there for one reason or another for a long time, and they become impatient; they decide that they do not want to sweep floors, or something of the sort. They would rather have a discharge from the service, but they feel that if they ask for a discharge, the kind of discharge they would receive would be under routine order 1029-12. namely, discharged at their own request. If a man takes that kind of discharge will it militate against him in the application of this gratuity? It does militate against him in other instances.

speechtext:
The only sort of discharge which disqualifies a man for war service gratuity is misconduct. May I add this word. I have not given my hon. friend the direct answer to his question because of the fact that I considered it was part of the demobilization plan. I do not want any doubt in anyone's mind that we are fully alive to the danger of having men's jobs filled by N.R.M.A. men. In that connection I may say that we intend to see to it as far as we possibly can that the danger is avoided. That will be one feature of the plan, and I want to make sure that the house understands that. I understand fully what my hon. friend says and certainly I will do everything I can, and I know that all the service departments will do what they can, to see to it that preference for jobs goes to men who have been overseas.

During that discussion we had the pros and cons of municipal public housing versus housing projects constructed under the direction of private interests. In reply to some of the statements that I made last evening, the hon. member for Halton still further attacked the competence of municipalities to go into this kind of thing and still further defended the idea that it should be done solely by private interests. I shall not argue the point at length, but I should like to bring the hon. member for Halton and other hon. members up to date on what is happening in this field in the world of to-day. I hold in my hand as one exhibit an interesting book put out by the Boston housing authority, showing the work that has been done in that city under that municipal housing body. On the fly leaf of

Housing
this book there is an interesting quotation from the United States Housing Act of 1937, a portion of which I should like to read:
It is hereby declared to be the policy of the United States to promote the general welfare of the nation by employing its funds and credit, ... to assist the several states and their political subdivisions to alleviate present and recurring unemployment and to remedy the unsafe and insanitary housing conditions. . . .
And so on. The point in the quotation to which I call attention is the deliberate policy of the United States government to assist the several states and their political subdivisions in this field. Under that legislation and under enabling legislation in the state of Massachusetts a good deal has been done most effectively and most satisfactorily in that state. If time permitted I could give hon. members a great deal of material out of this book which would prove of real interest. I have here also a copy of the eighth annual report of the New York city housing authority for the year 1941. Here again we have the housing problem attacked by a municipal housing authority. Surely there is no city in Canagla that can be faced with any greater housing problem or any greater slum clearance difficulties than the city of New York. Yet the report indicates considerable satisfaction so far as the public administration of housing projects of that city is concerned. I should like to read just two short quotations from a letter, contained in this report. The letter was written by the chairman of the New York city housing authority to Mayor LaGuardia of that city, and is dated January 15, 1942. The first quotation is as follows:
During 1941. with the aid of federal and city funds, 2.943 additional families were provided with low-rent, modern, sanitary housing in four new projects:	East River Houses,
Manhattan; Kingsborough Houses, Brooklyn; Clason Point Gardens, Bronx, and Wallabout Houses. Brooklyn (a defence housing project near the navy yard).
The next paragraph I quote is in reply to the statement of the hon. member for Halton that municipal authorities cannot manage rental projects satisfactorily. The quotation is as follows:
The authority now operates twelve completed projects with a total occupancy of 13,180 low-income families. Naturally, there are many human problems constantly arising in the relations of the authority with such a large group of tenants. These problems have been handled with patience and tact by the managers of the projects and with satisfaction to the tenants.
Another report that I have on my desk is also from the New York city housing authority. It deals particularly with the South Jamaica houses, one of the projects carried on
by that authority. Again the story of what has been done is a good one. There are pictures here that would be of interest to hon. members. They show the situation before and after the housing authority had done its work. These pictures tell a real story. I quote from this report:
The cost of South Jamaica houses is $2,196,000 of which ninety per cent is lent by the United States housing authority and ten per cent will be financed by the sale of 'bonds by. the New York city housing authority. This is an average total cost of $4,888.39 per dwelling unit and $1,222.10 per room. The cost will be repaid over a period of sixty years out of revenues of the project, and annual contributions made by the United States housing authority.
Rents are from $20.50 per month for a 2J room apartment to $25.75 per month for a 5J room apartment, which includes gas for cooking and electricity for lighting and refrigeration as well as heating and hot water. This averages $5.60 per room per month including utilities.
So one might go on with various sections of these reports of municipal public housing authorities in the United States to show that when we advocate this kind of thing we are not just propounding theory but are talking in the light of what is actually taking place in the world in which we live to-day. I feel that the position taken by the hon. member for Halton in defence of the government's refusal to consider supporting municipal bodies in this field is, to put it mildly, a voice out of the past.
Another document from which I should like to quote briefly is a circular which was sent out by the British ministry of health under date of March 4. 1943, to the housing authorities of the county councils of the United Kingdom. Hon. members should bear in mind that this circular was sent out right in the midst of the war, when it was not possible to do all the actual construction that one might like to have done, but it will be seen that the view of the United Kingdom government is that plans should be made for the building of homes as soon as the war is over, and that in their view the important people with whom the central government should deal are the housing authorities of the local councils. Let me quote one or two passages to make the position clear. This is what the ministry of health has to say to the county councils of England:
But it is clear that the need for houses is already substantial, and the minister is anxious ' that local authorities should now begin -to formulate plans so as to be in a position to make a quick start immediately conditions permit, whether during or after the war. I am accordingly to ask that the council, if they have not already done so, should review their housing needs and that they should concentrate on the preliminary arrangements necessary as a prac-
622S
Housing

tical measure to enable them to start on such part of the programme as would comprise a one year's building work as they are authorized to do so.	*
Then the two last paragraphs from this circular:
The minister will be glad to be informed in due course of the number of houses which the council have in mind for their first year's programme and of the extent to which they already have land in their possession available for these houses, or of the additional sites which they propose to acquire.
I am to add that directions have been given to the ministry's regional architects to continue to call on the local authorities in their region, as and when they can, to discuss with them their programme for housing after the rvar. If the council wish subsequently to discuss matters further, the minister will be glad to arrange for a deputation to be received by the ministry.
That is signed by L. F. Hearder, assistant secretary of the United Kingdom ministry of health. In that document are two points to which I call attention. First is the recognition by the central government in the United Kingdom of the important part to be played in housing by the local housing authorities of the county council. There is also in this circular a recognition of the necessity of planning the construction of houses. There you have the central government asking all the county councils to survey their needs and to report on those needs to the central government, so that the building of houses may be planned in the light of those needs. I mention that because to me it is in striking contrast to the lack of any plan in the housing legislation npw before us. As I said last evening, this measure will no doubt result in the building of many houses in Canada, and because those houses are needed we support the legislation. But I think hon. members who rose in their places to say that this was the finest housing legislation any government had ever brought down were, to say the least, a little extravagant in their statements.
I have before me as well some quotations from Lord Woolton, the British minister of reconstruction, similar to those which appear iri the circular to which I referred. For example, he said in December, 1943:
The next step is to advise local authorities What kind of houses they should build so that they can get further ahead* with their detailed plans. I can promise local governments that they will have the best advice on this matter that the central government are able to give them, and they will have that very quickly. . . .
1 emphasize again the view in the United Kingdom that there should be this close cooperation between the central government and the public housing authorities of the county councils.
In addition to the references to other countries I would mention the report of the subcommittee on housing and community planning of the James committee on reconstruction, in which it was urged that not only should there be planning in advance of any housing project but particular consideration would have to be given to all three levels of Canadian government. I quote:
It is important to recognize that actual achievement of great numbers of new houses constructed and operated on a sound basis depends upon a reasonable and cooperative division of labour between the three levels of Canadian government.
If there were time I might mention other parts of that portion of the report to indicate that the James committee recognized the important part to be played in any rational, satisfactory housing programme by the municipal councils, those who are closest to the people and to our housing problems. I regret very much that the government has taken what to my way of thinking is a retrograde step, by including in this legislation a provision that to all intents and purposes snubs the municipal bodies. The minister has stated his reason for this position; he is not satisfied that the municipal bodies can display the efficiency of the private limited-dividend housing corporations and the life insurance companies. We beg leave to differ with that. Some of us have had some experience in this field. We feel that greater reliance should be placed upon the municipal bodies, and that there should be the kind of cooperation with those bodies which is evident from the quotations I have read both from the United States and from the United Kingdom. '
I rose in part simply to reply to some of the comments that were made last night, and also that I might express my objection to the position embodied in section 12 of the bill; we favour instead the wider development of municipal public housing authorities.
