There are a few words in the first part of section 12 to which I should like to refer. I am going to try to direct my remarks not to the whole gamut of housing but to what this section calls for, namely slum clearance. Section 12 reads in part:
In order to assist in the clearance, replanning, rehabilitation- and modernization of slum areas or blighted or substandard areas in any municipality.
As I understand it, under subsection 3 the municipalities are to be advanced one-half of the purchase price of the slum area which is to be rebuilt on by the insurance company or other builders with whom the government may deal. Will the cities be able to take

Housing
over such areas by expropriation proceedings?
I have looked over slum areas in a great number of cities, but I should like to refer particularly to Toronto. Land fronting on the bay from Bathurst street, indeed from Simcoe street west, used to be a very high class residential district many years ago. The mansions of the rich people of those days, including the lieutenant governor, were south of King street. What drove those people away? The railways came in and their smoke drove out all residents who were able to move away. They went north until in time the city extended north for perhaps seven, eight or nine miles. This area is now occupied by people having low salaries or humble people who have no salaries at all.
I doubt if any insurance company or other builder could make houses pay in this area unless the railways were electrified and the smoke nuisance eliminated. Along the south bank of the Thames, and I believe also along the north bank, in London they have electrified the railroads. If this were followed out in Toronto, then I believe this so-called slum area could be rebuilt with houses and apartments to be occupied by people with low incomes or even by people with higher incomes. Buffalo is in much the same position as Toronto. In these cities people who work downtown in the office buildings and stores have to travel seven or eight miles to and from their work when it should be possible to build homes in areas where it would be cooler and where people would be closer to their work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better explain this. If a municipality wishes to acquire an area on which there are slums it may do so with the consent of the province and of the dominion. The consent of the dominion is necessary if we are to contribute one-half the excess acquisition cost. Demolition will be necessary, and if this cost and the cost of the land were to be borne by a limited-dividend corporation or a life insurance company it would be impossible to make the project pay. On the other hand, if only the cost of the land is to be paid by the limited-dividend corporation or the life insurance company it probably will be an economical investment.
Who is to pay the cost over and above that of the land? This bill provides that if the project is approved by us, by the province and by the municipality, we will contribute fifty per cent of what we call the excess acquisition cost. It is contemplated that the other fifty per cent will be provided by the municipality or by the province or by both. The only cost to the limited-dividend corporation or the life insurance company would be the cost of the land. The project is gone ahead with, and in the case of the life insurance company they get a guaranteed return of two and a half per cent. There are certain provisions as to how they must apply the amount they earn over a certain amount. In the case of the limited-dividend corporation, they get a loan from the government up to ninety per cent of the cost of the land and buildings. Under those favourable conditions they are enabled to charge low rents to tenants who occupy the buildings constituting the project.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.
speechtext:
This one area in Toronto covers a lot of territory.-Starting at Bathurst or even Simcoe street south of King street there are a large number of humble but very fine people residing in houses which perhaps should be condemned. Only $20,000,000 is being provided, but the minister said the other night that this was just a start. If this work is confined at the beginning to the four cities with over 200,000 of population, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal, and the amount is divided it will mean approximately $5,000,000 for each city; that would not go very far if we are to take in what the minister has just indicated.
I want to see a start made and I want to see a success made of it. It seems a pity that in those cities located on lakes or rivers or harbours use cannot be made of the land along the waterfront because of the railways. In many cities these districts are occupied by people who cannot pay any great amount of rent. That prompted my other question as to whether the electrification of railways might be considered under the provisions of this bill. The whole frontage of Toronto is taken up to-day with the railways; trains run along every half hour or oftener belching out great columns of smoke. I cannot imagine anybody taking over that land and using it for housing purposes. I should like to know if the minister has given any thought at all to the future electrification of our railways entering large cities like Toronto. The steam engines could be parked at Mimico on. the west or elsewhere, and at Scarboro on the east side of the city, and the trains brought in by electrical power. That would mean that the front of the city would be a desirable place to take over and erect housing on for our humble people who cannot pay a high rent but who nevertheless are entitled to every consideration possible for the sake of their health and the health of their families. These areas once cleared should have playgrounds, swimming pools and everything that would be beneficial
Housing

to the health of the children. Has the minister given any thought to that, or have any suggestions been made in connection with slum clearance to eliminate the smoke nuisance in the lower part of our big cities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOANS FOR CONSTRUCTION, REPAIR, ALTERATION, ETC.

I do not think the dominion government should assume responsibility for the elimination of the smoke nuisance or anything of that kind.
With regard to the amount that might be spent on slum clearance, $20,000,000 is provided for in the bill, but it should be noted that this amount is to take care of only half the excess acquisition cost of the land to be acquired for low-cost and moderate cost rental housing projects. An excess acquisition cost of $40,000,000 will make possible a substantial amount of slum clearance work, because it must be remembered that the land so acquired is to be sold to limited-dividend companies, life insurance companies or other approved lending institutions at fair and reasonable prices. If we assume that the excess acquisition cost is as large as half the total cost of the land acquired and cleared, section 12 of the bill makes possible the acquisition of land in our municipalities at a cost of $80,000,000 to provide a location for low-cost and moderate cost rental housing projects.

May I say one word with regard to paragraph (c) with respect to approval by the government of a province. I do not think that is comprehensive enough. In all worth-while schemes made for slum clearance, slum clearance is only one part of the main job. It has been the municipality or a planning board of the municipality that has made the plan, and I feel that first of all these loans should be restricted to municipalities or to districts that have made a plan, which plan is accepted by the province and by the dominion. That is very important. Ontario has a minister of planning, Mr. Dana Porter. I think this is one of the things that

Housing
might come under the department of reconstruction. The hon. member for Parkdale suggested the department of health but I think reconstruction would be the proper department. The dominion government should see to it that the money so spent shall do the maximum amount of good. It takes a very great deal of preliminary work before you can undertake such a big project as slum clearance, which requires the consideration of questions of various kinds such as different types of residences, single, family, double family, multiple family residences, and so on, and other questions such as light industry, or heavy industry on the other hand, obnoxious industry, commercial institutions, and so on. All these things must be considered in clearing slums. Unless they are considered, no matter how clear the slums or what houses you build, you will reproduce slum conditions. You must have the municipality undertake an over-all plan. In my opinion this is the whole crux of the bill. I am in favour of the bill as far as it goes, but more attention should be given to the municipal angle, and the dominion government should be quite careful not to undertake work in a municipality that has not a comprehensive plan. It must be more than a mere slum clearance plan. Take Toronto or Montreal. The whole topography of these cities is undergoing a change. It is a slow change, and the money invested in real estate is a long-term investment, so that it is very important that the house should be of equal livability value ten, fifteen, or twenty years from now. Unless you see to it that the district in which your houses are built does not become a blighted area by the construction of some obnoxious industry; unless the municipality passes enabling legislation to zone the area, then you will run into great danger that the money so spent will be lost and the houses so built will deteriorate.
There is another matter with regard to this clause which has not been mentioned. I refer to the outright renting of houses; the building of houses for rent and not for home owners. There is a large class of people in Canada, varying from time to time, who rent houses instead of owning them. There are young men who will come back and want to get married and to occupy one of those "wee white dream houses" that the national war finance committee spoke about in one of its advertisements in connection with the last victory loan. That is all right; but a man entering into business may often find himself tied up with long-term obligations in connection with the purchase of a house He may find after a year or two in one municipality or one location
that he is offered a much better job elsewhere, but he is obligated over a long term for the house he now occupies. He finds that buying and selling houses involves the loss of a great deal of principal value. speechtext:
Before the dinner recess I said a few words in connection with slum clearance, but the minister did not seem to think I knew what I was talking about. I have a few figures I should like to put on the record. This section deals with slum clearance, but I say that it will never do the

Housing

job it is supposed to do. Slum clearance cannot be carried on as a private enterprise; it has to be done in a different way altogether. Another point is that you must have some place for the people to go to when you carry out your slum clearance. If you are going to clear a space you must provide the people living there with other decent living conditions. It is not sufficient just to clear away the slums; you must provide decent surroundings, and playgrounds for the children. You must have low rentals; you must have a decent development, including playgrounds for the children and all that sort of thing, and you must have education among those who dwell in this new development so that they will not want to go back to slums again. It is not just a question of having people move from one building to another; they must be educated to appreciate these nicer surroundings. It will not do just to provide them with quarters to live in.
When I was speaking before six o'clock I had touched on what is being done in the United States. I intend to give a few more figures. The advisory committee on housing in Toronto is composed of Mrs. J. W. Bundy, Mr. F. D. Tolchard, Lieutenant-Colonel E. H. Marani, Mr. L. M. Wood and Mr. E. W. Sinfield.	These people have always been
interested in low-cost housing for the purpose of clearing slums, so that they know what they are talking about. Before the committee rose at six o'clock, I gave the estimated cost of doing some clearing of slums that has to be done in the city of Toronto. There are 900 rear and alley dwellings, assessed at $900,000, to be cleared away. Then they acquire ten blocks, containing 900 houses, assessed at $1,800,000. I am giving these figures to show how the thing works out. That makes a total of $2,700,000. The government pays half of that, or say $1,300,000. The estimated cost of putting up in place 1,800 new dwelling units is $4,050,000. That makes a total cost of S5,350,000 for the project, of which the dominion government pays $1,300,000, and the city or whoever buys the property pays the remainder.
Let us take taxes in the city of Toronto at 3| per cent. The- house costs $2,250 and the lot $722, or a total of $2,972. Try to build a house now for $2,250. You may be able to do it after the war when prices come down. The limited-dividend company will have to borrow the money at three per cent. I have allowed nothing for upkeep. Repayment over a period of forty years will amount to 4 per cent, without upkeep at all. So that we have taxes 34 per cent, interest 3 per cent, and

repayment 4 per cent, or a total of 104 per cent, and remember that that does not include upkeep. The total cost of the house and lot is $2,972, and 104 per cent of that gives a rental of aproximately $311, or practically $26 a month. That is not a low-cost house either. You cannot have low-cost housing; you cannot have slum clearance unless you give something to the slum people by way of education. You have to give them slum rentals, in the meantime they have to have some place where they can go, and if you do not give them slum rentals in nice surroundings they will go back to slum conditions. You have to give them some education.
I have received some information from the executive department of the division of housing at 80 Centre street, New York city. This is a summary of their views, and I am not going to go into the question of limited-dividend companies because I do not think we are interested in that at the moment. I am dealing now with the local housing authorities and what is to be done to meet the situation. Let me say that $26 a month is not a slum rental. As the minister said, he expects people to pay about one-fifth of their income a year in rent. Of. course one-fifth of the income of a man who has only a low income is a very much larger amount to him than one-fifth of the income of a man drawing $1,500 or $2,000 a year. The man with the bigger income has so much more left. I have been very much interested in this matter. I have studied conditions in my own riding in the city of Toronto and I know what has to be done. But it cannot be done under this plan of the government's. So far as this plan is concerned it is just so much camouflage. Now I quote from the summary. It is headed "local housing authorities" and reads:
The United States housing act embodies a plan for producing new housing at rents equivalent to those charged in the slums. It accomplishes this by authorizing the federal overnment to perform two separate financial unctions; that of banker and that of donor of annual rent subsidies. As banker, the USHA loans to the local housing authority, by purchase of its bonds, up to ninety per cent of the capital cost of a project. After a project is completed, the USHA assumes its second financial function. It grants annual subsidies in an amount sufficient to cover the difference between the annual cost (economic rent) and the rent which low-income families can afford to pay.
Local authorities were forbidden by the USHA to place any mortgages on public housing projects.
At first timidly, but then, as time passed, with increasing confidence, banks, insurance companies, and private investors have been buying local housing authority bonds. The financial arrangement originally contemplated, under which ninety per cent of the capital

Housing
funds were provided by the federal government and ten per cent by the investing public, has gradually been changed so that to-day it is not uncommon to have eighty per cent of the capital funds provided by the investing public and only twenty per cent by the federal government. Local housing authorities are able to market bonds running up to the year 1985 and they sell these bonds at interest costs which average less than two per cent. The way has thus *been paved for establishing the public housing programme of the post-war era on a basis of financing which will relieve the federal government almost wholly of the responsibility for providing the capital funds.
I give that as an example of confidence. They grant subsidies, or, as the summary says, "annual subsidies in an amount sufficient to cover the difference between the annual cost (economic rent) and the rent which low-income families can afford to pay." I have given these figures to show that you cannot possibly do that under this legislation. I have taken the figures of the National Housing Act, which allows four per cent of the cost for repayment, without any upkeep at all.
I think all my figures are correct, and I come to the conclusion that $26 a month is as low as you can go in a slum clearance project. It is based on an investigation by prominent men in the city of Toronto. I have had some experience in this housing business for a long time. As I told the minister last night, I have been connected with a Toronto housing company, and we have tried to do a good job, but the only reason why we have been able to keep our rents down is that the projects which we put up years ago were erected at a very much lower cost than would be required to-day, or even within the last fifteen years. That is why we have been able to maintain low rents; nevertheless we are losing money. The only solution of slum clearance is through some kind of subsidy by the federal government or other governments. After all, the government is not giving anything away by granting money at three per cent, because it can raise money at less than that rate. I admit that the government, by making these grants, is doing a good job in facilitating slum clearance, but that is part of the national job which should be done.
I do not wish to criticize this bill too much;
I believe it has some excellent features; but I could not let it pass without pointing out these things.

Section 25 deals with the general and special powers of the minister. Housing is ninety per cent a problem of giving local services. I suggest that an investigation be made of how municipalities can help out. I wish to refer to what the city of Toronto has done. As the committee knows, before the city of Toronto owned the street railway we had housing problems there. We gave to a radius of fifteen miles light, power

Housing
and transportation services. As the hon. member for St. Paul's saicl, we had to rely on private companies and others at the start. Public ownership solved the problem. By taking over the street railway which served only half of the old city, and by giving cheap light, water, sewers and power, and by the development of the new city in the other half we made considerable progress. We bought the street railway out; we bought out the buses; we bought out the radials, and we gave them light, power and transportation.
Under section 25, general and special powers of the minister, the minister will have authority to carry out investigations of the companies undertaking housing construction. Paragraph (b) of that section deals with studies to be made of investigations into housing conditions and housing accommodation. We should study the situation in the municipalities and see what the. municipalities have done and how they can surely solve the housing problem. They have done more for housing by developing their districts, cities and towns in Canada and their agencies than anybody else, provincial or federal. The city of Toronto is just an industrial city. In the olden days a private company owned the railway up to Bloor street. That was only one-third of the present city. The city expanded up to St. Clair avenue and then up as far as York Mills. The city of Toronto had to pay the whole cost of giving transportation, light, water, power, and all civic "services. We bought out the street railway which only served one-third of the old city. We bought out the privately-owned systems, the radials; there were eight or nine fares in the area now covered by the present city. What developed the city of Toronto? The building of the viaduct on Bloor street, the building of the bridge on Gerrard street, Dundas street, the high level bridge on Queen street, the waterfront improvement on which the city spent $33,000,000.
Under the general powers of the minister I hope that an investigation will be made of what the municipalities have been doing with regard to light, power and transportation and other municipal services to develop housing. Housing in Toronto has been developed by taking over the railways, as the Minister of Munitions and Supply knows, by giving water service, sewer service, buses and transportation. After all is said and done, the housing situation is ninety-five per cent a transportation, local service municipal problem. All these municipal services are given not only to the whole city of Toronto but free and without cost by Toronto to all three counties, to the riding of my hon. friend the Postmaster
General, York North, right up to Richmond Hill and transportation to lake Simcoe, which aided suburban housing. In Peel, the riding of my leader, we bought all the power companies, light, power, and transportation, as well as in the county of Ontario, the riding of the chairman of the banking and commerce committee.

He said: I do not know whether I should take up the time, but there has been some criticism of the scope of the bill on the ground that it is insufficient to meet the needs of the situation. I think those who criticize the bill on that ground fail to understand the provisions of the bill and of certain collateral legislation which has been enacted by or is now before this parliament, and have also failed to consider the appropriate parliamentary procedures in respect of appropriations of money out of the consolidated revenue fund.
Some hon. members have referred to the report of the subcommittee on housing and community planning of the advisory committee on reconstruction and have pointed out that this subcommittee recommended that a complete urban housing programme must contemplate the construction of 600,000 units in the first post-war decade, and that a minimum rural housing programme would require an additional 125,000 units. These are very high figures, and others have estimated that at least 300,000 housing units will be required, although it is true that there are some who think that even the figures given in the Curtis report are too low. The first thing to emphasize is that those who are making these estimates are talking, not about the first year or two after the war, but about the ten years following the termination of hostilities.
I am quite sure that if we brought down a bill that asked parliament to appropriate one or two billions of dollars for housing purposes over the next ten years, some hon. members who are now criticizing the appropriations asked for in this bill would criticize us, and I would say they would do so with a great deal of justification, for endeavouring to bind the hands of parliament over so long a period and for giving the executive arm of government so large an appropriation which could only be spent over a long period of years. The principle we have followed is, I think, a very

Housing
much sounder one. We have asked for what in our opinion is a very substantial appropriation, but it is one which is intended to take care of, say the next two or three years. It is asked for, moreover, in the full knowledge that if after a year, or two or three years, more funds are required, the government of the day can go back to parliament and ask for any further appropriations that may be required. These appropriations can then be made if parliament is satisfied, after a full review of experience under this measure, that the principles which it embodied are sound and desirable. That is my first point.
My second point is that the appropriations for which we are now asking will make possible a huge volume of construction in the next two or three years. Under part I of the bill we are asking for $100 millions which, as the house knows, means total joint loans of $400 million and a total building construction somewhat in excess of that amount. Under part IT we are asking an appropriation of $50 million for loans for rental housing purposes. If all these loans should take the form exclusively of joint loans with lending institutions under section 8 of the bill, this would mean total joint loans of $200 million and a volume of building construction probably considerably in excess of that amount. For the sake of this argument, however, let us assume that half of this appropriation goes into loans to limited-dividend housing corporations and only the remaining half into joint loans for ordinary rental housing. This would make possible a total volume of house building of something in excess of $125 million. I have now reached a total figure of at least $525 million and perhaps something in excess of that up to $600 million.
In addition, however, part II provides for investments in rental housing projects by life insurance companies and certain other designated approved lending institutions. If these institutions should take full advantage of the enabling powers thereby granted, we would have an additional volume of house building of a value something between $150 million and $200 million.
To this should be added, of course, the grants up to a maximum of $20 million for slum clearance purposes. I showed that the terms of the section really make possible the acquisition of land in municipalities to the amount of $80 million to provide the location for moderate or low-cost housing projects. I went into that this afternoon and showed that the $20 million contributed by us is only a start on this project.
In regard to rural housing, some hon. members have apparently overlooked the fact that the loans for rural housing are to be made
out of the appropriation of $100 million provided for in part I of the bill which, as I have already indicated, makes possible total joint loans of $400 million.
The appropriation of $5 million provided for in part III of the bill is merely for the purpose of covering the government's direct or contingent liabilities arising out of the contracts which it may enter into for the purpose of ensuring the production and sale at low cost of standardized units or components of houses intended to be sold to residents of rural areas.
In part IV of the bill we provide that the government may guarantee loans up to $100 million for the purpose of making repairs, alterations and additions to urban homes.
Adding all these appropriations together, and excluding the appropriations which will be necessary for carrying on the administration of the bill and which will be provided for in the main or supplementary estimates year by year, we get a total appropriation requested by the new bill of $275 million; but, as I have indicated, this appropriation will make possible a total volume of house building, housing repair and land clearance of at least $665 to $740 million, to which of course should be added another $150 to $200 million made possible by section 11 of the bill which enables life insurance companies and certain other approved lending institutions to buy land and develop thereon rental housing projects.
All this, however, does not take into account the fact that in the farm improvement loans bill we provided for the guarantee of loans to be made by banks up to a total amount of $250 million for the purpose of buying machinery and equipment, rural electrification and the making of other permanent improvements in connection with farms. I think it is beyond doubt that a substantial portion of this large amount will go not only for the repair, renovation and reequipment of farm houses but also for the building of new houses and of labourers' cottages on farms.
Finally, hon. members will note the substantial impetus which we are giving to the construction of new houses and the repair of old houses in connection with the veterans' reestablishment programme, the resolution in respect of which was discussed this morning.
When all these things are considered, I think it can safely be said that Canada is making preparation more adequate than, or at least as adequate as, the preparation made or being made by any other country to take care of the housing problem during the transition period immediately following the war.

Mr. CHURCH; On the first section of the bill, the short title, I raise the same objection which I did when it was first introduced. This bill went to the banking and commerce committee, and in that committee there was a wide difference of opinion as to the principle of the bill, its functions, scope and object. Industrial Development Bank
During the discussion of the bill in committee I do not notice here now the hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, whom I call "the admiral of the bay of Quinte", but he raised a very important principle. He was asked by the likable, learned and able man who is the deputy minister, Doctor Clark, about this first clause of the bill, "Does the hon. member think he knows more about banking than I do?"-which is a very humorous remark. I wish to point out to the [DOT]minister that if it were proposed that this bank could lend money without security it would be a very fine thing; is there anybody who does not want to borrow money without security? Why does not the minister lend some money under the bill to those who are in the house and those who are out of it who write us? We are to lend money under this new project of an industrial development bank, which does not develop anything, is not industrial and is not a bank at all. The lending is a straight gift, that is all it is.
My hon. friends here who are laughing on my right should get up and oppose the bill and say something. The hon. member for York West is here this evening; I can tell him-and I speak what I know-that in his riding there are shark loan companies charging two per cent a month. What do they do? Their practices are the same as the principle of this bill. They take a chattel mortgage from those who seek a loan; they take a bill of sale on goods and chattels for security to protect their two per cent a month charge.
What is the principle of the bill? If it were to swallow up all these various loan companies which are operating under federal charter and replace them by the industrial development bank, it would be a good thing and a blessing. But it is not. They are not doing that at all, and the existing banks and loan companies can do the business.
This is not a bank at all. We are simply lending money without security. It is a violation of the British North America Act and contrary to the interests of provincial institutions. There is no security for the advances made. It does not aid industrial workers at all. I object to the principle of the bill as set out in the preamble. This bill commends itself neither to the judgment of the country nor to that of the small private business men who are victimized by the shark loan companies without a chance to rehabilitate themselves, and wind up by being swallowed up in this bill.

speechtext: I was not able to attend the sessions of the banking and commerce committee, and I wonder whether consideration was given there to an alternative proposal that I put forward on the second reading. It was not advanced in the form of a definite proposal but rather as a suggestion for consideration by the committee. That suggestion was as to the advisability or otherwise of embarking upon a duplicate banking system across Canada as envisaged by section 8, involving staffs, branches and agents. I suggested at that time that consideration might properly be given to the question whether, by guarantee or otherwise, existing lending institutions could ibe utilized for the purposes of the legislation. The minister gave a detailed explanation either when the bill was introduced or perhaps on the second reading; I do not recall at which stage it was. At any rate, he discussed the question whether this guarantee or some similar system might be employed to loosen up credit-the method of government guarantees-without the duplication of services throughout Canada. One of the objections which have been made to this bill has been the fact that we are setting up a duplicate banking system to some extent. I realize that the argument may be met by the statement that it is only to a certain extent and that it does not represent anything like complete duplication. I would be inclined to demur to that argument. At any rate, I think some consideration might be given to the question. Perhaps it came up in the banking and commerce committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
It was argued at great
length in that committee, certain members of which were very much in favour of the government adopting the home improvement loan principle and the' principle of the farm improvement loans bill instead of setting up a government bank, so to speak. But the proposal was considered months before we decided to introduce this legislation at all, and it was also debated in the house. I remember giving the reason once before, in the month of May.
I am not sure that I stated it very well on that 
occasion and perhaps I cannot state it very well now, but the pool guarantee principle is generally regarded as more appropriate to a large number of small transactions of a more or less standardized type than to a small number of large transactions such as the ones that will be carried on by this bank. For instance, if we had adopted the other principle and one of the chartered banks made ten loans in the course of the year and the pool guarantee were applied, that we would protect them against loss up to the extent of ten per cent of those loans, I am doubtful whether it would be an inducement to the banks to make loans, because one very bad one would go beyond the ten per cent. That cannot very well happen in a very large number of small loans if reasonable care is taken. It is ten per cent in the farm improvement loans bill and five per cent under the home improvement section of the housing act. and as a matter of fact five per cent would have been abundant according to the subsequent experience under the old Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act. But I do not think that a pool guarantee of ten per cent would be any inducement to the chartered banks, nor do I think that individual guarantees of ten per cent would be an inducement or would be justifiable. As I said in the banking and commerce committee, I do not wish to lengthen too much the list of guarantees to private institutions, especially on transactions of this kind. For these big loans, to guarantee -a loss up to ten per cent would not look right. It would not look right to me and I would far rather have the government go into the business itself as it does here. I would not say that, probably, if we had to set up a thousand or two thousand branches; but there would be only a few branches of this bank, maybe one in each province.

I do not intend to press the matter at this stage. I felt that by bringing it to the minister's attention prior to the reference of the subject to the banking and commerce committee it would at least give that committee an opportunity to study it, because they are supposed to be somewhat expert now in matters of finance, if one can judge rightly by the volume of argument that seems to reach the press and other places from time to time, through the lengthy discussions we have had this spring and summer. I would point out to the minister that on the second reading I took a rather confident course in relation to the adoption of the principle of the industrial development bank, and one of the considerations that prompted me to do so was this. There is not much use in talking about priming the pump of industry

Industrial Development Bank
and keeping the wheels rolling unless you do something about it, and credit is one of the things that must be obtained. We might as well face it frankly. I was not quite sure that this was the best way to do it, but at least it was one way to do it. If we are to have the existing lending institutions guaranteed only for a certain amount, and if that did not prime the pump and keep the high level of national income and maximum production and expanding economy and all these things that are to be maintained when the war is over, then of course it would not meet the situation. The people of this country are going to expect that, when the war is over, there shall not be a falling off of production and national income and of the standards to which this country has now become accustomed during the war. They have tasted a new era of economy during the war. Having tasted -that economy, they like to have jobs; they like to have full employment. They are insistent that this shall continue. I am one who believes that we have to see that it continues. We shall run into some pretty difficult doldrums and perhaps reach economic chaos unless this is done. It is quite a test for private enterprise, free enterprise, free initiative, or whatever you like to call it. But as I see it, that is what has to be done in Canada.
So, far as this industrial bank is concerned I should like to have seen a little less duplication of the existing services, because duplication of existing services does not indicate that there will be the maximum efficiency. It was for that reason that I made the suggestion I did on that occasion. If, after close study, the banking and commerce committee has taken the position indicated by the minister, and if they felt that the other system would not meet the conditions and would not provide the remedy which I think is necessary to keep the wheels of business going, then I feel that I should bowr to the decision of the committee and raise no further objection at the moment, except to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the suggestion was made from this side of the house in an honest effort to see that if the best plan were finally adopted the suggestion might be considered at arriving at that best plan.
Mr. -ROSS (St. Paul's): Apropos of what the Minister of Finance has said, I understood from the governor this morning that the chartered banks were to be used to a certain extent and that losses were to be guaranteed and that they would share in them. I think he said this morning that where they were both entering into a loan he would like to
see the chartered banks bear some part of the loss. I understood from him that any losses would probably be shared.
I have been a member of the banking and commerce committee for some time. I have listened with great interest to what has gone on there. Very fine arguments pro and con took place on the bank bill. As I listened to those arguments, what impressed me more than anything else was the words of the governor of the Bank of Canada when he said that this was an experiment and that we would need to have many experiments.
I am in favour of anything that will encourage private enterprise. I think we need to encourage it as much as possible. What I am really worried about is this. If an outfit gets stuck a little bit and cannot get its funds in any other way, everybody will be running to the industrial development bank. I think we have to trust the governor and his directors to see to it that that is not done.
I should like to point out that the bank must be kept free from any kind of political patronage. That is one of the difficulties in an institution of this kind, particularly when it is a government bank and where influence might be brought to bear. We have to trust the government to see to it that this does not happen. I believe this bank might serve a useful purpose. However, the commercial banks are the ones that can be used to the greatest extent. This is an adjunct of the private banks. It will be more useful for small industrial businesses than for others.
My leader said that a great volume of business was done in the committee. It would be better to say that a huge number of words were spoken and that a lot of repetition went on. A lot of business could be done without so much repetition. The banking and commerce committee gave this bill a great deal of study. All one can do is to form his own conclusions from what was said there.

To what extent and by what means will the benefits of this bank be made available to the smaller communities? I understood the minister to say a few minutes ago that very few banks will be set up, possibly one in each province. Fundamentally our problem is in the smaller centres. Those communities should be rebuilt by enterprises being fostered in those centres. Those enterprises should consist of small businesses. They should be established there rather than in the congested cities. These banks will be set up as separate entities. Unless there is some machinery devised and cooperation insisted on to make that machinery accessible to the
Industrial Development Bank

smaller communities, the largest portion of our country needing help along this line will not be served at all.
I cannot see the necessity of setting up an industrial bank to lend only to those people and to those concerns in the larger communities to whom the chartered banks will not lend. Nor can I see where the smaller enterprises in the smaller communities will be able to take advantage of this bank unless there is much greater cooperation and organization to bring the benefits of this bank to those communities. I cannot help feeling that this war has taken an undue toll of the smaller centres of Canada and has congested our people and our enterprises in the big centres to the very great detriment of this dominion. Our biggest problem is to build up the smaller communities and to assist the agricultural areas by so doing. This can be done not by bringing the people from the rural sections into our congested cities, but by taking industries out to our smaller towns and villages so that our people may stay there. Has the minister given thought to that, and can he give us any enlightenment on that point? I could go on and express many different points of view and put forward arguments in favour of what I suggest, but at this very late date I do not feel like holding up the committee. I should like the minister to make it abundantly clear that what I have suggested will be kept in mind and that he will make every effort to make this industrial bank justify itself primarily and mainly in the smaller communities.

speechtext:
The person or corporation desiring a loan will get in touch with the bank probably by writing to its head office, which will be in Ottawa, or it may get in touch with the provincial branch and make its submissions in the usual way. If the size of the loan is such that there will have to be a little travelling either by the applicant or by a representative of the bank to look the enterprise over, that may take a little time. It is not the ordinary commercial banking business that will be carried on by this bank, with an office in every town or anything like that; nor would there be any need of that. The functions to be discharged by this bank are those which to some extent have been discharged by investment bankers rather than by commercial banks, and it is the kind of lending business that will require only a small number of branches.
I do not know that I can say anything about the other parts of the remarks of the hon. gentleman. He advocates the decentralization of industiy. The result of establishing an institution which will be available to make loans to small industries in the 
country would go some distance in preventing the concentration of industry. It would work in favour of decentralization rather than centralization.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: But the minister will appreciate the fact that this bank, according to his explanation, will be of very little if any use to the small communities. Certainly the small business man in the rural community is not going to use this bank to the extent I think we should have him use it. I believe that greater cooperation would be achieved with the existing chartered banks. I would not approve the industrial bank setting up branches in small communities, but I think that if we had greater cooperation and a better liaison between the chartered banks in the small communities and the industrial development bank it would bring this bank nearer the small individual enterprise, and would be much more useful in that regard than in the cities, where so many institutions now exist. We all know that investment bankers do very little in the way of promoting enterprise in rural communities. We also know that in the past the chartered banks have been criticized severely, and I think justly, because of the rigid requirements they have been compelled to exact in the small communities. I think the greatest cry of our people against the chartered banks to-day arises from the niggardly way in which they have dealt with industry in small communities. I do not think there is any question about that. I believe that the greatest cause of criticism of our banking institutions in the past has been the drying up of the lending power of the chartered banks in the smaller communities, and I think it should be one of the first and fundamental aims of the industrial development bank to remedy that situation. I do not believe that under this legislation that condition will be met to even a small degree.

speechtext: Yes; I have the amendment here, but I should like to refer to the principle. This section contains the whole pith of the bill; and when I supported this bill strongIyi I have forgotten whether it was at the resolution stage or on second reading-

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
-I had an idea that this proposed bank would be of great assistance in promoting the organization of industry. I am sorry to say I have lost that idea now. I do not see in this bill the value in regard to the promotion of industry that I thought I saw in it at the commencement. This bank is not going to do anything at all along the lines of the industrial organizations of the two great railways, the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. All through the years they have promoted and induced capital to organize businesses throughout the country. Many of our cities have their industrial commissions. We have had the Toronto industrial commission for many years. It has done a marvellous job and has been instrumental in bringing to Toronto-to use an arbitrary figure-anywhere from one hundred to two hundred and fifty industries of one kind or another. In my time the head of that commission was Mr. Charles M. Burton, president of the Robert Simpson Company, and under his chairmanship the commission did wonderful work. The city of Welland, and many other cities in Ontario have had industrial commissions for many years.
In the commencement I thought the purpose of this bank was to assist in the promotion of business, but now I cannot see that at all; I cannot see that we are going to get any real value out of this legislation. I really do not see anything in it any more. It has not the same vision I thought it had. If it does not do that, what is it going to do?

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: It should help business to carry on.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
No; business is not organized in that way. Business has to be promoted and organized and induced to go forward, as the industrial commissions have done. The chartered banks do everything else, but this bank does not come forward to try to initiate production in any way. What is it going to do? When I referred to the matter earlier in the evening the minister mentioned paragraph (a) of subsection 1 of this section,
which has to do with a person engaged in or about to engage in an industrial enterprise in Canada. There is no promotion in that. If a person who engages in or is about to engage in business goes to the bank and submits his proposal, the bank will first ask, "Why didn't you go to a chartered bank?" "Oh, well," the applicant may say, "I have been there and the chartered bank did not want to assist me in this matter and I come to this new industrial bank." If this bank is not engaged in the promotion or creation or organization of new business it will take little interest in what the promoter has to say. I was looking for something like the Toronto industrial commission but with finance behind it, or something like the Canadian Pacific or Canadian National industrial commission, all of which have done such magnificent work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: Why do they not keep on?

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: In my room I have the last report of the Toronto industrial commission and there is a list covering many pages of the businesses which have been started in Toronto alone. I imagine I was wrong when I thought this industrial bank was being organized for the promotion of business. As some one said earlier-I believe it was the hon. member for Carleton-if business is not going to be promoted, how are we to create the small businesses that the chartered banks will not have anything to do with?

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: Do you think the government should promote business?

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: I am not in favour of the government going into business on anything. My observation is that this is more or less of a farce if it does not assist in promoting business, and no one knows that better than the Minister of Munitions and Supply.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: I thought you were advocating that now.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: No, I am not; I am only advocating that there should be organization to assist private industry to carry on business. I imagine I let myself down when I approved this bill earlier in the session.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: I think what the. hon. member says is right. We are merely being given a shadow without any substance. With the limitations imposed I cannot see how this bank can perform any useful function that the chartered banks could not perform. If there is to be only an office of this bank in each province or thereabouts, how will it be able to lend advantageously to private enterprise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
Do not get too discouraged; just wait and see.
Industrial Development Bank

They ask what his inventory is and he tells them. They then tell him to increase his inventory by $40,000 and they will lend him another $20,000. He goes out to buy, and the people from whom he purchases feel that since he is good for it they can sell him another $40,000 worth of goods. We are doing nothing under this bill except to make it possible for those whom the chartered banks consider to be bad accounts to come to the dominion government, and perhaps if they have sufficient pull and prestige they will get some money. It is just a question of whether the dominion government will get anything out of it or not.

speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman
would follow section 22 of the industrial development bank bill as I read section 81 (1) of the Bank Act, which reads:

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL

There is no substantial
difference.

It is a different type of
loan.

That is the very point

But not in the same way, not as fully as we get reports from the department of insurance. subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
I believe that if we endorse the minister's attitude we are in
Mr. Ilomuth.]
effect setting up a board which is responsible only to the minister, about the particulars of whose work the members of this house cannot get particulars. It is important that when we set up an industrial development bank the board should be accountable in detail to parliament itself.	Here we are lending the
people's money to a borrower through the agency of the president of the bank, and not asking him to tell us how he lends it or how the accounts stand. This being a government bank, we should scrutinize its affairs in much more detail; the accounts should be presented in detail so that the facts can be referred to in the house if they are required. There should be sufficient particulars so that hon. members could refer any phase of the operations to a committee for investigation and to see how things are going on. Certainly there should be detail equivalent to that in the auditor general's report, and so that a matter could be referred to the public accounts committee and examined by it. If there is to be nothing beyond a summary of assets and liabilities, it will be a case of parliament having no knowledge of how the nation's money is being handled.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL

Industrial Development Bank
suggest that particulars of each mortgage account should be given in the board's annual return, instead of the report-which is a rather full return-that they make each year.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL

Here we are, as I say, giving out the money of our people through a board and not requiring that board to account to us for what they are doing.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext: I believe that there should be a broad general statement of the position of the accounts at the end of each year, as gone over by the auditor; but to undertake to divulge to parliament, and through parliament to the public, the intimate position of every company's business would be, to my mind, entirely impracticable.

subtopic: PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL CREDIT FACILITIES FOR. FIXED AND WORKING CAPITAL
speechtext:
But we are not divulging any secrets of a company's business. What we are doing is this; we are stating what money we have lent and what assets there are as security. Remember we are lending public money, and under those circumstances the public have the right to demand and to know where that money is going and what i3 being done with it. I could easily imagine the situation of some man who comes to this bank and gets a loan. The chartered banks have turned him down; but he puts up with this bank whatever collateral he has, collateral which the chartered banks would not accept, and it is accepted by this bank. There may be a little "pull" in regard to the getting of this loan, or a little pressure may be brought to bear. The first thing you know, someone, perhaps in mediocre circumstances, who is trying to finance a business in some small or large community, will suddenly branch out as an industrialist in that community; but he will do so with the people's money, and the people in that community ought to know why; they ought to know what it is all about. Parliament certainly ought to know what the bank does w-ith the money of the people of Canada, because the people who are working in that very community, working at their benches every day, are supplying the money to parliament to lend these men money with which to run their businesses. I come from a county in which practically ninety-five per sent of the businesses were started by people in a small way two or three generations ago. Men worked hard; they built up their businesses; everything they earned they put back
into their businesses. They never asked for any pap from any government. They worked hard and developed their businesses with the aid of loyal employees. Now we are to have a lot of upstart businesses financed at the expense of the taxpayers and without any report to parliament as to the position of their accounts. I do not think it is right.

Air service-civil aviation division-
396. Airways and airports-Construction and improvements, including lighting and radio facilities-capital, $2,035,800.
Will this be for the construction of new facilities or airports? If so, where will they be located?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speechtext:
This vote is confined entirely
at the present time to small extensions and capital repairs. About half the vote is required for improvements in lighting and short extensions to runways, and about half the increase represents facilities including certain
IMr. Abbott.]
radio beams such as the one from Winnipeg to Edmonton. There are no new airports involved.
Does the minister mean that the item pertains to T.C.A. alone.
Chiefly the airways that are now in use for transport purposes, practically all the main line of Trans-Canada-extensions to the main line.

Item agreed to.
Air service-civil aviation division-
Airways and airports-operation and maintenance-[DOT]
397. Civil aviation services, $891,495.
What does this cover?
This represents operating costs of airways that are operated by the Department of Transport. It is the cost of operating civilian airways.
Why the increase of $180,000?

There are more airports
involved. Certain military airports are turned over to the Department of Transport for operation, or are in process of being turned over.
Does it cover the same services as in the previous item?
Yes, but this includes all airports that are being operated by the Department of Transport. It includes a greater number of airports than are covered by the previous vote.
Is it the intention to turn over the others?

Yes. As soon as any military airports are surplus to military requirements they are turned over for operation in civilian aviation.
Mr. ROW'E: Is that the general policy of the government, to turn them over as they become available?
As they become surplus to military requirements.
Is it intended to use all these throughout Canada?

They are turned over in the first instance to the Department of Transport, and they determine the place of the airport in civil aviation and the value of the buildings on the airport to civil aviation. If there is no use for an ariport or building the Department of Transport declares the airport surplus to transport requirements and it goes to the War Assets Corporation for disposal. In the case of the field itself when it is likely to be

Supply-Transport
required for civil aviation and certain buildings are not required, these buildings are turned over by the Department of Transport to the War Assets Corporation for disposal.
So far none has been turned over to the War Assets Corporation?
I think not. No airports have been turned over to the War Assets Corporation, but there is a study going on as to certain buildings on airports which may be turned over.
Already sold?
No. They are under study.

These four items, 396,
397, 398 and 399, all pertain to government-operated airports?
Yes.
They have no reference to those operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway company in the north country?
No.
Do other planes besides government-operated planes use those airports?
Yes; they are for the use of government planes and other planes.
Is there a charge made for the use?
There is a schedule of fees for all airports. All aircraft landing on an airport pay a fee.
Do the Trans-Canada aeroplanes pay the same fee as the others do?
Trans-Canada Air Lines pay a schedule of fees on a monthly basis. It is $100 per plane per month. If there are five planes landing it is $500 a month.
It is $500 a month?
If there are five schedules into an airport; if it is one schedule it is $100.
It makes no difference how many times a week? That is just the regular planes going across every day, and so on?
A number of schedules per day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: How do the fees paid compare with the cost to the government of the service provided?

The situation is so confused with the use by military planes which pay no
fee that I doubt whether any of the airports are on a self-sustaining basis to-day, although before the war a number of airports were on a self-sustaining basis. After the war, when the operation is confined wholly to civilian services many of the airports will be on a selfsustaining basis.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: When the minister speaks of an airport does he include all the meteorological service, beams and so on provided by the government?
Yes; the operation of an airport involves the use of the beam which serves the airport.
Does the minister mean that there is commercial and civil aviation on the same fields as military aviation?
Yes.
That is where the increase occurs in this item?

No. Airports that are used for commercial aviation are in general operated by the- Department of Transport. The military have the privilege of using the airport. For example, Malton is a civilian airport; yet there is a training school there and the military use it. But it is operated by the Department of Transport. The same thing applies to Dorval. Dorval is used chiefly by United States planes being ferried to Europe. .It is operated by the Department of Transport as a civilian field.
What about the airport on Toronto island? Is that under this vote too?
That is owned by the city of Toronto. It is not operated by the Department of Transport. I believe it is under lease at the moment to the Royal Canadian Air Force.

Item agreed to.
Air service-civil aviation division-
Airways and airports-operation and maintenance-
308. Radio aviation services, $859,230.
Would the minister explain the $78,000 increase?

That is owing to the fact that additional beams have been installed during the past year. Three additional beams have been installed. They provide for the three new beams going in on the route from Winnipeg to Edmonton, Neepawa, Yorkton and Dafoe.

Is none of this vote for the far northwest country?
Supply-Transport
No.
How do planes going up in that country get their directions?
Beams have been installed, but they have been installed out of a war vote. The northwest staging route is a military expenditure.

I am contemplating making a trip very shortly by plane away up to the far north country. I am anxious to know that the plane I am going in will have all the scientific directions and so on. So far as I know it will be a Canadian Pacific plane. There are no other planes that operate in that country. I am speaking now of to Aklavik at the mouth of the Mackenzie river. Does the Canadian Pacific Railway company have to finance everything itself in the far north country, whereas the government under these four items pays 14,000,000 for other air lines? I am glad they do it. I have no fault to find with it. But the Canadian Pacific is the only air line operating in that great north country. Some air line must operate in it; otherwise folks will not be able to get in there. Has the Canadian Pacific to supply all its aviation arrangements and beams and so forth?

If my hon. friend is travelling over the northwest staging route he will travel on a military beam. All the facilities will be there but they are operated by the R.C.A.F. If he is travelling on the Mackenzie river route, these airports have just been taken over by the Department of Transport. They were built by the United States government. They have recently been taken over. I think he will hardly travel on beams between those airports at the moment. It is not a main route. It is a route built for a special purpose and it is not provided with radio beams.
As I understand it, I shall be travelling on Canadian Pacific planes.
That may be so.
Paying my way as a passenger.
You will be travelling on very good planes, with very good pilots and with a veiy good company, but you will have no radio beam.
How about the Toronto island airport? Is there a beam there?
There is no beam at Toronto.
Does the minister imply that there is no commercial planning in the Northwest Territories; that it is all R.C.A.F.?

No; there is plenty of planning and plenty of facilities but they happen to be operated by the R.C.A.P., because the traffic is ninety-five per cent military. There is very heavy traffic indeed on the northwest staging route, but it is chiefly military traffic, and as a matter of convenience the airports are operated by the R.C.A.F.
Does that mean from Edmonton to Norman Wells, or to White Horse?
Edmonton to White Horse.
The route I was speaking of is from Edmonton to Norman Wells and on down to Aklavik.
My hon. friend should travel in good weather on that route.
I am not going to discuss that with the company. The company operates the plane; I pay my money and I expect that they will take me there and bring me back.

Item agreed to.
Air service-civil aviation division

Airways and airports-operation and .maintenance-
SO:9. Meteorological aviation services, $475,000.
Is there anything being done with regard to assistance to boys going through schools? This vote is for the purpose of advanced aeronautical instruction. In what way will it work out?

This is the cost of the meteorological service for all Canada. It covers the cost of operating many hundreds of observation stations, the cost of war service and the appointment of staff. The training is arranged. I do not think it is by grants to schools particularly; I believe the department carries its own courses. During the war we have trained hundreds of new operators for this service and for military service.
Does it mean that grants will be made to private clubs, for instance?
I do not think we have come to that item yet. We are talking about item 399, meteorological service.

Now the minister has me interested in this. I cannot go to Aklavik, for instance, except by Canadian Pacific Air Lines; I cannot go by R.C.A.F. Do the Canadian Pacific planes receive this meteorological service?
Oh, yes.
Then this item would-

Help you quite a bit.

Supply-Transport
-provide for the furnishing of meteorological service to Canadian Pacific planes, as well as any others in that area?
Yes.
What is the difference between these two items? Here we have radio aviation services, and in the next item we have meteorological aviation services, $475,000.

Item 399 is the aviation service. That is a short-term service, forecasting the weather for about eight to ten hours ahead, with great accuracy. The other vote is for a service to farmers and citizens generally, forecasting the weather for much longer ahead, and it is less accurate for that reason.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is the work of the two coordinated?
Absolutely.

Item agreed to.
Air service-civil aviation division
k00. Grants for advanced aeronautical instruction and to aeroplane clubs, including grant of $5,000 to the Canadian Flying Clubs Association, $8,000.
This seems a very small item. Surely we give more support to these clubs than $8,000?

Before the war, many private flying clubs were assisted by the government. When the war began, the military undertook this training on a very much larger scale. Most of the flying clubs were made units of the military training, under an arrangement with the military authorities. Therefore this item has been cut down to the point where it merely pays the salary of the secretary of the association and a few administrative costs. There are no flying clubs operating to-day for the training of pilots except under military auspices.
There would be but for the war, would there not?
There will be when the war is over.
The government has no commitments at all to private clubs?
Not at the moment. As a matter of fact we give each club $100 a year to help keep the organization together.

It seems a very small
consideration.
They are not doing any business.

Air service-meteorological division-
402.	Grant to Kingston observatory, $500.
Is this for time?

No; we had an old arrangement with Kingston to perform scientific work for the meteorological service. The university undertakes certain work for which we have been paying $500 annually for some years.

Item agreed to.
Air service-radio division-
403.	Administration of the Radiotelegraph Act and regulations, $136,880.
Is this the item under which radio stations are licensed?
Yes.

I wish to ask the minister something about the situation in connection with the radio station at Halifax. As the minister probably knows, I was a member of the radio committee; and on June 28 Doctor Frigon, acting general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, made the statement before the committee that they were making a capital expenditure at Halifax to carry out essential services to the people of Nova Scotia and the maritimes generally, through their station there. Subsequently the newspapers carried the story that by some means or another an attempt was being made to block the erection of the C.B.C. station and to revive an old permit that had been granted to a private organization back in 1938. During the debate the Minister of National War Services did not seem very clear as to what really was the situation, and I thought under this item I would ask whether any licences have been granted at Halifax. It seems to me essential that the C.B.C., having arranged for the setting up of a transmitter there, should be the organization to go forward with the erection of this station. It is said that the other station might give satisfactory service to the community, but, after all, a private station gives only a certain part of its service to the community, while a C.B.C. station can render public service all day. I am not fully informed as to this situation, but I noticed the answer given by Doctor Frigon, and I followed very carefully the debate in which the senior member for Halifax took part, on the estimates of the Minister of National War Services. I should like to know the situation from the point of view of the Department of Transport, which is called upon to issue licences for the stations.
Supply-Transport

The Department of Transport issues licences under the Radio Act, after having obtained the recommendation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The situation at Halifax is that the Halifax Herald has had a licence for many years. It is the broadcasting corporation in Halifax. In 1939, I think, just immediately before the war, a licence was granted to the Halifax Chronicle. The work was not proceeded with because they could not get the plant and equipment, and the application lapsed. Recently we were advised of a new application from the Halifax Chronicle which came with the recommendation from the C.B.C. that the contract had been revised. I may say that the contract specified that there were no commitments as to any network. To my knowledge the C.B.C. have not applied for a wave-length or for a licence to build a radio station in Halifax. I know nothing about that. I heard they were to build one there, but as far as I am aware- and my memory is fairly good-I have no recollection of any application coming through from the C.B.C.
Mr. .COLDWELL: Doctor Frigon said:
. . . we are providing now for a provincial outlet in Nova Scotia, Halifax. The report has gone to the minister.
Then the senior member for Halifax asked:
Q. That is, you are making capital expenditure so as to carry out services of the second network ?
A. Right.
Q. Are there any others besides the one in Nova Scotia?
A. There is only one station, CJBC, which was not on the network before and which is being placed on the dominion network, and the one which we are building to provide an outlet in Halifax for the dominion network.
Doctor Frigon stated that they were providing an outlet.

My officers confirm my
memory that we have had no application from the C.B.C.
Do they already possess a permit for a station.
I am informed that the minister in charge of the C.B.C. confirms my understanding that no application for a frequency has been filed.
Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ORDER IN COUNCIL AUTHORIZING DENUNCIATION OF CONVENTION
speechtext:
I should like to table for the information of members of the house copy of P.C. 4666 of July 31, 1944, which authorized the Secretary of State for External Affairs to take steps in respect to denouncing the international convention relating to international exhibitions, which was signed at Paris on November 2, 1928. The purpose of the convention was to limit the number of inter-

Business of the House
national exhibitions and to establish a uniform code for their organization and administration. It applied only to exhibitions that were official or were officially recognized and lasted three weeks or longer. The contracting countries agTeed to withhold subsidies from every international exhibition coming within the scope of this convention which did not comply with its provisions. The convention was administered by an international bureau at Paris and jointly controlled by the contracting parties.
The Canadian government has decided to withdraw from the convention in view of other denunciations of the convention by other governments and with a view to clearing the ground for a new convention dealing with the same matters. In pursuance of minute of council, notification was deposited on July 1 with the various other parties to the convention with which Canada maintains friendly relations, of the termination of the convention on behalf of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I should be very happy to meet my hon. friend's wishes. He has referred to good luck and good management. My experience in public life has taught me there is nothing like cordial cooperation. If we have that I think there will be little doubt of our being able to complete the business perhaps by the end of this week without sacrificing any public interest.
As to the conclusion of the work this week it might help to make certain what otherwise would be a little doubtful if the house were agreeable to beginning its sitting an hour earlier this afternoon and to continuing its sitting for an hour after six o'clock. That does not mean that all hon. members will have to be in the house continuously. The British house, as one knows, sits through the dinner hour as a matter of ordinary procedure. If. when one o'clock comes, the house would be willing to adjourn until two o'clock, and possibly again at six agree to adjourn until seven, we would I believe make the progress which would help to ensure our completing the business late to-morrow night.

I have no objection to that for to-day. I would like to make this clear, however, that if at the end of to-day's sittings it looks as if we cannot complete our business by Saturday night, we ought to revert to reasonable hours, so that we can complete the session in an orderly way next week, if that is the earliest possible time of conclusion.

For some days this house has been sitting continuously from eleven in the morning until eleven at night, including Saturdays. I think most hon. members are feeling the strain of these continuous sessions. I know that I am and the members of my party are. I do not think the house should assemble at two o'clock, and I certainly do not think we should continue until seven. If we can finish the business within the ordinary hours of the house as we now have them, that is all right, but we should not prolong the hours of sitting
Business oj the House

beyond the present limits. It is physically impossible to stand this strain when we are giving to the house the attention which some of us are trying to give.

I took it for granted when I made my statement that there was unanimity in the house on that point. If there are hon. members who feel that the work is being pressed too much, we had better come to the conclusion that it is impossible to finish on Saturday night unless these hours are extended, having in mind that we should not as a parliament rush things too much. I mentioned that yesterday. I was agreeable, if the rest of the members were, to having the hours extended, but if the hours are not to be extended by unanimous consent it is physically impossible to close on Saturday night.

The estimates have been before the house since the beginning of the year; they have been discussed in large part under war appropriation and at other times, and it is not necessary to have a fresh discussion or any discussion of every item.
