speechtext: 36. Departmental administration, $410,189.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
At the risk of
holding up the committee, there are a number of matters that I should like to direct to the attention of the Prime Minister with a view to securing explanations which have not so far been given concerning certain matters in these estimates. I shall refrain from repetition of any of the arguments that have been advanced with respect to the whole field of external affairs.
Several matters have arisen during the last few days on which I think the Prime Minister should give some information. The first has to do with a meeting that recently took place in London of the shipping representatives' of the united nations to ensure continued availability of their tonnage resources for all purposes of the united nations. Canada was represented at that conference, the other governments being Belgium, Greece, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, the United Kingdom and the United States, as well as Denmark and the French committee of national liberation.
According to a press dispatch of August 8, the governments concerned declared that they accepted as a common responsibility the provision of shipping for all military and other tasks necessarily arising out of the completion of the war in Europe and the far east, and for the supplying of all liberated areas as well as of the united nations generally and the territories under their authority. I should like the Prime Minister to indicate the extent of the decisions arrived at at this conference and generally the point of view taken by Canada in relation thereto. This is, I submit, an important link in the chain of decisions that show the determination of Canada to continue in this war until the destruction not only of Germany but also of Japan is achieved.
At the risk of introducing a matter with respect to which the Prime Minister has stated that no information will be forthcoming at this time, I ask him to reconsider the question whether he is in a position to advise the people of Canada as to the continued use in the war against Japan of the veterans who are to-day overseas in Italy and France and who have served so long, so nobly and so well. I ask that question not in any desire to bring before the country any matter concerning which information should hot be furnished on the ground of disclosing our situation for the benefit of the enemy; but in the United States the situation is being freely discussed. It has been discussed in congress and by those in authority and the attitude taken has been that at the conclusion of hostilities in Europe there is bound to be a partial demobilization, and in particular that those who have served the longest will have an opportunity if they so desire to secure discharges from the army.
I wish also to ascertain from the Prime Minister whether he can furnish the committee with information regarding an international police force. He dealt at length with the question of international security and showed- and in this he represented the viewpoint of the Canadian people as a whole-the willingness of Canada to participate with the other nations of the united nations in a great scheme of international security. The experience after the last war showed that while in 1919 all the signatories to the league of nations accepted responsibilities, when it came to carrying those responsibilities into effect they failed to do so because there was not mobilized behind them the public opinion in their various counties. The United States have gone a long way in this connection in the last three years. A year ago when, as a member of the empire parliamentary association, I was in Washington, we met with Congressman Fulbright who introduced that now famous resolution in the House of Representatives setting out the stand , to be taken by the United States to assure the united nations of a united front after the war

in order to prevent future wars. While we in Canada have made a declaration to the same effect, so far as I know we have no official declaration as to what contribution Canada is to make. These are not matters of a partisan nature. If there is one subject that must be discussed in a non-partisan way, in a national way, it is the subject of external affairs, upon which we must endeavour by collaboration and cooperation to arrive at a common and definite point of view representative of the people of Canada as a whole.
In dealing with employment after the war Doctor George Weir suggested some months ago that when the war is over a large number of the men in the navy, the army and the air force in Canada will be assured of the opportunity to continue their careers in those services. In particular he referred to the fact that in going up and down the length and breadth of Canada he found that the Canadian people felt that Canada should contribute to an international force and that this force should come in the main from her air force which has achieved so much in this war under the British commonwealth scheme. Is the government in a position to advise what Canada's contribution will be? It may not be definitely known at this time, but is it intended that there shall be set up an international force in which Canada will loe represented to ensure peace in this world and punishment for all aggressor nations?
In view of the tremendous oil resources of the world and of the great importance of oil in war and peace, according to the Associated Press, Great Britain and the United States signed a pact on oil policy on August 8. According to the dispatch, this policy is designed to prevent peace-time disputes between these two allies and serve as a prime weapon to enforce peace. The dispatch goes on to say:
The agreement, negotiated by the acting secretary of state, Edward Stettinius, for the United States, and Lord Beaverbrook for Britain, is the first pact dealing directly with post-war trade and security.
Both countries agreed that it shall go into effect when eaih has notified the other "of its readiness".
The dispatch continues:
The agreement emphasizes the view that world security must remain uppermost in all international considerations, and make the distribution of oil "to all peaceable countries" subject to a future world organization to check aggression and maintain peace.
To what extent is Canada a party to this pact, and to what extent has she been consulted in reference to this very important matter? Had there been a control over the

oil resources of this world prior to the war, such as is contemplated by the agreement that was entered into recently by Great Britain and, the United States, the possibilities of aggressive war on the part of Germany would undoubtedly have been obviated to a considerable degree.
Another matter that has arisen since the Prime Minister made his speech on the subject of external relations has to do with civil air transportation within the empire after the war. The Prime Minister said the other day that through the session, from January to the present, matters of external relations had been discussed and because of that I am not going to make any formal speech to-day. I am merely asking questions on matters on which we have as yet no information. The subject of air transportation was dealt with at great length for many days, but within the last few days the Prime Minister of New Zealand, speaking in the parliament of that country, indicated that an arrangement had been arrived at-at least that is the way I interpret his words-between Canada, Australia and New Zealand, under which a Pacific all-red air line would be established. He went on to point out that application had already been made to the United States for the privilege of securing landing rights in Hawaii. One factor that kept back the development of an empire air route or an inter-empire air route in the Pacific from 1919 to 1939 was the fact that the United States refused to allow the nationals of any other country to fly over the Hawaiian islands. It was felt that in the interests of the defence of the Pacific, information gained through flying over the islands should be denied to Japan, and all nations were excluded, although when war came events proved that the Japanese had full information with regard to the Hawaiian islands. The step has been taken by the government of New Zealand, I believe in cooperation with Australia, to establish an all-red air line.	The press
dispatch, which I have not before me, indicates that the United Kingdom may participate in it. I asked the Minister of Munitions and Supply a question with regard to this matter yesterday, but I did not receive very much of an answer. In fact I received less information than the Prime Minister of New Zealand gave when he spoke in the parliament of that country. This is a matter of very great importance to the people of Canada, and generally speaking to the people of the empire. It is important to know how far we have gone and how far we shall go in establishing within the empire or within parts

Supply-External Affairs
of the empire a united air line in order to bind the empire closer together by closer communications than have heretofore existed.
I should like to refer to the empire council. All of us are in agreement that the conference of prime ministers was a most successful gathering and one which did much, and will, I I am sure, in. the years to come do more to bind the empire closer together than ever before. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, as I read the speech of Lord Halifax of January last, and the Prime Minister's speech delivered in this chamber the other day, I believe the Prime Minister and Lord Halifax in their respective fields are much closer together to-day than they were in January last.
There is agreement among members on all sides of the house, particularly so far as the empire as a whole is concerned, that our external affairs policy must be consistent with our interest. And there is no inconsistency if we so proceed as to ensure that British commonwealth traditions and ideals, and its way of life, shall in the years to come continue to exercise their power for good.
All of us are agreed that this is no time for recrimination in connection with what happened in the past. The war has proven that so far as Canada is concerned, the days of convenient detachment in the affairs of the world at large are at an end. Yet that view represented the attitude taken in Canada-an attitude which I describe as one of convenient detachment-between 1935 and 1939. We have learned that no nation by abstaining from world cooperation and world collaboration can prevent its becoming involved in any widespread war. That is why many of us believe there should be set up, sitting from time to time in London, in Ottawa and in other capitals of the empire, an empire council to collaborate together and to exchange information of mutual interest to the security, defence and welfare of the empire as a whole.
Listening to the Prime Minister one might conclude that the question of an empire council had been decided finally. Prime Minister Curtin, upon his return to Australia, and as reported by the Canadian Press on July 17, said that he-

echoed Marshal Smuts' declaration that "in an experience of forty years no imperial conference could compare with it in the magnitude of the issues raised and the spirit of mutual understanding which prevailed throughout."
Referring to his own proposal for a permanent empire consultative body, Mr. Curtin said the conference had agreed to consult with the respective governments on the suggested empire council and the possible centralization of empire cooperation on financial, economic and social questions.
Apparently therefore the decision as to whether or not a council or alternatively a secretariat shall be set up was not finally concluded by the conference of prime ministers. And if I am. right in that assumption, from what Prime Minister Curtin said, I would ask the Prime Minister of Canada whether or not, representing Canada, he would be prepared to consent or to accept the set-up of an empire council or secretariat representative of cabinet ministers from various parts of the empire, meeting from time to time in order to arrive at unity of policy-if necessary meeting continuously, subject to this, that whatever decisions are arrived at by the council shall be submitted to the respective governments in the various parts of the empire.
I see no sacrifice of autonomy in that. We talk so much about sovereignty and loss of sovereignty, and about danger to our autonomy. But, Mr. Chairman, when met with that argument the question which always suggests itself to me is this: Are we not prepared to trust our blood and kindred within the empire, as we are prepared to trust the nations without the empire, in a great international organization in order to secure peace and assure its perpetuation? I believe this, that not only on the ground of sentimental ties-and sentiment means much in the life of a people as well as in that of an individual -but also on the strict foundation of common interest there must be a closer cooperation between Great Britain and the dominion, whereby machinery shall be established so that the highest measure of unity of policy and unity of action in international and empire matters may be attained.
Canada secured equality of status under the statute of Westminster. But, as Lord Halifax stated "there was hardly any equivalent effort toward securing what I call equality of function." As I listened to the Prime Minister in a speech which I am sure will rank as a very great exposition of Canada's constitutional position, I take it that he has arrived at the position where he believes that it would be-
-ail immeasurable gain if on vital issues we could achieve a common foreign policy, expressed not by a single voice, but by the unison of many.
Those were the words of Lord Halifax in January last. In effect, as I understand them, they were the words of the Prime Minister of Canada in August 1944. And without there being any loss of sovereignty, and also without any suggestion of compulsion I believe that it should be extended as well to cover defence and empire communications.
I have already said that I do not share the view that closer ties with the empire mean domination by anyone, diminished sovereignty

or subservience to anyone. To me the hope for the future is in the extension of partnership in the empire and of its being fortified by closer collaboration-, through common endeavour, common idealism and a common desire to assure that the future shall be brighter than it was in the days between 1919 and 1939; that we endeavour by common representation and collaboration to arrive at a policy for the commonwealth, of the commonwealth and by the commonwealth. We should not do as we did between 1919 and 1939 when, because of Canada's abstention from active participation, policies were determined by one part of the empire and in the result the other parts of the empire, having had little to do with that policy, nevertheless followed the course decided upon.
I have already asked the Prime Minister whether the door is permanently closed to an empire council or a permanent secretariat. I do not mean that there should be a rigid organization, for this empire and commonwealth have not been built upon rigid formalism. They have been built through cooperation and gradual growth, and upon the determination to collaborate with each other. Freedom of the dominions would not be lost if men from all parts of the empire met together continuously, to the end that through diversity of opinion a unity of idealism in inter-empire and international affairs might be arrived at. While it is always dangerous to speculate as to what might have been, how often the thought occurs that the course of history might very well have been changed had there been a common direction and common effort in the matter of defence, participated in by all parts of "the empire, during the years when Hitler was rising to power. If Hitler had only known that the empire was united, that there was no division; if there had been a united voice for all parts of this empire, represented by such a council, to tell him what would happen if he were to transgress, the course of history might have been changed. This is speculation, and perhaps it is fruitless to indulge in it, but we should assure that in the future which we have in our making the mistakes of the past shall not be used as the foundation for our future policies.
There is just one other point in connection with the question of international security. On July 17, 1914, Mr. Cordell Hull, the secretary of state for the United States, announced that exploratory conversations on an international security organization for maintaining peace were under way and would culminate in a meeting in August in Washington. I do not know that the Prime Minister has yet

informed the house as to whether Canada is indirectly represented at that conference, for it seems to me this is a most important conference as far as Canada is concerned. Canada has a special interest in any conversations that take place in 'connection with post-war security, occupying as she does the strategic position of neighbour to both the United States and Russia. In their declaration of common aims, in the great charter of tjie commonwealth, the dominion premiers used these words:
We affirm that after the war a world organization -to maintain peace and security should be set up and endowed with the necessary power and authority to prevent aggression and violence.
That is a great aim and a great dedication by all parts of the empire. But promises, unless they are fulfilled; hopes, unless they are translated into action, are dangerous in times like these. Having regard to that declaration I believe at this time the Prime Minister should be in a position to let the rest of the empire know that Canada intends to contribute her share of the necessary manpower and what we have in the way of strategic bases to the end that there may be set up a police force, and that some of the police beats shall be located in the strategic airports within this dominion.
There were other matters with which I should like to have dealt, but I appreciate the opportunity the committee has given me to discuss these matters and I shall not proceed much further at this time. As one reads the casualty lists each day one is impressed with the fact that, without regard to racial origin, Canadians are living and dying for their country and their empire. Yet when these young Canadians return to this country, what do they come back to? They come back to a Canada which insists that they shall not designate themselves as Canadians but shall prefix their paternal national origin, regardless of the number of generations their families may have been in this country. A Canadian returning to Canada from a visit to the United States or from any part of the world is met at the border of this country by an immigration inspector who insists that before that Canadian can enter the country of his birth he has to say what is his paternal racial origin. In this regard I think we can learn something from the United States. We want to unify this country. Time and again the Prime Minister has declared for national unity, for doing away with the things that separate us. I do not believe we could do anything that would go further toward uniting the people of this nation than to have parliament make a declara-

Supply-External Affairs
tion as to the right of an individual to call himself a Canadian, irrespective of racial origin. That is what they have done in the United States. As I have said before, no one thinks of Mr. Roosevelt as a Dutch-American. No one thinks of General Eisenhower as a German-American. No one thinks of Mayor LaGuardia of New York as an Italian-American. They are great Americans. We perpetuate this thing every ten years in our census, the excuse being that it is necessary to have the information as to ethnic groups. How authentic is the information thus secured? Not very; for when a woman is married, irrespective of her racial origin, in the census she appears as belonging to the ethnic group of her husband. The necessity for ethnic information may have been important at one time, but if I may repeat the thought I expressed in the first speech I ever made in this house, if parliament wants to do one thing that will bring together people in this country of all origins, let it enact legislation to give Canadians the opportunity and privilege of calling themselves Canadians. In that way parliament would do more to bind this country together in the common idealism of a common purpose and common dedication than by anything else that could be done. Those who serve in the Canadian armed forces are proud of the "Canada" on their shoulder-straps, and without regard to hyphenated considerations. While they serve, they are Canadians. I ask the Prime Minister to round out this great programme which he has placed before the house in the last few days for the benefit and rehabilitation of our men who serve by making the necessary amendments which will once for all and without regard to origin enable men and women of this country to call themselves Canadians, and by so doing unite this country as never before.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say first of all to my hon. friend that I wholly agree with him that in these matters which relate to external affairs there should be as little of partisanship as possible. It is, however, inevitable that in our consideration of some international affairs we may look at matters from different angles. Some are strong in their conviction that centralization is the best way to build up the empire, while others of us are equally strong in our views that a measure of decentralization based on autonomy is as between all the parts a more effective way of preserving permanency and avoiding friction. I think we shall have to look to the record of the years to see which of the opposite points of view has on the whole most to commend it. These differences of view will exist and it is right that we should
debate their merits, but apart from that I believe all hon. members will agree that the tradition which they have sought to* follow [DOT] in the British House of Commons whereby foreign affairs are viewed as something which relates essentially to the nation as a whole in its relations with foreign nations, and keeping discussion therefore as far as possible from partisan considerations, is the correct and proper attitude to follow. I have tried to follow that tradition. I may have differed in the point of view that I have indicated from some other hon. members but I have never tried to make any aspect of external affairs a major party issue.
I wish to say in regard to the questions which my hon. friend has asked me that I would like to give a direct answer to every question in the sense of disclosing fully all that I know, but my hon. friend will realize, as all members of the house will realize, that throughout the period of the war there have been conferences and negotiations, exchanges of communications and .the like, not only between all parts of the British empire but between all of the united nations, more particularly those who are allied in the waging of war on the field of battle. From the beginning it has been essential for one to decide how far pronouncements should be made, in the first instance, from one or other of the dominions rather than from the government at Westminster, and how far announcements should be made by me in this House of Commons rather than by the President of the United States or the Prime Minister of Great Britain on matters which affect all their peoples just as completely as they affect the citizens of Canada. Knowing how meticulously careful both the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the President of the United States have been in making known major developments with respect to any aspect of the war or any aspect of the peace or of post-war policy without reaching agreement between themselves as to by whom the announcements were to be made, whether they should be made simultaneously, whether they should be made in several parts of the world-knowing that and much more which bears on the question of making decisions public, I have of necessity to exercise a degree of reserve in what I disclose which goes much further than my own personal inclination would go. I feel there is an obvious obligation which this government owes to the other governments having to do with these matters, and which our country owes to all the countries which are of the united nations. That is the sole reason why in some of these

Supply-External Affairs

matters I have not given and have felt that I was not entitled to give to the house as much in the way of what might be termed inside information as I otherwise would be ready and anxious to give.
I must add this further fact, that whatever is given out in this house on those matters is usually construed as something which necessarily immediately affects all different parts of the British empire, affects all the united nations if the question is large enough, and as such may give information to our enemies as well. I do not know how often I have heard in conferences the point of view stressed that by a little pronouncement here and a little pronouncement there- those who are most skilled in these matters are able to piece together in a very short time a pattern which pretty well discloses the whole. It is that pattern which at this time no one who is interested in what is going to be for permanent good would wish to have known to those against whom we are fighting. I think that will be quite clear to all hon. members. For that reason in answering my hon. friend this morning I may have to reply to one or two questions that he asked less completely than I otherwise would wish. However, as far as I remember his questions I shall mention them and seek to deal with them.
The first matter my hon. friend mentioned was the meeting which is being held in London on the question of shipping. As the committee is aware there has been throughout the period of the war between the different allied nations the closest kind of cooperation with respect to shipping in relation to war matters that it has been possible to have. The meeting in London has been for the purpose of carrying on into the immediate post-war period that same kind of cooperation. There will of necessity be need for quite as close if not closer cooperation in the matter of shipping between the shipping interests of the different countries once the great work of the liberation of Europe and the restoration of those countries gets under way. This meeting is obviously desirable to anticipate as largely as possible what will most effectively help to meet the emergency that will arise just as soon as European hostilities end, and this other great task is assumed by the nations that have been cooperating together up to the present.
My hon. friend asked me a question with respect, I take it, to the extent to which our armed forces would be used against Japan. That is a matter which I am not in a position to disclose at the present time. Any matter that relates to the disposition of our defence

forces would necessarily be one of which the department of defence would have the fullest knowledge and upon which it would not wish to give any information until the moment had come when agreement had been reached by all intending to contribute as to the extent of their contributions. But -this I will say, as is well understood, that the government has always assumed and said that the armed forces of Canada would be used to the end of the war, whether against the enemy in Europe or against the enemy in Asia, and that it is well known to be the policy of the government that our armed forces will continue to take their part in the war against Japan. There is this always to be kept in mind, that from the beginning of the war our forces have been employed in many parts of the world, but mainly in Europe, and that the United States forces have not been in the war as long as our forces have, also that the United States have large forces already employed in Asia, to an extent greater than there are British and other forces employed there. What disposition therefore will be made of armed forces as between the United States, the British and those of the different dominions I am not in a position to say at the moment. But I would make it perfectly clear that the policy of the government is to see that our appropriate part is taken in the war against Japan to the very close of the war.
My hon. friend asked whether I would tell him about the return of some of those who have -been longest overseas, whether they would be brought back first. I assume he was not in the house yesterday when the Minister of National Defence spoke on that matter. As I recall what the minister said, he made it clear that involved in this question was the matter of breaking up units, and that that was a consideration of which account would have to be taken before he could say who would come back first or who would come back later on. I think I should allow that matter to stand at the point at which the Minister of National Defence left it.
The next question asked by my hon. friend was the matter of an international police force. That question is bound up of course with the whole matter of post-war world organization and, as is well known, it is a subject which has been receiving for some time past the closest attention of the united nations, particularly those of the British commonwealth and the United States. The conference which is to be held in Washington relates to post-war organization and is an outcome of the Declaration of Moscow, at which it was agreed that representatives of the four great powers would

Supply-External Affairs
meet to discuss this matter in the first instance. There again, these matters follow a certain well-recognized procedure. From the beginning of the war it has been apparent that it would be impossible to have all the united nations taking exactly the same part or having the same voice in the discussion and settlement in a tentative way of some of these world questions. We have recognized that in the direction of the war, Mr. Churchill, the President, Mr. Stalin, and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, as the representatives of the four great powers, were in a different position- enjoyed, I might say, a certain priority in the consideration and discussion of these problems which affect us all. We have, I think wisely, recognized that fact, and instead of seeking to embarrass the working out of problems by at all times asserting that we must have equal rights and opportunities, we have rather sought to make it perfectly sure that in no particular were Canada's interests being in any -way overlooked; and being satisfied of that, being kept fully informed of what is taking place, we have proceeded on the lines of helpful cooperation, I might say behind the scenes, rather than out in the public arena. I would like to make this very clear, that I do not think there has been any matter of major concern-certainly none of immediate concern to Canada-in any of these international affairs in which we have not been kept very fully informed. There have been one or two or three or four slips here or there, where public announcements have been made by others a little sooner than perhaps they should have been made but, having regard to the vast organization which has had to carry on this work, I think the number of such embarrassing instances has been very few indeed. But we have been kept informed and we are informed to-day. We know the line which will be presented, for example, at Washington in regard to world organization by the officials who are discussing matters there. May I say that we know it in relation not merely to what may affect Canada but to what may affect any or all parts of the British commonwealth. At the meeting of prime ministers in London there was no question, unless it were questions related immediately to the conclusion of the war, which received more attention and discussion than matters relating to the post-war order, and particularly this great question of world organization; and there I think I might say, as the pronouncement at the end of the conference made clear, we were all in agreement on the general line that should be taken. There has been no difference of view that I can recall with respect to any authority that the officials at Washington will have at the present time.

They have their instructions; they are following them along lines that are known to South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the United Kingdom, and they will be presenting, with the other nations meeting at Washington, through the officials, points of view which have been fully discussed in advance.	*
Let me say at once that, had Canada insisted on being represented at the conference at Washington at this stage, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, as well as the lesser nations of the united nations, would have had an equal right to demand a like representation. After all, what is being done now is to try to bring into being some form of world organization which will be the best that can be devised. It would be going too far to say that the whole business is still in a nebulous state, because it is beginning to assume a very definite form, and that form has not been concealed from the governments of any of the countries concerned but rather is well known to them. It will not be definitely settled until there has been some opportunity to see, as between the powers which are meeting together, how far they are in common accord and what differences may still remain to be ironed out.
Let me repeat, the whole question of organizing world security is receiving the most anxious study of all the united nations. We have made it clear that Canada will do its full part in carrying out agreed security schemes, whether they involve the creation of an international police force or, alternatively, of measures for seeing that there will always be an overwhelming preponderance of power available to protect the peace. That goes as far as I think I shouldi go at the moment in indicating Canada's attitude toward a readiness to accept, with all the other nations that are united in the furtherance of world organization, such obligations as may be expected of them.
My hon. friend spoke about the agreement between the United States and Great Britain recently made with regard to oil resources, and asked if we were represented. That was an agreement between those two governments in a matter which is of vital concern to each of them. Canada is not in the same position as those two countries in the matter of oil resources. Canada is not a party to the United Kingdom-United States oil agreement, but we have been kept fully informed in regard to the discussions. We are not in fact an important oil producer, as we depend for four-fifths of our requirements upon imported supplies. The United States-United Kingdom agreement may well lead to a wider agreement,
Supply-External Affairs

including all oil-producing and all oil-consuming countries, in which case Canada would of course cooperate.
I think it must be clear that in these matters of agreements which affect many nations the right way to start is to begin with the two which are most concerned, and if agreement is concluded between them that of itself undoubtedly will help to further the next step. But if agreement is not concluded between the countries most concerned, it would serve very little purpose, I think, to have other countries intervene too soon in those matters.
My hon. friend has spoken about civil air transport within the empire after the war, and has referred to remarks of the Prime Minister of New Zealand, reported to have been made recently, as to some arrangement between Canada, Australia and New Zealand. I might point out that that rather helps to illustrate the danger of these matters being discussed prematurely in the parliaments of the different countries. I am not aware of any agreement, and I would want to see the statement made by the Prime Minister of New Zealand before commenting upon it in any way. We have discussed with New Zealand and Australia the importance of an arrangement which will ensure air transportation with these countries and an arrangement which will ensure that whatever we do is a part of a great cooperative effort.
The air routes which Canada should operate, or in the operation of which she should cooperate, is the subject of very thorough study and of examination with other interested governments and it would be premature to make any statement now with respect to the possibility of operating particular routes.
I think it would materially impair immediate and very important discussions that will be taking place if I were to say anything at this time which would lead anybody to gain from my words certain impressions which might not be justified at all. All I can say is that in this matter, as in everything that affects relations between countries of the commonwealth, there is, I believe, the strongest desire on the part of all to cooperate in the most effective way. Whether that cooperation will endure more effectively through some great centralized organization or by means of a series of cooperative organizations is something which I think will have to be considered very carefully.
The next question which my hon. friend asked was with reference to an empire council and a permanent secretariat. Here I must ask the hon. member whether, in presenting

the views he has stated, he is giving voice to the official opposition, or speaking for himself, or speaking for the leader of the Progressive Conservative party. He was out of the house the other evening when the matter came up and, at that time, I placed before the house the answer to some of those questions as given by the leader of the Progressive Conservative party. Perhaps I had better read again what I read at that time so that the hon. gentleman will know, if he is not already aware of them, what the views of the leader of the Progressive Conservative party are in this matter.
I said there had appeared in Maclean's magazine on May 1, 1944, a statement made by Mr. John Bracken on these very questions of Canada's relationship to Britain and the British commonwealth, and on the question of an imperial council, and the question of the "one voice". I shall read again the questions and answers as they appear in Maclean's, because I think this is very important. I have noticed that certain hon. gentlemen opposite would seek to have it appear that I am taking a view that suggests an isolationist attitude on Canada's part in commonwealth and empire affairs, and they direct their arguments at me in that light, or some of them do at any rate. The present leader of the Progressive Conservative party has made his view quite clear. I find that on most of these points it would look as though he had read what I said in the house in the debate on the address, and had been careful to frame his views in accordance with what I there expressed. At any rate, I give the questions and answers:
What should Canada's relationship be to Britain and the British commonwealth?
Answer: It should be that of an adult member of the commonwealth family. She should cooperate generously but she should retain the right to make her own decisions. She is bound however to the other members of the family by the ties which hold together any household that is loyal to worthy traditions and which looks back with pride to a good heritage. Canada's attitude should be one of willing and cheerful cooperation with other parts of the British commonwealth, freely associating with them and seeking every possible means to further the trade and peace and progress of the world, but wholly autonomous in her relations with them.
The next question is:
Question: Should the commonwealth set up an imperial council-
My hon. friend has spoken of that.
-as suggested by Australian Prime Minister John Curtin? If so, should this council have executive or merely advisory functions. Should its decisions be binding on commonwealth members ?

Supply-External Affairs
Answer: I am in favour of strengthening the ties which bind the nations of the commonwealth together and I believe that a technique of continuous consultation in matters of common interest should be developed. The present arrangements I regard as inadequate; we fight wars but we don't help to prevent them. I believe in frequent commonwealth conferences and closer cooperation toward common obpec-tives of a constructive character but I do not favour the establishment of any permanent agency which would unduly centralize the influence or increase the rigidity of the commonwealth structure.

Yes, that is right. I continue with the answer:
Such conferences as are held should be advisory and consultative and their findings should not be binding unless ajjproved by parliament.
Question: Should Canada be committed to fight in defence of the .interests of any part of the commonwealth?
Answer: Does this mean a prior commitment? I do not think the Canadian people would agree to a commitment which might precipitate them into a war, the causes or consequences of which they could not foresee.
In the commonwealth councils our efforts should be directed toward preventing war. In the contingency you raise, that of war affecting the interests of any part of the commonwealth, our position would inevitably incline us *to aid in preventing unjust aggression; but the decision should rest with the Canadian parliament. It would then know the existing circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate

speechtext:
Will my hon. friend allow me to state my position? What I wish to make clear is this, and I think it is
fundamental. I was attacked as strongly as any man in public life could have been attacked for the attitude I took before the declaration of war, for saying that I would wait to see what the war was about, and have parliament decide before any step was taken. I was told that leaving the matter to parliament was preposterous when we were dealing with a situation of the kind. Well, I held to my attitude. I claim that my attitude was wholly justified by the fact that parliament unanimously agreed to enter the war. If there ever was a policy that, in the light of subsequent events, was justified, it was the policy which was taken by myself and my colleagues, that, until we knew what the cause of the war Vas, and what it was about, and the relevant circumstances, we would make no commitment in advance, and that, when we came to make a statement of the government's view we would make it in parliament, and ask for the decision of the Canadian parliament on the issue. However, to return to Mr. Bracken.
It would then know, for example, whether the structure of the commonwealth was in danger, any international covenant to which we might have subscribed broken, and the degree to which our interests were affected. In the light of such circumstances it should make its decision.
That is exactly the position I took, and I am not at all sure that you will not find in what I have said on many previous occasions the exact words that appear there. Another question was:
At last year's session of parliament two opposing views on foreign policy became apparent-one, that commonwealth nations should speak with "one voice" in world affairs; the other, that Canada should develop her own foreign policy, which might not necessarily agree with the foreign policy of other commonwealth nations. What is you own view on this issue?
Answer: This question suggests there are only two alternatives. This is not necessarily so. In my opinion the best means for Canada to influence world affairs at the moment is in two directions: through her influence in the commonwealth family and through her individual relationships with all other nations, particularly the United States. These commonwealth nations should endeavour to reach common agreement with respect to peace, trade and other matters and I would hope they would generally succeed; but they should not be required to accept majority decisions except on the approval of their parliaments and they should not be denied consultation with other nations. In my opinion that is the most sane and practical mode of cooperation within the commonwealth and the most acceptable form of relationship with other nations. But our parliament must continue to be free to determine its own course.

I am very happy t,o.
Canada should take no steps toward further separation from the commonwealth. We should facilitate the freest possible consultation and collaboration of its autonomous parts.
That last sentence sets forth exactly the position that I have always taken. I take exception to the words: "should take no steps toward further separation from the commonwealth." I am not aware of any steps that have been taken toward separation from the commonwealth. All the steps that have been taken, so far as this administration is concerned, have been steps which we believed* would help to make the commonwealth a permanent institution in the world. I wish to repeat here what I said on Monday last. So far as the British Commonwealth is concerned I believe it to be the greatest agency for the maintenance of peace throughout the world that this world has ever known; and I hope with all my heart that as the years go by the association between the different nations of the commonwealth will become closer and closer, and that it will be an enduring commonweath for the good of the world.
I cannot express too strongly my feeling in that regard. It is a feeling that I have had all of my life. If hon. members would care to look at similar statements made at different times by me I shall be very happy to make them available; but I do not make a point of perpetually proclaiming my loyalty. I have not thought it necessary to do that. I have felt that actions were louder than words; and I should like to be remembered in this parliament in future years as one who in his every action in relation to affairs within the British empire has taken those steps which he believed would help to make that great cooperative commonwealth we know as the British commonwealth of nations an enduring instrument for peace, progress and prosperity throughout the world. I wish to see the British commonwealth endure and flourish, because I believe that this great community of nations joined by ties of similar ideals, aims and purposes and the great nation to the south, which share like ideals and aims, can work together, and that more than to any other nations, the world has to look to them for its future peace and security. That is the view I have always held.
My hon. friend referred to Lord Halifax, and the alleged difference of views between us, and in this connection spoke of secretariats. Let me read a few paragraphs from what I

said at the meeting of prime ministers in London and also what I said publicly in the address I made to both Houses of Parliament in Britain, which was broadcast to the world. These are my views on this matter of centralized secretariats.
From time to time it is suggested that we should seek new methods of communication and consultation.
I believe very strongly in close consultation, close cooperation, and effective coordination of policies. What more effective means of cooperation could have been found than those which, despite all the handicaps of war, have worked with such complete success.
It is true we have not, sitting in London continuously, a visible imperial war cabinet or council. But we have, what is much more important, though invisible, a continuing conference of the cabinets of the commonwealth. It is a conference of cabinets which deals, from day to day and, not infrequently, from hour to hour, with policies .of common concern.
When decisions are taken they are not the decisions of prime ministers or other individual ministers, meeting apart from their own colleagues and away from their own countries. They are decisions reached after mature consideration by all members of the cabinet of each country, with a full consciousness of their immediate responsibility to their respective parliaments. Let us, by all means, seek to improve where we can. But in considering new methods of organization we cannot be too careful to see that, to our own peoples, the new methods will not appear as an attempt to limit their freedom of decision or, to peoples outside the commonwealth, as an attempt to establish a separate bloc. Let us beware lest in changing the form we lose the substance; or, for appearance's sake, sacrifice reality.
I believe in the truth of those words as strongly as I believe in anything. I cannot understand how anyone, looking over the past twenty-five years, seeing how closely the different parts of the British empire have been brought together under the policies which have prevailed throughout this time, can wish to adopt any system which might prejudice, in any way, what up to the present has worked so successfully. The real test came when war came, and in the conduct of the war. In the course of this whole war where, I ask, has there been a single difference between Britain and Canada, between Australia and Canada, between New Zealand and Canada, between South Africa and Canada, from the beginning up to this very moment What finer cooperation could there possibly be? And that cooperation has come about, not through having some centralized secretariat in London directing the affairs of the war or any of the affairs of the commonwealth, but by the method that has grown up in recent years, whereby we have the freest and fullest day to day exchange of views and information between all these governments. As hon. members know, we have; the services being rendered by our high

Supply-External Affairs
commissioners in other countries of the commonwealth and by their high commissioners in our country. We have the exchange of communications between Mr. Churchill and myself as the leaders of government, and between myself and Mr. Curtin, Mr. Fraser and General Smuts. In addition we have the communications that come day by day, yes, hour by hour, from the secretary of state for the dominions to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the replies and other communications that are sent from here. And these matters are considered by the cabinet as a whole, and the decision that is made, where a decision is necessary, or the opinion that is expressed, where an opinion is sought, is the decision or opinion of gentlemen who are seated here in this House of Commons day by day, who may be questioned as I am being questioned at this moment by hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not think the peoples within the British empire have awakened as yet to a realization of how closely knit we are through these agencies of representation and communication in considering all the affairs that are of concern to the nations of the commonwealth. I might go on at length, but I think perhaps I have made the position clear.
My hon. friend referred to what he called, "convenient detachment from world affairs from 1932 to 1939." May I say to him that history will be the judge as to whether the position taken in those years was sound. I have nothing to take back with respect to Canada's attitude in regard to world affairs during any period this government has had the responsibility for Canada's attitude. A great many people like to hear themselves say, "If Hitler had known that Canada was going into this war, there would have been no war." I must say these people can have very little knowledge of what had been going on in the German war departments for decades, or of the extent to which even Hitler himself has been made, the tool of the German war machine. If anyone thinks that Germany went into this war because Canada had not declared, months in advance, that she would go into the war if Germany started a war against any country, he has a very limited view of the factors that weighed in bringing about this attempt to conquer the world. But may I tell my hon. friend that Germany had a very definite knowledge of what Canada's attitude would be in the event of war. I heard Mr. Anthony Eden, the British foreign minister, tell hon. members in this very chamber that he for one could not be too grateful for the part the Prime Minister of this country had taken in going to Germany and telling the German government what he
did. I have never sought to make any capital one way or the other out of matters of this kind, but I do tell this House of Commons to-day that my visit to Germany had as its objective to make it perfectly clear that, if there was a war of aggression, nothing in the world would keep the Canadian people from being at the side of Britain. That was known to the German government at that time, and my action in the matter was fully known to the British government; but I did not talk about it at the time, for it is just as well that some of these matters should not be spoken of until later years.
The attitude of this government and of Canada-I dlo not say it is the point of view of this government only, because it was held by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and by Sir Robert Borden as well as the present administration- was that our relations at the League of Nations and the positions that were to be taken there required the utmost caution and care. To have committed Canada, for example, as has been suggested, to instituting sanctions against Italy; to have been the country immediately responsible for such action, and to suggest that if we had been prepared to take it we might have averted this war, is not to appreciate the facts and to fail to realize what would have been said of Canada's action if as a consequence war had followed. Anyone who will look over the events of the last twenty-five or fifty years will not have any occasion to blush at the sane, rational, reasonable and helpful attitude Canada has taken on these matters.
The question of international security has been referred to. I have mentioned the exploratory conversations which are under way. Then in regard to any reference made by Mr. Curtin in London or elsewhere, let me repeat that while in London I made it clear that our government would be only too happy to explore any suggestions that might be made by Mr. Curtin or any of the other prime ministers on any subject whatever. I think perhaps what Mr. Curtin had in mind has never been quite fairly represented as far as he is concerned.

None at all. In fact, I should be delighted to see it furthered. But that is a different thing altogether from advocating a permanent secretariat in London which would be dealing with questions or programmes for all parts of the empire, and attempting to settle matters there. And it would be different from what was suggested this morning by my hon. friend, that we should have a council where cabinet ministers would be meeting in London. I think he went so far as to say that they might even meet continuously.
I feel particularly strongly, from a close study of this question, and after having to do with questions of the kind in a practical way, that while conferences are a good thing, the best place for a prime minister to be is in his own country at the time he is most needed there, and not to be away at a time which may be of most inconvenience to him and possibly prejudicial to his own nation.
I wish to conclude by referring to what my hon. friend said about hoping that we might, in some way, find it possible to have the citizens of this whole nation bound together

as Canadians and so recognized and recorded in all government records and registrations. He said that, without regard to racial origin, Canadians are living and dying for their country, and that, above everything else, we should see particularly as respects those brave men who have been fighting overseas, that upon their return they should be all classed as Canadians. He hoped that, irrespective of racial origin, they would be recognized as Canadians without having to put any prefixes before their names.
May I say to my hon. friend that in that I am in entire and wholehearted agreement with him. I cannot express too strongly the feeling I have that some of these practices which have been carried on by the census branch for statistical purposes, or possibly for ethnological purposes-I believe that is the way it is described-might be done away with. I would be happy to join with my hon. friend and with any others in seeking to do my part to see absolute recognition, or recognition made in an absolute way of men and women who were bom in this country, and those who have become Canadian citizens being regarded as Canadians first, foremost and all the time.
And may I say this to my hon. friend, that he has touched upon a very real subject, when he speaks of men who have fought and died as Canadians, irrespective of race and religion. I regret much to see in this country at the present time some gentlemen who are in positions of high respect, and who know better, seeking to raise matters of creed and race, with the suggestion that things are being done for people of one area rather than for those of another. May I say to this committee that if anyone wishes a battle on the question of whether we are to have one part of this country singled out as non-Canadian as against what of others is said to be Canadian, no one would welcome that fight any more than I would.
And anyone who raises the question of race to prejudice anyone of another race in this country is doing the greatest disservice that can be done to Canadiap unity and to Canadian nationality. And not only do I wish to see our people recognized as Canadians, but I also wish to see a Canadian flag recognized in this country. I would like to see it the flag that our Canadian men are fighting under to-day. We have a Canadian flag unfurled in battle to-day by our very brave men in Italy and in France. I think in time the people of this country of Canada will say we want to have as a Canadian flag the flag they are carrying in battle to-day.
And what is more, I would like to see a Canadian anthem, recognized as a Canadian

national anthem. I think we should sing "God Save The King" as the anthem of the British commonwealth or the British empire wherever in all parts of the empire the King is recognized as the sovereign head; but as a Canadian I also feel that as the Canadian national anthem I might rise and sing "O Canada".

One reference I
wish to make at the outset: The Prime Minister asked me whether I was speaking for myself or for the Progressive Conservative party. The views which I expressed to the committee regarding the empire-for, after all, in a matter of Canada's external relations there cannot be rigidity of view-are also the views of Mr. John Bracken, the leader of the party to which I belong.
The Prime Minister read an excerpt from Maclean's magazine to-day, and I wish to place on record, alongside of it, the statement made by the Hon. John Bracken in the early part of this year on the matter of empire policy of this party. This is what I read, as reported in the press on April 18, 1944:
John Bracken, national Progressive Conservative leader, outlining his party's policy on empire relationship last night urged "even closer" cooperation with other commonwealth nations.
Then he said:
"I am in favour,, therefore, of Canada acting, as an autonomous power, to strengthen the ties which bind the members of the commonwealth together and to this end I believe that a plan for continuous consultation in matters of common interest should be worked out by us all" he said in a statement.
"By that I mean consultation not just for purposes of thought whether described as exchange of views or as verbal collaboration, but definitely with a view to a meeting of minds on matters of practical policy. It has not be'en suggested, *as it could never be considered, that there should be such rigidity to any plan as would subtract from our sovereign rights."
There was one question I asked the Prime Minister, as to the stand he now takes on empire affairs, that he did not face. Is there any difference between that and what Lord Halifax spoke of in Toronto in January? Lord Halifax never said there should be a unity of viewpoint which would deny the right to various parts of the empire to their autonomy. But what he did ask was whether an empire policy could be achieved by a unity of ideas in respect of defence, communications and certain other matters, in order that a united front might be established in the empire. He went on to say:
Mr. Bracken denied that Lord Halifax had asked Canada to fall in line in any event.
Just in that connection the general idea which the government endeavoured to leave
with the people of Canada so far as Lord Halifax's speech was concerned was that he was trying to reduce Canada to the level of colonial status, and that she would be dictated to by other parts of the empire. On the contrary the attitude taken by Lord Halifax was that the empire should endeavour to secure equality of function. Mr. Bracken said:
Lord Halifax made no such request or even suggestion. Very definitely he recognized our completely autonomous position. He asked us to seek to agree with the other members of the commonwealth and invited our full cooperation at the table of the British nations in the determination of those features of commonwealth policy in -which all of us are concerned.
The Prime Minister objects to a phrase that I used in relation to the pre-war days. Canada refused in those days to sit down with the other parts of the empire and discuss imperial defence, according to Mr. Duncan Hall in his book on the British commonwealth. The Prime Minister says that it is idle to speculate on what would have happened, that it is foolish to think that things would have been different had Hitler known Canada's stand. I say, Mr. Chairman, that Hitler was entitled to rely on the speech made in the House of Commons on March 30, 1939, which indicated that Canada's attitude was this, that the Prime Minister thought it was foolish to expect that Canada should go to war to save Europe every twenty years. Everybody knew in 1938 what Hitler was going to do, and yet it was in 1938-was it not?-that the matter of the commonwealth air training plan came before this country.

speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved, the second: reading of bill No. 184, to provide for the payment of war service gratuities and for the grant of reestablishment credits to members of His Majesty's forces in respect of service during the present war.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really do not know that there is very much that one can add on the second reading of the bill to the discus. sion which has taken place on the resolution. The resolution was purposely made as full as possible in order that hon. members might get a general outline of what the plan is.
I can assure the house-and I am speaking now particularly with regard to the first part of the bill, which has to do with war service gratuities, but it also applies to the general scheme of the measure-that this measure is the result of long and earnest study. We have examined all the information which has been available regarding planning in the United Kingdom, in the United States, and in other dominions. We have studied the provisions of the measure on the same subject which was brought down after the last war. The plan which is covered by the bill is the outcome of no less than ten different plans which have been considered. That is to say, from time to time certain features have been adopted or discarded or changed, and this bill is the result of the tenth-and the final-draft of a plan with regard to war service gratuities and rehabilitation,	[DOT]
I want to put in concrete form and on record an outline of the plan.
First, as to its application. It applies only to those who have enlisted or who have been at any time obligated to service anywhere; that is to say, service without territorial limitation.
Firstly, it applies to the man who has enlisted, whether he is in Canada or overseas, but at different rates depending on where that service may have been rendered.
Secondly, it applies to men who may be obligated by being called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act for service anywhere, that is to say without any limitation as to territory. There again different rates apply to the portion of the service which may be in Canada and the portion which may be overseas.

War Service Gratuities
Thirdly, it does not apply to men who are called up for service in Canada unless and until they have enlisted for general service, or the area of their service has been extended under the National Resources Mobilization Act to include overseas.
Fourthly, it includes those who served in the offensive operations in the Aleutian islands, for the period of that service.
The plan, as has been indicated by the resolution, is divided into two parts: first, a cash grant as a war service gratuity, payable in monthly instalments, plus certain pay and allowances the rates of which will appear; secondly, in addition to those, a reestablishment credit which a man may take advantage of for certain specified purposes at any time within ten years. This reestablishment credit is an amount equal to the war service gratuity.
The basis on which the war service gratuity is paid is, first, $7.50 for each thirty days of service in respect of service in the western hemisphere; secondly, $15 for each thirty days of service in respect of service overseas and in the Aleutian islands; and thirdly, in addition, for each six months of service overseas or in the Aleutian islands, a man gets seven days' pay and allowances of rank.
That last feature is based on the fact that those serving overseas or in the Aleutian islands, or at least those serving overseas, have had no opportunity of obtaining leave to visit their families. This seven days' pay and allowance for each six months is to give them the equivalent of the leave they would have had if they had been in Canada and had had the opportunity to visit their families. Fourteen days a year is exactly comparable to the leave given as annual leave to those serving in this country, with a few exceptions. There are some special exceptions in which it is twenty-eight days per year.
The basis of the rehabilitation grant is one month's pay and allowances of rank. That grant, as has been indicated in the discussion on the resolution, is already in effect, and that will continue to be paid in addition to the payments I have already mentioned.
Then there comes the reestablishment credit, and as I have already said, that credit is an amount equal to the amount of the war service gratuity on the basis of $7.50 per month or $15 per month as the case may be. That is essentially a reestablishment matter, and the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) will be the minister who will deal with that in the discussion that will ensue. As I have already indicated to the committee, the long-term administration of the act, and that applies particularly to the reestablishment credit, will be under him.

speechtext: I take it that when the minister speaks of the minister of pensions he means the present minister, who will no doubt be given some identification, perhaps in relation to the Department of Veterans Affairs.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is perfectly right. The act provides that it is the minister of pensions or the minister of the Department of Veterans Affairs which has been established at this session. That reestablishment credit, I may say, provides an alternative to these other forms of reestablishment, and there is a considerable list, as the house will see in the bill, of uses to which the reestablishment credit can be put, and which it is hoped will assist materially in getting the individual settled in his community in post-war life.
Perhaps I should mention the principles on which the plan is founded. There were two alternatives in connection with war gratuities. One was a flat rate irrespective of rank; the other was a gratuity according to rank and based on pay and allowances of rank. No doubt good reasons could be advanced for either of these systems, but the government felt that to adhere rigidly to either of these plans could not be regarded as the fairest thing to do, and the plan therefore, as indicated in the resolution and in the bill, combines both principles. First, there is the basic gratuity-of a flat rate of S7.50 and $15, which gives a flat amount, regardless of rank, for all ranks with the same lengths of service in the western hemisphere and overseas; and, secondly, rank is given consideration in providing for pay and allowances of rank, for a certain number of days for those with overseas service and also in connection with the rehabilitation grant of one month's pay and allowances, which is already in effect.
Then there were two other principles, either of which might be considered: a simple cash grant and call it a day and say to the men, " That is the payment we are going to make; do what you like after that"; and the other would be to devote everything to rehabilitation measures, assistance in kind, rather than in cash, so to speak. Those two principles have been combined in the bill and we have therefore a substantial cash grant and along with that a credit for reestablishment purposes of an amount equal to the basic gratuity. It is felt again that the combination of the two ideas would be better than the adoption exclusively of either of them.
War Service Gratuities

In making a comparison with the gratuities payable at the time of the last war, I want it understood that I am offering no criticism whatever. The gratuities then were based on what I have no doubt was regarded as the best form in which the matter could be worked out. A grant was made almost immediately at the close of the war. But there are some anomalies in the provision made in the last war and we have had the benefit of an examination of those anomalies and a thorough exploration of the possibilities for improvement, and I should like to refer to some of these.
The first point is that gratuity in the last war was based entirely on pay and allowances of rank. In other words, the first alternative I mentioned a moment ago was adopted. That last war plan was one month's pay and allowances of rank for each year of service for those who served in Canada and two months' pay and allowances of pay and rank for each year for those whose service was partly overseas. The result was that there was a great disparity between the gratuity payable to officers and that received by the men.
I -may say that the United States in this war, as was indicated in the previous discussion, provided for mustering-out pay based on a flat rate for all ranks up to the rank of colonel, I think it was, and we have adopted the flat rate irrespective of rank for the basic gratuity and have given recognition to pay and allowances of rank in respect of payments for seven days for each six months of service overseas and in respect of the rehabilitation grant.
The second point to be noted is that in the last war there was a floor of $70 for single men and of $100 for married men. In other words, that was the minimum which was provided for each man.

speechtext: Was there any clothing allowance at that time?

speechtext:
At that time it was $35, the same as our original clothing allowance in this war.
We have not adopted that principle of the floor in this bill. It provides for allowances based on actual length of service and does not provide any floor.
A third point is that in the last war no one got pay and allowances in respect of service beyond three years. There was a ceiling. That is to say, the gratuity for four years' service was the same as the gratuity for three. Here again we have avoided that anomaly by putting in no arbitrary limitation on the period of service in respect of which the gratuity will be paid.

A fourth point is that in the last war the gratuity was so much per year of service and there was no proportionate gratuity allowed for parts of a year. A man serving twenty-four months received a gratuity of two years' service and a man serving twenty-three months received a gratuity for one year's service only, that is to say, only half of what the first man received, notwithstanding that both periods of service were almost identical in length. This measure endeavours to assess the service much more equitably by estimating the amount to be received in months and not in years.
One other difference in the provision made in the last war was that if a man got overseas his whole service was regarded as overseas service. That of course did make a substantial difference in a man's gratuity. In- this bill we double the overseas rate, but provide an additional amount for actual overseas service in the form of seven days' pay and allowances for each six months overseas, and we have felt that it would be better and fairer that the rate to be paid should depend on just what service is actually rendered in each particular theatre. Therefore $7.50 is provided for such service as is in Canada and the western hemisphere and $15 for such service as is overseas. In other words, there is not an artificial service created by reason of the fact that a man has at some time been overseas.

May I just add this. Having regard to my responsibilities, to me this bill is just as important as, if not more important, than any other measure that has come before this house. We have dealt with many other important measures, but I think this one takes second place to none. All our efforts in this war are directed toward the defeat of the enemy. That is the thing we are driving for, and the point is that the enemy cannot be defeated without fighting men. The culmination and summit of our activities against the enemy is the presence to-day of the fighting forces of Canada on sea, on land and in the air, adding their weight to the blows which are being rained on Hitler and the German army, in the east and in the south and west. The casualty lists that I have the sombre opportunity of reading every day tells the story of the courage and devotion of those men, and I may say of the women too. It is those men and women, and those in Canada who are doing their part by
War Service Gratuities

backing them up in the way of training, equipment and reinforcements, that this bill seeks to recognize. Many of those who have gone into the battle lines in the navy, the army and the air force will, alas, not come back, and it may be that more will join that heroic army of the fallen. Many will have suffered wounds, but most of them, whether or not they have been fortunate enough to escape injury, will have suffered ills or hardship, physical, mental or financial. They cannot escape that. These men and women who come back will, I hope and believe, be the backbone of post-war Canada. It seems to me we cannot dwell on that too much, because men who have done the things they have accomplished, and have gone through the hardships they have endured, and have shown the resolution they have displayed, are going to be a potent force in this dominion. We cannot hope either to repay or to make up to them in any material way what they have lost in those years in the separation from their homes and from their peace-time occupations. But we do say, and we try to say it in this bill, that this country must do all in its power to make sure that the change-over to civil life, when it comes, shall be as speedy and as successful as we can make it. It is with that objective in mind that I commend this bill to the house.

speechtext:
As I indicated yesterday, the committee which was dealing with it considered very carefully the matter of what some people call a combatant gratuity or bonus, and endeavoured to see if it were possible to draw any line or make any distinction or adopt any definition which would give special recognition in that respect. As I indicated, it finally came back to discussion of a flat amount regardless of ,pay and allowances for those who were overseas, no matter in what theatre of action. The view was that they all were more or less in a theatre of action, and the idea of a distinction in degrees of danger was discarded and the principle was adopted of double gratuity and the seven-day pay and allowances based directly on service over there, and rank

so far as pay and allowances were concerned. That one item of the seven days pay and allowances amounted to something like $50,000,000. I endeavoured to explain to the committee yesterday some of the difficulties of endeavouring to draw any line. I have no doubt that a lot of people would try, as we have tried, to see if they could reach any definition which would help and which would not at the same time have elements of hardship or elements of unfairness or elements of inequity. I think there is no way in which it can be done unless you took the individual man and had a board try his individual case to find out exactly what danger he was in at a particular time; because I can conceive of occasions of a man in a unit being at a particular time in danger when the rest of the unit was in comparative safety for the time being. Certain troops may be further up than the rest of the troops with whom they are serving, and consequently may be in more danger. You cannot adopt any rule having regard to actual contact with the enemy which will be fair and which will not include some who would not be entitled on the basis of that test, and would not at the same time exclude others who might be entitled. Therefore the provision of the bill distinguishes between overseas and Canada, first on the basis of risk and second on the basis of separation, to mention only two of the features. These are the fairest tests, the two principal tests that may be applied; and as I indicated we seem to be backed up in that by the fact that the United States have adopted the same idea. South Africa has not even gone that far but has made the allowance absolutely flat, regardless of area of service; and if I remember correctly New Zealand has done the same. They have not even attempted to differentiate between service overseas and service in the country. There is also the point that after the last war exactly the same distinction was adopted in the Canadian war gratuity scheme.
