Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to recognize the service of members of His Majesty's forces who have been on active service, and we support the government in this recognition. I should like to make a plea this afternoon, however, in behalf of those who bear the real brunt and pay the real cost of the war, but who are not recognized under this legislation. I am going to ask the government if they will not give consideration to the granting of gratuities to the next of kin of those who pay the supreme sacrifice. Parents who are actually dependents now come under the act and receive gratuities, but in thousands of

War Service Gratuities
cases the father is still earning a living, and because the boy has made no request for dependents' allowance his parents do not qualify under this legislation. All the mothers and fathers of our boys know anxiety and worry. If you have watched them, as I have, listening to the news over the radio, knowing that their boys are on bombing raids over enemy territory if you have seen their anxious expressions every time the mail man comes or the telegraph boy passes by, you must retalize something of what these people are going through. We can neve? repay them for the loss suffered when their sons pay the supreme sacrifice; a gratuity of any kind can be only a sort of token, but in many cases it would help a great deal.
I have in mind parents who are approaching the time when their ability to earn a living will be greatly diminished. I am thinking of fathers who have been incapacitated since their sons have gone on active service, and who have not had the opportunity to apply for dependents' allowance. The payment of a gratuity to the next of kin, I should say not less than that which would be paid to a soldier who had spent two years on active service, would do something to recognize the service of those who have lost their lives. Perhaps some of the parents would not want this money; they might prefer to donate it to a fund for the purpose of waging war against the causes of war, but in many cases where the parents are reaching their declining years, when they might have depended upon their sons to assist them in'some degree, the payment of a gratuity of that kind would be of great help. I do not think the expense would be very great, since the payments would be comparatively small, and if the government would give consideration to expanding the payment of these gratuities to take in the next of kin I am sure that action would be very favourably received. At least it would be a gesture; in some cases it would be a great help-

Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): I think hon. members generally regret that this bill has come before us in the dying hours of this session, for it is perhaps the most important measure to be brought before the house; it will mean so much to those who are doing so much for this country and for the world generally. Had the bill been brought in earlier it would have been given more publicity, and I believe the government would have changed their ideas in regard to some of its provisions. As the minister said yesterday, this is at least a gesture of appreciation on the part of the Canadian people of the service rendered by the men who have enlisted for active service and gone overseas. Yet we have imposed so many conditions upon the payment of these gratuities that in my opinion the scheme looks rather ridiculous.
Let us take the case of two men who enlisted for active service, and who served one year in Canada and two years overseas. As the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) said yesterday, each will receive a gratuity of $450; each will have a credit set up of another $450, making a total of $900 payable to each of them under certain conditions. Under section 9 of the act the credit must be used for one of the purposes there set out. A single man coming back may have no interest in a home, or in furniture, or in buying tools for a trade, or in furthering his education, or in any government scheme of insurance, or in any of the other matters dealt with in section 9. In that case he does not get any of that money. Yet someone else who wishes to buy a house or to do one of the things provided in the section will get twice as much money as the one who has no intention of doing any of those things.
Surely if we are going to give these men something in appreciation of what they have done for us and the country we should not hedge it in with provisions as to how they should spend the money. We should not say: We are going to supervise the spending of it; we are going to take charge of that part wipch is marked as credit; and if you do

War Service Gratuities
any of these things you will get so much money, but if you do not you will get only half as much as the other soldier who has seen the same length of service.
If we wish to treat these men right and fairly and equitably the only way we can do it is to give a lump sum. We must not say to them: We cannot trust you to spend this money in a proper way. We should say: This money is yours; do with it as you like. Had this bill been introduced earlier in the session I believe some of its provisions could have been given more consideration, and some of these things would have been changed. I protest against any government paying gratuities to men in our fighting forces and then saying to them, through legislation: We will give you this money, but we are going to see how you spend it. We had faith enough in them to let them go over there to risk their lives for us and for the country. Surely we can have the same faith in them, if they are given this money in a lump sum. Surely we need not hedge them in with a lot of provisions and stipulations as to how they must spend it.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) spoke to-day on the point I raised yesterday when the resolution was under consideration. I notice that in section 4 of the bill provision is made for the dependent, of those who have paid the supreme sacrifice, in the event of their receiving dependents' allowance or assigned pay. There are two problems coming within the scope of section 4 which I think the minister should take into serious consideration. I have in mind the case, for example, of the young airman who has paid the supreme sacrifice, but who may have served overseas only one month. After that length of service the grim reaper calls him, and in calculating his gratuity he would be entitled to payment only for a very limited period of service overseas. Although this young man has paid the supreme sacrifice, his dependents will be cut off from allowances by virtue of his death. The fact that the sons, brothers or husbands of these people have lost their lives on the field of battle, after only short service, should not deprive them of compensation. Young boys may have left to join the armed forces before making any financial contributions to the home; their parents may not have been dependent upon those young men at the time they enlisted. In such cases the next of kin, not having qualified as dependents, will lose a considerable portion of these benefits. In my view section 4 does not go far enough in dealing with such cases.

The dependent whose son returns is much more fortunate than the one whose son will never come back. In considering the provision for beneficent tokens of appreciation, limited as they are and inadequate as they must of necessity be, we should have given our first thought to the next of kin of those who have paid the supreme sacrifice. The fact that they have been killed in battle early in their term of service should not militate against the receipt of benefits by their next of kin. I suggest that these two points should be covered more fully than they are in section 4 of the bill.	.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on second reading there are some points I should like to bring to the attention of the house. May I say at the outset that there have been some grave errors made in connection with this bill. Under paragraphs (a), (b) and (c), now incorporated in parts I and II of the bill, members of the forces shall receive $7.50 for each 30-day service on the western hemisphere and S15 for the same length of service overseas. Those payments are- deferred. As I read the bill the mistake made is that these men will have to wait for their discharges before they receive those benefits. Many of the men will be wounded, . and they will not get their discharge papers immediately.
While this bill is commendable in many respects, I am afraid that in the larger cities it offers no direct assistance to the men until discharge papers are obtained. My contention is that the principle of the bill is all wrong. It involves process of gratuity and credit, together with rehabilitation, where it should be based on one broad principle, namely that upon discharge the soldier should be put back into the position he held when he signed up for war, in his attestation papers. I find no such principle in this bill. There are many mistakes in it. There is the large amount, of $350,000,000 allocated to the soldiers. But that is not the correct amount at all, because we have to take out those who are qualifying under the housing act, those who are qualifying under the veterans' land act, those who are going to universities or who are taking

War Service Gratuities
other forms of training in vocational pursuits. So that this sum will be reduced to only a portion of 8350,000,000 in direct aid.
The worst feature of the bill is the manner in which it gives the aid to the soldier when he arrives on the streets of his village or town, or on the farm. How will it help? This provision puts me very much in mind of the man who makes a will in which he gives a grant of $5,000 but ties it up so completely that it is not worth a five-cent piece until the beneficiary dies or until somebody else gets it. The same principle is found in this bill. Too many lawyers have had something to do with it-and I am not referring to the three able lawyers who are ministers of the crown; far from it. But there has been no attempt to do some direct and final things for these soldiers who come home. I see them on Yonge street and I see them in Ottawa, in other parts of the country and on the trains. I talk to them, and some of them tell me they have not received a cent yet for clothing. And yet there are some who are walking around the streets of Ottawa, who have five or six uniforms, but have never been out of Ottawa.
This allowance of $100 is not enough to buy an overcoat. I do not know where these men are going to get outfits for $100 in these days. In the first place that is not enough money to buy them, and in. the second place the supplies and equipment are not available. They cannot be fitted, and there are many other difficulties.
This bill is drawn up in such a way that it does not include certain young Canadians who should be included. Let us consider, for instance, those who after Munich, but before the war broke out, rushed to Great Britain when her rearmament began. Many of those men had just graduated in 1938 from Canadian universities. What did they do? They thought war was coming. Everybody knew it was coming. We in this House of Commons knew it was coming, but if we said so we would be called warmongers. I can tell you this, that these following classes should be added to the bill: First, those young Canadians who went overseas to join the British forces, many of them in cattle boats, at their own expense. Second, the merchant marine. There are a great many others who should be included. For instance, those who are serving with the imperials. Surely we should learn something from the last war, when many went overseas and served with the imperials, then
came back to Canada, where they had owned a home before the war. They are not included at all.
I have calculated what the $7.50 in respect of service performed in the western hemisphere and the $15 in respect of overseas service will amount to for a soldier who has been fighting in Africa or in France or Normandy for three years. It means that he will get a cash grant of $480 for three years when he comes home. What good will that be?
The resolution and this bill have been drafted by the three defence ministers, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Pensions and National Health and I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Five or six ministers have combined in drafting the bill and its terms of payment. The bill itself is a short one. It starts with a clause of definitions, defining "credit", "dependents' allowance", "overseas service", "forces", and so on. The definitions are not very long. Then we come to part I, which deals with the actual gratuity, and this part dealing with the terms of payment is very important. One section deals with the payment of gratuity in case of the death of a member of the forces. The dependents of every member of the forces who has been killed in this war should get the benefit of this cash gratuity as well as other benefits, particularly housing. In the city from which I come only one per cent of the houses are vacant. As the hon. member for Davenport said, the government gave a courteous hearing to the deputation which waited upon them from the city of Toronto with respect to housing. But you cannot build houses without all kinds of necessary municipal services, light, power, water, sewers, transportation and so on. That is the key to the whole housing situation, as everybody knows.
As I read the bill, the widow and children of a member of the forces who has been killed in this war will not qualify for the reestablishment credits provided for in part II of the bill. When the resolution was under discussion I referred to the way in which this country has been dealing with material needs. Parliament this session has provided $1,050,000,000 for material needs. We have provided for the soldiers only $350,000,000. A great many who should have been eligible to receive the benefits of this gratuity I am afraid will not come under the bill.
The Minister of Pensions and National Health has got out a splendid booklet and fifty copies have been ordered by the city council of Toronto for distribution among the heads of departments. I find in it a great

War Service Gratuities
deal of useful information in support of this bill. I have often spoken of university training. In the last war only about twenty per cent of the members of the forces had had secondary school education. The percentage is much higher in this war. I know that a great many enlisted in the city of Toronto who were attending our high schools and the university there. We had 900 young boys of seventeen, eighteen, nineteen and twenty years of age killed already who entered the forces from the secondary schools of Toronto. Some others of them, not home yet, have been only a year in the service and they will not get a very large cash gratuity, but they will qualify for the university training with small pay. This splendid booklet got out by the Minister of Pensions and National Health explains the principles in dealing with university education.
The sections of this bill which deal with reestablishment and rehabilitation credits cover a whole lot of people who will not actually get any benefits under the bill. The Prime Minister referred to a maintenance allowance for veterans and their families who are out of work. A great many of them will be out of work, particularly those who have come back and are not one hundred per cent physically efficient. I advocated when the war started that we should have a national system of insurance to take care of unemployment of soldiers, because I know what our experience was in the last war. A wounded soldier who was not one hundred per cent physically efficient had great difficulty in getting employment because employers did not want labour which was not one hundred per cent efficient. This class will have the same trouble in getting work after this war is over, but they would have been looked after if my resolution for a national system of insurance and to provide against unemployment for three years after the war had been adopted.
The bill is not broad enough. It does not give cash at the time it is needed to the soldier when he arrives back home and goes to his own city or town or farm. That is when he needs the cash, and three or four hundred dollars will not help him very much, especially if he has a bill of sale or chattel mortgage on which these shark loan companies are charging two or three per cent a month under legislation passed by this parliament. I hope that this bill will be a success but it does not reach all the people to whom I have referred and who should be included under the bill. It does not adopt the principle that this parliament ought to put the returned soldier back into the same financial position he was in when the war started. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to go on record as completely and entirely in favour of this bill. I know that it is the general desire of the house and the country that we should in a concrete form express our appreciation of the sacrifices that our men and women have voluntarily made in this war. At the same time I wish to state that there is no one in this chamber who regrets more than I do that the government have not seen fit to implement the terms of the National Resources Mobilization act and draft all who are enrolled in the army for overseas service. Mr. Speaker, I did not say anything on the resolution stage, because something the Prime Minister said during the course of his able speech in introducing this bill recalled to my mind the sons of four of my neighbours. One was a young hero named Robert Lockhart, one named William Winter, one named David Duncan, one named Murray Fitzpatrick. All these four boys have passed on, and in the presence of such tragedies, words seemed empty of meaning. However, if I do not say something in support of the bill my silence might be misconstrued.
The bill proposes a much better system of benefits for the soldiers who come back from this war than were available to those who returned from the last war. I remember very clearly what took place at that time. I used to come to Ottawa on many occasions in those days on behalf of the returned men of the riding in which I lived and from which a very large number enlisted. With that experience in mind, I compliment those who framed and those who were associated in framing this bill upon what it proposes. I do not feel competent to say that it is perfect, but it goes a considerable distance in the right direction, and I have no doubt that if it does not do all that is intended, future administrations will see that the situation is remedied.

War Service Gratuities
There are some aspects of it which I like very much. I compliment whoever is responsible for allowing ten years to the returned soldier to decide whether to apply for the reestablishment credit. Many of the boys who came back from the last war were anxious to get out of khaki and be done with the whole business, and I am afraid that many of them lost what were their rights. The allowance of a period of ten years in this measure is a step in the right direction.
Much has been said as to whether these heroes and heroines, when they come back, should be given all these benefits outright. I am of two minds on the matter. In two speeches yesterday the view was expressed that everything should be given to them at once and that they should do what they liked with it. I remember, following the last war, calling one day at a home where the young man had come back from overseas. He had been over there four years, and knew little more about what to do with money than a child would know. If my memory is correct he received something over $600. While I was talking to his mother he drove up to the door on a motorcycle with a sidecar. The mother said, "Where did you get that?" "Oh," he said, "I bought that to take you out." He had paid nearly six hundred dollars for that motorcycle. It was his right; he could do what he liked with the money, but the family were in humble circumstances and had a heavy mortgage on their home, and I have often wondered whether it was just right to distribute money in a lump sum or whether it would have been better for the government to try to protect such men against themselves.
Later on I had much to do with reparations connected with men of the merchant marine, and I came to Ottawa to make representations to the authorities on behalf of these men. I do not remember which government was in power; it makes no difference. Among those who received a grant was one woman whose husband had been killed in the discharge of his duty as a sailor of the merchant marine. I do not know how the amount of the grant was arrived at, but I understand that where ships are captured, those who are serving on the vessel which makes the capture draw large sums of money, as in the old days when sailors divided prize money among themselves. This lady-she was a fine woman, who lived in a humble home in my end of the city-received as her share $26,000. I pleaded with the authorities not to give her all the money outright, but rather to supply her with some ready cash and provide her with the interest on the money, or give her perhaps a thousand dollars a year; for I feared she would not know how
to handle such a large amount of capital. However, whoever was in charge of the distribution of the money did not want to be bothered with it; his attitude was, "Let them have it, let them squander it, let them tear it up or bum it, let them do what they like." The woman had no sooner got the money than someone, if I remember rightly, sold her a house for $17,000, and a furniture company sold her a large quantity of furniture for the house. To make a long story short, I am sure that both her house and her furniture were gone long before five or six years, and she was back where she had been when I first knew her. There is no sense to that, is there? An income of a thousand dollars a year for the rest of her life would have been a much more satisfactory provision. However, I am not going to say how much should be given, or whether it should all be given at once.
I am pleased with the provision for an outright cash gratuity which amounts to about $900 to a soldier or woman participant who serves overseas four or five years. It is a fairly substantial gratuity, and I assume that they can do as they like with it. I also approve the part of the bill which provides a credit, under section 9, to assist them to an equal amount to buy homes, et cetera. Many returned veterans of the last war who received gratuities put the money in small houses and so were able to become possessors of their own little homes, and that was a fine thing. Some men, like the young man I mentioned, did not do so, but the rest should not be condemned because a few spent their money unwisely. I strongly support section 9, which provides for the acquisition of a home, for its repair or .modernization, for the purchase of furniture, the provision of capital for a business, the purchase of tools, the purchase of a business, the payment of premiums, the purchase of special equipment, and any other purpose authorized by the governor in council. This must be all to the good. I hope that in framing these provisions, whoever drafted the bill conferred with and obtained the approval of the Canadian Legion and other returned soldier organizations, because they are far more competent than any civilian to suggest what should be done. If they have approved all this, it must be good.
The problem is huge. I am not going to say much about it because I am not competent [DOT]to do so. Nothing can compensate these men for what they have undergone. I have two nephews who are in the services. One of them was not nineteen when he enlisted. He is a pilot in the fleet air arm, and I have been told that casualties amongst these lads are heavy. I know that it is God's providence
War Service Gratuities

that in many cases the boys get back on their ship again from a fight. The other young man gave up a big position as a statistician in New York city. Like his cousin, he has the martial spirit, his heart was in the fight, and he came home and volunteered and is overseas. The other boy, of course, volunteered too.
What is one to say about these young men? No one can possibly figure in dollars and cents what they have gone through. Those who come home are happy in their good fortune; those who do not return-well, nothing can compensate them. The hon. member for York-ton, however, made a suggestion which I rather support and I do so partly because of the fact that at present I do not know exactly what the bill provides for.
As regards those who die leaving no next of kin who are entitled to their share, what is to be done with the contribution that would have gone to those men? If a large sum accrued to the honoured memory of such boys perhaps it could be set aside for the building of schools to educate the sons of those who do come back and who later on require assistance. In the last war three boys whom I knew very, well were all killed-they were Scotch- and their mother would not take anything all her life since the great war. She has just plodded along on a small farm and to this day has refused the compensation to which she is entitled of $40 a month. I suggest that there is no reason whatever why anyone should refuse to take that money. They are . entitled to it.
It would only be taking up the time of the house if I spoke any longer. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I could have sat down at the outset by merely observing that I fully support this measure. I support the best intentions of the bill, and I sincerely pray that it will bring the greatest possible comfort to all those who do come back, to 'their relatives and friends and to all who are entitled to it. I hope that what is planned for the rehabilitation of these young men will succeed in reestablishing them properly and that every one of them from the time he comes home and has received from his country that to which he is justly entitled, will try to forget the days that have gone and will concentrate on building up this great country, the richest in the world, with incomparable resources. I hope they will all make good and I hope too that a multitude of others from the old land will come with them and be equally successful.

Those who had assignment of pay, or assignment of pay and allowance, and who may lose their lives during the war must be considered. The gratuity can be paid to dependents coming within the classifications mentioned, but that is all contingent upon certain discretionary powers given the minister, who may determine what the administration of the regulations shall be.
What I wish to have clarified is this. In making these payments, is the question of necessitous circumstances to be one of the governing reasons why the minister may use his discretion to make the gratuity available to the classes here set out? Or will the bill be so administered that the Minister of Veterans Affaire shall be required to check dependents' allowance files and to pay to all those set out as dependents within the meaning of the regulations as indicated in clause 4? Or will this discretionary power give the minister such latitude as will enable him to determine whether the classifications for whom we are attempting to legislate here may be eligible or otherwise? I am afraid there is some ambiguity about this provision. If we are going to pay the gratuity to dependents as set out here, there is no necessity for discretionary powers on the part of the minister, and when such powers are set out I am led to believe that there may be certain qualifications that will determine the question whether a dependent may be brought within the scope of the regulations.
With regard to the point raised by the hon. pi ember for Yorkton, that service personnel who may lose their lives overseas should also be included in this principle, I am not so much concerned about that because I think the great majority of service personnel to-day in any of the services have an assignment of pay on coming back home. The number of those who have not an assignment is very small, and if I read this clause correctly I think we are protecting everyone who needs protection. There may be an isolated case here and there that should be taken care of -by those administering the regulations, but if I am not right in assuming that this question of necessitous circumstances, with all the ramifications of the pension act in determining eligibility in regard to dependents, will form a part of the picture: if it is mandatory and obligatory on the part of the minister who will [DOT] administer the regulations to take all the files of those coming within the meaning of dependent as defined in the dependents' allowance regulations, and set out in this clause, then the clause is all right. I wish to join in the many expressions of approval of the principle of the bill to do the very best we can for our returned men and for their dependents. Nothing that we can do in a material way will ever repay them for the sacrifice and suffering which they have undergone. I hope that at this time we shall do better for them than we did after the last war. It is a very depressing thing to see returned men begging on our streets, as I have seen on more than one occasion. I do not know whether or not the provisions of this bill can definitely prevent that. I believe it is wise not to give them a lump sunn at once, but if possible to spread it over in the form of an annuity to ensure that if employment is not provided for them they will at least be taken care of. adequately for the rest of their lives.
This morning the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) brought up the question of demobilization and the plan of demobilization and spoke of the principle "first in, first out." That would seem to be a desirable thing. The minister has, however, indicated that he and his associates have not yet been able to decide upon a plan of demobilization. May I express the hope that before long such a plan will be devised because, nothing could be more helpful to the morale of our men.
I notice that a distinction is made in this bill between men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act and those who have enlisted for active service, although the latter have not gone overseas. A definite distinction is drawn in regard to the grants that each will receive under this measure. This shows clearly that when the government said that these men of the home defence army were performing a very useful service in Canada by remaining in Canada, they realized there was a distinction between them and the active army; for otherwise the government's attitude is inconsistent when it denies the home army equal treatment with those who have enlisted but are still in. Canada and not serving overseas although willing to do so. I cannot reconcile the attitude of the government in saying on the one hand that these men are doing a useful service for their country by remaining here in the home army, and on the other hand in not giving them the same compensation or consideration that they give to the men. who remain home doing similar service but who have expressed their willingness to become active.

Nothing we do here under this measure can repay the men who have gone overseas; the most we can do will be too little. My greatest criticism, however, is that the bill has been brought in too late in the session. Such an important measure should have been brought in much sooner, at least two or three weeks ago, and hon. members would have had an opportunity to study it. It is all very well for a few groups of people to get together to study a matter, but after all the members of this House of Commons have their fingers on the pulse of their constituents all the time; they receive suggestions, which they are only too glad to pass on, and as we know from experience measures of this kind are often altered after being introduced. This is a non-partisan bill; we all want to do everything we can for our soldiers, but I should like to mention one or two points about it which do not seem quite right.
In the first place, the men who are discharged from the army want jobs more than anything else. We have the provision which states that a man shall be taken back into his job, and that his position shall be not worse than it would have been if he had not enlisted. That is not the way the clause has been interpreted, however. It has been held to mean that a man is to get his old job back again. On several occasions I have asked the government to clarify that provision, but so far nothing has been done. Then some parts of this bill contain too many restrictions of one kind or another, and it is hard to decide just what section 4 does mean. If a man lives he will be entitled to his gratuity; there is no doubt about that. If he dies, however, in certain circumstances his dependents will not receive this gratuity. I think that should be clarified. This gratuity belongs to the individual soldier, or to his heirs no matter who they are, to use as they wish.
Then, to deal with the other provision which was mentioned by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), why should we tell these men what they may do with this money? Why should we not let them have it to use as they wish? Heaven knows they have been over there long enough to deserve at least a portion of this money to spend as they see fit. In addition, there are

not nearly enough of these classifications under which they may spend this money. These men may want to do many things, but unless they come within the terms of section 9 they fall under the other provision, which says, "and any other purpose authorized by the governor in council," so that they have to go to the governor in council to find out how they may spend their gratuity.
Those are one or two points that occur to me in connection with this measure, but of course my greatest objection is the short time we are given to discuss this matter. We received this bill only this morning, and we cannot give jt proper study in this short time. We do not know what its ramifications are; we do not know how far it goes, or what is really in the mind of the government. That is the principal criticism. I venture to say this bill will have to be altered before it has been in force very long, and I suppose that will have to be done by order in council. That ought not to be necessary; the bill should be discussed at much greater length, and we should be given a much better opportunity to study it. On many occasions we have asked the government to let us know what they were going to do, and only now are we given an answer.
In connection with the clothing allowance, those returned men who were discharged and given only S35 will get nothing more. Those who were discharged and given S65 will get nothing more. Those discharged from now on will get $100. What will be paid those discharged six months from now-$120?	The
men who were discharged earlier need the clothing just as much as anyone else. How is this measure going to work out? I certainly support the bill, so far as that is concerned, but with these reservations.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I wish to return to my favourite subject, and I hope the minister will understand my motives. I feel pretty keenly in respect of one feature which in my opinion works an injustice. I do not suppose one can have a measure of this kind where there would not be some injustice. But the whole matter of gratuities having been decided on the basis of geography and of service in certain theatres, I think an injustice arises in respect of those who are actually in contact with the enemy in a major way. There cannot be much fault found with the proportionate manner in which the gratuities are to be given in certain instances, but I think in this legislation we are losing sight of one of the most powerful factors.
I draw to the attention of the committee and of the ministers this one case. Perhaps it is not fair to single out a particular case and I do so only to illustrate my argument. But take the air force. I am not sure that we are dealing justly with the air force by giving every person who happens to be serving in the force outside Canada exactly the same treatment without regard to the degree of danger in the service that he performs. I suppose that one of the most hazardous tasks of the air force is the bombing of enemy territory, and I am sure that there is hardly a night when the majority of the citizens of Canada are not concerned when they go to bed for the safety of the lads who are going out on these bombing raids over Germany. It is a terrifying experience to the ordinary civilian even to think of it. It is a job that calls for the highest kind of courage and heroism on the part of the man who undertakes it.
I am just wondering whether this bill meets that situation as it should be met. Without interfering with the present set-up of gratuities I think it would be possible to add something by way of a battle bonus which would recognize extremely hazardous service such as is performed by aircrew where it is found. I realize the difficulties which the government might have in arriving at what is actually
War Service Gratuities

battle-line service and what is not in all branches of the service; but even if errors were made in the direction of more liberal treatment and greater generosity I am sure that that would not worry many of the taxpayers in this country because, as I said when speaking on the resolution, it is not a question of what this nation can afford; it is a question of what these men and these women deserve, and having that thought definitely in mind I would ask the government if it is not possible for them to give consideration now, before this bill goes through the committee, to ironing out that type of injustice which I have just brought to the attention of the committee.
If we pass this bill without giving consideration to that and without amending the bill in such a way as to give some sort of battle-line bonus, I believe that the government and this bill are going to be in for some heavy criticism not only from those directly concerned with the gratuity but from the public generally. I think the government will realize that the argument I have put forward has a strong ' appeal to the public generally, and the government will have to provide a pretty powerful argument as an antidote because frankly I feel that this bill as it stands, in order to render justice to the men who have really come into contact with the enemy, needs amendment. Unless we do something along the lines I have suggested, I think we are doing. less than justice to the general situation. I do not wish to appear too insistent, but I really feel that the government will be making a mistake if they do not include in this legislation something in the way of a battle line bonus.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I have already dealt with that at length. I understand, and nobody understands better than the ministers and the officials who had to do with the matter, the difficulties in making a distinction. I sympathize with the idea put forward if it could be worked out and if you could make fair distinctions. But you have to have some sort of rules to work on unless you are going to make a different ruling for each different case and assess the degree of danger in which each particular man was. Nobody can express, not even the eloquence and earnestness of my hon. friend, the admiration we all feel for the great heroism of these airmen, but at the same time these men return to their bases to find their comrades suffering from robot bombs and from the blitz. Are those who suffer from robot bombs entitled to the bonus that my hon. friend speaks of? He says that the taxpayers would not worry about that. All right. Are the anti-aircraft men entitled to the bonus?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I have given consideration to that point. If my hon. friend brings that up his argument is not tenable because he would have to bring in all the civilians as well. They appear to be suffering from the robot bombs just as much as anybody else.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Is that not making my hon. friend's argument less tenable, not mine? He gets into a class where there may perhaps be as much right to compensation from the state as/or any other class so far as robot bombing is concerned. Surely my hon. friend sees the difficulty the 3iinute you start to make a separation into degrees of danger because a man will come along and say: I was just as much exposed to danger as that man, but I happened to be in a different classification, or I happened to be in a different territory. Just the other day we had thirteen men killed at a training centre in Canada by a premature bomb explosion and thirty-seven men wounded. Perhaps it would be said that a battle-line bonus for them would be fair because they had lost their lives in connection with the war. They might say: We took some risk; we did not know how much. I only mention these things to indicate how impossible it is to start making these distinctions, but if my hon. friend has any definition to suggest I am sure that we will look at it here. But I can assure him that we have worked at this thing with great care. This is no overnight plan. It is the principle we have adopted not because it is perfect but because we believe it is the most practicable principle to apply.
I come back to this. It is some testimony to the bill when I say that other countries have just had to adopt the same kind of test as we are doing. No doubt they all had before them the thought which my hon. friend has suggested. They have all been in exactly the same position and have had the same problems to consider and the same sort of service to reward.

It seems to me strange that in that rather involved sort of way the matter is disposed of, and I understand the disposal of it to be that the N.R.M.A. man is not included. The military forces in Canada are, surely, the active army, the enrolled army, and the reserve army

I shall have to fall back on the lawyers. I had nothing to do with the drafting of this section or the form in which it was put. The instructions were that N.R.M.A. men for service in Canada would not receive any gratuity. This is the bill which was evolved. I as a one-time lawyer now read the bill, and I find in section 3 that the only thing for which a man is given a gratuity is for every thirty days of service, and according to section 2	(i) the word
"service" meanstime served on active service in the forces while enlisted or obligated to serve without territorial limitation, or time served on active service in the Aleutian islands.
I know that the N.R.M.A. personnel called up for service in Canada are not "obligated to serve without territorial limitation" and therefore I conclude that they are not entitled to the gratuity under section 3. They are just not in there; that is all. The only service which is recognized by this bill as entitling a man to a gratuity is service without territorial limitation or time served in the Aleutians. subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: On the second reading of the bill I asked the minister to clarify this question of discretionary power in the minister. Can he make a statement now?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
As I understand it, it is this. You "have to find out whether or not there was a person who was entitled to dependents' allowance, not necessarily the person actually receiving it but the person who was entitled to it. In that regard, may I repeat what I said. In connection with the members of the C.W.A.C., even though they may not be entitled by reason of the fact that they are getting pay and allowances which puts them out of the dependents' allowance; nevertheless that disqualification does not apply in this case, and if they would have been entitled had they not been members of the C.W.A.C., then the amount of gratuity would be payable to the dependent. A third case is that the person
gets the gratuity if there has been an assignment of pay to the individual. What my hon. friend is asking is, to what does the exercise of discretion by the minister apply? I am always chary about giving legal opinions on the construction of statutes, because I recollect that there are courts all the way from the supreme court of a province to the Supreme Court of Canada and to the privy council to decide that I am wrong. However, I suggest that what this means is that the only discretion which the minister has is, after he finds one of these situations existing, namely, a person entitled to dependents' allowance, including a member of the C.W.A.C. in the circumstances I have spoken of, or a person to whom pay has been assigned, to decide for whose benefit the gratuity should be paid and whether to pay the gratuity direct to the dependent or person who would have been a dependent under ordinary circumstances, or whether the situation is such that it would be provident and proper to designate someone else to receive the gratuity. That is the only feature I know of to which discretion would apply.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Does that cover the case to which I referred on second reading, the passing on of the gratuity to next, of kin?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I would think so, yes; but it must be next of kin who are entitled to dependents' allowance.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is, the minister has the discretion of deciding whether or not they would be entitled to dependents' allowance.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: No; the statute fixes that. The statute does not give it to next of kin who are not entitled to receive dependents' allowance. Take a single man who has been killed. He may have a next of kin who is not entitled to dependents' allowance, perhaps an uncle. The minister has no discretion to decide that it be paid to the uncle. It is only persons who are entitled to dependents' allowance or to whom assigned pay has been made.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FOBCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: It would not cover the case of a young man who has been killed, who had parents at home but had not made an assignment of pay to them, even though the parents were really in a position where they might be dependent upon him if he came back.

Could the minister give us the percentage of men in the army who made pay assignments?
I have made a note of that and I shall try to secure the information.

Would there be a
possibility of widening that section in this way? Let us assume there is a mother who is receiving assigned pay or dependent's allowance from her son. The son is killed and within the next few years the father dies. Will it be possible for that mother to come back after the lapse of a few years and be included in this section?

My hon. friend knows, I think, that what would happen, in that case would be that the mother, the prospective dependent, would be entitled to pension as I understand it. I do not think it is contemplated under this legislation, and was not contemplated under the 1918 legislation in fact, that war services gratuity should revive and become payable. As one can readily realize, you have to provide for a great many other contingencies of different kinds. There might be a case where somebody became dependent or would be in a position where, if the soldier had been living, he would have contributed to their support, but you cannot provide for that in a war service gratuity. When you find somebody who is actually entitled to the dependents' allowance, it does seem that the person to whom you might pay this gratuity could be clearly identified in that way or as the person to whom pay had been .assigned, which indicates that the deceased had some interest in his or her welfare.

In view of what the minister said a few moments ago I think I am correct in assuming he is not anxious to give a legal opinion, but, having protested that, he then gave an opinion. I should like to place before the minister a set of facts. This is an actual case of a soldier, a father, who died in the service. He had enlisted for active service. His dependents were his wife and his son.

Excuse me; you are
referring to the husband.
The husband.
The soldier died who was the husband and the father?

The husband and father died. He left surviving him a wife and a son. The son is now in active service. The mother has died. Is the son entitled to receive the benefits under this act?
100-396i

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Is the son in the service now?
Yes.

The question is, who was entitled to receive the dependents' allowance at the time the father died, or who was receiving the assigned pay? One would have to know that. Was it the son or the wife? If the mother was receiving the dependents' allowance and is now dead, that leaves her out, as I understand it.
Yes.

There may have been dependents' allowances on account of the boy. If he were under sixteen, there would be dependents' allowance payable in respect of him. It would depend altogether on who was entitled to dependents' allowance, whether the boy was entitled to dependents' allowance at the time of death or before, or whether the boy directly or indirectly-I suppose indirectly-was receiving asssigned pay. I do not suppose it is effective now because he is a member of the forces.

Why is this amount of gratuity after death made discretionary? Why is the minister given discretionary powers? This is the way the section reads:
If a member of the forces dies on service or after discharge but before 'he has been paid war service gratuity in full, payment of all or any part of the gratuity or of the unpaid balance thereof may, in the discretion of the minister, ibe made. . . .
The minister is not in the same position as the governor in council. If the power rested with the governor in council the permissive "may" would be used, but as far as the minister is concerned, if it is to be mandatory should not the word be "shall"?

I should not have thought so. I thought the discretion of the minister applied to those he was selecting to whom the payment should be made, and) to the question of whether or not he should pay to that person or to somebody else on his or her behalf.

The words "in the discretion of the minister" are so separated from that portion of the paragraph which deals with the discretionary power that I think it is indifferently worded and not very well drafted. If the minister will just read it over he will see that it says:
If a member of the forces dies on service or after discharge but before he has been paid war service gratuity in full, payment of all or any part of the gratuity . . . may, in the discretion of the minister, be made . . .

In the first place I want
to say quite frankly that I think the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas is right when he suggests that my opinion was wrong in calling attention to the position of the words "in the discretion of." I am not sure that this does not mean there is absolute discretion in the minister in regard to making the payment, and that the discretion is not necessarily only in respect of the person to whom the payment shall be made.

That is exactly the point I make. The discretionary power, as the section is constituted at the moment, appears to me to be one that determines two matters. The first is whether or not a payment shall be made at all.

On section S-Deductions from gratuity.

I am suggesting an amendment to this section, to provide that the only amount which may be deducted from the war service gratuity is an overpayment of pay and allowances. As it stands at present, a deduction may be made on account of a debit balance standing in the service pay account of the member of the forces, or action might be taken under the act respecting debts to the crown. I am proposing an amendment which leaves out those two features and simply confines it to the overpayment of pay and allowances. I will ask my hon. friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health to move the amendment:
That section 5 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"The amount of any overpayment of pay or allowances made to a member or his dependents may, pursuant to the regulations of the governor in council in that behalf, be deducted from the war service gratuity."

Perhaps this point is not sufficiently important to mention, but I do not think the draftsmanship of this section is very good. It says:
Every member of the forces whose service included overseas service shall, upon discharge, be entitled . . .
I believe it should read, "Every member of the forces shall be entitled upon discharge."
I am strong on the way it is now; I like splitting verbs.
I know the theory of splitting infinitives had a powerful sponsor somewhere in the government, and now I have found out who it is.

On section 7-Manner of payment of gratuity.

I wonder if we could not remove some more hurdles here by giving the minister discretion to make these payments under certain circumstances. He is given a great deal of power all the way through this bill, and if a young man wanted to go home and set himself up in domestic happiness he should be able to get this money a little faster than is now provided. I wonder if there would be any objection to giving the minister discretion here.

I imagine my hon. friend would be willing to move that amendment provided that he was sure he would not be the minister himself. I cannot conceive of any power which would give a minister greater difficulty.
Let us take the case of a private, a married man with two children, who has one year of service overseas and one year in Canada. His

War Service Gratuities
gratuity is $270.00; plus S67.95, being seven days' pay and allowance for every six months of service overseas-or total of $337.95. He gets that in a little over 3 months, in monthly instalments of $108.12 each. I am taking the $108.12 because that is the amount of the rehabilitation grant and I presume that is equal to one month's pay. In addition he gets a rehabilitation grant, and a clothing allowance of $100 right away, so that he does not do too badly. His total is $546.07.
Is the payment of war service gratuities over a period of three months?

Yes, it might be four months, but not more. You can take any of them. The large ones, of course, generally come from the fact that the pay and allowances are larger, as well as the length of service. Therefore the monthly instalment is greater, and your divisor is greater, even though your quotient is correspondingly greater.

Has the minister the information with respect to a corporal? I have in mind the case of a corporal who was one year in Canada and four years overseas. His wife has been to see me twice about what I thought could be done to get a little home together as soon as he gets back. This man has two children. Where would he stand?
Well, if I promote him to sergeant for the time being I can give the information.
All right.

The total amount he
would get. outside of the reestablishment credit, would be $1,350.12. His gratuity alone would be $810. Then he gets $311, being seven days' pay and allowances for every six months of service overseas. That makes a total of $1,121. He would get his rehabilitation grant of $129.12 at the time of discharge, plus clothing allowance of $100, making $229.12. The next month he would get S129.12, divided into his $1,121. So that he would be about eight months in drawing that amount.
Then, he knows that the Dominion of Canada, is good for it and his money will be coming in at that time in monthly instalments. In addition to that, he has $S10 reestablishment credit which he can draw down for any of the purposes indicated. That does not have to be over a given period. If he has a purpose to which it ought to be devoted at once, he can draw it down immediately.

With respect to section 7 may I point out that there was nothing in the resolution to indicate whether part of this gratuity was paid in instalments, or whether it was to be paid in cash. I think most people felt that those who will be returning would have at their disposal a little more ready cash than is envisaged in this legislation.
I realize there are arguments on both sides in the matter, and I rise only to have one point clarified for my satisfaction. The minister said, in respect of men coming out of the forces on demobilization that, in so far as war service gratuities are concerned, three or four months would be required before the cash would be fully paid to them.
In one case it was six months.

That is the estimate, in any event, for a certain category. We have not yet come to the reestablishment credit mentioned by the minister as a cash possibility. My understanding, however, is that there are special strings attached to that. I am wondering whether or not this will not be a sort of let-down to our men who may have expected to be able to lay their hands on some cash as soon as they come out, for the purpose of reestablishing themselves.
I am not pressing the point specially, but I suggest that it should be made a little clearer than it has been, so far as reestablishment credits are concerned. I do not think that is a cash payment which could be called such. It looks to me as though the whole thing is on a sort of credit or instalment basis. There are three or four months for gratuities, and strings attached to the rehabilitation credit, and I am wondering what the man who comes out of the service and has an opportunity to utilize some cash quickly will think. We must remember that the civilian will have his victory bonds he can cash right away, and this may be a let-down for the men who have been in the services. Perhaps the minister might have some explanation?

I have made all the explanation I can make in the matter. The gratuity is absolutely sure. It is sure within a reasonable length of time. It is sure in specified amounts; it is sure to be paid; it is easily computed and quickly payable. It is exactly what he has been getting all along. It ensures no let-down in family income of 'any kind, and it provides payment over a reasonable number of months.
On the other hand, I think it is probably useful in the Canadian economy not to have it paid out in one lump; that is to say, to

have a tremendous amount of money in circulation immediately-and I am not blaming the men for spending it, at all. They have a perfect right to do that. But it would send everything sky-high if that were done. Spreading it over a reasonable length of time gives at once the assurance that he will get it, and enables him to get credit, and bank on it, in fulfilling whatever obligations he may wish to make. In addition to that, the reestablishment credit could be drawn down in cash, if the purposes were complied1 with.

I do not agree with the minister when he talks about everything going sky-high. We were told that with respect to family allowances that obstacle, with which we were concerned, did not enter into the matter. Therefore the question of any inflationary development-
They are paid monthly, just as these are.

I am not arguing otherwise. I am only saying that when the minister talks about sending everything sky-high I take issue with him, because this could not enter into the cost of production, and could not possibly lead to inflation, as the minister's words might indicate. I took it from what he said, when he referred to "sky-high"-
I did not suggest that.

Perhaps I misunderstood the minister. But when he spoke about things going sky-high in Canada, I naturally thought he was talking about the inflation of prices. And, that being so, while I did not wish to press or urge a change in the legislation, I would say that there are oases where, without question, the cash would come in extremely handy when the men leave the services. There are other cases which by his legislation the minister is evidently attempting to avoid. Those would be cases where men might get all their money at once and perhaps it was feared that it might not be utilized to the best advantage. I take it that, having weighed in the balance the possibilities of both methods, the government has decided that this is the better.

That is so. But I just wish to say this word about family allowances. If this gratuity were paid in a lump sum at the time of discharge it would be just the same as paying from four to six months' family allowances at one time.
This is not a matter of anything entering into the cost of production. It is a matter of trying to take account of the limited amount of goods on the market, and prevent-

ing the driving up of prices of goods by making an enormous amount of money available for spending at one time.

I think the comparison made by the minister was not a fortunate one. In one instance the payments will be regarded as income to the family. But in this particular case it is not just a matter of income, because this will be regarded by the many who will be rehabilitated as a first step toward gathering together some capital with which to rehabilitate themselves in a normal course of business. There is a distinct difference between family allowances and this gratuity which, in my opinion, is in an entirely different position.
But it is money nevertheless, and if it is available it can be spent.
What is meant by the words "payable in arrear".

That is to say the first
one would be payable one month after discharge. The rehabilitation grant is payable immediately upon discharge, and the first instalment of war services gratuity is payable one month after.

There would be no
time between the cessation of a soldier's pay and some income? There would be no time when he would have no income?

The first month is taken up with the rehabilitation grant, and his war service gratuity does not begin until the beginning of the second month. But along with the rehabilitation grant is the $100 for clothing grant.
What it really amounts to is the continuation for a while of the soldier's army pay into the peace-time period.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-Reestablishment credit.

I was pleased to hear the
minister say yesterday in reply to the hon. member for Edmonton East that men and women in the armed forces were to be treated alike, but line 23 of page 3 of the bill says "the total amount payable to him." If this is to apply to women and men equally we shall have to say "the total amount payable to him or her."
"Him" means "her".
May I have the assurance of the minister that men and women are to be treated equally?

Would the minister
explain why it is that any member of the armed forces who elects to take benefits under the Veterans' Land Act, or any educational, vocational or technical training benefits provided by parliament, shall not be eligible for the reestablishment credit?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The section outlines the various forms of reestablishment assistance that are provided, but there may be those who do hot wish to avail themselves of existing reestablishment provisions such as the Veterans' Land Act, educational, vocational or technical training. The idea underlying this is to provide for those who are unable or do not wish to avail themselves of the benefits already in existence such as possibly $2,320 under the Veterans' Land Act, or benefits in commercial fishing, and four or five different benefits under P.C. 7633. There are only three major benefits: educational, vocational or technical, and the Veterans' Land Act, including commercial fishing. Under the provisions of P.C. 7633 it is quite possible that a boy coming back from overseas, if he is exceptionally brilliant, because of a graduate or post-graduate course might be in receipt of four or five thousand dollars from the state, and a boy going on the land may possibly get $2,320 from the state. It was felt that in fairness to the others coming back and not going to the university or engaging in farming or fishing or taking vocational training, alternate benefits should be provided, and therefore these benefits are provided in section 9. That is the basic primary reason for the distinction here.

Suppose that he does not qualify under the educational, vocational or technical training benefits and becomes eligible for reestablishment credit; could he then of his own volition use that credit for educational purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes, for "any other purpose authorized by the governor in council".
What does that mean? There may be lots of things.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The words mean exactly what they say-for any other constructive purpose which would be of service to the returned fighting man and which the governor in council would approve.
He may not want to use it for any of these things. Does the credit not belong to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend is confusing two things. He is confusing the cash gratuity principle with the reestablishment credit. There are nine alternatives now, and there is a possibility of extending these alternatives. They are all concerned with the essential principle of reestablishment.

Section agreed to.
On section 9-Purposes for and time within which available.
I should like to see enumerated among these purposes doctor's and hospital bills which may have been piling up in the meantime.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We welcome suggestions such as the one made by my hon. friend. The government will be glad to consider any suggestion made by any hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is quite possible, but I think in practically every case it will be used because there is a period of ten years ini which it may be used, and the man who may not want to use it when he comes back may have to use it or be very glad to use it within two years time.
Has the soldier to show that he is entitled to it? Has he to produce documentary evidence?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The mere fact of his service is sufficient.

Will he have to produce a certificate to that effect? He may have a proposition that he will want to go into. What will he need to have in tangible form to show to the person with whom he wants to do business, that he is a returned man and entitled to the credit?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: His discharge certificate.
Will that indicate hovr long he has been in the service, and where, and the amount to which he is entitled?

Take the case of a
returned man who goes back to his old employment. I do not see how he can take advantage of this credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
He may bring back a war bride who wants to buy furniture.
War Service Gratuities
The minister did not do that.

A great deal of credit is due to the man who returns to his old job and we should give him any benefits that we can. He may want to set up house or enter into business or a profession, but perhaps that is all covered by the clause "any other purpose authorized by the governor in council".

The fact of the matter is that under clause 9 the man can manoeuvre to get this money unless you have a gestapo to look after him. The man may want to go into business, buy a small gas station on the comer. But the government says to him: We must first of all look into this and check up. Here we are by this bill saying to the returned men: Here is something of value to you, but we are going to see how you spend the money. I think it is ridiculous, nonsensical for us to say to the men: We are willing to trust you to go overseas and fight the battles of the country, to risk your life in preserving democracy, but when you come back we cannot trust you with this credit. There will be so much red tape, so much checking before the soldier can spend the money, that it is practically saying to the soldier: We cannot trust you to spend the money yourself. If this is a gratuity let us give it to the soldier.
We do.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
We do. My hon. friend used extreme language. He called this ridiculous. We had a committee of twenty-five veterans of the last war working on this for two and a half years and they were unanimous in preferring the principle of credits for reestablishment as against the principle of cash gratuities. Now they have both; they have the cash and the credit. After all, if we follow out the argument of the hon. member for Waterloo South, we can ask a man to go on the land to-day without seeing what the land is like; we can give freedom of action as to the type of farm he shall take up and where he will settle. But we are trustees for the national welfare, acting in the national interest and in the man's own interest, and we are applying to him the same rule we did in the Case of the Veterans' Land Act-the security and the welfare of the man himself.

In other words, they will not get as much as someone else who has served a similar length of time. They will get only half as much.
If this is being done as a token of appreciation to the men who have served in the armed forces, then surely we should not put any man in the position where he cannot get this money. A man may come back and have a home or a business to go to. He may desire nothing that is set out in section 9, but he may wish to buy a car so that he can enjoy the pleasure of taking his family out. Under this section he could not buy a car.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

That will give the minister an opportunity to say to Tom and Dick, "This is what you can do," but to Harry he can say, "You cannot do so and so." It is putting a tremendous power into the hands of the minister and we have done too much of that this session. Here is a single man who comes back from overseas and goes into a hospital in Canada. He may never get out again; he may spend the rest of his days there. He cannot go into any business or live in any house; he has no one dependent upon him for whom he would like to purchase a house; he does not get that extra money; he does not get that credit; yet lying in that hospital there might be times when he would like various little things that he cannot get under the clauses of this bill. If the minister says that he can under subparagraph (i), then why put the thing in at all? Why do so if it is to be made possible for them all to get it?
A week ago we passed legislation in this house for baby bonuses amounting to $250 million. There are men here who were called for service and who rushed into the bush and are in hiding until this war is over. When the war is over they will come out and will be granted an amnesty from any penalty. They will get married and raise babies and get the baby bonus, and there wfill be no check up on them as to how much baby bonus they get except the limitation as to the number of children in the family. subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

It has this to do with it, that those men who sneaked away are going to be in the public treasury with no check-up unless someone puts in a complaint to the department. The men who went over there and fought are told that if in certain circumstances they wTant this money they can get it. I think it is very unfair that the government should tell these men how they are to spend the money that a grateful country is giving them as a token of what they have done.
