fore, Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay Bast (Mr. MacKinnon):
That all the words after the word "therefor" in the twenty-eighth line on page 3 be deleted from section 9.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Speaking to the amendment, Mr. Chairman, this means the depriving of the veterans of Canada of some $350,000,000. If the mover of the amendment and the party to which he belongs are supporting that, then we want to know here and now. It means that the alternative benefits under this scheme are absolutely wiped out by the amendment of the hon. member for Waterloo South, because, this scheme, as has been pointed out, means $350,000,000 in straight cash gratuities, $50,000,000 for pay and allowances, and $350,000,000 for reestablishment benefits. The hon. member now wishes to strike out the portion of section 9 which deals with the rehabilitation gratuities. If that is what he wishes, then I wish to have a vote at once to see what position the Progressive Conservative party takes in this house with regard to depriving our Canadian soldiers, of $350,000,000.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is all rot.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
The minister, of course, jumps to his feet. I wish to say to him that he had better read the amendment. I think the purpose of the amendment ought to be clear to the committee generally. What the hon. member for Waterloo South has in mind -and I think the minister knows full well what he has in mind1-is that he wants to give $350,000,000 to the men who come back without any strings attached to it, as have been attached by this government. That is the motive behind the amendment and that is the meaning of the amendment. Let us be clear on that. When the government and the government's followers vote against this amendment, let me point out to the minister that this government is voting to put strings on this money and to attach conditions to it rather than to allow the money to go in cash to the veterans who come back. Therefore, may I throw back into his teeth the same language that he used when he was trying to accuse this party of depriving the soldiers of $350,000,000. Let me say to the government of this country that the soldiers, the sailors and the airmen who come back will know that the government is on trial to-night with respect to this matter. May I make clear and plain the motive and the meaning of the amendment which has been moved, namely, to give the money to the soldiers, sailors and airmen without strings attached 
to it. Let not the minister or' anyone else misrepresent the terms, the motives or the meaning of the amendment which my hon. friend has moved.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I should like to say a word on the amendment. First of all I should like to point out to the hon. member for Waterloo South, who, I am bound to say, made a very strong case this afternoon from his point of view, that ever since the last war there have been certain strings attached to certain benefits granted to returned soldiers. My hon. friend must know that; the leader of the opposition must know that. Ever since the last war, in addition to the gratuities which were payable to returned soldiers on their return to Canada, there were such things as vocational training and training allowances; there were such things as medical care, hospital care, surgical appliances and treatment; there were^ such things as benefits under the Soldier Settlement Act. In all of these cases there were certain strings attached, if my hon. friend wants to put it in that way. At all events, there were certain conditions that had to be fulfilled before the ex-service man would put himself in a position to take advantage of those benefits. I would point out this also, that to-day, before this bill is passed, there are a great many additional benefits available to returned soldiers. They were cited yesterday morning by the Prime Minister in his speech on the resolution. They are to be found in Hansard at page 6200. Some of them are the Veterans' Land Act-there is a string attached to that, if my hon. friend wants to call it that-out-of-work benefits, vocational and technical training benefits, the benefits of university training which a returned man may have, correspondence courses which he may take. There is the right to reinstatement in his former job. There is the right to preference in the civil service, and so on. These are all benefits which may accrue to an ex-service man, which do not accrue automatically, which can accrue only if certain conditions are complied with.
Speaking frankly to this committee, I am bound to say that when this whole matter was discussed-and it has been discussed for nearly six months-no fewer than ten separate schemes of treatment of ex-service men were suggested, some drawn up here, some suggested by the Canadian legion, some suggested by the services, the one that we are now presenting to the committee being the tenth in a series of schemes-I am bound to say to the hon. member for Waterloo South, who, as I have already said, made a very strong

War Service Gratuities
case this afternoon from his point of view, that my own judgment for a long time was not in accordance with the principle of .this bill. My feeling was that the benefits already provided for ex-service men in the statutes and in the orders in council of this country, pius one or two additions, to take care to some extent of the small business man and to take care of any professional man starting out, on his career, up to the present rehabilitation schemes, made what was virtually a complete rehabilitation programme. But I had thought that-and here is where I agreed with the hon. member for Waterloo South for a long time-more money should be given to the soldier in the way of cash gratuities. I did feel that the gratuities should be considerably higher than they are in this bill, and that these higher gratuities with the schemes under our statutes and under our orders in council, together with some assistance to the small business and professional man, would give us an excellent general plan. But on reflection and after full discussion with my colleagues of the government, with members of the civil service, returned soldiers and others, I came to the point of view which is expressed in this bill. The gratuities are considerably smaller than I originally hoped, but there are, in addition, these large credits available over a period of ten years.
The point that I rose to make on speaking to the amendment is that it is incorrect to say or to suggest that strings are now being attached for the first time to these benefits that are available to returned soldiers. I am as keen for the welfare of the returned soldier as anyone in this house. But I do not think it is unfair tO' suggest that if we are going to pay out money over a period of ten years we should lay down certain conditions, which I suggest are not onerous, and do not work any hardship, and which I am sure every returned soldier can readily accept if he w'ishes.

speechtext:
I should like to ask a question with regard to this section, which reads:
All or any part of the reestablishment credit herein provided for may, within a period of ten years from the date of the coming into force of this act, or of the date of his discharge, whichever is the later, be made available to or for the member of the forces eligible therefor for such of the following objects as, in the opinion of the minister or of such person or persons as he may designate for that purpose, are desirable in respect of the reestablishment of such member.
What is the reason for the insertion of the words "in the opinion of the minister or of such person or persons as he may designate for that purpose, are desirable in respect of
the reestablishment of such member"? Does this mean that every soldier will not be entitled to these benefits in the matter of the reestablishment credit, even if he qualifies and comes under the provisions of paragraphs (a) to (h) inclusive, unless the minister or some undetermined individual or individuals decide that he shall be so entitled? Personally I see no reason for those words in the section at all. The purposes in respect of which reestablishment credits will be considered and permitted are set forth in this section. Why is it necessary to add a further string, if you will, by providing that a soldier shall not be entitled to this reestablishment fund, even if he intends to use the money for one of the purposes set forth in these paragraphs, unless the minister or some other person so determines? In the first place I think those words should be deleted. They confer power upon the minister, or a person as yet undetermined, to decide each case on its own merits. As far as the amendment is concerned I certainly am not of the opinion, and I submit there is no justification for the opinion, that it is intended to take away from, the ex-service men and women of this country some $350,000,000. I imagine that statement was made by the minister perhaps in a moment of thoughtlessness, for to-day our irritation point is rather low, no doubt due to the temperature of this chamber. In any event I feel that the words to which I have referred should be deleted.

May I point out to the hon. member for Lake Centre that this committee has already passed section 8, and I believe the mover of the amendment has completely lost sight of the fact that section 8 deprives the recipient of these gratuities of the benefits of vocational training and the provisions of the Veterans' Land Act. Section 9 merely sets up other alternative benefits for those who are unable or do not choose to qualify for the benefits of the Veterans' Land Act, or vocational or technical training, as I pointed out before six o'clock. That is an important point. This is only an alternative series of benefits, I think about nine or ten in all, with the last one very generic in its terms.
Coming to the point raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre, I believe there is some merit in the second part of his remarks in regard to persons to be designated; but you must have advice and direction. This measure is essentially concerned with reestablishment, with the rebuilding of the lives of the boys who come back, in various endeavours; and I think they must have counsel. We have vocational counselors and guidance
War Service Gratuities

counselors in the department now, where we have nine or ten major benefits functioning already. We have these advisers for one purpose only; not to regiment anyone but to try and render all the assistance we can. We have personnel counsel in the hospitals to-day. to advise those who are wounded in regard to what they may desire to do. Someone mentioned that a few moments ago. The idea certainly is not to regiment anyone; it is to offer cooperation and assistance. I see no objection to the argument advanced by my hon. friend in regard to the other persons who may be designated, as mentioned in the section. If the power is left to the minister he is responsible to parliament and must answer to parliament, so that I think you must leave that power there. As far as I can see that should not be altered.

I think the minister must be left there, however, because he is responsible to parliament and he must do the advising, through his deputy minister and his counselors, purely for the purpose of assisting and reestablishing the veterans who come back. That is the only principle underlying this section. I think we are all agreed upon that point, and I believe my hon. friend from Lake Centre is right in his second point, that the section goes too far and allows too much latitude when it refers to such other persons as may be designated.

I drew up the amendment very hurriedly; I read over the provisions of the bill, and I thought this amendment would do what I should like to see done. I still feel, and I shall continue to feel, that when we are giving men gratuities for service in the armed forces, those gratuities should be equal to all and should not be predicated upon whether or not a man does something which under the act may be designated by the minister or by some board. If we are going to express our appreciation to our fighting men in this rather modest way, then let us make it apply to them equally; let us

see that they all get the same amount, and that some are not deprived of their share because they cannot come under the provisions of section 9. I realize that my amendment may be badly drawn, and I am prepared to withdraw it. Before this bill passes, however, I hope that the government will consider what I have said in regard to the necessity of seeing that everyone gets an equal amount of money under this legislation.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

I appreciate very much the spirit of cooperation shown by my hon. friend in withdrawing his amendment, but I am afraid he is confusing two things. He is confusing the gratuity with the reestablishment credit. Under this scheme everyone gets the same amount of gratuity, except that under one of the provisions there is reference to the amount of pay and allowances of the individual. In regard to the reestablishment credit everyone from the private to the general, from the airman to the air marshal, gets the same treatment and the same opportunity to avail himself of the credits that are available for reestablishment under this measure. So that when my hon. friend says that there is discrimination here, there is not; there is the greatest equality, more so than in any similar scheme proposed throughout the world, as I am sure hon. members realize.
Take the cash gratuities; they are the same for all, with no question of rank. The only difference arises in connection with the rehabilitation grant involved in this proposal, which has to do with the payment of seven days' pay and allowances. From the private to the field marshal, if we were fortunate enough to have one in Canada, they are all the same. You then come to credits, and they are the same for everybody. They are invited to take advantage of these nine or ten different schemes up to a period of ten years. Where is the discrimination there? It is equality of opportunity for everyone serving to-day in the fighting forces of Canada.

I shall read this paragraph. It states:
(a) The acquisition of a home . . .
(ii) if not under the National Housing Act, 1944, in an amount not exceeding two-thirds of the difference between the appraised value of the home as approved by the minister or the purchase price, whichever is the lower, and the amount of the encumbrance or encumbrances thereon, if any.
I ihave good reason to make reference to this, because in my community there are 785 war-time houses. There is some indication that soldiers who have already returned have expressed the desire to purchase some of these homes. Whether opportunity is given them or not, we are not quite sure. The president of Wartime Housing said that those houses would be torn down in six months. That was 'his statement to a citizens' committee of seventy-five people. And yet there is the offer to purchase some of these homes and put foundations under them. How is the appraised value of some of these homes built under the Wartime Housing Act to be arrived at? The section refers to "the appraised value of the home as approved by the minister", or some such person as the minister may designate. How are we to arrive at a price of a war-time house, When prices in Hull, Quebec, were over $4,000, while those in another centre were only $2,820? There will be a lot of confusion.
I am definitely of the opinion that if we had followed the suggestion of the minister and stopped at the words "for such of the following objects as" and deleted the latter part of the section, which is only going to make things cumbersome for the soldier who wants to buy a home of some kind, it would be much better. Yet he is placed in a position, under section 9 (a) (ii), where he has to go through all this trouble to buy some little cottage which has been erected, and which he might finance with his limited amount of money. I urge the minister and the government to simplify this situation for the man who will try to get himself a home. I know there are scores of them who are anticipating doing that. I am complaining particularly about section 9 (a) (ii), under which a man has to go through all kinds of cumbersome procedure with the minister.

That boy is penalized; he is stigmatized and he is deprived of what we are now providing for our service personnel. The thought I leave with the minister is that before this section should become operative a boy convicted by a civil court should at least be given a fair trial by national defence officials as to the justification for the sentence in the local magistrate's court. There should be some court of appeal. If I could sit down for fifteen minutes with the Minister of National Defence I could prove to him that he has lost at least two soldiers through the stupidity of a local magistrate right in this province, and all I am trying to provide for here is'a square deal on the part of military officials where service personnel are convicted by civil courts.

sentence of two years would have that effect. All I can say to my hon. friend is this, and it is not of very much use to him because it is general. Because of this additional penalty which is imposed on a man we shall endeavour to see that proceedings for discharges following commission of civil offences and conviction by civil courts are examined as carefully as possible. We shall see that instructions are sent out to that effect. I cannot promise that we shall have an army tribunal review the actual evidence before the court, but we shall look into it to see what the man's character is. Sometimes these fellows that commit offences are the best soldiers, and we do not want to drop them out of the ranks simply because they happen to get into trouble; nevertheless they must not get into trouble that extends over too long a period because in that case they are of no use to us.

I do not like a motion of this kind; I do not think the hon. gentleman quite realizes the responsibility he is taking. This is the law with regard to the gratuities of 1918; it is the law in effect with regard to the various rehabilitation provisions which are in force to-day, and I do not think we can quite take the responsibility of striking out a section which provides that you will not pay war service gratuities to men who are discharged for misconduct, naval personnel who have been sentenced to be discharged with ignominy or men who are discharged by reason of having been convicted by a civil court or by court
War Service Gratuities

martial during service. I do not understand the attitude taken. I know the case to which the hon. member for Lethbridge refers. He has had it before the House of Commons and I have had it before me. I do not agree with him in that matter. I have been through it from cellar to attic. He says that someone was railroaded out of the army and he does not want anyone to be disqualified on that account. Without in any respect derogating from the position that I have just taken in relation to that case, I have no doubt that men are convicted at times before civil courts in connection with matters in respect of which somebody else might have let them off. That happens. But when men are convicted it is not only the conviction that counts so far as the army is concerned. The question is whether or not they will be good soldiers. The army does not discharge men who are likely to be good soldiers, because it wants good soldiers. That is why we are here to see that the gratuity is paid in the most generous and ample terms possible for the benefit of the men who are giving service. What this section says is that if the offence has been so serious, if they have been convicted by a civil court and been sentenced for such a period that we cannot use them in the army, then we do not pay war service gratuity. My hon. friend may make his motion if he wishes to do so, although as a matter of fact it is out of order because it would mean an additional financial provision. The resolution that was passed by the house, on which the bill is founded, expressly provided this very thing, namely, that men would not be paid gratuity if they were guilty of misconduct. My hon. friend moves to delete the section and that would mean an increase in financial liability under the bill.
On that ground, without any other argument, I submit that the motion is out of order.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before you call the vote may I reply to what the minister said a moment ago? The argument that this section is sound because it resembles what was placed in the act after the war of 1914-18 is not valid. During the war of 1914-18 we did several things in the army which we are too much civilized to do to-day. There are a good many things we are doing in the army to-day that we shall not do in the next war because we shall be too civilized. I look on this measure as being an act of reward, not an act of punishment. Let us say that the boy is discharged. Is not the fact that he is discharged looked upon to-day by the army as being a punishment adequate to the crime. If the boy has been discharged for a misdemeanour, surely he has been punished. Why deprive him of the benefits which would naturally accrue to him under this bill and thereby punish him doubly? Surely there is no justice in that?

The Minister of National Defence is not correct in his interpretation of my views on this matter. I do not desire to test the decisions made by army or navy courts martial. I know enough about military affairs to realize that a man who is court-martialed gets a reasonably fair deal. I do not want an examination of all the cases, nor do I think there would have to be an examination of all cases. I have in mind the few who have grievances, who have perhaps been sentenced by local magistrates and as a result have been discharged from the service. You'might have one, two or a dozen cases, but I believe any man who is affected by these regulations should have the right to appeal; the door should not be closed. That is my point. If you go back through the discharges from the air force you will find that many men, because of the condition described by the hon. member for Lethbridge-nervous, worn to the breaking point-refused to go up, and as a result lost their commissions and left the service. I do not know how you discharge them; it may be for misconduct, or you may use some other term, but there will be quite a number of men dealt with in that way. I believe you will find a number of men who have grievances under this section, and I want to provide some machinery whereby they may have an opportunity of airing those grievances. As it is now drawn, this legislation closes the door completely. I do not visualize checking back on courts martial and all that kind of

stuff, but I am trying to insert into this legislation provision for a court of appeal. I feel so strongly on the matter that I should like

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I wish to point out that in England there have been some thirty thousand prosecutions in connection with breaches of war-time regulations, and that in Canada we have had about one-tenth that number of prosecutions for breaches of the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board. Offences against those regulations in time of war are not offences in days of peace. Would the provisions of this section rule out a man because he committed some minor breach of the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board, with all the controls and bureaucracy we have now? If that is the case I believe the section is really too drastic.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

I would agree with my
hon. friend if the section did mean what he evidently thinks it means. The offence for which a man was convicted must have been so serious that it showed he would not make an efficient soldier or his sentence would take him away from the service for so long that it would seriously impair his usefulness. Then he would have to be discharged from the army, the navy or the air force. The whole section is governed by the word "discharged" in the second line. If a man has been sentenced, even for an offence under the wartime prices and trade board regulations, which takes him away from service for a very long time, so that he cannot be of use as a soldier, sailor or airman, then paragraph (b) would apply. In practice, however, I do not think it would apply at all, because a man would hardly be discharged from_ any of the three services for an offence of the kind which my hon. friend has quite properly described as a war-time and not a peace-time offence.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I should like to point out that as the section stands now, without the amendment, the door is absolutely closed; that no man who has been convicted and sentenced by a civil court, and who as a result has been discharged, has any chance of coming under the bill no matter how just his case may be. This amendment would merely provide a loophole which would permit the minister to exercise a little discretion. After all, Canadian soldiers are just civilians who have put on the uniform. Most of them have not been accustomed to military discipline. Life in the army is apt to be more or less grating at times, and the sort of treatment and justice a soldier receives is so entirely different from what he has been accustomed to in civilian life that very often he builds up resentment against those exercising that control. Then very often when he gets away from that discipline he does foolish things, such as the instance pointed out to-night which involved nothing more than getting into a truck and'moving it three or four feet. The man who did that was convicted by a court in this dominion and sent to the penitentiary for one year. As a result he was discharged from the army. Surely that offence was not so great that it should entirely take away any opportunity he might have of getting the benefits of this legislation. We are trying to help these young lads to get back into civilian life. This amendment would not only provide a means whereby an unjust clause may have some justice in it, and I intend to support the amendment.

A number of young men in the forces to-day have left home for the first time. Before leaving home they were not accustomed to liquor, but since leaving home they have become accustomed to it. I believe that is one of the things that get many of these young fellows into trouble. They serve for four or five years; then as a result of some misdemeanor they are taken to court, with the results that have been described to-night. For that reason; because some provinces cannot find any better way to raise money than through the profits on the sale of liquor, I am satisfied that something should be done. The detention may be for a very short time, or for a long time. The word "detention" applies to anyone who is ^committed to the guardroom. I would suggest to the minister that under this section he is going to penalize many service men who have committed some small misdemeanours and who have been given forty-eight hours in the guardroom, or perhaps up to seven days or fourteen days. I do not wish to offer an amendment, because enough of them have been moved. But I would suggest that after the word "detention" the words "for a period greater than twenty-eight days" be added. Then we would be penalizing only the man who has committed a serious crime and would not be penalizing the man who possibly went out and got drunk, with the result that he was committed to the guardroom for possibly seven days, or forty-eight hours.
There is another feature to which I would direct attention. I notice the expression "or period of service in respect of which pay is forfeited". Forfeiture of pay has become rather a common, and I think unnecessarily common, type of punishment in the army during this war. A man may be absent without leave or late on a pass, and frequently
War Service Gratuities

his punishment is a forfeiture of two, three or four days' pay. The punishment would depend upon the length of absence without leave.
These are small crimes in. the normal life of many service men in this war. Even excellent soldiers have at one time or another been absent without leave for a day, or late on a pass, or committed some small crime for which they have suffered stoppages of pay, or have been committed to the guardroom for some hours, or possibly for two or three days. The expression in the section is too allembracing, and I would suggest that after the word "detention" the words "for a .period greater than twenty-eight days" be inserted, and that after the word "or" the word1 "like" be added. subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Would this section apply to gratuities of the same nature paid by other countries such as Russia and the United States? Some of our soldiers are having the difference between their army pay and what they receive in civil life made up by the municipalities or corporations for which they worked. For example, the municipality or corporation would give them S3.70 which, with their army pay of $1.30, would bring them up to the $5 they were earning in civil life. As I understand it, there is no deduction on account of these pecuniary benefits in Canada. Many of our soldiers are firemen and policemen, with pension and gratuity funds of their own. Lever Brothers, for instance, have a great system of helping soldiers, giving benefits and credits of all	kinds. It	is	the	finestsystem in Canada.	That will	not be	interfered with under this section?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Not at all. This applies only to grants by governments in respect of service with other than Canadian forces.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

states:
in respect of service performed with the naval, military or	air forces	of	any	suchdominion or power,	one-half of the	amount of

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I admit that it was an arbitrary division. They said: You must not take it all from the gratuity or all from the reestablishment credit. So that it is taken half from each. Then the question comes, how to apply the deduction and the rough and ready way to apply it is to take it half from the gratuity and half from the reestablishment credit.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That seems too rough and ready.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Many men may not take the reestablishment credit at all. They might get some other pecuniary benefits instead. In that case I do not think we should deduct one-half from the gratuity. I think the section should be amended accordingly.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: The bill expressly provides that a man has ten years within which to elect whether he will take reestablishment credit, and no soldier can say until the end of the ten years that he is not going to take the benefit of the reestablishment credit.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Off whatever credit would be available?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That is it.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
This is a clause that I
think needs clarification with regard to the question of domicile. What position are the men going to be in who left Canada and went over to England in 1936, 1937, 1938 or 1939 and enlisted in the Royal Air Force, served throughout the war and then came back here? Under this clause they would not be domiciled in Canada and they would not come under this provision. Yet one of the other acts that we passed granted to men in the like circumstances all the preferences given to members of the Canadian forces. Surely we should not debar these men from the benefits of this legislation because they went over to England between the years 1936 to 1939, and incidentally they were the backbone of the Royal Air Force in the darkest days of the war. We should not bar them from these gratuities.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
This would bar all the
men of the permanent force who were outside Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I should like to support what the hon. member for Waterloo South has just said. I know of my own knowledge several men who did that very thing, some enlisting in the Royal Air Force, some in the British navy. They were not domiciled in Canada in 1939.
War Service Gratuities

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: My hon. friend says that, but is it correct? Did they leave Canada to take up their domicile somewhere else?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: They went over there to join the Royal Air Force or British navy because they thought the war was coming on.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: That does not mean that they changed their domicile.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

Certainly they were
unless they intended not to return.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

My hon. friend asserted
positively that they were not domiciled in Canada. Domicile means that a man leaves his country intending to make his home somewhere else, or, putting it tihe other way, not intending to return. Did these men leave under those circumstances? If they did, why Should they have a gratuity now from Canada? The point is, they did not leave with that purpose. Therefore, they were domiciled in Canada in September, 1939.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I do not know what "domiciled" means.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I know that.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: Yes, I do not know, and all I am asking for is a clarification. These men went over to join the Royal Air Force, or the navy over there, because they believed that war was coming; not only that, but because they could not get into the forces here. You have to give them some consideration. As I understand it, the term "domicile" ordinarily means if you leave the country for a whole year, or something like that, you are out.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: You can leave for five years and not lose your domicile.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: So long as that is clear.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
I mean that you can leave for five years and not lose your domicile if you have not intended to lose it, but you can leave for ten minutes and lose your domicile if you leave with the intention of not returning. But I rather take it, from what I understand about these men, that they did not intend to deprive themselves of their Canadian

domicile. They simply jwent for the express and very laudable purpose of taking part in the war. Those are the men we are providing for here. If, however, they left-I say this seriously-to take up their domicile in the United Kingdom, or some other country with whose forces they became associated, I do not think it would be quite fair to have them come back some time and take a Canadian gratuity. That is the point. The whole question is, are they Canadians over there or are they Britishers in respect of their permanent home?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: My other question is this. I know of two of these men who married English wives.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: What I had in mind when I asked the minister the question was that a number of boys left my riding to join the Royal Navy and the Royal Air Force. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: All I want to be satisfied of is that these men who joined the British service, but with the intention of eventually coming back, have not lost their domicile.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: May I point out that a number of the boys who enlisted in the Royal Air Force went over to take the short service commissions, and we made special provision for them under the Pension Act amendments of 1941. I gave a press release with regard to the benefits. Under order in council P.C. 7633 we took the view that any Canadian boy who left Canada two or three or even four years prior to the outbreak of the war for the purpose of enlisting in His Majesty's imperial forces and returns to Canada upon his discharge will not have forfeited his domicile for the purposes of this order. Is that clear?

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext:
Yes, that is perfectly clear to me, but I wonder if such a regulation could be put in this bill.

War Service Gratuities

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I think we must distinguish clearly. We fire trying to benefit Canadians; that is really what this bill is for; and if a chap left here with intent to make his permanent home in another country he is not domiciled in Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: No. Well, I do not think they did that.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I do not think that man, no matter how laudable his services, should be entitled to come back here and reside here and say, "I am entitled to the Canadian war service gratuity because I have changed my mind and I intend to live here." But the man who left with intent to return is clearly domiciled in Canada, and that is the man we refer to when we say that the member of the forces who was domiciled in Canada on the 10th day of September, the day the war broke out, can come back and receive the benefits of the bill. As a matter of fact, that man could stay in the service over there for a good many years, then be discharged, and if he comes back within one year after his discharge he will be entitled to have the difference made up between the gratuity he receives there and the gratuity which is provided for in Canada.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE
speechtext: I just wanted that clear.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE

Air service-radio division-
J/03. Administration of the Radio Telegraph Act and regulations, $136,880.

Last night when the committee rose I asked that this item be held over. Something was said last night with regard to the situation at Halifax and the broadcasting station there, which I believe needs some clarification. The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party read into the record a statement made by Doctor Frigon of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. From the evidence taken in the radio committee and the statement made last night by the minister one wonders whether there is not an Ethiopian somewhere in the woodpile. The picture apparently is that an application for a broadcasting station must be made to the Department of Transport. That application would then be submitted to the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which would make a recommendation one way or the other. That recommendation would then come back to the Minister of Transport, and he has the power either to accept or to reject the recommendation. I understand that the Halifax Chronicle made an application for the right to establish a broadcasting station in that city; and I believe they were granted a licence but did not go ahead with the construction of the station. It was stated definitely by Doctor Frigon that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation intended to erect a station in Halifax. Rumour says they went so far as to bring the equipment there for that purpose. Anyway, a great deal of the equipment is there. The impression was left with hon. members that this station would likely be ready by the end of the year. According to the remarks made last night there is no record of an application by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to erect a broadcasting station in Halifax.
Although apparently no record of the application exists, yet Doctor Frigon says that such an application was made and that such a station is to be constructed. The application of the Halifax Chronicle is on file and has been passed on. I understand that they are hunting around to get the necessary material to construct the station. There is no record of the existence of an application from this great public ownership enterprise, this enterprise that Doctor Frigon has said on so many occasions can be so valuable to this country, and that makes one wonder just a little. I say this very seriously. Is the future of this great public ownership enterprise to be jeopardized to some extent for political expediency and that men who have strong leanings toward the government and a newspaper that has strong leanings toward the government are to get preference over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which is a nationally owned enterprise?
We have been told on many occasions by the Prime Minister and the minister in charge of this enterprise that it must be kept out of politics, that it must be kept separate and distinct from politics. We have been told of the great value it can be to the people. When we see such a picture as I have described, it makes one wonder if politics have not entered into the picture somewhere. The question is, is the Halifax Chronicle to build the station there, or is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to build the station? I believe we should get a definite answer on what is happening in Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speechtext:
I admit at once that I was in
error when I spoke last evening. I said at that time that to the best of my recollection the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation had not made an application for a wave length to the Department of Transport under this item. My officers called my attention to the fact that an application had been made and had been granted as of March 27, 1944, for a station of 100 watts on a wave length of 1,240 kilocycles. I had forgotten the fact. But actually the application was granted and is in good standing in favour of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. My officials tell me that the same difficulties which interfere with most broadcasting stations, namely, shortage of material and other difficulties, are responsible for delay. The matter is still under consideration but has not been brought to the final stage. My hon. friend is suggesting that there is some relation between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation application and the Halifax Chronicle application. There is no relation
Supply-Transport

whatever. It is not unusual to have three radio stations in a city the size of Halifax. The Halifax Chronicle application dates back to July 24, 1938, and was again renewed and recommended by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under date of July 4, 1944. The two are quite separate. The fact that neither of them is proceeding very rapidly is owing to the fact that it is imposible to obtain certain materials for broadcasting stations on account of war priorities.

The minister will realize
that as a result of his announcement last night it did look strange.

Quite so; I apologize for
the error.

In connection with the surveys that have been made on wave lengths and broadcasting in general, were they made by the minister's department or by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or how were they made?

The survey that my hon.
friend is referring to is, I believe, a survey of coverage. That was made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

I was not referring to a survey of coverage. I was referring to a .survey of frequencies and of the whole general picture. Was that made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or by the minister's department?

My department polices wave lengths and frequencies. If it has anything to do with wave lengths and frequencies under the Havana agreement, such a survey would be made by the department of which I am minister. If it is a survey in connection with coverage it would be made by the C.B.C. under the broadcasting act.

I have in mind a survey of the frequencies which can be allotted under the Havana agreement. What have we left in Canada; how many stations can we still have? Does that come under the minister's department? We were told in the committee that the judgment in connection with these matters was part of the job of the C.B.C.; that they had to be careful not to infringe upon the rights of the United States under the Havana agreement, and so on, although we know the power of the United States stations has been going up all the time. We have been told that the power of the United States stations was frozen in 1942; yet we hear that permits for increased power have been granted like nobody's business. The power of our stations
TMr. Howe.]
was frozen at 1,000 watts. My opinion, and that of a great many engineers in Canada, is that Canada has lost a good deal by the freezing of the power of our stations. No one thinks more of the C.B.C. than I do. I believe it is well run. I thought the set-up under which we had a board of governors, a chairman who had to do with policy, and a general manager who looked after matters of administration and who could? delegate power, was ideal. I understand^ as a matter of fact, that many months ago a recommendation was sent forward by the board of governors of the C.B.C. requesting the appointment of a general manager, although I am not absolutely sure of that.
Mr. LaFLECHE:	May I interrupt my
hon. friend to say that he is wrong?

The minister says that he has never received such a recommendation from the board of governors, and of course I accept his word. Now we are trying to create a new set-up, to fit the people we already have there. That is not the way to run a business. I believe the C.B.C. is run very well-
I would point out that this item has nothing to do with the C.B.C. and how it is run.

I quite agree with the minister, but I am pointing out that the minister has to do with such matters as frequencies and the allotment of channels. Those matters come under him entirely, and the C.B.C. has nothing to do with them. It is the job of the broadcasting corporation to say whether there shall be one, two or three radio stations in one town, but the decision as to how we shall use our channels and our power, so that the public may derive the greatest advantage, is something for the Department of Transport. We have stations in Canada whose power has been kept down, and which could render much greater service if they are allowed to increase their power. They would not interfere with the C.B.C. at all; on the contrary they would help it. I want to make sure that all our channels are not usurped by the country to the south, and there is no doubt that our rights are being encroached upon at the present time.

I should like to say a few words in connection with the matter brought up by the hon. member for Waterloo South. I am not as convinced of the correctness of the minister's answer as the hon. member apparently was, since he has now left the chamber. Personally I think there v is something wrong in the Halifax situation. Every-

Supply-Transport
one was pleased a few days ago when we learned that the personnel of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation were being jacked up by the appointment of a new general manager, a new assistant manager and a permanent full-time chairman, at a great deal of expense to the taxpayers of Canada. We all approved that because we felt that this organization was very important and capable, and should be staffed by full-time officials. If that assumption is correct, and this committee is justified in voting money for the upkeep of that organization-
This committee does not vote any money for the C.B.C.
The committee votes it.
No.

It does not operate on
nothing.
They collect fees from the listeners.

Well, those fees certainly do not cover the total expenditures of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The point I am getting at is that if it is the policy of the Canadian government to develop the airways of Canada along the lines suggested by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, then the advice of the technical officials should receive attention by those who are cooperating through the issuing of licences, and so forth. The whole set-up should work together. I was surprised to find on reading Hansard this morning that the minister was not aware of the fact that a licence had been granted to the C.B.C. for a station in Halifax, although I was glad to hear him clarify the position to-night. Of course I am not holding that little mistake against him; we are all liable to slip when speaking from memory. The point I am concerned about, however, is that radio reception in Nova Scotia from a provincial point of view leaves much to be desired, and we all want to improve it.
I was particularly pleased when on June 28 Doctor Frigon announced a second outlet for the city of Halifax. I was informed from a reliable source that a transmitter had been installed and that it could be put into operation on three hours' notice. The only thing holding it up, I understood, was the passing of an order in council to enable the work to go forward. I was led to believe that as far as the C.B.C. was concerned there was no shortage of the materials necessary to carry out the recommendation of Doctor Frigon. People in Novia Scotia became concerned as
to when this second outlet might be expected to commence operations. Then we were informed that a licence granted back in 1938 to the Halifax Chronicle, which had been allowed to lapse, had been revived. It is significant to me that while the C.B.C. licence was granted in March, as pointed out by the minister, it was not until July of this year that the Halifax Chronicle revived the possibility of going into that business.
I do not care how many private stations are operated in Nova Scotia; that is the business of those who want to put money into that game. But the recommendation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its acting general manager is the business of parliament and the Canadian people. I do not visualize any service to the people of Nova Scotia, from the point of view of better radio reception or better service for that province, from the station proposed by the Halifax Chronicle. I am not concerned about that; it is their business. I am convinced that the statement of the hon. member for Waterloo South is correct, that their concern is to augment the work of their newspaper and to promote whatever politics they may be interested in. We have not any jurisdiction over them. What they will use that radio for will be their own business, but we do have jurisdiction over the C.B.C. Would the minister inform the committee if it is correct or otherwise that a transmitter has been installed at Halifax, and that it could be put into operation within three or four hours by the C.B.C. If the operation of the C.B.C. station is to depend upon the securing of material by these other people, I do not think it will be possible to get that material to-day.
My information, from a reliable source, is that the people who are endeavouring to use the old franchise granted to the Halifax Chronicle have been dickering for a secondhand set of equipment at Edmonton, Alberta. That is their own business. But I should like to be assured by the minister that the hold-up in the C.B.C. station at Halifax, which means a public service for that province, and one recommended by the general manager of the company, is not for the purpose of enhancing the possibilities of establishing other stations.
I am looking for information. Can the people of Nova Scotia within a reasonable length of time expect the implementing of the decision made by the responsible head of the C.B.C.? The minister's statement that a city like Halifax requires three radio stations is, I think, ridiculous. That is not necessary in a city of that size. But if someone wishes to
Supply-Transport

spend money, and fool around with it, that is their own business. However, a time of war, when equipment is hard to get, and when personnel is scarce, owing to the requirements of the armed services, is not the time for local, private people to experiment, or to enter the game of radio.
I have had some confidence in the C.B.C., and in all these projects the government is slowly developing for the betterment of the Canadian people. I like to support those projects; but I hate to think that for the sake of promoting the interests of a particular group in Canada, progress in that field would be set to one side. I do not know the story but the minister should know it. If there is any truth in the statement that that transmitter is in Halifax, and that the order in council is being held back because of political pressure, it will shatter my confidence in the future development of radio in Canada, under government management. If that statement is not true, then it should be clarified. Would the minister give us some idea as to the correctness or otherwise of the fears I have expressed ?

May I make it clear once more that my duty is to administer the Radio Act. That act has nothing to do with broadcasting. It is the custodian of wave lengths assigned to Canada under the Havana agreement, and from time to time it issues radio licences assigning certain wave lengths, always on the recommendation of the C.B.C.
So far as Halifax is concerned, there has been one licence outstanding there for some time. In 1938 a licence was applied for, was recommended by the C.B.C. and was issued by my department. At the outbreak of war, possibly because of the difficulty of obtaining materials, that licence lapsed and was no longer outstanding. I found out this morning something I did not know yesterday, namely, that we did receive an application from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation some two or three months ago, that the licence was approved by the technical officers, and that it was issued to the C.B.C. Since that time we have received application for the restoration of the wave length previously granted to the Halifax Chronicle. After that application *was referred to the C.B.C. it was recommended favourably by that organization, and the wave length was issued to the Halifax Chronicle. So that there are outstanding at the present time three wave lengths assigned to three radio stations in the city of Halifax. That is all I know about the situation.
I have had no association with the C.B.C. for a number of years. Whether they have equipment on the ground or whether they

have not, I have not the faintest idea. I know there are a number of wave lengths which have been assigned over the last two or three years, and I know that none of those wave lengths is on the air, for the simple reason that it is impossible to obtain equipment. I will correct that by saying that fifteen wave lengths have been assigned since the beginning of the war, that six of them are on the air, and that the remaining nine are not on the air because they cannot obtain equipment. That is the information we have in this branch, and that is all the information I can give hon. members.
I would point out that the discussion affecting the C.B.C. should be on another item.
There have been many applications for increased power?
A great many of them have been granted.

Have they been granted to a maximum of their power? A year ago the radio committee recommended in its report that stations should be encouraged to come up to their full power under the Havana agreement. Is it within the power of the Department of Transport to say whether they should come up to their full power, because we were told in the radio committee that there was a certain amount of interference. Who has jurisdiction in the matter?

There again the Department of Transport would issue, the power permissible on each wave length, but as a matter of policy it accepts the advice of the C.B.C. The policy of the C.B.C. up to two or three months ago was that private stations should be limited to one kilowatt. Some two months ago, I believe it was, that policy was revised, possibly on the advice of the radio committee, and a recommendation was made to us that the one-kilowatt stations be stepped up to five kilowatts, provided that the wave length would jpermit a five-kilowatt station. We accepted1 that recommendation, and permits have been issued to those stations to go up to five kilowatts. I do not think any of them have increased, for the reason I gave before, namely the impossibility of buying equipment at this time. But as soon as the equipment is available I believe every one-kilowatt station will step up to five kilowatts, provided that it is on a wave length where a step-up is permissible.

The minister will understand that the Havana agreement will not last forever. I have forgotten when it runs out. But in order to protect our wave

Supply-T ransport
lengths we must be up to our power requirements on these stations, or else we shall not have bargaining power at a later time. I do not understand why the stations were allowed to go up to five kilowatts. I think some of them might have gone up to three, others to four, others to ten, others to fifty, and so on. That is why I asked as to who made the survey. I understand that a survey was made by the C.B.C. Who made it? We have dual control' here.

No survey was necessary. We know exactly what the permissible power is on every wave length in Canada. That is fixed under the Havana agreement. I think my hon. friend will not quarrel with the principle that the C.B.C. should set the policy so far as the power of broadcasting stations in Canada is concerned. If he accepts that principle I think he will admit that we are carrying out the proper policy in connection with the radio stations in Canada. I should like to take my hon. friend's advice, but we decided to take the advice of the C.B.C.

I do not put myself up as being an engineer, but I happen to know a little about the matter. There are a great many engineers in this country and there is great apprehension among them that we are losing channels. I do not know how complete the survey has been. I do not know why we should put these stations tip to five kilowatts all at once. I do not understand that at all. Different districts in the country, as the minister knows, are being treated in different ways. Last night I was listening to the radio in my room in this building and I could get only about two or three stations in Canada, but I could get plenty of stations in the United States. I got Schenectady and New York without any trouble. Are we using our power in this country to the fullest extent? I am all in favour of private broadcasting stations. What we have to do is to see that our facilities are used to the full in order to give the people of Canada the service to which they are entitled.

Item agreed to.
Air service-radio division
406. Issue of radio receiving licences-(Transport department only), $205,220.

We collected a little over $4,000,000 in licence fees last year and it cost the department $205,000 to collect that. It also cost the C.B.C. something. Altogether it cost $536,000 to collect $4,000,000 in licence fees. The principle in the old days was correct, that those who used the radio
should pay for it, but that principle to-day is out of date. There are plenty of people who do not have a radio but who listen to radio. Not only that, but the man who has only a $25 radio has to pay a licence fee of $2.50 just the same as the man who owns a $250 radio. The principle is wrong.
The same kind of music comes out of both sets.

And the man who has no radio at all hears the same kind of music over the radio because everybody listens to radio. I ask the minister if he thinks it is economic to spend $536,000 to collect $4,000,000 in licence fees. Yet those are the figures. How long would the Dominion of Canada last if it cost us in the same proportion to collect our taxes? Not only is the principle of the licence fee outmoded, but it is just a nuisance tax to have these fellows coming around to your place and asking, "Have, you your radio licence for this year?" The Department of Transport are also broadcasting over the radio: "Your licence is overdue and please go in and get it for this year; if you do not, we will take you to court'and sue you for the $2.50." The whole situation is ridiculous. Imagine spending $536,000 to collect $4,000,000! What nonsense! The cost of collection is nearly twenty per cent. If you want to continue this licence fee system, why not collect it on the number of radios each man has? If he has five radios let him pay on five radios. Or the fee could be based on the value of the radio. But there is no fairness in the present system and it ought to be done away with immediately. That is all there is to it.
Does not the revenue from the licence fees pay for the cost of collection? Why should we vote an additional sum?

The sum has to be voted by
parliament under the government accounting system. The equivalent is paid to the receiver general of Canada. It is recoverable, just like many other items.
Item agreed to.

Office of the coal controller-
Coal subsidies and subventions-
17.'t. Dominion fuel board, administration and investigations, $32,120.

['I think ths answer to that is that harvesting is over in Ontario before Manitoba, and it is over in Manitoba under normal conditions earlier than in Saskatchewan and Alberta. We have to move these men across the country, and it may be for that reason that facilities are not arranged at the present time.']

I do not know whether it is proper to ask this question under this item, but has there been any change in the coal situation in Canada? It has been causing

Supply-Munitions and Supply

considerable worry. Could the minister make a statement on the coal supplies for next winter?

The coal situation is very
difficult. It becomes increasingly difficult each year. We hope to have sufficient bituminous coal, but anthracite coal will be very short and we shall have to use great ingenuity in using coke and other substitutes for anthracite. I think we shall be able to protect the bituminous situation; I think our industries will be safe, but we ask householders to economize in every possible way and to use coal carefully and cooperate with us in using such substitutes for anthracite coal as we are able to make available.
There are people who use bituminous coal in their household furnaces. Would it be possible to have coils installed in furnaces to help out the coal situation?
W'e are making the material available as far as we can, but I cannot say that everyone will be able to get it.
I think it would be one way of helping out the coal shortage.

Item agreed to.
Office of the coal controller-
Goal subsidies and subventions-
175. Payments in connection with the movements of coal under conditions prescribed by the governor in council, $4,500,000.
['I think it would be one way of helping out the coal shortage.']
We cannot pass an item of $4,500,000 in a few minutes. It is nearly eleven o'clock.
We have been sitting here since eleven this morning. How long is this item going to take?
Perhaps we might compromise and take the item if it is not going to take long, but if it is going to take any length of time I think we should rise because we have had a heavy day.
This is a routine item voted each year.

Almost the entire coal
industry depends on this one item. It is a matter of the payment of subsidies, and some of us would like to discuss the coal situation as we see it to-day in relation to this subvention and what is to happen in the future. We have not the time to discuss that in two or three minutes.

This same item has been voted previously, but owing to the fact that the coal does not move the distances which it did move,

only about $1,800,000 was spent last year. I think there is no great principle involved. It is a principle which is capable of moving coal from Cape Breton to the eastern part of Quebec and from the prairies into Toronto, but it is not possible to move the coal, for reasons other than the subsidy. Ample money is provided, but I cannot think of anything which can be usefully discussed under this item.
The fact is that it is the only item under which we can discuss the coal industry, because were it not for these subventions there would be no coal industry in Canada.
I rise to a point of order. It is now after eleven o'clock, and if this is going to take any time I certainly think the committee should rise. I know I cannot stand this heat any longer.
Why does the hon. member not discuss it, if he wishes to discuss it?
I can discuss it if the minister wants to wait a little while.
Certainly.

speechtext: Go ahead.

I would not have any objection to letting this go through, because the possibilities are that the minister wants to leave town, or something, over the week-end, and wishes to get this through. There is an item under mines and resources for research into fuels. I think we could discuss anything under that item.
If the minister will give us that undertaking, that is all right.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE MOTION TO ADJOURN TO JANUARY 31, 1945, ON COMPLETION OF CURRENT BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I should like to make a motion similar to that which I have made at the conclusion of each session during the period of the war. Hon. members will see in the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday that I have'given notice of the motion. It is:
That when this house adjourns, on completion of current business of the session, it stand adjourned until Wednesday, January 31, 1945, at 3 o'clock in the afternoon, provided always that if it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with His Majesty's government, that the .public interest requires that the house should meet at an earlier time during the adjournment, Mr. Speaker may give notice that he is so satisfied, and thereupon the house shall meet at the time stated in such notice, and shall transact its business as if it had been duly adjourned to that time.

May I with the permission of the house lay on the table the names of 423 members of the Canadian Army to whom honours and awards for gallantry in action and devotion to duty have been granted by His Majesty'; and I would ask that, as has become the practice, these names be given a permanent record in Hansard.
It will be recalled that on March 6 I submitted a list of 481 awards to the house. The list I am presenting to-day comprises the honours and awards conferred on the members of the Canadian Army since that date. The house will perhaps be especially interested in this list because there are in it 107 awards for gallantry which are being published this morning for the first time. They include 17 awards of the Distinguished Service Order, two bars to the Military Cross, 27 Military Crosses, four Distinguished Conduct Medals, and 17 Military Medals.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE-PROPERTIES PLACED AT DISPOSAL OF CONTROLLERS- OPERATIONS TO RESUME MONDAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE-PROPERTIES PLACED AT DISPOSAL OF CONTROLLERS- OPERATIONS TO RESUME MONDAY
speechtext:
May I ask the Minister of
Labour a question? He was about to speak and perhaps he anticipates it. I read in the papers to-day that the minister would at nine o'clock this morning give a statement with respect to the Montreal tramways dispute. I was going to ask him whether he had made such a statement, and, if so, whether he would repeat it to the House of Commons, because we are very much interested in it.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE-PROPERTIES PLACED AT DISPOSAL OF CONTROLLERS- OPERATIONS TO RESUME MONDAY
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should say this. I thought it was my duty to tell the house first of the policy being adopted by the government to bring the strike to a conclusion, but in order to cooperate wifh the press-some of the newspapers go to press at ten and some at eleven-so that the people of Montreal might be fully informed, I gave them an advance notice of my statement, not to be released until 11.15. Unfortunately one of the agencies did not flay the game and gave the story out, notwithstanding the clear understanding .1 gave the press men when I met them.
I now table copy of an order in council passed by the cabinet yesterday appointing controllers who have been given the responsibility of seeing that street railway traffic is resumed in Montreal on Monday next, August 14.

The order in council directs the company to place its extensive properties at the disposal of the controllers and also requires the employees of the company to return to work on Monday morning.
The controllers named are E. L. Cousins, wartime administrator of Canadian Atlantic ports. Halifax; and J. E. St. Laurent, member of the National Harbours board, Ottawa.
The order in council, passed under authority of the War Measures Act, makes-it an offence for any person to refuse to resume work or to recommend to any person that work be not resumed, and also makes it an offence should the company refuse to place its properties at the disposal of the controllers. The employees are required to return to work under the terms and conditions prevailing at the time the strike occurred.
The disputing parties are now directed to recommence negotiations for a settlement with the controllers to remain in charge of operations of the Montreal Tramways system pending an agreement between the company and employees. If at the expiration of sixty days the controllers report to the Minister of Labour that there is no prospect of settlement, the matter will further be reviewed by the government.
I need scarcely say that the government has taken this action in the public interest. A continuation of the strike might well result in grave injury in two ways; further great inconvenience to the population of the district . of Montreal in not having local transportation facilities, and, war production, already seriously threatened, increasingly impaired if the strike continued.
The interests of employees and employer involved in the strike are decidedly secondary to the public welfare and convenience. The issue is not of sufficient importance to warrant a strike in war-time.
I want to make this point clear: the action of the government is not to be understood as lending support to the proposition that it intends to compel any worker to relinquish freedom of choice as to the union which he wishes to join, nor should the action be construed as any departure whatever from the principles laid down in the wartime labour regulations, which provide that employees and employer have freedom of contractual collective bargaining.
The public of Montreal are to be congratulated on the calm way in which they have accepted the inconvenience due to the strike and for readily accommodating themselves to the situation resulting therefrom.
I would like to add this precis of a telegram received from the city of Montreal and the

Questions
provincial government, Mr. Speaker: Under date of August 11, the Montreal Tramways company sent a lengthy telegram to my colleague the Minister of Justice. The company quoted in full a reply received from Fernand Dufresne, director of police services for the city of Montreal, indicating inability to comply with a request of the company for police protection sufficient to enable the company to resume operation of street cars and buses. Mr. Dufresne estimated that 1,200 police officers would be required and stated that he did not have the men available. He did offer such protection as could be afforded by any of the 800 officers regularly on his force, who could be spared for special assignment. In the same telegram from the company there is quoted in full a message received from Hon. Leon Casgrain, attorney-general of the province of Quebec. Mr. Casgrain stated that the dominion, under wartime labour regulations, had assumed jurisdiction over disputes of the type in question; and consequently the company must look to the dominion for police protection. However, he advised that the provincial police would carry out any duties falling to them as provided under section 51 of the defence of Canada regulations.
The request of the company to the dominion was that the civic and provincial authorities having declined to afford protection for passengers, operators and property, the federal government should afford the necessary protection.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS TO TRANSFER HELP TO WESTERN CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS TO TRANSFER HELP TO WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. I must apologize for not sending him ffotice, but owing to the urgency of the matter I hope he will overlook my oversight. Have arrangements been completed with the railway companies for the transportation of harvest help to western Canada? If not, how soon can we expect to have the arrangements completed? How many are expected to go west to help with the harvest?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS TO TRANSFER HELP TO WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I do not see any difficulty in connection with the arrangements with the railway companies. It is purely administrative. Last year we were able to get 5,000, but conditions were of such a nature that when it reached the point that 3,200 had gone, the western provinces asked us to send no more. I anticipate that we shall get as
many this year as we got last year. I am speaking of civilians, not the men in the armed forces.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS TO TRANSFER HELP TO WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I have been talking to some people who have been ready to go west and who have told me that the railway companies prevented them from taking advantage of the arrangements.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS TO TRANSFER HELP TO WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I think ths answer to that is that harvesting is over in Ontario before Manitoba, and it is over in Manitoba under normal conditions earlier than in Saskatchewan and Alberta. We have to move these men across the country, and it may be for that reason that facilities are not arranged at the present time.
