subtopic: EXTENSION OF AUTHORIZED INVESTMENTS IN UNITED STATES SECURITIES

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of bill No. 185, to amend The Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, 1942.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTENSION OF AUTHORIZED INVESTMENTS IN UNITED STATES SECURITIES
speechtext: May I ask the minister to give at this stage a full statement with respect to this matter? When the bill was introduced a number of questions were asked and some explanation given. Perhaps the minister might combine with the statement he made last night some information with respect to the original act of 1932, which I think is necessary at this time to lay the foundation upon which the discussion can be based.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: EXTENSION OF AUTHORIZED INVESTMENTS IN UNITED STATES SECURITIES
speechtext:
The information asked for is now found in the explanatory note in the bill. Section 60 of the act provides as follows:
(1) Save as hereinafter provided, any company registered under this act may invest its funds, or any portion thereof, in the purchase of
(c) ground rents, mortgages or hypothecs on real estate in Canada, or elsewhere where such company is carrying on its business, provided that the amount paid for any such mortgage or hypothec shall in no case exceed sixty per cent of the value of the real estate covered thereby;
Subsection 2 of section 60 reads at the present time:
Any such company may lend its funds or any portion thereof on the security of
(b) real estate or leaseholds for a term or terms of years or other estate or interest therein in Canada or elsewhere where the company is carrying on business; provided, however, that no such loan shall exceed sixty per cent of the value of the real estate or interest therein which forms the security for such loan, but this proviso shall not be deemed to prohibit a company from accepting as part payment for real estate sold by it, a mortgage or hypothec thereon for more than sixty per cent of the sale price of such real estate.
In other words, as the law stands at the present time the company may invest in mortgages on real estate, but only to an amount up to sixty per cent of the value of the real estate. It may also lend on the security of the real estate, but only up to an amount of sixty per cent of the value of such real estate. It will be noted that at the present time theTe is power to invest outside of Canada. Note the words, "or elsewhere, where such company is carrying on its business-"
Life Insurance Companies

The bill extends the powers of the companies in this way. At the present time they may only invest in real estate in the United States up to sixty per cent of the value. That provision debars them from investing on the security of real estate in the United States where the loan i? insured by the federal housing administration of the United States, and it is desirable to extend the powers of the companies to invest without that limitation of sixty per cent of the value provided the loan is insured by the federal administration of the United States. That is the purpose of the bill, and as I said last night the effect is merely to put our companies in a fair competitive position with regard to the United States companies who have the power to invest in these insured securities on real estate in the United States, and who do so heavily and increasingly. I may say that loans under title II of the national housing act of the United States, protected by the insurance provisions of that title, have been made since 1935. Up to date nearly four and a half billion of insured loans have been made. The usual rate borne by the mortgage is four and a half per cent, and after allowing for expenses and charges it is estimated that approximately three and a half per cent is the net yield to the lender. Under the act, if foreclosure becomes necessary the property is transferred to the administrator and a debenture is issued by the administrator to the lender bearing two and three-quarter per cent per annum interest and maturing three years after the maturity date of the mortgage, subject to redemption on three months' notice at the option of the administrator. The number of properties transferred up to date has been remarkably small, -4 of one per cent of the number of mortgages insured, and of those properties transferred 95 per cent have been sold, leaving less than two hundred out of the million properties mortgaged now on hand.
The Canadian companies are required to cover United States liabilities with deposits with governments or trustees there. Until recently, Canadian securities were permitted to form part of those deposits, but in later years the companies have been pressed to substitute United States securities for any Canadian securities now held and to cover increases in liabilities with United States securities only, and it has become a problem for the companies to get acceptable United States securities for that purpose to yield a rate equal to the rate on which their reserves are based, usually three per cent or at the most three and a half per cent. United States government bonds yield from two and a half per cent to two and three-quarters per cent and high

grade utility and corporation bonds approximately the same rate. State and municipal bonds, by reason of the tax exemption feature, yield substantially lower rates, .most of them less than two per cent.
The permission to the companies to lend on these mortgages will permit the Canadian companies to share in a comparatively remunerative investment field now open to all - United States companies with which the former are in competition. The loans in question will be made from the. proceeds of the United States business of the companies; even if any company should think of lending funds derived from its Canadian business on such mortgages the permission of the foreign exchange control board would have to be first obtained, but the yield rate on the mortgage is not sufficiently high to attract Canadian funds.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF AUTHORIZED INVESTMENTS IN UNITED STATES SECURITIES
speechtext:
I followed carefully the
explanation given by the minister, which seemed to indicate that in the United States

Life Insurance Companies
there is a different basis of lending in the insurance investment field from that which prevails in Canada. So far as I know we here do not have a situation quite comparable to the situation the minister described as existing in the United States. Up to the time the federal housing administration entered the guaranteed field, if I may call it that, in the United States, in connection with these loans, evidently the same provisions applied with respect to the protection of policyholders; that is, a sixty per cent ceiling was placed upon loans on real estate which are accepted by the insurance companies. That, of course, would be in compliance with certain legal protection which has been afforded trust funds of this character in both countries. The investments of the public in insurance companies in Canada and elsewhere are very large. The popularity of insurance as a means of saving and protection combined has increased during the years, and we have seen it reach the point where the savings of many people find their way first of all into the coffers of the insurance companies by way of premiums, and then from the insurance companies into investments such as those envisaged in this act.
One point which was not very clear to me I think has been clarified to' some extent by the minister's statements. When the bill was first introduced I was afraid we were inventing a departure from the system of protection which exists in Canada, under which the loan may not exceed sixty per cent of the value of the real estate, which was the system under which our companies operated in the United States.
I was fearful that perhaps the funds of those who are paying premiums in Canada might be utilized in a less protected fashion, when the company outside could utilize its funds for investment in the United States. But the minister points out that there is a definite limitation, a definite boundary line with respect to the investment of our funds in the United States, the same as there is in respect of the investment by the same company of United States funds in Canada. In other words, as I understand the minister's statement, this bill would apply only to the funds which are invested by a Canadian life insurance company doing business in the United States, but which will be utilized onlj' for United States investments. In other words unless the foreign exchange control board authorizes differently, this will prevent Canadian funds by way of premiums going into the investment market in the United States under a different system, and perhaps under a lesser protection-although it is not clear as to that-than we have in Canada.
My understanding-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-is that only funds of policyholders in the United States are the ones actually affected by this legislation, with the one exception, namely, in the event of this government's allowing, through the foreign exchange control board, a movement of funds from Canada to United States account to be invested in real estate there.
That, of course, is true now. But the first question which enters one's mind is that this legislation will apply for years to come. The foreign exchange control board will pass out of existence legally as soon as the War Measures Act becomes inoperative. This would be at some time after the War, or when the policy of the government then in power might be changed in respect of the movement of funds. So that the answer given by the minister is not the only possible answer in respect of the movement of Canadian funds for United States investment. It may be at this time, but it would not be in the future, when the war -is over. So that I suggest the minister's argument falls to the ground. If the operations of the foreign exchange control board would cease within the next year, this legislation would still be in operation, and there would be nothing to hinder investment in the United States of Canadian funds paid in by Canadian policyholders to a Canadian insurance company under the provisions of this bill, and on terms which may be less safe and less protected than provided by Canadian law. Has this phase of the matter been considered by the government, as to whether the law in respect of investments in the United States under this act is different from the law which applies if the money is invested in Canada?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the Postmaster General two questions. I hold in my hand the report of the Postmaster General for the year ending March 1943, which is the last report issued, and also the report for the year 1942. We might think that the one ending March, 1944 would now be available, but apparently it is not. I should like to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to a change that has occurred in the preparation of this report. I suppose there are some six or seven thousand post offices in Canada and the procedure for

many years past has been to divide the list of post offices into accounting offices and non-accounting offices, these, in turn being divided according to provinces.
I have some 100 post offices in my riding and when I wanted to look up a particular post office in the past all I had to do was to turn to the accounting or non-accounting section, and then look up the province in which I was interested. In the case of nonaccounting offices for British Columbia these occupied only three pages, and I could speedily find the post office I was interested in. I think the same thing must apply to every other hon. member. But the system has now been changed and if I desire to look up a particular post office I must go through about 100 pages. If this meant some saving of time or paper the change would be understandable, but it means neither. It may be dumbness on my part, but I cannot understand the reason for this change. I have spoken to other hon. members and I find they have the same obj ection to this new system. It is very troublesome and inconvenient and I cannot see where there is any economy of time or paper or anything like that.
While I am on my feet I will take the opportunity of dealing with another matter I have in mind and then the minister can answer them both at once. I hold in my hand a letter which is marked "copy" and which was sent to a country postmaster in my district. It is from the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, 422 Metropolitan Building, 837 West Hastings street, Vancouver, British Columbia, and is dated January 14, 1944. Then comes the name of the rural postmaster who was to be the victim of this scheme. I shall not give his name for fear there might be repercussions, but the minister has seen the letter. It reads:
Dear Sir:	I am circularizing all householders-
"All." Note what that would involve in work and expense.
-through post offices and rural routes soliciting support for our budget fund.
I am aware that postmasters and postmistresses take no active part in political movements, but you will no doubt be aware of some individual in your locality who would possibly be favourably inclined toward our movement, and perhaps you will be good enough to pass this letter along to him or her.
We require an individual in each district to assist us, and if they will communicate with this office I will see that they get supplies and any information they may require.
Yours very truly,
W. W. Lefeaux, Chairman, Finance Committee.
As they say, they are circularizing all householders and they address themselves to the

Supply-Post Office
country postmasters. This man is asked to break the law and imperil his job in order to advance the political and financial future of a political party. Hundreds of postmasters are fired after every election for taking part in politics during the election, but in twenty-three years I have only had two fired because of grave charges. One was suppressing my mail and he was also short in his. funds. This is from a party which sets itself up on a pedestal, both in the past and as to the future, a party which devotes a large portion of its time lecturing and damning the two old political parties. It is true that they have never had the opportunity to do the things which they accuse the old parties of doing because they have never been in power, and God willing I hope they never will be. Scripture says: "If these things be done in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?" I think that quotation can be applied most effectively to what these people are doing.
I hate to think what these people will do if they get a little more power. If some postmaster or postmistress should take a chance and do these things and they once got a hold over them it is only a step farther for them to come along and say, "How much mail is Tom Jones getting, and from whom?" There might be no limit to what they might do once they got in power. It will be noted that they say they are circularizing all householders through post offices and rural routes. Is it not most important for the purity of our elections that our post office officials shall be trustworthy?
I remember one occasion w'hen a postmaster was made a returning officer. I de>-manded an investigation after the election and it was found, first, that he had been drunk on election day; second, that he was short some considerable sum in his post office funds, and, third, that he.had not distributed political mail of mine which had been properly prepaid and addressed to people. He assumed that it was not wise for them to get it until after the election was over. The investigation was held unfortunately by political associates of this gentleman and he was not fired; he was allowed to resign. I was simple enough to let it go at that. A couple of years later he bobbed up again in another part of the riding and was recommended as a postmaster. I put it up to the officials here and said that I did not think a man with that pedigree was suitable for the position, but the reply I got back stated that the gentleman who had recommended him as postmaster was the very same inspector who had conducted the previous investigation and that as he had not been fired, there was really no black mark against him. I sent the letter I have read to the Postmaster General and I received an unsigned reply from
him stating that he did not approve of such proceedings. I should like to ask him what action was taken to prevent a recurrence of such a rapscallion piece of business.

With regard to the first question asked by the hon. member, I would say that some years ago the economy committee recommended that a change should be made in the method of setting out the post offices in the report. From a departmental point, of view it was found to be more convenient to list the post offices in alphabetical order rather than to follow the old system. However, in view of what the hon. member has said I shall be glad to reconsider the matter and discuss it with him.
In regard to the second matter, as soon as it was brought to my attention the district directors in all postal districts were advised that such action was incorrect, and it would be considered that if postmasters or postmistresses took such a course of action, they would be guilty of political interference if they did it for any party and would be liable to be dismissed for that reason. I think it has been made quite clear to them that that suggestion should not be followed by them unless they wish to place their positions in jeopardy.

Would the minister give the committee the new rates for the postmen and other services in the post offices of Toronto? There was something in the paper about it a few days ago. I should like the present rates and the new rates.

I am speaking on a point of order, and I do not think you have any right to interrupt me. I did not interrupt the minister when he was speaking on a point of order. Now I maintain that, knowing that situation, the minister instead of bringing forward his department at a suitable time to discuss these matters leaves them to the end, which would indicate that he considers the treatment of the wounded as less important than the Post Office Department.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There is certainly no point of order in what the hon. gentleman says. We are in committee of supply in the Post Office Department and the hon. gentleman raises a question of privilege. He knows that there can be no question of privilege in committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In order to prevent a false impression going out I wish to remind the committee, although it is entirely wrong to discuss the matter, that the hon. gentleman had a full opportunity to debate a certain question, and according to the rules of the house, once that subject has been disposed of for the session he has no right now to convey the impression that he has been deprived of full opportunity of debate.

I rise again to a point of order. I did not have a full opportunity to discuss the matter on a previous occasion because I *was told by the chairman that I had to make the charge general across the dominion instead of relating it specifically to the question of Christie street in Toronto.

The hon. member is
right in that.

speechtext:
I would ask hon. members to come down to the work before the

Surely the government

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The government will follow the procedure announced last night and concurred in. Hon. gentlemen will be given the fullest possible latitude and time to discuss any of the estimates.
I do not know how the government expects the opposition to cooperate when it takes the position that it does. That is not quite fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The order of procedure was announced last night and accepted by the house.

As to accepting the order of procedure announced, the minister knows that there is no such thing as acceptance of any order of procedure. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

Exactly as I thought.
The government is taking a dictatorial attitude to the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Canada, for they are a body of men who are imbued with a sincere desire to serve to the best of their ability. They advanced certain rates. One of them was the amount now mentioned by the minister, namely, $1,800. Am I to understand that the postman now starts at $1,200 and advances to $1,620?
Is that the letter carrier?

Yes, the senior letter
carrier. How long is he in the service before he becomes a senior?
It is a matter of promotion to. vacancies on merit.

The senior letter carrier
will now' commence at $1,620 and go to $1,800?
Yes.

That is an advance of
$180 over what the senior gets now. The senior letter carriers were asking for a maximum of $2,000. Am I right in that?

The representations made
were for $300 increase all round. This mattr has been dealt with, having received the recommendation of the joint council which was re-i cently set up comprising representatives of the government and representatives of the services in which there are three representatives of different branches of the Post Office organizations. We have letters of thanks, one from the heads or representatives of some of the organizations for this change. It is not all that they asked for but it has corrected' to a great extent the difficulty that has existed and has stopped men being brought in to work at less than $1,200 a year. The people in the lower incomes are the ones who will be helped most. The $l,020's are increased by $180. The hon. member has been interested in this matter for some time and he will agree that it will be a great help to raise the minimum from $1,020 to $1,200. That was one of the bad features and I am, and have been for some time, absolutely behind the increase. I am delighted that these changes have been made.

I am glad that this improvement has occurred in the minister's period of office, because many years ago* his celebrated grandfather made a change in the postal service and it is fitting that the grandson should emulate his example. I am glad that he has done what he has and I hope he will keep in mind improving the position of the men, because there is no country in the world that is served better by its postal employees than Canada. I am not discounting any other staff, but the outside letter carriers in Canada work in all kinds of weather, rain, or shine-

yesterday for example they were working in a temperature of 100 degrees-and they wear clothes that are not designed for the maximum of comfort in such temperatures. This is a step in the right direction. Have the new arrangements been made retroactive?

They are retroactive to
July 1.

I had been hoping that
they would be retroactive to the first of January for all senior clerks and all those who were on at that time. Has that been considered?

The matter has received a great, deal of attention. The hon. member will appreciate the difficulties in making changes, with price ceilings and wage control and so on. He will understand also thdt changes have to be considered in relation to wages in other branches of the government service throughout the country.

Some of these postal
employees in Toronto and, I presume, in Montreal and other big cities, have had additional duties imposed upon them in consequence of the war. Are they being compensated for that extra work entailed by war duties?

In some cases when men are fulfilling extra duties supplements are given in addition. Some of them have gone through; others have been recommended by the department and are under consideration by the treasury board. I agree with the hon. member when he says that the men have had added responsibilities and added work. He realizes that that cannot be entirely avoided. Inexperienced men cannot deliver mail efficiently. They have to learn their route; they have to learn the system. Experienced men are carrying a big share of the load. When increases come along I am glad to know that we are appreciative of what they are doing. They have helped out and have taken on those added duties because they know they are necessary. We have a large number of men who are in different branches of the armed service-some are on loan to other departments of the government-during this war. I wish to say that I appreciate the service that the men have given right across this country and the spirit they have shown. I refer not only to the men in the civil service but also to the postmasters in the small offices across Canada who help in every way they can and who cooperate in taking on more duties frequently without charge to the public treasury.

Will the Postmaster General give the committee an outline of the

procedure followed by the post office officials when a vacancy occurs and a new postmaster is appointed? What happens when applications are received? What investigations are carried on when the final appointment is made? Who has the final say?

I shall answer the last question first. If the office has a revenue of $3,000 or more the appointment is made by the civil service commission. If the revenue is less than $3,000 the appointment is made by the Postmaster General.
Outline the procedure with regard to what happens when there is a resignation. I presume applications are called for?

Of course the hon. member is fully aware that there is a soldiers' preference in all these cases. When a vacancy occurs the legion is notified. Then no action is taken, until the legion has been given a reasonable length of time to notify the returned soldiers organizations in that district so that men will have an opportunity for applying if they wish the position. If there is a suitable returned soldier he gets the preference over the civilian if he is a resident of the area to be served by the post office. The applicants are considered according to merit. Of course, the member or the defeated candidate of the government in power is notified. That has been the practice under every administration and is still the practice.

Has the minister had correspondence and communications from a citizen of Halifax who has been directing communications and complaints to the Prime Minister and the Postmaster General, and who on occasion has been good enough to send copies of the communications to me? The complaints made are fairly well detailed, and evidently the department has already received the information. I indicated earlier to the complainant that when the estimates of the Post Office Department came before the committee I would raise the question that has been brought to my attention. Without going into detail with respect to the matter perhaps the Postmaster General would give some explanation as to the probleins, difficulties and complaints that are dealt with in these letters and tell us what action he has taken or intends to take with respect to it.

I may say to the leader
of the opposition that I have seen these letters.

The complaints of Mr. Regan?

Yes. Investigations were made by the district director, affidavits obtained, and I shall be very glad to give my hon. friend the file for his decision.
My decision?
Yes.
I want your decision.
I can tell my hon. friend that it has been thoroughly investigated. I have not the file here but I shall be delighted to show it to my hon. friend for his information at any time.

Did the Postmaster
, General find the complaints substantiated when the investigation was made?

The original ones, no.
Certain other matters have come up and they are still under investigation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Did I hear the Postmaster General correctly a moment ago? Did he say that it is the policy of the government, when these vacancies occur, to notify either the government member or the government defeated candidate?
You did.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the policy? I can hardly believe it.
Certainly they are notified. Anybody can make a recommendation on a suitable person to be appointed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is one thing for anybody to make a recommendation; it is another thing for the government to take the initiative "on its own and literally to ask the government member in the constituency or the government defeated candidate for a recommendation. It seems to be far-fetched. I should think that the sitting member of the constituency concerned, and possibly some other defeated candidate, should be notified as well.

I asked the minister to outline the procedure completely with regard to these appointments. In his reply he did not refer to the superintendent. I want to know the various steps in the procedure where a resignation or a vacancy occurs in some other way. Would the minister go through the procedure from the beginning? First of all there is the call for applications, then there are recommendations. Following that there must be some kind of investigation to find out whether the applicants are qualified, and then the actual appointment. The minister has not given the position of the superintendent in
Supply-Post Office

regard to that at all. I should like to have the whole story given so that we shall know what procedure is followed.
After the applications are received? I presume it is from that time.
Received by whom?

Sometimes the applications are forwarded to the district director, and sometimes they come directly to Ottawa. All applications are considered and are referred to the district director, who usually sends an inspector to interview the applicants to find out their qualifications and make inquiries as to their ability to fill the position; to see what applications there are and who are returned soldiers. If there are returned soldier applic- [DOT] ants they are considered first. There is no use in going around to a lot of civilian applicants if there are suitable returned soldiers, because the returned soldier is going to get the position. Then the reports of the inspector are forwarded to the district director or superintendent, as the case may be, who in turn forwards them to the head of post office service at Ottawa.
Mr. CASTLEDEiN: And he makes his recommendation w'hen he forwards them; he recommends who is to get the position? The final decision, however,- does not rest with, him; his recommendation might be entirely overridden by other interference?

I would not put it in exactly that way. There is a departure from that procedure only when there is a dispute, and then of course the matter must be the responsibility of the Postmaster General.^ If there is a dispute on the question of entitlement, the recommendation would come from the head of post office service as to what course of action he thought should be followed, and he could come in and discuss the matter. However, the great majority of cases are dealt with entirely without submission to the minister's office at all.
And the returned soldier always gets the preference?
Yes; the suitable returned soldier always gets the preference.

I was greatly interested in the outline the Postmaster General gave in connection with the appointment of these postmasters. I understand that appointments in the revenue post offices are made through the civil service commission, but like the hon, member for Winnipeg North Centre I wras astounded to learn that appointments in the smaller post offices were sometimes of a political nature. Perhaps I was not as

surprised as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, however, because I have in my hand a sessional paper No. 224 dated Tuesday, March 14, 1944, which was brought down in reply to a motion standing in my name. In following the outline given by the minister in reply to the hon. member for Yorkton in regard to the procedure followed in these appointments, I was surprised when he neglected to inform the committee and the hon. member just what connection the Department of Agriculture had with the Post Office Department. I was not surprised to hear the Postmaster General say that defeated candidates were consulted in regard to the appointment of postmasters, but I did not know that our present Minister of Agriculture was a defeated candidate in the constituency of Humboldt. I should like to go through this return, giving the committee the essential information it contains, because I am quite sure the committee will be concerned about the matter.
First I have a copy of a letter which was sent to the provincial secretary of the Canadian Legion at Regina with respect to a vacancy in the Dafoe post office; that is the village of Dafoe, not the Dafoe airport. Mr. Chase, the provincial secretary of the Canadian Legion, was notified by the department that this vacancy was to be filled. That was all to the good; we appreciated this step. Then on August 2, 1943, the date on which the Canadian Legion secretary at Regina was notified, I have a copy of a letter addressed to the private secretary to the Minister of Agriculture at Ottawa, reading in part as follows:
Tile position of postmaster at Dafoe, electoral district of Humboldt, Saskatchewan, is vacant owing to the resignation of Mr. Cyril Lambe. Mr. Lambe has been on military leave and the office has been in the temporary charge of his wife, Mrs. Helen Maud Lambe since the 4th February, 1941. Mrs. Lambe now wishes to be relieved of her duties on the 15th August. As the appointment in this case rests with the Postmaster General, will you be so good as to submit as soon as possible for his consideration your minister's recommendation of a suitable person for appointment to this vacancy. An official nomination form is herewith.
I might add that I am sure the Minister of Agriculture was not in Ottawa at that time. Then on August 27 there is another letter addressed to the private secretary to the Minister of Agriculture:
Re Dafoe, Saskatchewan
With reference to the vacancy in the position of postmaster at the above mentioned office, permit me to inform you that an application has been received from Mr. William Ferdinand Werner, who states that he was born on the 29th January, 1890.

That is signed by George C. Avery, acting chief superintendent, post office service. The next letter is from Saskatoon to the chief superintendent of post office service, Ottawa: Re Dafoe, Saskatchewan
Referring to previous correspondence, in regard to the vacant position of postmaster at the above named office, especially to my letter of the 23rd instant, enclosing an application form 5-B completed by Mr. William Ferdinand Werner, I wish to advise .that the acting postmistress asked to be relieved of the office at the earliest possible date, and therefore, subject to the approval of the department, steps will be taken within the next few days to place the office temporarily in charge of Mr. Werner. Enclosed is a letter from Mr. W. E. Mason, secretary of the Dafoe branch of the Canadian Legion, to the effect that the branch is in favour of the appointment of Mr. Werner.
The next one is dated August 31, 1943, and is addressed to the private secretary to the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think this is absolutely out of order, but the hon. member is reading from a return which no doubt is available in the records of the House of Commons. This may be in order, but I doubt it very much, because after all the country has been put to some expense already in the preparation of this return, and I am sure most hon. members will be familiar with what is in it.

I want to assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I do not desire to place on record anything that does not concern this case, but I submit that in presenting the matter to the minister and the committee it is necessary to quote from the return in order to show that injustices are done in matters of this kind and that returned men are not always given the preference they are supposed to receive. I submit that subject to your approval, I may place this information on record without causing any undue hardship to anyone.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is not only the question of hardship; it is the question of whether or not the rules should be obeyed. Already some expense has been incurred by the country in having this return prepared and brought down, and I do not see that it is necessary for the hon. member to place it all on Hansard. There is no doubt that he has the right to base his argument upon the return, but I do not believe it is necessary to put all the information on Hansard again.
' Mr. BURTON: I intend to show that in this case the Canadian Legion at this point in Saskatchewan made a recommendation supporting the appointment of the man who had been the assistant in this office. They wished
to have him continue there, and here we have interference from the outside in connection with that appointment. To continue quoting from this return:
Private Secretary to
The Minister of Agriculture.
Re: Dafoe, Sask.
I am enclosing for your information copy of a letter from the Secretary of the Dafoe Branch of the Canadian Legion in favour of the appointment of Mr. W. F. Werner as postmaster at Dafoe.
As the acting postmistress desires to be relieved of the office at the earliest possible date, arrangements have been made for a temporary transfer to the charge of Mr. Werner.
Then we come to the next one, which is a memorandum stating:
Re Dafoe, Saskatchewan.
Mr. Parker, Private Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, telephoned and stated that his minister recommended J. B. Holfeld instead of Mr. Werner.
Then here is a telegram:
The District Superintendent of Post Service, Saskatoon, Sask.
Re Dafoe if not too late transfer office to Holfeld instead of Werner.
George C. Avery.
And then follows this letter:
Ottawa, September 3, 1943. District Superintendent. Saskatoon, Sask.
This will confirm telegram of September 2. reading as follows: "Re Dafoe if not too late transfer office to Holfeld instead of Werner." George C. Avery.
Here is another telegram:

George C. Avery.

Re Dafoe notwithstanding information your telegram third proceed with transfer to Holfeld.

Then we have this further letter:
Ottawa, September 10, 1943. Private Secretary to the Minister of
Agriculture, Ottawa.
In accordance with your minister's recommendation on the official nomination form, instructions have been issued for the appointment of Mr. J. B. Holfeld as postmaster at Dafoe, Sask.
Geo. C. Avery.
My submission is that in this instance the district postal superintendent wished to appoint a man who had been helping with that work, a man who had the recommendation of the Canadian Legion. Then there was interference and, as I have said, regardless of what the district superintendent had done, the Minister of Agriculture overrode the decision which had been made by the district superintendent and other officials of the Post Office Department. As a result there was appointed to that office a man who had not served overseas in a previous war, a man who had not been discharged from service in this war, and a man whose appointment was not approved by the people in that community. I have one other letter I should like to read, as follows:
Saskatoon, Sask., Sept. 25, 1943. Chief Superintendent, Post Office Service, Ottawa.
Re Dafoe, Sask., Post Office.
Enclosed for your kind attention is a petition bearing 128 signatures, protesting against the appointment of Mr. J. B. Holfeld to the position of postmaster at the above mentioned office.
J. H. Hunter.
I submit that when' we have interference of that kind, when the Post Office Department has men who are qualified and who should know the people they are dealing with, we should not find these little appointments- little two-by-four post office appointments- being interfered with by a man who never was a candidate in the constituency, who never was a member for the constituency, and who knows very little about the constituency. Yet he tells the people there who their postmaster shall be. I object to a procedure of that kind.
When I asked for this information, and the return was finally authorized, the Postmaster General said that with the usual reservations the information would be supplied. And if my memory serves me correctly the information was given and it was indicated that possibly all the information would not be supplied. The people in that district are satisfied that all the information is not supplied in the return. They reach that conclusion because they know that at the out-
break of war the Royal Canadian Mounted Police made a report with respect to this man who is now postmaster in that village. It will be noticed that that report is not in the files. I say that that is what the people believe. I do not know. The minister himself said when the return was brought down that possibly it would not be complete. I do say that this is not a healthy situation and the people do not like it, nor do they approve of it. The Canadian Legion has signified its willingness to have someone fill the position, and then they are overridden by a man who is not even connected with the Post Office Department. I want to know what connection he has.

If the hon. member had given me any intimation that he was going to discuss this matter I would have had the records here. He will appreciate that there are over 12,000 post offices, and I certainly cannot have all the files here concerning all of them. I cannot give him all the information he wants, but I shall be glad to make inquiries at once. That is all I can say at the present time.
Can the minister give any reasonable explanation to the committee why the minister of another department should have the say-so in the Post Office Department, as to who an appointee shall be?
The minister of another department does not have the say-so in my department, but he may have made a recommendation.

His recommendation is here,. as brought down in the return. It shows that the minister's official, one whom I have always considered an able official, hadl made an appointment. But because the minister of another department overrode the official's appointment, he had to bow to the appointment of someone else.
A district director could not make an appointment; he could make only a recommendation.

I realize that, but if we cannot have confidence in the men you have out there in the country, the men who are dealing with post offices day in and day out, and if we cannot have confidence in' those men being permitted to make proper recommendations, then I say we are getting into a>
bad state of affairs so far as the Post Office Department is concerned. And furthermore, if your men in charge find that when they want to do the right thing they are interfered

Supply-Post Office
with, even from outside the Post Office Department, you are reducing the efficiency of your personnel in other parts of the country.

My hon. friend would put permanent officials of the department in an almost impossible position. If the inspector made the appointment he w.ould have to take absolute responsibility. If he recommends a man who was a Liberal or a Conservative perhaps my hon. friend would object to him on that score. The inspector makes his inquiry and then reports to the head of the postal services in Ottawa. I will look into the matter the hon. member has brought up, but he will understand that I have not the details of all these cases right here.

I think circumstances alter < cases. I happen to have a vacancy in my constituency and I would be delighted to have a recommendation, even from the hon. member for Humboldt. It is easy for the hon. member to take one specific case in which a recommendation had been made by the legion. I honour the legion and I always consult them,, but it has not seen fit to make a recommendation for this particular vacancy. In these days of prosperity, positions in some of these smaller offices are not so attractive. It may be that somebody had ambitions and went through the procedure of having the legion help to get him an appointment, and now the hon. member makes a political hubbub about a particular appointment. I think all cases have to be analysed on their own merits and I hope that the argument advanced by the ht>n. member for Humboldt will not be applied to all cases. As I say, I have found it most difficult to fill this particular vacancy.

I appreciate what the minister has said, but I do not want him to think that I brought up this as an individual case. Despite what the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, this is not an isolated case. There has been altogether too much of this going on. I bring up this case as one of many that have occurred in years gone by.
If it was just an individual case I would be quite prepared to take it up with the minister, but this concerns a matter of apparent policy. The minister has permitted another minister to override the good judgment of his own officials. We are quite prepared to see that as far as possible these appointments are made on a non-political basis. He can say what he wants to say about the superintendent making the appointment, that one man may be a Conservative, a member of the C.C.E. or a Liberal, but we are quite prepared to have
100-400i
these appointments made by the civil service commission with the recommendation of the legion. In this case the recommendation of the legion was absolutely ignored and another man was forced into the position.
Will my hon. friend state that Warner who was recommended by the legion is a returned soldier?
No, I will not state that Mr. Warner is a returned soldier.
That was the inference.

The legion recommended
that Mr. Warner be considered.
I understand that in his own statement Mr. Warner said he was not a returned soldier.
Several returned men made application for the position but apparently they did not have a look in when the Minister of Agriculture asked that his appointee be considered.

I d'o not think my hon, friend is being fair to the legion when he makes the statement he did. He is saying apparently that the legion did recommend Warner, who is a civilian, in preference to returned men in the district who were suitable.

The members of that branch of the legion were quite willing that the man who had been helping in the post office should be given the position, but later when a man was appointed of whom the general public and the legion did not approve, the whole thing blew up. Then there were returned men who said, "If they are going to make this appointment, I am willing to serve," and they made application but they did not get any consideration.

I am not concerned with the particular case which has been brought to our attention by the hon. member for Humboldt; I am not interested in any particular case. So far as my own constituency is concerned I have not had any complaint, but I am concerned about the general principle about the application of patronage to the civil service of Canada. It seems to me that if we are to have an effective democracy that kind of thing cannot continue. There are more implications than are seen on the surface.
It has been called to my attention that when certain patronage agents offer to take up cases for individuals it is felt that they will be able to get more than the member



Supply-Post Office
[DOT]of parliament, particularly if the member is in the opposition. I have no complaint to make in that regard because any case I have taken up with any minister I have received very fair treatment. However, this matter has reached the point where some patronage agents find themselves financially benefited, and that is going too far.
Because there is political patronage many civil servants are tied down and prevented from giving expression to their own political views. I am sure other hon. members have met the same thing I have. As I have gone through my constituency individuals have come to me and whispered, "You know, I really should not be at this meeting, because I am a civil servant, but I thought I would like to come anyway." In one case I asked a gentleman if he would mind being chairman of the meeting, and he said, "Oh, no; I could not; you know I have a government job and that would not do." That sort of thing should not take place. I am not saying that this is true of all civil servants, but civil servants should be absolutely free to express themselves in' any way they want to, just as any other ordinary citizen is free to do. That would be the case if political patronage was completely eliminated.

I merely make this observation by way of suggestion, but I know that a large number of members have made reservations in order to get home to-night. It would be only with unanimous consent. Would the committee be inclined to sit on after one o'clock ?

If there are many hon. members with reservations, they got their reservations at their own risk, because I think I made pretty clear, yesterday and the day before, what view I took of this matter, and I did it because I recognized that everybody wants to get out to-night, but on the other hand I believe everybody takes the position, "We will get out to-night if the work is done, and done as it should be done, but if we cannot do it as it should be done by to-night of course we shall have to continue next week." There is no other rule or rule of thumb that can be applied, and I think we sjiall have to accept the situation as it is. There were 196 items left over from last night. That does not mean that they cannot all be dealt with, but if they cannot be dealt with properly they will have to be left over till next week. I believe that this is the frank, the proper and the appropriate position for anyone in the house to take.

I think the leader of the opposition is perfectly fair in his statement. I wonder whether as a measure of compromise the committee could reconvene at two o'clock. That would be a reasonable compromise, and I make the suggestion. Of course this can be done only with unanimous consent.
I am going to object to it, for several reasons. One is that very few hon. members would know that we were going to convene at two o'clock.
The bell is rung.

Most hon. members
understand that we shall meet at three o'clock, and I think we should meet at that hour. I may say that yesterday morning when the matter was discussed I made some objection to the proposed increase of sitting hours, but I thought that with cooperation we could get through to-day. But may I point out that yesterday morning one and a half hours were consumed by two members of the house, and to-day one or two items have occupied the entire morning.
Naturally consent has to be unanimous, and in view of what has been said we had better arrange to reconvene at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It "was said last night that the supplementary estimates to be brought in to-day would be tabled this morning. Will that be done?

I understand that they will be, although it is after one o'clock and they have not been tabled. I shall be glad to make inquiries and see that they are tabled at the earliest possible moment, which, I suppose, in view of the decision of the committee, will be three o'clock.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.
Progress reported.

Mr. BRL1CE: Mr. Chairman, I would like to say at the outset that it was a great disappointment to thousands of people in this country, particularly those in the low income group, that the national health insurance bill was not proceeded with during this session of parliament. In many sittings of the social security committee held last session we listened to some 117 witnesses, representing all phases of health activities, and went over very carefully the proposed draft bill. At the conclusion of last year's sitting we were given to understand that some members of the advisory committee, headed by Doctor Heagerty, an eminent physician and authority on health matters, would shortly proceed to o&cii province to discuss with them these proposals, and following this it was hoped that a conference would take place between the dominion and provincial governments to deal with the financial aspects of the bill. When we reconvened, this year we found that neither of these things had been done. I then called the attention of the minister of pensions and health to the urgent necessity of this conference being convened if we were to get this bill before parliament this session. Since then, no conference has been called, and although we have had many sittings and gone over the bill very thoroughly, and our chairman has laid it on the table of the house, it has not been considered by this parliament, for the reasons I have given.
If this bill had been passed it would have immediately brought relief to the many humble families suffering from sickness about whom the Prime Minister was so concerned when he brought in his baby bonus bill which is not to come into effect until July of next year.
AVhen the Minister of Pensions and National Health opposed my motion to adjourn the house to consider the treatment of our wounded, he gave as his reason that an opportunity would be given when his estimates were considered; and at last this opportunity comes to-day. Unfortunately several of our ex-service members who intended to participate in this debate have had to return home:	I refer to
the hon. member for Lake Centre, the hon. member for Vancouver South, and the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough.
In dealing with this question I intend to call as witnesses certain people who have
been making a special investigation of the situation at Christie street. First I will call Mr. 0. T. G. Williamson, secretary of the Canadian Corps Association, whose letter to the Globe and Mail is as follows:
The men in Christie Street hospital cannot be described as "humble poor" and yet they are deserving of rather more consideration than is being given them. A temporary lire trap overrun with cockroaches is hardly the place to which a grateful country should consign them. Far from being humble, they are proud. They have a proper pride in themselves and in their achievements. It is the task of us, who have remained at home in comfort, to see that they have no reason to lose their pride in the country they suffered to defend.
If there was the slightest necessity for them now to be housed in a factory building which has been a "temporary hospital since the last war they would take it with a grin. Many of them received their first dressing under fire in a slit trench. They can take it when they have to. Now the necessity is past. If energy and goodwill had been shown by the Department of Pensions and National Health, Sunnybrook hospital might be complete to-day.
Hospitals quite as large and permanent have been built in Australia and the United States in no more than six months. They go back to the outbreak of war. It is fair to the minister to say that he was warned of the necessity as long ago as March, 1943. Advised by deputies whose opinions at that time have since been shown to be without foundation, he stalled and procrastinated. When finally forced by public opinion to take action, he did so in ways which made it plain that he w-as sticking to his original intention of making the hospital a postwar project. To date, as far as actual construction is concerned, he has turned a sod and done some wholly unnecessary grading. It is now believed that tenders will be closed within a day or two for an up-patients building, a nurses' residence and the boiler plant. Even when these are complete, active treatment cases will still be relegated to Christie Street.
From an extensive knowledge of building practice. the writer wishes to say that a contract could immediately be placed for the construction of the main building.
Plans complete to the last detail are unnecessary. The structure could be comriienced at once with good prospect of it being enclosed before cold weather. The final details would be ready long before that time. Men being wounded in Normandy could easily receive treatment in Sunnybrook hospital by next April at latest if energy is now shown. The departments of defence have a responsibility in this matter which they must not overlook. They should take on the job and at once.
This appeared in the Globe and Mail on August 5. 1944. I wish now to read a few extracts from a letter written by Colonel C. E. Reynolds, immediate past-president of the Canadian Corps, in which he says:
I will stake my reputation as a construction man that the main treatment building at Sunnybrook hospital could be started at once and completed by the end of April of next year. To pretend otherwise is eyewash. Babies'

diapers apparently mean more than bloodstained bandages to the people of Ottawa responsible for the care of our fighting men.
Any decent Canadian must be heartsick at the callous disregard being shown toward the cream of our manhood.
I wish also to quote an extract from another letter written by Mr. O. T. G. Williamson a few days later than the one I have already read. He says:
The minister's statement, published on August 5, is misleading and calculated to promote complacency at a time when it is of the utmost importance that the public should be aware of the truth. As far as hospital accommodation is concerned, it is significant that Mr. Mackenzie speaks in terms of beds and not of buildings. That sufficient hospital space has not been provided is amply proved by the recent decision to convert hostels at Peterborough and Kingston for this purpose. Beds, as Mr. Mackenzie insists, may be available,, but suitable places to put them are not. The wards of Christie Street hospital are crowded far beyond the limits of decency and there are few empty beds. Within the last few days pressure had to be exerted to have three men in urgent need of operations, removed from Chorley Park to Christie Street. These men had been held for weeks in spite of their condition because beds were not available in Christie Street where the operations would be performed. Yet in spite of this situation Mr. Mackenzie is acquiring trumpery makeshifts instead of forcing the immediate construction of the active treatment wing at Sunnybrook Park. It is a sad outlook if every attaek on callous disregard for servicemen is to be dubbed political.
Tt should be noted that all those who have fought for a new hospital have fully appreciated that the medical and nursing services available have been unsurpassed in any Canadian hospital. The pity is that devoted doctors and nurses should be working under suc-h distressing circumstances.
That is the end of the quotation from Mr. Williamson's letter. May I add a word so that there can be no misunderstanding of my position in criticizing the inadequacy of the accommodation provided at Christie street. I have said before, and I repeat, that the surgical staff at Christie street is as expert and efficient as can be found in any part of the world. Operations of the most intricate and difficult character are done there by leading surgical specialists in the city of Toronto. The medical staff and those in charge of the X-ray department and laboratories are in every way most capable and efficient. The nursing staff is of the highest order and lives up to the best traditions of the nursing profession- In addition, the work of the voluntary aid detachment nurses is of a very high order, so that anything I say with respect to ,the accommodation provided for the wounded in that hospital must not be misconstrued as criticism of the staff.

Hamilton, who, if I mistake not, served as a medical officer in the last war. He states in part as follows:
Finally I wish to point out that to compare Christie Street hospital with hospitals in the United States housing returned American soldiers leaves a very bad impression. I do not think that soldiers want luxuries; all they want is comfort, good food and the most up-to-date scientific treatment. Many of them on returning complain that as long as they were in the army everything was satisfactory, but as soon as they were switched to pensions and national health the very opposite was the case. There is probably a good deal of truth in this observation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The whole thing is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Some statements are being made that are certainly out of order.

He says that the soldiers do not want luxuries such as are to be found in the million dollar Red Cross hospital at Cliveden, England, grand pianos, Persian rugs and so forth.
All they want is to be looked after and not kicked around from place to place until they are completely discouraged. Ask some of the Dieppe wounded, if they wish to verify this statement. Let us give some credit to the work that has been accomplished at Christie Street . . .
The rest conforms to what I said a moment ago about the efficient staff at Christie street.
Miraculous healing surgery has been an everyday occurrence there and up-to-date medical treatment in the past; but has it been brought up to date in the present?
As I said before, I have no criticism of the treatment; it is excellent. Now I should like to read another extract-and I am reading only extracts because of the time it would consume if I were to read in full all the letters that have appeared in the press, which are available to hon. members. Miss Ruth Mendel], Red Cross V.A.D., wrote a letter [DOT] which appeared on August 4, 1944, in the Globe and Mail under the caption "No Place For Ailing Veterans", which she opens with this statement:
Anyone who has ever visited patients at Christie Street hospital knows that the building is not fit to house sick men for weeks, months and sadly often years. But have we got the assurance that upon the new hospital's completion, the Red Chevron (Christie Street hospital's Davenport Road Annex) will be closed or will most of its patients, old sick veterans of the last war and a few younger veterans of this war be doomed to spend the rest of their days in tiny bare rooms lighted by inadequate windows, many of which face a wall three yards off? At

Supply-Pensions and Health
the Red Chevron many patients spend the greater part of the day in a long' narrow room ventilated by a very small window in one corner and a thoroughly inadequate air hole in one of the walls. On the bright and sunny morning while the unfortunate seven were outside for a few hours of fresh air this room was dark and the atmosphere terrible. The light from two small bulbs only emphasizes the gloom. For sane men the room would be a cruel sickening nightmare.

The minister said there were reports on the other side. On August 10, a man signing himself T. W. A. Milgate gave a report praising the staff of the hospital. He has been a patient there off and on for twenty-five years. He does not say anything about the accommodation of the hospital. All he'does is to praise the staff as I have done and as any other man who has gone through that institution and who speaks truthfully will do. Another man called Quinney did the same thing. I should now like to refer to what has been done there since last autumn. Eight months ago the citizens' committee of Toronto made
[Mr Ian Mackenzie.]
certain representations to the Department of Pensions and National Health. After -the situation was explained to them they agreed to a temporary building at Christie street, with the understanding that it be built at once. On June 2 the Public Works Department at Ottawa announced the awarding of a number of contracts; one was a temporary pavilion at Christie street to cost $128,789. It seems extraordinary -that it 'takes eight months before any work is done on this temporary structure, and that now we have the noise and dirt accompanying the building to add further to the tribulations of the soldiers who are occupying that hospital.
There are a number of others who have publicly given their opinion in regard to the hospital, which confirms the statement made by Miss Mendel, whose account I have read. They are: Mrs. Hugh Dalton Baker, Mrs. Healy Willan, Beth Avery, Miss Laura D. Flanagan and Mrs. Grace McCullagh. These letters express appreciation of the letter of Miss Mendel and others who have exposed the inadequacy of the accommodation at Christie street hospital. I shall not attempt to read them all.
Now for a moment I should like to refer to the offer made by Premier Drew of the mental hospital at St. Thomas, when those premises are evacuated by the R.C.A.F., in order to assist the department of pensions and health to provide additional accommodation for the wounded. I understand that offer has been accepted, and that the hospital soon will be in use as an auxiliary to help out dn the present situation. I think we are justified in assuming that a grave emergency has arisen in regard to hospital accommodation, which has not only necessitated the taking over of this St- Thomas hospital as soon as it is available, but also the conversion of two hostels formerly under the control of the Department of Munitions and Supply, one at Peterborough and the other at Kingston, which are expected to be transformed into up-to-date hospitals with operating rooms, X-ray equipment, laboratories and other accommodation for the care of our wounded within a period of six weeks. Well, I suggest that the minister and his associates will have to move much faster than they have moved in connection with Sunny-brook park if they are to get these hostels ready in six weeks. I doubt if that is possible; and even if it is possible it is only a temporary arrangement.
What I have been saying, together with many others, is that by this time we should have had adequate hospital accommodation for our wounded, at least equal to that provided for our civilians. We ask no more; but

certainly they are entitled to the same accommodation, the same comforts and all the things that go to make up an up-to-date hospital, that are available to the civilian population, and that has not been done. It should have been possible for the minister to look ahead and have these hospitals ready and waiting .when our wounded came home. I I think there is no excuse that will justify the fact that this matter has been delayed until we are approaching the sixth year of war. Other countries have been able to make such provision; it has been done in Australia and New Zealand, and in the press of to-day there is a reference to a hospital in Cleveland known as the Crile hospital, I presume named after the late Doctor Crile of Cleveland. This institution extends for a distance of eleven miles; it will accommodate five thousand people; it has all the modern conveniences, and it was built in the course of a few months. I do not understand why it was not possible to do the same thing here.

I will give them to the minister privately. I do not wish to publicize this man's name because I do not want him to suffer any more mental anguish through being disturbed by people making inquiries m regard to his injuries, or as a result of bringing his case up in the house. I am sure the minister will understand that. We will call this man Private Jones. On February 17. 1944, he was seriously wounded in Italy, receiving a compound fracture of the right knee joint and the lower end of the femur. His back was also dislocated. He was hospitalized in Italy from February 18 to May
24, 1944, and received the best of care though these hospitals were frequently under shell fire. He arrived in England on June 1, where he received excellent care in the hospitals until he was evacuated to Canada. He arrived in this country on July 8, and was taken to Chorley Park. On July 11 the cast was removed and a dry dressing applied to the wound. Later on there was a very considerable discharge from the wound, requiring daily dressings. About that time a board was held for the purpose of filling out his discharge papers. On July 28 he was again examined by a doctor who found dead bone, and informed him that this would have to be removed and that perhaps his leg might have to be amputated. It was decided also to give him penicillin treatment. When the doctor told him that he would have to undergo an operation to remove the dead bone the private replied, "All right. When do we start, and how long before it heals?" The doctor answered that it could take at least six months to heal, but it would have to wait until headquarters got around to it and a bed was available at Christie street hospital, because Chorley Park hospital has not properly equipped operating rooms for the purpose, and that this might mean a delay of a week or a month.

The other day the Minister of National Defence objected because I talked about Christie street hospital, and did not extend my criticism1 across Canada. I then referred to a situation in Montreal, and a statement made by Doctor Penfield which, I 'believe, confirmed the criticism I was making. In that connection the Gazette of May 30 contains the following:

There is one matter in respect of which the ex-service men of the last war are, in my opinion, in my riding at least, not getting a fair deal, and I wish to direct the minister's attention to it. Under the Soldier Settlement Act, 1919, a great deal of land was acquired. Much of the land in my province is owned by the farmers outright. They not only own the surface rights but the mineral rights. They acquired everything in the land from the centre of the earth below to the sky above, with the exception of gold and silver in the land. The entire land, surface and mineral rights were acquired by the soldier settlement board. When they sold the land they carried into the contracts those same terms; but when it came to conveying title-it was sold under agreements for sale- they withheld the mineral rights. I suggest that is not right. -The price paid for-that land was an entire price. It covered the minerals in the land and the surface rights. To withhold the mineral rights is improper and unjust. I suggest to the minister that it is just as wrong for the government to confiscate the property of a private individual as it is for one private individual to confiscate the property of another. It is just as wrong to take the property rights from a soldier wrongfully as it is to take them from any private individual. This is a matter which should be set right.
I wish to refer to a couple of sections of the Soldier Settlement Act. Paragraph (a) of section 16 reads as follows;
Where the parcel to be sold has been separately acquired the sale price shall be the cost of the parcel to the board.
[Mr Ian Mackenzie.!
Under that section the soldier settler who is purchasing the land would be entitled to the mineral rights as well as the surface rights. He is entitled to the entire land because it was bought entirely by the board. The two properties, mineral rights and surface rights, were not bought separately. They were bought as an entire deal from the board, and the government' is doing wrong in splitting it up and selling one part to the soldier settler and holding back the other part and not allowing the soldier settler to have it. They are withholding that under section 57, which is inconsistent with section 16 (a), which I have read. Section 57 says:
From all sales and grants of land made by the board, all mines and minerals shall be and shall be 4eemed to have been reserved, whether or not the instrument of sale or grant so specifies, and as respects any contract or agreement made by it with respect to land it shall not be deemed to have thereby impliedly covenanted or agreed to grant, sell or convey any mines or minerals whatever.
These are two inconsistent sections. Unfortunately the board is following section 57 rather than section 16(a). Can the minister not do something about it in order that the soldiers may receive justice under this section?

Yes, he gets $20 a month, but he lives under conditions such as no returned soldier should be asked to endure. When I hear all this talk of the last few days about taking care of the returned soldiers, and think of these two men, I just cannot figure out why they are not treated as they should be. Stevens enlisted on November 11, 1914; he was wounded in action in April, 1916, and sent down to No. 18 general hospital. He was offered leave thereafter, but instead of taking the leave to which he was entitled he went back into the line and was captured at Ypres on June 2. The department has the record.
What were the circumstances in this man's case? He and some others were in a dugout when the trench was captured by the Germans, who told them to come oht otherwise the# would throw grenades and blast them out. They came out; they were lined up against the trench, and perhaps because there were too many of them to be handled safely the Germans debated as to whether or not they should be shot. As a matter of fact they were getting ready to shoot these prisoners when a higher officer came along and stopped them.

What these men went through from that time until they were released in 1918 was worse than hell; I cannot picture it. For days they were compelled to carry out their own wounded, and they went through a great deal. Why the departmental officials here in Ottawa or those at Christie street hospital have kept these poor fellows suffering all through the years, starving to death, subsisting on what was not fit for returned soldiers, is something I cannot understand, when the act says they should be given the benefit of the doubt. In behalf of these men I saw the late General McDonald, than whom there was no finer or better loved administrator in the department. The last time I spoke to him here in Ottawa was shortly before he died, and I was in his home town of Banff on the day of his death, intending to call upon him and thank him for what he had told me before leaving Ottawa, as to what he was going to do for these two men. Well, nothing was done for them. He was very kind to them; I believe he and some others paid their expenses while here and paid their way back to Toronto. I am going to appeal to the minister once more. The department will not do a thing for these men. Whoever is in charge of these matters, with whom these people have to get in touch, will do nothing for them. I believe there is in the department a file of letters several feet high concerning these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: What was the reason given for turning them down?

I imagine it was because of the language they used in their letters; the information I get from the department is that they do not like the way the letters are written. I can well imagine men who have been turned down but who know they have a good case writing letters which would not be very well received by the department. I must say the men in the department have always been very courteous to me, and I could not wish for better officials than those with whom I have had to deal. But I should like to see these two cases settled. They are the only two of the kind I know of in all my contacts with the department since the great war that jjave not been settled. The department has always done its best in dealing with any case I have brought up, with the exception of these two men, who I am convinced have a one hundred per cent claim. They are not getting what they deserve. I am not going to blame anyone for that, but I would ask the minister to interest himself personally in these two cases, and not to pay any attention to the

letters that have been written in the past. Start all over again; if necessary bring them both to Ottawa, or send them to some hospital away from Toronto. I venture to say that the minister, with his sympathetic heart, will see that they get the benefit of the doubt, as they should under our legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I shall be glad to see that both cases are reviewed at once.
