In view of some of the statements made by the minister a few minutes ago I should like to offer a few further observations. The minister spoke of this being a political attack. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that as far as I am concerned it has nothing whatever to do with politics. I am a humanitarian, not a politician, and it is only on humanitarian grounds that I have ventured to intercede in behalf of the returned wounded men. The minister has mentioned the number of beds available for these men. I would say to him that it is not a question of the number of beds; the question is where you put those beds. You need suitable buildings, adequately equipped with modern conveniences, in which to house our wounded; and up to the present that situation has not been met.
I just want to refer to one other thing the minister mentioned in his very impassioned address. He referred to my work in the last war. I have no hesitation in inviting anyone to review the work I did in the last war.
And no apologies to make.

I suffered then, as many
people have at other times, from the politicians. And it was for political reasons and no other that I left the Canadian service and went to the British service. I say that because at that time my own party was in power, and the minister of militia was a Conservative.
When I was asked to investigate the situation in regard to the hospitals in England in 1916 I looked around and got hold of men who were familiar with the situation in England, in surgery, medicine, neurology, and other branches of the medical service. We made an investigation, and we reported the actual findings of our investigations, without colour. I asked the minister whether my report was to be a confidential one and he replied in the affirmative. As a consequence we simply

Supply-Pensions and Health
stated bald facts, without any veneer. Somebody took my report and handed it to a Liberal newspaper in Toronto. From day to day they published a certain section of that report. As a consequence of that there was a good deal of criticism in Canada with respect to the medical service overseas; and the minister in charge thought that to quiet that criticism the best thing he could do would be to appoint a board to inquire into the medical services which I had investigated. He selected as chairman for that purpose Sir William Babtie, a British medical officer who had been in charge of the medical services in Mesopotamia, and who was severely criticized for the mishandling of the wounded there and was relieved of his office. Three or four other medical officers, then in France, were brought back to England to join him. They did not investigate the hospitals we had investigated, but they sat in a room in St. James square and investigated me and my report. And upon that investigation they wrote a whitewashing report which was submitted to the minister and duly reported to Canada. The object was to quiet the unrest which some people felt, lest the wounded were not being properly taken care of.
We made twenty-four recommendations in that report. Those recommendations were made to remedy the defects we found in that service. Each of those recommendations was adopted, which proved conclusively that the criticisms which the recommendations were to remedy were well founded. Later on a certain junior medical officer who was at headquarters in London, Captain Andrew MacPhail, came to Canada and was given the job of writing the medical history of the, war.
He was not even a doctor, was he?
No, not even a doctor.
Order.

I am only replying, and I suggest I am quite in order. The minister made an attack upon me, and I am replying to his attack. I would not have mentioned this, had he not introduced the subject. Captain MacPhail wrote the first volume of what was to be the medical history of the war, and it was so prejudiced and so untrue that officers from all over Canada wrote to the press at that time complaining of inaccuracies and untrue statements contained therein. Amongst them was Colonel George Nasmith, of Toronto, who during the war rendered brilliant service in France, and was responsible for discovering the proper method of dealing with the first gas attack suffered by the Canadians overseas. I think perhaps the Minister of National War Services will recall that. He wrote a letter to the press in which he denied the accuracy of that so-called history. So many of these complaints were made to the department of government that they cancelled the commission to Captain MacPhail to complete the work with the result that he stepped out of the picture and did not continue to write the remainder of the history of the war. I think that is a complete answer to the criticism which has been made.
Following that I spent two years in France as consulting surgeon with the British army.

I have a few words to say in connection with this matter. Criticism can be levelled at any man in public life, and1 criticisms certainly are levelled at the minister. Nobody can question the hon. member for Parkdale, so far as his knowledge of hospitals is concerned. He is a reputable surgeon, and has defended himself here to-day in this House of Commons.
What is this, a nominating convention?
Well, so far as that is concerned-	.
Order, order.

-the hon. member needs no defence. He does not need any defence on medical grounds. I think everyone knows who he is; they know what he has done in a medical way. So far as the Department of Pensions and National Health and Christie street hospital are concerned he has not spoken in a partisan way. And neither will I.
There are none so blind as those who will not see. That is the whole point about it. It is true that there are vacancies at Christie street, but a good many of the boys would rather go home than stay there and have proper treatment. I go there quite often. One of my business partners was shot through the spine and could not walk, and he has been

there for many years. I used to go there to see him and the living conditions were disgraceful. We do not need to go into the details of these things. I do not know anything about the administration of the hospital, but I think it is pretty good. However, I should like to say a word about the doctors. A great many of them are giving a good deal of their time free and they are just about the finest men you can find in this country.
This afternoon the minister referred to the hon. member for Parkdale and his conspirators. I do not know who the hon. member's conspirators could be in connection with this matter. All you have to do is see what is in the press. This is not good enough for our returned men. Hon. members have been quoting a lot of papers, but I have here one of the finest papers that is written. It is a weekly newspaper published in Orillia where my dear old friend Stephen Leacock lived, the Packet and Times. The minister is laughing. He is Highland Scotch just like I am. I wish I had as good a command of English so that I could go after him the way he goes after some other members in this House of Commons. The first picture in this paper shows the view from the bed of an amputation case in an annex at Christie street hospital. A travelling crane and a derrick haul steel girders to two electric saws. How can a man sleep with the bang, bang, bang of those machines all the time? They would be slamming back and forth all over the place and yet this fellow has had an amputation. Every twenty minutes a train passes this hospital. The caption of this picture reads:
Tire wall of the main hospital building can be seen beyond this freight train as it chuffs smoke and soot to drift in through open windows and to cling to screens.
From the picture the track would appear to be no more than thirty feet from the building. The next picture shows what happens to a hand when it is wiped over the window sill, despite the valiant efforts of the staff to keep things clean. This is not from the Globe and Mail, the Toronto Telegram or anything like that; these pictures are in an independent weekly newspaper. I know these fellows and I know they know what they are talking about. I am approaching the situation on a non-partisan basis. This hospital should have been out of there years ago. We should have done something about it.
We have been spending millions and millions and billions and billions, and yet we cannot find two or three million dollars to put up a proper hospital for these fellows. That is all I have to say about the matter.

As I said before, I am going there again on November 11 and the minister and I are going to dig up another sod. These pictures show the conditions under which these returned men have to live. They are conditions which should not exist in any hospital. The hon. member for Parkdale who has just left will remember the great agitation we had in connection with the old general hospital in Toronto which was overrun by cockroaches and everything else. Finally, after a great deal of trouble wre got our present fine hospital. It always seems to take so much work to get rid of the conspirators that prevent these things from being done. The next picture is a view of the roof ward where twenty-seven bed cases; some of whom have been on their backs for more than a year, are housed. It states that they share three electric fans. There are twenty-seven bed cases and they share three electric fans. Just think of that-three electric fans! We kick because it is hot in the House of Commons. We have no electric fans here in the chamber, but we do have in our rooms.
Mr. MACDONALD (Brantford City); You must speak for yourself about electric fans.

What difference
does it make whether my party was in power or any other party was in power? The hospital is a disgrace. As a matter of fact it was taken over as an emergency and carried on by all parties. When this picture was taken most of the patients were out of the room. All you have to do is to look at these pictures to see the conditions under which these men are living. Are these the conditions to which we are going to bring our men back? As has been so convincingly said by other hon. members, it does not take much money to build a real hospital. At Gravenhurst, the old tuberculosis establishment, there are German prisoners at the present time. Why not put the German prisoners in- Christie street hospital and take our boys out to Gravenhurst? Why is it that in the city of Belleville, where we have quite a staff of letter carriers, some of them have been classed as temporary for a number of years? They are veterans. I understood that there was an arrangement by which at least ten per cent of the staff would be classed as temporary, but in this case about thirty per cent of our staff is temporary. I am advised by my officials that the reason is that there are no vacancies on the permanent staff at the present time. I return to the favourite subject of members like myself who have the honour to represent rural constituencies. I suppose there is no question that is brought closer to the average rural member, or that has been during the last few years, than the ' situation in connection with rural mail
couriers. This is not the first privilege I have had of saying a word on behalf of the rural mail courier, or inquiring of the minister in charge of these estimates about his plight or whether his condition had been bettered throughout the rural parts of the country.
While the rural mail courier is an underpaid contractor of the government, I believe that a good deal of sympathy is aroused on his behalf because there are few people who really come to know more closely the lives of the people in rural Canada than the rural mail courier. I remember very well when I was on the farm the part which he played on rural route No. 2, Brampton, Ontario, and he has played the same part in other districts throughout the country. The advent and the departure of the rural mail- courier to and from the farm was always* an important event, and perhaps it was more important in those days when the means of transportation were not quite as speedy or as available to the average farmer as they are now.
The rural mail courier has always been a very intimate influence in the life of rural Canada. Not only has he carried the mails, but the obliging rural mail courier always went a little farther. He has always done something extra that has not been contained in his contract. It does not always appear in black and white, but if you were to add up the little services, and those that are more considerable, in fact, the multitude of services and favours which the average rural mail courier performs, you would have a most imposing total, and I think every rural member in this house would support me in that statement. He has been faithful on six days of the week, rain or shine, in the most inclement sort of weather, and that is why there are so many who are always ready to take his part and to say a good word on his behalf.	[DOT]
Apart altogether from the position he has field in the esteem of rural communities, the system under which he has operated for a good many years, indeed from the beginning of the rural mail system, has been the cause of constant complaint and difficulty and criticism from time to time. I must confess- and I have gone as far as this in the house before-that the solution of the rural mail courier's difficulties has not been very easy. I think the present minister and past ministers as well will bear that out.
Problems have arisen from time to time and a multitude of solutions have been offered, even sometimes by those who are themselves intimately interested. It seems to me that the rural mail situation constitutes a very real challenge to this parliament and
Supply-Post Office

government. It is not enough for members of parliament and the government, year in and year out, to say that nothing can be done, that no light can be shedi on this problem, and that year after year, decade after decade, the rural mail courier must suffer in comparison with others from the point of view of the amount paid in urban sections for carrying the mails from door to door.
It is difficult to explain to the public why there should be a system whereby a man who carries His Majesty's mail along the sidewalks from door to door is paid on one basis- and I suggest that he 'has not always been paid very well at that-while the man who carries mail from farm to farm and from gate to gate should have to suffer in comparison as regards the remuneration he receives.
I do not wish to direct any special criticism at this time at this government any more than at any other government, although on this occasion the present minister has to take this responsibility, and I ask him to do so; nevertheless it is not sufficient to take refuge behind the old argument that there is no other way than the contract-tender system in connection with rural mail routes. I think that in many instances it has been little short of a national disgrace the way in which rural mail contracts have been whittled down to the point where it is hardly justifiable to allow a man to carry His Majesty's mail under the conditions that very often prevail.
I fancy the minister will say that there has been some improvement. Well, seeing that a difference has arisen in the cost of living as well as in operating rural mail routes, as compared with the situation that has existed previously, it would be strange indeed if something had not been done to alleviate the lot of the rural mail courier. I made a suggestion last year, but apparently the minister did not think very well of it because he did not take it up.
In' view of the fact that many different solutions have been offered for bringing the rural mail courier up to the position where he should be, and while there were divergencies of opinion as to what should be done, we as a parliament should not simply lie down in the face of a challenge of this kind and decline to do anything about it. We should at least appoint a select committee of the house to investigate the matter thoroughly. There can be no real reason why that should not be done. I asked the minister to do it last session. I was hopeful that there would be something done during the session just closing. Surely we cannot simply take it for granted that the

rural mail courier is to work under the same conditions as he has in the past. I should like to think that this parliament is at least big enough to measure up to its responsibilities. We should go into the whole matter and deal with it from the point of view of the public representatives in the house to see if we cannot do a better job and try to devise a better solution than has been offered by the Post Office Department. I ask the Postmaster General, if we are to have another session of this parliament, to see to it that one of the first committees to be set up at the next session will be a committee to go into the whole question of the rural mail couriers. I think that is something we can justifiably ask for, and something that the Postmaster General cannot justifiably refuse. If he decides that this is a move in the right direction and if this is to be the last session of this parliament he might have the preparatory work done so that the next Postmaster General will be able to carry on where the present minister has left off.

I should like to make a plea to the minister on behalf of some of the best of our people who do not get as good service as the rest of the country. I speak particularly of those farmers who happen to live on what we call a "dead-end street" a little off the main line. Generally speaking, they are just as good producers as the men on the main line, but they have to travel out to the corner to get their mail. In some cases the routes have been extended. The rural mail couriers go down those lines and retrace their steps, but in several instances in my particular part of the province applications have been made and have been refused. We were refused on one line where applications in connection with stub lines were granted a few years ago. When I think of the conditions under which our farmers and their wives are working to-day, often with only two of them on the farm, I say that they should not have to walk out to the corner to get their mail. They all like to read the daily paper if they have time. If they receive a communication that requires a reply they must walk back to the corner again. They are the partly forgotten people of the country. I earnestly ask the minister to take the plight of those people into consideration because they are obliged to tramp out in all kinds of weather. It is not too bad when they have children going to school, but on most farms the children are away to-day. I do not see why this service, which is a real service, and which is brought to the doors of our people, should not be made available to the farmers who are on these less accessible farms. I hope that the minister's department will give some consideration to these people.

I should like to say a few words on that question because it has come to my attention on numerous occasions. 'In the winter before last the snow was very heavy and it made it very difficult for the mail couriers to do their work. I believe that because of that hard winter some of the existing services were cut down last winter; but we did not have the same conditions last winter. There are two ways of looking at this problem. I believe the time is long past when every Canadian citizen should get the benefit of the. privileges to which he is entitled. These people who live on the dead-end streets or the side roads have the same inherent rights as every other citizen and they are entitled to this service. The rural mail couriers who, under our tender system, have been putting in bids for certain routes have said to the department that they are willing to give their services at reduced rates. Those mail couriers have to carry the mail in fine weather and foul, winter and summer. They are rendering an excellent service for a paltry amount. I say emphatically that it is almost a disgrace to the government to have that excellent type of man doing that type of work for such a small amount. The amount they receive is a mere pittance. The government should give consideration to giving the rural mail couriers compensation which would enable them at least to make ends meet. speechtext:

Then I should like to mention another matter which I might properly have brought up under the estimates of the Department of Finance, but since it is only a suggestion and I have no desire to initiate any discussion, perhaps I may mention it here. The matter has to do with the vexed problem of the tax on incomes of merchant seamen. I bring it up again only because since the debate on income tax took place in the house this matter seems to have caught the imagination and to have excited the sympathy of the people of Canada perhaps more than any other single thing that has come before parliament for a long time. The public realize, I think, what the merchant seamen have done; and because the matter has been brought out into the open in the house, where the skill of debate has been utilized in behalf of these men, the public have become pretty thoroughly aroused. Another point I desire to mention is this. It has been brought to my attention that prisoners of war are liable for arrears of income tax if they have not been paying the tax in connection with their general income. Perhaps the minister will not be in a position to answer the question I am about to ask, but I would ask him to consider this matter which has to do with income tax.

A member of the armed forces serving overseas is not liable to income tax on his service pay and allowances. If he had any tax liability before proceeding overseas, that is still standing against him on the books. No action, however, has been taken. He is not being pressed to pay it. No soldier overseas is being billed, but I must say it is still standing against his name on the books of the income tax division.

There may be cases
where the government may want to keep the liability alive. I can readily understand where a wealthy man may have enlisted and, having regard to his position, it might not be fair

Supply-Secretary of State
to relieve him of arrears. Generally speaking, however, I cannot conceive of cases of that kind coming up. It does seem to me, however, that we might readily wipe off those arrears which are in smaller amounts. I do not think we should be too niggardly, and I should like to see a generous attitude in this respect.

It came to my attention through an observation he made, so that I shall give him full credit and take none to myself. subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence)-for the Prime Minister- moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the senate to bill No. 184, to provide for the payment of war service gratuities and for the grant of reestablishment credits to members of His Majesty's forces in respect of service during the present war.
He said: The amendments made by the senate are to strike out section 25, which provided that the act should come into force on the 1st of October, 1944, and to substitute that this act shall come into force on the 1st day of January, 1945, or on any date between the 1st of October, 1944, and the 1st of January, 1945,' as may be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council.
The reason for the amendment is that on consultation, particularly in my own department, with the officers this morning, I find that it will be extremely difficult, and I think really likely to be detrimental to the best interests of a smooth running machine, to attempt to be ready to pay gratuities and to provide the necessary computations for the provision of reestablishment credits by October 1. This proposal is, therefore, that the date for coming into force of the act be extended until the 1st of January, but a provision is contained which authorizes the governor in council by proclamation to bring the act into force at an earlier date, not before October 1. While there may be the odd case of disadvantage in connection with that postponement of three months, I am satisfied that it will be to the advantage of the scheme as a whole and of the great mass of men and women whom it is intended to benefit by this legislation.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADIAN ARMED FORCES ACTIVE SERVICE PERSONNEL-PAYMENTS ON RETIREMENT OR DISCHARGE-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following the minister with respect to the amendment which the senate has made to this bill, I am in agreement with him having regard to the facts which he disclosed in his explanation. If, after
Supply-External Affairs

consideration, the departments of government affected find that their machinery for the purpose of administering this very important measure is apt to be inadequately set up on the 1st of October, J am in agreement with the minister that the measure should come into operation at a time when applications from veterans can be received and dealt with and the machinery is in perfect order, because I could readily understand the disappointments and discouragements which might occur if premature word went out stating that the 1st of October was the time when operations would commence, some plans had been laid on the assumption that that was the date, and it was then found that the situation could not be taken care of until later. I think it is best to postpone the commencement of the measure to a time when the administrative machinery can be actually put into operation and effect given to the measure in a practical way for those who are to benefit by it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: S6. Departmental administration, $410,189.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having one eye on the calendar and the other on the thermometer, I will endeavour to curtail my remarks. I will at least confine them to the one subject only, of great interest to the province from which I come.
When the Prime Minister, speaking the other day, announced his policy on that subject, I expressed my regret that I was compelled to speak without having seen his policy in writing, because the change of a word in a phrase might make quite a difference in the proper interpretation of the policy. I have now had an opportunity to study it carefully, and I wish to make one or two corrections or revisions of what I said the other day.
The Prime Minister laid down three principles in formulating his policy. The first one was, ,and I quote his own words, as reported in Hansard at page 5915:
... it would be unwise and undesirable, not only from the point of view of the people of British Columbia but also from that of persons-of Japanese origin themselves, to allow the Japanese population to be concentrated in that province after the war.
Further on, I quote again at page 5916:
... a maximum can be set on the number of persons of Japanese race to be allowed to return
(Mr. Graydon.]
to British Columbia, and persons of Japanese race can be given encouragement to move and remain elsewhere.
The whole matter is of so much importance to British Columbia that I want to emphasize certain points, because some people and perhaps some of the press have interpreted the Prime Minister's remarks in a way different from what he intended and rather in accordance with their own wishes, instead of giving a precise and definite account of what he really said-which of course is unfair both to the Prime Minister and to British Columbia.
For instance, let me note here that there is no guarantee expressed or implied, as some have translated it, that we in British Columbia would be allowed only to take the same pro-rated quota of Japanese to our population as the other provinces. Neither is it explained how either we or any of the other provinces can be compelled to take our due proportion, especially as regards those' provinces which have written agreements from the dominion government -that the Japs allowed into those provinces on account of war conditions shall be removed whenever a particular province asks - for such action. This constitutes a vital point on which we have no statement. After the war is over and peace is made, if we now accept that idea, that they are loyal, definite Canadian subjects, there will be no longer any opportunity of preventing them individually from drifting back into British Columbia, which I am sure a very large number of them would do. Indeed, the Prime Minister himself foresaw that because he said:
It would be most undesirable, I believe, to establish a permanent barrier to the movement within Canada of persons who have been lawfully admitted to Canada or who are nationals of Canada. Even the establishment of a temporary limitation would be - undesirable in principle, but as a practical question of policy it may well be inescapable.
He then goes on to say:
There is little doubt that with cooperation on the part of the provinces it can be made possible to settle the Japanese more or less evenly throughout Canada.
No doubt it could be done with the cooperation referred to; but, I ask the committee, have we not every reason to believe that this cooperation will not be forthcoming, especially when we see that every province which has up to date allowed -them to go in on account of the war has exacted the pledge that they will be moved out again on demand or at the close of the war? One can hardly expect much cooperation from a number of provinces who have exacted that pledge, and from other provinces who have not been consulted. That I consider to be one of the

Supply-External Affairs
greatest obstacles. As I said before, if Alberta wants them moved, to what place or province are they to be moved? British Columbia will stand strictly on its promised restriction, whatever that may be, and there is no reason to suppose that the other provinces would be willing to accept any quota at all. Therefore that leaves only one place that they could be moved to, and that is Japan.
But since I wrote those notes, I have received a newspaper from British Columbia containing an item to the effect that the acting premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. C. M. Fines, says that he is willing to cooperate with the dominion government in any reasonable way. However, he protects himself by so many qualifications that it practically does not amount to anything at all. He says that occupation might have something to do with it. He would not want fishermen, and that cuts out a good many. Then he said that he would not want them in colony settlements, and that is what the Japs want; and he ^ould not want any absorption of Japs so as to reduce labour standards.
Well, he has named three of the objections that we in British Columbia have against them. I do not know if his promised cooperation amounts to very much more than lip-service, but an idea comes to me here. Is it not Shakespeare who said that "like draws to like throughout the boundless deep?" I think it would be a grand idea to put the Japs and the C.C.F. together in Saskatchewan. They love each other; they are devoted to each other. It would seem, therefore, most appropriate to have them together. What a new heaven on earth it would mean for those people-who are outside Saskatchewan. Think of British Columbia.
Looking down the corridors of time I envision two conditions in British Columbia which we might achieve if we adopted the right plans now. Under one condition the place would be flooded again with Japanese as of old, Japanese who had drifted back individually

and it cannot be said that a so-called British subject cannot go where he likes in the dominion. They would all come back again and put our white fishermen out of business. The labour unions in the province are now getting satisfactory and workable agreements looking toward peace with their employers. But there is something else that people do not see, although, in my opinion, it is one of the worst evils. It would stop the importation into British Columbia of foreign capital or investment. The man with money to invest, tired of war-worn Europe, might say, "I will transport my business, my factory and my employees to some place in Canada." Then he looks around him to see where he will come; but he will not come to a place where, from a cursory investigation, he is convinced that there is growing up in substantial numbers a political philosophy that preaches that any private enterprise, any man who earns money or obtains money or properly gets ahead by hard industry and toil, is a blackguard who should be liquidated. When the prospective investor sees these things-and he has only to glance at the propaganda of my hon. friends to the left to be convinced that these things are taught here, seeing that one gentleman went to New York the other day and made a statement to that effect-what will that investor say? No one knows how many million dollars of investment with consequent employment were diverted from Canada on that occasion alone, when the gentleman I have mentioned went to New York. But if investors abroad see that these things exist they will say to themselves, "Well, we have not gone there yet. Those who are there now will have to put up with it, but we do not have to go and therefore we will keep out. We will keep aloof." Now that is one picture that I envisage.
Let us now look the other way and consider the British Columbia that might be. Let us consider the Japanese and the C.C.F. happily liquidating each other in Saskatchewan-more power to them. But British Columbia is the scene and home of prosperous white fishermen employed in numbers. It used to be said that we could not maintain the industry without the Japs. But if anyone says that now it is nonsense, because there are more white fishermen now than there were before, taking whites and Japs together before the war, and the white fishermen are happy and contented. In this other picture that I envisage I can see the labour unions growing in numbers, able to make suitable arrangements by means of trade agreements, cooperative movements in the way of labour and capital management, and possibly sharing in profits. They know exactly what their rights are and can maintain them, and capital has come to realize that it is much more likely to make money when employees are contented, so that capitalists will work with employees and there will not be any temptation to engage cheap labour such as was knocking at their doors in the shape of orientals. In short, it will be a place to which capital will come because it can make money without having to live in a state of continual dispute with cheap labour or unscrupulous politicians.

639S
Supply-External Affairs

It was Napoleon, who said-he enunciated the principle and he carried it out-that every soldier carried a marshal's baton in his knapsack; that is to say, he was capable of rising to the highest rank in the French army. And Napoleon lived up to that principle. We could say to the poor immigrant coming from the United States or from the old country or from any part of Europe, "Leave the place where they have wars every twenty years and come here. We invite you to come. We ask nothing more than your honesty and integrity, your thriftiness and willingness to work; and to any of these houses which perhaps suggest luxury to you, remember you have the key if only you will apply yourselves here. You will not be penalized by cheap labour on the one hand or dominating labour unions on the other."
I leave it to the house and the country to say which of these conditions that I envisage is the more attractive. Surely no objection could be made to putting the Japs in Saskatchewan because we have evidence of the support that the C.C.F. obtained from and the support that they give to the Japanese. Therefore they could not very well object to having them. In fact, their acting premier, although guardedly, has expressed the desire to have some of them. By all means let them go there. Put them all in.
I wish to refer now to the suggestion that has been made that the presence of 25,000 Japanese among twelve million Canadians could not be a menace. That sounds all right on the surface. But I have no doubt the same argument was used when there were only 25,000 negroes in the United States. I can remember reading of when that argument was used. They could have been deported then and there was a demand that the negroes should be deported. Well, there are twelve millions of them now and it is too late; and when the Japanese-Canadian population reaches twelve millions in Canada it will be impossible to talk about deportation of Japanese. It will be too late . then. The statesman that sees farthest ahead and outlines his policy in that regard is the one who is the most successful in the long pull, but perhaps not in the immediate future.
Th? second basic principle upon which the Prime Minister based his policy was that these Japanese who had remained loyal and refrained from active sabotage should be allowed to stay in Canada. The Prime Minister stated that he regarded that principle as fundamental. The obvious difficulty, of course, is, how are you to find out who amongst them are disloyal? A man may be utterly and entirely disloyal and treacherous, and there may be thousands and thousands of

them, but until you find them blowing up a bridge or doing something of that kind you cannot convict them of sabotage and conse-quentty of disloyalty. The method by which the Prime Minister suggested we could ascertain their loyalty or disloyalty in Canada was by an investigation by what he terms a quasi-judicial commission. I am fearful of quasi-judicial commissions. I have seen too many of them in British Columbia. Surely tfiis matter is important enough to have the highest judicial courts settle it. We have had too many of these quasi-judicial investigations dealing with situations in British Columbia. We had one to which I referred the other day. Before that gentleman reached British Columbia he said that he knew what the trouble was, that it was due to mob hysteria of a few people of the province. That included, incidentally, all of the members of parliament from that province, with one exception. You have met them; you have seen them here.	Do they give you the
impression of being likely to fall victims to mob hysteria? They all belong to different political parties and are nearly all of different racial origin; yet they are united on this question.
I have on my desk a quotation from a Vancouver paper. It appears in big headlines and is as follows: "Mayor Insists on Deportation of all Japanese." He was supported in that by most of his council. Vancouver is the third largest city in Canada. They are not all likely to be carried away by mob hysteria. "Government missing opportunity our children's children will regret", Mayor J. W. Cornett said, and he was supported by most of his council. These men cannot all be subject to mob hysteria. You might as well say that the people and the mayor of the city of Toronto are all suffering from mob hysteria. Let us be frank about this.
I would have no confidence whatever in a quasi-judicial commission of that type. The question has been raised and it has not been denied that- probabfy the -method adopted to find out a -man's loyalty would be to -ask him if he would take an oath of allegiance to the king and to this country; 3'et we all know or we should know that to a non-Christian, and especially an oriental non-Christian, the white man's oath means nothing at all. It is no more binding than asking you to put a postage stamp on a letter. You would do it willingly, would you not, if it were the price

Supply-External Affairs
of some advantage for you? The occidental oath to one believing in a different form of religion is of no effect.
I should like now to refer to two sessional papers that I hold in my hand as an illustration of how far we would go. These papers were laid on the table a short time ago. There is no feature of mob hysteria here. They are numbers 182F and 182G and were laid on the table on August 5. Number 182F asks the government the following question:
Was one NoborU Yamanoto, a twentymne year old Canadian-born Japanese, charged with refusing to obey an order of selective service officials and sentenced to a fine of one hundred dollars and costs or in default four months in gaol?
The answer is:
Yes. Persuasive efforts to induce the man to enter useful employment having failed.
I now wish to quote from the same sessional paper a letter that this man addressed to the hon. the Minister of Labour. Here is the letter:
Naboru Yamamoto, Registration No. 03283, Canadian born Japanese, Greenwood, B.C.,
May 22, 1944.
To the Honourable the Minister of Labour: -
I am very sorry to interrupt your precious time for stating my concerns, but I think you will be kind enough to listen and judge to what I state under the following order.
Now I am already twenty-one years old. Speaking from this standpoint I must be working or otherwise, be serving in the armed forces in this country, however, as I came here from Japan just before the war, 1940, after being educated eleven years school course there; I have no desire to be working for this country especially in this war time because such a work would be considered as though I were helping this country to win the .war against Japan.
This is the Canadian loyalty that they are supposed to respect once fhey have taken the oath. I continue:
I feel very sorry to Japan if I do work, as you might have been already noted that the Japanese have very strong patriotism ito their mothers country, especially in the war time; they are willing to offer everything that they have to their country even their life if they asked to do so.
You will notice that he classifies himself as a Japanese although he was bom in Canada. He says so himself, but he must classify himself as a Japanese. I continue:
There is no exception in my case to this conclusion particularly as I had been under the military training while in the school course there.
Here is a Canadian-born Japanese who says that he has taken his military training in Japan. The letter goes on:
I know that there is left only two ways by which I can keep my living in this country.
The first and best thing is to keep my studying until the end of war. By doing so, I would neither hurt Canada nor Japan. The next thing is to be interned or imprisoned until the end of war however this would hurt Canada.
Although I have no intention to hurt this country, there is no alternative course left for me, but to be interned or imprisoned if the selective service or commission (B.C. security commission) would force me to work.
I have professed my suggestion so that there will be left nothing indefinite between us.
Will you be kind enough to tell me if there is left any chance by which I could keep my study in the east? I hope to receive your answer as early as possible.
I have the honour to remain,
Your most obedient servant,
Naboru Yamamoto.
Apparently the Minister of Labour was not as speedy in getting a move on as this gentleman thought he should have been and evidently expected. He appears to have considerable respect for British law. He gets tired waiting for the minister to do something, so that he decides to do something about it and he writes another letter, this time to the national selective service offcer, and it is as follows:
No. 3 Building, Greenwood, B.C..
June 26, 1944.
National Selective Service Officer, Unemployment Insurance Commission,
Penticton, B.C.
Dear Sir:-
It has been long time since I received your order written on June 1, 1944, which ordered to me that I had have to go out to work the Midway sawmill from the June 7.
At that time I was still going to school and due to my special circumstances I did not go out to the work as I rvas directed.
Weeks later from the due date I was asked by the mounted police at Grand Forks the reason why I was not going. At that time I expressed my reason very clearly.
Then the two weeks passed but still there is no sign from the mounted police, also no sign from your office up to this moment.
I wonder what has happened.
He did not understand that he could play you for a sucker. I should not address that remark to the Minister of Labour because the letter is addressed to the national selective service officer. The letter continues:
Generally speaking if the man who refused the order of national selective service must be imprisoned at least six months.
I also have stated my reason fully to the Spanish consul general.
The Spanish consul general is the agent of the Spanish government, and the Spanish government is the nation that has kindly undertaken to look after the Japanese interest in the war, the same as we have Switzerland to look after our interest. They are allowed to do that. He is a Canadian-born
Supply-External Affairs

Japanese as he flaunts before the minister, but he does not go to the Canadian government to look after his rights, oh, no; he speaks to the Spanish consul general as a Jap appealing to that nation to look after his interests. It gives away the whole picture. You see the whole plan of these people who prate about their loyalty to the British empire, and when the time comes to fight they say they are not going to fight and they say they are loyal to Japan, although this particular man was actually born in Canada.
I go on with the letter:
Under these circumstances please notify me at once your regulation with regard to this case referring to my reason to the mounted police of Grand Forks.
Then he signs his name again.

This lad is twenty-one years of age and was born in Canada, and this is how he describes his loyalty to the country of his birth, to which I have no doubt he would swear allegiance if there were anything in it for him. He was born in Canada, but when it comes to a pinch he says quite openly that he owes his allegiance to the country of his forefathers. He says he has been trained to fight for it, and will not do anything else. I quoted the second letter, in which the writer asks the government why they do not take some steps in the matter. He says he has already stated his reasons fully to the agent of the country representing Japan, but he did not appeal to the Canadian government, as he should have done.
In speaking of this matter the other day, the Prime Minister said this commission would have to be careful in coming to a decision, that misunderstanding is not the same as traitorous intention. That is true, but I would pause here for a moment to put this definite question before the committee and the country. Would a man who would write letters such as I have read, as to which there can be no possibility of mistake or misunderstanding, expressing the sentiments that they did, be considered a loyal citizen of Canada? If he would, then you can pour your quasi-judicial commission down the sink for all the value it

will be. If, on the other hand, you are of opinion that this quasi-judicial commission would decide that he was disloyal, this demonstrates the complete uselessness of having the commission, because it is obvious that they never would have heard of this man at all. and of thousands like him, if the matter had not happened to come up in this peculiar and unusual way. As soon as the Japanese hear that they are to be interrogated by this commission there is no doubt in the world that they will have their answer down pat: yes, they love the king and everything Canadian, and they will swear to anything. They will swear loyalty to the king as readily as they would give utterance to an expression about the weather. Even if this commission were a strictly legal body it would be impossible for them to look into the minds or souls of the Japanese; and the Japanese, who are no fools, will speedily realize this and have their answers all ready. I know that when I write to my sister in the old country my letter is censored, and I do not write treason. This is not a case like that. The Prime Minister says that everything they do is known. Is it? They are allowed to publish a paper in Japanese in British Columbia. Can we read that? I believe that is going a long way. I do not know what was in their minds; heaven forbid that I should. ' I do know they thought enough of the importance of getting the early dope on what was going on -perhaps that is their national point of view -to take the trouble and risk being arrested, to sit in the gallery and take notes, which was against the rules. there in the first place. Mind you, they are representatives of a country with which we are at war. If the Prime Minister thinks that is all right, why cannot an ordinary man be allowed to sit up there and take notes?
The third basic principle laid down, by the Prime Minister, which I heartily endorse and have heard commented upon very favourably, is that the immigration of Japanese into this country should not be allowed after the war. But the people who so heartily approve perhaps failed to note the qualifying clause, where the Prime Minister said:
It is realized of course that no declaration of this type can or should be attempted which would be binding indefinitely into the future.
There is, of course, the well-known axiom that there is no law passed by man which subsequently cannot be repealed, unless we put it into the form of a constitution, and even that is liable to correction. I saw no necessity of putting that qualifying clause in there, unless, it was sort of to hold out a hope. I think it was regrettable that it was put in there, because there is plenty of time to make changes later on, and we all know that any law passed by man can be repealed by man.
I should like to conclude with a reiteration of what I said the other day. First, I said that we are not seeking to treat these Japanese with anything but strict justice, and as long as we do that we shall gain the respect of the oriental mind, On the other hand, if we show [DOT] fear it will be worse instead of better for our soldiers and civilians who are at present within their power, because that is the mentality of their native race.
Also, as I said the other day, as reported at page 5948 of Hansard, we should not be influenced in the slightest degree by the considerations of what possible trade we might or might not lose in the future. If we are to be so influenced, if that is to be the way we look at it, we are going back into the old policies of the time when the last peace was made, when each nation was trying to get ahead of the other by some advantage in trade.
I hope and believe that there will be little or none of that spirit at the peace table. I say we should look much further into the future than a trade agreement, but rather look to the humanities of the human race. Perhaps I might put it in these words, "Ye shall not sell our children's birthright for a mess of trade pottage."
I wish to give a few quotations, and they are all true. Every one of those substantiates 
my statement, and most of them are statements from Japanese law-not Canadian law. I quote:
A male of full seventeen years of age or upwards does not lose Japanese nationality, unless he had completed active service in the army, or navy, or unless he is under no obligation to serve.
That is not a Canadian statute; it is Japanese law-the 66th, I think it is.
And again:
A male of full seventeen years of age does not lose Japanese nationality unless he has performed his military service.
And again:
You will especially note the terms of article 24 which prescribes that Japanese nationality is not lost unless military service has been performed before naturalization.
That is not military service in Canada, but military service in Japan.
And I quote again.
Prior to that time

That was August 13, 1934.
-Japanese persons were frequently naturalized here who had not performed military service in Japan, and thus they became dual nationals.
Note that "dual nationals".
That order in council-
That was the order in council of August 13, 1!M,4.
*-provided, however, that no Japanese would be accepted for naturalization who did not have a certificate from the Japanese minister in Canada indicating that they had complied with Japanese military service requirements.
That last order in council is Canadian law. What would you think if Germany declared that we must not naturalize a man of German birth unless he had produced a certificate that he had performed his German military service?
It is said of one of the big religions in Canada-one of the great religions of the world-that if they have a child under their domination until he becomes seven years of age he will always live and certainly die of that same religion. It begins to look as though it was the same thing here.
This is no passing obscession; this is no mob hysteria. These are not the thoughts only of the member for Comox-Alberni. These are quotations from Japanese law supported by our order in council which was passed, and which provided-and this was in 1934, when the Prime Minister was not in power-that no one would get a naturalization certificate after that date unless he could produce a certificate of the Japanese consul in Canada, certifying that he had performed his military duty, and those military duties

Supply-External Affairs
were in Japan. If you knew how intense the military training is in Japan you would understand how there is so much difficulty for the Japanese citizen to grasp the ideals of the white man's civilization and Canadian citizenship.
I have just one more word to say. It is beginning to dawn on me in the last two or three days that the people of Canada, even members of parliament outside British Columbia, are not taking this matter seriously enough. They seem to think it should be confined only to British Columbia members. If they are so indifferent, then why should we in British Columbia worry so much?
The other day the hon. member for Lake Centre made a very fine speech in which he outlined the policy of his party, and referred to the statement which had been made by the Prime Minister. The hon. member made an excellent speech, covering the whole ground-with the exception that he did not mention that one question which is such a burning question to us in British Columbia. Well, if that is so, and if that is the view they take, we can be satisfied, and we shall be satisfied. If the government-this government or any other government-declares British Columbia a complete danger zone and prohibits any Japanese from living there, we would be satisfied, or at least silenced.
That is the situation as far as British Columbia is concerned. What you do to keep them somewhere else which is a matter of indifference to other members, will satisfy British Columbia if you make British Columbia for all time a danger zone and cut out all residence by those of Japanese origin. The solution is a poor one. It would be only the path of expediency, rather than of statesmanship, because statesmanship involves looking ahead to see what is best for the nation in the long run.
But in the meantime if the Prime Minister and this government -gave his announcement that he would declare British Columbia to be a danger zone, and keep all those of Japanese origin out of it, so far as British Columbia is concerned we would have very little kick. It is a poor thing, this path of expediency. But so far as we are concerned, it is the one we would accept. It would be easily enforced, and we would not be forever asking whether this man was loyal, or whether the other fellow was loyal. It would be just a matter of having a danger zone. And the history of international law would justify it, because British Columbia is the danger zone for all time against the intruder from the orient; it does not matter whether he ;s
Japanese, Chinese, or anything else. If you keep them out of there you prevent them from presenting any danger in the future.
I have overstepped my time, and I thank the committee for giving me this extra time. However, I feel very strongly in the matter, and I do hope the Prime Minister will take into consideration these matters I have mentioned.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the comprehensive statement made by the Prime Minister shows that, generally speaking, our government has followed a correct foreign policy. It is obvious that under present circumstances the first objective of our foreign policy is to win a victory along with the united nations as rapidly and as decisively as possible. Secondly, I believe that our policy in the postwar period aims to assure security for Canada and for the world through collaboration with the united nations, to promote such machinery as will unite these nations and guarantee them political, economic, social and cultural wellbeing for them and: for all other nations. The Labour Progressive party has on a number of occasions stated its position with regard to foreign policy, and1 I think I can give this in a few words as stated by Tim Buck, the national leader of the party:
The ideal toward which Canada's foreign policy should aim is that of Canada playing a democratic role as a sovereign state in a world association of sovereign states.
.Such an ideal does not exclude or contradict continued Canadian membership in the British commonwealth; on the contrary, it envisages development of Canada's role in the commonwealth to one of increasing importance. A member of the British commonwealth of nations, next door neighbour to the United States and a friendly near neighbour to the great confederation of Soviet socialist republics, Canada can and should be a link between the great democratic powers. To do that effectively she must not be subordinate in any way to any one of them. Canada's foreign policy must be based squarely upon Canada's national interests and needs.
If we approach Canada's foreign policy from that point of view it is then no more a ques-
[Mr. Coldwell.f
tion of whether Canada is a small nation or is to be a big power within an empire scheme. The real problem as I see it is that we are going to be either a nation speaking up independently and showing an interest in Canada and the world or we shall simply mouth what others say. The only thing that will make us great will be our independent position, based on Canada's interest. We have reached maturity during this war economically, politically and in many other ways. That is recognized throughout the world, and it is high time that we all recognized that from the point of view of foreign affairs we must accept the stature of full maturity.
Looking at the world at the present time, I believe it is necessary that we notice what is happening throughout the world. We must do this not just because we may want to go travelling over the globe but because what happens throughout the world affects us. We cannot disregard what happens in any part of the world, and it is therefore necessary that we look at what is happening in the various united nations and consider how we may best achieve victory and a state of peace.
Through the conferences at Moscow, Cairo and Teheran we have been given a pattern of collaboration, referred to by the Prime Minister. I wish to make it clear that this pattern of collaboration includes both great and small powers. We should not try to create the feeling that the large powers are going to run away with things and that the small powers will be left alone or will be oppressed by the large powers. I believe that to consider it from that point of view is to create ill-feeling and suspicion.
. There is a tendency at times to refer to the big powers as wolves and the little ones as lambs. I have not time to go back into history, but if I had I think I could show that there has been a number of wars fought by the little powers, wars that were inspired by reactionary governments. We must endeavour to see how we can collaborate best in the postwar period. The four powers in their declaration at Moscow* indicated how they intended to include the small nations. Parts one and four of that declaration read as follows:
1. That their united action, pledged for the prosecution of the war against their respective enemies will be continued for the organization and maintenance of peace and security.
4. That they recognize the necessity of establishing at the earliest practical date a general international organization based on the principle of sovereign equality of all peace loving states and open to membership by all such states large and small for the maintenance of international peace and security.

This was repeated at the Teheran conference in the following words:
We shall seek the cooperation and active participation of all nations, large and small, whose peoples in heart and mind are dedicated, as are our own people, to the elimination of tyranny and slavery, oppression and intolerance. We will welcome them as they may choose to come into the world family of democratic nations.
Here is something else:
Emerging from these friendly conferences we look with confidence to the day when all peoples of the world may live free lives untouched by tyranny and according to their varying desires and their own consciences.
Has the situation become better or worse since those conferences? If one wants to be pessimistic he will say that things have not become much better. It is true that there are many things that have not been remedied, but in my opinion many things have been improved. The difficult situation that existed in Jugoslavia has been changed since the conference, and in his last speech in the British House of Commons Prime Minister Churchill made it clear that this matter is well on the way to a final solution.
There is also the situation in Italy where Badioglio and King Emmanuel insisted on staying in power, where certain reactionaries behind them insisted that they stay in power. Since then, a government representing all sections of the Italian people has been established. While that government has not yet been given all the necessary power, it is trying to bring all sections of the Italian people together to help to drive the enemy from Italian soil.
There was the situation in France. We in Canada feel especially strongly about France. No doubt many of us were distressed about the situation that was created by hoisting Darlan. Peyrouton and others into power. Many of us could not see any reason for the use of these people. The other day in front of this house we heard Charles de Gaulle speaking. We believe that the fact of his standing and speaking there may be regarded as symbolizing the victory of the forces of progress over reaction, the victory of the heroic people of France.
Then there is the Polish situation. I know that this problem has not been solved, but there are good signs that it will be settled in a way which will satisfy all the-united nations and primarily the people of Poland. Not all is well as yet, but I am quite optimistic that even those things which are still wrong will be changed, because I have a lot of faith that
the peoples who have gone through this war do not mean to return to the conditions which prevailed before the war.
There is the problem of Italy. It is true that the Italian people now have a government, but some of the actions of others who are now in occupation of that country are not so reassuring. In many places the allied civil administration does not act in a manner most encouraging to anti-fascists. The other day I read a story by Matthews in the New York Times, written from Rome, that partisans, men who have risked their lives to destroy bridges and tear up tracks to help the Canadian and British forces, have been disarmed and left helpless. That sort of thing must not happen. These men, who had the "guts" to fight Mussolini, must be encouraged. They must be formed into an army to help us in the fighting, and given an opportunity of coming to the fore in their native land.
Here is a story of civil administration. A town was taken by Canadian troops. The Canadian civil administration entered the place and, finding a committee of anti-fascists had been set up, collaborated with it. The British took over the town and continued the collaboration, until one fine day the committee, taking seriously the statements of the Moscow conference about clearing fascists out of important jobs, sent a letter to the local bank asking them to "fire" fascist employees. What happened? This committee found themselves arrested and given gaol sentences; their office was closed, and they were informed that they had broken the regulations, because they had no business to send out letters. Somehow the true spirit of elaboration is still lacking. Too often there are officials in the civil administrations who come from business circles. Their minds generally being not of the most progressive type, they cannot understand these anti-fascist committees. That is not the best way of dealing with the problem of occupied Italy.
I should like to deal for a few minutes with the situation in Greece. We hear very little about it. There have been several refugee governments, at least three, I believe, in the period of a few weeks. The government was to include representatives of the fighting forces of Greece, the EAM. There have been troubles. Both the army and the navy revolted. They did not revolt because they did not want to fight; they revolted against a regime for which they did not want to fight. The result was that twenty-four sailors have been sentenced to death. Is that going to promote the unity of Greece? I have a feeling that British imperialist interests still believe they must have a hold on that area and feel it incumbent

Supply-External Affairs

upon them to tell the Greek people what sort of government they are to have or are not to have. That is not in accordance with the declaration made by the Teheran conference, that each people should have the right to the kind of government they wanted, and according to their own choice.
I do not know how soon the Polish situation will be cleared up. I have some personal knowledge of Poland, and I doubt whether Watson Kirkconnell, or Wilson Woodside, the C.B.C. commentator who, every chance he has, takes a crack at the Soviet Union as regards the Polish situation, or any other like-minded commentators, can tell me much about- it. I remember as a young boy that there were many streets in my native city which we did not dare t-o go up, because stones were -thrown at us. Jews could not pass along -those streets. I can recall that Jews had to put handkerchiefs around their beards, because there were anti-Semitic specialists in beard-clipping who went around with scissors to- clip the beards of orthodox Jews. Despite the fact that the present Polish government in London is made up of people from various parties, in the subordinate ranks of the diplomatic staff and among some of the officers there is a reactionary pro-fascist clique which we have to- take into consideration when we speak about Poland. These are the people who- want -to carry forward the policy of pre-war days in Poland. You do not have to- take my word for it. I am going to quote what Lloyd George had to say about Poland- in 1938. Writing that year in his book, "The Truth About -the Peace Treaties," David Lloyd George, former Prime Minister of Great Britain, said as follows, referring to the treatment of minorities:
Poland is one of the worst offenders. She actually repudiated the minority treaty at Geneva in 1934 by unilateral declaration in which her delegate laid down that the treaty would no longer be regarded as applicable to Poland.
One of her greatest breaches of faith relates to her treatment of the claim by the Ruthenes (or Ukrainians) to local autonomy for at least eastern Galicia. . . . There are some 6| millions of this race on her territory.
Such is his reference to the Ukrainians. As to the treatment of Jews, I have not time to go into that, but I have come across a number of articles, in the Manchester Guardian, the London Daily Herald and other journals, deal-1 ing with anti-Jewish pogroms. I do- not wish to dwell t-oo much upon the past, but the fact is that anti-Semitism still exists in the Polish army. Only a few months ago the British foreign secretary, Right Hon. Anthony Eden, admitted1 to the House of Commons that an anti-Semitic situation existed and that a number of Jews were going to transfer from

the Polish to -the British forces, but he hoped that the problem would be solved, because all the troops were about -to go into action.
There is a story in -the New York Times, appearing on March 19,	1944, by James
Alderidge, in which he tells about a colony of 134,000 Poles who had left the Soviet Union and gone to Iran. He writes:
The Polish camp was divided into classes . . . conditions got progressively worse as one's station was lower. The Jews were scattered into a Ghetto, the camp was run on totalitarian lines and you did what you were told. . . . When more than 300 Jewish children had been fixed up to go to Palestine the Polish elite who were very anti-Semitic put pressure on the Iraqui authorities not to allow the Jewish children to pass through Iraq to get to their destination.
To verify this, Quentin Reynolds writes in his book "The Curtain Rises," which appeared only a few months ago:
I knew, as everyone in Iran knew, what they did with some of our lend-lease and Red Cross equipment. I know that they cared for the Poles one way in Iran and for the Jewish people in quite a different way-oh, in quite a different way.
These are the words of Quentin Reynolds. I want to go a bit further and elaborate on this point because misunderstanding is created in Canada by people who are anti-Soviet on every occasion they get, especially in regard to the Polish situation. That is the thing they look for chiefly as a means of creating confusion. In this book "The Curtain Rises," Quentin Reynolds has a chapter called "Poland believed Goebbels." The stoiy about the ten thousand Poles who, it was claimed, had been murdered by the Russians is commented on by Quentin Reynolds in these words:
When we first heard this we yawned, and switched over to the Rome station. It was we thought just another of the good Doctor's bedtime stories. . . . Then we were shocked to see that the Polish government in London was actually taking the story seriously. Alexander Werth, Marjorie Shaw, Ralph Parker and two or three others who knew the Polish ambassador well hurried to his embassy. . . . He regretted the whole incident exceedingly but he emphasized the courteous treatment he had always received from the Soviet officials ... he told Alexander Werth that he did not for a moment believe Dr. Goebbels' story of 10,000 dead Polish officers.
In this chapter, Quentin Reynolds gives other facts about Soviet-Polish relations since 1941. He writes:
Soviet-Polish relations got off to a fresh and favourable start under the agreement of July 30 of that year.- The Sikorsky government said, in effect, "Well, for the moment we're allies fighting the same enemy. Let's let bygones be bygones until we sit at the peace table." All embassies were stationed in Kuibyshev t-hen. Moscow was too near the front. The Sikorsky government made the mistake of staffing its

embassy and its military mission with diplomats and officers who had always been identified with the avowedly anti-Soviet policies of Josef Beck. These gentlemen entirely lacked the gift of reticence.
Reynolds tells them about Kuibyshev, the temporary capital, during those days. He said that the Poles hated Russia and made no effort to conceal their feelings. He tells the story about the army in the Soviet Union -a Polish army on Soviet soil:
Meanwhile, what of that Polish army that was training? General Anders had little faith in the ability of the red army to withstand the full impact of the German blows which were increasing in fury each week. It was stated repeatedly that the German army would eventually smash Russia.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these were people who were happy in the belief that the Germans would eventually smash Russia and they would save their hides by withdrawing to Iran. Such people cannot deal with the Soviet Union. We here on this continent understand very well, when we are concerned about what happens in the Argentine because any such event disturbs the situation in the Americas. But very many in this country refuse to understand why the people of Soviet Russia do not feel so happy about having on their borders governments that are always plotting against them. Let me emphasize that, if anything, we want to learn from this whole Polish affair that the calamities of the past, which were due in very large measure to anti-Sovietism, must not be repeated in the future.
Unfortunately, anti-Sovietism is something to which too manj' still resort. But if we are to have peace in the future we must wipe this out completely. Because of that I felt rather peeved the other day when a little book came to my attention, bearing the title, "When the Iron is Hot", written by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore). I do not know what he tried to prove. I gather that his idea was that socialism is not good, but I do not know why he found it necessary to seek his materials in the events of 1925, 1926 and 1927, and slander fhe Soviet Union. AVhy should he use the arguments that were advanced by the worst enemies of the U.S.S.R. at that time in order to prove his point? That is beyond me. It does not help good relations, especially when such a book is sent out with the compliments of a member of the government.
