I do not like to mention names, but the person in question was Ernest Bertrand, K.C., P.C., M.P., who franked it and sent it out.
I should now like to turn to another country which has not been given very much attention in this discussion. I mean China. China is one of the four great powers, but if we speak frankly I think we will admit that the war in China is not going very well. President Roosevelt not so long ago made that admission, and I would say that the fact that certain appeasing elements, certain reactionary forces, are still active in Chungking, speaks for itself. Inflation is running riot there. In fact, it has reached catastrophic proportions, and I think members of- this house are old enough and responsible enough to be aware of these facts. The situation there is not very good. The rich refuse to lend their money, or they will not lend it except under compulsion, and there is little compulsion there. The other day a translation of a book written by Chiang Kai-shek came into my hands. I hope that Chiang Kai-shek has changed his mind since he wrote that book, because he does not express the kind of sentiment toward the western powers that one would expect. Generally, the situation there is not a healthy one. Vice-President Wallace visited him a short time ago and I hope that he was able to impiove the situation there.
I should like to say a little about the eighth route and fourth route armies. Very little is known about it in Canada; we should know more about it. Here is what Lieutenant-Colonel Carlson of the United States marines said about these armies a few months ago:
In the early years of the Sino-Japanese war I spent a number of months with this group. I found that its military successes were due in large measure to the democratic political action of the people and to the solid integrity of its leaders.
Recently I had a report from Professor Michael Lindsay formerly of the faculty of Yenehing university and now present with this group on the activities of the group up to the end of last year. Professor Lindsay tells me that the military agencies of this group, the eighth route and new fourth armies are containing about 350.000 Japanese troops. These Chinese armies operate for the most part in small mobile columns which engage the enemy daily. Activities have been extended northwest of Peiping and into southern Manchuria where they constitute a constant threat to the Japanese lines of communication with China. These armies with their militia units now number about one million men.
Hon. members may wonder why I am saying so much about China? I am saying it because I have heard hon. members ask, are we to participate in the war in the Pacific? Yes, we are. But we want everybody to fight. Everybody who wants to fight should be given an opportunity toifight. We want them to fight because that is the way in which we shall work better in the future-by speaking
Supply-External Affairs

of these issues; by seeing that China is united; by seeing that the troops who are holding back half of the Japanese army are given support. If we are giving mutual aid then we should give mutual aid to these groups as vrell as to the forces of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek.
Madame Sun Yat-sen, the wife of the great .eader of Chinese freedom, recently made an appeal to the American people and the American workers in which she said:
Insist that the products of their efforts, and the gifts they make to China shall be equally distributed to every force wherever situated, that is actively engaged in operations against Japan, and to no force that is otherwise engaged.
I wish to say a few words in passing about this Japanese rumpus. We are spending too much time on a small group of people in this country. We are wasting too much effort when we do not know what the post-war solution is to be. If the Cairo decisions are carried out, and I have no doubt they will be carried out; if Manchuria comes back to China, if Korea is made independent; if Formosa is taken away from Japan; if the Mitsui-Mitsubiski industrial enterprises are smashed; if Hirohito and the small group of Japanese war lords are dealt with, there will be no Japanese danger and there will be no reason to persecute here in Canada a group just because they happen to be of Japanese origin. Why were some of the Japanese supporters of Hirohito feeling so cocky in this country before the war? They were that way because they considered their country invincible, and we encouraged them by shipping scrap iron to Japan. While in Vancouver in 1938 I was to be interviewed On the air about Japanese espionage. I went to the radio station, but I got as far as the door only. The man who was to interview me told me that he was sorry, the mayor of the town- had intervened and the broadcast was cancelled. If we smash Japanese imperialism and the Japanese military clique we shall solve the Japanese problem in Canada too.
May I say a few words about another far eastern problem, India? I come back to the problem, shall we fight in the far east? Yes, w'e can send a lot of troops, but they cannot do as much as one-fifth, one-tenth or one one-hundredth as the solution of the Indian problem would achieve. Vice-President Wallace spoke abou(t that part of Asia not long ago. He said:
If the war ended to-morrovr Asia would find itself divided into free and subject divisions.
fMr. Rose.]
He declared that the latter would be India, the Dutch East Indies, Burma, Malaya, IndoChina and a great many small Pacific islands. Wallace said:
It is to our advantage not to perpetuate this division but to see -an orderly process of transition so that the area of free Asia will grow and the area of subject Asia constantly diminish.
A few days ago Mahatma Gandhi made some proposals-I would sajr those proposals were very moderate-calling for the setting up of a provisional Indian national government with the British viceroy retaining control over military affairs, and pledged not to renew the civil disobedience campaign during the war. He made separate proposals to the Moslems. There seems to be a means for solving the problem; and we in Canada, in the interests of the people of Canada and in the interests of the people of India and everywhere else, should say to the British government that we expect them to take up these negotiations and proposals. This is the finest way of cutting short the war in the far east; it is the finest way of having stability in the far east in the post-war period.
I wish to deal with one more area under British control. I have covered a large part of the world, and I shall conclude with this. I refer to Palestine. A number of hon. members have spoken on it and I wish to say a few words too. There are 600,000 Jewish people who live and toil in Palestine. People of various nationalities, Christians and others have travelled there, and they have come back and admired the things that were done by the Jewish people both agriculturally and industrially in that area. In the difficult days before El Alamein the people of Palestine looked after the repair of the machines of war for the British army. Tens of thousands of the sons of Palestine we^e fighting in the army. The Jewish settlement of Palestine has been cramped by the white paper. Jews have not the right to buy land, a lot that is worse than anywhere else in the world. They cannot emigrate to Palestine. Immigration is limited. I would say that Canada, together with the governments of Britain, the United States and Russia, should try to find a solution of the problem of those six hundred thousand people living in Palestine and those whp want to go there. I believe that a solution can be found on the basis of collaboration between the Arabs and the Jews, and I believe that this idea is becoming more and more popular with both these peoples. It is true that there are a few extremist elements among the Jewish people who talk about Palestine as their own hunting ground,

Supply-External Affairs
but they form a very small minority. I believe that we should do our best to help to find a solution of that problem.

speechtext: How would you suggest it should be done?

speechtext:
By suggesting that the great powers get together with representative groups of the Jewish and Arab leaders, trying to find some solution. I do not say it would be easy to get these people to come together, but at least we would be trying to solve the problem on a sound basis instead of on the basis of the white paper.
While I am on the question of the Jewish people in Palestine, I should like to say a word with regard to Jewish people in general and anti-Semitism, which must be driven from the earth once and for all. There should be no place for it in our world"' and at the peace table, or whatever the conference is called, anti-Semitism and the oppression of minorities by any one nation should be made a crime against all other nations. Our government should take a stand on this matter. After all, Hitler has used the Jewish issue to deceive the German people, and there are many would-be Hitlers who would like to use it again to-morrow. I see by the newspapers that in the city of Lublin, where I was brought up as a child, of the fifty thousand Jews who lived there before the war not one was alive when the Russians finally recaptured it from the Germans. While the Germans held that city they killed all the Jews, and to that city they brought Jews from all over Europe. The Russians found huge stoves in which Jews had been burned. So that I say that the evils of anti-Semitism and oppression against minorities are things against which we should all speak once and for all, things that must be discarded from civilized society. When we are united we are strong; when we are divided one from another we are weak. I want to cite this one example. When the Red army launched its offensive in white Russia, which brought it so close to German territory, its armies were commanded by four generals.

Then perhaps I may finish what I was about to" say. There was Bagramian, the Armenian; Chernyakhovsky, the Jew; Zakarov, the Russian, and Rokossovsky, the Pole; four generals leading one offensive, men of four nationalities fighting in white Russia, to help liberate the Polish people. That is the spirit we want to permeate throughout
Canada; that is the spirit we want in the world. With such equality and such opportunities in the new world it will be a better place for us to live in, as it must be.
I wish to conclude with the following quotation from a very fine book which I read the other day and which I recommend to hon. members for their vacation reading. It is "They Shall Not Sleep", by Leland Stowe. He concludes with these words:
Yes, yesterday is dead. But only the weak or the incurably greedy will weep for yesterday. To-morrow is a different day. It will belong only to those who are as clear of mind as they are strong of heart. To-day is dying as swiftly as those who fall and those who have fallen upon the fields of battle. If to-morrow is not a better as well as a different day, we can be sure that they shall not sleep.

The hon. member who has just taken his seat said something about supporting the movement of Jewish people from Poland to Palestine. That recalls to my mind a meeting I attended last winter in Toronto, a very large meeting of Jewish people at the Royal York hotel, one of the finest audiences it has been my pleasure to see. There were men from all over America, and I can say I was delighted to be there and delighted to meet the others who attended. At the conclusion of that gathering a very strong resolution was passed asking that Canada should support the programme of Jewish immigration to Palestine. I am entirely in accord with that sentiment, but I should not like to see all the Jewish people go to Palestine; I should like to see some of them come to Canada. In my own city of Toronto all I have to do is go down to the main business centre of the city, and there I see how much this country owes to the Jewish people who have come here. They have established great businesses. When I go to the university I see the great contribution they have made to education, to science and to music. In connection with the Jewish people I have always observed that when they come to Canada their first step is to learn our language and invest their money in business. I have seen many of them start very low on the ladder, and in their lifetimes rise to a very high position in business and all that go to make up this country. I have ' never had any animosity toward the Jewish people. There are Jewish people all around my neighbourhood; their sons have enlisted and are serving in the various branches of the armed services.
I cannot understand antagonism toward the Jews. I rose to say that from my own observation I have seen them make good in this country. I have seen them make a substantial contribution, in every walk of life, to
Supply*-External Affairs

the building up of this country. I have seen them participate in the defence of this country, and I would support a programme that might be initiated by the Prime Minister to help them. As I said a moment ago, I should like to see this government do something to help them migrate to Palestine, and to have some of them come to this country. I have not been to Palestine, although I am going there one day. I should like to see the city the Jewish people built there in a short time; I believe it is called Tel-aviv, and the wonderful gardens they have constructed out of a sandy desert, converting it into a prolific country by means of irrigation. I have said a great deal about irrigation, but I should probably learn something from what the Jews have done in turning the sandy wastes of Palestine into irrigated areas producing vast quantities of commodities.
This is what I rose to say to the Prime Minister. If he makes an effort along the lines of the resolution passed by the Zionist movement and endeavours to assist in the return of large numbers of Jewish people to Palestine, he will receive my support. I believe they deserve a great deal more from this country than they have been getting, in view of the vast contribution they have made to the progress of the world.
Mr. HANSEiLL:	I do not wish to take
a great deal of time on this item, although I must say I regard it as perhaps the most important we have had to discuss during the present session of parliament, in view of the times through which we are now passing. Yet I suppose it will be one of the least discussed of all items. Perhaps there is a reason for that for, after all, I believe most of us know very little about international relations.
In my constituency not long ago I made it a point, just as a matter of carrying out a little test, to ask a number of people what we were fighting for. I must confess that the answers they gave were not in the realm of superintelligence. One man would say, "Well, we are fighting a war against Hitler." Another would say, "We are fighting a war to defeat the enemy." Those were the answers I received. It seems to me that all international relations, so far as our people are concerned, are shrouded in a sort of mystery. We do not appear to know what is happening behind the scenes.
I can understand this, if that which goes on behind the scenes has to do with military strategy. But when conferences of a diplomatic nature are called, the people should be well informed as to what is happening at those conferences. Several very important conferences

have been held within the last few years. There was the conference at Casablanca. I do not know what happened there, and I doubt whether anybody else does-with the exception of those who attended. We were told, of course, that some great military strategy was being planned. Well, it occurs to me that perhaps the generals, admirals and air marshals would be the ones who would plan military strategy.
Then there was the great conference known as the Atlantic conference which gave birth to what was called the Atlantic charter. Somehow or another the Atlantic charter seems to have fallen into disrepute. In some sections of the world it is said that the Atlantic charter has failed. I question in my own mind wdiether that really was the object of the conference. When I look at the four freedoms I have to ask myself whether or not it wTas necessary to hold a conference in the middle of the Atlantic to decide that the peoples of the world are free from this and free from that.
Then there was the great Quebec conference, at which Canada and our Prime Minister played host. Certainly we were not told what took place behind the closed doors of that conference. As a matter of fact, when President Roosevelt, who, I suppose, was the one delegated to tell the world what did not happen, made his statement, he said that this time the enemy would know in due course what they had talked about.
Then there was the Teheran conference. Some little publicity has been given to it, but I doubt very much whether the people know a great deal about it. It seems to me that what we want, if we are to have an effective democracy, is an informed people. We need an informed public.	.	.
I am tempted to ask myself this question: What sort of information are the people getting? Any information they are getting with respect to international relations does not seem to come from officialdom. Most of it seems to come from all sorts of other sources. Stand at a modem newsstand in a railway station or on a street and look over the publications there offered for sale, and one will see that there is a lot of trash as reflected in certain types of literature dealing with foreign policy of foreign nations. What do we find? Well, I am quite certain that all that is publicized with respect to international relations only tends to confuse the public mind. I wish that our leaders would take the initiative and really inform the public as to what is happening. Tell our people, so that we may see the public reaction, and consequently move according to the wishes of an effective democracy.
That, I believe, is something that will make democracy more effective. A good deal has

Supply-External Affairs
been said with respect of certain announcements, and the timing thereof. Some little blame, rightly or wrongly, has behn focused upon the Prime Minister. I must confess I am not interested in that aspect of the matter.
I know that diplomatic relations are very delicate. Diplomats must be dressed properly; they must have their silk hats on properly, or they are not following the best form. I am not interested in whether the Prime Minister did rightly or wrongly in permitting an announcement to go out at a certain time.
I am quite willing to leave it to him, and trust him to do the right thing in that respect.
But what I am concerned about is the basis of the announcement. What I am concerned about is the subject matter dealt with by the diplomats of the various nations. And I would say now to the Prime Minister, for whom I have some regard-although I am not a Liberal-that he would do well for this country and for himself, and would do well for his party-if party could be brought into it-and would do well for the nation, if he were to attempt to give the public the entire diplomatic picture, in order that they may be informed as to where this country is going.
Might I now turn to the role of the philosopher? Perhaps I am a very weak sort of philosopher. I never did major in philosophy, and I have often thought that common sense will take one where some types of philosophy will not. But I say emphatically, and I do not think I am wrong, that the way I see the picture in the world to-day is that the whole world is lining up into two camps, each one with a particular programme for a particular desired end.
It may be that some well-intentioned people are the victims of one programme or the other. As I see it, one camp fosters a programme of driving the world toward what I have termed world statism. The other camp has its programme of effective democracy, or a world of free men. The one that is driving toward world statism has as its guiding principle that of compulsion. The one that seeks to bring about a world of free men has for its main principle that of inducement. There is all the difference in the world between the two.
That programme which tends toward bringing about a world statism means dictatorship from the top. It may not appear so now, but that is the inevitable result. A programme to have an effective democracy in every country that so desires that sort of thing must be a programme which gives the individual absolute freedom along with absolute security.
I offer no apology for saying that I regard Holy Writ as authentic and indisputable. One of the principles of divine creation was to make the individual created in the image of God a
personality with absolute freedom of will to choose. I do not think I need to take the time to repeat the story except to say that whether we want to take it as being symbolic or not, when man was created he was told that he could partake of all the trees of the garden. But we are reminded that the Creator said that there was one tree he should not touch. But the Creator did not place a fence around that tree and force man to stay away. Why? Because in the Great Almighty creative omniscience there was one principle that had to be realized, the dignity of man as a free moral agent. I will say philosophically that anything that tends to take away from or interfere with the dignity of a human being, to take away his freedom as an individual, is contrary to divine law.
I maintain that wherever the British flag has flown the great principles of freedom, equity, justice and peace have been its symbols. If we are to have an effective democracy it must be one where those great principles have free growth in our midst, the principle of the freedom of the individual, and the principles of equity, justice and lasting peace. I am quite aware that in many instances we have failed. I am quite aware that the privileges which have grown up under a free democracy have been abused. Nevertheless I say that any departure from the principle which recognizes the individual as a human being, as a free moral agent, will destroy democracy. When nations adhere to those great principles is what we mean by effective democracy.
An attempt is being made, and it has been going on for many decades, to destroy the British empire. The great underlying principles of British justice and democracy are as I have outlined and will always remain that. The one way to destroy freedom, the one way to destroy equity and justice in the world, the one way to take peace from the world would be to destroy the British empire.
The question is whether or not in our international relations we are to retain those vital Christian principles or whether we are to play into the hands of a world scheme for the setting up of world statism over which there will be, if the ultimate end is as I have pictured, a world dictatorship. I know the Prime Minister is well aware of this and we are all well aware that the old propaganda machine has been attempting to mould the minds of people to the bringing about of that international organization. It is all very well to talk about an international organization for peace, but we have to know what that international organization means, what its ultimate objective is, where it is likely to take us.
One thing is certain. If you delegate any power to an outside organization you cannot
Supply-External Affairs

delegate that power without losing it yourself. When you delegate $iat power to an international organization, all that is really needed is someone, to put it in a crude way, some great personage with a little more brains than the rest of them. The result will be tantamount to world dictatorship. I am convinced that what is being built is a programme to bring about a world state whereby each individual nation will surrender a certain amount of its sovereignty and power and, in addition, give that international organization a police force to force its will upon the rest of the world.
Personally I am against that. I often ask myself the question, as I view the matter along those lines, "Are we going to give our sons to fight in some war that in reality has nothing to do with us; are we going to give them to fight just because we have become tied to some sort of international organization?" Supposing some skirmish broke out in South America or in some other distant part of the globe. Are we going to give our sons to fight there just because we are tied to an international organization of that kind?
I know I shall not be contradicted when 1 say that that is the idea. I know that what is being propagandized is that this is an organization to ensure peace and world security. That sounds all very well, but I am wondering if in the end the idea is not to destroy the effectiveness of the British commonwealth of nations. I believe that it is. One thing is certain that what we need more than anything else is to remove the causes of war. My own common sense tells me that to simply build up an international organization, to give it a police force to impose its will upon the nations that are not in line, will not strike at the root of the matter. Such a programme presupposes that you are not going to get rid of the causes of war.
I have always had great respect for the British diplomat. When Mr. Anthony Eden was in Ottawa last year I had certain thoughts, but I did not think that was the occasion to raise anything by way of criticism. We must always be courteous to our visitors. In the speech he made in this chamber, he said, as reported on page 1748 of Hansard of April 1, 1943:
The League of Nations suffered, no doubt, from a number of human failings and shortcomings. We all do. However, what above all it lacked was a sufficiently wide inter -. national authority to express its decisions with conviction and an adequate force to see them executed.
Somebody has said that the failure of the League of Nations was because it did not have any teeth in it. Well, just as soon as

you begin to put teeth in anything, something is going to bite and something is going to be bitten; that is all there is to it. He goes on to say on the same page a little lower down:
It is essential that when this war is over the united nations should maintain sufficient force to ensure that neither Germany nor Italy nor Japan-
I do not know why he stopped there.

can ever plunge the world into war again.
The only redeeming feature about it is that he says " again." But why not include all nations?
The point I am trying to put over is that the term "force" is a very undesirable term, and the principle of force is simply antiChristian. I say again that we must remove the cause of war. The hon. member for Cartier said he believed that each nation should be permitted to lead its own life in its own form, be it democratic or some other. All right. If that is so, why all this talk about international organization? It does not " add up," to me. I do not want anyone to think I am against international collaboration and cooperation. I believe that you might have some sort of organization whereby the nations of the world can be represented around a conference table and have their problems and difficulties dealt with. But to say that the conference must make decisions and then have a police force to enforce those decisions means that we are to try to solve our internal problems by handing them over to somebody else. Personally I am against that.
One other thing which I should like to say is that nobody seems to know anything about what the peace issues are to be. I read some time ago a news item that Mr. Eden told the British House of "Commons that they were ready with their peace proposals, but he did not say what they were. I do not know the reason. I do not know why they should be shrouded in mystery, but we will give Mr. Eden the benefit of the doubt; it may be that there is something which it would not be advisable for us to know.
In the first place, I do not know whether there will be a peace table. If there is, I do not know whether there will be one or two. I do not expect that any peace conference is capable of disentangling international problems and settling the peace overnight. It will take a long time and the peace programme itself will stretch over some considerable period.
Since I have been functioning as a philosopher, although maybe a pretty poor one, maybe I can now turn politician. There is a question in my mind as to who will be at the peace table, if there is one, to represent

Canada. I hope I am not sounding a false note, but we have to look into the future. I say that no peace proposals should be made until they have been brought before parliament and the whole problem discussed, so that whoever represents Canada will reflect the democratic will. I have said that I do not know who will be there. If one may judge from recent elections there is no guarantee that the Liberal government will be returned to power if there is an election this fall-and I imagine there is going to be one. Our Liberal friends lost heavily in Saskatchewan and Quebec, and I do not believe that our Conservative friends have been as "progressive" as they thought they were going to be, while our C.C.F. friends lost heavily in Alberta *and Quebec, so that it is unlikely that they will form the next government.

I do not believe that the Prime Minister is going to that conference to propose the philosophy which I have outlined. My view of what he will do-and I cannot say that he is doing it unconsciously because he is too intelligent a man to do things unconsciously-is that he, too, may be a victim of a philosophy which is not too obvious in these days, that he may be the victim of influences causing him to advance a programme for a coming world socialist state with a world dictator. I hope that is not so, but. I also hope, no matter what government is in power, that by a gracious as well as a common sense act which
will be pleasing to the people of Canada, the present Prime Minister will be at least one of the delegation which will represent this country. But he should not go without obtaining the views of the people, and I do not believe those views can be ascertained by means of an election issue, because election issues become confused. This is an important matter. I suggest that whoever is the responsible Prime Minister should call in the leaders of every political party represented in this house and, if necessary, take days to thresh out the questions involved and ascertain the views of the people, so that he may go to the conference to bring about effective democracy in Canada and assure sovereign rights to each and every nation.
Having talked along political ideas for a moment, I am going to make this suggestion. I cannot make it to parliament. I cannot make it to the leaders of any party. All I could do would be to make it to the people of the country, and that is that the leader of every party be given an acclamation to this house in any forthcoming election. I do not know w'hy my hon. friend the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) should show forth his very hearty and1 pleasing laugh; but this, to my mind, is no laughing matter. I believe that the brains of Canada do not all repose in any one political party. I think we all have something to contribute in these days. If it were a peace-time election it would not matter to me whether one Prime Minister was thrown out and1 another put in, but we are living at a time when the1 war is gradually approaching its end and sooner or later, when the minds of the people are turned toward peace, we shall need in parliament the very best calibre of political leadership. That is why I am suggesting this. I hope that the Prime Minister returns to this house after the next election. I hope that Mr. Bracken will return.	,

They will not be embarrassing questions, and I am convinced that his answers will be such as I would give myself. May I say to this committee that if anyone wishes a battle on the question of whether we are to have one part of this country singled out as non-Canadian as against what of others is said to be Canadian, no one would welcome that fight any more than I -would.
And anyone who raises the question of race to prejudice anyone of another race in this country is doing the greatest disservice that can be done to Canadian unity and to Canadian nationality.
The question I wish to ask the Prime Minister first is whether, when he makes a statement of that kind, he is thinking of all the races that comprise our Canadian citizenship. When he spoke on that particular occasion his reference was to the fact that some of us are of French racial origin, and some of English racial origin or others of that group. But we have also in Canada people of many racial origins from Europe, such as the Ukrainians, and we have a few people of Japanese racial origin, some of Chinese racial origin, and some East Indians, who come from a part of the British empire. We have also in this countiy the descendants of the full-blooded Indians who were here before any of us were born, or before any of our ancestors migrated to Canada. In other words, Canada is a nation of a great many races. On this question of racial understanding the Prime Minister's record is pretty clear. He has just had a few commendations from the hon. member who has taken his seat, and I will not hesitate to add to them and say that so far as I know there is only one flaw in his record on the question of racial tolerance and understanding. I do not hold that altogether against him personally, because I still doubt whether he knew in the first instance about the inclusion of clause 5 in its original form in bill No. 135. That is the one flaw I refer to, for I still do not feel that the position the Prime Minister took in connection with that matter was consistent with his own life-time record and with the Liberal position both with respect to the franchise and with respect to racial matters. Apart from that I say that the Prime Minister has taken the liberal position-liberal with a small "1"-in this matter down through the years. I was very glad to hear his interjections to-night in the midst of the speech made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni when he pointed to some of the absurdities that the hon. member was uttering at that time.
Speaking of the Liberal position, I wish to quote from a Liberal newspaper. The day after we had the debate on the consequential amend-

It dealt with the amendments that had been made to bill No. 135 under this heading: "Better, But Not Right." I shall not go into the details so far as its comments on that issue are concerned because for the time being at any rate, that issue is closed and I am not anxious to antagonize the Prime Minister because I want his agreement with the position I am seeking to lay down. After recounting what had happened, the Free Press said this:
This seems like a small gain, -but it is an important one. The whole country has had a sharp lesson in what can happen if racialists are allowed to have their own way, and it will be hoped the lesson has been thoroughly learned. Racial discrimination is something Canada must do without if it wants to continue and to improve the strength and character of its democracy.
Later on, after referring to the history of that bill and what happened and to the way in which its iniquitous clause was slipped through, the editorial says:
This will not meet with universal approval, but, on balance, there may be a case-
-for what the government has proposed by way of an amendment. Then comes this conclusion:
But, the matter having been thus sharply raised, we invite our readers to consider whether the historic discrimination invoked bv British Columbia should be allowed to persist when the war is over. It is bad enough in itself, but the racialists who sponsored it and to-day strongly defend it have imprudently revealed their hand. They are prepared, as the record now clearly shows, to pursue certain groups of citizens beyond the limits of their own province and to open the door to the virtual destruction of the generally universal nature of the dominion franchise. They consider it quite proper that, if any province takes a dislike to any group inside its own borders, it can so legislate as to deprive the members of that group of the franchise no matter whether they live in the discriminating province or not.
This fragmentation of Canadian citizenship would carry us a long step forward to the destruction of the unity of the state and should not be tolerated in any form. When the war is over a most suitable project for liberal-minded men and women everywhere would be to advocate and support the extension of the dominion franchise to every citizen of Canada regardless of race and regardless of any provincial disqualifications that exist.
The Winnipeg Free Press, which has taken a strong position in this matter, is published in the city from which the Winnipeg Grenadiers went to Hong Kong. Few cities in Canada have as many homes in which there is
anxiety because their loved ones are in Japanese prison camps in Hong Kong. Few cities have as many homes where there is possibly as much bitterness toward the Japanese war lords because of what has happened to their loved ones. I represent a riding of that city. While the Free Press and I are usually at opposite poles, we agree in this instance and we take the position that we do because we feel and we know that even in the homes to which I have referred there are many who believe that in Canada we must rise above the racial discrimination, racial prejudice and racial hatred which have been displayed in this house at times by certain hon. members. Canada, of all countries, should be interested in broad understanding among racial groups. I have not the census figures before me, but I believe that there is no one racial group, so far as origin is concerned, which constitutes a majority of the people of this country. There are two or three groups which are very large, but we are a nation of many different backgrounds, and one might say that it is almost of necessity that we learn to get along well with each other and understand each other from one end of Canada to the other. I look upon this situation not just as a matter of compulsion but as a matter of opportunity. Much more important than racial origin or racial background is the basic fact of humanity. We have an opportunity presented to us by the very fact that there are so many different races in Canada to build a Canadian nationality which will be distinctively human and will have in it no element of racial discrimination, none of the kind of thing we are fighting in our war against Hitler and everything he stands for.
I say again I hope that the Prime Minister will amplify the statement he made the other day, making it clear, as the one who for the time being is the Prime Minister of Canada, that so far as he and his government are concerned he is prepared along with others of us to fight for a Canada in which there will be no drawing of any line as between various racial groups. There were some other points that I felt I should like to raise but perhaps I should let it go at that and express the hope that the Prime Minister will join with others of us in making it clear that whatever our feelings may be toward the Japanese war lords, so far as the citizens of Canada are concerned, whatever their racial origin, they are all Canadians and should be treated accordingly.
There is perhaps one other comment I should make before I sit down. Those who speak in this house against Canadians of

Japanese origin talk now only about the Japanese, but before the war some of those individuals were attacking not only our Canadians of Japanese origin, but Canadians of Chinese origin and Canadians of East Indian origin. Both of those groups have also been disfranchised in one province of this country. Therefore, what is being said now about those of Japanese background because we are at war with them is only a sample of the kind of thing that is possible on a larger scale and the kind of thing we do not want in this country. That sort of thing if it gets going knows no limits. It must be stopped before it gets started. I know the Prime Minister's instincts and sentiments are with me and with this group one hundred per cent on this matter; but I feel that because of the kind of speech that was made to-night and because of the speeches that are sometimes made by some hon. members of the Liberal party the Prime Minister should make a clear and definite statement along the line of the speech made a short while ago by his own parliamentary assistant, and along the line of the remarks made a short while ago by the hon. member for Trinity. In other words, the Prime Minister has many behind him, even as he has many on all sides of the house, who are liberal-minded so far as this issue is concerned and who want Canada to be a country in which no racial lines shall be drawn.

Then I will try to help the right hon. gentleman. I had intended during this debate to make some extended remarks with respect to our position in external affairs and particularly in regard to the commonwealth and empire, but perhaps to-night I can confine my remarks within a very narrow orbit because of the time at which this discussion arises.
I should like to say to the Prime Minister and the committee that the views of our national leader, which are the views of this party, have been placed on record by the Prime Minister on at least one or perhaps two occasions already, by reading the questions and answers that appeared in Maclean's magazine. Those views I desire to endorse. In addition, I should like to say that I believe it may be properly said that there has been a great deal of loose talk and of woolly

thinking in regard to the position of Canada in the commonwealth and empire. I believe there have been perhaps too many technicalities attached to the verbiage and phraseology used from time to time by public men in relation to our commonwealth relationships. And may I say further that a great many bogeys have been trotted out; a good many straw-stacks have been used to make straw men for various people and newspapers to knock down, particularly with respect to the so-called policies of our party in this dominion. So far as I know there is no one in Canada, at least I have heard of no one, who seriously proposes that, no matter what may be our relationship to the empire and the commonwealth now or in the days to come, the autonomy of Canada should be in any way impaired or prejudiced or interfered with. Anyone who advances a theory or policy of that kind must be thinking in terms of yesterday rather than in terms of to-day or to-morrow.
One reason why I asked the Prime Minister the question I did with respect to Mr. Curtin's proposal relative to an empire secretariat was that in my opinion very few people in Canada had any. real conception of what Mr. Curtin meant. If the average person in Canada had understood the proposed secretariat to mean some suggestion of rigidity with respect to the position of the empire, then I do not think anyone would have considered supporting that idea. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister indicate-I have not his words with me at the moment-that at least one of the possibilities in regard to the secretariat was that it might take the form of an empire or commonwealth reference library or research institution, where some of the details with respect to commonwealth affairs might be investigated and information made available in greater detail than is the case under the present system. But so far as the delegation to any commonwealth organization that might be set up of any of the sovereign powers of Canada or any other part of the commonwealth, I am quite sure that has never been entertained, certainly not as far as the policies of this party are concerned, because Canada is first of all an autonomous nation, and parliament must always have the final say with respect to what Canada shall do. In a word, I believe that deals with at least one of the matters raised by some people and^ newspapers in an effort to show that this party, or certain groups in Canada, have the idea that there should be some sort of commonwealth arrangement which would interfere with the autonomy of this nation. As I said before, that idea belongs to a past era and may well be forgotten.
I mentioned these questions in a brief general way during the debate on the speech

Supply-External Affairs
from the throne. I was going to elaborate those remarks to-night, but because of the lateness of the hour I shall not do so. On January 31, 1944, at page 20 of Hansard, I said:
It is well that the views of all sides should be carefully weighed and considered. The views of the government would be particularly welcome, but it is not our intention to embarrass our own Prime Minister, or the representatives of other parts of the commonwealth, by tossing controversial issues into this debate when common sense indicates that every effort must be made to secure a united front in a united Canada in a greater and more powerful British commonwealth.
These observations followed closely a similar statement of my leader, John Bracken, on January 25 of this year, in which he expressed the hope that such matters would not become the subject of small political discussion. The wisdom of public men generally adopting such a policy in a period as grave and critical as this I believe has since been abundantly proven. Prior to the meeting of commonwealth prime ministers my leader gave the considered views of our party. With the indulgence of the committee I should like to place those views on record, and with .that I shall rest my case instead of elaborating the matter further, as I had intended to do if the discussion had been brought on at a more convenient time. This is what Mr. Bracken said on that occasion:
I am proud that Canada is a member of the British family of nations. The courageous and noble leadership given by the British commonwealth to the world in this the most terrible of all crises has surely added to the pride we have always felt as sharers in its traditions and its goodly heritage.
In 1926 Canada, along with Great Britain and the other dominions, accepted the following as a just and worthy definition of the mutual relations, rights and responsibilities of members of this commonwealth-
This is the quotation:
They are autonomous communities within the British empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations.
Then he goes on to say:
These words mean, if they mean anything, that the governments of Britain and the dominions, functioning in full freedom from anything in the nature of control, are to have the close association of partnership for common interests and common purposes. Our principal common interest and common purpose is peace.
This country is properly proud of its independent sovereignty as expressed in the above definition, and that independent sovereignty we ought to exercise. Up to now we have failed in many respects to do so. Our colonial days are long past. Further, this country realizes that it is only vanity to parade the glories of
independent sovereignty and to ignore those responsibilities that independent sovereignty entails. This country also recognizes with pride the partnership and the duties of partnership involved in "free association" for common purposes. It is not only our duty but our interest to be loyal to that free association.
I believe also, and I am sure Canada believes, . in world organization for peace. Experience has proved that an effective world organization for peace is an objective very difficult to reach.
I.	however, am convinced we can reach the objective best, not by weakening or dividing the commonwealth, but by even closer cooperation with the other commonwealth nations. It would be a terrible responsibility-a responsibility which we could not take with dignity, with prudence or with honour-to choose a course which would be likely to lead to the impairment or weakening of that cooperation.
The line of conduct I have just outlined for this country is in full accord with our autonomous and sovereign rights-indeed, it is the intelligent evolution of those rights, the expression of our maturity as a nation.
I am in favour, therefore, of Canada acting as an autonomous power, to strengthen the ties which bind the members of the commonwealth together, and to this end I believe that a plan for continuous consultation in matters of common interest should be worked out by us all. By that I mean consultation not just for purposes of talk whether described as "exchange of views" or a verbal "collaboration" but definitely with a view to a meeting of minds on matters of practical policy. It has riot been suggested, and it could never be considered, that there should be such rigidity to any plan as would subtract from our sovereign rights. It has been suggested only that we, with other dominions and Great Britain, should frankly set forth our ideas or proposals and should seek to agree, if we can. on common principles of policy and especially of foreign policy, directed to the great purpose of world peace. On the rare occasions when in other years we have so tried we have succeeded. Surely it must be manifest that the failure of members of this commonwealth in the recent past to do that very thing has contributed to the catastrophe of this desolating war. No system, or lack of system, guilty of such a failure can set itself up as the highest evidence of our capacity to serve ourselves and mankind.
The Prime Minister has said that Lord Halifax asked us to make a "commitment", to fall in line, in any event, with a common policy for the commonwealth in all matters of our external relations. Lord Halifax made no such request or even suggestion.

completely autonomous position. He asked 'us to seek to agree with the other members of the commonwealth, and invited our full cooperation at the table of British nations in the determination of those features of commonwealth policy in which all of us are concerned.
I say Canada should not refuse to sit and act at that table. Canada should emerge from colonial habits and should not fear to take her responsibility as a full-grown nation and as a partner in this freely associated commonwealth. We have no reason to distrust our partners and we have now grown to a stature where surely we trust ourselves.
Our failure to function as a member of the British family will not promote the organization of another and better League of Nations; it is merely to lapse again into the trough of isolationism. Canada herself proved just shortly before this war that it is possible to be a fullpaying member of a league and to be isolationist still. The folly of isolationism is the great lesson that we and others must learn from the tragedy of these times. Sorrowful evidence of the consequences of this folly is visible daily in the mounting casualty lists. "
To these principles thus elaborated, by our leader, this party adheres. As ;he has from time to time stated, the government and parliament of Canada has a primary concern in all commonwealth and all other international relations, as well as in its own domestic affairs; and it should keep the interest and welfare of our own people in the forefront of all deliberations and decisions and, having thus firmly in mind, put forth vigorous efforts to increase our international trade and promote good will and permanent peace among all nations.
One of the things which has engrossed some of the newspapers in our land, and has formed part of our debate in the house, has been the famous speech of Lord Halifax. The difficulty I see with respect to the matter is one which I think is of importance to a great many people, and that is that it is so difficult to see the difference betwen the position which the Prime Minister has taken with respect to commonwealth relations and that set down by Lord Halifax himself. I have not tried to find differences. I tried to see where these two statesmen dealing with these matters found agreement, rather than division, and I found agreement.
But it does seem to me that the statement in the British House of Commons by Prime Minister Churchill and by Right Hon. Anthony Eden-and the Prime Minister will correct me if I am wrong-must, of course, be a reflection and an echo of those who took part in the empire meeting of prime ministers. Having that in mind, and taking that for granted, namely, that it is a true reflection, and a fair statement in respect of the decisions arrived at in the meeting of commonwealth prime mintMr. Oraydnn.'J
isters, may I just give one paragraph dealing with this matter, and put it on record at the present time.
Opening the debate on foreign affairs in the United Kingdom parliament on May 24 last, Mr. Churchill said of the London conference:
There was revealed a core of agreement which will enable the British empire and commonwealth to meet in discussion with other organizations in the world in a firmly knit array. We have advanced from vague generalities to more precise points and agreements and we are in position to carry on discussions with other countries within limits which we have imposed upon ourselves by this debate upon foreign affairs.
We, therefore, embark upon the present debate with the backing and hearty good will from all representatives of the commonwealth and empire.
Then on Thursday, May 25, in closing the debate, the Right Hon. Anthony Eden prefaced his statement oh post-war policies with these words:
When the victory is won the first task will be close collaboration between the British commonwealth-
And I wish to stress this, because it is an important part in his statement:
-collaboration between the British commonwealth. the United States, the Soviet Union and China-but in the main, so far as Europe is concerned, between the first three-to ensure that Germany cannot start this business again. I want to speak for a moment about cooperation between the three in particular-ourselves, the United States and the Soviet Union.
I had intended to go farther in connection with that, but I think it provides abundant evidence from the language employed in the debate by both of these statesmen that the deliberate use of the expression "British commonwealth" indicated that a full degree of consent and agreement on the course which they charted had been given and reached byr all at the commonwealth meeting.
As I said before, I wish to close this debate without extending it too far. But I should like to say this, that there has been much loose talk about one voice, a single voice, a bloc, and so on. I have watched carefully in the press from time to time and have seen in some instances where it is even magnified to the position where there is an assumption that when such words are used, autonomy in Canada is in some way interfered with.
So far as this party is concerned, the statement of our position is, I think, definite, in the questions and answers which the Prime Minister placed himself upon the record, in connection with this debate, and as answered by John Bracken himself. I think that makes

Supply-External Affairs
it abundantly clear with respect to the position which our party takes in connection with matters of this kind.
Before I conclude my remarks to-night I should like to make-

I seldom refuse to answer a question, but it is now ten minutes to eleven, and I wish to deal with the whole matter to-night, and perhaps might be able to close the debate.
On January 31, 1944, the Prime Minister took issue with the statement that had been made by Mr. Bracken to the effect that the Prime Minister had said that Lord Halifax had asked us to make a commitmeift, to fall in line in any event with a common policy for the commonwealth in all matters of our external relations. The Prime Minister's words are to be found on page 42 of Hansard of this year, when he said:
What would seem now to be suggested is that the prime Canadian commitment should be to pursue in all matters of external relations- "in foreign policy, defence, economic affairs, colonial questions and communications," to cite the words of Lord Halifax-a common policy to be framed and executed by all the governments of the commonwealth. I maintain that apart from all questions as to how that common policy is to be reached, or enforced, such a conception.runs counter to the establishment of effective world security, and therefore is opposed to the true interests of the commonwealth itself.
I wanted to put that on the record. That statement which the Prime Minister made there, and which I answered when he raised it in February or March of this year, is on all fours, if I may say so, with the statement which Mr. Bracken actually said he made in connection with the same matter.

I have no desire to enter into a controversy at the moment in connection with this. I have read this over very
carefully, and my interpretation is that the effect of both statements is to represent a parallel sentiment and a parallel meaning.
In closing, I want simply to say, to the committee and to the Prime Minister that it is perhaps unfortunate that these matters should come on at the end of a very lengthy, busy and pressing session. I am attributing no special responsibility with respect to that to any one, but if I had an opportunity- and if we are to go on next week perhaps I shall have-I should like to go farther into some of these matters. But I wish to deal with this matter and to indicate to the committee the position which was actually reached and which was reflected by the speeches made by Mr. Churchill and Mr. Eden in the British House of Commons. I think those are fair statements of the position which the commonwealth prime ministers took at their meeting some time ago. That is something which the Prime Minister perhaps may w'ant to deal with, and in order that he may have that opportunity perhaps I may be pardoned if I end my discussion at this moment.

speechtext:
I am not in favour of having this item carried at this time and I am going to tell the committee exactly why. I believe more damage has been done to public morale by the disgraceful squabbles that have occurred between the Liberal and Conservative ' parties about relationships between Canada and the empire than by any other matter that has come before Canada for discussion in the elections. I do not believe that the leaders of these two parties should discuss this matter until they are either one hundred per cent in agreement or one hundred per cent in disagreement. Then the people will know exactly where each one stands. Then there will not be any fighting in the elections between these two parties on, this issue.
I have listened with the greatest attention to the leader of the opposition and I have listened to the expressions of the Prime Minister. If there is any essential difference between the stand taken by the Prime Minister and by Mr. Bracken, the leader of the Conservative party, I must confess that I fail utterly to see it. If there is no difference, then why should not these two leaders say so on the floor of this house? If that were done, there might not be any disagreement over this matter in the election campaign.

speechtext:
That is all right; I am not talking about them. I feel strongly about this matter of imperial relations. From the

time I was a boy, from the time I first took any interest in politics, I have noticed this different approach to imperial relations. I have noticed that when you really studied what had been said by each side it was exactly the same thing. For example, Mr. Borden made a pronouncement about imperial relations in words and expressions that were identical to the words used by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I could not see any difference between the two. Yet by the time they got out to the constituency where I was and I went to the meetings and listened to the representatives of the two parties, you would have thought the one stood for a united Britain and the other wanted to tear the British empire all apart. There is no sense in that sort of thing and. we cannot hope to have a united Canada with that sort of thing.
It must be borne in mind that there are at least two prominent races in Canada. There is the Anglo-Saxon race and the Freneh-Canadian race, and the Ukrainians have increased to the extent of about 600,000. How are we to get these people to understand what we stand for if we quarrel about things like this? If these two leaders are prepared to make a statement that there is no difference and then fight the election on something about which there is a difference between the two parties, if there is such a thing as a difference between them, I will feel that something has been done even this late in the day. So that I am not in favour of passing this item, even though I sympathize, I must say, from the depths of my being with the Prime Minister in the position he is in. I do not believe that there has come before the house this year a problem of anything like the significance and importance which is attached to this particular problem at this moment, when you consider Canadian unity and the welfare of the British empire and harmonious relations between the empire and the rest of the world.
I think I have spoken with a little heat, but I mean every word I have said. I should like to see unity. If there is a difference between Liberals, Conservatives and C.C.F., we want to know what it is, and if there is a difference between them and what the Social Credit party stands for, we want to know what that is. We need to be very definite in this matter. If there is any one subject we ought not to quarrel about in election time, it is this particular matter of the relationship between Canada and the other members of the British empire and commonwealth.

speechtext:
I want	to	make anobservation or two with regard to the long , awaited statement of the Prime Minister that was contained in the Prime Minister's speech of August 4 dealing with the government's policy about	the Japanese.	At	this latedate in the	session	I am	not	going toexpand what	I have	to say	into	a speech,
but rather to endeavour to put on the record in a few words the reaction that I have to the statement.
I appreciate the fact that the government has definitely stated that it recognizes the Japanese question to be a national one. Whatever individual members of the ministry may have had in mind in the past with regard to it, there is no question that a considerable section of the Canadian public has looked upon this in the past as a provincial matter, as something with which British Columbia should deal.
[ therefore appreciate the fact that from now on it must be recognized that the dominion government looks upon it as a dominion question. I appreciate also the statement that in the Prime Minister's opinion the view of many in British Columbia that the Japanese should not be allowed to concentrate in that province was a reasonable one. The government's policy has been to endeavour to distribute the Japanese in the other eight provinces of Canada. In that regard I ask him not to forget that at the present time there are sixteen or seventeen thousand of those Japanese within British Columbia and that the smaller number has been distributed in other parts of Canada. Therefore whatever solution is arrived at, if we agree that it is not reasonable that a great majority of these people should still live in British Columbia, something will have to be done with the sixteen or seventeen thousand.
I would also remind the Prime Minister that the figures quoted-on which I cannot be accurate because I do not know exactly how many have been sent out-do not cover the Japanese resident in various parts of southern
British Columbia who did not come under the movement of Japanese from the protected area.
I appreciate also the statement that in future there should be no further immigration of Japanese to this country. It stands to reason that if this problem is to receive satisfactory settlement that must be the case. The operative part of this policy is that a quasi-judicial commission is to endeavour to investigate the loyalty of the Japanese now in Canada, and that the policy is to be continued and extended of placing these Japanese in different parts of Canada. What a task the government proposes to give to a quasijudicial commission to ascertain the loyalty of the Japanese! A great deal will depend on the personnel chosen for that commission. I cannot envy them their task. It would seem to me a most difficult thing to endeavour to ascertain the loyalty of the Japanese. In this morning's paper we have the considered opinion of President Roosevelt with regard to the Japanese as a nation and as a people. We are about to endeavour to ascertain the loyalty of certain thousands of Japanese. It is possible that some of them may help us.
Attention has been already drawn to the Canadian-born Japanese Yamamoto, who was convicted for refusing to obey an order of the selective service officer and who was fined with the alternative of a prison sentence. He took the prison sentence. In the course of the court's proceedings we were told that Yamamoto had written to the Minister of Labour stating that for him to obey such an order would be harmful to Japan, that his sympathies belonged to that country and that furthermore he would do nothing to harm her or assist Canada. If I could believe that the majority of the Japanese would declare them-in such fashion I would not look with such doubt on the success of the endeavour of a commission to decide on the loyalty of the Japanese. I trust that those appointed to the commission will not have the frame of mind which was found in some who in the past have been chosen as advisers by the dominion government, that type of thinking which appeared to result in the view that the opinion of British Columbians on the Japanese question was the result of hysteria, and that they should be smacked and ignored. I trust we have progressed beyond that stage and that the commission to be appointed'will be able to work on the information furnished by the mounted police and whatever they may be able to adduce from their interviews with the Japanese.

In 1937 a delegation of Japanese appeared before a committee of this house apropos of the Dominion Elections Act or the Dominion Franchise Act, The attention of one of them -and he, if you please, was a professor of English at Wisconsin university-was directed to this question of dual loyalty, the registration of children born in Canada, who are considered by a very great number of people to be Canadian citizens with no loyalty except to Canada. It was definitely ascertained that in his opinion the idea of registering children born in Canada with the Japanese authorities was not only desirable but convenient. I cannot look upon a child bom in any part of Canada, whose birth is registered in the country of his paternal origin, as having loyalty only to Canada. I wonder what the commission would have said of the Japanese envoy who in Washington, in December, 1941, was smiling and hissing at the secretary of state. I wonder if the commission to be set up would have been perfectly sure of his sincerity. I wonder what that commission would say with regard to that man's father and his ancestors, all of whom were steeped in the religion of Japan which has induced that people to believe themselves sent by some god to this earth in order to dominate at least the western part of the world. How is it possible to suppose that people of that nationality can come to' another country, Canada, and eschew all those doctrines which they have learned from the cradle? How is it possible to believe that these people can give wholehearted loyalty to this country? I find it very hard to place reliance upon the results of the work of a quasi-judicial commission. It should not be forgotten that these Japanese children who have now grown up and become parents have never entirely divested themselves of their loyalty to their ancestors; and as long as that is the case it seems to me impossible to believe that their loyalty to Canada now is something that can be ascertained by a quasijudicial commission.
The remainder of the operative part of the policy is that the dissemination of these people throughout the other eight provinces is to be carried forward, and they are to be largely removed from British Columbia. The difficulty there, of course, and it was touched upon by the Prime Minister, is that when all these war restrictions are removed; when we return to a period when the inhabitants of Canada will be able to move about at will, what can be done to prevent these seeded settlers from finding their way back to British Columbia, which province they have favoured hitherto?

The climate of British Columbia is always attractive, and they have made their opportunities in that province. This is a country of seasonal " occupation, and unquestionably their desire will be to return west of the mountains. Therefore it seems to me improbable that the policy pronounced by the government for dealing with the Japanese question can possibly succeed.
At the peace conference, as the Prime Minister has agreed, it will be possible to make some arrangement with regard to the Japanese in Canada. I am glad he acknowledged also the difficulties in regard to the problem of assimilation. In my opinion these people are not assimilable. Many years ago I saw something of the results of mixed marriages in the near east, and we have all read a great deal with regard to the Eurasian question in India and the countries nearby, in the islands of the Atlantic and the islands of the Pacific, not to be more specific than that. The horrors of the Eurasion question are so great that I woidd be ready to do well nigh anything to prevent that question getting a start in Canada. These mixed marriages are frowned upon and tabooed by both nations, but that does not prevent them from taking place, or from children being born to them. As a result we see half-breed children being born in Canada who will find little opportunity to work out their lives in this country on an equality with our children. Therefore in my opinion we must do every thing we can to dispose of this Japanese question at the peace conference in a way that will be satisfactory to Canada.

We are now entering a period which apparently is regarded by the united nations, and particularly the four great powers, as a time when the creation of a new peace organization is imminent and necessary. That this is contemplated is evidenced by the fact that in Washington during this month there will be a preliminary meeting of the four great powers. In the course of a debate on foreign affairs in the British House of Com-

Supply-External Affairs
mons on May 25 the Foreign Secretary had this to say with respect to the proposed peace organization:
I would like to leave with the committee just a few principles on which we suggest this future organization should be based. They are these: First, that the world organization must be designed, in the first instance, to prevent a recurrence of aggression by Germany and Japan and must be fully equipped with forces to meet the purpose.
In other words the organization was to have the strength and power for the purposes for which it was to be established. He continues:
Secondly, that to ensure this there must be close political and military cooperation between the United States, the Soviet Union, the Commonwealth and China-
An hon. Member: And France.
Mr. Eden: -and other powers; thirdly, that the responsibility in any future world organization must be related to power, and consequently the world organization should be constructed, on and around the four great powers I have mentioned, and all other peace-loving states should come in and play their part in the structure; fourthly, that the world organization should be flexible and not rigid, that is to say, that it should grow by practice and not try straight away to work to a fixed and rigid code or rule; and fifthly, that all the powers, great and small, included in the world organization, should strive for economic as well as for political collaboration.
On the basis of these quotations I wish to ask two questions of the Prime Minister: Does this vote No. 44, involving a sum of $214,600 for expenses of the League of Nations, mean we are going to make further contributions to the league? Will the League of Nations be disbanded, allowing this new organization to take its place, or will that new organization in some way work in conjunction with the league? I should like to know what the situation is, because we are here asked to contribute a large sum of money to the expenses of the League of Nations. At the same time I have no doubt in connection with the new' organization there will be heavy financial and military obligations. And if my supposition is correct, the new organization for peace as envisaged by the Foreign Secretary will be on a basis entirely different from that of the League of Nations. It is my understanding that it would be built up, not from a great assembly of nations coming together in a time of peace, but rather in a manner which has now been planned, namely that of the four great powers getting together to form a core, to operate as a nucleus for peace, and then as time goes on other nations being permitted to come in as circumstances permit. As I see it. this procedure would mean one of two things. Either the League of Nations will have to be
disbanded and this new organization take its place, or the two will have to be fitted together in some manner. It is my understanding that for the time being the league is simply carrying on until the new organization takes its place. There could hardly be room for both. I ask this question because there are many people in Canada who are making the inquiry.
I did not wish to extend the discussion on Saturday evening to any undue length, because I was desirous of giving to the government such measure of cooperation as I could1 in connection with the length of the session, but I believe I might be permitted now to repeat a question I asked some weeks ago, as to whether the representatives of the United Kingdom would also be in a position to represent the views of the British commonwealth, as well as those of the United Kingdom, at that conference of the four great powers. On the earlier occasion I understood the Prime Minister to say that the British commonwealth as such was not being represented, but that the representation was of the United Kingdom alone.
This brings me to a point discussed in Mr. Eden's statement. In every statement the Foreign Secretary has made concerning a new world organization he has been exceedingly careful, I think, never to use the words "Great Britain" or "the United Kingdom" in connection therewith. Coming on the heels of the statement of the Prime Minister of Great Britain, who spoke about the empire going forward in a firmly knit array, and that the prime ministers of the various parts of the commonwealth had reached what he called a core of agreement at the meeting, it was a normal procedure for the Foreign Secretary then to use words indicating that the four great powers were in cooperation to ensure that there must be close political and military cooperation between the United States, the Soviet union, the British commonwealth and China. I listened carefully to the Prime Minister's statement made a few days ago, when he referred to the fact that there was agreement and consent, and that there was no difference in the views of the various parts of the commonwealth on matters related to the setting up of a peace organization. At that time the Prime Minister did not indicate however whether the British representatives at the four-nation conference would go there with authority to express the views of the various nations in the commonwealth, and to speak on their behalf in the preliminary discussion.
It may be that when he used the word "British commonwealth" the Foreign Secretary had in
Supply-External Affairs

mind the fact that the United Kingdom representative would go there, knowing well the views of commonwealth prime ministers, and would act accordingly. I think it is rather important because the whole problem of how Canada shall fit into the new peace structure is involved. It seems to me that Canada has two ways of going into the peace organization. One is through the British commonwealth, as mentioned by the British foreign secretary, whereby we would be one of the great powers, and the other is to go in as one of the smaller nations.
I think the matter must be cleared up. Perhaps there is nothing serious with respect to it, but when the Prime Minister answers me he might indicate just how-Canada will eventually come in and what her part will be in the new organization. I am sorry to have asked so many questions at the one time but perhaps the Prime Minister has made a note of them. I will appreciate anything he can say at this time.
