speechtext:
First of all with regard to the position of the League of Nations and the new world organization that is to be created, obviously none of us knows how long the present war is going to last and we do not know how long after the war has concluded it will be before an international organization is set up for the purpose of maintaining peace throughout the world. Until the new organization assumes definite shape it may, I think, be regarded as without question that the League of Nations will continue to function, albeit to a very limited extent. There is no intention that I have learned of in the mind of any one which contemplates the coexistence of two great world organizations; one world organization undoubtedly is all that is expected, but just when the new organization will replace the other I cannot say.
Matters that are being considered at the present time in relation to the world organization do take into consideration the fact that already there is in the League of Nations a model on a certain scale and to a limited degree on which the new organization will be based and possibly in many particulars there will be a strong resemblance between the two. But until the world organization is actually in existence and approved by parliaments that will have to contribute towards its existence, the League of Nations will continue to operate as a world organization.
As to the other question asked by my hon. friend, I have made it clear that the conference which will be held shortly at Washington is a conference on the official level, that is to say, it will be a conference between officials of the four great powers. It is being carried

out in accordance with what was set forth in the declaration of Moscow where only the four powers are mentioned, the United Kingdom, the United States, China, and Russia. So far as the pending conference is concerned the British commonwealth as such will not be represented. It is not a conference between ministers but, as I have indicated, between officials for the purpose of working out a plan of organization.
While it is true that the British representatives will be representatives of Great Britain only, I think I have made it clear that they will have in their minds the point of view of the nations of the commonwealth with respect to the questions that will be discussed there. Fortunately these matters were considered fully at the meeting between the prime ministers in London, and there was general agreement with respect to them between the representatives of the nations of the commonwealth. that is to say, the United Kingdom. Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, with regard to broad essentials of the world organization that is to be brought into being. While it is true that the officials who will meet this month in Washington to discuss the world organization will be representatives only of the United Kingdom, it can be said that they are fully aware of the views of the nations of the commonwealth. I do not know whether there is any more my hon. friend wishes me to say.

I feel keenly about this. Our conception of democracy is that parliament is supreme, but somehow the mechanics of parliament are such that it seems to me that the government is supreme. I in my small way am going to insist that all commitments made by Canada with regard to her place in the post-war world shall be brought first to parliament.
These matters are very serious. It is not just a case of voting a quarter of a million dollars for the League of Nations. That is small stuff as compared to the ramifications

Supply-External Affairs
and implications involved in Canada's place in the post-war world. Personally I do not think that the Prime Minister or whoever it is that represents Canada at any international conference-perhaps one man with a few aides-should be able to commit the entire nation to anything. We have nine provinces, each one of which is a supreme state within its own rights. I can see difficulty if the government makes any commitments without first laying them before parliament and allowing them to be discussed and our views to be presented. I said the other day that I thought that the leader of every political party in this country should be brought into discussion with the Prime Minister. I would go further and say that I think the premiers of all the provinces should be brought in too. Surely we are not going to commit twelve million loyal Canadians to a policy about which they know very little but which in the end, perhaps generations hence, may wreck our nation as a nation. I just wanted to ask the Prime Minister that one question which I think he is prepared to answer. I hope that he will make it clear that commitments will be made only after parliament at least has had full opportunity to look into the whole matter and have the fullest possible discussion.

In a general
way may I say this, that in the beginning of foreign missions or representation abroad concern was primarily for ambassadors. The representative of the sovereign or head of the state in a foreign country was an ambassador. There grew up the custom of having as well ministers to less important countries and on less important missions. As time has gone on, the distinction between the functions of an ambassador and of a minister has practically ceased to exist. An ambassador had certain special rights in the matter of direct approach to the head of the state to which he was accredited, more, I imagine, of a ceremonial nature than anything else, but as I have said the necessity of maintaining the distinction between ambassador and minister has been lessening as the years have gone by. So far as the United States is concerned, which next to the United Kingdom receives perhaps the largest number of representatives from different countries, that country for some little time past has completely done away with that distinction by appointing to other countries on this continent ambassadors only, and it has readily accorded to the representatives of other countries in the United States the status of ambassador rather than that of minister. The United Kingdom in its representation at Washington has not only an ambassador as its chief representative but, particularly during the period of this war, has added to its diplomatic representation several ministers. There are I believe five or six ministers at Washington attached to the United Kingdom embassy in addition to the ambassador. That has made it apparent that the status of ambassador is somewhat higher than that of minister and that the functions of a minister have come to be slightly different from what they were when a country was represented only by a minister or by an ambassador.
We have felt that Canada certainly should not be the only country on this continent whose sovereign is represented at Washington by a minister when the heads of all the other countries on this continent are represented by

That was one of the reasons why the change was made at the time it was made, changing the status of our representative at Washington from that of minister to that of ambassador and the receiving of an ambassador from that country here. Of course the main reason was that we believed that the position of Canada as a nation holding a very high place among the nations of the world was being misunderstood by other nations in that we were represented only by a minister at the great capitals while other countries of lesser power and influence and standing in the world were represented by ambassadors.
In making appointments or in elevating the status of minister to that of ambassador the government proceeded by raising first the status of our representatives in certain nations which were our allies in the present war and were fighting with us, the United States being first, followed by Russia, China, and in South America, Brazil. The next group were from those other countries of the united nations which are immediately associated with us in the war. In the case of Belgium the minister, Baron Silvercruys, who represented that country from the beginning, was, as hon. members are aware, the dean of the diplomatic corps in Ottawa. He has been in the capital continuously, and it was felt that it would be a mark of recognition which we would like to give both to his country and to himself at this time to welcome him here as an ambassador.
What I have said will help to illustrate the necessity for the supplementary estimate we are asking for. With reference to Canadian representation abroad, and particularly with relation to Canada's trade, I do not know whether the Prime Minister or the government noticed a rather compelling editorial which appeared on July 29, 1944, in the Financial Post. I do not wish to read the editorial in full but it struck me as bringing to light an important matter. It inquired whether Canada's foreign trade machinery was ready in view of the uncertainty as to the closing of hostilities and the necessity for making arrangements for the post-war period, which considerations apparently prompted the article in question. The editorial says in part:
But what about that most important supplementary instrument of foreign trade-the Canadian government representation abroad- diplomatic and commercial? Is it ready? Has it the management, the staffing, the inspiration necessary to help Canadian business men raise our foreign trade to new high levels?
One sentence struck me as specially worthy of comment and one that should be brought to the attention of the committee and of the Prime Minister. It reads:
Canada's future depends on foreign trade. In the modern world trade and diplomacy are interdependent. The modern Canadian diplomat is no more only a tea-party lion than the modern trade commissioner is only a ringer of doorbells of prospective customers for Canada. It is high time that this critical issue of the organization of our foreign representation was taken up at once at a high government level.
I apologize for transgressing the rules in order to put that on the record, but it is a matter which I thought had an important bearing on the situation, and was stated more clearly than I might state it at the moment. That raises the question as to whether or not there should be a complete reorganization in the days to come of the whole matter of external affairs and trade and commerce because of the inter-relation of the two in our dealings with foreign countries. The Prime Minister mentioned some time ago that as time went on it would be necessary to divorce the Department of External Affairs from the office of Prime Minister. In making that move did he have in mind a complete reorganization which would carry with it a department in which the whole representation of Canada would be included'-in other words, that it would not be simply a matter of handling the diplomatic affairs of this country, political and otherwise, but one that would have to do with the equally important, perhaps the more important, problem of international trade itself.
We are now utilizing two distinct channels of representation abroad, one through the Department of Trade and Commerce and the other through the Department of External Affairs. Would the Prime Minister care to comment upon this, and indicate whether it would be possible from the standpoint of efficiency and ordinary diplomatic common sense to have the representation of Canada channelled through a larger and more comprehensive department where the services of all who represent this country overseas, in all foreign lands, would be utilized to the best possible advantage both as to external affairs and international politics and in the obtaining of a much larger share of international trade for this country?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The matter that my hon. friend has brought up is one that is of importance and I am glad that he has raised the question. May I say first of all that what Canada should do will have to be considered in relation to what other countries actually do in the matter of their diplomatic and trade relations. My hon. friend has asked if we could not in reorganizing bring together under one department of government all those branches of administration that relate to foreign affairs or external affairs, in particular diplomatic relationships and the commercial relationships of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I do not think that that would be possible, for a very obvious reason. The diplomatic representation under external affairs has to do with representation between governments, representation of the head of the state. All appointments from external affairs are to governments of other countries. They are not to commercial institutions or business agencies or private organizations or bodies, but to the heads of the governments of the different countries. I imagine that all countries will find it necessary to have a special representative of their governments as distinct from the business interests. In the Department of Trade and Commerce the commercial agents are representatives in the nature of agents for the promotion of trade, and as such their contacts are primarily with the great business concerns in the countries to which they are sent, through individuals as well as organizations.
It would not, so far as I can see at the moment, do to have those officials of the government, whose principal business is that of promoting trade, given the same status ' and position as the representatives of the government whose concern is with larger questions of policy that involve a consideration

Supply-External Affairs

of many things that lie altogether outside of trade. Government policy has to take account of all aspects of governmental relations that have a bearing on an immediate subject. At the same time there is every reason why these two departments of government should have their functions interrelated in a manner that will further the interest of both. That matter has received careful study by our officials over a considerable period of time. Anticipating a possible question on the matter I am prepared to give the committee a clearer and very full explanation.	[DOT]
War conditions, and the need to meet postwar conditions in the field of international tfade have made it necessary to reexamine the relations between the Canadian offices established abroad by the Department of External Affairs and the commercial intelligence service of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The government, more than a year ago, established a special committee from the two departments to study the question and to submit recommendations designed to promote closer cooperation between the services. This committee made a report, after studying the experiences of the governments of the other members of the British commonwealth and of the United States of America, as well as programmes for reforms which are being considered abroad. As a result of the information thus brought to the attention of the government, a special administrative committee has been set up, including three representatives from the Department of External Affairs and three from the Department of Trade and Commerce, with the deputy heads of the two departments as additional ex officio members. The special committee is charged with responsibility for working out practical measures for cooperation betw'een the two services. The effect of these plans so far as they have been developed should be clearly understood. They provide for the coordination of Canada's diplomatic and trade promotion services abroad -not for the merging of these two services into one. It goes without saying that there must be, both in Canada and abroad, the closest cooperation between the official representation maintained by the Department of External Affairs and the trade commissioner service. We are retaining the trade commissioner service as a specialized trade promotion organization under the full control of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and with such closer association of this service with the diplomatic service as will tend to strengthen both. Announcement has been made in the speech from the throne in regard to the strengthening of the trade commissioner service. It is generally agreed that strong rein-
forcement of this service will be required in the next few years. In fact it is not going too far to say that in the post-war period it will be essential for Canada to have the strongest department of trade and commerce we have ever had. The plans which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has now in hand for strengthening both the trade commissioner service abroad and the departmental organization at Ottawa are, accordingly, being advanced as rapidly as possible.
The types of problems, which emerge and are being dealt with by the interdepartmental committee, vary in different parts of the world. We may have a high commissioner and trade commissioner's offices in the same country. In some cases the trade commissioner's offices may be situated in the capital and may occupy the same premises as the high commissioner's office. In others, they may be separated. In other countries there may be a Canadian embassy or legation, with trade commissioner's offiqes either in the same place or in commercial centres in other parts of the country. In other places there may be Canadian consular offices established or under consideration. Where the offices are in different places, arrangements are made for periodic meetings. Where offices of the two departments are in the same place, every effort is being made to bring them under the same roof and to provide for close association in the work in which they are engaged. The committee is concerned with working out the instructions, which are issued to the heads of missions by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and to the trade commissioner's offices by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. These are designed to avoid overlapping and to promote consultation and cooperation. It is not possible to draw a hard and fast line between the work of the commercial intelligence service and the work of the Canadian diplomatic service. Both services gain where there are frequent consultations and where there is close cooperation in dealing with practical problems.
At the same time, the departments are working together in recruiting personnel from our armed forces. There are many young Canadians, in the navy, army and air force, who, by education, experience and ability, are well suited for the work of these two departments. Some of them would be immediately available upon discharge, and others will require additional education under the arrangements for rehabilitation and reeducation which have been established by the Department of Pensions and National Health. It is expected that the expanding needs of the commercial intelligence service and of the external affairs service will be largely met by personnel

Supply-External Affairs
obtained under this common recruiting policy.
As the young men come into the services, their work is being planned in such a manner, through interchange of personnel, as to ensure that they will have experience on both the diplomatic and the commercial intelligence side, and it is hoped that in the course of time there will be a large number of persons in both services suitable for senior posts for the diplomatic, consular and commercial services.
The development of a consular service and its special relationship with the commercial intelligence service will be a matter to be worked out carefully during the ensuing years. A consulate general has been established in New York and the arrangements there are working in a satisfactory manner. The office of the consulate general embraces the trade commissioner's office and the consular service proper. The trade commissioners in the office have been given consular rank and perform consular functions in addition to their usual duties. It is expected that the experience gained in New York will be of value, in the event that it is decided to open up consular offices at other points. Further, the experience which is being gained by the personnel of both departments under the arrangement for close cooperation, which has been in effect for some time, will mean that there will be a substantial number of personnel in the two departments sufficiently familiar with both commercial intelligence and consular work to facilitate the organization and establishment of other consulates.
I think my hon. friend will see that the government has seen very clearly what he has in mind and has left no stone unturned.
While I am speaking on Canada's relation with other countries there is one other matter that I would like to mention. Hon. members have no doubt seen items in the press concerning the arrival of Brazilian troops in Italy to join in the fight against the enemy. We in Canada, who have our own men fighting there, are proud to be able to welcome these soldiers from the south to the great battle that is being steadily and successfully fought. Our common participation in the war will do much to draw our two countries together, and our men, fighting side by side, will render firm and lasting the sense of comradeship between our peoples.

speechtext:
I believe it is recognized throughout the coal mining industry, and in other industries related to coal mining, that Canada has not yet arrived at a point where she has a satisfactory fuel policy. It is strange that although we have been living in Canada under constitutional government for so many years and with vast quantities of coal deposits, we have not been able to present to our people an adequate and proper fuel policy. Some months ago the Minister of Munitions and Supply announced that the government was in process of setting up a royal commission to investigate coal mining, particularly in its relationship to the post-war world. I find that there have already been set up in Canada eight distinct coal commissions, and m addition there have been set up five industrial disputes inquiries. In addition there have been forty-four boards of conciliation and investigation in respect of the industry. Putting these together it will be agreed that this industry has at least been looked into. I am not opposing the setting up of another coal commission, but I do oppose the setting up at tremendous cost of commissions whose reports are laid on the table and then filed, with no benefit to anyone except that which may be derived by the mice from chewing on them.
Repeatedly since coming to parliament I have noticed that commissions have been set up, and that the results have been as I have indicated. Some years ago an unemployment commission was established. It went to a tremendous amount of trouble and expense, but I have failed to see where parliament or the government brought down one bit of legislation as a consequence of its deliberations. Another commission investigated the wheat problem, and in doing so travelled across Canada, involving considerable trouble and expense. That report was laid on the table, but nothing flowed from it.
Evidently there must be some difficulty in the setting up of this commission, because months have passed since the original
announcement was made. No final announcement has been made concerning the meetings of the commission. Perhaps we will not have an opportunity to discuss this subject again until the next session of parliament; therefore I take this opportunity in the dying hours of this session to point out that if the commission is to do its work, and if any benefits are to flow from it, its report must be studied and acted upon. It will have to go into every detail of the coal-mining industry involving, as I see it, three distinct investigations. The commission will have to review the subject of markets-because if we do not have markets for our coal, the coal-mining industry cannot function, men will be laid off, and so on. That follows naturally. The commission will have to decide as to where permanent markets can be obtained. As I have looked into this matter for years I have been convinced that the market right at our door, our own Canadian market, is not being supplied with Canadian coal, and has not been for years. We realize of course that the war has made some difference in that condition. The commission must recognize that if the coal-mining industry is to be kept going we must have a market for our coal.
The second point is that the coal-mining industry must be kept solvent. My experience, which has involved my talking with coalmining operators and interested individuals, has led me-to .note that financially the coalmining industry of Canada is on the verge of folding up. A business should be able to realize at least a certain percentage on its investment. I am not free to say what the interest on coal-mining investments may be, but if it were known it would surprise many people in Canada. Therefore I say the commission should investigate whether or not the industry can remain solvent. If it were to fold up, an unemployment problem would develop in respect of coal miners.
We have talked about markets, and about keeping the industry solvent. A complaint came to me the other day which I would ask the minister to consider. Perhaps the responsibility would be that of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. There have not been railway cars available to transport the coal from the mines. I do not know how long this situation has existed, but I do know that in my particular area certain coal mines have had to close down in time of war. It is a rather strange thing that in time of war, when there is a national coal emergency, mines have to close down because they cannot get the railway equipment to haul their coal. I want the minister to find out just what is the trouble.
Supply

Mines and Resources

If the commission is to do its work properly it must discover where we can find adequate markets for our coal in order to keep the coal mining industry going. It must pay special attention to the interests of the coal miner. The coal miner must be kept employed, and at fair and agreeable wages. Not long ago there was a strike, and the commissioner appointed to look into the matter discovered that the coal industry could not afford to pay the miner what he was asking for. The commission agreed that the coal miners should have an increase, but it was passed on to the consumer. Perhaps that was the proper course to take, but I am contending that the commission should look into the problems facing the coal miner so that he may be kept regularly at work at fair and agreeable wages.
There is one other observation I should like to make. I would suggest to the labour organizations that they either have in their organizations or have access to the services of qualified actuaries and chartered accountants in order that they may examine the books of the industry in which they are employed. Because the manager of a corporation is able to get a new model car every year and is able to smoke big cigars the impression is that the company is making a mint of money. They may or may not be, and I suggest it would be beneficial to industry as well as to the labour organizations if management and labour could get together so that labour might have access to the books in order to see what profit is accruing to the company, what percentage is being made on the investment, and whether a raise in pay to the men would permit the company to remain solvent. Sometimes these corporations operate on a thin margin, and a decrease of a few cents in the price of coal may mean the difference between solvency and insolvency. I believe that many misunderstandings could be ironed out if this arrangement could be brought about.
That is all I am going to say on this item because I know we want to get through with the session. The royal commission should be directed to look into these aspects of the coal mining industry, paying special attention to the requirements of the coal miner as well to the solvency of the coal mining industry, so that we shall not have a repetition of what happened a few years ago, when the coal mining industry was operating only one, two or three days a week or sometimes not at all, and coal miners, who are qualified workmen, were on relief. Would the minister look into the matter of the supply of railway cars and see what the hold-up is? I have the promise of the Minister of Labour that there will be a

representative of the miners on this coal commission. That promise will be found'in Hansard, and I am going to ask that it be fulfilled.

I merely wanted to say to the minister that one of the most important matters to the province of Nova Scotia at the present time is the appointment of this royal commission, and unless the terms of reference to that commission are all-inclusive its appointment will be just a waste of time and a repetition of previous commissions' reports. The personnel of the commission is very important. You must have men who understand the industry, and understand the marketing of coal. Otherwise the evidence presented to the commission will be wasted because they will not realize its importance. I believe that the government is giving careful consideration to the personnel of the commission. It should not be so difficult. I could stand up and offhand, without any reference to papers, recommend a personnel that I know would be fair to all concerned and have due regard to the best interests of the men. It may be hard, of course, to get men who will suit the operators. But so far as the men are concerned, the miners' union in Nova Scotia has nothing to hide. They are interested in this commission and in its final recommendations from the standpoint of the best interests of the industry in Nova Scotia as it pertains to the economy of that whole province.
Personnel is important. But perhaps equally important are the terms of reference. If the terms of reference are not adequate, if it means just another examination of the coal mining set-up, we cannot expect much. It controls timber limits, steel, coal and iron. The company has some twenty-nine or thirty subsidiaries, and unless the whole picture is examined into we

When the committee rose at one o'clock I was making a few remarks on the coal situation. I was pointing out that in the matter of research into the mining industry, as far as Nova Scotia is concerned, the job is fairly complete, and in view of the fact that the federal government have definitely decided to set up a royal commission I think that the [Mr. Gillis.l
desires of the people of Nova Scotia should be given consideration in connection with the terms of reference. The mine workers' union, when they met the cabinet committee presided over by the Minister of Mines and Resources a few weeks ago, had a brief setting out their case, pointing out the possibilities of the industry, the difficulties that are to be faced in the post-war period, and offering a solution to the problem. But this was contingent upon proving to the federal government, through the medium of this proposed commission, that they have a case.
I do not suppose there is another industry in Canada that is subsidized to the same extent as the steel and coal industry in Nova Scotia, and that applies also to most of their subsidiary organizations. I think the time has come when, in addition to going into the public treasury to guarantee that these companies make a definite profit, the government must accept some responsibility to the public and see that the organization performs a public service.
It is only within the last few months that an exhaustive inquiry was made into the closing of the Trenton Car Works, a part of the Dominion Steel and1 Coal set-up. A brief was prepared in that case and it is a very informative one. The reason why I say that, in addition to subsidizing and guaranteeing profits, some regard must be had by the government to the question of guaranteeing to the people of Canada that the organization shall not only provide profits but shall perform a service to the public, is this. In this brief prepared by the steel workers union, examining the Trenton question alone-and that is a very small subsidiary of the Dominion Steel and Coal organization-it is pointed out, and I bring it to the minister's attention as an indication of some serious thinking on the part of the government in this matter of setting up a royal commission, that since April 1, 1939 a total of $40,019,015.99 had been paid to the Dominion Steel and Coal company by the dominion government in subsidies and for installation of plant and equipment. That is a good deal of money to have paid out since 1939. Operating subsidies amounted to $26,953,805.13, capital advanced on property, of which title is held' by the dominion government, $7,750,776.22, capital advanced on property of which title is held by the dominion government $5,313,434.64, making a total of S40,019,015.99.
The thing I am concerned about is that while operating subsidies have kept the industry moving during the period set out here, the

Supply-Mines and Resources
dominion government definitely haa an equity in plant and equipment made possible by direct federal assistance. It is the responsibility of the federal government to see that that plant and equipment is utilized in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole. '
An organization that receives so much money from the federal government is in my opinion responsible to some extent to those who are making it possible for it to operate. One of the main points in the miners' brief, and they went into the question thoroughly, is that the time has arrived in Nova Scotia for an examination of coal leases. A fact that was borne out very clearly in their brief was that in Alberta, where an examination was held into cost of production, when they got an increase in production they had a decrease in cost. That is a natural assumption, but in going over the figures for the Nova Scotia industry from 1929 to 1942 they found that while arguments were advanced by the company and others to show that, unless they could get a substantial increase in production, the possibilities were that they would not be able to continue operating, an examination of the figures for the period I mentioned, and the plotting of a graph from them, revealed that in Nova Scotia during that period when they got a fairly substantial increase in production they got an almost parallel increase in cost, and as production dropped, as it did in the last two or three years, they got a similar drop in costs.
There is an answer to that, I believe. At any rate, the miners' brief sets out an answer- obsolescent machinery, high cost mines, mines that are running out, where, in order to increase production it is necessary to step up the power, pumping facilities, and so on. All these factors tend to increase the cost, and vice versa as they drop off. That definitely tells us that if there is to be any prosperity in that industry new methods must be devised and new openings made.
I am glad to see in the supplementary estimates, and I might as well say it now to save time, that the minister has a substantial appropriation for the purpose of setting up a pilot plant for the hydrogenation process and getting everything from the coal that there is in it. That would partly solve the problem in Nova Scotia. It is essential that plants of this kind be established where the operation is carried on. Our coal should be coked. We should extract every valuable by-product that could be marketed in *the province where the fuel is produced. The time has come for the conservation of fuel in Nova Scotia. New openings should be found and the by-product
100-405	'
should be utilized to the greatest extent possible. That is something that we shall have to go into if the industry is to be operated on an economic basis. Because of our geographical position I cannot see how we can continue to drag our coal from east to west as long as the flow of trade is in the direction it is at the present time. The only way to make that industry in the province stand on its feet and compete with United States coal is to do as suggested by the miners, make a reciprocal agreement with the United States operators so that we might market our coal on the eastern American border in exchange for certain markets in central Canada. That principle could apply to the west as well. You are not considered patriotic when you talk that way, nevertheless it is an economic problem, and has a place in the discussions that take place on this problem in the future. I am going to let the matter rest because there is no need for me to try to prove to the minister that it is necessary. That has been done. The fact that the government has appointed this commission is positive proof that it recognizes the seriousness of the situation so far as Nova Scotia is concerned.
The western operation is something that I am not going to touch on. I am not familiar enough with it to discuss it. It is a totally different picture from that of Nova Scotia. In the west there are a lot of small operations; in Nova Scotia we have one organization, although there are some small ones. The solution of the problem in the east is an entirely different one from the west.
The last thought I wish to leave with the minister is that the personnel of the commission must be informed and capable men who will view the problem in the light of what it means to the whole of the country and not pull their punches in any direction. The miners are not asking for it, and the general public in the province are not asking for it. They want to see that industry rehabilitated to get the most out of it for Canada as a whole. The terms of reference of the commission must be broad enough to ehable it to go into all the ramifications of the company that controls the industry in Nova Scotia.

I was pleased to listen to the hon. member for Cape Breton South once again bring to the attention of the Minister of Mines and Resources the question of coal production as it applies to Nova Scotia. The hon. member for Cape Breton South is perhaps the best informed member from Nova Scotia on this subject. Coming as he does from that particular coal area of Cape Breton he is well

Supply-Mines and Resources

qualified to bring to the attention of the committee the questions that he has so ably dealt with. .
I could not follow what the hon. member meant when he was talking of the subsidiary companies of the Dominion Steel and Coal company. I could not understand what particular reference it might have to the coal production; but if the reference is broad enough so far as coal is concerned then I believe the royal commission that is to be set up by the government will serve a very useful purpose not only in Nova Scotia but in the dominion as a whole.
As the hon. member said1, coal production in Nova Scotia is confined largely to the four counties of Cumberland, Inverness, Pictou, and Cape Breton, and has been for twenty-five years. The apportionment of the water presupposes that each of the two nations shall construct works to fit themselves to make beneficial use of their share of the water. Supply-Indian Affairs

506. Medical-Indian hospitals and general care of Indians-further amount required, $235,400.
Mr. NEI'LL: I assure this committee that the sound of my voice is just as distasteful to myself as it is to the committee at this day and date, but I feel it my duty to bring up the subject. I claim that the Indian department have adopted a principle-no, a lack of principle-in dealing with certain Indian hospitals. To put it bluntly, they are chiselling on them, or trying to as far as they can. Naturally I think of the hospitals in my own district. We had. a fairly large hospital at Port Alberni which served a fairly large area. I remember that on a-tnumber of occasions we had to dig down into our own pockets because the hospital ran short of funds. I remember on one occasion putting up S75, and others put up more than that, because we felt that we had to keep the hospital alive, seeing that the charges were not adequate. That went on for a long time and these people we had to pay for were very often only recent comers or outsiders. That was all right, but the Indian department adopted the principle of not paying the ordinary standard rates for destitute Indians. They have no right to do that any more than destitute Scotsmen, if there are such, should demand a special rate for themselves. Scotsmen are not generally destitute; they only want and try to get what is coming to them. Owing to the increased population, saw mills starting up and so on, the town has grown to a large extent, and so they adopted the system of issuing contracts for individual workers in the saw mills and collecting the money through the payrolls, giving out private contracts to individuals like myself. I pay so much a year whether I need it or not, and then I do not get free treatment but only a reduced rate. In this way they were able to make both ends meet.
Time went on, however, and expenses rose. It is a union town now and the nurses belong to a union. They work three shifts a day and have to be paid accordingly. Well, does the department object to that? Will anyone object to that? The cost of living has gone up, the cost of running hospitals has increased. Again, does anyone deny that? The hospital had to do as everyone else has had to do; it had to raise its rates. They raised the contracts, and no one kicked about that. We have a board of control on which the ordinary contract holders are represented. They are represented and the mill people are represented, so that if there is any chance of overcharging you may be sure it will be noted and taken care of. But none of these people 
kicked. They realized that the increase was necessary. No one objected but our friends in the Indian department.
The fact is that they would not have to deal with more than four or five hundred Indians at the most in that neighbourhood, and at last the board, after showing a great deal of patience, called for a showdown. They said, "We cannot go on taking a loss on every Indian we handle and then piling it on to the workers." The result was that a delegation came from Ottawa to see the hospital board. I was present and I can prove these things. We were told a number of things. In the first place, it was said that the hospital was overpaid and overstaffed. Well, in a union town where the girls have a union rate you cannot talk about overpaying anybody, and a good many people would have kicked if they had been paid less. We were not out to pay any money that we did not have to, and we knew that we were not overpaying them.
Next they said that the institution was overstaffed, that those who were working there were not doing enough. They were working an eight-hour shift, and there is no complaint on that score. None of us kicked or said that there were too many nurses. We were satisfied to accept the situation that was caused by circumstances, but this authority three thousand miles away, who knew nothing about it, maintained that we were overstaffed and overpaid.
When this argument was disposed of, or at any rate when they could not find anything more to say on that point, they said that they could do it cheaper in dominion hospitals and we replied, "Go ahead, but where are they? Where are those hospitals in which you will take care of these people?" They talked about some place called Norway House and said that it could be done cheaper there. But Norway House is a long way from British Columbia anc^j|p did not know the conditions there whereas we did certainly know the conditions at home. Did they allow anything for capital expenditures which we had to pay in connection with the building of our hospital? I wonder if in Norway House they pay $7 a day for ordinary labour and sometimes up to $9. As I say, we do undoubtedly know what the conditions are at Port Alberni and neighbouring places, and we know that the costs could not be less.
Their next threat was that we had better be careful or they would take their patients elsewhere. We said, "Go to it, God bless you; but where will you take them?" The nearest place was Nanaimo, which is fifty-six miles away, and it would have been necessary for them to take patients there in an ambulance.

Supply-Indian Affairs
Now suppose they took an Indian woman in an ambulance at a cost of $25-and that would be the minimum-and paid the hospital costs for five or six da}-® in addition to that, and perhaps the ambulance back again at $25, would there be much profit in that transaction? Would it not be better for them to pay the extra two bits a day or whatever it might be and leave them at Port Albemi than to take them in an ambulance at the cost I have mentioned, possibly bringing them back if they were not sufficiently recovered?
The filial and damning argument was, "You had better be careful or we will build a hospital." Build a hospital t-hetel I was agent there for years and I may say that there were never more than 1,800 Indians on the whole west coast at any time and the number has diminished since then. To talk about building a hospital there is nonsense; some people would call it bluff. There are not enough Indians near Alberni to justify the building of a hospital.
Then there was another threat held out- or rather an appeal to our dignity and manhood. We were told that there was only so much money for the Indians and that if we insisted on a higher rate some Indians would have to go without hospitalization. I do not think there is any subject on which you can make a more sympathetic appeal than the question of assistance to Indians. "Lo! the poor Indian" is always good for a sympathetic hearing, and we were positively told or threatened, or whatever you like to call it, that only so much money would be voted for Indians and that if we insisted on our rights some poor Indian would have to go without hopitalization or with less.
These were the arguments that were put up to us, and I leave it to the committee to say what weight there is in any of them. The fact is that we simply wanted a reasonable rate. The inevitable happened. Three of these hospitals, of which there are five in my district in that vicinity, simply said to the department, "We are sorry, but we cannot find it in our mind, or in our doctrine, or in our bible why we in particular should treat Indians for less than cost any more than we should have to treat poor people generally for less than cost, but these Indians are wards of the government." And so finally these people put their foot down in these three hospitals and declared that after a certain date they would not take any more Indian patients except at the regular rate.
Observe, we were not asking for something excessive. Indeed, we were willing to take less than the standard rate. If I went to a hospital to-morrow I would pay more unless I got a
rake-off by paying in advance. But for the fictitious reasons that I have stated, the department wanted to pay us less than the reasonable and standard rate.
Now there is one argument that will be used and I had better combat it at once. The minister will say, "Ah! Destitute people in British Columbia don't pay that; why should we pay more than is paid by the destitute in that province?" The answer is very simple. The British Columbia government pay only $1.75 or something like that. The explanation is this. The $1.75 is not per destitute patient; it is per every patient day in the hospital. Even though a destitute never went there, we would get that low rate for every patient and in return we would have to treat all destitutes for nothing, no matter how many or few, It is a rough method of figuring throughout British Columbia, certainly at any rate in that area. The provincial government pays $1.75 for everyone who is treated, whether black, white, rich or poor, or anything else, and that makes the difference in the rate payable by the ordinary patient. You can understand that $1.75 per destitute patient is very different from $1.75 for every patient.
These hospital boards took it up with their people-in fact it was insisted upon by their constituents, so to speak-and notified the government that they would not take any more of their people except at the standard rates. What did the government do? They immediately climbed right down in the case of three. I have the records right here. They simply said: "Well, we think you have not made out a case; we think we could do it cheaper, and so on, but we cannot help ourselves. We will pay." It was too bad, was it not, asking them to pay the standard rates? In fact it was a little less than the standard rate. They did not give it to everybody. That is what I want to kick about. There are two hospitals, they are in that area run by the Catholics, and like all Catholic hospitals they are run very well indeed. No one has dared breathe a word about the way in which Catholic hospitals are run. I remember once when I was the Indian agent a Presbyterian missionary and his wife were contending with the Catholics about the schools, and there was a certain amount of ill will. The Presbyterian missionary's wife one day sent for me and asked me to call on her at a hospital, and when I went I was surprised to find that .she.was in a Catholic hospital. I said to her, "My, but I am surprised to see you here. I thought there was bad blood between you and the Catholics. How is it that you are here," She said, "Well, Mr. Neill, I am a sick woman and I go where
Supply-Indian Affairs

I get good treatment." That is a true statement. These godly Catholic women are serving there, ministering to the poor, and here we have the department cheaply and meanly trying to take advantage of them. It says to these people, "It does not cost you so much to run your hospital because the nuns work for next to nothing." That is a mighty poor excuse indeed. We have nothing to do with that. It is a well run hospital.
Then the other day I saw that one of them was written to in this manner:
"Come now, show us your costs." Well, the costs may not be very high, because instead of paying certain girls who belong to a union $125 a month, or something like that, they get nuns to work for next to nothing. "Show us your costs and we will think about it." They did not say that to Nanaimo or Port Alberni or Duncan. They simply said: "We will have to accept your price there." And it is a suitable rate. They settled the rate for these three hospitals but they are not giving these other people the rate at all. They bickered and said: "Show us your costs." Perhaps their costs are not comparable to the undenominational union run hospital. Nevertheless these Indians have to be taken care of. I do not think there is any cheaper form of chicanery than to refuse to pay these women the proper rate because they have not the vocal powers, or perhaps do not like to antagonize public sentiment by saying they will not take the patients. Of course that is part of their religion. They do not refuse to take in poor suffering humanity, and apparently the Indian department is taking advantage of them and refusing to pay the standard rates. If the Indian department or the minister can qualify that or dispute it, I shall be glad to hear it, because I have the data here. I have letters that were written; in one place they said they would pay the rates, but they wrote to the Catholic hospital and argued and deprecated the idea, and said, "Show us how you can justify rates like that." Let us hear the answer.

If we are being asked to pay an amount that we think is too much, is it unreasonable to ask hospital authorities to justify their figures? It may be so regarded by some. I do not think it is. All I do know is that we are endeavouring to increase substantially the medical service to the Indians of Canada. The committee knows as well as I do that we have been limited in the amount of money provided by parliament for this purpose. Naturally in those circumstances we have sought to make the money go as far as we could. At the same time I repeat to my hon. friend and to the committee that we want to pay and are will-

Supply-Indian Affairs
ing to pay the costs that are fair and reasonable in all circumstances. I may say this for the information of the committee. It seems clearly evident that in future years the federal government whose wards the Indians are will have to spend considerably more money for Indian hospital treatment than it has spent in the past. I am bound to add that our experience to date indicates that we can provide that treatment just as efficiently, just as completely in hospitals operated by the department as we can in outside hospitals, and there is no question of the comparison in costs. We operate our Indian hospitals substantially lower than what we are paying other hospitals.

The answer is no, so that we need not talk about it any more. Then the minister says, "We have spent considerably more on the treatment of Indians in recent years than we did before." Yes, we have done that. I have spent considerably more on fuel than I did a few years ago, but has that anything to do with it? Is that any precedent at all? How long has the Sardis hospital been running? What was the cost of it? What would be a fair amount for interest and depreciation? These are' merely trifles, I suppose, but leaving all those out the minister says treatment can be given for $2.23 a head.

No, $2.23 was the amount the minister mentioned, not counting these other items, at which we can only guess. Then to
buttress this figure of $2.23 and bring it up to the total of $3.50 the minister says these other items could be included. He is fond of saying, "What are the costs?" I ask him to show us the costs in this case, but he has not the' figures and cannot produce them. I am reminded of the young man just home from university, who thought he knew all about farming. He told the old man, who did not know much about law or books but who knew all about farming, that he was not running the farm right; that if he would do so and so the farm would show a profit. The old man looked over the scheme and said, "Well, son, you have forgotten only one thing; that is the rent, which amounts to $3,000." If you leave out the cost of buildings and the depreciation of course you can show a profit at $2.23. The minister also makes the bald statement that he can substantiate his statement, and in an endeavour to do so he says that hospitals can be operated for less in other provinces. Certainly they can, but I am not talking about other provinces; I am talking about Vancouver island and British Columbia. The minister wants to know the details of hospital costs, but I suggest it is none of his business what they are. He has gone into the market to buy service. If to-morrow I go to a saw mill' to buy lumber and am told that the price is $4,500; if I say, "I do not like that price; I want you to show me the cost of producing the lumber", they will tell me to go somewhere else for it. If I go to the saw mill around the corner, they will give me their price and no more. It is the competitive figure that counts. I have no doubt that in Hawaii or the Polynesian islands it could be done for less, but this is a matter of comparable cost. The Indian department is in the market to buy hospital services for destitute Indians. It cannot take these Indians to Quebec or Norway House or anywhere else; it can only compare the cost with that of some other neighbouring hospital.
The department did not like the cost at Port Albemi, and they said, "We will take them to Nanaimo." Well, if anything the cost there was a little higher, so the department said, "We are spending a lot of money for the hospitalization of Indians, and if we cannot get it at these rates we will have to cut down the hospitalization." I defy the minister to answer this question. Has he ever come to this house and asked for more money for the hospitalization of Indians, or any other aid for the Indians, when it has been denied him? The public are peculiarly sensitive in this regard; they are always willing to vote money for these purposes. If I wanted to do so I could go into several other matters in this
Supply-Indian Affairs

department, but I do not want to hold up the minister too long. The Indian Act is due for revision, and I think the Indian department is due for revision in many respects as well. But this is one matter we have immediately before us. The minister is trying to chisel these poor Catholic women, or perhaps I should not call them poor. They may be poor as far as money goes but they are rich in the grace of God. But we are taking advantage of them because they have no money and they have to yield in the matter; they cannot make a fuss about it and say, "Take your sick somewhere else." The minister says the cost of hospitalization is lower in Quebec, but these Indians cannot be taken to Quebec. I say the Comox hospital and the Campbell River hospital are being unfairly treated; let the minister deny that statement if he can. I do not care what the cost is; it is comparable with Nanaimo, which is seventy miles away, and with Port Alberni, which is one hundred and seventy miles away. Now the minister says this one wants so much and that one wants so much, so we will chisel these nuns in this Catholic hospital. Shame on him.

If my hon. friend seeks to convey the impression that because some very worthy sisters are running a hospital we are trying to shave them down and beat them down, simply because they are unable to advocate their own case, then I say he is giving this committee an impression which is wholly unwarranted and wholly outside the facts.

I suggest that if those in charge of this Catholic organization had been in a position to defy the minister as well, they would

At this late stage I apologize for rising; yet as one who is proud to be an honorary chief of the Indians I do not propose to let this occasion pass without saying something on behalf of these, the least vocal and least pugnacious of all Canadian citizens. I am not going to traverse all the complaints that have been uttered, many of which in my opinion are entirely legitimate; but I do not know of any class of people in Canada more appreciative of the difficulties under which this government are trying to carry on the. affairs of the nation, or more patient and tolerant in spite of the fact, which is quite true, that they are not treated as fairly as the situation warrants or as they deserve.
The minister has spoken about comparative costs of hospitalization. This prompts me to rise and say that on the reserve of the Stony Indians, of which I am an honorary chieftain, there is a very excellent hospital, on which the department is to be congratulated. It would have been difficult indeed to find a finer, neater, better equipped and, until a year ago, better administered hospital than the one on this reserve. But, alas, with the prohibition of the use of oil for heating; because of the cost of heating with coal; because of the difficulty of getting competent medical men and because of the shortage of nurses that very excellent hospital has remained with its doors closed, unless it has been reopened within the last week or two, and the several hundred Indians on that reserve have had no medical attention except in emergency cases, when a doctor from a neighbouring reserve some thirty or forty miles away has made special trips. I am sure this government will-and must perforce-give regard to the appeal of these poor people, many of whom are neglected and may die because of that neglect.
In the very fine memorial sent to the department by the Indian Association of Alberta there are a number of points to which they draw attention. I shall refer to only two, the first of which is the extension of social legislation to the Indians of Canada. In these days we have heard a good deal about social security, and measures we deem necessary and desirable for our Anglo-Saxon community and the other white citizens of Canada. Surely we should not forget our Indian brothers, and accord them the same or approximately the same consideration as we demand for the white population, by way of social security,

Supply-Indian Affairs
old age pensions, care for the blind and hospitalization. Why should they not receive the same care and consideration?
My second point is that I think the whole system of education of our Indian population is one which ought to be carefully scrutinized and reviewed, in the light of the admitted fact that the nomadic life of the Indians in Canada for the most part has ceased to exist except in the northwest territories. I say our educational system, designed to fit the Indians for a modern style of living, is one which needs complete overhauling.
On two other occasions I have referred to this matter. Our educational system for Indians does not fit them for the white man's way of life, and at the same time entirely unfits them for the Indians' way of life.
I pass on to one concluding observation on this subject. Because of the retreat of the furbearing animals along the east slope of the Rocky mountains, the reserve which at one time sufficed to sustain and maintain the Indian population no longer does. If these Indians are to subsist at all they must of necessity revert to grazing and agricultural pursuits. At this time they find themselves with reserves wholly unfitted for these purposes, with the result that they are quite incapable of maintaining themselves. On three different occasions I have urged the department to buy or purchase suitable agricultural and grazing lands upon which the Indians who are now ready and, as they have demonstrated, able and willing to engage in agricultural and grazing pursuits, may employ themselves. But they cannot do this until they have the land.
In this connection I would refer to the Stony reserve, with which I am mostly familiar, and I would say that the land is available. No finer management could be given to an Indian reserve than now exists out there; yet the man who operates it is only a grade 3 clerk in the department, and receiving remuneration as such. I say that is not good enough. We ought to be willing to pay competent men to look after these people, particularly when they have demonstrated their anxiety, their willingness and their ability to profit by any help given to them through education, which would fit them for modern agricultural pursuits.

Item agreed to.
159. Branch administration, $60,183.
