speechtext: As everyone knows, the Indians are wards of the government. They have no vote and no representatives in parliament. As such they are dependent entirely upon a sympathetic government and the sympathy of the members in that branch of government which deals with their affairs.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: If they had the vote they would be much better treated.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
I learn from different sources that Indians in eastern Canada are beginning to take their place in industry and agriculture. The Indians on the prairies, and especially in the northern parts, are still to a great extent sticking to their original habits of living by hunting, trapping and fishing. My information is that on the Pacific coast there are many instances in which they are fitting themselves into the white man's life, working as loggers and fishermen. From everywhere however one hears the same reports as to the desperate conditions of poverty under which they live. With the Indian population on the increase something should be done. It is neither possible nor desirable to treat them perpetually as alien enemies in our midst. Eventually they must be brought to a stage where they can mingle with the whites on terms of equality.
We owe a great deal to the Indians, because we got this great Canada of ours from them. In return we give the non-treaty Indians $5 per year in payment. This seems a very small amount, indeed in exchange for such a wonderful and rich country as Canada is. They are confined to their reserves, and the treatment handed out to them is far from satisfactory.
When the government made its agreement with the Indians they were promised education, medical care and living room as long as the sun shone in the sky, the grass grew and the rivers flowed. None of these promises has been carried out to the satisfaction of the Indians concerned. Changes take place rapidly these days, and since Indians live largely in the past and the present and give very little thought to the morrow, the mere process of making adjustments in methods of living made necessary by present-day conditions is beyond the powers of most of these men of the bush. Having been wards of the government for many years, they have grown accustomed to the care of the Indian Affairs branch. I would invite the committee for a few moments to consider some of the problems with which the Indians are faced. Their education is a difficult problem, but one which should not be incapable of solution if approached with intelligence and sympathy. Mother lore and later folk lore and the experience gained on the trap lines and the fishing grounds is the only education obtained on the reserves. There are two systems in operation, day schools and residential schools. Various religious bodies have cooperated with
Supply-Indian Affairs

the Indian department in establishing residential schools where prices of about $200 per year are paid per pupil. The day schools on the reserves, more especially in the north, are somewhat similar to the one-roomed schools in rural areas. They are up against the fact that the parents of the pupils travel most of the time and they do not believe in education. They must travel to earn their living and regular attendance at the schools suffers in consequence. This does not give the teacher much of a chance no matter how good he or she may be.
The residential school was created to overcome the difficulties experienced by the day schools. In these residential schools the pupils live together during the school year; they are away from their parents on the reserves. The boys and girls selected to go to these boarding schools are checked over by the doctor, that is, the children of parents who are agreeable to letting them go. Only the healthiest of the children are allowed to attend these schools. The children suffering from tuberculosis and other diseases are left at home.
These boys and girls return to the reserves from the residential schools at the age of sixteen years. The boys cannot hunt, trap or fish and the girls cannot keep house. All they have to show for their years at school is a superiority complex and a grouch. The children attending the day schools on the reserves receive the same education as those attending the residential schools and they have the opportunity of learning how to live under conditions existing on the reserves. The boys learn how to hunt, trap, fish and do other things essential to future life in the bush, and the girls learn how to bake bannocks under the primitive methods of cooking prevailing in the bush.
The boys and girls who attend the residential schools learn about agriculture and domestic science in addition to what is taught at the day school. They are well taken care of, they are given good clothing and good food, but in the north country there is no agriculture or no need for domestic science. Those things do not fit into the reserve picture of to-day. These children learn to speak English fluently but their parents speak only the native tongue. They become accustomed to the white man's ways. The girls have learned how to wash and cook by electricity, they have learned how to use many of the devices used in a modern home; the boys have seen modern agricultural implements at work, but in neither case do these children

have the opportunity to use the knowledge they obtain when they return to the environments they left.
I think there is a fault in this system which could be corrected by taking the more promising pupils and giving them further education. The boys could be taught trades in some of our trades schools and the girls could be trained as nurses or for some similar occupation. As men and women they could return as leaders in their communities. People who have studied the Indians assure me that there are some who show great promise and aptitude of becoming leaders in their communities.
The Indian will have to be fitted into our economy, and the sooner we start the better. It is to be hoped that the day is not far distant when every reserve will have its own day school. The best teachers should be encouraged to take up this work and they should be paid and treated so well that they will take on Indian teaching as a life work of a missionary nature. Outstanding Indian students should be helped to work for a university degree. They should have the opportunity to study and train themselves for the complex task of returning to their people who stand bewildered between two totally different cultures.
At the present time we have 260 Indian day schools and 80 Indian residential schools, with 16,876 pupils. From these figures it will be seen that there are not sufficient schools to start with. Indian children of school age number about 26,000, so it will be seen that there are 10,000 Indian children who are receiving no education whatever.
Coming to the matter of health on the Indian reserve, the Indians on the reserves appear to be incapable of protecting themselves against the white man's diseases. The prevalence of tuberculosis in all its forms is nothing less than appalling and largely accounts for the low rate of increase in the Indian population. You will find great numbers of children playing about the camps on the reserves, which indicates a high birth rate, but the departmental statistics show that the death rate is extremely high. Many of those babies and children will never reach maturity and those who do will have a poor chance of escaping the white plague.
In Manitoba, my own province, the Indians comprise only 2-2 per cent of the population, but the deaths from tuberculosis make up 31 per cent of the total deaths from that cause in the province. The reason is obvious. They have not built up immunity against the disease, and lack of intelligent maternal care, unsuitable and insufficient food produce the same

Supply-Indian Affairs
results on an Indian reserve as they do elsewhere. They have no appreciation of the ways of tuberculosis, and they have no knowledge of the dangers of infection or the importance of isolation of infected cases. They know nothing about the accepted methods of sanitation. Infected mothers can be seen nursing their babies on any reserve.
The log shacks used in the winter are so thoroughly chinked that the pure air is completely excluded and they are so overcrowded that they provide the most ideal breeding grounds for the disease. Their minds are so rooted in the past and so suspicious of the motives of the white man that they do not readily accept leadership from their white neighbours, who might be able to inform them as to the best precautions to take against this disease. We find from the departmental report that tuberculosis is the leading cause of death among the Indians, the death rate being ten to thirty times higher than that of the white population.
The great trouble seems to be lack of hospitals. We have approximately 500 beds for the hospitalization of the Indians and from the department we find that two-thirds of these are occupied by T.B. patients. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni this afternoon spoke of sending some of the Indians to Norway House. I have already drawn the attention of the department to the overcrowded conditions there. I said in the house a while ago that it was a sixteen-bed hospital, but I was corrected; it is a twenty-four-bed hospital. In that twenty-four-bed hospital there were forty-three patients when I was there. I saw them myself. So that there is no need for the hon. member to look to Norway H'ouse to help him out with a few beds.
The average number of deaths annually from tuberculosis among the Indians over the last five years is 815. On the basis of three beds per annual death, there are 2,445 treatment beds needed. Because of this the public as a whole is glad that a good 'bit has been done to check tuberculosis among the Indians and would endorse the expansion of the work. This is as it should be, for in spite of what has been done much more needs to be done.
Still, not forgetting that there is a war on, which has taxed the supply of doctors and nurses, we can only look on and make suggestions for the future. What will be most needed will be more frequent visits to isolated reserves by qualified doctors or nurses, or both, and more sanatoria; some in the north as well as some in the south, because it would be hard to convince an Indian at the Pas that he should go to Winnipeg for treatment when he is sick. There should also be health education
in the schools by visiting doctors or nurses and the medical officers should be empowered to compel the attendance of Indians at hospitals or clinics if necessary.
It will be very interesting to hear from the department when the nutrition programme being carried on at Rossville by the resident doctor, along with eminent doctors to the south of us, has been completed. What has been done to assure proper treatment of all Indians in Canada for trachoma and in the matter of nutrition? It is to be hoped that this may be the means of saving the eyesight of many Indians, and the nutritional work being carried on will benefit not only Manitoba but the whole north American continent.
Coming to the economic bleeds of the Indian, little can be done in any direction until a more satisfactory economic basis is laid for their life. As long as we have known the Indians they have depended for the means of subsistence on the bush and the lake. The coming of traders provided employment for them as freighters and enlarged their food supply by providing a market for their furs. These sources of food have gradually been disappearing. The aeroplane is supplanting the canoe for passenger and freight traffic. One makes a journey into the wilderness to-day in comfort in an hour or two which by canoe would require days, to say nothing of mosquitoes and black flies, portages and hard beds on the ground. There again the Indian has lost another source of revenue.
There are still plenty of fish in the lakes but should commercial fishing be encouraged in these lakes the Indians will have again lost a source of food supply. The distance from a market has kept these lakes from being a profitable commercial enterprise, but with the development of the aeroplane the fishing- in these lakes may become profitable.
A great deal could be accomplished by teachers, missionaries and doctors if a community centre could be established in each reserve. If a hall were secured suitable for handicraft studies, health classes, adult classes in English, reading and writing and indoor sports, boy and girl scout movements, it would be a step in the right direction. The Indians, never having had such a thing as a community centre, have no conception of what an important part it could play in their future life. If the government could start something like this on one or two reserves where there is a good leader, I am quite sure that the Indians could be got to cooperate.
The problem of the Indians' livelihood is more complex and difficult, and what must be
Supply-Indian Affairs

done depends in detail on the part of the country under consideration. But one principle unites all requirements, namely this, that while the Indian was free to roam at large he gained his living wandering freely where food could be found; now he is confined to a small area and must get the same living intensively.
One of the bright spots in the Indian situation to-day is the wonderful progress in , establishing the muskrat areas. To Tom Lamb of Moose Lake, Manitoba, a trader, born and living there, we give the credit of being the man to start this first. Having leased an island from the province of Manitoba he carried on his experiments in increasing the rat population.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext: And the beaver population, too.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
It is a wonderful story which no doubt most hon. members know, and I refrain from telling it again except to pay tribute to Mr. Lamb for the great work which he started.
The provincial and federal governments took up the idea and are developing similar schemes for the benefit of the Indians. The results have been excellent, and I have no doubt that further areas are being surveyed with the idea of making the Indian independent and able to earn his own living. The results have been so good that the government no doubt in the future will be able to get back their original investment.
I might say that in connection with this work there were eight beaver taken up to Fisher river, Manitoba, and let loose. When given their freedom three went one way and five went another way. The group of five kept travelling to a point sixty-five miles from where they got their freedom. At this point they built a dam which it would have cost the department $3,500 to construct. There had been a dam surveyed there and these beaver selected the very same spot. I want to appeal to the Minister of Natural Resources to see that all beaver are protected for the next five years. Beaver doing work like that are worth $700 each. The fur or skin of the beaver can never be considered when they can do such work as this. It has been the draining of these marshes, the ruthless trapping by all classes of people that have helped to deplete the northern country. If the beaver are protected and allowed their freedom I am sure it will return dividends a thousand-fold to the government and provide a livelihood for the Indians.

I wish to congratulate the government on the policy they have adopted, both provincial and dominion, to handle the furs for the Indians and to divide this money over into twelve payments. This is going to be a great lesson to the Indians, to learn that by getting their money by the month they will have something to spend every month in the year. As I said before, it has been a failing of the Indian that he does not look to to-morrow. In this way the families of the trappers have known for the first time the security of a small but regular monthly income which still can be supplemented as usual, of course, by casual labour or the sale of hay and wood. I see no reason why the plan should not work in other districts. It protects the Indians and enriches the country at the same time. It is to be hoped that the project will be manned and operated almost entirely by Indians, who are showing a great liking for the work. Something can be done by way of gardens and the patches of soil in the rocks, but the Indians are hunters and eaters of .meat rather than vegetarians and it is difficult to interest them in any form of agriculture. In the same way I believe that forestry and lumbering operations could be handled and developed and probably fisheries on slopes of the Rockies. It will be a matter of guiding them in the principles of preserving the resources entrusted to them so that they may become independent and take their place in Canadian life.
The Indian is not lazy and he will work and work hard at the kind of work that is natural to him. Canada owes at least this much to the people who are the true Canadians.
In closing I have one or two questions to ask the minister. I thought that the hon. member for Comox-jAlberni would have touched on this. The Indians in British Columbia are very much annoyed at having only $4.88 of groceries; that is to say, the Indian who cannot work is allowed $4.88 and no more. If he happens to have a wife and she cannot work he gets $6.30. I want the minister to look into that. That is a disgrace and there must be a slip-up somewhere: I went into this matter with the officials of the department and they have shown nje what a man is allowed, and I know that the men on the reserves are not getting what the department says they should get.
In a recent speech the minister said that there were good agents and bad agents. I hope he will clean out the bad agents and advance the good agents. The Indians in British Columbia have another grievance. In selling their goods they consider that, if I might use a vulgar expression, they are gypped. It takes $3.50 worth of wool to make a sweater. The

Supply-Indian Affairs
Indian has to sell that sweater for $4 and the product is sold in the stores for $7. That should be handled by the government.
I wish to call the attention of the minister to the deplorable conditions that exist in the northwest. I have here a quotation from Dorothy G. Steeves, M.L.A. of British Columbia, who said on her return from a visit:
The church is the most imposing building in Moosehide. Since the missionary went away it is served by a -blind Indian preacher, who is not very adequate, according to his fellow-villagers. On the wall are texts and written portions of the Scriptures, written in the Indian language, but in a different dialect from that used in the village. They cannot read them anyway so no harm is done. It seems symbolical of the stupid and illogical kind of Christianity we mete out to these people.
Here is a cesspool to be cleaned out in Canada and it seems clear that the problem must be attacked by bold and drastic measures. These places of corruption can only be cleansed by proper housing, modern health services, and education. It will not serve to send the children to mission schools, only to return to the conditions of the reservation. We must train hundreds of nurses, doctors and teachers, preferably Indians themselves, to go among these 'people and teach them better living.
May I also direct the attention of the minister to what appeared in the Ottawa Journal of March 24, 1944. I want him to contradict it if it is not true, because it has had a detrimental effect on every reserve in the dominion. It was carried in every newspaper. It dealt with the visit of a bishop to the department; and I quote from it the following:
"Most of the officials of the Indian branch," the letter continued, showed great sympathy but said.nothing could be done without the high approval of a certain Mr. Jackson, executive assistant to Mr. Crerar (Minister of Mines and Resources), and who seems to be somewhat of a half-appointed dictator over anything concerned with Indian welfare."
"Mr. Jackson told me the federal government was thoroughly acquainted with the situation among Indians on the upper Laird river and along the Dease river, and he readily admitted the Indians had been sadly neglected in the past. Yet, Mr. Jackson added, we must first win the war, and if I had any money to spare right now, I would have cannons built with it and let those Indians die rather than spend it at such a time on Indian welfare."

speechtext:
If he is an honorary Indian chief he should have reported this. I refer to two men named Fred Hudson and James Ward
on that reserve. Their numbers are respectively 230 and 398. These men lived on the reserve for eight years. They were put there under the policy of Doctor Scott and now they have an order to leave the reserve by November after living there all that time. They are classed as non-treaty. I would ask the minister to look into that.
Coming back to Manitoba, I have the assurance of the department here that an adult receives for a month:	twenty-four
pounds of flour; six pounds of rolled oats; one pound of baking powder; one pound of tea; two pounds of sugar; three pounds of lard; five pounds of beans, two pounds of rice; one pound of cheese; one dollar's worth of meat or fish; salt and matches. When I was there I saw destitute Indians receiving: twenty pounds of flour; 4 ounces of tea; 4 ounces of bacon; 2 bars of laundry soap per month. There, must be a bad agent somewhere, because the department assures me that the allowance for destitute Indians is as I have stated. In case the minister thinks that I am talking about someone who is not really destitute, in case there is any argument about it, I would refer him to Roderick Robertson, who was receiving that treatment, a blind man-stone blind.
I would ask the minister to be good enough to give to the Indians the answers which he promised eight weeks ago with regard to income tax and being called up for service. He knows that we have 1,S00 now serving in the army. Many of them have volunteered. They are now being called up. The minister promised in his speech on June 7 that he would give the Indians an answer in three weeks, and he has not done it yet.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is no one in this committee who would more gladly see those estimates carried than I, but I think it is necessary to take note of some of the remarks made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. With his general statement I have not very much fault to find. I do not think that his research into the history of the administration of the department has been complete or thorough; but there is no doubt that my hon. friend is genuinely interested in the welfare of the Indians and therefore I welcome his remarks to-day, some of which were constructive and some of which I might say were not very well founded.
On the general question of the welfare of the Indians, there has been, I am glad to note, a decided increase in interest throughout the whole country in the last few years. Not
Supply-Indian Affairs

quite nine years ago when this government took office practically nothing had been done in the way of specialized study of the incidence of tuberculosis among the Indians. At the present time we are spending more than half a million dollars in that particular field. We have made surveys and studies of the problem. Very little had been done in the way of examination into the nutritional side of the foods that the Indians were using. Extensive surveys have been carried out in the last few years in northern Manitoba. Those surveys were made with the assistance and cooperation of the Hudson Bay company and the Millbank institute of New York. The studies were carried out in a definite and scientific way, and very interesting results were achieved. The department has prepared under expert direction a biscuit that contains the important vitamins. These biscuits are distributed particularly for the use of children in the schools. Much more can be done in that direction.
The Indians, particularly in the northern parts of the provinces, are the ones who have suffered and are suffering the most. Their mode of livelihood is practically gone. What the hon. member for Selkirk said is quite true, namely, that the mode of life of the Indian has changed greatly. These changes have been thrust upon them. They have seen their trapping grounds go and their means of livelihood disappear. One of the things that I initiated-and I take considerable pride in it-when I came into the department was a study of the possibilities of the restoration of fur-bearing animals in the northern parts of those provinces. I am not going to tell the story to-day. Hon. members of the committee who are interested in it will find it pretty well set out in the reports of the reconstruction committee. Officers of the department appeared before the committee and gave detailed information as to what had been achieved in that direction. I am quite confident that by wise policies-if we get the cooperation of the provinces, and we are getting it in a very large way indeed-the fur-bearing animals can be brought back, and we shall have a market for fur in the future that will afford these people a fair standard of living. The department is spending a good deal of money, and has spent a good deal over the last several years on this work; but it is perhaps the most useful expenditure that the department has made.
On the general question of Indian administration in Canada, there is no doubt in my mind that the whole Indian Act needs a thorough revision. That was apparent to me

as long as five or six years ago. The departmental officials have been studying the act with a view to rewriting it and getting a new act. After all, the present act was passed many years ago when the problems of Indian administration were wholly different from what they are to-day. I hope that when the war is over and the preoccupations that engage the time of parliament and of members disappear with it, a revision of the Indian Act can be undertaken. It certainly should have the most serious consideration that can be given to it by the next parliament.
I do not know that I have very much more to add. I do not despair of the Indian problem. I admit that there is a problem. With improvements in sanitation, in medical care, in nutrition and ways of life the increase in the Indian population will accelerate year by year. It is simply a matter of common sense that the administration of Indian affairs take note of that fact and try by wise policy not only to give the Indians the means of becoming self-supporting but to bring about in his way of thinking, in his psychology, a desire on the part of the Indian to make himself self-supporting and become a full-fledged citizen of the country. These are problems that must be dealt with in the future. I wish merely to mention them briefly to-day in the consideration of those estimates.

I am sorry. My hon.
friend brought up two or three matters. If I understood him aright he gave an instance where an Indian paid $3.50 for wool in British Columbia, sold the product for $4 and it was retailed in the stores at $7. I should be very glad if my hon. friend would give the particulars of his information to the department, because I am advised that the sale of the products of the Indians-and it is substantial in quantity-is carefully watched by the Indian administration in British Columbia. That certainly is the case with fur in northern Manitoba.
My hon. friend was really not on very good ground when he did this. He read an extract from the Ottawa Journal of some day in March last purporting to give a statement by Bishop Coudert in Edmonton, I think it was, in which serious reflections were made on the Indian administration. I gave the press a statement about the matter. It may have escaped the notice of my hon. friend. Bishop Coudert was not correctly reported. When I read his statements it was quite evident that he had not been correctly reported. I deplore the practice of taking an article that appears

Supply-Indian Affairs
in a newspaper and placing it on the pages of Hansard as if were fact. If my hon. friend had made inquiry of myself or of the department he could have been satisfied on that point.	,

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Of course there has been a serious situation in the Yukon and the area from which the bishop comes, as well as in other parts of Canada. It has been difficult to get qualified medical men and nurses because in several instances they have not been available to send to these territories.
My hon. friend also referred to the case of two individuals in Alberta who he alleged were Indians and who had been removed from the Indian rolls; I think their names were Ward and Hodgson, on the Hobbema Indian reserve in Alberta. The fact of the matter is that these two persons were not Indians under the Indian Act, although they had come to live on the reserve. Years ago in the settlement they both accepted scrip, but they were halfbreeds. I do not wish to criticize past administrations, but these people were living on the reserve and were regarded as Indians, although as a matter of fact they were not Indians under the Indian Act. The department has a serious trust in that respect. The Indians are wards of the federal government, and that wardship is clearly set out in the Indian Act. If those who are not Indians, for instance half-breeds, are allowed to be treated as Indians, to share in band funds and other Indian property, then it is a distinct violation of the trust; and if the department permitted these people who are not Indians under the act to continue to participate in Indian benefits, the department would be leaving itself in a very wrong position indeed, wrong not only morally but legally. I do not know if my hon. friend was interested in any other point.

speechtext:
I should like to add a
word to what my colleague has said. I am very glad to hear the minister say that the revision of the Indian Act is under consideration, and I hope when that revision is under way, we may make some small contribution toward remedying some of the defects that have existed in the past. My plea is that the Indians be given an opportunity to make their own contribution to Canadian life, and I believe one of the first things that will have to be done is to give them some effective means of making their voice heard by the Canadian people. We know of things that have happened since this war began. The conscription of these men off Indian reserves, for instance, is something which I should say has hurt the attitude of the Indians toward the people of Canada. If these people had been taken into the confidence of the officials of the government, or if they had felt themselves worthy of even a vote in this country, then I think they would not have considered themselves mistreated. They have made several pleas to the government as to the status of the Indians with respect to being subject to conscription; and although we are now in the fifth year of the war, and the war is almost over, there has been nothing in the way of a satisfactory statement from the government which would contribute to a settlement of the matter. So that in the interval before the act is brought up for revision, which I hope will be next session, I trust that the officials of the department and the minister will study what our sister dominion of New Zealand has done in connection with the
Supply-Indian Affairs

Maoris. In New Zealand they have Maori representatives sitting in the house of representatives. These people are educated; among them are doctors, lawyers and scholars, taking their place in the life of the community, given an opportunity to express themselves and make their contribution in a real way.
I maintain that the Indians of North, America can show their white brothers many things that are wrong even in our economic set-up. I believe that the government policy of segregating these people on reserves has been wrong. Probably under the Indian Act the hands of the government are tied but, as the minister admits, the economic conditions on these reserves are far different to-day from what they were in the past. The opportunity to make a living does not now exist. I have been on these reserves; I have seen these Indians putting in their crops year after year. I have seen crop failures on those lands, and after three or four years the Indians began to wonder what it was all about. They are not all farmers; and I hope the minister has something more in mind than simply fur farming as a means of providing an economic lived-in od for these people. The Indians of this country have proved themselves skilled workers; they have become mechanics, steel workers and so on. They have various talents, just as their white brothers have. Their women make good nurses, teachers and social workers. They have proved themselves. They have ability and culture, but they have no opportunity to express themselves. Unfortunately, their economic conditions do not permit them even to improve their health standards. The minister, who has referred to the nutritional report from northern Manitoba, must know that the health condition of the Indians in Canada is far from satisfactory.
What my colleague has said is quite true. These thirty-eight doctors, many of whom are only on part time, are catering to about 38,000 Indians. Then, hospital and other medical services must be supplied. It is my submission that medical services for Indians, and health conditions among them must be cleared up, first of all. Proper nutritional standards must be maintained among these people, and they should be taught to take care of themselves.
Had the government at Ottawa done what was done in New Zealand, our Indians could have formed themselves into a regiment of their own. Some of them could have become leaders, and from among them 'Indian officers could have been trained. That would have meant much to these people. The fact is,

however, that the training they have received in Canada has been scarcely sufficient to render them available as officer material.
Indians have a great contribution to make. They are honest and, if given a chance, industrious. My colleague has said that next year when amendments are made to the Indian Act every effort should be made to straighten out the difficulties, and in doing so the cooperation of this group would be assured. Meantime something more effective should be done to remedy existing conditions.

I do not think it would be fair to let the item pass without tendering a word of compliment to the minister. From what one has heard to-day it might be thought that the department had been remiss in its duty. I know, of course, that improvements could be made, but I also know, after making an investigation into Indian affairs wider than has been made by most members, that the department, under the present minister, has advanced the position of the Indians. On the occasions I have made investigations in the last six or eight years, in respect of about twenty-five reservations, I have made a compilation of what in my opinion should be done, and while doing this I have seen considerable improvement in the position now occupied by the Indians in Canada.
Right along I have had in mind asking in due course for the setting up of a royal commission to thoroughly investigate Indian affairs in this country. Let it be understood that I am not finding fault with departmental officials. What I have in view is to improve the Indian set-up from beginning to end.
I have made surveys of these reservations -not just one or two of them, but no less than twenty-five, many of which were in remote areas. And this summer I am going to much more remote areas. I can say that since the present minister has taken control of the Indian affairs branch conditions have greatly improved, but there is room for more improvement.
Someone has referred to Indian representation, and with what was said I agree. In my view the time has come when they should be given representation. It has been pointed out that the Maoris have it. That is so, but they are an altogether different race from our Indians. Then, I believe the South African government has given representation to the Kaffirs to the extent of four members. So that when the minister looks into the matter he may come forward with a programme which will carry out what has been suggested by hon.

Supply-Indian Affairs
members to my left re Indian representation.
May I congratulate the hon. gentleman with the burr, the hon. member for Selkirk. Certainly he deserves credit for the research he has made in respect of the Indians. Then, too, the hon. member for Yorkton is deserving of commendation. These men have interested themselves in the problem of helping the Indians. The minister was right when he said it has been more particularly in the last few years-I am sure it was after I came to the House of Commons-that the branch has advanced the position of the Indians in Canada. It must be given credit for all it has done, and should be encouraged to go much farther.

Furthermore, my hon. friend has no right to attack the director. He has not so far attacked him to-day but he did on a previous occasion. I take full responsibility for what appeared in The Legionary, because the director spoke to me before the article was sent, and I authorized him to send it because I thought it was adding to the sum total of information on this question.

Supply-Soldier Settlement
I do not care what my hon. friend may say about myself. He is free to criticize me in any way he likes, and I am free to have my opinion of his criticism, but I think that it is scarcely fair for a member of this house to make an attack on an officer of this government, and, may I say, a very successful officer. I want to add this, that the ex-soldiers of the great war and the soldiers of the present war have no better friend in this country than the gentleman who is director of the veterans' land settlement, and I will stand by that statement in this house or anywhere else despite anything my hon. friend may say.
It may be of interest to the committee, because this question has created some controversy in the country if I give a few figures. This problem of giving clear title to soldiers of the last war is not one that can be lightly embarked upon. That is why I stated a moment ago that- we have not yet had time to consider fully the request of the delegation that came here. There are many aspects of that question which have to be considered.
I think it will be of interest to the committee to know that in the last five years since 1939 the total instalments due under soldier settlement sales were in round figures $5,230,000. Total payments made on those instalments due were $4,506,000. The prepayments made voluntarily, without any request or suggestion from the department, 'by these ex-soldiers who my hon. friend states were in a desperate plight and should therefore get free title to their land, amounted to $1,293,000. Furthermore, in the last five years 1,648 of these old soldiers have earned clear title to their land and have received clear title; and of those 1,648, 689 were granted1 clear title in the last fiscal year. These are facts that I wish to put before the committee because I do not wish it to get a wrong view of this whole matter.

speechtext:
I am glad that the minister is feeling the pinch of his sins. He has already envisioned what I am going to say on this occasion. His statement just now reminds me of what the old politician said when he was talking to a young man about to embark on a political career. He said, "When you have something worth while to tell you do not have to talk so loud, but when you have a poor case, yell like hell." I think the minister commenced to yell a little early.
I have referred on other occasions to this statement that appeared in that magazine. I did not have an opportunity at that time to say very much about it, but I felt, as soon as the matter was brought to my attention, that
I should make some objection to the article. I am objecting to it to-day. I say that it is a bitter pill and it would not go down very well if it had been printed, unaccompanied, entirely by itself. But in order that it might go down good we find that on the left-hand corner of the same page on which this statement appears there is a picture of the Governor General presenting to Carole Louise Hooey, of Toronto, the Distinguished Flying Cross won by her father, and she is proudly holding it in her hand. On the other side of the page is the winner of the Victoria Cross whom we had the pleasure of meeting in Ottawa a little over a month ago, Major Paul Triquet, V.C. That is a very nice setting for an article which is condemned from one end of Canada to the other, regardless of any statement which the minister or the director may make. Anything I have to say I am saying direct to the minister and to his director who is here. I am saying it in the house. I am not sending it to any magazine. The minister and the director are both here to question anything I may have to say.
I am now going to read the article and comment upon it as I go along. The article is headed, "Soldiers Settlement", by Gordon Murchison, director, Soldier Settlement and Veterans' Land Act. It is found on pages 10 and 11 of the May issue of The Legionary and says:
During the past several months a number of representations have been received by my minister, the Honourable T. A. Crerar, and by myself from or on behalf of an organization formed in Saskatoon last summer and known as the Soldier Settlers Association.
In case anyone should be in doubt about it, I want to say that other similar organizations have been in existence for a number of years. This is a brief from one that has been in existence since 1938. So that the organization ' which came to life in Saskatoon is not new by any means.
The article goes on :
This association has declared its policy by a resolution, part of which calls for the cancellation of all unpaid balances due or accruing in the agreements between soldier settlers and the director representing the dominion government. I understand the dominion executive of the Canadian Legion has received similar representations, and so that the situation from the standpoint of the government and the administration may be placed fairly before the Canadian Legion and the readers of The Legionary, the Honourable Mr. Crerar has authorized me to furnish you with an official statement.
First of all there is lack of evidence that the resolution and representations above referred to reflect the serious views of more than 10 per cent of soldier settlers, and, knowing the situation as I do, I am sure the great majority of the remaining 90 per cent
Supply-Soldier Settlement

must feel somewhat humiliated by the publicity being circulated by the few who for reasons best known to themselves and their friends endeavour to paint a dark and gloomy picture. What are the facts?
I question the figures given by the director when he says that he doubts that the resolution reflects the views of more than ten per cent of the soldier settlers. I say definitely that that is not correct. The article goes on:
I do not think that it is necessary to go further back than 1930 to review this situation in any detail. It is common knowledge that prior to 1930 successive governments had provided the means for the easement of soldier settlers' accounts tb an aggregate of several millions by way of interest remissions, reductions in the cost price of live stock and land revaluation. In 1930 there was a horizontal reduction of 30 per cent in the indebtedness of every soldier settler in Canada on record at that time. This particular write-off totalled $11,302,127.56.
During the difficult days of the thirties when farm revenue reached an all-time low due to price or climatic factors, soldier settlers-like tens of thousands of other farmers-were unable to meet contract indebtedness of one kind and another. A year's interest charges were cancelled in 1932 totalling $1,308,492.16, and commencing the following year a bonus plan was introduced which provided for a credit of $2 for every $1 .paid on matured instalments. This arrangement existed for a period of five years. Its value to the settlers concerned totalled $3,426,293.43.
Going over that paragraph, let me say that in 1932, the year in which these interest .payments were cancelled, the farmers of Canada received five per cent of the national income. I ask the minister and the director, how in the world can any farmer pay interest when they receive only such a small proportion of the national income? It is utterly impossible and the condition was entirely man-made.
Again we come to the credit of $2 for every $1 paid on the soldier's indebtedness. This benefited only those who had money to pay on their debts; the man who had no money received no benefit from that reduction. When he got this legislation through the house doing away with the two for one bonus in 1938 the Minister of Mines and Resources did not have the support of one member of any party, but the policy of the government was put into effect.
The article continues:
In 1935 the Farmers Creditors' Arrangement Act came into force, and soldier settlers 'had the same rights under the act as other farmers. Up to the end of 1937 only a limited number of soldier settlers availed themselves of this right, but commencing in 1938 no fewer than 3,504 settlers had their affairs adjusted-

May I say a word to the committee with reference to the question of adjournment. I believe hon. members are pretty well agreed that it should be possible to conclude the business of this part of the session before the day is over, but it may require something in the way of cooperation between the different parties. There is always difficulty in winding up the business of parliament before adjournment where bills require royal assent. In the first place, arrangements have to be made for the presence of the deputy of the governor general at a particular hour. This necessitates some notice. The other house must also assemble in advance. This procedure necessitates, in an endeavour to make the necessary arrangements, some preliminary and tentative undertakings on the part of the Prime Minister.
If there are any matters which hon. members think may involve discussion perhaps they could be mentioned at once so that they might be taken up before other items are proceeded with. If, however, the discussion is likely to be the regular discussion that is had on different items-and there are only comparatively few items left-there should be little difficulty in getting through fairly early to-night.
I might say that in the old days in this house, I have frequently known the house to sit until daybreak in order to conclude its business, and have seen that done two or three nights in succession. I take a little pride in the fact that I was the first one to bring forward in this house the proposal to adopt the rule that the sittings should conclude at eleven o'clock in the evening. That is a rule which is applicable from day to day throughout the entire session. However, in winding up the business of the house I think we must ask hon. members to cooperate with the government in seeking some finality, not for the advantage of anyone but for the convenience of all.
What I would suggest is that the house might agree to continue its sitting until seven o'clock, and meet again at eight, with the understanding that we would continue in session until business is conchided. If that were agreeable I should be very thankful and I am sure all hon. members would appreciate such a decision in almost equal measure. It would be most unfortunate, I suggest, if we had to continue over into another day or until very late to-night. If the house were agreeable I would suggest that we continue until seven and resume at eight.

speechtext: May I say that if there is anything the hon. member feels is being neglected or anything that is being overlooked, which should be discussed, I wholly withdraw what I have expressed in the way of a request. But simply to keep parliament going on from day to day, after the longest session this house has had in many years and where matters have been as far advanced as they have been in this session, creates I think a situation all aspects of which should be considered. My hon, friend mentions finance estimates. The estimates of the finance department have been before the house for months. We have discussed financial matters at great length throughout the entire session. If there is something in the estimates of the minister that is contentious we might be told about it at once so that the item could be brought on for discussion immediately. It does not follow that because sums of money are voted quickly members have not had an opportunity to consider the items to which they relate. I point this out only because I do not wish the government to be put in a false light before the country, while on the other hand I do desire, as leader of the government, to do all I can to accommodate the great majority if not all of the members of the house. To save public expense and the necessity of another day or two of sitting, if that involves having made now one or two addresses that might be delivered another day, the house might, I think, adopt the suggestion I have offered.

We have attempted to cooperate as best we could toward the closing of the session. I believe I made it clear on a previous occasion that so far as we are concerned it is a question of going as long as it is necessary in order to get the business of parliament done. There is a tendency sometimes to extend the sittings of the house, perhaps unconsciously and thoughtlessly, and sometimes not to the great advantage of the national interest.
My hon. friend mentioned amounts that were involved. I have never said -this in the house before, but I shall say it now because, to my mind, the amount of money involved is a wholly improper basis of assessing the extent to which time should be consumed in debates on estimates. Sometimes some of the smallest items involve the biggest principles. In the largest amounts sometimes there is very little to do but let them go through, because they have been properly understood by the house and the house is desirous of seeing them go through without needless delay.
I have seen parliament criticized wrongly by some outside and sometimes by hon. members inside because large amounts have gone through in a few minutes. That gives the public a wrong impression; it confuses the public mind when they are not aware of the exact situation with respect to estimates of this kind.
I rose to say that I hope no one outside will feel that when estimates are going through at this time, particularly when we consider that the very same principles have been debated on the war appropriation bill at considerable length, they are going through without being properly considered. If there were to be any curtailment of a real character at this time I would not agree to cooperate with the government even with respect to a matter of this kind. It is only because I believe that we have practically completed a proper study of these matters so far as the public is concerned
Supply-Soldier Settlement

that I am desirous of recording myself and my party as being ready to cooperate to have the session closed to-night if possible.
I may say to the Prime Minister that I think with one or two items in the case of pensions and national health and one item in legislation in which I am specially interested which should only take a few moments, there is, from my point of view, nothing much more, that has to be considered at any length. Therefore I wish to put myself on record in respect of this matter at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, had I been
allowed to continue I believe that I would have been finished by this time and the committee would have had the pleasure of hearing the pleasant voice of the minister instead of this rasping voice of mine. I w-as stating that:
... no fewer than 3,504 settlers had their affairs adjusted by total write-offs under this act of $6,754,851.28, made up of $3,281,990.92 in interest charges and $3,472,860.36 in reductions of principal. In the course of adjustment operations under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act extending over a period of approximately six years it was inevitable that some inequality of treatment would occur, either because the deterioration which had taken place was not fully taken into account or because in the alternative unsatisfactory farming conditions continued beyond reasonable expectations. Mainly, however, the break in the long spell of drought conditions and improved farm revenue closely synchronized with the outbreak of the war in 1939. There were some local exceptions to this, but that was the general situation.
During the early summer of 1942 a select committee of the House of Commons made inquiry into the affairs of soldier settlers as a result of which the government by executive order authorized the director on application by settlers to review the accounts of soldier settlers who continued to be faced with an unduly heavy burden, and, with the approval of the treasury board, to reduce these accounts to reasonable levels. Adjustments under this heading are now nearing completion, and it is estimated that approximately 1,600 soldier settlers, principally in Saskatchewan and Alberta, will benefit to a total of approximately $1,075,000. In 1,336 cases adjusted to date the reduction in debt has totalled $841,437.37.
Let me point out 'here, since the director neglected to do so, that in most cases those settlers have been slaves of this economic system, slaves of climatic conditions and other things for the past twenty-five years. Under the agreement they are allowed to continue for at least another twenty years. This means that a number of those settlers will be eighty to- ninety years old by the time they
[Mr. Graydon.j
have their contract completed, provided that conditions allow them to complete them at that time.
There is another recommendation that was made by the committee, I believe, and the director also neglected to give it, namely, that the settler should have a certain equity in his land after this adjustment is made. That equity, I believe, exceeded fifty per cent. I am not sure about that. If I am not correct in that impression the minister can correct me a little later on.
I continue with the article, under the heading of "A New Situation":
There is some realism about these extensive adjustments referred to above which no amount of argument can dispel, and there is abundant evidence that the realistic manner in which these adjustments were carried out, coupled with the general improvement in farming conditions. have, in fact brought about an entirely new situation.
Let me point out that improvements in farming conditions are not entirely responsible for the payments that have been made on soldier settlers' contracts.
It is generally agreed that a number of sons and daughters of those settlers are in the service, and a lot of their money has been used up to make good the contracts of their fathers who fought in the last war. It is also recognized by those who want to be fair that a number of sons and daughters of those same settlers took employment in munition factories and other places, and for that reason they have been able to make payments on their father's farms; otherwise we would have an entirely different situation. It took another war to bring about prosperity so that a small percentage of the settlers could claim titles to their land.
I continue:
What is the new record of soldier settlers in meeting the terms of their agreements during the past few years? I set out below the official record, which furnishes factual evidence that soldier settlers generally are the kind of people I have always known them to be-honest, reliable citizens who believe in fair play and the payment of their honest obligations]
May I pause for a moment. I agree entirely with that. I believe those soldier settlers are honest to the last man, but I also believe that they were saddled with conditions, because of an improvised land scheme which made it impossible for them to live up to the terms of their contract.
I continue with the article:
1.	In the fiscal year ending March 31, 1942, 7.314 soldier settlers had current instalments due totalling $1,039,050.75. Six thousand three hundred and four of these settlers paid $957,227.59 or 92 per cent of the current instalments due. and 1.504 of them made repayments of an additional $213,520,50.

Supply-Soldier Settlement
2.	In the fiscal year ending March 31, 1943, 6,860 soldier settlers had current instalments due totalling $983,103.54. Five thousand five hundred and fourteen of these settlers paid $841,110.25 or 85 per cent of the current instalments due, and 1,448 of them made prepayments of an additional $257,754.37.
3.	In the fiscal year which ended March 31. 1944, 6,364 soldier settlers had current instalments due totalling $860,871.83. To February 29, of this year, 5,612 of these settlers had paid $991,508.04 or 115-7 per cent of the current instalments due, and 2.066 of them had made prepayments of an additional $443,619.39.
4.	This record of performance means that soldier settlers are generally taking advantage of conditions and paying off their indebtedness. Since the outbreak of war, 1,528 of them have retired their loans in full and have secured the titles to their farms, and as time goes on the number will steadily increase.
I must give another fact that is not mentioned by the director in his article; that is, that a great deal of pressure has been applied on these settlers to make them pay up. A number of these men who have joined up for the second time, offering their all on the altar of sacrifice, as the result of an order in council have had to contribute a certain percentage of their dependents' allowance to be applied on their debt to the soldier settlement board. This may be denied once again as it was denied previously, on May 23. If that denial should be made this afternoon I should like to refer the minister to a particular case, M^42517, Corporal C. J. Lefley. I do not think the minister will take the trouble to investigate this case, however, because he wjll find that the result is against him. In this family there are eight children, six of whom are going to school and two of whom are too young to go to school. A short time ago their father was employed at the internment camp at Lethbridge, and $13 a month is being deducted from the dependents' allowance of that family to clear off the soldier settler's debt to the board. These facts were not given to the country by the director, and I think it only fair that they should be mentioned now. I continue reading:
In the face of the above factual information, what is the logic behind the argument that soldier settlers of record to-day should have their contract indebtedness cancelled, which means in effect legislation into ownership? Do the sponsors of the petition believe that this would be the end of the matter? Do they think for a moment that those who have paid for their farms, and all those who are meeting the terms of their agreements in full and on time or are prepaying their agreements, would stand quietly by and make no demand for a refund? I have received direct assurances that such demands would be made.
In all the discussions I have had concerning this matter with soldier settlers and others I have met only two people, namely the
Minister of Mines and Resources and the director, who have taken this stand. I question here the statement that a number of these men have stated that demands would be made for refunds. In order to obtain definite information I placed upon the order paper the following questions:
1.	From January 1, 1943, to May 31, 1944, how many requests from, (a) organizations; (b) individuals, have been received by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Mines and
. Resources, the director of soldier settlement and Veterans' Land Act, or any other department of the government, asking that veterans of great war one who now hold land under contract with the soldier settlement board be given titles without further payments?
The answer given was:
(a) 10; (b) 186 soldier settlers-60 other individuals.
My second question, on which I had hoped to get some information, although I was not disappointed when I did not get it, was
2.	During the same period, how many letters or other communications wTere received by the director or other departments of the government stating that if clear titles, as above requested, were granted, requests for refunds by those who have already paid up or are continuing to make payments, -would be made?
In asking that question I desired to get the names and addresses of those who had made such representations, with the intention of writing those people and finding out if they had actually done so and, if so, what was the basis for their argument. The answer was:
No record maintained. Representations have been made in confidence to the director and members of his staff.
If that information is available it should be produced so that we may know what is being done. The third question was:
3.	What are the names and addresses of those from whom such letters and communications have been received?
The answer is:
Answered by No. 2.
I believe that questionnaire will take care of itself. Now I read the last paragraph of this article, under the heading "No Change":
In conclusion I am authorized to say that the proposal is not deemed to be in the public interest and, consequently, it is not being entertained by the government. Therefore, the best advice I can offer to the soldier settlers concerned is to get into step with those who manifestly prefer securing title to their farms by complying with the terms of their agreements.
That information was given before the convention was held, and apparently before the minister and his committee had a chance to discuss the matter, so that I do not know whether the government is behind this. I hope not, because I am quite satisfied that a
Supply-Soldier Settlement

very high percentage of the members of the cabinet are favourable to cleaning up the mistakes of the old soldier settlement board before embarking upon the new programme under the Veterans' Land Act. Two months ago to-day, on June 14, I went into this matter in detail and placed quite a number of figures on record. To-day I am going to use just a few of those figures. The total number of men settled after the last war was 25,017. The total amount advanced by the government was $109,034,331. The total amount of principal repaid, up to March 31, 1944, was $50,507,493.20 and the total interest paid to the same date was $25,381,060.13. That covered the payments by soldier settlers and civilians who later bought the land, I might add in a number of cases at much less than half the original price to the soldier settler. I believe this is sufficient to indicate that the men were settled on that land originally with a load they could never hope to carry under the conditions to which they were subjected. In the case of soldier settlers the principal cancelled, under five or six different schemes, was $24,867,637.64, and the interest cancelled amounted to $19,234,239.77. That made a total cancellation of principal and interest of $44,101,877.41.
The cost of administration-and this is of interest to the whole country and was not given by the director in his article in The Legionary

was $27,346,763.64, making a total including cancellation of principal and interest and administration of $71,442,641.05. At the end of March, 1944, which was the end of the last fiscal year, the soldier settlers owed the government $7,715,954.01. At that time, in spite of the figures given by the minister today in regard to arrears, and the figures mentioned by the director in his article in The Legionary, there were arrears on account of soldier settlers amounting to $1,054,269.30. At that time we had remaining on the land some 6,153 of these settlers. Here also, in spite of the figures given to-day by the minister, it is interesting to note that up to the end of March of this year only a little over 4,000 of these 25,017 settlers had obtained title to their land, so that the general picture is not nearly so bright as the minister would have the committee believe. At this time, twenty-five years after fhe inception of the scheme, we still have 6,153 of these settlers under contract with the settlement board. That is approximately twenty-five per cent of the original number of settlers after twenty-five years of persecution. The minister did admit on one occasion that the scheme was a hastily improvised one. I have claimed, and still claim, that the land, implements and stock
[Mr. Fair. I
were bought at highly inflated prices, and that grain and other products since that time have been down to all-time low prices. Yet the settlers were still expected to make payments, and live up to the terms of their contracts. The average original debt of the settlers was $4,358.40. At the end of March of this year we found that- on an average they still owed $1,254, or twenty-nine per cent of the original amount. This is the figure, even after taking into consideration the cancellation of some $44,000,000. That is not a very bright picture. This amount of $1,254 is equal to approximately twenty-nine per cent of the original debt.
Another matter has not been touched upon before, one which I think I should mention at this time. I have in mind the soldiers who will come back from this war, and who will operate under the Veterans' Land Act. That soldier will have a grant of thirty-nine per cent of the total amount of his loan. I repeat that the soldier settler under the present Veterans' Land Act, if he takes full advantage of the legislation, will have a free grant of $2,320, which is equal to thirty-nine per cent of the amount of his loan. Under the old scheme there was no grant available, but we did have cancellations because of a faulty set-up.
I would ask the minister and the government to take these matters into consideration. I would also ask them to consider the fact that under the old act the settlers were charged five per cent on current loans and seven per cent on past-due accounts. So that in a very large ' percentage of cases the old soldier settlers from the first great war were paying twice the amount of interest that the veterans from this war will have to pay, because most of the payments of the old soldier settlers were in arrears.
I say to-day, as I said before, that 3i per cent is still too high a rate. So that the veterans from the first great war were charged more than twice what they should have been charged. I do not know whether I should go much farther in this connection. I believe the government is well aware of all the conditions. After this article had been published in The Legionary, and after the writer had made this trip to the west coast, we find a committee was set up out there, and that that committee framed a resolution. The resolution did not come before the convention. I do not know why. There were, however, some other resolutions which I understand were left over. This is the resolution:
Whereas any civilian at the age of 70 years, and burnt-out veterans at the age of 60 years, are presumed to be past the age where they may be expected to be self-supporting;
And whereas settlers under the Soldier Settlement Act have in many eases been resident

Supply-Soldier Settlement
on their holdings for a quarter of a century and are fast approaching the age -when they will be incapable of self-support;
And whereas under the new land act the new veteran is only called upon to pay 3J ,per cent interest, aqd after ten years' residence 25 per cent of his indebtedness is cancelled;
And whereas the soldier under the Soldier Settlement Act has had to pay, and is still paying 5 per cent interest;
Therefore be it resolved that, in order to be fair to our aging veterans and to bring the old and the new settlement acts more into line, the dominion government be asked to readjust the debts of the 6,153 original soldier settlers who have not paid for their lands, such readjustment to take into consideration the difference in interest rates charged under the said acts; and that following such readjustment the government be further asked to cancel the debts of those -original soldier settlers whose debt has been, or may hereafter be, reduced to 25 per cent of the original purchase price or the reduced purchase price, and that the interest rate to such veterans be reduced to 3J per cent.
This is signed by:
Mr. R. H. Inglis, Alberta.
Mr. B. V. Cameron. Ontario,
Mr. J. J. Macintosh, N.S.
Mr. G. A. Lauman, Manitoba,
Mr. George Noble, Quebec,
Mr. A. C. Stewart, Saskatchewan.
Mr. H. W. Ellis, British Columbia.
And the footnote says;
The committee wish to thank the comrades whose names appear below for their assistance in framing this resolution:
Mr. A. J. Sibley, North Battleford, Saskatchewan,
Mr. F. C. Highfield, Grandview, Manitoba.
Mr. A. R. Elridge. Ladner, British Columbia.
The two former were members of the delegation which visited this house recently.

speechtext:
The effort was entirely a voluntary one. Good care was taken to see that these men did not settle where they could effect organization, with the result that it was not possible to reach a number of them. I think the minister realizes that the petition was circulated during the winter months, and that those in charge of the petition had no records with respect to soldier settlers. However, if he will be good enough at a later date to give me a list of those settlers I believe I can prove to him that more than ten per cent -perhaps more than ninety per cent-of those soldier settlers are interested in getting clear titles. The fact that not more than 200 signed the petition is no indication whatsoever of the number who are in favour, because if the petition was not presented to them their names could not be there. When those settlers go to a meeting they have to travel at their own expense. Sometimes they have to go by team and sleigh. They are not privileged, as are government officials, to travel at government expense, and to live in the best hotels in the country while doing government business.
I am making one final appeal to-day to the government, although I do not know whether there is any use in making it to the Minister of Mines and Resources, because he has told me that there will be so much complaint, and I know from his attitude that he will not see that those titles are granted. I am sorry he has taken that stand. I know he is familiar with conditions, from practical experience. I point out to him. that the government is now about to embark upon another scheme connected with men coming back from this war who have offered their all on the altar of sacrifice. If the government is interested in the success of this new scheme, then I say, "For heaven's sake clean up the slums in the old one."
It will require $7,715,000 as at March 31 last to do this job. By doing that, the government will get away from the cost of administration, which cost has been so heavy in the past. Up to March 31 of this year administration costs as far as soldier settlers are concerned ran up to $27,340,763. Those are millions of the taxpayers' money, including taxes paid by those same soldier settlers. And there will be plenty of taxes still to be paid for the new programme. So that I am
Supply-Soldier Settlement

sorry the government has not seen fit to take more interest in the soldier settlers from the last war. I might say here that those old settlers say that it does not make so much difference to them, because it is only a matter of time until they will be pushed off the land, or occupying their six feet of mother earth. But they are interested in the success of the scheme under the Veterans' Land Act. I would also ask the government, however, to give clear title, without any further delay.
Twenty-nine per cent of the original amount involved still remains unpaid, after deductions. A number of the settlers are too old to work the land, and they certainly have suffered plenty in the past. The conditions which caused that suffering are man-made. Why continue man-made conditions and persecutions of those people to-day? Low prices for goods sold and high prices for goods they had to buy were responsible for their condition and, as I have said before, that was a man-made condition.
The bright circumstances outlined by the minister are entirely due to war conditions, and the fact that sons and daughters of those veterans, who are working in munitions plants, or in the services, are sending home to their mothers and fathers the money they earn, so that the bailiff may not come around and put those old people out on the road- something which has been done before in a number of cases. In the interests of Canada, in the interests of the soldier settlers of great war one and in an effort to pay only part of our obligation to the veterans of the present war, I ask the government to grant clear titles to those who hold land under the old scheme. I am going to suggest also what I have suggested before. If this scheme is to be a success you must have at its head a sympathetic administrator, and I do not feel you have that to-day. If the government want to make a success of this, then I suggest that they take cognizance of what I have said this afternoon.
