speechtext:
The minister gave certain figures about payments this afternoon, but when he is answering the hon. member for Battle River I should like him to say how many foreclosures there have been, in the past five years, particularly in the last year, and also how many men who settled on land were forced to give up. Sometimes their sons were able to take over, and sometimes they had to give up entirely. I want to know the number of cases where the soldier settler lost his equity between 1931 and 1940.

I wish to endorse what the hon. member has said. As he has stated practically what I intended to say, it is not necessary for me to repeat. However, there are one or two observations I should like to make which bear out what he has said in regard to the attitude of the government toward these soldier settlers. If proper treatment had been granted to these people I think they would have lifted their burdens. The figures given this afternoon by the minister prove conclusively that these men wanted to pay their debts and clear their land. It was just utterly impossible for them to do so because they had no source of income.
The number of men who came back from the last war and lost their land is nothing less than tragic. I know of one community to which twenty-five young men came back after the last war to take up land. They put in everything they had; they worked and slaved long hours, but to-day only three remain on the land out of the twenty-five. In at least eighty per cent of the cases where men have been forced off the land it is nothing but pure tragedy because the government failed to recognize the human side of the problem.
It was treated as a straight business proposition: "We must have the interest; we must have the money paid back. You have made an agreement and although there is no crop, you are standing in arrears." That was always the story. The figures given by the hon. member for Battle River prove conclusively that the old soldier settlement scheme was neither fair nor equitable. It was a failure so far as rehabilitating the soldiers of the last war was concerned. It did not recognize human values at all. It was a cold business proposition on the part of the government. It was simply a question of getting the interest and the money.
Adjustments were made, but they did not solve the problem for the men because they still had a pile of interest around their necks. The result of all this is that there are dozens of intensely bitter soldiers of the last war who have lost their equity after fighting and working for Canada. They are now approaching the latter years of their life and the tragedy of their position is a responsibility that the government will have to accept. Surely in the name of what is right those who are still on their land are entitled to clear titles. We would then stop all this constant bickering and fighting. It is true that some of those men were able to make their payments, but some of them had three or four sons to do the work for them while others had none. In most cases the sons were not paid at all.
By an order in council passed on March 19, 1941, the government gave power to the director of soldier settlement to take part of

Supply-Soldier Settlement
the dependents' allowances from soldiers who had taken up soldier settlement board land. The order in council reads as follows:
Accordingly the board recommend that notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained in any of the regulations providing for payment of dependents' or marriage allowances in respect of dependents' of members of the Canadian armed forces, that in all eases where the dependents of an enlisted person continue to occupy the farm for which such person is indebted to the director of soldier settlement and in respect of which the contract terms are not otherwise satisfactorily provided for, there may be deducted from the dependents' or marriage allowance amounts sufficient to provide for payment of taxes levied by the local taxing authority in respect of the property in question and interest accruing annually on indebtedness to the director of soldier settlement. such deductions to be made monthly and in no case to exceed $20 per month except with the consent of the dependents concerned.
The information that has come to me is that pressure was put on some of those dependents in a way that was not justified. The minister has probably received a copy of this, but I should like to refer him to two resolutions which were passed at the convention of the Canadian legion, British empire service league, held in Calgary from June 6 to 9. This reads as follows:
Report of Soldier Settlers' Committee
Your committee appointed to deal with soldier settlers' affairs has reviewed the many resolutions sent in by the various branches, dealing with settlers' affairs and we beg to submit the following resolutions dealing with same:
Resolution 1. Whereas the majority of original soldier settlers, who are still endeavouring to carry on under the soldier settlement scheme have now found it, owing to advanced years and the adverse conditions prevailing in agriculture, particularly the lack of parity prices, increasingly difficult to liquidate their indebtedness to the settlement board.
And whereas the settlers have struggled on through the years of drought conditions and low prices unprecedented in the agricultural history of this country and have now nothing to show for their years of toil and struggle but whatever equity they may have in the land which is liable to foreclosure.
Therefore be it resolved that we now petition the government to relieve the soldier settler of any further payments and that they be given the title deed to their land or. failing this, that a parliamentary committee in conjunction with representation from the dominion command of the Canadian legion, review the whole situation of the soldier settler with a view to alleviating their present financial difficulties.
Resolution 2. Whereas it has come to our notice that by order in council the soldier settlement board has been permitted to order deductions made from the pay and allowances of dependents of men now serving in the armed forces to be applied against land and taxes.
Therefore we ask that this order in council bo rescinded immediately, and that any sums of money so deducted be refunded.
I would like to know the total deductions that have been made from dependents' allowances under that order in council. I have dozens of letters I could read citing actual experiences. There should be some clause whereby if a veteran comes back under the Veterans' Land Act there should be an adjustment so that he will have an equity on parity prices, and also there should be a crop failure clause to take care of interest and principal payments in years when there is no crop at all. Otherwise I am afraid that we shall have to look forward to a continuation of what we had after the last war.
I should also like an assurance that something else might be done to make this new scheme a success, namely, that provision should be made under the Veterans' Land Act so that these men who have fought together and who, we hope, will soon be coming back will be given an opportunity, if they so desire, of working together, under direction and after training, on a cooperative farm where they can pool their activities and each make his contribution according to his own ability. Some of these men are good cattle men; some are good mechanics; some are good field men. I would suggest that some such scheme be surveyed with a view to putting it to work, which would be a great improvement over what we
had after the last war.

They were arguing like children when everybody knew where the trouble lay. What is the trouble with Canadian finance? The trouble we have now with banking is precisely that of international finance which has been denounced in the United States. Canadian companies have been denounced by the attorney general of the United States and here we are

discussing hidden reserves of the banks. The hidden reserves are a matter of a few millions while the debt created this year amounts to billions of dollars, and this is the work that serious members of parliament have done during the whole session. I know they have worked hard, but they have not worked any harder than members who were working on the election after Bennett was thrown out of power.
Hon. members worked for one whole session, if not two sessions, keeping at it day and night in order to improve the election act, but what did they do? They took the old one, after a year and a half or two years of work. The work done by the banking and commerce committee of this house this session is perfectly useless; it is childish. As one who had to fight with the potentates and pontiffs of finance in years gone by, when I had to denounce them in the caucus room-so much so that the day I told one of them to swallow what he had said about me he had a fit-I denounce the work of that committee. Now one of them is the boss of finance in this country and he holds the strings of international finance in his hands; yes, and he is not far from me now. He runs the whole show.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that committee should be instructed to reconsider its report, to make a new study of the matter in the light of what has been said1 privately by some of its members. Then its work will be useful to the country, because the Canadian people will know what is bad about finance. I do not mean to say that all banks are bad; not at all. Some banks are run in an honest way; but we see the president of one bank, who was chairman of the victory loan committee, becomes associated with the C.I.L. and then get away from the victory loan organization because he is too busy to look after that work; he is too busy sitting on the board of C.I.L. He takes advantage of the credit he got for the work he did in organizing the victory loan campaign, and now he sits on the board of C.I.L. to protect them. Against what? Against arrest? Against what has been done in the United States? Everybody knows this; it is in the press, so that I am not telling anything new. I am fed up with this situation. We must get to the bottom of it, and then we shall see that the marrow is rotten.

speechtext:
Well, sir, I will tell the minister again what I have told him before, that I have the highest possible regard for him.. He is one of the two or three most likable ministers in the cabinet. I say that with a great deal of pleasure.
On the other hand, how is it that last year the minister wrote me that Charlet would have his pension? He wrote that in August of last year-a year ago. He has received a small amount, but it is impossible for the returned man to get a proper pension from the Department of Pensions and National Health. I want the staff to be changed, from the deputy minister down. I have asked that before, and I ask it now, when they are in the house. I want a change of personnel in that department, so that the returned men may have justice.
I have been fighting for this man who came to me the other day and1 asked me to endorse a note. I am a poor man. A large part of my indemnity goes for the payment of taxes. We have no other source of revenue. I would like to be rich. I would like to be able to give money to those poor men, but it is not my duty to do that. It is the duty of the department. There is no excuse, when a man is entitled to a pension, according to the word of the minister, that this man should not receive a pension. I had to write a letter for this man, and address it to the bank manager, so that he may renew this man's small note.
How is it that it is impossible to get satisfaction from the commissioner? To-day I wrote a letter to the minister complaining about the information he has received from his officials regarding the case of a man suffering from a heart ailment. Afterwards this case was rearranged by the chairman of the board. When I brought this matter to the minister's attention for the first time he told me that this man had been examined by the army and that the case should be placed before the Department of National Defence.
But now it is not that, at all. It is a case where this man is refused a pension because of wrong information given to the Minister of Pensions and National Health by his officials, after consultation with the guilty
fMr. Pouliot.]
parties-those who are responsible for the fact that this man was not looked after and that he died without the assistance either of a chaplain or a doctor. It is a very sad case. It is a case with which the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence is familiar. My letter will probably be trans-scribed to-morrow. But in that letter I told the Minister of Pensions and National Health that the thing he should do would be to get in touch by telephone or otherwise with the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence, so as to get a true picture of this very sad case.
I have been fighting for the draftees, and I fight also for the soldiers. It is absurd that a member of parliament should have to give so much time to cases which are as clear as crystal water, and which should be decided favourably. How is it that the officials of the Department of Pensions and National Health find it so hard to understand, when these are typical cases of men who are wholly deserving of pensions? I think there should be a change. It took twelve months, and in the meantime legislation has been passed.
I have given credit to the minister, because some cases have been settled satisfactorily for the men. That is why I was pleased to say a good word for him. It is most unpleasant to say disagreeable things in the house all the time. It is much more satisfactory to speak otherwise, when occasion arises, and to say things which are pleasant, when one is satisfied that things are working well. But there must be a fate attached to certain deserving cases, when the men cannot secure the pensions to which they are entitled.
This case of Charlet is a case with which the minister must be familiar. This man received a small amount the other day, but the amount of pension is not yet settled. I hope the minister will give definite instructions to have it settled. Otherwise I shall stick to this case, and he may be sure that I will bring down the file and read it-and it is a big one- for the edification of members.
It is a strange thing; there is a man who is a high official in the department, a man who is supposed to be infallible and whose word is all-powerful. He gets more important according to the size of his staff. Naturally the deputy minister is the big boss in the department, because he has all the department around him-all the boys who smoke, and all the girls who knit. They are all around him, to give him more power. But when it comes to the case of a poor fellow who has been badly wounded in an accident, and who is entitled to redress of his wrongs at the hands

Supply*-Pensions and Health
of the state, how is it that Jean-Frangois Pouliot has to repeat the same thing so often in the House of Commons, without succeeding to make himself heard by the officials of the department?
I do not complain about the kind of correspondence I have received from the minister, because it is the finest of its kind. I do not complain about the style of it, but I regret that he is wrongly informed. I regret that he does not fire those who have been appointed as deputy heads in his department by R. B. Bennett.
When I must choose between the poor devil who has been wounded while serving his country and the big and powerful man who earns a big salary, I choose the weaker one. I choose the little soldier, and I fight for him because he is alone. The big man has the whole government to fight for him; he is all-powerful, because he has a big salary, one which amounts to several times the pension asked by the poor devil, who will not get it.
How many pensions were granted to men who were undeserving of them between 1919 and 1935? During this war we have had to fight to the utmost to get for those humble men who have been wounded in service what they are entitled to, according to the law-not the new law, but the old law which has been in existence since the last war. It is impossible to get justice for these men. We should fire the big ones; we should help the small ones and they should 'be helped right away. Why wait so long? Why say that we will wait for the benefits under the new legislation? There is the legislation which is in force and which could protect those poor devils who have been wounded, which should protect the mothers of dead soldiers, which should protect the wives and children of soldiers. Why not apply it now?
If the new legislation which is supposed to accomplish such marvellous things is enforced in the same way as the old legislation has been, no returned man will get any benefits from it. There is the case of Charles Pelletier, which I have mentioned. There are many others I could deal with, but I shall not impose on the committee to-night. These are cases of soldiers who have been wounded and who have written to me to ask that their wrongs and grievances be redressed. It is not a pleasure for me to do this; it is my duty and I do it now. I hope I shall have a satisfactory answer in connection with this young man who has been entitled to a pension since August of last year according to the word of the minister himself.
Then there is the case of Philippe Beaubien, one of the most shameful cases that occurred
in Lauzon camp in Quebec city. In that case I asked the minister of pensions to see to it that a pension was awarded to the mother. I ask that this wrong be redressed by firing those who have been so criminally negligent. I know the feeling of members and I am not going to impose on the committee which has been most kind to me. However, these are things that cannot be left over. This is the time to discuss them; it is our duty to discuss them and I will fight for them as much as I can.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal quietly with some of the observations of the hon. member for Temiscouata. I have not seen him here for the last three weeks. On frequent occasions he has submitted to me a list of twenty cases which I have personally investigated with the utmost sympathy and, if I may say so without any suggestion of boastfulness, some knowledge of pensions procedure extending over some thirty years. I may say that I want to vindicate the judgment of the pensions committee in every single case that was brought to my attention.
When my hon. friend suggests that there is any lack of human sympathy among those men I want to tell him that they are all men who fought with valour and distinction for their country in the former war. Six of the eight enlisted as private soldiers and fought as private soldiers. If any body of men in the Dominion of Canada would have sympathy and kindliness toward those claimants who come before them, it is the present members of the Canadian pension commission.
I wish to say a word also- about the deputy minister. He also is a returned soldier who fought with great distinction in the last war. I have been in the department for only four years, but I must say about my deputy minister that I have never had from him anything but the utmost human kindliness and sympathy toward the case of the returned man. That is the situation with regard to my deputy and the Canadian pension commissioners.
They are all returned soldiers just the same as certain members in all parties in the house. Whenever they are able under the regulations and under the statutes which this parliament has passed during the last twenty-five years to give the benefit of the doubt to the returned soldier, that is done. Why should they not? He is one of their comrades and that is their duty. I must protest against anyone coming up with these observations and animadversions and casting missiles of malice around this chamber at those whose duty it is to serve their comrades.
Supply-Pensions and Health

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I rise to a question of privilege. I did not throw any missiles of malice. That is not one of my defects, and I may have many. It is forbidden by the rules to impute motives to a member of parliament. I have treated the minister as my colleague, and he has no reason whatever to impute motives to the member for Temis-couata when he is fighting the case of the underdog. He may praise his deputy as much as he likes because that is his business, but he has no right according to the rules to cast aspersions on any member. I think I am far from being touchy, but I submit that the hon. member is infringing the rules by saying that I am casting missiles of malice at any one. I did not do that to the minister and I did not do it to his deputy. We are free to hold our own opinions, but I was not inspired by malice of any one when I made my observations and I ask the minister to withdraw what he has said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not see any point of order. There certainly is some rule that n member of the government's service should not be attacked on the floor of the House of Commons because it is not possible for him to defend himself. In this case the minister was defending some of his officials in his own department, and I do not think there is any point of order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: He was sheltering them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I was not sheltering
any one.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Not you, he.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I shall not take the time to east any compliments or brickbats at the minister because I think he has had his full quota of both this year, if not during the past few days, but there are two or three matters I should like to bring to his attention on the floor of this chamber. May I say that I regret that some of the matters I have to raise at this time concern individuals, but the only reason why I express any regret is that I know some hon. members object to our doing it. But these people are Canadian citizens, and they have asked specifically over a period of many months that their cases be raised in the high court of parliament because they feel they have not been dealt with as they should have been. I am sure the minister, the members of the government and all hon. members will agree that one of the principles of this parliament is that the case of the lowliest citizen in the land can be brought up for discussion here and for redress if it is possible to achieve it. Unfortunately these

matters come up at a late time, but when the appropriate item is called is the proper time for such a discussion, whether it be the first or the last day of the session.
First, I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a case which has been brought to his attention frequently over a period of several years. This is the case of Miss Mary Turnbull of MeMunn, Manitoba, in the constituency of the hon. member for Springfield, who among others has brought the matter to the attention of the minister and of the Prime Minister as well. This woman is the daughter of the late Acting Corporal John Turnbull, whose number was 859730. Miss Turnbull's father was a one hundred per cent pensioner for a period of many years. His illness was quite serious; in fact it affected him mentally. The result was that he was a very difficult patient to care for. He lived in an out-of-the-way place in Manitoba where his daughter cared for him over a period of a good many years. There is evidence which seems incontrovertible to me that her health was seriously impaired by the difficulties which she encountered in caring for her father during all those years. That his condition was attributable to war service was fully established by the fact 'that he was a one hundred per cent pensioner. I would say further that her claim to some consideration is supported by the fact that at the time of her father's death the balance owing to him was paid to her, and in addition she later was given a compassionate grant of $100. The information that I have in connection with that compassionate grant is that it was given without prejudice, but nevertheless it was given. The correspondence I have had, as well as other members, with the minister has brought out the technicality that this lady was not incapacitated before she reached the age of twenty-one. Apparently that is the technicality on the basis of which the commission finds it impossible to make any grant to Miss Turnbull.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Was the grant made by the Canadian pension commission or from the Scott fund?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I will read from the minister's letter to me dated January 22, 1943, with respect to the $100 grant:
She was also subsequently given a compassionate grant of $100, which was not intended as a payment to her for looking after her father as it is not the view of the commission that the state is under any obligation to pay children for looking after their parents.
I may say further that the most recent bit of material that has come into Miss Turnbull's

Supply*-Pensions and Health
hands is a recent issue of "Canada at War," in which she finds this sentence in reference to disability pensioners:
An additional attendance allowance for those needing the care of an attendant may be paid up to the sum of $750 a year.
Of course that is the present legislation. But the minister will appreciate the feeling of a woman in this position when she realizes that this kind of thing is being done now. When we are passing bills involving the expenditure of a good many hundreds of millions of dollars she cannot help feeling keenly that there is nothing for her after she has discharged not only her responsibility as a daughter to her father, but a responsibility for the country which he had served. For a good many years she took care of her father whose life was ruined by war service. Her own physical condition is impaired because of what she has done, and she feels that she has not been dealt with rightly because she has been simply told that technicalities stand in her way. She has also been told by the minister and by the Prime Minister that cases of her kind would be given consideration when amendments to the Pension Act were being drafted, but she has discovered that she has to wait a long while for any such changes to be drafted.
I appreciate what the minister said a few minutes ago in answer to the hon. member for Temiscouata that the members of the Canadian pension commission do their best within the regulations. We who are members of parliament and have seme idea about laws and regulations can understand that, but it is a pretty cold answer to the woman herself, as it is to others in similar situations.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It was not meant to be cold.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It simply means no.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I shall be glad to review that case at once.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am very glad to have that assurance from the minister. That was my point in raising this case even on this last night of the session. The minister has had the case before him a good many times, but I earnestly hope that in considering it further he will give as sympathetic and as favourable a decision as he possibly can.
Another case that I have been specifically asked to raise on the understanding that some people in this country have-and I say rightly so-that parliament is a high court where the grievances of a citizen can be discussed, is that of a wife of a soldier whose name I will not give but whose pension number is 104512. This is a case where the soldier is still living and is
in Deer Lodge hospital. His case is bordering on the mental, if not a mental case. There was a separation between the husband and the wife back in the late twenties or in the early thirties. My view about this separation, as about many other separations that have come to my attention, is that it was attributable to the war. The kind of experience that men went through made them in some instances, one might as well admit, difficult for their wives to live with, nr impossible for them to live with their wives, and there have been many troubles of this kind. In fact I have had instances somewhat similar to it of widows of veterans who have died to which Colonel Carmichael of the war veterans' allowance board has given favourable consideration. It i3 because there has been such favourable consideration given there that I mention this case, although it is slightly different because in this case the soldier is still living.
Although there was that separation the time came, about 1934, when by a court order the conjugal rights of the wife were restored to her. That was done by the court of appeal of Manitoba on November 12, 1934. In the meantime, unfortunately, the soldier had been admitted to Deer Lodge hospital less than a month before, on October 18, 1934. He has been in Deer Lodge hospital ever since. His condition is quite poor, bordering, as I have said, on a mental condition. The minister will notice, therefore, that it has been impossible for this man and wife to live together since the date of the court order. There again a technicality stands in the way. The regulations say that a wife in these circumstances can be given consideration only if husband and wife actually reside together. It seems to me that under these circumstances an effort should be made by the minister to find some way whereby the spirit at least of'the law might be interpreted in favour of the wife.
There has been some recognition of the validity of the case because in the first instance the wife had nothing to live on, and in due course she was awarded five dollars a month, which was the pension that had been awarded to the soldier. The commission agreed to pay it to her. Later, after I came into the picture and began this voluminous file of correspondence that I have in my hand, that five dollars was raised to twenty dollars a month. The consequence was that this lady was able to go off Winnipeg city relief, which she was very happy to do, having a bit of commendable pride. But she finds herself now with a total income of only twenty dollars a month, which is less than she was receiving before when she received the pension of five dollars and city relief. It seems to me that it ought
Supply-Pensions and Health

to be possible to pay a woman in such circumstances at least the S30.41, which is the amount paid to veterans' widows. In fact it has been suggested to her that if her husband were to die she might come into that category. That is a most unfortunate suggestion to have to make to a person, and accordingly I urge the minister to give favourable consideration to this case. I take it the minister's silence gives consent.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am listening very carefully to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not think that particular cases should be discussed when the minister shows his willingness to deal with these matters collectively.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I assure you, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take up much time. I do not wish to argue the point with you, but I suggest that this is in order under the item. This is the last night. If this matter had come on three months ago there would have been no argument on the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: This is the third time I have been before the house this session.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Not under departmental administration, civil estimates. This is the first time these estimates have been called this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not objecting.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Why not argue on principles rather than individual cases?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The principle underlying this, if the Minister of Labour wishes an answer, is that in these cases the department should not take the regulations as they stand as something final but should realize what these technical rejections mean to the people concerned, and should find a way of taking care of such deserving cases. However, this is the last of specific cases I will mention. This time it is a soldier of this war. I will give the number, 28222. In this instance the matter has been brought to the attention of the minister on several occasions by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). I raise it in his absence. In fact, it is the case which he mentioned in the house one night is a sample of something that ought to have oeen done without the intervention of a member, but which was taken care of after he brought it to the attention of the late General McDonald, who was formerly chairman of the pension commission. This is the situation with respect to this case, and the minister can
IMr. Knowles.]
look it up from the number I have given him. Pension was finally granted at a late date and it was made effective from May 1, 1942, which made it retroactive for a considerable period; but lately, within the past week or so, the pension has been discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: May I have the number?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I will repeat it: 28222. It has been discontinued on a technical ground. The man's condition is quite serious -the case is one of tuberculosis-and he is in a very serious plight. The secretary of my colleague the hon. member for York South has been in touch with the commission by telephone but without a great deal of satisfaction. So much has been done in this case, and so many things have been pointed out in regard to the justice of it, that I hope the minister will give it immediate consideration.
May I deal with one other matter. I said once before, when we were on another item, the civil service superannuation act, I believe, that I had received a number of briefs from and on behalf of the non-medical employees of the staff of Deer Lodge hospital, Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Those would be orderlies?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, and people in similar categories. I will not go into the long list of grievances presented because I am sure these briefs must have been presented to the minister as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I hope he will give consideration to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There were two main matters, one with respect to superannuation. I dare to hope that those problems have been taken care of by the recent superannuation legislation. Some are temporary permanents and people of that class. One sentence will give an idea of the kind of complaint they make. I quote:
Older employees are called upon to train newcomers whilst -being classed as unsuitable for -promotion.
That is a sample of the grievances which these people have.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is one of the biggest disappointments in our department.
Mr. KNOWLES,: What does the minister mean by that?

Supply-Pensions and Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Well, we have been trying for three years to get it remedied and we are on the eve of attaining that end. '

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Am I right in assuming that the minister has received all these briefs?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And that they are being given attention?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, indeed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And they will continue to receive attention?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think I shall succeed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am glad to hear that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Will the minister be good enough to revise the case of Charpentier and telephone to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence with regard to the case Beaulieu?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I shall be only too happy to do anything I can in the service in which I am engaged.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I thank the minister and I appreciate what he has done. When I speak as I have done I want to inform him that my only purpose is to bring to the attention of the committee some of the most deserving cases. I have not the time to bother about this or that individual. I want justice to prevail in the land and I want those who are in the army or have been in the army to be treated with fairness and justice and in a way that is satisfactory to them, which will bring in the social order that we hear so much about. But we shall get that only by looking after individual cases. We cannot help the soldiers by talking in the abstract; each man should have iirect and immediate assistance. I thank the ninister for what he has said. I appreciate it, and I will write to him again in regard to these cases. I hope that, as he has done in the past in some other cases, he will see that justice is done in the matter.

Item agreed to.
198. War veterans' allowance board, $169,771.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have had some correspondence from a person in New Brunswick who is interested in the extension of the terms and privileges of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I raise this question largely because my correspondent has brought it to my attention. Has the minister considered the extension of the privileges under that act to those who
have served not only in an actual theatre of war, which is the usual description, but in England or Canada as well? I will not pursue the matter further at the moment. I leave with the minister the suggestion that has come from my correspondent and perhaps when the time comes he will consider it in connection with prospective amendments to the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH

Mobilization branch-
199. Branch administration, $62,039.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: With regard to hospitalization other than at the larger centres where veterans are treated, what has the department in mind in connection with the use of local hospitals? In some cases the physicians are faced with an increase in the number of patients and they are becoming greatly concerned about their ability to provide the service which they anticipate on the return of the soldiers. Would the minister mind giving us a statement on the policy and what they intend to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In the last year the policy has been to identify the work more closely with local hospitals, especially in the smaller centres. One of the complaints we had in the Department of Pensions and National Health before I was identified with the department was that boys who were in local centres in the interior of the province had to come down to a coastal city or to the great centres of population in the provinces for hospitalization and treatment. So far as we can we are limiting that except for scientific and medical reasons where the case is more serious and we have to obtain the services of qualified specialists. We have developed as much as we can the assistance and encouragement of local centre treatment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Are you doing anything in the way of granting assistance to such hospitals to enlarge their accommodation?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No, not in every case. That is one of the difficult problems. We have done that provincially; we have not done it locally. We have done it in Edmonton, in Regina and in Ottawa by building a wing or a pavilion wing adjacent to very fine hospitals in each case where we have the benefit of the services of brilliant medical and surgical experts. That policy may be extended. In addition to that, of course, we
Supply-Pensions and Health

have ten or twelve major hospitals of our own which are being vastly extended. In addition to that w-e are building two of the biggest hospitals in Canada, the Sunnybrook in Toronto and the Currie hospital in Montreal., They will be two magnificent hospitals when finished.

Item agreed to.
Direct payments to veterans and dependents-
207. Widows' compassionate allowances to be paid under terms and conditions approved by the governor in council, $600,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The minister knows that this is another item that many of us in this house-I speak not only for myself-have been waiting for for many months during the present session, the item under which a grant is made to widows of veterans of the last war who died with a pension of fifty per cent or less. The first provision of something for those widows was made by a special vote last year to the amount of $20 a month, or in special cases up to $25. Under certain orders in council passed later that amount was raised this year to a maximum of $30.41 per month. A long battle was carried on by members of this house before I came here, and I have been glad to join in it. I am pleased that a start has been made. But I hope that the minister does not think that it is just a theme song on our part, when I say that the government really has not gone far enough.
May I ask this question: has the government given favourable consideration to the requests that were made following a meeting of the dominion council of the non-pensioned widows of great war veterans, held in Ottawa in the early part of March of this year? The requests made to the minister at that time were several. Perhaps I can state them briefly. They were, first, that the eligible age be reduced to fifty; second, that the allowance be paid to widows of veterans in this category irrespective of the place of service of the veteran. The point at issue there is the plight of the widow whose husband in the last war, shall we say, got to England and wanted to go to France but did not get there. It does seem most unfair to women in that position. The third request is that the amount be raised to $40 per month. Here again when these women realize the amount of money that we are able to find for other worthy objects, when they learn of the increasing acceptance of the concept of social security, they find it difficult to understand why the}' should be asked to exist on $30.41 per month. Remember that many of these
(Mr. Tan Mackenzie.]
women are in the age bracket of fifty-five to sixty, because the allowance starts at the age of fifty-five, and it is very hard for them to carry on on that amount.
The fourth recommendation is free hospitalization. The fifth has to do with a change respecting dependent children of such widows who at the present time are receiving allowances from provincial mothers' allowance boards. The next recommendation had to do with the plight of the deserted wives. This is very similar to the case that I was referring to a little while' ago, except that now we are speaking of the widow who was a deserted wife before she became a widow. It is similar to the previous case because there are many of these women whose husbands left them owing to a complete upset that occurred in the soldier's life as a result of his service in the war, definitely, in my mind, attributable to the kind of experience these men went through, and it does seem to me that consideration should be given them. The seventh suggestion was that this legislation be made permanent. As a matter of fact from the way it was introduced last year I thought that there might be a bill this year making it permanent, but instead of that we have this item, which is called the last night of the session.
The eighth suggestion is that representatives of the non-pensioned veterans' widows association be asked to sit in with the war veterans' allowance board, on certain occasions at any rate, to discuss matters of general policy relating to the administration of those allowances. I think that the minister will agree on that point; and I am sure that Colonel Carmichael would. I think that the visits these women made to Ottawa at their own expense have have been worth while. The minister at times may have thought that they were rather a nuisance, but he will admit that they have helped the government to bring into effect something that will at least begin to meet the sort of thing that Canada would want done for these people. That being so I suggest that their request that they be called in in an advisory fapacity is a commendable one and one that would help to improve this legislation.
The ninth request has to do with the plight of the widow of an imperial veteran where both the soldier before he died and the widow have lived in Canada for twenty years or more. I have had a number of cases in that category brought to my attention where the English ex-soldier and his bride came to Canada after the last war. The soldier had no pension. He died in the meantime and his widow is left without any chance to get any

Supply-Pensions and Health
assistance either from the United Kingdom government or from this government, although they are Canadians by reason of the fact of twenty years' residence or more. I hope this matter will be fully considered.
There are one or two other recommendations, but perhaps they are not as important as the ones that I have brought to the attention of the minister. He knows that this is a subject on which the hon. member for Davenport-, the hon. member for Trinity and many other hon. members of the house fee.l very keenly and have spoken on quite often. If it were earlier in the session the minister knows that this debate would go on all night. The way in which he could cut it short is by telling us that many if not all of the recommendations of these women are to be granted, or at least are being given active consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
May I very briefly refer to the point raised by my hon. friend. In the first place he mentioned the age of fifty instead of fifty-five. If he will read the order in council he will find that it says:
(a) that such widow has attained the age of fifty-five years or is so incapacitated by mental or physical disability as to be incapable of and unlikely to become capable of earning a livelihood.
So that there is very great leeway to deal with many cases.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I appreciate that, but it does not meet the request for a lowering of the age for all concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The second point my hon. friend raised was in connection with widow's of veterans v'ho served only in England. The position is that we cannot ver}' well extend that benefit to the widows until we extend it to the men themselves. I think that is clear; everyone should realize the situation. We must give it to the men themselves first.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: On that point I support the leader of the opposition in saying that that should be done without'delay.

Possibly I might agree. The third point was the question of the deserted wives. That is a most difficult problem, and as yet wTe have not- reached a solution, though wre have tried our best. The next point was the matter of permanent legislation. My hon. friend may take my assurance that this will all become permanent legislation, no matter what government may be in power. All these benefits will be embodied in the statutes of Canada. The last point raised by my hon-. friend was in
regard to some grant to assist the representatives of the non-pensioned widows. There is an item of $1,000 in the supplementary estimates to assist these ladies to come down here and place their grievance or their complaint before the government of the day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am very glad to hear that. The minister did not deal with the most important suggestion, however) which was that the amount of the allowance be increased to $10 per month.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That cannot be increased, of course, until the general range of veterans' allowances is raised. There must be some parity.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I agree, but the general range should be increased too.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that this grant of $1,000 to the non-pensioned widows is to assist a future delegation to present their case to the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is right. These ladies had to come down at their own expense. We thought it was rather unfair to ask them to do that, so that an amount of $1,000 was placed in the estimates for that purpose.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is an excellent idea. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre advanced certain arguments in their behalf, and I should like to join in the plea that justice be done these women. A number of them came to see me last year, and possibly the year before. Many hon. members of this house have taken a kindly interest in their case. Last year I had an opportunity of speaking in their behalf, and it is only because of the circumstances of the moment that I am not speaking at much greater length this evening. However, I should like the minister to understand that he will receive very general backing and support in parliament for any scheme that will give justice and equality to these women whose case I think presents a definite challenge to this government and this parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am glad indeed to see that the provisions have been widened and that the grant will be made to a greater number of women. I would strongly urge the minister to give consideration to those women who are not widows but who cannot live with their husbands, perhaps because their husbands are mentally ill or for similar reasons. There are a few women in this situation, and I think their case is exceptionally worthy of consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My hon. friend has presented a new appeal with which I was not familiar previously, but I shall be glad to take the matter into consideration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would repeat what he said about the case of the woman who was a deserted wife before she became a widow. I realize that the bachelor minister does not understand these things, but I am pressing this point because of one case in particular that I had some months ago. That was the case of a widow whose husband had deserted her before he died. As a matter of fact she was a Salvation Army officer. It was a matter of deep regret that this should have happened but it was due solely to the condition of her husband, which arose from the last war. This widow was in the further difficulty that while she had two sons serving in the present war, each had a wife and neither could afford to assign any money to her, so she had nothing of her own to live on. I mention this fact because I took up the case and fought it hard with Colonel Carmichael and his board which, eventually found a way to grant an allowance to this widow. I was very glad. But I have others whom the board have not found it possible to help out, on the ground of the technicality. It seems to me the minister should listen to the representations that have been made to-night from this side and by the hon. lady member for Edmonton East and see if the regulations cannot be changed to cover fully the case of the woman who was a deserted wife before becoming a widow.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The regulation now is that such widow was living-with or being maintained by her husband at the time of his death, or within a reasonable time thereof, provided that the board shall have discretion to waive this qualification in any case where circumstances exist which the board deem such as to make it just and reasonable so to do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
What is the date of that
regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: August 13, 1943.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: Yet in March of this year the widows still found it necessary to protest this matter.

speechtext: This is the last of the pension items, and I want to raise one question, though the matter is not covered by any of the regular items in the estimates. I realize that the circumstances under which the gratuities bill was debated did not give time for the reaction of certain sections of the country to reach parliament before the bill was finally passed, so that perhaps at this stage I may be permitted to put in a word for the veterans guard, who as far as I know were not mentioned in the discussion on the gratuities bill. These men are in a very special class, if I may say so. I mention this matter now because it is the only opportunity left at this late hour of presenting what I think is a case to be dealt with when amendments to the gratuities bill are considered by this or a succeeding government at the next session of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

In addition they are entitled to many other benefits. For instance, we extended the veterans' allowance and the provisions of the insurance act to cover them, so that I can say they have received more benefits than those who did not re-enlist in the present war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am anxious to have the
minister indicate to the committee, if he will, what contracts have been let, and the details of those contracts, with respect to the Sunny-brook Farm hospital. This matter is engaging the attention of the public at the moment perhaps to as great an extent as almost any

Supply-Pensions and Health
other of our many hospitalization problems. If the minister could give those details I would appreciate it, and it would be of great interest to the public generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I had information come to my hand a few moments ago that two contracts have been let so far. One was a grading or levelling contract for $14,000, let to a firm from Brampton. That is a purely preliminary contract. Then, a few days ago, on August 11, the main contract for the first unit was let, to the value of $2,887,000. That was let to the Redfern Construction company, and includes the preliminary units of a very great scheme which will amount to about $10,000,000 when it is completed. There will be a total cost, as I have said, of about $10,000,000, before all buildings are completed.
This first unit consists of a boiler house and engineering unit, what they call an up-patients building, and makes a provision for a total of 400 beds out of a total of 1,450 beds which will be finally developed in the institution when it is completed. When this hospital is finished it will probably be one of the largest in Canada.
As my hon. friend may know, we have acquired adjacent property for a health and occupational centre for that type of case which I have described on several occasions. We have bought eight or nine centres across Canada for the assistance of these cases who need some assistance to acquire again the desire for employment, and to develop fitness for employment. One is being built here in Ottawa-the Rideau occupational centre; one at Ste. Annes, one at London, Ontario, one at Toronto, one in British Columbia, one at Saint John, New Brunswick-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: One in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes, one in every province; but at the present time we have started with a project of five. We have not developed the whole project for every province, but we are going ahead as fast as possible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
When will the first
patients be admitted to Sunnybrook Farm hospital? I believe one of the real criticisms made with respect to hospitalization in that area is that the Sunnybrook Farm hospital was not got under way a3 early as it should have been. I remember the minister's arguing in the house that one of the reasons why nothing could be done a year ago was the question of priorities. Then, following that,
the priorities difficulty was apparently overcome, and late in the year the first sod was turned.
The real difficulty is that most people feel the hospital should have been commenced a good deal earlier, having in mind the possibility of casualties and the increased' need for hospitalization in Canada. For that reason I would say particularly to the minister that one of the chief grounds of complaint at the present time is that the original move was made too late. It becomes of vast importance therefore that we should know when the first patients will be admitted to Sunnybrook Farm hospital.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Of course I cannot give a definite assuranee in that regard; but I can say that the architects and contractors have been instructed to rush all work as fast as possible. I do not know if construction was commenced to-day, but I know it is to commence immediately, as a result of the contract I mentioned a moment ago. And I have every reason to believe that the second unit can be looked after very quickly indeed.
I can assure the committee that so far as this department is concerned, in cooperation with the defence services, and with the Department of Public Works, which is really in charge of construction, the purpose is to rush the construction of Sunnybrook Farm hospital as fast as it can be done. I am not a contractor or a construction man, and I cannot of course give a definite reply as to when we can have patients in there. But my hope would be that it would be as soon as possible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to have something a little more definite from the minister with respect to time. I know how difficult it is to estimate time, and sometimes it is even dangerous to do so. Nevertheless I think the public will not be satisfied unless some estimate is given as to the time when Sunnybrook Farm hospital will be able to take in some patients.
I wonder if the minister would go back to the time the matter was argued last session, when he told the committee that the difficulty was one of priorities. He said at that time that priorities could not have been arranged before, and the hospital got under way at an earlier time. That seemed to be a really serious complaint and I must confess it is difficult for me to see the reason why the work could not have been commenced earlier.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
For the same reason that they would not permit them to construct veterans' hospitals in the United States of America-exactly the
Supply-Pensions and Health

same reason as we had here. In company with my deputy minister I made a persona] visit to Washington a year ago to urge the necessity of obtaining priorities, especially in regard to Sunnybrook hospital at Toronto. We got the finest reception, but we were told that they had the same difficulties there, and that these were world conditions. They were found there, and they were found all over. I am glad to say we have now obtained a first priority in regard to labour and materials. That will be helpful to us.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Priorities are not holding it up now?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No; it is just a matter of plans and specifications. Then, of course, there would be difficulty in regard to labour; but the Department of Labour has been very helpful to us and has promised to give us every consideration in regard to getting available labour.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has the minister any approximate estimate as to when it will be finally completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: All I can tell is that it is commencing at once. How long it will take to build is a matter for a construction engineer to estimate. I can only say that every single expedition will be used and every pressure brought to bear. That is as far as I can go.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has an estimate been given by any competent engineer as to the possible time of opening the hospital for patients?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, I have not any.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister will see at once my reason for being so insistent in my inquiries. The public will brush aside all technicalities as to estimates by construction people. What they want to know is when patients will be allowed into Sunnybrook Farm hospital. Will they be allowed in in November, or next May, or a year from then, or when? They have no idea as to whether it will be years or months, or how long it may be. That is one of the reasons why I am so insistent in my inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The only estimate given me was somewhere in 1945, but I should not like to be bound by it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Has the minister under his hand the amount of assistance given to this problem in that area in connection with making available space for consumptive

patients, and space for critical surgical cases in Toronto General hospital and other hospitals in the Toronto area? Does the minister feel he has received the maximum of assistance from those charged with the responsibility of hospital administration in the Sunnybrook Farm area?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In reply to the leader of the opposition, first, I have received a note which states that the contract has been awarded for completion one year from to-day. I did not know that when I replied to my hon. friend before. That is the estimate made by the engineers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is that for the completion of the whole hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No; that is for the completion of the 400-bed unit. The rest will follow very quickly indeed.
The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) has asked a question, and I want to take this opportunity, on behalf of the members of the committee, to welcome him back to this assembly. I am sure that he, along with the hon. member for Wood Mountain who sits to his right, represented this parliament with great distinction when they visited our sister dominion. We are most happy to welcome them back here. In regard to the hon. member's question, I must say that he has been most cooperative with the Department of Pensions and National Health through offering the facilities of an institution to which he has devoted many of his years. I believe about 200 beds are to be made available in this hospital with which the hon. member has been associated for many years in a truly beneficent way. I want to express publicly the gratitude of the government for his efforts to assist us in that way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister will remember that I raised this matter a few months ago.. I think the departmental officials employed in this capacity have received a raw deal during the war. Their duties have increased and they are working longer hours. They are not in uniform and they have been refused the right to go into active service. Many of them volunteered their services but they were considered to be in essential work. When the war is over, those who are young men will be considered slackers because they are not recognized as being service personnel. In matters of promotion and so forth where preference is given to those who served in theatres of war, these young men who have been compelled to remain in their positions because the work they are performing is essential will lose out. Another thing to be considered is the matter of gratuities. The medical service is recognized as being entitled to these gratuities, but these men who render such valuable service at the ports, in many cases working harder than most other medical personnel, with the possible exception of those performing operations under fire, are not entitled. I think there should be an examination of their status.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH

This reminds me of a long distance call that I made last year with regard to butter. The production of butter was large enough but it was rationed. The wholesalers could not buy more because the cold storage warehouses were probably not large enough and the butter was purchased by the government from the farmers and then sold at a much higher price to the United States without the farmer receiving any further benefit. It is quite strange that it happens in this country. There has been a severe rationing of butter within the last few weeks and I cannot understand it. How is it that the government has purshased a large quantity of butter from the farmers of Canada which has been sold to the United States at a much higher price than that prevailing in Canada at the time without the Canadian farmers receiving any more benefit? That question has been asked many times.

I should like to say a word or two in regard to the price administration of agricultural products. I found on my trip to Australia and New Zealand that there was no subject that one heard more often than the price of agricultural products. AVherever
we went and wherever I addressed1 a meeting the one question that was asked was: "How are you in Canada able to keep the price of agricultural products so high, so much above the world price, because we sell our goods at the world price and they are much lower than what you people in Canada are obtaining for yours?" I was obliged under those conditions to explain why; but before I go on to explain why, I wish to give the committee the prices which the people in Australia and New Zealand are obtaining for their farm products, so that we may be able to get some idea as to whether Canada is being legislated properly or whether she is being poorly guided and governed. With regard to the prices which they are obtaining for their agricultural products-
Have you the cost of production?

Never mind the cost of production. I am giving you the prices that they are getting. You can find out the cost of production, you have plenty of time. In regard to butter, they receive for butter wholesale twenty-seven cents a pound or one shilling. sixpence. Butter retails at thirty cents a pound, or one shilling, eight pence. In Australia and New Zealand wheat sells for seventy-four cents a bushel. If they sell more than three thousand bushels they get a lot less; it runs down to sixty cents. I will not tell you, sir, what we are getting because you know as well as I do, about $1.25. They get three shillings and eight pence for barley, or about sixty-six cents; we get somewhere in the neighbourhood of seventy-nine cents. In Australia and New Zealand a steer weighing about a thousand pounds is sold for about $61.20. In Canada we get about $110 or SI 15 for a steer weighing that much, or nearly twice as much. In Australia and New Zealand a pig weighing 200 pounds sells for $21.60. It sells in our country for somewhere in the neighbourhood of $27 or $28. These are some of the prices which they receive for their agricultural products and they have a socialist government or a labour government, there. The only people who seem to be discriminated against in that country are the agriculturists or the farmers and not the labourers. They have a labour government. Wherever you go you find discontent. I never was in a country where I found more discontent among the farmers than I did in Australia and New Zealand.
I shall now give you what they pay for agricultural implements. The prices run something like this. These implements are manu-

factored and sold by the Massey-Harris company in that country. A hoe, 16-run small seeder drill, very few of which are manufactured in this country now sells for S375.30; a three-furrow disc plough sells for S412.20. An eight-foot binder, four-horse hitch, sells If or 8525.60; a mower, six-foot, sells for $202.95; a nine-foot rake sells for $79.65; a 26/36 horse-power 102 senior sunshine Massey Harris rubber tires sells for $2,187. In other words, the price of the agricultural implements that they have to buy is nearly one-third higher than in this country and the price of the goods which they have to sell is about one-third less. Is it any wonder that there is dissatisfaction in that country among the agricultural people with regard to the way in which they are being treated? On the other hand, some of our friends over in the corner do not seem to know that we sell our goods at the world's price too. The fact of the matter is that when England wants to buy wheat we ask her how much she is going to pay and we sell to her at the world's price. It may be 75 cents it may be seventy cents; it may be 80 cents; it may be SI.50. We sell it to them at the world price, whatever it is. Supposing the Englishman says he will pay us seventy-five cents; we take the other fifty cents, to make up the $1.25 that we receive, from the mutual aid appropriation. We do the same in connection with pork, beef, butter, cheese and all our farm produce. That is why we are able to get the prices we are receiving at the present time, regardless of what world prices may be. These are things I think we should tell our people, because they do not know how well they are being treated. In my opinion there was never a time in western Canada when the people had as much money as they have now. They should realize in what manner they are receiving the prices they are being paid for their products at the present time.
Would the minister please tell me why some Canadian butter has been sold to the United States at higher prices than those prevailing in Canada, without any extra benefit to Canadian farmers?

Mr. .ILSLEY: The Minister of National Defence was Minister of Finance for a period; and owing to his experience, as well as his outstanding ability and qualifications, it is thought desirable to have him named as Acting Minister of Finance in my absence. I am very grateful indeed to him for acting in my behalf when I am away.

That is the minister's view about it, and it is most complimentary to the Minister of National Defence, but the hon. gentleman does not touch the grave of the late Sir Sam Hughes, who was busy as Minister of Militia and who was never the perpetual Acting Minister of Finance.
Here is the reason I object to it. I believe that in time of war the job of Minister of National Defence must be a full-time job, and that a member of the cabinet who acts in both capacities must neglect one of them. Either the Minister of National Defence pays no attention to his duties as Acting Minister of Finance or the perpetual Acting Minister of Finance pays no attention to his duties as Minister of National Defence. I am reminded of a world character who has lost some of his popularity-Mussolini, who held five portfolios. The Acting Minister of Finance is the deputy Prime Minister, a fulltime job; he is Minister of National Defence, a full-time job, and he is Acting Minister of

So far as I am concerned, I know of no general rule. But I know the rule I applied to myself, and that rule was that immediately I accepted the portfolio of Minister of Finance I resigned every directorship I held, except one, and that one was in connection with a small company. I happened to be the executor of the estate of a gentleman who was president of that company, and whose widow I felt I should assist for the time being by continuing to act on that board.
