Saturday of next week will mark the twentieth anniversary of my election to the House of Commons for the county of Temiscouata, which I still represent. Sir, I have not changed. I am still a Liberal, as I have always been.
Order.

I wish the hon. member would come to his question of privilege. My understanding was that yesterday he explained his position. Now he is repeating it. I would ask the hon. member to state his question of privilege.
Yes. But yesterday I only expressed my regret at leaving my seat. Now I am saying why I am here.
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: There is no question of privilege in that.
I am afraid that is hardly a question of privilege.

Then if you will permit me, sir, I will go further and cite a precedent; it was when the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) was permitted to give his reasons for leaving the Conservative party some years ago. On that occasion he was listened to by the Chair. Now, sir, my point is that my Liberalism is a very definite doctrine, which may be entirely different from so-called Liberal policies.

Order. The hon. member is himself a student of parliamentary procedure, and he knows that what he now states, while it may be a matter for explanation to the house on another occasion, is not a question of privilege.

Then I will give it to the press, if they will take it.
PRIVILEGE-Mr. LaCROIX
Mr. WILFRID LaCROIX (Quebec-Montmorency) (Translation): I desire to state before this house that I am leaving the government side, where I have always sat while

The Ministry

preserving my independence of judgment and action to take a seat on the opposition side where I will continue to maintain the same attitude.
Any more?

subtopic: MOTION FOB RESCISSION OF ORDER PASSED ON JULY 24, 1944, FOR SATURDAY SITTINGS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION FOB RESCISSION OF ORDER PASSED ON JULY 24, 1944, FOR SATURDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: That the order passed on July 24, 1944, under which the house was allowed to sit on Saturday until the end of the present session, be rescinded, and that when the house rises on Friday, November 24, and every Friday thereafter, until the end of the session, it shall stand adjourned until the following Monday in accordance with standing order No. 2.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: REPORTED RESIGNATION OF HON. C. G. POWER- STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED RESIGNATION OF HON. C. G. POWER- STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention just one matter to the house by way of information. Some hon. members have asked me if the report in the press that the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) has tendered his resignation is correct and if the resignation has been accepted. I may say that the minister has tendered to me his resignation, but thus far I have not advised His Excellency that I think the resignation should be accepted. I wish further to consider the matter carefully.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORTED RESIGNATION OF HON. C. G. POWER- STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister if there has been any correspondence between the minister he mentions and himself in connection with this matter and, if so, will it be tabled in the house?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: REPORTED RESIGNATION OF HON. C. G. POWER- STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: It all depends upon what is meant by "correspondence". There should be two letters to have correspondence, and so far there has been only one. Should there be correspondence to table I shall see that it is tabled.

subtopic: REPORTED RESIGNATION OF HON. C. G. POWER- STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I would not like to see the Prime Minister limited. If he thinks the letter he has received from the minister should be tabled, we shall be glad to receive it even before he makes his reply.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: REPORTED RESIGNATION OF HON. C. G. POWER- STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
My hon. friend speaks about a letter that should be tabled. I have no letter that should be tabled because

I have not as yet advised His Excellency the Governor General that the resignation of the minister should be accepted.

subtopic: PETITIONS WITH RESPECT TO APPLICATION OF N.R.M.A. ACT
PETITIONS WITH RESPECT TO APPLICATION OF N.R.M.A. ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to present to the House of Commons and parliament assembled a petition, the prayer of which humbly requests that the draftee forces shall be at once dispatched overseas to the aid of our men now fighting at the front. This is signed by H. C. Baillie and many others.

subtopic: PETITIONS WITH RESPECT TO APPLICATION OF N.R.M.A. ACT
speechtext:
I wish to lay on the table a petition signed by Neil McLeod of Sarnia and several hundred others praying that full effect be given to what is commonly known as bill No. 80.
Mr. DOUGLAS G. ROSS (St. Paul's): I have a similar petition signed by several hundred persons requesting that bill No. 80 be implemented at once in order that the lives of our men overseas may be saved and reinforcements given to our troops.
Mr. II. R. JACKMAN (Rosedale): I have a similar petition from the constituency of Rosedale signed by approximately two hundred persons, and another from the constituency of Spadina bearing approximately sixty names.

maintopic: METHOD OF RAISING MEN FOR SERVICE OVERSEAS-

speechtext:
REFERENCE TO PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT on july 22, 1942
On the orders of the day:

maintopic: METHOD OF RAISING MEN FOR SERVICE OVERSEAS-
speechtext: When the Prime Minister speaks on his substantive motion on Monday next, notice of which is now on the order paper, I should like him to make clear a matter which is troubling me. At the .risk of taking some time to explain the position I would direct his attention to page 4564 of the House of Commons Hansard of July 22, 1942. At that time the mobilization bill was under discussion'-

maintopic: METHOD OF RAISING MEN FOR SERVICE OVERSEAS-
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: METHOD OF RAISING MEN FOR SERVICE OVERSEAS-
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member could give me some idea as to the relevancy of the statement he intends to make?

maintopic: METHOD OF RAISING MEN FOR SERVICE OVERSEAS-
speechtext: I have to lay the foundation. This is not intended in the slightest degree to embarrass the Prime Minister or anyone else.

maintopic: METHOD OF RAISING MEN FOR SERVICE OVERSEAS-
speechtext:

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE

speechtext: (Hon. A. G. L. McNaughton, Minister of National Defence, having again appeared before the house):

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want General McNaughton to believe that I am lacking in respect for him in any way. I would recall that on February 24, 1943, I was the one who suggested his promotion to full generalship. I did that for one reason, because of what had been said by the Prime Minister on November 14, 1941. I quote from page 4430 of Hansard of November 14, 1941, where the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
The general's last words to me were that I could depend upon it that he would take care to see that lives were not needlessly sacrificed. I remember those words very distinctly, that he as commander of the Canadian forces would take great care to see that lives were not needlessly sacrificed.
That is the action of a great man, that a commander in the field should not want to waste human lives. He knows the value of human life.
There is another thing that I would ask the general, and it is this, not to mention national unity in connection with conscription. I will qualify what I have said. It has been repeated over and over again that if conscription was not imposed in this country it was precisely to preserve national unity. What was meant by national unity? What was meant was that the province of Quebec was against conscription for overseas, and therefore conscription for overseas service should not be enforced?
In the first place. Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that we did not have from the very beginning of the war a well-balanced conscription, but a one-sided conscription. I regret very much the action of the Department of National Defence which has given emblems for service only to those who have volunteered, thereby indicating that all the others who were contributing to the war effort in other ways were slackers just because they had not enlisted in the army. That is a great mistake which was made at first.
Another mistake was to be afraid of the word "conscription". I prepared an article telling the draftees who were working in industries essential to the war effort what they had to do. That article was based on the regulations. But what did the director of
Reinforcements

mobilization say to me? He said: "The article is all right except that you call the draftees conscripts. They are not conscripts; they are mobilized." I have never played with words, sir, and I can never agree to that.
What I mean with regard to the disastrous effect of what has been said throughout Canada regarding conscription and national unity is this: The province of Quebec is not at all opposed to a well-balanced conscription where the value of the services of every man who is working in essential industry is recognized as a help to the war effort.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: As I understand the procedure that is to be followed to-day, questions are to be asked of General McNaughton. So far the hon. member for Temiscouata is making a speech which in my judgment would be more relevant when the motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister is being discussed on Monday. The procedure that has been adopted for yesterday and to-day was to enable members who desired information to question General McNaughton. Questions and answers are in order.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall come in just a few minutes to the conclusion of what I have to say. When on the one hand conscription is described as a good thing, and on the other hand the province of Quebec is described as opposed to conscription, and when what is described as a good thing is not imposed in this country on account of the opposition in Quebec, that is a great mistake which results in the province of Quebec being misjudged throughout the world. I hope that in the future there will be no politics mixed up with this question. I ask the general also not to play politics, and I know that he will not, because as a soldier he has gained a very high reputation indeed. I hope with all my heart that politics will be left entirely aside, and I would also ask the general to do something in his own department. The Canadian Army has been divided into three, following the suggestions made by the brass hats, who at one time I was not even allowed to refer to as pompous. I would ask the general to start a reform in the Department of National Defence to separate the chaff from the good wheat, which will be to the great benefit of this country. I would ask him to make a reform in his department, particularly in the medical corps, so that men who are unfit will not be kept in the army just to make the number greater. That is a great mistake. These men may be able to do very useful service, more useful service outside of the army than in it, and I hope that a free hand will be given in that matter.
[Mr. Pouliot.l
Now I want to make a request of the government. While I do not agree with their conscription policy, which was changed between four o'clock the day before yesterday and three o'clock yesterday, although no special danger during that short interval was indicated to us to account for the change, I hope, sir, that the present Minister of National Defence will be given a free hand to make in his department, in a spirit of justice, the reforms which have been so urgently needed since his predecessor took charge of the department, and in that he can rely on my full support.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I would like to direct a
question to General McNaughton. In this morning's Ottawa Journal the head line is "Volunteers to be Sent First-Use Zombies only to meet reinforcement deficiency." Yesterday when the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) was questioning the general he said, at page 6560 of Hansard:
Before I conclude may I say, without wishing to worry General McNaughton, 'because I know he must be weary, that there is one point which is still not clear to me, and that is this. No matter how many men you get from general service, no matter how many men you get from the young men who are coming of age, eighteen years and eighteen and one-half years, are the 16,000 trained men in the N.R.M.A. to go overseas whether they volunteer or not?
The answer was definite:	"The answer is,
yes." There is a difference of opinion apparently between the head line in this paper and the answer that was given here. My question is this. Regardless of how many men you get from general service or how many volunteer, do you still intend to send over 5,000 in December, 5,000 in January and 2,000 each month thereafter until the full complement of 16.000 shall have been sent? In other words, are these from the N.R.M.A. to be extra to those [DOT]that you recruit in the ordinary way?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for bringing that point to attention. Not only was it obscured in the press accounts, but there were certain other obscurities, for which I take full responsibility. Through my inexperience in parliamentary procedure I did not always convey what I intended. I should like, therefore, Mr. Speaker, to have the privilege of reading a short statement which I have made up following an analysis of the press reports. In reports which have appeared in the press there appears to be some confusion about one or two points which arose in a discussion yesterday, and I should like to make a brief statement to clear up those points.
I expressed a strong preference for our traditional voluntary system, and also my hope

Reinforcements
that it might not be necessary to use to the full extent the powers given to the Minister of National Defence in the order in council tabled yesterday. In some quarters my remarks have been interpreted as an intention on my part to scrape up men and use our general service men and to use them first even if they are not as well trained as N.R.M.A. men. That is not so. What I desired to convey was that I hoped trained N.R.M.A. men would volunteer for general service soon enough and in large enough numbers that it would not be necessary to send them overseas by compulsion. What I wish to make clear is that if adequately trained men do not volunteer in sufficient numbers the required numbers will be made up from the best-trained men we have. These will be detailed for service overseas under the order in council.
While the order in council extends the locality of service of all N.R.M.A. personnel, the maximum number the Minister of National Defence is authorized 'by the present order to dispatch overseas is 16,000. This power will be used to the extent that adequately trained men, whether now in the' N.R.M.A. or not, do not come forward as volunteers sufficiently rapidly to meet the numbers required. The maximum was fixed at 16,000 in order to provide adequate reserves. In addition to giving the reserves required by the time they are required, these numbers will also enable increased periods of rest for individuals and will provide the increased number needed to compensate for the men given leave to Canada as these proposals develop.
I can now give the house the composition generally of the first 10,000 of the additional reinforcements being dispatched in December and January to which I referred yesterday: 7,500 are fully trained infantry; 2,500 are well advanced in infantry training, and this training will be completed on arrival in the United Kingdom.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister has not answered the question of the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Mayhew); and I, too, am in the dark as to just what is to be the procedure. A straight answer to the question of that hon. member would relieve the minds of many of us.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I think we have come to the time when questions should be answered so that we can really understand. That question has not been answered. The point is, there is authorization for 16,000 to go over. Is that the total number of men who will be sent over 'between now and May? I think we should know whether it is or not. If it is, I for one would not be satisfied.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The 16,000 referred to are in addition to the presently-planned movements which are now being carried out.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I am not yet clear, Mr. Minister. [DOT]

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Hon. members may laugh if they like. We are not all as smart as some of the other fellows are. What I should like to know is what was asked by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C.: are the 16,000 to be sent now?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
We have a very considerable movement which was arranged and in full swing before yesterday. Since yesterday another planned movement of a total of
16,000	has been added to these movements. The planned movement-that is, the additional planned movement-comprises 5,000 in the month of December, 5,000 in the month of January, and 2,000 in each of the three succeeding months.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The 16,000 who are to go in December, January and the succeeding three months are to be taken out of the N.R.M.A.?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is right, sir. There will be included a few other personnel, naturally, because the officers are not in that category. There are officers and non-commissioned officers who are general service and must go with them.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is General McNaughton at liberty to disclose in public session the total number of reinforcements which will be added to the reinforcement pool between now and the end of next March?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That information is something which I cannot give in open session.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
(Bow River): I understand now that the 16,000 will be called up under this special order in council from N.R.
M.	A. personnel. I can quite see, if there were to be total conscription of all N.R.M.A. men, where officers would be authorized to pick certain individuals for the draft; but I am at a loss to know, and I should like the general to explain, what method is to be used to get these 16,000 from the N.R.M.A. It is general knowledge that in the past some of the methods used to get N.R.M.A. recruits to volunteer were not as they should have been. I was against any coercion or compulsion in that regard, and I am against that method now; I want to know how the general proposes to get these 16,000 out of the
N.	R.M.A. without conscripting "the whole works."
Reinforcements

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The units to comprise the first 10,000 of the N.R.M.A. for dispatch, as I indicated earlier, were selected this morning. Those units will shortly be in process of moving to concentration areas in eastern Canada. The men who wish to volunteer will be given every opportunity to do so. The others, the whole units including those men, will be dispatched on the dates which at the present time are being arranged.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That does not answer my question, if the general will pardon me for saying so. 1 wish to know the method used in making that selection. It makes a lot of difference.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The first consideration, the thing that stood uppermost in the minds of myself and the staff who were assisting me in the matter, is that we should get men who were as fully trained in infantry as possible. We have taken the best infantry soldiers we could get in the time available between now and the date of the sailing of the ships.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Would that depend, then, on the officer in command of that certain section? He can choose any man he desires. There may be two who are equally trained and he may desire to take one and leave the other. That would be a fair conclusion to come to. Would that be the situation?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: If, in the opinion of the officer in charge, a man were not up to the standard of training which we have laid down that man would be struck off strength of the draft, naturally.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That was not my point. Here are two men equally trained under the same officer. Only one is needed. What decision will be made in the choice of that one out of these two men?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: These movements are in essence based on the sending of the best trained personnel we can dispatch up to the numbers for whom we can get transportation. Therefore I do not think there is any invidious discrimination in the choice of individuals.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
In my opinion, the method which I believe will be carried out in the selecting of the 16,000 men is not the proper one. It seems to me that there will be more coercion and mistreatment in the choice of the 16,000 than there has been in the past in trying to get national defence men to volunteer. I am against that type of coercion and I can see plainly a great deal fMr. C. E. Johnston.]
of disunity arising from such action. Let me give a vivid illustration. Suppose you have one man in Quebec and another in some other province. No matter which of them is chosen there will be discontent. It is time for us to quit fooling around with the subject. All other parties have the blackest of war records in this regard, and I am proud to say that the Social Credit party is the only one than can stand with its head high.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I wish to be clear on this point. There are 5,000 men going overseas in Deoember, 5,000 in January and 6,000 later.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Are these men to be volunteers or are they men who will be taken out of N.R.M.A.? As from yesterday, when this order in council went into effect, will the voluntary system be continued, or will there still be N.R.M.A. men shifted to the concentration point ready for overseas? If we are sending over 16,000 under the conditions indicated, 8,000 fully trained, we are told, and
8.000	partly trained at the present time, and who will be fully trained in due course, is it not a fairly good bet that they will all volunteer before they go over? In other words, what you are doing in forcing the voluntary system on men who are actually called for compulsory service. That means, it seems to me, some coercion, the coercion being that they will proceed overseas either as conscripts or as volunteers, and they have the choice right up to the moment they leave as to which they will be. This is a strange way of going about the obtaining of the 16,000 men. I do not know where this is landing the house or the government, and if we are to have compulsion in the sending of men overseas I cannot understand why the government does not go the whole way. Where you have
16.000	who know they are going overseas and who are told that they may still become volunteers, you coerce them! into being volunteers. I am not yet clear as to whether the
16.000	who are going are to be men in the numbers of whom are included those who have already been told that they are going from general service. I am not clear on that point, and I believe some other members are in the same position. With regard to the other point, it strikes me as quite evident that men are going to be coerced into volunteering, and that is wrong. Let us be clear about what we are doing.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
May I answer first
the hon. gentleman's second question in which he asks whether the 16,000 are included in those now going over, or are additional. This

Reinforcements
16.000	which is engaging the attention of the house is in addition to the previous planned movements which include the general service personnel. The 16,000 is a new movement, on top of all other movements, which was initiated yesterday afternoon. The other point I can answer only by saying that under the authority of the order in council, and in order to provide the army in the field with the additional trained infantry reinforcements which are required in support of their operations, we are taking the
16.000	from trained infantry in this country and dispatching them. That personnel may, if they wish, convert to general service, that is, volunteer before they go.

speechtext:
Are they
not told that if they do not volunteer they will get no rehabilitation grant, and is not each commanding officer instructed to tell them that individually?

as Minister of National Defence. I leave myself in the judgment of the country. The country wants to know about this.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE

With your permission, sir, I am glad that the Prime Minister has clarified the position with respect

to the first portion of the question. Certainly only the Minister of National Defence could answer that part of the question with respect to the proposal that I suggest has been made. Whether it is true or not is another matter, but I will emphasize the fact that this is a form of cruel duress to make these men volunteer.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I would say to the hon. member he can be quite certain that no instructions of that sort would ever have been issued.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: "Would ever have been issued."

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Or has ever been issued. If he is aware of such an order being issued I should like it brought to my attention.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I will tell the minister that a high ranking officer, and I am not going to name him-

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No, I am not going to name him because he would be crucified by this government; make no mistake about that. I want the minister to understand this, that any man who talks to me talks at great peril to his personal position. Make no mistake about that. They are afraid to talk to me, General McNaughton, to give me factual information because they do not know what the gestapo might retaliate upon them. That is the situation in this country to-day. Private members of the forces are afraid to give me information. I hold in my hand information from an airman. He is in the gallery this afternoon. I do not know whether to produce it here or not, or to ask the question. These employment companies are being set up in order to provide an establishment to take in from the N.R.M.A. personnel in the lower categories, below the categories which can be posted to units of the combatant arms. The number is as yet uncertain, until we have more information as to the analysis of the physical categories of the men in question. About fifteen companies, each of a strength of approximately four hundred, are now being set up. That four hundred is an establishment; the strength will be very much less. As regards the work, I explained in the formal statement I made to the house that it would be these employment companies which we would use to fulfil requests for work to be done which was of national importance, and I indicated, and I think I should repeat, two important safeguards in that matter. The first is that for works outside the Department of National Defence I am in no position to say whether they are of national importance, so that we will look to the Minister of Reconstruction to teli us whether the work in question is something which we should undertake in order to help Canada's effort in the war. Second, I am very much concerned that no labour from our employment companies should be used which competes in any way with workmen who might get work at prevailing rates constituting remunerative employment, and so before we undertake any work we shall ask the Minister of Labour to assure us on that point.
