My understanding is that we are fighting for freedom from fear and freedom from want, and that means freedom of employment, or adequate maintenance whether the employment is there or not. These men, it is expected, are coming back to the same conditions which many of them left. But there is another point which I wished to raise. The minister stated further that the men who have been referred to are those who have been held in N.R.M.A. in order to ensure that men returning fom overseas shall have the first claim on remunerative employment; that they would be put at certain employment, and that the pay would be pay and allowances provided in military regulations. I should like to know if these men are working for private companies who will get the advantage of the additional pay, or where this additional pay will go?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The answer is that if there should be any difference of pay it will go to the credit of the public exchequer.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I have one other question for the minister. If my memory serves me aright, when the minister was speaking yesterday he said that the men in the N.R.M.A. were willing to serve overseas but not willing to enlist voluntarily. Has the minister ascertained the reason or reasons for this attitude? Is there any information on that? He mentioned a moment ago that officers were told to explain to these men their duty to the state. Were the officers instructed also to explain to these men the state's duty to them?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It is the responsibility of our officers so to do.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is any distinction to be made between men who enlist voluntarily from the N.R.M.A. and those who are sent overseas without volunteering?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I would say no. The situation is that in Canada, as soon as a man volunteers, he is given a G.S. badge to wear on his sleeve, the "G.S." standing for "general service". That badge is not worn in Canada by N.R.M.A. personnel who have not volunteered. Overseas wre do not wear any badges, and I see no reason for making any distinction once the man is overseas; in fact, I would be most averse to the institution of any distinction, because when a man goes on service we want him to become in all respects a member of the unit to which he is posted. I do not favour any distinction whatever.

R ein]or cements

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I was going to ask the minister that.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: What about the individual who returns-?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I think I have the floor for the moment.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The hen. member for York-Sunbury has been on his feet a good many times.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I believe I have Mr. Speaker's permission, and I want to ask a question.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I wish to ask another
question.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Acadia has the floor. He wishes to ask a question.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Will General McNaughton explain what will be the standing on his return of a man who was sent overseas without enlisting. Will he be allowed to wear the general service badge on his return?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: We are looking some distance ahead. One hopes that the N.R.M.A. business will be out of the road and liquidated. Frankly, however, I have not considered that point.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Where you take a man from N.R.M.A. and send him overseas and he is wounded, surely he should be entitled to the general service badge on his return, although he did not enlist for overseas service.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The hon. member has posed me a conundrum. I will look into it.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Will General McNaughton also give us a break-down of the 68,000 in the N.R.M.A., showing the dates on which these men were drafted, the numbers of those who were drafted in 1941, 1942, 1943 and 1944, so that we may get an idea of the core of resistance that is in there.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: May I ask that they be given by military districts?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I have not by me figures compiled in that form. I must answer the hon. gentleman's question by referring to the totals for all Canada. In 1941 there were
31,500	enrolments. Owing to conversions to general service, transfers to other services and discharges of meo, the 31,500 has decreased since then by 15,000, leaving still on N.R.M.A. strength, of enrolments of 1941, a total of 16,500. I must apologize to the house. I was giving the wrong figures, the figures at the
end of the year, rather than the figure that now remains. May I give them again for the purpose of greater clarity. In 1941 there were
31.500	enrolments and during the year total losses of 15,000. The strength at the end of the year was 16,500.
In 1942 there were 69,500 enrolments, with a wastage of 27,500, so that the situation at the end of 1942 was that, up until that time, that is, the 1941 and 1942 figures brought together, there were 101,000 enrolments and
42.500	struck off .the strength, leaving at the end of the year a strength of 58,500.
During 1943 there were 34,000 enrolments and 17,800 struck off strength, so that the situation) at the end of 1943 showed that the totals were: enrolments to that date, 135,000; struck off strength to that date, 60,300, with a net remaining strength at the end of the year 74,700.
I have the figures for 1944 up to September 27. The numbers taken on strength were approximately 15.000; the numbers struck off strength were 21,200, so that the totals to September 27, 1944, were in round numbers: enrolments 150,000; conversions to general service, 42,000; to other services, 6,000; discharges, 33,500; or total decreases of 81,500, leaving a net strength, as of September 27, 1944, of 68,500.
Of that 68.500, which represented the net strength on September 27, 1944, there were
8.500	on extended leave from duty from the depots, which left the net effective strength on the payrolls at 60,000. If I can combine the two questions, perhaps the hon. member would like me to cross-analyse by districts. I shall be glad to do that.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Thank you; I should like to have that.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I am analysing the figure of 60,000 net strength as of September 27, and I am going to give the figures for Ontario, Quebec, the maritimes, the prairie provinces and British Columbia, by the years in which the men entered the camps.
First of all, regarding the men who entered camps in 1941, there were in that 60,000 to which I have referred, as of September 27, 6,200 men remaining. Of these men, 900 came from military districts 1, 2 and 3, that is to say, practically the province of Ontario; 2,900 were from military districts 4 and 5; 400 from military districts 6 and 7; 1,700 from military districts 10, 12 and 13, that is to say the prairie provinces; 300 from British Columbia. These figures should add up to 6,200, being the number of men who entered N.R.M.A. in 1941 and were still on strength as of September 27 last.
Reinforcements

For 1942, there are 6,800 men from Ontario, 8,800 from Quebec, 1,800 from the maritimes, 6,200 from the prairies, 1,800 from British Columbia, or a total of 25,400.
Regarding the men who entered N.R.M.A. in 1943 the figures are: Ontario 4,900, Quebec 6,100, the maritimes 1,500, the prairies 4,200, British Columbia, 1,200, totalling 17,900.
For 1944, Ontario 2,400; Quebec, 5,000; the maritimes, 600; the prairies, 1,700; British Columbia, 800, making a total of 10,500. Therefore, if you cross-analyse your figure of 60,000 you will find that 6,200 of these men entered the N.R.M.A. in 1941, 25,400 in 1942, 17,900 in 1943 and 10,500 in 1944. I do not know whether the hon. member would like me to give these totals with respect to the provinces ilso.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Cross-analysing the figure of 60,000 in the other way you have Ontario providing 15,000 of the men; Quebec, 22,800; the maritimes, 4,300; the prairies, 13,800, and British Columbia, 4,100. May I say to hon. members that these are figures which I released to the press of Canada a few days ago in order that the public might have information in connection with this N.R.M.A. problem.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: In view of the fact that in recent months our casualties have been considerably greater than we had anticipated and apparently that rate of casualties is now considered normal, and in view of the fact that over a million men have already gone into the forces, has any consideration been given to the advisability of breaking up the first division as reinforcements?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I would say to the hon. member that no such project has been entertained.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Consideration has been given to the problem; it has been under consideration, surely. That was one of the alternatives. General McNaughton, as I understand it, to the course that is now being pursued.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
That was done in the last war, was it not? If the casualties continue to increase, to what extent are we to go in draining the manhood from this nation in providing reinforcements? Can the general visualize a time when the drain will become so great that we shall have to break up the fifth division or be prepared to drain every last man from this country in order to maintain reinforcements for an army that perhaps

is greater than we should provide for? Have we bitten off more than we can chew? I think that is a question which is of vital importance to the people of Canada to-day. I am not suggesting that this should be done; I am wondering what the pros and cons of the situation are.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I say to the hon. member it is an extraordinarily difficult question for any individual to stand on the floor of the house and answer. It is a matter that must be decided by the government in the full light of the circumstances as they develop. To use our man-power for carrying this war to a conclusion must be decided by the government as a whole from time to time in the light of every consideration.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: On a statistical basis do you know approximately what the rate of casualties is? They are considered normal, are they not? How long do you consider you can maintain the army at that rate? Can you carry on to the middle of next year if the war should go on for another year, or would you have to break up the fifth division?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Again that is a matter of developing policy in the light of circumstances when they come into existence, the progress of the war and so on. I would remind my hon. friend that the wastage figures which I gave were estimates and projections. It is true they are based on past experience which we obtained up to date, but there is no certainty about any of them. In fact I would say there is no certainty in anything related to war. It is a matter which those who are in charge must be guided by from moment to moment in order to bring about the result which the nation seeks, the defeat of the enemy who are threatening our civilization.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
May I ask an ancillary question to the one asked by the hon. member for Acadia with regard to N.R.M.A. personnel who are drafted and sent overseas? There is to be no distinction between the benefits they get and those the volunteers get so far as rehabilitation is concerned. That is correct? I agree with it. Then there is to be no distinction with regard to their uniforms. I entirely agree with that, because anybody who serves his country by fighting outside it deserves the highest credit, no matter how he is called. Will there be any changes in such things as regimental numbers, so that under no circumstances would there be any distinction whatsoever between the man who has volunteered, once he is fighting in any theatre

Reinforcements
of operation, once he goes overseas, and the N.R.M.A. men? As the minister knows, the N.R.M.A. men have boxcar numbers.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Yes. I have just learned one fact that I did not know before. I was under the impression that we gave the N.R.M.A, men when they came in a number to which they adhered. I am now informed that actually the numbers have been changed for those who volunteered. I agree with everything that the hon. member has said. Once a man goes overseas there must be no invidious distinction against him, and I will ask the officers to go into this matter and change these numbers immediately if that is an invidious distinction, so that anybody who may be sent overseas will have a number which is indistinguishable from anybody else's number.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
With regard to those draftees who have been called up over a period of time since the National Resources Mobilization Act was brought into effect in 1940, there have been, of necessity, thousands upon thousands of medical examinations. Is it correct that, since the shortage of man-power has become acknowledged and apparent, those who are in the lower categories immediately below those who are considered satisfactory medically are now to be reboarded and are at this moment actually being reboarded medically, with the idea that many of them may be raised to a higher category medically? That is going on to-day. I am not objecting to it. I think it ought to be done. I wish to know if it is true.
The other question in my mind was whether the standard of medical fitness might not, in the early stages and perhaps during the years 1941, 1942 and 1943, have been too high. I know of one or two men being categorized as C something-I am not familiar with the designations-and they looked A-l to me. They might have had some minor defect that was not noticeable. That is being done, is it not?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
They	are being
reviewed. People are being reboarded with a view to seeing that their categories are suitable for the employment we have for them.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Reboarded into the various grades?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Yes,	because a
man's medical category changes.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Yes,
quite so.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: And we want to have them adjusted to the realities.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Some may go up and some may go down.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Quite so.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: They are all being reboarded-those who have not actually gone into the army?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Well, actually it is just a medical examination; it is not a boarding.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Perhaps I have not used the correct term. However, the fact is that they are being medically re-examined?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: There is one further question I should like to ask, one which it seems to me is of importance. Certain young airmen have been in the Royal Canadian Air Force. The British commonwealth air training scheme, which is now about to be disbanded, constituted a very large force. There are about to be released, and in fact are now being released daily, very large numbers of young men, some of Whom have gone overseas and some who have not. These are men in A-l physical category; and yet they are being discharged, we will say, this day. Let us say that many of them will be twenty-one years of age, and in that category from which they would be callable. Are those men now automatically to be called up for draft into the army?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Men dischaiged
from the British commonwealth air training plan, so far as the Department of National Defence is concerned, become members of the general public.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
And unless they
wish to come forward voluntarily, and enlist
as other members of the general public do- and if so, they will be welcomed-

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: -they are not under our jurisdiction in any way, until they have been brought before us through selective service.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Then I shall ask this question of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) if he is here: are these men who are discharged from the R.C.A.F. immediately callable for draft into
Reinforcements

the N.R.M.A. army, in the event of their being medically fit? If the minister is not here, then perhaps his parliamentary assistant would answer-because I am sure he knows the answer.
Then, even if they are not medically [DOT] fit, are they to be recalled and reboarded or re-examined medically, with a view to pushing them into the army? These young men were volunteers, and they are greatly exercised over the fact that they are not going to be permitted to function as airmen. To a degree their morale is shattered. They are suffering from chagrin-and I am not placing any responsibility. I am simply trying as best I can to state a fact and a position.
I have every sympathy with these young men. They are high-spirited and patriotic individuals. They voluntarily enlisted to enter the armed services of Canada, and enlisted in that branch of the service in which they wished to serve, and to which they wanted to belong. Now, through no fault of their own, physically, mentally or otherwise, they are being discharged. They now find that they are being discharged from that service and placed back in private life. They do not want to go into the army; they want to go into the air force. What is their position to-day? To my mind it is a tragedy that these young men after two years' service, or twelve months' service, or whatever the case may be, some of whom have been overseas, are now brought back to Canada on the theory that there are too many of them for employment in the service for which they volunteered. That is a tragedy, and I have the greatest sympathy for those young men.
I am wondering if the position is as represented to me, namely, that they are now subject to the draft for the army, and to be placed in with those men whom, in days gone by, they spurned to join.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I can answer that question.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: With all due respect, let me point out that I am asking the Minister of Labour.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That point has been discussed this afternoon. However, the minister will be back in the house in only a few minutes. I am not aware of the discussion which took place in the last few conferences and, in view of the importance of the point raised, and the further fact that it involves a matter of policy, I should prefer to have the minister reply.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: And I am quite agreeable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The minister will be in the chamber in only a few minutes.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Then at that time I shall take the opportunity to restate my question.
I now turn to the subject of remustering, to which the Minister of National Defence referred yesterday, when he illustrated the basic training of an artilleryman, among others. I now call the minister's attention to the situation with respect to the volunteer who joined the forestry service, and who has been overseas in Scotland doing, I hope, useful work in the army. These men were trained woodsmen. They have been ordered to go into the infantry, and have been redrafted. Not one of those men ever had a day's basic training; they went directly into the forestry corps. How much training are they to have before they are put into the front line of infantry, and what is the position in respect of them? Perhaps the minister would tell me the whole story.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The situation in
respect of the forestry corps was that we had a considerable corps, as the hon. member knows, who were sent overseas, and were largely employed in Scotland.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Yes, I believe that is so.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The corps was
developed quite early in the war-1940 and 1941. I echo the sentiments expressed by the hon. member in respect of the wonderful work performed by that corps in providing lumber and wood for all needs in the United Kingdom. We have had the highest compliments from all sides in respect of our forestry corps. It is an effort of which Canada may well be. proud. Not only were those foresters, but those thousands of them in Scotland during the critical period of 1940 and early 1941 became an important part of the defence of that country.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I dare say.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
And while those men did not have basic training in accordance with the syllabi laid out, they were given every help and assistance by the Scottish command, under General Sir Andrew Thome, who commanded them. They were given instmctors, practice in the use of the rifle, and so on, and were given every inducement to make themselves thoroughly efficient for defence. In fact at one time they formed the only reserve force

Reinforcements
in the whole of the Scottish command. So that they had a very considerable training in infantry.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
They had
some, at all events.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Yes, some, at all
events. We knew that the work of tlhe members of the forestry corps overseas, that of cutting down trees, would in due course come to an end, because they had made a pretty big hole in the woods of Scotland. So that they were always regarded as eventually coming into the reinforcement stream for the Canadian Army-some into the infantry, others into the army service corps, and others into the technical arms of the service.
When the time came when they could be released from forestry work they came down to the south of England, and into the depots. Their standard of training was checked, and the decision was taken as to where they should be remustered. Proper training schedules were arranged. I have no doubt that all this was effectively done.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The minister is giving me the assurance-and that is all I want-that before these men are put into the front line of infantry, in a branch of the service for which they did not enlist- although I presume that under the terms of their enlistment they were liable-they will have ample training in the use of the weapons they will have to use? If the minister gives me that statement I shall be content on the point. I do not wish to see anybody put into the front line unless he knows something about the implements of war he has to use-outside his knowledge of the use of an axe. Of necessity, the physical standards of those men must be very high because of the work they have carried on in Scotland. They should make good men.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that we are taking every safeguard to ensure the adequacy of training of our reinforcements.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
That is
fair enough.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It will be our constant endeavour to see that there is no break in those safeguards.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Labour who has come into the chamber. A number of gallant young men, the very flower of our country-I say this without any disrespect to those who volunteered for service with the navy or the army-volunteered for
service with the R.C.A.F. under the British empire training scheme. The announcement has just been made that this scheme is to be brought to an end and these men are being discharged daily, some having been brought back to Canada for that purpose. They are A-l men, but they are discouraged by the fact that they are not to be permitted to serve in the service for which they volunteered. Their morale is down because of that. Once these men become ordinary citizens are they to be drafted into N.R.M.A.?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I get clearly the import of my hon. friend's question. As a matter of fact, discussions took place to-day with regard to the policy to be pursued. If they are brought to a finality next week I shall be glad to make an announcement in the House of Commons.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The minister is telling me that the matter is under consideration but has not yet been decided. I want to express the hope that consideration will be given to these young men. I trust that the government will take these men back into the R.C.A.F. should the opportunity arise. There is another matter I should like to inquire into in connection with the personnel of the R.C.A.F. but I do not know whether the minister can give me this information. It probably comes under the Department of National Defence for Air, but I do not see any spokesman for that department in the chamber, not even the minister's parliamentary assistant.
It has been reported to me that subsequent to the arrival of some R.C.A.F. in Lincolnshire, England, they received what, was termed commando training. This consisted of a course in the use of the Enfield rifle, the Sten gun and the Browning machine gun, as well as training with ack-ack or anti-aircraft guns. But it is reported to me that this training lasted for only ten days, when they were told by some one in authority that they would have to go to fight the Germans as guards around captured airports.
I want to know whether any men were put in the position of having to fight, the Germans with only ten days training in the use of the weapons they would have to use in that capacity? I think I can produce creditable witnesses to the fact that those men were ordered into positions of danger without sufficient training. If that is so, I want to know if the government is going to correct the situation.
It may be that the minister had nothing to do with this, and I doubt if he had. I would think it would come under the Department of National Defence for Air or it may be mixed
65S4
Reinforcements

up with the R.A.F. I am making what is more or less a summary of the whole situation. If the facts are as they have been represented to me then all I can say is that it is cruel to send men into positions of danger who have had only ten days instructions in the use of the weapons they would have to use in case they came into conflict with the enemy. If the minister does not know about this perhaps he will have some one else look into it and give me an answer.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I am not aware of
the circumstances.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Have instructions gone
out in the last three weeks to the different officers commanding the military" districts to cancel all leaves, including farm leave?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: How many of our Canadian boys have been loaned to the British army?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: There are really two schemes. There are 673 young officers on loan to the British army at the present time. Then there would be an additional number which would be variable and which we would not know of in Canada. These are individuals who are loaned to British staffs to help out from time to time in the various theatres. If the hon. member would like me to get the figure for any particular day' I shall be glad to do so.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I am more interested in knowing whether those young officers can get back into the Canadian army by making application. They- are serving under most trying circumstances at the present time.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Those officers were never off the strength of the Canadian army. They were posted for minimum periods of three to four months but they would be aligible to come back to the Canadian army an the expiration of the tour of duty which had been arranged for them.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I have a boy who has made -application two -or three -times to get back to the Canadian army. He has been wounded twice since D day and he wants to get back to the Canadian army because he has not received any mail or parcels from Canada. Although we have sent him over fifty parcels, the only one he received was one sent from the United States. Letters have been returned but the parcels have never been returned. Other boys in that pool are in the same position.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Would the hon. -member give me the particulars in order that I may investigate the circumstances?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I will.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It is only by having specific instances and carrying out thorough investigations that we can check on the system, particularly when our young men are away from our -own formations.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: When he came out of the hospital a few days ago he went down to the orderly room and they told him he was neither in the Canadian army nor in the British army. They said they had just sent twelve letters back home which had been received that morning.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Page the Postmaster General.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Can the Postmaster
General give me any information?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Was my hon. friend referring the case to me?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No, I was referring to the Postmaster General. Letters and parcels are not getting through to these young officers who have been loaned to the British army. We have sent our boy over fifty parcels and he has received only one, and that was sent from the United States. He has never received one from Canada, and over one hundred letters have been returned.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: We shall be only too pleased to look into this matter at once, but may I say to the hon. member that we do not handle mail for officers attached to the British army after it arrives in England or other destined country. The army postal corps and the Royal Canadian Air Force postal corps look after the mail for our troops, but if men are posted to other armies the hon. member will understand that the services of the army to which they are attached must be utilized.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is the reason why this boy wants to get back into the Canadian Army. I would ask General McNaughton what procedure he must go through to get back into the Canadian Army if there is any chance for him to do so.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member give me his full name and the unit in which he is now serving?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I should also like to ask the Minister of Labour a question. He told us last session that farm boys were not being

Reinforcements
called up. Actually farm boys are being called up all over this country, so far as I can learn;
I know they are from my own constituency. Furthermore when they make application to selective service or to the registrar when they are called up, even in the case of a family where three sons are serving and only one boy is left on the farm, no answer is received from the registrar until after the date to report. Then the boys have to go into the army and they are not released from the army. The general has told us that no order has gone out to cancel farm leaves, but all farm leaves in my constituency have been cancelled in the last three weeks and they have never been renewed. These boys have all been called up and have been granted no exemption.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I endeavoured to answer that in reply to a question put by the hon. member for Selkirk, but the hon. member for Waterloo South apparently did not want me to answer it. Let me say without qualification that we have the most liberal policy with respect to agricultural workers of any of the united nations. My hon. friend may have received complaints. I often get complaints from the industrial side. A man might say, "I am a machinist," and he may be the only man in the world who would say that he was a machinist. But if my hon. friend has any case in mind where he thinks that a real farmer is being called up, I would like to know the details.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: There are two or three questions I have been trying to ask. One was in reference to a remark made by General McNaughton with regard to the order in council when he first spoke. I thought I understood him to say that the order in council covered all the men in the N.R.M.A. I do not think he was putting a legal interpretation on the order in council, and I just wondered what led him to make that statement and just what he had in mind. Did I misunderstand him?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The answer is yes, to the best of my legal knowledge, although I do not claim to be an expert.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I want to understand just what the situation is, because, as I understand the order in council, it covers only N.R.M.A. to the numbers approved by the governor in council. It covers only such members of the N.R.M.A. as are specified and approved by the governor in council. It does not cover all the N.R.M.A. There is no action with regard to any of the N.R.M.A. except the 16,000, as I understand it. It does say that if further number of the N.R.M.A. are specified by the
governor in council and approved by. them, then the minister may require them to serve. But there is no action taken with regard to the N.R.M.A. beyond the 16,000 mentioned in this order in council.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is not the point this? The order in council is broad enough to cover all N.R.M.A., and the minister is now given by the order in council the right to deal with the numbers mentioned there and to deal with further numbers subject to the approval of the governor in council.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I say that that power always existed under the act. You did not need an order in council to authorize the governor in council to approve the numbers. That power has always been there. The only action which was taken in the order in council is the approval by the governor in council of N.R.M.A. personnel to the number of
16,000	who may from time to time hereafter be required for training, service or duty within the United Kingdom or in European or Mediterranean operational theatres. That is all that the order in council does, as I understand it. I do not want to argue a legal question, but I thought from a remark made by General McNaughton that he was misapprehending the terms of the order, or that there was something in it perhaps that I had missed.
Just one thing more. The suggestion was made I think from the other side of the house that all rehabilitation benefits should be extended to the men called up under this order as are extended to general service personnel. I wonder if that is quite right, when the men under this order are required to serve only in the United Kingdom and European and Mediterranean operational theatres whereas general service personnel have to serve the world over.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite correct. "Service" under section 2 of the War Service -Grants Act, 1944, is defined as follows:
"service" means time served on active service in the forces while enlisted or obligated to serve without territorial limitation, or time served on active service in the Aleutian islands.
That might have to be amended in the light of the statement made by the hon. member.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
The point is that these N.R.M.A. men get no war service gratuity Whatever under the order in council at the present time. The second is that if they enlist for general service they will get full war service gratuity. That brings me to my
Reinforcements

next question. Do I understand that the procedure is that, let us say, the Elgin battalion-I do not think there is such a battalion but we will take that name-is selected by you as one of the battalions which is to be included in the 16,000, and a notice goes from headquarters to the district and from the district to the battalion that the battalion and all the personnel therein are hereby required to serve? That goes. Then do I understand that after I, who happen to be a rear rank private in that battalion, receive notice that I am required to serve, and compulsorily, overseas, and am being dispatched overseas under this order in council, may then come in and volunteer? Do you think that is very much like "volunteering"? I did not see what the point was about it; that was all. I thought they were going to be given an opportunity to volunteer before they were told that they were conscripted. Can they now volunteer right up to the time they go into the line overseas?
You see what I mean? I want to see when the privilege of becoming a volunteer ceases. He is conscripted; he is dispatched overseas under this order; he is put on a boat and sent over there; he is still required to compulsorily serve; but somebody says, "Oh, but you have the right to volunteer". When does that right to volunteer end? Does it ever end? Can he volunteer after he is wounded and back in hospital; can he then be turned into a volunteer?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I must say the hon.
member is posing a legal conundrum that I would want some legal advice on.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No, it is not a legal point.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I would, think the actual extension of the man's service, which is what this is, to a new area, would take effect from when he went on board ship.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
No, extension of service
surely takes effect the minute he receives this requirement from the department, from the district: he has then become liable to serve since he is a person "to be dispatched" under the terms of the order. Do you intend, then, shall I say-I am not posing any legal question-that at some stage the right to volunteer should cease?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Well, I would think the actual extension of service would take place when the man went on board ship. He was beginning to go out of the territorial limits of Canada, and I would envisage that he had the full right to volunteer up to that time.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I do not see why there is a "full right" any time, as far as that goes. I do not know that it is any right at alL You have to stop it some time, surely. I must say that I never thought until the general spoke that there was any thought that after I had had my service extended and had become liable to and ordered overseas, then after that that I could be "converted"-that is the word they use-from N.R.M.A. to general service. I could hardly be said to be a very genuine "convert." I take it that there is no time at which that cannot be done? You have not decided on that?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No; I think that in a matter like that, which is one of precise definition, I must get the law officers of the crown and the department to advise me. I am not skilled on that matter.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: But it did seem to me it was quite inconsistent that a man who had actually been ordered overseas under the order-in-council could then become a "volunteer". It is like a man after being arrested by the sheriff saying, "I will go voluntarily", because the sheriff is right with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: May I say, with regard to the question dealing with gratuities, that if there is any doubt with regard to the statute-drafted by the Department of National Defence and not by the Department of Pensions and National Health-immediate action would be taken to ensure that these men would be entitled to gratuity.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The statute was drafted by the officers of both departments in collaboration. What I want to know is, even if immediate action were taken, is it right that men who are made liable by order in council for service only in the United Kingdom, Italy and northwestern Europe shall have exactly the same service gratuity as the men who voluntarily pledge themselves for service the world over? I do hot know that it is right that it should be the same.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: He is risking his life, is he not?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: He is risking his life, but in half the theatres. The volunteer who is now in Italy could be ordered to Japan or anywhere else. I suggest that my hon. friend consider it.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
We ought to have an answer to that. That is very important.

Reinforcements

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: General McNaughton, as I understand, you are training the additional 26,000; that is to say, there are the 42,000 who were mentioned by the Prime Minister and of these there are the 16,000 we are talking of here to-day who are infantrymen practically ready, and others who will soon be ready, for combat.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Very close to it.
Mr. RALSTON; That leaves 26,000 who are in the medical category for infantry and could be trained as such. Are those being trained?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: We are going ahead with those, with all the training we can.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: In order to provide for any possible contingency; is that right?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Absolutely right,

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: When you mentioned that this estimate was up until May, that was simply a planning date?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
That is the planning
date, yes.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Just a planning date. And the planning dates-

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It is as far ahead as we need to make provision at the moment, 'because as the plans become available we have plenty of time to affect the situation.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Planning dates are generally advanced or extended as the developments occur?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Quite so.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is, you may probably review the situation in January?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Absolutely.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: You spoke last night of the pools for May; I do not know whether it is the end of May. I wonder if you would look at your figures, because you mentioned that those pools for the United Kingdom, for Italy and for northwest Europe would be substantial pools at the end of May. I have in mind figures which I know about when I happened to be in this thing, and I do not think the figures could have changed very much. I understand there is some difference in respeot of casualties. But is there really any substantial pool at the end of May? I mean, there may be a few thousand men, but that is all. I am not asking you to give the figures, but I want you to check on that word "substantial" when you are referring to three different pools.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: These, of course, are figures which, as the hon. member knows, I cannot give in open session.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I did not ask it.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The table has been re-set since I took over the department, and the figures differ in several respects from the ones previously in effect. As the hon. member knows, we have been able to substitute actuals for forecasts, and we are thankful that the actuals were less than the forecasts in several respects. Then there are those additional dispatches we are talking about; the 16,000 comes in on the beneficial side of the ledger. What I would say to the hon. member is this, that the staffs are satisfied that the figures are sufficient. On top of the recommendations of the staff, small additions have been provided in order to free our hands in the matter of leave to Canada, and, if they wish to use them, for additional rest periods for individuals where there might, I think quite rightly, have been some doubt as to whether we were able to keep people out of the line for a sufficiently long time. I cannot say that was the case, that they were being sent back too soon, because I am assured it is not so; but I wanted to be abundantly certain that men were not under any conditions being rushed back into the lines too quickly.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I come back to my question which was with reference to the use of the word "substantial" when you assented to my question yesterday as to whether or not the pools in Italy, in northwest Europe and in the United Kingdom were substantial at the end of May. By the pools I mean what is over and above the number necessary to bring the units up to strength. Does the word "substantial" apply to all three pools?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Of course, as regards the distribution of the reinforcement reserves overseas in May, that is farther ahead than the break-down figures have been projected for. I am dealing with them here as a total overseas.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Total overseas, having regard to the possibilities. Suppose you had to provide a pool for one month's intense activity in Italy, two or three weeks' intense activity in northwest Europe, and for activities in the United Kingdom for six weeks, would you have anything like that at the end of May after bringing all units up to strength?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
We are getting
pretty close to things which it would be dangerous to discuss except under security.
65SS
R einforcements

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I am considering the word "substantial". You are looking at the figures. I cannot see them, but I have an idea what they are, if they are anything like the figures I have seen, and I must say that I questioned whether, when you looked at the figures, you would think that the word "substantial" -really applied to them.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The hon. member will take it from me that the figures are in accordance with the recommendations of the military advisers of the government. I have taken their recommendation absolutely without any influence by myself.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: With the idea of the war ending in May?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No, sir.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: With the idea of carrying on?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
If it is required,
and with the idea that in those periods, so far ahead as May, if in accordance with the developments of the situation we have kept at each stage a sufficient flexibility to bring the situation into balance should there be any indication of its going out of balance.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: What do you mean by flexibility?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Flexibility in the posting of reserves as among the three places where we must maintain -reserves, namely, behind the forces in Italy, behind the forces in northwest Europe, and reserves in the United Kingdom; as well as, in the fourth place, the men who are being trained in Canada for dispatch forward.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: When you spoke of something being countersigned by officers in the field, did you mean the rates of activity, the periods of activity?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: What I meant there was the expected wastage, in that case the periods of activity, to ensure absolutely that there was no doubt as between what was in the minds of our commanders as to what they were expected to do, and what the theatre commanders from whom they received orders had in mind,, so that we would be quite sure that full provision should be made. That was an arrangement entered into by the minister in his regime and I was very glad to see it in effect. I had therefore double assurance.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
It had nothing to do with numbers; it had to do with the projection by the commanders in the field of the number of

months or weeks of probable intense activity, the number of months of normal, and the number of months of quiet.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It was to ensure that we who have to make provision in Canada to meet calls for reinforcements without any possibility of doubt knew what was in the mind of the man who had to order those operations.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
And the request of the military advisers is practically the same as the request made by the chief of staff, Canadian military headquarters. His request was for
15.000	and you provide for 16,000.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I have not analysed recently the particular request to which the hon. member refers, because we have been dealing with the actual situation as it has developed, but I understand the figures are the same. Ours is a somewhat higher provision, about a thousand additional.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: You have started making arrangements for shipping the five thousand, have you?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I would like to say this, and I think the hon. member who is speaking can take it as great credit to the organization which he set up. I called the staff in the department together yesterday morning before I came up to make this announcement here. It was in the strictest confidence, naturally, and I outlined what was the intention, namely, that there should be added to the troops dispatched from Canada some 16,000 infantry, 5,000 to go in December,
5.000	to go in January, and 2,000 in each of the months thereafter. The highest priority was to be given to those who were fully trained and the next to those whose training could be completed as infantry in the shortest possible period in our establishments in the United Kingdom. I met those officers this morning and the proposition was completely worked out as regards the selection and dispatch of the first 10,000, namely, those to go in December and January. Knowing, as the hon. member does, the tremendous amount of detail which is required in working out a movement of that sort, it creates a wonderful feeling of confidence on the part of the minister who, after giving a general order of the kind, can go back the following morning and find that the thing is complete and is placed before him so that he has merely to say, "Yes, that is satisfactory."

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
That is what some people call "military red tape".

R einjorcemen ts

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: It is an amazing tribute to the organization you left me, Colonel Ralston.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I can say that I have had just the same experience of their excellent staff work, general. In this time table-I am not talking about sailing dates-what time do you expect it will take, beginning with medical boarding until the men are ready at the transit camp? What do they give you as the time table?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: The movement must start at once.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: What is the time table? How long will it take-all the preliminaries?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: About a month, and that enables us to provide embarkation leave and the usual privileges. There is no hysteria at all in the movement. That was what I was anxious to determine when I looked over the plan this morning. It is quite orderly.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Did you find that it had been organized for some time?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I suspect that is true.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I think you will find they had all their plans made for three weeks. You mentioned in your statement yesterday a possible prospective shortage of fully trained infantry which may go late in January or February next. I take it that means at that time, whenever the acute period comes, there will not be in the aggregate sufficient trained infantry immediately available to bring the units all fully up to strength.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: No. The references as to the prospective shortages which I have made -were references to the situation as it was forecast before we could count on this additional 16,000 to which I have referred.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I know that. Do not let us get the two things mixed up. I am talking about your reference as to the need. I am saying the shortage which you foresaw was a shortage indicated by the fact that without the 16,000 men that you would need in January or February, or whatever time it was, you would not have sufficient fully trained infantry available to keep the units up to strength.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: And the same thing applies in respect of the situation which you predicted later in the spring or early summer.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
You said there was another period when the infantry reserve behind the
troops may become low, meaning they would not be sufficient to bring the units up to strength.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: That is right. The anxiety regarding that situation has been relieved. Our minds are relieved of the anxiety by reason of this additional dispatch.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I was trying to get the
same thing exactly. I had the same anxiety that you had.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Do
you think, General McNaughton, it is wise to send men back into the front Line after they have been wounded three times? I know you will say that you have a rule in connection with that which reads something like this, that a man may apply for leave if he has been wounded three times but not trivially. A man may be wounded a half a dozen times or more and- I have noticed in the casualty lists boys in my own riding some of whom have been wounded more than three times. I do not think it is good for them. Many of them have written me and said: "For God's sake, get us out of the line; we have had enough."

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
I share the view
that the hon. member has expressed, and I shall make it my business to go into that scheme so that people who have been wounded the number of times he indicates will not be sent forward. They undoubtedly have played their part in this conflict. You will find some of them that you cannot hold back. They are wanting to go forward again.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Has
there been any definition of the word "trivially"? I understand that "trivially" may mean one or two toes off or a few fingers off. Is there any definition of the word?

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: I am not aware of the definition, but I shall have it checked up right away and let the hon. member know.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext: Is it not true that these pools of reserves or support overseas that you say are sufficient include men who are in hospital? You count them as your reserves and support.

maintopic: REINFORCEMENTS-QUESTIONING OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
No, sir. Let me say very definitely to the hon. member that the numbers on which we are working and to which I have referred as adequate reserves are people who are immediately available to go into the units in replacement or people who would be able to come in in the early part of the following month. There is a pool. We are breaking it down now for purposes of calculation into blocks of a month's length, setting

Reinforcements

the casualties not day by day but month by month, and therefore we have to put on the available side a double figure; that is, those who are available at the beginning of the month and those who are becoming available. Therefore the two come together. The staffs are satisfied as to the adequacy of those figures. That is, the units can be kept fully up to strength.

subtopic: RESIGNATION OP HON. C. G. POWER AS MINISTER OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESIGNATION OP HON. C. G. POWER AS MINISTER OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on Friday last I mentioned that a report which had appeared in the press to the effect that the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) had tendered his resignation was correct. I also intimated that I was very carefully considering the communication which I had received from the minister before taking any
100-414J	U
action upon it. My hope was that in the course of the week-end I might find it possible to persuade my colleague to reconsider his decision to tender his resignation, having regard to the exceptionally valuable service which as a member of the government he was in a position to render at this time of war. Unhappily I have not been able to persuade him to withdraw his letter of resignation, and in the circumstances I have had no alternative but to ask His Excellency to assent to its acceptance. I ask the house to grant me permission to read the letters which passed between the hon. member and myself with respect to his resignation and to table these communications at the end of the reading, and, also, to table copies of the order in council which has been passed to-day with respect to the minister's resignation -I quote:
Canada
Minister of National Defence for Air Ottawa,
23rd November, 1944.
Rt. Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ont.
My dear Prime Minister:
It is with the deepest regret that I ask you to accept my resignation as a member of your cabinet.
I am unable to accept the policy which the government has now adopted with respect to the National Resources Mobilization Act. I do not believe such a policy to be necessary at this time, nor will it save one single Canadian casualty.
I parted company with Colonel Ralston after the most mature consideration largely on the grounds that the number of troops which he reported as being required was comparatively so small, the means to remedy the situation without placing undue strain on the men at the front so readily available, and the end of the war so imminent that weighing everything in the balance we were not justified in provoking a national scission.
I cannot accept now from a new minister General McNaughton a recommendation which I reluctantly felt obliged to reject when made by an old comrade and tried associate Layton Ralston.
May I add that the task which you confided . to me in May 1940 of organizing the British commonwealth joint air training plan has now-been completed and the plan is being w-ound up. The Royal Canadian Air Force overseas has reached the peak of its expansion.
I shall always treasure the years of association with you and my colleagues and I thank you and them for all the kindness and consideration they have shown.
Yours sincerely,
Charles G. Power.

Reinforcements-Ministerial Changes
To that communication I replied this morning as follows:
Office of the Prime Minister Canada Ottawa,
November 27, 1944.
The Honourable C. G. Power, K.C., M.P.,
157 Daly Avenue,
Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Power:
I duly received, on the 23rd instant, your letter of that day tendering your resignation as a member of the government.
Since its receipt, I have, as you know, hoped that you might find it possible to reconsider your decision. I have felt that the importance of the service which, as a member of the government, you might have continued to render Canada's war effort would have outweighed the other considerations on which you felt it necessary to resign. As, however, you have come to the conclusion that you must adhere to your original decision, I have most reluctantly been obliged to advise the Governor General that your resignation should be accepted; to this advice His Excellency has civen his consent.
I need not say how great is any regret that so trusted a colleague and so dose a friend should leave the ministry at this time. This * regret will, I know, be shared by all members of the government.
On my own behalf and on theirs, I would like warmly to reciprocate the feelings you have expressed as to what the years of our association have meant to all of us personally; also to express appreciation of what your services in the ministry at a time of war have meant to our country and to the cause of freedom.
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: RESIGNATION OP HON. C. G. POWER AS MINISTER OP NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, it is a well known and clearly established custom for a retiring member of the ministry, if he so desires, to crave the indulgence of the Speaker and of the house to say a few words in clarification of the attitude which he has taken and I do now ask that the house permit me to make a few brief remarks on the subject matter which has been brought before it.
I thank the Prime Minister for his kindness and consideration. It is consistent with his character and tradition, and with the relationship which has existed between us for a period of over twenty-five years. I part with him in sorrow, not in anger. I shall never forget and never regret the long years of our association.
With respect to my colleagues-my excolleagues, I should say-in the ministry, we have been bound together by ties of amity and of friendship and I know that no difference of opinion on political matters will break or bend those ties of friendship. With respect to the officers, N.C.O.'s and airmen of the Department of National Defence for Air and

the civilian employees of that department as well as my own personal staff, I leave them also with regret but with thanks for the kindly cooperation which they have always extended to me. It has been a privilege to serve with them in the accomplishment of a great task, a privilege that I shall always hold dear.
In 1940 the tragic death of Norman Rogers would have been an irreparable loss to Canada's war effort if we had not had Colonel Ralston to replace him.
No two men could have worked more closely together than he and I did. Our fortuitous association was cemented into a close and intimate friendship by days of intense labour and white nights of anxiety. I am convinced that the course which my ex-colleague took was embarked upon after the most serious consideration and charted by the compass of honest, conscientious conviction.
When his recommendation was made it became the duty of the cabinet as a whole to deal with it as they deal with any matter brought forward by any minister in the interests of the department which he represents. The cabinet must take into consideration not only the departmental viewpoint 'but the effect of the recommendations made by the minister on the country as a whole.
It is in order that the divergent views and diversified interests inevitable in a country of the size and composition of Canada may find expression in the councils of the nation that all prime ministers endeavour to have as members of their cabinets representatives of every class and of every section.
It is clear that cabinet did give serious consideration to the recommendations of the minister. Discussion was continuous and lasted during many days. On November 2 the Prime Minister announced that Colonel Ralston had been replaced by General McNaughton as Minister of National Defence.
The former minister could not accommodate himself to the views of his colleagues and as an honourable man, and in pursuance of the doctrine of cabinet solidarity, took the only course which was open to him.
The decision of cabinet has now been changed. I, for opposite reasons to Colonel Ralston, but following his example, am leaving the cabinet also.
I do not propose to discuss the number of available reinforcements, nor the times and places where and when they will be required, nor at any length the method of raising them.
The strategy of General Eisenhower, the Supreme Commander of the allied forces, publicly proclaimed, is to strike the enemy again
NOVEMBER 27, 1944	6593
Reinforcements-Ministerial Changes
and again, and to give him no rest and no respite. We are informed that in order to carry out this Eisenhower plan of war, reinforcements must be available and at hand to refill battalions and units within twenty-four hours after the casualties occur.
I think I should draw to the attention of the house, and of the thousands of mothers, wives, sweethearts and dependents of those now in the front line, that this repeated return to battle, instead of making for fewer casualties among their loved ones, might very easily make for more. No commander will take his experienced men out of the unit and undertake an engagement with only the newly-arrived, however well trained they may be.
It seems to me that the logical thing, the reasonable thing, is to take the men out of the line temporarily to refit, to reequip, to rest, to recuperate and to refill the gaps in their ranks.
By all reports, the number required even of infantry, in which arm alone there is said to be a threatened deficiency, is comparatively small. The lowering of the rate of casualties by periods of comparative or total inactivity would wipe out the margin of deficit, if any exists, and restore the balance.
Neither ultimate victory nor national honour requires that Canadian troops should be in action every hour or every day, or even take part in every battle necessary to bring about final victory, especially when thousands of Europeans, fresh freed from the tyranny and the unspeakable terror of nazi occupation, are panting for vengeance on the oppressor.
It might be feared that the course I have suggested would lower the prestige and glory of Canada. In my opinion that glory and prestige has been for ever established by the deeds of our fighting men in every branch of the service. I cannot believe that this suggestion could be regarded as anything but common humanity and common sense having regard to all the circumstances.
It has been stated that casualties amongst the troops of some of our allies are greater than ours. Surely this war is something more than a competition in casualties amongst the allied nations.
I too have at heart the interests of the men at the front.
I shall not refer to my relations with the veterans of the last war. The records of this House of Commons during the past twenty-seven years are there for all to see.
With regard to my attitude towards the overseas forces in this war, the story is in the records of the Department of National Defence for Air. It is in the files of the British Air Ministry. It is in the instructions given by me to the commanding officers of the R.C.A.F.
overseas; and it deals largely with leave from the front, repatriation to Canada, and with representations' for relief from the undue risk involved in lengthened or repeated tours of duty of the R.C.A.F. aircrew, whether serving in our own Canadian squadrons or attached to RA.F. This attitude with respect to the R.C.A.F. is consistent with the views I hold with regard to the army.
If the course of systematic recuperation were taken, then the voluntary system which we have been following, which yielded more men last year than was ever estimated or even anticipated, and which in the words of the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. McNaughton) has not failed, would have sufficed at this stage of the war when by the most authoritative accounts victory is certain.
I gave to Colonel Ralston's report my most sincere and conscientious consideration.
I remained with the government and held firm to the policy to which I clearly understood it to be unreservedly committed. It was the policy on Wednesday morning last. It was the policy until Wednesday night. I could not change my matured consideration in a matter of minutes.
Conscription may be justified in moments of national crisis and in defence of one's country; and in the discussion of Bill 80 of 1942 I said so. It might have been justified at certain periods and phases of this war when we were on the brink of almost certain defeat. It might have been justified if D-day had been a smashing catastrophe instead of a brilliant success. But these days are now past. We have no right to tear this country asunder at this stage, and in this state of the war.
A word as to the consequences of this controversy. Millions of honest, decent people in all parts of Canada and of all shades of opinion are in the process of hating and reviling one another. Reason and sincere conviction have given way to hysteria on both sides. Cleavage between classes and between races has been driven deeper and deeper. The most tragic thing of all is the weakening of faith and confidence in public men-not only by the people of one province, but in all provinces; not only amongst those who hold one view, but in men and women of all sides of this unfortunate debate.
As to the cleavages to which J refer, I cherish and hold fast to the ideas of the chieftain under whose aegis I entered this house, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He could not and would not believe that as a Canadian he could belong to a party of one province only. With him, I cannot and will not subscribe to a purely isolationist provincial standpoint.

War Effort-Government Policy.
It may foe that for some time to come the day has gone when men of similar ideas and principles can meet and join in common action across the Ottawa river.
My hope, my prayer is that there will be no such outcome, and that with the advent of external victory and peace, peace and understanding may come within our own country.
