subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-MOTION, THE PRIME MINISTER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-MOTION, THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
. that this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
He said: Mr. Speaker, if anything were necessary to emphasize the gravity of the issue that has so suddenly arisen, it would most certainly be found in the words of my former colleague and all-time friend, the former minister of national defence for air (Mr. Power). He has given to the house, in a very few words, the real nature of the question which is before this House of Com-

mons at the present time. In a word, the issue of conscription has, once again, come to the fore, and it has brought to the fore once again the most serious kind of controversy which this parliament, has had, at different times, to face. The minister has drawn attention to the fact that he has resigned from the government for a reason diametrically opposed to that of the former minister of defence who resigned a short time before. I hope that this will make clear to the house, perhaps clearer than hon. members have realized thus far, *the nature of the position in which I, as Prime Minister of Canada at this time, have been placed in seeking to carry out what has been, above all else, the purpose of my work in public life, the maintenance of unity as far as that might be possible in the government of this country and in the Dominion of Canada itself.
Perhaps, owing to the fact that the question before us is of such great gravity, hon. gentlemen in different parts of the house will allow me to proceed with my remarks without interruption. If I should make a misstatement, I should, of course, wish to be instantly corrected, but, otherwise, I hope that hon. members will allow me to answer such questions as they may wish to ask at the conclusion of my remarks rather than in the course of them.
As the issue is one which is related almost exclusively to the question of the adoption of a measure of conscription at this time, it might be well, for an understanding of the reasons why some members of the government have taken different views, were I to review very briefly the development of this question since the beginning of the war. Here may I say that, from the outset, I have been conscious that what has been a source of division in the cabinet was but a reflection of what was certain to be a source of division in this House of Commons, and that-again- this House of Commons would be reflecting a source of division in all parts of this country. That is what has made and still makes the present question the most serious one with which this parliament, I believe, has been faced at any time.
Hon. members will recall that, before Canada entered the war, there had been much consideration of the attitude that should be taken by any government that might be in office should war come. It was anticipated that war might break out suddenly, and members of the government, and members of parliament other than those in the government, had to consider very carefully what attitude they would take in that event.
NOVEMBER 27, 1344	6595
War Effort-Government Policy
When the moment came, in September, 1939, and the house was brought together, it became my great and grave responsibility to ask members of this house unitedly to enter the war. I gave my reasons at the time why I believed it was a war that threatened human freedom and Christian civilization. I said that, in my opinion, it was a war which might spread to vast proportions and that nothing in history would be comparable to what we might be called upon to experience. When I asked this house to enter the war hon. members were all, I think, of one mind with respect to one of the conditions under which we would be prepared to take part in the conflict. It was that there should be no conscription for the sending of men overseas.
That was the position in September, 1939. Parliament met and had its discussions and the government was given and assumed the great task. But we had not been under way very long before we met with opposition from outside sources which, in my opinion, would have undermined any confidence which the public had in the administration. Realizing, therefore, that confidence was of the essence of the power of the government, I thought it advisable to seek that confidence from the source of our power, and to have parliament dissolved and an appeal made to the people.
When that appeal was made members of all parties appeared before the public and stated, I think, for the most part, what their position would be with regard to conscription. At any rate, members of the administration took the position that there should not be conscription for service overseas, and we took that position, not because of any statute, but because most of us, if indeed not all of us, had a moral obligation which we appreciated very deeply. We had given our word, no one more strongly than myself, speaking before the war broke out, that if war came the government would not resort to conscription for service overseas.
The government was returned by a very large majority. It had a mandate to carry on the war and to carry it on without resort to conscription. In the same year, early in the summer, the country received an appalling shock. France fell. And the world wakened up to the fact that the enemy we were fighting was an enemy whose power was vastly greater than the power required to dominate any one continent. It was a power which, unless it were overthrown, might dominate the world.
We, in Canada, were, at that time, supremely conscious of the fact that our own country might some day be invaded. Indeed, there was reason for the belief that, unless the might of Britain were able to protect us, we would
most certainly be invaded. In those circumstances, this parliament deemed it necessary to enact what is known as the National Resources Mobilization Act. That act was based on the principle of conscription, but it was conscription for service within Canada. The principle of conscription was certainly settled at that time and in that way so far as service within Canada itself was concerned.
That measure having been passed and the country having accepted it, the government continued with its great responsibility, seeking to avoid even the consideration of adopting the principle of conscription for service overseas. However, agitation arose in the country, an agitation for conscription. It was being represented that the government would resort to conscription, except for the moral obligations which some of its members had assumed. That was being given as the reason why this government was not in a position to carry out the power which it had under the law of the land. There has never been a moment at which the government has not had the legal power, but there was, up to that moment, a Very strong moral obligation. Now may I say that, as between legal obligation and moral obligation, if I find the two in conflict I shall, with God's help, maintain the moral obligation. Feeling very strongly that there might come a time, in the light of the developments of the war as they were then proceeding, when this moral obligation, so long as it lasted, might come to impede what was essential to the saving of this country and of human freedom throughout the world, I had my colleagues join me in proposing a plebiscite which would free us from any moral obligation that had existed up to that time. A plebiscite that would free our hands as individuals, a plebiscite that would free the hands of this parliament, as such. We sought to remove any question as to resorting or not resorting to conscription if that became necessary, because of some prior moral obligation.
The plebiscite was overwhelmingly carried. I have never been able to understand why any hon. members and newspapers should since have maintained, as some of them have maintained-not many but some-and great organizations throughout the country, even an organization as important as the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League, that there was as a result of the plebiscite, a mandate on the part of the country to the government to carry out conscription. That is an entire falsification, Mr. Speaker, of the interpretation of the plebiscite. Need I go farther at the moment than simply to quote a paragraph or two from a speech of my own to the people of Canada and one to this House of Commons
War Effort-Government Policy

in regard to the matter? On April 7, 1942, I made a nation-wide broadcast on the subject of the issue of the plebiscite. In the course of that address, as will be found on page 7 of the publication issued by the director of public information, I made this statement. The heading is "Canada's war effort being placed in false light."
And that brings me to the last of the questions to which you are awaiting a reply: "Why. after two and a half years of war, has it become necessary to have the restriction removed?"
The restriction therein referred to was the restriction which was attached to the National Resources Mobilization Act, which was that its provisions would not apply to the sending of men overseas. The government was asking that that restriction should be removed so that if the occasion should arise where the government believed the time had come when it was necessary to send men overseas it would be free to do so, free from all moral obligations, and of anything that could be cited as a moral obligation. Speaking on that point I said:
And that brings me to the last of the questions to which you are awaiting a reply. "Why, after two and a half years, has it become necessary to have the restriction removed?" One answer is that this restriction is being represented as the bar to an all-out effort on Canada's part. It makes no difference whether conscription for service overseas would add to Canada's total effort or not, the fact that the government is not free to consider its adoption is made to appear as limiting Canada's war effort.
At that time we were being told from certain sources that we were not going fast enough, that our war effort was restricted and limited. The alleged limitation was attributed by those who were back of the agitation at the time to this moral obligation not to resort to conscription. I was anxious, certainly, that the country should see that, if there was any limitation, it was for other reasons, national reasons. I was anxious also that the country should see that we were achieving a total war effort just as rapidly as a total war effort could be brought into being.
The truth, of course, is that our army to-day is just as large as it would have been if conscription for overseas service had been adopted. The absence of conscription for overseas service has not limited our war effort. The lack of power to impose such conscription has, however, placed our war effort in a wholly false light before our own citizens, and, what is worse, before our allies. In other words, conscription has been made the symbol of a total effort regardless of all Canada is doing to help win the war.
Then another heading: "Issue not conscription-but powers of government":
The issue at present is not conscription;-
LMr. Mackenzie King.]
This was said to the people of Canada before they cast their votes on the plebiscite.
The issue at present is not conscription; it is whether or not the government, subject to its responsibility to parliament, is to be free to decide that question itself in the light of all national considerations. The government is not asking you to say whether or not conscription should be adopted. That responsibility the government is asking you to leave to itself and to parliament, with entire freedom to decide the question on its merits.
The question of conscription, properly viewed, is a military question. The place to discuss it is in parliament. What the government now seeks for itself and for parliament is freedom to consider and debate and decide this question, like all other questions connected with the war, unrestricted by any pledge and in the light only of the needs of national security.
That was what was said to the people. I shall now quote what I said in this House of Commons in the presence of the then leaders of the different parties and of the members who were members of the House of Commons at that time. I shall cite only one or two paragraphs. When I was speaking on Wednesday, June 10, 1942, I said:
Let me now deal with the relationship of the plebiscite to conscription, and in particular as to whether a "yes" or "no" vote was a vote for or against conscription. On this point I should, first of all. remind hon. members of what was said in the course of the plebiscite campaign. Both in this house and throughout the country, it was made perfectly clear by myself as leader of the government, by the leader of the official opposition and by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and by members of their respective parties, that an affirmative vote was not a vote for conscription. I am afraid I cannot tell the house what stand the leader of the Social Credit party took. I have, however, found nothing in any of his utterances which would enable it to be said that he regarded an affirmative vote as a vote for conscription for service overseas.
Tihe question on the ballot is, however, the best answer as to whether or not the plebiscite was a vote for or against conscription.
The question on which the people of Canada were asked to express an opinion was:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
Clearly the plebiscite merely released the government from its obligation not to resort to conscription for service overseas. It did not commit the government to conscription for service overseas. The result of the plebiscite leaves no doubt as to the freedom of the government and of parliament to discuss the question of conscription for service overseas upon its merits. It equally leaves no doubt as to the freedom of the government and of parliament to decide, for or against conscription for service overseas, either conditionally or unconditionally.
I will not refer further to that subject, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to say, once and for all, that I do not think any good

War Effort-Government Policy
purpose is served by having the result of the plebiscite referred to a couple of years later in terms other than those which were not contradicted in this house at the time I made the statement to which I have just referred.
I come now to the. next step, which was the introduction and enactment of Bill 80. Bill 80 grew out of the discussions in this house following those that had taken place on the plebiscite. I should like to recall that Bill 80 was discussed in this house in June, 1942; that is, over two years ago. Bill 80 was introduced into the house in order to make it perfectly clear that the government would have thereafter the right to take such steps and actions with respect to. conscription as it might be necessary to take, either conscription in whole or conscription to a limited extent. That bill recognized the principle of conscription. At the time this house debated the whole question of conscription. We had a lengthy debate, and it was made very clear then that we were discussing the question of conscription and its possible use should that become necessary at a later time.
Why did the house take that step? The house, I believe, took that step just as it has taken every other step since the beginning of this war, in the light of the changing conditions of the world under the impact of war. The situation in 1941 was very different from what it was in 1940. In 1942 it was much graver than in 1941. No government with a sense of the responsibility that it should have would have wished to be left in any doubt as to its powers, should the necessity arise, to take any steps which might be needed in order to prevent a worse condition arising in our own country and throughout the world. That is why that measure was enacted.
May I make it clear that, in the course of that debate, different views were expressed by hon. members as to what the particular situation would be which might make it necessary to take action under that measure. Some, and I think I myself was one, spoke particularly in reference to the winning of the war. That was broadly the view which, I believe, a large number of us on this side took, that it would relate to the winning of the war itself. But specific references were also made, references which I shall mention a little later on, relating immediately to the reinforcement of troops, our own Canadian troops who would be serving in actual theatres of war overseas. Any statement that related to the winning of the war would necessarily, thereafter, have to be considered in the light of the particular pledge given at that time. I think I can best express the policy of the government, under that
measure, by saying that it represented not necessarily conscription but conscription if necessary; and may I add that in the minds of those who thought in terms of conscription if necessary, there was also the thought, ''and to the extent that might be necessary."
I shall leave that, at this point, and pass on to what followed after the bill was passed. The year 1942 went by and no action was necessary under the measure. All of 1943 went by and no action was necessary. The first seven months of this year, 1944, went by and there was no suggestion that anything was necessary under that measure by way of sending troops overseas in accordance with its provisions.

I am speaking for what was understood, certainly on this side of the house, in reference to the matter to which I have referred, and by the government as to the possibility of there being need for reinforcements.
That brings me to the immediate situation that has arisen, and here I wish to give to the house the sequence of the discussions that took place. As far as the government is concerned, there was nothing before it at any time up to October of this year which suggested that there would be any need for conscription to provide further reinforcements overseas. Let me make this perfectly clear. Colonel Ralston, the former minister of national defence, for a long time has believed that it might become necessary to resort to conscription for service overseas to provide necessary reinforcements. At different times when we have been discussing this matter he has made it clear that while not pressing anything of the kind as a matter

War Effort-Government Policy

of immediate need, he himself had a mental reservation as to the possibility of its becoming necessary to resort to conscriptioa at some time. It is due to the former minister that this should be known; it is due to the government also that it should be known that at no time, up to the period of which I am speaking, did the minister bring forward any recommendation, express or implied, for the sending overseas of further reinforce' ments under conscription. There is one point I wish to make clear-and here let me say that I am not going to try to go over the ground covered in the communications between Colonel Ralston and myself. What is set forth therein can be read by hon. members and need not be repeated at this time. But I do wish to make this statement, with which I am sure the former minister of national defence will be the first to agree: that when this question did come up, he and I were determined that it should not become a King-Ralston conflict or battle, as I have seen, it since described in the press. What has taken place in the discussions has been the consideration, the most careful and thoughtful consideration, of two opposing points of view, points of view that were opposed at the time of and have been opposed since the da}'s of the South African war: whether men should go overseas under voluntary enlistment, or whether resort might have to be had to compulsion. In all the discussions that wre have had, there has been nothing personal between the former minister of national defence and myself. To the extent that each has stood for a certain point of view we have been standing for points of view that we know are held in this country at the present time.
On August 7 of this year a recommendation was made to the government by the chief of staff that some seven hundred additional men should be made available for service in Italy. When that recommendation was made, I immediately asked if its acceptance would have any effect upon our man-power resources, whether it would result in any shortage of men in the event of some special demand coming for the reinforcing of men overseas. The government was given the most direct assurance at that time by the chief of staff, with the Minister of National Defence present, that there was no need for considering the question of additional reinforcements for overseas by compulsion.
Let me go a step farther. In September, from the tenth to the seventeenth, if I recall aright, a conference was held at Quebec between the Prime Minister of the United

Kingdom and the President of the United ' States. During the period of that conference there were meetings held between our own chiefs of staff and the chiefs of staff of the United Kingdom. There was also a conference held of the members of the war committee, at which our own chiefs of staff were present and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Mr. Churchill, along with the chiefs of the staff of the United Kingdom. That conference discussed questions related to the armed forces. It discussed matters related to the army, navy and air forces. The discussions were both particularly and generally mainly in reference to the war in the Pacific and what in that connection might be necessary.
One would have felt that, at a time when discussion was taking place on the reduction of the forces-because that obviously was one of the matters that was being carefully *considered, if there had been a possible inadequacy, in regard to needed reinforcement abroad for our army, that something would have been said of such a possible need. Nothing was said at that time which could give any member of the government of Canada reason to believe that we were nearing the time, or that we were fearing the time, when it might be necessary to resort to conscription to provide men for service overseas as reinforcements to our army.
I mention all this in order that the house may realize the impact of the shock that came upon the government a little later on, just as hon. members themselves must have felt the impact of the shock which has come to them in the last few days when they were told that they would have to face this question of sending men across the seas by conscription at this stage of the war.
After the Quebec conference there were persons in this country who began to make representations which were, to say the least, very distressing to the mothers, fathers and relatives of those who were fighting overseas and which must have been doubly distressing to the men who were serving in the armed forces. It was alleged that men in the army were not sufficiently trained and that, as a consequence, men were obliged to go into battle not adequately trained, or supported by men who were not adequately trained. I have always regretted that an immediate reply was not made to those statements, but it was not. I am inclined to believe that it was because the Minister of National Defence wished to be doubly sure before he made any reply. He had planned for some time to go overseas to visit the armies in

Italy and Europe to observe matters for himself. Hon. members will recall that the minister had not been long overseas before he sent back word that he did not think there was any justification for the statement that -men insufficiently trained were being sent into battle.
There the matter stood until October 13. At that time I received a cable from the Minister of National Defence giving me reassurance about the training of the men and stating that he felt perfectly satisfied with regard to the adequacy of the training which they had had. He stated, however, that he had become greatly concerned about the possible need for reinforcements and asked that I should see him as soon as he got back and arrange to have the war committee meet to hear his representations. He arrived back on Wednesday, October 18. That afternoon we had a conference in my office at which the minister told me that he had come to the conclusion that unless men could be secured very quickly by the voluntary method it would be necessary to invoke the National Resources Mobilization Act to send men overseas under compulsion. The next morning the same statement was made by the minister to the members of the war committee, and in the afternoon it was made to the members of the cabinet.
That was the first time that the members of the cabinet as a whole had had any thought of there being a probable necessity of men having to be sent overseas under Bill No. 80 to supply needed reinforcements. That explains why it took some little time before the discussions could get far enough for a decision to be reached one way or the other.
I want to make clear that the minister assured us that, as far as the records showed, the probability was that a critical situation would not arise until the beginning of the new year, but that he thought it might become acute at that time. I want that to be clearly understood so that hon. members in the house and people throughout the country will realize that, while the government has been giving this matter all the mature consideration that its great importance and grave significance necessitate, we have been running no risk so far as our fighting men overseas are concerned. I hope that it will be a complete assurance to their friends and relatives at home, to know that the time devoted to the discussion, which has taken place thus far, has not in any way prejudiced the position and security of our men overseas.
May I point out, as the former minister of national defence for air reminded us this afternoon, that this discussion came after five
100-415*
years of war under the voluntary enlistment method, and that it came on what was believed at the time to be the very eve of victory, of what we are being told from all sources would be ultimate victory, and that we were coming nearer to it every day. Do hon. members wonder that there was a difference of view in the cabinet at the time as to what was the best course to adopt? Let me say this, that the cabinet was quite prepared, once the facts had been la:d before its members by the minister, to accept the view that there was need for additional reinforcements being sent across. The difference that arose was one of method, whether in order to supply the additional numbers of men to reinforce the armies overseas we should abandon the voluntary enlistment method and accept full conscription under Bill 80, or intensify the existing system of securing the necessary reinforcements by voluntary enlistment. The question was: which of the two methods was preferable, or was there some way of meeting the situation other than by resorting to one extreme or the other.
I need not say that members of the cabinet gave their most earnest thought to the consideration of that problem day after day, and may I say that we were all conscious, at the time, of what failure to find a solution might mean.
I ask this house if it can conceive of any obligation that a ministry ever had placed upon it which was more onerous than the obligation to find some solution of this problem which would not involve a break-up of the government itself in a time of war. As I speak, I want hon. members to realize this, that new situations were being created within Canada which were very unsettling. A degree of unrest -was being organized the like of which has not been seen in the history of Canada before, not even in a political campaign. One may condemn this movement; the day will come when it will be exposed and will be fully condemned. But in a ministry, unfortunately, one cannot escape the responsibility that attaches to coping with every situation that -may arise, and a wholly new condition of affairs has arisen in this country as a result of the organized propaganda for conscription in Canada. A new condition and a very serious condition had arisen and it was one with the possible consequences of which the government has had to deal.
I want hon. members, in judging the action of the administration, to keep clearly in their minds what it was that we had to take account of. In speaking of what we might have to do
War Effort-Government Policy

if we had to act under bill 80, I used in this house the words that the government would act under that measure only when it deemed it was necessary and, I added, advisable so to do. Those two words carry great weight- necessary with regard to what was essential to the maintenance of our forces overseas, and advisable in the light of conditions not only in Europe but here in Canada and of what might be the consequences if we acted in any particular way. That brings me to what led to the resignation of the then minister of national defence.
May I pause to say this. It may appear to hon. members that I am disclosing matters that took place in cabinet council. I would not be going as far as I am this afternoon in these statements in disclosing what has taken place in cabinet council were it not for the fact that disclosures bearing on this matter have been made by the former minister of national defence, and were made known in a communication which was given to the press on the evening of Sunday, November 12. Up to that time, as hon. members will see by reading the correspondence between the minister and myself, I had felt that, following the constitutional practice with regard to the conditions under which matters in council could be disclosed, I would have had to advise His Excellency against permitting some of these matters to be made public. But once the disclosures were made in public my only decision could then be to ask His Excellency to permit the letters between the former minister of defence and myself to be published in their entirety. What I am saying to-day is based only on what has appeared in the publication of those letters and what had earlier been given to the public.
I might go at length into what was in the minds of the members of the cabinet in discussing this matter but it will be largely apparent to members what the arguments were. Naturally the members of the cabinet who felt that resort to conscription at this stage was not necessary supported that point of view by drawing attention to the five years of success that we have had under the voluntary system and to the fact that the war was obviously drawing near to a close. They called attention to statements that had been made by the Prime Minister of Britain that we were on the last Jap of the war, and to statements made by other leaders as to what they believed would be the further duration of the war. I should perhaps make it clear that it was about this time that Mr. Churchill added to what he had previously said that the war might take very much longer to finish than was anticipated. That again had its bearing on the discussions. But what I think members of the cabinet felt
fMr. Mackenzie Kina *
in particular was that Canada after all, as the former minister for air has pointed out this afternoon, had played very fine and noble part in this war, that we had carried our just burden in the war very well, and that we had failed in nothing that was possible to make Canada's war effort a total war effort. What seemed hardest to understand was how, after all we had done and were doing to make Canada's effort a total effort, we should suddenly have either to accept or to reject this obligation of sending additional men overseas under conscription, with all that any decision was certain to mean. We felt very strongly that up to that time nothing had been denied the army from the beginning of the war which the [DOT] minister of defence had requested as necessary for the fighting men overseas.
I can say this, and I am proud to say it. While I am not a military man I have relied with absolute confidence on the exceedingly able men of military experience whom I haye had around me in the departments of defence. When they have come forward with recommendations, while I have asked time and again whether we might not be going a little too far, I have always, after the assurances had been given that we were running no risk in regard to the question of our army being too large or the man-power problem coming to be critical later on, sought to have the recommendations met. Along with the rest of my colleagues I have accepted these representations in the best of faith, just as, I believe, they were given in the best of faith. I have done all that any man in my position, I believe, could do to make our army as complete, and the position of every man in it as secure, as it was possible to make it. This government has not only done all that could possibly be done with reference to the army, but the same is true in reference to our great contribution dn the air; the same is true of our great contribution on the sea; the same has been true in respect of our great contribution in the supply of munitions; the same has been true of what the people of this country have done in the matter of supplying food and other commodities that were necessary ; the same is true in regard to the tremendous financial obligations we have assumed-obligations, may I say, much larger than most people have even begun to realize at this time. It is true with respect to what we have done in the matter of mutual aid to our allies, something which no other country lias done in comparable measure; also of what we have done in the contribution to UNRRA to help to meet relief which is needed by those countries that have been under the heel of

War Effort-Government Policy
the conqueror and the oppressor. In no particular relating to the war effort anywhere have we done other than seek to make it a total effort, a maximum effort. Having done all that, naturally the ministers of the crown asked themselves, why must we run the risk of dividing this country over the particular request which is being made now and which may have such serious consequences; and that, as I have said, on what we are being led to believe is the eve of certain victory?
There was another argument which was very carefully considered, and it was this: what is the position of the war in Europe to-day? My former colleague the minister for air has said what I have said repeatedly, that if at the moment of the invasion, when everyone contemplated the possibility of life being unavoidably sacrificed on a great scale, a scale which at the time none of us could bear to face even in thought, our men had suffered great loss, lives had been sacrificed on a large scale and there had1 obviously been before our men the prospect of fighting on in Europe with their ranks depleted to liberate the countries there, I would not have lost one hour in bringing this House of Commons together and asking hon. members to support the government in sending the needed reinforcements at once, and I believe those reinforcements would have been granted without any division in this house. But what is the situation? Since the landing, which relatively speaking was carried through with amazingly small loss, France has been freed, Belgium has been freed, part of Holland has been freed, a , still larger part of Italy has been freed, Greece has been freed; in Yugoslavia the forces which were opposed to and fighting one another have been brought together and are working against the enemy; the satellite nations of Germany- Roumania and Bulgaria-instead of being at her side, have turned against her and are fighting against her to-day. Add to all that that Russia has driven the enemy off her soil and has invaded Germany and is fighting on German soil to-day. More than that, United States troops, British troops, Canadian troops, French troops, all of them to-day in some measure are fighting on German soil and conditions in Germany itself must be appalling. Do you wonder that some members of the cabinet found it difficult to appreciate why we should be asked to make this further contribution; and that particularly in the light of the experience of the introduction of conscription for overseas which we had in the last war? The adoption of conscription at that time was responsible for more disunity in this country
than any other step which has been taken in the history of Canada since confederation. With that example before us, do you think it was easy for any of us to come to the point of view that it was necessary at this time to adopt even a limited measure of conscription?
That, I think, gives a fair idea of what were some of the thoughts in the minds of members of the cabinet.
May I say further what was particularly in my own mind. I think it was true in some measure of my colleagues generally, but it was particularly true of myself because I have had to look at these questions as they relate to our national problems and our international relations. I had to think of what effect the taking of a step such as we are proposing to take at this moment might have on the future condition of this country in relation to the solution of its own problems and as regards its relations with other parts of the British commonwealth and other countries, and with all parts of the world. We are facing post-war problems on a scale that no man's imagination in this house, I believe, thus far has been able to grasp. We have the problems of the world organization of peace after the war is over. I have had to ask myself the question, what is going to be the effect of resort to conscription for overseas service at this time on the efforts that are now being put forward by Prime Minister Churchill, by President Roosevelt, by Marshal Stalin, and those associated with them, the greater and the lesser powers, to bring about that form of world organization which will keep the peace of this world, if our country, Canada, which has played the great part that we have played in this war, becomes divided. Our voice is not going to be a voice that will carry with it the weight and the influence which it was hoped, until a very short time ago, it would almost certainly carry in the solution of some of these great questions. This matter had to be considered in its bearing upon international problems as well as upon the problems of Canadian unity.
Let me continue with the discussion itself. As I have said, the cabinet were convinced by the minister as to the need of sending more men overseas. The division has arisen not over the question of need but over the question of method, as to how the needed reinforcements could best be supplied. A number of members of the cabinet believed they could be supplied by an intensification of the voluntary method; others did not. I will not labour the matter by seeking to outline the discussion or to explain why it was we took time and
War Effort-Government Policy

yet more time in consideration. Xet me come to this. We had reached the point where we were agreed, at least, that we would make a further appeal by the voluntary method for men and see what response we would get to that appeal. But the point on which we could not get final agreement was whether, before we began the appeal, we should fix a date within which the numbers would have to be supplied, and make that date known, or keep it secret to ourselves.
May I say that any appeal that begins with a confession of doubt as to its success is never likely to succeed. If we had been obliged to advertise to those *whom we were seeking to have come in of their own accord the fact that if they did not come within a certain time they would be conscripted, does anyone think that we would have obtained an adequate response as a result of such an appeal?
There are only two methods of obtaining results in matters that require governmental action; one is the voluntary method and the other is compulsion. When the Minister of Finance seeks to raise money for the country in order to carry on the war he takes advantage of both methods. He seeks to raise money in large sums by voluntary subscription, by voluntary loans; and if he does not succeed in getting money by voluntary loans then he has to raise it by taxation-compulsion. I have never heard an appeal being made under the victory loan campaigns-and we have had seven magnificent loans-which has been carried through by threat, the threat that unless the money was obtained by a certain date the people would have to bear extra taxes up to a certain amount at the end of that time. The same principle exactly was at stake in this matter. That was where, I think, we parted, where the minister and myself felt that we would have to part company. The minister repeatedly stated that he had not much faith, or any faith-I think I could go that far, that he had not faith, let me put it that way-in the voluntary method succeeding; and as day after day went by and we were still seeking to reach a course that would secure the needed reinforcements and keep us united, I was being told almost each day that unless we got a settlement the minister would have to resign, and would resign.
Now I come to the position in which I found myself as Prime Minister of Canada under those circumstances. Unfortunately, my good friend the Minister of National Defence for Air was suffering from an illness, followed later by an operation, and for the most part he was unable to be in the cabinet

while these discussions were on. I missed him very much at my side throughout that period. I had to face the fact that if the resignation of the Minister of National Defence took place, the Associate Minister of National Defence would not have been here to take *his place. But I had to face something more than that. I had to face this fact. All of us revered our colleague the Minister of National Defence, and may I say that many of us, including myself, personally loved him, and I had to face the fact that if he were to leave the cabinet his resignation would probably be followed by the resignations of other ministers. This is not something fanciful; this is something real, because the intimation was made very clearly that if Colonel Ralston went others would have to consider -whether they -would not have to go as well. I ask this House of Commons; I ask the people of Canada, where this country would be, at this time, if one minister after another, more particularly those who carried the greatest part of the responsibility of our war effort, had left the cabinet and I had been left thus handicapped with so great a load of responsibility for carrying on the war. The situation clearly was becoming one of utmost gravity so far as Canada's entire war effort was concerned.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that until I knew that it was only a matter of hours, at the most one or two days possibly, though I believe it was more nearly a matter of hours, that the Minister of National Defence would tender his resignation because we had not been able to agree on the last point to which I have referred-it was not until then that I asked myself: Is there any way of helping to save the appalling situation that may arise if the minister resigns? That situation I have just described. It was then and only then that I though there was one man in this country who might help to save that situation. Could I find as minister of national defence someone who the country had reason to believe had a knowledge of military affairs and knew the needs of the army, a man who understood relations between the state and the army which would also have to be considered? Until I thought of the one I did, I can tell hon. members that I had well nigh begun to despair of what could be done to save the situation.
It was then that I called in General McNaughton and told him the plight I was in, and the position of the government as I saw it, and asked whether he felt that by a voluntary appeal, which there was still time to make, we could find the necessary men. He told me he believed that they could be

War Effort-Government Policy
found, the numbers not being large, as my hon. friend the former minister of national defence for air has just said, and that an appeal launched in the proper way and carried on in the right spirit would bring forward the men. I asked him on the following day, or the same day, I have forgotten which, I had only two conversations with him, whether he would assume that responsibility himself if a crisis arose, whether he would come into the government and take on his shoulders the burden of making an appeal, with faith in it, believing that it might be successful.
I did not know then, and I do not know yet, what General McNaughton's politics are. I do not think he has been identified with any political party. I know him as a man of fine liberal outlook, of rare scientific ability and of great military experience, and I felt I owed it to the people of the country never to let this country get into the position, if it were possible to avoid it, where at a time of war Canada would be left without a minister of national defence and, possibly without several of the members of the cabinet who had carried on so large a part of the war effort.
It was when I told the cabinet that General McNaughton was prepared to assume this responsibility, that I thought that if we were going to make a public appeal we should lose no time because time was rapidly going by, that the minister said that if that was the case he thought he ought to tender his resignation at once, and it was tendered in the presence of my colleagues and myself. I received the written communication the next morning and I arranged to have the new minister sworn in on that morning as well.
Those are the circumstances of Colonel Ralston's resignation.
May I emphasize this fact to this house: That was crisis No. 1, a crisis which involved the possibility of Canada being left at a time of war without a ministry. I want to emphasize that. If one minister after the other had gone, if I had not been able to secure General McNaughton, who instantly brought confidence, I think, to the general public as he did to the ministry as a whole-had I not been able to do that, then I say this country would have found itself in a position where there would have been no government. Let me emphasize this fact further-this is something that this House of Commons and the country ought to know. I took great care to ask one colleague after the other, would he take the responsibility that was mine? I asked the minister of defence himself, would he take the responsibility of heading the government and putting through this particular measure? I was told by him that he would not. It is
very easy, may I say, to oppose a position hitherto assumed by a government and to propose new measures, but unless men are prepared to back their policies by taking responsibility for their enactment and carrying them out, they have no right, if members of a ministry, to leave a ministry in circumstances where as a consequence of their action the whole structure is almost certain to collapse.
We all have responsibilities. It is not the Prime Minister only that has responsibilities. I have made it plain that my power as a Prime Minister rests on the power and support that I can get from my colleagues, and the power and support that I can get from my colleagues of the cabinet, in turn, rests upon the power and support that this House of Commons is prepared to give them. The power which this House of Commons has rests upon the power and the will of the people of the country. Any man who takes responsibility must be prepared at all times to carry that responsibility, support it to the last degree or else make his appeal to the people themselves.
Then I asked myself the question: Shall I dissolve parliament; shall I ask for dissolution and appeal to the people? What was the answer to that question? The answer was this: Will a dissolution of parliament help the men who are ready to sacrifice their lives at the front, in order that we may preserve our freedom; will a dissolution help to get the reinforcements which we have been told by the minister of defence are necessary at this time? I could not see that it would. Indeed I have made it plain from the start that I hoped that until this war was over it would not be necessary to have a general election.
Colonel Ralston had not been out of the government for half a day before some of the papers carried the headlines: "Is Mr. King thinking of a general election?" Yes, I could have swept the whole province of Quebec, carried every seat in it. I could have carried seats from one end of this country to the other, and I have not the least doubt that I could have come back to this parliament as prime minister with a good majority as the result of an appeal in circumstances such as these. Would that have helped the men overseas? Would we not have had in this country the most bitter, the most cruel kind of political campaign? And let me say this, because I think this is important. Hon. members should remember it. This parliament has fixed a particularly long time for a political campaign, a particularly long time, over two months, according to the legislation we put through at this very session, before the writs are issued and are returnable. Then
War Effort-Government Policy

there remains the further time for bringing parliament together. I hope that hon. members will keep these things in mind. Two months and more of political warfare while we have international war raging at the same time. Can you imagine a situation more cruel to the people of this country than to have anything of that kind take place at this moment, more cruel to our fighting men overseas? I had to consider that; but I had to consider most of all-and I am going to speak of it again later this afternoon-whom I would advise His Excellency to call upon to form an alternative government. If I were to recommend that parliament dissolve, because I could no longer hope to carry on, the first question I would be asked by His Excellency the Governor General would be: Whom do you recommend? Well, I could not find one of my own colleagues who was prepared to take that responsibility. I do not know whether any gentlemen opposite would have been prepared to take it. I wonder if they would.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-MOTION, THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I am sorry, I mean resignation which probably would have been followed by a dissolution. The two are almost inseparable in my mind under the conditions of things as they are at the present time. And it is important that, as I say, hon. members should keep that in mind. The Prime Minister cannot hold office if he cannot get the support necessary, and I had to consider that situation at that time.
Well, having been fortunate enough to secure General McNaughton as Minister of Defence, the government then started to see what could be done in the way of a public appeal. General McNaughton himself began the appeal. Within two days after he had been sworn in he spoke at Amprior, and he spoke at Ottawa the next night. I prepared an address that I hoped might help to clear the situation a little by making apparent how *untrue and misleading were the statements that were being made about the N.R.M.A. men, the numbers that were involved, and the allegation that it was the Quebec men that were falling behind rather than that the situation was general as related to all the provinces. I tried to clear up some matters and to put the facts before the people, believing in the people. We appointed a committee of the cabinet to work with others 
to make plans whereby individual appeals could be made and made in an effective way. General McNaughton brought his officers from all parts of the country and explained to them that the policy of the government was a policy of voluntary enlistment. They have tried-or I believe many of them have, but I also believe some of them have not tried to get voluntary enlistments. That was the policy of the government. To make it succeed, all would have had to work for it for all they were worth.
How was the public appeal supported? The moment that we started on the public appeal, that moment the opposition to anything of the kind on the part of the interests that lie behind this organized effort to force conscription began to make itself felt in every direction-in the press, by meetings, resolutions by veterans' organizations, representations to members and so forth, with the result that instead of the appeal reaching the ears of the people, the ears of the people were dinned by the efforts that were being put forth by those who were determined they were going to have conscription no matter what the cost might be.
In the meantime I felt that it was desirable that this parliament should assemble. There has not been a day or a year since this war started when this parliament has not been kept intact. There has been no prorogation of any session until the time for each new session. There has been a continuing on and on so that the parliament of Canada would be ready to be brought together at any time. We have passed, another motion this afternoon which means that this parliament, when it is adjourned after this debate, will not have been prorogued but will continue until January 31 unless dissolved in the interval, so that hon. members can be brought together again if another situation develops which calls for their presence.
I felt the moment had come when the people's representatives should know that there was a very critical situation. We could not take chances on all that was involved in this situation. What was more we had come to the place where we could not longer take responsibility ourselves without sharing it with the members of this house. And that is what hon. members are here for this afternoon-to share the responsibility either of supporting the present government in its prosecution of Canada's war effort or of rejecting it. That responsibility is just as great upon every member of the House of Commons, no matter from where he comes, as it is upon the Prime Minister of this country at this time. Every single member is either

War Effort-Government Policy
helping to make it possible for a government in Canada to be maintained in this time of war without a crash in the middle of war, or he is helping make it impossible for the government to carry on.
We assembled here on Wednesday of last week. Up to that time I had thought that our public appeal would succeed. Here again I wish to make clear that we were further encouraged by the fact that some little progress had been made; men. were enlisting, it is true in small numbers, but once the move started I believe it would have followed through very rapidly. We were getting indications of what public opinion, if it were rightly guided, would have helped do, but we had to consider whether or not we could afford to run on much longer. As I have said., I believe with all my heart that a public appeal would have succeeded if we had received the support of hon. leaders opposite, if we had received the support of their following, if we had received the support of their press. Does anyone doubt that for one moment? I say we would have had the necessary men through voluntary enlistment but for the organized opposition that was taken to voluntary enlistment. From, this time on, those who have been responsible for this organized opposition will have on their heads the responsibility for what may follow in the present and over the years.
It was in these circumstances that the cabinet met parliament and that I asked my colleagues to meet me the evening after we had concluded the first day's sitting. I had a special reason for that. It was that General McNaughton himself, in conference with his staff, had come to the conclusion that it might be taking too great a chance not to act immediately. That presentation was made to the government, and with it I made a passionate appeal to every one of my colleagues-I think I may so describe it-not to press for any extreme position; to be as united as they possibly could, yielding up the extreme position, whether it was for all-out conscription under Bill 80 or whether it was for no conscription, realizing that there and then we were face to face with a situation which meant that if we could not agree and could not meet parliament the next day in as united a position as was possible, the only result would be that I would have to announce, on behalf of the government, that we were not in a position longer to carry on because the division in the cabinet was so complete as between those supporting the one point of view and those supporting the other.
That was crisis No. 2; and it was in those circumstances, as a result of the deliberations of that night, with members of council responding to the appeal to do everything possible to come to an agreement, that we were able to agree on the passing of an order in council which, without resorting to all-out conscription, would ensure the men at the front being guaranteed the necessary reinforcements. We were able to give this house that assurance immediately by passing an order in council under bill 80 which would enable the government to take such men as were needed, men highly trained- and others that might later be needed-and send them immediately overseas. That agreement was reached, and when the house opened the next day I was able to lay on the table the order in council which gave it expression and effect.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am interested in giving to the house a statement which I think will be illuminating. This is not the first occasion on which a Prime Minister has had to tell the country how very critical a situation has become and what is needed to meet it. One of the most critical situations with which Canada was ever faced was just prior to confederation, when Sir John A. Macdonald was Prime Minister of Canada- the united Canadas, Upper and Lower Canada. Sir John in his day, at a very early stage of his career, was in the position that he had to consider whether it was possible for government in Canada to be carried on at all.
I have in my hand an extract from a speech made by Sir John A. Macdonald on February 6, 1865, to the parliament of Canada, when, on behalf of the government of the day, he submitted the scheme of the confederation of all British North American provinces. Sir John began by observing that the scheme had been received in Canada with general if not universal approbation. The subject, he said, was not new; for years it had more or less attracted the attention of every statesman and politician of the provinces and had been looked upon as being the means of eventually deciding and settling very many of the vexed questions which had retarded the prosperity of the colonies as a whole and particularly the prosperity of Canada. The matter had first been introduced into the realm of practical politics by Mr., later Sir, Alexander Galt, in 1858. The subject did not begin to assume its later proportions until the summer of 1864.
Let me now quote textually from the speech which was made by Sir John A. Macdonald.
War Effort-Government Policy

It will be found in the debates on confederation of the British North American provinces, in the legislature of Canada, third session, eighth parliament, 1865, at page 26:
Then, men of all parties and all shades of politics became alarmed at the aspect of affairs. They found that such was the opposition between the two sections of the province

Canada under the union act, what is to-day Ontario and Quebec.
*-such was the danger of impending anarchy, in consequence of the irreconcilable differences of opinion with respect to representation by population between Upper Canada and Lower Canada, that unless some solution of the difficulty was arrived at. we would suffer under a succession of weak governments-weak in numerical support, weak in force, and weak in power of doing good. All were alarmed at this state of affairs. We had election after election-we had ministry after ministry-with the same result. . . . None were more impressed by this momentous state of affairs, and the grave apprehensions that existed of a state of anarchy destroying our credit, destroying our prosperity, destroying our progress, than were the members of this present house; and the leading statesmen on both sides seemed to have come to the common conclusion, that some step must be taken to relieve the country from the deadlock and impending anarchy that hung over us.
I give to the House of Commons to-day, Mr. Speaker, these words of Sir John A. Macdonald, as applicable to the situation in Canada at this hour. And when I speak of anarchy I use that term with the same meaning and significance that was given to it by Sir John A. Macdonald-a country without government. I say that unless this House of Commons can unite in reasonable measure to support an administration that can carry on at this stage of war we shall have to face the possibility of anarchy in Canada while our men are fighting overseas, giving their lives that we may maintain our free institutions and that we may have peace and concord through the years to come. Hon. gentlemen may belittle those words, but they are words, no matter to what party the one who uses them belongs, which are entitled to the greatest consideration that can be given. If, at a time when there was comparative peace throughout the world and Canada was on the threshold of her national life, there was danger that anarchy might develop in this country because the men of Quebec and the men of Ontario could not unite to compose their differences and no government could be found to carry on the administration of the country's affairs, how much greater is that possibility after five years of war, a war that still continues and at a time when we are in the midst of the most appalling phase of the

struggle? , How can you believe that there might not arise a situation much graver than any of us can begin to realize?
As I have said, that was the position under which the government decided to take the step it did. Let me make it clear that the step we took was taken under Bill No. 80. All that we have done is in accordance with what the government had said at the time would be done if a situation arose where it seemed to be necessary and advisable that such a step should be taken. We have been advised by the military authorities-as I have said, this question of conscription is a military question -that the step is necessary. I cannot speak of its being advisable except in the light of all the circumstances, but when I think of what may follow if this step is not taken, I think it is advisable.
Let me give to the house the statements which caused me to believe, and will, I think, cause the house to believe, that in this step which the government has taken we were carrying out our policy as announced to this house in 1942. So that there may be no doubt I will ask the house to bear with me while I read what I said at that time. I am sure that as I read hon. members will be somewhat impressed by what in all humility I believe was a measure of foresight as to the conditions that might arise before this war was over. What I am about to read was said over two years ago. We have been able to tide over some five years, but we come now to an hour of the war when I think this particular step is necessary. The policy was set forth in June, 1943, and it has been defined in the words, "not necessarily conscription, but conscription if necessary." And I might add the words, "to the extent only that it is necessary."
I spoke first in this house on this subject in the discussions on the plebiscite. What I said then will be found on page 826 of Hansard of February 25, 1942. I ask hon. members to note that date; it was as long ago as that. We are getting on to the point where it was nearly three years ago. I said:
For our programme this year, and up to March, 1943, there is an honest belief on the part of the government that we will be able to get the men by voluntary enlistment for service overseas, and will not have to resort to conscription. But no one can say how long this war is going to last. No one can say what particular turn it is going to take.
Then on page 3234 of Hansard of June 10, 1942, I am reported as follows:
Nothing, I think, could be plainer than that. It was made perfectly clear that the government had no thought of resorting to conscription for overseas service so long as the voluntary system continued to produce the
