War Effort-Government Policy '
necessary recruits; also, that we honestly believed the voluntary system would suffice to secure the necessary enlistments for the 1942-43 -programme. The government, however, wished to be free, without any breach of faith, to resort to conscription for overseas service should that become necessary to our national security and to the effectiveness of our war effort.
If the bill is amended as proposed, it is not the intention of the government to resort to conscription for service overseas unless circumstances should arise which would render the use of compulsion imperative, such, for example, as the maintenance of the necessary reinforcements for Canada's army overseas.
That is the statement that I made in the presence of hon. members as long ago as June 10, 1942, during the debate on Bill No. 80. I have said already that I am not a military man, that I have to rely for these matters upon the advice of my military advisers. That is the advice I have received, that it is necessary at this time for the maintenance of the necessary reinforcements for Canada's army overseas that we do resort to a measure of compulsion. Then on February 25, 1942, as reported on page 830 of Hansard,
I said:
The government is asking the people for a free hand in order that it may do in the circumstances as they may arise what is most in the interests of the people of Canada. We wish to make Canada's war effort as effective as it can possibly be made. What we shall do at any particular time will depend upon the course which we think at that time is necessary and advisable and most effective in Canada's war effort. That decision is not going to be made in the light of any one factor. It is going to be made in the light of all conditions as they exist and as they are known to the government at the time . . . that the government is going to do the thing that it believes is going to further to the uttermost Canada's war effort, all circumstances considered. May I say that when I say "all circumstances considered" I have in mind the conditions as they may exist in respect to the war in different theatres and the conditions that may exist in Canada itself.
Then I quote from page 832 of Hansard of February 25, 1942:
When we find that we cannot raise the required numbers of men for enlistment overseas by the voluntary method, and it is absolutely necessary to raise more men by other methods, then we will make our decision, present it to parliament and have it discussed on its merits'.
Then page 3227 of Hansard of June 10, 1942:
While full and complete powers for the exercise of compulsion are given to the governor in council by the act, under its provisions, it is left to the governor in council to decide when, and to what extent, it may be necessary or expedient to exercise the powers thus conferred. This will be equally true of the powers of the governor in council under the act as amended. The discretion of the government will remain precisely what it is at the present time.
Then page 3223 of Hansard of June 10, 1942:
The government does not believe that, to serve that end, conscription for overseas service is necessary at the present time. Moreover, it may never become necessary. But, in case it should ever become necessary, it is surely the part of wisdom that there should be no doubt Whatever of the power of the government to take the necessary action the moment the necessity to do so may arise. There should equally be no doubt that this power is derived from the present parliament rather than from a statute enacted in 1914.
The next paragraph'contains the expression of our policy which I have used. This is to be found on page 4011 of Hansard of July 7, 1942, and it reads:
If, in reference to the very difficult question of service overseas, anyone can conceive of a policy which is better calculated to serve the national interest than the one the government has formulated, and which is clearly and concisely expressed in the words: "Not necessarily conscription, but conscription if necessary", I shall be the first to advocate its acceptance. I can only say that nothing of the kind has been proposed by any hon. member in the course of the debate. Nor do I believe that anything better can be suggested. Indeed, the events of *the war, as well as all that has been said in the course of the debate, should have made it wholly apparent that, all circumstances taken into account, it is the only sound policy.
Having made clear the declaration of policy at that time, may I say that all we are doing at the moment is to carry out all that we were then pledged to do if the particular situation there set forth should arise, as it has now arisen.
There is one aspect which relates to the present- discussion I want to make plain, and it is this. It was made clear by the government at that time that there should be no second debate on conscription. The question of conscription was settled in the debate on Bill 80. What I made very clear at that time was that if the government felt that it was necessary to act it would act under order in council, but -that before the order in council would be put into force I would, if I were the leader of the government at the time, come to parliament and tell parliament that the order in council had been passed and ask parliament to give its support to the administration- not on all its policies but with respect to its war-time policy, so that, certainly* in the case of one like myself who has been known to stand so vigorously for the voluntary method, I might know that there was no doubt in the mind* of this House of Commons that I would see that what might be necessary would be duly carried out. To that extent I would* wish to have from this House of Commons some expression of its confidence.
War Effort-Government Policy

Let me read what in this connection I said in the House of Commons on July 7, 1942, as reported at page 4012 of Hansard:
If, at some future time, it became necessary in the judgment of the administration to apply conscription for service overseas, that step, it is to be presumed, would be to meet a situation which would permit of little, if anything, in the way of debate. Debate would involve delays at a moment when time had become a vital factor. Knowing that this is likely to be the case, had the government sought to postpone debate on overseas conscription until the hour of an emergency, hon. members might well have complained that on so controversial a question they were not being treated with the consideration to which the representatives of the people were entitled. It might have been said that their hands were being forced.
There is an additional reason why the debate on conscription for service overseas should take place upon the present bill rather than at a time-should the situation so demand -that the government may have reached the decision that the application of the compulsory method to military service overseas has become necessary. That reason is that the need would almost certainly arise in circumstances in which military considerations would prevent the disclosure in open debate of the factors on which the decision of the government was based. The government's judgment in the matter will necessarily depend, in very large part, on military information of the highest degree of secrecy. There is nothing more important in the movement of troops at a time of war than that all matters pertaining thereto should be surrounded with the utmost secrecy. Moreover it is not only Canada's position, and considerations of special interest to Canada, that have to be taken into account. Very careful account has to be taken of the hostile use the enemy may make of information disclosed, and of how far any disclosures on military matters may affect the position of every one of the united nations.
It has, I think, been made abundantly clear that, so far, at least, as the present administration is concerned, any decision respecting conscription for overseas service will not rest solely with the military authorities, but that any action taken under the present bill must and will be authorized by the Governor in Council. In other words, the decision will be the decision of the cabinet, subject always to its responsibility to parliament.
I have also already given to hon. members an assurance that all relevant factors would be taken into account by the cabinet in reaching a decision.
Then in the same debate, at page 4013 of Hansard, I said:
As to the right thing being done by the government at the right time, and in the right way, that, it seems to me, as I said in opening this debate, necessarily comes to be a matter of the degree of confidence which parliament and the people have in the administration charged with the responsibilities of carrying on the war. This does not constitute a reason for a second debate on the conscription issue. It is, however, the strongest of reasons why a government, once it has reached a .decision

that the needs of a situation demand a certain course of action on which opinion may be divided, should take the earliest possible opportunity of making perfectly sure that it enjoys the confidence of parliament, and that it may rely with certainty upon the support of parliament in giving effect to the decision reached.
I want hon. members to catch those words because they are significant. What the government is seeking to-day is not an expression of confidence in all of its policies, but we are asking the house to support the administration in giving effect to what has been decided. I went on, at page 4013 of Hansard:
Especially is this the case where widely divergent views have previously been expressed in the country, and also in parliament, on the wisdom of any discretionary power being given the administration; and where it is to be expected that differences will still exist concerning the 'wisdom of the decision.
If an administration is to begin to carry out its duties in the prosecution of a war, it cannot afford to be left in any doubt, at any time, as to the adequacy of its support by parliament, and least of all in a time of peril. The assurance of the confidenco of parliament is particularly necessary to the leader of a government where there is the slightest reason for him to doubt the extent to which he may be able to rely upon the support he will receive in the House of Commons.
I followed with these words, which appear at page 4014 of Hansard of July 7, 1942:
I intend, therefore, if the time should come when the government decides that it has become necessary to send overseas men who have not volunteered for general service, and I should be in office at the time, to ask my colleagues to join me in seeing that parliament is immediately informed of the government's decision. If parliament is not in session, I would do whatever lies within my power, to see that parliament is informed as soon as possible after the decision has been reached.
I intend, at the same time, to see that, before the administration assumes the additional responsibility of enforcing its decision, hon. members are given an opportunity, not for any second debate on the question of conscription, but of showing their confidence or want of confidence in the administration.
In following this course, I hope it will be agreed that I am fulfilling the spirit of an earlier undertaking given to parliament on February 25, that "when we find that we cannot raise the required numbers of men for enlistment overseas by the voluntary method, and it is absolutely necessary to raise more men by .other methods, then we will make our decision, present it to parliament, and have it discussed on its merits". The debate on the merits of conscription has, of necessity, come on the present bill. What really is important hereafter is that the government's decision should immediately be presented to parliament, and that the government should be prepared to stand or fall on its decision.
Just a few words more. I regret to quote at such length but the quotations do make clear to parliament the thought and the care with which a situation such as is presented was

War Effort-Government Policy
anticipated, and they leave nothing that is not definite and clear in regard to the government's duty in the course it is pursuing at this time. Again, at page 4564 of Hansard of July 22, 1942, I said:
When the government decides that it is necessary and advisable to resort to conscription as a method of raising men for service overseas, an order in council will be passed dealing with members of the forces as a whole. It will not be a matter of passing a series of orders in council, but one order in council will cover the entire force.
That is what has been done at this time, and it answers the question asked by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) a day or two ago. I went on at page 4565 of Hansard of July 22, 1942:
There is no submission to parliament, with regard to conscription. Let me make it perfectly clear that, so far as coming back to parliament for any purpose is concerned, there will be no coming back to parliament for a second debate on conscription, nor will there be any coming back to get the approval of parliament of the decision made. When the government makes its decision that decision is *made, and it will be carried out either by this government or by some other government. It will not have to be approved by parliament first. The question whether or not a ministry *headed by myself will enjoy sufficient confidence in the minds of hon. members of this House of Commons and of the people of this country to administer conscription, once it has been decided that conscription for service overseas shall be enforced, is a separate matter, and it is a matter on which I shall wish to have an expression of confidence.
Then, at page 4625 of Hansard of July 23, 1942, I said:
If that is the case let me say that I do not wish to assume any obligation that hon. members of this house have not full faith in my carrying out to the letter. May I say this to my fellow-members of the House of Commons: I have shirked no responsibility of any kind since this war came on that I believed to ibe in the national interest. I have not hesitated to ask this House of Commons for any measure [DOT]that I thought was essential in the national interest. . . .
I was taking a very grave responsibility when 1 came into this chamber and asked this House of Commons to support a policy which would carry Canada into the war. I had taken the greatest responsibility that any human being on earth can take, that of bringing his own country into the war. I did not shirk that responsibility because I believed it was in the interest of our country that we should take that step. And after three years of war-
It was three years then; it is after five years now:
-I ask my friends in this house to-night whether they think I was wrong in taking that step at that time.
I feel exactly the same about this matter of conscription for overseas service. Up to the present time I have not felt it necesary to conscript men for service overseas because our
Canadians were doing honour to themselves and to their country by enlisting for training for service anywhere in larger numbers than we could prepare them. But I say to-night that, with the world situation what it is, with 'the situation between Germany and Russia what it is at this moment, the situation in Egypt what it is at this moment, the situation on the Pacific as we know it to be at this moment, I would :be derelict to the responsibility which I bear to the country and to my fellow-members if I did not say to them that I believed it was absolutely in the interest of the country that the government should have power to take any step at any time that it deems necessary, so long as it takes that step in the light of its responsibility to parliament. If I am persuaded that it is necessary and desirable to resort to conscription of men for overseas service, I am going to support that view. But the minute I support that view, if it is the view of the cabinet, I wish to be able to come to this House of Commons and say: The cabinet has reached this decision; the next step will ibe to enforce it. Before that next step is taken I want this House of Commons to declare whether it has confidence in me as the head of the administration that is to carry out this policy of conscription or whether hon. members prefer to have another government in the place of the administration now in office. That is my conception of carrying out my responsibility to parliament. . . .
The people of this country will want to know two things: first, whether the head of the government that is carrying on this war has the confidence of the majority in this House of Commons, and second, where the members of this House of Commons stand, each one of them, not by their words but by their vote, on the question of the course that may be thought necessary by the administration in the winning of the war. And I intend, if it lies in my oower, to see that this House of Commons gets that opportunity, so that the people will know exactly where each and every one of us stands.
Then finally these words, as reported at page 462 of Hansard:
When this bill pases both houses, as I believe it will pass, and is assented to, the government will have been given by parliament power to conscript men for service overseas. That power will rest in the government. It will be there. The policy of the government is to exercise that power when it believes it necessary to do so, when it is necessary to resort to conscription to make Canada's war effort more effective. When the decision is made by the government- if and when it is made-that settles the matter as far as conscription is concerned. Conscription will have been enacted; the government will have declared that it is necessary for the carrying on of the war.
But the carrying out of a decision once it is made is a very different thing when a decision has been reached which places additional responsibilities on the ministry, responsibilities which must be faced by a responsible ministry in the light of all that has gone before, in the light of all that has taken place during this debate in this House of Commons, in the light, as my hon. friend the former Minister of National Defence for Air said this afternoon, of what is going to be
War Effort-Government Policy

the result of the enforcement of the order not only in the immediate future but through years to come.
I say, when all that responsibility is added to the responsibility already on the shoulders of the ministry, it is absolutely necessary that this House of Commons should say whether it is prepared to give its support to the administration to enable it to carry on with that extra responsibility, or whether it is going to withhold its support just at the time that support is most needed.
That, hon. members, is the position that we are in at this hour. This House of Commons will have to express its views as to whether it is prepared to support the present ministry in carrying out the provisions of the order in council which has been passed. Hon. members will have to take the responsibility which is theirs, with all the consequences that may flow from withholding support from the present administration, in the situation in Canada and in the world what it is at the present time.
That there may be no mistake as to what the order in council really does require, I shall give particulars as to its scope. I need not repeat the words of the order which is P.C. No. 8891; I think it will be found on examination that it contains precisely in its terms what in 1942 I said I would do. That order in council P.C. 8891 applies to all personnel who are serving or may serve in consequence of having been called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. Its enactment consequently accords with the procedure laid down in 1942, namely that the order in council deals with "the members of the forces as a whole". That is, one order in council covers the entire force. It was in reference to such an order in council that it was stipulated that the government would place the order before this house and that I would wish to be assured that I had the support of parliament in administering the order. The order in council authorizes the Minister of National Defence to dispatch overseas a maximum of 16,000 N.R.M.A. personnel. In calculating the number of N.R.M.A. personnel so dispatched of reinforcements men will be counted as N.R.M.A. personnel only if they have embarked on board ship without converting to general service. All N.R.M.A. personnel who convert to general service before embarkation will go overseas as volunteers. The additional numbers estimated to be required total 16,000, regardless of their status on leaving Canada.
The government, I contend, has surmounted	successfully two crises. There
have been two occasions on which the

ministry itself might have been obliged as a whole to resign, with what consequences I leave others to contemplate. The decision of this house will determine whether or not there is to be another crisis at this time of war, and that, a crisis greater than any other that has ever been on the horizon of Canada. I hope this House of Commons will keep in mind what it is they are here being asked to do. Let me follow my notes closely in this:	It
is to support the men overseas, and nothing more than that-these men, some of whom have been absent from their homes for over five years, these men who have been fighting in Europe under conditions of horror the like of which has rarely been known in the world's history, these gallant brave young men *of Canada who are offering their lives that liberty may be preserved, that human freedom may be preserved, that Christian civilization may be preserved. None of us can afford under any consideration ever to let any one of them down. When I asked this country to come into the war, I placed one solemn obligation on my own soul. It was this, that as long as it was in my power to do so, I would never fail to support the men who went to the front to fight; I have never failed them, and I am not going to fail them to-day.
It will not help the army to defeat the present government and possibly force a general election. I for one will not take that responsibility. Some one else will have to take it if I am obliged to resign. The government and the former Minister of National Defence are agreed that the army cannot wait for reinforcements for two or three months while any question is being decided at the polls. In the present situation every member with a sense of responsibility, who differs with the decision of the government, must therefore ask himself this question: "If I help to defeat the present government, do I believe that a majority of members can be found in this house who will support an alternative government which can carry on effectively the war-time duties of government?" For a responsible member, it is not enough to be prepared personally to support an alternative administration. He should also be satisfied in his own mind that an effective alternative government is possible.
There are only two possible ways of supporting the army; one is to follow the course proposed by the government, which we sincerely believe to be the right and effective

War Effort-Government Policy
method; the other is to replace the present administration by a government which can find sufficient reliable support in the present House of Commons to carry on Canada's war effort. Moreover, such a government would have the most solemn duty to see that conscription was enforced effectively before plunging the country into a general election.
That is the issue before the house. It is not the question of conscription; it is the question as to whether the present government should continue to conduct Canada's war effort, or whether the direction of that effort should be handed over at this stage of the war to another administration. In destroying the present government no one can tell who will compose an alternative government. No one can even say who would preside over the new government. We can be sure that a considerable number of the ministers in such a government would inevitably be new men without experience of our war-time administration; some would probably be men without any administrative experience; some probably would be without seats in parliament.
Any change in government involves a great deal of dislocation and inevitable delay in administration, and such dislocations and delays in every aspect of our war administration would be bound to be serious at this critical stage of the war. But it would be even more serious if it were found, after present government had been defeated, that the various elements which had combined to destroy it were incapable of agreeing upon an effective government to replace it. The country would then be without a government in war time. An election would be inevitable, and what would happen to Canada's magni-ficient war effort while an election of probably unparallelled bitterness was being fought?
The issue I have suggested is not a fanciful one. I have given a solemn and realistic picture of the alternatives which face this house. The government has made a decision we believe to be the right one in the light of our responsibilities. Hon. members must now make the decision which they believe to be right in the light of their responsibilities. In making our decision, we of the government have not been concerned about our personal or political fortunes. We have tried to make the decision which in the long run will best serve Canada and Canada's fighting men. The decision which rests with this House of Commons may determine the fate of our country for generations to come.
The hour has come to rise above considerations of party advantage and to rise above the emotions, often strong and honest
emotions of the hour, and to make a decision, without regard for our own futures, but solely in the interests of Canada. Let us not forget that, apart from giving the aid they so much need, it will be the poorest support we can give to our fighting men to weaken or destroy the country to which they will return. We must support our fighting men in war, but we have an equal duty to safeguard their future, and the future of their country.
Now I wish to emphasize what I have said about the undesirability of having an election in war time. If I had been looking for the political successes that sometimes come by seizing a particular moment to make an appeal to the people, I would not have waited until almost the last hour of the last session of parliament to bring on a general election. I have told my followers over and over again, when they were pressing me to bring on an election because it was then the moment to succeed, instead of waiting until the last hour, at the end of the last session, that such was not the course to follow. When I came back from England after being present at the conference of Prime Ministers and, again, after the legislation set forth in the speech from the throne in this session had been enacted, they urged upon me very strongly that it was then the moment to go to the country. But to all such overtures I replied, "This is not a time to think primarily of the success of a political party. It is a question of what is best for Canada, best for our fighting men overseas. We cannot afford, if we can possibly avoid it, short of running beyond the period fixed by the constitution, to bring on a national conflict of opinion while this great war continues."
That is not a new decision. When I spoke to members of my own party as long ago as September 27, 1943, over a year ago, and as I have said to them on different occasions since, and emphasized, both in this house and out of it, I said that in my opinion an election in war time was not advisable and, above all, an election that might involve the question of conscription. May I read some of the words which I used on the occasion to which I have just referred. Speaking to the National Liberal Federation at the Chateau Laurier on September 27, 1943, I said:
Speaking in the House of Commons on the morning of the day of adjournment,-
1943.
-I gave to the members of parliament and to the people of Canada a very clear and definite statement of the position as I then viewed it. I knew that before parliament reassembled in the new year, there would be much speculation as to what the government's course in relation to a general election might be. I was anxious that political controversy, certain to
War Effort-Government Policy

develop in the then approaching Ontario elections, and the federal by-elections, should not, regardless of results, be allowed, if at all possible, to divert the minds of the Canadian people from an utmost effort in the winning of the war, until final victory was achieved. Accordingly, I set forth in unequivocal words, my own view as to the course which I believed it to be the duty of the government to pursue. This view I expressed in the following words:
"While our fears about its outcome have lessened, the war, in a more immediate way, has been brought closer than ever to us. All arms of our fighting services are now in the thick of the conflict. Our fighting men are certain to continue in action on many fronts, until the enemy has surrendered. No one can say for how long that may be. Our men face a terrible ordeal of battle. Until victory is achieved, above all else, they must command a singleness of purpose in our hearts and minds, and the utmost that our country can give in their support."
I see no reason whatever to alter the course there outlined because of anything which has taken place, in either the federal or provincial political arenas, since these words were spoken. Indeed, all that has since taken place, in the arena of war, affords to my mind the strongest of reasons for adhering with greater determination than ever to the resolution there expressed. Let me repeat its words:
"Our men face a terrible ordeal of battle. Until victory is achieved, above all else, they must command a singleness of purpose in our hearts and minds, and the utmost that our country can give in their support."
It was in that light, and in that light alone, at the time of parliament's adjournment on July 24th-
1943.
-that I felt any question as to the time for a general election in Canada should be viewed. I hold to that opinion more strongly than ever to-day.
And then the following on page 27:
I am most anxious to take the country as completely as I can into my confidence in a matter so all-important as a general election at a time of war. All I can honestly say is that I trust it may not be necessary to hold a general election before the hour at which we may look forward to welcoming back, to their homeland, those of that great company of the sons and daughters of Canada who have survived the ordeal of battle in the different theatres of war. Whether a general election can be delayed until that time, I cannot say. I have indicated to you, as far as, at the moment I am able to foresee them the circumstances that will govern the decision.
We owe it to our fighting men to ensure, by our united support, the success of their arms. We owe this no less to the memory of those men who at sea, on land and in the air already have given their lives; and to those also who have given their strength or their liberty that we may continue to enjoy the freedom we have, and to provide for others a larger freedom than most men have yet enjoyed. This [DOT][DOT]an, I believe, be realized, if until victory is

achieved, our fighting men command a singleness of purpose in our hearts and minds and the utmost that our country can give in their support.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I heard my hon. friend the member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) laugh when I indicated that it might be difficult to find another government to carry on. He was not the only one, but his voice and accents are familiar to me and I caught it. But I did hear others along the same line. Perhaps they will not listen to any words of mine, but in reading the Conservative organ in this city shortly before the meeting of parliament, I think it was about the time the notice was sent out, I was very much impressed by an editorial which was published, and it seemed to me it was intended as something in the nature of an admonition addressed to hon. gentlemen opposite. I shall read it because they may listen to that voice where I am quite well aware they are not prepared to listen to mine. The article is pertinent to the present situation in this House of Commons. Hon. members will realize that, but do not think for one moment that I agree with what it says as to the position of the Progressive Conservative party; I do not, or as to the position of the government. What I am anxious about is that hon. members of that party should see how those of their friends who are looking in from without regard the present situation in this House of Commons. The editorial is entitled "Danger of Third Parties", and I have had something to say about that at different times, Mr. Speaker, which I do not take back. It is as follows:
One good may come from this crisis over reinforcements. The good of our people being shown the danger of third parties. And of groups.
Under a straight two-party system there would exist in parliament at the present time a single trained opposition, an alternative to the government strong enough to take over and carry on with the war in the event that the government resigned-or were defeated. As it is, what we have under this third party system is three opposition groups, plus other factions, with not a single one of them commanding enough support in the house to form or maintain a government.
It is no answer to say that the existing parliament is no longer a reflection of the mind of the country; that the Progressive Conservative party is vastly stronger in the country than in the house. For while that undoubtedly is true,-
And this is the part that I said I did not agree with.
-with the government's numerical superiority in the Commons hopelessly out of line with its position in the country-

War Effort-Government Policy
There again I do not agree.
-that could be no help in a situation under which, in the event of Mr. King refusing to carry on, the Governor General would be called upon to name somebody to succeed him. In such a contingency, and assuming that the Governor General found it necessary or desirable to name a successor from some party other than the Liberal party, an immediate election would be necessary-necessary because no one of the other parties could by any stretch of the imagination command enough support in the house to carry on.
Under a third party system, under groups, it must always be that way. Either one party must have more supporters than all the other parties combined, or you have government by minority-which means government by logrolling, by appeasement, by hand-to-mouth strategy.
Such a thing, bad under any circumstances, must mean impotence in time of crisis.

Just a moment. As I said, has not been in the House of Commons. And when I think that what we are seeking above all else is to help men overseas in what is needed at this time, I have to ask myself this: Would His Excellency feel that I was justified in making such a recommendation for one whose duty it would be immediately to form a government?
Now may I turn to hon. gentlemen, first on this side; to my colleagues in the cabinet? I am quite prepared that any one of you should take this responsibility if the house has greater confidence in you than it has in me. No man in the world would be more relieved to be free of responsibility at a time like this than I would, after carrying on for the years that I have, at the age I have reached; no one would be more relieved to have someone else carry my responsibility for a time. Unless, however, you are prepared to form another administration, I ask you to consider my position as leader of the Liberal administration. Now I ask my hon. friend the leader of the Progressive Conservative party opposite; I ask my hon. friend the leader of the Co-operative Commonwealth party; I ask my hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit group, each the leader of a body of members in this House of Commons: If I go to His Excellency the Governor General and tell him I can think of no one but the leader of the opposition or one of these other leaders to take on the responsibility of government, are you prepared to assume that responsibility? Unless you are, unless you feel that you can present to the country an alternative government worthy of its support at this time, I think you owe it to this administration to support it in carrying on the wartime administration and supporting the army overseas.
Let me make this perfectly clear, because we are all here as the representatives of the people of Canada. I ask you, what position will this country be in before many days have passed if the ministry of to-day is obliged to resign because it has not the support of the House of Commons? I have gone through two experiences within this past fortnight which caused me to realize that there was a possibility that the pillars of the temple of our Canadian national life might be drawn out from under and the structure come down, bringing disaster to the whole nation. I do not intend ever to go through that experience again. If anyone has ever gone through such an experience he will realize something of what it means to carry the load of responsibility that has been mine in this time of war. I am not going to plead with any man to give

me his support. Every man must answeT to his own conscience, as I must, but I owe it to this country to let the people know in the clearest and most unmistakable manner what the situation may be if this administration is not supported.
Now may I say just a word in conclusion te my hon. friend's from the province of Quebec. I have been told time and again that in my political actions I have been seeking to appease the province of Quebec or at all costs to retain its support. May I say that I have never, in any act of mine in this parliament, sought to take one step to please one particular province rather than another. Any step I have taken in any public act I have performed has been taken in the interests of Canada as a whole, not in the interests of any particular province. It is true that, to the best of my limited abilities, I have sought to have the people of Canada understand the province of Quebec. I have not reminded them very often, but I should like to remind them now, of the fact that if it had not been for the French-Ganadian people this Canada of ours would not be a part of the British Commonwealth to-day. If the French-speaking people of Canada had taken the stand that was taken by the English-speaking people of the thirteen colonies at the time of the war of American independence, and had joined them in declaring for independence, there would have been no Canada under the British flag to-day, and there would have been no separate Canadian nation. That is something it is worth while for the rest of the people of Canada to remember. More than that, if the French-speaking people of Canada had not successfully opposed with force the armed forces that came against Canada at that time, this country would not be under the British crown to-day. And may I go a step further and remind this house that not only at that time was Canada saved to the British crown, In the war of 1812-14, when forces from the country to the south invaded Canada, again the French-speaking people of Canada shouldered their muskets, went out and met the enemy and defeated him, and saved this country to the British crown. So I say for this, if in nothing else, something is owing on the part of the other provinces to the province of Quebec. Something is owing to them on the score of chivalry, a people who have been in this country for three hundred years and more, who were settled here for a hundred and fifty years before any number of British settlers came to the country. Look back over the history of those three hundred years, during which they have lived peaceably and

War Effort

Government Policy
quietly, always helping to do those things which would further the prosperity of their people and of this country. Those people met the situation that had to be met at the time of the transition of this country from the French flag to the British flag, and surely something is owing to them for the way in which they have played their part ever since as a part, a large part of the dominion as a whole.
May I say further that if at times, though not as often as I should, I have sought to defend the men and women of the province of Quebec from the ruthless, unprincipled and often brutal attacks that have been made upon them by some people from other parts of the country who ought to know much better, it has not been merely because of my desire to see fair play and justice and to prevent a course of action which is indefensible in every way; it has been in the firm conviction that one who belongs to the majority cannot do too much in protecting the rights of the minority. This country is composed of minorities. Canada cannot be governed unless the rights of minorities are respected. This country cannot be held together as a nation otherwise. It is not only the French Canadians who compose a minority. We have large minorities here of other races as well; and the responsible leader who has to do with the administration of affairs of this country who does not consider the rights of minorities will never be capable of holding this nation together. Think of their position in relation to the war; let us speak very frankly of what some of our French-Canadian friends have come to fear. It is not conscription as such that they are afraid of. They have submitted to conscription already under the National Resources Mobilization Act. They have accepted that situation, and they are obeying that law. But they look upon overseas conscription as. a symbol of domination by the majority. I hope my fellow Canadians will look at that aspect of it. They see, I think, the fact that for the most part they are French-speaking and of the Roman Catholic faith. On the other hand they see that those who are asking for conscription, those who will more or less have to do with command on the field of battle, are for the most part Protestant and English-speaking. Those are simple facts, but they express and account for a very great deal. If we want to do something that will keep our country together, we will keep that in mind all the time.

I do not wish to go any further with that subject. Speaking of my seeking to appease Quebec, let me say that in this parliament two or three steps have been taken which have been very difficult steps for me to take; they were certainly not taken to get the support of Quebec, but they were taken with the support that I had from the province of Quebec.
One of these was in connection with redistribution. I was responsible more than anyone else for asking this parliament to allow the question of redistribution to stand over until the war was over. Who stood to lose by that? The province of Quebec did, relatively to the rest of Canada. They accepted it. That was not an effort to appease Quebec; that was asking Quebec to join with the rest of Canada to prevent disunity and bitterness and discord. The members from Quebec and the Province of Quebec accepted it, and they accepted it in a graceful way.
I was the one who had the responsibility and duty of bringing in bill No. 80, the amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act. Bill No. 80 had as its principle the possibility of conscription for overseas. In bringing in that measure was I seeking to appease Quebec? was I pandering to Quebec? Look over in the opposite corner and you will see what happened after the bringing in of that measure. That measure was accepted by the great body of my friends here on this side of the house, but there were some who were unwilling to accept it. With that measure began the little rift within the lute of the Liberal party so far as this house was concerned. One minister from Quebec resigned; one member after another began voting against us, and to-day that rift has become wider and may become wider still in the course of this present discussion.
Am I seeking to appease Quebec when I ask this House of Commons to support the government after it has adopted this measure?
I hope I am not appealing in vain to my friends who have trusted me so firmly through the years that have passed to trust me again on this occasion. I think I know what is in their minds. They will ask me how I reconcile my attitude as a follower of Sir Wilfrid Laurier with my position to-day. They will ask me how I can take this action in the light of speeches which have been delivered from this very desk by the man who was my truest and closest friend through my whole political life, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. May I answer, not in my own words but in the words of St. Wilfrid Laurier and the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe.

War Effort-Government Policy
Let me quote from the first public address made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier after election to the leadership of the Liberal party. This address was delivered on August 2, 1887, at a political picnic at Somerset, Megantic county. I quote from page 355 of the "Life and Letters of Sir Wilfrid Laurier" by Oscar Douglas Skelton:
French-Canadians, I ask you one thing, that, while remembering that I, a French-Canadian, have been elected leader of the Liberal party of Canada, you will not lose sight of the fact that the limits of our common country are not confined to the province of Quebec, but that they extend to all the territory of Canada, and that our country is wherever the British flag waves in America. I ask you to remember this in order to remind you that your duty is simply and above all to be Canadians. To be Canadians! That was the object of confederation in the intention of its authors; the aim and end of confederation was to bring the different races closer together, to soften the asperities of their mutual relations and to connect the scattered groups of British subjects.
Again, speaking at the Monument National in Montreal on June 3, 1916, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
This, my compatriots, is what I ask-this is the entente cordiale I would have us achieve by service together. I have followed the ideal of conscience as prompted by m.v heart. Do not let us waver from the right line of conduct. I am older than most of you, and I am more than ever convinced that there is no real success but that which is based and has its foundations on right and justice and the generous instincts of the human heart. Let us unite to allay and, please God, to extinguish the prejudices that pull us apart, and do our utmost like real men and women to 'bring together the two elements in our country.
Come, my young compatriots, with these brave young men who offer their services-their lives -that France may live, that Britain may continue her noble and generous role and that heroic Belgium may be restored to her standing as a nation.
Those words were spoken in the course of the last war. To-day the call to my French-Canadian friends and colleagues is to a still wider service, to service not only for the salvation of France and Belgium but for the salvation of this world from domination by an enemy that would destroy human freedom and our Christian civilization.
Mr. Lapointe even before the war began, made a most realistic statement in the house to which I would ask you to listen. He was giving a word of guidance to his fellow citizens of the province of Quebec and to our country. It was given in relation to this very war, the fires of which even then were visible upon the distant horizon. This statement will be found on page 2469 of Hansard of March 31, 1939. It reads:
Canada is part of the world, and this planet mfortunately cannot be considered to-day as

an earthly paradise inhabited only by benevolent and rational beings of an altruistic turn of mind. It is not an oasis rich in natural resources used only to benefit mankind but never to excite the covetousness of predatory powers. The seven thousand mile flight from Egypt to Australia of three British service bombers is fresh in the memory of everyone. It is quite evident that Canada is now- well within the possible sphere of action of any military power of the first rank, should that power deem the action worth while. In this troubled period of history, Canadians cannot be mere spectators; they are vitally interested in the outcome of the tragedies enacted before their very eyes. Much of the bloodshed and misery that history records has been the direct result of honest, idealistic but impractical -wishful thinking. There is no reason on earth why pious aspirations, unsupported by anything more substantial, should be more effective protection for us than they proved to be for Abyssinia or China; and we must remember that even the excellent Czech army proved inadequate when left without support. So I say this, and I want my colleagues to hear and understand me: if there is one chance in a thousand that what our experts say could happen may occur, I should be a traitor to Canada, to my own people, if I would not help to provide against it.
That was said in 1939 by the closest, the truest and the most devoted friend I have had in, my political life. With how much greater emphasis would he, were he with us at this time, repeat his words to-day.
Mr. Lapointe at another time also said something that comes very close to home so far as I am concerned. His words are reported on page 961 of Hansard of February 24, 1941:
Perhaps I am more at liberty to speak than other members of the government because I would gladly give up my own place to someone else if that were the better course to pursue. I feel sure that those who know me well, realize that it is only a sense of duty that keeps me in the position I now bold.
I hope I can say that with equal truth myself. I should be happy indeed to have had some one take the responsibility that has been mine for so long a time. In years of membership I am now, excepting one, the oldest member of the privy council of Canada. I am to-day, excepting one, the oldest member in years of service in this House of Commons. For the past twenty-five years I have been the leader of my party and I am now in my eighteenth year of office as Prime Minister. In another few weeks, I shall have reached my seventieth year. As long as I can continue to serve my country in any capacity I shall do the best I can toward that end. But I tell you, honestly and frankly, that the load is getting heavier and heavier day by day, and to carry on at this time, I need all the support I can get from men who are like-minded in their thoughts and aims.

War Effort-Government Policy
Let me read what Mr. Lapointe said about an expeditionary force. This was on September 9, 1939, as reported at page 67 of Mansard of that date:
. . . Much has been said about an expeditionary force. Let me say first that I agree with what the Prime Minister said yesterday. Applications are pouring in-and they are coming from Quebec also-from people who want to enlist. Far from urging people to do so, we have so far taken the position that it is better to act in an orderly way, to avoid confusion and consult with those whom we want to help. But if the need comes, does any member of the house think any Canadian government, whether this or any other, could stop the thousands of volunteers who would like to fight for Britain and France? Does my hon. friend from Beauharnois-Laprairie believe that a government, even if he were a member of it, could resist the pressure from all parts of Canada for an expeditionary force? Unfortunately, or according to my own view, fortunately, this country has to be ruled by one government, and no government could stay in office if it refused to do what the large majority of Canadians wanted it to do.
All that Mr. Lapointe prophesied there has been fulfilled. There is not a word there that is not even truer to-day in its application than it was then. No government could stay in office if it refused to do what the great majority of Canadians wanted it to do. This was an appeal made in connection with an expeditionary force. Here the appeal is for the necessary reinforcements for those who have volunteered and who are prepared to sacrifice their lives that our country may be spared the curse of nazi domination.
I have spoken much too long. Without further delay, I beg to move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by Mr. Crerar:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
Let me say of this motion, it does not ask for approval of order in council P.C. 8891. That order was enacted in strict conformity with Bill 80, and the government's authority to take such action was specifically approved by the vote on Bill 80 in 1942. The issue of conscription is not being decided by this vote; it was settled two years ago.
The motion does not ask for an unlimited vote of confidence in the government. To do so- would be unfair to political opponents of the government who nevertheless are willing to aid the government in the vigorous prosecution of the war.
As I have said, the motion is not to be construed as an endorsation of government policies generally. So far as it relates to confidence in myself, that confidence is being expressed in relation to myself as one charged with responsibility of seeing that the policy set forth in the order in council P.C. 8891 is duly administered.
The motion does ask, and asks only, whether members are prepared to support the government in continuing to carry on Canada's war effort at this time.
Any member who votes against this motion is asking to have the present administration resign, and another administration immediately take its place.
Mr. Speaker, I am indeed grateful to hon. members for permitting me to continue until after six o'clock. We can probably arrange to have the evening sitting commence at 8.30 instead of at 8 o'clock.
Before we adjourn, however, I have one further quotation which with the permission of hon. members I should like to give to the house and then to repeat its words on behalf of myself.
This question of Canadians serving overseas which we have been discussing anew to-day came up for consideration for the first time in *this parliament as long ago as the South African war. Even prior to that much earlier in a smaller way in Sir John A. Macdonald's day. But at the time of the South African war Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking in different parts of Canada, made to the country in a confession of faith a statement of what he stood for and sought to stand for in Canadian life. I should like to conclude by reading these words uttered by Sir Wilfrid Laurier forty-four yeax's ago. They will be found in the "Life of Sir Wilfrid Laurier," by Peter McArthur, at page 97. The words were uttered by Sir Wilfrid on March 18, 1900:
If there is anything to which I have devoted my political life, it is to try to promote unity, harmony and amity between the diverse elements of this country. My friends can desert me, they can remove their confidence from me, they can withdraw the trust they have placed in my hands, but never shall I deviate from that line of policy. Whatever may be the consequences, whether loss of prestige, loss of popularity, or loss of power, I feel that I am in the right, and I know that a time will come when every man will render me full justice on that score.
May I repeat those words as my own, having in mind at this moment all that Sir Wilfrid Laurier meant to me as a leader, all that he meant to me as a friend, all that he meant to me as a great Canadian and a great statesman. I wish to address these words to this House of Commons to-day and I want them to be words that will be remembered of me by my fellow-citizens when I also am gone:
If there is anything to which I have devoted my political life, it is to try to promote unity, harmony and amity between the diverse elements of this country. My friends can desert me, they can remove their confidence from me, they can withdraw the trust they have placed
War Effort-Government Policy

in my hands, but never shall I deviate from that line of policy. Whatever may be the consequences, whether loss of prestige, loss of popularity, or loss of power, I feel that I am in the right, and I know that a -time will come when every man will render me full justice on that score.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at 8.30 p.m.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-MOTION, THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is perhaps the most important and momentous debate that any of us who sit in this parliament have participated in. I think I made it very clear in my first remarks at the opening of this adjourned session how serious I feel are my responsibilities and how important are the decisions which we are to make in this parliament, both to our men and women overseas and their dependents, and to the nation as a whole. I do not know how long this debate will last, but I hope that so long as it lasts this house will behave in both word and action as though every act were seen and every word heard by the troops who are fighting overseas to-night. This is peculiarly, I think, a parliament of those who fight for Canada, and indirectly of their dependents as well. Nowhere else and in no other section of our people is the interest keener or the concern greater than in that section which fights for us and that other section which waits for our fighters to return.
If I may add this personal note, it always seems to me unfortunate that we of, shall I say, middle age are refused enlistment in the army because of physical disabilities, and that the flower of our manhood, people who can be spared so much less easily than we who have reached the midday of life, have to pay the penalty and make the sacrifice and give the dangerous service for those of us who have to stay at home. It is one of the tragic circumstances of war. It seems to me it is too bad that some way cannot be found whereby those of us who mean so much less to this nation could be sacrificed, instead of those who mean so much more. I dare say that every man and woman in this house have felt, at one time or another during this war, the sentiment I am expressing now.
This crisis, which is of course the reinforcement crisis, is one which the government itself could have met and solved had it taken

the courage to do so without allowing it to reach the proportions that it has reached or disturbing and distressing our people, both here and overseas, in the long and tragic process. It is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that a debate is now in prospect on a subject which arouses this nation's passions and emphasizes in some respects, perhaps, its divisions. But this is a democratic assembly. We, the representatives of the people, have a right to be heard. Whatever may be the quantity of talk in this debate, let us hope at least that the quality will be high. From the very depth of my convictions I express the hope that when this parliament rises it will be possible to say of all of us, irrespective of where we sit in this chamber, that when it came to a matter of dealing with the troops overseas, parliament was able to let the party bars down once and for all and deal with this question on its merits for them and for the nation as a whole, rather than have any of its decisions influenced, even in the slightest, by artificial party divisions.
Due care and concern for national unity should be manifest in all our speeches. We have to make a fresh approach to this matter. For some considerable time, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said this afternoon, the question of national unity has loomed large in the eyes of our people. I should like every part of this nation to know-perhaps they might be more difficult to convince than my neighbours in the House of Commons, because we know each other personally-that those of us who take part in this debate-and I should like to think that this is the unanimous consensus of the house-have no hatred in our hearts for any single section or part of Canada. Let us 6ee that on all sides we do our best to keep any fissures in the national unity or any national divisions from growing deeper or wider because of things which we may carelessly say. Let us not forget that our enemies in this war do not happen to be Canadians; our enemies are the cruel aggressor nations of Germany and Japan; and let us conduct this debate with that thought definitely and properly in our minds.
Without indicating what in my opinion this debate should produce, or how it should be conducted, I would repeat the words of Mr. Churchill: "Let us keep our eye on the ball." There is still only one issue before this nation and that is the winning of the war. I have heard the Prime Minister speak of victory being , a certainty and I saw in the papers that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand), addressing an audience in his own province, is reported to have made the state-

War Effort-Government Policy
ment last week-he must have had some information which the Prime Minister did not have, certainly information which we have not had-that the war was won. That seems to me to be repeating a fallacy which I think we have committed on previous occasions in Canada, because this war has not yet been won. Victory is not here yet, and the Prime Minister himself this afternoon went so far as to speak of the appalling phase of the war that has yet to come.
The public want us to do a job in this parliament and they will not be satisfied with a half-finished job. I think they will demand that the job be cleaned up and completed once and for all because they do not like crises any more than the government does or we do. They do not want any more cabinet trouble. They do not want any more delays in providing help for our hard-pressed troops overseas. I thought in some of his remarks this afternoon the Prime Minister appeared to contemplate the possibility of another crisis such as this. But as regards the order in council which has just been passed and which is now law. if we leave this parliament with just that order, restricted as it is to
16,000	troops for reinforcements from N.R.-M.A., I do not think we shall have completed the job.
Moreover, I think it was quite clear from the Prime Minister's remarks this afternoon that when further troops are required for reinforcements, over and above the limited number of 16,000, other orders in council will have to be passed in order to provide those necessary reinforcements. The order in council itself contemplates that very thing. How many there will be is of course a matter of speculation so far as I am concerned, but let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that when we leave this parliament with an order in council such as we have now, which the Prime Minister says covers all those men, but which does not dispatch them or direct the remainder of them, then we are running ourselves right into a headwind again and it is quite possible and indeed probable that we shall have more cabinet crises for this nation to take care of in the future, as we have had in the past.
Having that definitely in mind, while the Prime Minister said that it was not his intention to bring these orders in council before parliament for ratificatipn, nevertheless if we are to have a cabinet crisis each time orders are extended, and if they are to be the same kind of cabinet crisis as this one, you may rest assured that we shall be very fortunate in this country if parliament does not have to be called upon to settle the dispute once more.
I say therefore that the job has not yet been done. More than that, the present government surrenders to a partial policy of overseas compulsory service which some have labelled in the newspapers as controlled conscription; but so far as the Prime Minister is concerned, with this change in policy on the part of the government, it seems to me *that this order in council is very much like an unwanted child, particularly as regards the Prime Minister-and I make no personal aspersions in that comparison. Not only is it an unwanted child but it is in the hands of a parent who is reluctant to look after it. .
I listened this afternoon with a good deal of interest to the Prime Minister's remarks, and I could not help thinking at times that we were almost intruders on the scene, because it did seem to me the Prime Minister was not always talking to parliament but was talking to a caucus of government supporters. As I listened to him I could not help feeling that his very attitude indicated a frame of mind, so far as this order in council is concerned, which I think is the kind of attitude from which one would not expect a very vigorous or enthusiastic administration of the order. It was not the bold, vigorous position taken by a man whose heart was in the order in council or in the legislation. A part of his speech I did not like because it looked too much like an apology rather than a support of the new legislation. Having that in mind, it seems to me that the question of confidence in the Prime Minister to carry out properly the terms of that legislation was left more in doubt this afternoon by his words than by anything that might be done over here to throw doubt upon it.
As regards the order in council, it is not very much wonder that we on this side of the house are desirous of having a full and complete job done. I shall not take the time of the house now to read the order in council which was passed when the expedition of Canadian troops went to Kiska. That order in council calling for troops from N.R.M.A. to go from Canada to the Aleutian islands and Alaska, including Kiska, was an all-out order, an order in council that did not deal only with 16,000 trained men. It was an order in council that did not pull any punches whatever. It was an order in council that put the entire N.R.M.A. personnel to whatever use was necessary in that territory or theatre of war. Why was it that the government did not do the same in this instance as they did in the Kiska incident? Why did they limit it? Why was not the same application made in this
War Effort-Government Policy

instance? I believe we are entitled to the same kind of order in council for Europe and the United Kingdom as we had for the Aleutians and Alaska. It would seem to me that we are in a much graver and more urgent position with respect to our forces at this time than we were on that occasion. When this order in council is contrasted with the Kiska order in council we find that this government has for some reason or another definitely pulled its punches and we, Mr. Speaker, are opposed to the pulling of punches in this last phase of our struggle in the war.
I believe it has been properly said that the present order in council establishes three armies for Canada. We have had a two-army system, a home defence army and a general service army. This order in council divides our home army until to-day we are faced with not two armies but actually three armies in Canada. As a matter of fact the time has gone when we can fiddle and fool with this kind of legislation. We should have one army in Canada, not three as the order in council now makes it. Therefore I wish to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Prime Minister that I join with those who have already expressed doubts as to where this piecemeal and appeasement	policy is	to	land	this
nation.

In so far as the 16,000 covered by the order in council are concerned there is no real guarantee that if more than the 16,000 are required we shall be free from cabinet trouble or more convulsions of public opinion or more crises. I believe that the present policy is confusing; the whole nation has great difficulty in even understanding the purport and the language of this order in council.
There is another matter. After the dizzy whirl which produced a certain government policy last Wednesday, still another one on Thursday and still an extension of that again

on Friday, I believe the public will be glad, if I may say so without offence, that the Prime Minister seems finally to have come to rest. But the lightning changes in government policy make it difficult for the people to keep abreast. It must be difficult for General McNaughton to keep abreast of the changes that have been initiated, because in the shuffle and various changes this government has lost two valuable ministers within one month and both for opposite reasons of policy. No single bold step has been taken with respect to this matter at any time. It has been a government retreat from trench to trench and from trench to trench.
I do not like to hear too much emphasis laid upon minimum requirements with respect to reinforcements. Too much emphasis has been laid upon the minimum and not enough upon the maximum. In mutual aid we went the whole hog, but on a more important issue we have gone only step by step and in a piecemeal fashion. It seems to me that this nation has not waged what one could call total war, despite what the Prime Minister suggested this afternoon, and this order in council does not completely cure that situation. It actually lowers the ceiling of pressure upon 16,000 men in the home defence army in the hope that some cabinet minister will be able to go into his riding and say that these have volunteered. It amounts to compulsion through pressure, or, as some have already said in the house, conscription by coercion.
It has been said, too, that the old policy of conscription if necessary but not necessarily conscription has now been changed to draftees if necessary, but not necessarily draftees. It may well have gone far enough into the area of overseas compulsory service to alienate those parts of Canada opposed to it and not far enough to satisfy those who see in its provisions a failure to go all out in solving the problem.
There is another problem that ought to be faced by this parliament and with which the Prime Minister has not dealt. When this war is over or when action in the Pacific arena gets under way, are those Canadians now serving in the European field of conflict to be asked to go to fight in the Pacific while men drafted under the N.R.M.A. remain in Canada? That is a problem, and that is a question which is being asked in letters which members of parliament generally receive from the battlefronts. The present shortage of reinforcements for units now in Europe prove conclusively, I believe, that another army for the Pacific war cannot be raised in Canada

War Effort-Government Policy
from the number of men available unless we use men now in service under the N.R.M.A.
I think the government owes an answer to this question to the men now fighting overseas and to those who have been away so long in service.
I should like to make one reference to that long-term service. I fancy that many members of this house have from time to time received letters from overseas with respect to that. Some of these men are celebrating their sixth Christmas overseas. At least a dozen of my close friends, unless they are in this next group that come over, will have spent their sixth Christmas in parts other than Canada. It is perhaps a matter for criticism that only 450 men should be coming back on Christmas leave; I believe a great many more who are facing their sixth Christmas overseas should be allowed to return on leave. To those at home this may not seem such an important matter, but I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that most of us do not like to spend one Christmas away from home even though we are still in this country. Think what must be the feelings of a man who has been overseas for five years, now facing the prospect of spending his sixth Christmas away from home!
Now if I may I should like to refer to a matter which was mentioned this afternoon by the Prime Minister. He dealt with a number of matters, and on one or two occasions I thought was somewhat careless and unfortunate in the language he used. Only a few days ago the Prime Minister asked to have expunged from the record certain statements made by an hon. member of this house; then this afternoon he went so far as not only to leave the suggestion but to make the statement that one of the alternatives to the defeat of this government and his resignation was anarchy in Canada. I do not know whether the Prime Minister had in mind the usual meaning that is attached to "anarchy," but in the public mind it might mean anything. Therefore I would ask the right hon. gentleman to have that word expunged from the parliamentary records, as a dangerous statement to make, because it seems to me anything could be taken from such a statement by a certain section of the public, anxious to pick up such statements made by prominent public men. The word carries two or three suggestive meanings which, even as leader of the opposition, I do not think I would be justified in using in this House of Commons. Of course that is nothing new for the Prime Minister. I do not want to hark back to 1935, because it may not have very much to do
with this debate, but in the last week of the election campaign of that year the Prime Minister caused to appear on great billboards across Canada advertisements reading: "Elect the Liberal party. Let Mackenzie King have a working majority. It is King or chaos." We had to wait for nine years, but in the end we got both. I do not think the Prime Minister should use the House of Commons as a sounding board for another election cry, "King or anarchy in Canada."

speechtext:
I am sorry there are hon. members in this house who desire to conduct themselves in this way at this time. I believe the great majority of hon. gentlemen take this matter very seriously, and I wish that could be said of all, because even in the opposition we have some rights to present our case.
The Prime Minister has brought into this house a motion of confidence in himself and his government, with respect to which motion I should like to say just a word. The right hon. gentleman made a strange suggestion regarding that vote of confidence. He said, "Of course it is not a complete vote of confidence; it is only a vote of confidence with respect to the administration of this particular order in council." I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Prime Minister that according to the Prime Minister himself this

War Effort-Government Policy

order in council now is law and in full operation, as far as it goes. The vote with, respect to the order in council is a vote of confidence in those who are to carry out the terms of that order in council. I think we who observed the Prime Minister's attitude this afternoon were left with very grave doubts in connection with the present position. In the first place the government in its motion intimates that a vigorous war effort is being conducted by the government and speaks of the maintenance of that vigorous effort. But as far as we are concerned the policy of this government does not go far enough in the direction of total war. I believe the wording of the motion should be altered in accordance with the terms of an amendment which I shall shortly offer this house. More than that, I believe the course which has been followed by the Prime Minister in regard to this whole matter has caused him to forfeit the confidence and faith of this Canadian parliament. It is rather difficult to know just what the government has in mind with respect to this motion of confidence. The motion was placed in the Votes and Proceedings by the Prime Minister while the government's policy was the voluntary system; it was introduced in the house after the government had adopted the new policy of compulsory overseas service. That in itself, I think, is enough to cast suspicion upon the whole question of the position of the government with respect to the confidence of this parliament.
I want to make it clear and plain, so plain that it cannot be misunderstood, that we in this party always have been ready and willing to cooperate with the government in every possible way relative to the war effort. In a war-time period, with one party carrying on the war, there is a duty and obligation placed upon the opposition to see that the government gives the maximum service and efficiency in the prosecution of the war. The very fact that that is the position and the relationship sometimes leads to misunderstandings as to the motives of both. I want to say to the Prime Minister, and to you, Mr. Speaker, that this opposition is prepared at all times to give to this government, or to any government that may have the direction of affairs in this parliament, the cooperation and help to which it is entitled in order to carry on the war. But our-great difficulty has been that this government has not gone far enough in the direction of total war. Our criticism has been directed largely in that direction and it will continue to be directed in that direction.

We want total war, but we have not been getting it from this government. I think the underlying reason for the lack of confidence in the administration of the Prime Minister is that he has not his heart in the legislation which has just been passed by order in council. It seems to me that he has lost the confidence of the house at this time. I should like to bring my remarks to a close by quoting the favorite newspaper of the Prime Minister. He used the Ottawa Journal as part of his argument this afternoon, and I wish to quote with approval from an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal this morning. I quote:
If Mr. King and General McNaughton still don't believe in the compulsion principle, then are they the people to be carrying out this order in council? Here we have a minister of defence coming to parliament and saying to it in effect: "I am going to carry out this policy, but I don't believe in it-am against its principle". We say as plainly as we can that General McNaughton would show more of integrity, certainly more of logic, if lie said instead: "I don't believe in the principle of this policy; you had better get somebody to carry it out who does believe in it." And that goes for Mr. King.

I intend at this stage to move an amendment to the motion of confidence moved by the Prime Minister. This motion is seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and reads:
