subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-MOTION, THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we assembled a few days ago we endeavoured to approach the problem which faces parliament with open minds. We have listened to the evidence that has been placed before the house and have endeavoured to reach an opinion which will be in the nature of an intelligent appraisal of what we have learned during the days we have been assembled. To-night I shall try to place before the house what we believe as a result of the discussion we heard during the three days of last week.
NOVEMBER 27, 1944	6623
War Effort-Government Policy
I want to say at the outset that in our opinion the issue before parliament is reinforcements, not conscription. When the National Resources Mobilization Act was adopted in 1940 the government was given authority to conscript men, their property and resources for the purposes of war. In varying numbers and classes and for various purposes young Canadians have been conscripted already. As we predicted at the time, the government has not used the wide powers conferred upon it by the act to impose a total war effort by conscripting the financial institutions, the war industries and accumulated wealth. The outcome of the long investigation earlier this session into the chartered banks resulted merely in the confirmation of their special privileges and charters for another ten years.
Let us be clear then that the problem before parliament is not whether men shall be conscripted, but whether men already conscripted are needed and shall be dispatched as reinforcements for our armies now engaged in war, in Europe, the Mediterranean and Great Britain. Let me repeat, because I want to get this as clearly as I can before the house, that the issue is not conscription; it is reinforcements.
The principle of conscription was adopted in 1940 when the National Resources Mobilization Act was passed. As the Prime Minister suggested this afternoon, the plebiscite gave approval to the members of this house as well as to the government to send conscripted men beyond the boundaries of this country if necessary. When bill No. 80 was adopted subsequently the government was given the right to use reinforcements if, as and when needed.
We have held the view throughout that when human beings are compelled to lay their lives on the altar of our national sacrifice, industry, the financial institutions and accumulated wealth should be compelled to do the same thing at the same time and on the same terms. But parliament has not accepted that policy which, may I say, had we been in power would have been put into effect several years ago, and should be put into effect now to secure some equality of sacrifice to win the war and to ensure adequate preparations for full employment when the war ends.
Because this was not done, the present situation faces us. Total war at least would have demanded that a thorough inventory should have been taken long ago of all our resources. We should have decided the best contribution that this country could make and then decided what man-power we should need to expand our
100-416J
agricultural and industrial activities and to maintain an army, navy and air force at an appropriate strength in the theatres of war. This was never done.
A gesture was made when Canadians were compelled to register in 1940, but no effective use was ever made of the result and no comprehensive appraisal was ever made of our economic resources or of our anticipated contributions in the economic field. For many months we received orders for goods from our own armed services and from our allies, while our military commitments were expanded regardless of what might be expected of us in other fields. We have now reached the position in which, under similar circumstances, Canada found herself in 1917.
But all that is gone and done. We are now faced with an immediate problem. When, shortly after the member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) resigned as Minister of National Defence, I urged the calling of parliament. I did so because I regarded the matter of reinforcements as so vital that parliament, and not alone the government, should be apprised of the situation in all its aspects and take responsibility for all that should be done. In other words, the problem is the responsibility not of the government alone but of this parliament as a whole.	.
I think members of the house will agree with me-and perhaps we have received some criticism because we have remained silent- that we took no part in the recent discussion throughout the country based on supposition and on rumour. We joined in no chorus of the hymn of hate against conscripted men who had not volunteered for service overseas. We know there are among those young men ones who should have come forward. But let us not forget that there are some among them known to me, and I am certain to some members sitting in all parts of this house, whose sick or aged parents on the farm or in other circumstances require their assistance at various times and at various seasons. As long as they remained in Canada, leave for such purposes was always a possibility. To my certain knowledge some of these men have been torn between their duty to their country and the necessities of their homes, sometimes involving, too, a consideration of the needs of the country in the production of foodstuffs and other supplies. It is quite possible that under the order in council passed last week such men will still be tom between their sense of duty in one direction or the other. They may still wait until the vital decision is made for them, and in the meantime I am afraid they will be subjected to all
War Effort

Government Policy

the epithets which some persons and some sections of the press may hurl at them. I have no desire to defend men who are not doing their duty, but I must in justice to-night draw the attention of the house to a condition which we know to exist in the defence army.
Then, too, the order in council extends the service of the home defence army to Britain, Europe and the Mediterranean area. What the decision was that was arrived at Quebec regarding the use of Canadian troops in the Pacific area, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) implied a few minutes ago, we simply do not know. We have learned from the press that we are to take part in the war against Japan. But what Canadian troops are to be used there? Are the men who have spent five years abroad going to proceed to that theatre of war, and how large a force is contemplated? In any event whatever army is sent, reinforcements will be needed for it. Where and how are they to be secured?
The government says that it hopes to obtain the 16,000 reinforcements needed now from volunteers from the N.R.M.A. men. But some may not volunteer because by compulsion they will be available for service only in the United Kingdom, in Europe and in the Mediterranean area and will not be obliged to serve in the Pacific war as general service volunteers may be. The question of the Pacific war and the part we are expected to play in it was one I intended to ask about in a private sitting because it obviously is a problem which has a bearing on the problem now before us.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that too many questions remain unanswered as it is. General McNaughton told us that 16,000 reinforcements would take us up to the month of May, and in reply to the hon. member for Prince he said that in May the reinforcement pool would be' substantial. He told us that he had a table which he wanted to place before the house but could not do so in a public sitting because the enemy could deduce from it our expected casualties and hence deduce also the plans of our armies and indeed those of our allies during the next few months. The former Minister of National Defence, who of course is in possession of figures not available to private -members on the government benches, although they may be later figures than those used by the present Minister of National Defence, which are not available to hon. members, was I thought obviously not satisfied with General McNaughton's assurances. Yet because the official opposition objected to receiving vital information in private sittings of the house we are not in possession of all the facts. To say that in war time this house should have no more information

upon which to base its judgment than the general public has is in my opinion a view which is utterly irresponsible. Since the government is but the executive responsible to parliament, logically the official opposition should also refuse to allow the government to withhold any secret information regarding military operations from the house in public session. But the public examination of General McNaughton convinced me that reinforcements are needed and that for various reasons, some of which I have already given, the voluntary system of raising reinforcements for our forces overseas is inadequate. Let us be frank about it. All parties represented in this house repudiated in 1940 the poLicy of conscription of men for overseas service-all parties. There were no exceptions.

speechtext:
We shall see if I am
wrong. I have in my hand two statements
issued by my hon. friends to the left. One was issued in Edmonton on October 23, 1939, after a caucus of the Social Credit members of which my hon. friend the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) was chairman. He issued the statement, which contained three points, and the third point was this:
To this end the conscription of money and material wealth as defined below-
And a definition is given below.
-be made effective without unnecessary delay and before the conscription of man-power is considered.
Afterwards the leader of the party, Premier Aberhart of Alberta, thought it necessary to issue another public statement. This is what he said on May 1, 1940:
The Alberta followers of the New Democracy movement were definitely opposed to conscription of man-power and so declared themselves.
It was Major Herridge's persistence in this national service idea that placed him outside the New Democracy movement and lost him his election.
Major Herridge is no longer regarded in Alberta as the New Democracy leader, and he will be obliged to seek other followers for his national service policy outside the ranks of New Democracy supporters.
The New Democracy movement is definitely opposed to Major Herridge's national service proposals, and the conscription of man-power.
Let us be frank about it; all parties represented in this house repudiated conscription of man-power for overseas service in 1940. There were no exceptions. Now, the support we owe the gallant men in the firing lines demands immediate reinforcement. Whatever

War Effort-Government Policy
that support entails must be undertaken. That is our view; and we therefore place it before the house in the form of a subamendment, moved by myself, seconded by Mr. Maclnnis:
That all the words of the amendment after the word "that" in the first line thereof be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"The following words be added to the motion: which in the opinion of this house requires the immediate removal of all distinctions between drafted and volunteer personnel, thus making the entire home defence army available for reinforcements overseas, and requires further the total mobilization of all the resources of Canada, material and financial as well as human, to ensure a total war effort, adequate reestablishment of the members of our fighting forces, and full employment after the war."
From the discussion last week we cannot accept the order in council as a sound or proper policy to meet the needs of the armed forces. If 16.000 trained men are required between now and next May; if, as now seems likely, the war against Germany is prolonged beyond that time, and if, as has been intimated, we are obligated to play some. part in the war against Japan, further reinforcements will be needed. Why then pass an order in council which fails to do all that may be necessary and satisfies no one? To my mind it looks less than adequate and certainly is not statesmanlike in this grave hour. If it is done to placate the anti-conscriptionist followers of the government, it fails miserably; and if it is done to assure our armies of vigorous support in the war effort, it fails equally. To my mind the government has merely invited the obvious criticism that it is trying to play politics through a great war crisis when statesmanship of the highest order was demanded. If the government had come to parliament and stated frankly that unexpected casualties in the infantry had made it necessary to make available the N.R.M.A. army for immediate and subsequent reinforcement and presented the facts as they were partly given to the house by General McNaughton last week, they would have had the respect of the entire country and of all hon. members who have come to this house with unbiased minds. As it is, they have largely forfeited that respect.
The leader of the opposition said that instead of having two armies, we were going to have three. No, we are not. Instead of having two armies we are going to have four. First, there are the general service men who have already volunteered for service anywhere. Second, there will be those among the 16,000 trained men in the home defence army who, under the threat of compulsory service, will volunteer now for service. Third, there are the men of the same army who do not volunteer but are going to be drafted for service in the
United Kingdom, Europe and the Mediterranean. Fourth, the fifty-two thousand or so who are in the home defence forces in Canada. Then, there will be three types of service men actually in the battle line. There will be general service men; there will be new volunteers from draftees, and there will be men drafted to the fighting front. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is confusion worse confounded and is a policy which neither this house nor the country can support. That is why our amendment seeks to change the policy into one which removes all distinctions as to service and to benefits, and that to some degree is where our amendment differs from the amendment of the official opposition. Indeed, it differs in other respects too, because we leave the government's main motion in and amend it, giving particulars of what we think is a vigorous war effort. The government's policy is bad because it discriminates between men who have been called to serve under the same law and under the same conditions. This will cause endless confusion now and, in my opinion, grave difficulties in the future.
Since it is obvious that sufficient reinforcements can be obtained only in one way, why not place all the men on the same footing? If we are ordering 16,000 home defence personnel overseas, all in the same category should be liable to the same service and should be treated on exactly the same basis. Then there could be no sense of discrimination. But if parliament exercises such a power it merely emphasizes anew the obligations which it has to all the fighting forces and which it has made no proper preparations to fulfil. So far no adequate steps have been taken to ensure a total war effort, nor has this parliament made adequate reestablishment proposals involving plans for full employment when the war ends. Indeed, certain men are being led to believe officially that their return to civil life now will give them the first choice of jobs which will be difficult to obtain, when general demobilization takes place and the labour market becomes congested. Throughout the war fear of post-war conditions has interfered with recruiting and the government has neither plan nor policy to remove or even to mitigate to a sufficient extent this fear. How, then, can this house be expected to vote confidence in the government's policy-for that is what the motion says-to maintain a vigorous war effort when its proposals in all respects fall far short of obvious requirements?
I have said something regarding the government's policy, and I have tried to sum up the conclusions to which we came after having
War Effort-Government Policy

listened to the questions and the answers thereto last week. As to the official opposition as the alternative to the government, may I say, Mr. Speaker, that their own irresponsibility during this controversy and this debate makes it impossible for this house or the country to place any confidence in their intentions or ability. Personally, I think theirs has been a really shocking display of political manoeuvring. Some of their highly placed friends and a section of the press supporting them have done their best to inflame sectional differences and hatreds. Some of their pleas for support of the splendid and brave men who are serving this country on land, in the air, and on the sea have to me a hollow sound. They and their friends said the same things after the last war, but when the war was over how did they treat the boys who came back? They were in power, too, from 1930 to 1935. How did they treat the thousands of boys, the men who are fighting this country's battles to-day?
Seven weeks ago to-morrow two of my colleagues and I visited the Canadian cemetery at Dieppe. There, on a pleasant slope looking toward the setting sun, we saw hundreds of white crosses row on row. The place was beautifully kept, but not all of the crosses had yet been lettered. I knew that some of the boys whom I had known and taught had found their last resting place in that foreign field. We walked up and down the rows reading the names, and I noted this. They lay together there irrespective of race, tongue or creed. Here was a boy whose name told of his British origin while next was a lad whose name was of French or Ukrainian or even of German origin. There were many, many names, Mr. Speaker, that told me the boys that lay there came from the province of Quebec; many, many names of boys from my prairie province and other parts of Canada; and of course I was particularly interested in the names of those, who perished in the South Saskatchewan Regiment and in the Winnipeg Rifles. I knew that among them were boys who had probably been condemned to the relief camps and had ridden the rods. Some perhaps in their bitter hunger and distress had joined the trek to Ottawa in 1935 when my hon. friends of the Conservative party were in power. Then they asked foi the right to live, the right to earn their daily bread, and the government of my hon. friends gave thqm tear-gas bombs. Thus, knowing the record of the Conservative party.
I assess their present pleas and I rather think the country and our fighting men and women will assess them too.
(Mr. Cold well.]
Another thought I had as I viewed those crosses. Here I saw young men, the very flower of our manhood, lying together united in death. There was no distinction there of race or creed or colour. They were just Canadian lads who had died for their country. Why, oh why cannot we who are left behind in this country, to enjoy the freedom for which they died, live together? Those who in the midst of war engage in the setting of race against race, creed against creed and colour against colour in this land are in my opinion unworthy of the living and the dead.
Before I sit down may I say something else in connection with the visit we paid across the seas two months ago when we saw those splendid Canadian boys. We saw how brilliantly they were led, we saw how finely they behaved. We heard from Belgian and French people whom we met how highly they were respected, and we got a great thrill as we drove all the several hundred miles from Brussels right through the battle areas to see everywhere signpoints with the arrow on the maple leaf of Canada.
May I say here, too, Mr. Speaker, that these boys whom we are talking of reinforcing overseas, suffering as they are, are well cared for when they are wounded or sick. Our hospitals are a credit to Canada, to the doctors who man them, to the stretcher-bearers and to the gallant little nurses who do the job of tending the wounded at the battlefront. I thought I should just like to interject these words.
In conclusion, let me say this. For ourselves in this party we intend to give all the support we can to those who are fighting our battles overseas, in regard to reinforcements, whatever that involves, then to provide decently for those loved ones they leave behind and to prepare for those who return a Canada in which they may find security and opportunities for the free and abundant life for which they believe they fight beyond the seas.
Mr. Speaker, if we fail in this, their sacrifices, their suffering and their victory will have been again in vain.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-MOTION, THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
We are really discussing a resolution which reads as follows:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), wisely took pains to define what he meant by government policy. He made it clear that he meant only the order in council which undertakes to send overseas by coercion some
16,000	N.R.M.A. men. Had he not so specified the house would have taken the resolution at its face value and it would have concluded, I would presume, that we were to support the whole of the government's policy in connection with the conduct of the war. Now, what apparently does that policy mean, Mr. Speaker? It is really" altogether too bad that the Canadian people have been exercised so deeply over the conscription issue. Let no one imagine for a moment that we do not stand for the adequate support of the boys overseas. But it is a terrible pity, with all the other monstrous dangers which are threatening the Canadian people at the present time and which ought to be exercising them to the very depths of their being,
that not a word is being said about any of those things, but the attention of the people is being concentrated on 16,000 men. This, I am afraid, indicates pure politics. As I said when we first arrived at Ottawa we were going to listen and endeavour to find out what was underneath all of this. The behaviour of the Progressive Conservatives has impressed me also, as it did the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).
I must say that there are several things about this whole situation that fill me with misgiving. I believe it was on November 14 or 15 that, according to press reports, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) journeyed to Chicago and made a remark which certainly indicated to me that there was a good deal more politics under this whole crisis than there was real need for men; the speech of the former Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) this afternoon gave a certain amount of support to that idea, and the speech of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand) not very long ago gave another hint that there were men in the cabinet who were not very much impressed by the urgent need for men. I do not know and the ordinary citizen on the street in the Dominion of Canada does not know. He has to depend on the men in public life to inform him regarding these matters. But on the face of it, it does look strange that this nation should have been exercised from coast to coast over the matter of conscription at the present time when issues which will affect our lives and liberties for generations are not even being mentioned in the press.
What would government policy apparently stand for if the Prime. Minister had not accurately defined it to-day? Here are some of the things: the debt structure which he mentioned this afternoon as having already attained alarming proportions. Yet almost at the time when this crisis developed over conscription we were adding to the indebtedness of this nation in terms of billions and everyone was being led to believe that by so doing we were performing a patriotic act. What were we doing? We were building up a vast debt which the boys will return from overseas after fighting the war and pay for. Yet we are supposed to be doing these things for the boys overseas. It needs some explaining.
Then the government stands for a taxation structure which is tyrannical and destructive. Yet we are not agitated against that as you would think the papers should agitate us. The newspapers seem to feel that is all right, and the public men seem to think it is all right.
War Effort-Government Policy

Yet we are being told in stray radio speeches by someone every once in a while who gets co use the radio that we must be prepared to keep the income tax just where it is after the war. That is serious. Another aspect of government policy is insecurity. Apparently it is going to prevail after the war for no provision has been made up to the present time for any change whatsoever in our economic or financial system -which would justify anyone in supposing that conditions are going to be better after the war than they were before. Also centralization of power has proceeded in Canada and is being advocated in the world at a rate that would alarm anyone if he could only be allowed to see how serious it is. Yet never a word is uttered in the newspapers about that, and it probably will take away from the boys the very thing they are fighting and giving their lives for. This is a dreadfully serious matter. Why is it that we are not told all over this country by the newspapers that Canada's sovereignty is to be destroyed? Why is it that the newspapers are not telling us that the government is apparently definitely aiming to destroy the British empire, to disintegrate it? We hear nothing about that. Why is it that we do not hear anything at all about the fact that when we finish with this war, as far as the set-up which is now being erected is concerned it will be so nearly like the League of Nations' set-up after the last war that we shall begin immediately preparing for another war, or at least our enemies will? We will wait until they strike before we are prepared. Why are not all these things told? They are all in government policy. Before the Prime Minister took pains to define this matter clearly I was genuinely alarmed lest this was the sort of thing for which we were going to be asked to vote.
When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) mentioned the way the Conservatives had dealt with the lads who were marching east when they reached Regina, I was led to think of the way the government at present in power treated the boys in the Vancouver post office. They asked for bread; they were given tear-gas bombs, and then perhaps some of them died at Dieppe. These are serious matters, to which everybody who wishes to get this tangle straightened out should be giving some attention.
Since we are discussing the whole question of conscription at the present time, I think it is perhaps fitting that I should refer to the stand that has been taken by members of our group since the beginning. First may I point out that in February, 1936, members of this group, and I as the leader, made an announcement in Edmonton, which I believe can be

found in the Edmonton Journal and Edmonton Bulletin of February 12 of that year, in which we pointed out that this country ought to begin to prepare for war. If we had time to go through the newspaper comment of that time we would be quite surprised to find that those loyal newspapers, which should have been on the watch to warn the people of the coming conflict, instead of saying, "Here is a voice calling for something sound," endeavoured in their headlines and their editorial comment to discredit those who had thus manifested vision and courage in warning this country that we should be prepared. If we had started to prepare at that time we could have saved perhaps thousands of lives which have since been lost owing to the fact that we were not adequately prepared. That is the stand this group has -taken. We have never consciously played politics in the matter of war or conscription. We have always endeavoured to discover the truth and to make that truth known, regardless of what it cost. So that when we were confronted with the war in 1939 we took a strong stand in favour of national selective service which would guarantee equality of service and sacrifice. May I read from the records of those days. At page 48 of Hansard for the special session of 1939, during which war was declared, I find these words:
A good deal has ibeen made of the fact that the Social Credit organization in Edmonton and the social credit organization here, with New Democracy, have announced that they support conscription. I have noticed, however, that all too few have observed that the conscription is of the three distinct elements of our national life. The first is finance, with all that the word implies; the second is industry, with all that this word implies, and the third is manpower. The three must go together. Each of these is as necessary to the other two as is the third leg of a three-legged stool. If one is applied without the other two, only inequality, disaster and chaos will result. In conscription, in universal service, we will find the only way to avoid injustice, discrimination and class distinction.
That, I believe, indicates pretty clearly the stand taken by the Social Credit group. Here is another excerpt from the same page, for those who are interested:
Therefore, the New Democracy declares that justice, equality and effectiveness depend upon conscription of finance, industry and man-power.
And again on page 49:
We must do all we can and go where we are asked to go, in order to meet the enemy of religion, of freedom and of race. It is stupid and insincere to draw7 a distinction between home and foreign service. There can be no distinction.
I think those excerpts place the stand of the Social Credit group at the outbreak of

War Effort-Government Policy
war before the public with sufficient definiteness. And though the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar read some statements made in Edmonton, let me reaffirm that in parliament the Social Credit members have never receded from the stand they took in 1939.
One matter, I believe, does require some attention. A measure which might have been sound when war broke out may not be sound now, after the war has been conducted by false methods for four or five years. I am not, therefore, arguing that the policy we advocated at the outbreak of war would necessarily clear up the difficulties which the government has encountered as a result of pursuing a false policy. So many injustices have taken place during this war; so much bitterness has been engendered by reason of knowledge of those injustices, that the temper of the Canadian people both in and out of the army is genuinely dangerous at the present time. Had the government adopted the methods which this group advocated I believe they would have avoided many of the things which now threaten national unity as well as our peace and happiness. I am not saying, therefore, at this time huw we of this group are going to vote. We are still going to watch and study, to see, if we possibly can, what it is that lies under this whole thing.
A few moments ago I stated that the policy of the government apparently involved some very objectionable things. May I just refer to one or two of those things. First is the post-war programme of the government. During the last few months I have come into contact with a number of boys who have been overseas, who have been injured and who are in receipt of pensions. I have talked with the boys about their condition, physical, mental and spiritual; then I have regarded the pensions they have been given, and I have hung my head in shame to think that boys who fought engagements like the Dieppe affair should be turned off with such meagre pensions as must simply fire the minds of the men in the service to madness. Yet this government, in charge of a man who talks about a "new order", is condoning that kind of thing and apparently is contemplating it for the after-war. That simply is not good enough. When we hear about boys out in British Columbia and in other parts of the country staging parades, tearing down and burning the union jack and so on, let us remember that the cause of that reaction is partly this shameful injustice to which they have seen their fellows subjected already. I will not go into details in. this regard tonight, but may do so at a future time. If we want this war conducted as the resolution
says, with vigour, I tell you we shall have to change our ways with respect to the boys who are coming home from overseas, or their comrades will arise in wrath and do something for which we shall all be sorry.
May I again direct your attention to one statement I made and which perhaps may be challenged. I said a while ago that there was a definite aim apparently on the part of this government, or the powers that are behind it whatever they are, to destroy the British commonwealth of nations. I believe that that statement will need a little elaboration. As evidence of the truth of what I said may I refer to the Brett-on Woods conference. Some will say that that has nothing to do with the war effort. Can it be conceived that men who are fighting and giving their lives to rid us of abominations such as are contemplated in the Bretton Woods conference can go forward and fight with the courage and confidence they would have if they had not read of such things? Therefore, I believe that this Bretton Woods question has a vital bearing on our war effort. It is going to affect the war effort more and more as the days go on and people generally get to know what is being done.
I should like to read some excerpts for the information of hon. members who do not happen to have read an article by Paul Einzig, a famous writer on economics in the old country. This has been Teprinted with the kind permission of the Daily Express of London from its issue of Thursday, August 10, 1944. It is entitled, "1925 and All That- Only Far, Far Worse." I quote;
A .plain man's guide to the menace of Bretton Woods.
It must be clear to those, who understand the meaning of the report of the Bretton Woods international monetary conference, published in a white paper before the Bank holiday, that the experts of forty-four nations have agreed on a return to the gold standard after the war.
How do you suppose the boy in the battle line will feel when he knows that he is fighting for the return of the gold standard? How do you think the fathers and mothers of the boys who have given their lives will feel? An inspiring prospect, is it not? Let me go on:
Unfortunately, very -few laymen can possibly understand the report. If the public were to realize what it is being led into it would raise its voice in a powerful protest, instead of allowing the experts a free hand to do their worst as they did in 1925.
Why is it that we did not read any protest against the Bretton Woods conference in any of the great papers in the Dominion of Canada? Why is it that no government spokesman found it worth his while to tell us about this thing over the radio? Why

War Effort-Government Policy

was the report couched in language which the ordinary man would be unable to understand? It just does not look very good, does it? Yet it seems to be part of the government policy, for no protest was lodged against this conference. They sent the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and a number of others there. They apparently took part in the conference and came home satisfied; yet this is what Paul Einzig has written about the conference. There are many things in this pamphlet which I am sure hon. members would like to read; I shall not take the time of the house to-night to read it in full. However, may I read a little farther on:
Yet, once the plan, is translated into intelligible English and is denuded of all camouflage, every layman of normal intelligence is bound to realize that it is -the gold standard, the full gold standard, and nothing but the gold standard.
Admittedly, it is a different gold standard from the one we abandoned in 1931, just as the gold standard adopted in 1925 was different from the one suspended in 1914. But the changes are, for the most part, considerably for the worse.
How does that make the members of this house feel whose boys are fighting and dying? Yet apparently this government is quite in sympathy with the Bretton Woods affair. May I read another passage which should impress all members, as follows:
Worst of all, the British experts have agreed to the insertion of an entirely new provision into the final draft of the plan, under which it will become impossible for this country to escape the consequences of their folly by withdrawing from the fund.
Under article XI the board of international financiers is given powers to declare economic war on Great Britain should she devalue sterling against the board's wishes!
All the united nations (including, let it be noted, the British dominions) will have to undertake to boycott and blockade this country in such event!
How do we feel about an agreement under which at the instructions of an international ooard, consisting of men like Sir Otto Neimeyer and others, this Dominion of Canada would have to boycott Great Britain and declare economic warfare on her? Can anj'one by any stretch of the imagination conceive that that is a thing worth fighting and dying for? I continue:
Is it really conceivable that parliament could pass such a suicidal measure?
It all depends on whether the public overcomes its natural reluctance to penetrate behind the smoke-screen of the experts' findings, and discovers for itself what is being planned against its vital interests.
The return to the gold standard under a cloud of obscurity must be prevented if this generation and the next are to enjoy the hard-earned fruits of victory.

Hon. members will now understand why I protested a few moments ago against arousing public opinion from coast to coast in Canada for political reasons over the matter of conscription in order to send 16,000 men overseas while matters of this kind are left in obscurity.
The Prime Minister will say in extenuation, "We will bring the matter to parliament." Should this government bring in a measure embodying the findings of Bretton Woods, every last one of those on the Liberal side would stand up and bow and vote for the thing no matter what it meant. It will be impossible to stop it; the steam roller will operate. It will not matter a particle how much anybody in parliament knows about it; when he rises to explain it Liberals and others will not listen. What guarantee of the people's protection will be given by bringing the Bretton Woods matter before parliament? A similar steam roller process I suppose will be employed over in England too.
Bretton Woods is one of the elements of government policy. I do not want to spend too much time on this sort of thing. What we are concerned with in this house is to get men overseas. I still believe that a great many of the men who are reluctant to-day to go overseas have been embittered by reason of the things that are occurring right in this country, that are being advocated or condoned by the government of Canada, such as this gold standard proposal. So that we ought to give a good deal of attention to this matter, too. I think I have shown from the quotations I have read from Paul Einzig, if he is an authority-and I think he is-that Canadian sovereignty is being threatened by this monetary agreement. It would be different if it were necessary, but it is not necessary, as those who are well informed on monetary matters know full well. The sovereignty of Canada is being threatened not only by the monetary agreement but also by that iniquitous rqeeting at Dumbarton Oaks not very long ago. Do you know what Dumbarton Oaks stands for? It stands for the building up of an international police force which will be able to move in and subdue Canada if she wants to introduce, let us say, social credit or any other measure that her people want to introduce. This international police force will be under the dictates and direction of this group of international scallywags that will have charge of the international financial arrangements; I will wager that these international scallywags will get themselves appointed without any member of this house being able to do anything about it; and they will keep themselves in office in spite of all the

War Effort-Government Policy
efforts of all the members of this house. Once we allow this thing to be fastened upon us our freedom will be gone. This is a serious matter.
The Prime Minister this afternoon spoke of building up organizations to prevent wars in the future, and I presume that a part of these organizations will be this international monetary stabilization scheme and organization proposed at Bretton Woods and the international police force proposed at Dumbarton Oaks.
Let us examine this Dumbarton Oaks affair a little farther. Let us suppose that we get Russia with her 192 million people, China with her 400 million people, Japan and India with their teeming millions, and a few more countries all going into this big international organization and that they have votes in proportion to their populations. The Anglo-Saxon peoples will then be binding themselves up in an international organization in which other peoples will be able to outvote them ten to one. The Anglo-Saxon peoples are paying with their lives for the winning of this war to bring about a situation of that sort!
These are serious matters. I am not detracting for a moment from the seriousness of the conscription issue and the conduct of the war. I am just urging the members of this house to be warned that we look beneath the surface before it is too late. It is easy to see how the British commonwealth would be destroyed if the members of the commonwealth are under this international organization and have to do what they are told to do rather than what they want to do, in order to pull together.
There is one other serious matter. There is the possibility of another war. After the end of the first great war we lulled ourselves into security with slogans and catchwords that were used during the war. It was "a war to save democracy," "a war to end war," and the boys of my generation went into it and gave their glorious young lives in that war to end war. Then we built up a League of Nations to guarantee "collective security," so that we would never have war any more. All that the League of Nations did was to lull the Anglo-Saxon peoples into repose, so that they neglected to be prepared while their enemies prepared. That did occur. There is no guarantee that this united nations scheme, which is only a glorified league of nations, will not have the identical result. We have just barely saved ourselves in this war, and that by the grace and assistance of God Almighty. Let us go on for another twenty years in which more diabolical instruments of war are perfected and the art of using them learned by other nations, and then imagine what will happen if they strike while
we are unprepared. It may be argued that an international police force will take care of that. But what kind of international police force would it have taken to stop Hitler when he struck? It would take a pretty tidy sized international police force. Who are to be the members of this international police force, and who is to pay for its upkeep? I sat in this house when it was next to impossible for this house to get through a paltry sixty or seventy million dollar appropriation for war preparations. Is it to be supposed thaf the members of the united nations organization will contribute any more generously to the upkeep of an international police force than they formerly did? I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that we are not heading towards international security by building up a supra-national organization, called a "United Nations" organization. What we shall be doing by building up an organization of that kind will be heading inevitably into chaos because it will mean the destruction of everything we hold dear.
There will be members of this house who will disagree with me when I say that there are three distinct types of international power, each and every one of which is seeking to destroy the freedom of all mankind. I will not name those three in public, but if any member cares to ask me privately I will tell him the names of the three. It is these three that we can expect to be working through the agents who are organizing the Bretton Woods affair, Dumbarton Oaks and the rest of them, and they are putting out propaganda all over this land which fairly screams at you through the pages of the press and over the radio, to prepare the people for this international organization that will take away all our liberty. Is it to be supposed that the boys in the forces do not know about some of these things? Is it to be supposed that my boy does not know when I know? Of course they know, and it takes away a lot of the enthusiasm of these young men, especially of those who have not yet enlisted or gone over.
These are some of the things that Social Crediters think about when we are called upon to vote in support of the government's policy in conducting a vigorous war effort. I say, Mr. Speaker, that much remains to be uncovered yet. The people of Canada have not begun to learn what is behind this crisis. Social Crediters will watch a,little longer and listen a little further and perhaps we shall learn even yet what lies underneath it all. I promise you, Mr. Speaker, and I promise the government and every member of this house and every man and woman outside it that when we do find what is the right thing to do we will do it regardless of politics.

speechtext:
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Speaker, after the sharp differences of viewpoint that have arisen in recent days, the house I believe will turn with relief to a matter on which there will be only one viewpoint, and that one of pleasure and of pride in the achievements of a young Canadian army officer overseas. I refer to Major David Vivian Currie, of the 29th Canadian Armoured Regiment (South Alberta Regiment), who has been awarded the Victoria Cross.
The record exemplifies the opportunities for advancement available to young men in this democratic nation. Born in Sutherland, Saskatchewan, he graduated in due course from the Moose Jaw technical school, and for ten years prior to appointment to commissioned rank in the active army in January, 1940, was employed as an expert automobile mechanic and welder. Through merit, his promotion has been rapid, and he attained field rank early in the present year.
I should like now to read, on behalf of the Minister of National Defence, who is not here, the official citation:
The King has, been graciously pleased to approve the award of the Victoria Cross to:

Major David Vivian Currie,
29th Canadian Armoured Reconnaissance
Regiment (South Alberta Regiment).
In Normandy on 18th August, 1944, Major Currie was in command of a small mixed force of Canadian tanks, self-propelled anti-tank guns, and infantry which was ordered to cut one of the main escape routes from the Falaise pocket. The force was held up by strong enemy resistance in the village of St. Lambert sur Dives and two tanks were knocked out by 88-mm. guns. Major Currie immediately entered the village alone on foot at last light through the enemy outposts to reconnoitre the German defences and to extricate the crews of the disabled tanks which he succeeded in doing in spite of heavy mortar fire.
Early the following morning, without any previous artillery bombardment, Major Currie personally led an attack on the village in the face of fierce opposition from enemy tank guns and infantry and by noon had succeeded in seizing and consolidating a position half-way inside of the village.
During the next thirty-six hours the Germans hurled one counter attack after another against the Canadian force but so skilfully had Major Currie organized his defensive position that these attacks were repulsed with severe casualties to the enemy after heavy fighting.
At dusk on the 20th August the Germans attempted to mount a final assault on the Canadian positions but the attacking force was routed before it could even be deployed. Seven enemy tanks, twelve 88-mm. guns and forty vehicles were destroyed, three hundred Germans were killed, five hundred wounded and two thousand one hundred captured. Major Currie then promptly ordered an attack and completed the capture of the village, thus denying the Chambois-Trun escape route to the remnants of two German armies cut off in the Falaise pocket.
Throughout three days and nights of fierce fighting Major Currie's gallant conduct and contempt for danger set a magnificent example to all ranks of the force under his command.
On one occasion he personally directed the fire of his command tank on to a tiger tank which had been harassing his position and succeeded in knocking it out. During another attack while the guns of his command tank were taking on other targets at longer ranges, he used a rifle from the turret to deal with individual snipers who had infiltrated to within fifty yards of his headquarters. The only time reinforcements were able to get through to his force he himself led the forty men forward into their positions and explained the importance of their tasks as a part of the defence; when during the next attack these new reinforcements withdrew under the intense fire brought down by the enemy, he personally collected them and led them forward into position again where, inspired by his leadership, they held for the remainder of the battle. His employment of the artillery support which became available after his original attack went in was typical of his cool calculation of the risks involved in every situation. At one time, despite the fact that short rounds were falling within fifteen yards of his own tank, he ordered fire from medium artillery to continue because of its devastating effect upon the attacking enemy in his immediate area.
Throughout the operations the casualties to Major Currie's force were heavy. However, he never considered the possibility of failure or﻿NOVEMBER 27, 1944	6635
Army-Reports of Disturbances
allowed it to enter tlie minds of his men. In the words of one of his non-commissioned officers, "We- knew at one stage that it was going to be a fight to the finish but he was so cool about it, it was impossible for us to get excited. Since all the officers under his command were either killed or wounded during the action, Major Currie had virtually no respite from his duties and in fact obtained only one hour's sleep during the entire period. [DOT] Nevertheless, he did not permit his fatigue to become apparent to his troops and throughout the action took every opportunity to visit weapon pits and other defensive posts to talk to his men, to advise them as to the best use of their weapons and to cheer them with words of encouragement. When his force was finally relieved and he was satisfied that the turnover was complete he fell asleep on his feet and collapsed.
There can be no doubt that the success of the attack on and stand against the enemy at St. Lambert Sur Dives can largely be attributed to this officer's coolness, inspired leadership and skilful use of the limited weapons at his disposal.
The courage and devotion to duty shown by Major Currie during a prolonged period of heavy fighting were outstanding, and had a far-reaching effect on the successful outcome of the battle.

speechtext: I desire to direct to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, who I presume is representing the Minister of National Defence, or to the Prime Minister, an important and urgent question with respect to a matter of urgent public importance. speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, on Thursday of last week, the day that General McNaiughton was first in the house, I made certain assertions and allegations as to the representations that were being made, or were supposed to have been made, according to the evidence and information I had, by commanding officers in the various units with respect to voluntary enlistment. It will be recalled that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and myself had a somewhat heated exchange, which personally I much regret. I wish to say that because I do not want to live in a battle of that kind all the time. In the course of my remarks I stated it was my understanding that when these men were asked to volunteer it had been represented to them that rehabilitation grants would be denied them. I say this because a gallant officer who is the district officer commanding military district No. 7 feels that my remarks have misinterpreted his position. I know that gentleman, and know the service he has rendered in this great cause since he was appointed by my friend the former minister of national defence, over the heads of perhaps higher officials, to be the district officer commanding that military district. I make this explanation in justice to him as well as to myself. I understand that my improper use -I am going to take as full responsibility as I can-of terminology led me into error. I did not mean what I said; I meant something entirely different, namely, that they were to be told they would be refused the cash gratuity. Having said this, I hope the whole position will have been made perfectly clear.
