subtopic: TOLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, November 27, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort, and the proposed amendment of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: TOLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I desire to give my ruling with regard to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The motion before the house, moved by the Prime Minister, is:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved in amendment thereto:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following words substituted instead thereof:
"This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice."	.
To this the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) moved in amendment:
That all the wTords of the amendment after the word "that" in the first line thereof be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"The following words be added to the motion: which in the opinion of this house requires the immediate removal of all distinctions between drafted and volunteer personnel, thus making the entire home defence army available for reinforcements overseas, and requires further the total mobilization of all the resources of Canada, material and financial as well as human, to ensure a total war effort, adequate reestablishment of the members of our fighting forces, and full employment after the war."
It will be noticed that the leader of the opposition moved that certain words dealing with the same subject matter of the main

motion be added to that motion. The leader of the C.C.F. group moved' that certain words, some of which such as "and requires further the total mobilization of all resources of Canada material and financial" introduce other features, be added to the main motion. As this is foreign to the subject matter of the main amendment it cannot be moved at this stage of the proceedings, though it is relevant to the main motion. May says, page 285:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed.
The amendment to the amendment is in the nature of an amendment to the main motion,
and the hon. member must wait until the first amendment be negatived before his amendment can be offered. If the main amendment, instead of a substitution, was an addition to the main motion, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar might .move another addition different from, but relevant to, the main amendment. This often happens on the address in reply, where the wording of the main motion is unalterable; but in this case the house is asked to aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort, and the official opposition objects on the ground that the government has not provided for adequate and trained reinforcements. The leader of the C.C.F. party asks that this proposition be eliminated, and he gives certain reasons for voting against the main motion. He cannot adopt that course; he must first endeavour to have the amendment negatived or amended in a substantial manner, or otherwise disposed of, before moving his own amendment to the main motion. This theory is confirmed by May (page 291) who says:
An amendment to a proposed amendment cannot be moved if it proposes to leave out all the words of such proposed amendment, but in such a case the first amendment must be negatived before the second can be offered.
My attention has been directed to the amendments moved on 9th March, 1943, which will be found at pages 142 and 143 of the Journals of that date. The motion was made for the Speaker to leave the chair. An amendment was moved to the effect that government-created money be established, and a subamendment was proposed declaring that the banking system be nationalized. There were other considerations in both propositions, but they were akin and relevant to each other. They were allowed. In the question now under consideration the amendment proposes a substitution of the main motion, and the subamendment proposes an addition to the main

War Effort-Government Policy
motion. The question is not the same as in March, 1943; the two propositions are separate motions, and must be voted upon accordingly. 1 was also referred to the debate on the address in reply, this session, pages 42 and 43, Votes and Proceedings, and to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition and the subamendment moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party. The same objection applies as I have stated with regard to the amendment and subamendment of 9th March, 1943. < In the question now before the house, if the house accepts the subamendment the main amendment would be eliminated and the only question before the house would then be the main motion as amended by the subamendment. The result would be that the mover of the main amendment would be deprived of his right to obtain, an expression of opinion, either original or in an amended form, by the house on the policy stated in his amendment. For these reasons I rule that the subamendment is not in order at this time.

subtopic: TOLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing the debate on the motion now before the house I should like first to say what a pleasure and privilege it is once again to attend this Canadian parliament after four years spent on active service with the Canadian Army.
I was in England in September and October of 1940. I saw the German planes attacking by day and night. I saw the small but gallant R.A.F. force the Germans to resort to night bombing only. I saw London, that long-suffering city, burn at night, the last Sunday of the year 1940; and then that last big German attack in the early summer of 1941 when the House, of Commons at Westminster, the mother of parliaments, was destroyed. During that same period the destruction of Coventry and Plymouth and the burning of Bristol were suffered by the people of Britain. Then the organization of the air defences of the British isles forced the attackers slowly but surely from over England, and air superiority was gained over the much battered island. Then Germany attacked Russia, and Russia was called upon to take her share of the load so as to lighten the burden resting on the shoulders of England. The result was that only hit and run raids at long intervals came to the people of England. Then came December of 1941, Pearl Harbor, and the entry of the United States into the conflict; the arrival of the Americans and the Flying Fortresses in England; and the building of greater airports, which the Canadian engineers helped to construct so rapidly. Then followed August,
1942, and Dieppe, where the second Canadian division shouldered the great attack on the fortress of Europe, and made history and undying glory for Canada.
I saw the Canadians being trained for the job to come, where brigades were moved swiftly and smoothly from the south coast of England to the rugged hills of Scotland. I saw the Canadian Army move their artillery in one scheme after another. And then one day in the early morning broadcast of July 10, 1943, the world was informed that an allied army had landed in Sicily, the British on the right, the Americans on the left and the Canadian troops, consisting of the first Canadian division and the first Canadian armoured brigade attacking in the centre. Then followed September 3, and at daybreak the First Canadian Division landed at Reggio di Calabria, on the Italian mainland. Then in quick succession Pottenza, Spitzenola, Foggia, Motta, Campobasso, Castropignano, Torella, Molise and Agnone. Then a rest before the great battles along the Adriatic. A year ago now, on the part of the first Canadian division and the first Canadian armoured brigade, there was a rustle of preparations for that big show which was coming. Orders were issued and a quick move was made to the Adriatic. Then followed in succession the Sangro, San Vito, the Mora, Ortona and the Arielli. Then followed that long period of holding the winter line, that cemetery at the southern approach to Ortona which the Canadians left behind when they moved to Caserta in preparation for the battles that still were to come. Again there followed in quick succession the Gustav line, the fall of Cassino, the crashing through of the Hitler line, Pontecorvo, and onward to Rome -history written by Canadians in Italy. Then came the news on the radio on D-day, that morning in June the whole world had been looking forward to. While this initial attack was taking place on the Normandy coast the Canadians in Italy went into a rest period. After that short rest there was a quick push to Florence. The great 8th Army moved to the Adriatic and into the Gothic line, over the Metaurus beyond Pesaro and onward toward Bologna.
I served with the first Canadian division. I know the work that our infantry men have done. At this time I would like to draw to your attention an item that appears all too frequently in press reports of the world, "Slight activity-only a few patrols sent out". If you, Mr. Speaker, were one of the members of that patrol, you would not think it slight. Day in and day out infantrymen and engineers are going forward, clearing the
War Effort-Government Policy

way for the army to pass. Those are the men we must reinforce; those are the men who carry the load; those are the men who swept Jerry out of his dugout. They are the men who advance against the nazi war machine with nothing but the air and their skill to protect them from German fire. When this war is over, may the infantrymen hold the place of honour. They are the men who have been doing and are doing it the hard way. *
In fairness, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say at this time that I have spoken at some length respecting the activities of the first Canadian division because that is the one with which I served. It is an infantry division, and in a short time many of those soldiers will be starting their sixth year overseas. They are looking to the day when they will be back with their families. That is why it is necessary to send the required reinforcements to support our troops overseas.
I should like to place on record at this time some of the things I saw and heard when in England in September of this year. I saw the damage done by the robomb to communities in the south and east of England, the same area which received such a heavy bombing in the early years of the war. Once again that area is under terrific strain and pressure. I saw the damage, the havoc, the destruction and hardships the people have been suffering. V-day was coming even closer-and then came the robomb. The people of London will long remember the tragedy at the Guards' chapel, the robombs at Waterloo Station and the Lewisham market,.-all incidents in the suffering of the civilian population of England.
Anyone who has seen action in the combat areas, anyone who has seen the suffering and devastation in southern England, wants to see the war finished as quickly as possible. Speaking as a service man, and only for myself, I should like to give my impressions of the support the army has received from the official opposition in this house.
On Monday of this week the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) interrupted the Prime Minister, and those interruptions and the replies are reported at page 6597 of Hansard. Let me read a few lines to show what was said:
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): That is not a correct statement, because in this house I moved an amendment to the address in the session of 1942, calling for complete national selective service. I want to correct a misstatement.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	Complete national
selective service, as I understand it-
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): For the army in any theatre of war, for agriculture and for industry. That is a matter of record.

Mr. Mackenzie King: Well, perhaps I may speak for myself and allow the hon. member to speak for himself.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury):	I say the
record speaks for me.
I should like hon. members to look at that record. I have looked up the amendment moved by the hon. member for York-Sunbury on January 26, 1942, and I want to read it. This is what I find:
And the question being proposed:
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury), seconded by Mr. Stirling, moved in amendment thereto: That the following words be added to the address:
"This house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers, instead of giving to the country the leadership so essential at a time properly described in the speech from the throne, as the gravest crisis in the world's history, on the contrary, have sought to evade their responsibility by holding a plebiscite, which, in the view of this house, is the negation of responsible government.
And this house regrets that Your Excellency'* advisers have not seen fit to recommend to parliament without delay additional measures designed to:
(a) completely mobilize the wealth and material resources and, on a selective basis, the full man and woman power of the nation, to the end that the natioit may wage total war in any theatre of war.
I thought it desirable to look up the amendment moved on February 1, 1943, by the present leader of the opposition, after Mr. Bracken became leader of the Progressive Conservative party. It is in these words:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed (a) to provide an adequate plan for the effective use of Canada's man and woman power; (b) to adopt and carry through a national labour policy which will ensure maximum production and give to labour its rightful position as one of the major partners in our Canadian democracy; and (c) to provide adequate measures whereby Canadian agriculture can make its maximum war contribution and receive a fair share of the national income.
That is the record. To me as a soldier those are weak motions. They are facing both ways. They are trying to give the impression to one side that the Conservative party favours conscription and to the other side that it is not in favour of conscription. The Conservative party now seeks to get credit for wanting total war, but its record shows that it has never come out directly for conscription.
What has, been the position of the government? At every stage the government has given the army the support it needs without cheap heroics. They are doing that to-day. The government avoided conscription for overseas as long as it was possible to do so without endangering support for the army. But since 1942 the government said that it would use

IFar Effort-Government Policy
coascription if necessary. The Prime Minister has never hidden behind smoke screens like selective services or other phrases which mean different things to different men. The Prime Minister has been straightforward. He has called things by their right names. When he means conscription he calls it conscription, not something else. When conscription for overseas became necessary the government took the responsibility and passed the order in council.
But that is not all. The government has done everything necessary in all directions to make Canada's effort an all-out effort. Let me remind the house of what Mr. Churchill said on that subject. I quote from page 72 of ''Onwards to Victory" by the Right Honourable Winston S. Churchill:
March 6, 1943.
(A Message to Mr. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada, who had congratulated Mr. Churchill on his recovery from illness):
I am deeply touched by your very generous message, and I send to you and to all members of the parliament of Canada my heartfelt thanks. I recall with gratitude the warmth of the reception which you all gave me when I visited Canada in December, 1941. In the darkest days Canada, under your leadership, remained confident and true. Now the days are brighter; and when victory is won you will be able to look back with just pride upon a record surpassed by none.
Then in a radio address from Quebec on August 31, 1943, Mr. Churchill said:
I have also had the advantage of conferring with the Prime Minister of Canada, Mr. Mackenzie King, that experienced statesman who led the dominion instantly and unitedly into the war, and of sitting on several occasions with his cabinet, and the British and Canadian staffs have been over the whole ground of the war together. The contribution which Canada has made to the combined effort of the British commonwealth and empire in these tremendous times has deeply touched the heart of the mother country and of all the other members of our widespread family of states and races.
From the darkest days the Canadian army, growing stronger year by year, has played an indispensable part in guarding our British homeland from invasion. Now it is fighting with distinction in wider and ever-widening fields. The empire air training organization, which has been a wonderful success, has found its seat in Canada, and has welcomed the flower of the manhood of Great Britain, of Australia, and New Zealand to her spacious flying fields and to comradeship with her own gallant sons.
Canada has become in the course of this war an important seafaring nation, building many scores of -warships and merchant ships, some of them thousands of miles from salt water, and sending them forth manned by hardy Canadian seamen to guard the Atlantic convoys and our vital life-line across the ocean. The munition industries of Canada have played a most important part in our war economy. Last, but not least, Canada has relieved Great Britain of what would otherwise have been a debt for
these munitions of no less than $2,000,000,000.
All this, of course, was dictated by no law. It came from no treaty or formal obligation. It sprang in perfect freedom from sentiment and tradition and a generous resolve to serve the future of mankind.
That will be found at page 224 of the same publication. I should like to quote from the Ottawa Evening Citizen, Tuesday, November 28, as follows:
Canada's Effort "Magnificent"-Churchill
London, November 28-(CP)-Prime Minister Churchill to-day told the House of Commons he realized "the magnificent character of the Canadian war effort."
This resolution is not a vote on conscription. That is water over the dam; that issue was settled by the government on its own responsibility. The government is now asking for support in continuing the war effort-to finish the job. I believe that this government is incomparably better than any alternative to finish the job. I want a Liberal government to guarantee the future of Canada; no hybrid Union government, no soulless, heartless, conglomeration of office holders can do this. Our aim is to destroy the barbarism and error of nazism and take steps to prevent their rise again. Our aim is to strengthen and advance civilization and justice and assure security to all mankind.	*
Change is the law of life. We are living in a period of great changes, but any change must be in the right direction. Twenty-five years' leadership have given the Prime Minister experience without destroying vision. As proof let me quote from his speech before the members of both houses of parliament at Westminster on May 11, 1944:
Let us, by all means, seek to improve where we can. But in considering new methods of. organization we cannot be too careful to see that, to our own peoples, the new methods will not appear as an attempt to limit their freedom of decision or, to peoples outside the Commonwealth, as an attempt to establish a separate bloc. Let us beware lest in changing the form we lose the substance; or, for appearance's sake, sacrifice reality.
Those words are applicable to the situation in this house to-day. What has already been done at this session in making provision for the future of the service men, in advancing social security for everyone in Canada and in laying foundations for full employment and enlarged opportunities, give concrete evidence of the aim of the government to make Canada a land -where the four freedoms will be the birthright of all who live within its borders. I am therefore supporting the motion now before the house.
War Effort-Government Policy

subtopic: TOLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for London, (Mr. Johnston) who has just preceded me, and I know I voice the sentiments of all the members of this party and the house as a whole when I say we are delighted to see him back after his wonderful service overseas during the last four years.
The hon. gentleman has said that the issue to-day is not conscription, that that is water over the dam. Literally we cannot help but agree with him in that statement, but there is no doubt that the administration of a form of conscription is the burning issue today. This is a serious session. It is as unexpected as it might have been made unnecessary. I agree to a considerable extent with what was said the other day by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and with much of what has just been said by the hon. member for London. In many respects Canada's war effort has been magnificent. In many respects it has won the admiration, the esteem and the respect not only of our allies but of the whole world. Of the gallantry of our men at sea, in the senior service; of the fearlessness of those gentlemen of the air who fought against great odds at the beginning of the war and are still doing such a masterly job; of the sturdiness, the stubbornness and the bravery of our infantry and our army generally, there is no doubt. I realize as I speak that there is not an hon. member but who has a direct and personal interest in this war. I know there are members of the government who have lost what they valued most.
These are indeed serious times. The courage of the mothers of this country at this time should not be forgotten. The determination of our people in general, their attitude from the very beginning of the war. their determination to enter upon the side of Britain, the bulwark of civilization in those dark days, will be remembered and recorded in the pages of history in the years to come. The genius of our mechanics and artisans in industrial production has enabled us to attain productive capacities beyond the imagination of the most optimistic at the beginning of the war. These things are written indelibly in the history of our progress in these last five awful years.
But we are not here to boast about our achievements. We are here to finish the job. We are here to face the last desperate test of a struggle which will decide the fate of civilization itself. I cannot put the issue in better words than have been used by Mr. 
Alexander Walker, C.B.E., dominion president of the Canadian Legion, whose statement contains these words:
Only one thing matters now and that is getting reinforcements into the front line just as speedily as it is possible to do so. Anyone who still doubts this vital issue for reinforcements has only to look at the daily casualty lists and remember that, for every name appearing, a reinforcement must be found or an already war-weary soldier must do double duty.
He further states:
It is a vital burning issue, upon the immediate solution of which will depend first, the lives of our sous and brothers overseas, and second, the honour of Canada, both in relation to her self respect as a nation and to the degree of esteem in which she will be held by the governments and people of the united nations when the war is over.
He concludes:
The fate of our army overseas, and indeed Canada's future as a united nation, is now hanging in the balance.
That is the issue. It far transcends advantage to any party. It far transcends the dickering and manoeuvring for position or the clever strategy of the government which is now in power with the lopsided support of enormous numbers in this house. Having that in view, and realizing the seriousness of the situation this afternoon, I speak to this house and to this country for the Progressive Conservative party, with which I am associated ; and I say that no suggestion which I am about to make has any reference to what the hon. member for London (Mr. Johnston) has intimated with reference to a national government, but is wholly an offer of cooperation provided the right leadership is found, and is made without any request or suggestion of union government.
The Progressive Conservative party, with the full authority of its leader, John Bracken, and with the unanimous voice of its representation in this parliament, hereby declares that in this hour of national crisis, when the fortunes of political parties must be subordinated to the national weal, it stands prepared to cooperate with any government which, under leadership that will ensure equality of service, offers proof of will and determination to send to our soldiers overseas the reinforcements which our war commitments demand.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the position of the party to which I belong. I am proud to say that we stand foursquare for a policy which will equalize conditions among our armed forces, which will equalize conditions of selfrespect, of honour of service and of sacrifice,

War Effort-Government Policy
and give to the remainder of this war a united front in the battles overseas through that united stand here in Canada.
I listened with much interest to the remarks the other day of the Prime Minister. I have for the right hon. gentleman keen respect, and for almost a quarter of a century he has reciprocated this attitude. But may I say that his speech on this vital issue bristled with fear, doubt and uncertainty as to where this country was going, and I would point out, with the keenest respect, that we have only to look back and realize where the government has been standing to understand why he was nervous, why he almost shivered and shrank from his duty on this occasion. The hon. member for London has just told us that when the Prime Minister speaks about conscription everybody knows whait he means. That is news, let me say, to a distressed Canada at the present time. I well recall the statements which were made before the -war by the Prime Minister and his supporters. However, last year he informed us in this house that he had told Mr. Hitler himself that if he ever attacked Britain, Canada would be at her side.

speechtext:
Yes. I heard Mr. Eden speak, but I did not hear the Prime Minister speak- not at that. time. I heard him only four years afterwards. I look back and I see that some time ago, away back in 1939, the Prime Minister stated, as reported in Hansard at page 22 -and I agree with what he said:
If Britain goes down there will in time be no freedom on this continent.
He further said, in a broadcast on October 27, 1939, just after the beginning of the war:
We see forces loosed upon the world which, if not subdued and conquered overseas, sooner or later would be at our very doors.
With that also I agree. Later, on June 13, 1941,-Hansard, page 3931,-he stated:
This war will be won or lost ... on the shores and in the skies of Britain. The battlements are in the Atlantic and the English channel. Freedom falls only if Britain falls.
Again I agree with him. In September, 1941, speaking in the Mansion House in London., the Prime Minister said:
The policy of the Canadian government is to have our troops serve in those theatres where, viewing the war as a whole, it is believed their services will count most.
These are statements with which one cannot disagree. In fact, with most of the right hon. gentleman's statements one cannot disagree, and I am not disagreeing with them. But I am condemning his lack of action. On November 12, 1941, the Prime Minsiter said, in spite of these facts:
So far as I am concerned, without any consultation of the people on that subject, I do not intend to take the responsibility of supporting any policy of conscription for service overseas.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister also said:
It is alw'ays well, however, to be prepared as far in advance as may be possible for any contingency. . . . To defeat the enemy overseas is the objective of Canada's armed forces.
But, Mr. Speaker, later on the Prime Minister said: It is clear that the need for home defence has passed. And then we had the famous plebiscite, and the Prime Minister said the other day in his speech that there has never been a time since 1941 that this government has not had the legal power to enforce conscription if necessary. The hon. member for London has said to-day, however, that that is water under the bridge; conscription has been passed; and, as he intimates, the Prime Minister passed conscription. Indeed, it was his conscription that took the boys from the farm and the factory, from the forest and from the store, from the school and from our mines and from every enterprise in this dominion. He put in conscription, he brought on a plebiscite and had a substantial majority on it. As he said the other day, he has had that power from 1941, but he had the moral obligation, and he wanted to be relieved of that moral obligation in 1942. He was then released from the moral obligation, as he stated, so that it would leave him free in every way; and evidently he was released in every way, because by order in council
War Effort-Government Policy

P.C. 1867 he authorized the dispatch to Jamaica of personnel called out for training and service under N.R.M.A. Again on March 12, 1943, by order in council P.C. 2003, he authorized the dispatch of troops to Newfoundland. On April 20, 1943, he authorized the'dispatch to Alaska of personnel called out for training, service or duty pursuant to N.R.M.A., not restricting this to any specific number of men. Then there was an order in council extending the above to include the Aleutian islands, and there was also the famous order in council that has been passed recently. I say, therefore, that we have had no great conversion to any new administration of this policy.
I regret as deeply as does any other member of this house the resignations that have been handed in to the government. I regret the resignation of the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston), a gallant soldier of the last war and a gentleman who has served diligently in this war. I regret the resignation of the former minister of national defence for air (Mr. Power). It is regrettable that at this period in the war it should be necessary for two of the most important men in the cabinet, the two fighting men to resign. But the ex-minister of national defence has struggled with this problem, and no doubt struggled all the harder because of the uncertainty that has surrounded him by reason of the policy of his government. He went overseas expecting, as it was rumoured, to spend six weeks there, but he rushed back in three weeks-why? Because he realized that the situation was critical. He rushed back straight to his government and to his friend the Prime Minister and urged upon the right hon. gentleman the need of men. He had seen at first hand exactly what the picture was and he knew that we must depart from the policy of the voluntary system.
One would think that the old slogans of the Prime Minister would have been reviewed in the light of events-that we should have conscription if necessary but not necessarily conscription, that we should have conscription when we needed it and when we knew what the need was. The man who had stood beside him for a quarter of a century, a man whom he trusted, his friend, the ex-minister of national defence, on whom he had depended in this crucial year, offered his advice and that advice was rejected. Why wars his advice rejected at the eleventh hour? Why did the Prime Minister forsake him? The Prime Minister said that one of the reasons was that the ex-minister of national defence had assured him previously that this would not

happen until after the new year. In his speech the other day he said: I was assured there would be no such need until after the new year. He went further and said: I want this house and the country to know that we have been thinking about this. We have been thinking about it for a long time, but Mr. Ralston said that he would not break the news to us until after the new year. I do not want to be unfair to the right hon. gentleman, but those were his statements as I understood them.

speechtext:
I understand the issue, perhaps not as well as the Prime Minister understands it but better than he thinks I do, and I .will say with all deference that I have learned to follow his words cautiously and carefully. What he has just said is true. No man can tell the truth more skilfully than he. Let me say this. The Prime Minister knows what the situation is, as does every member of this house. But the ex-minister of national defence resigned from his government because in his opinion the crisis would arise so soon that plans for troops to go must be made now. The issue is so clear that it must appeal to every Canadian, just as it appeals to every member of this house. It pleads for a solution.
We know that troops could not be dispatched and disembarked overseas before the end of December and therefore the month of December was not the immediate problem. But should we wait until January to be told of a shortage of reinforcements? No. The Prime Minister said that another reason why he did not take the advice of the ex-minister of national defence was this, and I quote: I want the house and the country to know that we have been thinking about this all along. He said he wanted the people to know that the reason why he did not accept the advice, after five years of -war, was that we were now on the very eve of victory; therefore why should we do as suggested. He said we were on the very eve of victory; why should we do it now? Further, he said: What we had to decide in the cabinet was not only the necessity overseas but

War Effort-Government Policy
exactly what conditions existed right here in Canada. He emphasized that. I say therefore that the speech bristled with fear, doubt and uncertainty. Am I unfair to him?

speechtext:
-as we are about the political and other uncertainties in Canada. You cannot blow hot and cold. You cannot say on the one hand that you have made such great strides, as the Minister of Finance can well say with respect to the sale of victory bonds. Every loan has been oversubscribed. How can you talk about what the Red Cross has done in this country; how can you say that our industrial enterprise has done marvels in providing munitions and supplies; how can you boast about the determination and industry of the Canadian people, the genius of our mechanics and the soundness of the business executive across the country who have made our war effort the success that it has been, and at the same time talk about the uncertainties in Canada? These people have led the government instead of the government leading them for the last five years. How can you boast about that on one hand and say to the world on the other hand that so far as the necessity for man-power is concerned we have to think of conditions at home and then try to escape the responsibility for those conditions?
The man who has been in power in this country for so long says that the conditions are caused by an organized conspiracy. A conspiracy by whom? The press of Canada? The Canadian Legion? The boys who have returned from overseas? Who are the conspirators? Where is this conspiracy? _

speechtext: A Tory conspiracy.

subtopic: TOLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING

speechtext:
Somebody says, "a Tory
conspiracy". Yes, I have heard you say that before. It is not worthy of an answer, Mr. Speaker, because the hon. member knows where this party has stood. He knows where it stands to-day, and if there was any doubt about it I have made it clear to you now. We are not seeking power; we are not seeking authority. What we are seeking is to have this government do the duty that lies clearly before it, and get on with this war. We did not call this session of parliament. It was called because one of the senior cabinet ministers left the government because it had faltered in its duty. It was called when another cabinet minister left because you floundered in your compromise. That is why they left you. One left because you compromised; the other left because you faltered. There is no organized conspiracy against this government, Mr. Speaker. There is an organized determination across the country that we shall finish this job. I think this afternoon of the Right Hon. Winston Churchill. Would not the Canadian people prefer that the
War Effort

Government Policy

Prime Minister should come out and tell us: All I can offer you at this time is blood, sweat and tears, than that he should say on the floor of this house that the necessity makes him throw the responsibility on parliament?
Who has replaced the hon. gentleman who has resigned as minister of national defence? A man who said he had faith in the voluntary system the day before he came into the house and now asks us to support him in a compulsory policy. He came into the house with unanimous consent. This government cannot hide behind such smokescreens. You cannot hide behind secret sessions of parliament. The public of Canada know where you stand. They know about the vacillating, twisting, squirming, floundering and faltering policy of this government. Everybody in Canada knows. The boys in service overseas are almost weeping about it. They write back home and ask us what is happening in Canada. Why should we humiliate them in their hour of greatest crisis?
The Minister of National Defence-and I have every respect and regard for him-has been a great scientist. He is a cultured gentleman. He was nervous the other day. I say that because after he left us the first day we were more confused than when he came into the house. It was, not any fault of his. It was because he was making his first appearance in the house under such peculiar circumstances. But I remember one thing he did say-

Yes, Mr. Churchill said that victory may not be achieved until well on into next summer. The Prime Minister is thinking about the first statement Mr. Churchill made. The Prime Minister is six months behind on this particular issue.
The new Minister of National Defence spoke to the house and said for five years he had faith in the voluntary system, and then in five hours admitted that he had been converted to the compulsory system. We are now asked as a people to endorse and support him, to endorse a policy for which the former minister of national defence was let out. It is the most ridiculous spectacle that this country has ever faced-toying and- flirting with our destiny while our boys are dying. Yes, Mr. Speaker, he said that the fighting was much heavier than we had expected. He now comes in and asks us to endorse the sending overseas of only 16,000 men. He says the loss of life will be great. The future is dark and difficult, yet the other day another minister of the crown, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand) said that the war is already won.

I will not deal with that
further; the statement aroused the whole United States, but if I were sitting where hon. gentlemen are sitting I would not laugh very heartily at that one. Then we have the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) another gallant supporter of the government. If anyone thinks there is consistency in this government let them listen to what that hon. gentleman said in 1942:
I am convinced that we all want to win the war and that we are all prepared to submit to any measure which may be absolutely necessary for that purpose. . . . No thinking person can, therefore, have any objection to the government resorting to conscription for overseas service in the event of absolute necessity.
Then only the other day the same hon. gentleman said:
Mr. Ralston has visited the battlefields overseas and upon his return has communicated to his cabinet colleagues reports of an extremely serious nature. . . . We in conscience could not accept what he recommended us to do. ... If the federal government had decided to send draftees as reinforcements overseas, the majority of the, people of Quebec would have deemed themselves deceived by their Englishspeaking compatriots.

speechtext: But this is your owm Minister of Justice. I have as much regard for the province of Quebec as my hon. friend has. Never within or without this house have I reflected upon your province. I have said that your noble people, who win Victoria Crosses just as other people do, have been misled and fooled for twenty-five years by the right hon. Prime Minister. I ask the hon. gentleman, or any other hon. member from the province of Quebec-

subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Is that what you have always said?

subtopic: TOLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Oh, get up or shut up. If any minister from the province of Quebec can speak for the Minister of Justice in his absence, I ask him to rise now and tell us where the minister stands at the present time. Does he want to change his mind again? Does he support this degree of conscription, or does his silence indicate another resignation coming up? We have even heard from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson), who said it was possible the time might come, and that if it did the government would adopt without equivocation the same method of raising men for our overseas forces that has been followed in connection with the home defence army. I ask the minister if he now supports this policy, as this is something else again. This is the third time he has changed. Does he stick with that, or is he waiting now for a
fourth policy? Then in 1942 I heard the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) say in this house:
When in my view conscription for overseas service is essential to the safety of the state and the preservation of our way of life, I will express my opinion in no uncertain terms.
Why does he now remain in conspicuous silence, while his colleagues bid him a last and loud farewell? Then we have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the famous champion of the middle of the road. Where does he stand to-day? Does he still stand in the middle of the road? Does he stand for sending more men overseas, or is he going to confine it to just this 16,000? These are the last shreds by which this faltering government hangs; from crag to crag they flounder; from one point of despair to another they hesitate, and from one national humiliation to another they retreat. I would remind them of one awful advertisement in connection with these gallant young men-and I say gallant young men advisedly, for I have every sympathy for these boys who have been so often rudely termed "zombies." These boys have been misled; they have not been approached fairly, but they have as gallant hearts for battle as many of the men overseas. They are waiting for uniform conscription, as they said this morning in Vancouver. In that connection I think of that advertisement, paid for with the money of the taxpayers, pleading with them, intimidating them, coercing them as well as conscripting them: "Have I the guts?" Then I say to these hon. gentlemen who are left, these lesser lights of the former cabinet: when this house adjourns, go out and get a mirror, look at yourselves and ask yourselves the same question.
Was it any wonder the Prime Minister, in his speech the other day, turned his back to those of us who understand his motives, and talked to his former colleagues? Is it any wonder that he pleaded: now, at my time of life, you should support me. Is it any wonder that he resurrected from the graveyard of the political life of this dominion the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the great Sir John A. Macdonald, to take what they did in days of peace in order to justify him for what he has done in time of war? Is it any wonder that he fears anarchy may follow his regime? We have anarchy in this country now, Mr. Speaker, and the Prime Minister has lost the confidence of the people of this dominion. The other day he spoke as though he were indispensable, but in that regard let me say that I have seen governments come and I have seen governments go. I know the right hon. gentleman knows, and he knows that I know, that he
War Effort-Government Policy

does not have to name his successor. In this house he turned and asked his colleagues which one would take on the job. He has not the right to ask anybody else. The governor general has the right, though he has not the duty, to ask the Prime Minister to recommend, and the governor general does not have to accept that recommendation unless he sees fit to do so. Surely no one is indispensable. This is not a dynasty; this is a democracy. The Prime Minister pleads for a rubber-stamped approval by a colossal majority before his government is smothered by the avalanche of dissension so obvious throughout . the country.
Then we have the Japanese situation; I see my time is going, but not long ago in the city of Quebec a conference was held. Mr. Churchill said:
And Mr. Mackenzie King and his cabinet likewise have insisted that they should take the part assigned to them.
I have not time to deal with that matter now, but some three years ago we declared war on Japan, and now Canada still waits for a policy in connection with its execution.

War Effort-Government Policy
And this was at the time of the fall of France. So I say to the leader of the C.C.F. party: Did he kneel among those white crosses and repent of having taken that position, to assume the changed position he described the other day in this house?
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the house for its attention. The issue, sir, is clear. The challenge is definite. Our duty is at hand. We must keep faith with our boys. We must not flirt with destiny. We must not fail our boys and humiliate our country. Our national dignity is at stake.
Mr. VICTOR' QUELCH (Acadia): Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has asked the house to aid the government in maintaining a vigorous war effort. He asks for an endorsation of the government's general policy in that regard. He made his position clear when he spoke on November 27, as reported at page 6617 of Hansard in these words:
As I have said, the motion is not to be construed as an endorsation of government policies generally. So far as it relates to confidence in myself, that confidence is being expressed in relation to myself as one charged with responsibility of seeing that the policy set forth in the order in council P.C. 8891 is duly administered.
And again:
Any member who votes against this motion is asking to have the present administration resign, and another administration immediately take its place.
No matter what the Prime Minister may have said, I believe that in many parts of this country a vote for the Prime Minister's motion will be regarded as a vote in favour of sending the personnel of the N.R.M.A. overseas-and vice versa, where a vote is against the motion.
We have now a situation where reinforcements are needed overseas immediately, and I believe that P.C. 8891 is sufficient to meet the needs of that situation. Furthermore we have had the assurance of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McNaughton) that the 26,000 of the N.R.M.A. personnel not covered by the order in council will be put immediately into the training stream, and made available if and when required.
This group would have preferred an order in council which would have made all men called up under the N.R.M.A. available for overseas service. We realize, however, that an urgent situation has developed, a situation in which reinforcements are needed overseas immediately, and we are prepared to support the government in seeing that those reinforcements' are sent. We are also prepared to
support - the government in averting a crisis which might very well bring on an election which would split the country from one end to the other. An issue such as this should not be placed before the people at this time. It would be my hope that when an election does come it would be on an issue which is clear-cut, so that the people may vote with some degree of intelligence.
It has been suggested that we could support the amendment offered by the Progressive Conservative party, which would ensure that the whole of the personnel of the N.R.M.A. be sent overseas. I think it is clear, however, that support for that amendment would in many places be regarded as showing confidence in the Progressive Conservative party-and members of this group have absolutely no confidence in that party. We have not forgotten their record between 1930 and 1935, their policy of belt-tightening in the face of actual physical want and destitution. We have not forgotten that that party failed to give leadership early in 1940. Furthermore, after they were defeated they immediately began to embarrass the government, and they have been, trying to embarrass it ever since that time, throughout the period of the war. Their sole purpose seems to have been to capitalize on the crisis that has developed.
P.C. 8891 is being blamed for the wave of discontent sweeping the country to-day. I would say that the order in council has merely brought the matter out into the open. For some years, since the beginning of the war, discontent has been spreading, and that situation has been largely the result of the manner in which policies have been administered, and especially those policies relating to recruiting.
The government's policy from the very beginning in connection with this question has been one of appeasement. A policy of appeasement, whether national or international, is in reality a policy of cowardice; it neither satisfies the appeased nor does it satisfy those who are attempting to appease. It earns the contempt of the appeased and the wrath of those who are sacrificed as a result of the appeasement.
From the beginning the government has consistently opposed conscription for overseas service. Apparently it is a strong supporter of the voluntary system. But let me stress this fact, that it has indulged in what I would describe as despicable practices, in an effort to compel people to volunteer. In addition to that its policy has, from the very beginning, been one of flogging the willing horse.
What has been the consequence of that policy? The result has been this, that in
War Effort-Government Policy

various parts of Canada we find families in which the whole of the manhood of those families has been wiped out; and then across the road you may have a family that has made no contribution. That is bound to be the result of flogging the willing horse with your so-called voluntary system. It is that kind of thing that is stirring up so much resentment in the country to-day, when you see these families bereaved of all their sons and perhaps the husband as well.
The policy of the Prime Minister, or perhaps I should say of the government, created a problem in the men that were called up under the N.R.M.A. Ever since those men were called up a campaign of abuse has been carried on against them. The reason why so many of those men are refusing to enlist to-day is not that they are cowards, it is that they are burning with resentment because of the policy which has been applied.
Do not let us forget that in the early stages of this scheme many men were obtained under false pretences. I think it was in 1941 when the four months' training plan was first put into operation. Men were asked to leave the farm to serve under that scheme, to take up four months' training and then be in position to return to the farm in the spring. Many boys, wishing to cooperate with the government, refrained from asking for postponements. They went into the training stream, and what happened? After they were in there the government froze them there for the duration. Many of those boys would have been eligible for postponement had it not been for the fact that they were asked to cooperate with the government and they did cooperate. But they were penalized for cooperating. That is what happened at the very start of the scheme. Men were got in under false pretences and they have been burning with resentment ever since. When you have a few men in a crowd burning with resentment, that resentment grows and filters through the rest.
We are told that volunteers make better soldiers than conscripts. Are we prepared to say that the Canadian soldier is a better soldier than the United States or Russian or British soldier? I do not think any one of us would dare to say that. Under this policy a man will be considered a volunteer up to a certain hour, but after that he becomes a conscript. Will you say that if a man volunteers before twelve o'clock he will be a better soldier than he would if he were conscripted five minutes later? That is the situation as we have it to-day.
We are told that conscription failed in the last war. I can speak only from personal

experience, but I do know that on September 2, 1918, just before we launched an attack on the Drocourt-Queant line I received a large number of reinforcements. I did not care whether those men were conscripts or volunteers. I and the company were glad to welcome them. We were not of the opinion that conscription had failed. The only fault we had to find was that these men had received only a comparatively few weeks training. That was because conscription had not been put into force early enough; it was not as a result of conscription.
I agree that the voluntary system is the best method to use in order to obtain men for a raiding party or a small expeditionary force; but when you are going into a total war which will require every man that is available, then I do not see how the voluntary system can- be maintained on an equitable basis. Certainly you cannot expect to have equality of service and sacrifice under the voluntary system which may result in all the men of one family going overseas and none from another.
Under P.C. 8891 the government still supports the voluntary system; it is still going to try to get N.R.M.A. men to enlist. Will the man who is practically forced to enlist be a better soldier than the man who is conscripted? As I have already pointed out, that is bound to be the situation which will develop as a result of the order in council. In spite of the fact that men are being called up you are still going to flog the willing horse. There will be nothing to prevent the last remaining son in a family from enlisting for overseas. That boy may have lost two or three brothers and want revenge. If two or three sons from a family have gone overseas the remaining son should not be allowed to go. Instead of doing everything to make it possible for that son to enlist, we should refuse to allow him to enlist. Under the present system all the boys in one family may be enlisting while other families will be permitted to continue to disregard their obligations or responsibilities.
The Liberal party is continually emphasizing the fact that Canada has made a magnificent war effort. I think we will all agree that our war effort has been a glorious one, but I take issue with the statement that we should support the Liberal party in an election because the Liberal party has made a magnificent war effort. I think in many cases our magnificent war effort has been in spite of the government's policies rather than as a result of them. I will give two or three examples to prove my contention.
NOVEMBER 29, 1944	6651
War Effort-Government Policy
Let us go back to the early days of the war and remember that for the first three years agricultural prices were maintained at a ruinously low figure. In spite of that injustice, agriculture cooperated and expanded its production. I would say that agriculture made that effort in spite of the injustices that it had suffered rather than as a result of the government's policies at that time. The same thing may be said with regard to labour. Since the start of the war labour has suffered many injustices, but in spite of those injustices labour has made a tremendous contribution to the war. Again you can say that that contribution was made in spite of rather than as a result of Liberal policies.
I should like to refer to the treatment that our soldiers and their dependents have received since the start of the war. The mistreatment which some of our soldiers and their dependents have received has caused a great deal of indignation. At the start of this session I referred to many cases and asked that these injustices be remedied before they caused further resentment. Apparently the government has no intention of altering certain policies which have proved so detrimental to the welfare of the soldier.
Let me refer to the order in council which was passed in 1940 and which amended the Pension Act. That order in council removed the insurance principle. I understand it was introduced on the recommendation of the Department of Finance. Up until the passing of that order in council a soldier was insured from the time he put on his uniform until he took it off. After the passing of that order in council a man serving in Canada was insured only against disability incurred as a result of military duty. As a result of the policy incorporated in that order in council many thousands of soldiers have been refused pensions on the ground that their disabilities were incurred while they were not on military duty.
Take the situation in the last war. During the last war those men would have been eligible for pension. Then again, thousands of soldiers have been refused pensions, and perhaps their dependents as well, on the ground that their disability was of pre-enlistment origin. That is not the law in England. There the category of the man upon enlistment is recognized as his real condition, and if that condition deteriorates he is pensionable. Should a man in this country enter the army as A-l and his condition deteriorate, if it can be proven that that deterioration was due, say to an accident which happened prior to
his enlistment, we refuse to give him a pension. If so, it is not the law in England, and I think it is high time that that law should be changed in this country. Many of these men are put through a form of third degree in order to try to prove that the disability they suffer from upon their discharge was incurred prior to enlistment. The only reason for passing either of those orders in council-the one regarding pre-enlistment origin and the one regarding the insurance principle-was to save the country a few million dollars, and to do so at the expense of the soldier and his dependents.
Then, one might refer to the condition of the old soldier settlers of the last war. I believe every hon. member is familiar with that situation. I do not think any member is proud of it. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) has brought this question forcibly before the house on several occasions. I am reminded that when a delegation came here to interview the cabinet last summer they were given the assurance of the cabinet that every consideration would be given to their request. I was there when they met the cabinet, and afterwards, and the men were jubilant. They said, "That is good; we are going to be given free title to our land." I told them then and there not to be over-optimistic. I told them, "Governments have a peculiar way of failing to carry out promises which you think they have been made". It was only a short time afterwards that a statement appeared in the Legionary magazine under the pen of the director of the Veterans Land Act which told the men that the government had no intention of giving them clear title to their land. It would have been far better if the government, when they met these soldiers, had explained that situation then and there instead of encouraging them to believe free titles were going to be given; because that is merely storing up future resentments.
All the things I have referred to have created a great deal of dissatisfaction throughout this country as a result of the injustices. So again I stress that the glorious war effort of Canada in many regards has been in spite of the policies of the Liberal government rather than as a result of them.
Before I sit down I intend to move an amendment which, I believe, would largely rectify the condition that I have referred to; but before I propose the amendment I wish to make a statement in clarification of a certain situation that exists in this country:
We, the members of the Social Credit party in this house, in 1940 were elected entirely from the province of Alberta. At that time

War Effort-Government Policy
no national social credit movement had been launched. However, in April of this year a national convention in Toronto set up the Social Credit Association of Canada, which is not a political party machine but is an association of autonomous provincial and federal constituency organizations, as the name implies. This association has not had an opportunity of submitting its policy to the people of Canada for their endorsation; hence no member is among us to speak for the Social Credit Association of Canada.
In all that any of this group have said in this house, in all that I have said in this address, and in the contents of the amendment we are about to propose, we simply have represented and do represent the policies of this group of Social Credit members of parliament and not necessarily those of the Social Credit Association of Canada.
On this question of Canada's war effort this group has been entirely consistent from the earliest days of our presence in this house. In what we now propose as a sane and sensible policy to be followed by the government of Canada from this day forth to ensure a maximum war effort, we believe we are voicing the will of the vast majority of Canadians, and certainly the will of the majority of the Social Crediters who elected us. But we realize now that there may be groups of Social Crediters in various parts of Canada not represented here who may not entirely agree with our proposals, hence we cannot presume to speak for them until they have been given memberships in our caucus through the mechanics of an election.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "house" in the amendment be struck out and the following words substituted instead thereof:
"requires the government to give immediate effect to the following policy:
1.	The unqualified assurance to our men on the battle fronts that they will receive at once ample material supplies, and adequate reinforcements; and the use of all persons in any of Canada's armed services in any theatre of war in which they may be required.
2.	The unqualified assurance, backed by appropriate action, that:
(a)	Upon demobilization the active service men and women in the armed services, together with their families, will be ensured economic security, together with adequate grants and proper opportunities for training to enable them to reestablish themselves in the country's economic life;
(b)	Adequate pensions and free medical care will be given to all persons whose health has been impaired during active service in the Canadian forces from any cause -whatsoever;

(c)	The dependents of all men killed in action or who have died in active service in the Canadian forces will be provided with economic independence for life.
(d)	The foregoing will constitute a first charge on the nation.
3.	The assurance to the people of Canada, by immediate action to that end, that following the war the abundant productive resources of the country will be used to the full, and that the resulting goods and services will be equitably distributed to ensure every Canadian economic security with full freedom.
4.	The assurance that government wartime controls, bureaucracy regimentation and oppressive taxation will be discontinued as rapidly as possible after the war, and that the peace-time economy will be based on a proper democracy free from state domination of the people's lives.
5.	Immediate steps to establish the necessary reforms to our financial system without which the foregoing will be impossible."

speechtext:
My remarks will be brief. I do not need to speak at any length to repeat what I have stated a hundred times in and out of the house. I foresaw long ago the events which are now taking place and I have frequently warned the government and the people. During the sessions of 1937 and 1938, I consistently opposed the increase in military estimates, maintaining an unyielding opposition to any attempt to drag us into foreign wars. I have fought unremittingly for the repeal of section 64 of the Militia Act, at the very time when an attempt was being made to lead us into believing that the increase in military estimates was intended for the defence of Canada and of Canada only. On September 9, 1939, I denounced with all my strength Canada's participation in the war, and I even moved an amendment to that effect.
Alone the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. LaCroix) supported my efforts against participation which necessarily was to bring about the unjust and disloyal conscription which has been in force since 1940 and, finally, the present disaster.
As the result of Canada's participation in the war, the government has spent sixteen billion dollars; agriculture has lost over half a million workers, male and female; families are broken up, while mothers and daughters are toiling in factories, and thousands of our young men are being sacrificed on foreign soil. And who are responsible for this appalling situation? Those who failed to support our amendment against participation in the war and our amendments against mobilization, on June 18 and 19, 1940.

War Effort-Government Policy
Protests are being heard against conscription, not only from Quebec but from all sections of the country. I am still opposed to conscription with as much strength as I deployed in opposing the increase in defence estimates, participation and mobilization. 1 cannot find words sufficiently scathing to condemn this new reversal of policy by a government which, at the end of its term of office, imposes this evil and anti-national measure. Never has a government broken so many pledges. Never has it thus sowed doubt and suspicion. A self-respecting administration, if they have any regard for the people, do not resort to all possible roundabout means to abuse the good faith of those under their jurisdiction. In whom will our people repose their trust if they lose confidence in the government?
One last word. Since Canada has started participating in the war, we have lost all our prerogatives. We have reverted to century-old colonialism. Our country, thanks to the acts and errors of the government, is now trailing for good in the wake of the Empire to the great satisfaction of our partisans of colonialism. Let us hope that we may forsake this chaotic situation to unfurl at last a Canadian flag in an independent country, mistress of its own destinies. Whether we wish it or not, the deep reactions of the postwar period are bound to bring about the independence of Canada.
At last, because they have camouflaged the facts, the government who have willingly declared war must inevitably be led to conscription. Let them shoulder their dreadful responsibility in this matter, which they share with those who have refused to support the amendment I moved against participation in the war, on September 9, 1939. Their attitude at that time has been and still is the main cause of conscription. If, in 1917, a similar measure was a tremendous mistake, to use the expressions of the former Minister of Justice, it is doubly wrong to-day. The experience of the last war should have been a warning to the administration. The Canadian people, after seeing the economical structure of their country threatened, besides shouldering too heavy a burden of taxes and loans must, by the expressed will of their government, pay the blood tax. Such are the deferred, but dire results of the military and financial imperialism laid down as a creed by the very people who claimed they were opposing it.
Personally, I shall maintain the attitude I have taken, resolved to fight to the end against this unjustifiable measure.

speechtext:
From what has been said it is obvious that we all agree that the country and the people are faced by a very grave crisis. It is the crisis of reinforcements and also the crisis of national unity, and this crisis of national unity is one that we should consider seriously because of its effect upon the people of Canada and upon the morale both of the people at home and of the troops overseas.
My party, the Labour Progressive party, has done everything in its power, in whatever it has said or written, to encourage the greatest number of men to join the army, to undertake general service. Our party has no N.R.M.A. men. We in this party, in the course of the plebiscite, carried on a campaign for a "yes" vote, and I believe that if at that time the necessary steps had been taken of explaining to the people of Quebec the character of the war, the people of Quebec would have looked upon the war through different glasses.
When we speak of reinforcements, I suggest that we should stick to the issue of reinforcements and not try to introduce any other questions. I am referring, for instance, to the issue of the conscription of wealth, resources and machines. By introducing these additional phrases, by raising these additional demands we are helping to create doubt in the minds of young people whether or not it pays them to join. We do not need any additional frills. There is a problem before us, the problem of reinforcements, the problem of men -needed for overseas. That, as I understand it, is the issue before the house to-day.
In considering the problem of reinforcements it is necessary that we should look upon Canada as it is and not as we might want it to be. It is unfair to try to compare Canada with Britain or the United States. We have in Canada a two-nation state and it is about time that every member of this house recognized that fact. There are French-Canadian people and English-speaking people in this country and we have to recognize that. It is something which of course does not exist either in the United States or in Great Britain. We have French-Canadian people who have reason to be very suspicious of wars because of what has happened in the past when they were forced to participate in wars that were not among the most popular of conflicts. We have to realize that, but we must also realize that these same people have grievances that have not been corrected. If those problems had been faced I would say that our approach to the problem of reinforcements and conscription would be a different one from what it is to-day.

War Effort-Government Policy
The French-Canadian people and the province of Quebec have been slandered in the past few months as never before. The press in the eight provinces of our country has been carrying on a vicious campaign about Quebec and Quebec zombies. That is all we have heard. Having travelled a bit in Ontario I can appreciate the fact that this terrific unCanadian agitation is bearing fruit. When you meet the average man or woman you hear nothing but insults against Quebec. I would say that campaign is not an accident. It is not a spontaneous campaign. It is an organized campaign. I do not believe in the theory of spontaneity. Things do not happen just by themselves; they are organized. They have been organized in the eight provinces by the leaders of the Progressive Conservative party. It started a few months ago on the issue of family allowances. At that time Premier Drew of Ontario said: "Ontario will not pay for Quebec zombies". Then came a terrific intensification of this sort of thing in which he nearly broke his neck. He then decided to go overseas and to come back with a new issue, the issue of reinforcements. I am not denying the issue of reinforcements, but I do not like how it came to be raised. Premier Drew came back to this country, and at about the same time Major Connie Smythe came back and in a public statement told the country that untrained men were sent to the front. If I understand military law I should think it would have been more proper for the major to take this matter up with the proper authorities than to go into politics, but that was not done. When N.R.M.A. men parade we hear talk of mutiny, but when officers break every rule nobody says anything about mutiny or treason.
When the people of Quebec are attacked- and of course it is always a French-Canadian problem-it is time that we tried to understand that the isolationist feeling of the people of that province is not something that has just happened. It was nurtured. It was nurtured not only by French-Canadian leaders, but by English-Canadian leaders. I am not trying to raise any issue between the two, but let us have the facts. When French-Canadian workers wanted to join a union of fellow workers of other nationalities, Englishspeaking or others, along came big trusts, controlled not by Freneh-Canadians but by English-Canadians-Dominion Textiles is an example; you know the names connected with that firm, Sir Charles Gordon, the late Sir Herbert Holt and others-and told them to join the Catholic syndicates. They were iso-

lated not only from the rest of Canada but from their fellow workers in the same province.
