speechtext:
The companies. Again, the Aluminum company, a new industrial giant, did the same thing. The workers were told that the company preferred to deal with the Catholic syndicates to keep those workers isolated and pay them lower wages. When we look at our province we see the following: If our people's health is not as good as it is in the other provinces, or if their educational levels are not as high we find that an English-Canadian has always held the pursestrings of the province. Let us know the facts. I give those facts not to excuse a single individual who does not join the army, who does not leave the N.R.M.A. ranks and go voluntarily, but to show that poison has been spread throughout the country against the province. That is the work of the same Tory elements who have profited in the past by the isolationism of the people.
The people of our province have had a bigger dose of fascist propaganda than any other people. Here again I am going to make a very serious charge. I was a candidate in the general elections of 1935. I followed the election campaign quite closely. Some literature was distributed at the time by the Conservative party. The heading of the bulletins issued was, "Renaissance Nationale". In eight provinces it was the Conservative party and in Quebec it was the nationalists and the "Renaissance Nationale". These bulletins which were spread around every part of the province were edited by no other than Hitler's aide in Canada, Adrien Arcand. Was that the way to prepare the people of Quebec to be ready to participate in a just war? The Hon. Sam Gobeil, leader of the Conservative party in Quebec, wrote some of the most open pro-Hitler pamphlets written by any politician in this country. These are facts. Nobody can deny them. I am not trying to cover up the weaknesses of the Liberals in our province in helping to create confusion, but I say it is necessary that we know all who have been responsible for the way in which the people of our province think and act.
We have had other fascist materials, of the type of La Nation, one of the worst fascist sheets in our province, edited by a young man named Paul Bouchard, from whose writings I have had occasion to read previously. Paul Bouchard ran in a by-election in

War Effort-Government Policy
Lotbiniere in 1937, at which time his campaign was financed by the leader of the Conservative party, Maurice Dupre. What is more, at a libel trial in connection with some item that appeared in La Nation, Pierre Ohaloult testified that he received support for that vicious sheet of his from none other than the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion), who was at one time linked up with the Conservative party and whose policies, I would say, are just the other side of the Tory, anti-reform policies. I do not care if the new party organized by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay is called les Groupements des Independents; from past experience in our province, and after looking at some of the people in that new movement, I -would say it is exactly the other side of the Conservative party in this country, with one sort of party in Quebec and another sort of party in the other eight provinces.
I am going to give more facts. During the last provincial election campaign Maurice Duplessis issued posters throughout the province showing men coming back to this country on crutches as a result of the Liberal war policy. The same Montreal Gazette which is now so loudly demanding conscription did not mind what was being done by Maurice Duplessis because that served certain interests. I am going to go farther and say that I wonder if the expropriation of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power company had anything to do with contributions from English-speaking Canadians going into the coffers of the Duplessis anti-war machine. I have very little doubt in that regard, and the cime may come when I will give more facts in that connection.
While talking about the sort of confusion being spread among our people due to power politics, by the Tories, I do not want to cover up the faults of the Liberal party. In a pamphlet which I wrote in 1942 I set out what I thought should be done in our province in order to have our people become willing participants in the war. I said:
It is necessary that the government enact measures to remove the grievances of the French-Canadian people in regard to lower wage standards, in regard to the need for rapid training of large sections of workers in war industries to be able to do skilled work, and to help influence a change from the present outmoded and inadequate educational system to a modern and compulsory system; that it remove all inequalities with respect to the French language in the armed forces, set up special French-Canadian units officered by French Canadians and a special French-Canadian military college.
100-418J
While some improvements have been made, many of the statements I made in 1942 still hold good to-day. If these things had been done we would have had French units; we would have had greater numbers of men enlisting voluntarily instead of remaining under the N.R.M.A. While pointing to these weaknesses of the Liberal party and many more criticisms I have heard, I want to say that if there is anything wrong with the Canadian situation or the Quebec situation, surely the Tories cannot remedy it.
Despite such a background and some weaknesses of approach to the French-Canadian people, they have done splendidly in this war, and it is about time we recognized that fact. Who will deny the heroism of Lieutenant-Colonel Triquet? Who will deny the heroism of Colonel Menard? Who will deny the heroism of the French-Canadian units overseas? I have here a book entitled "French Canadian Wings," which gives the names of fifty-one French Canadians who have received -the distinguished flying cross, the air force cross and the distinguished flying medal. On a number of occasions in this house I have also emphasized what Quebec is doing in connection with giving our men the weapons with which to fight to victory. We have done a great deal. Not very long ago General Eisenhower spoke about the need for more and more shells, but somehow in the Canadian press, in the midst of this fight, it became "man-power." I saw the original statement in one of the United States papers, and all that Eisenhower spoke about was the need for more shells with which to pulverize the Siegfried line. On a number of occasions in this house I have pointed out what Quebec is doing in regard to. the production of shells, guns and all those things that make for victory. When our men have plenty of equipment they are more confident in battle. I want to read part of a letter I received from a friend of mine whe has since been reported killed in action. He said:
I have been writing this sitting comfortably in my carrier, taking in some sun, and to the symphony of our artillery giving hell to the jerries. We have lots of artillery that is playing havoc with him. One really has to listen to the ceaseless fire from an endless number of guns to appreciate what it means. There are stories that German prisoners have asked to be shown our "automatic" artillery. . . .
Then he says:
We have complete mastery of the air, planes, planes and more planes. We are well equipped and there are many of us. We have lots of everything-.including guts.
These are the words of a man who has beeD in action, a man who on August 13 of this year was reported killed.

speechtext:
: In France. We of Quebec have helped give our men these weapons. Let me read from the Financial Post about the role of Quebec as a producer of the weapons of war:
Quebec builds four of Canada's nine types of aeroplanes; both types of tanks, all our aerial bombs. The province has the largest plant in the British commonwealth completely producing 25-pounder guns from the scrap pile to the finished products, two of the largest shell-filling plants and two great small arms ammunition plants. Some half dozen shipyards are producing cargo vessels, corvettes, mine sweepers and torpedo boats. Most of the boots worn by the Canadian armed forces are made in Quebec. A large part of the uniforms are also made in the province. In addition Quebec turns out parachutes, shells, cartridge cases, trench mortars, trench mortar bombs, and a large part of Canada's chemical and explosives output, electrical and radio equipment, fuses and primers. The province has the largest aluminum 6melter in the world.
And the men and women of our province are toiling daily, not always under the finest conditions; but they do not kick. We have had very few strikes in Quebec. The people have been happy to produce these things, in order to make sure that our men have as much amuni-tion as they need.
I want to emphasize that the conditions under which they work are difficult. Only last week, while I was in Montreal, a woman came to see me. She told me she had been working on the Mosquito aircraft. The exposed parts of her body were covered with a rash, which followed as a result of her work. That was not very pleasant. But those people keep on working. Many more like her suffer similarly as a result of these new types of work. And all this is done, Mr. Speaker, by those people who are being insulted by elements that are trying to play politics.
Let me return to the question in connection with the shortage of shells. Since I came to the house I have always insisted that we should have more rather than less of everything; that we should plan to have a surplus, rather than that our men should run short. In connection with shells I said this on June 13, in the discussion on Mutual Aid.
Why the reduction at this time? When men of the united nations are involved in the hardest of battles why should we at this time decide that this reduction is justifiable? Materials will be expected at a great rate and we should have no illusions. At Cassino we learned that planes were good but that we need more and more guns and shells. We learned at Sicily that we need a lot of automotive equipment. It is better to have more than less.
That was the attitude I took in June. Of course there is only one misfortune, namely, that Canada sometimes takes pointers from some of the other powers as to what we should produce. We do not have all the

say; but I believe we would have even less if the Tories were in power. They would follow the dictates of London without a murmur. I would say that at least we have tried to speak up much more as an independent country.
One thing further: in attacking Quebec people say that that province has given a smaller share of recruits, that they have not given enough. I would again refresh the minds of some hon. members in respect of something I said when we were discussing the estimates of the Department of Labour. These were my words:
This house has become practically a missing persons' bureau with people wanting to find out exactly how many have not reported for military service. It has become a battle over figures. I hol'd no brief for men who do not report for army service, but I rather detect an attempt to slur the province of Quebec.
Of course this process of slurring Quebec has been intensified since that time. Then I continued:
Apparently very few hon. members of this house took any notice of the figures in regard to the number of men in the province of Quebec who are not fit for military service. In the city of Montreal only thirty per cent of the men were in category A, while in Toronto the figure was 49-6.
I appeal to all hon. members to try to understand these facts. People in Quebec are victims of certain conditions for which, to a great extent, English-speaking Canadians are responsible.
While giving all these facts, I do not wish for one minute to have anyone get the idea that we do not need the reinforcements. We do need them. Our men deserve to have a rest, and they deserve to have those reinforcements as soon as possible. The only problem is: should we at this stage of the war, when leaders of the united nations who should know more than we do about these matters have said that this is the last lap of the war in Europe, create the worst possible spirit of disunity in an effort to get those reinforcements? Should we not try to get them in the best possible manner?
I like the methods used by the Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaPleche), who has gone out to get French Canadians to volunteer, much better than those of hon. members who sit here and attack, attack, attack, every attempt to induce such men to come forward as volunteers. Much more would have been achieved if we had taken seriously the appeal for volunteers. Those 16,000 would have come forward if some had not played politics. Has politics been played? Let us see. An appeal was made after General
NOVEMBER 29, 1944	6657
War Effort-Government Policy
McNaughton took over the job. The answer was immediately one of insults against a great man, against a general.
I now turn to a quotation from the Windsor Star of November 7, which tells the following story:
"General A. G. L. McNaughton's appeal to war veterans to support him in getting the younger generation to take up this 'honourable obligation' and volunteer for active service is so outrageous that I can hardly speak about it", Major Everett Bristol, past dominion commander of the Canadian Legion said yesterday; "Veterans are not going to lend themselves to such an ignoble task."
That is the way they regard the process of having people come forward as volunteers- an "ignoble task". They were not interested in reinforcements. They were interested in bringing down the government, and in having an election so that they could ride to power, not for the good of the men who have gone overseas, but so that they could bring us back to the old iron-heel Bennett days. This was the answer of some of the people who are inspired by the Tories. And there was a similar response from Tories throughout the country-nothing but insults.
We had a reflection of it in the house the other day. I would say that last Thursday was one of my saddest days in this chamber, when men in it treated a great general as if he were a traitor.

speechtext: And a culprit and a criminal.

speechtext:
Yes, and a culprit and a criminal. I said to myself, "How would they treat a simple worker?" I know how they would treat him. But how many people are there who do know? This is the way they have treated the architect of our army, a man who kept up the morale of our men during a long period of inactivity, and kept it at the highest pitch. I was told, in letters, that when the men heard General McNaughton was coming to visit a unit they were always happy to see their father. It was General McNaughton who, in those dark days, came forward with the slogan that the Canadian troops were a dagger pointed at the heart of Berlin. How encouraging that was to all of usl It was he who, through Dieppe, was able to give the united nations those lessons which saved hundreds of thousands of lives. It was he who, after Dieppe, when some of the great, so-called military specialists were saying that it would take millions of casualties to invade the coast, said, "If we had gone there to stay, we could have made it stick." I may be wrong in this, but I have read in the press that it was also he who advocated that we ought not to
split the army, and that we should have one powerful Canadian unit to go into action. If his advice had been taken, maybe we would not be faced to-day with the reinforcement crisis.
We need reinforcements. We now have the new order in council which will give us 16,000 men. I think everybody should be satisfied; that is, if he really wants reinforcements and does not want to force an election on the conscription issue. We all want to see our men reinforced and provided with the necessary equipment in this final stage of the war. We are the only country where such a crisis exists at this time. This does not help morale; it simply tears it down. That is why I and my party will support this order in council and work for its success.
I did' not act like some hon. members. Over the week-end I spoke at one time to about 2,500 people, and then on Sunday afternoon I went up to speak in the French-Canadian part of Montreal. I told those people that if they had friends or relatives in the N.R.M.A. they should tell them to volunteer. We want a solution that will give us a united Canada to-day and a united Canada during the post-war period, not a solution that will force a conscription election and rip our country apart and maybe keep it apart for another twenty-five years.
The only ones who would gain from such ' an election would be those whose interest it is to keep us apart. Whenever the English and French people have stood together, all the people benefited; whenever they have been torn apart, every one has suffered with the exception of those who wanted them to be torn apart. There must be greater national unity if our men are to get needed reinforcements, and if the people of Canada are to achieve security and peace in the post-war period.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
I was saying that when I came home from overseas I reported to the Prime Minister and to my other colleagues in the war committee and the cabinet that we needed an additional 15,000 trained infantry as reinforcements overseas as quickly as We could get them there. That immediate need still exists. That is the issue to which I intended to direct exclusively any remarks I had to make. I shall not forget it, and I shall not let the house forget it.
In his address the Prime Minister devoted considerable attention to my humble self. I know I am only a very minor incident in connection with this discussion, but I feel that these matters-which were quite extraneous, and added nothing, I thought, to assist the house in coming to a conclusion on the paramount question-ought to be dealt with, because the Prime Minister, by bringing them up, must have thought that they would in some way influence the vote of some hon. members. I do not think so myself, but I may be wrong. I feel, therefore, that hon. members should have what I can give them about the facts as I know them. I will mention, then, those points first, not because they come first in order of importance, but just to get them out of the way so that we shall not stumble over them in seeking the path to be taken on the main question. Please do not think for an instant that I am going to be deflected by them.
One of the points the Prime Minister mentioned was the matter of council secrecy, and he suggested that all he was saying was based on the fact that the member for Prince had in a public declaration made some statements with regard to what had taken place in

council, and said he felt that he would have to deal with the same matters from his own point of view. Let me say to you, Mr. Speaker, that what I said in my public statement on November 12 was as the result of what the Prime Minister had said in his radio broadcast on November 8 with regard to matters which had taken place in council. In other words, his statement, his disclosures, did not follow mine; mine followed his.
I am not going to take very much time except just to refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the speech made by the Prime Minister on November 8 to indicate to you that the Prime Minister felt it was permissible in a public speech to refer to what had taken place in council; and, as I told him in the letter which I wrote to him on November 14:
Regarding privy council secrecy, I feel I ought to point out that your own speech of November 8 contains references to matters treated, debated and resolved in council discussion, and I am sure these references would not have been made had you not considered that they were permissible.
Now, as regards those references in the Prime Minister's speech to which I will refer, I am finding no fault with him, but I ask him and I ask the house to find no fault with me if I dealt in my statement of November 12 with the same matters that the Prime Minister had already dealt with in his radio speech of November 8-matters which took place in council. I have here the pamphlet of his speech of November 8, and on page 5 I quote:
Colonel Ralston's report to the government-
That must have been a report to council.
-disclosed an immediate problem which had to be faced.
That certainly is giving the contents in a negative way of a report to council.
That problem

That is, the problem which Colonel Ralston had reported.
-is to find the means of speeding up the flow of fully trained infantry reinforcements-
That must all have been in the report.
-to meet, not an actual shortage-
Which would indicate that the report had indicated that there was no actual shortage.

of reinforcements now but a possible shortage in the next few months.
Now that in brief immediately puts on the public record what the Prime Minister says that Mr. Ralston reported to council, and I submit-and I had no difficulty in coming to a conclusion-that if it were permissible for the Prime Minister to publish that summary to the public, it was equally permissible for
NOVEMBER 29, 1944	6659
War Effort-Government Policy
Mr. Ralston to publish what he did say to council in connection with these very matters; otherwise it would mean that someone would state that So-and-so did not say so-and-so in council, and the other man would be barred absolutely from contradicting it because of council secrecy. A statement of the negative is just as much a statement of what took place in council as a statement of the positive. If there is a statement that Mr. Ralston disclosed, not an actual shortage of reinforcements, an opportunity must be given for the man whose statement is referred to to say what he did say. Also, the term "possible shortage in the next few months" gives, I should think, the individual referred to an opportunity to say what he did say about that.
On page 6 I read:
Colonel Ralston had grave doubts of our ability to keep up the flow of reinforcements in the next few months by voluntary means.
Where was that said-in public or in council? That is a statement of what took place in council.
He considered therefore-
And this must have been in council.
-that he had no alternative but to recommend that draftees should be sent overseas as reinforcements.
I am skipping a part of the paragraph.
Days of anxious deliberation were devoted to an exploration of all possible alternatives.
All that must have taken place in council. Then he goes on:
The recommendation made by Colonel Ralston was not accepted.
Which of course was in council. Then on page 7 I quote again:
Let me give you some facts and figures which were before the government in reaching its decision.
Then the Prime Minister proceeds to give to the public what he says are the facts and figures which were before the government in its deliberations. Those are all matters which were "treated, debated and resolved" in council. and those were all made public by the Prime Minister to the public of Canada. I do not think one can be reprimanded for dealing with the same matters and giving one's own version of what took place.
I have not much more to say on that because I shall be dealing with the matters to which the Prime Minister referred in his address, but the two things that struck me as needing correction were, first, the statement in effect that Mr. Ralston had reported that there was no actual shortage of reinforcements and, second, the statement that Mr. Ralston
had reported that there was a possible shortage of reinforcements in the next few months. Both those statements, I felt, left an impression which was not in accordance with what I had stated. With regard to the matter of an actual shortage at the time, I have indicated to the public, as I indicated to my colleagues, that there was an actual shortage, that the reinforcement pools were down very much, if not wholly depleted. You cannot say that there is not a shortage simply because you may have fifty men on one side of the ledger or the other, so far as the strength of units is concerned, because in both theatres of war they are supposed to maintain pools, and the situation which I reported was a short-term position in November which showed that they were nothing more than just about square in actual unit strengths with nothing for the pools, while the situation in December showed that, taking all the men who would be available in the reinforcement pools and everywhere else, trained men in the United Kingdom and in both battle areas, and adding them all together, there would still be a considerable shortage before you could fill up the strength of the units, without allowing anything at all for the pools. It seemed to me that was a situation which indicated an actual shortage of reinforcements, and second, indicated that the "possible shortage in the next few months" was really a "probable shortage at the end of December." These were the two points that I made in the statement which I issued to the press; and I make no apologies to the house or to my former colleagues in the cabinet for having done that in view of the fact that the Prime Minister attempted to epitomize my report to council in that short paragraph to which I have referred. In other words, Mr. Speaker, I think in this debate so far and especially in the Prime Minister's speech the other night the doors of the privy council have been pretty well opened and there is not very much that has taken place there, which one recollects, that has not been revealed to the house and to the public. What I wish to say is this: that what is all right for the Prime Minister of Canada, I am sure he will admit, ought to be quite all right for a humble ex-minister.

subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: All right for Canada, too.

subtopic: TOLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
One of the other points is the matter which was mentioned in the Prime Minister's speech and which was contained in his correspondence, namely, the fact that there had not been sufficient notice to the cabinet or to the war committee of the reinforcement situation and of the likelihood of N.R.M.A. men being required. I am dealing with this

War Effort-Government Policy
now as an extraneous point because I do not think it has anything to do with the debate. In the first place and in the last place I submit that it is wholly irrelevant to the question which this house is called on to decide. The question is whether or not troops for reinforcements are going to be sent. If there was something wrong, something reprehensible, if there was bad faith on the part of the minister, that is a thing for which he should incur the odium and the opprobrium which come from it. But to say that has anything to do with the debate and should be introduced here is, I think, wholly wrong. But I do wish to say that in connection with some of the statements made the Prime Minister is not quite accurate and I should like to correct them in justice to the officers and in justice to myself. He said that there was nothing before the cabinet or the war committee at any time up to August of this year, suggesting that there would be any further need for reinforcements overseas. I think I have quoted him correctly. Well, Mr. Speaker, Hansard, which I have in my hand, gives it differently from the way I took it down and perhaps I am wrong about this. I thought the Prime Minister said that the cabinet had nothing at any time up to August of this year suggesting that there would be any need for further reinforcements. I see that Hansard at page 6597 says:
As far as the government is concerned, there was nothing before it at any time up to October of this year which suggested that there would be any need for conscription to provide further reinforcements overseas.
I think the Prime Minister is wrong about that. In June I brought to the attention of the war committee advice which had been received from the chief of staff that further forecasts had been made into 1945 and that they would indicate the necessity for a heavier call on reinforcements. He did consider that we were all right up to October, but he pointed out that the question would arise as to whether we would have to break up a formation or send N.R.M.A. men over. He considered that we could await developments of the war before reaching a decision, and he suggested additional efforts, mentioning infantry particularly. Then steps were taken by the three defence ministers to arrange so that air force and navy recruiting would be slowed down for the benefit of the army. That was in June, 1944, and the Prime Minister suggests that so far as the government is concerned there was nothing before it with regard to the need for conscription, no suggestion that there would be any need for conscription to provide further reinforcements up to October. The Prime Minister has forgotten that telegram. I think I mentioned it at another session.

He said we received direct assurance on August 3 that there was no need for considering the question of additional reinforcements for service overseas by compulsion. I think those are his exact words. Yes; at page 6598 of Hansard the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
The government was given the most direct assurance at that time by the chief of staff, with the Minister of National Defence present, that there was no need for considering the question of additional reinforcements for overseas by compulsion.
All I can say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Prime Minister is that I have quite a distinct recollection of that meeting, and I myself-and I can only give my word for it- am satisfied that the reference to reinforcements by compulsion was not used in any way on that occasion. My memory is just as fallible as anybody else's, but I am quite satisfied1-and I have made some inquiries about it -that the Prime Minister is mistaken in connection with that, and that there was no discussion at that meeting with regard to reinforcements for overseas by compulsion. There was a proposal at that meeting to constitute an infantry brigade by combining certain existing units in Italy; that is to say, they were existing units and it was proposed to put them into a brigade instead of having them operate as they were operating at that time separately or within other formations. The proposal involved something under six hundred additional, and it might involve up to March, 1945, something like nine hundred additional reinforcements. It is quite true that the chief of staff in making that recommendation and in making his recommendations to the war committee that day did report the over-all reinforcement position as entirely satisfactory. I am sure that he did so in the very best of faith. The Prime Minister has been good enough to acknowledge that, because at page 6600 of Hansard he says:
Along with the rest of my colleagues I have accepted these representations in the best of faith, just as, I believe, they were given in the best of faith.
I want to stop here to say that I inquired about the formation of that brigade when I was in Italy, and the corps commander there assured me that the casualties suffered by that brigade operating as infantry had been no higher than the casualties which had been estimated for them when they had been operating as separate units.
The chief of staff at that time indicated that the only part of the reinforcement problem which concerned him at the moment was reinforcements for the French-speaking infantry battalions; and the chief of staff's explanation, both to the Prime Minister and to the

War Effort-Government Policy
war committee and myself since that time is that the unexpectedly high proportion of infantry casualties which have occurred threw his calculations and expectations out and that the fact that this high proportion continued so long rendered it impossible for him to reestablish the pools by remustering from other arms. I wish to say this for the chief of staff at Canadian military headquarters, General Stuart; I know of no officer in the Canadian army with a finer reputation or who has more loyally, more faithfully and more efficiently carried on his duties. He has recognized what the policy of this country was. He has endeavoured to carry it out to the very best of his ability. He has remustered men; he has seen that N.R.MA. men were put in the place of general service personnel; he has pulled general service personnel out of every position from which they could possibly be spared, and replaced them with either low category men or men of the N.R.M.A., and generally he has endeavoured to make the voluntary system work to the very limit. He was in charge in England at the time, in August. He had to be vested with that responsibility there. He accepted that responsibility and in my judgment made the very best contribution that an officer could make to meet that situation over there. It was absolutely essential that the administration be left in his hands and in the hands of Canadian military headquarters. It could not be done from here. I know General Stuart feels that if he had to do over again what he has done in the last year, in endeavouring to maintain Canada's army and generally in connection with the administration of Canadian military headquarters, he would do exactly the same thing.
The Prime Minister also mentioned the Quebec conference and suggested that some notice should have been given at that time if there was an apprehension with regard to the reinforcement situation. I point out first that the Quebec conference had not the faintest thing to do with the battles going on in Europe. The Quebec conference was a meeting between the representatives of the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada with respect to Pacific operations. I have examined the minutes of the war committee and there is not a reference-except one that has anything to do with Europe. That concerns Italy, and it has no reference to reinforcements or to anything which would affect reinforcements. There is no reference whatever to any thing or any subject which was brought up which would give an opportunity or afford a place for the discussion of reinforcements if an apprehension existed. As a matter of fact, of course, reinforcements would be a domestic matter which would be discussed at meetings of the war committee. We held meetings of the war committee every week, and that was the place to discuss the matter of reinforcements or anything else which had t*o do with the Canadian army.
So much for the Quebec conference. At the same time, however, I had a report that the Prime Minister had made some statement which I felt might indicate some change of policy with regard to N.R.M.A. men. This is mentioned in the correspondence, so that I am not disclosing anything I should not. I went to the Prime Minister at Quebec with regard to that very matter, because I have always been insistent that the N.R.M.A. men should be held as potential reserves; and I was assured by the Prime Minister at that time that what he had stated in 1942 still stood with regard to N.R.M.A. men and the possibility of their being used as potential reinforcements. I mention that to indicate that perhaps I have been a nuisance more than anything else in connection with this matter, mentioning it so frequently, but certainly if there has been any red light to hold out I have endeavoured to hold it out. In September, after the conference, a situation did develop which gave me concern. A report came from overseas as to the number of infantry reinforcements on hand. I was disturbed by it. I made calculations with regard to how many would be in Italy and how many would be in the United Kingdom. I should pause here to say that we in Canada do not keep the records of the pools in the United Kingdom and Italy. Those are dealt with in the United Kingdom, because they are close to the battle line; they know, what the needs are; they know what the forecast of activity is, and they are the ones best able to judge what dispatches should be made to Italy and what dispatches should be made to the United Kingdom. I endeavoured to make a calculation, and I took that calculation with me when I went to Italy.
As I say, a situation did develop in September, after the Quebec conference, as I was advised by the then adjutant general. I did not withhold that from my colleagues. I was at the war committee, I think the day before I left for the United Kingdom, and at that meeting of that committee there was a discussion about the N.R.M.A. men. I advised them there that on account of our heavy infantry casualties I could not consent to the release of any trained N.R.M.A. men,



War Effort-Government Policy
that they must be maintained in order to provide against the uncertainties then existing on account of that report.

speechtext: On what date in September?

subtopic: TOLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
That was September 22, I think; and a day or two before that at a meeting of the cabinet I believe the matter did come up incidental to some other matter which had been mentioned there. Those are the matters to which I refer, and they indicate that the situation was not altogether unmentioned to the cabinet, although I admit quite frankly that had the situation been as I discovered since, and as I reported it to the cabinet after I came back, certainly I would have reported it at once. All I can say is that the fact that I did not know it and did not report it sooner means that I did not sooner recommend the action that I did. I would have done it just that much quicker had I known what was the situation.
I want to say that there was a telegram which came to me in August and which I did not bring to the attention of the cabinet. It is my own fault. I brought it to the attention of the cabinet when it came to my attention the second time. It was a telegram which advised that there was a serious shortage in the strength of the infantry units and that remustering was rapidly going on. It indicated that two-thirds of the shortage would be made up in six days, I think it was, and the balance in about two weeks, and asked me to authorize the use of general duty infantry tradesmen for the purpose of helping to clear up the situation on account of these heavy casualties. If I remember correctly it was a Sunday morning, and I simply initialled the telegram and handed it back to the chief of the general staff. The telegram concluded by stating that everything would be all right in three weeks. As a matter of fact, if I had known as much then as I know now I would have realized that this meant it would be unlikely that the pools would be built up, although if it had come to my mind at all I would have thought that the men who were being trained in England would be coming in again in three weeks, and that this was simply a situation to be tided over at that time. I say quite frankly that I did not tell the cabinet about it. There was no possible reason for my withholding it, but I want to mention all these matters so that the house may have no doubt as to the exact position. I did bring it to the attention of the cabinet when it was brought to my attention again, but

that was after I had come back. As a matter
of fact, I brought it to the attention of the cabinet when I asked for approval of the paying of the infantry tradesmen.
I want to say that the department has carried its own load in connection with the administration of the army, as every department has to do. The department has tried to solve its own problems. I have hung out the red light whenever I thought it was necessary, and I think some people have an idea that I have been almost too anxious to hold out the red light sometimes, that perhaps I have cried "wolf, wolf," when there was no wolf. Nevertheless I have consistently maintained the position, as the Prime Minister was good enough to say the other night, that I could not undertake that the Canadian army would be always wholly reinforced by volunteers, but that the time might come when N.R.M.A. men would be utilized. I have not hesitated to say that in this house time after time, I think in the minds of some people almost ad nauseam, because I wanted it distinctly understood that this was what I was banking on. The Prime Minister has been good enough to indicate that; and I feel that he and my former colleagues will accept my assurance that I have not withheld anything from them which I considered required attention from the cabinet or the war committee. As soon as I was really concerned about this matter I told them promptly. I cut a trip which would have taken six or seven weeks, at least, down to three and a half weeks. When I got back to London from the continent I stayed only three days, in order that I might come home immediately. On October 13 I wired the Prime Minister to let him know I was coming, having left Canada only on September 23, and asking if I might have an opportunity of meeting my cabinet colleagues at once, indicating to him generally what was the nature of the trouble. I say it is all very well to be wise after the event. Rut I can only say that if I had had hindsight I would have recommended this action just that much earlier. After having said all that, I am coming back to this-and hon. members may wonder why I am dealing with it so fully. I did not expect the Prime Minister would have made so much of it himself. But the Prime Minister took time the other night- and quite a bit of it-to impress upon the house the fact that the cabinet had not known about this matter, and made a very positive statement about it. I believe in justice to myself and in justice to my officers I at least ought to make an explanation about it, even though it is a matter which is irrelevant.

War Effort-Government Policy
I understand the point the Prime Minister was making was that it came as a great shock, and it took the cabinet longer to consider it. I am only pointing out that at least a month before I had mentioned it to the war committee, directly, I had indicated that there were heavier infantry casualties, and that in view of the uncertainty of the situation these men might be needed. I had gone over and I had found that uncertainty had become a reality.
I think all hon. members will remember what I have said in the house from time to time. I have stood in my place and defended the voluntary system. I have worked just as hard as I possibly could to support it. I started out in 1942 at the time of the plebiscite, speaking about it. As a matter of fact, before that one hon. member on the other side mentioned it just on the eve of a recruiting campaign, and I think I was the first man on this side of the house to stand up and take a member in this house to task for having advocated conscription in the earlier days of the war.

I have ever since defended the voluntary system. I wish to say that if in fact the voluntary system has failed, as I leel it has failed, so far as being a dependable source for infantry reinforcements at least- and do not understand me to say that it has failed entirely, but failed to be a dependable source for infantry reinforcements for the army at this stage of the war, and having regard to what is ahead of us-that does not make me take back what I have said with regard to the desirability of having a voluntary army, if we could have one. The very fact that over 500,000 men have enlisted voluntarily in the Canadian army, and that in these there are 42,000 N.R.M.A. men is some indication someone has done some work in connection with the matter. Then of course, as someone has reminded me, there are enlistments in the navy and the air force. The air force is something in the neighbourhood of 200,000, and the navy about 75,000.
This is not the main issue in this matter- the matter of notice to the cabinet. But it did come as a shock to the Prime Minister, and I can understand that, with the many things he has to consider. Those who are running the departments have these matters laid on our shoulders, and we endeavour to carry them. I wish to say to you that it came as a shock to me, too, when I went to the battle areas. And when I came back to
100-419J
C.M.H.Q. and went over the figures there with the officers, and found what I believed was a situation requiring radical measures, I came home and so reported. So much for the reference the Prime Minister has made to what I said to the cabinet.
I wish now to mention a matter which gave me some real concern. The Prime Minister in his statement-I really do not know why he did it; I am at a loss, frankly, to understand it, because it is not like him-said:
I took great care to ask one colleague after the other would he take the responsibility that was mine. I asked the minister of defence himself, would he take the responsibility of heading the government and nutting through this particular measure? I was told by him that he would not. It is very easy, may I say, to oppose a position hitherto assumed by a government and to propose new measures, but unless men are prepared to back their policies by taking responsibility for their enactment and carrying them out, they have no right, if members of a ministry, to leave a ministry in circumstances where as a consequence of their action the whole structure is almost certain to collapse.
That is the strangest doctrine I have ever heard enunciated in this house. If I were not respectful of the Prime Minister I would call it just plain nonsense; I will call it rhetoric, instead. I do not think anybody could imagine what the effect of a policy of that kind would be. In the first place if there was any impression that the Prime Minister asked all his colleagues, since he has told what took place let me say that he asked three colleagues. He did not ask any more. I do not know whether the fact that-

speechtext:
I wish to say this, that I am going into this matter because in reading the castigation by the Prime Minister of Canada what does he say? He says:
It .is very easy, may I say, to oppose a position hitherto assumed by a government and to propose new measures, but unless men are prepared to back their policies by taking responsibility for their enactments and carrying them out, they have no right, if members of a ministry, to leave a ministry in circumstances where as a consequence of their action the whole structure is almost certain to collapse.
Let us see what the situation was? Was anybody, opposing a position hitherto taken by the government? I was proposing to carry out the policy of the government, which tfas the policy of sending N.R.M.A. men, if necessary. I was not opposing any position which had hitherto been taken by the government.
Then the other suggestion is that I was proposing a new measure, a measure which had not been proposed or had not been contemplated by the government. I was not proposing ahy new measure. I was proposing a measure which had been forecast by the Prime Minister himself in 1942. It was a measure stating that conscription should be imposed, if necessary. WThen the Prime Minister of Canada rises in his place and takes me to task for having indicated that I would have to resign if the policy were not carried out, I submit he is taking a position which is absolutely untenable. It simply means that if a man proposes to carry out the policy of the government and his colleagues do not agree he must stay in the government or else be prepared to accept the prime ministership of Canada. I say that that position is a position

which cannot be upheld or supported. It means that a man joining the government enters into an obligation that once there he has to stay, no matter what policies are adopted, even though it means repudiating his own convictions and pledges. The only way he can get out is to agree to Accept the prime ministership and1 form and lead another government.
I am speaking strongly about this because there is not very much in the Prime Minister's speech to which I have any objection. He puts his point of view and that is all right. But it is something else again when the Prime Minister in a casual conversation makes a quick interjection at a cabinet meeting and asks somebody whether he will accept the prime ministership and then rises in his place on the floor of this house and says that a man should not be left in the cabinet because he did not accept that invitation, because he did not say, "yes." I submit that is doing that member an injustice with regard to which I think he has a right to defend himself.
