speechtext:
The Prime Minister can make his own statement with regard to what took place at other meetings of the cabinet. I am discussing the meeting of the cabinet, the procedure of which the Prime Minister disclosed. I am not discussing any other meetings of the cabinet.
I say that that proposition is not a proposition which can be upheld. I want to say further that I am complaining now of the Prime Minister having brought this up, having held this against me and having told the people of Canada that I was derelict in my duty because, having made a statement to this house and having undertaken a certain policy which I believed was the policy of the government and although my colleagues would not agree I must stay in the cabinet unless I was willing to take the responsibility of forming a government on a casual invitation such as I have described.
I want to say that if the proposition were that a man had to stay in the government or ' else be prepared to form a government and lead a party it would be a serious deterrent to men undertaking cabinet responsibilities. It means that cabinet marriage is till death or defeat or acceptance of the prime ministership
NOVEMBER 29, 1944	6665
War Effort-Government Policy
doth us part. That would be the individual's position. On the other hand, the Prime Minister could cut the knot at any time and transfer his affections elsewhere.
I am speaking with regard to my own position. Mr. Speaker, the matter of assuming further responsibilities is for the individual man according to his own conscience or his own sense of his own capabilities and shortcomings. It is not a matter of a rule to be laid down by the Prime Minister or to be dictated by anybody else. I undertook the task of Minister of National Defence at the request of the Prime Minister on the tragic death of my friend, the late Norman Rogers.
I have carried on the job and given my best to it. Whether I have succeeded, history will have to judge. I confess that I should have liked to finish the task, but that has not been possible.
I know a few of my own weaknesses. One of the many perhaps is that I am not flexible enough. I was born that way. I am too old to change. I have not any ambition but to be a good Canadian, and I know my place is not on the dizzy heights of leadership but in the more humble valleys working with my fellow citizens. I have no inclination, much less aspiration for preferment in public life, and such modest services as I have given have been from a feeling of duty and a hope that I am contributing something, within my capacity, to this land of ours. I neither felt nor feel any duty to take on responsibility for which I am convinced I am not suited.
I am saying this in case there is any more answer needed to the Prime Minister's snap invitation. I have dealt with it in that way.
I have been serious about it, because, as I said a moment ago, I felt that as a colleague I was entitled to something better than that from the Prime Minister in view of all that has taken place between us. I understand, of course, that he had his tremendous difficulties, but I had mine.
The situation which I had been facing in the last two months meant the most serious and vital decision of my whole public life. If I may be quite frank about it, when I did make this recommendation I foresaw that there would be resentment from my friends, that there would be a good deal of, shall I say chortling or at least some satisfaction on the part of my political opponents. Worst of all, I would not have the opportunity of finishing the job which I had taken on. But I had to make that decision, and I am saying , that in the presence of the Prime Minister to let him know, as I know he does know, that I have had some difficulties as well as he.
When I left the cabinet it was not with any sense of any dereliction of duty, or that I would have to stay and form a ministry. It was made quite clear to me that the place for me was not inside, but outside the cabinet.
I do not think I am going to take much of the time of the house with the matter of the resignation. The Prime Minister has dealt with it at some length himself. It was all dealt with in the correspondence. It has been gone into thoroughly, but there is one impression which the Prime Minister left which I should like to clear up. The impression which I gathered was that he indicated that the difficulty between us and the point on which we parted was a question as to the time limit which should be given for the appeal which was proposed to be made in connection with N.R.M.A. recruiting.
I mention this only for the purpose of clearing this up once and for all if I can. It is quite clear from the correspondence that that was not the issue on which I felt I had to leave the cabinet. The basis of my resignation was the refusal to accept my recommendation. I have no complaint about that, since the cabinet had a perfect right to refuse it. When the question of making an appeal came up I put before my colleagues two points; one was a practical one, namely, the practicability of the appeal and the delay which would follow and the likelihood of success. The other point concerned the policy. We discussed the matter for some time. I do not need to go into the details here because I shall go into them later on in connection with another point.
We discussed the matter of the appeal for some time. I pointed' out the necessity of having these men at once. The time which would be taken in making an appeal; the experience which we had had in the past; the fact that an appeal was nothing new, that the department had been constantly making appeals to N.R.M.A. men; the fact that when you enlisted an N.R.M.A. man you could not be sure that he would be a trained infantry man, he might be a gunner, an army service corps man or something else; the fact that the man might not be physically fit-all these things had to be taken into consideration. It made for uncertainty and delay which was extremely dangerous from, my point of view having regard to the urgent need which I knew existed.
We had made arrangements in the hope that the recommendation would be accepted in time for a sailing on November 27, but that necessitated the taking of some preliminary action by way of medical examinations on November 1. I pointed out that if that were delayed it meant a delay of another
War Effort-Government Policy

month. Well, we discussed that matter; the appeal was still pressed, and I asked for overnight to. consider that matter. Then I wanted to know, where do you go from there? Supposing the appeal is made, what is the policy of the government? Is the policy of the government that if the appeal is made, and fails; in other words, if there are not sufficient general service men to send the number, 15,000. I had asked for, is it the policy of the government that N.R.M.A. men be sent? And I could get no assurance on that point at all.
Further than that, I found that the government as a whole, certain colleagues excepted, did not consider that the government was bound to that policy by the Prime Minister's speech in 1942. The Prime Minister interjected there, I think, or indicated that it was all a matter of the heart that a man put into it, that that was really what was the important thing, that he had been consulting General McNaughton and that General McNaughton felt that he could get these men by voluntary means, and he mentioned something about a previous resignation of two years ago which had not yet been withdrawn. I rather got the impression that he thought he might accept that, but he did not say so in so many words and went on to speak of General McNaughton again and that he was willing to take on and that he thought he should be invited to do so. Of course I promptly indicated to him that I would send him my resignation at once.
That is the conclusion of the story of the resignation, and I hope that the matter will not be rehashed again, because it is not at all important. I am out of the government, as far as that goes. I have been allowed to serve this country-and I thank the Prime Minister publicly for it, as I did in my letter of resignation-at perhaps the most serious and crucial time in her history. I have appreciated that. I have appreciated the associations that I have made. I have no regrets whatever. To me it seems that the matter of my resignation or the exact circumstances of it are neither here nor there, but that also seems to have had to be discussed all over again the other night, along with these other side issues I have referred to. What I thought was much more important was the question of the need of these men and how they should be sent.
These are the matters, although they are really outside the general issue, to which the Prime Minister referred and to which I felt I had to refer.

I wish now to refer to a statement which the Prime Minister made again the other night m connection with this matter of shortage. I want to correct it, because I am afraid the house and perhaps the country may get the idea that there is no shortage until the end of the year. As reported at page 6599 of Hansard, he said:
I want to make clear that the minister assured us that, as far as the records showed, the probability was that a critical situation would not arise until the beginning of the new year, but that he thought it might become acute at that time.
I am afraid that I have again to take issue with the Prime Minister. I was more concerned than anything else about the immediacy and urgency of the shortage. I remembered the discussions which had taken place and the statements which had been made. I recall the discussions which took place in cabinet. I presume that it is my fault that I did not make it clear, but I do remember some of the discussions, and there is no doubt in my mind but that I made it clear beyond per-adventure that an actual shortage existed owing to the fact that the pools were down and that we were just on the thin edge. I remember having pointed out that there was a short term as well as a long term problem. I remember that it was said, "Well, we are doing pretty well if we keep them up to strength." I explained the pools and why they were formed. I remember that the chief of staff's own memorandum mentioned that the 15,000 were wanted for an infantry pool. I remember that he also mentioned the fact that he wanted to send to Italy so many men for the purpose of forming a pool there, and so many men to France. I remember that I took occasion on almost the last day to read to council a memorandum from the present adjutant general on the necessity for maintaining pools, and I endeavoured to impress on everybody concerned that there was at present an actual immediate need to build up the pools, not just a probable "critical situation which would not arise until the beginning of the new year." The point was that we could not meet the need immediately because we could not get those men over soon enough, but if we took prompt steps it would reassure our men and our commanders.
With regard to the Prime Minister's statement that there was a possible shortage in the next few months, I have already indicated that a probable considerable shortage was ahead in December and that it was getting worse every month from then until May. I pointed out that the units would be down in strength, not

War Effort-Government Policy
in the next few months but in the next eight weeks, and that the units went down further each month.
I submit that the statement by the Prime Minister on Monday gives an entirely wrong impression. What we have to show to this house and to this country in order to get support for the sending of these men is, not what the situation is if we get the 16,000, but what the situation will be if we do not get them. That is what I had been endeavouring to show to the Prime Minister and to council and, so far as I could, in the statement I made to the press in correction of the Prime Minister's statement, and that is what I want to refer to now, in order to come to what is really -the heart of the matter, namely, the situation with regard to our need.
Here are some of the conditions which make these men necessary. First, the reserves or the pools of trained infantry reinforcements which had been established overseas have been almost if not entirely depleted to the point of exhaustion. Additional infantry reinforcements are needed at once to reestablish them. Second, the forecasts show that we are sailing so close to the wind that it would appear that by the end of January not only shall we be without reserves, but our infantry units themselves will be in the aggregate slightly under strength. When I left the cabinet the figures showed that there would be a considerable shortage by the end of December; I mean a shortage in the strength of the units themselves, with no pools whatever. I referred to this in my public statement of November 12. I understand that since that time the estimates of casualties have been revised downward and the departure of certain detachments being remustered in the United Kingdom has been hastened, so that now the estimates for the end of December show an aggregate surplus; that means, a surplus over the strength of the units, not over the strength of the pools. It means some surplus to apply to the pools, which, however, would disappear in January, even after using up all the trained infantry now available. That means there would be no pool whatever of trained infantry reserves at the end of January.
When I left the cabinet I forecast that we would have a small deficit even at the end of November. That would be within a month after the statement made by the Prime Minister. In other words, when I retired we faced a situation where we might reasonably expect to have just about enough men to fill units to the end of November, but with no real reserves. During December the position
would get worse, and at the end of December not only would we have no pool, but the units
themselves would be under strength, and the unit strength in the aggregates would grow weaker month by month in 1945. The only substantial difference between the figures compiled before I left the cabinet and the figures of the day before order in council P.C. 8891 was passed is that any actual shortage in units strengths develops, under the new figures, in January instead of December. The point is that even on the revised figures there is a substantial shortage for December because the aggregate surplus is far too small a number to provide sufficient pools in the battle areas in the United Kingdom.
The tight position now' forecast for January or February gets tighter each month of 1945, and by the end of May we find ourselves with the units under strength to the extent of several thousand and with no trained reinforcements immediately available. To use the minister's expression, we shall be "far more than going into the red-quite deep". Any reinforcements which might be prospectively available have to be earmarked to meet prospective casualties.
Now these statistics may change. They have changed since I left the cabinet. They are, after all, statistics. They can never be proved or disproved. What they do show is that in reinforcements for infantry we are working with no "backlog", instead of having an adequate reserve as we have for every other branch of activity either in war or in business. The fact that we may have paper figures which would show that we might from time to time get together enough men in the aggregate to bring the units up to strength if they were concentrated in one area is not good enough. We must have a margin and a substantial one.
Would we think for instance that our medical people were doing their job if the stores of, say, anaesthetic were maintained only on the basis that the quantity kept on hand would just about serve the average number of patients who would be expected per day? Would we not expect them to add twenty-five per cent or fifty per cent to be sure that some wounded soldier would not be placed on the operating table only to find that he was one more than was expected, and that he would have to wait until they sent to the stores in Rome, or perhaps until a ship came in bringing additional supplies from the United Kingdom? You say that is absurd. Is it any more -absurd than to try to comfort ourselves with the statistical conclusion that at the end of any month our units should be pretty well up to strength, subject to "ifs"
War Effort-Government Policy

like the following: if the casualties are no higher than expected; if casualties are incurred in numbers and times to correspond with the days when reinforcements become available; if the convoy arrives on time; if it brings as many as are needed; if the other battle area does not ask for some of the men we are expecting; if there are no interruptions or delays in training; if some of the training is omitted; if those who have been wounded and are counted on as returning from hospital are sufficiently hardened; if restriction of leave is imposed; and if there is no sickness, absence or other wastage among the reinforcements. Mr. Speaker, it is those "ifs" and some more which make reinforcement pools or reserves absolutely necessary.
The need for these additional reinforcements did not arise from having suffered more casualties in the aggregate than had been forecasted. The need arises because the casualties incurred by the infantry have been a very much higher proportion of the aggregate casualties than had been estimated, and the estimates for the future are based on that experience. Those estimates of casualties had been made on the most careful calculations based on experience in various theatres and1 in consultation with the war office. It has turned out, and this applies to our allies as well, that while the estimates with regard to the other arms of the service have been adequate, the basis of those estimates for infantry casualties has proved from actual experience to be in error.
I want to stop hgre to emphasize the necessity for having adequate reinforcement pools or reserves overseas, both in the United Kingdom and in the battle areas, and in that connection to say something of the actual conditions which I found while in Italy, northwest Europe and the United Kingdom.
It can be stated without qualification that reserves or pools of trained reinforcements are a fundamental part of the organization of any field army, just as much as reserves of ammunition or equipment. An army cannot just depend for reinforcements on the periodic arrival of ships and the number they carry. There must be some substantial cushion to provide for numberless contingencies which must be guarded against. The reinforcement reserve in the United Kingdom is the heart of the reinforcement organization overseas, and it supplies the smaller pools in the battle areas. These battle area pools are absolutely essential. The pools are intended to provide a reservoir directly behind the forward area from which reinforcements can be drawn promptly as casualties are incurred.

Reinforcements are sent from the United Kingdom pool to the battle areas periodically. In Italy, they are received only once a month; in northwest Europe once a week. These periodic dispatches of reinforcements may not come in time or in sufficient numbers to be available to replace current casualties. Arrival of reinforcements may be delayed. Losses may at certain times be exceptionally heavy. It is most desirable that losses be replaced quickly. If they are not replaced, there are less men for the job, with the consequent additional strain. If they are not replaced, morale is bound to be lowered. It is all very well to say that units may be filled up by the end of the month or the end of the week, but what about the days and nights in between? And so pools of reinforcements in the battle areas ensure that reinforcements are available to the units when needed. It ensures that they are not dependent for their reinforcements on the arrival of a convoy, or the uncertainties of how many the convoy will bring due to shortages in the United Kingdom or in another battle area.
It means everything to men in the line to see new men come in beside them to fill the gaps while the battle is on. The men can understand shortages if they know that there are no reinforcements available, but it is different-and I found this particularly in Italy-when the men know that we have these trained infantry men of the N.R.M.A. in Canada who can be made available.
In Italy I visited the reinforcement unit and most of the infantry battalions. I talked with the men themselves, and time and again I got that same story-about having to go back in the line repeatedly, or not having leave, or being short-handed, when trained N.R.M.A. men could be made available to give them relief.
At the end of September, just before I left Italy, the pool of trained infantry reinforcements was down to between ten and fifteen per cent of what had been planned, and infantry reinforcements were so scarce in the United Kingdom that the only addition they were getting was in the monthly convoy to arrive in about two weeks, bringing not even enough trained infantry men to meet the casualties which would have been incurred in those two weeks.
The corps commander in Italy pressed strongly that the pool be reestablished in the area sufficiently strong to relieve the tight situation and ensure prompt replacement of day-to-day casualties.
In northwest Europe the acting army commander impressed on me another reason for

War Effort-Government Policy
maintaining an adequate pool in the battle area; that even well-trained reinforcements coming into the line for the first time have to be helped and advised by their battle experienced comrades. He made the point that if the unit is allowed to get down in strength through reinforcements not coming in promptly it puts an added strain on men in the unit to absorb a large number of new men coming in all at once, and fighting efficiency is lowered.
In a word, casualties should be replaced promptly as they occur so that there would be smaller numbers to be absorbed, instead of allowing shortages to accumulate and expecting a weakened unit to absorb a large total at one time. This was another reason making it so necessary to reestablish an adequate pool immediately available behind the units. Fighting efficiency calls for continual instead of periodic reinforcement.
The acting army commander also explained to me that shortages in the infantry battalions were generally due to casualties suffered by the rifle companies of the battalion. He pointed out that the fighting personnel of the rifle companies numbered only about sixty per cent of the battalion and that, although a shortage might appear to be a small proportion of the whole battalion, it would be a much heavier proportion of these fighting personnel, with a corresponding weakening effect on the capacity of the battalion for aggressive action.
The acting army commander pressed very strongly for a minimum infantry pool at a figure which I considered entirely warranted.
I found that on account of the heavy infantry casualties, the infantry reinforcement pool which had been established in France on D-day had been completely exhausted, and that at one time there had been aggregate shortages in the units themselves of over 3,000. This had been gradually overcome in aggregate numbers, but not in individual units, by vigorous efforts to retrain men from other arms as infantry. No pool had been built up. The week I was there, there would be sufficient infantry in aggregate numbers available in the area to bring the units up to strength. To do so would leave only about ten per cent of what should have been on hand to provide the pool for which the acting army commander had asked. Some people have the idea that striving to keep units up to strength means trying to achieve an ideal condition. They think of experiences in the last war when units held the line with strength substantially reduced. Experience in the last war is no guide. In the last war
battles were short, the objectives were limited and long static periods intervened. In this war a battle is a series of continuous offensive operations, or, to put it the other way, a battle is a continuous series of offensive operations. That makes it most necessary that units, while they are in the battle, be reinforced on the move to keep up the momentum of the operation and each unit's fighting efficiency. That does not mean that units are kept in the line a longer time than they should be. They are withdrawn and replaced constantly by other units. It only means that, while they are there, the activity is more intense, and to support men and the success of the operation the ranks should be filled up promptly.
Just here I wish to mention one point with regard to the reinforcement system. An impression that I feel sure is wrong has got abroad with regard to the system which is in practice overseas. I am speaking now both of Italy and of northwest Europe, because the system in Italy was copied in northwest Europe. There is the idea in some quarters that when the battalion itself wants men it requisitions the brigade, and the brigade requisitions the division, and the division the corps, and then the corps requisitions the echelon. Well, that is absolutely fallacious. What is done is this: the reinforcements generally are under the reinforcement group which is directly under the second echelon, the second echelon being located fairly well back. That reinforcement group is fairly well up but in, shall I say, a comparatively secluded and safe place. The reinforcement group throws off forward battalions of infantry, artillery, army service corps, and so on at the army road-head. From there again there are sent further forward into the corps area or into the divisional area companies of reinforcements to be directly behind the units so that they will be available, not to be sent from away back at the group, but available immediately to be sent to the different units themselves. The requisition does not come from the brigade to division to corps to army; the requisition comes direct from the unit to second echelon which has charge of the distribution. Second echelon immediately advises the people having charge of these men up in the corps or divisional area to release direct to the unit. In other words, in requisitioning men the unit by-passes brigade and division and corps and army, and requisitions straight back to second echelon, and in filling the requisition second echelon gives orders direct to the people in charge of the reinforcements, away up in the forward area behind the units,
War Effort-Government Policy

and these men are released direct to the units. That is how speedily it is done under the system we have. All that you need are two things, transport and men, and you will get your reinforcements very quickly indeed. We had a situation in France at one time where the group was so far back and the forward troops were moving so fast that it took about six days to get the reinforcements up. When I was there the reinforcements were in the forward reinforcement battalion within about ten miles of the front line. The reinforcements in the corps and divisional areas would be even nearer to the front. Please do not get the idea that units get down in strength and have to wait a week for all these requisitions to go back to the brigade. There is a complete shortcut between the units and the second echelon which has charge of all the reinforcements.
I have spoken of Italy and I have spoken of France. Now a word about the main pool in the United Kingdom. That pool has to be kept up, so that it can supply and maintain, and, if the need should arise, supplement the battle area pools. The pool in the United Kingdom, through the battle area pools, has to be sufficient to provide against shortages in strength which may be anticipated for a month or two ahead; it has to meet the successive and increasing monthly shortages in strength anticipated in 1945; it has to meet unexpected situations when battle casualties may be more than estimated; it has to meet the additional wastage due to increased sickness in the winter months; it has also to provide replacements for men with long service overseas who may be given well deserved leave, and generally it has to afford assurance of man-power against all the other contingencies I have mentioned. The plain fact was that under the stress due to the unexpectedly high proportion of infantry casualties it had not been possible, with the volunteer resources available, to reestablish any adequate pool of trained infantry in the United Kingdom. Nor on the estimates presented by the department were there prospects of any such infantry pool being established unless large numbers of trained N.R.M.A. infantry men were utilized. All the infantry reinforcements which could be made available have had to be sent forward just as rapidly as possible from the United Kingdom to the battle areas to replace casualties. The result was that the infantry units of the Canadian army were operating not with any adequate pool of trained available reinforcements immediately behind them, but rather on a hand-to-mouth system dependent on

what could be supplied direct from time to time with the precarious uncertainties of retraining, shipping, sickness, and the impossibilities of accurate distribution between the two battle areas.
Further than that, as indicated, it looks now as if by the end of January there will be no pool at all. From then on there will be a shortage in the aggregate strength of the infantry units which will increase month by month. When I was talking about the pool I was talking about the aggregate pool, and I was not content to make plans based on leaving the infantry units of the Canadian army in any such risky position with regard to reinforcements. We do not take chances on ammunition and equipment. We make excellent and right provisions for ample reserves. You cannot afford to take chances when human lives are at stake. Furthermore, we have to remember that in Italy to-day there are over ten thousand men who have been overseas for more than four years and in the battle areas more than six months. I talked with many of these men. I told them I would give the matter of leave attention as soon as I returned. When I got back the plan for leave was worked out in consultation with my officers. A day or two before my retirement word was received that transportation arrangements could be provided. The plan was awaiting the opportunity to be presented to the war committee at the time I resigned. Since that time I understand it is the same plan which has been approved and announced by my successor.
These men in Italy deserve the utmost consideration, and if the sending of these N.R.M.A. men as reinforcements can help to relieve the strain on them, then I think we are in duty bound to send them.
These are some of the conditions I found in the field. That is a bit of the background from which I felt we must plan for the future.
I consulted General Eisenhower; I consulted General Sir Henry Maitland Wilson; I consulted General Montgomery; I consulted General, now Field Marshal, Alexander and I consulted General McCreery as to the future and I consulted our own commanders as well. Before I finish I am going to mention a word with regard to the prospects of the future course of the war.
After visiting the battle areas I consulted with the chief of staff, Canadian military headquarters, General Stuart. He and his officers had been making every endeavour to meet the changed situation in infantry by re-must.ering from other arms, and had succeeded in providing sufficient numbers of trained

War Effort-Government Policy
infantry in northwest Europe to create a small surplus over the unit strengths. He found, however, that by this process he was not able to reestablish pools and at the same time keep units up to strength. He had reviewed the situation with his officers, and before I went to Belgium I had been over the whole position with him.
On my return from Belgium on October 12 we had further conferences, examining the figures and endeavouring to assess the needs, and the possibilities of meeting them with the resources at hand and what were estimated to be prospectively available. As a result of these conferences, I cabled the Prime Minister on October 13 indicating my apprehensions about the reinforcement situation and that I was coming back to Canada immediately. I left for Canada on the 16th, arriving on the 18th, accompanied by the chief of staff, Canadian military headquarters, and saw the Prime Minister that afternoon.
On the 19th the chief of staff, Canadian military headquarters, made a written report to me that, after going over the situation, the only solution which he could see was to find an additional 15,000 trained infantry reinforcements to add to the total infantry reinforcement pool overseas on or before December 31, 1944. He also asked for a certain addition to each of the monthly dispatches of reinforcements from Canada in 1945. He recommended that if the numbers required could not be found in the general service personnel in Canada, the terms of service of the N.R.M.A. personnel be extended to include overseas service in any theatre.
In view of my observations in the battle areas, and after most careful consideration of the figures and of all the relevant factors, I placed this recommendation of the chief of staff, C.M.H.Q., before the war committee at a meeting held the same day, October 19, which was continued on the 20th, and then before a special meeting of the cabinet on October 24. The question then arose as to the source from which these trained infantry men could be obtained before December 31. Here was the situation. Fifteen thousand trained infantrymen were needed at once to build up the overseas pool. Commencing January 1, 1945, a certain additional number of trained infantrymen wore needed to be included in the ordinary monthly dispatches of reinforcements from Canada. The chief of the general staff, General Murchie; the adjutant general, General Walford, and their officers made an exhaustive examination of all possibilities of finding the 15,000 trained infantry reinforcements for the pool and the
monthly increase for the first six months of 1945, as required by the chief of staff, C.M.H.Q. They were able to provide only sufficient to meet the monthly increases. This was accomplished by demoting non-commissioned officers and utilizing infantry tradesmen, although paying them respectively at the rates for N.C.O.'s and tradesmen for a certain period; by accelerating dispatch of certain infantry; by dispatching certain other arms for retraining as infantry in the United Kingdom. Only about seven hundred of these would be available in the battle area in January and the bulk in February and March. The net result was that this additional 4,500 did not provide anything towards the 15,000 pool, since it would just meet for a five-month .period the additional monthly increase that had been asked for by the chief of staff, C.M.H.Q.
The chief of the general staff suggested two possible courses of action. One was the reduction of infantry battalions from four rifle companies to three, making corresponding reductions in the strength of the units in other arms. The other was the disbanding of one infantry division. He stated a number of weighty objections to either of these courses. He pointed out that the adoption of either of them was a matter of government policy, and that before a decision was reached to accept either of these suggestions it was essential that the field commanders be consulted. I agreed with the objections of the chief of the general staff to either of these courses. I considered further that when trained N.R.M.A. men were available, Canada's duty at this crucial period of the war was to support our men in the line, and that our obligation to them, to ourselves and to our allies was not to relax but to go on with the task to help shorten the war.
The third suggestion made by the chief .of the general staff was to extend the terms of service of the N.R.M.A. personnel to permit their dispatch overseas. While recognizing that it was a matter of government policy, he stated that, based on purely military considerations, the adoption of this course in his opinion would meet the requirements which the chief of staff, C.M.H.Q., had put forward, both as to numbers and without disruption of the organization and fighting efficiency of the Canadian army. To make a long story short, every available source from which trained infantrymen might be procured was examined, Canada, the United Kingdom and the battle areas themselves. The conclusion was that we had exhausted those possibilities, as far as immediate need was concerned.
War Effort-Government Policy

As is well known there must be ten soldiers, or nearly that many, in the lines of communication, at the bases, in support and in the various services which are vital for the purpose of servicing the troops to every man in the front line, but generally speaking most of those ten men do not meet the specific standards lor the front.
I thought that perhaps when my successor took over he would find some possible source of supply which had been overlooked; but, from what the house knows, I think he has come to the same conclusion that I did. So when people ask me why a few thousand infantrymen could not be supplied from the many, many thousands of soldiers in Canada and'the United Kingdom, while I could go over the figures and tell them where all these men are situated, what they are doing and what their qualifications are, I think the short and quick and, I hope, convincing answer is that the present Minister of National Defence, with his experience, has made the same inquiries and has become convinced that men are not available from these sources to meet the immediate problem.
It was under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, that I considered I had no other alternative but to recommend that N.R.M.A. personnel be made available, and I did so. There were 8,000 N.R.M.A. infantrymen who could be ready for combat at an early date, and 8,000 more who could be ready in a month's time. In addition, there were 26,000 N.R.M.A. men considered suitable material as infantry reinforcements who could be remustered and trained as infantry. I thought no time should be lost in getting them to the United Kingdom. The immediate position was that there was a lack of reserves. We were living from hand to mouth. The prospective position was that there would be not only a lack of reserves but shortages in strength even before these N.R.M.A. men could reach the battle areas. The best estimate was that at least two months would elapse from the time it was decided to send the men until they could reach the battle areas. That is, if the decision were made, say on November 1, the first 8,000 men could not be available in the battle area until between January 1 and January 15. Every day that went by meant one more day in which the infantry units of the Canadian army would be without assurance of adequate reinforcement provision. In the hope of favourable action, and in order to have everything in readiness for sending these additional trained infantrymen overseas at the earliest date possible, I had tentative arrangements made for a special sailing near the end of November. The whole

matter was thoroughly discussed at many meetings, both of the war committee and of the cabinet; my recommendation was not accepted and, as the house and the country know, my retirement as minister took place on November 1.
Let me recall here that these 15,000 men would be, as it were, a lump-sum addition to our reinforcement reserves. The need could not be met by the gradual dispatch of these men on the monthly instalment plan. They were in addition to all the general service men who could be provided by the regular monthly dispatches, and they were in addition to the extra 4,500 which had been found by the chief of the general staff. The only source from which to get them was from the trained N.R.M.A. infantrymen whom we had been holding in Canada as potential reinforcements.
That was the situation before the cabinet. It was under these circumstances that it was suggested that a further appeal be made to N.R.M.A. men to enlist. I want to point out what the house already knows, since it has been discussed so much, that there was only one group sufficiently trained to qualify to meet the urgen need, and! that was the N.R.M.A. infantrymen. I must confess I felt that the appeal would be impracticable and futile. The only question was whether or not the appeal ought to be made in order to say that every effort had been put forth. This is what I told my colleagues when we were discussing the appeal. A little while ago I said that I made two points. One was the practical point; the other was the question of policy, as to what would happen if the appeal failed. In the Department of National Defence we had a good deal of experience with regard to the enlisting of these N.R.M.A. men. Altogether we had enlisted about 42,000 of them. Most of these had enlisted in the early stages of training while, as one might say, they were in the receptive stage and had not acquired fixed ideas. We had enlisted 6,500 since D-day; 2.915 in June, and they were down to 850 by October. The total number we had enlisted from April to October was 10,016, or an average of something like 1,400 a month. But it must be remembered that these N.R.MA. men whom we enlisted were not all infantry; they were artillery', army service corps and every arm of the service; they were men in A category, men in lower categories for other services, categories too low for infantry, and so on. So that from the over-all members of N.R.M.A. men who enlisted we cannot judge very much as to how many infantrymen we might get.

War Effort-Government Policy
Well, we had attempts at recruiting regiments. We appealed in particular to a Frenchspeaking regiment, offering that they should go overseas if 500 enlisted; that was the usual offer we made. A very few enlisted. I want to sa.y that was not confined to the Frenchspeaking units. We had exactly the same experience with an English-speaking unit. Perhaps a few more offered to enlist, that is to sayi conditionally, if 500 went over, but in each instance I can say that we had less than fifty' unconditional offers of enlistment.
There was a good deal of talk in this house about the experience we had had out west in connection with the brigade which went to Iiiska. We had there a brigade which had gone on offensive operations, which had been with the United States troops, and which had been regarded as top-hole, so far as troops were concerned. These men deported themselves magnificently, and there were very few desertions when they sailed. They got along splendidly when they got there, and went through their training manoeuvres in the Aleutians. But those men who were prepared to take on that Pacific operation, on the morning they landed at Kiska, just happened to find that the Jap was not there.
There was a group we thought would be interested in, and anxious perhaps to go overseas, if they could go as a unit. Well, what did we do? We put on a campaign-and I assure you, it was not any sideshow. We had three V.C.'s there-Major-General Pearkes, Colonel McGregor and Major Triquet. We had padres, officers, N.C.O.'s-everybody-to see these men and to interview them individually. Each battalion was vying with the other to see how many men they could get to enlist to go over. Out of a total strength of, I believe, 2,432, the total enlistments which we got from the brigade amounted to 769. That was a three weeks' campaign. And these were not all infantrymen; it included men in other arms of the service who belonged to the brigade, as well.
We knew only too well the likelihood-or rather the unlikelihood-of any possible campaign which would produce 15,000 trained infantrymen, or anything approaching that number.

speechtext:
Yes, last May. In that case what we finally did was this: we enlisted men from other units on the west coast,
filled the Kiska units up, and they did go over as a brigade. They had worked so hard in the campaign that we thought they might go over, and we did send them over as a brigade.
I only mention this to the house-and may I add that the government knew that this was the experience we had had. It may be that we were dumb recruiters. It may be that we did not know our business, and that our officers did not know their business. Certainly they tried, and they gave a report in connection with the whole operation which indicated what the difficulties were, a report which, it seems to me, would be helpful to anj'body who was going to undertake a special campaign again. The house will not forget, however, that the campaign has really been going on continuously and the N.R.M.A. men we have been enlisting month by month have been the result of continued faithful efforts.
I come back to this: we had that experience. In order to get just as much information as possible as to the possible prospects of fresh endeavours, we communicated direct with the general officer in each of the districts of the Pacific command, to ascertain from him what he thought of the possibility of a campaign- a campaign not on a military level, but one in which the Prime Minister would take part, in which the Minister of National Defence would take part, and in which other ministers would take part. The campaign was suggested for ten daj's. I suggested it for ten days, and he suggested no campaign was any good for ten days. Finally he said that he thought if the campaign went on for three weeks, with all these other agencies engaged that it might be possible-he could not promise anything-but he would say that at the outside you might get 1,500 trained infantrymen.
That was the situation, and those were the reports which we had. Those were the reports we had to consider in connection with this appeal. On the other hand was the fact that every day which went by meant that these men were just one day later in getting to the battle area. These men could be coming in in dribbles of ten on one day, twenty on the next and fifty on the next, and you would not be able to handle it administratively. You would have to wait until the last man came, or until you got at least 1,000 or 2,000. The result was that it did seem to be administratively impracticable, and the prospects of success seemed absolutely negligible. That was the situation.
Hon. members know what took place. General MeNaughton came in, and he felt that these men could be got by voluntary
War Effort-Government Policy

enlistment. He made a speech at Amprior in which he indicated the desire to get volunteers. At that time he did not mention the N.R.M.A. men at all. Later he spoke at Ottawa. At that time he did mention N.R.M.A. men; his remarks were not addressed directly to them, but he was saying that encouragement would be given to those men to come in.
Then the Prime Minister made an address on November 8 in which he did address these men and their families directly, and asked for their support. The D.O.C.'s came in on November 14. and a report was made and the matter discussed. I think the minister felt that he got some encouragement from that, because he made an announcement that the conference had considered the subject, and that there was confirmation in his mind of the idea that these men coiuld be got by voluntary enlistment. That was the position with regard to the matter of the appeal, about which I referred when I mentioned my resignation.
The minister had advised the Prime Minister on October 31 of his belief that the men could be obtained by voluntary enlistment. I knew the experience we had had-and the government knew, too. The minister took over on November 2. He knew that we were specially short of infantry, and that untrained infantry would not do. He would know that if our troops were out of the line now they would probably be in in January, and that these troops would be most useful to them; and if they were to be obtained by voluntary enlistment the enlistments had to be rapid and effective. The speech at Arn-prior was on November 5, I believe it was, and then he spoke again in Ottawa either on the next night or on the night following that.
Then, as I say, on November 14, the D.O.C.'s came in. That means that nearly a month after I came home the first really active step was taken to get N.R.M.A. men to enlist voluntarily. As I have already said, if these men were sent on November 1 they would not get to the battle area, to be of much use to reestablish pools which were going to be short in December.
As I have said, after conference with the D.O.C.'s the minister in a press statement indicated that his belief was confirmed more than ever in continuing the voluntary policy to provide reinforcements. That was on November 17. But within a week, namely on November 23, the minister came to this house and advised us that the D.O.C.'s had told him frankly that they had not much hope that
I Mr. Ralston.]
our requirements would be met, but that they had loyally undertaken to make another effort. Then he went on to say:
This they have now done, and I must admit that the results have not been adequate. I am advised that there are very many N.R.M.A. men who will not volunteer under present circumstances but who are quite willing to be sent overseas.
I was not in that campaign at all; but I want to say this that the Prime Minister did mention-and I do not think he was quite fair to the officers-that the officers had not cooperated-

speechtext:
Yes, some of them. I do not know about them all. But I know some who would cooperate to the very limit, no matter what you asked them to do, if it were for the army. And I do not think, with regard to the great bulk of the officers-and not only the officers, but the staffs as well- that the government, or any of us, can have any complaint with the way in which they endeavoured to carry on, under the conditions which I have described.
The Prime Minister also mentioned the big interests or the big influences. Well, as he knows, probably the biggest influence or perhaps the most important was the Canadian Legion, which felt that they could not take part in the campaign. They had their own reasons for that. I assure you that I never had very much of the support of the Canadian Legion in connection with volunteer campaigns, but they did not take the strong attitude which they took in connection with this campaign. There were practical conditions which were fairly well known and which were I think fairly well appreciated.
It all adds up to this: I felt that from November 1 until November 14 no step was taken to get the district officers commanding together, the men who knew more about this thing than anybody else. I felt that that was a very serious delay which could hardly be explained. I came home and perhaps I was too anxious about this thing, but I did have it on my soul and I did believe that these men ought to go. I still believe that they ought to go and I believe that they could have been gotten away on November 27 if action had been taken promptly. We had the whole programme and the whole time table worked out.
I do feel badly that the first address which was made by the minister was simply an address indicating that the best hope was the voluntary system and asking everybody to help. I am not criticising the minister; I

War Effort-Government Policy
am not saying this harshly; I am simply saying what I felt. I felt that the only place to go for these men was the camps in the west, because that is where the men were.
It seems to me that the first thing that should have been done in connection with the campaign was for the minister to have flown out there immediately to gather his officers together. That was not done. The Arnprior speech was made and then the Ottawa speech, and then the Prime Minister's speech was made on November 8. As I say, that appealed to these men, but you cannot do recruiting at long distance, either for general service or for N.R.M.A. men. It is like an evangelistic meeting; you have to have hand to hand work. Apparently it was felt that ever}' effort and every expedient had been exhausted. I felt that there had been a series of delays and that is what concerned me in connection with the matter-and I am speaking very mildly. I had considered that if there were to be prospective success a very large number of men had to be obtained by a certain time and it had to be short.
I felt that neither the Prime Minister nor the minister recognized the necessity for the promptness of action which was essential in order to meet this urgent situation. I want to credit the minister with this: after three weeks, when he found that his advice in connection with this matter was wrong, he said so forthrightly, both to the house and to the government.
On November 23, the same day the minister spoke to the house, order in council P.C. 8891 was passed and laid on the table of the house. It authorized the minister to dispatch overseas to the United Kingdom and/or to Europe and/or the Mediterranean theatres such personnel in such numbers as may be approved by the governor in council who are serving under the N.R.M.A. or who are or may be from time to time hereafter required in the opinion of the minister for training, service or duty within the localities of service I have just mentioned.
The number of 16,000 was expressly provided by the order in council. It provided for the further approval by the governor in council for the sending of those who might hereafter be required in the opinion of the minister. I had asked on October 19 for 15,000 men immediately. The question arises at once whether, if such action had been taken by the governor in council while I was still minister, I would have accepted it, and the answer is that undoubtedly I would have accepted it, not because I considered it was
satisfactory or a proper way to deal with the matter but because, above everything else, I was concerned in getting those 15,000 men just as quickly as possible.
I would have felt that as the minister responsible for the administration of the army I could not afford, in the interests of the troops themselves, to have rejected such action, but I certainly would have registered the strongest protest possible against the halfhearted, piecemeal method adopted. I would have pointed out that, once the decision was made to secure the service of N.R.M.A. men, once it was extended overseas, that decision should not apply to any one group of men in the N.R.M.A. but should apply to that force as a whole. To apply it just to part of the force was to perpetuate the system of two different armies for Canada.
That was inherent so long as the N.R.M.A. were obligated only for service in Canada. There was then a clear and uniform distinction between all N.R.M.A. men and volunteers. The former were for service in Canada and the latter were for service overseas, but the moment the principle was accepted that N.R.M.A. men were for overseas service, then in my view it should be carried through by actually obligating alt the men for overseas service and helping to remove the rankling distinction which would be even more pronounced against those who still retained the status of service in Canada only.
I would have pointed out that the result would be to create an additional division in the Canadian army. First, there would be general service men for service anywhere. Then there would be N.R.M.A. men for service in certain designated theatres. Then, there would be N.R.M.A. men for service in Canada only. All the difficulties that have existed, not only in administration, discipline and the utilization of non-commissioned officers, but in the sense of discrimination where there are different areas of service, would be multiplied. Further than that, there would be complaints of discrimination in selecting certain N.R.M.A. men and extending the scope of their service, while leaving others with only the obligation to serve in Canada.
This was not my idea alone. It was envisaged by the Prime Minister in 1942. When he was asked a question by Mr. Douglas, he replied, as reported on page 4564 of Hansard.'.
When the government decides that it is necessary and advisable to resort to conscription as a method of raising men for service overseas, an order in council will be passed dealing with members of the forces as a whole. It will not be a matter of passing a series of orders in council, but one order in council will cover the entire force.
War Effort[DOT]-Government Policy

My second objection would have been that if the N.R.M.A. men are to be used overseas, they should be subject to exactly the same scope of service as the general service personnel. I believe that these objections hold good to-day, and I urge upon the government just as strongly as I can the adoption of the procedure which the Prime Minister promised would be adopted, that of passing one order in council and making it applicable to the whole force.
Notwithstanding these objections, it was so important beyond anything else to have these men immediately that I would have accepted the action taken and battled out, if I may use that expression, the objections I have stated in an endeavour to secure the method which I consider should have been adopted.
I come now to the motion and amendment before the house. I did not know there was a subamendment and I have not seen it. My one objective and determination, and I may say struggle, from the day I arrived home from overseas has been to get additional trained infantry men overseas quickly to reinforce our magnificent fighting men. That still is my objective whether I am in office or out of it. In the midst of all the confusion and contradictions and upsetting incidents of the last five years I have been determined to keep my eye on the ball. I considered, and so recommended, that it was necessary to send N.R.M.A. men for that purpose.
My immediate objective was to get the additional 15,000 men from the N.R.M.A. trained infantry. To-day, if the declarations of the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence mean what I understand them to mean, the sending of 16,000 additional men from N.R.M.A. as rapidly as they can be dispatched is assured, and the principle is laid down by order in council that N.R.M.A. men are to be available for reinforcement purposes, and it is said by the minister that further numbers will be sent as required. I do not think the principle is laid down by the order in council itself that they are all included in the order in council, but the principle has been established by the order in council that N.R.M.A. men are available, and the minister has said that further numbers will be sent as required.
That result has been achieved by a combination of circumstances unique in the history of this dominion. Public opinion has made itself felt so powerfully that it could not be disregarded. The resolute stand of certain former colleagues in the cabinet has put that mighty influence into positive action. Any part that I have had could only succeed because of the vigorous and staunch support of those two forces.

I am far from satisfied with the delay which these three weeks have cost and with the lack of a sense of urgency which has been shown. I am far from satisfied with the piecemeal method that has been adopted or the halting attitude it indicates. I have already stated my objections to that method. But, now that at last action has been taken, I am determined that neither my dissatisfaction nor those objections are going to deflect me into doing anything which may in the slightest delay further the sending forward of these reinforcements.
With that paramount objective before me I have considered well how I should vote on the motion before the house, and on the subamendment-which, I understand, has been ruled out of order-and the amendment, in order to get the one thing accomplished which matters most. I can speak now only of the amendment and the motion.
I can say this regarding the amendment. I have already indicated my opinion of the advantages of the method it proposes. I believe the time has come when the proper course is to make all N.R.M.A. men subject to the obligation to serve overseas. I have registered that opinion. But to vote for the amendment is far more than registering that opinion. The amendment is, in fact, a motion of want of confidence because if it were carried, the government's motion would be lost; and the government, instead of driving ahead, as it must do, to dispatch the 16,000 reinforcements from the N.R.M.A. and the further reinforcements required from time to time, would cease to function, and the whole matter of dispatching these men, which I have so earnestly advocated, would be thrown into the realm of uncertainty and suspense.
I have come to the conclusion that I will not by my vote permit that to happen. I have worked too hard in my humble way to help to bring about the changed policy of the government to jeopardize or give any excuse for delaying the prompt dispatch of these 16,000 men overseas. If the amendment were carried, I confess that I cannot, and I doubt if anyone can foresee clearly or with any reasonable certainty what would happen about the sending of these men. There would follow attempts to form a new government, the probable necessity of any new government having the assurance of the support of the house, and the delays and uncertainties which are inevitable in a course of that kind. Or, instead of the formation of a new government there might be dissolution of the house and a general election. Either one of these alternatives, while some people might regard them as preferable to the present situation, would constitute in my

War Effort-Government Policy
judgment a definite deterrent to the quick dispatch of these reinforcements. That action, in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of the great body of members of this house, and of the country at large, is at the moment the supreme consideration. I was not asking for a change of government at this crucial period of the war. I wanted reinforcements and I wanted them quickly. I was not asking for a general election, to plunge this country into acute political turmoil for the next two months. It was reinforcements I wanted.
If this house supports the amendment it renders abortive, for the time being at least, all that has been won, and the goal-the sending of these men who are urgently needed overseas-which is now directly ini sight, will be lost in the thickest of confusion and ' political controversy. I want to be practical, and to vote against the motion either indirectly by voting for the amendment or by voting "no" on the motion itself, would, in my opinion, be voting for delays and confusion and greater uncertainty in the sending of these needed reinforcements for our troops overseas.
To put it bluntly, I think that, unsatisfactory though the method is, action is more important than method, and I believe that these men will be dispatched more quickly and more certainly if this house completes the action which the government has at last taken, by approving the motion, than by any other course which the house can take at the present time.
With the powers under this order in council sanctioned by this house, there can be no excuse that trained men are not available. There can be no excuse for straining at getting the last volunteer or for curtailing such privileges as would be granted when manpower is adequate, and there can be no excuse for not extending further the provisions for leave for men in the battle areas, with long service overseas. There is one thing more, and that is that I doubt if the minister's programme of dispatch is sufficiently rapid to provide all he should have to reestablish reinforcement pools as quickly as that should be done, having regard to the conditions which face him now and in the near future.
He will be held responsible for accelerating the dispatch in every way. And one other point I am assuming, unless the Prime Minister states otherwise, that if the government motion carries, the future orders in council specifying additional numbers of men will be passed and put into effect without any reference back again to this house for a vote of confidence or other approval.

speechtext:
I take that to be clear from the minister's statements to the house.
I have mentioned these points specially, but what I want to emphasize is this, that this house and the people of this country, and I myself, will hold the government-and particularly the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence-to strict account for carrying out vigorously and without wavering their declared intention to reinforce the army with well-trained men from the N.R.M.A. to the fullest and fastest extent possible.
It is on this understanding and for these reasons, and one other, namely, the confidence which I have in certain of my former colleagues, who have contributed in no small degree to the changed attitude of the government, that I shall vote against the amendment and for the motion.
Mr. Speaker, the war is not over. Our efforts in the days before us must not be relaxed for a moment. A desperately stubborn enemy faces us in Italy and northwest Europe fighting on every hill, before every village and for every farm. We must go all out to beat him back into his corner, and the more he is cornered the bitterer will be his defence until he is finally overcome.
Such pauses as have occurred in the advance into the Low Countries have been the inevitable result of a fast-moving campaign handicapped by lack of full facilities for supply. There is no thought of retiring to winter quarters and digging in.
Mr. Churchill said on November 15, "The new fact that stares me in the face is that extremely heavy fighting is continuing week by week and will certainly last for a long time". General Eisenhower on November 21 said, "There is a job here for every man fit for battle that we can bring in, and it's up lo every man back home to give him everything he needs-that is my prescription for victory."
That prescription must be for us all. There is no easy road to peace. The German army has proved that it can absorb terrible punishment and still come up fighting. Our men in Italy have a saying that they are always attacking the last hill, and that when they reach the top they always find that the Germans have built another behind it.
We must jostle him, hurry him, harry him, pound him, give him no rest, give him no time, give him no chance to build up successive lines of resistance. We must keep him on the run. It is not an easy task. It is one that will require the last ounce of strength that we can put forward. Driving him into his corner is not enough. We must build up
War Effort-Government Policy

all the weight, all the power and all the determination we can muster for the knockout and victory and peace.
Just for a moment, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word about the Canadian army. There was placed on to-day's Hansard, so that it might become for all time part of the records of this parliament, the story of the great exploit of Major David Vivian Currie, which won for that yioung Canadian army officer the empire's highest battle honour, the Victoria Cross. Leading a mixed force of tanks, infantry and men from other units, with all his officers either killed or wounded under repeated attack by German tanks, German guns and other German formations, for three days and three nights this officer rallied and led his men, visiting them, advising them, encouraging them, and at the end he had the supreme satisfaction of seeing that his task had been accomplished. The position had been held and the escape route of a large number of Germans cut off.
That officer was born with no silver spoon in his mouth. He was, in civilian life, an automobile mechanic and welder. He is typical of the Canadian army, an army of civilians, who have turned themselves into soldiers and who in the process bring honour to themselves and glory to the land of their birth.
That citation, Mr. Speaker, which stands on Hansard, factual and formal though it is, impressed one thing on our minds with stark and striking reality. That one thing is the fierceness of the struggle in which our men and our allies are engaged. This man had to fight alone. All his other officers were killed or wounded. Alone for three days he and his gallant band of Canadians had to face the full might of the enemy's attack. It is because such attacks are being made and will continue to be made until the power of Germany is finally broken that I press the urgency of the situation that now confronts us, that I urge this house to lose no further time in taking the steps necessary to give our men overseas the utmost, assistance and support. It was because I had seen for myself the conditions under which our men fought; it was because I felt that no one should ever be able to say that we had failed in our duty to these men, that I took the position which I did on my return from my last visit overseas. When this war is over, and when men like Major Currie and those fighting with him in all three services return to Canada, the destiny of this nation will largely have to be shaped and directed by them. They will have to take their places in the public affairs of this dominion. The tasks of peace will fall to their younger and stronger and fresher hands. They will be great tasks,

tasks calling for every last item of strength and skill and courage. When they lay aside their arms and assume the duties and responsibilities of civilians and citizens I and we all want to be able to look them in the face and say ,"We did not fail you." I want and we all want them to feel that Canada was worth fighting for and worth living for-worth, if needs be, dying for. We want these men to feel, when they return, that they have come back to a land which was proud of them, a land which appreciates their heroic service, a land that has proved that appreciation not by words only but by its deeds and by its actions on their behalf and in their support.
If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, since probably this is the last time that I shall have an opportunity of addressing the house on matters of this kind, I should like if I might to put on Hansard a message which I sent to all ranks of the Canadian army and civilian staffs and also a recognition of the services of the officers. This was the message I sent to all ranks of the army and civilian staffs of the Department of National Defence everywhere:
On relinquishing the duties of Minister of National Defence, I want to express to all ranks of the Canadian army and to the members of the civilian staffs my most sincere appreciation of their whole-hearted devotion to duty during the arduous time of preparation and through the fiery tests of battle.
To our fighting troops, I pay highest tribute and send humble admiration for their endurance, their courage and their amazing achievements in the face of unprecedented difficulties. With them I remember also the skilful and self-sacrificing labours of medical officers and nurses and the devotion of the padres and members of the auxiliary services.
To those who have toiled without reserve in the less spectacular but highly important tasks of organization and training and supply, I express deepest appreciation. Their work has been to fortify Canada's men and women on the battle lines.
As my distinguished successor, Genera! McNaughton, takes over the responsibilities of the department, I confidently ask every man and woman to give to him the same unflagging help and intelligent industry that has meant so much to me and to Canada during my four and a half years of office.
There may be many long days and many rough places before the enemy is completely overcome. The Canadian army will never falter until the task is done. I am proud indeed to have been associated with this grand company of fighters and -workers for victory. Good luck, great success, and my warmest thanks to you all.
I want, if I may, to put on record my sin-cerest appreciation of the work which has been done by the officers of the Canadian army. The accomplishment of the army in the field stands out as a magnificent example of hard fighting in the most difficult circumstances, but I wish to speak more particularly at the moment of the faithful work of the staff and

War Effort-Government Policy
others responsible for counsel and advice in our endeavour to support the men in the battle areas. From the officers in the lines of communication back through the administrative training establishments overseas and from there back to Canada and throughout the country, all have worked faithfully and tirelessly and with no other purpose than to see to it that the men in the battle positions wanted for nothing that could be supplied them. The burden of this work has fallen most heavily on the shoulders of the chief advisers. But everywhere throughout the administrative staffs, officers and men have worked long hours, often with no apparent recognition but always unselfishly and with high purpose to ensure that men, ammunition and supplies were available when they were wanted and when they were needed.
To the army commander, to the former chief of staff at C.M.H.Q. and the officers who worked with him, to the chief of the general staff and the heads of the branches at national defence headquarters, to the general officers commanding, to the district officers commanding and camp commanders in Canada and to all the officers and men who have loyally carried out the work under their direction, I extend my warmest and most heartfelt thanks.
As regards the men of the Canadian army, I have seen them at close range. I know their walk and their talk. I know their bearing. There is no swaggering, but there is quiet confidence born of having proved themselves and the fact that they know it. I visited the men in Italy who have been there for sixteen months. Over ten thousand of them lead with four years overseas service and more than six months in the battle area. These men and their comrades have gone from Pachino to Rimini. By day and by night, over rough, tough ground against a battling enemy they have kept on driving forward. Mile after mile and height after height have been taken. Sometimes the assaulting battalions have only gotten half way up, but their comrades came through and completed the task. Even with ranks thinned they never wavered. To-night they are in the midst of the ditches and the hedges and the dykes of the soaked Po plain. They are fighting on and holding down German divisions. If they did not fight on, those enemy divisions would add to the strength of the hun forces which their comrades would have to meet on the threshold of Germany.
In northw'est Europe the army has had a succession of holding, gruelling, fighting and dearly won successes: Caen, Falaise, Trun Gap, Bois de Londres, the occupation of
Dieppe, siege of Calais and Cap Gris Nez and that most intricate difficult operation on the Scheldt, every foot desperately contested, and every enemy resistance overcome. The way was finally paved to the use of the key port of Antwerp as the base of great operations.
In Italy and in France, in Belgium and in Holland, and on the edge of Germany, sometimes under strength, but with indomitable courage, they have endured the strain. The days will come soon when the great battles- the last we hope-will be fought. And, Mr. Speaker, there will be gaps in the ranks. Those gaps cannot wait for the men to be trained and transported to fill them. I tell you and you know it, and this house knows it, that on the estimates there will not be enough trained volunteers to fill those gaps. But we have in Canada to-day the trained infantry men *who have all these years been enrolled as potential reinforcements for such a time as this. They have never said they would not go. They say they will go when they are sent. They were to be sent if necessary, and the responsibility for making the decision for them is on the shoulders of every hon. member of this house. Part of them are to be sent now. We are assured by the minister that the rest will follow if required. He has assured this house that while he still hopes the voluntary method will be effective-I am quoting his words now-"my first duty, my first purpose is to maintain our forces overseas to the strength which has been decided; and those forces will be maintained by any method." Again I lay it on the government, and particularly on the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence, Mr. McNaughton, that there be no halting and no delay in providing amply for the needs. We cannot escape it; not only the N.R.MA. men, but our own men in Italy, Belgium and Holland are awaiting the decision of this house. I said, Mr. Speaker, that there would be gaps in the ranks. Each man in this house has the responsibility for saying by his vote whether those gaps will be filled.
