I am sure this House of Commons to-night has found itself for the most part in the utmost agreement with the great speech which the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) has just concluded. I am satisfied that the reactions which I myself had to that speech will in a large measure be the reactions of the country when they read it to-morrow. I was pleased indeed that the remarks of the hon. member for Prince were, for the most part, altogether moderate, because after the

War Effort-Government Policy
attempts that have been made from time to time during the last four or five days to shoulder upon him responsibility for a situation which everyone of us, I am sure, now agrees exists, he might have been forgiven if he had shown considerable heat and resentment. I must say that for myself I do not think I could have shown such forbearance or Christian spirit as he exhibited. That merely illustrates the difference in temperament between us.
Certain things have emerged from this speech which, I am sure, will commend themselves to the country, and, I am satisfied, to the membership of this house. One of those things is that beyond peradventure infantry reinforcements are needed and needed badly and are now overdue; that is to say, the preparation for sending them over, and the country will hold responsible for that delay and for any bloodshed that occurs as a result of that delay two men, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the present Minister of National Defence, Mr. McNaughton. Make no mistake about that. Six precious weeks have been lost.
There are other portions of the speech to which I desire to refer, and perhaps to analyse at some considerable length. I crave the indulgence of the house at this hour, ten-thirty by the clock, to ask for the adjournment of the debate. I could go on, but I confess to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the hon. members of this house, that I have been greatly stirred by parts of the speech of the former Minister of National Defence. I have a keen desire to analyse that speech to do him justice and to commend portions of it- and it will be the major portion-in which he laid the position before this parliament. Therefore, sir, I propose at this time, with, I believe, the concurrence of the Prime Minister, the adjournment of the debate.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, November 29, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this house will aid the government in its

War Effort-Government Policy
policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort, and the proposed amendment of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Quelch.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I wish to make a ruling on the amendment to the amendment, submitted by Mr. Quelch seconded by Mr. Shav.
The motion before the house is:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
Mr. Graydon moved an amendment as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following words substituted instead thereof: this house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice.
Mr. Quelch moved an amendment to the amendment. The first paragraph of the subamendment is as follows:
The unqualified assurance to our men on the battle fronts that they will receive at once ample material supplies, and adequate reinforcements; and the use of all persons in any of Canada's armed services in any theatre of war in which they may be required.
It has relevancy in that it refers to the motion and the amendment, but it is qualified by the other sections of the subamendment which deal with policies following the war, and have no relevancy either to the main motion or to the amendment. One cannot approve and disapprove the same document and the amendment to the amendment must be considered in its entirety.
Paragraphs 2, 3, 4 and 5 of the amendment to the amendment should be brought before the house in the form of a substantive motion. The object of the motion is to aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort. The amendment to the amendment deals with matters which are intended as peace-time policies.
I would refer to a decision by the Hon. Mr. Black, the Speaker, on May 4, 1934, page 640 of Beauohesne's third edition, which decided that on a motion to appoint a select committee for the purposes of considering the accounts of a government-owned railway, an amendment to empower the committee to consider also the accounts of a private company is out of order and should be brought before the house as a substantive motion.
On May 21, 1940, I gave a ruling which will be found on page 647 of Beauchesne's third edition. I ruled an amendment out of order on the ground that an amendment must
not raise any question which can only be raised by a distinct motion, after notice.
The amendment to the amendment which we are now considering raises questions which can only be raised by a motion after notice.
Yesterday I ruled the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) out of order, and the opinions which I then gave are equally applicable to the amendment to the amendment which we are now considering and I would repeat if the house accepts the subamendment the main amendment would be eliminated and the only question before the house would then be the main motion as amended by the subamendment. The result would be that the mover of the main amendment would be deprived of his right to obtain an expression of opinion either original or in an amended form by the house on the policy stated in his amendment.
For these reasons I rule that the subamendment is not in order.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I rise to-day to take part in a debate on a subject which is one of the most important that has ever been brought before the house or the country. I do so because I realize that tremendous events are now taking place and that the possibility of good or ill that may flow from the deliberations in this House of Commons at this special session may be of the greatest importance. I hope that what I may say to-day will be wise and judicial. I trust that I shall not be offensive even if I speak strongly.
I rise first to say that the issue before this house and the country-and in my view the only issue-is that which relates to steady reinforcements for the armed forces overseas, and that no other issue should' be allowed to becloud it. Notwithstanding the invitation of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) to curtail the discussion, I believe it is imperative and in the national interest that the views of my colleagues and myself should be fully presented to this house. I reaffirm the fundamental principle that is embodied in the amendment to the resolution now before the house, namely, that reinforcements for our armed forces overseas should be pressed to its ultimate and logical conclusion without limitations of any character or equivocations or reservations, mental or otherwise.
I wish to say further that the offer which was made yesterday by my colleague, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) on behalf of the leader of the National Progres-
War Effort-Government Policy

give Conservative party, to cooperate with any government that will fully implement the policy of adequate and immediate reinforcements, still stands, and it is not a mere political gesture.
In the course of his speech on Monday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that the convulsion in the country was an engineered convulsion. So far as I am able to ascertain from the facts I deny that assertion from A to Z. I say that the convulsion which has swept over this country in the last three or four w eks, and which is still foremost in the heart and mind of every member of our community who is thinking about it-and I believe that includes the entire population of this country-is based upon a condition that has been growing in intensity ever since D-day. I think this whole thing started because of reports given by servicemen overseas in letters to their relatives. I know that in my own community reports were received from men in the northwestern European theatre of war to the effect that reinforcements then on the ground were wholly inadequate; and I certainly believe the communications which I myself have received from overseas, notwithstanding the position on paper, notwithstanding the theoretical position that has been given to us in secret session and open session, indicate that there is and has been inadequate provision in the northwestern European theatre of war to meet the ever-increasing casualty lists that are flowing in daily. I suggest that the only organized campaign which focused the attention of the public on this immense issue was that which flowed from the Canadian Legion. If there is any body of public opinion in this country that has the right to focus attention on so vital an issue as this, surely it is the veterans of the last war, who know what reinforcements mean, and whose position cannot be better emphasized than was done by the magnificent speech of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) last evening.
To say that there is a cabal among certain elements of this country outside of this house who want to seize the reins of power is to say something that could not be farther from the truth. If that were so certainly some communications would have been had with the membership of this party. I want to give assurance to this house and to the country that none of us has ever been approached to form a conspiracy simply for the purpose of getting rid of the present Prime Minister. What public opinion outside of this house has done *-and expression has been given to it by the great metropolitan newspapers of Canada-is to focus attention on a critical situation which

we now know existed, and which still exists and will not be adequately taken care of by the right-about-face policy of the Prime Minister and those of his cabinet colleagues who have turned face -with him.
I listened to the Prime Minister's speech with the utmost attention. I shall have something to say about it presently. During the course of that speech I asked myself this question when he was making a plea, not directed to me especially but to his own faltering followers, to the effect that they should vote confidence in him.

speechtext:
Possibly
they will. But he was making a plea to his followers to vote confidence in him, not on the policy that, was in effect on November 22 when he put his motion on the order paper. What was the policy then? The policy then was a continuation of the voluntary system of reinforcements for the army overseas. Is there any dispute about that? That was the fundamental basis of the resolution of confidence that is now before this house. Then something happened, to use the words of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power)-and I regret that he is not in his seat-in a matter of moments, and a right-about-face was made by the Prime Minister and the majority of his colleagues. A position was taken which the hon. member for Quebec South felt he could not support; that was, they reversed the traditional policy of the Prime Minister and his government which had been in effect since before the war started. They dumped into the debris of past history the policy of voluntary enlistment and adopted, after a gunshot wedding, the, policy they had derided for five long years. In the light of that I ask myself this question. How can I vote confidence in a government which has one policy at halfpast six Thursday evening and another policy, diametrically opposed, at. half-past ten of the same evening?

I have
read Hansard for 1942; I helped make Hansard for 1942, and that brings me to a point which I might as well deal with now. In January, 1942, I had the honour of moving in this house a resolution which I have under my hand, which definitely declared the position of this party with respect to this great man-power question that has been before this country ever since that time, and that has been bedevilled by the actions of this government from time to time. We made it abso-

War Effort-Government Policy
lutely clear that the time would come-and the time has come-when this whole question of reinforcements necessitated by casualties overseas would have to be met man-fashion, and that in our view, having regard to the position which undoubtedly would develop but which did not develop for several years, in due course of time this country would find that the voluntary system would fail and resort would have to be had to the only other alternative. What was the position in 1940? Up to the fall of Dunkirk the war effort of this government was a moderate war effort in accordance with the pledges that were made to their supporters in the province of Quebec.

speechtext: Absolutely. If you do not believe me I will page the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) and he will give you day and date. I am not going to thresh over that old straw, except to follow it up by saying that after Dunkirk there was an entire reversal of the attitude of the government, and very properly so. That was brought about by two reasons. The first was the force of public opinion in Canada, which was shocked at what was taking place on the continent. Then I venture to claim the credit, along with my colleague the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), for having had a very large measure of success in reshaping the policy of this government.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
All right; hon. members may laugh, but as long as I live I will never forget the day my colleague and I interviewed the Prime Minister and made certain requests or demands whatever you wish to call them, and out of those requests and demands there evolved the mobilization act. I asked the Prime Minister to take authority from the parliament of Canada to assume any and every power that might be absolutely necessary for this nation to wage total war, on the theory that not only was this country itself in danger but that civilization was in danger and that the enemy ought to be met and defeated in the only theatre of war where we could make an effective defence of our own country as well as of the principles of liberty and civilization to which we all adhere.
We got the mobilization act, but we got it with a hamstringing limitation that outraged patriotic public opinion in Canada. Public opinion flared up against that limitation. What was the result? The result was the plebiscite. I venture to say that if the Prime Minister had
asked this house to be released from that limitation his request would have been granted unanimously. Perhaps I am too optimistic in saying that, but I know that as far as this party is concerned unanimous consent would have been given without reservation. Well, we had the plebiscite. The Prime Minister said that the plebiscite gave his government no mandate for the inception of a policy of conscription. On the face of the technical aspects, I agree. On the face of the question submitted to the electors, technically speaking that is correct. But the reaction of public opinion to the vote, from one end of Canada to the other save and except one portion of this nation, was that the government had a green light and a mandate from the people of this country to go ahead and put into effect a man-power .policy that would result in the total utilization of all our forces, our man-power forces, in every field of human endeavour that was necessary to win this war. The Prime Minister resisted that mandate in and out of season, in and out of his cabinet. From his own standpoint he was justified, because the Canadian army was not in action and up to D-day the casualties were very limited.
I well remember the debate on bill 80. I well remember the stand taken by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) on that occasion. I well remember the speech made by the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston). I well remember the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and I well remember the speech made by the hon. member for Quebec South. All these hon. gentlemen endorsed the principle for which we were contending at that time, but in order to preserve the solidarity of the cabinet and because at that time the pressure for reinforcements was not as great as it would have been had the casualties been greater, they were content to let the situation ride on the theory that when it became tense; when the situation became such that reinforcements were required, the necessary order in council would be adopted by the government of this country, and these men of the home army I shall not insult them by calling them zombies; I never have done so publicly-would be utilized to the fullest possible extent as a result of the conditions that would then exist. That was the meaning taken by the hon. member for Prince from the Prime Minister's statement, "not necessarily conscription, but conscription if necessary." If necessary why? Not because of conditions in Canada; not because of conditions in the Liberal party ^in Canada or certain supporters of the Liberal party, but because of conditions in the actual theatre of

War Effort-Government Policy
war, where men were going to be needed urgently and in full measure. That was the understanding of ninety per cent of the people of this country in regard to the Prime Minister's reservation.
The Canadian forces went into action in Italy some thirteen or fourteen months ago; I have not the exact date in mind. A very much larger force had the honour and the glory of taking part in the invasion of northwest Europe. I knew then in my own heart- and I am sure every hon. member in the house who is true to himself, his own thoughts, his own reason and his own convictions was in the same position-that the sternest part of this great European war was about to begin, and that that was the only theatre of war in which this great battle would be waged and won. I knew in my own heart, as I am sure the former minister of national defence knew in his, that when that great day came, the casualties suffered by the gallant Canadian army, and especially the infantry branch, would not only carry sadness to a great many homes in Canada, but would also place additional responsibilities upon the government of the day to see to it that the position of our fighting men was taken care of to the utmost extent of the capabilities of the Canadian people.
That is what I am striving for to-day. I am not going to thresh out here this afternoon the old question of conscription, because I have neither the time nor the desire to do it. We already have conscription. And by the same token the principle of conscription was written into the laws of this country before parliament was summoned. I point to the Militia Act, the terms of which are invoked by the order in council now before parliament. The principle of conscription is inscribed in the mobilization act, now that the limitation is taken away from it.
Let us not deceive ourselves by saying that this is a debate on conscription. Conscription is an accomplished fact; it is the law of Canada and the will of the Canadian people. Now we have before us this one problem: How shall we give effective support to the law of the country and the will of the great majority of the people of Canada? Immediately we are faced with this problem: How shall we fully implement the law, and action under the law?
That was the issue round which the battle waged in the cabinet. I know what the oath of a privy councillor is; I know it is a most searching oath. But the lid was opened first, to a degree, by the Prime Minister in his radio speech, and then by the hon. member

for Prince. And surely the hon. member for Prince was justified, as he claimed, in lifting the veil further. Through the correspondence we have had revealed the issue raised within the cabinet. But I suspect that only half the story has been told. I suspect that we do not know all of it, and that we probably never will. I am not pausing now to ask that it all be told; but I do know that the minister of national defence of that day parted company with his colleagues on a matter of profound and fundamental principle.
I shall not allude to the manner of his going. Some say he was kicked out; possibly it can bear that interpretation. But I prefer to say this-and to say it in his honour-that when he found he could not carry the convictions of his leader in the policy which he advocated, one which he knew was fundamental and absolutely necessary, man-fashion he resigned his portfolio, although it was the wish of his heart to carry the war effort through to its conclusion. That privilege was denied him. It was denied on what grounds? On the ground that the Prime Minister determinedly set his face against full implementation of the pledge he made to the country in June of 1942.

the Prime Minister for allowing me to proceed, because there are some things I still desire to say, though not at afty great length.

Is there any doubt in the mind of any hon. member in this house who heard that speech, is there any doubt in the minds of the public generally who have now read that speech, that the hon. member for Prince, the former minister of national defence, was right in the position he took, and that the Prime Minister was wrong in the position he took? The hon. member for Prince demonstrated beyond peradventure that that policy of voluntary enlistment had failed. Any man who assumes that he did not prove the proposition which he laid down, which he supported by evidence that has not been controverted' here, is wholly at fault, if my judgment and intellect are to be trusted. I want to say to the Prime Minister that his radio speech and the communications he had with his former Minister of National Defence were, in the light of the speech of the hon. member for Prince, based upon false premises, upon premises which he cannot substantiate here.
As a lawyer who has for many years been accustomed to producing evidence in court I think I know something about the question of the weight of evidence and the credibility which should be attached to evidence. It is my view, and I hold it without equivocation or reservation, that the hon. member for Prince proved last night, and in the interchange of letters, beyond peradventure that which I am striving for to-day, that is, the establishment of the principle of reinforcements and more- reinforcements now for the men who are fighting overseas for you and me. The situation outlined by the Prime Minister in his radio speech and in his correspondence was intended to support and uphold a position which he changed in a matter of minutes. For what policy are we now voting?

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: There may be another before the vote.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: I could not vote confidence on the basis of the policy of the government on November 24 because that was a negation of the facts as we knew them then and know them now. That position has been abandoned. Why? Has it been abandoned on a question of principle? I put that to the Prime Minister. Did he abandon his support of the voluntary system because he believed that the voluntary system was no longer a good system? The answer cries ''No" to high heaven. He reaffirmed his faith in the voluntary system in the speech he made to this house on Monday afternoon last. Was it on the basis that General McNaughton, himself a declared believer in the voluntary principle, could do the impossible? General McNaughton was very frank with us in the house. Of course he would be frank because he is not a politician-yet. He will rapidly become one if he stays in the company he is now keeping. I have no doubt in the world that General McNaughton was sincere when he expressed the opinion to the Prime Minister, and subsequently to the public of Canada, that he could get volunteers for the reinforcements so urgently needed overseas. I do not question his sincerity in that connection; all I question is his judgment. I will go further and say that when he made the statements he did at Arnprior and at Ottawa, General McNaughton had been away from the front for over a year; he was out of touch with public opinion in the country, and he had not the true facts of the position before him.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: He said so himself.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Subsequently in this chamber he admitted in man-fashion that his information was wrong, and he reversed his position. The government suddenly, in a matter of minutes, to use the language of the hon. .member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), reversed its traditional policy and decided to work under the order in council that was laid on the table on Thursday last. That certainly was a sudden conversion. Talk about the conversion of Saul of Tarsus; Saul had nothing on the Prime Minister of this country. I have never known as complete a reversal of policy in the whole history of this Dominion of Canada. I defy you to find a parallel for the proposition which has been presented here.
They were either right on November 22, or they were wrong. They were either right on November 24, or they were wrong. According to the Prime Minister, and according to the statement made by General McNaughton, they came to the conclusion that they were

War Effort-Government Policy
wrong in their premises, and they then took up the policy that they had derided for years; they adopted it as their own child. They did this notwithstanding the fact that they had both given expression to the conviction that the policy was in every respect a bad policy for Canada. They became the foster fathers of this policy.
I ask the right hon. gentleman and I ask the members of this, house: how can you trust those two men to put into effect a policy of great national import when they have both declared that they have no belief in it, a policy which the Prime Minister has condemned for years and years? How can I vote confidence in a government which is putting into effect a policy in which the leader says he does not believe? The two things are incompatible. All you have to do to get the answer is to state the proposition. There cannot be any faith in a government which, at the point of a gun levelled against them by members of the cabinet itself, some of whom I am looking at this very afternoon, reverses itself overnight. What faith can this country have that the government will put such a policy into effect and carry it through to a successful conclusion, without evasion, without equivocation or discrimination? It just cannot be done; the people of this country understand that it cannot be done, and I would like to prophesy that it will not be done.
I regret more than I can say, and I say this more in sorrow than in anger, that the member for Prince who made such a valiant defence of the principles and objective which he espoused, and who last night established beyond peradventure the soundness of the position that he advocated in the cabinet and outside-I regret that he has retired to Torres Vedras and that he is not going to carry through. That is not- like the member for Prince! The member for Prince has always impressed me' as having great determination. If you do not believe that, just look at the shape of his jaw! I have always understood from my study of physiognomy that a man with a jaw shaped like his had great determination in his make-up, and I am sure he has. But I regret to say that the member for Prince is not carrying through. The country expects something more from him. He realizes that the carrying through of the policy which he extracted at the point of a gun from the Prime Minister depends upon certain colleagues of his in the cabinet, and I am just afraid that those colleagues have not enough strength or power in the cabinet to see that that policy is carried through. I am afraid
that when the meeting of this house is over and there comes a lull, when things are quieted down in the country, as the government hopes they will quieten down, the policy of reinforcements laid on the table on Thursday last will be more or less forgotten.
I have read and reread that order in council, and I say that it is not a clear, distinct and unequivocal statement of the principle which the member for Prince asked for. The member for Prince asked that all these N.R.M.A. men be made available for active service overseas in the theatres of war-all of them, not merely 16,000. He asked that all of them be made immediately available. Has he got that? I suggest that a proper interpretation of that- order in council shows that it is directive and not mandatory, that it may be implemented or may not be fully implemented in spite of the declaration made here last night and by General McNaughton; and if the government can get enough of these home defence troops tQ volunteer they will be used, as General McNaughton told us in his first statement, which impressed me as the truth, only to make up the deficit. There is no assurance in the order in council or anywhere else that the 'rest of these N.R.M.A. men who are physically fit will ever be utilized in the active army of this country-and that is what we want. We want this order in council to go all-out, and we want the government to implement it on that basis. I venture to say to the Prime Minister that the public will not be satisfied with anything less. If that is negatived by the government it will only be transferring the battlefield to the country, because the veterans of this war, and I am sure from my information the men overseas, want that and just that and nothing less than that, and will never be satisfied with anything less than that.
And so I tell the Prime Minister that we intend to press with all the force and all the vigour at our command to have him go all-out in the utilization of the home army men so that there never may be any doubt that there will always be a reservoir from which reinforcements may from time to time be dispatched overseas to take care of critical situations on the battlefield which I am' afraid are only just beginning. Is there anybody within sound of my voice to-day who believes that this war will be over in January, February or March?

War Effort-Government Policy

I hoped it would be. I have loved ones over there, like everyone else in this house, and we all hoped that we would see them again. But there is no certainty as to when victory will come. Take a map and sketch a circle around Germany and you will agree with me that the battle zone to-day is just on the perimeter of fortress Germany. The heart of Germany, shattered as it may be by the gallant bombings of the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F., is' still unconquered and our men have a long way to go before they march into Berlin. The casualties will be heart-rending to many. The thought I have in the back of my mind is that we must never in word or thought or by lack of action desert them, and we can only fully support them if we have an order in council passed that will once and for all make these men available as reinforcements in any theatre of war. I am not including Japan as one of those theatres of war, because that is another consideration altogether. I am reminded, however, that Canada was one of the first of the belligerent nations to declare war against Japan, and that Canada probably has done the least among the allied nations to make war on Japan.

The only issue now is that full implementation shall be given to the policy that the government has now adopted.
War Effort-Government Policy

The former minister of national defence had grave doubts as to the sufficiency and efficiency of this order in council. I shall not take the time of the house to analyse it as I had intended to do. He had grave doubts last night as to the sufficiency of the order in council to carry forward a steady stream of reinforcements out of these N.R.M.A. men before and after the 16,000 approved and now authorized go overseas. That is why he put the Prime Minister under questioning. If hon. members will turn to page 6677 of Hansard they will find what he said. He served notice on the Prime Minister that with the powers of this order in council sanctioned by this house there can be no excuse for trained men not being available. Here are his words:
With the powers under this order in council sanctioned by this house, there can be no excuse that trained men are not available. There can be no excuse for straining at getting the last volunteer or for curtailing such privileges as would he granted when man-power is adequate, and there can be no excuse for not extending further the provisions for leave for men in the battle areas, with long service overseas. There is one thing more, and that is that I doubt if the minister's programme of dispatch is sufficiently rapid to provide all he should have to reestablish reinforcement pools as quickly as that should be done, having regard to the conditions which face him now and in the near future.
He had grave doubts as to the efficiency of the order in council from the point of view of time. I think that is a fair interpretation of it. Then he went on and raised a note of warning to the Minister of National Defence, his successor in office. He said:
He will be held responsible for accelerating the dispatch in every way.
Then he went on:
And one other point I am assuming, unless the Prime Minister states otherwise, that if the government motion carries, the future orders in council specifying additional numbers of men will be passed and put into effect without any reference back again to this house for a vote of confidence or other approval.
The Prime Minister answered:
That is correct.
On what basis does he make that assumption? There is no undertaking by the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence that a further order in council will be passed at the expiration of the order in council sending over the 16,000 men or at any time. Parliament will be away and he will do as he likes. What I wish this government to do before this vote is taken is to give a solemn undertaking that the order in council-and this is what I asked the Prime Minister to do the other night-will be clarified, and that

there shall be not the slightest cause for doubt as to the mandatory authority of the order in council to take every man that is necessary should the occasion arise, and before it arises, to reinforce our men overseas. It is because I think there is an equivocal position, among other reasons, that I propose to vote against this motion of confidence.

speechtext:
Sanity and reason are seldom present at the birth of great national or parliamentary crises. The present instance is a further proof that mass emotional outbursts may develop into a situation such as to cause certain steps to be taken in the govemings of the nation which may in turn incite other people to react in a way such as to cause friction and unrest.
For five years now this country has been at war. For five years this parliament has, on the whole, heard few dissenting voices to a war effort as efficient as it could be made. For five years Canada's participation in the war, whether in the military, in the industrial, in the agricultural, or in the financial field, has been acclaimed by the united nations leaders as a most wonderful achievement, which has taken a young country from the ranks of the new-born nations into the status of a full-grown power which stands now fifth in importance in. military and economic strength. This has been done, Mr. Speaker, because the country as a whole understood not only that Canada's participation in the war was unavoidable, but that it was necessary in order to safeguard the nation against tyranny and slavery. This has been done because the country was whole-heartedly behind the methods followed by the government up to now in its management of the war.
Let us first look at the Canadian accomplishment in the military field, As in all other countries, the navy and the air force were on a voluntary basis; yet Canada has enlarged its navy a. hundredfold and its naval personnel numbers to-day about 90,000. The R.C.A.F. grew rapidly on a voluntary basis under the guidance of the former minister of defence for air (Mr. Power) and has 'become one of the most efficient weapons of the allies. The commonwealth air training plan, also under the authority of the former minister, has been a source of strength of the air forces of Britain and of all the other parts of the commonwealth, This is all part of our country's achievements in the last five years, and it was done without an3r form of compulsion. In passing I may say that the personnel of
the air force now numbers about 200,000. As to the 'Canadian army proper it numbers at present about 400,000 men for general service, which means service overseas, all enlisted by the voluntary system.
After the fall of France we put on the statute book a measure prescribing compulsory service for the defence of Canada in Canada and the territorial waters thereof. Everyone in this country subscribed to this measure, because no Canadian has ever objected to fighting in the defence of his own country. The trouble in Canada started when the conscriptionist elements in the cabinet yielded to the pressure of the Tory press and forced the government to bring in bill 80. Events have proved that there was no real urgency in regard to that bill, since two years and four months elapsed after it was passed, over the opposition of myself and quite a number of other hon. members, 'before further pressure and the threat of a cabinet rupture 'brought about an order in council applying bill 80 to the extent of sending 16,000 men overseas between now and the end of January.
The whole country is in agreement as to the aim and duty of the Canadian people to do all they can to bring the war to a speedy successful conclusion. The only thing, that has ever divided us is the method by which the Canadian army should be recruited for service overseas. In the last war this question split the nation asunder, leaving scars which took years to heal, some of which were still painful when the present war started. The same question split the British nation in 1916; the measure providing, conscription in England was passed only eighteen months after the start of the last war, following a long debate which brought about the resignation of some members of the cabinet on the principle of conscription. In this war it is still the question that divides public opinion in many, if not all, of the British dominions; and the Tory press, the Orange lodges and the technocracy groups cannot blame the French Canadians or Quebec for the situation which exists in other parts of the empire.
I have often thought, Mr. Speaker, that my compatriots of English origin should be thankful for the presence of the French-Canadian element in this country. That is so not only because Canada was discovered, explored and settled by them; not only because, five years after the fall of Quebec, French Canadians refused to help the American colonies in their war of independence, though it might be noted that had they accepted American arms and agreed with
War Effort-Government Policy

the suggestion of the emissaries sent from the Lafayette group in France and fought with the American forces, there were so few British soldiers in the country at the time that there might have been no Canada to-day. English Canadians should be thankful not only because we fought side by side with the British in 1812; not only for the contribution we have made generally to Canadian history, Canadian culture and the development and advancement of the country. They should be grateful to us, as an agent of unity among themselves, as a sort of national scapegoat on which to blame everything that goes wrong. Any isolationist doctrines preached in Canada must always be of French origin, according to the press. In the United States Colonel McCormick, Cissie and Joe Patterson, Hamilton Fish, Lindbergh and even the beautiful Clare Boothe Luce can always be called isolationists; there is never any attack on their racial group. In Canada, however, if some man of the type of Groulx or Laurendeau gives an isolationist statement to the press, immediately you see all through English Canada, "French Canadians against war effort." They blame it on the whole racial group.
In Britain, in Northern Ireland, in Australia, in New Zealand and in South Africa, people have opposed to the limit conscription during this war, and they have prevented the passage of measures imposing conscription for; overseas service in some of the dominions, while in South Africa they have prevented the imposition of conscription of any kind; yet there are no French Canadians in those countries, there is no Quebec that can be blamed. In Canada a question which could remain only the subject of discussion as to the merits or demerits of a principle has become the cause of racial disunity and parochial prejudices.
Let us see first from official statements what opinions were expressed on the subject by leaders in the British isles and the commonwealth. Two years ago during the debate on bill 80 I gave many such quotations; to-day I shall give only one. In 1916 Mr. Asquith, the prime minister, was speaking in the House of Commons. At that time, sixteen months after the beginning of the war, he said:
My objection to the employment of compulsion for the purpose of recruiting the army under existing' conditions has not been based at all upon abstract attachment to a principle. It is based upon an entirely different ground, namely, that the employment of compulsion under existing conditions would forfeit what I regard to be of supreme and capital importance, that is,

the maintenance of the national unity. That again is an abstract objection, but when translated into concrete terms-
I beg of my hon. friends that they note this. Many hon. members are smiling these days, when we talk of national unity, but this is not just an abstract expression. Mr. Asquith said:
-when translated into concrete terms it means this; if you were to apply, I do not speak of any particular method, but any method of coercion or compulsion, without something in the nature, I will not say of universal, but of general consent, you would defeat your oven purpose.
That was not the statement of a nationalist from Quebec; it was the statement of the prime minister of Great Britain during the last war.
When I spoke during the debate on bill 80 two years ago and gave the quotation I just read one hon. member asked: "Can you quote Churchill on this?" I had not under my hand the book m which I could find that reference, so I had to let it pass at that time. To-day I have it, however. On May 20, 1941, when Mr. Churchill was asked in the House of Commons whether he would not reconsider the question of conscription for Northern Ireland and whether he would make any statement about it, he replied:
The question has for some time past engaged the attention ,of His Majesty's government, and I hope to be in a position to make a statement on the first sitting day after this week.
The next week, on May 27, 1941, Mr. Churchill said:
My right hon. friend the member for Antrim had a question on the order paper about the application of conscription to Northern Ireland. I said a week ago that this matter had been engaging our attention. We have made a number of inquiries in various directions, with the result that we have come to the conclusion that at the present time, although there can be no dispute about our rights or about the merits, it would be more trouble than it is worth to enforce such a policy.
This is the statement in the British House of Commons by none other than the foremost leader of the allied nations in this war. Now let us go to Australia. Unfortunately we have not all the Hansards of Australia, but I believe hon. members will trust me if I quote from the Journal of the Parliaments of the Empire. After the first year of the war the government of Australia decided to recall all their troops, serving on all fronts, and to bring them back to Australia. They already had. as we have in this country, compulsory service for Australia. On February 12, 1943, they passed a law imposing compulsion for service in the southwest Pacific zone, but a few months later a proposal was made by a

XVar Effort-Government Policy
member named Blackburn, who I do not think possibly could have been French, in these words, and I would ask hon. members to mark the similarity between Australia and Canada in this regard:
That this house, reaffirming the policy upon which the majority of its members were elected, oppose the imposition of any form of compulsory service outside of Australia and the territories of the commonwealth.
That was at a time when they had American armies and the American navy fighting alongside them in the Pacific. And yet people got up in the house and proposed that the application of conscription for the south Pacific zone be restricted, and that from now on they would all stay in Australia as it was when the conscription law was first enacted.
Again let me quote from the Journal of the Parliaments of the Empire, because we do not have the official report of debates of South Africa for these last years. Not later than March of this year Prime Minister Smuts declared this, as reported in the Journal:
The Prime Minister went on to speak of South Africa's war effort, and explained that while they had to-day larger forces in the field than at any previous period in the war, it was not easy to keep them up to full strength for various reasons. For one thing, they were volunteer forces. They could not conscript their armies, their people, as other countries were doing.
That was in a British dominion that has filled its engagements. There was no conscription, and no French Canada which prevented it.
Now we come to something of even greater interest, and more closely connected with the situation in Canada. I again quote from the Journal of the Parliaments of the Empire, where, under date of March 3, 1943, I find this, in summarizing the speech of Mr. S. G. Holland, leader of the opposition in New Zealand:
He had said before, and he repeated it, that there was no justification for the number of men under arms in New Zealand.
Then the Minister of Industries and Commerce for New Zealand, the Hon. D. G. Sullivan, is summarized in this fashion:
They were critical of the extent to which men were being used in the armed forces-there was a cry that not enough was being done. Now there had come a sudden change in the criticism, and they were told that the government had entered into too heavy commitments. .	.	.
To-day-
And that was in 1943-
*-it looked as if the security of the dominion was better than it had been and might justify some relaxation in the matter of military commitments. But they could not afford to relax entirely.
That was a year and six months ago. There was a member of the government speaking of relaxing. The government could not say what numbers of men they were going to allot to the various services, and that the rest of the people were to go into industry.
Now let us come to the causes of differences of attitude in Canada on the methods of recruiting the army-and not as much on the question of principle as on its reaction among certain elements in this vast country which comprise one-third of the population. I refer of course to my own French-Ganadian compatriots.
I recall earlier that during the American revolutionary war French Canadians remained loyal. The same happened in 1812, when we fought side by side with our friends the British who were in Canada. But from 1812 to 1898 there .has been no war in which Canada has been called upon to participate. For eighty-six years, for three generations of men there has been no war in which Canada, either for the empire or for its own defence, has been called upon to participate. Now, as you know very well-and it is a known historical fact-during those eighty-six years no encouragement was ever given to anybody of French-Canadian origin in Canada to join the army, for fear he might use unwisely some knowledge he would have acquired, despite what they did in 1812. But we have in a club to which I belong in Quebec, the Garrison club, a frame containing the names of men who were on the walls of Quebec on such-and-such a night in 1850. In that list there is not one French name. There have been a few sons of families who had not chosen to make serious studies in law or medicine, or one of the other arts, who went into the army and took commissions, but we had a very small number of militiamen. In fact I discovered the other day that one of my ancestors was in the army in 1792, and died while serving. I cannot be sure whether he died at war or not.
These things are to be taken into account. In 1898 when the South African war broke out there was little sympathy for it in French Canada. We now find that a large proportion of broadminded British people believe that the South African war was a war of conquest and an unjust war. Canada stood in the same position as it did at the start of the present cabinet crisis. Laurier was faced with a difficult position and menaced with a rupture of his cabinet, and he had to send forces over there. So far as the break up of unity in the country on military matters is concerned, that is the starting point.

War Effort-Government Policy

That is the moment the trouble started. Youl saw Bourassa going around Quebec, spreading! trouble, spreading nationalist sentiment and separatist sentiment. You saw this sentiment growing and growing in the elections of 1904, 1908 and 1911. In 1911 they succeeded in destroying Laurier in that province. Some of our opponents say that the Liberals are responsible because in Quebec the people are against conscription. I would ask whether or not the Liberals, by keeping for French Canada a political outlet in following a large national party, have not served the country well. If they had not taken the attitude they took in 1917 the whole of the province of Quebec would have gone nationalist and separatist, and we French Canadians would have suffered from it. Canada as a whole would have suffered. But due to the broadmindedness and the understanding of Laurier, Who gave them an outlet in a national party, French Canadians were kept in a frame of mind which permitted them to collaborate in confederation, and they carried on for twenty-seven years in that fashion.
We are not responsible for conscription. That has been started by the nationalists, and by those people who believe that there should be two countries in Canada instead of one. But we of the Liberal party have fought against it. Laurier maintained national unity. He felt it was his duty to maintain a political outlet by means of a national party for French Canadians. And because of that attitude we were able afterwards to reestablish and reunite with the rest of Canada in cordial relations, and to play the part which has been played, under this government, from 1921 to the present.
I now come to the situation the government had to face prior to its passing order in council 8891. For five years, as I said before, the country has contributed an efficient war effort under the guiding hand of the Prime Minister. Yet for five years a powerful machine has been at work trying to undermine public confidence in the Prime Minister-and I say this, no matter what the hon. member for York-Sun-bury (Mr. Hanson) may say. I say that it has been at work trying to undermine public confidence in the Prime Minister, and to convince the country that everything would go wrong unless a union government were formed, or unless a Tory administration were in authority. A rumour-spreading, lie-whispering, mud-slinging monster has run amok unscrupulously risking to wreck the whole effort of the country, and with only one aim in view: the destroying at all costs of confidence in the Prime Minister, and the promotion by all means of Tory Conservative interests.

This campaign, waged relentlessly has laid the foundation for the attacks repeatedly made in the house in the name of patriotism and national duty on the methods followed by the government in recruiting the army. Unable to attack the governmental record of administering the war effort without scandal and the squandering of public moneys; unable to find fault with the economic policies of the government; unable to deny the wonderful industrial production directed by the government, which supplied our armies and those of our allies with weapons of war; unable to attack the achievements brought about in the agricultural field by the wise planning of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner); unable to question the efficiency of the management of the air training plan and the R.C.A.F. by the former Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), or the splendid record of the Canadian navy, the Tory Conservative machine has pinned its hope of success on dividing Canadians among themselves on the question of conscription for overseas service. The old motto, "divide in, order to govern," was again to the fore. No matter how much the welfare of the country would have to suffer, no matter how much the war effort might be hampered, the one question, the only question that was' apt to divide public opinion in Canada had to be brought forward and made into a symbol of disunity. Distrust had to be sown in one part of the country against the other, and vice versa.
While in English Canada the Tory organization, supported by the Tory press, represented the government as not waging an efficient war effort, and acceding to the views of Quebec in the matter of compulsory service, in French Canada the people who through all their political life had been friendly to the Tories are masquerading as independents. They are accusing the government, and I use their own words, of "betraying Quebec." They criticize the whole war effort and accuse those of us who have supported all government measures exclusive of bill No. 80 of being tools of English Canada and of causing great harm to our racial group. You will see them probably during this debate doing the same thing and asking us to disapprove all that we have co-operated in doing in the execution of the war effort. They have campaigned against Godbout in the same way and have based all their attacks on Godbout's approval of the war effort. The present premier of Quebec, Mr. Duplessis, has said that if he had been premier at the time the N.R. M.A. would not have been enacted, that it was not necessary; that bill No. SO would

War Effort-Government Policy
not have been enacted because he would have been strong enough to prevent it. Now the cry is raised in Quebec: "Duplessis is back in power and the government has been forced to implement bill No. 80 and Duplessis could not prevent it."
We therefore have to face a monster with two heads and two bodies but with one common aim-to destroy confidence in the government in order to get into power.
I think I can say that most of us in Quebec of the Liberal faith have done our best toward the war effort. We have fought and campaigned to have all the measures pertaining to the carrying out of the war understood and approved by our population. The only point on which we differed from our colleagues of the other provinces was in connection with bill No. 80 and the latest order in council authorizing the sending of N.R.M.A. men overseas.
If I believed that when that order in council was passed the security of Canada was at stake unless we sent a few more thousand men overseas, I could have approved it and tried to have it understood in my province. But I cannot believe that, nor can I believe that without these few men the outcome of the war will be changed or even delayed.
The whole trouble is that our military experts want to make good the commitments they have made, even if they prove to be too large. I think personally, although I am not a strategist or technician in warfare, that the spreading out of our forces on two vastly different theatres of war was a great error of judgment. Instead of having two divisions in the Mediterranean area in Italy and three l'n western Europe, I think we should have had them all on the same front in a Canadian army. For one thing it would simplify the question of reinforcement pools, and, secondly, it would permit the keeping of three or four divisions in the line while one or two were withdrawn temporarily "to refit, to reequip, to rest, to recuperate and to refill the gaps in their ranks," as was said by the former minister of national defence for air.
By sending these divisions alternately to the front and withdrawing others, our men would not be subjected to the strain they have had to endure. The sending of 16,000 unseasoned troops will not change the procedure followed at present or make for more security for those who are now there. If we have taken too large a chunk of the front, let us be sensible and correct our mistake. With a population of twelve million, Canada has not at its disposal the vast reservoirs of men that the Russians or the Americans have, and cannot be expected to compete with them.
100-421J
I am not in such bad company in saying this. As I stated earlier, the Minister of Industries and Commerce for New Zealand, speaking for the government, and the leader of the opposition, both spoke of relaxing their military effort because the country was no longer in danger. Canada is no more subjected to danger from the outside than is New Zealand. I admit that we have to do our utmost in other theatres of war to help bring victory about, but let us not do it in i way to endanger the success of the whole war. effort, industrial, agricultural as well as military, by enforcing methods which do not, as Mr. Asquith said in 1916, meet with the approval of all the population or which, iij the words of Mr. Churchill, speaking of northern Ireland, would cause more trouble than it would produce good results.
I personally am convinced that by order in council 8891 the government has taken steps that were not necessary for the security of the country or imperative for the winning of the war; therefore I cannot approve the action of the government in this regard.
Let us look at another element that entered into the decision of the cabinet and to which both the Prime Minister and General McNaughton have referred-the mounting wave of public opinion, growing into an hysterical panic in certain parts of the country, and provoked and kept alive by the Tory press. This is all based upon the wrong belief that unless the N.R.M.A. recruits are sent overseas, the sons and relatives of good patriotic Canadians will be incurring more dangers in the battle line. The creation of this artificial state of mind will bring grave responsibilities upon those who have built it up for political purposes. I would be the last to ignore the seriousness of such a condition prevailing in the country. I despise those who have brought it about, but I have sympathy for the government which has had to face it. I understand the difficulties, but I am forced to say in all honesty that if such a situation existed, if such an impasse had been reached when public opinion was dangerously split into opposite and irreconcilable views, if a change in policy had to be faced, it might have been better, in order to preserve the confidence of the nation in those whose business it is to run the country, to give way to others to apply such measures.
I say this reluctantly because I have more confidence in the Prime Minister than in any other man in public life, and I know that my constituents, except for the passing of bill 80 and order in council 8891, even now have more confidence in the Prime Minister than in any other leader. They believe he is a

War Effort-Government Policy
good administrator of the nation, yet they cannot understand or excuse a man whose personal opinions are admittedly, even at this moment, favourable to the voluntary method, weakening under the pressure of his conscrip-tionist ministers. My fear is that this conduct will increase that tendency in the public of a province to distrust the statements and declarations of public men, while in the rest of the country it will appease but temporarily the worries of those whose attitude on this question has reached a state of hysteria.
I regret all the more that I feel compelled to say this to the Prime Minister because my whole mature life has been spent in the surroundings of this cabinet. I arrived in Ottawa in 1925 and I was here until 1930. I was here again from 1935 to 1940. All that time I was under the then minister of justice, the late Mr. Lapointe. I have seen the close association of Mr. Lapointe with the Prime Minister. I have seen them working in harmony and unity, whether in Canada in an effort to bring about better relations in this country between the component elements of the nation, or whether it was in London during the imperial conferences of 1926 and 1937. They then worked in unison to have this nation recognized as an independent state equal to Great Britain and united to the mother country only by bonds of a common allegiance to the crown.
I know the role the Prime Minister has played in the building of a strong and prosperous Canada. I consider that his imprint on Canadian history will be considered the most remarkable of modern time. I am convinced of his sincerity when he says:
If there is anything to which I have devoted my political life it is to try to promote unity, harmony and amity between the diverse elements of this country.
I think history will recognize that that is so.
I wish to say in passing that I am convinced that had not Lapointe's health been impaired and had not his death deprived Canada of one of its most able sons, his weight in the councils of the nation would have strengthened the will of the Prime Minister to prevent some of the measures which have divided us and at times taken our minds away from Canada's wonderful accomplishments in the war. Never has a man's passing away been so sadly felt, especially when we realize that his presence might have been such an agent of cohesion and of unity. [DOT]
It is all very well to quote some of his words, but I want to say to the Prime Minister that other words spoken by him have had even a stronger influence upon his province. I need not quote them to-day, now

that conscription is law, and it is the duty of every good Canadian not to arouse people against the law of the land.
I regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot see my way clear to voting with the government on this occasion. I have said and I will repeat that I am taking this stand reluctantly because of my admiration and sympathy for the Prime Minister. I wish also to state that I am not doing this only to please the people I represent, because my proximity to public men, to which I referred a moment ago, has taught me that public favour is fickle and of little consolation if one's acts are not based on conviction. The attacks of the so-called Independents and the Nationalists in Quebec on the former minister for air, who made the painful but conscientious gesture of parting with friends on a matter of principle, are another proof that the value of one's actions is always judged according to a person's prejudices and is readily distorted for political motives. I am taking this stand solely because in conscience I think it is the only logical one for me to take.
I repeat that I have confidence in the Prime Minister. .1 will go so far as to state that I do not think that Canada could have at this moment a better leader. I am convinced also that he is best suited of any national leader to represent Canada at the peace table and to reorganize things in the post-war period. But as I said, I consider that voting for the main motion as it is drafted means an approval of all the government's actions up to the date of the vote, and that includes the passing of order in council 8891, and no sophism or specious reasoning can change this fact. Just as I have been opposed to bill No. 80, I am not convinced that order in council 8891 is necessary for the security of Canada or advisable at this oUge of the war, having regard to conditions existing in the country. I cannot find it logical for me to vote for the main motion, and even less so, of course, for the amendment moved by the Progressive Conservative leader. But lest this attitude be construed as a disapproval of the efficient pursuit of the war, instead of just a difference of opinion as to the method of recruiting the army and an opposition to conscription for overseas service as provided for in bill No. 80 and in order in council 8891, I do now move, seconded by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker):
That all the words of the amendment after the word "that" in the first line thereof be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house will aid in maintaining an efficient war effort but it does not approve of compulsory service overseas."

War Effort-Government Policy

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to try to answer the arguments of the member for Rellechasse, (Mr. Picard) who has just preceded me and has moved an amendment. All I wish to say is that should the amendment be adopted by the House of Commons the effect would be that Canada would be deserting her boys overseas; and neither I nor any other member of the Progressive Conservative party in this house, nor any Tory so-called from coast to coast, has the slightest intention or deserting our lads overseas no matter whatever else may hefall.
In this debate several members have been rather flippant in their remarks about Tories and Toryism. May I say to them and to this house and to the Canadian people that there is one thing about the Tories and that is that whenever the call to arms goes out, whenever this country is in danger, there is no doubt that the Tories in Canada will do their share and that their sons will give their share of the blood that has to be given. That is one of the main reasons why I am proud to be a Tory.
This afternoon I propose to speak as a representative of one of the greatest constituencies in Canada, a constituency which has already given hundreds of lives in this war and has thousands of young men overseas; also as a representative from a province which has given to the armed forces of this nation 45-8 per cent of its total male population between the ages of eighteen and forty-five- a percentage second only to that of the great little province of Prince Edward Island.
I speak also as an infantryman in the last war and as one who is vitally and personally interested in many of the young Canadians who are now in the infantry or about to go into the infantry units overseas and whose lives are in danger at this time, whose lives may be snuffed out needlessly if the wrong action is taken by the House of Commons on the issue before it to-day.
There are two things upon which the House of Commons and the country should insist now. They are these: in the first place, that the 16,000 N.R.M.A. trained infantry personnel should be dispatched overseas at once, instead of by monthly instalments extending through the spring months to next April. The latter course is the compromise plan that has been proposed by the new Minister of National Defence, Mr. McNaughton, and obviously it means that these fully trained infantrymen are not to be sent to the front as quickly as they could be.
The second is this, that before the house ^adjourns an order in council should be passed
requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel, whether now or hereafter enrolled, to serve in any theatre of war. This is absolutely vital, because, over and above the 16,000 to which reference has been made, there are the 26,000 N.R.M.A. men who are fit to be remustered into the infantry and to go overseas to reinforce our infantry troops there. There are llso young men who will be called up under the N.R.M.A. every day from now, and the position1 should be such that they too can be sent to reinforce the infantry. If this nation is to be certain of reinforcing its men overseas, then these 26,000 men and the new draftees are needed and they will have to go overseas. That has been made perfectly clear not only by the former Minister of National Defence but also by the present minister. These are the two points I wish to stress before the house to-day.
Now I plan to say something in support of my proposals. When the ex-minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) came back from overseas he gave the government a warning. The whole story is out now, or at least there is enough of it to make the picture about as bad as it could be. He warned the cabinet that a substantial number of additional trained infantry were needed overseas. He did not say they were needed in the future; he said they were needed quickly. Repeatedly, in his statements to the public, to the press, and in his speech yesterday, he has stressed the time element and emphasized that there was great urgency. He pointed out that there was going to be a shortage overseas in the units at the end of December or early in January and he asked that N.R.M.A. troops be sent. That was the obvious thing to do, because these N.R.M.A. troops are the best trained infantrymen in Canada. They were and still are the only big block of trained troops available as a reserve either in Canada or overseas. In my own province of British Columbia we have had the sixth division. The men of that division have had training by brigades. They have had battle training and combat training of every description. One of their commanders said a week ago:
We have the largest body of home defence troops here who have been trained purely for combat duty. They are in a high state of training and discipline and would be almost immediately ready to go.
The ex-minister had1 a plan to meet this situation. It was in the first place to send
8,000	fully trained infantrymen during the present month of November. They would have been on the high seas now if he had had his way and the support of the cabinet. He said last night that they were to sail from the

War Effort-Government Policy
shores of Canada on November 27 and they would have been in the line early in January. He explained clearly that they would have made up the shortage in our units at the present time soon after January 1 and would have reestablished the pools in the battle areas.
The second part of his plan was to send
8,000	more of these men during the month of December. By that time they too would have been fully trained infantrymen. That would have meant that in all there would have been 16,000 fully trained infantrymen overseas before the end of the year. Then the remaining 26,000 in Canada were to be remustered under his plan and made available and trained as infantrymen so that they would be ready for overseas as quickly as possible.
In his speech last night, at page 6672, the ex-minister said with reference to these 26,000:
In addition, there were 20.000 N.R.M.A. men considered suitable material as infantry reinforcements who could be remustered and trained as infantry. I thought-
And these are the key words.

no time should be lost in getting them to the United Kingdom.
So that he had a clear-cut honest plan for meeting the tragic situation in which he found our lads overseas.
What was done about it by the cabinet? One would think that any Canadian cabinet would have agreed at once to his plan, thereby giving the boys overseas the benefit of the doubt. We have always contended in .the house that the lads who came back from the last war were entitled to the benefit of the doubt in connection with applications for pension, and so on. That of course was quite correct. How much more important it is that the lads now overseas doing the fighting and offering their lives should get the benefit of the doubt. But they did not get it; the government did not give them the benefit of the doubt. The government had a duty to make certain that these men overseas were adequately reinforced in time. And remember what it meant to take a chance in the way the government did take a chance. It meant risking tired men having to carry on without proper rest out of the line. It meant, as one press correspondent from Italy said the other day, that one volunteer rifleman had to try to do the job of two. It meant that wounded men had to go back to the line before their wounds were properly healed. It meant reinforcements being used who had not had full training or who were in a poorer state of training . than men in the N.R.M.A.
fMr. Green.]
I have here a letter from the Women's Auxiliary of the British Columbia Regiment, the Duke of Connaught's Own Rifles. The menfolk of these women are serving in Holland as the 28th Canadian Armoured Regiment (B.C.R.). This is a regiment with a wonderful record in the last war, the old 7th Canadian infantry battalion, one of the outstanding regiments of Canada. With reference to the situation of their husbands and sons, these women write to me:
Our husbands and sons, as the 28th Canadian Armoured Regiment (B.C.R.), are fighting to-day in Holland. We know-
And these women are in a position to know, because they hear from their husbands and sons.
We know they are understrength and we know too many of the costly expedients that have been adopted in an attempt to keep it and other regiments near establishment.
What was done by the cabinet? There was delay, there was talk, Colonel Ralston was forced out, General McNaughton was brought in. Then there followed three more weeks of delay. Finally the cabinet made a partial surrender and by this very act of surrender proved that Colonel Ralston was right. In fact there is not an hon. member in this house who can honestly say to-day that Colonel Ralston was not right. His stand has been justified time and again since we. assembled here a little over a week ago. The cabinet made this partial surrender only after tremendous pressure from the Canadian people who will not brook uncertainty or delay in giving help to their boys overseas.
There has been quite a lot of talk about disunity in this issue. The suggestion is made that because one province feels one way the other eight should hang back and not press for adequate reinforcements for their boys overseas. If that is to be the law in Canada; if a minority can have that vetoing power over the majority when the lives of the sons of Canada are at stake then there will be no nation of Canada very long. We cannot have a nation if the minority is to have its way on a vital issue of this kind.
On the second day of this session the government brought in a plan which is set out in P.C. 8891. This plan permits them to send overseas a maximum of 16,000 N.R.M.A. personnel ; but the real policy of the government was laid down by General McNaughton the other night and will be found at page 6534 of Hansard, and I draw the attention of the hon. members from my own province to this statement particularly. The real policy is as follows:

War Effort-Government Policy
The policy is to have voluntary service, and there will be an extension of that principle only where it is necessary to met deficiencies in our army overseas.
I emphasize the word "only"1. This plan is a political compromise, Mr. Speaker. There can be no compromise with death overseas. That is out for our boys over there and I suggest that it should be out for the government in Canada.
Then to go on with the plan which was brought in by the new Minister of National
Defence, General McNaughton: In the first place he arbitrarily postpones the shortage to the end of January or early in February. Colonel Ralston said that it would be at the end of December or in January. The evidence we have heard in the house proves conclusively that Colonel Ralston is right. The new minister says: "Oh, no, the shortage is at the end of January or early in February." He cuts Colonel Ralston's first 8,000 fully trained infantrymen almost in half, to 5,000, and they are not to be all N.R.M.A. troops. Some of those are to be general service personnel. Several times during his remarks General McNaughton made it perfectly clear that some at any rate of this first draft would be general service personnel. They are now going in December rather than in November. There you have another month's delay. It all adds up to this, that only 5,000 of those fully trained infantrymen who are so badly needed overseas now, instead of Colonel Ralston's 16,000, are to be available for the critical period. That is the difference between the plans of the former Minister of National Defence and the present one. It is a difference of 11,000 fully trained infantrymen available overseas where they are needed at once.
In the meantime the regular reinforcement stream is to go over. I suppose so many thousand will be going every month. One would have thought that General McNaughton would put in that stream the other fully trained infantrymen. Instead of that this reinforcement stream is to contain only general service personnel. That will be found in the general's statement on page 6571 of Hansard. All of this reinforcement stream are to be general service men who probably are not so well trained as the N.R.M.A. infantrymen in Canada, and many of whom no doubt will be such men as ordnance men or carpenters who have been carrying on really as tradesmen for two or three years. They are in no physical condition to go over right away. They have not the proper military training. They are being rushed over to fill the gap while these fully trained N.R.M.A. infantrymen are being left here. It will also include the young lads
of eighteen and a half years who are being called up and rushed over because they had enough spirit to volunteer for service anywhere. That is what this wonderful new policy means in human lives.
Then under the compromise plan 5,000 N.R.M.A. men are to go over in January less certain general service personnel. We do not know whether there will be 4,000 N.R.M.A. men or 4,500 or 3,500. We have no idea how many there will be.
