subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
No provision whatever is made under the compromise plan for sending over the 26,000 who are to be remustered. Nor is there any provision for sending over those who will be enrolled from now on as N.R.M.A. personnel. Under the order in council there is no power to send these other men over. Before that is done there must be another approval by the cabinet. Perhaps there will have to be an approval for each additional 1,000 men. I should say that for all practical purposes it will be impossible to get such approval. The cabinet is hopelessly

War Effort-Government Policy
divided on this question. Some of them are so bitter and determined about it that they can delay, or perhaps prevent the sending of one man over the 16,000. At best, even if additional men are sent, there will be argument and delay, and at that time there may not be a minister with enough backbone to resign because the right thing is not being done. Then the Canadian people will never know until it is too late how they have been let down by their own cabinet.
Obviously the proper thing and the Canadian thing to do is to provide that these
26,000	men and those enrolled in the N.R.M.A. hereafter can be sent overseas as reinforcements. They are absolutely necessary to make certain that there are adequate numbers of men in the reinforcement pools. This house can do no less than make certain. We have no right to gamble with the lives of our young men. General McNaughton himself stated that there would be a second shortage of men overseas late in the spring or in the early summer. That will be .found at page 6520 of Hansard. He said:
Should casualties continue at the higher rates, there is a possible prospective shortage of fully trained infantry, which may come late in January or early in February next.
And that prospective shortage is under his new compromise plan. Just yesterday we had Prime Minister Churchill warn us that the war would run into the summer. Some time before he had said "early summer". Yesterday he said, "Take out the word 'early' and leave it that the war will run into the summer." Everyone knows the terribly costly fighting there is likely to be in the interim.
Apparently the government is hoping for additional volunteers to meet that second prospective shortage. At the same page General McNaughton said:
The forecasts have not as yet been carried through the summer, and all I can now say is that the situation then %vill depend on the rate of recruiting for general service in December and in the following months.
Yet it is almost certain that all the volunteers enlisting from now on will be required to keep up the regular reinforcement stream. So that I repeat, Mr. Speaker, and I submit that it cannot be disproved, that the new plan is obviously a political compromise. It is a cunning political subterfuge; and if it proves to be an inadequate compromise the mistake will be paid for not by the members of the cabinet or the members of this house, but with the lives of young Canadians overseas, through lack of adequate, trained reinforcements. This house and the Canadian people must never permit any government to gamble with the lives of our sons.

There is only one way to make certain of these adequate and continuous trained reinforcements. That is to do just as we have suggested in our amendment and require all N.R.M.A. personnel, whether now or hereafter enrolled, to serve in any theatre, of war. This is what the great majority of the Canadian people want. This is what the majority of the members of this house want and what they would vote for if they were free of the party whip. The Canadian people have long since seen the folly and deceit of this two-army ' system. No government policy could have been more demoralizing to a people. For some time past the draftee army has been a huge, costly diversion to try to satisfy eight provinces and at the same time not offend Quebec. In both respects it has failed. The man-power policy of the present government has set province against province, the general service soldier against the draftee, and now the new1 compromise plan is setting draftee against draftee. The man-power policy of the Canadian government has brought about the meanest, lowest kinds of compulsion, both in trying to force these young men to go active and now in the treatment of the draftees themselves. It has brought about this situation, that with ample, fully trained infantry in Canada, it has allowed our boys overseas to go short of trained reinforcements and has forced into the line young Canadian lads not fully trained. Yet under the government's compromise policy the N.R.M.A. plan is to continue, if you please; we are still, to have the two-army, system. There is still to be the coaxing and the bluffing of men to go active. There is still to. be all the bitterness, all the inequality of service and sacrifice, and this plan is to be administered by a government that has been greatly weakened by the loss of two of its key. ministers and by the events of the last month.
I appeal to the private members of this house of all parties. We cannot go back to our constituencies leaving this question.of reinforcements in the air, where it is now. We must make absolutely certain in the first place that all the trained infantry draftees are sent over from Canada at once, and in the second place that all N.R.M.A. personnel, whether now or hereafter enrolled, are required to serve in any theatre of war. This would mean that wre would have only one army for Canada, and I hope then we would have an army in which all our young men are given equal treatment. This is the only way to make certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements for our army overseas.

War Effort-Government Policy
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say the -time has come, and in fact is long since past, for the government of Canada, -the House of Commons of Canada and the parliament of Canada to adopt an honest, courageous manpower policy that is in line with the straightforwardness of the Canadian people.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I doubt whether in the whole history of Canada any other administration have made as great a direct contribution, in the loss of members of their own families, as the present administration; and it ill becomes the official opposition to speak as they have through the mouth of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). I would remind them- now, when they are talking in such brave language, that the official opposition went to the country in 1940 under a leader who was not beyond asking for support in the province of Quebec on the ground) that there would be no overseas conscription. He took that stand as the leader of the party, and he was supported by his party. We had the spectacle after that of the acting leader of the party rising in his place in the house and, after being elected on that pledge, inviting the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to break the pledge and to vote for overseas conscription, without in any way consulting the people. That is not consistent
with the language used by the last speaker. Why did their leader at that time take the stand he did, if it was not in order to try to preserve national unity? If it was all right for the late Doctor Manion, the leader of the Conservative party at that time, and under whom they went to the country on- the issue of preserving national unity, is it not a proper procedure to-day?
After a great deal of anxious consideration I have decided) to support and to second the motion moved by the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Picard), that "this house will aid in maintaining an efficient war effort, but that it does not approve of compulsory service overseas."
During the 1940 election campaign I, in company with practically every member of the house, sought the support of the people on the understanding that if they would support our war effort they could rest assured that it would be conducted on a voluntary basis, and that there would not be conscription for overseas service. Not only did we have the assurance of our own leader to that effect, but also the leader of the then Conservative party took that stand, and so did the leader of the C.C.F. I thought I was quite safe in inviting votes in my support, as supporting the government in its war effort, but on the definite promise that there should not be conscription for overseas service. On that basis the support of the whole country was sought.
I well remember that in September, 1939, there was some worry as to whether or not the country could enter the war as a united unit, because of what had happened at the time of the last war when, after war was declared, conscription was imposed by the majority upon the minority. It was because of our experience in the last war that these explicit pledges were given to the Canadian people, in order that they might support the war effort unitedly on that basis.
Those pledges were given in this chamber, in my hearing. And when the premier of one of the provinces of this country attacked the war effort of the government and went to an election on the issue, some of the leading members of the administration went into Quebec and asked for the support of that province of the war on a voluntary basis. In that they achieved an overwhelming victory, and the people of this country from one end to the other applauded- that action. No fault at all was found with it.
Then in 1940 we went to the country on the very same policy. I believe that when people make a deal with their eyes open that deal should be respected. If we have

War Effort-Government Policy
gone into this war as a partnership on an agreed voluntary basis; if we have done our very best on that basis, and received the support of the whole country on that basis, then nothing short of actual danger to the country's existence, or a loss of the war, would justify our departing from that position.
Some people might say it was an unwise thing to do. But if at that time or in 1940 the British government had been asked whether it would rather have the support of Canada on a voluntary basis, through her declaration of war, or have Canada abstain from coming into the war because we could not unite in our effort and because we could not go in on an unqualified basis, but preferred to wait outside the war for two years, as did our great ally to the south, I venture to say that the British government would have said to us, "By all means come in on our side at this crucial time." I am satisfied that we went into it at that time as a united people, because we were able to come to that understanding. I am satisfied, further, that it was because we were at the side of Great Britain in 1940, when she was on the verge of suffering defeat; that it was because Canada stood at her side with the one trained organization in the British isles-the First Division, which was fully equipped and ready to operate, and which was the only organization in that position-and that it was because our airmen were in the skies and our navy in the seas, that the situation was saved. It was just that iittle bit of extra support, I believe, that did it. That was a crucial time, and I believe perhaps the decision of our leaders at the outbreak of war may very well have prevented our losing the war in 1940.
I submit, however, that to-day we are not in that crucial position-and I make that submission most sincerely. The two conditions which might have justified us in not living up to our pledge to the Canadian people to the effect that there would not be compulsion for overseas service, namely the conditions, first that our very existence as a country is in danger or, second, that we are in danger of losing the war, do not now exist.
Having given that pledge, and having received the support of our people, which perhaps enabled us to avoid losing the war at a crucial time, through our being at the side of Britain and our commonwealth, we are not now justified in departing from that pledge merely because we think it is preferable to do otherwise, now that the crisis has passed. I do not think that is a proper way to treat the Canadian people.
It is not a matter of balancing between what is better and what is not so good. If

we are not absolutely in a position where, to save ourselves or to keep from losing the war, we must impose conscription, then I think we are in duty bound to adhere to the pledges we gave at that time. I do not think anyone would argue that we are not now assured of victory. I do not think the sending of those 16,000 extra men for the support of the infantry would make the difference between victory and defeat.

speechtext: I was there last time, and I offered my services and gave them for two years this time. I have given altogether over four years of my life in the service of my country. I do not want any such interruptions.

speechtext: Then you ought to know, in that case.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
And I do know. I know how much harm conscription did when it was attempted at the time of the last war, and just how little good it did.
If I may be permitted to proceed without interruption-and it was quite uncalled for- I would say that Australia, which has been in greater danger than Canada has been, still has not seen fit to impose conscription on her fighting forces for service north of the equator. This means that they are not in a position to send by compulsion men to fight on the islands of Japan, where only Japan can be defeated. Yet Australia manages to keep her forces reinforced, despite the fact that she has not yet imposed conscription. In addition to that there is the fact that she has a far greater proportion of her troops who are not enlisted for overseas services than has Canada at the present time.
Let us now consider South Africa. She manages to fight her war and keep her troops in the field. And I suggest again that South Africa still is in greater danger than Canada is to-day.
Then, what about Northern Ireland? There, again, there is no conscription to send troops for overseas service. And in none of these cases so far as I know have specific pledges been given to the people that there would not be conscription for overseas, as it has been given to the people of Canada.
To insist that we must send 16,000 troops overseas in spite of the pledges we gave at one stage in the war, and to pretend that it is a matter of life and death when, as a result of. actions in which we have taken part, hundreds of thousands of Europeans have been freed, and are now in a position to fight and

War Effort-Government Policy
are anxious to fight is to raise an issue which is unjustified in the light of Canadian history. We are telling them that their efforts must be limited because we cannot give them the arms for which they are pleading. All those people are willing and ready to fight; there are probably 200,000 or perhaps 500,000 Frenchmen and Belgians who are crying out for arms and equipment in order to take their part in defeating the foe.
The argument for overseas conscription is based upon several different grounds. One is that if we do not pass this measure we shall not have adequate reinforcements for five divisions, or practically six divisions when you take into account the corps and army troops. The first thing I should like to suggest is that in my humble judgment the figures which have been given to me do not indicate that we cannot adequately reinforce those five divisions by using men who have already enlisted or are now enlisting, who are trained and ready to go. I am satisfied that a reasonable period of more or less non-active fighting and holding the line which Canadians might be permitted to do in the light of their tremendous exertions since D-day, the acquiring of the channel bases and the capturing of the Scheldt estuary, would enable that lag in infantry reinforcements to be overtaken.
We have been assured over and over again that the over-all reinforcement situation is adequate and satisfactory, that there have been more infantry casualties proportionately than casualties in the other services. We have been told that these people can be remustered and be ready after something like six weeks training. I submit that the deficiency with regard to the infantry could be made up by our troops remaining for a short time more or less inactive to rest as they are at the present time. They would not need to remain inactive very much longer to have a position where all would be well so far as the infantry is concerned. That is leaving out of account what can also be done by remustering.
The suggestion has been made that Canada is under obligation to have her troops fighting continuously in the line. I would call attention to the fact that the United States 9th army just went into action recently. There is no obligation upon an army to be fighting continuously day in and day out. The Canadian corps during the last war withdrew from the line some time in April, 1918, and did not go back until August 8.	*

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: There were some divisions in the line all that time.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
There was one part of one division in the line part of the time, but the
bulk of the Canadian corps was out of the line. It was thrown in at the Germans with such strength as the spearhead of the allied attack on August 8 that it broke them. I fancy that we are entering a period on the western front when climate, mud and so on are going to restrict activities somewhat whether we like it or not. I make the prediction that if the finding of the general staff that the over-all reinforcement situation was satisfactory was correct, that there was sufficient provision for over-all reinforcements, then the present situation is such that with a reallocation of a proper number of men to the infantry there will be no difficulty about providing adequate reinforcements without sending over 16,000 draftees by compulsion. I am not alone in that thought. A member of the cabinet who has resigned, the former minister of national defence for air (Mr. Power), said this when speaking in the house recently:
By all reports, the number required even of infantry, in which arm alone there is said to be a threatened deficiency, is comparatively small. The lowering of the rate of casualties by periods of comparative or total inactivity would wipe out the margin of deficit, if any exists, and restore the balance:
The former Minister of National Defence for Air undoubtedly has the confidence of the people of this country and I feel sure that we can accept his statement at its face value. As far as I am concerned no figures have been given me to show that those figures are incorrect.
There is another thing I should like to draw to the attention of the house. There is nothing magical about five divisions. I find it difficult to understand why at a time when we are actually sending back to civil life thousands and thousands of fully trained aircrew it is felt necessary in order to make a proper war effort to send over 16,000 unwilling infantry men. Put those aircrew men into bombers and fighter planes, and I submit that they will make a greater contribution toward the defeat of Germany than two or three times their number of unwilling draftees who are sent overseas by compulsion by virtue of the decision of this government.
If our only purpose is to make the greatest possible contribution to winning the war, why do we persist in reinforcing five divisions and demobilizing thousands of trained aircrew? It seems to me, and I have a right to this opinion, that it would have been far better to break up one of those divisions if necessary to provide reinforcements that way, and use these trained aircrew who would have done much more damage to Germany than
War Effort-Government Policy

a division which might be broken up in order to provide reinforcements for the boys in the line or 16,000 draftees sent over by compulsion.
There is nothing unchangeable about having five divisions in an army. There is nothing set about it. It is a matter of our making our greatest contribution, and I suggest that the way to do that would be to make use of these men who are willing and anxious to fight instead of putting the emphasis upon these unwilling men.
This demand for conscription for overseas service is also made upon the ground of equality of service and sacufice. Attacks have been made upon French-speaking Canadians and upon other Canadians of foreign origin. The suggestion is made that the only way to have equality of sacrifice is by the use of compulsion. Despite the fact that over fifty per cent of the people of Saskatchewan are of non-English speaking origin, that province does not need to take a back seat to any other province in her contribution to the war.
Of those who have been killed in action and who are presumed 'to be dead from the constituency of Rosthern that have come to my attention-and that is all I can speak of- to the total of fifty, the proportions are as follows:
Per cent
English, Irish, Scotch and other
English-speaking origin	 26
Ukrainian	 18
French-speaking	 12
Mennonite	  12
German	 20
Scandinavian	 4
Hungarian	 8
I put these figures on the record to show that we are building up a nation of Canadians regardless of their racial origin. These figures show that uhder a policy of allowing people to offer themselves freely in the defence of their country there has been a response from all peoples regardless of their religious beliefs or racial origin.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, when I think of the thousands of young people of the Roman Catholic faith who have laid down their lives in the defence of their country in this war I deplore the activities of a certain gentleman by the name of Shields who is going up and down this country maligning the people of that faith, and I contend that men of all parties, not only of the Liberal party but of the official opposition and of all parties in this house, should make it clear that they disapprove these unwarranted1 attacks upon people of another faith who have made such a splendid contribution not only by their sweat but by

their blood and sacrifice in the winning of this war and in sustaining and building up the country in time of peace.
As I say, the volunteer method was" working magnificently in this country. No other country in the world of our strength, of our population and our wealth, has made the wonderful contribution that this country has made, and on a voluntary basis. Will anybody here say that, had we been faced with the disunity that an attempt to force compulsion at the start of the war would have brought about, we could have accomplished anything like the magnificent effort we have made in this war? Nobody will say that; and since we have gone into the war on that basis my regret is that there should have been carried on a campaign which did not start yesterday, when apparently there was more need than formerly for reinforcements, but was going on two years ago, yes, three years ago, since when there has been an insistent demand for conscription and attacks upon the Prime Minister because he would not impose conscription. The present opportunity has been seized upon because it was thought that at last the great Prime Minister of this country, who has led this country in a war effort that I say is unparalleled in the experience of all countries of the world for a country of our population anji wealth could be overthrown, his party broken behind him, and he himself driven from public life. Incidentally I have no doubt that the forces of reaction which hate and oppose that great programme of social and humanitarian measures which the Prime Minister has laid before parliament this session saw in this agitation for conscription an opportunity of destroying the greatest Prime Minister that Canada has ever seen.
A great deal has been said about the home defence troops, and a great deal has been said in bitter criticism of them. Many of them are known to me. Some of them served with me while I served in the army in the present war. I know why a lot of them have refused to go active. It is because they were called up when they felt that they were absolutely needed at home. I know cases where the last boy at home in the family, with a brother overseas, has been called up, leaving the aged father and mother to attempt to carry on the farm alone. Some of them have brothers paratroopers, and others have brothers in different branches of the armed forces. I know their situation intimately. They considered that if they went active and went overseas they could no longer help their aged parents or families to make a living on the farm. They refused to go active. They believe that they never should

War Effort-Government Policy
have been called up, and if it had not been for the activity of certain people in Saskatchewan who were not carrying out the government's policy but instead were calling people up from the farm who never should have been called up, hundreds of these young men who are in the home defence army never wmuld have been called up at all. I know whereof I am speaking.
On January 14, 1943, a reinforcement arrived at one of the battalions on the west coast. They numbered 195, and at the time I made my canvass there were exactly thirty on fatigue . and other duties, leaving 165, and of that 165 only seventeen were not farmers-and that in spite of the well-established policy of the government that young farmers should not be called up if they were needed at home on the farm. Of that 165, thirty-eight had already received postponements on the ground that their services were necessary on the farm. Yet they were called up and placed in the home defence army. That is one of the reasons why a lot of these boys, some of whom have brothers overseas, have refused to volunteer. I deplore the attacks on these boys, calling them zombies and all the rest of it, as most of them are fine young fellows.

speechtext:
I wish to summarize some of the arguments which I used before the dinner hour as to why I oppose the government's policy as outlined in order in council 8891 providing for a limited measure of compulsory service overseas. I argued that such a measure was not absolutely necessary in order to defend the existence of our country or to achieve victory and that therefore it should not have been brought in at all.
In a country composed as ours is, so largely of minorities, the utmost good faith must be maintained in the treatment of those minorities, and if an undertaking is given to minorities and is to be broken without overriding and overwhelming reasons, then the very basis upon which a country is constituted as ours is, in large part of minorities, will be broken down and we shall not be united; we shall be a country made up of warring factions. I say therefore that, in view of pledges given at the commencement of the war, this measure should not have been introduced because there was no need for it from the point of view of defending the country against external enemies or for the purpose of achieving victory.
I also argued that it was very doubtful whether this measure ultimately would provide more reinforcements for overseas than would have been obtained had we continued with the voluntary system. What will develop in the days that lie ahead will in my opinion demonstrate the truth of that statement. I argued that if we break up the unity of this country, in which an amazing amount of work has been accomplished in our war effort, we shall not be able to make the same contribution to assisting the other united nations in winning that we have made as a united dominion. One of our greatest contributions has been in the direction of providing foodstuffs for our allies, providing shipping and munitions of war, and so on. On that basis we have made a contribution which I think transcends that of any other nation of similar population and similar wealth. If we disrupt our unity at this time, anything that we may accomplish as a result of that will not compare with what we could still do as a united nation. What we can do united would far outweigh any little good that might be obtained by securing a few more men, if we do secure them, for overseas service by the method of compulsion.
After all, each of us is entitled to his own opinion; but in the light of the figures given by the general staff with regard to the general reinforcement situation, if those figures are correct, I am not satisfied that there is any necessity for us to resort to this measure in order to make up the deficiency in infantry reinforcements resulting from a wrong allotment of men in the last four or five months. I am satisfied that a dispassionate examination of those figures will show that a reasonable amount of remustering, together with a reasonable chance given our troops to serve for a short time in a quieter part of the front, would have enabled us to meet that slight discrepancy in lack of infantry reinforcements without resorting to this policy of compulsion.
If we were to return to civil life thousands of men, many of whom have been taken from our farms, they could make a great contribution to the cause of the allies in the production of food and in providing other necessary supplies-the men who do not desire to volunteer to go overseas. In my opinion it would be better to have those men return to civil life than to carry out the proposed return, in effect, to civil life of thousands of trained aircrew men from the R.C.A.F. Those men in the air force who are anxious to take a real part in the war could be given a chance, and their contribution would far outweigh the
TVar Effort-Government Policy

contribution that may be made through the dispatch of these men by compulsion for service overseas.
There is no reason to insist on having five divisions in the army at any cost, and a fixed and lesser number than we would provide in the air force. Our contribution should have been based upon an endeavour to do our utmost on the basis on which we started out and which we have carried on so successfully up to the present time. We could have made a greater contribution on that basis than we can by the introduction of this measure of compulsory service.
Then there is the question that we face a troubled world. We may have to face another such time as we faced in 1939. I hope that will never happen, but I did hope that we would meet this crisis if it comes as a united nation. Had we been able to do so we could have faced whatever the future had in store for us, with every confidence in our ability to meet the events that might come. Now, however, we have broken up the unity of the country, how badly I do not know, I hope that irreparable damage has not been done. Such damage may have been brought about but I hope not. At any rate it is very greatly to the credit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that he held out against this measure as long as he possibly could. History, I believe, has already recorded that the attempt at conscription in the last war was a failure and did more harm than good, and history will record once more that this attempt at conscription in the present war will have been an equal if not a greater failure. It was imposed upon a Prime Minister who saw its dangers and resisted it to the very last. History will give him the greatest amount of credit for the fight he put up in that regard. I repeat, I hope the damage that has been done, if any, has not been irreparable. I trust we shall be able to get together and co-operate, regardless of racial origin or religious creed, so that we can build up a country worthy of the volunteers who have gone forth to defend us against our enemies. To use the words of the former minister of national defence for air (Mr. Power) when he addressed the house last, I would express the hope and prayer that "with the advent of external victory and peace, peace and understanding may come within oui own country."

Since the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) moved his amendment to-day I have been considering the question of the relevancy of it. The amendment as moved by Mr. Picard, seconded by Mr. Tucker, was:

That all the words of the amendment after the word "that" in the first line thereof be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house will aid in maintaining an efficient war effort but it does not approve of compulsory service overseas."
The first requisite of an amendment is that it must be connected with government administration. The amendment as proposed does not connect the government with the maintenance of the war effort. It is of no purpose to make such propositions in the house because they are in their nature hypothetical. The words I have already quoted from the amendment are, "This house will aid in maintaining an efficient war effort."
The amendment is not complete in its form. It is the expression of a general opinion which may be moved in any public body but has no connection with the business of the house.
The object of the house is to suggest, approve or disapprove of the government's policy. The amendment does not relate to government action, is irrelevant to both the amendment and the main motion.
For these reasons, together with those already given in connection, with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar and the hon. member for Acadia. I find the amendment out of order and I so rule.

I am not without realization of the gravity of the situation and the anxiety which exists in the minds of many people in Canada, as well as in the minds of the hon. members who represent the people of Canada in this House of Commons, but I felt that I could not give a silent vote on a motion of this kind and that it was my duty to express my opinion in all sincerity and frankness and to make my position clearly known before the house and the country. I hope that I am well enough known by all hon. members of this house for them to understand that even if I use a certain amount of heat in the expression of my personal and sincere opinion it is not due to the fact that I have any rancour in my mind toward any hon. member who does not share my views, or that I want to exercise any kind of vengeance against anybody with whom I have been associated in the past. I cannot ' avoid becoming heated when expressing views at any meeting. I cannot imitate other people when they express their views coldly, calmly and without raising their voices. At times I envy them, and particularly the former Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralstoii). I cannot bring myself to believe that being in

War Effort-Government Policy
the situation, in which he was yesterday, I could have reasoned my case as calmly as he did. Our temperaments are not the same. At times I regret that I have not the temperament of those who are capable of arguing their case as the former Minister of National Defence did.
It was refreshing, Mr. Speaker, to listen to a speech like the one which was delivered before and after six o'clock by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). It is not very often that we French Canadians hear in this House of Commons an Englishspeaking voice defending the position that we are taking, expressing views which are similar to those that we entertain and using the same arguments that we ourselves are using in support of our own ideas. I thank him for the kindness of his speech, which, nevertheless was a very strong one from the point of view of reason and knowledge, as well as being an expression of real Canadianism. I congratulate him upon his frankness in expressing his point of view and upon having argued SO' well, so clearly and so energetically in support of it.
I also desire to congratulate the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard), who made an excellent speech and who has expressed to a very large extent sentiments which are mine at this time as they were when I debated bill 80.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if it were permitted to an humble member of the House of Commons to congratulate you as a judge of our procedure; if it were permitted to a lawyer arguing a case before a court to congratulate a judge upon the wisdom of his decision, I would congratulate you upon the decisions that you have been rendering in declaring out of order the subamendments which have been proposed to the motion of confidence moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). In most cases what is the object or rather what is the effect of these amendments? I am sure they are proposed in good faith, but what is the result? It is purely and simply to becloud the issue and prevent the common people from understanding what is really at stake before parliament. I have had enough experience in this House of Commons to notice that the public do not always understand what is going on in the house, because of the beclouding of issues which is caused by numerous and successive amendments and subamendments, which most of the time drown the question under a lot of words and are only an enunciation of principles and programmes w'hich are the very opposite of the object that those who have moved the motion have had in mind. I claim, Mr. Speaker,
that if the rules of the house permit amendments and subamendments to a motion of this kind, in reason and in common sense, they should be modified to allow the government to be free to ask for a vote of confidence according to their wording of the motion, and then not have to face a vote Oi confidence on a motion amended expressing the views of opposing parties.
The government has come before the house asking for a vote of confidence. We shall vote on it, and we should vote on it the way it has been drafted, and not be afraid to say "yes" or "no" and express clearly the approval or disapproval of the government's policy. I see no necessity of an amendment to bring into the light the word "conscription". The word "conscription" is in the wording of the motion. The word itself is not there, but the spirit is there bfecause the motion of the Prime Minister reads as follows:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous w'ar effort.
"Its policy". What is the policy of the government to-day? A policy of conscription for service overseas. That is the policy of the government; and an hon. member rising in his place in this house and voting for the motion made by the Prime Minister would vote for the policy of conscription, because the policy of the government is a policy of conscription as it has been stated by the Prime Minister himself and as it is stated by the order in council which is before the house at the present time. There is no possible escape from that position. Those who are disposed to vote for the government and thereby vote confidence in the government on that motion should be able to face the situation squarely and not try to vacillate or hesitate and try to hide behind some amendment or subamendment. They should face the issue as it is. It is sufficiently important to deserve full consideration and a frank vote on the part of members representing the electors of Canada.
I am probably one of those who have been accused by some hon. members and particularly by the press, of not having properly led the province of Quebec, of not having given proper direction to the people of that province. They say that Quebec is in such a state of mind because of the attitude of her leaders. In a very humble way I have been for a certain time one of the leaders of public opinion in the province of Quebec, and before this House of Commons I have nothing to retract; I have no excuses to offer; I have nothing to take back from what I have told the electors of my province. What I said there wTas approved by the Prime Minister, with whom I was then

War Effort-Government Policy
associated. What I said there was approved by the leader of the opposition during the last electoral campaign. There was no divergence of view as between Liberals and Conservatives in regard to conscription for service overseas. We all said that this policy was no good for Canada; that it had been a failure in the past and would be a failure in the future. Why agitate that question before those who are not well informed, and say that Quebec is in this position because its leaders have not been true to their duty? I have been true to my duty, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier has been, as Ernest Lapointe has been and as others have been. We have spoken the truth, and what we have said in the province of Quebec we have repeated on each occasion and at every opportunity that has been given us in other sections of Canada, with the same courage, the same conviction and the same feeling of a real Canadianism.
I feel somewhat proud, Mr. Speaker, to have been able to face the electors of the province of Quebec at certain times with policies which were not very popular. I remember the days of 1939. The policy of the government, which had decided to participate in the war, was not well understood at that time, and there was some agitation. The late Ernest Lapointe and your humble servant went to the province of Quebec to explain the position of the government; to aid our fellow-countrymen in understanding the situation; and what did we get? We got the approval of the province of Quebec, in favour of Canada participating in the war. It was not an easy task, let me tell you, to argue with our fellow-countrymen in the province of Quebec at. that time, but we did it. We did not shirk our responsibility ; we did not turn away from the task. We faced the situation as we found it, and we argued with the people of Quebec, with a large amount of success. Since that time we have continued to do so, and there has been no trouble in my province, even though a certain number of my compatriots felt that they had been unfairly treated, that they had been insulted, that they were being called zombies by people who were irresponsible and who never had the courage to face the electorate in any section of Canada.
Let me say this, Mr. Speaker. We are accused of not having furnished as many soldiers as other sections of Canada. My answer to that statement is that the flow of blood on the battlefield is never measured by arithmetical calculations. That is not the way to appreciate the sacrifices of a section of the population of a country. In Montreal the other night I made a statement which I am going to repeat now, because I am not

afraid to repeat here anything I say outside the house. We have done more than you English-speaking Canadians of British descent. You have only obeyed the call of blood. You have answered the sentiments of your heart and mind. What we have done could only be done through reasoning, and judging the situation as a judge would do when deciding a case presented to him. It is not a case of reasoning with you; it is a case of sentiment, and I understand you. For a moment, if you wish to understand me and the French Canadians, reverse the picture, if you please. Try to imagine Canada as part of a French empire, with the descendants of British citizens in the minority. Can you tell me that if that French empire, of which you would be part, were in danger you would be as enthusiastic in defending that empire as wrnuld be the Canadians of French descent? To any man who would say that he would have the same views and sentiments I would reply that he is not sincere.
Think of the position in which we are placed. Think of the concessions which the French Canadians and their representatives have been making to bring about and maintain unity in this great land of ours. I have no time to enumerate them all, but go over in your minds the concessions that were made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, by Ernest Lapointe and by myself, at the risk of losing support and, indeed, with the loss of support in certain quarters of my province. We are here in the House of Commons, all friends, and as members of a family capable of understanding the truth. Where are your concessions, you British Canadians, in favour of the French Canadians? What have you ever done to preserve unity between the two great races in Canada? Unity has been maintained owing to concessions made by French Canadians in this House of Commons and elsewhere. These are strong words, but they are the truth and no one can dispute them. The political history of our country is there to sustain my statement.
We are in a difficult situation, but it is no more difficult in the province of Quebec than in the province of British Columbia or in the province of Nova Scotia, where not very long ago, when soldiers were parading the streets of a city, a young girl called them zombies. One of them left the ranks and, with his rifle, broke the window from which that young girl was insulting the soldiers who were walking on the street. There is no more agitation in Quebec; there is less agitation in Quebec.
I know that for the last two of three days the newspapers have said that the troubles in British Columbia are attributable to a

It would be impossible for a handful of French-Canadian soldiers to cause any trouble or create any difficulty in British Columbia if there had not been sympathizers among members of the majority in that province. The facts are there; you cannot deny them. When the first demonstration took place in Vernon the Canadian English newspapers said that over ninety per cent of the soldiers were of English descent.
There is no use in trying to evade the issue, and to throw the blame on us in the province of Quebec. That problem is largely political. And, Mr. Speaker, I have still ringing in my ears the speech of the man who has been doing a lot for the war effort of Canada, and without whom we would perhaps be in a worse position than we are at the present time. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) is not the lowest man in this house; he is not the Iorvest man in the cabinet of the Prime Minister, and he said, even in the United States, that this agitation was mostly political. I say the word of that man deserves consideration. That man deserves respect.
I have the greatest respect in the world for Colonel Ralston. He is a man of his word, an honest and sincere man. That is what I have said in the province of Quebec. So Iy believe. I know him well enough to say that. But I am under the impression that, even in the face of the wonderful record of Colonel Ralston, the record of the Minister of Munitions and Supply is still more important, and that he has done even more to help the war effort of Canada. He said it was political agitation. In all sincerity, and without wishing to hurt the feelings of anyone, I must say that I am afraid this has now become a political issue on both sides. I regret having to say that.
One thing has been made clear during this debate, and that is that conscription is here. It has been here since 1942, no matter what may have been said in my province. It has been here and it has been applied since 1942 in connection with the Aleutian islands. Conscription is the law of the land. The Prime
Minister has said so in his speech, and there is no denial of it. It is here to such an extent that, in making his motion for confidence, the Prime Minister said to members of the House of Commons: You are not voting for conscription; it is a thing of the past; this is not the question to-day; you are just voting to-day to express your opinion as to whom you think would be best qualified to carry from now on the war effort of Canada. That is a clear indication, if one requires one, that conscription has been with us since 1942. It has been with us not only in principle but in effect. And, as I have already said, it has been put into operation in connection with the Aleutian islands, and other places where our troops have been sent.
I cannot understand why, after five years of our admirable contribution to the war, a contribution which has caused countries' throughout the world to compliment Canada and to express their surprise with respect to our achievement, it becomes necessary, practically at the end of the war, to propose conscription, a policy concerning which we had been hesitating arid vacillating for so long.
A few days ago the distinguished Prime Minister of Great Britain spoke. His words were brought to us by the newspapers, and also by a gallant soldier from the other side, the hon. member for London (Mr. Johnston), who spoke the other day. Mr. Churchill said in the House of Commons in London that the character-not the war effort-that the character of the war effort of Canada was admirable. That is what he said. It was a compliment to our system of voluntarily waging war, and it was that system which caused the Prime Minister of England to say that the character of the war effort of Canada is admirable.
It is, in fact, admirable. Why should we now change our policy? Oh, we have heard many touching words about the soldiers on the other side. Mr. Speaker, the soldiers on the other side have gone there of their own free will, and in glory. They have not waited for conscription. They have gone there, prompted by a conviction that was in them. They have volunteered to help their country and to help the empire and-if rve want to speak poetically-to help assure the freedom of the world. But, Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to think that those who have been gallant enough to hasten to the other side voluntarily are now changing their minds and asking that others be sent to help them, through coercion. That does not properly represent the feeling of the soldiers of Canada on the other side.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
It is said that the crisis facing us at the moment is due to two main causes: first, the necessity for reinforcements, and, second, the trouble existing in the country and the necessity of avoiding crisis No. 2. Crisis No. 2 is the threatened resignation of a certain number of ministers who share the views of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston). The hon. member for Prince indicated that himself in the speech he de-

livered yesterday. Is it not an extraordinary spectacle to hear a minister who has resigned say: I am going to vote for the government and against the amendment of the opposition in order to expedite the sending of soldiers to the other side, and in order not to lose any time in sending reinforcements across the ocean; but I am not entirely satisfied; I am going to keep my eye on the ball; I am going to watch the government in this connection, and I rely on those in the cabinet who share mv views to see that that policy is put into effect without any slowing down?
Is that not a most extraordinary situation? A man' resigns from the Cabinet, leaving behind him three or four men who share his views and who, if necessary, will extend the crisis in which we are at the present time. So extraordinary a situation has never before existed in Canada and I doubt if it will ever exist in the future. Speaking for myself and for many other Canadians, I say that this country is entitled to know who precipitated the crisis, who caused the change in policy of the government, who brought about the decision which was given to us on November 23.
We were called here to consider a policy of voluntary service which was to be explained to us by General McNaughton. I have not the time to refer to the tragedy we witnessed when General McNaughton was forced to explain and justify a policy of conscription when it had been announced the day before that he was going to explain and justify a policy of voluntary service. The day after we came here we had a policy of conscription; that is what was explained instead of a policy of voluntary service. General McNaughton had to explain the policy of coercion and conscription which the government had decided to put into effect. Who was responsible for that? Was it those whom the former minister of national defence left behind him to watch the fort after he had decided to get away from the situation? The public of Canada ought to know who those ministers are who share the same views as the hon. member for Prince and who were ready to resign from the government. We ought to know them. They ought to stand up and take their responsibility before this house and before the country.	-
It is said that an election is to be feared. An election was held in the United States, as was said this afternoon, and elections have been held elsewhere. An election was held here in 1917 and no one was killed. Laurier fought for his policy in 1917. He was defeated, but he accepted his defeat gracefully. He did not lose any prestige in Canada; he was even greater than he was before. His name is

War Effort-Government Policy
greater in Canadian history because he had the courage of his own convictions. The Prime Minister has quoted the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the late Ernest Lapointe in an effort to justify his attitude, in an effort to justify this policy of conscription. He should have quoted the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Lapointe in favour of the voluntary system and denouncing the very stand which two or three ministers have forced him to take and who threatened to resign if conscription were not put into effect.
Why are we in need of reinforcements? After the death of the late Norman Rogers, the Department of National Defence was divided into three departments, with a minister at the head of each. Those three departments competed for recruits for their particular services, and that is the cause of our trouble. We tried to do too much for a country of our size and population. As an hon. member from western Canada said the other day, probably we undertook too much. If that is the position, why not, like men, adopt a policy such as has been adopted by Australia and reduce the extent of our activities on the other side? Why should we try to compete in a race with Britain, the United States and Russia to win the laurels of victory, to try to win a crown of greatness, when in reality we are only a colony in the British empire, and are not, as I said when speaking on bill 80 in the House of Commons, really an independent and sovereign country? Why should we try to have a war effort which will be superior to the w'ar effort of any other allied country participating in this war? There is no sense in that, Mr. Speaker. We have gone beyond our capacity. We have not enough material for the coat that we have been trying to put on the Canadian people. Let us be more generous to our own people; let us be more reasonable; let us act in accordance with what we can really do. Let. us not be ashamed of doing what the Prime Minister of Australia did, when accompanied by his own general staff, he discussed with Mr. Churchill and Mr. Roosevelt and their respective staffs the possibility of reducing the numbers of Australia's armed forces in order to help the civilian and war industries of Australia. Why should we not take a similar attitude? That would have been the manly attitude, instead of following the impractical policy we are attempting to put into effect.
Something has been said about an election. Why bring up that issue at this time? Well, Mr. Speaker, can any member of this house be unaware of the fact that the government has been preparing for an election for the last six months and that all the documentary procedure necessary for an election is already in the hands of the returning officers? Even the ballots are there, ready to have the names of the candidates printed on them. The Liberal organization in Ottawa has been restaffed, and a man from the province of Quebec has been brought in from the eastern townships to prepare French-Canadian literature to be distributed in the province of Quebec. I have received a certain amount of that literature, preparing an appeal to the electorate. Why should we be afraid of an election? The sooner we have one, the sooner the clouded atmosphere in which we are now living and have been living for the past five weeks or more will disappear and the sooner we shall be able to follow a policy that will be in the best interests of Canada as well as in the best interests of the allied nations. I am not afraid of an election, whatever opposition may be reserved for me, whatever opposition I may meet from men coming from the party with which I have been for so long closely associated. I have not ceased to be a Liberal, but I contend that my party, alas, has been moving toward the other side, towards the imperial and Tory spirit.
My time is running short, Mr. Speaker, and there are many other things I had in mind to speak of, but I want to observe your ruling and show that I am an obedient servant of Your Honour.
Let me in conclusion say just a word about my friend and former colleague, the former Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), and I am sure that he will pardon me for this reference. I listened to his address with very great attention. Without moving from my chair, throughout the whole length of his speech I followed it as best I could with my limited knowledge and understanding of the English language. He made a good speech, possibly not, as good as the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) suggested this afternoon, but on the whole it was a very good speech. At least it was the speech of a very sincere and trustworthy man, a man who, whatever his opinions may be, deserves the respect and the confidence of every member of this house, and I will be the first one to pay him that compliment. But when the Prime Minister raised the point that probably he, (Col. Ralston), had been a little slow in bringing before the Prime Minister and the cabinet the gravity of the situation I thought that part of my friend's speech was a bit weak. He did not bring forward anything very definite to show that he had long before informed the Prime Minister of the crisis that was looming up on
War Effort

Government Policy

the horizon. He said that he did not want to disband the draftees. Well, he said that when I was a member of the government in 1942, when there was no request for conscription from the military authorities. All that he has brought to the house, except for the statement made on his return on October 18, are things that he has been saying since 1942, and there was nothing definite about them, nothing to justify the Prime Minister in thinking that there was a real danger threatening as a result of not having the necessary reserves for the reinforcement pools on the other side. I repeat that my good friend was a little bit weak in that part of his speech. Perhaps he can justify himself, in saying that his officers were not any more pressing in their demands. In my humble judgment that is the situation; he was not very strong in his' argument in answering the Prime Minister on that point.
I want you, Mr. Speaker, to allow me just a moment or two more, and I am most appreciative of the kindness of hon. members in sitting and listening to me. I am not probably in age the oldest member of this House of Commons, but I am the only one who has been sitting continuously in this house for over thirty-three years. Let me say that I am older than the Prime Minister from the point of view of continuous sitting in this House of Commons. I have the profound satisfaction of having done everything I could to discharge the duties of my office, and to be honest with my fellow Canadians, to be frank with my people. And now, in the evening of my life, we have reached a time of crisis in Canada, the consequences of which I can very readily foresee. I have never taken offence when any man opposed his views strongly against mine. I have never taken offence when members of the House of Commons objected strongly to my views. We cannot always be of the same mind; we cannot always be of the same opinion; we cannot always entertain the same sentiments and feelings in our hearts and minds. Being human beings, we are bound to have differences among ourselves. But the best thing to do is to try to reconcile as much as is humanly possible the conflicting opinions that we hold and to try to unite in this country, and bring together as much, as is humanly possible, the different elements composing the population of Canada.
There are not only English-speaking and French-speaking people in this country. People of other races form part of the population and they have become good citizens of Canada and are ready to express real Canadian views. In the evening of my life, from the point of

view of age and of parliamentary service, let me through you, Mr. Speaker, and from my place in the House of Commons, address just a word to the citizens of the province of Quebec and ask them, whatever may be their sentiments, whatever may be their feelings at the present time, to be calm,, to take things easy, to reflect before acting, and to remember that they are not only citizens of the province of Quebec but at the same time citizens of Canada as a whole, who desire to see their country in the not distant future, and with the will of all concerned, become a great and independent country.
They are as much interested as I am, as much interested as others are in the future of our great land, and they should do all they can to help to build up, on the foundation of confederation, a great and prosperous country which, with the help of God and the concerted effort of those who are in authority, before long will be a country of -which we shall be proud and in which we shall have great honour.
I ask my fellow-Canadians in the province of Quebec to be firm. They have a right to be firm. I ask them to be energetic. They have a right to be energetic, and nobody can deprive them of the freedom of speech, of the freedom of expression of their own opinions, even if they do not agree with the majority of the citizens of Canada. But they ought to express those opinions in all sincerity and in all honesty and be careful not to hurt too much the feelings of the majority of the citizens of this countiy. I know, from my long experience in parliament, that the people of the province of Quebec, the French Canadians, have many friends among the English-speaking population of Canada. They have many friends in all the provinces from one ocean to the other, wffio on many occasions have expressed that friendship, and their understanding of our situation, of our state of mind, of our mentality, of our point of view. I say to my French-Canadian compatriots: Be careful my friends, my brothers; be careful not to lose the advantage of the friendship which we now enjoy to a greater extent than ever -before in the English speaking provinces of Canada. Let us speak openly; let us respect the opinions of others, but let us be careful not to cause any damage to property, not to injure the life of anyone. Let us await in calm and patience the hour when we shall be in a position to express as Canadians and as electors our opinion of what has been done to-day and what may be done to-morrow.
Having these sentiments in mind, I hope, with all the sincerity I am capable of, and pray from the bottom of my heart, that a guiding

War Effort-Government Policy
light will appear upon the horizon of our country, to rise high in our sky and that under such a sign of salvation, men of good will may get together, dispense with the military caste, which is a source of trouble, and reach a brotherly understanding between Canadians of all races and creeds in making Canada a great and glorious country. That guiding light, I also pray, will help us to think of Canada first and always, before thinking of any other country, however great that country may be.
In the present crisis, which is causing so much trouble in the world, if you put aside the brilliant rhetoric of the leaders of the great allied nations, you will find back of their literary utterances, behind all their fine words, and more particularly at all the conventions that are taking place at present to deal with the aftermath of the war, the clearly expressed desire to promote the interests of their respective countries. Those great leaders and their followers are thinking of their respective countries first and are doing what is best, each in the interests of his own country. Let us imitate them and think of our country first of all and of the welfare and greatness of our beloved land.
Mr. MAXIME RAYMOND (Beauharnois-
Laprairie) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, the
Prime Minister, after having read to the house the order in council "directing" the Minster of National Defence to send to the various theeatres of war in Europe and the Mediter-ranian, 16,000 recruits already trained under the Mobilization Act, 1940, for the defence of Canada, requests parliament to support him by a vote of approval and confidence.
To enjoy the confidence of someone, one must deserve it. Could it be claimed that the government who do not fulfil their undertakings, who violate their most solemn pledges, deserve a measure of confidence? Surely not, and I shall quote the testimony of the Prime Minister himself in this connection.
On January 26, 1942, he stated, as reported in Hansard:
The present unhappy state of the world is, in large part, the result of broken pledges. Nazi Germany has erected bad faith and the broken pledge into a principle of action.
And, on April 8, 1942, he added in a radio speech:
It is the trust reposed by the people in the given word of the government that has maintained national unity.
In the Prime Minister's own terms, the present unhappy state of the world is the result of broken pledges.
Let us briefly review the pledges taken. I shall quote brief excerpts from speeches delivered in the House of Commons by the Prime Minister, in which he repeats his pledges concerning conscription for overseas service. Here is what he said on February 25, 1942:
When the war came in Europe and this parliament met to decide whether Canada would enter the war or not, a declaration was made by the government of the day that, if Canada did enter the war, there would not be compulsory service for overseas, but that service for overseas would be by voluntary enlistment. . . . No more solemn undertaking could possibly have been given by the people. . . .
