subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
My colleagues and I .	.	. have made it
equally clear that service outside Canada in the armed forces of Canada at sea, on land and in the air . . . shall be freely undertaken.
Before war came, the government gave a solemn pledge that in the event of war, we would follow that policy.
When the war came the pledge was solemnly reaffirmed. At the general elections during the war itself, that policy received the overwhelming approval of the people of Canada.
In the light of these statements, these pledges and these undertakings, is it possible to give the government a sincere vote of confidence which would constitute an endorsation of the order in council implementing conscription for overseas service? For my part, it would be breaking faith with my constituents.
The Prime Minister claims that he has been relieved of his pledges by the plebiscite. I have already proved to this house that such was not the case, and I have based my contention on quotations, some in particular from Mr. Lapointe's speeches. They represented a pact for the duration of the war, the fulfilment of which he could be relieved by the anti-conscriptionists alone. However, his claim is disproved by his own words since, on Monday last, he stated again that the plebiscite did not refer to conscription.

War Effort-Government Policy
In. that event, how could he be relieved, by the plebiscite, of his undertakings concerning conscription? He, has no mandate to impose conscription; on the contrary, the elections of 1940 from which his mandate originates, directs him to avoid conscription.
The plebiscite has provided additional evidence of the small measure of confidence that may be given to the Prime Minister's statements.	.
During the plebiscite campaign, he formally stated over the radio on April 24, 1942, that the plebiscite did not refer to conscription, and he added:
Surely you cannot allow parades of young men carrying banners and shouting "Down with conscription" to weigh on your decision, "when this question is not even involved.
However, a few days after the vote, he introduced bill No. SO, implying conscription for overseas service, stating that it was a logical sequence to the plebiscite vote.
Sometimes he says yes, sometimes he says no, according to the needs of the moment, and he requests our confidence. Thus the public are being deceived by actions which are contrary to previous statements.
A review of the developments which have taken place in recent years shows how we have been misled. Before the outbreak of the war, our self-governing status was loudly proclaimed and the Prime Minister did not scruple to say that we had nothing to do with foreign wars. But in 1938 war clouds were gathering in Europe and we learned long afterwards, in a speech delivered by the Prime Minister at Prince Albert, in 1941, that if England had gone to war he would have favoured our entry into the struggle. This is a peculiar sort of self government. We go to war when England goes to war; when she refrains, we also refrain.
Last May, 1944, the Prime Minister said before the British parliament in London that "we had entered the war of our own free will and not as the result of a formal obligation." But on September 1, 1939, two days before England declared war, the Prime Minister stated that in the event Great Britain went to war to fight aggression, the government had already decided to request parliament for authority to cooperate closely with Great Britain. We are free, declared the Prime Minister, but each time England decides to go to war, we go to war. A peculiar freedom.
In other words, the Prime Minister endorses the principle of self government in his statements and imperialistic tendencies in his acts.
During the special session of September, 1939, when I opposed participation in the war, I said: "If we approve participation, it will

lead us to conscription, if the war lasts long enough." Mr. Lapointe replied that those who, notwithstanding his statements against conscription, claimed that conscription would be passed, sowed the seed of disunity. Unfortunately, my predictions have materialized. Conscription is in our statutes and it is being implemented.
The government proceeded step by step, ending up with this order in council. According to the statements made by members of the government during the general election of 1940, our participation was to be moderate, but it has now become an all-out affair.
The mobilization act, passed in June 1940, which was intended specifically for the defence of Canada in Canada only, has become, following the passage of bill 80, a conscription measure for overseas service and it has been used to blackmail and intimidate N.R.M.A. men into enlisting for overseas service.
Although they had been trained for the defence of Canada within Canada, the N.R.M.A. men, or should I say the conscripts, found themselves overnight, following the passage of bill 80 in 1942, subject to overseas service. However, in governmental circles, it was still claimed that we were operating under the voluntary system. Some voluntary system I It was conscription camouflaged in various ways such as the unfair persecutions of men who refused to volunteer for overseas service, as it was frequently proved to this house. But the Minister of National Defence replied that he did not intend to interfere with the methods of recruiting for overseas service. Moreover, he was forced to admit that called-up men were meant to be used as reinforcements overseas.
As recently as November 8 last, in a broadcast, the Prime Minister, after stating "that he was now sure that there was no longer any need for men for home defence" added: "We shall continue to call up young men as soon as they have reached military age, for training and compulsory service." However, the members of the government were still repeating that the voluntary system was in force.
Why, therefore, draft these men who are not needed for home defence unless it be exclusively for overseas service? If they had wanted to enlist voluntarily, they need not have been conscripted.
I thought that quibbling would at last be abandoned after the passing of the order in council of November 23 ordering the dispatch overseas of 16,000 men drafted under the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940. But no, the Minister of Justice in a statement to the press again resorts to quibbling. "The

TEar Effort-Government Policy
order in council," he said, "authorizes the dispatch to Europe of 16,000 men drafted under the N.R.M. Act if a sufficient number of volunteers, from among those draftees or from elsewhere, should there remain any elsewhere, who are well enough trained do not come forward in time to be included in the new detachments about to leave". Such a statement is liable to mislead the public.
In the first place, the order in council not only authorizes but orders, let no one forget it, the dispatch of 16,000 men drafted under the N.R.M. Act. It is not stated therein "if a sufficient number of volunteers do not come forward"; the word "if" is not used, it is purely and simply an order to dispatch them overseas. Moreover, those 16,000 men are recruited among draftees. There cannot be any talk about volunteers. According to the Oxford dictionary, a volunteer is "a person who voluntarily enters military service". Now, all those who have been called for training under the N.R.M. Act of 1940 are conscripts.
The impression is given that they will be asked, before they leave, to sign as volunteers. What a joke! They are already conscripted for overseas service. The order to dispatch them has been issued.
It is just as if, before the execution of a man sentenced to die, one asked him if,he were willing to put the rope around his own neck.
I beg the government to be frank enough to call a spade a spade. They have labelled the conscription measure a mobilization act. Conscripts have been termed recruits, and conscription is now being described as conditional voluntary service.
Let us put an end to this quibbling and dodging, if we would not have the people lose all trust in public men.
The Prime Minister spoke of a cabinet crisis. Another will develop, one far mpre baneful to the country, the confidence crisis which the Prime Minister has been nursing along these past few years through his deceitful attitudes, at one time equivocal, at another time inconsistent. In a speech I made on June 18th, 1942, I warned the government against such a crisis, which was already being felt. It has been intensified and the action taken by the government in passing the order in council of November 23rd but adds fuel to the fire.
Why should conscription be applied more strictly by the direct method now in use? Is it to increase a war effort which has already reached exaggerated proportions? Anyone computing our contribution can assert that our war effort, in terms of our population and
resources, surpasses that of any of our allies. So the Prime Minister has stated over and over again with great pride. In financial sacrifices, we are second to none, as I have indicated to the house by means of comparative tables which have never been disproved. Besides, they were based on official figures.
Alone among British dominions, alone among the allies, we have presented England with billion dollar gifts. Yet, we have no material interests to defend in the war.
The losses we have sustained in manpower, in terms of our population, are no less than those of any of our allies. Still we pay the price for the mistakes of others who brought about the war. Our soldiers have been sent to every battlefield-they have been at HongKong, at Dieppe, in Africa, in Italy, in India, et cetera-in short, wherever a battle has been fought, and yet it is not considered enough.
If we must resort to conscription to supply the army with reinforcements, it means that too much is asked of Canadian troops. A country with a population of eleven and a half million cannot play the part of world policeman. It is high time we realized this and limited our front-line activity rather than consider conscription. Strange to see, the government resorts to this measure at a time when the other British dominions who have a greater stake in this war than our own not only have refrained from resorting to conscription for overseas service but have decided to reduce the strength of their armed forces.
No reason was overlooked in order to justify our participation in this war on an exaggerated scale; the loftiest of humanitarian motives were appealed to; we were told that we were defending freedom, civilization, small nations, et cetera, et cetera-
The facts speak for themselves.
We declared war against Germany because England had done so, and because Poland had been invaded. However, barely a fortnight later, we witnessed unmoved the invasion of that country by Russia. Three months later, on November 30, 1939, we witnessed the dastardly attack against Finland by Russia. Later on, in June, 1940, the Baltic states, Lithuania, Latvia and Esthonia, were in turn invaded by Russia, despite a pact of mutual assistance dated October 10, 1939, between the U.S.S.R. and these Baltic states. About the same time, Russia annexed Bessarabia which she had taken away from Rumania. Those are facts.
In conclusion, Germany invades Poland and we go to war against her. Russia violates the boundaries of six countries, including Poland,

War Effort-Government Policy
hut instead of fighting her, we welcome her as an ally and extend our help to her. That is another inconsistency which gives us grounds to question the alleged motives of our participation in the present war, and which is not calculated to enhance confidence in public men.
The latest action of the government will increase the disunion which already exists. A nation has the right to compel its citizens to fight for its defence but not for the defence of other countries, especially when that nation has already accomplished a war effort of such magnitude.
Confederation was based on two fundamental principles: provincial autonomy and respect for the rights of minorities, and from a national standpoint, autonomy of Canada with regard to England.
Who are those who threaten national unity? They are the people who think as imperialists rather than as Canadians. I do not hesitate to say that in Canada there is but one way of fostering national unity, and it is to act as Canadians. Before closing, I wish to voice a thought which I have already expressed in this house.
Canadians of French extraction are first of all Canadians; they are devoted to their country, Canada, and they want to develop it in harmony and peace with Canadians of other racial origin. They do not like war but, as history shows, they do not fear it when their territory has to be defended. They object, however, to being compelled to defend other people's territory by bringing ruin on themselves.
Too often has the Prime Minister resorted to the argument in favour of national unity, to find justification now in asking for a vote of confidence on a policy most likely to destroy that unity.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not originally my intention to take part in this debate, but some remarks made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) and by the leader of the C.C.F. group (Mr. Coldwell) have caused me to change my mind.
Before proceeding further, however, I should like to pay my compliments to the hon. member for London (Mr. Johnston) upon his maiden effort yesterday. It is a measure of his service to Canada that, having been a member of the House of Commons for four and a half years, this has been his first opportunity to address the house. I for one believe that his effort was one of such distinction as to equal his war record.

May I also make a few remarks respecting the address to-night of the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin). All of us envy his manifest talents, and we know that those talents have been and will be used in his own province to uphold the honour and dignity of the House of Commons. But there is one thing I should like to say, something which affects me rather closely.
The hon. member did say-and I regret it, and with respect must disagree-that soldiers overseas as a whole do not or may not understand what they are fighting for. There are many things I am not sure of in this world; but there is one thing of which I am sure, and that is that there are not any soldiers overseas who do not understand what they are fighting for.
When the order in council was passed and made public last week I had thought there would not be much debate, because the leader of the opposition had appealed to us to eliminate politics. The order in council so firmly and clearly carried out the policy of the government, as I have known it for the past two years, that I therefore considered there would not be much difficulty. To the contrary, however, we now have an amendment, in these words:
This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice.
This amendment divides itself into three parts, and I believe it is an attempt to combine two ideas, so as to becloud both of them.
It says, first of all, that we have failed to provide trained and adequate reinforcements by requiring certain actions in respect of N.R.M.A. personnel. It is true that the order in council does not require certain services of N.R.M.A. personnel, but it is not true to say that this government has not provided adequate and trained reinforcements.
On that point I should like to digress, and give my own experiences overseas as an illustration. In England there is a reinforcement unit for all arms of the service. I speak particularly of the Canadian Armoured Corps. Many months ago, before we went into action, the reinforcement unit would have only a few men in it; officers and men would come to me and say, "The reinforcement unit is empty; why dio we not have concsriptioni?" I would counsel patience and very shortly another ship would come from Canada, with the result that the reinforcement unit would be filled. As the recruits received their additional train-

War Effort-Government Policy
ing and went forward to the field units, the reinforcement unit would become depleted and we would have the same scene reenacted by the same officers and the same men. There would be the same gloomy outlook and then another ship would arrive to fill the reinforcement unit. No matter how often that happened, they just could not believe that it would happen again next month.
To some extent that is the situation which I have found in this house on the two or three occasions that I have been here. It seems that the opposition and a section of the press have created at regular intervals a thought in the minds of some of the public that all was lost, that the future was black and that nothing would do but that this government, powerful though it may be, should give way to another government of an indefinite and, may I say, dubious origin. When these so-called crises are over, I often wonder what they were all about. This government, aided by the united efforts of the Canadian people, has gone forward in its own way and produced a war effort second to none in the world. Perhaps the opposition members are a bit like my friends overseas, they just will not believe the evidence of their own senses.
However, there is a significant difference between this amendment to our motion and amendments moved in the past, as referred to yesterday by the hon. member for London (Mr. Johnston). As he said, those amendments provided for national selective service which could mean different things to different men. This amendment makes no reference to that subject; it speaks only of N.R.M.A. personnel. I am wondering if national selective service has been thrown overboard by the official opposition as they have so many times thrown overboard other platforms, programmes and leaders.
There is another feature of the amendment about which I should like to speak, namely, the reference to the government failing to assure equality of service and sacrifice. I must apologize if I have not heard my hon. friends' explanations in bygone times as to just what that phrase means, but my own experience has been that there is no system which will provide for equality of sacrifice. The best of us is always the most daring; the best will always go forward recklessly. He will take additional risks for the sake of his comrades and nothing will make him act any differently.
Reference is made also to equality of service. For many reasons that may sound good, but I do not know of any system which will provide for equality of service. Service
is best given by the man who wishes to give it, and any job is best done by the man who wants to do that job. I am not suggesting that the N.R.M.A. personnel would not make good soldiers; they will; but I repeat that we want initiative; we want enterprise; we want every man doing the job that his heart and soul is in.
Reference is made also to adequate and trained reinforcements. During the past few days I have heard the Minister of National Defence, Mr. McNaughton, say that 16,000 draftees are all that he requires for the present emergency. The hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) will correct me if I am wrong when I say that he recommended some
15,000	men a short while ago. When both those gentlemen are in substantial agreement I am prepared to reject the amendment which says that we have not provided trained and adequate reinforcements. I hope the house will forgive me for referring to something I said about two years ago about the present Minister of National Defence and the former Minister of National Defence. I was speaking about the Canadian army and its probable use in the future and I said:
It will be led by young officers who, with their troops, have been trained for that day by one of the greatest soldiers of the British empire. More than that our army had been planned and equipped by one of the ministers of this government who knows what an army ought to be and has created it accordingly.
I am glad that both these gentlemen have given the house and the country the benefit of their wisdom and experience. I do not know of any other two men- who are held in such high regard with respect to the planning and use of the Canadian Army. As I say, when they are in substantial agreement I feel completely safe in adopting their opinion.
I should like to say something about reinforcements as I understood them overseas. We in the armoured corps never had any difficulty about reinforcements. In Normandy trained reinforcements in sufficient numbers were available at all times and in all places. I understand that since July 25-prior to that I can speak from personal knowledge-there has been no shortage, nor has there been any shortage anywhere except with respect to infantry. That shortage does not exist to-day, but it is said it will exist ini the immediate future and for that reason this government has met the emergency, I believe, to the satisfaction of this country.
I have heard it said many times in the past that with one good battle there would not be reinforcements enough for the Canadian Army.

War Effort-Government Policy

We fought a good many battles; the Canadian Army stood up to its losses; they beat the Germans and they will continue to do so.
I should like to speak for a moment about the most persistent campaign which has been waged with respect to trained personnel or, in the words of the people I refer to, untrained personnel, that have been sent abroad. This campaign has been directed to the next-of-kin of our soldiers, the intention being to discredit this government by saying that soldiers now fighting in the Canadian Army have not had a fair chance, were not sufficiently trained for the. occasion.
I do not know of a commander in the Canadian Army who would take the responsibility of sending untrained men into battle. Every reinforcement unit commander is personally responsible for seeing that every man who leaves the unit has been adequately trained. This campaign of misrepresentation is to my mind explained to some extent by the attitude which was displayed in this house last week by the official opposition. They came here on Wednesday, and the look on their faces plainly showed that they meant and expected to enjoy this session of parliament. The look on their faces belied entirely the expressed desire of their leader that they should eschew politics. With an expressed desire that there be no politics, that the sole purpose was to provide reinforcements for the men overseas, one would have thought that under those circumstances they would have applauded the announcement that this government was going to send reinforcements. But instead, the announcement in this house was received by them in silence. I think one hon. member said something about surrender.
May I refer for a moment to the campaign
which was waged at least in the province of Ontario, attempting to show that the home defence army was a problem that pertained almost exclusively to the province of Quebec. Surely the publication of the figures that
15,000	of the home defence army are from Ontario and 22,000 from Quebec shows clearly that it is not exclusively a Quebec problem. There was one feature of this campaign that was particularly discreditable. In the province of Quebec there are many wives, mothers and sweethearts who are daily awaiting mail from their loved ones abroad just as eagerly as those in the other provinces, and just as anxiously fearing a telegram from national defence headquarters. I had the honour to serve in Normandy alongside French-Canadian units, and I want to tell the house that they served just as co'^-ageously, just as stubbornly and just

as effectively as we did. I would have thought that when I got back to this country Canadians would have been showing publicly our respect and admiration for the French Canadians, but on the contrary, I found a campaign being conducted which could only add to the burdens of their next-of-kin in the province of Quebec by deriding that province for the very considerable effort it has made in the Canadian armed forces.
With respect to the voluntary system of enlistments, I was astonished at the suggestion that this government had made a change of face. I never doubted at any time that the first and foremost intention of this government was to reinforce our army whenever reinforcements were necessary, and this is the first time since the war began that any responsible person has suggested that we needed to use any other method of obtaining reinforcements than the voluntary system. This government has provided reinforcements by a different method with a minimum of delay. It is true that the Prime Minister did everything he could to make the voluntary system work, and I doubt if we can hold that against him. I for one do not. It is also my opinion that we should not hold against him the fact that we are at present dispatching only 16,000 draftees overseas, because that is all that are required in the present emergency.
Something has been said in the house as to the necessity of equality of conditions. Personally I favour the voluntary system and want it encouraged and continued. I understand that as a result of the efforts of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche) some 500 French-Canadian draftees have enlisted for active service. All I can say in my own riding is that if the province of Ontario will do likewise we shall have a very good army. I understand also that whereas three weeks ago our weekly enlistments from the home defence army were at the rate of 170 they have now reached over 800, and I hope that keeps up. I would much prefer, and I know that the men overseas would much prefer, that every soldier reaching France and Italy would come as a volunteer, and I would not agree to any system which would take away from the present draftee or young man reaching military age the right to volunteer to serve this country.
The leader of the C.C.F. group suggested in his remarks that we had three or four armies. I am sorry, but I cannot understand that. It seems to me that there are 'but two. First, we have the general service men who are liable to serve in any theatre of war any-

War Effort-Government Policy
where. Second, we have all the N.R.M.A. men. who are liable for service in Canada and in the European theatres of war. 1^ Canada there are something like 60,000 draftees and a number of thousands of general service men. Among the general service men there are a good many who, because of their age or medical category or ability, are not fit for the front line. Let us be realistic and not send them. There is no use in depriving these men of the amenities of home by sending them abroad, because they would only add to the burden of maintaining our army overseas, which in my opinion should consist of the largest number of fighting personnel and the smallest number of administrative personnel consonant with efficiency. Similarly among the 60,000 draftees there will be a good many who for the same reasons cannot at any time be sent to the front line. For that reason the order in council, as I understand it, provided that the Minister of National Defence should have the right of selection, and I know his first choice will be to send abroad the best trained and the best fitted men to fight in the front line.
To come to the main motion before the house, it is, as defined by the Prime Minister, a vote of confidence that he is asking, based solely on a vigorous war programme. He has expressly limited the motion to that interpretation. In so doing I think he has done less than justice to himself. He has deprived himself of a very considerable advantage by excluding a vote of the great confidence which this house enjoys in his known ability, in his advanced social programme and the extensive and generous treatment that he is giving to wounded and discharged servicemen. But those considerations having been excluded there remains but one question before usv Has this government met the wishes of the Canadian people in the past and in this present emergency in such a way as to be acceptable to them.? I defy any member of the opposition to say that any other government could have done better than this government has done in the past four-and-a-half or five years. I will go farther and say that in no other democratic country engaged in this war has any government received so little substantial criticism as has this government. It must be obvious, from what has been said in this house to-night- and from the antagonisms which have been arising in the country during the past two or three weeks, that no party could carry on government in this country unless it were truly representative of all sections of our people; and, Mr. Speaker, I-say that there is no government which has done so 100-422J
much as this one in the past and is doing so much at present to represent all sections of this country and to smooth the way between the two great racial groups in Canada, to provide an adequate social programme for the future, and to compose the economic differences between our different groups. For that reason it seems to me it would be fatal to assume that any other government could carry on at this time. This government and this government alone is capable of keeping the Canadian people united behind a maximum and effective war effort, and that to me is the deciding factor to-night. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am going to vote against all the amendments and for the main motion.

First of all I wish to pay my respects to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I understand that he has been, at the front and has been wounded. But the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris) has without a doubt tried his very best to befuddle the issue that is before the house at the present time. He has absolutely befuddled the issue.
Oh, oh.
You can laugh as much as you like, you on the government benches-
Do not get excited.

I am not getting excited, but what did the hon. gentleman say? He said there were plenty , of reinforcements overseas, but he was speaking only of the armoured units. That is all he was speaking about; that is all he said. That is all he knew about; that is the only unit he was in. But that is not the issue at stake to-day. What we are here for in this sitting is to try to get infantry reinforcements for our boys overseas as quickly as possible. They should have been there two or three months ago, and a returned man rises in his place and says we have plenty of reinforcements. He mentioned the fact that the former Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) asked for only 15,000 men. Let the hon. member not go out of the chamber; I want to tell him where he is wrong. Fifteen thousand men; that is all the former minister asked for. Yes; but he asked for those immediately, and he is surprised that they have not already been sent overseas. But the hon. gentleman mentions 16,000 men who are in this order in council and, as we were told in the house, the 16,000 men are supposed to last until May of next year.
War Effort-Government Policy
No.
Yes; that is true. Sixteen thousand; that is what the order in council said.; that is what you were told right here on the floor of the house.
Address the Chair.

You
come out of your tunnel and you will be all right. All you have done is sit in your chair throughout this session and last session and make a noise. The hon. member said there were plenty of reserves overseas. Well, we had General McNaught-on on this floor and he said there were not plenty of reserves overseas for our forces. We had the former minister of national defence on the floor and he said there were not enough infantry reinforcements there. You had your own Prime Minister say the same thing, and he is right at your shoulder now. Yet you belie his own words; you absolutely belie his words.
You missed part of the speech; he said the same thing.

The Minister of Agriculture can get up and, make a speech afterwards. The hon. member also mentioned the faces of the opposition when he came into the house; he said there were smiles on those faces. Well, there were smiles on those faces and I will tell, you why. Members of the opposition have been very much concerned over the condition of things as they are overseas and have been doing their very best to try to cover up their feelings, and I do not think any member of this house has any right to rise in his place and, try to belittle a person because once in a while there is a smile on his face. The hon. member also took exception to the fact that the opposition said there were two armies. There are two armies and there always will be as long as. this government is in power. The order in council takes just 16,000 of the
68,000	or 70,000 of the N.R.M.A., and it still leaves two armies. Some people say there are four armies, but I will not go into that at the present time.
The hon. member also praises the present government. He said that no government could have done better in the war effort than this one. All I can say to him is that no government could have done worse. I can say this, however, and I will say it in all fairness to the people of Canada. Canada has done wonderfully well in this war-not the government; the government has not done it. In spite of the government Canada has done a good job.
In 1942 we were told that if this government ever had a change of heart in regard

to the sending of men overseas parliament would be called together and there would be a vote tfind no debate. We were called together, and the first thing we had was a speech by the Prime Minister, a speech that will go down in history-
Hear, hear.

You say, "hear, hear". Yes; it will go down in history as the swan song of the Liberal government. It was a speech which the boys overseas will wonder at, a speech which the boys in the fighting fronts will wonder at. I will not say they are wondering what they are fighting for, but they will wonder what kind of government we have here at home. That speech must have been a humdinger. I heard it and it was like the speech of the hoe. member for Grey-Bruce, a rather befuddling speech. The Prime Minister, through the wartime information board, had 87,000 copies printed, and an official of the board said that the speech was regarded as factual and nonpolitical, making public a considerable number of facts and figures which had not been known. The former Minister of National Defence certainly showed that it was not factual, that the whole set-up of the Prime Minister was absolutely out of line and not just according to the facts.
I wonder what the director of salvage would say to the Prime Minister of the country for issuing 87,000 of these booklets. I have one of them here. They were sent out to schools and to different organizations. Now, the salvage organization pleads with the people to save paper because it is needed for shells and bombs, but the Prime Minister does not practise what his different organizations try to preach.
With reference to reserves overseas, I am going to read an extract from a letter, not written this year but dated December, 1943. The hon. member over there said that all troops were sent over thoroughly trained.
Did you say 1917?
I was wondering where you were in 1917.
He was not even a zombie.	,

No, I was not a zombie in 1917. This is from a major of the Canadian army now invalided home:

War Effort-Government Policy
The class of men we get as reinforcements are pitiable. Some of them have been in our branch of the service for three years and we have to teach them gun drill in the front line. The system of training over there must be all wrong, or the people responsible slacking on their job or lamentably ignorant of what a soldier should know. It is rather unfair to expect us to train them here under fire; certainly unfair to the men, and they are a good type of men, too.
Then he goes on:
We have had a terrible struggle to capture Ortona, in my opinion the toughest the Canadians have ever experienced.
That man has been invalided home and will never be able to walk again.
The speech of the former Minister of National Defence showed exactly what kind of man the Prime Minister is. When the Prime Minister heard that the fathers, mothers, widows, wives and children of the men fighting overseas were demanding that help be sent to their sons, husbands, fathers and friends, then and then only did he have a right-about-face, and he had that only when his members told him that they would not have one chance in the world of ever getting elected unless he did have a right-about-face. A chameleon changes colour to correspond with his surroundings; the Prime Minister of Canada changes his face. The Prime Minister watches to see the way the wind is blowing and then he tries to blow the easiest way.
We must have support for our men overseas and we must have it at once. The powers-that-be seem to have a different idea about sending the N.R.M.A. men overseas. I shall not go into the order in council because I have not the time, but we need the men at once to support our troops overseas. There are men over there who have been in hospital not three times but many times. There are men listed on the casualty lists as being wounded and in hospital who, when the lists have been checked, have never been wounded at all. They have been put in hospital because they were absolutely exhausted. I know of one man who was marked down as wounded, but he was in hospital from sheer exhaustion because he went through eleven days and nights without sleep and proper food. They had two days' food for eleven days. They were going so fast they could not be caught up with. That was the time they needed reserves.
There is no reason under the sun why we should fool ourselves in thinking that this war will be over soon. We have to remember that our men and our allies are getting into German territory, and the closer they get to that territory and the farther they get into it the harder the Germans are going to fight. They know that at this time there will be no armistice; it will be unconditional surrender and you can rest assured that the Germans will fight to the very last ditch. Our infantrymen are fighting at the present time without any rest or let-up. Just the other day I obtained this casualty list which I hold in my hand, and on it I read the names of two Peterborough boys, one Roy Moore, 43 Frank street, Peterborough, and the other his brother, Edward Moore, at the same address. That is a common occurrence in casualty lists to-day. We find one, two, three or more boys of a family wounded and perhaps two or more wiped out. I have kept track of the casualties in the Peterborough area. I have a book here giving the names in alphabetical order. The pages of that book have been practically filled since June; some of the men are wounded, some missing and some killed, and some seriously wounded. When you see a casualty list like that it is all the more reason why we should get support for these men who are fighting for us.
I have here an extract from a letter of an intelligence officer. I have the letten on my desk upstairs. I shall read only part of it, as follows:
If the people only knew how true Connie Smythe's charges were I'm inclined to think that the pot would soon boil over.
I may say right here that the pot has boiled over.
The section that I am with covers the* reinforcement units, and having covered that area for more than a year now, I am in a position to know something about what Smythe was talking about. And you can imagine the effect it is having on the boys, knowing they are playing politics back home and the situation so critical here.
By that he meant the King government. The men overseas are doing a wonderful job. One reason why I am very much interested in seeing that support is sent over is that I have here a list of the men in the Canadian army overseas from Peterborough city only. The list covers thirty-three pages up to January of last year of men from Peterborough only, not counting the county. Canada has an obligation to these boys. Some of them are dead, passed to the great beyond, having sacrificed all for their country. We have an obligation to all the boys overseas and to their wives, children, fathers, mothers and relatives. We cannot let them down.
I have received letters and telephone calls saying that the Prime Minister, in not wishing to support our boys overseas, must have a very cold heart. I will not say he is coldblooded, and I shall tell you why. Last summer when the temperature was running

War Effort-Government Policy
around 98, 100 and 105 degrees in the House of Commons chamber the Prime Minister came into this house on one occasion, wearing a tweed suit and vest, when every hon. member was fanning himself trying to keep cool. One day one of the hon. members said: "How can he wear a vest in this weather?" And another hon. member a short distance away said: "It is quite understandable; that man could not have red blood in his veins, he must have ice water."
There is a limit to this, Mr. Speaker. Let me make this observation to my hon. friend: I do not remember his name being mentioned in the dispatches in the last war.
(Peterborough West): No; it was never mentioned in the dispatches in the last war; neither was the Prime Minister's.
He was doing something.
I am just telling you the story people across this country' are telling at the present time.
You are the same age as myself; what were you doing in 1917? I should like to know if what I say is true.

Just keep on talking. We have in hospitals overseas some of those men who fought at Dieppe. I know of two brothers who fought together there, and came through safely. Then they went to France. One was killed before his brother's eyes, and only a few weeks later the other was wounded. Another brother was in Italy, and he is missing. One family in my district has five boys overseas already; one still remains in Canada, but he has signed to go overseas.
Have you lost your place?

No, I have not lost my place; I am watching the time, because I want to make this as short as possible. Both in this house and outside the question has been asked, why are the people of the rest of Canada so bitter against the French Canadians.
They are not.
That is perfectly correct; they are not bitter against the French Canadians, but they are bitter against the Prime Minister and his government which has played favourites with the French Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That is not so.
That is so. Only this session in this house I had occasion to ask why in Quebec creameries were allowed to collect .cream every other day-
For goodness' sake get on with the war.
-while in Ontario they were allowed to collect cream only once every four days.
It is the same in Quebec.
It is not.
It has always been the same.

Not according to the wartime prices and trade board. There are many other similar instances I could mention, but I am not going into them to-night. That matter has been brought up, however, and I wanted to answer it. The Prime Minister and his government are to blame for any disunity that exists in this country.
I intend to vote for the amendment offered by my party. We ask for no favouritism toward anyone; that all be treated alike; that all be given the same chance, no matter who or what they are. It should be all for one and one for all immediately. We must give our fighting forces support, and continued support. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has chipped in a number of times, but at this time I do not think it is right to play politics. This is a time for action. Men should be on their way overseas right now, but General McNaughton said that help would not get over there until late in January.
In conclusion, let me say that I am not going to vote for the main motion, after hearing the Prime Minister's speech, in which he said he did not know the conditions overseas; after hearing him blame somebody else for his own neglect; after listening to the speech of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston), and after the secret session. All these things convince me that it is not right to vote for the motion. I am more than ever convinced that the boys overseas need help, and need it right away. If this government cannot conduct an all-out war effort instead of party action, as they have been doing or attempting to do, then I say it is time to change governments. The Prime Minister says there will be anarchy in this land if there is a change of government I doubt that very much. I have faith in the Canadian people, even if the Prime Minister has not.
NOVEMBER 30, 1944	6723
War Effort-Government Policy

Mr. Speaker, the inevitable has happened. The time of reckoning was bound to come, and it is already upon the doorstep of this government. In my opinion this is the result of not having an honest man-power policy from the very start of this war. To me, as to many others, it is the result of political promises made by all parties. At the very outset of the war we were told what a terrible conflict lay ahead. Promises were made that we would never have conscription. Those pronlises should not have been made. I have never hesitated to tell the members of this house and the people of Canada just what my views were. I set forth those views very clearly during my election campaign, during the debate on the plebiscite, and during the debate on bill 80. I would refer hon. members to pages 300 and 301 of Hansard for February 3, 1942; to page 725 of Hansard for February 19, 1942; to pages 3961, 3962 and 3963 of Hansard for July 6, 1942, when I spoke in support of bill 80. At all times in expressing my views on conscription I have been mindful of the position in which hon. members from the province of Quebec found themselves. In this connection I call to the attention of the government the courageous statement made by the hon. member for Belleehasse (Mr. Picard) as it appears in Hansard for June 24, 1942, at page 3671:
If they had talked of Canadian interests in the war, they might have been able to convince the French Canadians to accept a compulsory measure at this time; but not having contributed to bring that about, I do not think the government can expect its supporters from the province of Quebec to go back to our people now and attempt to convince them overnight that conscription for overseas service had become a matter of life or death for Canada. I would be willing to risk myself in such an effort if I had received any help before. But I cannot do it in a week. You cannot all of a sudden, overnight as it were, change the lifelong sentiments of a people.
There, Mr. Speaker, was a frank request for a little help and assistance in order that the hon. member might clearly outline to his people the policy of the government. I wonder what help and assistance, if any, he and the other hon. members from -that province received. We are asked to support a motion which is in effect a vote of confidence. We are told that the fact that this order in council has been passed and is in effect has nothing to do with the vote of confidence; apparently we are going -to accept this order in council, along with many' thousands of others, for what it is worth. It is to be regretted that we, as the elected representatives of the people of Canada, were denied the privilege of expressing our views on this measure by a vote in this
house. Only- when the government does accept the will of the majority of the elected members can democracy in its true form prevail. However, we are told that we shall have to support the government's policy-or else! I wonder just where is -that true form of democracy which we often speak of and for which we are fighting. Yet, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the wording of this resolution is almost the same as that given by the government in the British House of Commons, through the motion of Mr. Attlee on June 27, 1942. That was a vote of confidence by all parties to carry on their coalition government and not along partisan lines.
The last few days we have listened to some startling evidence, and I for one, have no hesitancy in stating my confidence in the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston). His great anxiety at all times has been to make sure that the boys in the service receive ample reinforcements. I have heard him speak often in this house, and' I am sure all members will agree as to his fine qualities and above all his sincerity. Why, then, was this order in council not given to the former minister of national defence? We heard the evidence that this was all he was asking, for the present. Then, may I ask, what was it that changed the government's decision?
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I am in full accord as to the purpose of the amendment to the main motion, and would have supported it. However, after hearing the grave situation as outlined by the former minister of national defence, I consider that the real issue before the house at this time is to see that reinforcements are sent overseas without further delay. I feel it my duty also to put aside any personal views and differences in this regard and to express the same views as the former minister has done. I will therefore vote for the main motion, but I want to make it very clear that I am doing so not as a party supporter but as a duty I owe to Canada and the fighting forces who are fighting for that love of freedom and way of living which is so dear to us all.
Canada's part in this war has been greatly to the credit of the Canadian people. The discreditable part has been in party politics. What the great majority of the people of Canada want is action-and action at once.
Ever since the last war I have felt that conscription was the only fair way of mobilizing man-power. I know there have always been two different views on conscription, and I would like to close my remarks by quoting from what Abraham Lincoln said:
War Effort-Government Policy

Canadian Army
that I shall fulfil my duty to my electors, my race, my province and my country Canada, which I love above all and which, I hope, will become independent in the near future.
On motion of Mr. Mayhew the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
Friday, December 1, 1944
The house met at three o'clock.

maintopic: CANADIAN ARMY (RESERVE) INQUIRY AS TO FUTURE ACTIVITIES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CANADIAN ARMY (RESERVE) INQUIRY AS TO FUTURE ACTIVITIES
speechtext:
I desire to direct a question to
the Acting Minister of National Defence, but I do not see him in his seat at the moment. Perhaps some other minister may be able to answer on behalf of the government. It has been brought to my attention on more than one occasion during the last month or so that the situation with respect to Canada's reserve army, formerly known as the non-permanent active militia, is becoming more acute as the days go on. I am told that in some centres the attendance is tapering off and in the minds of both officers and men there is a feeling of uncertainty as to the future of the reserve army. They are awaiting at the moment a full declaration of government policy with respect to the part this army- is to play in the future in Canada. The patriotic citizens who are giving much valuable time from their civilian activities to maintain this volunteer citizen army have made an important contribution to our war effort, and I think some clarification of -their position is in order. I would therefore ask that the government make a declaration in the matter so that a definite and clear-cut policy will be known to the officers, to the men and to the Canadian public.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, November 30, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon.
War Effort-Government Policy

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I think that everyone in this house will be in accord with my first remarks. I am sure that all hon. members noticed in the press this morning that Major Alan Chambers, member for Nanaimo, the county next to the constituency which I have the honour to represent, has won the Distinguished Service Order. He has brought great credit to himself, honour to the country, and honour and distinction to his own constituency as well as my own. I am extremely proud therefore to be able to refer to it at this moment. Further, I have a telegram from Major Chambers which he wishes me to read to the house. He has been in the army for over four years, and has been overseas for two years. He was with the Canadian troops in Sicily and is now serving in northwest Europe, where he has distinguished himself as is evidenced by this citation to-day. Before reading this cable I want to make two observations in connection with it, one as to the place from which it was sent and the other as to the time at which it was sent He was overseas and therefore was not subject to the many demands that have been *made upon the rest of us in this house. Whatever decision he arrived at was his .own decision. I should like hon. membens also to note the date it was sent. It was written in London on November 18, five days before this session reconvened. His wire is as follows:
Reference special session. Regret military service France prevents attendance. Quote my stand on question remains same as stated my speech Ottawa May fourth, namely when the army requires trained reinforcements they must be available. If the only trained men available are required for battle and will not volunteer they must be sent anyway and sent in time to meet the battle demands.
What I have to say from now on must not be confused with the statement of Major Chambers. Each hon. member of this house must stand on his own feet and do what he thinks best. So, Mr. Speaker, may I now state my own position as clearly as possible.
In 1942 I urged the people of my constituency of Victoria to vote yes on the plebiscite. Further, I voted with the government in support of bill No. 80. Before coming east last January to attend the 1944 session I told my, executive that in my opinion the issue of conscription would be before the house before the end of the session. I thought it would be remarkable if Canada were able to undertake an offensive with all her forces, and maintain all her wartime industry, including

shipbuilding, the building of planes and all the wastage on the battle line, without a weakness being discovered somewhere. It was on that premise that I told my executive that if the man-power situation was such that reinforcements were demanded and we could not get them under the voluntary system. I would be supporting conscription. That situation has now arisen. We have been told by both the former and the present Minister of National Defence that there is a serious shortage of men in the infantry; therefore I am supporting the order in council, and I support it as I understand it. Having questioned the Minister of National Defence in this house and having listened to his statement, I understand the order and the policy of the government to be that all physically fit men in the N.R.M.A. will be put into training camps and properly trained and conditioned, and that
16,000	will be sent over between now and May 1, 1945, with more to be sent over if and when necessary. If my understanding of the order is not correct I ask to be corrected, because on that understanding I am supporting the resolution of the Prime Minister.
I referred to the 1942 plebiscite and to my support of bill No. 80 to indicate that I have not been a victim of pressure from any source whatever, though one must take into consideration the opinion of the majority of one's constituents. In all this, however, I hear but one voice other than the dictates of my own conscience and the workings of my own mind; that is the voice of Canada's bravest sons calling for help while they are fighting our battle for freedom. In my opinion that help must be forthcoming, regardless of any consequences. I do not blame the government for stopping to consider alternatives in this matter of reinforcements, if there are any, to consider what might be the result in this country, and to count carefully the cost to Canada as a whole before taking this stand. To me that has taken real courage, greater courage than was required by those who faced the same situation in 1917, because we know what happened then and we can perhaps judge more accurately what may happen in the future. I will give this government my full and best support as long as it endeavours in every way possible to get. sufficient men overseas to support and relieve those already there. When a man is obliged to leave the fighting front there must be some other equally

War Effort-Government Policy
reliable and equally well trained man to whom he can throw the torch. I believe the present government can and will do that, and until I think differently I will support it.
I want to emphasize here that I have never been an advocate of limiting our war effort, either as to money, material or man-power. I think perhaps some hon. members will remember a letter which was circulated early in the war, quoting excerpts from a speech I made in my home city, in which I said that Canada should be prepared to give Great Britain anything she wanted that we could give her, and that we should mark the cost on our cuff until the war is over. My position in that regard has not changed. I maintain it, not only in respect of goods or foodstuffs or munitions, but in respect of the supplies of men.
I realize that in taking this position I am intimating that I am not satisfied with the aid that has been given to Great Britain. The fact is that I am quite satisfied; but I think it would have been better for us had we proceeded in another fashion. When we come to settle the cost of sending materials and supplies to Great Britain we must remember the long past, when to so great an extent Canada was dependent upon the mother country for protection and support, and even for financing. We shall have also to consider the present; because this is not Great Britain's war; it is a war of freedom-loving peoples against the oppressors. Therefore our support ia not given to Great Britain but rather to ourselves. If we take these two items we find that we almost wipe out any credit balance which might have been placed on our side of the ledger. And if we add to that what is going to happen in the future-our desir-e to continue trade with Great Britain and our desire that at this time she should have everything she needs in the way of foodstuffs, building materials, and everything else, then I think that whether we wish it or not we would have to write off the balance.
I repeat that I would not have limited our contribution, and that I do not see how we can limit it, when we promised at the beginning of the war that we would go shoulder to shoulder all the way, to the maximum of our materials and man-power, and to the end of the struggle. How, then, can we impose any limitations?
Let me say a word or two about conscription. Much has been made of the point that at heart the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie
100-423J
King) is not one who believes in compulsion, and that General McNaughton, who has taken over the portfolio of national defence, is not in favour of it. I wonder who among Anglo-Saxons is in favour of compulsion? We adopt it when we have to-and this is one time when we have to. But unless conditions warrant it I do not think that at heart any of us wants to say, "you must do this" or "you must do that", whether it be to fight or to do something else.
It is my belief that, a condition has developed to-day under which we have to say to the 60,000 young men in Canada under the N.R.M.A. that when we are in desperate straits we cannot tolerate a group of that size not doing its share.
I should like at this point to read a paragraph from a letter I received this morning, and which I believe sets out the two sides of the question. It saj's:
My two sons, Ernie and Frank, were the only two who cared to stay on the farm with me. I found it very hard to get along alone.
Her husband was an ex-soldier, and he has gone.
We hope Frank will be entitled to come on leave at Christmas, as he enlisted on September 3. 1939. I might say we have six sons in the army and one in the navy.
Now, in view of those facts one could argue against conscription. Here is a family of loyal people, people who are possibly more emotional than some others-and these can be found in other parts of Canada. I know of similar situations in Quebec where through their emotions people have gone beyond their limits. In my view they should not have been allowed to do so much. We should not permit seven boys from one family to serve in the armed services; and had we had a selective process that might not have happened.
But it can also be argued: Have these seven boys the obligation to fight for all that Canada stands for in the way of freedom and advantages, in the opportunities it offers for establishing homes, and in education? Have they that right? Is there any justice to have all seven of them fighting, while probably a neighbouring boy does not fight, and still enjoys those same privileges in Canada? I think you will agree with me, sir, that the subject can be argued both ways. I agree with General McNaughton when he says that he will hold open the doors for voluntary enlistment. We have enlisted in this country under the voluntary system over 900.000 young men and women. We have 60.000 under the
War Effort-Government Policy

N.R.M.A., or less than seven per cent. Are we now going to close the doors for voluntary-enlistment to all the young boys who come of age 'between now and the end of the war, or shall we give them the opportunity to say for themselves, "Yes, of my own accord) I am going to enlist. I am not going to wait to be forced, through conscription." I believe we should leave the door open to the boys with spirit and patriotism who would enlist voluntarily.
I have heard it argued in the house that we might have proceeded in a different fashion, that we could have shortened our lines. I am not a military man, but I think that is one argument to which one might easily pay some attention. Probably we could strike harder and oftener if our forces were less scattered, but not being a military man I have to accept the advice of those who have been over there. Suppose we do shorten our line; suppose we take out our men every once in a while to give them a rest-God knows I would like to see that done; suppose we treat them as they should be treated, we still have not got over the fact that there are 60,000 men here in Canada. I do not believe that all those
60,000	are unwilling to fight. I should be surprised if one-fifth of them actually did not want to go over. But no matter how small the proportion may be, they should be called up.
I want to say a word about the general service men. I met quite a few of them when I was home. Some of these men have been in the army for two, three and four years. One man who came into my office just before I left for Ottawa had the white chevron and four red chevrons, indicating that he had had five years' service in the Canadian army. He also had the maple leaf on his ribbon. I assumed that he had been overseas but he told me that he had got that for a Cook's tour. Two other boys who came in to see me had not been over either. They told me that the Department of National Defence had1 asked) them to try to convince the N.R.M.A. boys to go active. They said, "What chance have we to convince those boys? They merely say that we are hiding behind the general service badge on our uniform; behind our backs they will say that we, not they, are the zombies."
Just here may I say that I think that word should be barred from use in this house. No Canadian who is good enough to wear the king's uniform should be called a zombie. These boys went to Kiska when they were asked to go. They went up there, on a draft put into effect by an order in council similar

to the order in council we have here. They were prepared to meet the Japs quite bravely, and it is not their fault that the Japs ran away. I was in Gordon Head when these boys came back from Kiska. .At that time the word "zombie" was becoming quite popular, but not one of those boys knew its meaning. I doubt if one out of a hundred knows its meaning to-day. Let somebody give the Canadian people the actual meaning of that word and then let us in the House of Commons refrain from using it.
That is the position in which you put the general service men. They have no chance of recruiting these other men when they , are up against that. But there is something else to be considered. One of these men who came in to see me was quite well known to me. He holds the rank of colonel, and he told me that during the five years he had been serving in Canada the difference between what he received as an officer serving in Canada and what he would have received had he been serving overseas amounted to S13,000-made up pf income tax and loss of gratuities. I think you will find that quite a number of these young officers, non-commissioned officers and men will be ready to go over. While some of them may be hiding behind their general service badges, I believe the number is comparatively few.
I want to say one word about the resolution itself. It reads:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
There are two points in that motion of which every hon. member should take notice. I do not think they have been mentioned as yet. The first is that there is a definite promise by the government that it will maintain the momentum of Canada's war effort in order that it may become one of the greatest war efforts of any country of like size in the world. If they fall down in that promise, I as a supporter of the government will not hesitate to tell them about it. The second point is that an appeal is made in the motion to every member of this house, regardless of party or regardless of where he comes from, ,to exert every effort to help this government to maintain this war effort. When a member gets up in this house and votes against this motion he mukt act according to his own conscience.

Let me quote from a statement which I think the hon. member will accept. I read from page 6610 of Hansard:
I need not repeat the order which is P.C. No. 8891; I think it will be found on examination that it contains precisely what I said in terms I would do in 1942. The order in council P.C. 8891 applies to all personnel who are serving or may serve in consequence of having been called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. *
And then one or two lines further on:
That is, one order in council covers the entire force.
Mr. G.S. WHITE (Hastings-Peterborough): Mr. Speaker, first I would like to refer briefly to certain remarks which have been made this week by some hon. members. Let me refer first to the hon. member for London (Mr. Johnston). In his remarks on Wednesday he stated that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to conscription, everyone knew what he meant. I find on page 6606 of Hansard of November 27 the word "conscription" as defined by the Prime Minister. He says:
The policy was set forth in June, 1943-
I believe he meant 1942:
-and it has been defined in the words:
"not necessarily conscription, but conscription if necessary. And I might add the words, "to the extent only that it is necessary."
The word "necessary" appears twice and I will not attempt to put my own definition upon it. Instead, I will quote from the correspondence, filed in this house, between the Prime Minister and the Hon. J. L. Ralston. At page 8 of the correspondence the following appears in a letter from Colonel Ralston to the Prime Minister on November 6.

speechtext: Order. Yesterday, and I presume the same will happen to-day, there was constant reference to the hon. and gallant member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) by name.
