speechtext: You are wise.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
-but I feel that I must do everything in my power to see that reinforcements are provided for our lads overseas. There is nothing I will not do, at any time, no matter what may be the sacrifice, to see that these reinforcements are provided. I cannot follow the argument of the hon. member for Prince, who left the cabinet, who pointed out all the inaccuracies of the Prime Minister' up to a given point, but then said, "I must support this government because the Prime Minister has made another promise, and I must give him another chance." I just cannot support that halting attitude, which was taken also by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., the hon. member for Lambton West and others, including the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), who went right to the brink, who stated that they believed what

War Effort-Government Policy
is embodied in our amendment but simply could not agree with this party. The amendment I intend to support reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war, and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice.
A moment ago I believed the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) cut in with a remark which I ignored at the time, because I had not much longer to speak. He stated that I was wise in not wanting an election. This government has an up-to-date political organization in operation. As the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) stated last evening, they have had all their publicity ready for many months; as a matter of fact I believe the Prime Minister indicated the other evening that they could have had an election two years ago and that he would have swept the country. I know something of the reports coming to the head office of this Liberal organization in regard to the situation throughout the country, and after studying the Prime Minister's proposal it seems to me that he is more concerned about winning an election than about reinforcements for overseas. I believe that to be a true statement of fact. While I do not want an election, I have no fear of one. However, I am more concerned about reinforcements, although I cannot be bluffed by the Prime Minister or any other member of the government on this issue at this time.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house, moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), asks that this house shall aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort. As one of those coming from the main soldier city of the dominion, a city which in two wars has contributed so many men, I regret to say that I cannot support the motion. I have come to that conclusion purely from the point of view of the soldiers. This house knows very well the steps that were taken by this government from the time it came to office in 1935 until the outbreak of war and since; and the policy has not been by any means productive of a vigorous war effort, nor have they maintained it.
As far as voluntary recruiting is concerned, I do not believe it was given the chance it should have had. As you very properly said in a ruling the other evening, Mr. Speaker, it is the duty of this house either to approve or to disapprove the policy of the government. That is also the duty of this opposition,
because often in the past criticism has been a tonic that has caused the government to take action. I am glad that the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) has been vindicated in the action he took, that his judgment and wisdom in regard to overseas reinforcements have been upheld, but he should have gone farther. I have never, during the last war or between the wars or during this war, spoken on this matter as a partisan, nor am I a partisan in the strict sense of that word. My duty is to the soldiers overseas. As the former minister said in the last two lines of the letter he wrote to the Prime Minister, his first duty as a minister was to the troops overseas. I believe that in that stand he has the overwhelming support of the people of Canada. In my opinion the way the minister was turned out of office, after having taken the stand he did, was not creditable to the Liberal party or to the government of this country. I believe that the verdict of the people as a whole is that the House of Commons is better than the cabinet; they have shown that in the last two weeks. The House of Commons is vastly superior to the government of the day, and the public, back in the constituencies, are far better than the House of Commons; they know more than we do. The other day I referred to the great losses that have been suffered. Over a thousand boys from the secondary schools of my city have lost their lives during the present war. In almost every block in my constituency there has been a casualty during this war, some boy wounded, missing or killed. I believe that the present government on the man-power question and equality of service has been everything by fits and starts, and nothing very long.
I was not very anxious to take part in this debate and would not have done so but for the large number of letters I have received since we adjourned last August, and the casualties we have suffered in the Mediterranean area, in the low countries and in France. I have been astounded and almost appalled to read the daily reports issued by the government showing the casualties suffered. In days like these I believe moderation should be the supreme law for all, but we should be sane and honest with one another and with our soldiers overseas. I speak what I believe to be the truth. I would not hurt or offend any person in this house by any remark I might make, but we cannot all think alike, and I must say, temperately and moderately, that what I believe to be the truth should be said in a crisis such as this. I believe that we should pursue a policy of malice toward none and charity toward all, even though we cannot see each other's point
6744	COMMONS
War Effort-Government Policy
of view. It has been said that England invented the phrase, "His Majesty's Loyal Opposition", and that took place under a Tory government, with Danby who invented the party system. This made criticism of the administration as much a part of parliamentary life as the administration itself. As I have said, in times past criticism has stirred this government to action.
As I said in the house the other day, the government has turned a complete somersault from voluntary service to conscription, and I must say that does no credit to the party system. In less than twenty-four hours the government of the day and the new minister made a complete change. I did not ask the new minister any questions; I did not want to do so; I felt sorry for him in attempting a hard task, since I had known him for so long. I believe that it is an error in wisdom and judgment on his part, and it would have been far better if he had left things as they were, and not accepted office. He would have received more support from the soldiers' and the people of this country.	,
As I survey the ups and downs of our man-power policy since the beginning of the war I am reminded of the words of Tennyson's "In Memoriam":
Let knowledge grow from more to more.
That is badly needed in the House of Commons to-day, in connection with this question. But Tennyson, in his "In Memoriam," justifies the wishes and the judgment of those on the opposite benches who have supported a total war, and all-out aid for our soldiers overseas. He says:
Our little systems have their day
They have their day and cease to be;
They are but broken lights of thee,
And thou, 0 Lord, art more than they.
This system of voluntary enlistment had run its course months and months ago. Why did Brigadier Mess resign? I can remember that before the house adjourned in August the former Minister of National Defence projected a most elaborate publicity programme in an effort to do his utmost to put the voluntary recruiting system on its feet. Appeals were made in the secondary schools. I am sorry to say that it would have been far better if they had stayed out of the schools.
However, a real effort was made. That system was dead and gone long ago, beyond recall. I saw the stores and rooms which were opened in support of voluntary recruiting. Day by day I passed those stores, but I never saw a soul in them, with the exception
[Mr. Church.}
of some officials. I do not criticize the officers of the department, because I know they did their best. But I believe that system of voluntary enlistment was finished, in this country.
I can remember meeting hundreds of
soldiers who have returned home with wounds, after the heavy fighting in Italy, France and the low countries. I have seen them at the railway stations as they have travelled on the trains, as they have been in hospitals and in their homes, and I have received many letters from overseas. One after another has told me that the voluntary system was wrong and unfair, that it was unjust and produced inequalities of service and treatment. They have pointed out that it has used people on one side of the street in one way and the people on the other side in another way, without any equality of service and sacrifice. That was where the first mistake was made. We should have had a different system from the beginning of the war.
This is a changing war. It changes from day to day, from week to week and from month to month. That applies, too, to the equipment and the instruments of war. Something should have been done long ago to remedy the present situation. As I see it, this is not a conscription debate. One day in the house I asked the Minister of Justice of that day about this matter. I believe that was at a time shortly before the outbreak of war. In reply to my question he told me that the conscription act of 1917 was still on the statute books, and it is also in the Militia Act and in the N.R.M.A. I believe my question to that effect could be found in Hansard.
Then, we have had conscription for home defence and defence of adjacent territory since the passage of bill No. 80. In addition to that we have had it through the draftees' policy which has been followed for the last two years. But, after condemning the former Minister of National Defence the government turns right around and adopts the policy of conscription, which in my opinion is not total conscription at all under their order in council.
There is no use in our trying to trifle with the public in that fashion. We are told that
60.000	draftees have been called, and of that number the Prime Minister admits that
42.000	are available for army training. Sixteen thousand of them have had some training, another 8,000 are almost completely trained, and 8,000 more about half trained. Twenty-four thousand of them require further training, but in a few months would be ready to take their place in the line.

War Effort-Government Policy
I am not one who will join in voting in favour of this motion. My vote will be a strictly non-partisan vote, but I will vote against the motion. I am not going to join in any "Te Deum" of praise. I am not joining in any hallelujah chorus, because it was the people back in the constituencies and the press who compelled the government of the day last week to reverse its policy.
Between the two wars the profession of arms was openly laughed at in this chamber. Some said that it was demoralizing, and that all public bodies should oppose it. Those people even went into the schools and supported the policy of pacifism. I am a humble member of a church which agrees with the thirty-nine articles, one of which states that it is lawful for Christian men at the command of the magistrates to take up arms and to serve in the wars.
When I see the efforts which have been made to secure volunteers I must say I am at a loss to understand how the voluntary system lasted as long as it did, because it is not adapted to a war like this. I admit that the resolution now before us is skilfully drawn, but it is full of pitfalls, and it does not mean what it says.
What has been the policy of the government? One day it is a policy of voluntary enlistment, and the next day it is a policy of conscription. There are different points of view; first there is your own view, there is the right view, and there is the other fellow's view. And let us not forget the other fellows' view, and have respect for it. There is "change and decay in all around I see" in this building. This is a most important question that has been placed before the people of Canada. From the start the government has attempted to wage a Liberal war; it did not want any help or advice from the opposition. The result was that the government has not waged the war effort it should have waged.
During two wars and in the period of depression between those wars I supported national service, and equality of service and sacrifice. The people want to know the truth, the whole truth arid nothing but the truth, about this matter. This problem is their problem. But the government could not make up its mind last week, even for twenty-four hours. It is conducting the war, and it is a duty of the government to conduct that war overseas, so long as it is the government of the day.
In the last war a million men went from the dominions to fight. We know that 130,000 of them fell on the field of battle. They went there under their own status, sovereignty and autonomy. They went to the side of the
mother country; her cause was the cause of all, and what they did changed the history of the whole civilized world.
I can remember quite well the period between the two wars when 200,000 youth were coming out of our high schools every year. I can recall the actions of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and his supporters. The other day he attacked the Conservative party, or the Progressive Conservative party as it is now called. We do not need to be called the Progressive Conservative party because we have always been progressive. Some of us between the two wars advocated a policy of rearmament, national service, full publicity of foreign affairs, complete service and sacrifice and of every citizen doing his duty. The dictators solved the unemployment problem in their countries by preparing for war, and we should solve our unemployment problem by preparing for peace.
We must use our natural resources to even out the trade cycle. I contended that full use should be made of the 200,000 youth who were coming out of the high schools yearly during Hitler's ascension to power from 1935 to 1939. I contended that they should have military training instead of having to ride the rods. An apprenticeship system extending over three to five years should have been set up. These youths could have learned a trade and gained some knowledge of our key industries. They should have been given this training, along with their board and lodging and some pocket money, and deferred pay and physical and military training during the depression that engulfed the whole world.
If that action had been taken when the war broke out we would have had 25,000 trained mechanics and pilots for our air force. But nothing was done and I never heard the gentlemen to my left make any protest. Most of them were not even in the house then; some were. They believed in complete pacifism. They thought the war would never come. They argued that we could depend upon Washington and the league for any defence that we needed. Why have we had to go through all .these elaborate ceremonials during the past month?
Since the war started we have had a plebiscite; then we had a census; then we had bill No. 80, and then we had a national selective service register. All this was done when it was the plain duty of the government to wage a total war with total conscription. There should have been a policy of sending adequate reinforcements overseas weekly and monthly as they were needed. These reinforcements should have been sent to our troops who

War Effort-Government Policy
had borne the heat and burden of the day, some of them for nearly four or five years.
What did the government do? It showed a magnificent disregard for the need of a proper survey to show the true facts, and it relied on tradition for the conduct of the war. It operated on old and obsolete war rules; it took the provincial and parochial view of the man-power situation, and there has been no equality of service or sacrifice. It has resorted to the old system since 1640. When I review the situation, when I recall the excuses, coma, inertia, doubt, fear, delays, procrastinations, postponements, fireworks and somersaults that have taken place, I am driven to believe that the government's action is something like what a soldier said of the charge of the Light Brigade which he witnessed: "C'est magnifique, mais ce n'est pas la guerre." "It is magnificent, but it is not war."
That has been the policy of the government for some time until the minister gave a proper report. Everybody knew that reinforcements were urgently required. Everybody knew that reserves were needed overseas, but until the report of the minister was brought down, nothing was done. The minister had a plan to do it now and do it right, to do it for all time, for yesterday, to-day and forever-to provide total reinforcements of draftees at once.
I have no further confidence that the government will ever solve this question. The whole policy of the Prime Minister has been nothing but shadow-boxing and window-dressing at a time when the main issue has been the absolute and immediate need for reinforcements overseas.
We should not speculate too much about the end of the war, even though Mr. Churchill tells us that it may end by next summer. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand) made a prediction, but I do not know whether he was telling a fish story. He said that the war was about at an end. As I say, that may be a fish story in connection with which he is an expert, but the fact is that we should not be prophesying about the end of this war.
No doubt the German army will be beaten. The dictators made the greatest preparations for this war, but we sat and did nothing. The democracies which had made no preparations have beaten the dictators at least so far. If the necessary reinforcements were provided, the war would be shortened. No one can tell when the Germans will capitulate. They are a tough crowd of thugs and murderers, ten times as tough as they were from 1914 to 1918. They are the toughest crowd that has ever been turned out in the history of mili-

tary warfare. A bunch of terrorists, brigands and murderers are now at the head of Germany. They have seized power and they can keep going much longer. They are going to keep going; the fighting will be much harder, and our casualties will be much greater.
Nobody has as yet offered any plan as to how Germany will be curbed after this war. Fortunately the war is being carried to them, but after the war is over we are likely to have lots of trouble with them. One good thing is that many of the young Germans who would be likely to give us the most trouble are being destroyed. Russia and Poland have a plan; they are going to keep one or two million Germans and make them work to rebuild their countries. Those Germans will have to work just for their food and clothing. The same policy should be followed by the low countries, France, Czechoslovakia, Belgium and Norway. Camps of these Germans should be established to rebuild these different countries.
I have a few constructive remarks to make to the government in this connection, but before I do so I should like to refer to the fact that Mr. Churchill has just had another birthday. There is one thing about the British constitution; the British have acted the same way in this war as they did in the Crimean war when they put out the Quaker and they put in the pugilist. This pugilist had a birthday yesterday, and he is the one pugilist who is going to give these dictators a complete knockout in a very few months. I have every respect for our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) expressed yesterday. One great advantage of the constitution of the mother country is the fact that in peace or war it can change itself to meet any circumstance or situation. It is said that the British cabinet under Aberdeen during the Crimean war was the greatest cabinet since the Reform Act, 1836; yet that cabinet was put out.
As Sir Walter Bagehot says in his textbook, "The Law and English Constitution":
Under a cabinet constitution at a sudden emergency this people can choose a ruler for the occasion. It is quite possible and even likely that he would not be ruler before the occasion. The great qualities, the imperious will, the rapid energy, the eager nature fit for a great crisis are not required-are impediments-in common times. A Lord Liverpool is better in everyday politics than a Chatham- a Louis Philippe far better than a Napoleon. By the structure of the world we often want, at the sudden occurrence of a grave tempest, to change the helmsman-to replace the pilot of the calm by the pilot of the storm. In England we have had so few catastrophies since our constitution attained maturity, that we hardly appreciate this latent excellence. We have not needed a Cavour to rule a revolution [DOT]-a representative man above all men fit for

War Effort-Government Policy
a great occasion, and by a natural legal mode brought in to rule. But even in England, at what was the nearest to a great sudden crisis which we have had of late years-at the Crimean difficulty-we used this inherent power. We abolished the Aberdeen cabinet, the ablest we have had, perhaps since the Reform Act- a cabinet not only adapted, but eminently adapted, for every sort of merit then wanted, who, when he feels the steady power of England behind him will advance without reluctance, and will strike without restraint. As was said at the time, "we turned out the Quaker, and put in the pugilist."
During the first days of this parliament one hon. member used some remarks which I did not then concur in. The statement was made that the ministry should resign. I take issue with this position. As I have said before, the people elected this government with 178 seats. They were elected by the Canadian people, and therefore the responsibility rests upon the government to conduct the war as long as they are the government and to make an allout effort so that our troops shall receive the necessary reinforcements.
I agree with what the member for Dufferin-Simcoe said with reference to the Prime Minister. I believe in moderation, especially in these days, and I have already given my reasons why we cannot all share the same views. I suggest to the government, however, that the army needs men. There are too many men now in the R.C.A.F. Why could we not have a division of R.C.A.F. infantry organized? I have seen dozens of these young fellows just out of high school, and many of them spent all summer aUd all fall erecting wooden structures in connection with the training in No. 1 manning pool. They were devoting their time to this work night and day. I suggest that a ground division of R.C.A.F. infantry could be organized, because I have seen many of these lads marking time day after day and they would be glad to go active.
I would ask the government, what has been done to transfer available men from the R.C.A.F. for service overseas. Another thing I would point out to the government is that only about one-eighth of one per cent of the men overseas are getting home this Christmas. I suggest, in order to aid recruiting, that something should be done to extend the time of our soldiers in Canada over Christmas and New Year. They should have three or four days additional for travelling. I have seen letters from mothers in my constituency saying that their boys just managed to get home from the maritimes and had to go back on Christmas evening.
These serving men should be looked after by the government. Why can there not be more transportation for them? Transportation
is provided for different people travelling all over Canada. Look at the control boards. The trains throughout the country are crowded with people who could very well make room for our fighting men. We have people travelling with missions to the old land and to the United States. In fact, we have in Washington a small expeditionary force there. There is no trouble about transportation for them; why should our soldiers overseas not get transportation home with all the aid our navy and shipping can give if we had reinforcements?
As regards these 16,000 men for whom the order in council makes provision, we could raise from fifty to sixty or seventy thousand men if we went about it properly. Many of our young soldiers of eighteen or nineteen years of age are being killed, and others have been overseas for three, four and five years. They should be brought home for keeps, and something should be done about that immediately.
This is a war that is changing from month to month and I should like to see some clarification of this order in council. I do not want to bother the new minister with questions, but there is one important matter that I would bring to his attention. I would ask him this question: Does a civilian lose his rights when he joins the army? When the war broke out we had no army, no navy, no air force, nothing; we had to start from scratch. We have a citizens army in this country because we had to start from scratch. But it seems that when certain soldier people discuss matters of vital concern to the country action is taken to curb them. If they wish to express an opinion concerning a military question, the question of volunteer service versus compulsion, steps are taken to prevent them from expressing their views. Should all their civilian rights be taken away from them because they join the army? No one has any right to take away the rights of our citizens. They have not done so in the United States. Look at the campaign that has been carried on in that country. No such attempt has been made to prevent men from expressing their views. Nor have I heard of any such action having been taken in England. I hope the new order will be cancelled.
I brought this matter to the attention of the former minister. I pointed out to him that apparently a citizen has no rights when he joins the army. The former minister two years ago abrogated the order and it became of no effect. The same should be done here.
May I offer some other suggestions to the government. I would say: Keep out of the secondary schools for recruiting. The secon-

War Effort-Government Policy
daryi schools have cadet corps, military training and all that kind of thing, but for those of sixteen and seventeen, the application was refused by the board of education for Toronto.
I have yet to hear anyone sum up the cardinal principles of the new elaborate recruiting policy. Another thing I object to is this. I know some of the commanding officers; I have known some of them for a great many years. I do not believe that it was wise to use any compulsion to adopt a system that was through, with respect to these commanding officers when they came to Ottawa, in the discussion with the new minister. One of these men came from Winnipeg, a fine citizen and) a good soldier, and he has resigned. He would not put up with it. I venture to say that if some of these men could tell us what was going on at that time hon. members would agree with me that instead of having the new minister here we should have had the commanding officers. I am sure they could tell more than the present minister. I have not spoken ten words to him since the war started, but I have always had a great respect for him. I believe, however, that he showed poor judgment in becoming a politician.
We should have the reports of the heads of military districts before us. I asked the former minister a question about this in the house with reference to the dispatch of troops to Italy and why they were kept in England for four years. I asked why it was that we had no soldiers with General Montgomery in the march across the desert in Africa when there were tens of thousands of Australians and New Zealanders, Indians and troops from South Africa. There were none from Canada. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I believe he said that in any event it was not the duty or the function of the commanding officer overseas but primarily the duty and function of the minister. I think he answered the question correctly. I have always had a great admiration and respect for the people of Quebec. I have expressed it on many occasions, during both the present war and the last war. In the debate on August 4 last on foreign affairs I said that France would always be a great nation, and made other remarks in that connection; and I compliment the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) upon having called yesterday upon the citizens of his province to obey the law, remain calm and not destroy property or use unlawful means.
Let it not be forgotten that Britain has sustained half the losses on the sea and in the air while some of our present allies were neutral; and, as I have reminded the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. 
LaCroix), but for the mother country during two years after Dunkirk, we would have known the awful horrors of war on our own soil, not only in Quebec but in Ontario and the maritimes; we would have suffered the gestapo, the whip, the loud speaker, the concentration camp, and the removal of thousands and tens of thousands of our citizens to Germany to work.

speechtext: May I rise to a question of privilege? It has to do with the question of the amendment which was moved to a government motion this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Justice. As my hon. friend moved the amendment it occurred to me that it was a strange procedure, having regard to the fact that no notice had been given of his resignation as a parliamentary assistant. I asked him then- I do not know whether the Prime Minister was in the chamber at the time-if he had resigned, and he said that he had. It seemed to me that it was a pretty important point, because it was a major amendment against the government motion made by the right-hand man of one of the major ministers of the crown. I do not think it is enough for my hon. friend to say that he has resigned; I think the resignation must be accepted by the government; I do not believe that a parliamentary assistant can just walk out of his job while he is moving an amendment and afterwards move back into the position again, without the public-in common street parlance-feeling that there is "a nigger in the woodpile" with respect to the whole matter. I do not want the Minister of Justice to be suspected by the public as being one of those who were engineering a move of that kind, and I think the fact that the parliamentary assistant has resigned-

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Leader of the Government in the Senate
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. GRAYDON REFERENCE TO AMENDMENT MOVED BY A PARLIAMENTARY ASSISTANT TO A GOVERNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
With regard to the questions my hon. friend has raised, I recall that the parliamentary assistant to the former Minister of National Defence also tendered his resignation. He did it for Teasons of his association with the minister, and asked me if I would accept it. At the time I was not too sure whether it was desirable to accept it, and I was far from sure that it was the custom in the British parliament with respect to parliamentary assistants to have resignations necessarily follow the resignation of the ministers whose assistants they were. I wrote Mr. Macdonald that I was in doubt about just what the procedure should be. I said, as far as I recollect it, that as parliament might not be lasting very long, I doubted whether there was any necessity one way or the other. Mr. Macdonald was himself not too sure of the course he should take. However, he did subsequently say that he wished to have his resignation accepted, and I accepted it.
I must say that I do not think there is any Teason why a parliamentary assistant should not be just as free as a minister or any member of parliament to take whatever course he wishes to take in giving expression to his views in parliament. There is no reason why *a hon. member who holds the position of parliamentary assistant should tender his
resignation just because he intends to make a motion in the house. I can understand a parliamentary assistant feeling that he would wish to have his motives above question and that no doubt should be left in the mind of anyone that he wished to be free and untrammelled in the attitude that he would take either for or against a particular course in the house. The hon. member wrote me to that effect; he stated that he wished to be released from a position where anyone could misunderstand the motive that he might have in-he did not say, as I remember, in bringing forward a motion; it was, in any course he might take during the present crisis. When I read his letter I replied to him that I would have a word with the Minister of Justice about it; that, seeing that he wished to have perfect freedom and not to be misunderstood or his actions misinterpreted in any way, if the Minister of Justice were agreeable I would be agreeable to releasing him from his duties. But I very much hope that this crisis is not going to last indefinitely, and I am also hoping that circumstances may be such that the government may be in a position to ask the hon. member to reconsider his position later on. Certainly we are not going to adopt a course in this house whereby, if a member of the House of Commons becomes the assistant of a minister, he is thereby to be hamstrung in the matter of his perfect freedom to introduce a motion or to refrain from introducing a motion.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Justice as I understand his purpose, wishes to prevent any doubt or suspicion from arising as to his perfect freedom of action. He has taken that course and will be released from duty in order that his actions may stand out as something being done without fear or favour in any direction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday
my hon. friend asked me if I would give to the house the correspondence between Mr. Jean, parliamentary: assistant to the Minister of Justice, and myself. On Friday afternoon, December 1, I received the following letter addressed to myself, as Prime Minister:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I deeply regret to have to tender my resignation as Parliamentary Assistant to the Honourable the Minister of Justice.
You will understand, I feel confident, that during the present crisis I may think it preferable to release myself from any administrative connection with the government, in order to take my responsibilities as a member of parliament with full liberty of conscience.
I wish to thank you very sincerely for having entrusted me with this position of parliamentary assistant. It was indeed a privilege to have the opportunity of serving in my humble way under your administration.
Yours very truly,
Joseph Jean.
To this communication I replied on the same date, December 1 in the afternoon, as follows:
Joseph Jean, Esq., M.P.,
Parliamentary Assistant to
The Minister of Justice,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Jean:
I have just received your letter of to-day.
I can understand your desire to be perfectly free to take or to refrain from taking, without fear or favour and without the appearance of either, any particular course of action you may deem advisable in the present crisis.
While I do not believe that to maintain such a position it is necessary for you to be released from the duties you have assumed as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Justice, I shall nevertheless be pleased to discuss the matter with my colleague, and if Mr. St. Laurent agrees that to ensure against the possibility of any misinterpretation or misrepresentation of your position, it is advisable to release you from your duties as his Parliamentary Assistant, I shall act accordingly.
I need not say that, except for the reasons expressed in your letter, I would not consider, as I know the Minister of Justice would not consider, taking any action which would deprive the government of your valuable services, which, I need not assure you, have been deeply appreciated by the Minister and myself.
With kindest regards,
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King
The Parliamentary Assistant's resignation was accepted, and an order in council was passed to that effect, dating the resignation as from December 1.

subtopic: THE WAR
subsubtopic: POLICY OP THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the undeniable seriousness of the happenings which have motivated the sudden summoning of the house is such that we realize, perhaps more than ever before, the weight of responsibility which is ours. Last Monday, before making to the house his outspoken and remarkable statement as to the present situation, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) while referring to the resignation of the former minister of defence, spoke as follows:
If anything were necessary to emphasize the gravity of the issue that has so suddenly arisen, it would most certainly be found in the words of my former colleague and all-time friend, the former minister of national defence for air (Mr. Power). He has brought to the house, in a very few *words, the real nature of the question which is before this House of Commons at the present time. In a word, the issue of conscription has, once again, come to the fore, and it has brought to the fore once again the most serious kind of controversy which this parliament has had at different times to face.
However, Mr. Speaker, at the very outset of the present conflict, and even before, as well as in 1940, when the various parties were soliciting the support of our citizens, the leaders themselves, recalling sorry past experiences and knowing full well that nothing more than conscription could provoke the most serious kind of controversy which this parliament has had at different times to face, took the positive and solemn pledge, in clear, precise and explicit terms, of never under any circumstances resorting to conscription in Canada again. I wish to put on record those very
tMr. Mackenzie King.]
pledges made by the ones who had authority to make them in the name of the people of Canada. At page 2426 of Hansard for 1939 we find this statement by the Prime Minister himself:
In a war to save the liberty of others, and thus our own, we should not sacrifice our own liberty or our own unity. . . . Profits could and would be rigidly controlled, and profiteering suppressed. But men's lives a,nd men's wills cannot be put on the same basis as goods and profits. . . . Let me say that so long as this government may be in power, no such measure will be enacted.
At the very same session, and debating the same subject before the house, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, whose passing we so deplored in Quebec, and who was then minister of justice as well as, I believe, the recognized leader and spokesman for the province of Quebec, had this to say :
Now I am going to touch a subject which is a delicate one. The French Canadians will never agree that any government has the right to force them to military service on the other side of the ocean. In 1917 that was my view, and I have never altered it. I believe that conscription in 1917 was a blunder of frightful magnitude, and that we are still reaping the sad and sorry results of that ill-conceived policy. I was pleased that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition-
And that was the late Doctor Manion-
-said yesterday what I have myself learned, that the results did not in any way justify the taking of the risk.
And a little further on, Mr. Lapointe had this to say as reported on page 2468 of Hansard of March 31, 1939:
I think I am true to my concept of Canadian unity when I say that I shall always fight against this policy: I would not be a member of a government that would enact it; and not only that, but I say with all my responsibility to the people of Canada that 1 would oppose any government that would enforce i,t.
For the benefit of all hon. members, and particularly for the benefit of the loyal opposition which is seated, sir, to your left, I should like to quote what the leader of the Conservative party said on this question. I may have to quote Mr. Manion at length, but it is necessary' in order to make my point quite clear. This is what Mr. Manion said, as reported on page 2440 of Hansard of 1939:
There is the extreme view that we should, that we must, participate in all the wars of Great Britain to the last man and the last dollar, without question or discussion. That is condensing the viewpoint to a definite statement. but I think I am stating it fairly. The other extreme view is that we must participate in no war unless we are directly attacked.
And again:
Considering all these facts, and remembering the strong view's held by 'both extreme sides, I

War Effort-Government Policy
see a very grave danger to the dominion unless some fair compromise policy is adopted. It seems to me that persistence in either of these extreme views, to the ignoring of the very large group who have the other extreme view, means the disruption of Canada, possibly civil war in ease there was an international war in which Britain was engaged, perhaps the ultimate break-up of the British Empire. In the last war the conscription of men to go to the front caused violent racial antagonisms, much disharmony, bitterness and misunderstanding- conditions from which as yet we have not wholly recovered; and on top of that I believe I am expressing the opinion of authorities when I say that it was of no real value so far as the empire was concerned.
Mr. Manion had this to say in conclusion:
It seems to me, therefore, that we must adopt a sane middle course in order to preserve a united Canada and, indeed, to maintain this empire. The policy that I suggest is the one which I gave three days ago in an interview: first, that there should be no conscription of Canadians to serve outside the borders of Canada; second, that we should have full cooperation with the British Empire short of the conscription of men to serve outside our borders.
In view of these statements, I ask any man who is willing to think for a moment whether it is surprising that the initial feeling of amazement created by the unexpected adoption of order in council P.C. 8891 should now be replaced by a deep and general feeling of distrust? The people who placed their trust in us rightly feel that they have been deceived. Is it not elementary and logical that they should arrive at this inevitable conclusion when they are confronted with the events of the last few days? How could we be so misguided as to think that it could be otherwise? In fact, only a few hours before the introduction of this compulsory measure the most competent authorities on the matter expressed their unfailing faith in the voluntary system.
Has it not been by the use of the voluntary system that our country has been in a position to raise such an excellent, such a gallant, such a marvellous army, and that our Prime Minister was in a position only a short while ago, speaking before the representatives of the United Kingdom and the member nations of the British commonwealth, to express the pride of Canada in this army? I ask how it is that this system has become discredited overnight after having given such splendid results. In the light of the statement made by the Prime Minister last Monday, some parts of which I shall quote, it is no wonder that our gallant soldiers who are fighting for us have been denied the results they have been expecting from the voluntary system of recruiting.
After the appointment of General McNaughton as Minister of National Defence -that great soldier, that picked man, that keen
patriot who in the worst crises of his country always answers "here" to the call of duty, this is what happened. First, let me refer to what was said by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), and I quote from page 31 of Hansard of May 20, 1940:
May I pause here to pay a tribute to the government for having appointed him to lead the first division. I have great confidence in General McNaughton, and so have the Canadian public. As evidence of my wanting to he fair, let me say that they could not have made a better appointment. The Canadian people applauded the appointment of General McNaughton.
After the appointment of General McNaughton as Minister of National Defence this is what happened, and I quote the words of the Prime Minister as reported on page 6604 of Hansard of November 27, 1944:
General McNaughton brought his officers from all parts of the country and explained to them that the policy of the government was a policy of voluntary enlistment. They have tried-^-or I believe many of them have, but I also believe some of them have not tried to get voluntary enlistments. That was the policy of the government to make it succeed, all would have had to work for it with all he was worth.
How was the public appeal supported? The moment that we started on the public appeal, that moment the opposition to anything of the kind-
I ask the house to note these words:
-on the part of the interests that lie behind this organized effort to force conscription began to make itself felt in every direction-in the press, by meetings, resolutions by veterans' organizations, representations to members and so forth, with the result that instead of the appeal reaching the ears of the people, the ears of the people were dinned by the efforts that were being put forth by those who were determined they were going to have conscription no matter what the cost might be.
Can we believe in the sincerity of those who claim that conscription is necessary, no matter what the cost may ibe, in order that our fighting men should get the required reinforcements, when they themselves systematically opposed the public appeal and deliberately refused their cooperation when that was requested in order to get reinforcements by the voluntary system?
I wish the house to understand and the whole country to know that the rebuffs did not come from the province of Quebec. For the information of the house I quote from a statement given to the Canadian Press by Brigadier Edmond Blais, O.C., military district No. 5, Quebec. This statement was published in the Ottawa Journal of Wednesday, November 22, under the heading "Blais confident Quebec will furnish support battalions":
Brigadier Blais, O.C. military district No. 5 here, said to-day he had "complete confidence"
War Effort-Government Policy

speechtext:
It is not my intention to follow in detail the remarks of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Trem-

War Effort-Government Policy
blay) who has just taken his seat; but I do take exception particularly to one remark that he made, namely, that in the different camps throughout Canada there has been discrimination so far as the French Canadians and the English Canadians are concerned. I have had the honour to command two large camps in Canada. I have had both French and English Canadians in these camps, and I can say truthfully to this house that I do not know of one instance where there was any difference between these! two races. They have played together, worked together, drilled together and slept together, and never has there been any trouble between them. Therefore I feel that in justice to the Canadian people, both English and French, I should make this statement. I know also that overseas our men feel they are all Canadians and that there is no difficulty of the kind the hon. member has mentioned.
Before I enter on my general remarks this afternoon I should like to refer to a matter which is perhaps rather personal. In the course of his fine address a few days ago the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston), the former minister of national defence, expressed his regret that he could not finish the job he had undertaken as minister of national defence. He also extended to the officers and men who had worked under him for the last four or five years a word of thanks. I should like to say to the hon. member for Prince-I see he is busy at the moment-that as one of the officers who has worked under his department for the last four years it is a matter of personal regret to me that he has not been able to finish the work which he undertook. I wish to extend to him my personal thanks for the help which I received as an officer while working under him. I would not presume, Mr. Speaker, to speak for all officers and men in the Canadian Army, but I feel he has had the respect and admiration of practically all of the officers and men who have served under him. I am sure that he has their respect in the stand which he has taken on this reinforcement matter. But that respect may be dimmed because of the action which he feels it is now incumbent upon him to take. I do not think he is carrying his ideas to their logical conclusion; I do not think he has gone far enough.
This is not a question of voluntarism versus conscription. So far as this country is concerned the question of conscription has been settled. But we still have the two systems in vogue in Canada, and I wish to make my own position clear. The hon. member for Dorchester referred to our leader in 1939. I
say without any hesitation, Mr. Speaker, that I disagreed with my leader in 1939 so far as conscription was concerned. In my own constituency-and it is well known in New Brunswick-I ran against an anti-conscriptionist and under a conscription platform. Therefore my attitude has been consistent throughout.
I should also like to quote from my remarks of 1942 when the question of the plebiscite was before the house. I quoted then and I shall quote now a statement which was made by Abraham Lincoln in 1863. I think that statement is just as true to-day as it was then. He said-I am quoting from page 165 of Hansard of January 29, 1942:
Voluntarism is the unprincipled dodge of cowardly politicians. It' has ground up the choicest seed corn of the nation. It has consumed the young, the generous, the patriotic, the intelligent and the grave. It has wasted the best moral, social and political elements of the republic, and left the cowards, the shirkers and the money-makers to stay at home and propagate their kind.

speechtext:
At that time there was a vote of confidence before the British house as there is a vote of confidence before this

War Effort-Government Policy

house at the moment. What happened in England at that time? Here is what I said on that occasion:
When Churchill came before the British House of Commons for a vote of confidence, the vote stood 464 to 1-practically unanimous. Why? Because Churchill makes and leads public opinion in that country. It vras a magnificent tribute to a great leader and a great statesman, a man who tells his people what is needed and sees that those needs are carried out, as far as is possible for him to do so. He offers no apologies or excuses. He said to them, "I make no promises". I commend that to the people of this dominion and to the members of this house. We make too many promises. If we had not made promises which we could not fulfil, we would not have been in the position in which we are to-day. A wise man is Mr. Churchill. He makes no promises, and he holds no plebiscite in his country during war time to find out whether he should be relieved of those promises to satisfy new conditions.
I quote these words, Mr. Speaker, to show that we have not had the leadership in this country since the war started that we should have had. Great Britain has had the leadership of Mr. Churchill. He has not only given leadership to his own people, he has given leadership to the world. The United States has had the leadership of Mr. Roosevelt, their great president. Russia 'has had the leadership of Mr. Stalin. In this country we just drift along without any leadership and without anything definitely settled.
Going back to the issue of voluntary enlistment, the hon. member for Dorchester said that it did not receive the support of this dominion. I would ask him, where did it receive that support? I can speak for my own province, and I think I know something of the maritimes generally; I know that in those little provinces by the sea the voluntary system has been a success. In some towns there is hardly a young man left to carry on the ordinary work, ordinary employment, and I know that men from outside the maritime provinces have been brought in to carry on the work in the pulp mills, in the woods, and in other industries because our own young men are absent; they are not there to do that work because they are overseas fighting. When anyone says therefore that the voluntary system has not been a success in our particular provinces he is saying something that is an absolute mistake. So far as Canada is concerned it has been a failure from the very beginning.
The other night I listened to the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose) when he said that he had spoken to 2.500 people here a few days ago-2,500 young French Canadians, or to the Freneh-Canadian people-and it occurred, to me at that time that this hon. member might very well have spoken to other nationals in

this country than French Canadians. He would have been well qualified to speak to them, because there are other nationals who have not done as well as some of our French-Canadian people.

speechtext:
If I had one drop of Freneh-Canadian blood in me I would have resented it, knowing what I do. Let us be Canadians. The Minister of National War Services has been going out in the last two or three weeks making passionate appeals. The point I am making is these hon. members are just four years too late. It has also been mentioned in the house that the military authorities in the different districts did not give the support to the measure which they should. I can only speak for two military districts, and perhaps I have no authority to speak for them except for information I have myself. In district No. 7 there has been an effort in the last four or five years to obtain all the recruits they could from N.R.M.A. men who have come into service, and I know that the results have been very satisfactoiy. I also know that in district No. 6, when this order went out asking the district officers commanding and other military men. in the districts to try to get as many recruits as they could, the district officer commanding No. 6 called every camp commander and commandant into Halifax. The matter was explained to them, and while some of the officers started to grumble a little at first, the officer commanding said to them: "This is a matter which it is not for us to question in any way. I do not know what your personal opinions are and I have no intention- of giving my personal opinions. This is the policy of the government and we are asked to carry it out, and as good soldiers it is our duty to do our best to see that it is carried out."
These were the instructions given at that meeting, and I know that at that meeting plans were laid for every commanding officer to go out and try to do his best to get N.R.M.A. men in his command to go active. I remember one commanding officer who stood up and said: "It is going to be a very hard job, and I will tell you why. My men are veterans." We were all amazed at that, but he went on to explain. He said: "I mean they are veterans in this sense. They have been

War Effort-Government Policy
through many campaigns. First, they were asked to enlist when they were members at the basic training centre. Afterwards there were attempts to enlist them and get as many of them as possible when they were in the advanced training centre. Efforts were made to get them when they were in units before they came to me, and now that they are in my outfit there is nothing but the hard core left and it is impossible for us to get more men."
The situation which that officer explained as to his men was the situation all across the country, and while the present Minister of National Defence may not have known it I am quite sure it was known to the former minister of national defence, as it was known to practically every senior officer from one end of Canada to the other.
As to the need of men, I think it was known that there was a need of men even before the member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) went overseas. He had his fears at that time and he went to England, to Italy and to France. What did he find? He found that our reserve pool was empty in England, that it was practically empty in Italy, and practically empty in France, and at what time? Not at a time when there was no fighting going on but when there was the severest fighting that Canadian troops have engaged in during this war. Is it any wonder that he hurried back	to	Canada and	placed beforethe Prime Minister the situation as he found it? To the people of Canada and to us, the only wonder	is	that nothing	was	done atthat time. The hon. member suggested that there should	be	15,000 men.	He	did notsuggest that	they should be	sent	over in
December. He did not suggest that they be sent over in January, 5,000 of them. He did not suggest that for the three succeeding months there be 2,000. The minister came back to this country and told the government that 15,000 men were needed immediately to fill the pools and give a backing of reserves to the men who were fighting overseas.
And there is hard fighting. I listened the other day to the Minister of National Defence as he described the great west wall where thousands and tens of thousands of slave labour in the last three years have been building a wall of concrete and steel, built in depth, and, as he said, where guns can play in every direction. This is certainly going to be an enormous task for all troops, allied and Canadian.
But besides the west wall there is also the matter that General Eisenhower has told us about, the matter of crossing the Rhine. He says it will be one of the most stupendous 100-4254
and one of the hardest of military operations carried on in a great many years. I point out these things to show the great need of men at the present time and the need of keeping up our reserves until the war is over.
I contend that we are not sending even this small number soon enough. The government should have adopted on October 13 even this meagre policy which they are now adopting. I know something about the time it takes for men to get from the west coast over to England, or to the pools. I know something of the funnel through which men are poured out of Canada into ships to cross the Atlantic. It takes practically eight days to move across this country, and then they will give these men embarkation leave, which means another week. It takes another one or two weeks to cross, all taking up four weeks, and when the men arrive in England, after being on the train for a week and at their homes for another week, after waiting for a boat, and after crossing, they are in no condition then for service. It takes two months to get these men into the lines. I say this should have been started long ago, instead of just now.
Then again, if five thousand men are selected from the troops on the west coast, what assurance have we that five thousand men will reach the ships at Halifax or whatever the port may be? My practical experience, even with men who have volunteered, is that the number reaching the ships will be far short of that. They have to be medically examined again when -they land at the transit camp. The other day General McNaughton spoke of sickness, measles, mumps, and so on. Hundreds of men will be quarantined as a result of these diseases. There is also the question of men absent without leave. These men coming from the west coast will be dispersed to every little hamlet and village across Canada. I know in days past, even with men who- had volunteered, after they came from the training camps in the west and went home, dozens and dozens were absent without leave for long periods of time, and in fact many have not shown up at the camps since. What will be the situation among these men, with the attitude they are taking toward going overseas? I say there will be not hundreds but thousands of men who will never land at the port of embarkation in time.

speechtext:
It is going to be an abnormal thing and greatly accentuated under these conditions. The men who went before volunteered. These men are being forced to go, against their will. What would have happened if the total N.R.M.A. personnel had been selected; what would have been the result? It would have been what the minister asked for; we would have every pool filled back of the lines. The pool in England would have been filled; the pool in Italy would have been filled; the pool in France would have been filled; every fighting unit at the front would have been up to strength. It would mean also that wounded men, who at present are being sent back to the line after recovering from their wounds, would have more time in which to recuperate. They are being sent back much sooner than they should be, I believe, and much sooner than they would be if we had plenty of reinforcements. It would mean also that more men would return home. The former minister of national defence has recommended that 450 men be sent home each month, and I commend him for that action. Many of these men have been overseas for four and five years. Four hundred and fifty is only a drop in the bucket, only one man in a hundred. If more men were sent over, more men could be brought home1 for a rest. These men aTe being sent home for only thirty days. I have had some experience in that connection. Men who have been brought back-on prisoner of war escort, or on compassionate grounds, and who are being sent back overseas, are complaining bitterly. They say they have not time to settle their domestic affairs, and I want to say to this house that many domestic affairs will have to be settled when this war is -over. These men have not time to look after their business. They come home for some particular work they wish done. By the time they get straightened away and come to do -the work they want to do, it is time to leave. They have come to me by the dozen, trying to get their time extended. I say that not thirty days but sixty days should be granted these men, and this could be done if this government would send over the number of reinforcements required.
Then there is the question of better selection. Among military men there is a process known as scraping the pot, and for the last three or four months we in Canada have been scraping the pot to get men. What do we mean by that expression? Well, when a commanding officer builds up his establishment sometimes he finds a young man who, while physically fit and able to pass all the examina-

tions, still is not considered strong enough for combat training. It may be that he is just out of school, so that he is kept as a clerk in the orderly room, or put in the quartermaster's stores, or sent to the army service stores. This goes on in every camp across Canada. Again, a commanding officer may find a man thirty or thirty-five years of age who would be considered a little too old to. undertake the strenuous training of the camp, and he is given special duties. He may be in category A, but he will be put in the cookhouse, or given some other more or less sheltered job. These are the men we have been scraping from the pot for the last three or four months. These are the -men who are now being given training and sent over to reinforce our boys at the front, when the most strenuous fighting is going on that our army has ever seen. Not long ago in my own camp 300 of these men came in. I remarked to some of my officers that they did not look to me like satisfactory reinforcements for the infantry. Just a few days later 500 other men came in. I saw them march past my window in the orderly room, and remarked to my adjutant, " That is a fine looking lot of men, as good looking as any men we have had in this camp for some time. They will make good reinforcements." He replied, " Those men are not reinforcements. They have been sent over here from Sussex to help with the apple picking." They were young, virile men who would have .made splendid reinforcements for any unit. There was no comparison between the two groups. We were sending ever three hundred men whom we had scraped out of the pot, yet here were these five hundred men, twenty, twenty-one and twenty-two years of age, being sent out to pick apples.
Then there is the question of families who have lost sons overseas. Just- before I left Windsor I was called long distance by my wife in Sussex. She had been visited by a man who had been wounded during the last war and who had five sons overseas in this war. Within two months two of his sons were killed in action; the second was reported killed just the day before he went to see my wife. Another son had been wounded twice and was back in the front line. He wanted to see if I could not get in touch with someone in order to have the son who had been wounded twice removed from the front line and put in a safe place. He said. " If anything happens to this boy it will kill my wife." That is not an isolated case; there are many similar cases across Canada. Again I say, if we had sufficient reinforcements and reserves such men would not have to go back into the lines: there would be plenty of men to go in and do the fighting. To me, and I think to almost any military man who has any knowledge of the

War Effort-Government Policy
subject, these 16,000 men we propose sending overseas are considered too little and, for some purposes, also too late.
I do not wish to weary the house, Mr. Speaker. I listened with great respect and attention the other day to the former minister of national defence. I was intrigued by this statement of his:
I know a few of my own weaknesses. One of the many perhaps is that I am not flexible enough. I was born that way. I am too old to change.
It is a good thing for this country that the hon. member was born inflexible. It is a good thing for the men overseas that he was born inflexible; because, while we have not a full loaf, through his inflexible effort I feel we are getting half a loaf. But I do not think his speech carried him entirely to a logical conclusion. I should like to have seen him maintain his inflexibility to the extent of accepting the Prime Minister's challenge to form a government. Had he done so I can assure him he would have had great support from the people of Canada, and would have had support from members who sit in this chamber. Things have come to a strange pass when the will of one man in this country can nullify and frustrate the will of the great majority of the people.
We are asked to vote confidence in the policies of the government; we are asked to vote confidence in the Prime Minister. We are asked to vote confidence in what is even less than half a measure, and in no way meets the requirements of the men overseas. This is a policy which has encouraged, indirectly-but nevertheless I believe has encouraged-young men in one part of Canada to tear down the flag and to trample it into the dust, to tear down the flag of a country which for one whole year stood alone, the flag which has been carried into France, into Belgium, and into Holland. The British flag is not being torn down in any of those countries. I can remember, and every other returned man will remember, that at the time of the last war we entered certain liberated parts of Belgium and France. I remember well the efforts made by those people to honour that flag. Paper was scarce at that time; but the people found bits of paper, coloured it and made British and American flags. They took pieces of coloured cloth and sewed them together in an effort to make something which would resemble the British flag.
We are asked to vote confidence in a government which has kept two armies in this country, one to fight and one to do nothing. We are asked to vote confidence in a policy
which has cost the overburdened taxpayers of this country between $150,000,000 and $200,000,000 each year-and for no useful purpose; a policy which has made us the laughing stock of other nations; a policy which has made us ashamed before our own people.
The house should support the all-out policy of reinforcements as recommended in the amendment proposed by the official opposition. What would it do? First it would assure our men overseas that they would have ample reinforcements. Second, it would assure mothers and parents-yes, the people of Canada-that their boys overseas would have all the required reinforcements. Third, as one hon. member has said, it would assure that there would be no discrimination in the N.R.M.A., and that all men would be used the same. That is what the carrying out of the amendment of the opposition party would do for the people of Canada.
The other night I listened to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) speak about the call of blood. Well, this is a call of Canadian blood. Surely we are a Canadian people. We may be French Canadian, British Canadian, [DOT] Jewish Canadian, or whatever you wish, but the fact is that we are a Canadian people, and it is the blood of those Canadians overseas that is calling. It is Canadian blood calling for reinforcements, sending out a Macedonian call, asking us to come over and help them. Fifteen or sixteen thousand men scattered over this period of time is not enough. The only answer this house should give is that which would bring about full implementation of the amendment submitted by the official opposition, and the sending of badly needed reinforcements consisting of those men in Canada upon whose training we have spent so much,

Mr. Speaker, May I first of all compliment the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Brooks). I have not heard him speak often in the house, and I think the house is not richer for the infrequency of his utterances. His manner of speaking to us this afternoon has been such as to indicate that. We know him to be warm-hearted and unquestionably sincere, and I have no hesitation in expressing my compliments to him. That is not to say however that I agree with a very great deal of what he has said. I believe upon further consideration he will realize that he has been over-ve'hement on many points, and that he has been equally vehement when inaccurate as when 'accurate. On the whole that means that he is most often, inaccurately over-vehement.

War Effort-Government Policy
The hon. member quoted Lincoln as having said "Voluntarism is the unprincipled dodge of cowardly politicians." He was inaccurate on that. Speaking in this chamber on February 5, 1942, after using this quotation, the present Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) said:
This language has been used in a number of newspapers, the first reference to it having been found in the Canadian Airmen; and when we tried to track it down we found that the man who had written the article had lost his notes. I have in my hand a letter from the library of congress indicating that the most careful search has been made of Lincoln's speeches, correspondence and books, and there is no reference to any such statement in anything that Lincoln ever said.
