speechtext:
I shall deal in just a moment with the hon. member who has interrupted. As was stated at that time by the Minister of Health and Welfare, there may be some synthetic logic in that statement, just the same. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) had a perfect right to speak as he did, and to use as. his own expression the words: "Voluntarism is the unprincipled dodge of cowardly politicians"-which would mean that it is his view that all his colleagues,.or practically all of them, including the hon. member who has just interrupted, are of that stripe. There was practically no one in the Conservative party who did not adopt the idea of vdluntarism, and it was as much then a dodge of cowardly politicians as it is on this day of Our Lord.
I rose mainly to record my opinion upon the matter of confidence or no confidence in this government, and upon allied subjects that have arisen in the debate. I have no hesitation in saying that I shall vote for the main motion and against any amendment that I have seen so far. The position taken by the government in applying the overseas features of the mobilization act to draftees in Canada comes close to the policy that I have advocated for a long time. Despite some of the remarks that have been made previously in this debate I would have thought that I was the first person in this house to espouse publicly the idea of sending draftees over the water. However, in view of what the last speaker said, that he campaigned on that basis in 1939, it would appear that he preceded me. At any rate I shall not quarrel over precedence. It is a fact that I advocated such a policy for a long time before the date of the plebiscite and again at the time of the plebiscite. I advanced the same view when

bill No. 80 was before the house. So that I have been consistent, and my attitude is well known.
I see quite clearly that the order in council before the house indubitably does apply to all N.R.M.A. personnel, so far as liability is concerned, with an immediate movement of 16,000, which is the admitted number that is now required. The last speaker made reference to the wastage between the commencement of the movement and the point of embarkation. I would point out that since the order obviously does apply to all, unquestionably more than 16,000 will be dispatched to the points of embarkation to allow for all forms of wastage which have been mentioned by him.
In view of the fact that, as I have said, the order does apply to all N.R.M.A. personnel so far as liability is concerned, the Conservative amendment is, as is usual with that party's offerings, "off the beam." It is right enough in showing that Burma, India, China and Japan are not dealt with. That is the only merit the amendment has in the circumstances of the case, if that can be called a merit. I do not, however, regard it as a merit; I look upon that as a demerit. I consider that this is not the time to discuss the methods of carrying on the war with Japan, and I might well question the wisdom of using these same methods to aid three hundred million Chinese. At any rate, this is not the time.
I shall vote for the main motion for the reasons advanced by the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston), and also because I am fully convinced now that our boys will indeed be adequately and fully reinforced by the dispatch of troops to their side. As support for my view I should like to quote a sentence or two from an article by John Bird which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune, a man and a paper by no means friendly to this government. I quote from the Winnipeg Tribune of November 29, 1944, as follows:
First and foremost our men overseas are going to get reinforcements. That is what this is all about in the nation's mind. All these political manoeuvrings are garbage compared with the essential thing, reinforcements. That has been taken care of.
Whenever it has arisen this has proved to be one of the most difficult subjects to deal with in Canadian life. We are all agreed about that. There have been misunderstandings on both sides of the Ottawa river. The Prime Minister has said that some people regard this matter as a symbol of domination of the French-speaking minority by the Englishspeaking majority. I do wish most fervently

War Effort-Government Policy
that they would wipe out all such thoughts from their minds. There is no sound reason for them.
The position is this: A situation has arisen- its cause does not matter for the moment- where it is necessary to reinforce, to succour, to aid our boys who are making great the name of Canada. The expression, "our boys" applies to our French-speakers as well as to our English-speakers. The Canada whose name they are making great belongs to us all.
To harbour such thoughts is really to nurse a persecution complex, and that is unworthy of the great characters in French-Canadian history. It is complained sometimes that English Canada does not understand French Canada; and there is an element of truth in the charge. We should do better, and we will try to do better; but I ask my friends from the province of Quebec-of whom I have many, and I value their friendship most highly-to try a little harder also to understand us. As a beginning I would implore them to stop thinking of us as not being simply and integrally Canadians.-We are nothing else. Above all I ask them to stop thinking of the Reverend Tommy Shields and the Globe and Mail as though they truly represented u$. They do not. The one is serving some kind of financial crowd and the other is a mere bigot. Remember that such people are the cross we have to bear; give us your sympathy because of that, not your adverse judgment. Better still, do not give them another thought.
I cannot subscribe to the idea which has been advanced that a conspiracy in the form of a pressure campaign caused this crisis. When infantry casualties were fifty per cent over expectations a crisis was inevitable. Only 34,000 infantry were involved and the monthly losses were 5,000 instead of an expected 2,500. In those circumstances we were of necessity marching forward to a crisis of some sort. But concerted action there most certainly was. Right across Canada all the agents of the cabal that wants a chore-boy union government swung into action. This was their devil-sent chance. Any historian in the future reading our papers will have no difficulty in coming to that conclusion. It is amusing to note the reason given by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) a few days ago, when he was acting opposition leader, for rejecting the claim that there had been a conspiracy. The reason he gave was that neither he nor any of the members of his party had been approached to join the conspiracy, and therefore no cabal
could have been operating. Of course the failure of the modern emulators of Guy Fawkes to make contact with the members of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition does not support a denial of the conspiracy, but the hon. member's delineation of himself and his colleagues as the natural people to be lined up by conspirators is indeed interesting from an interested person.
For quite other reasons I would accept his statement wholeheartedly that he and his colleagues were not approached. It is natural that his self-estimate would be different from my appreciation of the situation. My view is that the wilful men who were desirous of wrecking things knew that they could count on these thirty-nine; that they would fall into line quite readily. "Why consult sheep," they would say. The Port Hope Conservative meeting, you remember, bypassed the elected Conservatives, and Meighen did not consult them when he picked Bracken.
Most people have a desire to be practical, and they must be so if there is to be any advance at all. When we come to talk of things practical and of people practical we have to think of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), in my own province, for his im-practicality stands out at once; it sticks out like a sore thumb. According to him, the only solution for to-day's problem is a general election. He may say that he did not say that, but he will be only thoughtless if he denies it was his proposal. He urged that the Prime Minister resign and that he suggest to His Excellency that John Bracken be asked to form a government. Mr. John Bracken! Mr. Bracken, who so far in his meanderings and peregrinations and wanderings has not seen fit, or managed, to have himself made a member of this house which the hon. member for Souris wants him to lead. The hon. member's suggestion is that Mr. Bracken will bring in several new men at once-another new defence minister-and other defence ministers-Mr. McTague probably as Minister of Labour-with the Department of Munitions and Supply, and its air problems added, to have a new head-and so on with all the rest. Most of these men he wants to be with Mr. Bracken are not even members of parliament! As soon as they are sworn in, the country is to have an election, during which all the sails of the departmental ships are to flap idly in the wind. For an election is certain. Mr. Bracken would have to meet the house at once. That is elementary. There may be political uncertainties, but the attitude of this House of Commons toward John Bracken is not one of them. No one will follow Bracken.

speechtext:
Perhaps it would be
proper if we took time out to laugh at and with the hon. member.
This Mr. Bracken who has been mentioned in the midst of this crisis was not found in a place where he could help. Every member of the House of Commons has been in deep travail of spirit these many days. I except no one from that, whether his views are as mine or whether they are contrary to mine. It is a fact that all members of parliament, of whatever shade of opinion, have been in deep travail of spirit these many days. John Bracken could only employ his time at a party convention getting ready for an election. He seeks to supplant the present member for Neepawa (Mr. MacKenzie). The measure of the two men can be gauged' by the activities of Bracken the electioneer, contrasted with MacKenzie the member for Neepawa, who walked away from his constituency convention to come here to attend to the nation's business. He was not obsessed by self.
It was at that Conservative convention that Mr. Bracken used the word "cowardly" with reference to the Prime Minister. Of all men he should not speak that way. That he is acting without responsibility does not absolve him. I realize that he is as irresponsible as the Globe and Mail and the Reverend Shields whom I have mentioned. But we do not need a microscope to detect the characteristics that distinguish Mr. Bracken from all other people.
Just consider the position. This leader and this Conservative party are unique in the history of political parties in Canada-unique in the history of political parties in England- unique in the history of political parties in any part of the British empire-or in the United States-unique in the history of political parties anywhere in the world. There

have been probably thousands of political parties and maybe tens of thousands of leaders, but never from the earliest time to now has there ever been a party or a leader whose sole attribute or claim for notice was fear, nothing but fear. To make an egregious case rise still higher, just note the nature of the fear. The fear is not that Mr. Bracken may endeavour to enter the precincts of this chamber from some constituency and be defeated. That is not the fear. It is that if he were to ran for election he would actually be elected; that he would be chosen to represent a Canadian community and have to assume some responsibility for his words and deeds which, of course, they know would be ruinous, both for the party and for the man.

The nature of their fear indeed accentuates the uniqueness of the political phenomenon I have described.
As a footnote to this story, without bothering to reply to the hon. member who has interrupted, may I direct Your Honour's attention to a brief history of a peculiar naval strategy. Some people think that the Italian fleet did not give a very good account of itself in this war. Well, it did not get hurt, did it? It stayed in harbour; and if the Italian admirals had kept it in harbour more closely it would have finished this war completely scatheless. Even as it was, that fleet was nearly intact when peace came for it. Now, that strategy of the Italian admiralty is the source, and spring, and motive, and inspiration of the managers of the Conservative party and of its leader. They have emulated it well. By reason of such close imitation they will finish probably just about as the Italian fleet did, in just about the same position or nearly the same, as when they started. With respect to honour and with respect to pride of service their position will likewise be identical with that of those home-staying seamen.
, I had not intended to speak in this fashion. I rarely do so. Had it not been that persons sitting to my left in the Conservative party, have continuously since this session started undertaken to fight an election in this house with their organizer, John Bracken, on the hustings, I should not have done so, but I think it is about time it stopped. I believe I have not spoken in this manner before and I hope it will not be necessary for me to do so again; but if these people are to continue the tactics which they started some days ago and to engage in mud-slinging and epithets instead of

War Effort-Government Policy
reasoned argument, then it will be necessary, distasteful as it may be, to turn attention to them again.
There is one other point I wish to mention. Unfortunately at the moment we have not a regular minister of defence in the house. I agree that it is regrettable. However, I should like to draw something to the attention of the government which I believe should be corrected. We are going to carry on-I believe it is right that we should-a voluntary system and an N.R.M.A. system. By the way, I think that policy is right for this reason. There are numbers of people who will yet desire to volunteer, and I think they would desire to be able to keep the distinction 'between being called up and being volunteers.

speechtext:
I find that we have
established, perhaps unwittingly and unintentionally, a distinction between men who are discharged on coming back from overseas and men who are discharged after having spent all their time in Canada. When I was in Winnipeg I ran into a number of cases of men who had come back. They had been getting trades pay. Their rate was two dollars a day. Because they were not promptly discharged they were reduced to one dollar and fifty cents a day, the pay of an efficient soldier. It is very important to such men because apparently it affects the seven days' pay and allowances for each six months of service. Also, should there be hospital treatment some time in the future, to which they are entitled, it would affect that, because, as every person knows, while they are in hospital they are on pay and allowances. The rate of pay 'both for the seven day grant and when in hospital is the rate upon discharge. The contrary seems to be the case of men whose service has been purely Canadian. True, in the case of those men they do not get the seven days' pay and allowances; therefore there is nothing to consider in that connection, but usually that man gets discharged within the necessary time limit and is not penalized in any way.
I have a memorandum from the paymaster's office in which he seems to controvert the idea I am putting forward, but upon a close reading it is not fully controverted. What I have been describing is apparently a fact because people are going out of the army with that much less money in their pockets.
I wish to say, in closing, that that condition should be corrected and corrected at once, and when corrected it should be made retroactive to every person of the class I have described who has been discharged so far. I am quite sure that it will be agreed by everyone that this is just elementary justice. I only add, in closing, that with respect to justice just as with respect to charity, the maxim, " He gives twice who gives quickly," applies with full force. Therefore I ask the government to lose no time in correcting the situation.

speechtext:
When this special sitting of parliament was called it was assumed by the Canadian people, I think, and by the hon. members of this house that we were being convened for the purpose of considering reinforcements and the method by which adequate reinforcements could be sent overseas as quickly as possible. The temperature of the Canadian people was running quite high on that issue. Various reasons have been advanced in this chamber for the precipitation of the crisis. Some hon. members, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), have intimated that it was deliberately organized by certain sections of the Canadian press and certain other interests who have been seeking to divide the Canadian people on the question of conscription ever since the war began. I believe that there is much truth in that assumption. I saw something of it during my own campaign in February, 1942. I am convinced, however, that that is not the whole truth, nor does such an assumption account for the full upsurge of public opinion on this question in some of our provinces.
There have been and still are many people in this country who believe honestly that conscription is the only way of securing sufficient man-power with as little discrimination and as little inequality of sacrifice as possible in a modern war. There are many others who believe that conscription of man-power should be accompanied by other forms of conscription. These people-and I include myself in both groups-are still of that opinion. It is also true that many people in all the provinces, not in one only, do not believe in the conscription of man-power for overseas service under any circumstances. I take it that they too are sincere. They have every right, with the rest of us, to hold that opinion. They also have every right to express that opinion. It is true that certain interests intent on securing the conscription of manpower, regardless of the consequences-more intent indeed on the conscription of manpower than on securing any other form of conscription'-have put forth considerable
War Effort-Government Policy

effort to bring this question to the front. Some of the spokesmen of those interests who have shouted loudest and most consistently for the conscription of man-power have, in almost the same breath, shouted loudly for a reduction in excess profits and other taxes.
The campaign for the conscription of manpower slackened off in 1942 and 1943, for two reasons. First there was no immediate and apparent need of reinforcements. More important, I think, those chiefly interested in that campaign feared that an intensified demand for the conscription of man-power would also lead to a public demand for other forms of conscription that they themselves did not welcome. While there was a willingness on the part of the Canadian people to accede to conscription of man-power if needed, there was also a considerable public demand that such conscription should be accompanied by other forms of conscription. I personally know of large numbers of industrial workers and large numbers of farmers who have seen on every hand wealth being accumulated out of the war and who were and are still opposed to the conscription of man-power without a corresponding conscription of wealth. Emphasis on conscription, and certainly public opinion regarding the sending of trained men overseas immediately for reinforcements, has changed somewhat in recent weeks. That change has not been brought about entirely by the organized efforts of those who have been pressing, even if at times half-heartedly, for man-power conscription only. The government itself has played into the hands of these interests, whether because of the division of the Canadian army which made three reinforcement pools necessary and which, on the evidence of General McNaughton himself, complicates the question of reinforcement, or whether because the voluntary system failed, or because the government was not kept informed of the extent to which the reinforcement pools were being depleted during July, August and September, or probably for all three reasons together the government itself has played into the hands of those who wanted man-power conscription only.
It was not in my opinion the organized efforts of these interests, whose efforts found little response with the Canadian public during the early years of the war, but the failure of the government and its military staff to provide adequate reinforcement pools during the past few months, that has precipitated this crisis. Added to that is the fact that the first intimation of the need came not from the general staff to the government and from the government to the Canadian priblic. The first intimation came to the Canadian

public in letters sent from overseas to relatives in all parts of Canada.
I still cannot understand why even the Minister of National Defence was not properly informed of the actual conditions until he went overseas and saw them for himself. If one wanted to be critical one could readily infer that the organized efforts to secure conscription were not all confined to interests in this country. Once that need became known to the Canadian public through letters from overseas that public, already having too little confidence in the government's policy, became intent on securing what reinforcements were needed by whatever means were necessary. During the first few days of this sitting I received from my constituents more than one thousand requests for the sending of N.R.M.A. men overseas immediately. These people were not all organized; hundreds of these letters came from constituents who had worked for me during my election on a policy of total conscription. These citizens saw the possibility of their men overseas suffering unduly for lack of reinforcements. That situation took precedence over all other considerations.
At the time we were called together it was assumed that the government would stand by its policy of voluntary enlistment; but in view of the situation into which the government had gotten itself, I fail to see how it could, having regard to the opinion of the majority of the Canadian people, have chosen any course other than that of sending men already trained overseas immediately. I admit quite frankly that I for one was pleased to . be able to write to my constituents and tell them I was sure they would be relieved to know that by virtue of this order in council tabled on November 23 reinforcements would immediately be made available in sufficient numbers to meet at least the immediate emergency.
I am confident that these people, whose genuine concern was the welfare of their loved ones overseas, would be grateful for that measure of relief. It is not for me to judge whether or not the high command, by dividing our Canadian army, has made the reinforcement of that army too difficult. That can only be judged later when the history of this war is written and when more information is available to the public. It is a matter requiring the careful study and consideration of the government. It is not for me to judge whether the military authorities have exhausted all the possibilities of the voluntary system. What I know is that the voluntary system as it exists to-day has become a voluntary system in name and theory only. I cannot for the life of me see how a man who
DECEMBER 4, 1944	6767
War Effort-Government Policy
is given a limited time in which to become a volunteer or go overseas as a conscript can -still be called a volunteer when he volunteers under such measures of compulsion.
The .facts are that our army has been divided; the voluntary system had failed to provide reinforcements; men at the front were suffering and were likely to suffer more for need of reinforcements. To meet that need I can see no other adequate means than that of sending men already trained. We had a situation which the majority of the Canadian people could not accept with any degree of complacency.
The question now before the house is whether or not we shall support the government "with respect to its war-time policy"- these are the words used by the minister on page 6607 of Hansard; and more particularly in "giving effect to what has been decided"- page 6608 of Hansard. I presume the Prime Minister means by "what has been decided" order in council P.C. 8891. And what reasons does the Prime Minister give for our supporting him? He tells us at page 6610 that it will not help the army to defeat the government. Then he assures us again-I quote from page 6613:
If I cannot get enough support out of my own party to feel sure that the men of my own party are behind me without depending on those who are politically opposed, then my resignation will go in to the Governor General. . . .
Again, at page 6614 of Hansard the Prime Minister implied, though he did not actually say, that at present there was no one in the cabinet to whom he could turn to form another government if he should be defeated. He further implied that no one in the entire country could be found to assume that responsibility. I want to ask, Mr. Speaker, if it is really true that after leading his party for twenty-five years, during eighteen of which he has been in office, the Prime Minister has no other colleague sufficiently trained and experienced to take his place should he, for any reason, be taken from us at a critical period in our history. Or is it equally true that there is not in this country another man who could step into the breach caused by the Prime Minister's removal from office? Surely if true that is a tragic situation for a democracy. I think we have the right to consider whether that is the actual situation or whether the Prime Minister was merely rehearsing some of the arguments he intends to use in the next federal election. We have had other great men in Canadian history whose loss has been felt, but this is the first time in our history that I can recall any man, however great, claiming to be indispensable. In
my opinion the Prime Minister's argument is a weak one on which to appeal for support. We cannot feel justified in voting, on those grounds, to support a policy of which we do not approve.
The former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) has given us the same argument in other words. We are told that we must vote confidence in this particular policy, as represented by this order in council, and confidence in the present ministry to enforce it, even though the hon. gentleman himself admitted that he is not satisfied that the order in- council will meet all our future needs, unless it is supplemented by others. Nor did he evidence great confidence in some members of the present cabinet to carry out that order. But he told us that failure to support the government would cause delay in getting reinforcements overseas. On the other hand General McNaughton told us, the second day he was before the house, that action had been taken already; that certain units already had been ordered to concentration depots for dispatch overseas and that these units would go overseas whether or not they volunteered. The former minister gave us to understand that all these details had been worked out by his staff before General McNaughton took over and before the order in council was passed. If that be so, would a change of ministry really result in delay? Already two important war ministers have left the cabinet, not because this house has given a vote of no confidence. We are obliged to ask ourselves whether a no confidence vote on this particular policy really would have any drastic effect in connection with the enforcement of this order in council.
In my opinion the Prime Minister and the former minister of national defence are attempting to place this house in a very awkward position. Under threat of failing our boys overseas we must vote confidence in a government policy in which we may or may not have confidence, but in which the men in the forces with whom I have spoken certainly have no confidence. Those of us in the opposition groups are in a still more difficult position by reason of the Prime Minister's statement that he will not carry on if he does not get sufficient support from members of his own party. We in the opposition are in the position that even if we vote confidence in his policy, for the purpose of hastening reinforcements overseas, the Prime Minister may still refuse to carry on if he does not get sufficient support from his own followers in this house. In my opinion the Prime Minister and the government can be
676S
War Effort-Government Policy

assured of a vote of confidence if they will bring in a more straightforward, forthright policy that will provide reinforcements and bring about a more vigorous prosecution of the war than we have had so far. If the Prime Minister is concerned only with providing adequate reinforcements at the earliest possible day, and with maintaining a vigorous war policy, I think he can obtain the full support of a majority of this house by passing a forthright order in council which will remove all doubt as to the matter of reinforcements and provide for a much more vigorous war effort, a policy which will mobilize the resources of this country behind that war effort to an extent to which they have not been mobilized as yet. At page 6602 of Hansard the Prime Minister said:
There are only two methods of obtaining results . . . one is the voluntary method and the other is compulsion.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the order in council tabled on November 23 does not commit the government to one or the other; it does not call for either conscription or a voluntary effort. It merely coerces men into voluntary enlistment. It can only result in further discrimination, inequality of sacrifice, and dissatisfaction. Nor have we any assurance that this measure will meet the future reinforcement needs. That will depend, I think, upon whether we accept the general tenor of the statements made by the present Minister of National Defence on the first or second day he appeared before the house. I realize, of course, the minister's difficulty in having to revise, on a few hours' notice, a speech quite evidently prepared in defence of the voluntary system, and then using it to defend this hybrid order in council.
'Many of our constituents are asking us to-day if the government, in its reluctance to enforce the terms of this order in council, will continue to comb volunteers from other branches of the forces. That in reality is the policy the government has been following. Men have been forced into the infantry from the army service corps, the medical corps, the artillery and other corps, merely because they had volunteered.
I should like to give the house one case in point. This is the military story of a young soldier, regimental number H-18581, and the information is given to me in a letter from his brother, who is now a flying officer in the R.C.A.F. This boy enlisted in the Royal Canadian Artillery on December 20, 1943, and was trained as a transport driver. After his basic and advanced training as such he was posted overseas, arriving in England on July 2, 1944, and while there continued his training

as a transport driver. The following facts are taken from letters written by this soldier to his parents and brothers.
On August 12:
I have been moved to a new place with fellows from the armoured car corps, engineers, army service corps and even the air force. We did not know why we were moved, but we are apparently now in the infantry, the Rocky Mountain Rangers, a western outfit.
On August 16:
We have again been moved to another station, still in Yorkshire, a new place just recently opened up.
And from his letter of August 17:
As yet we have had no infantry training.
And again on September 3, two weeks later:
They are sending us overseas in a few days and I don't want to go. Don't think I am yellow, but we have had so little training that I hardly know one end of a rifle from the other. Guess I'll have to trust in God and keep ducking.
Then on September 11:
My new address is 2-C.B.R.G. We crossed the channel 7th September landing on a beach about 3.30 a.m. Only three of the fellows that trained with me in the artillery are not here.
Then, again on September 14:
I am now with the Black Watch of Canada.
That young man was killed in action in Belgium on October 9, one month ?nd two days after he crossed the channel with, according to his own words, not enough training to be able to tell one end of a rifle from the other. Our constituents are asking whether this kind of combing and remustering will continue while the government tries to bolster the number of volunteers. I say it is unfair to the men themselves, and unfair to the units to which they are attached.
Reference has been made to the subject of a general election. I do not believe the majority of the people of Canada want a general election fought on the conscription issue. They do however want legislation or an order in council which beyond all shadow of a doubt will provide adequate reinforcements for the future, as well as the present, and legislation which will mobilize all the resources of the country for the further prosecution of the war. I feel certain a majority of members in this chamber would support such a measure were it introduced by the government.. In my opinion that is the only form of conscription that can possibly receive the support of the majority of Canadians in all the provinces. From this special session of parliament the country wants two realities; first the

War Effort-Government Policy
type of legislation to which I have referred and, second, a ministry in sympathy with that legislation, one upon which they know they can rely to carry it out. Anything less will not satisfy the majority of the people of Canada, nor can it satisfy the majority of members of the house, regardless of how they vote, by reason of their desire to stand by our men overseas.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not often refer to what has been said by other hon. members; but on this occasion I shall allude briefly to what two previous speakers have said. My first observations are directed to the remarks of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) who has just taken his seat. He has not always been so fixed in his opinion respecting full-out support for overseas. Although I did not look up the reference before coming to the house, as I had not anticipated what he would say, still I have a clear recollection that he and his party voted unanimously against the amendment of the Progressive Conservative party in 1942, which called for all-out enlistment, all-out financial support, and1 all-out support all along the line.
However, I do support what the hon. member said respecting the present-perhaps I should say recent-voluntary system. I have made inquiries all across Canada about the voluntary system. On other occasions I have said that more than once I have been shocked beyond measure by the methods used to force young men in Canada to enlist in the active army, or even to enlist at all. From the beginning I have felt that this is every man's war, and that each and every one of us should give the same service, or should serve where best he can carry on, in the opinion of the authorities.
I was r.ot surprised by the hon. member's opening remarks, wherein in my judgment he again proceeded to attack employers of labour. Not having been an employer of labour the hon. member, in common with most members of his party, entertains the idea that all employers of labour-I believe he referred to them as industrialists-are everything they should not be. However, those of us who have given employment to large numbers of men [DOT] know differently. We know that the vast majority of industrialists have rendered a great service to Canada, and I believe that knowledge is shared by those Who are employed.
May I now refer, but only briefly, to the address of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank). It is not my habit to use unkind expressions in respect of anyone. I am sure hon. members know that in my record in this chamber I have refrained at
all times from making personal attacks. The fact is that I have held a high opinion of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. On numerous occasions he has delivered excellent addresses in the house. They have contained much information, and have been a credit to him. So that I was especially sorry to-day to hear him make two personal attacks, one of which was upon the Reverend Doctor Shields. It is not my business to defend Doctor Shields, because he is quite able to defend himself, and I have no doubt that in due time he will take the hon. member to task. But to call Doctor Shields a fake or a faker, as I thought he said, is not, in my judgment, proper language to employ in respect of anyone outside the house who is not here to defend himself.
Then the hon. member referred to the Toronto Globe and Mail. What I shall say about that newspaper I can say, too, about a multitude of other newspapers in Canada. So long as I have read it-and that covers a good number of years-the Globe and Mail has been a stout defender of British connection. It has stood in defence of the maintenance of British connection and British ideals. I will go further and say that unde^ present conditions, as well as in the past, I am convinced that the Globe and Mail is absolutely unpurchasable by anyone who may have the funds with which to purchase it. I mean its editorial and other opinions are not purchasable. If they were purchasable I am sure the large number of full-page government advertisements which have appeared in the Globe and Mail from time to time since war broke out would have had an effect long ago. I am sure that the editorial columns of the Globe and Mail, of the Toronto Telegram or other papers could not be influenced even though this or any other government purchased every full page of advertising space available. I am sorry indeed to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre attack this great newspaper. It is a great newspaper.
Now to my own remarks. When I decided to go home on Friday evening I arranged with the whip of this party to try to get fifteen or twenty minutes, either to-day or to-morrow, because I did not expect to be here on Wednesday. At that time I felt that I would not take over fifteen or twenty minutes, but in the meantime I have been home. I cannot speak for other ridings, but I am sure that any member from Ontario who went home to his constituency, especially a member from Toronto where the enlistments have been almost en masse, got such an earful that it would take more than fifteen or twenty minutes to say what he would want to say.
War Effort-Government Policy

Anyone who attends a theatre in Ottawa, Toronto, Hamilton or any other Ontario city will be greatly surprised at the indication of the unpopularity of certain members of this government when their pictures are thrown on the screen. When the picture of the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) is shown he gets a great hand, but when the pictures of certain other members of this government are thrown on the screen they get anything but a hand. I was sorry to see these demonstrations of opposition to certain members of this government.
In my opinion we came here for three purposes: first, to find out why the voluntary system broke down; second, to hear of the programme to send adequate reinforcements overseas and, third, to hear why the former minister of national defence was ousted from the cabinet. By Wednesday we shall have been here for two weeks and up to now we have heard many speeches. One took over three hours; two of them took more or less an hour each, and many others have gone forty minutes. I believe the shortest one I heard was the one delivered by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray).
What are the startling and stark facts that came out of those speeches. I took the trouble to read the speech of the former minister of national defence quite carefully because it was full of information. As I read through it I said to myself that he was making a masterly . address, that he was giving the Canadian people a great deal of information with which to back up their opinion about this matter. But as I came near the end of his speech and read where he said he was going to vote for the motion, I said to myself, "This is figuratively a grand example of the cow that gave a fourteen-quart pail of milk and then put her foot in it." I was sorry when I reached that point because he had done extremely well up to then.
Here are the facts as I wrote them down, and I have tried to put them in chronological order. No. 1: In June, 1944, the minister was advised by the chief of staff that heavier reinforcements were required, were urgently necessary. He in turn advised the war cabinet, perhaps not just on that day. No. 2: In June he discussed with the other two defence ministers their letting up a little on their recruiting to allow him to obtain more infantry recruits. No. 3: during the summer a programme was initiated-I am not sure whether this was initiated by the former minister or the staff-of remustering from one branch of the service to the other.

22 he advised the war cabinet, which apparently at that time was discussing what could be done with the N.R.M.A. personnel, that he could not allow the N.R.M.A. personnel to be interfered with, that he might need them for infantry reinforcements, or words to that effect. No. 6: On September 23 he sailed for overseas to examine the situation on the various fronts. I congratulate him upon taking that action because that is what a minister should do; he should make himself familiar with everything that is required.
No. 4: In August he received a telegram from overseas, which later he presented to the cabinet, stating that a serious shortage existed in the units overseas. No. 5: On September
No. 7: On October 13, having made his inquiries, he cabled to the Prime Minister-I presume stating that he wps returning shortly -that he desired a meeting of the cabinet in order to place before them the results of his inquiries overseas. I believe he arrived home on October 18. No. 8: On October 19 he received a report from the chief of the general staff that the only solution of and remedy for the question of the depleted pools and the low numbers in the units overseas would be the taking of 15,000 personnel from the N.R.M.A., and he so reported to the government.
No. 9: Then followed a week of what I pre-surpe were hectic discussions behind closed doors in the cabinet, during which the minister tried to convince his colleagues that he had to have 15.000 N.R.M.A. men. I have no doubt that he supported his proposal with the best of arguments. No. 10: On November 1 the minister either was asked to retire or resigned voluntarily. I do not know which it was and I imagine the public will never know just what happened. No. 11: On November 3 the new minister came into office and abandoned the proposal of the former minister. The new minister Redded to carry on the voluntary system which the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) has aptly described as anything but-a voluntary system. However, it was put into effect in any event.
No. 12. On November 23 last we had P.C. 8S91 brought down by the government, which meant an abandonment of their previous support of the voluntary system and the adoption of compulsory service overseas of some 16,000 men of the N.R.M.A. That was a piecemeal measure.
The next fact was that the minister stated in the course of his remarks that there are overseas in the Canadian army now-I presume on two fronts-some ten thousand men who have been overseas for from four to five

War Effort-Government Policy
years. Further inquiries showed that many wounded soldiers, because of lack of sufficient reinforcements in the pools, had to be sent back again into the front lines before their wounds were wholly healed.
Lastly was the fact that the units were generally undermanned.
There in startling chronological order is the stark statement of what the minister found overseas and I am sure that Canadian people everywhere who read his address were startled by his revelations. I know the people of my riding were, and I believe they read every word of it because those with whom I came in contact when I was home on Saturday all seemed to know all about it.
The new Minister of National Defence decided to carry on with his fetish of the voluntary system.
Davenport riding is a great riding, Your Honour, and the men of Davenport riding have enlisted almost en masse in this war as they did in the last. In the last war enlistments were particularly heavy in the north end of the riding, which had been settled by many thousands from the old land, some of whom had not been here very long, and when war broke out they volunteered to a man for service overseas to fight with the British empire, because that is what it means. We cannot fight a war in Canada, Your Honour. If Canada is to fight, we want to keep the war out of Canada, and the only way in which we can do that is to fight the battle on the high seas and on the battlefields of Europe.
The people of my riding have enlisted en masse in this war also. I know one family with seven sons, everyone of whom is in the service. I know of another family with six sons, everyone of whom is in the service. I know many families who have five sons in the service, and numerous families in my riding have four sons in the service, or three sons or two sons, and many of course have given their only son. Davenport is a riding that all down through its history has rallied to the defence of the empire and its men have volunteered to go anywhere to fight. To volunteer to fight in Canada only-I do not know what kind of fighting that would be. But the men of my riding have volunteered to fight overseas. That is the kind of man who helps to hold this empire together. Davenport riding has sent so many overseas that its branch of the British Empire Service League, the Earlscourt branch, is one of the largest in the British empire, and close by are two other branches of the British Empire Service League, which is an indication of the
martial spirit of the people of my riding. I am proud to represent them because my own Scottish blood goes back generation after generation, and in all countries we have been a military race.
About three weeks ago I attended a commencement meeting in Oakwood collegiate, in my riding, where every year I give gold medals to students for oratory, and at that meeting they read off the list-about 1,000 names-of the young lads of Oakwood collegiate and roundabout who have enlisted in this war, some seventy to ninety of whom have already made the supreme sacrifice. How many have enlisted from the other collegiate in my riding, Bloor street collegiate, I do not know, but the number must be great. If every school in Canada had enlistments of its students to the same extent there perhaps would have been no necessity for compulsory service in this country, and the fact that they did not enlist in as large numbers as the young lads did from the collegiates in Davenport has forced the young men from my constituency to enlist to the extent that they have. I am proud of the young heroes who sat on the platform of Oakwood collegiate a few weeks ago, some of them having come back from overseas. Consequently, Your Honour, Davenport riding certainly needs little compulsion. I do not know how many more could enlist from my riding, certainly not very many. From the very beginning they have been in favour of all-out service, not only by Davenport, but by every other riding.
There have been cases of men holding so-called key positions who have not enlisted. On one occasion I was in a factory where I saw a notice posted up to the effect that if any employee felt that his position was of great importance to the war effort, if he spokh to so-and-so in the company, arrangements would be made to keep him in the plant in his present position, I know the case of a hairdresser who is now holding a key position in an aeroplane factory. He has to do with assembling wings. I cannot imagine how a hairdresser can be indispensable in the building of aeroplanes when so many mechanics and women are available to do that work. That man should have been in the army if he is eligible. There are many cases like that in Canada, of men holding so-called key positions who have been aided and abetted in holding on to those positions.
I want to mention the case of a man who came to see me last night because his is typical of thousands. Cases of this sort have
War Effort-Government Policy

been mentioned before but are worth repeating. This man is in the air force. He is a university graduate, a capable and brilliant young man. He succeeded in passing all the tests required of him in the air force and went on and studied the course. He has been in the air force for two years, but now he has been mustered out. He told me last night that he had been ordered out of the air force and that he must remuster into the infantry. His case is only one of many, and I think this treatment of these young men is wholly unfair. Thousands of these young men have spent a long time preparing themselves for the air force or for some other particular branch of the service, perhaps following in their father's footsteps in the last war; and now all of a sudden, because we have not had compulsory service in this country, and because there have not been sufficient enlistments in the infantry service, these young men who have served a year or more fitting themselves for a particular branch of the service are mustered out and remustered into the infantry. My hon. friend the member for York South mem tioned the case of a young artillery man, and his case was typical of many.
Something was said about petitions, letters and the like. I received over 10,000 names. Nobody can tell me that these men and women sent letters and signed their names to petitions just for the mere fun of doing it. I give them credit for sincerity. I believe the vast majority of them are fathers, mothers, wives, sisters and brothers of men overseas. They have had, as I have had, many letters from overseas bearing out what the former minister said, that units were undermanned and the wounded were being sent back before they were restored to health. I met a father on the street in November. I hope he does not read what I am now going to say. He felt very badly, naturally. His son wrote that he was badly wounded but that he had recovered. Then he received another letter from the son saying that he had been ordered back into the front line again. In the letter to his father he intimated to me:
I am not quite well, but am ordered back to the front. I am still wearing the bandage on my arm, but God has been good to me. He saved my life in all the actions I have been in and I trust Him to do it again.
He was sent back into the line with a bandage on his arm. Well, the father received a message a few days ago that his son was killed. He was unfit to go into the line, but because of lack of reinforcements he was sent back. I wish to ask who is responsible for that.

speechtext:
Well, I am not going to place the responsibility. But there is something wrong with the whole organization in the country when such conditions obtain, that a boy has to go into the line again, again and again until he is shot to death.
Another father came to see me on Sunday. His boy has been over there for three years. He has been wounded twice. The first time he was wounded very badly. He was placed on board ship to go to England for recuperation, I presume, but the unit became so depleted and the pool so empty that, after being on the ship for two days, he was taken off and sent back into the line again. In a letter to his father the boy writes something like this:
I was too weak to go into the line. On getting there I was too faint. . . .
I presume, to go right in close. I am not familiar with the military set-up although I listened very carefully to the former minister's description of it. They told the boy he would get along more quickly if he were within sound of the guns. His father said:
It is too bad. Within sound of the guns. He may easily get killed listening to the guns and not actually taking part in combat.
There is the situation, and as someone has previously said, a large part of the agitation going on in Canada to see that the fighting men overseas are adequately reinforced, as is their right, comes from the receipt of letters from overseas by parents. The newspapers obtained these letters. I give credit to the Toronto papers, Your Honour, for having the courage to publish these letters. They have published hundreds of them. They have come from ridings all around the city. I believe it is the publication of these letters that has stirred up public opinion as I have never seen it stirred up before. It would do anyone good to go to a theatre in Toronto these days. In an Ottawa theatre on Thursday or Friday night and in both these fighting cities that have sent multitudes of boys overseas it would do your heart good to see them cheer when the picture of the former minister of national defence is thrown on the screen, and I am sure you would feel badly as I did, to hear the boos when other pictures are thrown on the screen. That is public opinion, and public opinion in Ontario today-I cannot speak for the other provinces- has been worked up as it has never been before..
The former minister of national defence said the other night that he would watch the new minister. I myself have not a lot of confidence in the new minister. He stood on the floor of this house on two or three different

War Effort-Government Policy
occasions and took time to point out his adherence to the voluntary system. I cannot have a lot of faith in a man of that kind enforcing the compulsory system. I would have had faith in the former minister because he recommended it and his recommendation was accepted by the incoming minister twenty-two days too late. The former minister said his programme called for the sending overseas of troops on November 27 to support the men over there. His recommendation called for troops from the N.R.M.A. personnel. A whole month has gone by, and dear knows how much time will go by before these men go overseas. Major Conny Smythe brought up something like this before. I have heard his remarks discounted, but they were well supported on Saturday by Major "Tiger" Welsh. His remarks appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of Saturday last and I shall quote some of them:
As typical of conditions, a draft of replacements Him an anti-aircraft unit was sent to his anti-tank unit and, apart from not knowing anti-tank weapons or methods, turned out to be "largely cooks and clerks with little knowledge of ack-ack and had to be sent back to regimental headquarters."
If that is a statement of fact-it is not for me to say, but here is a reputable major making the statement-then I say it is a sad state of affairs. It is a terrible thing to have the units overseas undermanned and the pools in the same condition. I do not think any father in this house who has a son fighting overseas would want to see his son supported so ineffectively.
Further on, the major says:
But our infantry has been reinforced, insufficiently. of course, with untrained men or men trained in other highly specialized technique such as artillery, while artillery itself suffered from lack of trained men. There is all the difference in the world in this war between numerical reinforcements and trained reinforcements.
I have no doubt that this is right. I do not know anything about it. I for one am deeply sorry that our Prime Minister for whom I have and have had a particularly warm personal regard, did not do exactly as the President of the United States did. I remember that during the presidential campaign of 1940 the President of the United States, if I remember correctly-I have not written his remarks down, although I heard them-and his opponent the late Mr. Willkie, told the people of the United States in the summer of 1940 that they could not think of sending American boys overseas to fight again on the fields of Europe. No, they could not think of it, but
once they got into the war they did it immediately.

We have been attacked
from the beginning. They did it immediately. Had the Prime Minister of this country, particularly after the plebiscite vote which was so overwhelmingly in favour of an all-out effort, come out for all-out service, as the military service vote called upon him to do, I believe he would have had almost the united support of this country to carry on an all-out war effort. I wish he had done it, but he did not do it and here we are to-day with I do not know what. I have little confidence that the proposal is to be carried out because the new minister said, in answer to my question and questions of other hon. members, that in regard to the 16,000 from the N.R.M.A. he would send them if required to fill up the units. That is not what the people want. The former minister said that there were 10,000 men overseas who had been there for four years, and God knows it is time that they had the chance to get back home for a rest. They cannot get back here again if we are to send over only 16,000. God knows, a boy wounded two or thr times should not be sent up a fourth or fifth time, but I have here the report of one lad who was injured for the sixth time. On Saturday I went to see many people. I had received many letters and I went to see some of those who had written to me. One mother told me that her son had been fighting for seventeen months and had been in hospital six times and she said it was enough to make her see red. Is it any wonder? This is everybody's war.
Someone spoke about enlistments. Well, I am not going to discuss enlistments by provinces, but I will say this. I went across to the other side south of the 45th parallel of latitude in the state of Maine, in Vermont, in New Hampshire and in Massachusetts, where there are large numbers of good people, good citizens, who formerly came from the province of Quebec. I am sorry I mentioned that province because there are few who have a warmer feeling for the province and for the people of Quebec than I have. I will not be guilty of saying an unkind word about them. I have never done so and I never will. But on the other side, south of the 45th parallel of latitude, former Quebecers are enlisting because they have to. There is no trouble there. They are fighting. And in the United States there are some six million people of German extraction and five million people of Italian extraction. Altogether there are
War Effort-Government Policy

approximately fifteen million people of axis extraction, but there is no trouble there. They are marching up and enlisting because they are called upon to do so.

In spite of what the minister has said, they are all subject to be called up under their system.
However, to proceed with what I was saying, another lady told me that one of her sons had been overseas for almost five years and she thinks it is time he had a chance to come home. I agree with her. Any young man overseas for four or five years ought to be able to come back, but this is not possible if you are sending only 16,000 from the N.R.M.A. The public -want the whole of the eligible N.R.M.A. to go overseas and then their husbands and sons and brothers overseas for four years and more will have a chance to come home. The former minister said something of that sort himself. I have another report of a lad who was overseas in the air force for two years and was thrown out. One man told me that he has four sons overseas and he said, "For God's sake, get tough; we cannot win this war unless we are tough; we cannot win it by pussy-footing." I wish I could do something in some capacity; I would be glad to do it. I have another report of a husband who had been overseas for about five years. He is now forty years of age. In my opinion all those of forty years and four years or more overseas should be home for a rest.
The workman is not given a chance. He goes to selective service and is sent on a job and he has to go. Why is it not the same in the army? It should be the same. That is precisely the question that one man, the father of two sons, asked me. I have a letter from a mother who has twin sons in Italy. They have been overseas for three and a half years. I do not see why her two sons should remain there so long without a furlough while others are not sent at all.
In conclusion, may I say this. When I was home on Saturday I read in the newspapers

something about a proposal that had been made in the other house, to use the language that we are obliged to use with reference to that place, to the effect that the life of this parliament be extended. I am utterly opposed to the extension of the life of parliament. I do not believe in it and I have never done so. I listened to what the Prime Minister said so ably when the matter was mentioned before, and I could not agree with him if he went back on what he said on that occasion.

Mr. Speaker, I think I have attended certainly as many and perhaps more of the sessions of this house in uniform than any other of the uniformed members. In all my appearances here, and in the considerable number of times I have spoken, I have attempted to keep such remarks as I had to make, in the house free from any suggestion that I have at any time used the experience it has been my privilege to have in the armed forces of the country for my own advantage or for political purposes. I make no apology for the fact, and it is a fact, that in such contributions as I have made to the debates of this house during the last four sessions I have attempted1 to keep as free as possible from purely political discussions, not because I am not interested in political discussion or that I see any great objection to it, but because I have felt that at times this might have proved to be a limitation on the service I was anxious to give and was endeavouring to give to the armed forces in my capacity as a soldier. To-night I do not propose to depart from that practice, although I make no promises for the immediate future.
During these years, I have, of course, made political speeches in my own constituency in the nature of reports to my constituents, and have taken part in the political activities of my constituency. But I am most anxious that the single purpose I have in mind in coming to this session of the house shall not be confused with any other issues which might be in my mind.

War Effort-Government Policy
In 1942 my constituents in Winnipeg South indicated by a ratio of approximately twelve to one their desire that this government should take any and every step, including conscription, to assure adequate reinforcements to our soldiers overseas; arid in the debate on bill No. 80 I stated that I would advocate and support conscription if it were required in order to reinforce our forces overseas. The people of my constituency, and I as their member, meant what we said'-literally. I have never at any time qualified that declaration. I have supported the government in the light of that fact, and because I have believed in the policies of the government and in the leader of the government. I make no boast and offer no apology for saying that to me Canada, her sons and her honour are a first consideration. I have not cried "wolf" when there was no wolf, and I have no intention now or at any subsequent time of accepting less than that which in my judgment is adequate to meet the need as I see it.
After nearly four and a half years in uniform, mainly in Canada but also in New foundland and Great Britain, I am not ignorant of the Canadian army, its personnel, its organization, the composition of the forces, their capabilities and their needs. I am not unaware of the contribution Canada has made in other phases of the war effort. I appreciate the extremes of opinion that' exist in this country. I know that much of this opinion is real and is based upon honest conviction. I also know that too much of it has its basis in prejudice and emotional stress. It has not taken me the nearly ten years I have been in this House of Commons to realize that in this house an hon. member is all too seldom placed in the position where he can give a simple yes or no to any proposition that comes before him. I am aware that it is the responsibility' of an hon. member to think in terms of to-morrow as well as of to-day; that the duty of an hon. member is not only to the living but also to those as yet unborn.
For me, Mr. Speaker, the issue in this session is simple. On the facts as I understand them I was and am unwilling to take the risk, which in my judgment we would be forced to take, if at this time we refused to resort to conscription of N.R.M.A. personnel to reinforce our overseas army. For me the hour has struck which, when I spoke on bill No. 80 in 1942, I realized might come. May I add that neither at that time nor at any time since have I had the slightest doubt that the Prime Minister of this country meant what he said, as I in my humble capacity meant what I said, during that debate in 1942:
"Conscription if necessary." My decision in regard to conscription was taken during the course of that debate. It was my own decision, and it left me with no problem once the facts were made clear, as they have been since the beginning of this session. [DOT] I am gratified, therefore, although not surprised, that this government has kept its pledge. The crux of the matter before us this session is the question of reinforcements. The question of conscription was settled in 1942.
I have said that I am impressed with the need for a dependable stream of reinforcements. I cast my first vote in France as a youngster of nineteen or twenty. I knew what it meant to be one of seventeen people standing up to do a job which should have been done by fifty people. I do not pretend to think that a conscript, except in individual cases, is man for man the equal of a volunteer soldier, but I, do know what it means to a man standing in the position in which I once stood to feel completely confident that somebody is standing behind him, that the people at home have not abandoned him and that in point of numbers, whether or not in point of efficiency, the chain of support is not broken, so that he does not have the feeling of being forgotten or abandoned. I will leave no stone unturned, as far as my influence may go, to see that this assurance is in the minds of the men who volunteer to fight for this country. But I differ sharply from those who suggest that the man in action to-day does not know what he is fighting for. I do not suppose any army ever organized anywhere knew as well what they are fighting for as does the present Canadian army. I do not think it requires the fanaticism which is common in some armies. We know what can happen under the pressure of fanatic appeal, and I know from experience as well as from observation how fanatic appeal will break against the solid phalanx of men who know why they are there, men who know that behind them stands a country from which they know reinforcements will come.
The number to be sent now is in my opinion adequate to meet the need. My interpretation of the order in council-and the government's statement leaves no doubt-is that all of the N.R.M.A. men now serving, or yet to be enrolled, are and will be available as required in the United Kingdom, in Europe and in the Mediterranean. It is clear that this is conscription, with all that it implies; and 1 deprecate greatly the statements of some of our hon. friends in the opposition who attempt to make it appear that that is not what it is.
I accept the fact that behind those 16,000 men who have now been notified by the
War Effort-Government Policy

government that they are to proceed as reinforcements stand another 26,000 who are in process of being readied for a similar departure, if and when their services are required in the field of battle. Whether they go as volunteers or conscripts is only of psychological importance, because these are the 42,000 bodies, the 42,000 physical beings or personnel who were not standing in line. And, according to my interpretation of the order in council-and I think I can understand what I read1-those who did not stand in line now stand in line. That, to me, is accomplishment of the essential thing, namely a dependable stream of reinforcements, bringing new confidence to those who fight.
Now, to those who declare that this government will not proceed along the lines I have accepted, I can only say that I believe it will. Because I believe it, I will vbte confidence in the government; I will vote confidence in those men who, in my judgment, are not only best qualified to carry out this policy, but also in fact the only government which could give effect to the policy I desire, definitely, positively and in time.
For those who have reached this decision only after heart-searching-and some, I feel quite sure, in some trepidation-I have only this to say, this question to ask: Is it reasonable to doubt that he who has swallowed the camel will strain at the gnat? Conscription, by the application of the extension of territory to N.R.M.A. personnel is, in my opinion, clear and concise; and any attempt to belittle or becloud the issue is not in the interest of that to which all of us who assembled here in this chamber on November 22, gave, at least, lip-service. We were here to see that the men who needed reinforcements would get them.
Some one has spoken of this vote of confidence as "suspended sentence". I shall not advertise the publication which used that expression, because it has been very well advertised in the house recently. May I hasten to add that I do not hold this view. I have no doubt of the sincerity of purpose behind the declaration of the order in council. If I did not have that confidence I would vote for the amendment.
Now, as always, as a private member, I, and those whom I represent in the house, may say and do say to those to whom we give our trust: You must not fail us. Mr. Speaker, I have no fear that they will fail, and for that reason I shall vote for the main motion.

Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln) : Mr. Speaker, before I engage the attention of the house on the more specific subject now under discussion I want to digress for a moment to bring to the attention of the government a matter which has just come to my notice, through the mail. I have reference to a communication just received from overseas dealing with discrimination, as they call it, against the volunteer fire service which went overseas, after having quit their good jobs in this country. These men are urgently appealing to the government to. place them in the same position, for gratuities and other benefits, as members of the armed forces are entitled to. I bring this matter to the attention of the government, simply because of the urgent plea which has just reached me from overseas.
I consider it the duty of every hon. member to reflect the view of his constituency as best he can with respect to the issue now before parliament. Last week I returned home with the determination that I would satisfy myself as to the actual sentiments of the people in my constituency'-because, after all, that is what we are expected to reflect. I returned home and held consultations with some of the heads of organizations that have written me in the past two or three weeks. I have no doubt the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has received, as I have, copies of many resolutions, which I shall not quote in detail. However, these are groups such as associations of business men and women, Daughters of the Empire, veterans' organizations of all descriptions, and scores of individuals. I say that these represent a true cross-section of my constituency. I say, further, that their representations have not been made on a political basis.
The opinions expressed in the resolutions I have received-and I repeat that I believe copies have been sent to the Prime Minister- are supported by letters received by mothers and fathers from their boys overseas. If the Prime Minister will summarize the intent and purpose in these resolutions I believe he will agree with me that he will have a clear conception of actually what is in the minds of the people from my constituency-and what I believe is fairly well representative of the whole of Canada. They want reinforcements sent overseas at once, and they want no limitations on those reinforcements. I imagine the Prime Minister has received several hundred copies of the ballot which was prepared by the Canadian Legion. This was published in my
DECEMBER 4, 1944	6777
War Effort-Government Policy
local paper, alongside one addressed to myself. The one addressed to me was dated November 16 and it reads:
As the member of the federal riding of the county of Lincoln, I call on you to do all in your power to have the home defence army made completely active immediately, and available for overseas forthwith. I ask you demand a recorded vote on this subject, if brought up in parliament.
That was signed by one of my responsible constituents. As I say, alongside that was another ballot addressed to the Prime Minister which reads:
As a citizen of Canada I request that you make the home defence army completely active immediately, and available for overseas forthwith.
Those were both signed by the same individual who is known to me personally. That is the sentiment expressed by the people of my constituency. Never in my experience have I seen the people in my constituency wrought up to the extent they are at the present time. I was interested in what the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) said this afternoon but I do not intend to be quite as modest I do not think that what has happened has anything to do with the Prime Minister personally; it is simply an expression against the policy he is following. All one has to do is to go to a picture show to find out what happens when the Prime Minister's picture appears on the screen. As I Say, I have never seen the people so wrought up. I repeat that all this is not against the Prime Minister personally, it is simply because of the serious situation that has arisen overseas.
Over the week-end I found the people of my country definitely thankful for the revelations made by the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston), for the clear and concise way in which he has presented the situation to them. Even though the former minister of national defence has revealed the means by which these conclusions, ending up in the order in council, were arrived at; even though he has revealed part of what occurred in the war committee when there was no doubt something in the way of an internal war started, the people are not satisfied with the back-tracking he indulged in at the finish of his speech. I say this in all sincerity. I am simply trying to indicate how these people whom I made it my business to get in touch with over the week-end are thinking.
The Prime Minister knows that there has been a wave of adverse public opinion sweeping across the country because of the evasions of the government during the past few weeks. The true situation has now been revealed. The Prime Minister, may try to lay that on the
doorstep of the official opposition, if he likes; he may say it is a malicious press, if he likes; perhaps he may criticize the Canadian Legion, but I want to say that not only the Canadian Legion but every veterans' organization in the country have taken the same stand. Surely the Prime Minister knows that as well as I.
For the moment let us leave out the reference he made to the official opposition and to the press. May I pause here to say that perhaps we owe a debt of gratitude to the press, to the scores of papers across this country which have taken a firm stand on this situation. I want to say a word about the veterans' organizations in particular. These organizations are made up of the fathers and mothers of the boys overseas. Many of the fathers served in the last war; they served well and they know what war is. Among this group is to be found the true basis of the unrest that has swept across this country. I say that advisedly because I found out where this criticism is coming from. As I say, in the statement made by the hon. member for Prince the true reason for this unrest has been revealed.
The present Minister of National Defence, Mr. McNaughton, has admitted up to a poipt that this situation does exist and is of a serious nature. The Prime Minister admits it; but he still appears to evade the issue; he still appears to be trying to avoid sending all-out reinforcements to the boys overseas. I say most definitely that because of this evasion the people of this country have lost faith in the Prime Minister and in this government.

When we met here on November 22 no one suspected that the government would execute a somersault on the question of voluntary service overnight and that on November 23 the Prime Minister would introduce the order in council at three o'clock in the afternoon, providing for the drafting of 16,000 N.R.M.A. men for service overseas. Perhaps there was somebody behind the scenes who knew what was going on, but whatever was happening behind the scenes or in the war committee or elsewhere between November 22 and November 23 was not revealed until the government indicated the reversal of its policy on voluntary service on November 23. Within twenty-four hours this drastic change had come. Then followed the

admission of General McNaughton to this chamber, and it was quite evident that he had not changed his mind on the voluntary system; in fact, he said so in this chamber. Almost his first words on November 23 in this chamber indicated his stand on this matter. I interpreted the words of the new Minister of National Defence to this group of people as meaning that he did not believe in the reversal of policy of the government which had been made within twenty-four hours, and I indicated what General McNaughton said he intended to do in carrying out the overnight reversal of policy of the government. I was asked on what I based my opinion, and by good luck I happened to have in my brief case a copy of Hansard of Thursday, November 23.
