subsubtopic: POLICY OP THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
I interpreted the stand of the new Minister of National Defence on the government's overnight change of policy; I was asked on what I based my opinion, and so I turned to page 6529 of Hansard of November 23, where in the second column I find that General McNaughton, in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), said this:
What is correct is this: where we have general service personnel, N.R.M.A., who have converted, if they are entirely suitable and are up to the standards of training which we require of them-and that cannot be stated in simple terms across the whole business, because some of the training will take advantage of facilities. We shall have people at certain stages in Canada, and certain places, and as regards others we shall want to use our facilities in England for working out. As long as there are suitable general service personnel available to fill the requirements, it is our intention to use them. We propose to make good whatever deficiencies there are from N.R.M.A. personnel.
It was on that assertion by General McNaughton and others that I based my opinion. Then I went on to read the next two questions, on the same page of HansaYd, as follows:
Mr. Green:	So that the government's policy
means this, that there may not be any N.R.M.A. personnel sent over at all between now and next May?
Mr. McNaughton: Perfectly correct-if there were, as I see signs developing already to indicate, a most satisfactory start in the conversion of N.R.M.A. men. We would not use this authority, then, in any way, and I would be the most thankful man in this room.

War Effort-Government Policy
Mr. Green: N.R.M.A. men will not be sent overseas if you can possibly avoid it?
Mr. McNaughton:	I have no intention of
using compulsion except to meet a deficiency, and having regard to the purpose we have of maintaining the strength of our armies overseas.
It was upon1 these statements of General MeNaughton's that I based my opinion. I also pointed out, without giving away any secrets, that what had happened in the secret session only strengthened that opinion. That was as far as I went. I think any hon. member who was present at the secret session will agree that the information given in secret only strengthened the position that I took. Then I was referred to the address which the hon. member for Prince made in this house and I repeated as nearly as I could some of the statements that he had made. I pointed out that he had particularly stressed to the house the urgency of the situation, and that he had told us about the war behind the scenes here in Ottawa, and I undertook to see that those present at the meeting got copies not only of the Prime Minister's speech but the speech of the former minister of national defence, which promise I carried out. So that they are in a position to form' their own conclusions as to what I told them. I was asked if the speech of the former minister of national defence was available and I said, "yes, in limited numbers." Then I was asked this question-I think the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) referred to it-if I did not think that the speech of the hon. member for Prince should be circulated across this country, in the manner referred to by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough. I stated that I entirely agreed. They did not know of the suggestion the hon. member had made; the idea came from themselves, and I thought it was a worthy one. Perhaps the Prime Minister will even yet consider it worth while carrying out. I suggested to my audience that they might write to the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, and gave them his address, but they did not think it worth while; they said I appeared to have all the facts, and they would be glad to have a few copies of the speech.
There is confusion of mind among our people; it is growing, and with that confusion their anger is also on the increase. I tell the Prime Minister that it is directed against the government and that he must take personal responsibility for it.
A highly respectable and reputable citizen, a prominent business man in my constituency, rose to his feet in this meeting and asked permission to read a letter and then to ask a
question. He had just received the letter from his son in Italy. It stated that the hon. member for Prince, whom I will refer to as the former minister of national defence, had been in Italy one week earlier and had left the assurance that he would deal with the urgent situation immediately upon his return to Canada. Apparently this boy had that definite impression. I think the hon. member for Prince is to be commended for giving that assurance to the boys, for goodness knows they needed it. I need not remind the house to what extent the hon. member kept his word to the troops; he did so, perhaps, up to a point. The reason why he did not go farther was not 'of his own making, and it is obvious to the house. The Prime Minister and a number of the members of the war committee would not allow compulsion to be put into effect for overseas reinforcements. That is the statement I made to the meeting, and I believe it is correct. Some time between six p.m. on November 22 and three p.m. on November 23 the government changed their opinion. I pause to wonder if it did change its opinion, or was it a case of compulsion of another form? I do not know; I leave it to the house to decide. I am not so sure that there was an actual change of heart. Anyway, stormy scenes were enacted, and resulted in Canada losing a very capable minister of national defence, a man who assiduously applied himself to the job before him, a man who took the trouble to go overseas and get first-hand information and who assured the boys over there that he would stand back of them. What is more, according to this letter, they had the impression that these reinforcements would be over soon. I ask hon. members if the former minister of national defence did not make it clear to this house that reinforcements were going forward at once, in goodly numbers. I was asked if I really believed that- the former minister of national defence intended to implement his promises. My answer was that he had staked his public career on it and resigned his office on the strength of it, so that I felt that the hon. member had conscientiously tried to discharge his duties and carry out the promises which he had made. Not much more need be said on that point. Events followed, and they continue to follow. People are aroused as never before. The end is not yet.
I desire to convey this to General McNaughton in a kindly way, and if I transgress a little in referring to him I crave his pardon. But the boy who wrote this letter, and who has been in Italy for a year and a half, spoke of General McNaughton as "their Andy," and he added that "if Colonel Ralston had left
War Effort-Government Policy

'Our Andy' on the job the boys in Italy would not be crying out for help at the present time." I leave it to the judgment of this house and of the people of Canada to what extent that is true. To my mind the irony of the. situation is appalling.

I wonder what the boys in France, Belgium, Holland and elsewhere overseas are going to say when they read the speeches of the Prime Minister, the former minister of national defence and the present Minister of National Defence. They should have all this information; yes, and I am going to make sure that they do get it all. Then we shall wait for the next mail and see just what the boys overseas have to say on the general situation.
I see that the Prime Minister gave an indication that his motion would be one for an all-out vigorous war effort. He implemented that statement by using the same phraseology in the motion he presented to the house, but he skilfully avoided any reference to voluntary enlistment or anything of that kind. Yet every hon. member knows that that was the policy of the government up to three o'clock on November 23.
Then he referred to the marvellous war effort which Canada had made. Many of us know something about the marvellous accomplishments of Canada. I know something about what has been done by the manufacturers, by the farmers, by the factory workers, and by the women; but I often wonder, when listening to their speeches, whether the Prime Minister and some members of his government

I do not say, all

are afflicted with the same superiority complex-

Well, this is a superiority complex, I fear. I wonder if they think that all the great and valiant achievements of our manufacturers, industrial workers, women and farmers would never have been effected if their government had not been in power. It is ridiculous to think that the same people could not do the job under any administration. After all these marvellous achievements-I say, by the people-we are now missing the boat on the most important issue, namely, reinforcements for our weary and worn-out boys overseas, particularly in the infantry. This is on the eve of victory, so the Prime Minister says. I say that we have a long, hard and tough road ahead of us, and the Minister of National Defence so

told us. He pointed out to us in this house, partly in secret session and partly in open session, some of the things we have to combat before we are through. However, the Prime Minister still seems to think we are on the eve of victory. He speaks of anarchy unless we vote confidence in the handling of the reinforcement crisis overseas. Well, the house knows now whether it can vote confidence in the government or not, and if it is satisfied with the way in which this situation is handled, that is up to every individual member. But I say that when they get home to their constituents some of them may find the picture a little different.
We will take the Prime Minister at his word, unless he is skilfully evading again, as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe says he is. Be that as it may, the people accept the statement of the Prime Minister that we are not to have an election. My people accept that statement; I accept it. But my people will not accept and I will not accept the deliberate evasion of the issue to get reinforcements overseas to our boys at once. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, the boys overseas will not accept it either, and I can produce many letters here. On behalf of my people I call on the Prime Minister to accept the principles embodied in the amendment moved by the official opposition to get behind our weary lads overseas by making every man in the defence of Canada army, called up now and in the future, available in any theatre of war.
In 1942 the Prime Minister declared that but one order in council would be required if compulsory service was necessary. Does the Prime Minister still say this is not necessary? How can he, when he has overnight passed a restrictive order in council accepting the principle, one which the new Minister of National Defence states openly he is not particularly in sympathy with? The statement was made in the house on the afternoon the order in council was passed. I call upon the Prime Minister-

War Effort-Government Policy
challenge for an election the Prime Minister can take it or leave it. speechtext:
I cannot help remembering that it was two years ago last week, on November 30, 1942, that I was elected as member of the House of Commons for the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay. I believe I can assert that I have fulfilled as well as possible the mandate that was given me, although the task of representing the people for the past two years has not been a very easy one. I know that my coming to this house did not please everybody, but I believe no one can deny that I have been faithful to my electors in taking the stand I have taken during the past two years.
I believe in democracy. I therefore believe that we are here to be the spokesman for our electors and not to be the tools of a party or of some outside interests. I must say that I was never so happy as I am now to be independent of all political groups and thus to be enabled to speak freely. That is the reason why I will do my utmost to discuss on its merits the question that is before the house to-day, not forgetting the gravity of the hour.
I will also try to refrain from rousing passions, because I believe that at a time like this those who take this opportunity to play politics for the benefit of one group or another render very bad service to their fellow citizens. I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, and to offer my congratulations upon, and my thanks for, the magnificent speech delivered last week by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). In this connection I wish to congratulate also the member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris). These hon. gentlemen have shown us that in spite of the malicious campaign of the last few weeks there are still in other provinces men of good will who can understand the sentiments of the French-Canadians, together with the fundamental basis of Canadian unity.
Before proceeding further, I should like to call the attention of the house to the meaning of the amendment moved by the leader of
the opposition (Mr. Graydon) and the subamendment moved by the member for Mercier (Mr. Jean). As regards the amendment of the opposition, I should like to know if those who wish to support it are aware of the fact that in doing so they will admit that the government has already ordered all the personnel of home defence to go overseas. In fact, if I take the amendment and endeavour to understand it I shall try to read it in a different way from that in which it is worded, and it would read as follows:
This house is of the opinion that by requiring all the N.R.MA. personnel, whether now or hereafter enrolled, to serve in any theatre of war, the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements and has failed to ensure equality of service and sacrifice.
Do you not think the members should be entitled to. know exactly whether the Progressive Conservatives do admit that the government has already conscripted for overseas all the N.R.M.A. personnel?
With regard to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Mercier, if we deal with it as I have dealt with the wording of the amendment moved by the opposition, in order that we may understand what it means, this is what we get:
This house is of the opinion that by using to the best advantage the general service personnel in Canada and the volunteers overseas, without resorting to conscription for service overseas, the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements.
I think the electors of Mercier will be glad to know what their member really wants in connection with the prosecution of the war; and by the amendment he has moved they will learn that their member has found that the present government has not done enough up to date, but that what he wants is a much more vigorous effort with conscription for overseas, because his motion constitutes blame on the government for not having imposed conscription for overseas.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before beginning my remarks on the present debate, I wish to deal with a statement made last week by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose), in which he referred to me. The hon. gentleman has often alluded to my activities in the political field and as recently as last week he stated that I had fascist leanings. I wish to say to the hon. member for Cartier that, before questioning other people's loyalty, he should think of what and where he was at the beginning of the war. On the other hand, I do not admit that the hon. member for Cartier has the right to speak for French Canadians in this house.

IFar Effort-Government Policy

Mr. Speaker, we must, no doubt, ask ourselves to what purpose we are gathered here at present, and the answer to this question is to be found in the statement of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), made on Wednesday, November 22, in which he listed the reasons for the recall of parliament at this time.
I find at page 6505 of Hansard the following statement made by the Prime Minister:
Mr. Speaker, the present meeting of the House of Commons has been occasioned by the controversy which has arisen out of the resignation on November 1 of the Hon. J. L. Ralston as Minister of National Defence, and the desirability of affording to hon. members an opportunity of discussing all matters in reference thereto, and in reference to the situation which has since arisen, and which is a matter of first importance to parliament and the people of Canada.
Now, what was that controversy between the right hon. the Prime Minister and the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston)? The explanation is to be found in a letter tabled on the same day in the House of Commons, and recorded at page 6506 of Hansard. I shall read the end of a paragraph which enlightens us upon the nature of the said controversy. I quote:
The only difference-
I am reading from a letter written to the Hon. J. L. Ralston by the right hon. the Prime Minister.
The only difference which exists is one of the method or methods of meeting this fundamental vital necessity.
That is the reinforcements for our troops overseas. I repeat:
The only difference which exists is one of the method or methods of meeting this fundamental vital necessity.
Now, what happened? After this meeting of Wednesday, November 22, we returned here and Thursday, the 23rd, in the midst of a most impressive silence, the famous order in council 8891 was read. It is my contention that from then on, the reason for which we had been called here no longer held inasmuch as the disagreement which had existed regarding the methods of reinforcement for our troops overseas had been dispelled or was no longer of any account. For that matter, it is the former minister of national defence who so informed us, in a statement which he made on November 23, page 6524 of Hansard:
I know a little about the things about which General McNaughton has been talking. There is little difference between him and me. The only difference as I understand it, is that the genera^ said there was a difference between us respecting policies. I think he rather attributed to me the policy of conscription for conscrip-

tion's sake or conscription whether necessary or not. My policy has always been, and it has been frequently announced in this house, conscription when necessary, and I was following that policy when I made the recommendation I did w'hieh was not accepted by the government. I hope that the general will accept that correction, because there is no difference between him and me so far as the matter of policy is concerned. I understand his policy to be the same, that is to say, conscription when necessary.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that after the sitting of November 23 the controversy no longer existed, and it was also obvious that there was no longer any reason for the debate which was to take place thereafter.	.

speechtext:
The hon.
member must know that there was a substantial difference. The former minister of national defence wished to send overseas, I understand, 42,000 N.R.M.A. men instead of 16,000.
Mr. DORION (Translation) On the strength of the statement made and repeated by the former minister of national defence-and I do not think that I am mistaken-more has been granted to the present Minister of National Defence, Mr. McNaughton, than has been requested by the former incumbent. Unless I am mistaken, the former minister of national defence had requested 15,000 men, but his successor was allowed 16.000. But the figure is of no consequence whatever. As I said before, a decision has been taken on the matter of principle, and all that remained for us to do was to take cognizance of the settlement of a disagreement between the former minister of national defence and the right hon. the Prime Minister. So definitely indeed had the matter been settled that order in council 8891 authorizes the Minister of National Defence to send overseas all necessary troops, all the men he sees fit to dispatch, without the necessity of again referring the matter to the house.
The proper interpretation of this official document will be easier, I believe, if we seek the spirit in which it was made. In order to get a better understanding of it, I refer to certain statements made some time ago by the former minister of national defence and his colleague of the naval services (Mr. Macdonald). First, I shall quote the following words of Hon. Mr. Ralston as reported in Le Soleil, of July 28, 1940:
Our front line is on the English channel and we must place on that line all we have even if it means running short here, stated the hon. Mr. Ralston, Minister of National Defence, to-day.
This was according to a Canadian Press dispatch from Ottawa. Here is another statement, by a minister still a member of the

War Effort-Government Policy
cabinet, reproduced in the Montreal Standard of October 24, 1940, Hon. Mr. Macdonald is reported as saying:
We have sent men, ships, guns and aircraft overseas and we shall send more and more as long as there remains a Canadian dollar unspent and a single Canadian citizen to talre the defence of freedom.
Mr. Speaker, I claim that the moment order in council 8891 was tabled, the die was cast, and in view of present and past statements of authorized persons, I say that this order must be constructed according to said declaration, and that, therefore, the ensuing debate is absolutely unwarranted. Not only is this debate unwarranted since November 23, but I blame the government for starting a discussion which has provoked a campaign of abuse toward the province of Quebec. It is probable that, had we returned! home on November 23, the outburst of fanaticism sweeping certain sections of the country might have been avoided.
In support of this contention, I shall quote a few words from one of hundreds and hundreds of letters, which in my opinion serve no useful purpose, which we receive every morning: '
Canada must not permit the province of Quebec to blockade the national support of our armed forces overseas.	.
The blame is always placed on the province of Quebec. And this abusive and fanatical campaign against Quebec continues. I repeat that if this debate had not been started, we would not have been called here in Ottawa to receive such letters which come from all sections of the dominion and there would not be such a campaign by eight provinces against the province of Quebec. Further, the present debate is absolutely useless for, after all, this issue of conscription which has been discussed for two weeks, has been settled definitely and in principle long ago. To my mind it was first settled by the visit made by the right hon. the Prime Minister to Hitler in 1937, about which we knew nothing before August 11, 1944. What took place during that visit? I wish to repeat the statement made in this house on August 11 of this year by the right hon. the Prime Minister:
I do tell this House of Commons to-day that my visit to Germany had as its objective to make it perfectly clear that, if there was a war of aggression, nothing in the world would keep the Canadian people from being at the side of Britain. That was known to the German government at that time, and my action in the matter was fully known to the British government; but I did not talk about it at the time, for it is just as well that some of these matters should not be spoken of until later years.
100-426J
Now, Mr. Speaker, from that very moment, not only had the principle of participation in the war been decided upon as the result of a visit of the right hon. the Prime Minister to Hitler, but the principle of the enforcement of .conscription, with all the consequences it entails to-day, had by that very fact been accepted.
Another happening also shows that this debate is useless because, once more, this discussion on conscription is only the consequence or the outgrowth of what has taken place in the last five years. The declaration of war by the Canadian government in 1939 could1 not but involve the enforcement of conscription for overseas service with which we are faced today. Is there a level-headed man in this country who, in 1939, when Canada declared war, has not immediately said to himself: No matter what is being said, no matter what the people of this country may do, conscription for overseas service will certainly be resorted *to before long.
A third event to which I refer is the mobilization act of 1940. Again I say that at that time conscription was necessarily decided upon. Therefore, this debate that has been going on since last week is absolutely useless. The Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons for Wednesday, June 19, 1940, give us the following account of what happened then:
The house then resumed consideration in committee of the whole of Bill No. 43. an act to confer certain powers upon the governor in council for the mobilization of national resources in the present war:
And the debate continuing.
Objection was raised against a ruling by the chairman of the committee (Mr. Vien) on a point of order, and an appeal being made to the house:
Mr. Speaker resumed the chair and the chairman of the committee made the following report:
When the committee was discussing section 2 of Bill No. 43, an act to confer certain powers upon the governor in council for the mobilization of national resources in the present war, Mr. Lacombe moved the following amendment: "That all the words after "Whereas" be deleted and the following substituted therefor: 'the government's war policy must be free and voluntary'." The chairman ruled that proposed amendment out of order because it could not be moved during the discussion of section 2 of the bill, and in view of the fact that, under the provisions of rule 76 of the house, consideration of the preamble is left until all the clauses have been disposed of.
Reference to the record of that time shows that the right hon. the Prime Minister himself, on that day, requested that a vote be taken on the motion of Mr. Lacombe to find out, so he said, who were in favour of it. The Votes and Proceedings record that two members, only two, voted against participation in

the war: Mr. Liguori Lacombe, member for Laval-Two Mountains and Mr. Wilfrid LaCroix, member for Quebec-Montmorency. The vote was taken on Mr. Lacombe's motion, as requested by the Prime Minister. The fourth event which gave rise to the present situation is the speech from the throne of 1942, in which the government announced the holding of a plebiscite to request that the Canadian people release them from past pledges. On page 2, column 1 of Hansard for 1942, the following paragraph is to be found in the speech from the throne:
My ministers accordingly will seek, from the people, by means of a plebiscite, release from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service.
When the vote was taken, on the main motion moved by Mr. Fournier (Hull) the following members from the province of Quebec voted against the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As for the others, they naturally voted in favour of the address. Bertrand (Terrebonne) LaCroix (Quebec-Bourget	Montmorency)
d'Anjou	Lizotte
Gauthier	Parent
Lacombe	Pouliot
Lacroix (Beauee)	Raymond
Roy
They are the only ones who, at that time attempted, but too late already, to oppose the law of conscription, the enforcement of which we are deploring this very day.
That is why I say that this conscription issue has been determined-it was determined, as I said before, by all the incidents to which I just referred. In conclusion, it is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that we were very far from that free, voluntary and moderate war effort promised in the speeches delivered by Liberal leaders on the declaration of war. In September, 1939, the war which was to be waged was a pink and easy war, according to statements made by the public men of those days and those who were responsible for the administration of national affairs. All that has changed, unless there was nothing true in all that, if we are to judge by. the situation which is laid upon us to-day.
Mr. Speaker, I heard the other day the Prime Minister evoke the memory of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and of the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe in an attempt to convince the hon. members of the province of Quebec to give him their support at this juncture. If the Prime Minister had cared to put before the house what' purported to be the opinion of the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, he would no doubt have referred to a speech which he delivered on September 9, 1939, and he would have detached the following excerpt. I quote:
To those who criticize me to-day and who claim that I have changed my views, let me say that I am quite willing to show them the text of the speeches which I made on many occasions during the war. The change came on the conscription issue, which unfortunately was projected into the field at the time and which has sown the seed of discord of which even to-day we are reaping the bitter fruit.
And a little further on, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe said:
Every speech that has been made has shown that this will be a gigantic conflict.
He was aware therefore of the enormous war effort Canada would have to make. In spite of that, he made the following statement:
If Canadians go to the front line of battle they will go voluntarily as Canadians, under the control of Canada, commanded by Canadians and maintained by the Dominion of Canada.
And further on he added:
The other school consists of those who also close their eyes to realities and are promoting courses which disunite Canada-because such measures will never be accepted or enforced by and in a most important section of the country. The whole province of Quebec-and I speak with all the responsibility and all the solemnity I can give to my words-will never agree to accept compulsory service or conscription outside Canada. I will go farther than that: When I say the whole province of Quebec I mean that I personally agree with them. I am authorized by my colleagues in the cabinet
[Mr. Dorion.l

War Effort-Government Policy
from the province of Quebec to say that we will never agree to conscription and will never he members or supporters of a government that will try to enforce it.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, had the right hon. the Prime Minister really been drawing his inspiration from the acts and policies of the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, he would not have attempted, the other day, to take advantage of certain statements, to request of the members from the province of Quebec a vote of confidence on the conscription motion that is presently before the house.
Numerous sub-amendments were offered in the course of the debate. Of course, I do not wish to make an exhaustive review of those that were ruled out of order. As regards the sub-amendment of the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Jean) I said a moment ago how it should be viewed. Nevertheless, those subamendments which were submitted to us gave us the opportunity of wondering what are the real tenets of the groups which advocated them. The first was drafted by the C.C.F. party. It was immediately apparent that, in view of the theory I have just expounded, we could not support it, for it stemmed from the doctrine and principles which form the basis of the general policy of the C.C.F. party, a policy that, to me, appears unacceptable, especially by the province of Quebec. As far as I am concerned, I take this opportunity to disclaim any misconstruction, as attempted in certain quarters, of statements I have previously made, and which I do not deny, but which must be given their true meaning. I must say that I am far remote from the C.C.F. party as I cannot accept, the socialist doctrine of that party. I am in favour of private enterprise provided it is duly controlled by the government, because otherwise-and that is to a certain extent, the situation which obtains to-day-it is rather private enterprise which controls the government. For my part, I wish that the development of private enterprise should continue in this country, but. as I say, under the rigid control of the government in power.
As regards the amendment of the Progressive Conservative party, I said a few moments ago what if amounts to. That amendment is nothing short of a request to the House of Commons to put all our manpower at the disposal of the government, so as to provide our armies overseas with an increasingly large number of men, regardless of the country's needs and regardless of consequences. The aim is to deprive this country of its manpower, no more, no less, but to'whose benefit? I wonder.
That is why that amendment moved by the Conservative party can certainly not have our support.
In regard to the main motion, it is obvious that, for several reasons, we cannot support it. The chief reason is that its adoption would constitute a vote of confidence in a government whose policy is absolutely opposed and contrary to that it advocated during the 1940 electoral campaign. Hence, we claim that the present government has no mandate to enforce the policy which it now carries out. We should vote against this motion because all the members sitting in this house have not been elected to enforce the present policy of the government. Therefore, if we wish to comply with the mandate with which we have been entrusted, if we wish to be honest with our electors, we must of necessity vote against the main motion.
The second reason why we must vote against this motion is that we claim that at the present time we have gone much too far in a war effort entirely out of proportion with our means; and that in 1939 and after 1940 in particular the dominion government has made commitments which far exceeded this country's abilities and resources. In 1939 as in 1940, if we had not rushed in blindly in order to display an unimpeachable loyalty by doing more for the war effort than any other country in the world, if we had remained within the reasonable limits of a war effort in keeping with the resources and manpower of the country, I contend that we would not find ourselves in the present emergency. What will the principle laid down in order in council 8891 lead us to? I read in the newspapers the other day that, according to certain figures which were supposed to be official, we had at the present time about 900,000 men in the armed forces. Any country which has 10 per cent of its total population under arms has reached the limit of its effort according to experts in vital statistics. Although we are at war because parliament has so decreed we are not really threatened in this country. If we consider, as it has often been stated in this house during the last two sessions, that we have fed the European countries and raised an army which almost reaches the limit of 10 per cent of our population, that is why I say that before the end of the war is reached, we shall find out, but too late, unfortunately, that we have gone far beyond our means.
Another reason for voting against this motion of confidence is our claim that the present government, in spite of what they have endeavoured to represent to our people,
67S6

War Effort-Government Policy
is not the administration conducive to national unity. I shall go further and assert that the Liberal party, now in power, is a factor of national disunity. If the present situation, which we deplore, exists in our country, it is because for more than thirty years the Liberal party in the province of Quebec has stirred up and encouraged grievances, to gain political advantages. For the last thirty years the province of Quebec, as I pointed out in greater detail in a speech I made here on February 10, 1944, no elections, either federal or provincial, were held in which the Liberal party did not exploit to its advantage the feeling opposed to all participation in external wars. Evidence of unfailing loyalty is now the order of the day, as was demonstrated a short while ago by the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Picard) who saw fit in his speech, to attack the independent members who sit in the house. I quote the following from page 6694 of Hansard:
.	.	. in French Canada the people who
through all their political life had been friendly to the Tories are masquerading as independents. They are accusing the government, and I use their own words, of "betraying Quebec." They criticize the whole war effort and accuse those of us who have supported all government measures exclusive of Bill No. 80 of being tools of English Canada and of causing great harm to our racial group.
The hon. gentleman, whose party for thirty years campaigned in the province of Quebec asking the people to vote against the party responsible for war in 1914-1918, now tries to assume a feeling of loyalty, which dims that of our most imperialistic fellow citizens. There is another passage I wish to quote from his address. On page 6695, I find the following:
Now the cry is raised in Quebec: "Duplessis is back in power, the government has been forced to implement Bill No. 80 and Duplessis could not prevent it."
Does the hon. member for Bellechasse wish to insinuate that we have conscription to-day because the Union Nationale is in power in Quebec? This places a terrible responsibility upon the federal government. These were the words uttered in this house on November 30, in the speech,to which I refer.
Recently, at a meeting held in his constituency, he again attempted to make political capital out of the 1914 war. I find in Le Soleil of November 25, 1944, the following:
Mr. Picard thanked all his friends for having expressed their opinion. He cautioned his audience against fomentors of discord, against the so-called independents, who are Conservatives in disguise, and the heirs of those Tories who in 1917 spoke against conscription but voted for it.
He is now trying again to raise that prejudice on which the province of Quebec has been fed for thirty years by the Liberal party. In that report from Le Soleil this most laughable explanation was given by the hon. member of the fact that he had not crossed the floor of the house, as some other members had done:
Some hon. members have seen fit to cross the floor of the house to sit on the opposition side. That is but a gesture. A member can just as well uphold his principles while keeping his seat, and moreover, in my ease

And here is the comic part of the statement. -the seat which I now occupy is already on the left of the Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, we have another reason for voting against the motion of confidence, and it is because I claim that, since the beginning of this war, the government-and the responsibility therefor weighs especially on the ministers from the province of Quebec-has never taken the trouble to indicate true figures about the share of the province of Quebec in the war effort. At the beginning of November, when the Prime Minister spoke over the radio, I heard some statistics which had already been requested in this house but which we had not been given because it was said that their disclosure would have been detrimental to the public interest.
Had the ministers from Quebec taken care to show under its true light the nature of that province's contribution to the war effort, I claim that it would have been possible, in a large measure, to prevent the campaign of abuse and fanaticism which is so apparent at the present time.
This is another reason why I propose to vote against the main motion.
Another thing. It is obvious, in all this, that the French-Canadian ministers who have broken their pledges to the province of Quebec, their constituents and their fellow-citizens, have not done everything in their power to prevent the passing of order in council 8S91. Moreover I am convinced that if the ministers from the province of Quebec had not been afraid and had had the courage to defend what it is their duty to uphold in this house, this order in council would probably never have been passed. I say that if the right hon. the Prime Minister had also had the courage to defend the stand which he had consistently taken since the outbreak of war, I am convinced that he would readily have obtained the vote of confidence which he intended to request on November 22 in support of the voluntary system. If the right hon. the Prime Minister had had the courage to maintain.the stand which he

War Effort-Government Policy
had taken since the beginning of the war and if it had been necessary to go to the country, I am convinced that he would have been returned to power with an even larger majority than he has today.

Certainly. We must not depend too much on this campaign of political frenzy stirred up at the present time to ascertain the real feelings of the Canadian people. We must realize also that in the English-speaking provinces, there are people who understand the situation. That is why I claim that they lacked courage or tried, once again, to deceive the whole country.
(Text) In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize the fact that, very fortunately, a certain press together with some individuals, seem to have seized this question of reinforcements to raise an anti-racial struggle in this country.
We often hear of Canadian unity in these days, and I wonder if those who preach it very loudly know what it is.
One must not forget that unity does not mean unification.
One must not forget that, in this country, there are two races with two different mentalities.
The French Canadians do understand that the English Canadians can still hold some close ties with the country they left not long ago, even if it be one or two generations ago, but it must be understood that you will never make Britishers out of the French Canadians.
I am sure that if our English-speaking fellow citizens went to the trouble of learning and of knowing the sentiments of the French Canadians, they would refrain from raising such issues as the one with which we are now confronted.
I am one of those who believe that there can still be understanding between the two races. But the majority must not try to overrule the minority and force it to submit to all its wishes.
Democracy, in a country like ours, cannot mean the domination of the majority over the minority; there must always be some understanding between the two; otherwise, it is not democracy; it is tyranny.

Before I do so, my good friend the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion)

speechtext:
Yes, in 1939 as well as in 1940 and 1944.
After a few opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I will now resume the debate before the house. Bill No. SO, passed in 1942 by the present parliament, recognized the principle of the conscription of man-power for overseas service. Like a number of other Liberal members, I voted against bill No. 80 and against conscription, as evidenced by the records of the house. Therefore, I am able to state to-day that I have been as good as my word and that I have not broken faith with my constituents to whom I had promised that I would not vote in favour of a compulsory measure.
The right hon. the Prime Minister gave his word that, before bill No. 80 was put into effect, the House of Commons would be consulted and an order in council passed to that end. For five years the right hon. the Prime Minister managed to steer clear of the reefs. For five years he has faced the storm and held the fort against the might of various opposition groups which tried to force the enactment of such a measure. Yet, a few months prior to the end of the war, he gives in before the pro-conscription push. Order in council 8891

was passed on November 23, authorizing the Minister of National Defence to conscript
16,000	additional N.M.R.A. recruits. I emphasize the word "additional", for it implies additional commitments as far as the men are concerned. I claim, therefore, that the hon. Minister of National Defence now has the right to call 16,000 additional draftees.
Mr. Speaker, here is a full right-about-turn on the policy announced a few days earlier, here is conscription as denounced by the leader of the Liberal party for the past twenty-five years as well as by the late Hon. Ernest Lapointe, the late Hon. Fernand Rinfret and others. Here is conscription as I censured it myself, in this house, in my speeches to my constituents and in the newspaper of my riding. Here is conscription against which I have agreed to struggle unless it is absolutely necessary to save Canada, our beloved homeland.
I admit, with regret, that the explanations advanced by our military authorities and ministers, far from satisfying me that conscription is necessary to save Canada, have convinced me more than ever that the right hon. the Prime Minister and the Liberal government have been the victims of fully ripened and premeditated schemes, that the former minister of national defence has failed to rise to the occasion and could not curb the tory influence of the military bureaucracy which controls our army. Even in June 1944, it would have been easy to foresee and avoid the catastrophe and the conflict which now threatens to disrupt the Canadian confederation, had proper action been taken.
The former minister of defence (Mr. Ralston) admits that he was informed in June 1944 that reinforcements would be required at the end of the year, that is in December. What did he do? Did he take any action with a view of promoting voluntary enlistments? As far as I know, he did nothing of the kind. He admitted having received in August a telegram informing him that the situation was becoming worse, he admitted at page 6662 of Hansard that he did not communicate that telegram to the war cabinet. It was only after the receipt of a second telegram that he decided to submit the latter to his colleagues. Meanwhile did he do anything to promote voluntary enlistments? No, as far as I know, he did nothing. At page 6597 of Hansard, the right hon. the Prime Minister stated that it was not before the month of October that the former minister of defence submitted for the first time to the cabinet the matter of conscription draftees. Ever since June, conscription was in the mind of the former min-

War Effort-Government Policy
ister of defence, and he then had to do something. But did he do anything with a view of promoting voluntary enlistments among French Canadians whose units seemed to have suffered particularly heavy casualties on the Italian front? No, in that respect again, he did nothing. And furthermore I wish to congratulate the Minister of National Defence for admitting frankly, as shown by page 6661 of Hansard, that the government does not possess at arm}' headquarters, here in Canada, figures and data showing the number of reinforcements in the United Kingdom and Italy, so that one ' day he decided to make a tour of the European fronts to ascertain the situation of our armies which even our government did not know.
I feel that the war cabinet, the government and the people were deliberately left under a false sense of security. We have been left in a state of doubt, of uncertainty. Daily reports of our casualties and reinforcements should have been available here in Ottawa, so as to enable us to reinforce our brave soldiers on twenty-four hours' notice. There has been in this regard an unpardonable lack of organization, the serious consequences of which must be borne today, and which, in the judgment of the country unfortunately fall upon the shoulders of a man who is not responsible for it, the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada. The chiefs of staffs of our army should alone bear the full responsibility.
I have carefully listened to certain speeches, which invariably implied-but never adduced positive evidence-that the province of Quebec did not do its share in this war.
We did more than our share in agreeing to the declaration of war, but did so on the express and essential condition, that there be no conscription for overseas service. Mr. Speaker, we assented to mobilization for service in Canada, for the mobilization act was based on the unavoidable duty every man in this country is required to fulfil, since he must defend the soil he loves and cherishes. In the province of Quebec, we accepted the taxes, we concurred in the loans, in fact, we subscribed generously. We agreed to the gifts of raw materials, guns, shells and so on, made to our allies totalling one billion dollars in 1942, one billion in 1943, and. $800,000,000 in 1944. We accepted our share of responsibility in this war, Mr Speaker, and cooperated in the maintenance of national unity in the country, a condition essential to the success of the gigantic task we had undertaken in the interest of humanity as a whole.
We did not jib when French Canadians were asked to enlist that they might defend the cause of humanity, but was anything done to promote voluntary enlistment in Quebec? Not
to my knowledge. On the contrary, I assert that everything was tried to discourage any attraction French Canadians might feel for service in the active army. '
As a matter of fact, I know young draftees who could not speak a word of English, but who were sent to English-speaking units and dispatched, like so many heads of cattle, to the Pacific coast, in hostile surroundings, where they could not feel at home, and if perchance they did not obey orders given in a language they did not understand those young French Canadians were frequently made a laughing stock for English-speaking members of the active army. How could our compatriots be expected to volunteer in such unfavourable circumstances, when they were sent to places far remote from their province.
The Prime Minister said that the voluntary system failed on account of the campaign waged, after the appointment of the Minister of Defence, by the Tory organization of the other provinces which incited the people to follow their basest impulses. That campaign was-launched by the Tories. In February, 1944, the Saskatchewan Conservative association passed a resolution calling for conscription for. overseas service. On June 19, at Guelph, Ontario, Messrs. Bracken and McTague both demanded, in a public meeting, conscription for overseas service. On June 20, Colonel Drew, speaking in Winnipeg, also demanded- the immediate enforcement of conscription for draftees. On June 27, at Ottawa, Mr. McTague again took up the cudgels for conscription and upbraided Mr. King for his stubbornness in refusing to send draftees overseas. On October 5, in Toronto, Colonel Drew made another plea for conscription, and on October 10, in Montreal, Mr. McTague blamed Mr. King for his failure to enforce conscription.
I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that this clique which for years'has been opposing the present government is much more anxious to bring about the defeat of the Right. Hon. Mr. King than to see the downfall of Hitler. I know that my views will not be shared in some quarters, but I am sincere about it.
These incidental remarks must not, however, make us lose sight of the only issue: the motion of confidence moved by the right hon. the Prime Minister, which reads as follows:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
The vigorous war effort mentioned implies the order in council passed on November 23. Now, this order embodies the decision of the government to implement conscription for

War Effort-Government Policy

overseas service. As I have stated, I am not convinced that such a measure is necessary and timely; this half-measure is only one step removed from the total conscription demanded by the Conservatives in their amendment which reads as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following words substituted instead thereof:
"This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice."
Then comes the motion of the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Jean) in which I concur wholeheartedly; it is worded as follows:
That all the words of the amendment after the word "reinforcements" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"by using to the best advantage the general service personnel in Canada and the volunteers overseas without resorting to conscription for service overseas."
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with the first two proposals which both include constituent elements of a measure I do not endorse. I will, nevertheless, vote for the sub-amendment moved by the hon. member for Mercier and against the amendment submitted by the Tory party. I do not, however, forget the wonderful achievement for which the right hon. the Prime Minister deserves credit in this war. Surely our people understand the difficult situation with which he is faced, and sympathized with him. The right hon. the Prime Minister no doubt realizes the unbearable position in which have been placed many of his supporters who have constantly stood by him in times of stress. He is aware that a group of our colleagues, of whom I am one, have received a very definite, clear and explicit mandate. I have concluded a solemn agreement with my constituents, and I do not want it to be said that I betrayed them.
