subtopic: THE WAR
subsubtopic: POLICY OP THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Earlier speakers have stated that the subject of this debate is not the principle of conscription, as that has already been decided. It was decided in the debate on bill No. 80 in 1942 when the government was given power to introduce conscription for overseas service if necessary. To-day's debate centres rather on the problem of supplying immediate, adequate trained reinforcements to the army overseas. I myself was overseas when the debate on bill No. 80 took place, so that perhaps the house will pardon me for a minute if I take time to make clear my stand on the issue of conscription.

At the outbreak of war I believed in the voluntary system of enlisting the army, the air force and the navy in this country, and like almost every other member of the house I campaigned on that issue in the spring of 1940. Those, of course, were the days of the so-called phony war, when we all had a Maginot-line complex and felt that we could blockade the Germans into submission with little use of man-power. At that time the only bitterness in our armed services was among those who had volunteered and could not get into the service because they were so flooded with recruits.
At the time of the fall of France, however, my attitude towards conscription changed very greatly, and that change was crystallized by my service overseas. In Britain I saw democracy at war where everyone shouldered the responsibility assigned to them according to their ability to carry that burden. Those medically fit took part in the fighting services as they were directed; those who were unfit, those who were too young, those who were too old, those who had special abilities were directed into employment by the state, with fire-watching and A.R.P. work in addition, men and women alike.
Out of this equality of service and sacrifice came unity, a real unity such as Britain has never seen before, people of every class united by common sacrifice in a common aim, a unity which gave the people of Britain the courage to stand the dark days of the blitz undaunted and unafraid. I therefore declare myself unreservedly in favour of total conscription in time of war, and I intend to adhere to this belief even more strongly in time of peace because I am quite sure that if every Canadian citizen knew in time of peace that if war came he would be obliged to take his full share of the fighting and the sacrifices, then our people in peace time would be all the more resolved that this nation should pursue a course which would avoid war.
There are many I know who sincerely believe that the enforcement of total conscription in this country will set one part of the country against the other and contribute to national disunity. I feel that there is much more serious threat to national unity; if we do not have some uniformity of service and sacrifice it will not be one section of the country against all the rest; it will be a bitterness in every street of every city, town and hamlet in this land, a bitterness between the men and the families of the men who have volunteered and those who have shirked every appeal to carry part of this nation's burden.
Coming now to the matter of adequate, trained reinforcements, I do not intend to use

War Effort-Government Policy
any of the welter of figures which have been given to this house in the last few days. Like my friend the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), I cannot remember which figures I learned in open session and may use, and which I learned in closed session and may not use. One fact, however, has emerged during this session; that is, that the Canadian infantry overseas are perilously short of trained reinforcements, and that immediate action must be taken to sustain them. This news is supposed to have surprised the cabinet. It surprised the people of Canada even more, for two reasons. First, in the press appeared the news that the Canadian army overseas was short of reinforcements, and at the same time we were told that we had in this country 130,000 general service men. together with 70,000 conscripts. How could we be short of men overseas with such a reserve in this country? I know our military men in this house have given a break-down of all those soldiers into so many categories; we are assured that the army has combed out all the fit fighting men from the more than
130,000	general service who are available, and we are told that these men number only some 5.000. The people of Canada do not accept that, and I do not accept it either, because there is a much simpler standard, which was given in the press at the same time, in regard to the use of man-power. I refer to the announcement of the winding up of the British commonwealth air training plan, which was undoubtedly one of Canada's greatest contributions to the fighting front in this war. The press announced that the scheme was being wound up; that we had trained so many aircrew there was no need to continue the scheme. Everyone here knows the long and intricate training needed to fit aircrew for battle; the many instructors needed both in the air and on the ground; the very great number of groundcrew required to service the aircraft and man the fields. But this plan, which turned out over a quarter of a million graduates, at its very peak used 101,000 men. So that the people of Canada may well wonder what the army is doing with 130,000 general service soldiers in this country, and may well feel, as I feel, that the army has not used its man-power as well as the air force.
There is a second cause of bewilderment, also more or less connected with the air force. At this time the people of Canada see one branch of our armed services, the army, desperately pleading for men. Such is its desperation that we are here in special session because of that crisis. At the same time in the daily press the announcement is made 100-4271
thai another branch of our armed services is refusing to enlist men and, more than that, is discharging 70,000 of the very type of men the army is trying so desperately to get. What is the reason for this? Why should the air force find it so easy to get recruits and the army find it so difficult? It is not simply a matter of comparison, the army against the air force; it goes a little deeper than that. Since the start of the war every little break has been given the air force. From the start they were better dressed. Airmen wore collars and ties; they travelled tourist while soldiers travelled colonist; they were paid better; they got more commissions and faster promotions. Airmen slept between sheets while soldiers slept between blankets. All these little things built up and made the air force a very much more attractive service for the young chap who wanted to serve his country. These things, I think, were principally due to the driving force of just one man, the former minister for air, whom I regard as the greatest single loss the air force has sustained in this war.
If this preferential treatment had brought no good result of course I would be very-much against it, but there is at least this to be said for it; it caused the army and navy to raise their standards a little in the direction of those of the air force. There is, however, one difference which is of very great importance in the present discussion of reinforcements. The former minister brushed over it very quickly in his statement, when he said that all anyone needed to do was read the records of the joint air training scheme to see what his attitude was. I refer particularly to the matter of relief from operational fatigue. Let me explain this. During the battle of Britain the planes and the pilots were so few that the dauntless few fighter boys of the Royal Air Force went up again and again against the enemy without rest or respite, until they were finally shot down. The same thing, of course, was true in the early days of bomber command. They had few planes and few pilots, so that the same men went out night after night against Germany. But as the production of planes and aircrew increased the R.A.F. were able to set up a definite tour of operations, 200 hours of combat for a fighter pilot and thirty trips for a bomber crew. That meant that aircrew no longer had to go on and on until the law of averages caught up with them and they were killed. At the end of a tour they were taken off and given a rest; then they served a period as instructors and finally came back to fight again.
Our former minister went further than that, however, and fought for recognition of the

War Effort-Government Policy

principle that no set standard of operations could apply to all men alike. Some lads take thirty trips right in their stride with no apparent ill effects at all. Others do suffer from fatigue. After all, these Canadian boys of our aircrew are not professional killers of the nazi stamp. They are just boys, gently reared in Canadian homes; and some find after a few trips that the strain of taking those bombers up night after night, through flak and searchlights and night fighters, then limping back home with a crippled plane, together with the strain of seeing their comrades wounded and killed in the same aircraft and the strain of coming back in the morning and seeing that comrades in other aircraft did not return, mounted until finally the condition called operational fatigue set in. Our minister fought for recognition of the principle that for those chaps their operational tour was honourably ended, and to that end he instructed the R.C.A.F. squadron and flight commanders and squadron doctors to watch carefully so that, when this fatigue set in, the man should not be expected to continue until the end of his tour, which would be unfair to him, unfair to the crew and unfair to this country. Instead, he is immediately given a rest and leave at home, then a tour of instruction, after which.he is fit to go back and fight again.
Therefore, in calculating the supply of reinforcements necessary for the air force squadrons, there were two calculations to be made: reinforcements for casualties, namely deaths, injuries and sickness, and reinforcements for relief. In this house, in both open and secret session, there has been a long discussion of the problem of reinforcements for the army. In every case the gauge has been simply the number of casualties. If our reinforcements exceeded the casualties, things were satisfactory; if our reinforcements were not up to our casualties, the situation was grave. When the honourable and gallant member for London (Mr. Johnston) made his maiden speech in this house, after four years of service overseas, he recited just a few of the major battles fought by the Canadian first division in Sicily and Italy, starting at Pacliino and Agira, across the straits of Messina and up the Italian boot; dogged fighting, village by village, hill by hill, river by river, when quite apart from the bombing, the shelling, the strafing and the mines expected in warfare, the spirit of every soldier is tried by the heat and cold, the dreary monotony of army life, the mud, the sand, the filth, the endless diet of bully beef, the remoteness from everything left behind in Canada. But there is no operational relief
fMr. Sinclair 1
for our men in the infantry as in the air force, because we have not adequate reinforcements.
Nothing can illustrate this better at this time than a letter which was passed on to me through the courtesy of my good friend the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), to whom it was addressed, although the writer is a constituent of mine. She did not write me, probably because she thought I would be unsympathetic. I have already communicated the contents of this letter to the Minister of National Defence, and I shall be very glad to table the letter if anyone wishes me to do so. This woman writes of a neighbour's boy:
The father fought in the last war and is a total disability veteran. The three boys are in the service, two overseas, one in the navy just back from overseas. The boy I am going to speak of is about twenty-five, in the Seaforths, went over in the first draft, in 1939, a volunteer, has seen action and plenty of it. He was in England for quite some time and as a dispatch rider was in a serious accident necessitating his being in a plaster east for six months due to two cracked vertebrae and a fractured shoulder. He went back into action after that, landed in Italy and was wounded in both hands; still did not get home, and has seen continuous action since. His mother received a letter the other (lay saying he was in prison. It appears he was in an advance with some other chaps. He was on the roof of a building and a shell blew these other two chaps to pieces, all over this boy, and stunned him. He was badly shocked over this affair and begged to be allowed to come home. His nerve is gone and, as they refused his request he said he cotdd not go ill the line again, as he had had enough. Now the boy is far from being a coward, but he told his mother that he has seen so much blood and dead and dying he can't stand any more. . . . Five years seems a long time for a boy to be away from home. The Christmas at home would give him heart to go back and fight again.
I can say flatly that if this lad were in the air force that condition of operational fatigue would not have been permitted to go to that extent. The other evening I had the unpardonable rudeness to interrupt the magnificent speech delivered by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vereheres (Mr. Cardin) when he said he did not believe that volunteer soldiers would want to be relieved by conscripts. Does anyone think that soldier would care whether it was a conscript or a volunteer who gave him respite from the lines?
The army now announces that those with over five j'ears overseas service may be brought home, 450 at Christmas, and 250 each month thereafter, if shipping permits, if the reinforcement situation permits-and a series of other ifs, which the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) recounted the other day. At the present time we have over 10.000 men overseas who have been there for four years or more.

War Effort-Government Policy
So that even if the "ifs" come through it will . take three years to bring those troops home in rotation, for one month's leave. Some of the chaps can therefore look forward to serving seven years overseas before they will get home for a month's leave. And all this happens because we have not got sufficient reinforcements -not just to replace the casualties, but to bring relief to those who have done the fighting over there for so long.
It is for this reason I believe reinforcements should be provided not just to replace the number of casualties, but two or three times that number to stand behind the men who are fighting, so that there may be a rotation of front-line men. If it is the policy of supreme command to hammer, hammer, hammer the enemy without respite, I do not think it is the business of a member of this house to criticize that policy. But it is the business of this house to see that it is not the same Canadian lads in the line who are doing all the hammer, hammer, hammer and that they are replaced and rotated with fresh men. And so I cannot be content with a policy which is going to supply only 16,000 reinforcements from the N.R.M.A. army until next May.
The air force has gone one step farther now than have the other services. It has announced a policy of retirement to take place immediately. It is to apply first of all to those with overseas service, second to those with more than three years' home service, and then two years service. Those with more than two years home service will then be free from military call-up, although this week that period has been raised to three years home service.
While as an airman I am happy to see the air force again take the lead, yet as a member of parliament I cannot approve. Every volunteer in the armed services, whether he be in the navy, the army or the air force, joined the service to fight for his country, in the service of his choice, for the duration of the war. I cannot justify airmen having two years home service being discharged to civilian life, while a man in the Seaforths, overseas for five years, who has been on the job for that length of time, does not get that chance. Again, of course, this is a matter of reinforcements. If the army had reinforcements they, too, might properly be released, if they had given long service. I believe that any system of retirement and discharge now brought to bear, should be uniformly applicable to all three branches of the armed services.
At the present time we find great discontent among N.R.M.A. soldiers because, at last, some of them are called to give active service. At the same time, for the first time we have real discontent in the air force, but for the very
opposite reason. Some of them feel that they have not had an opportunity yet to give that service they had hoped to give when they joined.
Every man who joined the air force joined as a volunteer. He enlisted to do overseas service, and most of them, there is no doubt, expected to be overseas within a short time. However, because of the demands of the British commonwealth air training plan over
100,000	of them were kept in this country. Most of them, however, had hoped that some day they wotdd get overseas. Now ahead of them they see discharge. And with a feeling of self-reproach-and hon. members know there is no reproach as bitter as that-many of these men now feel that they have almost a zombie taint, because their service has been confined to Canada.
The question is what to do with these men. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) suggested the other night that they be kept in the air force, and that our blows against Germany should be increased. There is a limit to the number of men we can put into the air force, in aircrew. At the present time in Canada there is a great surplus of aircrew. Overseas there are three operational aircrew, at least, for every operational aircraft. The tremendous supply of bombs and petrol needed to supply our daily raids of thousands of bomber and fighter aircraft, over Europe, are undoubtedly taxing our supply lines to the limit. Sending more aircrew overseas would simply add to the congestion and the strain on supplies. If there is one thing this war has taught us it is this, that victory will not be won through air power alone. In the end we still need the men on the ground, who go ahead of the tanks, to achieve victory.
Then, why are not these airmen transferred to the army, where they are needed? In our army, as General McNaughton has said, there have been transfers from ordnance and from service corps and other branches, to the infantry. But because we have not full conscription we do not transfer men from the air force to the army, as they do in Great Britain. Someone will say: If these men are so anxious to serve, why do they not join the army themselves? Quite a few have, but there are one or two very simple reasons why more have not done this.
First, there is the attitude of many airmen who say this: Why should we volunteer a second time, and this time not in the service of our choice, when there are 70,000 trained soldiers in this country who have never volunteered, even once, for any service? Bringing in total conscription would dispel that attitude.
67&4
War Effort-Government Policy

Second, there is an understandable reluc- [DOT] tance to serve in a new service, under strange regulations, after serving years in the air force.
The third reason is a much more direct one, namely the matter of pay. General McNaughton has explained that when a noncommissioned officer from some other branch in the army is remustered to infantry, as a private, his pay is held at the old level for six months. The air force has done better than that. When they remuster a man from aircrew they protect his pay until he can regain the rank he held formerly. But when a man transfers from the air force to the army he falls back to private rank-which does not 'bother him, particularly. But his pay also falls back to SI.50, and that makes a lot of difference to him. These men, when they joined the air force, adjusted themselves to their pay of $1.50. As they served in the air force and their rank went up, their pay went up, too, and they and their families took on new obligations. It would be unfair to ask these men to drop back to SI.50 a day on volunteering a second time.
To circumvent these conditions I made a suggestion some weeks ago to the former Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), that an R.C.A.F. regiment be raised, similar to the R.A.F. regiment of Britain, or the Herman Goering division of the German luftwaffe, open only to men now in the air force or the air cadets. While it would be just another army infantry unit, as far as fighting is concerned, yet within the regiment it would still be air force. The R.A.F. regiment have preserved that illusion by allowing the men to keep their blue caps, to keep the R.A.F. regimental numbers, to keep their R.A.F. designations of rank, and certainly our regiment could do the same. Such a regiment would have many attractions to R.C.A.F. personnel which the ordinary army service would not have. It would still be the air force in spirit; it would be a unit of men who speak a common language. It would be a proud unit composed of men who have volunteered, not once but twice in the one war to serve their country. It would be a unit which would require very little training, because all the ground-crew and aircrew have elementary training in ground warfare and, of course, are accustomed to military discipline. It would be the only chance offered to many thousands of keen men in the air force, who have been kept through no fault of their own at desks and shops in Canada, to get active service overseas.
The R.A.F. regiment in England serves only for aerodrome protection, but in Libya and in Sicily they gave valiant service right in the

line. There were no infantry troops in the Afrika Korps in Libya which were equal to the Herman Goering division. We have a much better example at home in the United States marines. After all, they are only soldiers recruited from the navy. If the conditions I have outlined are met I believe an R.C.A.F. regiment could be raised at least of brigade strength within a month.
There is one other reason why I believe the whole N.R.M.A. army should be placed on active service. I think practically everyone in Canada is agreed that in any system of demobilization of our armed services the basis should be first in, first out. The air force is now carrying out this policy with its announced system of retirements and discharges. General McNaughton has announced that that will be his policy for the army. Therefore, this can only mean that he intends to keep the N.R.M.A. conscripts who do not go overseas, in uniform in Canada until every volunteer is demobilized. This means that either they are to be kept in uniform in idleness at a tremendous cost to the taxpayer, or they are to be farmed out in labour battalions as Hitler did in pre-war Germany, to be placed at work in civilian industry or in the construction of public works.
Nothing is gained financially by putting soldiers into industry. By the time you provide for a soldier's pay, his allowances, for dependents' allowances, for food, clothing, medical and dental care, there is very little difference between that and the usual labour pay.	_
While the use of soldiers may be justified in cases of national catastrophe such as floods and fires, it is difficult to justify the use of soldiers in civilian industry or on government works. I want to make myself very clear on this issue. I am not one of the military caste who believe that Canada's only worth-while contribution can be made by sending every able-bodied man into the firing line. Modern warfare is fought with much more than just men. Canada has made a magnificent contribution in the production of food and munitions and other implements of war, a contribution which many of our allies cannot make because they have not our resources and our factories. Certainly we shall not be helping to end the war quickly if we so drain our man-power for the fighting fronts that we cannot maintain our obligations for food and munitions.
It may be that we have over-reached ourselves in supplying men for the armed services. Other countries have done this, but they have acknowledged that they have done this and taken action to correct the situation.

War Effort-Government Policy
Gallant little New Zealand has made a contribution on the fighting front which I think is unequalled by any other united nation, but they found they had over-reached themselves and they returned men to the farm and the factory. If we are in a like position, then we should do the same. It is not the conscript who should be returned to civilian life; it is those who have given the longest service in the army, the air force and the navy. They are the ones who should be sent back.
Nor should these men come from just one branch of the service, the air force. The Minister of National Defence for Air should have no difficulty in justifying his sensible policy for the air force, but can the Minister of National Defence tell the army in Italy and the army in northern Europe that airmen with short service, some of them going into the civilian air reserve with just fifteen months' service, are to be discharged to civilian life, while chaps overseas with five years' service are to be given no hope of relief or discharge or leave? Can the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services tell his sailors who have served five bitter winters in the little ships out on the north Atlantic that this course is fair? Can the Prime Minister tell the families of these soldiers and sailors that it is fair to demobilize airmen who have had only short service and allow them to pick the cream of the civilian jobs now available, whilst these men are kept overseas?
When New Zealand retired her men. she retired them on the basis of length and character of service. The men of the army of the Nile, the men who fought in Greece and Crete, who marched under Montgomery and Auchinleck, were the ones who were given first choice at retirement. So must we do. If the entire N.R.M.A. army was placed on active service, then we could have an orderly process of discharge based on length and character of service. There would then be no necessity of holding 70,000 men in idleness all over the country, nor would there be any necessity of using labour battalions in industry.
Summing up, I believe that if the whole N.R.M.A. army is placed on active service, adequate and trained reinforcements in excess of those required to meet any casualties will be available, and so a proper system of operational fatigue relief could be set up for the army. Second, I think it will give a great lift to the morale of the men overseas, and even a greater lift to the morale of their families here in Canada if they know that adequate reinforcements are on the way.
Third, with the full use of the N.R.M.A. army I am quite sure that very quickly volunteers would come forward from the air force if they could do so under the conditions I have outlined.
Lastly, demobilization on a straight basis of length and character of service could be easily carried out without holding men in idleness or without putting them Hitler fashion into labour battalions to be used in industry.
If the order in council had put the whole N.R.M.A. army on active service without reference to any theatre of operation, then I would not have spoken to-day and I am sure that this debate would have been wound up a week ago. There have been vague and evasive assurances given at long length to the effect that the order in council did not necessarily limit the reinforcements to be obtained from the N.R.M.A. army to 16,000, that other orders in council could be passed if necessary. Apparently that word "necessary" has been a difficult word for this house to understand.
If that is the case, how much simpler and more direct it would have been not to mention any number but simply to put the N.R.M.A. army on active service? May I remind the house that no orders in council are necessary to send any size draft of general service men overseas-they just go. I am even more opposed to the restriction on the theatres of operation. There is no mention at all of Japan. Active service men in all branches of the service enlisted voluntarily for service anywhere and I cannot understand this sudden restriction in the service of conscripts. The government has announced already its policy for the Japanese war. It is that volunteers are to be called afresh. This means that brave and willing hearts who have fought so long will be again expected to volunteer, while those who have shirked all calls to duty will be again protected.
Let us look ahead to the Japanese war. If, as may happen, one phase of that war goes against us and we are short of reinforcements for one branch of the armed services, are we to have this sorry spectacle of parliament convened once again to make conscripts available for the Japanese war?
In conclusion, I find that the issue before the house is immediate and continued supply of adequate trained reinforcements for the Canadian army overseas. There are those in the house who think the government is doing too much; there are others in the house who think it is doing enough; and there are some in the house who feel that it is doing too little. If it were simply a matter of voting for or against the government motion, those who think the government is doing too much and those who think the government is doing too
War Effort-Government Policy

little in this matter would be lumped in the same position, so that I think it is quite proper that amendments are being put forward to clarify the situation. I quite agree, however, with the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres when he says that some of the amendments have done nothing but becloud the issue. The C.C.F. and Social Credit amendments tack on bits of their social philosophies and give ample reason to appeal to both conseription-ists and anti-conscriptionists in the next election.
The Conservative amendment-perhaps I should not say Conservative because if it were Conservative I would have no hesitation in voting against it because I am not a Conservative. I am a Liberal and a supporter of this Liberal government, but I need not go into detail to discuss the position of a government supporter who is not in complete accord with the government on one feature of its policy, as that has already been admirably done by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) and the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris). I need but say that my supporters have no doubt of my Liberalism because they nominated me last week knowing the stand I take on this question.
The issue is not Liberalism versus Socialism or Toryism. I realize that several of my Liberal colleagues have made speeches which indicated that they felt very much as I do on this issue, that all conscripts should immediately be placed on active service at the disposal of the chiefs of staffs, but in the closing moments of their speeches they have found reasons why they should not go that far but should support the government motion. I feel, like some of them, that some elements of the Tory party are striving to make political capital out of this crisis, but I do not feel that this motive is at all confined to the Conservative party in this house. I feel, like them, that the government policy on this subject is vague and elusive, and it is precisely because of this that I want to make sure to the people I represent that there is nothing vague or elusive or evasive about the stand I take.
The amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition states:
This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice.
I think hon. members will realize that this sums up in simple and direct language the
IMr. Sinclair.]
views I have advanced this evening, and as I cannot talk one way and vote another way I shall therefore vote for that amendment.
If that amendment is defeated I shall vote for the government motion, with the realization that half a loaf is better than no loaf at all, that 16,000 reinforcements out of the conscript army is better than no reinforcements at all out of the conscript army.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising to speak after the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), I want to express my deep and sincere appreciation of the splendid, lucid and clear-cut stand that he has taken on the issue before us to-night. I am sure that every member of this house must have been thrilled by the references of this man who has served his country overseas and has seen the workings of conscription in Great Britain, who has seen the policy which the government there have put before their people under the inspired leadership of the Right Hon. Winston Churchill. He has given to the house, I believe, a true, lucid, frank and forthright view of our armed forces. May I in turn humbly, yes apologetically, give what I conceive to be the viewpoint of the home front.
If there was any doubt as to the immediate need of trained reinforcements for our army before November 22 last, that doubt has now been dispelled. Doubt has given way to alarm. The former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston), after five years of loyal obedience to the will of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), after having made a thorough investigation of the situation overseas with respect to reinforcements and having come back and exhausted his efforts, even his patience, in trying to abide by the wishes of his colleagues that he support the voluntary' system of enlistments for overseas service, has reluctantly resigned his office in despair at the government's policy. He recommended the sending of 15,000 N.R.M.A. men at once, and more to follow monthly, as reinforcements for our men overseas. His fear of catastrophe drove him to leave the government. The courage of his colleagues in dealing w'ith that recommendation of his, faltered, and thereby they lost a true and trusted colleague. The Prime Minister then called on General McNaughton to continue the policy of voluntary enlistments which the former minister of national defence after five years of effort had found to be a failure. General McNaughton assumed the responsibility, in his own words, without full knowledge of the task. He, too, tried the voluntary system. Three weeks

War Effort-Government Policy
passed by and that system did not prove a success. His failure brought panic throughout Canada. It brought about the summoning of the 245 members of this House of Commons to an emergency session. A party caucus was called by the government. Urgent cabinet council meetings were called and P.C. 8891 was passed. What did it do? It vindicated the stand taken by the former minister of national defence. It showed that the voluntary system had failed. It proved that trained reinforcements were required at once. It proved that more would be required later. It threw voluntary service out of the window. It changed the government's policy overnight. That order in council provided for the compulsory sending overseas of 16,000 N.R.M.A. personnel within the next six months, if, as and when required. But in the words of the new Minister of National Defence not one of these men should be sent over, yes unless against his will or against his hopes, because General McNaughton would be a happy man if none of them were compelled to go overseas. I refer to the arguments of the hon. member for Vancouver North in answer to that proposition.
What did the order in council not do? It did not adopt the recommendation of the former minister of national defence. It did not in any way cure the situation he found. It did not provide for the sending overseas of
15,000	N.R.M.A. men now, with more to follow monthly. It did not pacify public opinion. It did not give assurances of adequate trained reinforcements in the future for service overseas. Yet we are now asked to vote confidence in the government on its policy. What policy, may I ask? The order in council was passed and tabled at a time when this government, on November 22, were emphatically adhering to the voluntary system. The Prime Minister was emphatic in his denunciation of any compulsion for sending N.R.M.A. men overseas. On that basis was the notice of motion tabled in this house? Or are we asked to have confidence in the rightabout-face policy of the government in casting out of the window their pet theory of voluntary enlistment, in rejecting a minister of national defence who for five years had persistently tried to meet the wishes of the Prime Minister and his colleagues, who had done all he could, under their philosophy, with all his military officials, to make, if his power could make, voluntary service fill the bill, and had failed? Or are we asked to vote confidence in the piecemeal present-day solution, a hand-to-mouth policy of compulsion, grudgingly conceded and not given with a spirit which would show a will to make it work? The Minister of National Defence,
on November 23, the first day of his appearance in the house, showed us beyond any doubt that his spirit was not in the act.
Our spirit, Mr. Speaker, must be in the war. Our spirit must be with our men overseas. Our spirit must be to accomplish this task. It cannot be in anything less than that. And then they ask us to support what government? A government headed by the present Prime Minister who, time and again, has said he would not head any government that would bring in compulsion for overseas service, and who has convinced the members of this house that he is not a believer in compulsion. Yet he would have members of this house and citizens all over the Dominion of Canada believe that he js the man who is saving them from the compulsory method of service overseas. Or are we asked to vote confidence in a government of nineteen cabinet ministers who, having served five years, bring us to this war-time emergency, having seen the panic which has arisen among the people to-day, having seen this special session called and witnessed the about-face of the government itself, have not yet risen to their feet in this chamber to explain to the people how they have discharged their duty in their respective portfolios? Is it not remarkable that the Prime Minister, alone in his cabinet excepting for the deposed one, the discharged one or the resigned one, has stood in this house to give the Canadian people their impressions of this situation?
How can we vote for a government with a party following of 167 members among whom there are none willing to accept the leadership, and none willing to accept the responsibility of following any other leadership than the present Prime Minister, a government that will have no other leader than the present Prime Minister, a government who, in the words of the Prime Minister himself, are to have King or anarchy? This is a sad spectacle.
The former minister lost faith in his colleagues and left them. The ministers who remain have lost faith in themselves as leaders. None of the nineteen will aceept the challenge of the Prime Minister-if, which I doubt, it was seriously given-to accept their responsibility in this day of emergency, to do their best to form a cabinet, to form a government, to solicit support, to carry their country through this crisis.
The people have lost faith in all of them. The army, the war veterans, the legion, the public press-denounced as it has been by the Prime Minister-have lost faith in him. The people of Canada have lost faith in all of them.

War Effort-Government Policy
I cannot understand the situation. Surely Canadian soldiers and Canadian people deserve better things from the Canadian parliament. Surely the Prime Minister is not the only man in Canada who is indispensable. Surely there are men in this house and in this country able to lead the government; and surely there are hon. members willing and anxious to rise to the occasion and provide a leader who will satisfy public opinion and the spirit of our armed forces, our veterans and our newspaper publications, yes, who will give us the inspiration, the leadership and the courage of a Churchill or a Roosevelt.
We are invited to abhor the very idea of an election. Yet our great neighbour to the south can go through an election in time of war, and under our great British institutions we have seen minister after minister resign from the cabinet of Great Britain, accepting the honourable situation of being at odds with their colleagues, and the country carried on.
I do not think there is any doubt in the mind of any Canadian that, in the cabinet to-day we have three schools of thought. How, then, can there be cabinet solidarity? There is the King-McNaughton school, which will accept pressure under conditions of panic and will adopt the policy of compulsorily forcing some 16,000 N.R.M.A. men overseas, and yet they are against compulsion. Then there is the Colonel Ralston school, composed of those who, like the hon. member for Vancouver North, originally believed in the success of the voluntary system but have faced realities with courage, with conviction, with patriotism and with loyalty, and, abandoning the hope of voluntary service, have accepted the necessity at a time of crisis of recommending and adopting compulsory service overseas. We have also the Major Power school-I wonder how many of the cabinet belong to it

who say in effect that we Canadians, for the sake of those who hold the opposite principle as a fundamental article of faith, must, regardless of circumstances, oppose at any cost compulsion for overseas service. In the cabinet those three schools of thought were definitely in opposition to and in collision with each other. How under those circumstances can there be cabinet solidarity? This is not a healthy condition; it is not right; it is not fair to our Canadian soldiers or our Canadian people.
I say the Prime Minister has lost the confidence of all the Canadian people and should resign. Another should take his place, pledged to a courageous, all-out compulsory service policy. It would then be the duty and the honour of all hon. members to lend to a new man or to new men all our faith, all

our support, all our hope and all our inspiration in carrying out to the utmost our commitments, our responsibilities and our obligations in connection with this war.
Six weeks have elapsed since the emergency arose. This parliament has been called to send our soldiers the necessary aid and to reassure our people. We members who have met have been asked to take courage in our teeth and convert action into achievement. Have we done it yet? Certainly not. We should do it now.
Possibly this war could be won without Canada. Possibly we could diminish our efforts and restrict our undertakings and let our other allies carry our load. Surely no Canadian can bow to this. What right would we then have to celebrate victory? What right would we then have to a seat at the peace table? What claim would we have to a say as to what policy should be pursued in post-war reconstruction or as to the form of the peace terms? Canadians should not tolerate the thought. We must perish the very thought of detracting, of diminishing, of withdrawing from any of our commitments, any of our obligations or any of our duties. We must do our utmost. Domestic unrest is alleged as one reason why we should pull our punches. Surely domestic unrest should not interfere with the life struggle, the struggle for existence itself, which is our responsibility to-day and which, in the words of the Minister of National Defence, is increasing daily. The toughest struggle is yet ahead, he says.
How fortunate we are in Canada to-day. Our homes are all here. Our civilians are not enslaved. Our living conditions are satisfactory. We have no aeroplane attacks; we have no submarine attacks; we have no artillery bombardment and no robot bombs. Not one house has been destroyed by enemy action. In the motherland one-third of the homes have been destroyed. They have suffered all this; we have suffered none. Our army has fought in a general way, in an extensive way, only since D-day, since July last, although two divisions did valiant service in Italy. But we did not have any allout intensive fighting until D-day in July last, and yet our shortage of reinforcements commenced to pile up the following month.
What excuse is there for this government in our having had this crisis arise at all? What reason have we to fear anarchy, in the words of the Prime Minister, because of our failure to follow him? What right have we to slacken our efforts? Now is the time for us members to get a government in Canada which will inspire our people to their utmost effort. Now is the time for this house to

Canadian Forces
show courage. The Prime Minister has lost the confidence of the people. Now is the time to get and to assist a government under a courageous and inspiring leader. It is not a time to let party allegiance or personal prejudices interfere with our national duty. It is not a time for any member of this house to go home and say that he felt, because the past had produced certain results, that the crisis would work itself out, that our Deity would do the job for us or that our allies would accept our responsibility. '
We at home cannot afford to be rubber stamps for the present policies of the present government under the present leadership. I think the situation is very well set out in an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal, a part of which I will read with the indulgence of the house. It appeared on Friday, December 1, 1944, in a journal which I believe more than any other paper has been quoted by members of this house, yes, and by the Prime Minister himself only recently. I quote:
For what parliament knows, and what the country knows, is that all the hurt and humiliation of these weeks would have been avoided had Mr. King, in the first place, kept his pledges-accepted Colonel Ralston's recommendations, and used the authority which the country gave him in 1942. The flouting of pledges; the protracted cabinet debates; the discreditable .dismissal of Ralston; the pitiful fiasco with General McNaughton; the spectable of parliament summoned to do one thing and then asked to do another; the tragic rancour and unrest throughout the country; the misrepresentation throughout the world of the Canadian war heart; the possible fatal delay in sending reinforcements-for all of this evil Mr. King, with his political evasions and manoeuvres, is directly and wholly responsible. If there be those to doubt this, let them read the speech of Mr. King's former Minister of Defence-the most damning indictment of a public leader ever pronounced in the Canadian parliament in our time.
Whether the Journal be right or whether it be wrong, there is not a member in this house who cannot say that the opinion therein expressed is a very popular one with a large section of the Canadian people. I ask therefore, how can. we expect unity, solidarity, devotion to duty and our utmost effort under those circumstances? I think that we members of the House of Commons, coming here for this short time, must do something. If we do not take courageous action now, the future of Canada will be upon our heads.
On motion of Mr. Diefenbaker the debate was adjourned.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, December 5, 1944.
The house met at three o'clock.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CANADIAN FORCES
subsubtopic: RESERVE ARMY-STATEMENT OF POLICY AS TO ITS ROLE IN THE FUTURE
speechtext:
I think the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald) promised yesterday, that if possible, he would give some report, or lay on the table a declaration of government policy with respect to Canada's reserve army. I should be very glad if he would do so at this time.
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Acting Minister of National Defence): Mr. Speaker, speaking for the Minister of National Defence, Mr. McNaughton, I should like to give to the house a short statement as to the policy of that department as regards the reserve army.
1.	In so far as our post-war military commitments and requirements can be foreseen at present, the reserve army will continue to play the same important role which it performed in the years before the war, and which it has so abundantly fulfilled during the anxious days of this war.
2.	In this connection I would refer the house to the statement appearing in Hansard of February 14, 1944, in regard to the reserve army, and made by the then minister of
Canadian Forces

national defence. In that statement the splendid contribution to the war effort by that force was brought to the notice of the house. Its role was stated as follows:
(a)	To maintain throughout the country continued interest in the Canadian Army and its activities, and to set the example to all citizens of preparedness at all times.
(b)	To provide a continuing flow of reinforcements, for the forces overseas, by training young men of preenlistment age.
(c)	To back up the civil authority responsible for the enforcement of law and order, if required.
(d)	As a trained reserve to support the active forces available for the defence of Canada if the military situation should deteriorate.
(e)	As a basis for expansion of the active army should the necessity arise.
3.	It is intended to modernize the reserve army and to develop the efficiency of the force.
4.	The reserve army is the name now given to that portion of the pre-war non permanent active militia which has not been mobilized for active service. The non permanent active militia is the framework of our national military organization in peace time. It is the policy to ensure the continuation in the postwar period of this framework which will then become again the major portion of our military forces. The men who have gone from these reserve units and who now fill the ranks of the mobilized active units will return to the reserve army and they and their units will find their military family association maintained so that there will be no break in the continuity of service and tradition of each regiment.
5.	It is not possible at this time to assure each regiment individually that it will be continued or that it will be continued in its present type. The organization of our forces must depend upon our needs and must reflect modern tactical organization, and it is always possible that units may be required to change their type. However, to the greatest possible extent present units of the reserve army will be perpetuated in some continuing role. These are matters which are kept under constant review by the responsible military staff.
6.	It is hoped that this statement will give assurance to the members of the reserve army that their work is important and that it is in the national interest that it should be continued; and that it is the intention of

this government to protect the continuity of the reserve units to the greatest extent possible in the post-war period.

speechtext: I desire to draw another matter to the attention of the government, which might also be treated as a notice and dealt with later at greater length than they may care to deal with it at the moment. I refer to the congestion of cattle which is so acute at present in the stockyards across Canada. In this connection I would mention-the shortage of stable accommodation for live stock during the coming winter months, and also the fact that I understand a number of farm organizations have brought this situation to the attention of the government and have asked that the government give consideration to the lifting of the embargo on the export of beef cattle from Canada to the United States, even if it is only a temporary measure, in order to relieve the situation which seems to be so serious. speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :

speechtext:
I am sorry I was not in the house when the leader of the opposition began his question, but I take it he is asking for information as to the position in relation to the marketing of beef cattle and the possibility of reopening the American market.
Yesterday I made a statement to the agricultural conference being held in this city at the present time. This is the conference that has been held each year since the beginning of the war, to lay out plans for the succeeding year. Plans are now being laid out for the crop year 1945, beginning in the spring. At that meeting of representatives of the different farm organizations and the provincial departments of agriculture, I stated that last week we consulted with the persons in Washington who are concerned with this matter, and the information we received was to the effect that they are experiencing just as great difficulty in handling cattle through their processing plants as we are experiencing on this side of the line, and the suggestion was made that we should not send beef cattle to the United States at the present time. That is the attitude taken there, and of course we are respecting that attitude. On the other hand, we have had representatives of the British government here for some considerable time now, off and on, suggesting that they are most anxious to have our beef in Great Britain. This year we have sent Britain 103,000,000 pounds of processed beef, which represents more live cattle than we have ever sent, at least in recent years, to the United States and Britain combined. We have an agreement with Britain under which they will take all the surplus beef we care to seqd them during 1945, and only at the end of last week they and we entered into an understanding that a similar agreement will be made for 1946. This means there is a market in Great Britain for all the surplus beef which is in sight at present in Canada, and there is a need for that beef in Great Britain from the point of view of the prosecution of the war. It is the wish of the Americans that we should process that beef and send it to Britain ourselves, rather than send it to the United States to have it processed and sent to Britain under their lend-lease arrangement. There is just as great difficulty being experienced in the United States, both in relation to labour and in relation to plant capacity, as there is in Canada. So that the three-way understanding is that we should market this beef in Britain if at all possible, and an attempt is being made to do so. The marketing agreements are being concluded which will make this possible.
6S02

Beef Cattle
The extra cattle that are on the markets across Canada at the present are not finished beef cattle. Any blockades on the market have resulted from the fact that for some reason or other people have been marketing very considerable numbers of cows, younger cattle and plain beef cattle. These are not the cattle for which there is likely to be any demand in the United States, to begin with, or which there is sufficient demand for here at present. As many of these cattle as can be turned into beef are being boned and put in the form of processed beef that can be shipped to Britain and utilized as food at the present time. Because we are able to announce that there is a market assured for 1946 we believe that at least the yearling cattle will be got off the market and fed by someone somewhere else. The assurance is given that the present price for finished beef will prevail right through 1946, so that farmers who have been looking for the war to end within the next three or four or probably six months and were therefore anxious to get out of the production of beef because they felt that there would not be a market for beef towards the end of next year now have the assurance, because of the arrangement entered into with Britain, that they can go on and feed their cattle and get rid of them at as good a price two years hence as they can get now. We believe that that will aid considerably in getting some of the stock cleared off the markets. In any case the suggested solution that has been made of opening the American market is not available to us at the present time.

speechtext: Following the reply just given by the Minister of Agriculture in connection with the prices for live stock sold on the markets and for which the packers are guaranteed their prices by the meat board, may I ask if any guarantee has been given to the farmers or the live stock producers as to the price they shall receive when they sell their live cattle on the market?

speechtext:
The present position is that there is a ceiling price on beef right across Canada, and under the agreement which we have with Britain the price at which beef. , 
is being sold is related to that ceiling price.
I am speaking of finished cattle ready for slaughter. The price that is being paid for finished cattle on the markets right across Canada is a price which bears a proper relationship to the price at which beef is selling on the market. I have had correspondence from the province of Alberta no later than to-day; in fact, I answered one of these letters just before coming down to the house, indicating that there is little complaint with regard to the price obtained for cattle ready for slaughter. The complaint is with respect to cattle brought on to the market which are not ready for slaughter and which somebody must take off the market and feed before they can be sold on the market. There is no way that I know of in which we can compel one farmer to pay a higher price for feeder cattle to another farmer who wants to get rid of them when the deal is between those two farmers directly. They may live side by side. There is no feasible way of doing that unless we had someone at every place where this exchange of cattle takes place to grade the cattle and establish their value. But so far as cattle brought into the packing plants and sold ready for slaughter are concerned there is a proper relationship between the price of the cattle and the price of the beef that is sold from those cattle.

speechtext:
It contained
significant information which the people of Canada were entitled to have, and which it was desirable to have made known as widely as possible. If the appeal was to be effective it was obviously necessary that it should have a wide measure of public support.
The distribution of the broadcast by the wartime information board was at the instance of the cabinet committee which had been formed to further the appeal for voluntary enlistments. If ever distribution was justified it was justified in the case of a speech making a national appeal on a matter of urgency, the importance of which was everywhere recognized.
Hon. members may be interested to know that in the twenty-six days since November 8, the date on which the broadcast was made, 6,297 men have volunteered for general service in the .Canadian army, and of this number 2,701 are from the N.R.M.A., and 3,596 from the general public and the reserve army. These figures I understand represent the largest enlistment for a similar period since the outbreak of war.
May I say to the hon. member for Parkdale that in giving what he will recognize was an immediate reply to his question of yesterday I was misled by its wording as to the particular speech to which he had reference. My hon. friend's question was as follows:
I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. In order that the public may have both sides of the issue fairly before them, will the Prime Minister direct the wartime information board to publish and circulate 87,000 copies of the speech made in this house by the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) on November 29, 1944? This would correspond to the number of copies of the Prime Minister's speech, in defence of the voluntary system, as given over the radio on November 8.
I thought for the moment by his reference to something corresponding to a speech delivered in this house that the hon. member was referring to the speech that I made in the house and to the speech that the former minister of national defence made in this house. The speech I made in the house has not been distributed, so far as I am aware. In reply to the statements I made in my broadcast over the radio, the former minister of national defence issued a statement on November 12, just a few days later. So far as my first statement was concerned and the first statement of the former minister of national defence, those two statements correspond and both have been given fully to the public.

speechtext: Arising out of information I have received, I should like to ask the Minister of Labour what is the position regarding older people who have been employed during war time, in so far as benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act are concerned, if they are laid off work because of age or declining efficiency.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: *UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT-POSITION OF UNEMPLOYED ELDERLY WORKERS
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for
Vancouver East for having given me notice of the question. One of the principal conditions for the receipt of benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act is that the claimant is capable of and available to work, but unable
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
to obtain suitable employment. That is in section 28, subsection 3 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940. If an elderly person made claim for benefit, the official handling the claim would look at his employment history, and if he had been recently employed that would be evidence that he was capable of and available for work. If an employer laid him off because of declining efficiency, it might be-and each case would have to be judged on its merits-that suitable employment for the claimant would be of a slightly lighter nature than his previous employment, possibly with some modification of his employment conditions. There is no age ceiling under the act, and we have in fact paid benefits to claimants who were about eighty years of age. It should be remembered that unemployment insurance is protection for employable people who become unemployed; it is not intended as a substitute for health insurance or for old age pensions, which are separate parts of the social security scheme.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, December 4, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Jean.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: THE WAR
subsubtopic: POLICY OP THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in resuming this debate at this time I intend to refrain as far as possible from anything in the nature of repetition; also, as is always my custom, from anything of a personal nature. I believe, after having read the debates in 1917 in connection with the Military' Service Act, that this debate in the main has been on a very high plane, and one worthy of the highest traditions of parliamentary government in this country. On all sides of this house, regardless of where we sit, hon. members have made sacrifices in this war and their families have been affected as possibly never before in any war in our history. When we in this house can do what we did the other evening, when those who disagree with the member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) can listen to a message of sincerity from him, and those who disagree with the member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) can give him the hearing which he received, parliamentary government in this
country has touched a high plane in the discussion of public affairs.
I am going to epitomize in a very few words the stand I shall take to-day. I believe, sir, that the vast majority of the people of the country do not want partial conscription; they demand impartial conscription. They demand reinforcements. The trust that rests upon us on behalf of those who serve cannot be discharged by accepting order in council 8891, which in its very essence establishes rationed conscription, politically designed and by its very nature denying equality of service and of sacrifice everywhere in Canada. That order in council perpetuates the discrimination and the inequality of service that characterize the administration of the N.R.M.A. in Canada. By selecting 16,000 to go overseas and failing to say to the rest that they too shall be trained and sent overseas according to their training and fitness, we endanger the last vestige of unity in this country.
I believe that the keystone of Canadian unity must be equality of service. Racial dominance will never bring unity in Canada and there is no question of racial dominance in the demand on the part of His Majesty's opposition that the principle of equality of service and of sacrifice everywhere in this dominion shall be made a reality. I say that if out of this order in council there comes a continuation of the kind of administration that we have had in the past under the N.R.M.A., the order in council will do still more towards arousing the passions of the Canadian people.
To-day this country, as a result of the unfairness in which the administration of the National Resources Mobilization Act has been conducted, is tom by grievances, some legitimate and others accompanied by prejudice and by senseless bigotry, and I ask you sir, and through you the government, even at this late hour, to ensure that all provinces in Canada shall be equal under this administration; for only through equality among all the provinces will there be Canadian unity-and by equality I mean equality in responsibility as well as in benefits.
I try to understand the argument of those who look at the matter from another point of view; I try to appreciate what they have in mind; but I cannot understand the point of view of any member of- this house who denies the common responsibility which every individual in this country has to the service of the state. Indeed a common responsibility is part of the law of the country, and it was brought in by members from the province of Quebec who demanded that in the build-
War Effort-Government Policy

mg of this country, that in the assuring of equal sacrifice, that principle should be embodied in the law of the land. And it is.
I am going to refer to the Militia Act, because I believe that much of the talk in opposition to conscription fails to take into consideration the fact that conscription for service overseas has been a part of the law of the country since 1868, with the responsibility of every person in Canada to serve. That legislation was introduced by the Hon., afterwards Sir Georges Etienne Cartier, who gave Canadians a message that should resound to-day. That message was that there can be no confederation, there can be no unity as between two divergent races, unless there is a common acceptance of our equality and of responsibility of service to the state by all.
Under the Militia Act everyone between the ages of eighteen and sixty is liable for service. In passing it provides that anyone chosen to serve by ballot may secure someone to be his substitute in military service. That is still the law of the country. I come now to the sections in question. Section 64 reads:
The governor in council may place the militia-	[DOT]
Which is defined as the military forces of Canada.
-or any part thereof on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
Emergency is defined as a condition of war, invasion, riot or insurrection.
Who placed that portion of the act on the statute book of Canada? Another great Canadian of French origin, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in 1904. Yet my friends rise in this house and say that there is no responsibility for service beyond the confines of Canada. The legislation to which I refer was first the product of the mind of the Hon. Georges Etienne Cartier and secondly the product of the mind, as a result of experience, of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I would point out that Mr., afterwards Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, who was minister of justice at the time, made the following statement in the debate on the Militia Act in 1904- quoted at page 2194 of Hansard of 1917:
The governor in council may send the militia of Canada out of Canada at any time when deemed necessary for the defence of Canada. If, in the opinion of the governor in council, it should be necessary, because of a war going on in India, to send our militia out there for the defence of Canada, they may, in the exercise of their discretion, do it, because they are the sole judges of what is necessary to be done in defence of Canada. But we do not think it advisable that that power should be absolute

and unrestrictedly in the hands of the governor in council. We think it advisable that the period during which they may exercise that power should be restricted and that parliament should be called together and be consulted at the earliest opportunity. Parliament must he summoned in fifteen days and then the whole matter will be in the hands of the people's representatives.
In other words, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick recognized that under this act-and the government is proceeding under this act to-day-contained in the Militia Act our militia may be sent for service anywhere in the world. The last section of order in council 8891 reads as follows:
Further, all personnel so dispatched or who may at any time be dispatched are, pursuant to section 64 of the Militia Act, hereby placed on active service beyond Canada for the defence thereof.
I should like the Prime Minister to explain whether parliament was called together pursuant to the powers contained in section 66 of the Militia Act, which provides the following:
Whenever the governor in council places the militia, or any part thereof, on active service, if parliament is then separated by such adjournment of prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for the meeting of parliament within fifteen days. . . .
Was parliament called together pursuant to that section of the Militia Act, after the decision of the government to send these men overseas?

speechtext:
The provision is
still there, Mr. Speaker. No one can be sent beyond Canada unless parliament is called together within the period named therein.
In 1917 Sir Wilfrid Laurier accepted that principle. He accepted the principle that our men should serve anywhere in the world for the defence of Canada. All he asked was that there should be a referendum to determine what the people of Canada wanted. Well, we have had a referendum in Canada on the question of conscription. The Prime Minister himself admitted that fact on January 26, 1942. Towards the end of his speech he was dealing with the submission of the plebiscite question to the people of Canada. He said, as reported on page 51 of Hansard:
It will be seen that in seeking freedom for itself to act on all matters pertaining to war in accordance with its judgment, the government is taking a course which will remove all legitimate excuse for controversy, and the course best calculated to maintain the unity of the country in this time of war.
Mr. Homuth: Then what will they do?
Mr. Mackenzie King:	That will depend in
part upon what my hon. friend and those who are round him will do.

War Effort-Government Policy
Mr. Homuth: Do not worry about us.
Mr. Mackenzie King: I am quite prepared to trust the people; my hon. friend certainly is not. Just here may I pause to say that if my hon. friend is afraid that the people will pronounce against conscription, for that is what he has in his mind, and he is still prepared to have conscription put into force without any reference to the people, then I should like to know how he expects that the unity of this country is going to be maintained.
In other words, what that means is this: On January 25, 1942, the Prime Minister in submitting the question of the plebiscite to the Canadian people was endeavouring to secure from them a vote on the question of conscription, and he so stated. It is true that in June, some months later, after the result of the vote, he said that at no time had there been any intention on the part of the government to consider the vote as one on conscription.
Every condition necessary to the carrying into effect of the Militia Act has been met. We have the law; we have had the referendum. Now at a period in our history when the reinforcement situation is as serious as it is the government produces an order in council; it is rationed conscription. In one part of Canada the government can say it covers only 16,000; in another part of Canada it can say, as General McNaughton said, it may not cover anybody, and in still other parts of Canada those who support it will be able to say: Well, it covers everybody if you read it carefully. Rationed conscription will not meet the demand; rationed conscription will not assure unity in this country; rationed conscription will destroy unity. The Prime Minister should answer this question. He has answered it only indirectly so far. He failed to answer it the other day when it was put by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Mayhew) in the course of a very fine address. The question to which the people of Canada have a right to an answer, not by explanation, not by evasion, but by direct answer, is this: Do you or do you not intend that every man in Canada called up under the N.R.M.A. who is fit for overseas service shall be rendered available to be sent overseas?
To-day the Prime Minister said that there had been a very large enlistment during the past few days. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there have been enlistments, but I ask you to understand the circumstances under which that enlistment is taking place. I have a letter here which will give some indication qs to why these 2,701 N.R.M.A. men enlisted during the past few days.

speechtext:
So far as the hon. member is concerned I am not going to enter into any controversy with him. I am dealing with a member of a cabinet which is supposedly based on solidarity, but where there is such a diversity of opinion as indicated by statements appearing in the press in the month of November. Because of that diversity I find it impossible to understand how they are able to hang together.
When I was interrupted I was dealing with the question of enlistments, which the Prime Minister mentioned to-day. Here is the kind of representation that is being made to these N.R.M.A. men. They used to have what they called the N.R.M.A. squeeze. But that squeeze is no longer in existence. To-day-and I take the responsibility for saying this-and for the last few days, representations are being made to the N.R.M.A. men at Petawawa. They have been advised that if they now enlist,
War Effort-Government Policy

instead of being sent overseas compulsorily they will have their enlistment for active service antedated six months. The result is that instead of receiving only $7.50 per month, beginning now their allowances are to be dated back six months.

speechtext:
Furthermore, the
representation is being made that if they enlist now they can secure the voluntary service medal in one year instead of eighteen months. Furthermore, the non-commissioned officers in the home defence army at Peta-wawa have been advised that if they go active their ranks will be confirmed. The only active men who can have confirmed ranks to-day are those in a low category, who are unfit for overseas service. This type of conduct is discrimination against the men who volunteered in the service of this country.
In his great speech the other evening the hon. and gallant member for Prince (Mr. Ralston) gave us more than a peep into cabinet council: he opened the door. He did not have to tell us as much as he did, because the speeches of certain members during the last month have revealed the attitude of members of the cabinet. I shall now refer to them briefly. They reveal that there is no unity in the cabinet! Unity there must be, if this legislation is to be enforced fearlessly, definitely and assuredly, to maintain our reinforcement situation overseas. Are the ministers in agreement? I have been amazed at the silence of the ministers of the crown in this debate. The hon. and gallant Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche) made a speech the other day in which he said this:
I hope that not a French-Canadian conscript is sent overseas. Reinforcements are needed, and should come as volunteers.
He has continued a campaign such as that to which I have just referred.
Then, we have the statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) who, by the way, since making that speech on November 6, has been even more silent than usual. This is what he said, as reported by the press and undenied, as was the statement allegedly made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand), until it was denied to-day in part. This is the statement of the Minister of Justice:
Colonel Ralston, who is a great Canadian, believed that a coercive measure had become necessary to provide our armies with reinforcements should the war last several months longer. I am convinced that if the government had agreed to look at the question in this light, the vast majority of the province of Quebec would
I Mr. Differ! baker.]
have felt that they were betrayed by their English-speaking fellow-citizens. That would have been disastrous. .	.	. They may be
mistaken, but they will not betray you.
That is the statement made November 6. Let me turn to it again, where he said that there was but one line of action, and that was volunteer action. Then he added this:
National unity would have received a destructive blow in such a way that it might have taken decades to rebuild it.
Sir, through you I ask the Minister of Justice this question: Was he speaking for the record on November 8, or has he, too, changed his opinion since that time? What is the reason for the change? To-day we have conscription, partial though it be. Is he to-day of the same opinion as he was then?
And now we come to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), who delivered an address in Chicago in which he said that so far as this question was concerned it was a political question rather than a question of meeting an urgent need. Well, Mr. Speaker, he had before him the representations of the hon. member for Prince. He had before him General Stuart's memorandum of October. He had before him General Murchie's memorandum of October. And yet he said it was a political question rather than an urgent need. Has there been any change in his views since November 16, when that speech was made?
