maintopic: QUESTIONS WITH RESPECT TO EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT AND DISSOLUTION
subtopic: THE WAR
subsubtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess the hon. member for Prince drew my attention to the fact that I had not quoted all of the extract which I read, that
War Effort-Government Policy

starting where I did I may have attributed unfairly to him a sense of self-importance which he would be the last to claim. I am glad to have this opportunity of giving the question in full, and I quote from page 6677 of Hansard as follows:
I have mentioned these points specially, but what I want to emphasize is this, that this house and the people of this country, and I myself, will hold the government-and particularly the Prime Minister and the Minister _ of National Defence-to strict account for carrying out vigorously and without wavering their declared intention to reinforce the army with well-trained men from the N.R.M.A. to the fullest and fastest extent possible.
That in no way changes the point I was endeavouring to make, namely, that the hon. member is seized with great responsibility, perhaps more so than any other hon. member, in the action he proposes to take on the motion and the amendment now before the house. No one is more willing to sacrifice himself for the men overseas than the hon. member for Prince. As in the last war when he was colonel of his battalion, he would not ask any man to do anything which he would not himself do. So that he should not now accept a trust or be an example to others to accept the same when a breach of that trust will mean a lack of needed reinforcements overseas. Having failed in the cabinet, how does the hon. member expect to succeed in his objective outside the cabinet?
Was there ever a vote of confidence in this house which was not supported by speeches by the various ministers of the crown? The Prime Minister made a speech when he introduced the motion, and that speech was subsequently devastated by the hon. member for Prince. Mention has been made already in this house, of the speeches which were made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) before the passing of the order in council, and he alone has spoken in this debate. Mention was also made of the speech of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand) and the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who spoke of our material contribution to this war.
May I remind the Minister of Agriculture that mutual aid is but a measure of how many less men relatively Canada has on the fighting fronts as compared with some of our allies. Do not prate about war production, particularly about our gifts, until you measure our relative contribution on the fighting front. Let the ministers who may be for or against the application of a full manpower policy in Canada stand up and be counted.
Usually in an important debate, and surely this is the most important debate this parliament has seen, ministers start oS at three o'clock in order that what they say may be

the highlight of the day. In this debate they are singularly silent. What have they to be ashamed of? Are they endeavouring to put themselves in a position where they can say to one part of the country that they are in favour of sending reinforcements and to another that they are against compulsion? One should not accept the fruits of office without also accepting the responsibilities.
The people of Canada are entitled to know just where each member of the cabinet stands on this vital issue; otherwise how can they place any reliance in their future actions which may decide whether or not their sons and husbands are to have a fighting chance? Let each member of the cabinet definitely declare himself. The public have no right to make assumptions. A vote on the motion as worded does not mean taking a stand on further reinforcements.. In the case of the former Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), when I heard of his resignation I did not know whether it was because the government had gone too far for him or whether, when he said in his great speech in favour of the plebiscite in 1942, he felt that the time might come when he might have to part company with his constituency, that he thought the government had not gone far enough.
I think most of us understand where the Minister of Agriculture stands in this matter, but he has not declared himself in open session. Policies hang on personalities and it is impossible to divorce one from the other or to speak of one without the other. The public are demanding that the various ministers who support the policy of "Conscription when necessary" and interpret "necessary" as needed reinforcements hereafter as well as now should speak; otherwise how are they to be identified beyond peradventure of doubt? The Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson), the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock), the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), and the Minister of Health and Social Welfare (Mr. Claxton)-what of them? And what of the position of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand)? Given the same information, and the information is now common knowledge, I am sure that many of these gentlemen will have the same instinctive reaction that I have. We should all hang our heads in eternal shame if we let down our sons and brothers overseas. That and nothing else counts: The former Minister of National Defence has not named them, but he knows

With an administration unfriendly to the order under which it operates, can the people of Canada expect a just carrying out of that order in council? The German war, to say nothing of the Japanese war, may last much longer than any of us expect. Is this government making available the greatest number of men possible who will be ready as trained reinforcements six months or a year from now? Where is the cabinet solidarity or the consistency on which the hon. member for Prince is relying? What was his own experience, according to his statement at page 6664 of Hansard:
Let us see what the situation was. Was anybody opposing a position hitherto taken by the government? I was proposing to carry out the policy of the government, which was the policy of sending N.R.M.A. men if necessary. I was not opposing any position which had hitherto been taken by the government.
And then later on, at page 6665:
It was made quite clear to me that the place for me was not inside, but outside the cabinet.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) believes in cabinet solidarity when it suits 'his book, but not when it does not. After the former minister's statement, how can the people of Canada have confidence in the exercise of a power given to the Prime Minister under the National Resources Mobilization Act and the War Measures Act? What interpretation will be again put on "necessary" and on "advisable in the best interests of Canada"?
Let me give the last and most recent example of the Prime Minister's political evasiveness. On page 6677 of Hansard I find this statement by the hon. member for Prince:
There is one thing more, and that is that I doubt if the minister's programme of dispatch is sufficiently rapid to provide all he should have to reestablish reinforcement pools as quickly as that should be done, having regard to the conditions which face him now and in the near future.
He will be held responsible for accelerating the dispatch in every way. And one other point I am assuming, unless the Prime Minister states otherwise, that if the government motion carries, the future orders in council specifying additional numbers of men will be passed and put into effect without any reference back again to this house for a vote of confidence or other approval.
To which the Prime Minister replied:
That is correct.
Then the 'hon. member for Prince continued:
I take that to be clear from the minister's statements to the house.
I have mentioned these points specially, but what I want to emphasize is this, that this house and the people of this country, and I myself, will hold the government-and particularly the Prime Minister and the Minister^ of National Defence-to strict account for carrying

out vigorously and without wavering their declared intention to reinforce the army with well-trained men from the N.R.M.A. to the fullest and fastest extent possible.
It is on this understanding and for these reasons, and one other, namely the confidence which I have in certain of my former colleagues, who have contributed in no small degree to the changed attitude of the government, that I shall vote against the amendment and for the motion.
But what did the Prime Minister say yesterday in answer to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), who said, as reported in Hansard at page 6809:
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has kept very quiet on this subject but the other day Mr. Charles Bishop, a distinguished member of the press gallery said:	"Sixteen
thousand is the limit for the Honourable J. G. Gardiner." We should like to know whether 16,000 is the limit and also whether or not any promise has been made to anyone that no more will be sent. [DOT]
To which the Prime Minister replied:
May I answer my hon. friend at once? I have made no promise to anyone.
Does that not fly in the face of the statement in reply to the hon. member for Prince, reported on page 6677 of Hansard, namely, "That is correct"? But if one examines that statement one can see that it can be taken to refer to the procedure under order in council rather than to the substance, namely that additional numbers of N.R.MA. men will be sent overseas as reinforcements. This country is tired of dealing with words; and the hon. member for Prince, in view of the Prime Minister's statement, "I have made no- promise to anyone", can no longer be held bound by his undertaking to support- the government motion.
What is the opinion of the individual cabinet ministers on this vital subject? Either we have the essentials of cabinet government or we have not. The cabinet is of divergent views. The people of Canada can have no assurance of what the policy of that cabinet is as to overseas reinforcements. It is a situation which is untenable and one which cannot be tolerated in view of the fact that the lives of our fighting men hang on which way a majority of those holding divided opinions are swayed. No; a government cannot exist where there is no unanimity of opinion on a matter of such grave policy. A cabinet divided against itself will not stand.
Liberal members can have no assurance. I ask them to put it on the low grounds of political expediency, that a clear, definite order in council should be passed doing away with the two-army system in Canada. I ask them to put it on the highest ground, needed reinforcements for overseas, which means all available reinforcements.
DECEMBER 6, 1944	6867
War Effort-Government Policy
The hon. member for Prince has said that much as he agrees with the ideas expressed in our amendment, he will not vote for it because it would be a vote of want of confidence in the government and that, if it were defeated, the whole matter of dispatching the 16,000 reinforcements from the N.R.M.A. would be thrown into the realm of uncertainty and suspense. As has already been pointed out, the Dominion of New Zealand, the Commonwealth of Australia and the United States of America have all had general elections during the war. In no case has the election interfered with the carrying on of a vigorous war effort.
So much for the general principle; what of its particular application at this time to Canada?

maintopic: QUESTIONS WITH RESPECT TO EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT AND DISSOLUTION
subtopic: THE WAR
subsubtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's time his expired.
Mr. G. A. CRUICKSHANK (Fraser Valley); Mr. Speaker, I do not think any soldier member need apologize for taking the time of the house to declare his stand on the reinforcement problem. I want to repeat, reinforcement-not conscription. I think it will be equally obvious that the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) must have prepared his speech before this agreement to shorten the debate came into effect. We have had conscription in effect for some time, the only trouble being, as I see it, that it is conscription for a limited number and for a limited area.
At all times I have stated that I believe the volunteer soldier to be superior to the conscripted one. I still believe that, and always will. The time has come, however, when all that matters is that the infantry shall have help, either volunteers, or men from the N.R.M.A. or both. Nothing else now matters but that the infantry shall be guaranteed1 all possible reinforcements.
Early in the war I took exception to Canada endeavouring to maintain an army. I said that, with the man-power drain to maintain a large and splendid navy and air force, with the man-power drain to maintain an expanded war industry, and with the man-power drain to supply food on a scale such as we in Canada had never been called upon to supply it, we could not also maintain an army.
In the last war we were unable to maintain four divisions with proper and ample reinforcements without breaking up the fifth division. Why try now to maintain six or seven divisions? I believe that the most effective fighting weapon you can have is not only a well-trained army but one that has at all times ample reinforcements, and that, above all, the
men serving in the army should know that they have an ample supply of reserves both immediately adjacent to the units and in the reserve. Does any hon. member believe that the infantry think now they have ample reserves immediately available? Surely everyone knows that our infantry have not sufficient reserves now available-not here but across the ocean where they are needed.
Surely it is the wish of every Canadian that we at once make provision, by voluntary methods or by conscription or by any other method, to ensure that the men have not too little reinforcements and too late. Rather they should have too many and too soon.
It is not clear to me now, and it never has been, wny, our staff did not make ample provision for sufficient reinforcements for such a very small percentage of our army that was in the infantry. It would appear to me that too much of their time was taken up with concentrating on the promotion of some of those in the higher ranks. I do know that if we had as big a reserve as we have of generals and colonels protecting the Lord Elgin hotel we would have plenty of reserves everywhere.
Why is it that after all this time we have only 8,000 trained men available and 8,000 almost trained men available in the N.R.M.A. from these large and expensive camps, with the instructors that we have? It does not make sense to me, and it has not been explained properly what the staffs were doing to permit such a condition to arise. It is no use speaking of mistakes in the past. It is time now to speak, however, in order that we may not repeat the mistakes we made previously. I do not claim to have any more military knowledge or experience than any soldier member of the house, but I do say that the people of Canada, and the men who will return after the war, will never forget. And why should they? If we send over 5,000 men now, perhaps that will give an ample reserve under present conditions. But what if the ship is sunk? Here I bring as my witness no less a person than the hon. and gallant member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Lapointe), who last night, in my opinion, made one of the finest and most eloquent speeches delivered in this house. Let me say that as a soldier the hon. and gallant member need take a back seat to no soldier member in this house at any time. Last night the hon. member pointed out that reinforcements were delayed to him, for a short period fortunately, because one of the barges had been sunk. Now we are talking of sending over a driblet of 5,000 men. What if the ship is sunk when taking over those 5,000? What if an epidemic

War Effort-Government Policy
of mumps or diphtheria hits the men? What if they should suffer untold casualties in the battle that lies ahead? I do not think any member would care to predict what casualties may occur in the terrible war that we are still facing-and let me say, without claiming any knowledge as a military man: Do not think for a moment that the hardest part of the fighting is not ahead of the Canadian army.
Will anyone say that none of these possibilities may become a reality? I for one will not accept the responsibility of saying to the men or to their families at home afterwards that we thought help would arrive in time.
My riding was not unanimous for the plebiscite; it was about seventy per cent for and thirty per cent against; and here let me say a word for the Canadian Legion. Unfortunately there was left by two members of this house an inference not altogether favourable to the legion. I do not think they intended it, for possibly they spoke without knowledge. The government asked me to go back to my riding and endeavour to get a favourable vote at the time of the plebiscite. I in turn asked the Canadian Legion to put over the campaign and they did so in their own time, by their own efforts, and at their own expense. There are many fine organizations in Canada, but there is no organization so exclusive or so favoured as the Canadian Legion, for the simple reason that no one can get into it by right of money or of might, or anything else. The only way you can be a member of Canada's finest organization is by right of service in His Majesty's forces.
Nothing matters but that our men should have reinforcements and that these should be sent to them right away. I am trying to-night to obey what I gather is the understanding as the aftermath of the meeting of the Prime Minister and the two other leaders concerned, and I sincerely hope that the rest of his followers will keep faith as I do and not take too long in speaking. But having listened to some of the eastern members I may tell the Prime Minister and the other leaders that I have not much hope of their wish being fulfilled.
I was told twice by the leading isolationist in the house, my hon. friend in the corner, that I would not be re-elected. I would sooner be defeated doing what I think is right than be re-elected doing what I think is wrong. This, I believe, the fathers and mothers of our soldiers will approve, to the disappointment of my isolationist friend in the comer when the election rolls along. But no matter, my own Liberal association approve my stand in this matter; what happens to me is im-

material. The important thing to every member of the house is not his own political future but the future of the men who are serving overseas.
The day on which the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) resigned I was asked my stand on the controversy as we read it in the press and heard it over the radio, and from what I said on that day it would be easy for me to vote otherwise than I intend to vote now. I said at that time that I had every confidence in the former minister. He had just made a trip overseas and, I presumed, had consulted his advisers, and if he said that reinforcements were needed, and needed now, there was only one answer- send them. Later, speaking to the Canadian Legion just before I left, I made a statement which I should like to quote from the daily press of Vancouver under the heading, "I Have All Confidence in Ralston."
Mr. Cruickshank, Liberal member for the Fraser Valley, said that until he has attended the special session and has heard first hand the details of the reinforcement situation, there was little he could add to his previous statements on the matter.
I have every confidence in Colonel Ralston, and with a vivid recollection of the terrible shortage of reinforcements while serving in mud and water during the last war, it is my opinion that nothing must be allowed to stand in the way of sending every volunteer or conscripted man necessary to maintain our units at full strength.
Colonel Ralston was a noted soldier during the last war, has headed our department of national defence that raised, equipped and trained our splendid army.
He has made a personal investigation and after consultation with his staff has made the definite statement that more men are needed now. That is good enough for me. Nothing else is as important as seeing that our Canadian boys have every support.
Since then the hon. member for Prince has spoken and stated his stand, and now I must state mine. I have a vivid recollection of the shortage of man-power during the last war and the need of ample reinforcements. I had to make a decision, a decision caused by lack of ample reinforcements at the time, a decision far more difficult than the one I have to make to-day. The day we entered the Courcellette area it was my duty as company sergeant-major to tell the men that because of the heavy battle expected and our shortage of men no matter who was wounded no one was to be detailed to take him to the nearest dressing station. It was up to the wounded man himself to try to struggle back at night, alone through mud and shell fire as best he could to where stretcher parties might find him. Every soldier of the last war remembers when going into the line the delays caused by

confined himself in Laurier House, it was the man who was his right arm but who was a sick man, who died a year later, whom he asked to go throughout Canada and preach the doctrines of the Liberal party. In the winter of 1940 Liberalism was not preached throughout the land by the Prime Minister, the leader of the Liberal party; it was preached by a French Canadian of my county, Ernest Lapointe, as the then leader in spirit of the government. He was practically the leader of the government at that time, as he had led the government so ably in the house when the Prime Minister was defeated in 1925, after his speech at Richmond Hill. Mr. Lapointe was a sick man; he had been a sick man for years, but still he undertook that task. He did not do so only to keep the party in power; he did it for a noble cause. I am sure he was sincere. He was ready to do anything to promote Liberalism in this country.
I was deeply moved by the brilliant speech which was delivered yesterday by the son of Ernest Lapointe, and which was a vindication of his memory. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Lapointe), that gallant officer, has proved that courage may be found in the House of Commons as well as on the battlefields of Europe. He was not one who had been overseas on a Cook's tour surrounded by brass hats. He was in the thick of the battle, during which half his unit was killed. He ;ame back to tell this house things that had ;o be told. They were told in a way that was worthy of his father, worthy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, worthy of the grandfather of the Prime Minister and of all the great men who have been in public life in this country. I pay the same tribute to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Halle). The hon. member for Lotbiniere came from the western front. The other hon. member, Lieutenant Colonel Halle, came straight from Italy. Here we have two men who have been witnesses of the war, in the thick of battle. I respect and believe them, more than I believe the brass hats who infest general headquarters here in Ottawa, who have never been in any theatre of war but who want young men to be sent overseas to take their places there. I well remember that I was called to order by the Prime Minister because I said the brass hats were pompous. What a thing! I told him then that if these men were shedding their blood for their country, it was in scratching their fingers with red tape.
What is the feeling in this country, Mr. Speaker? There are two groups of people, those who favour conscription and those who

oppose it. Those who favour conscription cannot understand the gossip which we witness in this house between old men who have passed military age, who give their views and relate their experiences and say, "Well, you said this." "No, I said that." "No, I said this." "No, you said that." It is like, "After you, my dear Gaston." "After you, my dear Alphonse." It is most incredible. That sort of thing earns the contempt of the people of Canada. They are strongly against it, and they are not interested in such things being said in this house. They are interested in what is done by the government, things of which the government is ashamed. When since the beginning of the war have we had the truth about the policy of the government? I remember distinctly, sir, that at first conscription was not mentioned; it was not even included under mobilization. We were to have the mobilization of our natural and material resources for the greatest possible war effort, but no conscription whatever. That is what was being said. I am on record in that connection; the Prime Minister himself has put on record what I said in caucus before conscription was imposed.
Before concluding my remarks I must say that the advice of the Liberal party has never been sought in regard to any measure brought down by the government, while the advice of the opposition has been obtained. The Prime Minister said in this house that in caucus I had proposed to raise a regiment for the defence of Canada in my constituency within a week. That was about June 18 or June 20; I have the record in my house, but I know it so well that I do not need to read the book. Hon. members will remember it also. I offered to raise a regiment in my own county, and the Prime Minister told me that that would be the greatest possible mistake, that it would hamper the work of the farmers, the lumbermen, those working in essential war industries making munitions and arms, and so forth. What the Prime Minister said was plausible, but on the other hand all the men and women who have done so much for the war effort have been and are still being ignored by the government. Apparently their contribution does not count. From the start of the war the only ones who were doing their duty toward the war effort, according to the government, according to the wartime information board, according to the CBC and according to all government publications, were not those who had complied with the law, the young men who were first called recruits, then draftees and then N.R.M.A. men; it was only those who had volunteered even though they
DECEMBER 6, 1944	6871
War Effort-Government Policy
remained in Ottawa to wage a war for increases in salaries, allowances, bonuses and all that. Those were the brave men.
At the start of things there was a misconstruction of words. The word "conscription" was only a reminder of the abuse which the Quebec people had taken under the so-called union government in 1917, 1918 and 1919.
About a month ago I met a prominent Tory in Toronto. He asked me how I could justify what had been said by Mr. Lapointe to the effect that the hands of Arthur Meighen were dripping with blood. I told him that in the first place I did not know whether Mr. Lapointe had used that language, but whether he had or not I knew that it was true. After the war was over, there were men paid by the Department of Justice of the Meighen government to run after draftees and shoot at them. Imagine that! The allied forces had stopped firing on the battlefields of Europe, but here in Canada because some farmers had not forgotten the pledge of Borden not to impose conscription on farmers they were treated like convicts, they were treated like the enemy. When I was elected in 1924 one of the first letters I wrote was to Mr. Lapointe asking for the files in connection with those individuals who had been paid by the government to shoot at their brothers. What did Mr. Lapointe tell me? He said, "Jean-Frangois, the war is over, we must have peace in this country, do not insist on having those files." That was the language used by Mr. Lapointe in answer to my request.
To summarize my point let me use an expression which once fell from the lips of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). It may seem to us that we have done too much. If too much has been done it has been to excuse the government for not having imposed conscription according to the letter as well as the spirit of the law. That was the guiding star of the policy of the government, the fear of an offensive by the Tory party. They are not dangerous. I stood alone before their most powerful man, R. B. Bennett. I am still here and he is across the sea, and not in the army.
The Prime Minister is witness to the fact that I have fought battles for the Liberal party. He will remember that all the great leaders of the Tory party came to speak against Jean-Frangois Pouliot in Temiscouata county. First there was the Calvinist Arthur Meighen, then there was the bombastic R. B. Bennett and then the non-conscriptionist, R. J. Manion. They all came; they were listened to, but when the time came to vote they were all forgotten.
I have tried to help the Prime Minister in every way. Many times I have helped to
make matters smooth for him. How many times did I warn him against oncoming danger? I did that many times, not for anything in return but simply for the satisfaction of my own conscience, my own patriotism and because of the friendship that existed between us. Very often I was subjected to humiliation because I delayed leaving the party.
The Prime Minister must remember when he toured the Gaspe peninsula in 1932 or 1933. I sent him a wire asking if he would meet some of my constituents at my, home. He graciously acceded to my request and one night, although the weather was very bad, about eight hundred people came to my home to shake hands with him and with Mr. Lapointe. The Prime Minister must remember that for a time I used to send his photograph as a wedding gift to young couples in my county. The Prime Minister must remember also that I have deprived myself of valuable books on the occasion of his birthdays as a token of my admiration for him.
But that is not all. In 1930 when Mr. Houde, who is now running for mayor of Montreal, was leader of the provincial Conservative party in Quebec, it was suggested that the Liberal members should support his opponents in the Montreal election. I succeeded in having a different order given and all members except one decided to refrain from taking any part in the campaign. When the general election came around I went to see Mr. Houde, and at my request-the Prime Minister with another member of the cabinet was informed of the matter at the time

Mr. Houde refrained from taking any part in the federal campaign. Imagine, sir, he was elected by 42,000; he was the leader of the provincial group. All that was done to help the Liberal members on the island of Montreal, and it was done by the member for Temiscouata from away off in the country, just for the sake of the party and to prevent the party from being humiliated more than it was. Mr. Houde kept his word and kept away from the fight, and when that bombastic Bennett came to Maisonneuve Mayor Houde refused to preside at the meeting.
Afterwards, at the time of the padlock law, when the late Mr. Lapointe was ready to deal with the matter in a summary way, I sent a memorandum to the Prime Minister to inform him of the danger of such action. But I pass quickly over that.
In the provincial election of 1934, after the Prime Minister had stated in my presence at a meeting in the Chateau Laurier which was presided over by the late George P. Graham, that Mr. Hepburn was his leader in Ontario, I campaigned for Mr. Hepburn
War Effort-Government Policy

because I thought it would be a good thing for the party, and in the following year I returned to Ontario counties to speak for some of my colleagues in this house in the federal election. Two weeks before the date of the election, at a general meeting which had been organized by one of my best friends, the late Harry Anderson of the old Globe, I predicted, and it proved to be true, that sixty out of sixty-five supporters of the Liberal party would be elected in the province of Quebec on October 14. That was not only published in the Toronto papers but carried by the press agencies and published all over Canada.
I regret, very much, Mr. Speaker, that from the beginning of the war the government has boosted only those who would volunteer and has ignored the others who are doing so much for the war effort here in Canada- our farmers, our railwaymen and those engaged in other war industries. They have been ignored completely. Why? The man in the cab of a locomotive and all the members of the train crews are exposing their lives daily, just as do those who work on explosives in munitions plants and so on, but these men are considered slackers. I have had to fight for them, and I did secure amendments to the national war services regulations which benefited not only my own constituents of Temiscouata but even the constituents of those members who dare to insult the province of Quebec at the present time. That is on record. I shall not show the letters of appreciation that I have received from officials of the department concerned; I shall keep them. But, sir, if I am here to-night it is because I have suffered mental cruelties for so long in belonging to a party which has been ignored by the Prime Minister from the start of the war. I do not know whether he takes the same attitude with his colleagues in the cabinet. If so, I understand why they are divided.
I remember that in 1936 Miss Agnes MacPhail, referring in the house to the election posters of 1935, on which were the three words "King or chaos", said that the wording should have been "King and chaos". I was scandalized at the time. I did not believe that that could ever be true. But now here it is; we have it.
Did I not warn the Prime Minister three and a half years ago, on the afternoon of February 21, 1941, that he was to be stabbed in the back? On that occasion did I not warn all the English-speaking colleagues of the Prime Minister, including the minister for naval affairs, the then minister of pensions, the
fMr. Pouliot.]
Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and even the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and many others? I did so because I had confidence in the Prime Minister, because I still hoped against hope that he would be true, not to his promises, but to our expectations. But, sir, on that memorable occasion the former minister of national defence was not defended by any one of his colleagues in the cabinet. He was defended by the then leader of the opposition, to whom the Prime Minister paid such a tribute when he left the leadership.
Not only that, but when the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) said that the Prime Minister was not qualified to be prime minister in time of war, that the one who was qualified was his colleague, the then minister of finance, and the late minister of national defence, who read the book that the hon. member for Parkdale had in his hand? Who brought embarrassment to the hon. member for Parkdale just to save the skin of the Prime Minister if it was not the member for Temiscouata himself?
My colleagues may be surprised that that was some time after I had left the Liberal caucus. Why did I do so? I did so for a very good reason, because there is no freedom of speech in that room. I was prevented by the Prime Minister himself from saying what I thought of the then minister of national defence, that he was incompetent. Since I was precluded from expressing that judgment in that room I could not breathe there any more, and I left.
I returned last spring to offer my good wishes and to say godspeed to the Prime Minister before he left for England. I did not want the death of a sinner; I wanted his conversion. But here we see the Liberal party embodied in a man who takes advice from his bitterest opponents, until he falls in a muddle. We are in a muddle now. Who is responsible for it? The Prime Minister cannot cast any blame on me, because I warned him. I warned him against himself. He did not listen to me. He listened to the opposite party, the party that is now making an amendment for his downfall.
I could speak for hours on this subject; I could speak for days and weeks and months. But I will conclude by reminding the house that the time has come for the "Great Divide". The members of the cabinet live in a false security. Ottawa has always ignored the public opinion of the Canadian people, but I can tell you they are fed up; they want a change; they want leadership. It is the time of the "Great Divide". The Liberal party as a party-I do not speak of my old friends

War Effort-Government Policy
who belong to it-is dead. The Prime Minister has killed it. It is just as dead as the Tory party.

maintopic: QUESTIONS WITH RESPECT TO EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT AND DISSOLUTION
subtopic: THE WAR
subsubtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 17, 1919, death came to a great Canadian statesman, one whom the gracious queen Victoria had called the "silver-tongued speaker", Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
We reverently preserve many a memory of that great public man who spent long beautiful years in Arthabaska, a town of my constituency which will always be proud to have numbered among its citizens this great Canadian, this famous patriot, who has remained the symbol of national unity and a model of straightforwardness and fair play toward all nationalities and sectional groups in our fair country.
This illustrious Canadian has bequeathed his political will and testament to his successor. In it he condemned conscription. The original of this document is in the hands of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) who, in accepting the legacy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, agreed to abide by the tenets of his last will. For a quarter of a century, a copy of the political will of this great Canadian citizen has been in the hands of every member of the Liberal party and has been quoted in numberless speeches in every election campaign.
In 1940, as every other Liberal, I was given a copy of this document and I visited the most remote corners of my constituency. Knowing the pledges taken by my leaders, I told every one of my constituents, men and women alike, that the Liberal party would never pass conscription for overseas service, adding that, if it ever did, I would oppose with all my strength any government which would endeavour to apply such a measure.
In June, 1940, in view of the fact that the events which had occurred since the outbreak of the present war had given rise to an extraordinary crisis and that the national security of Canada was in jeopardy, the government introduced Bill 43 entitled "An Act conferring certain powers upon the governor in council for mobilization of national resources in the present war," in other words, the Mobilization Act. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that at the time,
I supported the enactment of that measure, which was also unanimously supported by all the political parties of the loyal opposition.
On January 22, 1942, at the opening of the third session of the 19th parliament, one of the features of the speech from the throne was the announcement that a plebiscite would be held in regard to the utilization of man-power.
I understood that the government were asking the people to release them from their former pledges in regard to overseas service. It would have been preferable to my mind if the government had asked directly to the people: "Are you for or against conscription for overseas service?" But inasmuch as the government was asking the electors whether they agreed to release it from its pledges in this connection, I was under the impression that both questions were synonymous, even though the one selected appeared ambiguous. I voted for the holding of the plebiscite, inasmuch as it was merely a public expression of opinion which gave me an opportunity to ascertain the views of my constituents when they were being asked by the government whether or not they were willing to release it from its former pledges in regard to overseas military service.
Fully conscious of my duty and responsibility, I addressed myself to my electorate during the plebiscite campaign,, in spite of the fact that I was then in very poor health, endeavoured to explain to them that they were free to vote as they saw fit, to think as they liked in this matter, but that, as far as I was concerned, I could not accept the responsibility of an affirmative vote to the plebiscite question and would vote against it. My personal opinion was supported by 98 per cent of the electorate in my riding. The province of Quebec refused, by an overwhelming majority, to release the government from its pledge.
On the day following the plebiscite, a bill to authorize conscription for overseas service was introduced in the house. It was claimed that, in view of the result of the plebiscite, such was the decision of the electorate. How can this lame explanation be reconciled with the interpretation which, at that time, the Right Hon. Prime Minister himself gave to the plebiscite question in asserting that conscription was not the issue at stake? Had it been so, could the government feel released from a solemn pledge when the only electors to whom the guarantee had been given formally refused to cancel it? Such was Quebec's decision.
Bill 80 advocated the repeal of section 3 and, once this had been struck out, the Canadian mobilization act would have authorized' compulsory service in any theatre of war, that is to say, conscription.
I voted against Bill 80 in the house, in other words against conscription, and I am proud of it, for in so doing, I honoured the mandate which I had received from my supporters.
On November 23, 1944, a date which, to my mind, marks a "national tragedy", the present government passed order in council No. 8891,
War Effort-Government Policy

providing for the dispatch overseas of 16,000 draftees. I have said, Mr. Speaker, that it was a surrender to the blackmail of the con-scriptionist gang and to the collective frenzy of the eight English-speaking provinces, thoroughly aroused against the French-speaking province.
Fully aware of my responsibility, I say that I shall never be a party to this breach of the plighted word by the imperialists within the government and the opposition. The latter showed no regard for the memory of Laurier, who, during his whole life opposed that banfeul measure, and in this I shall meet the wishes of my constituents who elected me on the principle of no conscription for overseas service.
I shall therefore vote against the main motion, which requests us to support the whole war policy of the government, including order in council No. 8891 which provides for the dispatch overseas of 16,000 draftees, just as I voted against Bill No. 80, that is against conscription for overseas service.
I realize, of course, that the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada was the victim of a foul conspiracy hatched by a majority blinded by old prejudices and by new political-military and financial schemes.
My convictions are those of a liberal, and I shall remain a liberal. From now on, I reserve the right to pass judgment on the war policy as time and circumstances may warrant. I know that the right hon. the Prime Minister and his cabinet have done great things. I heartily approve of the general administration of the country in war time, such as the exemption granted to farmers' sons, industrial workers, war plants employees, commercial employees, and heads of families. I also support the social measures, such as family allowances, and post-war plans. Finally, I do not hesitate to say that the present head of the Government is still, to my mind, the only one who can lead our great country to a prosperous destiny.
Mr. Speaker, on every occasion when a national issue or a difficult situation arose, even if detrimental to some of their legitimate and acknowledged rights, French Canadians have yielded ground; they have set an example of generosity and patriotism in order to maintain and strengthen perfect unity between the two great races of this countiy. However, whatever our interest in a principle so important and so vital as that of national unity, there comes a time, tragic, indeed, when one can no longer afford to yield without accepting complete surrender. Self-denial, in the case of the individual, may assume the form of an almost supreme unsel-

fishness but, in the case of a nation, it must not become cowardice or treason. Much has been asked of French Canadians since Confederation and much has been received from them. But, let it be noted that their survival as a race is more important than anything else, that their hearts are filled with national pride, that in their veins flows a blood inherited from heroes who sacrificed all but their honour.
Mr. Speaker, my ancestors came from France in 1616, that is more than three centuries ago. I am a citizen of the province of Quebec; I speak the French language which I have learned with respect and devotion on my mother's knees. I have the right and the duty to love my mother tongue and I would be despicable if I failed to fulfill that obligation. I have the same respect for those who speak another language, which they love so dearly and have learned in the same way.
Must we be divided simply because the accident of birth has made us to pray to God with a different accent and in a different language? When we speak of our mother, it is with equal love, equal devotion and the same feeling of gratitude. We use the same words even if we choose them from different languages. In both cases, the tongue is but the interpreter of the heart. National unity is in the heart, not in the language or the customs. Our forefathers brought Christian civilization to this land. They built villages in spite of the red man's bow, hatchet and scalping-knife. Without any mechanical instruments, they made the earth produce food and disgorge part of its treasures; they set up business enterprises and industries. They built the country in which we live happily to-day.
Our political background is no less replete with glorious pages. As to our part in world affairs, it has been getting more and more important for a number of years until to-day Canada ranks among the first nations of the world.
At this very hour, thousands of our gallant men are giving their all to free the nations crushed by the enemy and to make possible for us a new order in which we shall know liberty, peace and happiness.
Nothing can deprive us of our tongue, our faith and our traditions. We must not forget that Canada stretches from Halifax to Vancouver, from the Arctic to the forty-fifth parallel. It is all this Canada, so great, so rich, so beautiful, so full of promises that we must love. Our patriotism should not be confined to a small part of the country where life is good, where we are rich in historical

War Effort-Government Policy
associations, but which is not the only part of Canada where our forefathers have written glorious pages.
Canada for Canadians. Let us, Mr. Speaker, set this sane example of enlightened and intelligent patriotism whenever, as in this instance, we 6ee a group foolishly attempt, through blind imperialism, to pass such a baneful bill of conscription, a bill which is anti-Canadian and a cause of national disunity.
Fellow-Cansdians, we have reached the turning point. As a representative of Quebec, I appeal to you in these grave hours. Let us not be disunited, but rather let us stand1 side by side; let us not pass a law that would disrupt our national unity; let us consider our country's future, and have faith in our ability to achieve national unity in this country of ours. If we are able to perform a national miracle of this sort, we shall be all the more justified in proclaiming ourselves the builders of our country.
On March 22, 1943, in a speech which I made in this house, I said:
I feel bound to make the following statement: as long as my leader, the right hon. Prime Minister refrains from putting conscription into force for overseas service, I shall remain among his most_ faithful followers; however, I must say to him that if he ever gives way to the imperialists, even though they be members of the present government, or to the opposition, and puts conscription into force for overseas service, it shall be my painful duty to fight him, for I am opposed to conscription for overseas service and as a gentleman, and a man of honour I shall keep my pledge: in other words.
I shall discharge the trust reposed in me bv my constituents in this respect.
I will therefore vote against the main motion, by which we are asked to approve the government's entire war policy, including order in council 8891, with regard to the sending of 16,000 recruits overseas; I shall vote against it for the same reason I voted against Bill No. 80, namely because I oppose conscription for service overseas.

subsubtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate I should like the government to take my remarks as constructive criticism, because I know perfectly well that every hon. member must do everything in his power to bring this war to a successful conclusion. In speaking of reinforcements which are necessary, from the information we have had in public and private sessions of this house, I think it is really more a matter of man-power than reinforcements. Have we bitten off more than we can chew? I think we have. We have built a navy which is a great credit to Canada; we have built an air force second to none, and we have built an army that is one of the finest in the world
to-day. Our navy and air force have ample reserves. They have perhaps more than they need to-day. But the army, and the infantry particularly, need' reinforcements in the worst way. We have other commitments as well. We have increased our merchant marine by nearly one hundred percent. We are supplying our armed forces and the allied nations with tanks, guns, shells, ships, et cetera, which need a huge industrial army to carry on. Then there are the armed forces to feed, the food arrangements with Britain and other allied nations which need a land army to maintain. Can we take any more men from indhstiy or from agriculture without cutting down our supplies? I am quite sure that we cannot do it.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said in the house yesterday that further agreements had been made with Britain to supply more beef in 1946. I asked General Mc-h aiughton about the policy of the Department of National Defence with regard to men essential to agriculture. Hon. members will find that at page 6576 of Hansard. He assured me that the department was establishing a reserve list of N.R.M.A. men who could be posted to *agriculture. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has also assured me that that will be taken care of. I do not question the word of General McNaughton, nor do I question the word of the Minister of Labour, but the men are still going into the army every day. If the men who are called for a medical examination are found to be fit they are put into the army, men who should be producing food for Britain and the armed forces. You can imagine the position a man is in. He goes for his medical and he is in the army. They say, "Well, ask for a postponement."
I know there are a lot of commanding officers among the membership of this house and I have been four years in the army myself. A commanding officer is not the best person to whom to go to ask for anything, especially when you are only a recruit sent from the mobilization board to take your basic training. During his basic training that man cannot do anything about a postponement. At the end of his eight weeks of basic training he is told, "Well, you are in the army now; we have trained you; forget about the farm." That is the position to-day. I am quite sure that hon. members on both sides of the house will agree with me in that.
I have a letter from one of my constituents who is a young farmer, married and the operator^ of a farm. He has had agricultural leave which expired on November 1. He reapplied for an extension to carry on his farming operations and they have granted him leave to

War Effort-Government Policy
January 2. If he is essential on the farm from November to January 2, he is just as essential after January. When that case was before the mobilization board the judge thought he should be sent back to agriculture to carry on his agricultural occupation, but the military representative said, "Oh, no, that man will have to get an old man or a younger man under military age to carry on the work on that farm."
We then come to the N.R.M.A. men who have been getting spring and fall leave to help to sow and harvest their crops. If this supply of man-power is taken farm production will drop and it is dropping to-day. It is down now from last year.
I should like to read a letter covering the point I am trying to explain:
My son is the only able-bodied man on a 1,900 acre farm-900 under cultivation and 100 _n cultivated grass. We have 150 odd cattle, about 40 hogs and 13 horses. The cattle are < mostly beef cattle, but we winter them under farm conditions, that is, we feed, water and shelter them, instead of letting them get down to hide and bones during the winter. 1 have one son in the active army, I believe now overseas. I am crippled myself, so that 1 can only do light work, and I have a crippled son also unfit for manual labour. The cultivated acreage of this farm has already been reduced by 400 acres since the start of the war. You can see what I am up against if they bold my son tor further military service, and I know there are many more up against the same conditions.
To rob the land army of these men who are essential to the success of our food programme will be nothing less than disastrous. Yesterday in the house the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was asked questions in regard to the congestion at the various stock yards. This situation is due largely to the scarcity of men on the farms. If more men are taken we shall have still greater congestion at the stockyards, because more unfinished cattle will be coming on the market. The minister said there was a good outlet for finished cattle, but the unfinished cattle are coming on to the market in great numbers. Why? Because no help is available to feed them on the farm. Visit any of our abattoirs across Canada any day and you will find them slaughtering milch cows that should be kept on the farms and milked next summer to aid in the production of cream or butter or cheese. You will also find young sows coming on the market which should be kept on the farms and bred in order that we might have more bacon for Britain. But when the help is not there they cannot feed themselves, because in this country we cannot run our stock outside. They have to be cared for in the winter and we have to put up the feed in the summer. Trace that unfinished stock to which
[Mr. Btyce.)
the Minister of Agriculture referred yesterday back to where it came from. Go to the farmer who sent it in; ask him why he did so. You will find that he had a son who joined up in 1939, and that the next son was called up. You may find that the farmer was sixty-five years of age in 1939 and now is seventy years old, and that it is impossible for him to carry on any longer. If you read the papers to-day you saw that not eighteen miles from here a man seventy-five years of age, bringing in his wood, was trampled to death by his horse last night. That is what we have all over this dominion to-day, with the farms being stripped of the man-power that should be there.
On March 24, 1942, according to Hansard at page 1567, the Prime Minister declared that men essential to or employed in agriculture on March 23, 1942, would be left on the farms. That regulation has not. been complied with as it should have been. I wonder if the new regulations which are promised this parliament will be lived up to. The government has been asked repeatedly to establish some standard of production on the farms throughout Canada, for which there should be a guaranteed minimum man-power. There appears to be a lack of co-ordination between the Department of Labour, which operates selective service, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of National Defence which established six divisions in the field and now finds itself short of reinforcements. I want it understood by the members of this house that I am in favour of sending all the reinforcements needed for our men overseas. Anything less would be a betrayal of the gallant men of this country who have offered their lives and are now in desperate need of reinforcement.
Coming back to the farm situation and the production of food, in my own province I had something to do with this as agricultural representative on the mobilization board. When a man applied for postponement he was given a questionnaire as to his farming operations, which questionnaire he was asked to fill in. By going over that questionnaire you could immediately understand that man's farming operations. If the board considered his production insufficient they advised him to increase his production or go into the army. This policy increased production, and could now be used as a yardstick in connection with the production of food on the farm. The greatest failure of this government has been its failure properly to estimate its man-power needs at home and in the armed forces, and then take a firm stand to meet those needs from its man-power resources.

Mr. Speaker, at a time when
millions of soldiers are fighting on the various battlefronts, when the government in London cites the Canadian war effort as. an example to all other Allied nations, we wonder what can be the meaning of the agitation stirred up around this matter of conscription or, to be more accurate, around the dispatch by compulsion of 16,000 Canadian draftees.
The explanation is as simple as the young men who are to be sacrificed: the enforcement of conscription for service overseas indicates that Toronto's imperialistic Tories have triumphed, they who, since the outbreak of the war, in collusion with certain interests known to us, never stopped sabotaging our voluntary system. maintopic: QUESTIONS WITH RESPECT TO EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT AND DISSOLUTION
subtopic: THE WAR
subsubtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Some will note with surprise that the people of Quebec, though inexorably opposed to conscription for overseas service, are and will remain quiet. Soon, however- for the end of the war is at hand-those same capitalists will beg the province of Quebec to save them from socialism 'which never fails to sweep a divided nation. Will the province of Quebec respond this time? I wonder.
To-day, regardless of the way in which we choose to look at the problem, the house is asked to endorse the conscription policy for the present and for the future. Personally, I have always been, and I am still, opposed to conscription for several reasons. I cannot accept conscription because, as the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself has admitted, there is no assurance that our war effort has not been out of proportion to our resources, and, if so, instead of increasing our forces we should revise them in keeping with our available manpower.
I cannot accept conscription because, to my mind, if the senior minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) had shown as much foresight as his colleagues in charge of the Department of National Defence for Air and the Department of National Defence for Naval Services, the present critical situation would not have occurred, and I say that it is not up to the youth of this country to make good the mistakes of a minister who looked to the other side of the house for guidance.
I cannot accept conscription because it is a measure utterly inconsistent with the liberalism of Laurier which I have upheld for over thirty years.
I could not close my brief remarks without comparing certain thoughts expressed at twenty-seven years' interval. In 1917, I happened to be in Grand'Mere, on Chamberland street, in front of the office of the Englishspeaking soldiers sent from Toronto to apprehend our conscripts. Three old Liberal leaders, who happened to pass by, pointing to those soldiers who were carrying revolvers in their belts, told me in their simple but always forceful language: "Young man, this conscription measure is not of our doing."
Tuesday, November 21, 1944, again at Grand'Mere, where I was about to entrain for Ottawa, I ran across another old French-Canadian Liberal leader who was immensely proud of the fact that three of his sons are now serving in the active army and who said to me: "You are going to Ottawa, Mr. Member of Parliament. The news from there is good." It was still good at the time. He added: "Conscription is not of our doing."
Mr. Speaker, from my seat as Liberal member from the constituency of St. Maurice-Lafleche, I repeat: "Conscription is not of my doing", and I shall vote against the motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before continuing my remarks in French I should like to say to the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), who said to-night that we were the isolationist lads in this corner of the house, that if the members now sitting in this comer of the house were to be called isolationists, then it was also true that the Liberal party for the past five years should have sat in this corner because we were sharing the same views, except some members, on matters similar to the one that we are now discussing.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, on no occasion during the last twenty-seven years have the people's representatives been faced with a responsibility as heavy as the one which devolves upon us at this time. It is therefore the duty of each one among us to face the situation calmly, following the dictates of his conscience, judgment and intelligence. I shall express my thoughts very briefly, because I do not think it is necessary, in upholding our cause, to repeat all the arguments which have already been expounded in this debate. ' I merely wish to state the reasons which lead me to believe that I can no longer give my support to the present government.
After passing the order in council whereby the draftees called under the Mobilization Act are to be dispatched overseas, the government requests us to endorse its policy by a vote of confidence. To my mind the issue now being

6S78

War Effort-Government Policy
discussed has a military and a political side. An endeavour has been made, in this house, to advance the argument that the morale of our troops overseas was greatly affected by the lack of reinforcements. I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that I am not sufficiently well informed to pass judgment on military matters, but I cannot understand how the dispatch, during the next six months, of 16,000 unwilling draftees will improve the morale of our troops. I believe the right hon. the Prime Minister himself (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated, as has been repeated over and over again, that they would not be enthusiastically welcomed by the volunteers they were to join. In addition, it was claimed that their presence might cause disunity if not dissension among jur fighting units.	_
Moreover, the problem with which we are faced to-day means that the government lacked foresight in pursuing a war effort out of proportion with our means and blundered in the assignment of the troops available.
The crux of the argument, however, is the political aspect of the matter, since it is evident, as we are well aware and as several well-informed1 people have pointed out, that conscription, in short, is but a shield which has screened those who, for the past four years, under the cloak of patriotism, advocated its enforcement in the hope of coming into power.
In the speech which I delivered in this house on Bill No. 80, I said that if the government yielded on one point of its program, it would find it hard in the future not to yield all along the line. Unfortunately, my predictions have materialized and to-day we are faced with this hard fact: we have conscription.
I need not recall all the solemn pledges of the leader of the government and of his chief associates, to the effect that conscription would never be resorted to. These statements are still too fresh in the minds of each one of us, and I still remember the radio speeches of our leaders, during which they repeated their unshakable opposition to conscription.
It would be inconsistent to claim that after having broken so many pledges and solemn promises, the present government could expect from us a vote of confidence, especially since it has not been shown that conscription was necessary to an allied victory. I still think that the voluntary system would have proved adequate if its application had been entrusted to people who believed in it and if means in keeping with the circumstances had been used.
We are called upon to-day to support a "vigorous effort" in the prosecution of the war. I am wondering what is implied by the 
word "vigorous". Are we to gather from that expression that we have not, so far, done our utmost to help our troops and our allies? One has only to peruse, the statistics prepared by the various departments to realize that Canada, in every field, has neglected nothing to encourage a war effort which, in proportion to her population, has surpassed that of all other allied nations. This is the reason for statements published in the press from well-informed and authoritative people, such as Mr. Roosevelt, Mr. Churchill-and others who said, in effect, that our war effort was not only most commendable but that it bordered on the miraculous.

All honest and sincere people now know that since the war's outbreak a sly and dishonest campaign has been waged in this country in order to make it appear to the other provinces that Quebec has refused to do its share in the present conflict. Mr. Speaker, from my seat in this house, I want to protest with all the power at my command against this slanderous campaign aimed at my province. I think, on the contrary, that Quebec is entitled to feel proud of its contribution to the Canadian war effort. As regards our contribution of men for the armed forces, I believe we have done well, and nobody can criticize us, in the light of the facts stated in this house by the honourable member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin).
The Right Honourable the Prime Minister had, quite recently, words of high praise to speak about the province of Quebec, and he

War Effort-Government Policy
very aptly stated, in connection with minorities, that "our country being composed of minorities, its administration would be impossible if the rights of those minorities were not respected."
After all these commendations, in view of all the sufferings we have endured so far, the Prime Minister should not have yielded; he should have held his own against the agitation, for the safeguard of the principles he had always upheld. One fights for his principles, one falls for them, but one never surrenders.
Personally, I trusted him. Apart from his statesmanship, this confidence was based on the historical fact that, in 1917, under circumstances identical to those of the present time, he was among those who, with Laurier, had struggled for the very cause that we are struggling for to-day. Be well assured, Mr. Speaker, that we do not light-heartedly forsake a leader which commanded both our admiration and our respect. However, as in the present situation, everyone must follow the dictates of his conscience and judgment, I cannot put my trust in the leader of the government for the carrying out of the new policy he has just adopted. For my part I have also made promises and given pledges which I intend to keep.
I understood from the speech of the former minister of national defence, that there still are in the cabinet, ministers who had led their leader to alter his policy and that, therefore, he would no more be free to uphold, among his colleagues, the principles which have heretofore been admitted and * advocated by all true Liberals.
