maintopic: QUESTIONS WITH RESPECT TO EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT AND DISSOLUTION
subtopic: THE WAR
subsubtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were called here to this special session for the purpose, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) puts it, of discussing the controversy which had arisen out of the resignation of the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston). We have since heard from the Prime Minister and the former minister, of national defence; and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, and I think the country feels that the forced resignation of the former minister of national defence was unjust. The position which he took within the cabinet has been wholly vindicated and the policy which he advocated has now been adopted in halfmeasure.
The question we now have to decide is whether we have confidence in the Prime Minister and his government, confidence that they will carry through even this half-measure, whether they will carry out their present policy with respect to reinforcements and whether that policy is fair and adequate. There has been much serious and thoughtful debate; some excellent speeches have been made, and soon hon. members will have an opportunity of recording their votes.
Some members of the house have protested against the holding of a secret session. I myself was not in favour of a secret session because I felt that we had already sufficient facts to enable us to make a decision, but I also felt that it could do little harm. The further information I gathered at the secret session only served to strengthen my opinion that reinforcements are desperately needed for our troops overseas. I do not think anyone who attended that secret session or heard the discussions that took place in the house could have failed to be so impressed. The former minister of national defence, the hon. member for Prince, further confirmed my views on the reinforcement question. I do not think any political or other consideration could alter the fact that replacements and reinforcements for our troops overseas are needed, and needed now, not some time in the future. Valuable time has been lost.
One of the matters I wish to discuss is the statement of the Prime Minister in which he said, in effect, that a measure of unrest was

War Effort-Government Policy
being organized the like of which had not been seen in the history of Canada, and that a new condition of affairs had arisen as a result of organized propaganda. I resent that, because it was not organized by propaganda and the measure of unrest was not organized. I know of no such effort. The situation is not the result of organization; it is a general building up of public opinion based on facts which came to the people at home. It started before the plebiscite. It began through the foresight of many men and women in this country who knew what happened during the last war, who saw how the voluntary system had fallen down at the most critical stage of that war, who had watched the subsequent developments, and were far-sighted enough to desire that such a situation should be provided against, before we reached & critical stage in the present war. There was no organized propaganda about it.
In 1942 when the plebiscite was taken the same situation obtained, except that the government was not forced to take action. The taking of the plebiscite appeased the people by leaving the impression-despite the Prime Minister's speeches and denials-that the government were given a mandate from the people to enact conscription for any theatre of war. That was the belief of the people when they voted on the plebiscite. At that time I remarked that if we had leadership I believed that we would have in embryo a united nation, and that unity could be obtained by the government taking full responsibility and enacting all necessary measures for the safety of the state. I pointed out that if those measures were not taken we would have all kinds of turmoil as time went on. What I pointed out in my speech against a plebiscite has been justified by the events. We should have faced the issue at that time rather than be compelled to face it at a time like this.
I repeat that there has been no organized propaganda. What the Prime Minister hears to-day is simply the voice of the people as echoed by the press of the country. Ever since 1942 there has been an uneasy feeling among the people, who knew that the voluntary system might break down and that when our troops o'verseas were actually engaged in combat they might be short of reinforcements. This uneasiness spread to those whose sons and husbands and wives and sweethearts and friends and relations in general were over in Great Britain. It was not an organized propaganda. After our troops started to fight in Italy letters came back complaining of shortage of reinforcements. Many of the men who served in Italy had been overseas since 1939. They had been through hard

fighting and were due for leave. Then came D-day, and more statements and letters were received by those at home. Some of these communications were extremely alarming. Statements were made to the press by prominent people; among them, Conn Smythe made a very serious charge, and I think it resulted in action. But the unrest was not organized. I could read letters which I have had from time to time pointing out the seriousness of the situation, but there is no opportunity to do so now.
The whole course of events culminated in the present crisis. I do not need to go through the whole chronology of what happened since the former minister of national defence came home. That has been talked about here and we know just what happened. I will give the former minister credit for having made arrangements for the dispatch of N.R.M.A. reinforcements on November 27. He informed the cabinet of the serious situation, but it was only on November 23 that action was taken, and much valuable time has been lost. Now we have a rationed conscription. It has been said that had conscription been imposed some time ago-and it should have been put in effect long ago- there might have been civil disturbances in Canada. It has been said that even under this hybrid order in council which has now been passed such incidents may occur. It has been suggested that trouble might arise between men of the N.R.MA. who would be sent over and the troops who are now overseas. I do not think so, but if I know the temper of our forces overseas, and I have some information from letters I receive and directly from men who are returning to this country, the trouble we might have here now will amount to nothing compared with what will happen when the fighting men come home if reinforcements are denied them. The government and the Prime Minister will be held strictly responsible.
Another point to which I wish to direct attention is the tortuous methods used by the Prime Minister in his speech with respect to the voting of members of the House of Commons; the propaganda about what will happen if any hon. member votes against the government. What did the Prime Minister say in the course of his address? He said, as reported in Hansard, at page 6613;
I am happy beyond all words for one thing: it is that the responsibility from now on is largely off the shoulders of the ministry and is in an even greater degree upon the shoulders of hon. members of the House of Commons. They will be the ones who will have to determine whether or not this ministry is to continue to carry on the war effort of this country for a further

War Effort-Government Policy
period of time, and administer this order in council, or whether some other ministry is to take its place.
The Prime Minister here throws the responsibility on the house membership as a whole. But he is leaving the door open, as he always does, so that the blame will attach to the members of the opposition or any other hon. member who votes against him, if he has an adverse vote. See what he says in the [DOT] very next breath:
If I cannot get enough support out of my own party to feel sure that the men of my own party are behind me-
Mark those words.
-without depending on those who are politically opposed, then my resignation will go in to the Governor General. . . .
Just what does this mean? In effect these words exonerate every other member but the members of his own party. So that we shall have no blame, I want that known throughout the country, in order that if anything happens and the Prime Minister is defeated in the House of Commons it will not be our fault, because he would not take our support anyway. He is so used to an overwhelming Liberal majority that he has no need for opposition support. It has always been a Liberal war and he intends to keep it so. He does not care if 'he gets our support, and yet he is always complaining because we do not give him that support. That propaganda has gone out to the people, and I hope they understand that it will not be our fault if he is defeated, but only the fault of his own members in the .house.
He makes it clear that unless he gets the support of his own party he will resign. Why does he try to cajole us into voting not to send replacements overseas, not to implement bill No. 80, in an endeavour to make it appear in the eyes of the country that we are lacking in patriotism and are callous about the gallant men fighting our battles overseas if we do not vote "yes", if we do not vote against our conscience for a Prime Minister and a cabinet in whom we and the country have lost faith and confidence?
That brings me to another point. To say the least, I was shocked, and I am sure the house and' the country must have been shocked, when the Prime Minister told us thaj, there is no one to succeed him in the event of his resigning. He says he has canvassed the situation and finds that none of his colleagues will succeed him. What of his cabinet? Have they given their consideration to this situation? What is their thought in the matter? The Prime Minister cannot do anything about it. What will they do? Suppose the Prime Minister became incapacitated, or suppose he died? What then would be the course they would follow? They are the executive of parliament charged with the administration of the affairs of the country. Whom will they select to succeed the Prime Minister in any of these events? Up to the present time have they and the Prime Minister ever discussed the situation as to who is to be his successor, or have they nothing to say in the matter? Has the axe been held over their heads so long that they dare not open their mouths on this situation, or have great big juicy carrots of office been dangled before their eyes to keep them in line?
Is there any one among the 170 members of the Liberal party in the house who is capable of discharging that office? What kind of business administration can be expected from such a cabinet? Who is the understudy? Is there a business head or board of directors in any institution in Canada who would not be facing disaster if they_ were so neglectful of their duty as not to provide for a similar situation in the event of the resignation, death or incapacitation of their chief executive, seeing to it that there should be a successor?
The responsibility is on the cabinet, not on us, to see to it that there is someone who can succeed the Prime Minister in any of these eventualities.
There is another question. Conscription for overseas has always been the law of the land, limited only by the government, and the order in council just passed by the government giving a measure of conscription for overseas service would seem to relieve the anxiety which has been felt by many people, in that it will in the meantime guarantee the necessary reinforcements, although the delay which has taken place is serious. It may provide needed reinforcements at the early part of the year.
The order in council has now reinforced the law, and what happens politically will have nothing to do with the enforcement of that law. It would not matter if this house were dissolved. The personnel is there in the department to administer the law as it is. The deputy minister and the staff of the various " forces are there and the business of the country will not stop. If any such thing should happen, or could happen, then it is about time that we changed our constitution.
The people of Canada gave an overwhelming mandate through the plebiscite. Perhaps it was a good thing the plebiscite was taken, because the mandate is there, and the wishes of the majority of the people must be carried out, namely, that adequate reinforcements
War Effort-Government Policy

shall be made available, not here in Canada but overseas. Whether the method is right, fair, just or discriminating will not matter in the meantime; and, in the words of the hon. member for Prince, the people of the country and I will hold the government and especially the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence personally responsible to see to that. As a matter of fact, it has been expressed in the press that if the house were dissolved our troops would not go overseas.
I think the law of the land must be carried out.
One has only to study the order in council and it must be plain that it is a further example of the government's man-power muddle. This policy, has resulted in inequality of sacrifice and it is also threatening to weaken the moral fibre of future generations. It is lowering the character and manhood of the N.R.M.A. men. No democracy can effectively and successfully wage wrar unless it can and does command every citizen in, any capacity in any theatre of combat to which he may be directed by the government. I would bring to the attention of the house the point of view that was taken on June 5, 1941, by the board of education of the city of Toronto when it received a letter from the then minister of national defence with regard to recruiting activities in the schools of the city. This was their considered reply:	The board of
education respectfully suggested that the most satisfactory solution to the recruiting problem, for parents and students alike, would be found in the application by the government of the principle of universal selective national service.
The question before the house has nothing to do with this. We are asked to vote confidence in the leader of a government and in his cabinet when he has lost the confidence of the majority of the people of Canada-a cabinet divided against itself, a cabinet, I venture to say, that has not even confidence in itself. We are asked to vote confidence in a leader who has been forced to bring in a measure which he does not believe in, and he has no heart in the thing he is doing.
It is a measure which he is forced to bring in as a means of appeasement in such a way as to appease different sections of the country in the hope of retaining power, a measure of such a discriminatory character as to be scandalous. And when I say this I am not pointing my, finger at any province. Never in the history of Canada nor, I suppose, in the history of any other British parliament has a Prime Minister been given such a castigation in a polite way. Never has a Prime Minister been shown up as having misrepresented the truth to the people of Canada in a radio address, 87,000 copies of which

have been distributed to the public, and in the speech which he gave to parliament, as has been done by the dismissed minister of national defence. How can I vote confidence under these circumstances? How can I vote confidence that the reinforcements and replacements necessary will be continued to be sent overseas to our hard-pressed forces?
I will say this, however, if the Prime Minister will bring in an order in council making universal selective service anywhere effective, end the farce of the two-army system, put into effect equality of service and sacrifice, for there is none up to the present time, end this discrimination, ensure that reinforcements and replacements in adequate numbers are made available I will give my cooperation.	.
With regard to the order in council itself, it makes available for overseas 16,000 N.R.M.A. troops. Just what does that mean? It simply means a continuation of the compulsory volunteer method that has been used. Previously it was coercion of the worst kind. Now it is bribery, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his speech the other day.
Never have I heard such a shocking expose of a state of affairs as was given by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Just imagine, in order to get these men to volunteer, the date of enlistment is dated back six months if the N.R.M.A. men will enlist now! The result is that instead of receiving $7.50 a month beginning now, the allowance is dated back six months. The military service medal is given in one year instead of eighteen months and the non-commissioned officer ranks are confirmed.
This order in council P.C. 8891 by its very scope is an affront	to	parliament	and anundeserved reflection	on	the	people	of thiscountry of whatever	race or	creed.	It willnot get rid of the controversy and has the uncertainty as to future action. Our troops are still abandoned	to	the	uncertainty of
voluntary enlistment at the most critical stage of the war. The country is humiliated and disgraced.

of Quebec. It was, "Send the slackers of Quebec overseas." In 1944 we have come back with a new slogan, "Send the Zombies of Quebec overseas." I saw the Quebec riots in 1917. I saw very respectable citizens being shot down at night, coming peacefully through the streets of Quebec with their arms upraised, unarmed, and men were using the famous Vickers machine guns on the population of Quebec. These things, Mr. Speaker, happened in the constituency of Quebec West, which is a part of the old constituency of Quebec East, which was divided in the redistribution of 1911 and which was represented in this House of Commons for over forty years by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
I recall when I was following the debates of 1917 that it was the old chieftain who would lead me to the chief doorman so that I would obtain a seat in the front row. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier saw how I used to follow the debates of the House of Commons in those days with such attention he said to me, "My boy, some day you will come to parliament to sit in the house instead of in the gallery," and he added, "Remember that conscription is a measure contrary to Liberal principles." I have never forgotten that schooling, or the schooling that I had from the Liberal party. Is it strange that, coming into the House of Commons with such a background, I had the firm resolution that never would I make a step which would lead me eventually to vote for a law of conscription? I still recall the first speech that I made in 1937, when I said to the Liberal party, following the return of our minister from the unveiling of the Vimy monument when we greatly increased military expenditures: "We are tailoring the first sleeve of a military uniform that will some day lead us to conscription." I was told at that time that I had no knowledge of international affairs; that we were not to go into a war; that not a single one of those armaments would leave the country; that it was for the defence of Canada and for the shores of Canada. I can still recall the words of the man who was at that time the inspiration, if not the guiding star of our province. I can still recall the declaration of the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe when we were discussing this matter of armaments. When we were pointing repeatedly to him and the danger ahead, he said, "The French Canadians will never agree that any government has the right to force them to military service on the other side of the ocean." I believe he was right. Mr. Lapointe said:
I think I am true to my concept of Canadian unity when I say that I shall always fight against this policy; I would not be a member
of a government that would enact it; and not only that, but I say with all my responsibility to the people of Canada that I would oppose any government that would enforce it.
That is what we are doing to-day. In order that my English friends may understand our state of mind, listen to the schooling we have had. Mr. Lapointe went further and said:
I agree -with what was said yesterday by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and what was said by Mr. Bruce of Australia, that the time for expeditionary forces overseas is certainly past. . . .
This is not a declaration dating back twenty-five or forty years. It was made in this House.of Commons, with the approval of the Conservative party as well as that of the Liberal party, in 1939. Can my friends who speak the English language not understand that with the schooling which was given for more than thirty years in the province of Quebec, and which was repeated here in this national forum, you cannot go to the people with a law like this and just state that you can send them overseas against their will. That is the explanation of all these increases in armaments which have been so ably exposed from time to time, and which I voted against. With every step we went further and further. Finally when we came here on the declaration of war we found that all this schooling had been wrong. Those who came here without any knowledge of national or international affairs, back-benchers who had not been to imperial or international peace conferences, saw their humble judgment justified by events. That is why, true to my commitments, true to what I have said in my constituency and what I would have said in any other part of Canada, from the schooling we have had, I voted against sending troops overseas. Also in accordance with that schooling I voted that the way to help the British empire was not by sending soldiers but by producing arms, munitions of all kinds, ships, aeroplanes and all the different things an army needs. In that philosophy we were supported not only by our leaders in Canada but by the then Prime Minister of Australia.
Following the sending of the first contingent we found ourselves caught in a current so strong that we could not row against it. We were carried by a stream so powerful that eventually we had to go on to an expeditionary force much greater, and to spend millions and millions of dollars. I still recall that at the time we thought by spending $1,000,000 a day on the war we were making the maximum effort our country could make. To-day we are spending $14,000,000 a day, and to some people it is still just a reasonable effort.

I did not want to take a chance in these matters. I stood on the principles on which I was elected, which were the Liberal principles of Laurier, and which were maintained at the time by King and Lapointe. That is why I have never, in any circumstances, indulged' in a vote that would lead me to what we are called upon to deal with to-day. At the time of the plebiscite I voted three times in one day against the Liberal party. I seconded' the motion of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) that the bill be given the six months' hoist. I campaigned in the province of Quebec for a "no" vote and told my electors that I did not want to be relieved of the commitments I had made. I said to them, "If you believe that King is right and1 you give me a 'yes' vote I will accept it as a mandate to vote for conscription. But if, as I ask, you give me a 'no' vote I will go back to parliament and if ever the Liberal party introduces a measure or an order in council to send a single soldier from Canada overseas against his will I will cross the floor of the house and leave the Liberal party."
I was the first member, Mr. Speaker, to leave the Liberal party on the day the Prime Minister tabled the order in council, and I was followed by the hon. members for Temiscouata, Levis and Quebec-Montmorency. I recall that my gesture was interpreted in different ways in certain quarters. Lately Prime Minister Churchill, in discussing the plans for the House of Commons to be built in England, said that he wanted a square chamber with a broad aisle, with the opposition on one side and the government on the other, so that when a member crossed the floor of the house it would be very noticeable; and. he added, "I have crossed the floor of the house twice in my career." So that I say my crossing of the floor means that in accordance with the instructions and the schooling I have received I will fight the Liberal party on this conscription issue. I will fight it without any appeal to prejudice. I will fight it honestly without indulging in personalities against any members of the government or any members of the House of Commons who do not share my views. It is the privilege of each to judge this question as he sees fit, and I am not going to try to raise in my province any prejudice against any one of English, Irish, Scotch, or any other nationality in this house because he does not think as I do. On the other hand, I want it to be known that when I crossed the floor of the house I knew I would be far away from the smiles of the

ministers. If I was not making a move that led to honours, I was at least making a move that kept me a man of honour.
In closing, may I commend the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Lapointe) for the marvellous speech he made yesterday. Belonging to no party, I am ready to welcome the expression of honest attitudes in the house, and I think the hon. member is deserving of acclamation at the next election because of the stand he has taken. His father rose in his place in this house on a debate similar to this when he was about the same age as his son now is. The other day the hon. member for Riehelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) was referring to the guiding star that may come out of this debate in parliament. I would say to the younger generation of my province as well as of Canada that in the hon. member for Lotbiniere they have a star that should lead the younger generation. He was in France on D-day; he has fought with his soldiers and he knows the reactions of those men. He. has seen what war is and yet, when he comes back here, even though he is still a soldier, he makes the claim that we should not have conscription.
I wish also to commend the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Tremblay), who are both veterans of the last war and of this war. I realize how difficult their situation is compared with that of a civilian, but they have been broad-minded enough to judge the situation according to their conscience. I believe these men are entitled to the highest consideration for the position they have taken, and I highly commend them.
I intend to vote for the subamendment of the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Jean). While I do not concur in all its trimmings, it does contain a point which I cannot overlook-it condemns conscription for overseas service. As far as the amendment and the main motion are concerned, I will vote against them without any malice, ill feeling or otherwise. I will vote against them in accordance with my conscience. By that I shall be simply following the whole philosophy of my political life; I shall be following the whole philosophy of my party. When I crossed the floor of the house I asked myself if, along with my other friends, we did not really compose the Liberal party since my other hon. friends on the other side had completely changed their political philosophy on conscription.
On motion of Mr. Macdonald (Halifax) the debate was adjourned.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, December 6, consideration, of the motion) of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this house will aid the government in the policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort,
War Effort-Government Policy
and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Jean.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the votes on the motion and the amendments before^ us, but I think it advisable to make my stand on them perfectly clear.
The motion is:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
The Prime Minister has announced that he regards the motion as one of confidence.
This meeting of the house has been brought about by the recommendation of the former minister of national defence that N.R.M.A. personnel be made available for overseas service. It may be useful to consider the situation that existed early in 1942. It was a grave hour in the fortunes of the allied nations. A rapid expansion of our armed forces was then taking place, and furnished the background for the crisis that has developed.
In the speech from the throne at the opening of the third session of this parliament, in January, 1942, it was stated that we would be asked to approve a programme for further increases in the armed forces involving an expansion of the establishment of the Canadian army overseas; and that the government would seek from the people, by means of a plebiscite, release from any obligations arising out of past commitments respecting the methods of raising men for military service. It must have been in contemplation then that when the Canadian army was created there would be the possibility of the need for conscription in order to provide for its maintenance.
In the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced that it was proposed to create overseas a Canadian army of two army corps-one army corps to comprise three infantry divisions and two army tank brigades and the other corps to consist of two armoured divisions-together with all necessary auxiliary units to serve the two corps.
Shortly thereafter, the Canadian Army was established and. on its establishment, the government and the country became committed to its maintenance. From this commitment and from the great increase in infantry casualties in northwestern Europe over those forecast by army authorities have directly resulted our present difficulties with respect to infantry reinforcements.
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
I think it important for the government to keep this in mind when determining the nature and extent of our participation in the war in the Pacific.
I took part in the debate on the address to which I have referred', and dealt particularly with the plebiscite. I supported the action the government proposed to take, and expressed the view that, having sought the confidence of the people on the faith of its pledge not to impose conscription, the government would not be justified in bringing conscription into effect without first obtaining a release from such pledge.
I also spoke of conscription. Let me read two sentences from my remarks which I believe are pertinent. I am reported on page 584 of Hansard of February 13, 1942, as having said:
It may be necessary for us to have conscription for overseas service. It will become necessary, if sufficient numbers do not continue to come forward voluntarily to provide necessary reinforcements or to permit us to put forth our most effective war effort.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Some of our members are having difficulty in hearing my hon. friend. Would' it be possible to have first of all a little more order in the chamber? And he might attempt to speak a little louder, or come to the front seats, because we are very anxious to hear him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
It may be more convenient to speak from a different seat.
We had the plebiscite. The voting took place in April, 1942. This was not a long time ago. However, many people seem to have forgetten what the electors were asked to pass upon. They say it was a vote on conscription. It has been clearly proved in this debate that it was not. .Certainly, it was made plain to my constituents that it was not. My colleague (Mr. Isnor) and I addressed' an open letter to the electors of the county of Halifax. It was published in the Halifax newspapers. In our letter, while urging an affirmative vote, we said: "Such a vote does not mean a vote for any political party, and you are not asked to say whether you believe in conscription for overseas service."
The government got the release it sought. The result of the vote was to give the government the moral right to impose conscription. It already had the legal right under the War Measures Act. The government decided, and I think rightly, that before any steps would be taken to bring conscription for overseas into effect, the implied restrictions on the government's freedom of action in the
6S89

War Effort-Government Policy
National Resources Mobilization Act should first be removed. Bill No. 80 to amend the act by removing these restrictions was introduced in this house and received the assent of parliament.
A lengthy debate took place on bill 80. On page 3234 of Hansard, June 10, 1942, the Prime Minister is reported to have spoken as follows:
The government, however, wished to be free, without any breach of faith, to resort to conscription for overseas service should that become necesary to our national security and to the effectiveness of our war effort.
If the bill is amended as proposed, it is not the intention of the government to resort to conscription for service overseas unless circumstances should arise which would render the use of compulsion imperative, such, for example, as the maintenance of the necessary reinforcements for Canada's army overseas.
I am not going to refer to other parts of the Prime Minister's speech. I think that the sentences which I have read make it clear that the policy of the government was to impose conscription if such a course were necessary to maintain reinforcements for our army overseas.
Declarations of this policy by members of the government constituted a pledge that the army would be maintained. I realize that a great deal of emotion is mixed with the question of reinforcements. No member in his senses would want to say anything that might stir up more feeling. I shall content myself by saying this-our fighting men who went overseas freely and voluntarily to protect our liberty and ensure our freedom are entitled to our fullest support. They were assured that we would not fail them.	.
The need has arisen for the dispatch of additional infantry reinforcements overseas to meet requirements early in the new year. Casualties in that arm of the service have exceeded estimates. The action taken by the government in passing P.C. 8891 will, I believe, ensure adequate reinforcements for our infantry overseas up to the month of May. The order in council approves of the dispatch to the United Kingdom, European and Mediterranean theatres of 16,000 N.R.M.A. personnel. Provision can be made by order in council without reference to this house for the dispatch of additional personnel should the need arise.
The issue before us is whether the government should be allowed to carry out its policy, and particularly whether the passing of P.C. 8891 in pursuance of that policy should be approved. I have no difficulty in reaching a conclusion. I accept without any reservation the assurance given to us by General McNaughton that our army overseas will be
maintained. I accept likewise without any reservation the assurance of the Prime Minister that further orders in council for the dispatch of men overseas will not have to be referred to this house for approval. I approve fully P.C. 8891 and the action to be taken thereunder.
May I digress here to say how fortunate it was that N.R.M.A. personnel were available in Canada to meet the emergency that developed overseas. It is fortunate that the former minister of national defence and the government resisted the efforts made in this house earlier this year to have the N.R.M.A. draftees demobilized and sent back to civilian employment. The draftees have performed important and essential work in Canada and elsewhere. They provided 42,000 enlistments for general service in the army and 6,000 for other services-48,000 men in all. They provided most of the Kiska task force. They have served in operational units in the defence of our coasts and in Newfoundland and elsewhere. They have served in large numbers in our home war establishment doing work of the highest importance. Most of all they have been and are to-day the potential reserve of reinforcements for our army overseas.
I shall vote against the subamendment. I shall also vote against the vague amendment of the official opposition. When we met here on November 22, their leader made the following motion:
That this house is of the opinion that the full provisions .of the National Resources Mobilization Act should be put into effect forthwith;
And that all trained troops in the Canadian home defence army should immediately be dispatched for reinforcements overseas.
He was, however, by the rules of the house precluded from going ahead1 with the motion at that time.
When, the government announced in this house the passing of P.C. 8891, the amendment now before us was moved. The leader of the opposition did not elaborate, but if his amendment means what it says, it means that N.R.M.A. personnel should be conscripted to serve in any part of the world. The amendment contemplates the extension of their scope of service to any theatre of war. The member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), acting leader of the opposition, stated that he did not include Japan as one of the theatres of war. He was not prepared to say, in answer to questions from the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), whether China and India were included. I think his hesitation supports the charge that has been made that the present amendment is a purely political one.

War naturally engenders tension and nervousness, and in that atmosphere thereby created there is an active and pernicious element that thrives well and enjoys as at present its traditional feast in a mass of division, hatred and race antagonism. The Conservative party has had several loud speakers for the element which stands for total war, but to use the words of Mr. Roberts, total war means " total war for our youth only." This government has waged total war, but in the eyes of that element of which I just spoke total war, again to use the words of Mr. Roberts, " begins and ends with the lives of our young men."
The present situation has been discussed in every aspect and I do not wish to repeat what has been said. Suffice it to say that I make my declaration the declaration of the exminister of national defence for air (Mr. Power). I believe that our country has undertaken too much, at least in the infantry field. In the first place there was overzeal. Then there was deceit or carelessness, and then finally there was this mass conspiracy to make the voluntary system fail. I cannot help expressing the few thoughts I have in mind. Addressing myself to the ex-minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) I wish to say this: Before
he left for Italy and France there had been admittedly a prolonged remustering for reinforcing our infantry. That prolonged remustering should have been sufficient warning to him that something was going wrong. It lasted, from what we have been told, from the month of June on. In addition, I say this: If we had not such an army as our recruit army I am certain that the ex-minister of national defence with his ability, his intelligence, and his knowledge of military affairs, would have found a way of settling this difficulty and avoided any kind of catastrophe. In the third1 place, looking at the Conservative opposition, I wish to say that the effort which was made to spoil the voluntary system was an act bordering on crime. I have thought and spoken a great deal about this conscription matter since I came to this house. It is only the lack of hair that saved my head from turning grey. I think what Struck me the most was something my own son said. It was a simple thought. He said that while a government has the duty of imposing conscription for the defence of its home front, it has no right to impose conscription to send its citizens to fight outside the country's boundaries. By the way, England has always been in favour of the voluntary system and it seems to me that England never imposed conscription unless she was attacked on her own soil.
In order to bring the present crisis to a climax a group of people have succeeded in putting my own province of Quebec and her inhabitants more or less on trial-her inhabitants who are the sons and descendants of the pioneers of North America. Yet we have committed no offence; we have hurt nobody; we have lived as usual, letting others alone and just asking to be left alone. On certain questions we have views different from those of other people, for instance on conscription, but that is our privilege. But in spite of all that has been said the province of Quebec has done well in this war, indeed very much better than might have been expected bearing in mind what took place in 1917. After all, we do not ask much. We just wish to live peaceably. We are not wealthy but we are rich enough to be independent. We have never enriched ourselves and we do not want to enrich ourselves by war contracts. But the lack of war contracts does not enrage us as it has enraged some other sections of the Canadian people. The fact is that whenever there was trouble in our country between the different races it never came from us but because somebody always wanted to interfere with our way of living and our way of thinking.

I would name also the former chief organizer of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec, Mr. Arsenault, who left the ranks of the Conservative party some few months ago because, he said, he could not stay with these people who tried to set race against race.
Looking back to what happened some years ago and facing what is happening now, which is just a repetition of history, I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that I am bound to respect, my pledges respecting conscription in order to show my good faith as contrasted with the bad faith of some of my predecessors of the Conservative party. I repeat, the point I wish to make is that the attitude which is prevalent in the province of Quebec at the present time is due to the work of the Conservatives of the province of Quebec during the past years, and that work was helped by Conservatives in other parts of this country.
Because of what has been said both in this house and outside, the statement the other day by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) that the attitude of Quebec was due to the Liberals, and because of what was written in the order in council which was sent to us recently by the government of the province of Quebec, which was to the same effect, I wish to say it is time that some of us protested against this false impression that the Liberal party is responsible for the attitude of French Canadians concerning the prosecution of the war and conscription.

speechtext:
In 1930 Mr. Bennett appointed Mr. Blondin, speaker of the senate, as a further reward for services rendered the
flag, and to the flag wavers, whoever and wherever they are-and we know where most of them are.
I say these things took place some years ago, when I was young. But I well remember the influence of these Conservatives, disguised as nationalists, upon opinion in the province of Quebec. And my constituency was not alone in this.
Let me refer to a few others who were leading the nationalist party at that time. There were Mr. Monk, Mr. Pelletier, Mr. Lavergne, Mr. Rainville, and others. When they came here, after having worked as nationalists in Quebec, and having formed that opinion-which the Progressive-Conservative party deplores, to-day-most of them were appointed either as ministers or as senators, as a reward for the good services they had rendered their party.
I denounce in this house those who have been guilty, and I denounce them outside the house-and particularly that phantom leader, John Bracken, who every now and then, but always from a distance, has been throwing political robots against the government. I accuse a group of Canadians, well guided by the Conservative party, of having been unkind and unfair to Quebec. I accuse them of setting English Canadians against French Canadians. I say it is shameful, and that it has been the base work of the Conservative party to make Quebec an object of hatred on account of an attitude for which that party is responsible. It is time the other side of the picture were shown, and that the truth be stated about these super-loyalists who, in these last few years, have succeeded in making conscription a political issue.'
As confirmation of what I said I shall quote David Maclellan of the Halifax Chronicle, a major in the Canadian Army:
As a Canadian with as much British blood as the most energetic flag-waver in the land-
I am not the only one who has used that expression-
-it strikes me that English speaking Canadians may well hang their heads in shame for the stupid, nasty smear campaign against Quebec. Tolerance that has somehow taken root in the Canadian army overseas is, and has been, sadly lacking here. It is a tragedy that many Canadians cannot capture the spirit and resolution which animates their sons and brothers overseas.
Quebec's attitude toward conscription has been no secret for many years, yet, completely ignoring the fact that almost two-thirds of the home defence troops come from other provinces, some Canadians have been vicious enough to pour abuse, all the abuse, on the steadfast, warm-hearted people of Quebec.
For a minority speaking another tongue and subscribing to another faith the record of cooperation of Quebec residents has been
War Effort-Government Policy

splendid. The record of relations between English and French-speaking Canadians has been blotted repeatedly by the pin pricks, the rude remarks and the stinging insults that have been hurled at Quebec. Regardless of right or wrong, Quebec has every right to be resentful; and the amazing circumstance is that she had not permitted herself to give more forceful evidence of her resentment.
The Canadian voluntary system has worked throughout this war. It can continue to work if given a real chance. One thing is more important than the controversy agitating Canada to-day, and that is the Canadian nation.
There is one thing I forgot to say while I was discussing the campaign waged by the Tories in Quebec in 1911, who were disguised as nationalists. May I give further proof. Mr. Lavergne, who was one of the leaders of the nationalist party, long after the election wrote this in his memoirs respecting the 1911 campaign:
In 1911 when the Tories of the other provinces began to feel that Laurier in Quebec was losing ground to the nationalists, they redoubled their help to us and money flew in abundance into the nationalist electoral treasury.
We have now come to a difficult pass. We are asked to vote in respect of a motion of confidence, and also in respect of some amendments. The government's motion is:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort
A vigorous war effort since Wednesday, November 22, has comprised a partial, mitigated or restricted system of conscription for overseas service. The order in council passed on that date reads in part as follows:
And whereas it has now become necessary, in order to ensure provision of adequate reserves to meet requirements for the reinforcement of the Canadian forces fighting in Europe and in the Mediterranean, to extend the locality of service of certain personnel who have been called out for training, service or duty, pursuant to the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940.
Now therefore His Excellency the Governor General in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of National Defence ... is pleased to order and doth hereby order as follows:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any other statute, law, regulation or order, the Minister of National Defence is hereby authorized and directed to dispatch to the following localities of service, namely: the United Kingdom and/or to European and/or Mediterranean operational theatres, such personnel, in such numbers as may be approved by the governor^ in council (the number hereby approved being sixteen thousand).
It will be noted that the number is limited to 16,000 and that there is a further restriction as to the theatres of war. This does not satisfy the opposition, because they wish to send all recruits overseas. They claim that the order in council or the decision of the government is not sufficient. They want to conscript the

whole army of recruits and send them anywhere in the world, to India, to China, to Burma or to any other theatre of war. The Conservative amendment reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice.
Equality of service and sacrifice has been discussed before, but as far as the province of Quebec is concerned we say that before talking about equality of service and sacrifice there should be equality of advantage and privilege. I know that some people, particularly those to my left, will say that we have all the privileges and advantages that we ought to have, but we say we have not. In order to stop for all time the talk that is going on inside and outside the house, a commission of outstanding citizens should be appointed to study the grievances of the citizens of the province of Quebec. Of course I will not vote for the amendment of the Conservative party, and I do not think they expect me to vote for it. I am ready to vote for amendments against conscription as long as they are definite and clear, but I shall not vote for an amendment which states that it is against conscription and then mixes up that question with other matters. In such case I shall not hesitate to vote against the amendment.
I come now to the main motion, which is much more serious. It was Burke who wrote and spoke on the duties and responsibilities of members of the House of Commons. In spite of what Burke said, and in opposition to what he said, I have decided to look upon my constituency as the source of my authority, at least on certain vital questions in connection with which I have been given a definite mandate by my constituency. I promised my constituents, I gave them my word of honour- if a word of honour is not to -mean anyr thing, I wonder where this world is going to-that I would vote against any move or measure connected with conscription. Up to this time I have not deceived my electors in any way. I have fulfilled my preelection pledges, and on this vital question of conscription it is not my intention to attempt to split hairs and find an excuse or justification for violating that principle.
I am sorry, but I find it impossible to vote confidence in some of the ministers who have been for conscription and who are yet ready to keep up the fight for total conscription.

speechtext:
I am glad you have not anything to do with the present government. I wish to say that I still have confidence in the Prime Minister. He is an honest and respectable man; he is an outstanding and illustrious statesman who would have reached top honours wherever he might be. The larger the field of effort, the more his superiority would have manifested itself. Above all he is a real and true Canadian. He has devoted the best part of his life to the cause of unity. For years and years the people of Canada will be grateful to him for the social legislation which he has placed on the statute books. Labourers, the toilers of the soil, the masses of the people, the poorer classes, all these will enjoy the advantages of the social legislation introduced by the Prime Minister and will forever bless his name. I hope everyone in the house will understand me when I say that it is painful for me to vote against the Prime Minister. I am faced with having to sacrifice one of two things, fidelity to my party or fidelity to my word of honour, and I choose to keep my word.
This conscription issue which has been systematically kept alive by the Conservative party has created political and racial strife in Canada, yet I take comfort in knowing that there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians, yes, millions, who are still determined to keep steady and to maintain harmony between the two large racial groups in Canada.
I have no apology to make for my stand on conscription, although I realize that the opinions on conscription unfortunately follow differences in race. The two large racial groups have conflicting views on the subject. As a Canadian proud of my origin I shall forever be thankful to my electors for having given me this happy opportunity of paying tribute to those magnificent and sympathetic and broadminded Liberals in this house who have been considerate, particularly in connection with this delicate question of conscription, who have at all times shown themselves ready and willing and anxious to extend to French Canada the warm handshake of good will and understanding.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of this short ssesion I intended not to take part in the debate, which has become nothing but the utmost uselessness. But since an amendment and subamendments had been moved to the main motion, and after listening to the speeches of hon. members of this chamber, I cannot refrain from saying a few words on the whole situation.
I have said that the debate is useless; the question involved in this debate having been decided definitively on the second day of this session. In support of my contention, Mr. Speaker, I will read what was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on Njovember 27, reported at page 6617 of Hansard. The Prime Minister read his motion, which is as follows:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
And he said:
Let me say of this motion, it does not ask for approval of order in council P.C. 8891. That order was enacted in strict conformity with Bill 80, and the government's authority to take such action was specifically approved by the vote on Bill 80 in 1942. The issue of conscription is not being decided by this vote: it was settled two years ago.
So that the Prime Minister has definitely established that this vote of confidence on the main motion does not mean disapproval or approval of conscription, which was adopted in 1942 and was put into force two weeks ago. Therefore it is too late to debate the question, and in my humble opinion all the speeches we can make against or for it are nothing but fiction and trickery.
I have been listening very carefully to most of the speeches which have been made in this house by hon. members from Quebec and from other parts of Canada. I shall come later on to the speeches and the attitude of the Tory party; but I want to begin with the speeches made by the members from Quebec. I have never seen such lack of logic. I will give examples. Listen to the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle). He accused the Tory party of being responsible for conscription being enforced in Canada to-day. Other hon. members have made similar contentions every day since the debate began. Well, if we look at the figures of how the parties stand in this house we must admit this, that in the general election of 1940 the Liberal party was returned to power with some one hundred and eighty members while the Conservative party returned about forty members. If these forty members have been strong enough to impose upon the Prime Minister and the whole country that law of conscription which we have to-day, it means that the one hundred and eighty Liberal members, if they are not just as much Tories as the Conservative members, were very weak, so weak that it is shameful to have to avow it. I cannot understand how forty members can be stronger than one hundred and eighty members with such so-called
War Effort-Government Policy

great leadership as that of the Prime Minister. There is something wrong, something illogical in these statements.
That is not all. Hon. members from Quebec who still remain with the Liberal party have, in most of the speeches they have made, praised the Prime Minister for his great achievements in the past five years, yet they say that they are opposed to conscription to-day, which conscription has been prepared step by step from 1937 until now. It is too late, fifteen days after conscription was put into force, to say that we are against it when we have voted for the government on most of the war measures which have led to conscription. Those who supported the government in 1939 when it introduced the declaration of war opened the door to conscription. Those who voted for the mobilization act in 1910 welcomed conscription. Those who voted for the speech from the throne in 1942, which pertained to the holding of a plebiscite, confirmed conscription, and, in so doing, permitted it to become the master of the place. Those who, after bill 80 was adopted, voted for the annual budget, gave at the same time their entire support to that measure of conscription, since the Prime Minister in having that bill adopted had given notice, "I am passing this bill, not to enforce it now but to give the government the right to enforce it if ever it becomes necessary." So that the measure could be put into force at any time, and it was bound to come, because the moment that bill 80 was -passed no one could vote subsidies to the government without taking responsibility for conscription if ever it was imposed. So that it is of no use, two weeks after it has been put into force, to say "I am against it." It is of no use for the Liberal party with its one hundred and eighty members to accuse others of being responsible for it, because they have supported every war measure. The declaration of war was adopted unanimously except by two-or, to be fair, by three-hon. members, the late Mr. Woodsworth, the hon. member for . Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix), and the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe). These latter two Liberal members alone voted against the general mobilization of our human and material resources; all the other Liberal members took the responsibility from which they are trying to get away to-day; and it is of no use for them to try to escape that responsibility. They helped to launch the boat, they helped to head it into the stream, and now that it strikes the reef of conscription they
(Mr. Roy.]
are trying to escape, and say, "I did not want to betray and I will not betray my electors;' It is a little too late, I am afraid.
As to the word "betray," I should like to add something, Mr. Speaker. On November 23, when the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) spoke to a question of privilege, he said that the Prime Minister had betrayed Quebec. Later on in the day the Prime Minister had those words expunged from Hansard. Here is what I read in the Liberal newspaper of Montreal, Le Canada, on November 6, reporting a speech that was delivered by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) in Quebec on the Saturday before, that is to say, the 4th. The Minister of Justice is reported as having said:
Je suis convaincu, dit le ministre, que si le gouvernement avait accepte cette maniere de voir, Fimmense majorite de la province de Quebec se serait erue trahie.
That is to say: "I am convinced, said the minister, that if the government had accepted this way of proceeding, the immense majority of the province of Quebec would have considered itself as betrayed." Well, if it was right for the Minister of Justice to make that judgment, had conscription been passed on the advice of the former minister of national defence, I am right in saying, and I dare to say to-d-ay, that the province of Quebec has been betrayed, and I challenge the Prime Minister to expunge those words from Hansard.
The Liberal members of Quebec are praising the Prime Minister, saying that he is the greatest Canadian, that he has made a great achievement in the past five years-which great -achievement includes the passage of conscription; this must not be forgotten-, and they are trying to make out in this house, as did the hon. member for Cham-bly-Rouville, that the Prime Minister is a martyr to- national unity. What a fine national unity we have at present in this country ! So they are trying to make people believe that the present Prime Minister is not the -one responsible for conscription, that he is a martyr of Canadiian-ism. Those are things I cannot understand. If the -people of Quebec had an opportunity to be present in this house and to look, as I have done so often, at the one bench which has been occupied since the death of the late Mr. Lapointe, by the Prime Minister and his bosom friend, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), they would not believe that the Prime Minister is such a martyr to Canadianism and that conscription has been imposed upon him by only thirty-nine Tories in this house. I recall that the very Minister of Mines and Resources is one of the Liberal members who joined with the Conservative party to form
689"

the union government in 1917 which passed conscription at that time. In Quebec the union government of 1917 has become such a scarecrow to the people of the province that they would approach only in fear the former member of the union government of that time who sits to-day with the Prime Minister as his bosom friend. That is the state of mind created in the people of Quebec by the Liberals with regard to the union government of 1917. But the Prime Minister is perfectly at ease with that hon. gentleman, because they are both conscriptionists in this war as they were in the war of 1914-1918. I say both of them, because this is what I have just read in the memoirs of Robert Laird Borden, published in 1938, at page 995: '
During those days the Liberals were in convention to select a leader and on August 7 I learned that Mr. Mackenzie King had been elected by 476 votes, defeating Mr. Fielding, who received 438 votes. I extract the following from my diary for August 7: "Quebec and Mr. Mackenzie have killed Mr. Fielding."
By Mr. Mackenzie he means the Prime Minister, Mr. Mackenzie King.

speechtext:
We know what his conduct has been and that of the Liberal party for the last twenty-five years. We know further what has been his war policy since 1937. He has betrayed, to use the word used by the Minister of Justice in Quebec on November 4.
Coming to the subamendment which we are called upon to vote on, I should like to put myself on record and submit to the house my understanding of it. I should be glad to be corrected if I am wrong because I should like to be fair and just to the hon. member for Merrier who proposed it. The subamendment reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain-
And I emphasize these words, "has not made certain".
-of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by using to the best advantage the general service personnel in Canada and the volunteers overseas without resorting to conscription for service overseas.
That is dear, "has not made certain without resorting to conscription for service overseas". This subamendment is confusing; it seems to blame the government for not imposing conscription in time; therefore I will vote against it.
I now come to the amendment moved by the Progressive Conservative party. That amendment seems to concentrate on one point only. I shall read it all, Mr. Speaker:
This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice.
The government is blamed for not having assured equality of sacrifice. Everybody understands that this .is addressed to the province of Quebec. I am (not surprised, of course. I know the Progressive Conservative party. I was with it for a whale after I was elected to the house, believing in the promises of the Hon. Mir. Manion, who was against conscription. I had to leave the party in 1941 because it had gone back to oonscriptionist policy. I know the mentality of the party. I respect the opinion of anyone as to the kind or form of patriotism he likes, although I do not believe in the form of patriotism that has been preached in some parts of Canada for a long time-that is imperialism. We do not live In England or in France, or, I should like to say to the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose), in Russia. We have been for too long in this country, which was settled by we French Canadians to accept as professors of patriotism newcomers of ten, fifteen or twenty years, who at the outset of the war were against participation in it but who have now joined in that war because Russia is at war. We are not ready to accept direction from these people or to have them

War Effort-Government Policy
tell us what to do-. The true Canadians know who we are; we know that our patriotism is truly Canadian, that is all.
As to this request for equality of service and sacrifice, I aim amazed to find it appearing in the amendment. Must I recall to you. Mr. Speaker, and to all the Progressive Conservatives that we have made sacrifices in the past. We. have shared in the service of our country. We have rendered all kinds of service, but whatever we have done has never been recognized in the way it should. We are never given credit for it. And yet, what we are doing at the present time is just as much as the rest of Canada is doing. In 1792. 1812 and 1814 as has been recalled time and time again by prime ministers and others; it was referred to by Sir Robert Borden and by the present Prime Minister a few days ago-French Canadians were faithful to the oath given to the British -crown because we were not republican, because we were royalists and wanted to maintain in this country a royalist regime, because we intended to preserve our country we fought against some English people who had revolted against the British crown. We even fought against some French people who wanted us to fight against the English regime. We stood for the British -crown and ever since from time to time, we have been give-n credit by high personalities, such as -the prime ministers -of the country. Yes, that is well known; but, does it help us to-day in the mind of the imperialists? What do we see to-d-ay, and what did we see in 1914? In spite of the fact -that French Canadian regimen-ts brought the most sparkling glory to Canada in the last war the same clique in Toronto and elsewhere are criticizing the French Canadians for not doing -their share. It is only a clique; it is not all the English speaking population. We have had -proof of -that right in this house. We have heard -two English speaking hon. members praise the French Canadians and give -them credit for what they did in the past. We have -read -articles in many -newspapers, articles written by English writers giving us credit f-o-r w-h-a-t we have done and talking to us with -respect and politeness. One I should like to mention is Mr. Ma-clellan of the Halifax Chronicle.
The clique to which I refer waged a campaign against Quebec in the last war and is still waging a campaign against Quebec today. They are helped in that campaign by the communist party in Canada which offered its services and its help to the Liberal party as it did to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party last summer. The C.C.F. party
rMr. Roy.]
rebuked them, but the Liberal party has not done so. When I see that kind of campaign being waged against Quebec, I say what is the use of the French Canadian doing as much as he has been doing to try to bring peace and harmony in this country, asking his English speaking brothers to join with him to build up a countiy that should be ours? That should be our ultimate ambition, but it seems to be of no use with those who do not understand our patriotism. They refuse to recognize what we have done in the past, how faithful we have been to the British crown, though we never embraced imperialism, and we never shall. We think we are right and we believe this will be shown in the future, and earlier than we may think. We should always fight for Cana-dianism; it ought to be the supreme ambition of any nation to be something by itself. Who can find his pride in the title of colonial? That is one thing we do not understand. Being truly Canadian, as we are, as we always have been, we have never listened to any imperialistic propaganda, whether it came from France or from England. We are called fascists or nazis by newcomers, or by the little clique of fanatics, but it d-oes not matter. We are none of them. Truly Canadians we are, and true to our country we will remain. We have proved time and time again that we are ready to fight for it at any time with anyone. My contention is that the dignity of each group deserves respect and should be respected. That is all we ask. This very question that divides Canada so bitterly is nothing but a hatred campaign. All we hear is equality of service and sacrifice. All we hear in the newspapers, in the house and1 on the street is Quebec- Quebec-Quebec. Coming up on the train from Montreal on Monday morning, and I have two witnesses, the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. LaCroix) and the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion), I was told "Whether Quebec likes it or not, you are going to get conscription." Well, we know we are going to get it, but my appeal to the house at this critical juncture in our history is this: As there are no reasons for sending a few conscripts against their will abroad to fight overseas for a cause in which they do not understand what interests they have, and at the very time when Great Britain is demobilizing two million of her men, I say that it is a most dangerous disservice to do to our country. If we are Canadians, even if we like England, for God's sake do not let us bring this bitter division into Canada w'hich may do -more harm than any good- we can ever hope t-o do by sending a few men overseas.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I shall vote against the subamendment moved by the hon. mem-

War Effort-Government Policy
ber for Mercier (Mr. Jean) because it calls for conscription, or rather blames the government for not having imposed conscription sooner. I shall also vote against the Progressive-Conservative amendment, and I shall vote against the main motion too because in my opinion whoever applies conscription in this country against our will, against the true interests of Canada, and thereby brings about disunity in this country is doing the greatest harm which this country has suffered for years. I do not care which party enforces conscription. I am against it.. The Liberal party has changed its policy on this question. That party with its 180 members is responsible for this conscription measure and I am going to blame that party and that government for it by voting against it.
