speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening just before the adjournment the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggested that speeches to-day should be few in number, short and to the point in order that we may conclude to-day. I am glad, Mr. Speaker, that I have so many agreeing with me when I say that. I accept the Prime Minister's challenge and I throw the challenge to those who are now applauding me, for I am one of those who believe that this session should have concluded a week ago. We could have done our job and been back home by now. I shall take only a minute and a half.
This morning we have listened' to two speeches which did not help one iota in getting a single man to reinforce our men overseas. I think that the speech of the hon. mmeber for Champlain (Mr. Brunelle) who indulged in a tirade against the Conservative party, was disgraceful. It was the kind of speech that does not tend to bring unity to Canada. It was the kind of speech that will make this parliament, if that sort of talk goes on, a laughing stock in the eyes of the people of Canada, and let me say that I was surprised to see the Prime Minister and one or two other ministers around him applauding the speech of the hon. member for Champlain.
This is an unprecedented session, at a critical period. The Prime Minister has termed it "the present crisis". We were called here to learn what the exact situation was with respect to reinforcements. We heard the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston), the former minister of national defence, review the situation as he found it on his trip overseas. He reported to the house what he saw, and I think we all came to the conclusion that the all-important need was adequate reinforcements immediately-not after some further period of delay. He asked for
15.000	reinforcements from the N.R.M.A.
Then we heard from the Prime Minister, and after he had concluded we learned that he has not had the confidence of his own cabinet since the first day of October last. There have been two resignations from the cabinet for opposite reasons, which shows conclusively that there is no confidence in the cabinet itself in the government.
Even now we have received no definite assurance from the Prime Minister or the members of his cabinet that further orders in council will be passed if necessary to see that the required reinforcements go to our fighting men.
The Progressive-Conservative amendment sets forth distinctly what is required at the present time to meet the emergency. We must not fail our fighting men, and I, Mr. Speaker, intend to do all within my power to see that the reinforcements are sent overseas as speedily as possible. I could if I had time read many letters that I have received from relatives of men who have been overseas for four-and-a-half to five years-and I wonder how many of them got past the censorship. These mothers and fathers and wives know the situation. They know that the situation is as the former minister of national defence explained it to the house. I therefore conclude by saying that I am going to support the Progressive-Conservative amendment which I think meets the situation. It reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice.
I believe, sir, that that is the all-important thing at the present time, and I am therefore going to vote for that amendment.
Mr. WILFRID LaCROIX (Quebec-Montmorency) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, to
understand fully the motives which have inspired the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Jean), I feel it my duty to read a statement of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), as reported in Hansard of Friday, December 1, 1944, on page 6749. Here is what he said about the resignation of the hon. member for Mercier as Parliamentary Secretary:
When I read his letter I replied to him that I would have a word with the Minister of Justice about it; that, seeing that he wished
War Effort-Government Policy

to have perfect freedom and not to be misunderstood or his actions misinterpreted in any way, if the Minister of Justice were agreeable I would be agreeable to releasing him from his duties. But I very much hope that this crisis is not going to last indefinitely, and I am also hoping that circumstances may be such that the government may be in a position ^ to ask the hon. member to reconsider his position later on.
I want to emphasize the following words of the right hon. the Prime Minister, which I quote again:
I hope that the circumstances may be such that the government may be in a position to ask the hon. member to reconsider his position later on.
The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Mercier, the first part of which is already included in the amendment proposed by the conservative party, reads as follows:
That this house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by using to the best advantage the general service personnel in Canada and the volunteers overseas without resorting to conscription for service overseas.
In my opinion, this subamendment means that we are not satisfied with the Canadian war effort, because the government has not made certain of adequate reinforcements, and that we recommend a more vigorous war effort.
We are asked more and more reinforcements at a time when two million Frenchmen remain idle witnesses to the liberation of their country while they are beseeching us, through their president General DeGaulle, for weapons and ammunition to fight against Germany.
Why should we keep on sacrificing more Canadian lives when Frenchmen, Belgians, and Dutchmen are more than willing to take their revenge?
Why not gradually withdraw our troops from the front and give to the people of formerly occupied countries the opportunity of squaring accounts with the Germans, thereby affording our men a rest which they have well deserved?
Therefore, the hon. members of the house who vote for the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Mercier wish to tell the government that the administration should' pursue the war effort with even more energy and they thereby create for themselves a reason for supporting, by a subamendment, the very policy advocated by the government's motion which reads as follows:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.

It is as though the right hon. the Prime Minister had secretly told his supporters: "the crisis has subsided, I no -longer need your votes, speak, act and vote without paying any attention to me, but so as to lull and mislead the opinion of the people in your Quebec constituencies."
I shall therefore vote against all amendments and subamendments, as well as against the main motion, because I have always opposed and still oppose every form of participation.
I must also stress the reasons which the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) has put forward for supporting the government. Those are words which the electors from the province of Quebec will surely remember when the time comes for the Liberal party to give an account of its administration. Here is what the former minister of national defence said to justify the fact that he will support the King government, as can be seen in Hansard for November 29, 1944, page 6677:
I believe that these men will be dispatched more quickly and more certainly if this house completes the action which the government has at last taken, by approving the motion, than bj' any other course which the house can take at the present time.
I also wish to draw attention to the talks of the former minister of national defence with the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada, as recorded on the same page. I quote the statement of the former minister of national defence:
4nd one other point I am assuming, unless the Prime Minister states otherwise, that if the government motion carries, the future orders in council specifying additional numbers of men will be passed and put into effect without any reference back again to this house for a vote of confidence or other approval.
The Prime Minister replied:
That is correct.
The former minister of national defence further stated:
I take that to be clear from the minister's statements to the house.
I have mentioned these points specially, but what I want to emphasize is this, that this house and the people of this counrty, and 1 myself, will hold the government-and particularly the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence-to strict account for carrying out vigorously and without wavering then-declared intention to reinforce the army with well-trained men from the N.R.M.A. to the fullest and fastest extent possible.
After that, Mr. Speaker, there is no comment that we could make; we can only await the next election.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

War Effort-Government Policy
The house resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I have just seen the statement made by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) in which he referred to the Memoirs of Sir Robert Borden, and then said:
This citation from the memoirs of Robert Laird Borden has never been denied by the present Prime Minister.
The citation he gave from the Memoirs of Sir Robert Borden was this:
I was told in the summer of 1917 by an intimate friend of King that he (King) was ready to join the proposed union government.
The hon. member (Mr. Roy) then went on to say that that statement in the Memoirs of Sir Robert Borden had never been denied by me. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a scintilla of truth' in it. There is no mention made of who the intimate friend was who is mentioned by Sir Robert Borden, but I have no doubt that someone must have made some such statement to Sir Robert Borden or he would not have included it in his memoirs. May I say that there was never a man in this country who was more constantly, steadily and unequivocally with Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and more opposed as he was to union government than myself.
While I am speaking may I say that I was one of those who were approached to enter the union government. When spoken to, I gave a most emphatic reply that I would not consider any suggestion of the kind.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, this bouse has been called to vote on the government's motion requesting the support of its members for the prosecution of a vigorous war effort.
Since the outbreak of war, our nation's war effort has been vigorous enough to deserve the gratitude and admiration of our allies and their leaders. In a proportion which it would be useless to estimate, this contribution concurred in putting an end to the conquest and subjection of millions of human beings. It helped to ward off a seemingly inevitable catastrophe. To-day, the conquered people recover their freedom and the time is at hand when an heretofore invincible foe will be faced with defeat.
, Could the situation ever have become so favourably to the nations united against the nazi menace without the gigantic effort of our country? If the strength of Canada is taken into account, its war effort has truly been gigantic.
Our varied and abundant materials have been used on every battlefield. In addition to the heavy burden of military production, our country has fed millions of people deprived of the necessities of life by the enemy's wanton destruction. Our population of about twelve million contributed nearly a million Canadians to the armed forces. Through our air training plan, we supplied the allied air forces with trained airmen who have been successful in mastering the formidable German luftwaffe. Countless convoys have reached harbour under the protection of our navy and due to the gallant deeds of our merchant marine.
In the air, on land and on the sea, our airmen our soldiers and sailors have accomplished heroic feats of arms. All the greater their legitimate pride in these achievements, and all the greater our admiration for those heroes, whether famed or obscure, when each chose freely, and uncoerced by any law, to serve in his country's armed forces and1 to defend the cause of justice and liberty.
Canadians from all provinces have shared in this magnificent war effort. Like her sister provinces, Quebec has assumed her just share of the common sacrifice. An imposing number of her sons have enlisted in the armed forces. On the battlefields they have shed their blood alongside other Canadians. They have added heroic pages to the glorious history written by their elders who fought in 1914-1918.
The workers and industrialists of Quebec have done an efficient job as regards war production. In spite of labour shortage, our farmers have redoubled their efforts in order to help feed the peoples of Europe. The people of Quebec have readily accepted heavy taxation and they have subscribed to the victory loans.
French Canadians have ungrudgingly done their fair share. And yet they have not the same reasons as their English-speaking fellow-citizens to be interested in the present war. They did not demand Canada's participation in this war, they have merely accepted it, knowing that such was the wish of the majority and realizing also that their liberty, their civilization, and their national, political and economic interests were at stake.
Their effort is none the less effective and their share in the common sacrifice that much more admirable. Let those who advocate equality of sacrifice for Quebec and the other provinces open their eyes and shed the prejudices in which they are steeped; they will then be forced to recognize that the achievement of Quebec and of French Canadians throughout the country in the present war is
bS02

War Effort-Government Policy
truly remarkable. They have fulfilled the agreements which devolved upon them as parties to the Confederation pact.
In pursuing the war, however, French Canadians have not altered their feeling of antipathy against conscription for overseas service. The people of Quebec clearly expressed1 their ideas on the matter during the plebiscite campaign of April, 1942, and such an attitude can be justified and understood. French Canadians make it a point of honour, for they know that they constitute a minority. If some advocates of conscription are convinced that compulsion is the most effective and fairest method of waging war, how many, on the other hand, urge its enforcement only to assert their supremacy over the minority.
Moreover, French Canadians know, from the experience of 1917, that conscription brought them unfair and1 iniquitous treatment. Their objection to such a system has only been strengthened. On the other hand, political leaders of both racial groups and of all parties have fostered the development of this feeling among French Canadians. Are we to interpret Quebec's attitude towards conscription as one of cowardice or as a refusal to fulfil a national duty? Such a statement would be unfair and mistaken since French Canadians have enlisted for active service in large numbers and1 are still doing so.
Now, on November 23 last, the government through an order in council, enacted conscription for overseas service, under the pretext that in the near future our infantry troops might need to be reinforced with 16,000 men.
Therefore, the vote on the government's motion implies approval or disapproval of that conscription principle. In March, 1940, I was elected on the clear-cut understanding that I would oppose conscription. My electors did' not release me from that pledge at the time of the plebiscite. I respected their will in voting against Bill No. 80. I shall abide by it in voting against the government's motion.
During the present debate I have been unable to acquire the conviction that conscription was indispensable to victory. Besides, is it not being demanded by people of whom an overwhelming majority have not the least knowledge of the data connected with the military problem involved? This debate and the campaign waged throughout the country on the conscription issue have confirmed me in the following conviction: conscription has been used by certain groups as a pretext for rousing public opinion in the secret hope that, as a result of the solemn promises made by members of the govem-

ment that conscription would not be resorted to, the Prime Minister would be faced with a crisis that would bring about the downfall of his government. In some quarters, what is desired is the downfall of the Prime Minister rather than the dispatch of reinforcements for our troops.
Consequently, in voting .against the main motion, I intend to voice my opposition to the enforcement of conscription, without however wishing to condemn the government's policy as a whole.
Considered as a whole and without taking into account that issue of conscription, the policy of the present government is worthy of the gratitude and admiration of the Canadian nation, if one bears in .mind the intricacies of international policy and the complexity of our national and economic life. As a" matter of fact, the government has directed our war effort without upsetting our economic system; it has fought inflation successfully and has consistently sought to plan for a better post-war world.
Nor do I intend, through my vote, to take a stand which might contribute to the isolation of my province. Isolationism can only bring trouble, worry and misfortune to my fellow-citizens.
In conclusion, I express the hope that this momentary crisis which has stirred the country mav afford all Canadians an opportunity ot realizing that the development of our national life is primarily dependent on unity which, in turn, requires a mutual understanding ase on good faith and the respect of the rights of all.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so much has already been said in the current debate, and a great deal that should not have been said, that I am rather hesitant about adding any further remarks at this late date.
I do, however, wish clearly to record my stand regarding conscription for overseas service. During the 1940 election campaign I took no definite stand, but immediately after the evacuation at Dunkirk and the capitulation of France, I realized that this war was something more terrible than any of us could possibly have conceived at the outset.
I have felt, above all, that we as Canadians must not fail those gallant men who have volunteered for service overseas, and that when reinforcements are needed we should not hesitate to see that they are sent. Therefore, when bill 80 was being debated, I spoke unequivocally in favour of conscription of

War Effort-Government Policy
men for overseas service, as can be found in Hansard of June 15, 1942, page 3365, when I said:	[DOT]
Personally I am in favour of conscription in spite of the fact that it proved to be a failure in the last war. I consider it to be by far the fairest, most equitable and surest way of raising an army or obtaining reinforcements.
Again, when debating the soldier gratuity bill on August 11, 1944, page 6286 of Hansard, I am reported as follows:
At the same time I wish to state that there is no one in this chamber who regrets more than I that the government has not seen fit to implement the terms of the National Resources Mobilization Act and draft all who are enrolled in the army for overseas service.
Before the member for Prince (Mr. Ralston), the former minister of national defence, a man for whom I have the highest regard, resigned, I sent a telegram to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on October 30, 1944, advising him of my position on the matter of sending draftees overseas, and I came to Ottawa fully prepared to break with my party if necessary. At this point I wish to emphasize the fact that my opinion was formed long ago and that I was not browbeaten into making the public statement I did on November 7, 1944, either by pressure groups or by any campaign carried on by a certain section of the Ontario press.
Since this house adjourned on August 14, I have had the privilege of sailing on a Canadian naval frigate from the Pacific coast of Canada to the Atlantic coast. For three and one-half weeks I lived with the men on board and talked to all arid sundry, from the captain to the lowliest stoker. Before going aboard, I was particular that no one should know, apart from the officers, of my political affiliation, as I was most anxious that the men would feel free to talk with me. I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians can feel proud of the new ships being added to the Canadian navy, but especially of the men who are serving on these ships.
The vast majority of the crew had seen active service on the north Atlantic convoy run, and many had been on the most hazardous and disagreeable route of all, namely, convoying ships around the coast of Norway to Murmansk, Russia.
Some have gone through the harrowing experience of being torpedoed, and there were very few who had not been in active combat. I was told of one trip on a minesweeper where, out of forty-eight days in mid-winter, forty-five were spent at sea. To me the spirit of these men is magnificent. They do not expect any great concessions to be made them upon their return to civil life and seem quite satisfied
with the rehabilitation schemes offered them. There was one thing, however, that eclipsed all other matters in their minds, and that was that while every hour in the day they were being asked to risk their lives, there were others in uniform who were living comfortably and drawing army pay without having to make sacrifices of any kind. Although they were resentful of this inequality of service, nevertheless their reactions could not be termed spiteful in any sense of the word because they all feel that this is a matter of simple justice; and with them, Mr. Speaker, I must agree.
At this point I should like to pay high tribute to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald). He has built up the Canadian navy from a handful of old obsolete ships to a force that now ranks third among the united nations. I cannot praise too highly the esprit de corps existing in the navy, brought about to a very large degree by methods used in recruiting and training for this branch of our service under the guidance of a most capable minister. In passing, it is worthy of note, that during this readjustment of personnel in the other two branches of service, the navy has recruited neither too many nor too few men and women. Of the 92,000 enlisted in the navy, 38,000 are afloat and
54,000	ashore; the latter figure of course includes Wrens. Actually excluding those under training from consideration, 47-5 per cent of the personnel of the navy is afloat, which shows a phenomenally large percentage in actual combat service.
The frigate I was aboard landed at an Atlantic port on September 22, the very day that the following interesting item appeared in the newspapers of Canada, which I shall quote from the Halifax Chronicle of September 22, 1944:
Canadian Affairs Interest Germans Hon. Angus L. Macdonald Gets Much Publicity in Nazi Press
A general interest in Canadian affairs, with particular emphasis on the northwest, and in personalities on Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, Minister of Naval Affairs, is currently being shown by the German press, according to a letter received yesterday from Fit. Lt. Kingsley E. Brown, R.C.A.F., a former staff member of the Halifax Chronicle, now a prisoner of war in Germany.	.
"Angus L. Macdonald receives more publicity in the German press than any other Canadian," said Fit. Lt. Brown. "His work in building up the Canadian navy, is described in almost flattering terms, and one newspaper, the Berliner Boersen Zeitung, describes Angus L. as working with quiet self-confidence and determination toward his goal. The same article declares that Canada is 'fated by nature to become a great sea power'."
War Effort-Government Policy

Further to my personal contacts with the men in the Canadian navy, regarding their attitude towards the men enrolled under the N.R.M.A., can be added the observations I have received by letter from men in the R.C.A.F. and those serving overseas in the army.
Unfortunately, however, there are all too many civilians in Canada clamouring for an all-out conscription of man-power for overseas service who themselves are giving very little or no thought to their contribution to Canada's all-out war effort. I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Brockville Recorder and Times of November 6, 1944, and which logically sets forth that all zombies are not to be found in the army:
- The term "zombie" is one of contempt now widely applied to young men of military age and the proper physical qualifications who decline to bear their share of national responsibilities in time of war by volunteering for general military service.
How many of the older people of both sexes who ridicule and censure these "zombies" can themselves say that they are doing all they possibly can to fight and win the war? How many of them refrain from presenting themselves at blood clinics to save the lives of the men overseas when it is quite within their power to do so? How many of them are by no means above cheating on their food or gasoline rations when both are short because of the pressing needs overseas? How many of them do not object to chiselling a bit on prices in disregard of the ceilings which have been established and held so far that Canada may be properly mobilized for the winning of the vTar?
How many of these civilians are ready to perjure themselves in order to secure tires to which they are not entitled and which remain in short supply because of overseas demands? How many of them decline to cooperate in salvage campaigns for the benefit of the overseas operations, or refuse to assist in Red Cross workrooms, grumble and cheat about their wartime taxes and offer the flimsiest excuses for their failure to buy victory bonds when they are well able to lend their country this Vital assistance?
All of Canada's "zombies" are not in the home defence army by any means. There are thousands more of them all over the map in practically every community, people who, although well able to do so, decline to bear their full share of responsibility when their country is at war or who chisel and cheat at the expense of their country and its fighting men. They should be very careful about the criticism they direct towards the young Canadians who decline to volunteer for general service when they themselves are by no means free of stigma.
And now I would like to call to the attention of this house still another type of zombie, the political leader who directs his party by remote control and during this critical period fulfils his war service by holding party organization meetings from one end of Canada to the other. Surely his place should be right
JMr. Fulford.]
here in this chamber where he would be made to retract irresponsible remarks such as were made last night over the C.B.C.
In conclusion, I need hardly mention that I have no intention whatsoever of voting for the subamendment now before this house, nor do I intend to be duped by the political trickery of the reactionary Tory party in voting for its amendment in that party's futile attempt to gain the reins of power.
I am supporting the main motion because I am positive in my own mind that the government intends to see that adequate reinforcements reach our gallant fighting men on the western front in Europe. We can already see the effect that P.C. 8891 has had on the personnel of the N.R.M.A. and civilian population alike, by the tremendous recent increase in enlistments for active service. This is a very gratifying aspect, but the government is bound to send 16,000 N.R.M.A. men in excess of the original estimate for reinforcements and, should more be required, more will be senU-even should further orders in council have to be passed.
Conscription for overseas service is an accomplished fact and a vote of confidence in the government will allow the Prime Minister to continue to lead Canada in a war effort that has been a source of amazement and an inspiration to the rest of the civilized world.

It is not very often that in this house we have witnessed a debate of such great importance. As one of the generation mainly concerned with the object of the discussion, I feel it my duty to participate in this debate. I intend to try to do so in English, but that compels me, Mr. Speaker, to appeal to your sympathy and to the best of your good will, and if in the course of my remarks it happens unfortunately that I say something that may hurt the feelings of any hon. members with whom I have the honour to sit in this house, or of any of our Canadian citizens outside this parliament, please do not impute it to any ill will on my part but to a lack of ability to speak the beautiful language that you, sir, speak so magnificently.
It is my definite intention to try to follow the example that was given by most hon. members who have already spoken since we were called to meet in this house.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING

speechtext:
I have listened with pleasure to
most of the speeches that have been delivered

War Effort-Government Policy
and I have been pleased to observe that most hon. members who have spoken so far did so as good Canadians and in the way that speeches ought to be made. This is an example which I feel bound to follow and I shall try to deserve the same compliment.
I appreciate the fact that it has always been rather difficult in our country to be a good Canadian. If we consider the difficulties of our national life we shall realize that the conditions under which we are living in Canada are exceptional. I imagine that it must be very easy in Great Britain to be a good Britisher. It must be very easy in the United States to be a good American, and very probably ft must be rather an easy thing even in Germany to be a good German and in France to be a good Frenchman. In Canada, however, it is different by reason of the fact that we are two races, that we speak two languages, and that we have not all the same religious creed. I understand that in our country it is rather difficult to suggest the real formula of the best Canadianism and I am perfectly well open to understand the point of view of anyone. In times such as these through which we are now passing I do not think that any of us can be anything but real Canadians. This is the very spirit that has inspired the humble remarks that I shall make to you this afternoon.
The proposition that is put to us can be summarized in this way. The government has decided to call the members of parliament, the representatives of the Canadian people, to determine this question, to find out whether we are ready to support the government in maintaining its present policy in connection with the war, which is nothing but conscription. I intend to oppose that proposition, and if you will kindly permit me, Mr. Speaker, I will give some of the reasons I have for doing what I intend to do.
I do not find that policy useful for the army; on the contrary I find it useless for the army and most unfair to the Canadian people. So far as the army is concerned, I must admit that I am far from being an expert qualified to talk about it, but I have heard since the beginning of this session so many people who were in the same position that I think I am entitled to discuss the question just the same. But we have heard experts, the best we have in Canada", the present Minister of .National Defence, Mr. McNaughton, for whom I have the greatest respect, and the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) for whom I have a great deal of admiration, because I have always admired men who have opinions and
who have the courage to stand or fall for them. What did we learn from these two experts whose competence cannot be denied? They did not agree, Mr. Speaker. They were divided in their opinions. Before November 22 we were told by the builder of the Canadian army, by the first man responsible for the victories of the Canadian Army on the different fronts, that conscription was not necessary; that there was no question yet that we should apply that form of policy for reinforcements overseas. The views of the other individual were just the opposite, and now we are placed in the position where we have to face the responsibility and to make up our own minds and act according to our own conscience.
We were told, Mr. Speaker, with a bit of exaggeration, that the Canadian Army fighting overseas at the present moment was in a desperate condition. We were told that if we did not send a few thousand more Canadians to help them that this will be the last and that our soldiers would, be practically wiped out from the battlefields. I can hardly admit or conceive such a thing. If we take what was told to us prior to November 22 and what is told to us now, and if we consider the news that is coming to us through the newspapers about the way things are going on the battle front, I am inclined to think that what has changed, is not the war condition but rather the political condition in our country, and I do not feel that that is sufficient for me to take the step of voting in favour of the government on a measure such as the one now before us.
Let us assume that the condition in which the Canadian Army is fighting overseas is absolutely desperate; let us assume that we have to send reinforcements as we are proposing to do now, we have 900,000 soldiers who have enlisted voluntarily.

subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Not in the front line.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
We have the American army with millions of soldiers, we have the British army with millions of soldiers and we have to think of the other armies of Russia fighting on the other front. If these soldiers, millions and millions of them, do not succeed in achieving the work they have begun, I cannot admit that this handful of Canadians will be successful. The real reason why our armies overseas are placed in the position in which they are to-day is not that they lack reinforcements. I am rather of the opinion that since the beginning of the war Canadian soldiers have been given too much

War Effort-Government Policy
to do. We have to consider that the Canadian front covers a lot of territory. It goes from Hong Kong to Dieppe, passing by Africa, fighting in the Mediterranean sea, fighting the battle of Sicily, and still fighting to-day in Italy. We were at Dieppe; we were in Normandy; we were in Belgium; we were in Holland, and to-day we are in Germany. I am not surprised to see that we are beginning to be short of men, because we have undertaken too much, as was so ably and eloquently presented by my best friend, the hon. member for Riehelieu-Ver-cheres (Mr. Cardin). We have undertaken too much, Mr. Speaker, and the proposition that the government puts before us is not a remedy for the situation. I cannot believe that the situation is what we are told it is.
We learned about the situation of our armies at the front from the newspapers before we learned it from the headquarters of the army. If it is true that our armies are in a desperate situation, I have enough confidence in the Americans and the British to come to our help. After all, there would be nothing to be ashamed of in the Canadians being helped over there when we consider what we have achieved since the beginning of the war. There is not, I believe, a single allied nation we have not helped in some way, since the beginning of this war in 1939. Among the united nations we Canadians have done the most for the war. We were in it at the very beginning, two years before the United States. We have given our money, we have sent our men. We were asked to give the tools. We gave the tools. I do not wish to be sarcastic, because I hate that kind of argument. However, it seems to me as if after giving the tools we will have to finish the job.
I come now to the second part of what I intend to say, Mr. Speaker. I said at the beginning of my remarks that I am going to vote against the main motion, firstly, because I find it useless for the army,_ and secondly, because I find it most unfair to the Canadian people. We are now reaching the beginning of the policy of the last man. Probably in a few months from now it will be the policy of the last cent. I do admit the responsibility of our country in connection with this conflict. I admit that as Canadians we have some duties to perform in order to help the civilized and Christian nations. But those duties do not go beyond our responsibility. Where are our responsibilities in the war? Those responsibilities were really created by the treaty of Versailles which was not cooked up on this side of the

Atlantic. We were not responsible for the mistakes made in that treaty. As a French author has said, the surgeons of Versailles forgot the abscess in the belly of the European continent. That abscess consisted of the 65,000,000 Germans who faced 45,000,000 Frenchmen.
The Germans had not felt the effects of the war. There had been no fighting on their home soil. Every opportunity was given to them to rebuild their army. It is not the fault of the Canadian people that the French were prevented from recovering from Germany that to which they were entitled by the treaty of Versailles. We are not to blame because Germany failed to carry out the provisions of the treaty of Versailles. We were not among those who forced the French to retire from the Ruhr. As a former premier of Ontario said, we were not responsible for the financiers of Great Britain, at a time when 6,000,000 good Britishers were almost starving, lending money to Hitler in order to permit him to build up his army and train it for the work he has been doing these last few years.
It is most unfair to put upon the shoulders of the Canadian people this heavy burden which should be placed only on the shoulders of those responsible for this war. When I voted for the declaration of war on Germany I believed that it was to prevent this country from becoming a German and nazi province.
I realized at that time that there were certain dangers facing us, that we had a duty to help Great Britain to force the enemy to stay on the continent. We have done that job, and more. We have contributed magnificently in the liberating of half a dozen nations on the European continent. They could not do the job themselves and it was up to us to help them, but the job is done. Those nations are free, but where are their soldiers?
I believe that they should enlist voluntarily. But if they have become soldiers to continue the fight, to finish the job, where have they gone? The Canadian Army is now in a bad position, we are told that it is in desperate straits, but where are those people whom we have helped so generously? After all we have done I do not think there is any reason to be ashamed of in expecting some help from them at this time.
I realize that human beings are liable to make mistakes, but I want it understood that I am not fighting for the province of Quebec alone. I am not fighting for the city of Montreal or my constituency, only I am fighting for the Canadian people. If I speak like this I do so because I want you to believe

War Effort-Government Policy
that I have no other feeling but that of honest Canadianism. I speak for all of Canada when I ask the members of this house to vote against the measure proposed by the government. I do not pretend that I speak in the name of Quebec or any other province. I am not going to make a small provincial problem into a national problem, and I certainly am not going to make it into an imperial problem. It is not an imperial problem; it is not a world problem; it is not a provincial problem, it is a Canadian problem and as a Canadian member of the Canadian parliament, considering what our nation has done'since the beginning of the war, I must refuse to support this measure. I repeat the words of the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe. I will vote against conscription; I will never admit conscription to send Canadians overseas. More than that I will fight any government that would force Canadians to go overseas. Our soldiers are there and no doubt more will enlist. But we have no right to force those who want" to stay here to go overseas. They are free men and the most solemn commitments were made by all political parties, with the exception of one, by the Tories, the Liberals and all political parties that they -would not have to go. They accepted' that pledge.
Some hon. members will say that the situation has changed, but I do not think it has. Because of propaganda in the newspapers some of the mothers, sisters, fathers and sweethearts of boys overseas have been led to believe that if this step is not taken their boys overseas will suffer. But that is not the, case. To-day the Canadian people have been poisoned with propaganda, as they were in 1921, in 1925, in 1940, and again in 1942 where, right in the very heart of the province of Ontario, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was defeated. At that time we were at war. We were fighting against Germany, and the situation did not look as good as it does to-day. The Canadian people rejected all those who were advocating conscription for overseas. I admit that in certain parts of our country the minds of the people have changed, not because of the situation at the bottlefronts, not because Canada is not doing its utmost to win the war, not because we have refused to do our share, but because of propaganda.
After the war they will realize the position in which they are placed to-day by some of their fellow-citizens whom I do not consider worthy of being classed as good1 Canadians. After this war, exactly as they did after 1917, they will realize the mistake they have made. We know that in 1917 in certain parts of
Canada public opinion was poisoned' as it is to-day. Those who can recall the debates which took place in the House of Commons at that time will remember that exactly the same arguments were used, exactly the same reasoning, exactly the same propositions. But within a few months after the war public opinion realized it had been misled by propaganda, and since 1917, by all Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific conscription has been considered a shameful disaster, despite the fact that, as to-day, it was sought by many Canadians. They were misled at that time; they were misinformed. When they realized that they had been . made the victims of propaganda they voted against those who put conscription into effect. The same is happening to-day; history is repeating itself, because conditions are the same to-day as they were then.
I admit, of course, that many among the people living in this land are in favour of conscription, just as they were in 1917. But to-day if they favour conscription they do so for exactly the same reasons as were offered in that earlier year, namely because they are badly led and because they have been poisoned by propaganda. I say that a few months after the war is over we will see exactly the same reaction-take my word for it-because the situation to-day is exactly the same as it was then. The government will appear shameful in the eyes of all real Canadians, because it will be seen that it has fallen into the ditch, into the hole, because it has been afraid of some Canadians who have tried to put it in a bad position- Canadians who have been playing the cheapest kind of political game, and that is all.
While there is still time, I urge the government to change its mind. It is not sufficient to put a drop of water into the ocean-a handful of Canadians. What is that in war as we see it to-day? What does conscription mean to the Canadian people? After the war we will know what it means, as we knew after the war of 1914-18. We have not forgotten the first conscription measure, and we are going to remember the second one.
I feel I must apologize, Mr. Speaker, for having spoken too long and perhaps too loudly. I ask you, sir, to believe that what I said has come from the bottom of my heart. I shall take the action I have indicated because deep in my heart I hold the honest belief that it is by so doing I best serve my country at the present time.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING
subsubtopic: VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate at this time,
690S
War Effort-Government Policy

my object is not to delay the proceedings of the house, but to state the reasons for the vote I shall be called upon to cast, either on the main motion, on the amendment introduced by the Progressive-Conservative party, or, on the sub-amendment moved by the hon. member for Montreal-Mercier (Mr. Jean).
The Progressive-Conservative party's amendment reads as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the government has not made certain of adequate and continuous trained reinforcements by requiring all N.R.M.A. personnel whether now or hereafter enrolled to serve in any theatre of war and has failed to assure equality of service and sacrifice.	.
Mr. Speaker, if that amendment were carried, it would mean that all draftees now on strength or to be called in future under the N.R.M. Act, would have to serve on any theatre of war, be it in India, China or the Philippines, apart from the European theatre where Canadian troops are now fighting. It is unfortunate that such an amendment should have been moved. I believe that, under the present circumstances, far from promoting national unity, that amendment will tend to disrupt it and, should this happen, it will inevitably conduce to a lessening rather than to the maintenance or the increase of our war effort.
It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that this whole campaign for conscription is the doing of a group with a thirst for power and who, in such a campaign, would use the Province of Quebec as a means of splitting the country, at least for some years to come.
In that campaign, the Conservative party, under the guise of patriotism, is expecting to come into office and implement anew its reactionary policies which have always consisted and still consist in the protection of a privileged group at the expense of the general public.
Therefore, I shall have no hesitation in voting against the amendment of the Progressive Conservative party.
Then there is the subamendment introduced by the hon. member for Mercier. I regret that the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) should have attempted to give this amendment a meaning other than the one it contains. In order, therefore to enlighten you on the matter, and to prove that it really has the meaning which the mover intended to give it, I shall refer to an editorial taken from the issue of Tuesday, December 5, of the Ottawa newspaper Le Droit. It bears the signature of Mr. L'Heureux. Here is what it says, with reference to the subamendment of Mr. Jean:

There can be no misunderstanding. That amendment is obviously a motion of want of confidence in the government who is charged with having wrecked the voluntary system' and with having been brought, by a wrong distribution of our man-power resources, to resort to conscription for overseas.
Such is Le Droit's editorial opinion on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Mercier. I will therefore vote for the subamendment.
The main motion reads as follows:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
I would have voted for it had order in council 8891 not been passed. This order authorizes the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McNaughton) to conscript up to 16,000 draftees if volunteer enlistments are insufficient to provide adequate reinforcements for our infantry fighting in northwestern Europe and in Italy. As I said during the debate on Bill No. 80, against which I voted, I agreed at the time of the 1940 election to oppose any proposal advocating conscription for overseas service; I shall remain faithful to my pledge and I intend to keep the promise made to my constituents who honoured me by choosing me as their representative and by placing their trust in me.
True, the number of men needed is not great, and according to the information supplied by General McNaughton, reinforcements are doubtlessly required in order to keep the various Canadian units in action. But would it not have been possible to withdraw our men temporarily from the front lines to enable them to reequip themselves, rest, recuperate and bring their units up to strength? Such a respite would have allowed the new Minister of National Defence to make necessary arrangements and to resort to the voluntary system in which he has confidence, and undoubtedly he would have made a success of it.
If the voluntary system has not been as successful as was expected it is probably because the former minister of national defence lacked faith in the system, and success is seldom attained where confidence is lacking. The former minister may have known that a large number of the senior officers in the various camps of the country did not favour the voluntary system; on the contrary, they took advantage of every opportunity to discourage voluntary enlistments. In support of my contention, I may say that some time ago two French-Canadian recruiting officers went to a camp in British Columbia to secure the voluntary enlistment of French Canadians, but without avail. Why were they unsuccessful? Because the officers of the camp barred

War Effort-Government Policy
them from entering the premises and interviewing their fellow citizens. In view of this, it becomes evident that voluntary enlistment has been systematically discouraged for political reasons alone and surely not from patriotic motives.
Speaking of patriotism, I wish to state that the province of Quebec is just as patriotic as any other, a fact that it has proven over and over again and especially on two memorable occasions which I do not intend to recall at the moment. In the present conflict, its citizens have done their duty. However, how often are insults hurled at them by certain sections of the press and a number of ignorant fanatics?
I said I would be brief for I do not wish to delay the work of the house. I repeat in closing that I have always opposed and will continue to oppose conscription for overseas service. It is not through personal interest that I take that stand, in the hope that my sons may be exempted from military service, for, Mr. Speaker, three of them have enlisted voluntarily; one was in Holland the last time I heard from him, last Friday.
In opposing conscription I am upholding a principle which has inspired all my life: for the French Canadians and for myself what counts above all else is national pride.
(Text)

Mr. Speaker, I have followed with close attention the drama that has been enacted on the floor of this house since parliament reassembled, and while it is not my intention to speak at any length in this debate I have come to certain conclusions that I propose to place upon the record. But before I do so I wish to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) on the speech he made in this house yesterday afternoon. I do not care to deal in superlatives but in my opinion his speech will do more to promote national unity in this country than any other speech or any article that has been written in this country for many j'ears past. I know and he knows that the speech he made will be severely criticized and unfairly criticized in some cases, but I believe that it is only by stating facts and by appealing to reason-not by relying on worn-out political doctrines and appealing to prejudices-that unity can be achieved in this country. There are occasions when events make former promises and former policies uncouth. This I believe is such an occasion.
I have never criticized or blamed, either in this house or outside of it, the majority of the people in the province of Quebec for the stand they have taken on this issue. I
have not agreed with the stand they have taken; I have been very much opposed to it. But I realize that you cannot preach one policy to one part of the country year in and year out, that you cannot make solemn promises to the people in one part of this country year in and year out, and then expect them in the twinkling of an eye or in a very short time to change their opinions. I do not blame or criticize them but I do blame and I do criticize the leaders and the public men in their province who preached those doctrines to them and made those promises to them.
In this country, as in many countries, there are bound to be great differences of opinion arising from differences in racial origin, religious and other prejudices, differences over political issues and differences over systems of government. These differences of opinion are bound to arise and at times lead to great bitterness; but in any free and democratic country I fail to understand why they should lead to national disunity, no matter how great these differences may be. I believe that in a free and democratic country, and Canada is a free and democratic country, there is one foundation, and one foundation only, upon which national unity can be based, and that is that when the representatives of the people in parliament declare war, all Canadians must be prepared to fight and, if necessary, die for their country. Unless all Canadians are prepared to go forth and fight when Canada declares war, unless they are prepared to subscribe to the doctrine Of equality of sacrifice, there can be no unity in this country. The basis of unity in this country can be found only in the principle that in a time of war there must be equality of sacrifice and that all able-bodied men must be prepared to meet the enemy wherever he is to be found and to fight him until peace is declared. Until we are in agreement on this principle I believe that the words "national unity" can have very little meaning in this country.
To state briefly the conclusions I have come to as a result of what I have heard on the floor of the house during this debate: The first is that the need for trained men overseas is imperative and that the voluntary system has failed to supply the number required. The second is that there has been a dangerous and an unjustifiable delay in providing the needed reinforcements. The third is that the stand taken by the former minister of national defence, the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston), to obtain those reinforcements has been vindicated. He has rendered. I believe, a great service to his country. He

War Effort-Government Policy

has proved himself again to be a loyal- and patriotic Canadian, who has placed the needs of our army and the honour of our country ahead of personal ambition or party consideration.
The fourth conclusion I have come to is this, and I do not think much emphasis has been laid upon it here: I am of the opinion from what I have heard that in one respect at least our army organization should be improved. We have learned during the course of this debate that we do not keep records in Canada of our reinforcement pools overseas. I believe it is important that such records be kept in order that the government know the true position of affairs. It should not be necessary for the Minister of National Defence or any other minister to go overseas to learn what our reinforcement position is and the strength of our army in the field. The former minister of national defence told us that what he learned when he went to the battle areas came as a shock to him, and when he went over the figures at Canadian military headquarters in England he found that the situation required radical measures. I think and believe that those figures and this information should have been available here, and that steps should be taken to have it made available, and that when it is obtained, the Minister of National Defence and the war committee should keep it before them so they will know how our reinforcement position overseas stands and the number of men we hare in the reinforcement pools.
The order in council which has been tabled by the government gives approval for the sending of 16,000 men overseas. In my opinion it is not a satisfactory solution of this problem. It is a compromise. It can be '[DOT]egarded only as a temporary adjustment. It is only a partial policy of overseas conscription. It may allay for a time the force of the spontaneous upsurge of public opinion that took place throughout this country when the people were led to believe that the Prime Minister and his government did not intend to send any of our home defence army overseas, but I do not think it will be satisfactory to the people of this country when it is fully understood. The order in council does not make certain of adequate and continuous reinforcements or require men called up to serve in any theatre of war. It has been described, and correctly described I think, by the former minister of national defence as "a half-hearted, piecemeal method." He said he was far from satisfied with the halting attitude it indicates. I agree fully with the objection he has taken to it and with the objections which have been taken to it by

the leader of the opposition and other hon. members on this side and in other quarters of the house. I do not think, however, that any useful purpose could' be served by taking up the time of the house in repeating those objections.
It is plain that it was an aroused public opinion that forced the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his cabinet to introduce this order in council. The Prime Minister preferred it either to resigning his office or to calling an election. The Minister of National Defence, who has the duty of carrying out this order, said the day it was tabled in this house, as reported in Hansard of November 23, page 6529:
I am a confirmed believer in a system of voluntary service for the Canadian army.
In all seriousness I fail to understand how a man who is a confirmed believer in the voluntary system can in conscience and in honour carry out this order in council which makes provision for conscription for overseas service.
I have heard the views of the Minister of Agriculture and I have read in the press the speeches which were made by the Minister of Fisheries, the Minister of Munitions and Supply and other members of the government. I do not propose to review them this afternoon, because they have been placed on the records of this house, but I will say this, that I do not see how, when you have in the cabinet some members who are opposed to this order in council, some members who support it because they were forced to do so, and only some members who believe in it, that we can have confidence that the government will carry it out or see that it is properly carried out. If members of the cabinet hold1 these and similar views, how can we have confidence that the government will send trained reinforcements overseas in sufficient numbers and thereby maintain a vigorous war effort?
I propose to vote against the motion and support the amendment; and may I point out in conclusion that any person who votes against the amendment of the opposition votes against conscription for overseas service.

Mr. Speaker, I anticipate a little applause from some hon. gentlemen opposite when I say that my remarks are going to be very brief. I am not going to follow the remarks of the last speaker, the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen), except to say that his speech was the most tolerant and the least bitter of any speech that has been made so far by members opposite.

War Effort-Government Policy
I was elected by a very large majority for the constituency of Kings in 1940 to come to Ottawa to support the Liberal party, under the leadership of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and in 1942 that government was released from its commitments in regard to conscription. A few weeks ago I was again given the nomination for my own riding and I pledged myself that when I came to Ottawa I would support the Liberal party. If I had not done that I would not have been given the nomination for the next election.
On Tuesday night last we were privileged1 to listen to an able speech delivered by the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Lapointe), who is himself an officer fresh from the battlefront opposing the Germans. He told us that conscription was unnecessary, undesirable and uncalled for at the present time, and I do not believe that the soldiers at the front are asking to be reinforced by conscripts at this stage of the war.
Opposition members have been telling us about numerous letters they have been receiving from soldiers overseas asking for reinforcements to come quickly. I think there are in the fighting lines as many soldiers per capita of population from my constituency as there are from any other constituency in Canada, and I have received no such letters. I have received letters from wives and mothers asking that their husbands or their sons who are overseas be sent home for a rest if they have been over for four or five years, and I am glad to note that that is the policy of the new Minister of National Defence.
I am sorry that I cannot support the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Jean), although personally I favour the voluntary system, and I want to see a united Canada, but this is not a free-for-all system of government. We are told by those who should know that the voluntary system has fallen down. That should not have happened after five years of wise planning. That is, of course, my own opinion, but regardless of the comparative merits or demerits of voluntary enlistment and the conscription system I do not believe that compulsion would have been necessary at this late stage of the war if someone had not blundered. I do not think the Prime Minister of Canada was the one who blundered, although it might have meant disaster to him and to Canada. However, in accepting the resignation of the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) and appointing in his place a man of General McNaughton's well known anticonscription views, the Prime Minister has
100-434J
proven his sincerity in the belief that the voluntary system had not so suddenly fallen down, and it is hard to believe that it did.
If the motion before the house carries we shall continue to have a voluntary system as well as power in the hands of the Minister of National Defence to send reinforcements overseas from the home defence army if necessary. If the amendment carries we shall have total conscription and nothing else for anywhere in the world in the hands of Tory exploiters and profiteers as we had it after 1917, with its abuses and scandals, which will never* be forgotten.
If compulsion is inevitable, of the two evils I intend to choose the lesser and to vote for the motion of the Prime Minister, thereby permitting our unsurpassed war effort to be pursued without interruption until final victory is achieved over Germany, which I believe could have been done under the voluntary system properly managed.
In other words, I intend to stand by the Prime Minister of Canada, and that is what the vast majority of my constituents want me to do. I am glad to see the Prime Minister in such good form and that he knows when he should relax, for on Monday night when the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher) was reading to him a merciless lecture, prepared no doubt at Bracken House, the Prime Minister, who had heard the same type of speech recited on several occasions recently, fell sound asleep and continued to sleep for ten minutes until precisely eleven o'clock, when he awoke, apparently much refreshed, which reminds me that repetition is one of the best treatments for insomnia. Try it. If you go to bed tonight and cannot sleep, repeat over and over again one of those little prayers that you learned at your mother's knees and you will soon be in dreamland.

I do not intend to prolong the debate. My only reason for rising at this time is to clarify the position I am going to take when called upon to vote on the amendment to the amendment now before the house. I propose to vote for the subamendment of the hon. member for Mercier, not that I so much like the wording of it or the manner in which he has expressed his views; but in the main I claim that the subamendment contains an expression of opinion in favour of the continuance of the voluntary system and, second, an expression against compulsion, against conscription. Therefore while admitting that the wording of the subamendment has not been very happy-in fact, it is poor-I ap-
War Effort-Government Policy

prove its substance and will favour it because it includes the two main points upon which my own conviction remains.

I declare the amendment to the amendment lost. The question is on the amendment. All those in favour of the amendment will please say "aye".
