speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to move an amendment to the main motion which will call for the addition of certain words to that motion. The words which I suggest to be added were moved in the form of a subamendment by the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) on November 27. Although that subamendment was ruled out of order by Your Honour at that stage of the proceedings, the content and the significance of our proposal will already be familiar to hon. members.
I should like to state briefly our reasons for introducing this amendment at this time. We feel on the one hand that the Prime Minister's motion which is now before the house is ambiguous in its wording, and that it presents the house with no real issue upon which hon. members must make a decision. On the other hand we feel that there are certain very real issues before the Canadian people at this time, and that this House of Commons should come to a decision on those real issues. As we see it, the real issues are two. First of all, now that partial conscription for overseas service has been made the law of the land there are a number of matters relating to the application of conscription which need to be cleared up. We feel that a straight-forward statement of the position should be made and that all distinctions and discrimination between drafted and volunteer personnel should be removed. Further, now that Canada has taken the step of conscripting manpower for overseas service, we are convinced that the people of this country look for this parliament and this government to take the step which should have been taken beforehand, and certainly should not be delayed, namely conscription of wealth and industry, in order that we may be assured of a total war effort, adequate reestablishment of the members of our fighting forces, and full employment after the war.
I made the statement a moment ago that we do not see in the motion now before the house, as moved by the Prime Minister, a real issue, and I should like to document that statement by a few references to statements made by the Prime Minister in his speech

on November 27 when he moved the main motion. First of all, the vote on the motion before us is not a vote on the principle of conscription. That has been affirmed by many hon. members. The Prime Minister stated it clearly, at page 6617 of Hansard*'
The issue of conscription is not being decided by this vote; it was settled two years ago.
In the second place the vote on the motion now before us is not a vote for or against order in council P.C. 8891. Again I quote what the Prime Minister said, at page 6617 of Hansard of November 27:
Let me say of this motion, it does not ask for approval of order in council P.C. 8891.
In the third place, the vote on the motion which is now before us does not call for confidence in the government with respect to all of its policies. The Prime Minister, as reported at page 6608 of Hansard, said:
What the government is seeking to-day is not an expression of confidence in all of its policies.
Further, at page 6617 he said:
The motion does not ask for an unlimited vote of confidence in the government.
Later on, on the same page, he said:
The motion is not to be construed as an endorsation of government policies generally.
If the vote on the motion of the Prime Minister is not a vote on conscription, not a vote of approval or disapproval of order in council 8891, and not a vote of confidence in the government generally, what is the vote which is asked of this house in the motion now before us? The Prime Minister made it quite clear. He pointed out that it is not a vote of confidence in the government by means of which the house is asked to approve or disapprove of the government for having brought in P.C. 8891; it is simply a vote of confidence in the government as the administration to be entrusted with giving effect to a law that is already part of the law of this country. Frankly I do not quite understand why so many of the Liberal members find it difficult to vote confidence in their leader, entirely apart from what the rest of us may think of him, when he put it in that way for them. He made it clear in a number of places in his speech on November 27 that the issue before the house was simply whether the present government should continue to conduct Canada's war effort, and without quoting him verbatim, he used such words as "to give effect to the decision that has already been made". So that what this house is asked for is not a vote of confidence in the government generally, not a vote of confidence in the government because it passed P.C. 8891, but simply a vote of confidence in the govern-

War Effort-Government Policy
ment as a tool to administer a law which is now in effect, as if they were not even responsible for it.-
These times are serious, and we do not feel that is an important enough measure to be the main vote of this special sitting of parliament. We feel that parliament should be called upon to decide on the more burning questions which are before the country. I may say, in passing, that this issue as to whether or not confidence is to be voted in the administration as a means of carrying out this order in council might have been worthy of our consideration but for the fact that the Prime Minister himself as much as told those of us who are not in the Liberal fold that it is none of our business anyway, for on page 6613 of Hansard he said:
If I cannot get enough support out of my own party to feel sure that the men of my own party are behind me without depending on those who' are politically opposed, then my resignation will go in to the Governor General. . . .
This means that even if the government were to be sustained by this House of Commons, but if that vote in order to be a majority, required some who were not on the government side of the house, the Prime Minister would offer his resignation. In other words, the decision as to whether or not this administration is the one to carry out the terms of this order in council, according to the way the Prime Minister has put it, rests solely with the Liberal party. We feel that this is turning a serious crisis such as we have had in this country into a melodrama when one realizes that this house contains an overwhelming majority of members who are prepared to vote confidence in the present administration and in the present Prime Minister.
Some members have suggested from this side of the house that the words of the Prime Minister exonerate opposition members from any blame if the government is defeated. We do not feel that way about it. In fact, we do not feel that his statement absolves us in this group from our duty and responsibility as representatives of a large section of the Canadian people. We feel, notwithstanding the way in which this has been treated as a Liberal family affair, that it is our duty to present to parliament and to the government what we regard as the issues before the people at the present time, and so it	is because	of that	belief that	atthis stage	of the proceedings	we	present	tothe house	again the	amendment	which was moved on	November	27.
May I emphasize that we do this in no perfunctory sense. The people of Canada will be interested to know how the members of other groups vote on this amendment. For example, I hold in my hand a telegram which I received a few days ago, among the many communications that hon. members have been receiving during this sitting. It happens to come from the Orange Lodge of Greater Winnipeg, but I ask my hon. friends from the province of Quebec to listen closely as I read this telegram and to note the absence of any prejudice of any kind from it. I also ask my hon. friends of thp Progressive Conservative party to listen closely to what these members of the Loyal Orange Lodge in the city from which I come are asking at this time. The telegram is dated at Winnipeg, December 2, and addressed to me at Ottawa. It reads as follows:
Whereas the Canadian government over its man-power policy seems to have lost the confidence of practically the entire personnel of the fighting services and whereas the Canadian public appears to be in a state of revolt against the government and whereas the government seems to be in a liquid state of mind, therefore this county Orange Lodge of Greater Winnipeg and district in annual sessions tins thirtieth day of November, 1944, unanimously urge the government that the only solution to their problem of equality in waging total war is the application of conscription of wealth, industry and man-power. We further urge the government that to regain the confidence and respect of the nation it should adopt such a policy immediately.
County of Winnipeg Loyal Orange Lodge C 64 C. G. Perry, Secretary.
It is in the spirit of that telegram that we move our amendment at this time. It is not a motion of confidence or non-confidence in the government. It proposes that certain words be added to the main motion. We feel that these words should be added, and if they are we will vote for the motion as amended by the addition of these words. We are doing this in part to make our position clear and also because we feel that the people of Canada would like all the hon. members of this house to make their position clear on this twofold question of a clean breast of the policy of conscription and total conscription of wealth and industry as well as man-power to ensure a total war effort, adequate reestablishment and full employment in the post war period. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South'(Mr. Gillis), that the following words be added to the motion :
which in the opinion of this house requires the immediate removal of all distinctions between drafted and volunteer personnel, thus making the entire home defence army available for reinforcements overseas, and requires
War Effort-Government Policy

further the total mobilization of all the resources of Canada, material and financial as well as human, to ensure a total war effort, adequate reestablishment of the members of our fighting forces, and full employment after the war.

In the moment when I have been considering this amendment, I should like the hon. gentleman who has moved it to give me his comments thereon in the light of the subamendment which has already been decided and disposed of by the house. It dealt with using to the best advantage the general service personnel in Canada and the volunteers -overseas without resorting to conscription for overseas service. The hon. member's amendment deals with drafted and volunteer personnel, thus making the entire home defence army available for reinforcements overseas, and requires further the total mobilization of all the resources of Canada, material and financial as well as human. The issue of volunteers has been raised by the subamendment and the issue of conscription was raised in the amendment. The amendment which the hon. member has submitted to the house, as I see it, requires both human resources and material resources to be used. One portion of it has already been decided by the house. I have already ruled that one cannot approve and disapprove the same proposition, but that the document which deals with it must be considered in its entirety. If one portion of the amendment is out of order it renders the whole of it out of order, and the house has decided the question in the subamendment. Unless the hon. member can show me some reason other than those I have already stated I shall have to rule this amendment out of order, but I shall be glad to hear him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it strikes
me that the house has made only a partial decision on the conscription question by the two votes taken thus far to-day. If the position that Your Honour is now taking is valid it seems to me that the issue was decided by the vote on the subamendment and that there should not have been a vote on the amendment. I would point out further that the amendment which I have moved accepts what is implied in the main motion, namely, an en-dorsation of conscription as far as it has gone. The issue of the main motion, whatever that issue is, has not yet been decided by the house. I would suggest that the ruling that you are making on the basis of the votes already taken on the subamendment and on the amendment would have a bearing on the vote to be taken on the main motion if you are to be consistent.
fWr. Knowles.]
In this amendment we are asking for an extension of what is implied by the main motion still before the house. It does not rule on the basic question of conscription of man-power; it accepts what we have and asks for a clearing up of its provisions and an extension of the principle of conscription to cover wealth and industry as well. It strikes me, Mr. Speaker, that it should be declared in order. If Your Honour will recall when the amendment made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was ruled out of order you said that the amendment was not in order at that time but that it could be offered after the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) had been disposed of. We have reached that stage. I realize that in the meantime a subamendment was moved1 by the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Jean), but in Your Honour's comments just now you referred also to the bearing of the vote on the amendment on this question. If the terms of the amendment did hot stand in the way at the time Your Honour made your ruling on November 29 it seems to me it should not be made to apply now. I suggest Your Honour should consider that my amendment adds relevant words to the main motion and should be declared in order.

Before Your Honour
makes this ruling may I add a word? It seems to me that during this debate Your Honour has interpreted the rules so strictly that hon. members who disagree with the motions or amendments made thus far are prohibited from their inherent right in this parliament of expressing their points of view and of giving support to them by means of their votes.
I wish to add this word to the contentions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The motion is:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
By that motion we are asked to endorse the policy of the government. We indicate clearly that we consider a vigorous war effort as one involving something other than what the government has undertaken. We are of the opinion that a vigorous war effort not only requires the sending of drafted men overseas but requires further that industry and wealth shall be placed on the altar of our national sacrifice as well as the lives of the young men of this country. Since we believe that the policy needs extension in those respects we have moved an amendment to that effect.
I suggest that under the traditions of this parliament and according to those rules of procedure in debate which I have been able
Ii917

War Effort-Government Policy
to read and study

I have given some thought to the rules of procedure-we are being denied by your ruling the right to express what we think is involved in a policy of vigorous prosecution of the war. I contend, with all due respect to the Chair, that our amendment is in order.

When the amendment was moved previously by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) I stated that the first portion of that amendment might conceivably be within the rules of the house and be accepted as an amendment to the main motion, but I was clearly of the opinion that the amendment as then constituted was not in order. Since the production of that amendment by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar the house has had under consideration a subamendment. That subamendment has been voted upon and it is now a decision of the house. It referred to part of the contents of the amendment now before us. The thirteenth edition of May, page 292, has this to say:
It is a rule, in both houses, which is essential to the due performance of their duties, that no question or bill shall be offered that is substantially the same as one on which their judgment has already been expressed in the current session.
That is a salutary ruling to prevent duplication of debate. Reference was made to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Jean). I did not give a ruling on that amendment because I was satisfied that it was in order. It referred to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), and proposed to insert an alternative proposition to that contained in the amendment. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre reads in part:
. . . and requires further the total mobilization of all the resources of Canada, material and financial as well as human, to ensure a total war effort, adequate reestablishment of the members of our fighting forces, and full employment after the war.
It has embodied within its terms the terms of the subamendment which has already been voted upon and which is now a decision of the house. May I say that in my rulings with regard to amendments being brought before the house I have not been concerned with the merits of any of them. I have been concerned solely with and have directed my thoughts toward the procedure that was necessary to bring the amendments within the rules of the house. In this case I am clearly of the opinion that the amendment is out of order.
I must respectfully and regretfully appeal your ruling.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I have read a statement made by the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) this afternoon with regard to the sending of dodgers by mail. There is a gentleman by the name of Mr. Robert Rumilly, translator and well-known author, who would appreciate being heard under oath to establish that the dodger was in a franked letter containing also a letter from Mr. Coleman, Under-Secretary of State.

subtopic: POLICY OF THE GOVERNMENT IN MAINTAINING A VIGOROUS WAR EFFORT-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF THE PRIME MINISTER.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie 
King) that this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
Mrs. DORISE W. NIELSEN (North Bat-tleford): Mr. Speaker, a little while ago our newspapers in this country carried a Canadian Press news item dated July 29, and headed "With the Canadians in France," which read:
In a neat bit of team play that began six days before the British-Canadian drive south of Caen July 25, French-speaking troops of a Quebec battalion paved the way for the capture of Verrieres by Ontario troops by attacking and holding two hillside farms about 1,000 yards north and northwest of the town.
A company commanded by Maj. J. P. C. Gauthier of Montreal was consolidating south of the Beauvoir farm when the Germans loosed a terrific concentration of mortar and gunfire along the whole of this front. Other men under Major J. A. Dextrase of Montreal had pushed on ahead but enemy fire pinned them down on the south side of the crest of the ridge. . . . The farm was held despite attacks by five tanks which remained dug in on the south side of the farm for 48 hours and in the face of heavy mortar and artillery fire. The tanks were finally forced to withdraw due to the aggressiveness of White's (Ontario) company. Troteval was attacked and captured by Major Dextrase's company July 24 and later Ontario troops passed through the position to go and capture Verrieres.
To my mind, in that short excerpt was the very spirit of Canadian unity. It is in my opinion the duty of all of us not only to maintain the Canadian army but in the doing of it to maintain the same spirit of unity among those of us who work together on the home front as animates our men who fight abroad. That to me is a most important thing.
We have in this country a very well-known Canadian journalist by the name of Mr. Leslie Roberts. He has written a book on the famous Canadian flying ace of Malta, "Buzz" Beurling, and has just returned from five months with the armed forces overseas to find Canada in the middle of this crisis. In an article which appears in the Canadian Mining Reporter, Mr. Leslie Roberts has this to say about the crisis-I quote just a short portion:
What first impresses the returning traveller, setting foot in the home country after five months' absence and stepping across a troopship gangway into the middle of the conscription crisis, is that Canada has suddenly gone stark, screaming mad.
What currently goes on in parliament and press is no patriotic filibuster but sheer political gangsterism, led by men ready to divide and destroy Canada if in the process they can also kill King.
Give them their heads and they will destroy Canada, ruin our hope of nationhood, at the hour when we stand not merely at the portal of peace, but at the gateway of our country's greatness

War Effort-Government Policy
If to hold us together he has compromised, attempting to hold the scales in balance between us, let us thank whatever gods we profess (and most of the leaders of the anti-King claque have no god but Mammon) that we have a leader who cherishes the unity of Canada, for without unity we perish, even in the hour of victory.
I agree very much with what he says.
At the beginning of this debate the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose) placed on record the position taken by the Labour Progressive party on this issue. As a member of that party I wish to endorse all that he has said, and in calling attention to the contributions made to the war by the people of the province of Quebec I also wish to associate myself with his remarks.
What I am going to say now I naturally say as a westerner and as a member from Saskatchewan, but the more I think about these things the more I realize the similarity between the people all over this country, never mind which province they happen to live in.
Western Canada is very proud of its contribution to this war in food for victory. Besides the thousands of volunteers who have gone from the prairies we had until quite recently about 13,800 draftees. Let me give the house one or two reasons why we had this number. In one. part of my country where we have no railways and where the roads are so bad that you cannot travel after a rainy spell, there was in a little town a young blacksmith and an acetylene welder. He had not volunteered because he was needed so desperately in that part of the country for repairing farm implements. Finally he was drafted, and after he was drafted the people of the district sent a petition to me asking if I could get him exempted for a while, because the . only other place they could get their implements mended by an acetylene welder was twenty-five or thirty miles away. Therefore I wrote to the board in Saskatchewan and got him an exemption for a while. He went back, and soon afterwards I received a letter from a woman who lived in that district. She was very bitter. She said, "My three sons have already gone, and now this boy is allowed to come back." What hurt her so badly was this: she said, "that boy got the priest of his village to telephone to Ottawa to get all the French-Canadian members to have him exempted.' It was I who got his exemption, and I am neither a priest nor French-speaking. But her anxiety and concern over her three boys, and the injustice which she felt because three of hers had gone away, while some also were
100-435J
kept on the farms, were canalized into race hatred and religious prejudice. I regretted it terribly.
I know of a couple of Ukrainian lads who had been the sole workers on their farms ever since they left school, because their fathers were old and unable to work. They did not volunteer. Their families could not live without them. Finally they received notices to be drafted and attend for their medical examinations. They went to the reeve of the village and said, "If we leave home our families will starve; what can we do?" The reeve of that particular area was an English-speaking man. This was after March 22, 1942. Those boys should have been frozen on the farms; they were eligible for such treatment; but the reeve is one of those English-speaking people who used to say, "Let those darned foreigners go; why should our boys fight, while they hide on the farms?"
These things are very bad. I am sorry that among a certain section of our English-speaking people there is a tendency to consider they are a little superior if they think as Britishers, when they should realize that their greatest duty, no, not their duty, their greatest privilege should be to think first and always as Canadians. Only a small percentage of them are involved in this kind of thing, but they have stirred up antagonism and prevented many a good boy from volunteering.
Of course these things are the result of mistakes in government, policy for which the cabinet must take full responsibility. I am not trying to absolve the government from blame. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has made mistakes, so has Mr. Roosevelt, so has Mr. Churchill. Churchill is making an awful mistake right now in interfering in Greece and in Belgium. But I say with confidence that if the democratic forces in any country are sufficiently strong and vigilant and courageous, they can and will correct the mistakes of leaders. That can be done. We must blame ourselves to some extent if in our war effort there have been inequalities and injustices which have provided fertile ground for those who now seek to stir up disunity in this country for their own political ends.
I regret as much as any French-speaking person in this country the slanderous attacks which have been made upon the people of the province of Quebec during this crisis, and I want the French-speaking people of Canada to know there are many English-speaking people in this country whose greatest desire is to persist in trying to keep alive and build the unity of our two great nations into a greater

War Effort-Government Policy
and a finer Canadianism. It is quite possible that with wiser policies earlier in the war our whole country might have accepted conscription. If we had had or if we had created a basis of real economic and social equality in the province of Quebec and the rest of Canada we might all of us have accepted conscription, on the basis of each man's fitness to become either a fighter, a food producer or a producer of war materials. In this way we would have had an army whose size was regulated by our ability to have behind that army the food producers and the producers of war materials, and too great commitments by way of an army would have been avoided. But the government did not do that. Perhaps they could not do it; at the time it was not possible to estimate these things. But I still maintain that we could have done better than we did.
Now the situation is different. We are nearing the end of this war, and I am one of those who, after sitting through these public sittings and the secret sitting, feel that the man who built the Canadian Army, and1 who is now our new Minister of National Defence (Mr. McNaughton), is the man who will not let that army down. I have great confidence in him. But I will say this: I hope sincerely that if there remain, among the high command within the ranks of the army, any officers who think more of their allegiance to the Tory party than they do of Canada. General McNaughton will see to it that they never have another opportunity of disturbing the confidence of our boys and of this nation. As to those who resigned from their positions of trust, which they should have held during this crisis, I think we are well rid of them, and if there are any others like them I hope they will be relieved of their duties.
Why did the Progressive-Conservative party create a political crisis when the problem of reinforcements arose? In my opinion it was because they have seen that the people of Canada are on the march, because they have seen the beginning of reforms during the early part of this present session; and how they have hated them! You will remember the crusade which has been waged by the Tory premier of Ontario against family allowances. That should indicate the stand of the Tories toward reform. What a blow to the great Canadian Pacific interests in this country that we should have decided that Trans-Canada Air Lines, a government-owned company, should1 control Canadian airways after this War! These Tories see in the new industrial bank and in our farm credit arrangements a threat to the chartered banks and to the trusts whose mouthpiece they are. Those

were the real issues over which the Tory party was concerned The reinforcement issue was but a patriotic cloak in which they wrapped themselves to strut before the Canadian people. If there is one thing more than any other calculated to upset the magnificent efforts of our war workers, our farmers, and all our people, including the boys overseas, it is to plunge and precipitate this country into an orgy of hysterical campaigning on the question of conscription, at this date, so near the winning of the war.	.
There are some westerners, I believe, who, because the Tory party is discredited1 in the west, say, "Oh, well, the Tories, if they go before the people with an honest presentation of their programme, could not possibly win an election." I think this recent Tory manoeuvre should teach them that it is quite possible for the Progressive-Conservatives to try to force an election on a dishonest issue, and in that way to win thousands of honest people to their support who fail to see what is behind this cloak of patriotism. Such in my opinion is their present manoeuvre, and I am happy to know that at least for the time being it is foiled.
It has been said in the past, and truly said, that patriotism sometimes becomes the last refuge of scoundrels. In my opinion nothing so closely approaching fascist tactics has ever been witnessed in Canada, and' I hope very much that I never again have to sit in this chamber and witness another exhibition of , mob rowdyism and speaking to the galleries such as we had to listen to when the spokesmen of the Tory party were questioning General McNaughton. It was a disgraceful exhibition.
The industrial workers of Canada have already seen the truth behind this crisis; and on my desk, and I know on the desk of the Prime Minister because I have received copies of them, are a good many resolutions from the organized' trades unions of Canada-from both the province of Quebec and the rest of Canada-supporting the government's action at this time. From both the province of Quebec and the rest of Canada, among broad sections of our people, among the industrial workers, farmers, business and professional men and white-collar workers, there is seen the great necessity for maintaining unity in Canada.
It is true that order in council 8891 is a compromise. It is more than some Frenchspeaking people feel they should be called upon to support; it is a little less than some English-speaking people feel is necessary. But do the French and English battalions on the

War Effort-Government Policy
fighting fronts squabble as to which of them should bear most of the brunt of battle? No. Together they do the job that has to be done. It is an example that we might well follow here on the home front.
This order in council does ensure, first of all, reinforcements to the men. Second, it does leave room for what I hope will be a great voluntary movement of young men in this country toward the army. Third, a thing I am more happy about than anything else, it destroys utterly and defeats for the time being the Tory manoeuvre.
When victory is assured, this country will welcome an election. It will be good to have one, to go again to the people with the real issues that face them-yes, not conscription, but the real issues that face the people. The programme discussed then will be what kind of government will direct our foreign and domestic policies in the years to come after the war to bring the kind of peace for which we have fought.
At the next election, from wide sections of our people representatives will be elected from the ranks of organized labour, from farmers, from people's parties like the C.C.F., the Labour Progressive party, the Social Credit party, and they must work together with that section of progressive forces within the Liberal party who will work for international collaboration for the maintenance of peace and for the continuance of our markets and our trade as well as for reforms on the home front, to bring social security to our people. Together such forces can isolate and destroy and send dowfn to oblivion this Tory gang. If those forces in this country who want progress, who feel that it is time to leave the status quo and go forward, work together they can help to keep peace, to extend our markets, to increase farm income, to continue jobs and employment and to give us a national health scheme, better pensions for old age and for the blind as well as for our mothers, and they can rebuild our city and rural slums and provide better education.
If we do these things we shall have achieved something great and Canada will have taken a great step forward. It will not be socialism. No; but it will be a step forward, and that is what eighty or ninety per cent of our people in Canada are willing and ready to do; it is what they want. Such forces working together can lead our nation forward with the rest of the world to progress and security. It is in the best interests of Canada's fighting people here and abroad; it is in the best interests of unity; it is in the best interests of our people, which are so far above political
considerations, that, I say, Mr. Speaker, every honest person in this house to-night should support the motion of the Prime Minister.

Following the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) as I do, with the type of speech which I shall make, I do not expect to receive the same applause from the Liberal government or the Liberal benches as she has been given, and in making the type of speech I am going to make I want no reflection to be cast upon my patriotism. I will say to my hon. friend that the Labour Progressive party in this country has no comer on patriotism. Furthermore, I would simply make this statement in all kindness, that if patriotism is the refuge of scoundrels I should like to know where the communists were when Great Britain had her back against the wall. The term "fascist" is used very often by so-called patriotic speakers. I wish to know where the Labour Progressive party were, the communists, when fascism was riding roughshod over France and over the lowlands, and when the battle of Britain was on.
In this debate I realize that the issue before us is one of the most serious that perhaps this parliament has ever had before it. We are living in serious times and dealing with tremendous problems. The problems and the times, being what they are, do not permit of anyone, much less the government which is facing those problems, playing the game of politics, toying with the feelings of the people, the lives of the men and the destiny of the nation.
It is with this in mind that I have to decide whether or not I am to vote confidence in the present administration. The present situation with which this parliament is faced is, I believe, the result of a series of political moves which the leader of the present administration has made over the past year. I am not going to take a lot of time to go into all the details of the past, but perhaps I have only to go back to 1940 when parliament was called in the regular way and sat for half a day, whereupon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) sent us all back home on the flimsy pretence that a resolution had been passed in the Ontario legislature, and when asked why he had called us here anyway the the answer was: Oh, well, of course, he had made a great promise that he would not go to the country without first calling parliament. At that time we were fighting a war, but the election was called. May I say that that election was fought on the basis of a "no conscription" issue, and1 when the Prime Minister was returned to power with the biggest
War Effort-Government Policy

majority that this country has ever seen it was because he promised the country that he would not tolerate'conscription.
It is all very well to talk about the way the war has gone; it is all very well to talk about these things now, but I ask the simple question: Did the Prime Minister not know at that time that we were face to face with one of the most powerful war machines the world has ever seen? He should have known it, because he was Secretary of State for External Affairs at the time. He had gone over to Germany himself, although if he went on a Cooks' tour they would not show him all that. The group with whom I have the honour to be associated recognized the danger. We went to the country too; to the best of our ability we portrayed the truth as we saw it, and that was that since we had declared war on the greatest war machine the world has ever seen we would1 need every available dollar, every available part of our national resources as well as every man in his proper place. However, the Prime Minister's party was returned. Some of us got back; some of us did not. Then in 1942 when the battle of Britain was on-the nazis had walked roughshod through France and the Netherlands- the war was going seriously against us and something had to be done. Public opinion had undergone a change and so the bright idea was thought .up to put over a plebiscite in this country. However, it was not until Britain had1 been driven from continental Europe that public opinion turned that way. The plebiscite was put on, and may I say it was a plebiscite which nobody seemed to understand. When we were discussing what should be on the ballot, the question on which the people of Canada would have to vote, it was an open secret that the cabinet had burned the midnight oil in an attempt to put a proper question on the ballot paper. Eventually they put that question to which I am inclined to think the right hon. the Prime Minister is accustomed, a question that can be read and1 interpreted in any way he wishes it to be interpreted.
I would suggest that there are not a half dozen people in Canada to-day who can tell you what was on the ballot paper during the plebiscite. It was not intended that anyone should understand it. As a matter of fact, when some hon. members of this group moved an amendment to the question on the ballot paper in order to clarify the thing we received the answer: Oh, no, no, that could not be done; and the government side of the house voted against any clarification of it.

Speaking of plebiscites, may I digress foi a moment to tell the house that I put ovei a plebiscite of my own.
Did it cost a million and a half?

No, it did not; it cost a few dollars. When I recognized that we would have to come to this session of parliament and that the question to be decided was whether or not we should conscript the draftees, I immediately circularized my constituency. I should say that I did not write to everybody; I have a mailing list of nearly one thousand names, not all of them my supporters, although, of course, most of them are! I sent out a little card. I will send it over to the Prime Minister so that he can see it. One side of the card reads:
Dear sir or madam:
Parliament has been hurriedly called in special session to discuss and vote on the manpower problem. In order to know the feeling of my constituency in this matter I would appreciate having you mark the back of this card with either "yes" or "no" to the question asked. This will help me to vote according to the majority wishes of my riding. You may sign your name if you w'ish, although this is not necessary. . . .
The question on the reverse side was not the type of question that was put on the plebiscite of 1942. This was one that the people could understand:
Are you in favour of conscripting draftees for military services overseas? Mark yes or no.
There you have it, no bones about it, no quibbling, no getting around it, under it or over it, "yes" or "no." Quite a number of these have been returned, and I find that between ninety and ninety-one per cent told me to vote "yes," while between nine and ten per cent said, "no." I must be fair to those who indicate "no" votes. Many of them, besides sending in their card, wrote to me to explain their position, and I will say that most of the letters I received explaining the "no" vote were sensible letters. The people who wanted to tell me why they did not want the draftees conscripted were people, some of whom I knew, whose judgment I could trust. Some of the arguments in the letters I regarded as sound. I am not going to say that there are not two' sides to this question. I believe those who said, "no" did have some argument, and I am not wholly out of accord with my Quebec friends on this. I think they have an argument too. And may I say when we are talking about this national unity, I am just as concerned about the national unity of this country as anyone else is, and I am just as concerned about the future of this country as anyone else is.
DECEMBER 7, 1944	6923
War Effort-Government Policy
Let me get back to the main thread of my speech. When the plebiscite of 1942 was put over on this country what did the Liberal party do? Did they simply leave it with the people to vote "yes" or "no"? They did not. They went throughout the country urging everyone to vote "yes." They went throughout the country urging everyone to place upon them the, responsibility of conscription for overseas when that time became necessary. They did that. They invited responsibility. The question is, why were they so anxious to get a "yes" vote in 1942 when they were not prepared to implement the "yes" vote as long after as November 22, 1944? Another question: the right hon. the Prime Minister of this country cries oiit, "Anarchy, anarchy, anarchy!" Did he not know that there might be a possibility of such a thing when he was calling on the people of 1942 to vote "yes" for the conscription of men for overseas service? Why cry "anarchy" now? A couple of years or so too late, I fancy.
Parliament was summoned in consequence thereof and the government brought down their national resources mobilization bill. That was supposed to implement the plebiscite vote. I refer to bill No. 80. That was simply another attempt to lead the people to believe that the Liberal party were about to do something.
I want the house to note a most significant thing. When bill No. 80 w'as brought down in 1942 the Prime Minister said, "I am not going to put this bill into effect until I get a vote of confidence from this parliament." I maintain that that promise has been broken, and I will tell hon. members how. When parliament was summoned a week or two ago it was summoned for the purpose of voting confidence in the Prime Minister's voluntary system. He was calling parliament to seek endorsation of his position as against the position taken by the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston). That was what it was all about.
The funny thing about it i*>
that the right hon. gentleman recognized that he would have difficulty in getting the confidence of his own party in his voluntary system. Before asking parliament for a vote of confidence to give effect to bill No. 80 as he said he would, he passes an order in council while parliament is sitting right under his nose. I ask: why this strange procedure? The only answer I can find is that it was a political expedient to keep his party and cabinet together.
Now a word with respect to the resignation of the former minister of national defence. When the Minister of National Defence reported conditions overseas to the government why did not the Prime Minister tell the country the truth about the situation? Why did he not go on the air, for instance? Spot announcements could have been made that the Prime Minister of Canada wanted to talk to the nation on a particular night, or something of that kind. I would not have objected to a little build-up for the Prime Minister on an occasion of that kind. Why did he not say to the country, now, .fellow Canadians, my minister has brought back a report from the fighting fronts that the situation there is so-and-so and so-and-so; he informs me this and that; now, fellow Canadians, on the basis of what my minister has told me I am afraid I shall have to call parliament together in order to get their confidence, for the time has now come to put bill No. 80 into effect.
If the Prime Minister had done that, not only would he have been able to gather unto himself not only the confidence of the people of Canada, he would have had their admiration as well. What did he do instead? When the thing began to boil, when the former minister of national defence was out of office, the people began to weigh the situation and ask, What is all this about? The Prime Minister then went on the air, taking the attitude that he must play safe with his party. He went on the air and attempted to justify his position as against that of the former minister of national defence.
The Prime Minister may argue against that if he wishes, and as I think he tried to do the other day when the question of the circularizing of his speech by the war information board was before the house. We were told that this was an attempt to get Canada to stand behind him when he was calling for volunteers. I should like to read one or two statements the Prime Minister made when talking over the air. The first was:
I now come to the question: Is there an adequate reserve of reinforcements for the army ? In_ the opinion of the military authorities, no difficulty is likely to arise except in relation to reinforcements for the infantry. Infantry reinforcements have been adequate to meet requirements to date. But, during his recent visit to the army overseas, Colonel Ralston learned that to provide replacements for future casualties at present rate, the flow of infantry reinforcements from Canada should be accelerated. One fact needs to be emphasized. There is not an overall shortage of potential reinforcements. Many thousands of men are in training now and enlistments are continuing at an encouraging rate. Because we eannot tell how long the war may last, we must, as long as a possible need may arise, continue to recruit men for the army to keep up the supply of reinforcements. But recent recruits and those who enlist from now' on will not be available until they are trained.
War Effort-Government Policy

Colonel Ralston's report to the government disclosed an immediate problem which had to be faced. That problem is to find the means of speeding up the flow of fully trained infantry reinforcements to meet, not an actual shortage of reinforcements now, but a possible shortage in the next few months.
Is that not designed to support the Prime Minister's position against the position of his former minister of national defence?
The question many of you will ask at once, is: why not send overseas some of the draftees who are fully trained in Canada under the National Resources Mobilization Act?
That will seem to many of you the easiest way of meeting the problem. It is not, however, in accord with the policy of keeping our army overseas a 100 per cent voluntary army if we possibly- can. The voluntary system of raising our overseas forces has produced splendid results during five years of war. We have always believed that Canada's forces, having begun as voluntary forces, would be more effective, and that the country would be more united in their support, if we continued to rely upon the voluntary system for reinforcements as long as the voluntary system continued to be effective.
Is that paragraph not designed to state the government's position over against that of the former minister? How much more do I have to read?
Colonel Ralston had grave doubts of our ability to keep up the flow of reinforcements in the next few months by voluntary means. He considered, therefore, that he had no alternative but to recommend that draftees should be sent overseas as reinforcements.
Is that not designed to argue his position over against that of the former minister of national defence?
When I realized that unless Colonel Ralston's recommendation were accepted by the cabinet, his resignation would follow, I felt it to be my duty as Prime Minister to seek the most expert advice I believed to be available.
Is that not designed to substantiate the Prime Minister's position over against that of his former minister? And again:
It is important to remember that the former minister of national defence and the present minister have precisely the same objective in view; they differ only as to the means of reaching that goal.
Is that not designed to substantiate the government's position over against that of his former minister? To be fair I must say this, too, that before the Prime Minister concluded he did bring forward a passionate appeal for the country to support him in his call for volunteers.. I shall read the last part of his speech:
It is the government's responsibility to make the decision as to the best methods of supporting Canada's army overseas. No decision could possibly please everyone. We have made the decision which we believe will best support the army and contribute most effectively to an utmost national effort in the winning of the 
war. But to achieve these ends, we shall need-the help and cooperation of the people as a whole.
It is true that that appeal was put out to the people. If the Prime Minister states that this essentially was an appeal for the support of his voluntary system and not an argument pitting his judgment against that of his colleague, then all I say is this, that if he now has to admit that his appeal failed that is an admission that the country did not have confidence in him.
We were called here on November 22. The correspondence between the Prime Minister and his former minister of national defence was read. It took the greater part of an afternoon to read it. That night the crisis came, and that crisis was a party crisis. On the basis of that party crisis an order iD council was passed reversing the policy the government had held just a few hours before. When next day I questioned the Prime Minister as to whether, if he had passed this order in council when the former minister had reported to him on his return from overseas, his resignation would have been necessary, I could not get an answer for a few minutes. I did not get one until I insisted, and then just what was the answer? The answer was -well, I was going to use a term which I shall not use, because I must be polite. I shall use a term the former minister of national defence used, and say that the Prime Minister's answer was simply nonsense. He said that you cannot tell now what you might have been able to do a month or two months previously. As a matter of fact, it was only three weeks prior to that that the minister had resigned', and only two weeks prior to that that the Prime Minister had gone on the air.
Had the situation changed in those three weeks? Had the ranks overseas been depleted in those three weeks, or in the two weeks between the broadcast and the order in council? Were the men overseas finding it less difficult or more difficult? Had anything changed in respect of the reinforcements situation? I think no. There was only one change, and that was a change in the attitude of the people of Canada, and the attitude of certain ranks within the Liberal party.
Then, must I conclude that this order in council was passed because the reinforcement situation demanded it, or because there was a split in his party, and because his cabinet demanded it? Am I now to vote confidence in a government of that kind?
Just another word concerning the resignation. Subsequent events have proved that the resignation of the former minister of

national defence would not have been necessary if the Prime Minister had been honest with the people of Canada-well, I should not say "honest"; I will say that it would not have been necessary if he had been fair with the people of this country, when the report was given to him by his minister.
Therefore I say this, that my view of this whole debate from the beginning is that the fate of the government very largely hinged on which way the former minister of national defence was going to put his support. What did he do? Well, he did, I believe, the gentlemanly thing. He proved his case, and then said, "I am not going to break with the Prime Minister and my party. I am voting confidence in him." The strange thing about it is that the former minister of national defence is the one man who has very largely saved the Prime Minister and the Liberal party from disgrace. And another strange thing about it is that he is the man who was fired. Am I now going to turn around and be asked to vote confidence in that government?
Now a word about the motion of the Prime Minister. It was placed on the Votes and Proceedings before the order in council was passed. I maintain that when the motion was placed there the Prime Minister was seeking the confidence of this house on his voluntary system. The order in council was then passed, but the motion has not been changed, and now the Prime Minister seeks the confidence of the house for his partial conscription policy. Personally, I fail to see how a motion which was designed to seek the confidence of the House of Commons in the government's voluntary system, can now be used for a vote of confidence from the housp on the government's conscription policy. I fail to see that; it is not logical.
I am not going to vote for what I call a double-barreled motion. Read it for yourselves. We have read it several times, but let us read it again:
That this house will aid the government in its policy of maintaining a vigorous war effort.
What does that mean? It means he has got you both going and coming. It is going to be heck if you do and heck if you don't. If you vote against the motion, because you have not confidence in the government, what will some go out and say? They will say. "See those men? Well, they voted against the policy the Prime Minister wanted to bring in so as to reinforce the troops overseas." And if you vote in favour of the motion the people in my constituency and in yours, and all the rest of them, will say, "See those men there? Well, they voted confidence in the government." So it is heck if you do.
and heck if you don't. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is a double-barreled motion and, so far as I am concerned, I am not going to be forced to have to choose which barrel to look down, and especially when I do not know which trigger he is going to pull.
May I now say a word about voting confidence in the government? Since when, under our party system, did the present Prime Minister ever want to plead with anyone in the opposition to vote confidence in him? It is a different matter when his own ranks are beginning to be depleted. Is he now coming to the opposition and saying, Please come over and help me; vote confidence in me, and fill up my depleted ranks? Well, hon. gentlemen, you may vote confidence if you wish- but please excuse me.
Now the Prime Minister cries "anarchy"; he cries "election", and the danger of being without a government. Well, since when did the Prime Minister become so concerned about when he should hold an election? If he comes to the opposition now and says, "Do not hold an election now; I do not want to hold an election now, because it would be suicide in Canada to do so." If he puts up the big bogey man, I say, What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. When he does want to hold an election why does he not come to us and say: Gentlemen, I want to know if it is right for me to hold an election now? It must work both ways. I do not want to be mean with the Prime Minister; I know that he has a tremendous burden and I sympathize with him in his position. Upon his shoulders is the responsibility of running Canada's part in the war. All I am going to say is that it is my firm conviction that when it comes to an election-
He will win.

I do not know. Perhaps the Prime Minister will win. I was not careful enough about my little pauses that time. I was going to say that when it comes to an election the Prime Minister will not think twice about the day of holding it so long as he thinks it is a good' day for him. He would hold it on Christmas day or to-morrow or any day next month if he thought that was a good day for him. I would not be surprised if there was an election before we are supposed to resume here on January 31. If it suits the Liberal party the election will be called; do not worry about that.
Another cry is: Reinforcements are needed and we cannot hold them up. Who is holding up reinforcements? Did it hold up reinforcements in the United States when they held an

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate, and I hope I shall not run over my forty minutes because, as you know, I usually do not take that long. But we feel that it is necessary under the circumstances to move an amendment, so that I now move, seconded by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) that the motion be amended, as follows:
1.	By inserting after the word "house", where it anpears in the first line, the following words:
"while not being requested to support all the [DOT] policies of the government".
2.	By deleting all the words following the word "government" and substituting therefor the following
"in sending immediately adequate reinforcements to our men overseas, and will also aid the government at all such times as it wages a vigorous war effort against the totalitarian powers; an effort consistent with Canada's ability and position in the world."
The motion will then read:
That this house, while not being requested to support all the policies of the government, will aid the government in sending immediately adequate reinforcements to our men overseas, and will also aid the government at all such times as it wages a vigorous war effort against the totalitarian powers; an effort consistent with Canada's ability and position in the world.
The reasons why we desire to move this amendment to the main motion have been stated clearly by the hon. member for Macleod. As the main motion now reads, it is impossible to know what is required of the house. It reminds us very much of the motion that was put at the time of the plebiscite. We did not consider at that time that the question which was put to the public was intelligible. We did not think it was fair. Certainly there was confusion all over the country over it. At the time the plebiscite was held, nobody in the country understood what it was about, not even the members of this house. I recall that even in this house the members of the government did not know what it was about. It was definitely stated by the former minister of national defence that the government itself did not know; at least some of them were not clear on the issue. Now, surely our English language is not so lacking in words to make things clear and explicit to the public.
Had I been prepared to speak here this evening I could have quoted contradictions in the Prime Minister's speech which would be clear evidence of the fact that one cannot put too great trust in the wording of that motion. Accordingly it is our intention that

the amendment which we have offered shall clarify the whole problem. It will permit hon. members who desire to support the government in a clear and unmistakable position to know exactly what they are voting for. Certainly there is not a member of the group to which I have the honour to belong that is not fully in favour of sending all the reinforcements necessary to our troops overseas, and I doubt-if there are many hon. members who are of a different opinion on that matter. But we are not in favour of supporting the government in all its policies; I would hate to be associated with some of those which the government has undertaken. I would hate to be associated with the attitude which this government and other parties represented in this house took at the time war broke out, in 1939. I recall only too vividly our stand here when we asked for an all-out war effort. We stood alone at that time, and when the plebiscite came on we were criticized here because of our action, but we were the only party in Canada which went out and explained the facts as we understood them to the people. We were the only party, I repeat, which, when the plebiscite was taken, explained the facts to the people and, in conformity with the practices of a democratic country, said to them, "You tell us how you want us to vote," and abided by that decision. The rest of the membership of this house went out and told the people to vote "yes", and when they did vote "yes", some of them came back to the house and voted against the passing of bill 80, contrary to the decision democratically registered by the people. It may be that there was an excuse for them: they could justly say, nobody knew what it was about. The purpose of this amendment to the main motion is to put the question fairly and squarely not only before the members of this house but before all the people of Canada. We are only too anxious to send all the needed reinforcements, but we do not. think we should be compelled, as the hon. member for Macleod said, to vote for a two-barreled resolution, when you do not know which trigger the Prime Minister is going to pull, although you can depend upon it that he will pull the one which suits him.
The amendment which we have made does not in any way deflect from the policy of sending reinforcements, but it does make the issue clear. The Prime Minister said in the course of his speech that to vote for his motion did not imply support of all the government policies, but the motion does not so state, and our amendment is intended to clarify that position and make it clear to
hon. members that by voting to send the required reinforcements they will not be obligated to vote confidence in the other policies of the government.

I shall not inflict another forty-minute speech on the house. As I said before, I do not like the wording of the motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister and yet, realizing the tremendous problem he has, I wish to give him all the support I can. I am speaking now for myself and not for my group; my group can vote the way they want to; but I am not going to vote confidence in the government on the basis of the present motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister. He may not want my little vote; it may not make a particle of difference-

Not very much.
Mr. HA.NSELL: -nevertheless my vote is going to be determined on the basis of what the Prime Minister wants to do with the amendment. All I am asking the Prime Minister to do is to take one tiny step, a step which will readjust this motion, whereby he will put into the motion what he promised in his speech, namely, that he was not demanding the house to vote confidence in all the administration did. The next is a slight addition which says that we will also support his government in waging "a vigorous war effort against the totalitarian powers"; and it adds this, too, "at all such times" as it wages a vigorous war effort, because I do not think we should be forced to vote confidence in the government in carrying on its war effort and let it carry on just as it wants to; it is to be "at all such times as it wages a vigorous war effort" that we will support them. Then there is this little addition. You know there is an opinion in Canada that we embarked upon too ambitious a war programme. I do not know whether we did or not, but I do not think we should be called upon to do more than our share in a world war. Other nations are at war on our side. So that we are merely adding, "an effort consistent with Canada's ability and position in the world." It is a slight change. Personally I will give the government every possible weight of support I can in my own small way if they will reword their motion, and this amendment is exactly what that will do. If they vote against this amendment I cannot vote confidence in the government.

Mr. Speaker, to-night we are called upon to pass judgment on a motion of confidence moved by the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in support of the direct enforcement of the conscription act for overseas service. After all, it is purely and simply a vote for or against conscription.
Many amendments and subamendments have been moved. This afternoon, we have voted on the progressive-conservative party's amendment which involved conscription for overseas service and, together, with the members of our group, I voted against that amendment because we are opposed to conscription.
We have also had to vote on a subamendment moved by the hon. member for Mont-real-Mereier (Mr. Jean). I voted for that subamendment although I did not like its wording and I did not agree with its full purport; I supported it only because it expressed some blame against the government for having resorted to conscription for overseas service. That is the sole meaning of the vote cast by myself and the members of our group on that subamendment; it was a vote against conscription. But it seems to me that, at this stage of the proceedings, it would be advisable to put an end to the moving of amendments and subamendments, because the house has had several opportunities to vote for or against conscription on an amendment and a subamendment and it should now have an opportunity to vote on the motion of confidence moved by the right hon. the Prime Minister, which also implies a vote for or against conscription. Further amendments can but create confusion in the mind of the public and, for my part, I would agree to all amendments and subamendments which will be introduced from now on being set aside by the Speaker.
I wish to reply to a statement made by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) in his speech of last Monday. He declared that the only two members who had voted against participation in the war-he said voted mind you-were Mr. Liguori Lacombe, member for Laval-Two-Mountains, and Mr. Wilfrid LaCroix, member for Quebec-Mont-morency. Not only is this statement at variance with the facts, but it may unfairly lead the public to believe that only the member for Laval-Two-Mountains and the member for Quebec-Montmorency have opposed Canada's participation in the war. I do not intend to deal at length with that matter, but I shall
	.
merely report the facts as published in Hansard, the official record of the debates of the house.
In September, 1939, after England had declared war, a special session of Parliament was called. On September 7, the speech from the throne was read to the house and the debate was adjourned until the next day. On that very next day, as soon as the house had met, I took the first formal step against Canada's participation in military operations abroad by tabling a petition, signed by thousands of people opposed to Canadian participation in any extra-territorial war; I refer to page 6 of Hansard where the following petition is recorded:
Petition
Opposition to participation by Canada in any extraterritorial war
Mr. Maxime Raymond (Beauharnois-La-prairie): I desire to lay on the table a petition signed by thousands of citizens against participation by Canada in any extraterritorial war.
The public can judge whether the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie opposed Canada's participation in the war.
The following day, September 9, when the discussion was resumed, I continued to protest against Canada's participation in a European war, and the text of my speech can be found on page 58 of Hansard. I was the first member from the province of Quebec to speak in the house against Canada's participation in the present war.
The debate on the speech from the throne ended the evening of September 9. Shortly before ten o'clock, after having ascertained the number of members who wished to take part in the debate and having made sure that the discussion was to last until midnight, I went to the editor of Hansard to check up the English translation of a speech I had made in the afternoon.
At about 10.15, or rather, between 10.15 and 10.30, I heard the bell ring and bolted for the house. On my way there, I met members who were coming out and who told me that the debate had abruptly come to an end. Certain hon. members who were listed to speak had decided not to and the debate had suddenly ended without the vote being registered. Now every member of this house is aware that, when a vote is called, the bell rings to summon the members who want to register their vote.

I quote the words he used in concluding his speech:
Yes, I have boys of my own, and I hope they are not cowards, but if any of those boys, not from cowardice but really through belief, is willing to take his stand on this matter and, if necessary, to face a concentration camp or a firing squad, I shall be more proud of that boy than if he enlisted for the war.
I cannot see how it could be inferred that Mr. Woodsworth, the member for Winnipeg North Centre, who had delivered one of the most courageous and energetic speeches heard in this house on that occasion, was not opposed to our participation in the war.
(Translation): Germany had not yet invaded Russia at the time.

On September 11, the acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) brought down estimates amounting to 8100.000,000 for war expenditures and requested that the said amount be applied, among other things, to the conduct of naval, military' and air operations, in or beyond Canada. This is to be found on page 91 of Hansard, special session of 1939.
On the same day, as reported on page 100 of Hansard, I rose in this house to move an amendment. Here is what I said:
Mr. Maxime Raymond (Beaukarnois-La-prairie): Mr. Chairman, as I have already stated my attitude against participation of Canada in the present war I shall not at this time make any additional observations. May I therefore propose an amendment to the resolution before the committee. I move to amend the resolution by striking out in subparagraph (b) the words "or beyond".
This means that I did not want the appropriation to be used outside Canada, in a war waged outside Canada.
The amendment was ruled out of order and, a short time after, on the same day, the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. McNeil) moved an amendment drawn in approximately the same terms and having the same effect. That amendment can be found on page 103 of Hansard. As can be seen at page 110, there was a vote which was the only one taken during that session; it was recorded while we were sitting in committee on the amendment of Mr. McNeil and the said amendment was negatived by a vote of 151 against and 16 for. Sixteen hon. members thus voted against Canada's participation in the war, ten from the province of Quebec and six from other provinces. My hon. friend the member for Quebec West and South (Mr. Parent) was included among those from the province of Quebec.
I have no intention of commenting on the facts which I have just mentioned, but I was anxious to state in this house, so that the public may know, from the official record of the house, what happened at the time and in order that should some one claim that the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains and the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, whom I do not want to deprive of the credit they deserve, were the only ones who opposed participation in the war, the public may judge whether or not I have from the very beginning been against our participation in the war.

Mr. Speaker, I did not approve the subamendment presented by the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Jean) and did not approve either the Progressive Conservative amendment. Nor do I approve the main motion. I believe Canada has undertaken a war effort that imperils all our resources. We have no right to sacrifice thus the economy of our nation and the live forces of our manpower. I remain consistent with my principles. I opposed participation and mobilization, and my opinion has not changed in the meantime.
Close to a million Canadians are enlisted in the armed services. Our young men are falling by the thousands on the battlefields of Europe. We are being bled white both by taxation and by demands on our manpower, and this subamendment was asking us to do even more. Those who approved participation and mobilization-they were within their rights-as	did	the	hon.	member	forBeauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond), could easily feel they were supporting the principle involved when they voted for the subamendment presented	by	the	hon.	member	for
Mercier.

I say, Mr. Speaker, that we have assumed too heavy a burden in this unfortunate adventure which I denounced in this house on September 9, 1939. I knew that our participation in the war would inevitably drag us into conscription. I did all in my power to save our youth from the application of this measure by opposing participation which was to give rise to conscription. In this critical hour, fraught with fearful consequences for Canada, I repeat'-with all due deference to the hon. member for Beauhamois-La-prairie-that alone the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) supported me. Always frank, always loyal, always logical, he was again my sole support against conscription on June 19, 1940. If only the members who will vote against the confidence motion of the government now under discussion had supported my amendments against participation and against mobilization, we would have been spared this tragedy and my hon. friends would not now be compelled to express their lack of confidence in their own leader. I shall act as I always did. If I acted otherwise I would not be true to myself and I would belie my whole past.

I do say, once again, that such a myth which the "delayed-action, patriots", if I may borrow an apt expression, try to use as a mantle, should be destroyed at all cost. Those are the "pure" and "untouchable" people. Do not ever enter their ranks.
Finally, if the honourable member for Beauharnois-Laprairie has seen fit to assume the responsibility of supporting the amendment moved by the honourable member for Mercier, I shall not begrudge him the liberty to do so. I respect his opinion. He has, in taking such action, followed and maintained the course he has always taken- in this house, he has supported participation and mobilization.
You voted for conscription.

I have been considering carefully the amendment moved by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), and seconded by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), but since its terms are so peculiar I thought I should like a little time for its consideration. During the course of this debate I have already had to enunciate the principle that one cannot approve or disapprove the same document, and that it must be considered in its entirety. I have enunciated that doctrine twice, in respect of two amendments. The amendment now before I he house says:
While not being requested to support all the policies of the government.
The form in which that is drawn is rather vague; but vagueness in itself does not make an amendment irrelevant. However, I take it that what is intended by the words is that they do not approve all other policies of the government, and to that extent they express disapproval of the main motion now before the house.
Then the amendment deals with the main motion and states that this house will aid the governmentin sending immediately adequate reinforcements to our men overseas, and will also aid the government at all such times as it wages a vigorous war effort against the totalitarian powers.
That, in effect, is an approval of the main motion. Then, part of the last sentence reads:
an effort consistent with Canada's ability and position in the world.
In other words it is imposing, or submitting to the house what is a general principle, and is not dealing with the matter in the main motion.
In 1932 the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black), who was then Speaker of the house, was dealing with an amendment then made by the former minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston), and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). He ruled as follows:
Amendments to the motion for the approval of a trade agreement ruled out because it partly approved the main motion, was an expanded negative of certain stipulations of the agreement and was declaratory of general principles which can only be approved on certain specified motions.
In the light of that decision, and also because of the phraseology employed' in the amendment now before the house, I find that the amendment disapproves the government's policy in the words:
while not being requested to support all the policies of the government

And later in the amendment approve the government's policy in the words:
And will also aid the government at all such times as it wages a vigorous war effort against the totalitarian powers.
And then it imports the general principle:
An effort consistent with Canada's ability and position in the world.
For these reasons I rule the amendment out of order.

War Effort-Government Policy

Mr. Speaker, every eare was taken to draft this amendment in accordance with the rules. It looks to me as though surely this government resolution should be open to amendment, and that in making your ruling you have rendered it almost impossible to amend the government's resolution. I believe that Your Honour is thereby laying down a principle in parliament which is unsound, and I therefore most respectfully challenge your decision.

Order. In dealing with this amendment I have considered it only as 1 view the rules, and not in connection with its merits, as I already said to-day when dealing with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I have carefully considered the amendment, and have come to my conclusion. I cannot allow any discussion of my ruling, except by challenge.
Then I most respectfully appeal from Your Honour's ruling.

I have ruled the amendment moved by Mr. Johnston, seconded by Mr. Hansell, out of order on the ground that there was imported into it a negative disapproval of the main motion, while in the midst of it there was an approval of the main motion, and in the third place in the last line of the amendment there was enunciated a general principle. I ruled that these were inconsistent and irrelevant, and therefore ruled the amendment out of order.
